## Volume front matter

### Series title page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully corrected by comparison with one another and with several manuscript codices; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume and each author of any importance; embellished with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any theme may be seen at a glance, and the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual scriptural books and in what places in their works. This is the most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others when one considers the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the modest price, and above all this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library gathers together six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.*

**SECOND SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. —The Latin edition is sold for 1,200 French francs; the Greek-Latin for 1,300. —The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; in the third [series], however, they are presented only in Latin translation.

# ISIDORE MERCATOR

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. V]

### Selection and critical assessment by Heinrich Denzinger, professor of theology at the University of Würzburg, of what recent critics have established concerning the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals

**1.** By a remarkable turn of events in our own time, those very men who formerly attributed the Pseudo-Isidorian materials to the fraud of the pontiffs in order to attack the prerogatives of the Roman see now, more successfully and more subtly than anyone else, point out their genuine origin. Nevertheless, most of them have not advanced so far as to admit that the Roman pontiffs did not favor a fraud already accepted by many, or that the privileges of the Roman see did not thereby gain more than was proper. Indeed, the matter is so tangled that even all Catholics have not yet reached such clarity as to concede that these Decretals introduced at least some alteration into ecclesiastical discipline.

Therefore, in order as far as possible to put an end to such long-standing prejudices, we have decided to precede the publication of the Decretals by gathering together what recent critics have done well and submitting what seems less satisfactory to us to a new examination. There will consequently be three matters briefly requiring our investigation:

1. Where, when, and chiefly for what purpose were the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals composed?  
2. Did the Roman pontiffs of that period favor the fraud once it had been perpetrated?  
3. If the pontiffs had no part whatsoever in the fraud, did the Decretals themselves at least introduce something new in what they teach concerning papal authority?

## § I

**2.** It is useful to divide the various recent opinions concerning the origin of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection chiefly into three classes.

The first class consists of those who, fewer in number and virtually abandoned by everyone, assert that the Decretals were composed at Rome to increase papal power. To this group belong the Catholic of unfortunate reputation Antonius Theiner [Note: [Col. V] *On the Pseudo-Isidorian Collection of Canons* by Antonius Theiner—please distinguish him from his brother Augustine. Breslau, 1827.] and H. E. Eichhorn [Note: [Col. V] *Proceedings of the Berlin Academy*, year 1834, and in Savigny’s *Journal for Historical Legal Scholarship*, vol. IX, no. II, pp. 119 ff.]. They nevertheless add that the Decretals originated at Rome in the eighth century and were enlarged in the middle of the ninth century by a certain Frankish cleric.

Others portray Pseudo-Isidore as almost entirely innocent. Among these must be named A. Walter [Note: [Col. V] Walter, *Church Law*, 10th ed., § 79.] and Rosshirt [Note: [Col. V] C. T. Rosshirt, *On the False Decretals*, preliminary notice, Heidelberg, 1847; and *On the Ecclesiastical-Law Sources of the First Millennium: On the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals*, Heidelberg, 1849.], the former professor at Bonn and the latter at Heidelberg. Walter holds that our author—whom he suspects of having been Benedict the Levite, compiler of the Pseudo-Capitularies—intended nothing more than a complete collection of canons embracing the discipline of the Church, and concentrated especially on matters that at that time were being more seriously neglected. Rosshirt agrees for the most part. From a Bamberg codex discovered by him, he believes he has established that our Mercator first employed, for the most part, apocryphal materials, which he considers chiefly to have been of Greek origin [Col. VI], and that at that time it was not regarded as fraud to compose such documents when genuine materials were lacking, provided that the documents suited the persons and circumstances.

The celebrated defender of the faith Möhler must also be added to this group [Note: [Col. VI] *Fragments from and concerning Pseudo-Isidore*, *Tübingen Quarterly*, 1829, no. 3, and year 1832, no. 1.]. He considers the Decretals a pious fraud undertaken for the good of ecclesiastical liberty. For, since in those most grievous times all human and divine things were being confused and all authority of the living was held in contempt, that author brought forward persons of venerable antiquity, as it were, to protest against the prevailing disorder.

Authors of the third class admit a genuine fraud, but one that neither proceeded from Rome nor intended Roman advantage. Some of them—Spittler [Note: [Col. VI] *History of Canon Law*.], Plank [Note: [Col. VI] *History of the Christian-Ecclesiastical Constitution of Society*, vol. II, p. 800 ff.], and Drosle-Hulshoff [Note: [Col. VI] *Principles of Common Ecclesiastical Law*.]—say that the Decretals were directed against metropolitan power. Others, such as Knust [Note: [Col. VI] Knust, *On the Sources and Purpose of the Pseudo-Isidorian Collection*, Göttingen, 1832.], who likewise calls Benedict the Levite of Mainz the author, think that they were forged to vindicate the rights of bishops both against secular and against synodal tribunals.

To this group belong also those who seem, more than the others, to have indicated to us the genuine source of the Decretals. A. Wasserschleben [Note: [Col. VI] W., *Contributions to the History of the False Decretals*, Breslau, 1844.] and Gfrörer [Note: [Col. VI] Gfrörer, *Freiburg Theological Journal*, 1847; *Investigation into the Age, Origin, and Purpose of the Decretals of False Isidore*, Freiburg, 1848; and *History of the East- and West-Frankish Carolingians*, Freiburg, 1848, vol. I.] hold that Otgar, or Autgar, archbishop of Mainz, had the Decretals collected after the assembly of Thionville in 835, in order to vindicate the primatial rights of the see of Mainz in Germany and further to defend the rights of bishops against princes and synods. A man who deserves honorable mention, Karl Hefele, approaches this opinion as the more probable [Note: [Col. VI] Hefele, *Tübingen Theological Journal*, year 1847, no. 4], although, with the modesty and moderation of judgment characteristic of him, he does not conceal the difficulties.

Following these guides, we establish three principal points for resolving this riddle: first, that the Decretals were composed neither at Rome nor in the eighth century; second, that they were composed in the middle of the ninth century in Frankish territory; and third, that it appears highly probable that Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, was their author in the moral sense, as they say.

Those who say that Pseudo-Isidore was compiled at Rome in the eighth century rely chiefly on the argument that the so-called Chapters of Hadrian I, or of Angilram of Metz [Note: [Col. VI] See Mansi, vol. XII, p. 904 ff.], were excerpted from Pseudo-Isidore, while, according to several codices [Note: [Col. VI] Cf. the Ballerini, *On the Ancient Collections and Collectors of Canons*, part III, chap. 6, § 2, no. 8, at the end of the works of Saint Leo, *Patrology*, vol. LVI, col. 244.], these same chapters had been handed over at Rome by Hadrian I to Angilram.

Nevertheless, Wasserschleben has conclusively shown that the codex inscription which states that they were presented to the pope by Angilram should be preferred, when Angilram was at Rome in 785 to have the accusation against him removed. For the rules found in them agree much more with the discipline prevailing in the Frankish kingdom, especially concerning provincial synods, than with that which the pontiffs were then defending. Indeed, some provisions seem less favorable to papal rights, such as Chapters 6, 20, 27, and 28. Finally, the sources from which the chapters were drawn are not those from which a Roman pontiff would have drawn them—for example, the decrees of the Spanish and Gallican synods, the Visigothic Law, and the Alarician Breviary. Indeed, some writers [Note: [Col. VI] Knust, Walter, Rettberg, *Church History of Germany*, vol. I, appendix, and, before them, the Ballerini, cited above.] believe that these chapters belong to a later period and were fabricated by Mercator himself.

The argument based on the alleged fact that the Chapters of Angilram were composed at Rome is therefore invalid; the place accordingly fails. But it is also false that they were excerpted from Mercator himself; hence the date fails as well. There is nothing in them that agrees with the purpose and principles of Pseudo-Isidore, especially concerning accusations against bishops. For the passages in two chapters that are found to have been taken from Isidore, Wasserschleben testifies that they are absent from one codex of better quality and were interpolated later. Indeed, some provisions contradict Isidore, such as Chapters 6, 12, 27, and 28. On the contrary, it is evident that Isidore drew from Angilram, since at times, where Angilram cites his sources more accurately, Isidore reproduces them in variously altered form.

Nor do Theiner and Eichhorn fare better when they argue that certain parts of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection—such as the Pseudo-Clementine letters, the Donation of Constantine, and the Acts of Sylvester—had already been cited by eighth-century witnesses, such as Hadrian I in a letter addressed to Charlemagne, a capitulary of 806, and certain statements of Agobard of Lyon and Theodulf of Orléans. For it is sufficiently established that such documents had already been fabricated before Isidore, who not only deceived others but was himself deceived in many matters.

Those who wish the documents of Mercator to have existed already in the eighth century are easily shown to be later than the author of the Decretals. Here belongs the collection of canons of Remedius of Chur, said to have been written at Charlemagne’s command, since the title on which that opinion rests is plainly fabricated [Note: [Col. VI] Thus the Ballerini, cited above, chap. 4, § 4, no. 13, *Patrology*, vol. LVI, col. 249; with Knust, Wasserschleben, Richter, Walter, Kunssmann, *The Collection of Canons of Remedius of Chur*, Tübingen, 1836.]. The argument drawn from a letter of Gregory IV to the bishops of Gaul and Germany in 832 must also be placed here [Col. VII], if it is spurious, as Richter holds. But even if we suppose it genuine, it is by no means clear whether it derived from Isidore or Isidore from it.

Finally, Eichhorn seemed to himself to have accomplished something significant in proving the same point when he thought he had discovered that the *Liber Pontificalis*, which Mercator used above all, was unknown outside Italy. This is entirely false, since the Venerable Bede used it in the eighth century, and Gallican codices from the same period are not lacking.

But why waste time refuting such petty arguments, when two pontiffs, in the years 850 and 863, while themselves listing the canonical authorities used by the Roman Church, mention only the decretals contained in the enlarged Dionysian collection?

Thus Leo IV, in his second letter to the bishops of Britain [Note: [Col. VII] Mansi, vol. XIV, 884]:

> “It is not proper for anyone to judge from the booklets and commentaries of others and to abandon the canons of the holy councils or the rules of the decretals—that is, those which are held among us together with them in the canon and which we use in all ecclesiastical judgments: those of the Apostles, of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Chalcedon, Sardica, Carthage, and Africa, together with the rules of the Roman bishops: Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, and Simplicius. These are altogether the authorities by which bishops judge and by which bishops and clergy alike are judged. For if some unusual matter should arise or occur that could in no way be settled by these authorities, then, if statements of Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, or other similarly holy doctors like those whom you have mentioned should be found, they are to be retained and promulgated with courage, or such matters are to be referred to the apostolic see.”

Nor was Nicholas I, bishop, any less explicit in a letter to Hincmar of Reims in 863 [Note: [Col. VII] Mansi, vol. XV, 374]:

> “Moreover, we decree and establish that no one may dare or be able with impunity to seek or await the judgments of others, or to accept ordinances contrary to the canons from elsewhere, or to flee irregularly to other provinces, but only in accordance with what has been promulgated in the canonical definitions of Nicaea and the other councils, and what has been decreed in the constitutions of the blessed Roman pontiffs Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Boniface, Leo, Hilary, Gelasius, Gregory, and the others, without prejudice in any matter to the right of the apostolic see.”

What need is there, then, of a longer examination, when the pontiffs themselves show themselves entirely alien to such a fabrication—at least, which is sufficient for our present purpose, down to the year 863, by which time the Pseudo-Isidorian materials had certainly been disseminated throughout Gaul?

**3.** Having removed the obstacles, let us proceed to positive arguments and determine when and where Pseudo-Isidore was fabricated. It seems especially certain, from the arguments assembled by the Ballerini [Note: [Col. VII] Cited above, § 4, no. 14, *Patrology*, vol. LIV, col. 250.], Knust, and Wasserschleben, that the cradle of the fraud must be sought in Frankish territory. For all the codices, including the Vatican codex no. 630, which is the oldest of all, originated there. The Decretals are first cited by Frankish authors. The sources from which Pseudo-Isidore drew are the decrees of the councils of Spain and Gaul, the Alarician Breviary with Anian’s interpretation, the collection of canons of Quesnell, and the letters of Saint Boniface of Mainz concerning the Carolingian kingdom.

The Hispanic Collection, which Pseudo-Isidore made the foundation of his work, appears in his version with those alterations that are found in codices of Gallican origin [Note: [Col. VII] The Ballerini, in the same place and no. 19, col. 255 D.]. His language likewise betrays a Frankish origin: for example, *missi* are called *legati* (“legates”); *seniores* is used for feudal lords; *comites* is read in the sense that then prevailed; and the words *venire* (“to come”), *habere* (“to have”), *modernus* (“modern”), and *custodire* (“to guard”) are employed according to Franko-German usage.

In establishing the date of the fraud, we have an indisputable *terminus ad quem* in the Assembly of Quierzy of 857, which certainly used the Pseudo-Decretals. Blondel, the Ballerini, Wasserschleben, and Gfrörer placed the *terminus a quo* in the Paris synod of 829; Walter in the letter of Gregory IV of 832; and Knust in the synod of Aachen of 836, because the impostor seems to have drawn from those sources.

But such an argument does not seem sufficiently solid. For in cases of this kind one must ask which of two sources that agree so closely that one must depend on the other was followed by the other, and which preceded. It is therefore enough for our present purpose to establish that Pseudo-Isidore came to light somewhat before the Assembly of Quierzy, in the middle of the ninth century.

**4.** To look deeply into the darkness concealing the period, author, and purpose of the Pseudo-Decretals, we must turn our attention to another forger of the same age, who seems closely connected with Pseudo-Isidore. This is Benedict, the Levite of Mainz [Note: [Col. VII] See his work in Baluze, *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, and in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, vol. IV, p. 39, appendix.]. As he himself says in the preface to his work, at the command of his archbishop Otgar he undertook to prepare a new collection of capitularies, supplementing the compilation of Ansegisus, from notes formerly gathered by Archbishop Riculf.

These alleged Capitularies, however [Col. VIII], are materials scraped together from everywhere in the manner of Pseudo-Isidore. Approximately one-twentieth of them—namely, fifty-seven capitularies—are taken from Pseudo-Isidore, so that a connection between the two impostors cannot be denied; one may almost say that the same person fabricated both the canons and the capitularies, proposing to disseminate the same principles and attain the same end by forging both ecclesiastical and civil laws.

Hincmar of Reims joins the two books and attributes them to the same author in his treatise against Hincmar of Laon. In chapter 24 he calls the Pseudo-Isidorian compilation a book of letters collected by Isidore, which Riculf, bishop of Mainz, had obtained from Spain and brought to these regions, just as he had obtained the royal capitularies.

Once this is established, it will be possible to confine the origin of the Pseudo-Isidorian work within narrower limits. Benedict the Levite repeatedly testifies [Note: [Col. VIII] Pertz, edition II, b, pp. 39–40] that he wrote his work after the death of Louis the Pious, while his sons were reigning—sons whom he already calls kings—at the command of Archbishop Otgar. Now Louis died in 840 and Otgar in 847. The intervening period must therefore be assigned to the composition of Benedict the Levite’s work, and Pseudo-Isidore, which he used, must have preceded it by some time.

**5.** Yet this will be the least benefit that our question derives from the connection between Benedict and Pseudo-Isidore. We can already see some trace of the author; from the circumstances of the times and places we can now extract his purpose and determine with the greatest precision the period in which the work was composed.

Two men could have collaborated in fabricating the Pseudo-Isidorian materials: Riculf, who gathered the notes from which Benedict, and therefore his parent or brother Pseudo-Isidore, drew; and Otgar, whom Benedict admits to have imposed the work upon him.

Hincmar the Elder, and most of the earlier writers after him, already suspected Riculf of being the author of the Decretals. He wrote in his treatise against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24:

> “But if you collected such things as seemed appropriate to you from the aforesaid judgments of Angilram and the frequently mentioned letters, by cutting them up, transposing them, and disorganizing them, because perhaps you thought that no one else possessed the same judgments or the letters themselves, and therefore believed that you could freely gather such things, the matter is astonishing, since this land is full of those very judgments, just as it is full of the book of letters collected by Isidore, which Riculf, bishop of Mainz, industriously obtained from Spain, as he did the royal capitularies, and caused these regions to be filled with it.”

Yet it is absolutely certain that Hincmar erred here and confused the Pseudo-Isidorian collection with the genuine Hispanic collection.

For it is established from historical records [Note: [Col. VIII] Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, I, 315, and *Supporting Documents*, no. 78] that in 788 Rachio, bishop of Strasbourg and a suffragan of Riculf, arranged for the genuine Isidorian collection of canons to be written. It is highly probable that this was the autograph which Hincmar claims Riculf brought from Spain.

Moreover, during the period when Riculf occupied the see of Mainz—from 787 to 813—the circumstances were not those presupposed by Pseudo-Isidore: namely, that priests were being oppressed, ecclesiastical property seized, and similar abuses being committed. Such things did not occur under Charlemagne’s rule.

Blondel infers that Riculf introduced something new from Book VII of the Capitularies, 281, where he is said to have brought forward at the Assembly of Worms a letter of Gregory of which there had been no previous or subsequent record. But this was a genuine letter of Gregory II to Saint Boniface.

Benedict does indeed say in the preface to his Capitularies:

> “These chapters, which we have endeavored to gather together in the following three books, we found scattered in various places and on various sheets, just as they had been issued in various synods and general assemblies; and especially we found them deposited in the archive of the holy metropolitan Church of Mainz by Riculf, metropolitan of that holy see, and finally discovered by Autgar, his second successor and kinsman. We preferred to insert them in this little work in the form written above.”

But who is so blind as not to see that this was fabricated by the impostor in order to lend authority to his fictions, when it was so widely known that Riculf had brought from Spain a collection of canons previously unknown in those regions? Finally, Benedict does not even claim that he drew everything from Riculf’s notes, but says that he found materials in various places and documents.

**6.** The matter appears entirely different if we consider Otgar’s character and the events of his life. It is manifest that the impostor pursued two aims: to free bishops from secular [Note: [Col. VIII] Letter 1 and 2 of Pius; Letter 1 of Pontian; Letter 1 of Zephyrinus.] and synodal [Note: [Col. VIII] Letter 5 of Damasus; Letter 1 of Julius; Letter 1 and 4 of Zephyrinus and Damasus; Letter 2 of Sixtus.] tribunals and false accusations, and to protect their property from seizure by secular powers [Note: [Col. VIII] Letter 2 of Pius; Letter 2 of Zephyrinus; cf. the Preface]; and to exalt the primates, whom he is the first to teach should be introduced on a wider scale [Note: [Col. VIII] Letter of Anicetus to the bishops of Gaul: “Let no archbishops be called primates except those who preside over the chief cities whose bishops the apostles and their successors regularly established as patriarchs and primates, unless some nation should thereafter be converted to the faith and, because of the multitude of its people, it should be necessary to establish a primate for it. The others, however, who have obtained other metropolitan sees, should not be called primates but metropolitans.” Mansi, vol. I, 684. —Letter 1 of Clement; Letter 2 of Julius, chap. 12; Letter 1 of Felix II, chap. 12; Letter of the Egyptians to Felix II; Letter 1 of Victor. [Col. IX] Letter 1 of Sixtus II; Letter 1 of Felix I; Benedict the Levite, book II, canons 309 and 381; book III, canons 83, 89, 156, 171, 314, 321, 439, and 460.], whom he wishes to be judges to whom appeal from a metropolitan’s judgment may be made.

[Col. IX] The other two aims that he appears to have pursued—defending papal authority and the right of appeal, and diminishing the prerogatives of metropolitans—are plainly secondary and subordinate to the former. For he has recourse to the pontiffs because he trusts that bishops will find in them the strongest protection against their oppressors. Hence he also defends so fiercely the greater cases of bishops, which are reserved to the pontiffs.

If we compare all this with Otgar’s age and life, we shall see that it corresponds like wax impressed by a seal.

When Louis the Pious had fathered by his second wife Judith a son, Charles, later called the Bald, he and the empress sought to secure a portion of the empire for the son of the second marriage. Consequently, the sons of Irmengard, his first wife, to whom he had divided the empire by the law of 817 concerning the succession, took up arms against their father.

Many prelates stood on their side: the abbots Wala, Hilduin, and Elizachar, and the bishops Ebbo of Reims, Agobard of Lyon, Jesse of Amiens, and Otgar of Mainz. Matters were brought to such a point that the emperor was compelled to perform public penance, chiefly at the urging of Ebbo of Reims.

When the emperor had been miserably oppressed, the minds of his subjects and of his sons Louis and Pippin changed for the better, so that he was restored to the kingdom. Then, at the Synod of Thionville in 835, Ebbo was deposed after confessing in writing that he was unworthy of the episcopate; the others suffered penalties in various ways. Otgar, humbly asking pardon, was released after a brief imprisonment.

After Louis’s death, a new quarrel broke out among his sons. Lothair sought to subject the whole kingdom of Charlemagne to himself, while Louis and Charles claimed their respective portions. In this conflict Otgar, continually striving to preserve the unity of the empire, was on Lothair’s side and, as Nikardus testifies [Note: [Col. IX] *History*, II, 7; Pertz II, 659], was the most hostile of all opponents of Louis the German. Thus, even after Lothair had been defeated, Otgar went with the other vassals of Lothair toward the Rhine in order to prevent Louis from crossing the river. When affairs went badly, he fled from Louis’s anger. Only after the Treaty of Verdun did he return to Louis’s favor. Certainly, in 845 we find him exercising episcopal office and enjoying Louis’s favor.

It is scarcely worthwhile to prove from the synods and authors of the same period how badly the Churches were treated amid such great disorders and in such a barbarous age, and how their property and ministers scarcely fared better. Hence the complaints about churches that had been despoiled.

Nor is it surprising that, after the decrees of the Synod of Thionville had been issued against Otgar and his associates, he attacked the judgments of synods and amassed such a mass of material concerning the forms of trials to be held against bishops that either it would avert the blow directed against him or, rather, demonstrate that the blow had been unjustly delivered.

There are also certain passages in the Decretals which, as Hefele shows [Note: [Col. IX] Cited above, p. 627], seem clear enough to point directly to Ebbo’s confession and deposition. For Pseudo-Alexander writes [Note: [Col. IX] Letter 1]:

> “Likewise, if writings of this kind have in any way been extorted from such persons through fear, fraud, or force, or if they have been written or confirmed by them through whatever ingenuity so that they might be able to free themselves, we judge that this shall bring them no prejudice or disadvantage whatsoever; nor do we permit them ever, by God’s authority and that of the holy apostles and their successors, to suffer any disgrace or accusation on this account, or any sequestration of their property.”

Indeed, certain things in the Decretals seem to us to concern the first see and the principle that it should be judged by no one—things that may depend upon the events of that period.

Gregory IV, having come from Italy in order to reconcile peace between the father and his sons, was detained by Lothair and seemed to favor the sons. The German prelates who supported Louis rose up against him and went so far as to plan the excommunication of the pontiff.

It was then that Wala, abbot of Corbie, whom we mentioned above among the adherents of the sons, offered the pontiff a collection of authorities in 833. These authorities demonstrated that the pontiff possessed all the eminent authority and living power of blessed Peter, that he judged everyone, and that he was judged by no one. Later, our Isidore likewise gathered together materials of this kind.

The other end that Pseudo-Isidore set before himself, and that the Levite Benedict likewise advanced, was, as we were saying, to vindicate for the Church of Mainz genuine primatial rights similar to those enjoyed in Africa by the metropolitan of Carthage, and in other regions by the papal vicars of the Roman patriarchate. How aptly this applies to Otgar we shall see if we inquire what the fate of this dignity at the see of Mainz was from Saint Boniface down to Otgar himself.

That most holy apostle of Germany received from Pope Zachary the see of Mainz, elevated to metropolitan status, to which the Churches of Tongeren, Cologne, Worms, Speyer, and Utrecht were to be subject, together with all those German peoples whom he had converted—namely, the recently established sees of Würzburg, Büraburg, Erfurt, and Eichstätt, to which Augsburg, Constance, Chur, and Strasbourg were later added. This was truly a primatial authority, since the Churches of an entire nation were subject to Mainz.

Soon afterward, however, while Lullus, Boniface’s successor, occupied the see, Hadrian I separated the diocese of Utrecht from the metropolitan see of Mainz and subjected it to the Church of Cologne. Indeed, that authority of an apostolic vicar and primate does not seem to have passed to Boniface’s successors, as Blascus has splendidly shown [Col. X] in chapter 7 of his dissertation on the Collection of Isidore Mercator.

[Note: [Col. X] Carolus Blascus, *On the Collection of Canons of Isidore Mercator: A Commentary*, in Galland, *On the Ancient Collections of Canons*, collection of dissertations, vol. II, Mainz edition, 1790.]

Nevertheless, Mainz retained the first place among the sees of the Frankish Empire for a long time, as the same author shows more fully in chapter 13. Accordingly, it was easy for Boniface’s successor to conceive the ambition of demanding that Boniface’s prerogatives should both remain with him and be restored to him. Riculfus, who succeeded Lullus, unwillingly saw Salzburg and Cologne elevated to metropolitan status.

While Otgar occupied the see, the greater part of Mainz’s suffragans was about to be taken away from it, and consequently its metropolitan diocese diminished, since Louis the German claimed the trans-Rhenish regions of the empire as his own, whereas ecclesiastical provinces generally tended to follow the boundaries of kingdoms. Hence Otgar was so devoted to the unity of the empire and opposed to Louis the Pious when he granted Alsace, Swabia, and part of Burgundy to his son Charles, while favoring Lothar, since he desired the entire inheritance of Charlemagne.

You will find this expressed especially clearly in the Decretals. He introduces Pope Pelagius II speaking and explaining what constitutes a legitimate ecclesiastical province:

[Note: [Col. X] Letter otherwise numbered 8.]

> “Furthermore, brothers, concerning the matter of the province about which you formerly wished to consult the Apostolic See, it seems to us that it has been sufficiently treated by our holy predecessors. But since you have again thought it right to question our mediocrity on the same matter, know that a definite province is one that has ten or eleven cities, one king, and an equal number of lesser authorities under him; and one bishop, together with ten or eleven other suffragan bishops as judges, to whose judgment all cases of bishops and of the other priests, as well as the cases of the cities, are referred, so that all these matters may be justly decided by them with one harmonious voice, unless an appeal has been made by those who are to be judged to a higher authority. Therefore no province ought to be degraded or dishonored, but each should have within itself its own judges, priests, and bishops, each according to his proper order.”

Yet in the fourth year after the peace of Verdun—which, in accordance with Otgar’s wishes, prevented the province of Mainz from being divided—his successor Rabanus Maurus, while holding a synod at Mainz, had eleven suffragans: Salomo of Worms, Gebhard of Speyer, Gozbald of Würzburg, Otgar of Eichstätt, Baturad of Paderborn, Ebo of Hildesheim, Haymo of Halberstadt, Waltgar of Verden, Gerbrath of Chur, Lanto of Augsburg, and Salomo of Constance.

[Note: [Col. X] Harzheim, *German Councils*, II, at p. 152.]

In a word, he had precisely as many bishops subject to him as Pseudo-Pelagius wished to constitute a province. Note also that the Pseudo-Decretal requires a province to be under the authority of a single king. It further requires that the cities in which primates are to sit should already have been major and primary cities before Christ’s coming.

[Note: [Col. X] Letter 11; Stephen I, chapter 4; Anacletus, letter 2, chapter 4.]

There were, moreover, people who derived Mainz’s origin from Magontius, the son of Hercules, or from Magog, the son of Japheth, or from the Magi expelled from Trier. Certainly, at some time before the birth of Christ, it was given the status of a city by a certain Drusus. Add to this the statement in the letter of Anicetus cited above, that a primate is not to be admitted except those established by the apostles, unless among a people converted later whose number is so great that it requires such a head; and you will have Mainz and its province almost perfectly portrayed.

Nor will it be difficult for us to explain why, after the peace of Verdun, we see Otgar abstaining from such frauds, reconciling himself with Louis the German, and why there was then, both from his successor Rabanus and for a long time afterward in Germany, a profound silence concerning the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals. The explanation is that the peace of Verdun introduced such a division of the empire as left the extent of the province of Mainz entirely untouched. At that point the very inventor of the fraud neglected his own wares, since they had become useless to him.

If we consider all these matters together, it seems most probable that Otgar of Mainz was at least the moral cause of the Decretals. Whether Benedict the Levite himself was Mercator, as Walter, Knust, and others plausibly maintain, I would not presume to decide, nor do I think that it can ever be established with certainty. The suspicion is certainly favored by the fact that he freely altered and translated the Pseudo-Isidorian sections he used, as one does who is employing his own compositions and citing them not word for word, rather than one who is copying the work of another.

It is now clear that the Decretals and Benedict’s later Capitularies were composed neither before the assembly at Thionville in 835 nor after the peace of Verdun in 834. Finally, whether they were later expanded, as Gfrörer suspects, by Wenilo of Sens—who himself aspired to primatial authority in Gaul, as did his successor Ansegisus—and by Rothad of Soissons, is scarcely something anyone can determine; nor is this suspicion based on arguments capable of persuading a prudent person.

Once these points have been established, we cannot agree with those who portray that Mercator as so entirely harmless. Who could persuade himself that a man who introduced such a lie into the world was so dove-like in simplicity that, while lying, he scarcely thought himself to be acting rightly? We know nothing of pious frauds, nor do we believe that they have ever belonged to the pious. Still less should it be said that such falsehoods were then regarded not as frauds but as a certain method of setting forth one’s own principles.

[Col. XI] Finally, the passage in Pseudo-Isidore’s preface from which the distinguished Rosshirt attempts to demonstrate that these wares were drawn from Greek sources proves absolutely nothing.

[Note: [Col. XI] *Ibid.*, p. 52.]

For the author of that preface speaks of councils, not of decretal letters. Here are his words:

> “Those councils, however, which were published in the Greek style, we find to have been interpreted or written out in more than threefold or fourfold form. But if the truth is to be sought, let us follow the style of the Greeks from among the many, and imitate their expressions and copies, and so forth.”

The documents that he produced from the Bamberg manuscripts, in which Pseudo-Decretals supposedly occur before Mercator, were written after him, since they concern the ordinations of Formosus. But that little work, recovered from the Bamberg manuscripts, which he supposes to have been wholly unknown and earlier than Pseudo-Isidore, from which Mercator drew, is nothing other than the first book of Auxilius on the ordinations of Formosus, written long after Mercator. Therefore, although it is true that Pseudo-Isidore made use of many materials already in existence, it must not be said that he did not combine very much on his own initiative.

### 7.

Let us now hear what the distinguished Hefele has brought forward by way of objection, though in the form of a doubt and while himself favoring our hypothesis.

[Note: [Col. XI] *Ibid.*, p. 628.]

There are, he says, so many sections in the Pseudo-Decretals that in no way serve the author’s alleged purpose; the fact that metropolitan authority is so greatly diminished does not fit Otgar, who himself was a metropolitan; and Benedict the Levite, whom we suppose to have been associated with Isidore, is even less likely to have been hostile to metropolitans. It would be strange, if Otgar were the author of the Decretals, for them to have been wholly ignored by his successor Rabanus, and indeed for no use to have been made of them in Germany for a long time afterward, so that at the synod of Gerstungen in 1085 the German bishops, together with the papal legate, mentioned them only with a certain disdain.

But who does not know that such forgers mix in many things that are indifferent and appear harmless with those matters that they chiefly intend to implant in people’s minds, lest the evil purpose, exposed too openly and too nakedly, should immediately become apparent? There is no reason for surprise that Isidore diminishes metropolitans, since he claims for himself the higher authority of a primate.

Nevertheless, I would not say that the Decretals directly oppose metropolitans or synods, whose celebration they emphatically urge.

[Note: [Col. XI] Anacletus, letter 1; Felix, letter 1; Julius, letter 2.]

Their sole intention is that synodal judgments should not be conducted arbitrarily, that there should be no refuge from unjust sentences, and that judgment should not be exercised in another province—as had occurred at Thionville. Indeed, he wishes cases to be brought first before the metropolitan, then before the synod, afterward before the primate, and finally before the pope, unless an appeal has been made immediately to him.

[Note: [Col. XI] Compare Pelagius I, letter 8.]

Therefore it is not correct to object that Benedict the Levite was less hostile to metropolitans. Add that it is in no way certain that he was the same person as Isidore; consequently, it is not unreasonable to allow some difference between them. Finally, the subject matter of the Pseudo-Capitularies was different.

Gfrörer has admirably explained why the collection of Pseudo-Decretals was passed over in silence by the German bishops and by Rabanus, and finally abandoned even by Otgar himself. Nothing needs to be added to what we excerpted from him above, except that most of the German bishops stood on the side of Louis the Pious and, later, of his namesake son. Consequently, the collection could not so readily have been sent to them or received by them as to Otgar’s associates living in Neustria, among whom it was later widely disseminated, once it had been abandoned by its author after being received back into Louis’s favor.

It is also false that the German bishops either neglected or despised the Decretals until 1085 and afterward. For at the synod of Cologne in 887 they used Anacletus’s letter; at Mainz in 888, Urban’s letter; and finally, at Tribur in 895, several Pseudo-Isidorian decretals. We omit other points that are easily resolved, for the sake of brevity.

## § II.

Although almost all critics now admit that the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals were invented neither at Rome nor for the service of the popes, many nevertheless maintain that several popes later favored them and used them for their own advantage. Wasserschleben believes that Sergius II, as early as 844, wished to create Drogo, bishop of Metz, as primate of Gaul and vicar of the Apostolic See, according to the principles of Pseudo-Isidorian law. Yet nothing appears in the records of those proceedings that bears the distinctive mark of the Decretals, nor was the dignity that the pope was seeking for Drogo so novel.

The letter of Nicholas I to the Gauls concerning the case of Thietgaud of Trier, which cites a Pseudo-Decretal of Alexander I and which Hontheim assigns to the year 861, is of doubtful authenticity.

[Note: [Col. XI] In Hontheim, *History of Trier*, vol. I, p. 197.]

Kunstmann considers it to belong to Nicholas II, since what is said there concerning the bishop of Trier fits not Thietgaud but Eberhard, who was captured by Count Conrad of Luxembourg.

[Note: [Col. XI] *Neue Sion*, 1845, no. 54.]

The matter is settled by the year 863, when Nicholas, writing to Hincmar of Reims, enumerated only the Decretals of the Hadrianic collection, as we reported above; thus the Roman pontiffs plainly knew nothing of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection. At almost the same time, Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, consulted that same pope about a Pseudo-Isidorian decretal of Melchiades in these words:

[Col. XII]

[Note: [Col. XII] Mansi, vol. XV, p. 397.]

> “It is said that Pope Melchiades decreed that no pontiff should ever be deposed without the consent of the Roman pope. Therefore we beg you to be so kind as to send us his statutes in full, just as they are preserved among you.”

The pope, replying to Wenilo and his fellow bishops, to whom Lupus had written in conjunction, says nothing at all about this matter—certainly either because he did not find the decretal, or, if you prefer, because the response sent to Lupus has perished. Nevertheless, the same conclusion follows: when replying to Wenilo, Nicholas deliberately refrained from using a decretal that so strongly favored papal authority.

### 9.

Hence many believe that Nicholas finally learned of the Decretals from Rothad of Soissons, while Rothad was staying at Rome after appealing against Hincmar of Reims. So Gfrörer and Spittler maintain.

[Note: [Col. XII] Spittler, *History of Canon Law*, p. 256.]

Whatever the truth may be, it is certain that in 865, when writing to the Gallican bishops concerning Rothad’s case, Nicholas refuted Hincmar’s contention that the decretals of the popes were without force if they were not contained in the canonical code—that is, in the Hadrianic collection. These are his words:

[Note: [Col. XII] Mansi, vol. XV, pp. 694–695.]

> “Yet, to speak to you while preserving with you the charity rooted in our hearts, we are grieved that you have set this aside, and we rightly reprove you for having, in this matter, despised the decrees of various prelates of the Apostolic See. For far be it from us not to embrace, with due reverence and the greatest discernment, the decretal constitutions or any explanations concerning ecclesiastical discipline of anyone who has persevered in the Catholic faith until the last day of his life—writings which holy Roman Church has preserved from ancient times and entrusted to us also for safekeeping, and which it venerates as having been properly deposited in its archives and ancient records . . . . . Although some of you have written that those decretals of the ancient pontiffs are not contained in the entire body of the canonical code, you yourselves use them indiscriminately whenever you see them supporting your purpose, and now claim that they are less acceptable only when they diminish the authority of the Apostolic See and support your own privileges. For some of their writings are preserved with us, and they are known to set before us not only the decrees of any Roman pontiffs whatsoever, but even those of earlier authorities, in their own cases.”

Nor is there any need, with Kunstmann, to say that Nicholas here had no reference at all to the Pseudo-Decretals, for the very tenor of his words refutes that view.

Nevertheless, anyone who concludes from this that Nicholas accepted the Decretals themselves or ever used them is seriously mistaken. Hefele indeed cites Nicholas’s letter to Charles the Bald from the same year, in which he supposedly uses a Pseudo-Decretal of Julius.

[Note: [Col. XII] Letter 40; Mansi, vol. XV, p. 658.]

But, with all respect to that distinguished scholar, nowhere in the false Decretals could we find what Nicholas reports about Julius. The words convey nothing more than a brief narrative of events, which he took either from the *Tripartite History* or from the genuine letter of Julius to the Orientals. Here are the words:

> “Pope Julius also, writing to the Orientals, urged the presence of both parties—that is, Athanasius and his opponents—so that, with both parties present, the accused might be heard and, after being condemned by all, might thereafter be restrained from the priesthood.”

In another letter of the same year to the Gauls, he cited a genuine decretal of Julius. Nicholas never used the Decretals and never invokes any one of them by specific mention, although the opportunity arose so many times.

As for that letter addressed to Hincmar, which is the only one in which the pope refers to the Pseudo-Decretals, there are two points that must be made.

First of all, it must be noted that Nicholas displays only a confused and general knowledge of those Decretals, and does not appear ever to have had them before his eyes except in a few passages cited by Hincmar. He speaks of them only once, and then in certain general terms.

The second point, which must be regarded as most important, is that Nicholas is not concerned at all with the authenticity of the Decretals. He merely attacks the principle asserted by Hincmar: that the decretals, even if genuine, were without authority because they had not been received into the canonical code, namely, the Hadrianic collection. Nicholas left entirely untouched the question of the authenticity of the Decretals, acting with the utmost prudence so as neither to admit doubtful matters inconsiderately nor to reject them rashly. No occasion had been given for him to address that question. For Hincmar himself did not then doubt their authenticity. Although these events took place in 865, when writing to Charles the Bald around 868 he still invoked the Pseudo-Decretals of Urban, Lucius, and Stephen as authoritative support.

[Note: [Col. XII] Letter 29.]

Gfrörer indeed thinks that Hincmar did not dare to attack the authenticity of the Decretals publicly after Nicholas I had defended them, and that he at least admitted them as a subsidiary source of law.

[Note: [Col. XII] *Ibid.*, pp. 172, 185.]

But if this had been so, he would certainly have remained silent, not used them—as in fact he did. The same point is confirmed by the work that Hincmar opposed to the booklet composed by his nephew Hincmar of Laon from the Pseudo-Isidorian materials at the synod of Attigny in 870.

He does not in any way attack the authenticity of the Decretals or of Angilram’s Capitularies, which had been joined to the Decretals:

[Col. XIII]

> “But if,” he says, “you collected such passages as seemed suitable to you from the aforesaid judgments of Angilram and the frequently mentioned letters by cutting them up, reversing their order, and disorganizing them, because perhaps you thought that no one else possessed the same judgments or the very letters before you, and therefore believed that you could freely collect such things, the matter is remarkable, since this land is full of those very judgments, just as it is full of the book of collected letters by Isidore, which Bishop Riculfus of Mainz obtained after it had been brought from Spain, as he was diligent in such matters and in royal capitularies also, and caused these regions to be filled with them.”

[Note: [Col. XIII] Chapter 24.]

You see that Hincmar still regarded the Capitularies as a genuine collection of Isidore, and reproved the younger Hincmar only for having used them improperly, just as he had used Angilram’s capitularies.

He himself uses the Decretals of Clement, Anacletus, Zephyrinus, Stephen, and others to establish that metropolitan bishops owe due obedience.

[Note: [Col. XIII] Chapters 11–15.]

What Hincmar’s position was, however, is clear from the same work. His whole purpose is to show that only those canons are to be followed “which the Apostolic See . . . . . and the whole Catholic Church calls canons,” and which are found “in our books, which our ancestors received from the Apostolic See for observance.”

[Note: [Col. XIII] Vol. II, p. 543, Sirmond edition.]

Hincmar distinguishes between canons and decretal letters, relying on the fact that Gelasius, when speaking at the Roman synod about books to be received and not received, says that councils are to be received and guarded, whereas decretal letters are to be received with reverence.

[Note: [Col. XIII] Chapters 25–26.]

He interprets the passage of Leo, which Nicholas had cited in writing to the bishops of Gaul, as meaning that the decrees of the popes have force insofar as they agree with the general statutes of the Church; that it is one thing to give laws and another to decide this or that matter according to laws already given. The decisions of councils, he holds, are the supreme rule of ecclesiastical law, and the See of Peter cannot prescribe anything contrary to the authority of councils.

Hincmar calls the booklet extracted by his nephew from the Pseudo-Isidorian materials “a mousetrap set around all metropolitans,”

[Note: [Col. XIII] Chapter 10; *Works*, vol. II, p. 813.]

 but not because he considered the Decretals themselves fraudulent. Rather, as we saw above, the testimonies had been excerpted and collected in such a way that many passages were omitted which insisted upon the suffragans’ due subjection to the metropolitans.

[Note: [Col. XIII] Compare chapters 11–19.]

Indeed, he attacks the Decretals themselves, not because he regarded them as inauthentic, but because he thought them inconsistent with the councils. Apart from the councils, he held, the popes had nothing to define, and he attributed no authority to them on the ground that they had not been received into the canonical code; consequently, they had no force against the rights of metropolitans and synods.

From this we must derive the standard by which that letter in which Nicholas speaks of the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals is to be interpreted. Since the controversy between the pope and Hincmar did not at all concern their authenticity, Nicholas should not be considered to have defended their authenticity.

Finally, in 872 Hincmar, writing a letter in the name of Charles the Bald to Hadrian II, attacked the authenticity of the Decretals in a text full of invective and anger. He insisted that the Sacred Scriptures, the tradition of the Fathers, and the definitions of councils were to be followed:

> “Whatever,” he says, “has been compiled or fabricated by someone else, we recognize not only as to be rejected but also as to be refuted.”

[Note: [Col. XIII] Works, vol. II, pp. 701–706.]

But do not forget that these words were spoken seven full years after Nicholas’s letter.

As for the popes who followed, they must truly be said to have neglected Isidore’s Decretals. The complete collection was neither known nor established at Rome until the middle of the eleventh century, after the passage of a long period had silenced every doubt and the collection had been admitted through the common usage of all—and consequently had been received into the canonical collections of Regino, the Prümian, and Burchard of Worms.

[Note: [Col. XIII] Compare Carolus Blascus, dissertation, chapter 3, p. 18.]

Nicholas I, John VIII, and even Saint Gregory VII denied that fornicating and murderous clerics were to be restored, contrary to what Pseudo-Isidore teaches in the second letter of Callistus and in the addition to the letter of Gregory the Great to Secundinus.

[Note: [Col. XIII] Nicholas I, letter to Arduicus of Vaison, in D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. 12, and letter to the German bishops, in Martène, *Collection of Ancient Writers*, vol. I.]

[Note: [Col. XIII] John VIII, letter to the bishop of Le Mans, chapter 4, distinction 50.]

[Note: [Col. XIII] Gregory VII, letter to the bishop of Lincoln, book VII, letter 34.]

John the Roman deacon, who wrote the life of Saint Gregory and dedicated it to John VIII, treats accusations and judgments on the basis of Gregory’s conduct and teaching, yet says nothing about what is presented on this subject in Pseudo-Isidore’s letter of Gregory to Felix of Messina.

[Note: [Col. XIII] Book 4, chapters 5–6.]

What he presents elsewhere concerning the degrees and impediments of kinship, which resembles that letter, he derived not from it but from Egbert.

[Note: [Col. XIII] Book 2, chapter 10.]

Of the popes before the time of Leo IX, we find only Hadrian II and Stephen V citing false decretals. Hadrian, in a letter written to the synod of Douzy concerning the case of Actard of Tours in 871, invokes a letter of Pope Anterus.

[Note: [Col. XIII] Letter 32, in Mansi, vol. XV, col. 852.]

Nevertheless, since he cites nothing Pseudo-Isidorian elsewhere, although opportunities arose very frequently, it must be said that he had not seen the complete collection and knew this isolated passage only because Actard had brought it to his attention.

[Col. XIV]

Add that this occurred a full year before Hincmar first attacked the authenticity of the collection.

The other pontiff, Stephen V, writing to Luitpert, bishop of Mainz, about the number of the Nicene canons, says on the authority of Athanasius that there were seventy; this is found in the Isidorian letter of Athanasius to Pope Mark.

[Note: [Col. XIV] In Ivo, p. 4, chapter 232, and Gratian, canon 13, distinction 16.]

But since he cites neither Mark’s own letter nor those of Julius or Felix II, which also bore upon the matter, what we said about Hadrian applies equally here. Nor should it be overlooked that both popes did this in matters that touched the rights of the primacy least of all, and that, although the fraud concerning the seventy Nicene canons was introduced into the West by Mercator, it had nevertheless arisen in the East long before.

Auxilius, who wrote a booklet on the ordinations of Formosus at the beginning of the tenth century, cites only one letter of Anterus, while passing over letters that might have been of great usefulness to him—the second of Evaristus, the second of Callistus, and the first of Pelagius II. He therefore seems to have drawn from the letter of Hadrian II, who had cited the same letter in the same case concerning the transfer of bishops.

The *Lives of the Pontiffs* attributed to Liutprand of Cremona, an author of the tenth century, which make extensive use of the Pseudo-Isidorian materials, are not Liutprand’s, as everyone acknowledges, but belong to some unknown German.

Indeed, as late as 1085 Otto, cardinal-bishop of Ostia and papal legate—who later became Pope Urban II—spoke of the Pseudo-Isidorian materials at the synod of Gerstungen only contemptuously, using these words:

> “Those passages of Scripture whose testimony we have used have always been recognized as objects of reverence in the Church, and their authors are by no means obscure or of uncertain name.”

You see how, over the course of two centuries, the popes must truly be said to have been ignorant of and to have neglected the collection itself, using its testimonies only once or twice, insofar as others brought them to their attention. Indeed, the collection itself was not accepted in Italy at all.

We are not unaware that our opponents insist forcefully upon this point: that although the popes did not accept the wording of the Decretals, they nevertheless accepted their principles, and that they spread Isidorian law far and wide. But we shall vindicate them from this accusation if we show briefly that papal authority did not derive its origin from the Decretals, but that for a much longer period the Roman pontiffs had already exercised those prerogatives which, in the middle of the ninth century, they defended against Hincmar—prerogatives which are such that they necessarily flow from the very nature of the primacy.

## § III.

Even many Protestants do not deny that the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals contributed nothing new to the popes.

[Note: [Col. XIV] Luden, *General History*, vol. II, book II, chapter 10; *History of the German People*, vol. V, p. 473. Leo, *Universal History*, vol. II, p. 100; Gfrörer, *ibid.*, p. 213; Schönemann on Böhmer, *Principles of Canon Law*, seventh edition, § 122, note b.]

For it is clear that such frauds would not be accepted so widely by people unless they contained things already accepted by many. Certainly, if the Decretals had taught matters that at that time were completely unheard of and could not be defended by any documents of antiquity, how could the fraud not have been immediately exposed to everyone’s eyes?

What is more, it is now certain that Pseudo-Isidore was less a forger in creating new things than in composing new constructions from ancient documents and attributing to foreign authors things that had genuinely been said or written. He placed the genuine collection of Isidore, which Riculfus of Mainz had brought from Spain, as the foundation of his compilation. The rest he scraped together from the authentic Decretals of the popes, the genuine acts of councils, and the writings of the Fathers; from the Capitularies of the Franks, the Theodosian Code, the Breviary of Alaric and its commentators; from the Rule of Saint Benedict and the *Book of the Pontiffs*; and from certain genuine letters of the patriarchs of Constantinople, Saint Boniface, and his friends.

The acts of Sylvester that he used are indeed false, but by then they had already been accepted by everyone. How, then, could the ideas have been so new, when even the words were not new? We do not deny that Pseudo-Isidorian law contains certain matters that were only implicitly present in the earliest discipline, and others of which only rare examples were supplied in the first centuries of the Church.

Nevertheless, changes of this kind in ecclesiastical discipline had already been introduced, or were beginning to be introduced, before the Decretals were composed, according to the changing circumstances of the times. The compiler’s sole purpose was to defend and promote them, along with many other matters already admitted into ecclesiastical law and sanctioned by the popes when they most certainly still knew nothing of the Decretals—matters that would have been accepted even if Pseudo-Isidore had never written.

Indeed, for a long period Pseudo-Isidore had no authority at all in Italy or Germany.

These general remarks against the Protestants and Febronians should suffice. Earlier critics—such as the Ballerini, Blascus, and Zaccaria—have already labored sufficiently to defend the rights of the primacy attacked on the basis of the Pseudo-Decretals. We shall refrain here from repeating what has been said so many times, and shall undertake only to resolve certain more subtle difficulties that are occasionally raised even by Catholics.

[Note: [Col. XIV] Compare Walter, *Canon Law*, § 92.]

Many of our own writers concede, as they must, that appeals to the Roman pontiff were always admitted. Nevertheless, Hincmar was already arguing that, according to the norm of the ancient discipline, the pope ought to delegate judges in the province to hear the case, and that it was not lawful—as Pseudo-Isidore so often declaims—to exclude suspected judges by an appeal made before sentence had been pronounced.

[Col. XV]

[Note: [Col. XV] Letter of Anicetus, chapter 3; first letter of Victor, chapter 3; letter of Sixtus II; second letter of Julius, chapter 3, verse 10; first letter of Felix II, chapter 19—in which passages Pseudo-Isidore imitates the Council of Chalcedon, canons 9 and 17; third letter of Fabian, chapter 2; second letter of Felix I; third letter of Sixtus III—which are taken verbatim from the Interpretation of the Theodosian Code, book 11, title 30, concerning appeals; first letter of Eleutherius, chapter 3; first letter of Felix I, chapter 8, from the Interpretation of the Novels of Marcian, book III, title 7, section 1.]

But the first point is altogether false, since canon 8 of Sardica expressly says: “If he should declare that his case ought to be heard in the city of Rome,” and very frequent examples from antiquity are not lacking. The second point must be rejected no less decisively, since traces of this right—which follows from the very nature of any judgment—and definite examples of it occur in the earliest times, before the Decretals had either been fabricated or spread in every direction.

Leo IV had already established the following in 850, when treating of the judgments of bishops:

[Note: [Col. XV] Letter 2.]

> “And if among those whom men have declared worthy of condemnation there should be a bishop who has requested that his case be heard in the presence of the bishop of the Roman See, no one shall presume to pronounce a final sentence against him; rather, we decree that he be heard without fail.”

This ruling admits an appeal before sentence has been delivered, or the transfer of the case, and sends the hearing itself—that is, the investigation of the proceedings—to Rome, if he so wishes.

Likewise, in 835 Gregory IV had established the following in favor of Aldric of Le Mans, who was being harassed by many:

[Note: [Col. XV] Letter 1.]

> “We command,” he says, “that if any of Aldric’s rivals should wickedly attempt to accuse Aldric, bishop of the Church of Le Mans, then, in honor of the memory of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the Roman Church, over which its privilege and the authority of our office preside, he may, after being heard by the primate of the diocese, appeal to us if necessary and, by our authority, conduct and conclude his proceedings either before us or before legates sent from our side, according to the decrees of the Fathers. No one shall judge him, or presume to judge him, before this has occurred. But if anything grave and intolerable—which God forbid—should be brought against him, our judgment must be awaited, so that nothing may first be decided concerning one who has fled to the bosom of the holy Church of Rome and implored its aid, until it has been commanded by the authority of that same Church, which has so bestowed its functions upon other Churches that they have been called to share in its solicitude, not in the fullness of its power.”

You see how he grants Aldric that, if he wishes, the hearing alone may remain with the synod, while the sentence is reserved to himself.

Such, namely, was the condition of the times that it became necessary for the cases of bishops to be brought more and more before the Apostolic See. A rough and barbarous storm had preceded, during which no synods had been held in Gaul for eighty years, as Saint Boniface testifies.

[Note: [Col. XV] Letter 49 to Zachary.]

It was he who recalled the celebration of synods from oblivion. Once the former order had been restored, however, metropolitan bishops very often abused their right, especially since they frequently depended upon secular authority or were unable to protect the innocent. For this reason it was no longer expedient to hand bishops over to the arbitrary will of just anyone, leaving them no way out of their difficulties.

In the same way, I would have you resolve the difficulty that troubles others—namely, the claim that a new right was introduced because Pseudo-Isidore sends absolutely all episcopal cases, and not merely doubtful ones, to the cases reserved to the popes as major cases, and because he holds that sentences in such cases cannot be pronounced by synods unless the pope grants permission.

[Note: [Col. XV] Letter of Eleutherius, chapter 1, verse 2; letter of Victor I, chapter 1, verse 3; letter of Zephyrinus, chapter 1; letter of Sixtus III, chapter 1; letter of Marcellus, chapter 1; letter of Julius, chapter 1, verse 2; preface to Julius’s letter 1; letter of Felix II, chapters 17–18; letter of Damasus, chapter 4, verse 2.]

Nevertheless, Isidore was not the only person to demand this at that time. The Council of Troyes, consisting of six provinces and held in 867, in which Hincmar himself took part, asked Nicholas I not to permit a bishop to be deposed without the consent of the Roman See. It is manifest that this was done not to weaken metropolitans and councils, but to avert the force of kings and nobles, so that they might have a stronger protection in the Roman pontiff. They do indeed appeal to the Decretals; but Hincmar himself, who had already rejected their authority, and none of his associates would have adopted such a right, indeed would have demanded it, if it had followed from the Decretals alone and had not also been seen as necessary from the whole condition of the times. Gregory IV had already acted in the same way in the letter mentioned above. For he derives, in a lengthy discussion, the basis of the privilege granted to Aldric of Le Mans from the principle that major cases are to be reserved, by decree of the Fathers, to the Roman pontiffs:

“Rulers of the Church are rather to be awaited and corrected than immediately judged without consultation with us, since the canons of the holy Fathers, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, command that greater matters and more difficult outcomes of cases be suspended pending our decision and brought to an end under our direction . . . . . By the present command we prescribe nothing new, but confirm those things which seem formerly to have been granted, since no one doubts that not only episcopal litigation but every matter concerning holy religion ought to be referred to the Apostolic See, as to the head of the Churches.”

Among the Greeks, who certainly could not have been deceived by those Decretals, the same discipline had already become established: episcopal cases were reserved to the patriarchs, as had been decreed by the Fourth Council of Constantinople in 869 [Note: [Col. XV] Canon 26.].

[Col. XVI] Finally, they call a new rule the one which establishes that all synods, even particular ones, are to be held only by the authority of the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. XVI] Julius, Letter 2, chapter 29. Letter of the Egyptians to Felix II. Marcellus, Letter 1, 2. Damasus, Letter 4, chapter 2.]. Yet this he drew from the Tripartite History, which says that “the ecclesiastical rule commands that councils ought not to be celebrated apart from the decision of the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. XVI] Book IV, chapters 9, 19].” Pseudo-Isidore appears indeed to have understood this in such a way as to require the pontiff’s express permission. But even this had already begun to be both required and observed at that time, before the Decretals had arisen. In a letter to the bishops beyond the Alps, by which in 844 Sergius II appointed Drogo of Metz his vicar in Gaul and Germany, he says, among other things:

“To him we entrust our authority in convening general synods throughout all parts of the aforesaid regions, and whatever shall have been defined by a provincial synod, we decree that it be brought without delay to his knowledge.”

Writing to Hincmar [Note: [Col. XVI] Mansi, vol. XIV, col. 886.], Leo IV declares that he will not confirm the Council of Soissons, both for other reasons and “because legates of the Apostolic See were not present there.” In the same letter he delegates Peter of Spoleto and the bishop of Arezzo of the same name to remedy the defect.

We also see this acknowledged in the words of Nicholas I:

“[Note: [Col. XVI] Letter 17, in the same volume, vol. XV, p. 278; cf. Letters 28, 19, 22.] Your royal excellence recently sent word to our apostleship that we should deign to dispatch legates from our side for the completion of the synod.”

This was also conscientiously observed by Saint Boniface. Not only for the synods which he presided over in Gaul [Note: [Col. XVI] Letters 49, 63. Zacharias, Letters 2, 9.], but also for those which, already archbishop, he held in Germany [Note: [Col. XVI] Gregory III, Letters 4, 7.], he sought and obtained the authority of the Apostolic See. That he accomplished little in this matter is evident from the fact that afterward it did not pass into practice that the pontiff’s special command and authority should be required with such strictness [Note: [Col. XVI] Cf. Thomassinus, *Vetus et nova Ecclesiae disciplina*, vol. II, book III, chapter 57; Blascus, *De Collectione canonum Isidori*.].

Among the unheard-of innovations introduced by Pseudo-Isidore, Theiner included the proposition that the First See is judged by no one on earth. Yet Pseudo-Isidore expounded that doctrine only in the Acts of Sylvester [Note: [Col. XVI] Canon of Sylvester, chapters 3, 20.], which, although apocryphal, are nevertheless no older than he is. The same point is also found stated repeatedly in genuine documents from before Isidore [Note: [Col. XVI] Gelasius, Letter IV to Faustus; Letter 14 to Dardanus. Roman Synod under Symmachus, 501. Ennodius, *Apologetic Libellus*, 502. Avitus of Vienne, Letter to the Senate, 502.]. When Leo III was accused, the Fathers of the Roman synod convened by Charlemagne only a few years earlier, in 800, refused to judge him. When Gregory IV had been terrified by the threats of the German bishops, Wala, abbot of Corbie, presented in 803 a collection of documents demonstrating that the Roman pontiffs are judged by no one. Otgar, or whoever the Mainz compiler of the Decretals was, had been imbued with this same doctrine by Saint Boniface himself, the apostle of Germany. For from his statements the following pronouncement concerning the Roman pontiff has been handed down:

“Since he himself is to judge all, he is to be judged by no one [Note: [Col. XVI] In Cardinal Deusdedit, book I, *De Rebus ecclesiasticis*, chapter 231. Nauclerus, *Generatio* 26. Gratian, chapter 6, distinction 40.].”

Nor did he invent the dignity of the primacy—something which would certainly have been rejected by everyone—for something of this kind had long been found among apostolic vicars, and even more nearly in the primate of Africa, who in dignity and name was precisely what the Pseudo-Decretals of the Church of Mainz proposed to claim for themselves.

From all this, then, let us conclude that Pseudo-Isidore did not effect a change in ecclesiastical discipline, but expressed and defended a change already made, and accompanied it as it was beginning.

[Col. XVI]

D. GEORG PHILLIPS, TREATISE ON THE PSEUDO-ISIDORIAN COLLECTION.

(Translated from the German work *Kirchenrecht*, Regensburg, 1851, p. 61, into Latin.)

I. The Collection Described

[Col. XVI] Because of the considerable benefit derived from it, the Spanish Collection necessarily had to spread quickly beyond the boundaries within which it originated [Col. XVII] [Note: [Col. XVII] Hincmar of Reims writes to his nephew Hincmar of Laon (HINCMAR OF REIMS, *Opusculum* LV, chapter against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24, *Works*, vol. II, p. 476): “But if you collected such things from the aforesaid judgments and frequently mentioned letters by cutting them off, putting them out of order, and disarranging them because you perhaps thought that no one besides yourself possessed the same judgments or the letters themselves, and therefore believed that you could freely collect such things, this is astonishing, for this land is full of those very judgments, just as it is full of the book of letters collected by Isidore, which Bishop Riculf of Mainz obtained after it had been brought from Spain, being diligent in such matters as he was in royal capitularies, and caused these regions to be filled with it.”]. The first of all to have a copy of it rewritten was Rachio, bishop of Strasbourg, in 787. Through the efforts of Riculf, archbishop of Mainz and Rachio’s metropolitan, it was multiplied and propagated throughout the entire Frankish kingdom. The preface of Rachio’s manuscript, which still survives, first contains the *Order for Celebrating a Council*, taken from the Fourth Council of Toledo [Note: [Col. XVII] Council of Toledo IV, 633, chapter 4.]. This was perhaps because the copyist of the codex had the Frankish kingdom especially in mind, since he proposed that councils be organized according to the model of the Spanish councils [Note: [Col. XVII] It is regrettable that Koch communicated citations from Rachio’s codex so sparingly. It would be of great interest to know whether anything was read in the preface that was not unlike the words of Pseudo-Isidore in his own preface: “At the beginning of this volume we have placed the manner in which a council is celebrated among us, so that those who wish to follow our order may know how they ought to conduct it.” By these words the author seems to imply that he is writing among foreigners. The manuscript codices of the Spanish Collection found in Spain display the order of which Pseudo-Isidore speaks only in the acts of the Fourth Council of Toledo. Cf. Batterini, part IV, chapter 4, § 4, no. 16, p. 519.].

This codex of Rachio, copied from the Spanish Collection, did not proceed beyond the Twelfth Council of Toledo (681). In general, however, Frankish manuscripts include the Thirteenth Council (683), but not the Fourteenth Council of Toledo (686). Such manuscripts, enlarged by several false decretals and other apocryphal materials, were circulated everywhere in the Frankish kingdom toward the end of the ninth century under the name of the Collection of Isidore [Note: [Col. XVII] Hincmar of Reims, *Opusculum* XLVIII, chapter 21 (vol. II, p. 793). For it is written in a certain sermon without the name of its excerptor, concerning the deeds of Saint Sylvester, which Bishop Isidore of Seville collected together with the letters of the pontiffs of the Roman See, from Saint Clement to Blessed Gregory, that the same Saint Sylvester had decreed that no layman should dare to bring an accusation against a cleric.].

It remains disputed whether that name had previously been attached to the genuine Spanish Collection [Note: [Col. XVII] This is still entirely unknown. Cf. Arevalo, *Isidoriana*, chapter 91 (*Works of Saint Isidore*, vol. II, p. 176, note 18).], or whether it was called by that name from the time when, in the preface later attached to the work, Isidore is introduced speaking as its author [Note: [Col. XVII] In Merlin: “Isidore, servant of Christ, to his fellow servant and reader” (Gratian also reads it this way as far as this word in canon *Placuit*, distinction 16, canon 4), “and to his faithful relative in the Lord, greeting.” On the addition “Mercator” or “Peccator,” see the text above and the following notes. Instead of *fideli*, another reading has *fidei*; and instead of *lectori*, Arevalo [Col. XVII] (*loc. cit.*, *Works*, vol. VI, p. 607) reads *Hectori*. No bishop of that name is known in Isidore’s time; in 516 a certain Hector appears as bishop of Carthage at the Council of Tarragona (see Harduin, *Councils*, vol. II, col. 1043).]. For this reason, in more recent times, the name of Pseudo-Isidore was given to the enlarged Spanish Collection [Note: [Col. XVII] The sole edition is this: MERLIN, *The First Volume of the Four General Councils, and Also of Forty-Seven Authentic Provincial Councils; Likewise of the Decrees of Sixty-Nine Pontiffs, from the Apostles and Their Canons up to Zacharias I, with Isidore as Author. Also the Golden Bull of Emperor Charles IV Concerning the Election of the King of the Romans*. Paris, 1523; Cologne, 1530, 2 vols., folio. Paris, 1535, 2 vols., octavo (from the printing office of the honorable man Francis Regnault). That edition adopted many fragments lacking in the older manuscripts. Cf. Camus, “Notice of Manuscripts Containing Collections of Canons and Decretals” (*Notices et Extraits des Manuscrits de la Bibliothèque nationale*, vol. VI, p. 270, note 12). See also Ballerini, *loc. cit.*, chapter 7, p. 559 ff.].

Some historians honor Isidore II of Setabis or Xàtiva (683), the bishop, with authorship of this work [Note: [Col. XVII] See Blascus, *loc. cit.*, chapter 6, p. 35. Cf. also Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol. VIII, p. 48 ff.]. This opinion, however, has no greater claim to credibility than the one that attributes the collection of canons itself to him. It would not be highly improbable that he, like others, attempted at different times to complete the earlier Spanish Collection and carried it through as far as the Thirteenth Council of Toledo [Note: [Col. XVII] He attended the Fifteenth Council of Toledo in 688 (Harduin, *Councils*, vol. III, col. 1771); given the chronology, he could have been one of those who worked anew on the Spanish Collection. He is distinct from Isidore I, whom he succeeded (677–682; Council of Toledo XII, 681, col. 1726).], so that the name Isidore, attached to the Collection, became confused with the name of the holy bishop of Seville [Note: [Col. XVII] The Modena codex, like the Vatican codex: “Here begins the preface of Saint Isidore’s book.” See Zaccaria, *loc. cit.*, vol. 42: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, here begins the preface of Saint Isidore’s book.”].
