This is merely a supposition, which, on examination, advances no farther than the limits of conjecture set against the opposing view. The principal fact is that the compiler of that enlarged Spanish Collection, as the ninth century presents him to us, called himself either Mercator [Note: [Col. XVII] One codex among those of Arevalo reads *Mercatus* (Arevalo, *loc. cit.*, p. 209, note 52).] or Peccator. The former reading is supported by the most ancient manuscripts [Note: [Col. XVII] Arevalo, *loc. cit*.]; the latter by the custom, very common among the bishops and monks of this century, of styling themselves “Sinner” [Note: [Col. XVII] See Elipandus’s letter to Migetius, no. 10 (in Flórez, *loc. cit.*, vol. V, p. 531): “But concerning priests, when you assert that they call themselves sinners, how can they be truly holy? Or if they confess that they are sinners, why do they presume to approach the ministry?” See also Blascus, *loc. cit.*, p. 35 ff.; Devoti, *Jus canonicum universum*, Prolegomena, chapter 18, § 15, note 1 (vol. I, p. 357). See the Council in Trullo, 692: “Andrew the sinner, Philip the bishop, and many others” (Harduin, [Col. XVIII] *Councils*, vol. III, col. 1702). Rachio of Strasbourg likewise styled himself Peccator; see Koch, *loc. cit.*, p. 174. See especially the subscriptions to Chrodegang’s privilege of 751 (in Harduin, col. 2008).], that is, of designating themselves by the surname Peccator.

[Col. XVIII] Among the oldest copies of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection is the Vatican codex (630), transferred from Gaul to Rome. It is believed to have originated during the reign of Nicholas I (858–862) [Note: [Col. XVIII] Not much more recent, and certainly not later than 881, is the cathedral codex of Modena, mentioned by Zaccaria, *loc. cit.*, pp. 284, 291; it too originated in Gaul. Like the Bamberg codex mentioned above (see Rosshirt, *loc. cit.*, p. 49), it contains only decretals. The Modena manuscript does not appear to have been examined by scholars with the care it deserved. Pertz (*Archive of the Society for German Historiography*, vol. V, p. 34) was unable to visit the cathedral library of Modena during his journey; the codex is not mentioned in any of the other volumes of the *Annals*.].

In this manuscript [Note: [Col. XVIII] Concerning this codex, see the Ballerini, *loc. cit.*, chapter 6, § 5, no. 16; d’Aguirre, *Councils of Spain*, “Plan of the Work,” no. 9, p. 5; Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum manuscriptorum*, vol. I, p. 128; Camus, *loc. cit.*, p. 288 (“Comparative Table of the Five Manuscripts with Merlin’s Edition”). See also Rosshirt, *loc. cit.*, p. 51. He considers the manuscript not so ancient. See also Wasserschleben, *loc. cit.*, p. 25, who judges the Modena codex to be less important than it is commonly considered.], the method of compilation is indicated as follows. The Collection is divided into three parts. The work is preceded, in the manner of a preface, by various short writings: a list of the supreme pontiffs down to Nicholas I; various materials concerning ecumenical and particular councils, intermingled with several authentic fragments of the Spanish Collection; then a description of the provinces of the Roman Empire; and a letter of Luitard of Vence to Wenilo of Rouen. There follows a preface bearing the name of Isidore Mercator. In it the author declares that he undertook his work at the urging both of many—eighty—bishops and of other priests [Note: [Col. XVIII] Preface: “I am compelled by many bishops as well as by the other servants of Christ to collect the judgments of the canons and make one thing out of many. But I want you to know that eighty bishops compelled me to begin and complete this work,” and so forth. In Merlin. The shorter preface presented by Arevalo, *loc. cit.*, p. 607, suggests that it is the original and that the longer preface arose from it. Arevalo’s opinion does not seem to have been especially accepted by Richter (*Jus ecclesiasticum*, chapter 69, note 4). The matter remains disputed.]; in order that, with all ecclesiastical discipline collected into one body, he might leave a doctrinal work for bishops, priests, and laypeople [Note: [Col. XVIII] In the following words of his preface Merlin indicates the purpose that the compiler set for himself: “So that the discipline of the ecclesiastical order, collected and arranged by us into one body, might instruct holy prelates by the rules of the Fathers; that ministers obedient to the Church, or the people, might be imbued with spiritual examples; and that they might not be deceived by the depravity of wicked men. For many, weighed down by depravity and greed, have oppressed priests by accusing them. Therefore the holy Fathers established laws which they called holy canons. Many accuse others for the very purpose of excusing themselves through them or enriching themselves from their goods. But many good Christians remain silent and bear the sins of others which they know because they are often deprived of the evidence by which they could prove before ecclesiastical judges what they themselves know, since, although certain things are true, judges are nevertheless not to believe them unless they are demonstrated by definite indications, unless they are proved by manifest judgment, unless they are made public according to judicial procedure. For no one who has been stripped of his possessions or expelled from his own see by force or terror may, before everything taken from him has been restored to him by law and he himself has long enjoyed his honors peacefully and has been regularly restored to his own see, be accused, summoned, judged, or condemned according to canonical regulation, until he has been allowed to enjoy it freely for a considerable time.” (The preface in Arevalo, after the passage cited in the preceding note, moves on to the following, which is also abridged there.) “Hence ecclesiastical history, composed by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, says concerning a certain woman who was accused by her husband on the charge of unchastity: It was commanded or forbidden by an imperial law that she should first be permitted to arrange her household affairs freely for a considerable time, and only afterward answer the charges brought against her. All laws, ecclesiastical as well as civil and public, prescribe this. If all these harmonious provisions were set down, the days would run out before the task was completed and the letter would become excessively long. Nevertheless, from the many we have judged it appropriate to insert some for the instruction of others. Thus Saint Leo, bishop of the Roman Church, says in the letter sent to the Council of Chalcedon, and so forth. If such provisions have been established for women and secular persons, they have been granted much more to ecclesiastical men and priests. These same ecclesiastical laws also prescribe this. Likewise, canonical authority completely rejects accusers and accusations which the laws of the world prohibit. The authority to convene synods has been entrusted by a special power to the Apostolic See, and we read that no synod is valid which has not been convened or supported by its authority. Canonical authority attests this; ecclesiastical history confirms it; the holy Fathers affirm it.”].

To this preface is appended the petition of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, to Damasus, together with a letter, asking that he obtain both the earlier decretals and the response of the Roman pontiff. Damasus’s rescript follows, along with the *Order for Celebrating a Council* and another enumeration of synods. Finally, two spurious letters are read, attributed to Jerome and Damasus.

The division of this Collection into three parts, whereas the Spanish Collection consists of only two, arose from the fact that the latter begins with the Council of Nicaea; in the Pseudo-Isidorian Collection, by contrast, a series of decretals is placed before that council [Note: [Col. XVIII] Merlin’s preface: “Then we inserted the decrees of certain letters of apostolic men, namely Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, and the other apostles, whose letters we have thus far been able to find, down to Pope Sylvester. The same things were also decreed by the ancient apostles who lived before the Council of Nicaea.”]. These, together with the fifty apostolic canons added here [Note: [Col. XVIII] The Bamberg codex does not contain them. See Rosshirt, *loc. cit.*, p. 52.], constitute the first part. These decretals, fifty-nine in number, are attributed to thirty supreme pontiffs, from Clement I [Note: [Col. XVIII] On the Clementine letters, see the Ballerini, *loc. cit.*, no. 18.] through Melchiades [Note: [Col. XVIII] The Bamberg codex continues through Damasus. Rosshirt, *loc. cit.*, p. 52.] (314) [Note: [Col. XVIII] This method of proceeding had been indicated in Dionysius’s distinguished collection.]. The decretals are followed by a treatise on the primitive Church [Col. XIX] and the Council of Nicaea, which Gratian, deceived by the arrangement, counted among the decretals of Melchiades [Note: [Col. XIX] Ballerini, *loc. cit.*, no. 19, p. 547.]. The first part concludes with the spurious letters of the donation of the emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. XIX] See canon *Constantinus*, distinction 96, canon 14. Cf. Biener, *De collectionibus canonum Ecclesiae Graecae*, § 14, pp. 72 ff.].

The second part, namely the collection of councils, begins with a fragment of the preface of the Spanish Collection [Note: [Col. XIX] “Canons of the general councils,” and so forth.], as well as with another fragment of the Quesnellian Collection [Note: [Col. XIX] “The letter or preface of the Council of Nicaea to the most blessed Sylvester.”]. In all other respects this part differs in nothing from the first part of the Spanish Collection. The division is the same in both, and the series of councils is also the same [Note: [Col. XIX] In addition to all the Greek councils contained in the Spanish Collection, Pseudo-Isidore presents the following: Councils of Carthage I–VII and of Milevis; Councils of Arles I–III; Valence, Turin, Riez, Orange, Vaison I; Agde and Orléans I; Elvira, Tarragona, Girona, Zaragoza I; Lérida, Valence, Toledo I–XIII; Braga I and II; the Capitula of Martin of Braga III (675); Seville I and II.].

In the third part, a preface was likewise taken from the Spanish Collection. The Acts of Sylvester (335) follow, together with the decretals of that pope and of the supreme pontiffs who followed him, down to Gregory II (731). During the pontificate of the latter, thirty-five further spurious fragments were added. Up to this point the original manuscript is rightly recognized. There follows a blank leaf; then, written in the same hand, the fifth and sixth spurious synods of Symmachus and certain apologetic writings concerning that pope, together with two letters of his. After another blank leaf, certain spurious capitula of Angelramnus (176) are read; then eighty judgments concerning proceedings against bishops and clerics, as well as other fragments of lesser importance [Note: [Col. XIX] Cf. Möhler, *loc. cit.*, pp. 285–304; Walter, *loc. cit.*, § 95, p. 187, § 98.].

The Pseudo-Isidorian Collection is much more extensive than the Spanish Collection, since the spurious decretals contain many discussions of dogmatic and moral matters, namely: ordination, baptism, confirmation, marriage and sacrifice, fasting, the Paschal solemnity, the discovery of the cross, the translation of the bodies of the apostles, chrism, blessed water, the consecration of churches, and the blessing of crops, sacred vessels, and ornaments.

The Isidorian Collection is especially distinguished by the fact that it develops and orders with the greatest precision those matters which concern the constitution of the Church. It discusses the primacy of the apostle Peter, as well as that of his successors in the Roman See; the individual degrees of the hierarchy; and, above all, primates, accusations and proceedings against bishops and laypeople, their appeals to the pope, and their relationship with him concerning provincial councils.

II. The Pseudo-Isidorian Collection Concerning the Sources of Ecclesiastical Law

The spurious decretals by which the Spanish Collection had been enlarged, both at its beginning and in later times, caused little disturbance and, once certain impractical propositions had been set aside, gained acceptance everywhere, since they were in no way opposed to ecclesiastical discipline [Note: [Col. XIX] Cf. Döllinger, *Liber instructionis historiae ecclesiasticae*, vol. II, p. 46; Hefele, *loc. cit.*, p. 593; Rosshirt, *loc. cit.*, p. 36.]. Pseudo-Isidore’s positions concerning the divine origin of the apostolate, the succession of the episcopate [Note: [Col. XIX] Accordingly, according to Pseudo-Isidore, bishops are in no way regarded as delegates of the Roman See. [Col. XIX] Cf. Walter, *loc. cit.*, p. 201, note y.], and the divinely instituted primacy of the Roman pontiff—who, as the head of the Church, is subject to no judge on earth and imposes laws upon the universal Church—are the same as those supplied by Sacred Scripture, the holy Fathers, witnesses of tradition, and the authentic sources of ecclesiastical law [Note: [Col. XIX] In two places—Anacletus, Letter 3, chapter 2 (canon *In novo*, distinction 21), and chapter 3 (canon *Sacrosancta*, “Inter,” 5)—the following words occur: “The apostles wished him [Peter] to be their leader.” Since the two chapters exalt the divine institution of the primacy in a particularly emphatic manner, they attempt to signify the agreement between the will of the apostles and the divine will; but there does not appear to be any mention of election. (Walter, *loc. cit.*, p. 199, note o.)].

Other propositions which at first sight seem to have the character of novelty, when examined, prove to be such as one will find universally attested either in still earlier sources or in the actual practice then approved [Note: [Col. XIX] See Walter, *loc. cit.*, § 98, for an exposition of these sources.]. Other propositions, moreover, flow as necessary corollaries from the fundamental principles of the constitution of the Church, so that it matters little whether they had been expressed in the form of a canon or decretal. From this it follows that, once everything has been properly elucidated, scarcely anything new remains in Pseudo-Isidore’s doctrine [Note: [Col. XIX] Cf. Hefele, *loc. cit.*, vol. V, p. 640, etc.], except for one or another proposition, for example: “No layman is permitted to accuse a cleric.” This, however, never passed into practice [Note: [Col. XIX] For example, Clement, Letter 1 (canon *Beatus*, 5, chapter 5, question 1). Cf. Walter, *loc. cit.*, p. 209, note p.].

In that Collection, however, one will find several propositions concerning the relationship of bishops with the Roman primacy which are regarded as entirely new and attributed to Pseudo-Isidore. Thus one reads the following proposition, although it was never applied in practice: “Provincial councils may not be convened without the consent of the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. XIX] Julius, Letter 1, chapter 2 (canon *Dudum*, part 9, chapter 3, question 6). Letter 2, preface: “Councils ought in no way to be celebrated apart from the decision of the Roman pontiff.” (In Merlin, fol. 162A.) Chapter 29 (canon *Regula* 2, distinction 17). See also the passage cited above (§ 173, note 89). Cf. Walter, *loc. cit.*, vol. V, p. 202, note e at the end.], or at least require his approval for the validity of the acts conducted in the synod.” Then: “In accusations against [Col. XX] bishops, the provincial councils have jurisdiction only over the investigation [Note: [Col. XX] Some have falsely claimed that Pseudo-Isidore wished to remove episcopal cases entirely from provincial councils. See Walter, *loc. cit.*, p. 201, note c.], and over the transmission of that investigation to the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. XX] For example, Eleutherius, Letter 1, chapter 2 (canon *Quamvis*, part 7, chapter 3, question 5). Cf. Walter, *loc. cit.*, p. 205, note s.]. The right of the supreme pontiff, however, is [Note: [Col. XX] Julius, Letter 1, chapter 2.] to decide all episcopal trials himself, as major cases; but an accused bishop has the right, not only after the judgment of the council but already before it, to appeal to the supreme pontiff whenever he regards his judges as either hostile or suspect [Note: [Col. XX] For example, Victor, Letter 1, chapter 3 (chapter *Si quis*, part 7, chapter 2). Cf. Walter, *loc. cit.*, p. 204, note q.].”

These propositions, by universal agreement, lead back to an almost unquestionable principle: since the episcopate is of divine institution, and by virtue of that institution is intimately joined to its head, the successor of Peter, it cannot be torn away from this union—which is necessary for the salvation of the Church—by any authority, ecclesiastical or civil. It must indeed be admitted that, given the condition of the Frankish Empire [Note: [Col. XX] “Concerning the history of Germany,” vol. II, p. 302, etc.], the dignity of the metropolitans, resting upon a merely historical institution and making the bishops participants in a kind of primatial authority, could not fail to hinder, even with respect to political administration, the union between the pope and the bishops. Apart from the actual truth of the matter and the certainty of this principle, however, and without any longer considering the condition of the Frankish kingdom, the question is whether the first of the propositions mentioned above, which are canonically expressed in the spurious decretals, should be attributed to Pseudo-Isidore.

The supreme pontiff Nicholas I, a contemporary of Pseudo-Isidore, expressed these very propositions almost word for word in an address delivered on Christmas Eve in 864 in the Basilica of Saint Mary Major [Note: [Col. XX] Nicholas I, *Sermon on the Case of Rothadus* (Harduin, *Councils*, vol. V, col. 585.)], as well as in a letter sent to the bishops of the Franks concerning the affairs of Rothadus [Note: [Col. XX] Nicholas I, Letter 42, to all the bishops of Gaul (Harduin, *loc. cit.*, col. 590 ff.)], the bishop of Soissons [Note: [Col. XX] On the case of Rothadus of Soissons, see Gess, *On the Life and Distinguished Writings of Hincmar of Reims*, § 10, p. 239, etc.; Hefele in the *Freiburg Ecclesiastical Lexicon*, vol. V, p. 205, etc.], who had appealed to the Apostolic See after his deposition [Note: [Col. XX] Cf. Kunstmann in *N. Sion*, p. 245, etc., where the matter is treated more fully and specifically.].

With respect to matters more directly concerning the convocation of councils and the confirmation of their decisions, Nicholas I expressly says:

“A general council—that is, a council of all the bishops of all the provinces of the kingdom—cannot be convened without the command of the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. XX] The sermon cited, col. 585: “For this reason, when a general council had been convened—which no one is permitted to call without the command of the Apostolic See [Col. XX]—the bishops summoned this man, Rothadus, whom, at the royal suggestion of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, they had caused to assemble, so that he might give an account of that priest before the synod.”].”

Indeed, long before this pontiff, the same principle concerning councils of every kind without distinction had been sanctioned in the *Tripartite History* [Note: [Col. XX] Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, book IV, chapter 9, no. 19 (from Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 8, no. 17). See Walter, *loc. cit.*, p. 202, note e.]. Moreover, even if matters had not stood thus previously, this proposition, correctly understood, contains a principle so true and incontrovertible that it would require neither the address of the supreme pontiff, nor the *Tripartite History*, nor any other earlier document. For, on the one hand, it cannot be denied that many councils have been convened without the prior consent of the supreme pontiff and have issued valid decrees without his confirmation—a practice that continued down to the present day. On the other hand, it is no less certain that no decision in the Church is valid if the supreme pontiff, as the head of the episcopate, contradicts it. If it has any force, it has that force because the supreme pontiff has approved it either tacitly or expressly. If, therefore, some supreme pontiff, following the example of Nicholas I and earlier documents [Note: [Col. XX] Canon *Confidimus* 1, chapter 25, question 1 (Gelasius, 495).], were to state this proposition concerning synods, because just as dangerous arrangements had formerly existed in the Frankish kingdom, so now a danger to the unity of the episcopate might arise from them, he would rightly be exercising a right most conducive to the salvation of the Church. Even if the compiler, placed in these circumstances, saw and expressed such a proposition earlier than himself, he would indeed have erred by giving it the form of a decretal, but he ought not on this account to be accused of novelty.

The remaining propositions mentioned above concern cases involving bishops who are summoned to trial before provincial councils properly convened by the metropolitan. In these cases—therefore designated by Pseudo-Isidore as “major cases”—an appeal is made to the supreme pontiff. Hence it is clear that the councils have jurisdiction over the ordering of the litigation, while judgment belongs exclusively to the pope [Note: [Col. XX] Walter, *loc. cit.*, p. 205, note 1, speaking of the Fourth Council of Constantinople in 869, chapter 26, observes that in the East, where the authority of the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals certainly carried no weight, discipline had been altered in a more stringent manner, and that bishops there were subject to the immediate judgment of the patriarch.]. Nicholas I explicitly adhered to this doctrine as a right already prevailing everywhere [Note: [Col. XX] Kunstmann, *loc. cit.*, p. 246.].

After the sentence had been pronounced, we by no means concede that the right of appeal, once sanctioned by law in the Council of Sardica [Note: [Col. XX] Justellus thought it appropriate to cut away several leaves from the manuscript he used, and thus the Council of Sardica appeared only in mutilated form. See Kunstmann, cited above, p. 241.] [Note: [Col. XX] Council of Sardica, canon 3. — Compare Walter, cited above, § 19, p. 44, note a.] was abolished by Charlemagne [Col. XXI] [Note: [Col. XXI] For example, Gfroerer (cited above, p. 5).], as some maintain [Note: [Col. XXI] Cf. Rettberg, *Church History of Germany*, II, 596.]. The Council of Chalcedon [Note: [Col. XXI] Council of Chalcedon, canon 9. — Compare Walter, cited above, § 93, p. 204, note q.] had granted bishops the power to appeal to a primate or patriarch before sentence had been delivered; how much more, then, to the supreme pontiff of the Church. Just as Gregory IV [Note: [Col. XXI] *Canon Decreto* II, c. 2, q. 5 (Gregory IV, year 832).] and Leo II [Note: [Col. XXI] *Canon Nullam* 3, C. 2, q. 4 (Leo IV, year 850).], so too Nicholas I—and indeed with the same intention as the Council—decreed that an appeal should be made to the pope in episcopal cases. As he himself observes, he drew this doctrine from the letter of Leo the Great to Anastasius of Thessalonica [Note: [Col. XXI] Leo the Great, letter 14 to Athanasius: “For, since you were free to suspend the more important matters and the more difficult cases while awaiting our decision,” etc.], where the discussion concerns more serious affairs and more difficult disputes [Note: [Col. XXI] See also Innocent I, *Letter to Victricius*; and, for the later period, *Canon Concilia* 6, D. 17 (Ennodius, *Apologia for the Roman Synod IV*—see Richter, *Church Law*, § 24, note 7),] specifically belonging to major cases. In this matter, therefore, just as Leo and every Roman pontiff after him would have determined, had circumstances required it, so Nicholas determined according to his right. And the same man who had earlier warned Hincmar of Reims in his reply that, “even if Rothad had never appealed” [Note: [Col. XXI] Nicholas I, letter 23: “Certainly Your Blessedness ought, when you had examined Rothad so many times, to have honored the memory of Saint Peter by writing, and to have awaited his judgment in every way, even if that same Rothad had never appealed.”], nevertheless had to await his judgment from Rome—he now answered the bishops of the Franks, who distinguished between episcopal cases and metropolitan cases, asserting that only the latter were major cases, in these excellent words: “But it is said …” etc. See Nicholas’s letter 75.

In establishing these principles, therefore, he exercised the power granted to him by God according to the needs of the times [Note: [Col. XXI] Walter rightly observes, cited above, p. 205, note u: “Their minds had been brought to this conclusion both by preceding events and by consideration of the remarkable dignity of bishops, so that episcopal judgments came to be regarded as major cases,” etc.], without there being any need for him to rely upon the authority of decretals issued by his predecessors or of any ecumenical council. Since, then, he established the same principles—and indeed in similar words—as the pontiff just mentioned, he must not be accused of falling into any charge of novelty, least of all of a kind that would have endangered ecclesiastical discipline.

Meanwhile, some maintained that Nicholas I had borrowed his statements from Pseudo-Isidore [Note: [Col. XXI] Wasserschleben, cited above, p. 76 and following. — Eichhorn, cited above, p. 179.]; indeed, on the basis of these statements they argued that the spurious decretals had not merely been in force at Rome but had also been issued there. But this alleged partnership between Nicholas I and Pseudo-Isidore [Note: [Col. XXI] Because he was unaware of the spurious decretals, the pope was seized by anxious doubt when a certain decretal of Melchiades was requested from him. — Compare Walter, cited above, § 95, p. 188, note b; Hefele, cited above, p. 649; Kunstmann, cited above, p. 243.] is supported by no arguments whatsoever [Note: [Col. XXI] See Blasco, cited above, chapter 3, p. 24 and following. [Col. XXI] From one passage alone in his letter to the bishops of Gaul it might be inferred that he was not unfamiliar with these decretals; but the argument drawn from it is exceedingly weak. For the text reads as follows (see Kunstmann, cited above, p. 247): “For we possess some of their writings, which are known to prefer in their cases not only the decrees of any Roman pontiffs whatsoever, but also those of their predecessors.”]. We have already shown that the pope spoke while relying upon an entirely different foundation and employing different sources. For the statements he brought forward concerning episcopal judgments he supported by the force of pontifical law, whereas Pseudo-Isidore considers only the interests of bishops. Nicholas had no need of Pseudo-Isidore’s work for establishing laws, any more than did the other supreme pontiffs, since it was not they but the bishops of the Franks who resorted to the spurious decretals—above all Hincmar of Reims, who cites them when they favor his own opinions, but who, when they do not, attacks not necessarily their authenticity but at least their authority [Note: [Col. XXI] Compare Hefele, cited above, p. 637; Kunstmann, *Remedius of Chur*, p. 9; see also Gess, cited above, chapter 11, p. 271 and following.]. Moreover, the testimony concerning the spurious decretals given by the legate of the supreme pontiff at the assembly of Gerstungen (1085), with the Saxon bishops in agreement, makes clear that the collection possessed extremely little authority at that time. Finally, when, as the eleventh century was already drawing to a close, those decretals, together with many additions—both authentic and apocryphal—had entered the widely circulated collections of canon law, you find them cited by the supreme pontiffs. Nicholas II did this especially; for that reason, distinguish him carefully from his predecessor of the same name.

From this it follows that the Church’s constitution and discipline grew day by day, supported not by any assistance from Pseudo-Isidore [Note: [Col. XXI] Compare Kunstmann, *On the Synod of Gerstungen* (Freiburg Journal, vol. IV, p. 116); *Fragments beside Pseudo-Isidore*, p. 254. — In the manuscript published by Kunstmann, the Saint-Emmeram manuscript, he had said: “They hoped, however, that what had been done could not at present be detected because those statements of Isidore did not belong to those more eminent authorities, and therefore were less discussed and more obscure.” — At the end one reads: “Your Prudence knows that those statements of Scripture, whose testimony we have used, have always been held in known reverence in the Church, and that their author is by no means obscure or of uncertain name.”], but upon a divine foundation, and that the Pseudo-Isidorian collection is improperly counted among the genuine sources of ecclesiastical law. It should also be added that the spurious decretals circulated only in the western part of the Frankish kingdom. Among the Germans and Italians, only very rare manuscript copies could be found, and even these were plainly derived from the Frankish region. It is said that no copies of Pseudo-Isidore reached the Spaniards at all until they had already appeared in print [Note: [Col. XXI] Compare De la Serna Santander, cited above, § 6, no. 145, p. 90 and following. — What should be thought of the manuscripts Madrid A. 151 (Pertz, *Archive*, vol. 8, p. 771) and Toledo 15 n. 16 (ibid., p. 822), where Isidore the bishop is named in the text but Mercator in the index—and of manuscripts Avranches 109 (p. 381) and Bologna 109 (p. 406), where the two are confused?]. Besides, everyone knows that for several centuries the collection of decretals was customarily attributed to Saint Isidore [Col. XXII], and that no one took the trouble to ask whether the acts composing it were or were not the acts of a genuine author. Since that age was wholly untrained in the art of diplomatics, and if that ignorance cannot be counted as a fault, what difference does it make whether Anacletus or Leo, Evaristus or Gregory, Telesphorus or Nicholas first uttered each individual statement?

## III. Summary of the Critical Assessment

Until the fifteenth century, the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals were regarded as genuine. John Wycliffe seems to have suspected that they were spurious [Note: [Col. XXII] He said: “The decretal letters are apocryphal and lead people astray from the faith of Christ, and the clerics who study them are fools.” — Compare Blasco, cited above, chapter 5, p. 30; Ballerini, cited above, part IV, chapter 6, § 1, no. 2.]; nevertheless, nothing more can properly be inferred from his arguments than the hatred with which he pursued all papal laws. First of all, Nicholas of Cusa [Note: [Col. XXII] *On Catholic Concordance*, book III, chapter 3. — The Dominican Katteisen may have preceded him. See Blasco, cited above, p. 32. — As for the letter of Clement, Peter the Eater had already entertained doubts.] (+1464) and, after him, John de Turrecremata [Note: [Col. XXII] *Summa of the Church*, book II, chapter 101. — See the note above by the learned Justus Fontinianus, preface to John de Turrecremata’s fifth book of Gratian’s *Decree*; Düx in the *Freiburg Lexicon*, vol. 5, p. 742 and following.] (+1468) apparently began to suspect interpolation in the decretals of the most ancient pontiffs. Once the collection had appeared in print, it came under more exacting criticism—first from Erasmus, then from the Magdeburg Centuriators, and also from several Frenchmen, including Dumoulin [Note: [Col. XXII] *Decretals*, edition of 1554, on c. 2, D. 22. — Compare Walter, cited above, § 96, p. 190, note g.] and Lecomte. Through their efforts, there is now no room for doubt that the decretals were adulterated [Note: [Col. XXII] Richter, *On the Correction of Gratian*, Leipzig, 1835, p. 26.]. But because of their ignorance of history and ecclesiastical law, and still more because of the controversies concerning faith that had then arisen among the Germans, together with the Gallican opinions that were already spreading among the French, they interpreted the recently discovered adulteration in a hostile manner. They wanted to convict the compiler of falsehood and to make the Church’s constitution—and especially the primacy of the pontiff—rest upon no other foundation than the writings of Pseudo-Isidore. Thus, in attacking the divine foundations of the Church, he unwittingly supplied weapons to perverse and deceitful men. If he truly undertook his labor for the purpose of strengthening the Church, then the Church has rightly grieved over the uselessness of his work down to the present day [Note: [Col. XXII] Very serious Catholic writers held that the entire discipline of the Church had been changed by Pseudo-Isidore [Col. XXII].]

At the beginning of the seventeenth century, the interpolation could no longer be denied. The Jesuit Franciscus Torres did succeed in freeing Pseudo-Isidore from the accusation of heresy [Note: [Col. XXII] Blasco, cited above, p. 33.], but by no means in establishing the authenticity of the decretals. Indeed, he furnished an opening to the Calvinist Blondel [Note: [Col. XXII] See above the article by the learned Haas in the *Freiburg Church Lexicon*, vol. 2, p. 47 and following.], who, in a very learned and bitter refutation, demonstrated with irrefutable arguments that the decretals had been adulterated and disclosed the sources from which Pseudo-Isidore had drawn them.

With a much more fruitless effort, Bonaventura Malvasia [Note: [Col. XXII] The work was entitled *A Message of Truth Sent to David Blondel*. Rome, 1635, octavo. — Cardinal d’Aguirre also wrote in this sense (*Hispanic Councils*, vol. I).], of the Order of Saint Francis, once again labored to prove the authenticity of the decretals, even while more learned Catholic writers were undermining it critically with greater diligence than Blondel [Note: [Col. XXII] Compare Zaccaria, cited above, p. 298.]. Among these, with no one offering serious opposition, the leading place was held by the brothers Ballerini, priests of Verona; among more recent writers, Walter showed himself their equal [Note: [Col. XXII] Knust also discussed this matter learnedly; Rosshirt gave an excellent review of him, cited above, p. 9.].

Through these and similar investigations by learned men, the present subject has been thoroughly examined, and many other important questions concerning Pseudo-Isidore’s sources, date, and homeland have been settled. Nevertheless, until a new edition accurately taken from the manuscripts is produced, the clarification of some questions will remain desirable—if, indeed, they can be clarified at all.

The principal documents discovered by recent critics concern the sources from which Pseudo-Isidore drew [Note: [Col. XXII] Compare Blondel, cited above, prolegomena, chapter 12; Knust, cited above, p. 16; Walter, cited above, § 98, in the notes.] and the manner in which the adulteration occurred. It is obvious in itself that he was not the author of many spurious acts that were already before everyone’s eyes before Pseudo-Isidore’s time [Note: [Col. XXII] See the testimony according to Ballerini in Walter, cited above, § 95, p. 185, note o; Richter, cited above, § 69, no. 1.], for example, the Donation of Constantine. It is therefore probable that the spurious decretals were not issued all at once but appeared gradually over time [Note: [Col. XXII] Compare Zaccaria in the *Critical Yearbooks for German Jurisprudence*, year 1846, p. 822.], and that several other documents by an unknown author likewise preceded Pseudo-Isidore. It should also be added that Greek manuscripts of such decretals were in circulation [Note: [Col. XXII] Compare Rosshirt, cited above, p. 8 and pp. 44, 47, 48.].

Nevertheless, because not a few of the supposed decretals cannot be attributed to Pseudo-Isidore, he is not thereby freed from every taint of interpolation; he is merely farther removed from blame. There are, however, other arguments of no lesser weight by which it is proved that, since the sixteenth century, many have unjustly fastened upon Pseudo-Isidore the charge of hatred or fraud. The matter is plainly otherwise if one grants what cannot be denied: that the collection of the decretals as a whole is not far removed from the truth [Note: [Col. XXII] Rosshirt, cited above, p. 56.]. For in the case of many decretals actually issued by pontiffs of a later age, the compiler assigned an earlier date; and other documents issued in earlier centuries and received by tradition he skillfully recast into the form of decretals. The compiler, therefore, ought not to be judged more harshly than those through whose work the canons of the apostles and the constitutions became known to us. The principal material for composing the book was supplied by the historical works of Rufinus and Cassiodorus, which were then disseminated throughout the Church, as well as by the lives of the supreme pontiffs discussed in the *Liber pontificalis* [Note: [Col. XXIII] Edited by Bianchini, Rome, 1718, four folio volumes; Muratori, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, vol. III, part I, Milan, 1723; Giovanni Vignoli, three volumes, Rome, 1724. — Compare Ciampini, *Examination of the Book of Pontiffs*, Rome, 1688; Devoti, *Universal Canon Law*, prologue, chapter 18, § 23, note 5 (vol. I, p. 370); *The Origins of the Roman Church*, chapter 9, p. 320, chapter 10, p. 338.], whose very words—and often only those words—are found in Pseudo-Isidore [Note: [Col. XXIII] For example, Anastasius I’s letter to the bishops of Burgos. See Walter, cited above, § 97, p. 196, note a.]. In addition to these, his sources were Sacred Scripture, the works of the Fathers, the statements of the councils, and the *Breviary of Roman Law* used by the Visigoths.

It is therefore clear that Pseudo-Isidore used many apocryphal documents that were readily available, as well as decretals by uncertain authors. He seems not to have composed any decretal from his own material, but only from material taken from elsewhere [Note: [Col. XXIII] Hefele, cited above, p. 592.]. If fraud lies hidden somewhere, that should not yet be considered proved; but in order to judge it fairly, one must attend to the time when the interpolation entered the work. How many documents from apocryphal sources appeared at that time not so much to deceive minds as to establish some truth [Note: [Col. XXIII] Rosshirt, cited above, p. X, no. 2.]!

The interpretation of Roman law published in the Visigothic idiom, which Pseudo-Isidore follows, clearly indicates that the whole collection originated in Spain or Gaul. This opinion is not weakened by arguments drawn from the *Book of Pontiffs*, which both the English and the Gauls used [Note: [Col. XXIII] Compare Bunsen, *Description of the City of Rome*, p. 208.] [Note: [Col. XXIII] As Eichhorn did; Walter, cited above, § 192, note r, contradicts him. — Compare Knust, cited above, p. 8; Kunstmann, *Remedius of Chur*.]. Spanish writers, who boast of the holy Isidore as their own, vehemently oppose those who maintain that the most shameless deceiver—who was not ashamed to assume the name of a holy man—was born in Spain [Note: [Col. XXIII] De la Serna, cited above, § 6, no. 140 and following.]. But what purpose would such laborious effort serve? The unmistakable traces of manuscripts of Gallic origin [Note: [Col. XXIII] It would be an irrefutable argument if what Richter suggests were proved: that Pseudo-Isidore used the Vulgate edition revised by Alcuin.], the idioms, and the spurious decretals brought forward only by Gallic authors—do they not make it plain that the kingdom of the Franks was Pseudo-Isidore’s native soil [Note: [Col. XXIII] Compare Ballerini, part III, chapter 6, no. 14, p. 541 and following; Walter, § 97, pp. 191–192; Richter, § 70, p. 126; Wasserschleben, p. 42 and following; Hefele, p. 607; also Möhler, p. 371 and following.]? Why, then, has that absurd hypothesis still found supporters in recent times [Note: [Col. XXIII] See Theiner and Eichhorn, whose words were cited above; against them, Walter, cited above, § 97, p. 192, notes r and s, p. 194, note x; Richter, cited above, § 70, note 9; Wasserschleben, p. 44 and following; Hefele, p. 609.]—the hypothesis advanced by Febronius [Note: [Col. XXIII] Zaccaria wrote of him, p. 288: “But what imposture is darker and more malicious than all the Isidorian impostures, and that of Febronius, who has the audacity to assert that the collection was issued at Rome?”] out of hatred for the Holy See, according to which the collection had already existed in complete form in the seventh century? [Note: [Col. XXIII] See Wasserschleben, p. 55, against this view.] Yet everyone can see that the Council of Paris (829) preceded our compiler. And does it not follow, from the fact that Pseudo-Isidore was first solemnly mentioned at the Council of Chiersy [Note: [Col. XXIII] In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, vol. III, p. 452, and Hardouin, *Councils*, vol. V, column 118.] (857), that his date may be inferred in some general way? It is disputed whether the compiler drew something from the Council of Aachen, or the council from the author [Note: [Col. XXIII] As Wasserschleben holds, and long before him Daude, *Universal History*, reflection 10 on book III, chapter 2.]. The first view is all the less distant from the truth [Note: [Col. XXIII] See Knust, pp. 38–40; Kunstmann, *Fragments*, p. 250; *Remedius of Chur*, p. 11.] because the zeal with which he discusses each matter pertaining to primates can scarcely be explained otherwise than by the restoration, in 844, of the primatial see of Metz [Note: [Col. XXIII] Compare Walter, cited above, § 97, p. 194; § 98, p. 198, note m.]. Since it is otherwise no less probable that Pseudo-Isidore was acquainted with the treatise on chorepiscopi [Note: [Col. XXIII] Pseudo-Isidore strongly opposes the chorepiscopi. See Kunstmann, *Fragments*, p. 258; *Bonn Church Lexicon*, vol. 4, p. 691.] published by Rabanus Maurus [Note: [Col. XXIII] See above the learned Kunstmann, *Rabanus Maurus: A Historical Monograph*, Mainz, 1841.] between the years 845 and 849, while the aforesaid abbot and archbishop was entirely unaware of the spurious decretals, the collection is rightly believed to have been completed only in the middle of the ninth century.

Some have maintained that the collection was compiled at Mainz [Note: [Col. XXIII] Kunstmann, *Fragments*, p. 254.]. But this opinion is refuted by the fact that Pseudo-Isidore was unknown to Rabanus Maurus, who succeeded the deceased Otgar as archbishop of Mainz. It is not denied that the Mainz deacon Benedict, in his collection of capitularies published between the years 840 and 847, expressed statements not unlike those of Pseudo-Isidore; indeed, he asserted that his statements had been drawn from notes written by Riculph on canon law. These notes, once stored in the archive of the Church of Mainz, were later discovered by Otgar. But the statements of the deacon Benedict and of Pseudo-Isidore do not agree so closely that one cannot distinguish one from the other [Note: [Col. XXIII] See Benedict the Levite’s preface.], since both, although differing in their principles, may have drawn from the same source. Besides, in our own time there have been those who, reviving a long-obscured hypothesis [Note: [Col. XXIII] Blasco already defended it in chapter 6, p. 44; among more recent writers, Wasserschleben defended it learnedly and sharply. Compare Gfrörer, p. 42. See the following note.], have said that the archbishop Otgar himself was the author, while Benedict was merely the editor of the work. They are opposed by arguments of no slight weight [Note: [Col. XXIII] These arguments are assembled in Hefele, p. 628, although he favors the hypothesis to some extent, p. 635.].

If anyone wishes to consider what we said above, from which it emerges that Pseudo-Isidore was by birth a Frank [Col. XXIV], two facts present themselves that make it credible that the book first appeared in the western part of the kingdom of Charles the Bald [Note: [Col. XXIV] Compare Kunstmann, p. 254; Hefele, pp. 631–636.]: namely, that the oldest manuscripts were written in the Frankish idiom and that Pseudo-Isidore is first found cited there. Indeed, if it were granted—which, however, cannot be granted in the sense in which the matter is commonly understood—that the author wrote with the intention of attacking metropolitan authority, scarcely anyone would be unwilling to admit that Rothad of Soissons [Note: [Col. XXIV] It happened only by chance that a document concerning Rothad survived in which he calls himself a sinner.] had assisted Pseudo-Isidore [Note: [Col. XXIV] Gfrörer too, although he held that the spurious decretals originated at Mainz, believes that the Pseudo-Isidorian collection was completed by Rothad.].

On this matter, let each person abound in his own opinion. It does, however, seem worth noting that the hypothesis which imagines Otgar as the author of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection rests upon no arguments, unless perhaps upon the fact that the bishop of Mainz favored hierarchical authority [Note: [Col. XXIV] Compare Walter, § 97, p. 195, note y.]. Yet in this matter of no great importance the critics labored most intensely: namely, to determine what Pseudo-Isidore’s genuine purpose had been in composing the work. If he had wished deliberately to deceive, he would not have shrunk from any means, however bad, provided that they promoted papal rights, attacked the authority of councils, favored primates, depressed metropolitans, or provided assistance to clergy oppressed by the laity [Note: [Col. XXIV] Walter rightly observes, p. 197, note f, that one might add: “To increase piety, perfect Christian morals, order divine worship, and place the Church’s possessions in safety. For all these matters are discussed at length and in serious language in the spurious decretals.” Hefele, p. 595, discusses the various motives that encouraged Pseudo-Isidore to compose the work.]. Whatever any critic intended to extract from Pseudo-Isidore, he extracted; hence it is clear how accurately the author had praised himself when he said that he wished to write “a work very useful to bishops, clergy, and laity, embracing the whole discipline of the Church.” And in fact, considering the state of the Church at that time in the Frankish kingdom, he accomplished this in his own manner, since he believed that what was lacking in the books of ecclesiastical law ought to be supplied from more recent sources, which, however, he had not examined with complete understanding [Note: [Col. XXIV] Rosshirt, p. 19.]. In this labor, as has been observed, the words of the *Book of Pontiffs* served him both as foundation and as rule [Note: [Col. XXIV] Döllinger, *Textbook of Church History*, vol. 2, p. 46.].

Finally, learned men have not been lacking who suspected that some affinity lay between the nauseating fiction concerning Pope Joan [Note: [Col. XXIV] Blasco, cited above, chapter 16, p. 135 and following; Gfrörer, *History of the Carolingians*, vol. 1, p. 288; concerning the commentary itself, Haas in the *Freiburg Church Lexicon*, vol. 5, p. 705 and following.] and the Pseudo-Isidorian collection. Believing the story to be nothing more than a genuine fiction, they suppose that the collection of the spurious decretals is allegorically represented under the figure of the fictitious pope’s spurious son [Note: [Col. XXIV] See above the learned Rosshirt, p. 60 and following.]. Let each person abound in his own opinion [Note: [Col. XXIV] Devoti, § 5, p. 358, does not entirely reject the hypothesis.].

# ISIDORE MERCATOR’S COLLECTION OF DECRETALS

*(In Merlin, Collection of Councils, Cologne, 1530.)*

[Col. 0001]

## DEDICATORY LETTER OF JACOB MERLIN, DOCTOR

[Col. 0001] To the Most Reverend Fathers in Christ and my most excellent lords, Stephen and Francis Poncher, most circumspect bishops of the Churches of Sens and Paris, Jacobus Merlin, doctor of theology, sends respectful greetings.

I have not concealed from myself that nothing could be more advantageous to the commonwealth than to bring together in one volume the institutions of the holy councils and orthodox pontiffs—some of which blessed Isidore long ago assembled into one collection, while others you, most reverend Father, have delivered for publication, sealed with lead. For these materials present, with such abundance and such Catholic spirit, everything that either wears down the errors of mortals or can restore a world already almost collapsed, so that everyone may now readily possess what will slay heresies and heretics, humble the proud, wear out the pleasure-seekers, rouse the sluggish, empty the ambitious, and capture the little foxes that are destroying the ecclesiastical vineyard.

If, therefore, anyone henceforth attempts to ward off and drive monsters from the commonwealth, what could be more excellent than David’s stones, which this Jordan supplies in such abundance? If someone likewise tries to satisfy the prayers of the hungry, what could be more abundant or sweeter than the riches brought by this ship arriving from the most distant shores? But if someone desires the path and splendor of truth, by which the darkness of error may rightly be expelled and depart far away with its authors, what could be clearer than the judgments of the Fathers and ancestors, which, moved by the Holy Spirit, they gathered into this heap?

Here, like flowers gathered from a meadow full of every kind, one may easily collect whatever contributes to ecclesiastical affairs, whatever is useful for restraining vices and extinguishing the fires of desire. Here, if you dig only a little, an outstanding pearl will immediately appear. Here you will see all the heretics whom the devil has raised up slain, pierced, and cast down. Here you will recognize the enemies of the rites and sacraments of the orthodox Church, beaten and half-dead. Here you will easily draw out whatever is needed to defend the rights of the Church’s Bridegroom, the liberties of his bride, and everything else that promotes the peaceful fellowship of human beings.

Here, like little children dashed against a rock, Novatus, the Elkesaites, Sabellius, Cerinthus, and Nepotianus are crushed together with Paul of Samosata. Here, lest the spark of Arian perfidy should eventually produce a great conflagration, Photinus, Eunomius, Hebion, and Montanus perish in ancient death. Here, like animals lurking in a very dense forest, the orthodox are hidden; like bears, they tear and rend Pelagius, Apollinaris, Priscillian, Nestorius, and the Cataphrygians, together with the sons of Jericho. Here Eutyches, Manichaeus, the Acephali, Dioscorus, and Theodore are cast down. Here Severus of Aquileia is slain by the sword of Phinehas. Here the Monothelites are brought down by the jawbone of an ass. Here Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Macarius are caught like little foxes. Here the perfidious Hussites, the insane Wycliffites, and the apostate and schismatic Bohemians, together with all their descendants, are struck by a perpetual anathema as a single offspring.

Here the tyranny of kings and emperors is restrained as by bit and bridle. Here the luxury of bishops and pontiffs is exposed. If rulers disagree, sincere peace lies hidden here. If bishops dispute about primacy, here the angel of great counsel reveals who ought to be placed above the others. If the pestilential weeds begin to weaken the Lord’s field, the evangelical father soon arises and orders them gathered into bundles to be given to the fire. Once those supreme authorities—namely, rulers and pontiffs—have tasted their force and character, they will immediately rouse ecclesiastical power, which, although so often admonished long ago by the Council of Basel, was unable to recover its strength; once roused, it finally brandished its arm and will not withdraw its hand from the undertaking until it has found the drachma once lost—that is, the truth of life, doctrine, and justice.

Since, then, so abundant and useful an antidote for the commonwealth is expected from such materials, I considered it fitting to offer through you, most reverend Fathers, who possess the truest scar of Christ and strive with supreme efforts to restore and illuminate holy Jerusalem, the most elect bride of Christ, after driving away every disguise of error, this small labor of ours to the commonwealth. I expected to obtain no small reward, provided that from your pupil—whose spirit his shoulders scarcely support—you should draw, through whatever studies he possesses, arguments like honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone, by which heresies may be driven from the seats of the Gauls, truth may flourish again, and empty, insignificant disputes may disappear.

Receive, therefore, excellent Fathers, these nocturnal labors of ours, which in my judgment will benefit ecclesiastical affairs and indeed the whole world, so that learned and unlearned alike may readily find in them what delights them; and so that they may likewise strengthen, protect, and defend themselves against the pestilence of the fury of I know not what men; so that every seedbed of error may at once cease and be cut away; so that wars may yield to peace, schisms to unity, and error to truth; so that the light of truth may shine in Zion, and the true furnace of zeal may be recognized in Jerusalem—namely Christ, who, amid winds and storms, may once again and again, I pray, command

[Col. 0003]

# ORIGIN OF THE GENERAL COUNCILS

When councils began to be held, and concerning the four councils.

[Col. 0003A] The canons of the general councils began in the time of Constantine. For in the preceding years, while persecution raged, no opportunity was given for teaching the peoples; thereafter Christianity was divided into various heresies, because the bishops were not permitted to assemble together except in the time of the aforementioned emperor. For he granted Christians permission to assemble freely. Under him also the holy Fathers, coming together at the Council of Nicaea from the whole world, handed down, in accordance with the evangelical and apostolic faith, the Creed that follows after the Apostles.

There are, moreover, four principal councils, from which the Churches possess the fullest teaching of the faith, both concerning the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and concerning the incarnation of the aforesaid Son and our Savior.

The first of these is the Nicene Synod of three hundred and eighteen bishops, held under Constantine Augustus. In it the blasphemy of the Arian perfidy was condemned, by which Arius asserted the inequality of the Holy Trinity; and that the Son of God is consubstantial with God the Father was defined by the same holy synod through the Creed. [Col. 0003B]

The second synod consisted of one hundred and fifty Fathers, assembled at Constantinople under the elder Theodosius. It condemned Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, and demonstrated that the same Paraclete is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, giving a fuller form of the Creed, which all Greece and Latinity proclaim in the Churches. [Col. 0004A]

The third synod was the First of Ephesus, consisting of two hundred bishops, held under Theodosius Augustus the Younger. It condemned Nestorius, who asserted two persons in Christ, with a just anathema, showing that one person of our Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures.

The fourth synod was that of Chalcedon, consisting of six hundred and thirty priests, held under the emperor Marcian. In it the same judgment of the Fathers condemned Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who declared that the Word of the Lord and the flesh have one nature, as well as his defender Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, and Nestorius himself together with the other heretics. The synod proclaimed that Christ the Lord was born of the Virgin in such a way that we confess in him the substance of both the divine and the human nature.

These, as we have said, are the four principal and venerable synods embracing the Catholic faith. But if there are any councils that the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have established, they remain firmly established in every respect after the authority of these four. Their acts, moreover, are contained here, preserved in this collection. [Col. 0004B]

### Again, concerning the principal synods: where, for what causes, at what times, and under whose authority they were held

[Col. 0003]

[Col. 0003B] The first synod was held at Nicaea, consisting of three hundred and eighteen Fathers, against Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, who asserted three degrees in the Trinity: namely, the Father as greater, the Son as lesser, and the Holy Spirit as a creature. It was held in the time of the emperor Constantine, Silvester, Roman pope, Macarius of Jerusalem, and Alexander of Constantinople. After condemning the heresy, they established twenty canons. The principal author of these was the aforementioned holy bishop Alexander.

The second was held at Constantinople, consisting of one hundred and fifty Fathers, against Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God. It was held in the time of the emperors Gratian and Theodosius, Damasus, Roman pope, Cyril of Jerusalem, and Nectarius of Constantinople. After condemning the heresy, they established three canons. The principal author of these was Nectarius of Constantinople.

The third was held at Ephesus, consisting of two hundred Fathers, against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, [Col. 0003C] who said that the blessed virgin Mary was not the Mother of God but only the mother of a human being, thus making one person belong to the flesh and another to the divinity. It was held in the time of the emperor Theodosius the Great, Celestine, Roman pope, Juvenal of Constantinople, and Cyril of Alexandria. They composed twelve chapters against the blasphemies of Nestorius, and an equal number of chapters anathematizing them, under the authority of the same holy Cyril. [Col. 0004B]

The fourth was held at Chalcedon, consisting of six hundred and thirty Fathers, against Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who asserted that Christ, after assuming humanity, did not exist from two natures but that only the divine nature remained in him. It was held in the time of the emperor Marcian, Leo, Roman pope, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Anatolius of Constantinople. After condemning the heresy, they established twenty-seven canons. The principal author of these was the same holy Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople.

The fifth was held at Constantinople against Theodore of Mopsuestia and all the heretics. Theodore said that the Word was one God and Christ another, and denied that the holy Virgin Mary had been the Mother of God. It was held in the time of the emperor Justinian, Vigilius the pope, Domnus of Antioch, and Eutychius of Constantinople. They wrote fourteen chapters, anathematizing the blasphemies of Theodore and his associates. [Col. 0004C]

The sixth was held at Constantinople, consisting of one hundred and fifty Fathers, against Macarius, bishop of Antioch, and his associates, who falsely maintained, under a mistaken supposition, that there is one will and one operation in Christ. It was held in the time of the emperor Constantine, Agatho, Roman pope, and George of Constantinople. After condemning the heresy, they wrote eight chapters in the form of an anathema.

### Again, a notice of the synods whose acts are contained in this codex

[Col. 0003]

[Col. 0003C] The first notice concerns the Aquitanian synod, which is said to have taken place before Nicaea but is placed after it because of the greater authority [Col. 0004C] of the latter. In it eighteen Fathers established twenty-four canons. Their principal author was Vitalis, bishop of Antioch. [Col. 0005A]

The second was the Neocaesarean synod, which is read as having occurred after the Aquitanian and Nicene synods. In it sixteen Fathers established fourteen canons. Their principal author was Vitalis of Salamis.

The third was the Gangrian synod, which is read as having occurred after Nicaea. In it sixteen Fathers established twenty-one canons because of certain ecclesiastical necessities, chiefly against Eustathius, who said that no one living in the married state, nor any believer who did not renounce everything he possessed, could have hope in the Lord, along with many other poisonous teachings that would take too long to enumerate.

The fourth was the Sardican synod, in which forty Fathers established twenty-one canons. Its principal authors were Hosius, bishop of Corduba, and Vincentius, bishop of Capua and legate of the holy Roman Church.

The fifth was the Antiochene synod, in which thirty Fathers established twenty-five canons. Its principal author was Eusebius, bishop of Palestine.

The sixth was the Laodicean synod, in which twenty-two Fathers [Col. 0005B] established forty-nine canons. Its principal author was Theodosius, bishop.

The seventh was the Carthaginian synod, in which two hundred and seventeen Fathers established thirty-three canons. Its principal author was Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, is also read to have been present at this same synod, in the time of Honorius Augustus.

The eighth was the African synod under Theodosius Augustus the Younger. In it two hundred and fourteen Fathers read out and confirmed one hundred and five canons, which are said to have been composed through various councils of the African province [Col. 0006A] in the time of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

The ninth was the Arelate synod, in which the Fathers established canons, and so forth. Its principal authors were Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, and Saint Marinus, bishop of Arles, as some assert, in the time of Constantine Augustus.

The tenth was likewise held at Arles, in which nineteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

The eleventh was likewise held at Arles, in which sixteen Fathers established canons.

The twelfth was likewise held at Arles, in the village of Ortinsicum, in which eleven Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

The thirteenth was likewise held at Arles, in which nineteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Sapardus, bishop of Arles.

The fourteenth was the synod of Orange, in which sixteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Bishop Hilary.

The sixteenth was the synod of Agde, in which thirty-four Fathers [Col. 0006B] established canons. Its principal author was Bishop Caesarius.

The seventeenth was the synod of Orléans, in which seventy-two Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Aurelius, bishop of Arles, in the time of King Clovis.

The eighteenth was likewise held at Orléans, in which thirty-one Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Melanius, bishop of Rennes.

The nineteenth was likewise held at Orléans, in which twenty-three Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Saint Albinus, bishop of Angers.

[Col. 0005]

## HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF AURELIUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE, TO POPE DAMASUS

[Col. 0005B] To the most reverend pope Damasus, Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

Our humility implores the glory of the apostolic see and the favor of your eminence that you may deign to send us in writing the decrees that you are able to find, from the death of the blessed prince of the Apostles, Peter, up to the beginning of your sanctity’s pontificate, in accordance with the authority of the apostolic see, which we have learned is governed through the holiness of your wisdom. [Col. 0006B]

Thus, through the nobility and prudence of your sanctity, we may be able to know what was decreed in the aforesaid holy see during the aforementioned periods, and who acted against the ordinances of the canons of the Apostles. Fare well, most holy pope, and pray for us, most loving father.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, and read at Rome on the Nones of May.

[Col. 0005]

## DAMASUS’S RESCRIPT TO AURELIUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

[Col. 0005C] To the most blessed brother and fellow bishop Aurelius, Damasus.

We have received the writings of your holiness with the reverence due to them. In them we recognized, as was fitting, your thirst for reverence and prudence concerning the apostolic ordinances. For this reason we have sent some of the things you requested, and we wish to send some others when you write again.

Nevertheless, we have omitted none of the decrees of our predecessors from the death of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, concerning which we have not sent you something through Ammonius the presbyter and Felix the deacon under specified seals. We wish you to preserve these and command that they be proclaimed and published to others, so that all may keep and observe them inviolate with the reverence due to them, and so that they may be carefully honored by all in future times. For those who voluntarily violate the canons are judged gravely by the holy Fathers and condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and gift they were dictated. For those who, not compelled by necessity, [Col. 0005D] but willingly, as has been stated, act insolently against these same holy canons, presume to speak or act, or freely consent to those wishing to do so, seem not improperly to blaspheme the Holy Spirit. Such presumption is plainly one kind of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0006C] since, as has already been mentioned, it acts against him by whose impulse and grace those same holy canons were produced.

The devil’s wickedness, however, often deceives many subtly, and so frequently mocks the imprudence of certain people through an appearance of piety that it persuades them to accept harmful things in place of beneficial ones. Therefore we must faithfully know and diligently handle the norm of the holy canons, which were fashioned by the Spirit of God and consecrated by universal reverence, lest in any way we transgress the statutes of the holy Fathers without unavoidable necessity—which God forbid—but, walking most faithfully by them, may deserve, with those who composed them through divine inspiration, to possess the glory of reward and the abundance of labor, with the Lord’s help and through their merits.

When these matters have thus been duly considered and, by our deliberation, brought to the knowledge of your churches, it is altogether fitting that you obey the rules of those same holy canons, lest the negligence of certain people cause you to oppose them in anything. Rather, may your wise and sound teaching—which desires you to please God in all things—show you to be their fellow heirs and fellow sharers in the heavenly kingdom, and faithful collaborators in the sees. [Col. 0006D]

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourth consulship of Gratian and Ciritus [possibly Cyritius].

[Col. 0007]

## [COLLECTION OF DECRETALS]

### ISIDORE’S PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING WORK

[Col. 0007A] Isidore, servant of Christ, sends greeting in the Lord to his fellow servant, reader, and faithful kinsman.

I am compelled by many people, both bishops and other servants of Christ, to collect the pronouncements of the canons, reduce them to a single volume, and make one collection from many. But this greatly troubles me: different interpretations produce different formulations, and although the meaning is one, the formulations differ, some being longer and others shorter. We have found that those councils which were issued in Greek have been interpreted and written down more than threefold or fourfold.

If truth is to be sought from many versions, let us follow the style of the Greeks and imitate their expressions and copies. Otherwise, let those who have as many copies as there are codices speak and explain for themselves. [Col. 0007B] It seems to us, however, that when they differ in our language, unity and truth should be sought from those in whose language they are known to have been issued. This is what we have done, and, just as we found them from their true teachers, we have taken care to insert them into the volume to which this preface is attached.

The Greek word *canon* is called *regula* in Latin. It is called a rule because it leads rightly and never draws one elsewhere. Others say that it is called a rule either because it rules, or because it provides a norm for living, or because it corrects something distorted and crooked.

The word *synod* is interpreted from the Greek as “company” or “heaven.” *Concilium*, however, is a name derived from common intention, because all direct the gaze of their minds toward one thing. The *cilium* is the eyelash of the eye. Hence those who disagree among themselves do not hold a *concilium*, because they do not have one mind. A *coetus* is a gathering or assembly, from *coire*, that is, from coming together in one place; hence it is called a *conventus*, because all come together there. Thus a gathering, assembly, or council derives from the association of many into one.

At the beginning of this volume we have set out how a council is celebrated among us, so that those who wish to follow our procedure may know how they ought to conduct it. But those who choose to conduct it better should do what they judge through a just, canonical, and most wise deliberation.

Finally, because of their authority, we have placed before the other councils the canons called those of the Apostles, although some call them apocryphal, because many accept them, and the holy Fathers strengthened their pronouncements with synodal authority and placed them among the canonical constitutions.

Next we inserted the decrees of certain letters of apostolic men—namely Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, and the other apostolic men—which we have so far been able to find, down to Pope Silvester. Afterwards we placed the Nicene Synod, because of the authority of that great council. Then we arrange beneath the view of this volume the chapters of various Greek and Latin councils, [Col. 0008A] both those held earlier and those held later, distinguished according to their order of numbers and times. We also append the remaining decrees of the Roman pontiffs down to Saint Gregory, together with certain letters of his, in which there is an authority not inferior to that of councils because of the eminence of the apostolic see.

Thus the discipline of the ecclesiastical order, gathered and organized by us into one collection, may instruct holy prelates in the rules of their fathers; obedient ministers and peoples of the Church may be imbued with spiritual examples; and they may not be deceived by the perversities of wicked men.

For many, crushed by wickedness and greed, have oppressed priests by accusing them. Therefore the holy Fathers established laws that they called holy canons. Many accuse others for this reason: either to excuse themselves through them or to enrich themselves with their possessions. Many good Christians remain silent and bear the sins of others that they know because they are often abandoned by the evidence by which they cannot prove to ecclesiastical judges what they themselves know. For although certain things are true, they are not to be believed by judges unless they are demonstrated by definite indications, unless they are proven by manifest judgment, unless they are made public according to judicial procedure.

No one who has been stripped of his possessions, or driven by force or fear from his own see, can be accused, summoned, judged, or condemned according to canonical regulation before everything taken from him has been restored by law, before he has long enjoyed his honors peacefully, and, having been regularly restored to his own see, has freely possessed its honor for a considerable time. [Col. 0008C]

Thus the Ecclesiastical History, composed by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, says concerning a certain woman who was accused by her husband on account of her chastity: “An ordinance, or prohibition, was issued by the emperor through a law, that she should first be permitted to arrange her household affairs freely for a considerable time, and only then answer the charges brought against her.” All these laws, both ecclesiastical and civil and public, give the same command.

If all the harmonizing material were set down, the days would run out first, and the letter would become excessively long. Nevertheless, we have judged it appropriate to insert here certain passages from many sources, as an encouragement to others.

For Saint Leo, bishop of the Roman Church, says in the letter sent to the Council of Chalcedon, whose beginning is: “Leo the bishop to the Chalcedonian synod. Indeed, most beloved, I had desired”—and so forth. Among other things he bears witness in this way:

“Since we are not unaware that the condition of many Churches has been disturbed by wicked rivalries, and that very many brothers have been unjustly driven from their sees, carried into exile, and replaced by others in the place of those who survived, let the medicine of justice first be applied to these wounds. Let no one be deprived of his own possessions in such a way that another uses what belongs to him. Let everyone abandon such an error, so that no one’s honor should perish; rather, let the proper right of the earlier bishops be restored to them with all their privileges.”

The ancient apostolic men who lived before the Nicene Synod also established the same thing. The same is stated by the synod held at Larissa under Valerian. Very many Roman synods bear witness to the same, and Pope Symmachus and the other holy Fathers established the same. To avoid excessive length, we have postponed inserting their lengthy statutes here. Anyone who wishes to know and read these matters more fully will be able to find and read them in their own sources.

For us, these things are sufficient in this preface. Just as, from many weapons, a soldier is satisfied with those he can suitably carry upon himself, so one or two judgments—or as many as may then be necessary—are sufficient for us from many judgments. For just as we defeat an enemy with one or two weapons, so with one or two judgments full of authority we overcome an adversary.

If these provisions have been established concerning women and secular persons, they have been granted all the more to ecclesiastical men and priests. These same ecclesiastical laws command them, and the laws of the world give the same instruction. Likewise, the canonical authority utterly rejects accusers and accusations that the laws of the world prohibit.

The authority to convene synods has been entrusted by a special power to the apostolic see, and we do not read that any synod is valid which was not convened or supported by its authority. This is attested by canonical authority, [Col. 0009C] strengthened by ecclesiastical history, and confirmed by the holy Fathers.

I also wish you to know—and this is necessary for the eighty bishops who compelled me to begin and complete this work, as well as for all the remaining priests of the Lord—that we have found more than the twenty chapters of the Nicene Synod that are possessed among us, and we read in the decrees of Pope Julius that there ought to be seventy chapters of that same synod. We have placed that letter, in its proper order among the other decrees of the Apostles, for examination by those who investigate these matters and by all who wish to know them.

That there are more than twenty chapters of the Council of Nicaea is found in many places. For it is read in the Constantinopolitan council as follows:

“It is evident that the matters belonging to each province are to be administered by the synod of that province, just as it is established by the Nicene Council.”

It is also read in the letter of Pope Innocent addressed to Victricius, bishop of Rouen:

“If any causes or disputes should arise between clerics and laypeople, or between clerics of either the higher or the lower orders, it has been decided that, according to the Nicene Synod, judgment should be concluded after all the bishops of the same province have assembled,”

and so forth.

The bishop Theophilus of Alexandria, of blessed memory, also mentions in his letters that it was established at the Council of Nicaea that, from the eighth day before the Ides of March until the Nones of April—that is, for twenty-eight days—whatever moon should arise in any intermediate period, it should be taken as the beginning of the first month. The fourteenth day, however, was to be carefully sought from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April until the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May. If it fell on a Saturday, Easter was to be celebrated on the following Sunday, that is, on the fifteenth day of the moon. He also wrote that if the thirteenth day of the moon of that same month, that is, of the first month, fell on a Sunday, Easter was unquestionably to be celebrated after that week had been carried over to another Sunday. [Col. 0010A]

By these and many other examples it is clear that there are more than twenty chapters of the Nicene Council, and that the aforementioned letter of Pope Julius is genuine.

Certain men from among our brotherhood in the East also testified to us that they had seen a Nicene Council larger than the four Gospels, containing the sessions of the bishops, the introductions, the judgments of complaints, the definitions and constitutions, and also their subscriptions. [Col. 0010B]

They confirmed that the great Council of Chalcedon was written according to its likeness, and finally that other councils were held at Constantinople: one under the emperor Justinian against the opponents of God—Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius—and another in the time of Pope Agatho and the emperor Constantine against the bishop Macarius, his disciple Stephen, and the remaining bishops, who sowed weeds among the Churches instead of wheat, mixed wine with water and gave their neighbor a drink of troubled overturning, and, like wolves, pretended to be lambs. Falsehood was offered, while truth was rejected as falsehood.

It is also necessary to know—although certain matters are not thereby invalidated—that there are four principal councils, from which the Churches possess the fullest teaching of the faith, both concerning the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and concerning the incarnation of the aforesaid Son and our Savior.

The first of these is the Nicene Synod of three hundred and eighteen bishops, held under Constantine Augustus. In it the blasphemy of the Arian perfidy was condemned, by which the same Arius asserted the inequality of the Holy Trinity; and the same holy synod defined through the Creed that the Son, God, is consubstantial with God the Father. [Col. 0010C]

The second synod consisted of one hundred and fifty Fathers, assembled at Constantinople under the elder Theodosius.
