It condemned Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is the Lord, and demonstrated that the same Paraclete is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, giving a fuller form of the Creed, which all Greece and Latinity proclaim in the Churches. [Col. 0010D]

The third synod was the First of Ephesus, consisting of two hundred bishops, held under Theodosius Augustus the Younger. It condemned Nestorius, who asserted two persons in Christ, with a just anathema, showing that one person of our Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures.

The fourth was the Chalcedonian Synod, consisting of six hundred and thirty priests, held under the emperor Marcian. In it the same judgment of the Fathers condemned Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who declared that the Word of God and the flesh have one nature, as well as his defender Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, and Nestorius again together with the other heretics. The same synod proclaimed that Christ the Lord was born of the Virgin in such a way that the natures are contained in one divine and human substance. [Col. 0011A]

These, as we have said, are the four principal and venerable synods embracing the Catholic faith. But if there are any councils that the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have established, they remain firmly established in every respect after the authority of these four. [Col. 0012A]

First, as has been stated, the order for celebrating a council has been inserted, and afterwards come the canons of the Apostles and of the earliest apostolic men, that is, in order from Saint Clement through Saint Silvester.

## HERE BEGIN THE CANONS, THAT IS, THE ECCLESIASTICAL RULES, ESTABLISHED BY THE HOLY FATHERS AND COLLECTED BY ISIDORE INTO THE BODY OF A SINGLE CODE (C)

[Col. 0011]

## 1. THE PROCEDURE FOR CELEBRATING A COUNCIL (C)

[Col. 0011B] At the first hour of the day, before sunrise, everyone is to be expelled from the church. After all the doors have been closed, except for one entrance through which the priests must enter, doorkeepers shall stand there. All the bishops shall assemble and enter together, and shall sit according to the order of their appointment.

After all the bishops have entered and taken their seats, the presbyters whom the matter requires to enter shall then be summoned; no deacon shall insert himself among them. After these, approved deacons whom the order requires to be present shall enter. When a circle has been formed by the bishops’ seats, the presbyters shall sit behind them. The metropolitan shall choose which of them may sit with him; those so chosen may judge and decide matters together with him.

The deacons shall stand in the sight of the bishops. Then the laypeople who have deserved, by the council’s election, to be present shall enter. The notaries whom the procedure requires for reading or recording shall also enter. Once the doors have been closed and the priests are seated in prolonged silence, with their whole hearts turned toward the Lord, the archdeacon shall say, “Pray.” Immediately all shall prostrate themselves on the ground, both bishops and presbyters. After praying for a long time in silence, with tears and sighs, one of the senior bishops shall rise and openly pour out a prayer to the Lord, while all are still lying on the ground, saying this prayer:

### Prayer

We are present, holy Lord Spirit; we are present, held indeed by the enormity of sin, but gathered together in a special way in your name. Come to us and be with us; deign to enter our hearts; teach us what we should do, where we should go, and show us what we ought to accomplish, so that, with your help, we may be able to please you in all things. Be the salvation, adviser, and accomplisher of our judgments—you who alone, with God the Father and his Son, possess the glorious name.

Do not allow us to be disturbers of justice, since you love the highest equity, [Col. 0011D] so that ignorance may not draw us to the left, favoritism may not bend us, and acceptance of a gift or of a person may not corrupt us. Rather, join us effectively to yourself through the gift of your grace alone, so that we may be one in you and deviate from the truth in nothing. Thus, gathered in your name, may we uphold justice in all things with a moderation governed by mercy, so that here our judgment may disagree with you in nothing, and in the future we may receive everlasting rewards for what we have done well.

In this prayer the Lord’s Prayer is not to be said, nor a blessing, but only the prayer itself is to be confirmed. When the prayer has ended and all have answered “Amen,” the archdeacon shall again say: “Rise.” Immediately all shall rise, and, with complete fear of God and discipline, both bishops and presbyters shall sit.

When all have thus seated themselves silently in their places, a deacon dressed in white shall bring forward into the midst the book of the canons and announce the chapters concerning the business of councils: namely, from the Third Council of Toledo, era XVIII; likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo, era III; likewise from the chapters of the eastern regions, which Bishop Martin translated from Greek into Latin, era XVIII, concerning the holding of a synod; likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, era XVIII; likewise from the Council of Agde, era XXV or XXVI; or some other canon that may seem more suitable to the metropolitan, so that it may be read.

When the headings have been completed, the metropolitan bishop shall address the council with an exhortation, saying:

“Behold, most holy priests: after offering our prayers to God, I address your fraternity with a devout exhortation, and I adjure you by the divine name to receive with all piety those things that are said to you by us concerning God, the sacred orders, or holy conduct, and to intend to carry them out with the highest reverence.

“But if perhaps one of you should think differently from what has been said, let him bring forward without any scruple of contention, in the fellowship of us all, the very matters about which he has doubts, so that, with God’s help, he may either be taught or teach. [Col. 0012D]

“Next I address and beseech you with a similar adjuration: let none of you, in judging, accept a person, or, moved by any favoritism or gift, knowingly turn away or depart from just judgment. Rather, with complete piety, reconsider whatever matter is brought before our assembly for judgment, so that neither contentious disagreement may find a place among us for the overthrow of justice, nor the vigor or diligence of our procedure grow lukewarm in seeking equity.”

After this exhortation, all the presbyters, deacons, and religious persons who are present shall enter to hear the teaching. Then the archdeacon shall read the first canon of the Eleventh Council of Toledo, era I, so that the council may not be disturbed by tumult. When this canon has been read, the Council of Ephesus shall be read in order.

Afterwards, let there likewise be a conference and instruction concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity, and also concerning the orders of ministries, so that unity in this same observance may be maintained in all sees. For these purposes, as the time of day permits, the letters of Pope Leo to Bishop Flavian concerning the errors of Eutyches and the mystery of the Trinity are also to be read. The canons concerning the unity of ministries are likewise to be read, and nothing else is to be taken up beforehand until all these matters have been explained.

For the entire three days of the litanies, nothing else is to be done or discussed except the conference concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity and concerning the orders, whether sacred or relating to the established ministries. These matters are to be divided throughout all three days, so that nothing else—as has been said—is considered except the question of the matters mentioned above. The reading appropriate to the order and to the matter being investigated must always precede.

After this, on the fourth day, the remaining matters are to be admitted in order. Thus all the religious persons who have attended the council on the preceding days for spiritual instruction shall go outside, while certain presbyters whom the metropolitan has approved for honor remain seated in the council.

On each of those three days of the rogations and litanies, the bishops or presbyters, with an admonisher, shall first prostrate themselves in prayer. Then, after the metropolitan has collected the prayer, they shall rise and hold a conference only on divine matters, as has been said. On the remaining days, while everyone is present, the prayer is to be collected, and then, once seated, they shall consider the business of the cases justly and religiously.

There shall be no tumult, either among those who are conferring or among those who are standing by. In the same manner and order as was set out above, everyone shall enter the council on each successive day.

For if any of the remaining presbyters or deacons, clerics, or laypeople who have stood outside should think that the council ought to be appealed to concerning any matter, they shall make their case known to the archdeacon of the metropolitan church, and he shall announce it to the council. Then permission shall be granted to those persons to enter one at a time and present their case.

No bishop, however, shall withdraw from the common assembly before the general hour of withdrawal arrives.

No one shall dare to dissolve the council until everything has been determined, so that whatever is concluded by common deliberation may be subscribed by the hands of each individual bishop. Nevertheless, two or three days before dissolving the council, they shall all carefully reconsider all the constitutions they have issued, lest they have offended in anything.

Likewise, on the day when the council is to be concluded, the canons established in the holy synod shall be reread publicly before the church. When these have been completed, the response in the choir shall be: “Amen.” Then, returning to the place where they sat in the council, they shall subscribe the canons themselves.

The metropolitan shall also admonish them concerning the coming Easter, on what day it will occur. They shall likewise be admonished when they are to come in the following year to hold the council. Bishops are also to be chosen who shall celebrate with the metropolitan the feast of the Nativity of the Lord and holy Easter.

After this, when the archdeacon says, “Pray,” they shall all prostrate themselves together on the ground. After praying for a very long time, one of the senior men shall say this prayer:

### Prayer
There is no power of the human conscience, Lord, that can carry out the judgments of your will without fault. And therefore, because your eyes have seen our imperfection, we ask you to reckon as perfection what we earnestly desire to conclude with a perfect end of justice. We asked you to meet us at the beginning of our proceedings; we also entreat you to be present at the conclusion of our judgments, so that you may spare our ignorance, pardon our error, and grant perfect effectiveness in action to our perfect vows. [Col. 0014C] And because, with conscience gnawing at us, we waste away lest ignorance may have drawn us into error or perhaps rash willing have driven us to turn aside from justice, therefore we ask and beseech you: if we have incurred any offense in this solemn assembly of the council, may you deign to pardon it and make it forgivable, so that, when we are about to dissolve the council we have assembled, we may first be absolved from all the bonds of our sins, so that forgiveness may follow those who have transgressed, and everlasting reward those who confess to you.

To this prayer let the prayer “Our Father” be added; and while all are still lying prostrate, let this blessing be pronounced.

**Blessing**

May Christ, the Son of God, who is the beginning and the end, grant you the fullness of charity. Amen. And may he who brought you to the completion of this council make you absolved from every stain of sin. Amen. And, having been made freer from every guilt and also absolved through the gift of the Holy Spirit, may you return unharmed in a happy return to the resting places of your sees. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this, whose kingdom and dominion remain forever and ever. Amen.

When these things had been completed, and the archdeacon had said, “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us go in peace,” all immediately rose together; with the metropolitan seated, beginning with him, they all gave one another the kiss. Having thus given one another peace, the assembly of the council was dissolved.

[Col. 0015A] **Prayer for the second day**

Bowing the knees of our hearts before you, Lord, we ask that we may accomplish the good required of us by you; that, always advancing with ready diligence, we may make the subtle judgment of lofty discernment, and, loving mercy, may shine through efforts pleasing to you.

[Col. 0016A] **Prayer for the third day**

Proclaiming to you, Lord, with the voices of inward cries, we unanimously ask that, strengthened by the favor of your grace, we may become fearless heralds of your power and may be able to speak your word with complete confidence.

[Col. 0015]

## 2. THE CANONS OF THE APOSTLES BEGIN, PROCLAIMED THROUGH POPE CLEMENT

[Col. 0015B] **I. A bishop shall be ordained by two or three bishops.**

**II.** A presbyter shall be ordained by one bishop, and likewise a deacon and the other clerics.

**III.** If any bishop or presbyter offers upon the altar anything other than what the Lord ordained in the sacrifice—that is, either honey, or milk, or beer instead of wine, or prepared foods, or birds, or any animals, or vegetables—acting contrary to the Lord’s constitution, let him be deposed at the proper time.

**IV.** It is not permitted to offer anything upon the altar except new ears of grain, grapes, and oil for the lamps, and incense, at the time when the sacred offering is celebrated.

**V.** All other fruits shall be sent to the bishop and presbyters at the house of firstfruits [Col. 0015C], and shall not be offered upon the altar. It is certain, however, that the bishop and presbyters shall distribute them to the deacons and the other clerics.

**VI.** A bishop or presbyter shall by no means put away his own wife under the pretext of religion. If he does put her away, let him be excommunicated; and if he persists, let him be deposed.

**VII.** A bishop, presbyter, or deacon shall by no means undertake secular concerns; otherwise, let him be deposed.

**VIII.** If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon celebrates the holy day of Easter with the Jews before the spring equinox, let him be deposed.

**IX.** If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or anyone from the priestly order, after the offering has been made, does not communicate [Col. 0015D], let him either state the reason—if it is reasonable, let him receive pardon—or, if he does not state it, let him be deprived of communion, as one who has become a cause of injury to the people, giving rise to suspicion concerning the one who offered the sacrifice that he did not offer rightly.

**X.** All the faithful who enter the church and hear the Scriptures, but do not persevere in prayer and do not receive holy communion, ought to be deprived of communion, as those who stir up disturbances in the Church.

**XI.** If anyone prays together in the same house, even with an excommunicated person, let him be deprived of communion.

**XII.** If anyone prays together with a condemned cleric as though with a cleric, let him be condemned.

**XIII.** If any cleric or layman, suspended from communion or communicating, hastens to another city and is received on account of letters of recommendation, both those who received him and the one who was received shall be deprived of communion. In the case of an excommunicated person, the correction itself shall be prolonged, since he has lied and misled the Church of God.

**XIV.** A bishop is not permitted to invade another parish, abandoning his own, even if compelled by many, unless perhaps someone urges him for a reasonable cause—as one who might bring greater benefit to those established there and foresee some advancement in the matter of religion. Let him not attempt this on his own, but accomplish it by the judgment and earnest petition of many bishops.

**XV.** If any presbyter or deacon, or anyone from the number of the clerics, leaves his own parish [Col. 0016C] and goes to another, and completely transfers himself to dwell in a foreign parish without the knowledge of his bishop, we do not permit him to minister any longer, especially if, summoned by his bishop, he refuses to return and persists in his restlessness. Nevertheless, let him communicate there as a layman.

**XVI.** If the bishop with whom it is established that they have remained treats the decree of cessation against them as nothing and receives them as clerics, let him be deprived of communion as a teacher of disorder.

**XVII.** If anyone, after baptism, has entered into a second marriage or has kept a concubine, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor at all belong to the number of those who serve in sacred ministry.

[Col. 0016D] **XVIII.** If anyone takes a widow who has been cast out, or a prostitute, or a slave woman, or any woman belonging to those who are devoted to public spectacles, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor belong to the number of those who serve in sacred ministry.

**XIX.** Whoever takes two sisters in marriage, or his brother’s daughter, cannot be a cleric.

**XX.** Let a cleric who serves as a surety be expelled.

**XXI.** If a eunuch was made so through the plots of men, or if his male organs were cut off during persecution, or if he was born so and is worthy, let him become a bishop.

**XXII.** If anyone has castrated himself—that is, if anyone has cut off his own male organs—let him not become a cleric, because he is the murderer of himself [Col. 0017A] and an enemy of God’s creation.

**XXIII.** If anyone, while a cleric, castrates himself, let him be utterly condemned, because he is his own murderer.

**XXIV.** Let a layman who castrates himself be deprived of communion for three years, because he has proved an assailant of his own life.

**XXV.** A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who is caught in fornication, perjury, or theft shall be deposed, but shall not be deprived of communion; for Scripture says: “The Lord will not judge twice for the same thing.”

**XXVI.** Likewise, let the other clerics also be subject to this condition.

**XXVII.** Concerning marriages, we prescribe that those who have been advanced to the clergy may, if they wish, take wives—but only readers and singers.

**XXVIII.** We prescribe that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who strikes faithful people when they offend, or unbelievers when they act wickedly, and who wishes to be feared by such means, be deposed from his office, because God nowhere taught us this. On the contrary, when he was struck, he did not strike back; when he was cursed, he did not curse; when he suffered, he did not threaten.

**XXIX.** If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been justly deposed for definite crimes dares to take up again the ministry formerly entrusted to him, let him be completely cut off from the Church.

**XXX.** If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, let him be deposed [Col. 0017C], and his ordainer also; let both be cut off from communion in every way, as Simon Magus was by Peter.

**XXXI.** If any bishop, making use of secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed, and let all who communicate with him be separated.

**XXXII.** If any presbyter, despising his bishop, gathers the people separately and raises another altar, having no grounds on which to accuse the bishop in the matter of piety and justice, let him be deposed as one who loves pre-eminence. For he is a tyrant; and let all the other clerics who agree with such a person be deposed, while the laypeople shall be separated. This, however, should be done after the bishop has entreated him once, twice, and three times.

**XXXIII.** If any presbyter or deacon has been separated by his bishop [Col. 0017D], no other bishop may receive him; he may be received only by the one who separated him, unless perhaps that bishop who is known to have separated him has died.

**XXXIV.** No foreign bishop, presbyter, or deacon shall be received without letters of recommendation. When they bring written documents, let them be examined most carefully, and let them be received if they have proved to be preachers of piety. If not, do not even supply them with necessities, and do not admit them to communion in any way, because many things arise through stealth.

**XXXV.** It is fitting that the bishops of each nation know who among them is considered first, whom they should regard as a head, and that they do nothing beyond his knowledge except those matters that belong to each one’s own parish and to the villages subject to it. Nor should he do anything in their parishes without the knowledge of all. Thus there will be unanimity, and God will be glorified through Christ in the Holy Spirit.

**XXXVI.** A bishop must not dare to perform ordinations outside his own boundaries, in cities and villages that are subject to him by no right. If he is convicted of having done this without the knowledge of those who hold those cities and villages, let both he and those ordained by him be deposed.

**XXXVII.** If any bishop does not accept the office and care of the people entrusted to him, let him be deprived of communion until he consents and offers obedience. The same applies to a presbyter and a deacon. But if he proceeds and is not received—not on account of his own judgment but because of the people’s malice—let him himself remain a bishop; but let the clerics of the city be deprived of communion, because they were not instructors of the disobedient people.

**XXXVIII.** Councils of bishops shall be held twice a year, so that they may examine among themselves the doctrines of piety and remove ecclesiastical disputes as they arise: once in the fourth week after Pentecost, and the second time on the twelfth day of the month Hyperberetaeus—that is, according to the Romans, the fourth day before the Ides of October.

**XXXIX.** The bishop shall have charge of all ecclesiastical affairs and shall administer them as in the sight of God [Col. 0018C]. He may not take anything at all from these things, nor give to his own relatives what belongs to God. If they are poor, let provision be made for them as for the poor; but on their account let the affairs of the Church not be plundered.

**XL.** Presbyters and deacons shall not attempt to do anything without the bishop. For the Lord’s people have been entrusted to him, and he will render an account for their souls. But let the bishop’s own property, if indeed he has any, be clear, and likewise the Lord’s property, so that the bishop may have the authority, when dying, to leave his own possessions as he wishes and to whomever he wishes, lest what is shown to belong to the bishop be lost under the pretext of ecclesiastical property. For perhaps he has a wife, children, relatives, or servants, and it is just before God and human beings that neither the Church should suffer loss through ignorance of the bishop’s affairs, nor the bishop or his relatives be proscribed under the pretext of the Church and fall into legal cases concerning him, so that his death may be subjected to the injuries of evil reputation.

**XLI.** We prescribe that the bishop have ecclesiastical property in his power. For if human souls have been entrusted to him as precious, much more ought he to take care of money, so that, under his authority, everything may be distributed to those in need through the presbyters and deacons and administered with fear and every diligence. From these resources, let him himself also receive what he needs—if indeed he needs anything—for his necessities and for the use of visiting brothers [Col. 0019A], so that he may lack nothing at all. For the law of God commands that those who serve the altar should be fed from the altar, since no soldier takes up arms against enemies at his own expense (1 Corinthians 9).

**XLII.** A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who devotes himself to gambling or drunkenness shall either desist or certainly be condemned.

**XLIII.** A subdeacon, reader, or singer who does similar things shall either desist or be deprived of communion; likewise a layman.

**XLIV.** A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who exacts interest from debtors shall either desist or certainly be condemned.

**XLV.** A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who prays with heretics shall merely be deprived of communion. [Col. 0019B] But if he has urged them, as though they were clerics, to act or pray, let him be condemned.

**3 XLVI.** We prescribe that a bishop or presbyter who accepts the baptism of heretics be condemned. “For what fellowship has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer have with an unbeliever?” (2 Corinthians 7:15).

[Col. 0020A] **XLVII.** If a bishop or presbyter rebaptizes someone who has received baptism according to the truth, or fails to baptize someone polluted by the impious, let him be deposed, as one who mocks the cross and death of the Lord and does not rightly distinguish true priests from false priests.

**XLVIII.** If any layman puts away his own wife and marries another, or one dismissed by another, let him be deprived of communion.

**XLIX.** If any bishop or presbyter does not baptize according to the Lord’s command in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, but in three principles without a beginning, or in three Sons, or in three Paracletes, let him be expelled.

**L.** If any bishop or presbyter does not celebrate baptism with the triple immersion of the one mystery, but immerses once in the baptism that is understood to be given into the Lord’s death, let him be deposed. For the Lord did not say to us, “Baptize into my death,” but, “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

[Col. 0019]

# THE FIRST LETTER OF CLEMENT TO JAMES, THE BROTHER OF THE LORD, BEGINS

[Col. 0019B] Clement to James, lord bishop of bishops, governing the holy Church of the Hebrews at Jerusalem [Col. 0019C], and also all the Churches founded everywhere by God’s providence, together with the Fathers, deacons, and all the other Fathers: may peace always be with you.

I inform you, lord, that Simon Peter—who, by the merit of true faith and by virtue of his uncorrupted preaching, was declared to be the foundation of the Church, and for this reason was also surnamed Peter by the mouth of the Lord—was the first of the apostles, the firstfruits of the Lord’s choice. To him God the Father first revealed the Son (Matthew 16:17); to him Christ appropriately granted blessedness, because he was called and chosen, made the Lord’s guest and companion, a good and most approved disciple. As the mightiest of all, he was commanded to illuminate the world’s darker western region, and he was able fully to carry out the command. But how long shall I prolong my speech while shrinking from reporting what is sad, though it is necessary, even if late, to bring it forth?

This same Peter, then, who, because of the immense love he bore toward all human beings, did not cease publicly and with complete confidence, even in opposition to the tyrant, to proclaim the good of the whole world, and brought the King of all ages throughout the earth, even to the knowledge of this very city of Rome, so that it too might be saved—this Peter, I say, wishing to suffer for piety, brought his present life to an end. In those very days when he sensed that his end was approaching, while he was present in the assembly of the brothers, he took hold of my hand and suddenly stood up before the ears of the whole Church and spoke these words:

“Hear me, my brothers and fellow servants, because, as I have been taught by the one who sent me, my Lord and teacher Jesus Christ, the day of my death is near. I ordain this Clement as your bishop [Col. 0020C], and to him alone I hand over the chair of my preaching and teaching. He has been my companion in everything from beginning to end, and through this he has recognized the truth of all my preaching. He has faithfully persevered as my partner in everything. Among all others I have found him to be one who worships the Lord, loves human beings, is chaste, devoted to the study of learning, sober, kind, just, patient, and able to endure the injuries of many, even among those who are instructed in the word of the Lord.

Therefore I hand over to him the authority to bind and loose that was entrusted to me by the Lord, so that whatever he decrees on earth concerning anything may be decreed also in heaven. For he will bind what ought to be bound and loose what ought to be loosed, since he knows the rule of the Church exactly. Hear him, therefore, knowing that whoever grieves the teacher of truth sins against Christ and provokes God, the Father of all; for this reason he will also lose his life. The one who presides over the others ought to act in the place of a physician and not be stirred by the fury of a wild beast.”

When he had said this, I fell at his feet and begged him, excusing myself and declining the honor or authority of the chair. But he answered:

“Do not ask me for this. It has been appointed that this be done, and all the more because you excuse yourself. For this chair does not seek one who desires it and boldly pursues it, but one adorned with good character and learned in speech. If there were someone else better, if another assistant had stood by me so diligently, if someone else had undertaken the explanation of my teaching so fully and had learned the Church’s arrangements from me so plainly, then, having such a person, I would not need to compel you to undertake a good work that you do not wish to accept. It is therefore pointless to seek another, since I have offered you first to God as the firstfruits of those who are being saved through me from the Gentiles, and especially of this city.

Consider also this: if, fearing the danger of sin, you refuse to accept the governance of the Church, be certain that you sin more by evading the people of God, who are like people placed amid the waves and in danger, when you are able to help them, considering only yourself and not providing what is beneficial to all in common. Be certain that you must accept every danger, because I too will not cease entreating for the salvation of all. The sooner you obey me, therefore, the sooner you will relieve me of the burden and sorrow of my labor [Col. 0021B].

I also know this, O Clement: I will bring upon you the weariness, troubles, dangers, and reproaches of an uneducated and unteachable crowd. Nevertheless, I know how steadfastly and courageously you will endure them, looking toward the other hope that prepares for you with God the crown of patience.

I also want you to see clearly with me, in accordance with reason, when Christ most greatly needs your labor: now, when the enemy is stirring up war against his bride, or in the future, when Christ will already triumph after victory and will no longer need anyone’s labor. Who, even of limited understanding, would not perceive that this is the time in which Christ requires your service? Therefore, with your whole mind, offer your labor in the present necessity and give assistance in the battles to the excellent King, who will grant magnificent rewards after victory.

Gladly, then, accept the office of bishop, especially since you have learned the Church’s arrangements from me with sound understanding, so that the salvation of those who have fled to the Lord through us may not waver at all. Nevertheless, I thought it necessary to remind you briefly before everyone of the order of this administration.

You must live irreproachably and strive with the greatest zeal to cast away all the occupations of this life: do not become a guarantor; do not become an advocate in lawsuits; do not become entangled in any worldly business through any occupation whatsoever. For Christ does not wish to ordain you today as a judge or examiner of secular affairs, lest, suffocated by the present concerns of human beings, you be unable to devote yourself to the word of God and, according to the rule of truth, distinguish the good from the evil.

Let the laypeople undertake for one another those works which, as we explained above, do not suit you—that is, let laypeople undertake them—and let no one occupy you with anything that would remove you from those studies through which salvation is given to all. For just as it is a charge of impiety for you, neglecting the study of the word of God, to undertake secular concerns, so it is a sin for each layperson not to serve the others faithfully, even in matters belonging to the common use of life.

In order to make you secure and free for the duties you owe, let all labor together. If laypeople do not understand this by themselves, they must be instructed through the deacons, so that they may leave to you the concerns of the Church alone, which you will be able to administer as is fitting [Col. 0022A] and to serve the word of truth more abundantly and diligently. For if you are occupied with worldly cares, you will deceive both yourself and those who listen to you. You will not be able to distinguish fully for each person the things that pertain to salvation; and as a result you will be deposed as one who has not taught what pertains to human salvation, while the disciples will perish through ignorance.

Therefore devote yourself solely to this: teach the word of God at the proper time and without interruption, through which they may attain salvation. Let them receive your words with such reverence as those who know that you are the ambassador and herald of truth, and that whatever you bind on earth is bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose is loosed there also. For you, as I said, will bind what ought to be bound and loose what is expedient to loose. Let these and similar admonitions be addressed to you who preside.

Let the following be addressed to the presbyters.

Above all, let them devote themselves to chastity and join young men to wives, so that they may forestall the heat of burning youth by the law of marriage. Nor should they neglect to take care of those who are more advanced in age, because in many people, even when the body has grown old, desire remains vigorous. Therefore it is necessary to beware and forestall the possibility that the stain of fornication, having found an opportunity, may spread among us like the worst poison, lest a hidden fire of adultery grow hot within us.

And what is more serious among all sins than adultery? It holds the second place in punishments, since the first belongs to those who depart from God, even if they have lived soberly. Therefore, you presbyters, cultivate and adorn the Church, the bride of Christ, for chastity. By “bride” I mean the entire assembly of the Church. If she is found chaste by her bridegroom, she will be honored by him with immense gifts and presents, and you, as ministers of the bride and friends of the bridegroom, will rejoice in great joy and gladness. But if this bride is found stained by sins, she will not be handed over to the royal marriage-bed as unworthy, while you will suffer punishment if, through your negligence or indolence, the cruel contagion of sin has crept in.

Therefore, above all, take care of sobriety and chastity. For fornication is considered a very grave crime before God. It has many forms, as Clement himself will carefully explain to you. Nevertheless, the first form of adultery is for a man not to be content with his own wife alone, and for a woman not to preserve herself for her own husband alone.

If anyone is chaste, he can become humane and merciful, and through this can himself obtain eternal mercy from God. Indeed, just as the poison of adultery is more destructive than all evils, so brotherly love and charity hold the summit of all good. Therefore love all your brothers, and regard everyone with religious devotion and mercy. Show yourselves as fathers to orphans; provide widows with the care of husbands, supplying what is necessary with complete chastity. Join younger widows to husbands in marriage.

For those who do not know crafts, seek out honorable opportunities by which they may obtain the food necessary for life. Provide work for craftsmen; show mercy to the weak. I know that you will do all these things if you establish charity in your hearts before everything else and above all. The greatest encouragement for receiving and possessing this charity will be to make your food and table common among yourselves frequently, and, as far as each one is able, to share your bread and salt with your brothers more often. For charity is especially acquired through these things, and the cause of every good consists in such fellowship. Where there is peace and goodness, there is salvation. Therefore make your food common with those who are brothers according to the Lord, because through these temporal services you will merit eternal joys through the fruits of peace and charity.

Be much more diligent in feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and helping those who are in prison as far as possible. Receive strangers very readily into your homes. And, not to mention everything individually, charity itself will teach you to do every good thing if it is in you, just as, conversely, hatred teaches those who are alienated from salvation to do every evil.

If any of the brothers have disputes among themselves, let them not be judged before secular judges; rather, whatever the matter may be, let it be settled before the presbyters of the Church, and let them obey their decisions in every way.

Above all, flee greed, which separates people from eternal goods through the opportunity of present gain [Col. 0023C]. Keep weights, measures, and balances completely just according to each place; faithfully restore deposits. You will fulfill all these things, and anything similar to them, carefully and diligently only if you continually turn the future judgment of God over in your heart. For who could sin if he always placed God’s judgment before his eyes? What is certainly to be done at the end of the world, so that at last those who have acted well in this life may obtain the goods that have been stored up, while sinners may obtain the punishments prepared for them—we cannot doubt at all that these things will come to pass. For a true prophet foretold all these things to us.

Therefore, you who are disciples of the true prophets, above all cast disagreements and dissensions of spirit from your hearts, for from them every evil work proceeds; preserve kindness and simplicity with your whole mind. If, however, the heart, resentment, unbelief, or any other evil of those we mentioned above has secretly crept into someone, let the person who cares for his soul not be ashamed to confess it to the one who can heal him through the word of the Lord and salutary counsel, so that, with complete faith and good works, he may escape the punishments of eternal fire and reach the rewards of perpetual life.

Let the deacons of the Church be like the eyes of the bishop, going about and observing with modesty the conduct of the entire Church, and carefully investigating whether they see anyone becoming close to the precipice and near to sin, so that they may report this to the bishop and he may admonish the one who is about to fall into the precipice, so that he may be recalled and not fall into sin. Let them also admonish and encourage those who are more negligent and those who come less often to hear the word of God and do not diligently gather for the bishop’s instruction.

For if they are constant in hearing, they gain not only the profits of eternal life from salutary admonition, but also whatever sadnesses or sorrows arise from the necessities of the present life and the disasters of the times—whatever they carry fixed in their hearts like arrows through their own speeches—all these things are cast away by the preaching of truth and purified by the teaching and instruction of eternal life. Otherwise, if they withdraw their hearing from the word of God for a long time and remain in the worship of vices, they will undoubtedly be occupied by thorns and briars [Col. 0024B]. And for what else is such land prepared except for fire?

Let the deacons, therefore, as we said, have concern for these matters. But let them diligently seek out those who are sick in the body and inform the people about them if the people are unaware, so that they too may visit them and provide what is necessary, with the knowledge of the one who presides. If they do this secretly as well, they will not sin.

Let them likewise inform the bishop about strangers who need to be refreshed, and let the other matters pertaining to the worship and discipline of the Church be the concern of the deacons.

Those who catechize—that is, those who instruct beginners by the word—must first themselves be instructed. For human souls are at stake, and the one who teaches and instructs inexperienced souls must be such that he can adapt himself to the ability of the learners and direct the order of his speech according to the capacity of his hearer. Therefore he himself must be especially well educated and thoroughly learned, irreproachable, mature, fearless, as you yourselves will find this Clement to be after me.

It would be a great task if I were now to go through individually what each person ought to possess. Nevertheless, this is what above all I desire to be preserved in common by all of you: that you maintain concord. Through this alone you can enter the harbor of rest and dwell in the city of the highest King, whose name is Peace.

For the whole condition of the Church resembles a great ship which, across a wave-tossed sea, carries men from various places and regions who are hastening toward one city of the powerful kingdom.

Let the Lord himself, almighty God, be the master of this ship; let Christ be the pilot. Then let the bishop fulfill the office of the helmsman at the prow; let the presbyters occupy the place of sailors, and the deacons that of stewards. Let those who catechize be compared with recruiters of sailors; let the multitude of the entire brotherhood be like the passengers. Let the sea itself represent this world; let the variety of winds and storms represent various temptations; let persecutions, tribulations, and dangers correspond to the waves.

Let the earthly spirits that blow either from torrents or from valleys represent the words of false prophets, deceivers, or corrupt doctrine. Let the promontories and rugged places represent those who hold authority in the world, judges who threaten dangers and deaths [Col. 0025A]. Let the “two-sea” regions—places battered by the double tides of deceptive waves—be compared with those who are uncertain in mind and wavering concerning the truth of the promises, and with those who examine our faith by irrational reasoning. Let hypocrites and deceitful people be regarded as like pirates.

The swift whirlpool, the Tartarean Charybdis, shipwrecks dashed against rocks, and deadly overturnings—what else should they be considered but sins?

It remains, therefore, that this ship may safely enter the harbor of the desired city with a prosperous course. It is fitting to pour out a prayer to God so that those who sail may deserve to be heard. But a person will deserve to be heard by God only if his prayers themselves are supported by good character and good works.

Above all, while the passengers—that is, the laypeople—remain quietly and silently in their respective places, let them not, through restlessness and disorderly, useless wandering, begin to roam about everywhere, lest they either hinder the sailors from their duty or, because of their disturbance, cause the ship, pressed toward one side, to sink.

Let the recruiters of sailors remind them about wages, and let the deacons neglect nothing that pertains to diligence or discipline. Let the presbyters, like sailors, carefully arrange each matter for the ship’s instruction and prepare what must be sought at its proper time. Let the bishop, like the helmsman at the prow, watchfully and diligently keep the words of Christ the pilot.

Let the Lord Savior, the pilot of his Church, be loved by all, and let the whole Church trust and obey his commands and orders alone. Let all continually implore God for favorable winds [Col. 0025C], so that those who sail may overcome every tribulation and every danger, sailing as upon the deep sea of this world and the ocean of human life, in which they must hunger and thirst, endure nakedness, and tolerate bodily diseases and illnesses.

Moreover, they must often struggle against the plots and deceit of human beings, knowing that they will sometimes have to scatter and at other times gather themselves together; they must also endure vomiting and contusions. For, because of the confusion of sins and the rejection of crimes, like bile badly gathered in the entrails, an expulsion must be made, and every bitterness of sin hidden within must be utterly cast out from the heart, if it has perhaps been gathered there from evil desires like harmful foods. When someone has vomited and cast it out, he will be freed from the sickness of a great disease—provided that after the vomiting he takes what belongs to health.

Yet know, all of you, that the bishop labors above all of you, because each one of you bears his own labor, but he bears both his own and that of each individual. Therefore, O Clement, since you know that you can benefit everyone, help each person as best you can and relieve each one, for you carry the burden and anxiety of them all. Hence, as I now impose this administration upon you, I know that I am receiving grace more than I am offering it. But be confident and bear it bravely, certain that you will receive the reward of your labor when you have brought this [Col. 0026A] ship safely into the harbor of rest, where you will receive wages and rewards for the salvation of all, if here you keep watch for the safety of all. Thus, if many of the brothers hate you because of the strictness of justice, you will not be harmed by this; rather, through such hatred the love of God will be won for you. Therefore strive all the more and avoid being praised by the wicked or loved by those who act most evilly; instead, because of your administration of justice and the most equitable rule of discipline, may you deserve to be commended by Christ. When he had said these and very many similar things, he again turned toward the people and said:

But you also, dearest brothers and my fellow servants, obey in all things this man who presides over you in order to teach the truth. Know that whoever grieves him does not receive Christ, who entrusted to him the chair of teaching; and whoever has not received Christ will be judged not to have received God the Father either [Col. 0026B] (Luke 9:48). Therefore neither will he himself be received into the kingdom of heaven. For this reason, make every effort always to attend every assembly, lest you be condemned by Christ the Judge as negligent and idle. When you gather, frequently go to Clement, and all of you take care to be of one mind with him and to show him genuine support with the greatest zeal, knowing that on account of you individually the enemy attacks him alone all the more and stirs up greater battles against him. You must therefore strive with the greatest zeal so that, bound to him by every bond of love, you may cling to him with the fullest affection. You also must persevere as one in complete harmony, so that all of you may more easily agree, with one accord and [Col. 0026C] unanimity, to obey him. In this way you may attain salvation, and he may more readily lift the burden of the charge imposed upon him with you obeying him.

You yourselves must also understand certain things, if there are matters that, because of the plots of evil people, he cannot state more openly and plainly. For example, if he is hostile to one of the wicked because of that person’s actions, do not expect him to say to you, “Do not be friends with him.” Rather, you must observe this prudently, observe his will without associating with that person, and withdraw from the person toward whom you perceive him to be hostile. Nor should you speak with those with whom he does not speak, so that each person who is at fault, while wishing to retain the friendship of all of you, may hasten to be reconciled with him who presides over everyone, and thereby return to salvation and [Col. 0026D] health once he begins to obey the admonitions of the one who presides. But if someone is friendly with those with whom he is not friendly, and speaks with those with whom he does not speak, he too is one of those who wished to destroy the Church of God; and although he may appear to be with you in body, in mind and spirit he is against you. This enemy is much more wicked than those outside, who are openly hostile; for under the appearance of friendship he performs hostile acts, and he scatters and devastates the Church.

And when he had said this, in the midst of everyone he laid his hands upon me and compelled me, with great embarrassment, to sit in his chair. When I had sat down, he again said to me:

“I beg [Col. 0027A] you, O Clement, before all who are present, that after I have brought this present life to its natural end, you briefly describe for James, the brother of the Lord, either what concerns the beginning of your faith or also what sort of disposition you had before the faith; and likewise how you were my companion from the beginning to the end of my journeys and actions; what you, as an attentive listener, received in each city while I was disputing; what order there was in my preaching, whether of words or of deeds; and what end overtook me in this city. As I have said, do not hesitate to send him everything that you can, briefly gathered together. Nor should you fear that he might be excessively saddened by my departure, since he certainly does not doubt that I endure it out of devotion. It will, however, be a great consolation to him if he learns [Col. 0027B] that after me someone has not taken up my chair who is inexperienced, uneducated, ignorant of the mystery of the divine word, unaware of the discipline of ecclesiastical order, or unacquainted with the rule of doctrine. For he knows that, if an uneducated man receives the office of teacher, the disciples and hearers, enveloped in the darkness of ignorance, will undoubtedly sink into destruction.”

Therefore I, my lord James, having received these commands from him, was obliged to fulfill what he had ordered by informing you, and by briefly gathering together both these matters and those which, as he passed through each city, he either uttered in his preaching or accomplished through the power of his deeds. Although, at his command, I have already sent you a fuller account of many of these matters under the very title that he ordered to be attached, namely, *Clement’s Itinerary*, not *Peter’s Preaching* [Col. 0027C], he has now also commanded me to set them forth. With the Lord’s help, I shall begin.

“Repent,” he said, “and practice true repentance.” Therefore all people who are designated by the name Christian must truly believe and confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as one God and Lord; they must love him with their whole mind, whole heart, and whole strength, and love their neighbors as themselves. Those who are teachable must acquire whatever is necessary to advance toward these things and toward perfect doctrine.

For faith and love are the foundation of all goodness. “Without faith no one will be able to please God” (Hebrews 11:6).

When Christ had risen and ascended into heaven [Col. 0027D], and the Holy Spirit had been sent and knowledge of languages had been granted to the apostles, while they were still together in one place each of them, expressing what he believed, composed the creed that the faithful Church now holds, so that, when they departed from one another, they might preach this rule among all nations. Thus, reviewing the whole of the Catholic faith—in which the integrity of belief is established, the equality of the one almighty God, that is, of the holy Trinity, is declared, and the mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God is set forth: how, for the salvation of the human race, he descended from heaven in time and deigned to be born of a Virgin; in what order and at what time he came forth; how, after being buried, he rose again; how he ascended bodily into heaven itself and sat at the right hand of the Father; how he will come as judge; how he has granted remission of sins to those reborn through sacred baptism; and how the resurrection of the human race in that same flesh will take place unto eternal life—they taught it in this way [Col. 0028A]. For *symbolum* in Greek means “collection” in Latin. These holy Apostles, as has been said, beneficially composed it among themselves through the Holy Spirit. It is also called a “sign,” because by it the person who believes rightly is identified.

Therefore, for all believers, salvation of souls and everlasting life are prepared through good works in accordance with what is contained in the aforesaid creed. Thus, what is placed at the beginning of that same creed—“I believe in God the Father almighty”—is shown at the very outset as a glorious testimony of faith and its foundation, because the person who believes rightly will be able to be saved. “For whoever approaches [Col. 0028B] God must believe” (Hebrews 11:6), since “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10). Hence the prophet says: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Psalm 115:10). And again: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17). Also: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Luke 24:25). In human affairs, therefore, no undertaking is begun unless it is believed that all the labor will reach its intended result; consequently, one must believe in God, from whom both the present life and the future life are granted.

“God” is the designation of an eternal substance, or of divine fear. God, therefore, is without beginning, without end, simple, incorporeal, and incomprehensible. But when you hear “Father,” recognize that he truly has a Son begotten, just as one is called a possessor [Col. 0028C] who possesses something, and a lord who has someone over whom he rules. “God the Father,” therefore, is the name of a hidden mystery, whose true Son is the Word, the mirror, the character, and the living image of the living Father—like the Father in all things, of the same nature, begotten in divinity, and in every respect co-equal with his begetter. One must not ask how he begot the Son, a matter unknown even to the angels and hidden from the prophets. Hence it was said: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). This hidden origin, together with his own Son, is known only by the one who begot him. God is not to be subjected to our investigation but believed in, since even within ourselves we do not know how what we know comes to be, or how our wisdom, talent, understanding, counsel, or mind generates a word. It is enough to know that light begot radiance [Col. 0028D], as the Prophet says: “From the womb, before the morning star, in the splendors of the holy ones, I begot you” (Psalm 123:3). And again: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him”; and afterward: “He was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 4:36, 38).

It is therefore necessary for each person to love God with all his heart and all his soul, as has been prescribed, and with all his strength, and to love his neighbor as himself. The Lord answered one of the scribes and said: “The first commandment of all is: ‘Hear, Israel: The Lord your God is one God, and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength.’ This is the first commandment. The second [Col. 0029A] is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these” (Mark 12:29–31).

This is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices. Hence it is also written in the Old Testament: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16), and the Lord says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matthew 7:12). Through these two commandments, malice is restrained by the one, and benevolence is propagated by the other, so that no one may inflict evil but may bestow good. The first commandment is to beware of causing harm; the second is to provide what is good. “For if you do not love the brother whom you see, how can you love God whom you do not see?” (1 John 4:20.) Thus he teaches us [Col. 0029B] to exercise our care without abandoning your care, and to love us in such a way that love of one’s neighbor is not neglected. For the love of God is compared with death, as Wisdom says: “Love is strong as death” (Song of Songs 8). This is because, just as death violently separates the soul from the body, so the love of God separates the soul from worldly and carnal love. “For whoever loves me,” says the Lord, “will keep my commandments” (John 14:23). Whoever despises God’s commandments does not love God; hence it is written: “Do not suppose that you remain in my love if you do not keep my commandments” (John 15:10). Nor do we love a king if we hate his laws. Nor can a person known to fall short in love of his neighbor love the Lord with his whole heart, because through love of the [Col. 0029C] Lord one arrives at the charity of Christ.

Since, as was said earlier, the whole law and the prophets depend upon these two commandments, all who are teachable, and not yet perfectly instructed, must be directed toward fulfilling them, so that they themselves may be taught, prudently instruct others, and be able to teach perfectly, in accordance with the prophet Daniel, who says: “The people who know their God will prevail and act, and those who are learned among the people will teach many” (Daniel 11:32). As has already been said, all who are teachable, though not yet taught, must become so; but Christ taught that priests must be more learned than the rest of the people, saying: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matthew 15:14). He commanded teachers who are the priests, the salt of the earth and the light of the world, to glorify God the Father through the splendor of their works [Col. 0029D]. Concerning them the Lord says: “Blessed are you when they curse you, persecute you, and say every evil thing against you falsely because of me. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you” (Luke 6:23). “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be salted? It is no longer useful for anything except to be thrown outside and trampled by people. A city cannot be hidden when it is set upon a mountain; nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house and so that those who enter may see the light. Thus let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works [Col. 0030A] and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:13–14).

He commanded us to send bishops to each city where he had not sent them, men learned and prudent as serpents, simple as doves, in accordance with the Lord’s command. We have begun to do this and, with the Lord’s help, shall continue to do so. You, for your part, appoint and send bishops throughout your dioceses, because we shall attend to other regions, as he himself ordered us to do. We shall send some to Gaul and Spain, and we wish to direct others to Germany, Italy, and the remaining peoples. Wherever we learn that the peoples are more savage and rebellious, we must send men wiser and stricter. They do not cease daily [Col. 0030B] to sow divine seeds, to win many for Christ, and to lead them to the right faith and the way of truth, so that they may be able to present more sheaves to the Lord.

In those cities where, formerly among the pagans, their chief priests and principal teachers of the law held authority, he commanded that primates of the bishops, or patriarchs, be installed, who would handle the judgments of the other bishops and the more important affairs whenever necessity required, dealing with them in matters of faith; and, in accordance with God’s will and the arrangements established by the holy apostles, they would decide matters so that no one might be unjustly endangered. In those cities where, formerly among the aforesaid peoples, there had been chief priests of a lesser rank, he commanded archbishops to be instituted in place of the primates already mentioned, so that they might enjoy not merely primacy but also the name of archbishops [Col. 0030C]. He taught that the judgments of bishops, as mentioned above, and the greater affairs of the Churches should be transferred to the aforementioned primates or patriarchs if the bishops themselves objected, or had some fear, or regarded these or other persons with suspicion, so that no one might perish to his harm. In each city, moreover, he commanded that one bishop, not two, three, or more, be established. Such men would possess not the title of primates, archbishops, or metropolitans—for they did not govern lesser cities—but only the name of bishops, since even among the apostles the arrangement was not equal, but one presided over all. He established this one provision: that bishops should not be installed in villages, fortified settlements, or small cities, lest their name become dishonored. He said that the Lord had taught that bishops [Col. 0030D] hold the place of the apostles, and he indicated that presbyters ought to occupy the place of the remaining disciples. If anyone scandalized one of these, he preached that the gravest punishment should be inflicted upon him. He instructed that all should love and help one another, and that no one should withdraw from helping a brother.

He prohibited true murderers, adulterers, all bound by criminal ties, and those who were not their equals from harassing or accusing them, saying that the Lord taught that no one should inflict anything upon him except his equals. “For the disciple is not above the teacher” (Matthew 10:24), nor ought anyone in any way to inflict an injury upon him [Col. 0031A]. He asked that all infamous persons and those whom the leading authorities of secular law did not admit, as well as laypeople, should always be kept away from accusing and harassing them, and he commanded that all such persons be subject to them. He taught that the life of all priests must be superior, holier, and distinct from that of secular and lay people; that spiritual persons and priests must always be placed above carnal and lay persons, and must remain so. “For it should be regarded as a very small matter for us to be examined and judged by such people, or by any human tribunal” (1 Corinthians 4:3). He said that those of greater rank could in no way be accused or judged by those of lesser rank. For he said that this was prohibited not only by the divine laws but also by secular laws. Therefore he judged all who willingly violated the divine laws and voluntarily [Col. 0031B] disturbed the sacred institutions unworthy of ecclesiastical discipline and holy communion. But he said that those who carried them out and obeyed them were worthy of these laws, of the other laws, and of every good thing. Hence he called the prophets as witnesses:

“Hear, O heavens, and listen, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: ‘I nourished and exalted sons, but they rejected me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; Israel has not known me, my people has not understood. Woe to the sinful nation, the people laden with iniquity, the wicked seed, the criminal children. They have abandoned the Lord, they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, they have turned backward. Why should I strike you further, as you add transgression? Every head is sick, and every heart is grieving; from the sole [Col. 0031C] of the foot to the crown there is no health in it, but wound, bruise, and swollen sore. It has not been bound up, treated with medicine, or softened with oil. Your land is desolate, your cities are burned with fire; foreigners devour your country before your eyes, and it will be laid waste like a land devastated by an enemy, and abandoned’” (Isaiah 1:2 and following). “Woe,” he says, “to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isaiah 6:21). “Therefore my people have been led away captive because they had no knowledge; its nobles have perished from hunger, and its multitude has dried up from thirst. Therefore the underworld has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without limit; its strong ones, its people, and its lofty [Col. 0031D] and glorious ones descend to it. A person will be bowed down, a man will be humbled, and the eyes of the lofty will be brought low. The Lord will be exalted in judgment, and the holy God will be sanctified in justice” (Isaiah 5:13 and following).”

He prohibited carnal persons from resisting spiritual persons. Concerning those who raised their necks against their teachers and elders, he spoke by way of the example of the devil:

“Your pride has been dragged down to the underworld; your corpse has fallen beneath you. Beneath you worms will be spread, and worms will be your covering. How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who used to rise in the morning? You have fallen to the earth, you who wounded the nations. You who said in your heart: ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne. I will sit upon the mountain of the Testament, on the sides [Col. 0032A] of the north. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’ Yet you will be dragged down to hell, into the depths of the pit. Those who see you will bow toward you and look upon you: ‘Is this the man who troubled the earth, who shook kingdoms, who made the world a desert and destroyed its cities, who did not open the prison to his captives?’”

He strictly prohibited drunkenness and preached that those drunk in body and spirit were dead. Concerning them he also said by way of example:

“Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they are inflamed with wine. ‘Harp and lyre, tambourine and flute, and wine are in your banquets, but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands’” (Isaiah 5:11 and following). And again: “Woe to you who are [Col. 0032B] mighty for drinking wine and strong men for mixing drunkenness, who justify the wicked for gifts and take justice away from the just. Therefore, just as the tongue of fire devours straw and the heat of the flame consumes it, so their root will be like embers and their shoot will rise like dust. For they have cast away the law of the Lord of hosts and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel. Therefore the anger of the Lord has been kindled against his people; he has stretched out his hand against them and struck them. The mountains were shaken, and their corpses became like refuse in the middle of the streets. In all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out” (ibid., 22 and following).

He taught that no presbyter in the parish of any bishop should do anything without the bishop’s permission [Col. 0032C], and, by the Lord’s institution, taught that all presbyters must obey their own bishops in everything and without delay. He taught this. For no one should desire or presume upon what belongs to another, but each person should be content with what is his and with those entrusted to him. He instructed: “No one should do anything to another except what he would wish to be done to himself” (Tobit 4:16). He proclaimed that everyone must preserve the holy Church immaculate, and said that bishops are its keys. For they have the power to shut heaven and open its gates, because they have become the keys of heaven.

He taught that no one should remove them, because they are the eyes of the Lord, and whoever touches them touches the pupil of his eye (Zechariah 2:8). He said that the Lord himself had taught [Col. 0032D] how great a punishment is deserved by one who causes them to stumble, where he says:

“Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be plunged into the depths of the sea. Woe to the world because of scandals; for scandals must come, but woe to that person through whom the scandal comes. If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to be sent into the fire of Gehenna. And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life lame than, having two feet, to be sent into the eternal fire. And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be sent into the fire of Gehenna. See that you do not despise one of these little ones” (Matthew 18:6 and following) [Col. 0033A]. “Amen, I say to you: Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven. Again I say to you: If two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:18 and following).”

And again he speaks through the prophet, saying: “Heaven was terrified at this, and was struck with an even greater horror, says the Lord: ‘O intolerable wickedness! O tongue speaking iniquity against the Lord, and mind [Col. 0033B] lifting up its horn on high.’” And again: “Place, O man, a door and a bolt upon your tongue; cease lifting up your horn on high and speaking against the Lord and your neighbor. How long will you insult the suffering Christ and the brothers?” (Ecclesiasticus 28:28 and following.) Thus, by sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience, you sin grievously against Christ; made liable to judgment, you will become infamous and will rightly be rejected.

And again he speaks through the Prophet, saying:

“But you shall be called priests of the Lord; you shall be called ministers of our God. You will consume the strength of the nations and boast in their glory. In place of your double shame they will praise their portion; therefore they shall possess double things in their land, and everlasting joy shall be theirs. For I am the [Col. 0033C] Lord, who love judgment and hate robbery for burnt offering; I will give their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them. Their seed will be known among the nations, and their offspring among the peoples. All who see them will recognize them, because they are the seed whom the Lord has blessed. Rejoicing, I will rejoice, and my soul will exult in my God, because he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and wrapped me in the robe of justice, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride decorated with her jewels. For just as the earth brings forth its shoot and just as a garden causes its seed to sprout, so the Lord God will make justice and praise sprout before all the nations” (Isaiah 61:6 and following).

He said that these men were to be judged or removed by the Lord alone [Col. 0033D], and not by others, because they belong to him and not to another. For who is there who judges another person’s servant? Even if human beings do not endure such things, neither does the God of gods and Lord of lords tolerate them in any way. Hence he said that the prophets were his witnesses, through whom the Lord speaks:

“Behold, I have tested you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty. For my own sake I shall act, so that I may not be blasphemed, and I shall not give my glory to another. Hear me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I call. I myself, I am the first, and I am the last. My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured out the heavens. I shall call them, and they shall stand together” (Isaiah 48:10 and following). “The islands shall wait for me, and they shall support my arm. My salvation [Col. 0034A] shall be everlasting, and my justice shall not fail” (Isaiah 51:5–6).

“Hear me, you who know justice, people who have my law in their hearts. Do not fear the reproaches of people, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. For just as a garment, so the worm will consume them; and just as wool, so the moth will devour them. But my salvation shall be everlasting, and my justice from generation to generation” (ibid., 7–8).

And again:

“My life is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment will pass away from my God. Do you not know, or have you not heard? The eternal God, the Lord, who created the boundaries of the earth, will not grow faint or weary, and there is no searching out his wisdom. He gives strength to the weary and increases power for those who lack strength. Boys [Col. 0034B] will faint and grow weary, and young men will fall in weakness. But those who hope in the Lord will change their strength; they will take up wings like eagles. They will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not faint. Let the islands pass over to me, and let the nations change their strength; let them draw near, and then speak. Let us approach together for judgment” (Isaiah 40:27 and following).

He taught that the Lord himself condemns through the prophet those who forbid these men or attempt to remove or condemn them, and that they remain condemned until they make satisfaction to them and to the Church, where he says:

“They chose such things in their ways, and their soul delighted in their abominations. Therefore I too will choose their mockeries and bring condemnation upon them, because I called them and they did not listen; they did evil in my sight and chose what I did not [Col. 0034C] want. Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word. Your brothers who hate you and cast you out because of my name have said: ‘Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see your joy.’ But they themselves shall be confounded” (Isaiah 66:3–5). “For my prelates shall not labor in vain amid confusion, because they are the seed of the Lord’s blessings. Before they call, I shall answer; while they are still speaking, I shall hear” (Isaiah 65:23–24).

He said that the Lord had chosen them to glorify him, sow the divine commandments, and preach the Gospel, not to be forbidden or troubled, since whoever injures them injures the one whose embassy they carry (2 Corinthians 5:20). He urged them to preach continually and announce the Lord’s commandments without interruption. He indicated that they should display their good works before [Col. 0034D] people and maintain a good conscience before God. He commanded all the rulers of the earth and all people to obey them, bow their heads to them, and become their helpers, so that all might be shown together to be faithful and co-workers in the law of the Lord, lest it be said of them:

“Let all who fight against you be confounded and ashamed; they shall be as though they were not, and the men who oppose you shall perish. You will seek them and will not find the rebellious men who oppose you. They shall be as though they were not, and like the destruction of a man fighting against you” (Isaiah 41:11–12).

Therefore he declared that everyone who opposed them was condemned and infamous until making satisfaction, and commanded that, unless they converted, they should be excluded from the thresholds of the Church.

[Col. 0035A] He said that there were three kinds of murder, and taught that their punishment would be evident. Just as he clearly identified murderers and killers of their brothers as murderers, so also he declared that those who slandered or hated them were murderers, because the person who kills his brother, the person who hates him, and the person who slanders him are shown equally to be murderers.

He urged everyone to abstain from carnal desires that wage war against the soul (1 Peter 2:11), and to show all people their good and innocent conduct. He indicated that everyone should love one another attentively from the heart and taught that they should have true brotherhood among themselves. This was his daily preaching, among his other divine teachings, and I have taken care to communicate it to you also as his example, dearest brother:

“Among the other seeds and concerns of good works is this: as much as each person understands and is able, he should love God with all the depths of his inmost heart and entrails, as was said earlier, and his neighbor as himself. He taught that a person must deny himself, for himself, in order to follow Jesus Christ our Lord, must prefer nothing to his love, must speak the truth with heart and mouth, and must always entrust his whole self to the Lord. He instructed each person to guard the actions of his life at every hour and firmly to know that God observes him in every place. When evil thoughts come to his heart, he must immediately dash them against Christ and disclose them to the priests of the Lord.”

He taught them to guard their mouths from evil or wicked speech and not to speak vain or false words, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11); to hear the divine words willingly, [Col. 0035C] and willingly to obey their priests, and to be obedient. He taught them frequently to devote themselves to preaching, prayer, and reading, and to perform genuine works of almsgiving. “Do not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Gal. 5:16), but break one’s own will; when he sees something good in himself, let him attribute it to God, not to himself, and let him acknowledge the evil he has done and reckon it to himself. He taught them not to love speaking much, but to guard their lips lest they speak deceit or evil; to fear the day of judgment, to dread Gehenna, to desire eternal life with every longing; not to kill, not to commit adultery, not to steal, not to covet what belongs to another, and not to give false testimony (Exod. 20:13 ff.), but to honor all human beings; to guard the body; not to embrace vain and fleeting [Col. 0035D] pleasures; to love fasting and holy vigils; to refresh the poor, clothe the naked, visit the sick, give drink to the thirsty, bury the dead, carefully perform their funerals, pray for them, and give alms.
