He taught them to console the afflicted, strengthen them with their own goods, and keep themselves apart from evil deeds; not to be proud, “not given to wine” (Tit. 1:7), nor excessively gluttonous, nor sleepy, nor lazy, nor murmurers, nor slanderers, because whoever slanders kills not only himself but many others; not to carry anger through to action, nor to reserve time for wrath. Not to harbor deceit in the heart, nor to offer false peace; not to abandon charity, nor to swear, lest one perhaps become perjured—which God forbid. Not to repay evil with evil [Col. 0036A], nor to inflict injury, but patiently to endure injury inflicted; to love enemies; not to curse those who curse them in return, but rather to bless them; and to endure persecution for the sake of justice.

To love charity and hate no one, because “whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). To flee arrogance and not harbor evil zeal. Not to practice envy, nor to love contention. To return to peace with those with whom they disagree before sunset, and never to despair of God’s mercy. To venerate elders and love the younger. To instruct and love their bishops, their priests, all the remaining ministers of the Church, and the entire people entrusted to them in the divine words and commandments; and to love all these—their bishops—as their own eyes, because [Col. 0036B] they are their eyes. To obey their commands in all things, even if they themselves act otherwise—which God forbid—remembering that command of the Lord: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:3).

If the bishops themselves deviate from these things, they are not to be reproved or accused, but borne with, unless they have erred in the faith. These, therefore, are above those; not those above these, since one who is greater cannot be accused or judged by one who is lesser. Let no one exalt himself against his teachers and masters, because “the disciple must not be above his teacher” (Matt. 10:24), nor can he be. Let no one wish to be called holy before he is holy; rather, let him first become so, that he may be called so more truthfully. One must fulfill daily, by one’s deeds, the commandments of the Lord and of teachers and masters, and pray in Christ’s name for one’s enemies. For the obedience and humility shown to masters are offered to the Lord.

[Col. 0036C] “The fear of the Lord will delight and will give joy and gladness for length of days. It will be well with the one who fears the Lord at the end, and on the day of his death he will be blessed” (Sir. 1:12–13). Woe to the fainthearted, who have not believed God, who resist his commandments, and who are disobedient and obstinate toward those who carry out his commission; therefore they are not protected by him. Woe to those who have lost endurance, who have abandoned the straight paths and turned aside to crooked ways. And what will they do when the Lord begins to inspect them?

Those who fear the Lord will not be incredulous toward his word, and those who love him will keep his way. Those who fear the Lord will seek what pleases him, and those who love him [Col. 0036D] will be filled with his law. Those who fear the Lord will prepare their hearts and sanctify their souls in his sight. Those who fear the Lord keep his commandments and will have patience until his visitation, saying: “If we do not repent, we shall fall into the hands of the Lord, and not into the hands of men; for according to his greatness, so is his mercy also with him” (Sir. 2:15 ff.).

“Come,” he says, “children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:12). “Walk while you have the light of life, lest the darkness of death overtake you” (John 12:35). “Whoever desires life and wishes to see good days, let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking [Col. 0037A] deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good, let him seek peace and pursue it, because the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33:13 ff.). Therefore, do not become like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding. But rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous, and glory, all you upright in heart (Ps. 31:11).

“For many will come from the east and the west”—the Lord saying this—“and from the north and the south, and they will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Matt. 8).

For this reason I beseech you, dearest brother, to teach this order of preaching and the days of absolution with the greatest care, so that the souls of human beings, by God’s hidden power, may recognize whom they ought to love before they are taught. The accounting of deeds, however, is entrusted to the power and judgment of each individual, and this is their own responsibility; but the desire for the teacher of truth is given by the heavenly Father. Salvation consists in doing the will of the one whose love and desire you have conceived by God’s gift, lest that saying of his be spoken against us, the same saying he uttered: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?”

It is therefore each person’s proper duty to become perfect in the Church according to what our Lord has given, reaping the divine seeds, so that the saying mentioned above may not be spoken of us, but rather the saying our Lord uttered elsewhere: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. 13:52).

“Therefore,” he says, “let no one obstruct the order, occupy a place irrationally, or exchange the proper sequence of times. Rather, let us first seek what his justice and his will are, so that we may be filled with good works and God’s grace. For God is present to those who think rightly and do good, since [Col. 0038A] he reveals himself to them. If someone wishes, before correcting his own deeds, to inquire into matters that he cannot discover, his inquiry will be foolish and ineffectual. For the time is short, and God’s judgment is concerned with deeds, not questions. Therefore let us first seek above all what we ought to do and how we ought to act, so that we may deserve to attain eternal life. For if we spend this brief time of life on empty and useless questions, we shall undoubtedly go to the Lord empty and devoid of good works, where judgment will be made concerning our deeds; for each matter has its own time and place. This is the place of deeds; this is the time of merit; the future age is [the time] of reward. Let him therefore run along the way of the Lord’s commandments, and let no one depart from the institutions of those commandments [Col. 0038B] or from the teaching of the Holy Spirit. Therefore our hearts and bodies must be prepared and made ready for obedience to his holy commandments, to their bishops, and to those mentioned above, so that he may command his grace to provide us assistance, and so that all who flee the punishment of Gehenna may be able to reach eternal life.”

Thus, dearest brother James, I received these things from the mouth of Saint Peter as he gave the command, and I have taken pains to explain them to you as you wished, so that you may command that everything be kept undefiled, because ecclesiastical affairs ought not to be carried out carelessly but diligently. Let no one therefore believe that he can neglect or disregard these commandments without danger to himself, because, by God’s judgment, whoever has neglected ecclesiastical decrees will suffer the torments of eternal fire. Whoever listens to you, as the minister of Christ Jesus commanded, will receive glory. But whoever does not listen to you, indeed to the Lord speaking through you, will receive condemnation for himself. We must therefore all take care and pay attention to what is expedient forever, so that through patience we may share in Christ’s sufferings and deserve to be companions of his kingdom. Amen.

# LETTER OF POPE CLEMENT TO JAMES, THE BROTHER OF THE LORD  
## On Consecrated Vestments and Vessels

[Col. 0037]

[Col. 0037D] Clement, prelate of the Roman Church, to James, bishop of Jerusalem.

Since we have received from the blessed apostle Peter, the father of all the apostles, who received the keys of the heavenly kingdom, instruction concerning how we ought to preserve the sacraments that are administered among holy things, it is fitting that we in turn instruct you systematically concerning them.

For the sacraments of the divine mysteries have been entrusted to three ranks: the priest, the deacon, and the minister. With fear and trembling, together with the clergy, they must guard the remaining fragments of the Lord’s body, lest any decay be found in the sacristy; for when the portion of the Lord’s body is handled carelessly, a grave injury is inflicted. If the communion of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ is distributed carelessly, and the priest does not take care to admonish concerning the lesser duties, [Col. 0038D] he is to be struck with the grievous wound of humiliation meriting a severe anathema.

Certainly, as many holocausts should be offered on the altar as ought to suffice for the people. If any remain, they are not to be kept until the following day, but are to be consumed with fear and trembling by the clergy and with diligence. Those who consume the remnants of the Lord’s body left in the sacristy must not immediately come to eat ordinary food, lest they suppose that they may mix with the holy portion food that, digested through the intestines, is discharged into the latrine. If the Lord’s portion is eaten in the morning, the ministers who consumed it are to fast until the sixth hour. If they receive it at the third or fourth hour, they are to fast until evening. Thus, through secret consecration, the eternal sacraments are to be preserved.

Concerning sacred vessels, the following procedure is to be observed: the altar [Col. 0039A] cloth, the cathedra, the candelabrum, and the veil, if worn out through age, are to be given to the fire, since it is not permitted to treat improperly those things that have been in the sanctuary; rather, everything is to be committed to the fire. Their ashes, too, are to be placed in the baptistery, where no one passes, or thrown into a wall or into cavities in the pavement, lest they be defiled by the feet of those entering.

Let no cleric, through ignorance, suppose that the altar cloth should be wrapped around a dead person, nor let a deacon wish to cover his shoulders with what was on the altar, or with what was given for the Lord’s table. Whoever does this, even lightly and as though it were nothing, and handles the divine mysteries carelessly, shall be excluded from the Lord’s altar for three years and six months, struck with a grave anathema. If a priest does not admonish the cleric, he is to be excommunicated for ten years and five [Col. 0039B] months, because he did not admonish him concerning the ministries of the Lord’s sacraments entrusted to him; afterward he is to be reconciled to Mother Church with great and grievous humility.

The altar cloths and veils that have become soiled in the service of the sanctuary are to be washed by deacons together with humble ministers near the sacristy. They must not carry the veils of the Lord’s table outside the sacristy, lest perhaps dust from the Lord’s body fall improperly from the linen while it is washed outside, and this become a sin for the person doing it. Therefore we command the ministers to guard these holy things carefully within the sacristy. A new basin is to be obtained, and it is to touch nothing else. That basin is not to be used for washing anything except what pertains to the service of the Lord’s altar: only the altar cloths are to be washed in it, [Col. 0039C] and the door veils in another.

The doorkeepers are to take care of the door veils, following the admonition of their superiors, so that no negligent or ignorant person may carelessly wipe his hands on the veil of the door of the Lord’s house. Everyone is immediately to be restrained and taught that the veil of the court of the Lord’s house is holy.

We also command that fragments of the Lord’s offerings never be placed at table for an outsider, whether cleric or layperson. How do you know—when you distribute the sacristy’s loaves indiscriminately to the unworthy—how do you know whether they are clean from women? David too, when he was questioned by the priest Abimelech as he asked for loaves to eat, was asked whether he was free from a woman; when he professed that he had been clean for three days, he ate the bread of the Presence.

[Col. 0039D] For the Lord’s mysteries, such men are to be chosen as did not know their wives sexually before ordination. If, after ordination, a minister should happen to enter his own wife’s bed, he is not to enter the thresholds of the sacristy, become a partaker in the sacrifice, touch the altar, receive the offering of the holocaust from those offering it, or approach the portion of the Lord’s body. Rather, he is to bring water to the priests for their hands, close the doors from outside, perform lesser duties, and not carry a pitcher or chalice to the altar.

If any priest or deacon should sell, after taking it away, the sacristy’s linen or veil, he is to be considered like Judas Iscariot. Whoever does this deed out of greed should know that he will suffer the [Col. 0040A] punishment of the aforementioned Judas.

Let no cleric approach a woman’s dwelling alone, or hurry there without the command of a superior officer. Nor should a priest meet alone with a woman alone; rather, bringing two witnesses, he is to visit the sick woman. He must not converse privately with a woman alone, nor should an archdeacon or deacon, under the pretext of humble service, frequently visit the homes of married women, nor should married women perhaps communicate anything secret through his clerics or household servants. If this becomes known, he is to be deposed and she is to be barred from the thresholds of the church. If there should be some intercession, it is to be brought before the bishop. If she is someone whom he ought to visit through a pious intervention, he himself may go. Otherwise, he is to send someone from his own household, together with two or three [Col. 0040B] who ought to know of the matter. Certainly no cleric is to enter to visit a sick woman except with two or three companions.

Nevertheless, no one is to live with a strange woman unless she is a close relative or sister. This must be done with great vigilance. We are not ignorant of Satan’s malice. All these ministries are to be completed with ecclesiastical gentleness. For God’s business ought not to be carried out carelessly.

Again and again we give instructions concerning the fragments of the Lord’s body. The minister is to prepare the chalice appointed for bringing the Lord’s blood with complete cleanliness in the service, lest a chalice that has not been properly washed become a sin for the deacon who offers it. Everything must be fulfilled with the entire decorum that we have set out above. Clerics are to be chosen for the ministry who [Col. 0040C] are worthy and able to handle the Lord’s consecrated things. For it is better for a priest to have a few ministers who can worthily perform God’s work than many useless ones who bring a heavy burden upon the one who ordained them.

From the beginning of the letter up to this point I have assigned matters concerning the sacraments for careful observation, so that no mouse droppings may appear among the fragments of the Lord’s portion, nor may anything putrid remain through the negligence of the clergy; and so that those who come wishing to receive medicine for themselves, when they see something putrid, may not appear to receive it with greater ridicule and disgust and thus fall more deeply into sin through the negligence of the clergy. Therefore let no cleric henceforth disregard these matters or dare in any way to neglect them, but let him willingly fulfill what has been commanded and in no way handle the divine consecrated things [Col. 0040D] carelessly.

Therefore both young and old ought to be very concerned about these matters and about their entire conduct, conversion, and repentance, and ought to act sufficiently so that they may carry these things out worthily. For the rest, both clerics and laypeople should adorn their souls with the worthiest ornaments: namely, with the doctrines of truth, the beauty of chastity, the splendor of justice, the brightness of piety, and all the other qualities with which a rational mind ought to be adorned. In addition, they should avoid the company of the dishonorable and the faithless, associate with the faithful, and frequent those gatherings where chastity, justice, and piety are discussed.

They should pray to God with all their heart in hope, ask him for what is fitting, give him thanks, and show true repentance [Col. 0041A] for past actions; if possible, they should also assist their repentance to some degree through acts of mercy toward the poor. Through these things forgiveness will be granted more readily, and forgiveness will sooner be shown to the merciful. If the person who comes to repentance is of advanced age, he ought all the more to give thanks to God. Since the full force of carnal desire has passed for him, having received knowledge of the truth, no struggle of combat remains through which he must restrain the bodily impulses rising against the soul. It remains for him to exercise himself in the knowledge of truth and works of mercy, so that he may bear fruits worthy of repentance.

Let him not think that evidence of conversion is shown in the length of time, rather than in the firmness of devotion and purpose. For minds are manifest to God, because he does not [Col. 0041B] calculate the measure of time but of souls. He himself tests whether someone, after hearing the preaching of truth, did not delay or waste time through negligence, but immediately—or, if one may say so, in that very moment—began to dread the past, desired the future, and burned with love for the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore let no one among you delay any longer or look back, but gladly approach the Gospel of the kingdom of God. Let the poor person not say, “When I have become rich, then I shall convert.” God does not ask money of you, but a merciful soul and a pious mind. Nor should the rich postpone his conversion on account of worldly concerns, while he considers how he will distribute the abundance of his crops. Let him not say within himself, “What shall I do? Where shall I store my fruits?” Nor let him say to his [Col. 0041C] soul: “You have many good things stored up for many years; feast and rejoice.” For it will be said to him: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and whose will those things be that you have prepared?” (Luke 12:19–20).

Therefore every age, every sex, and every condition should hasten to repentance in order to obtain eternal life. Let the young be grateful for this: that, in the very surge of their desires, they submit their necks to the yoke of discipline. Let the old also be praiseworthy, changing, for God’s love, the long-established habits in which they have been wrongly ensnared. Let no one delay; let no one hesitate. For what reason is there to hesitate in doing good? A person whose conscience is troubled, while he seems to himself to suffer no punishment, believes that the Lord does not judge; yet to abuse God’s patience and fail to understand the goodness of the one who spares is already a great [Col. 0041D] condemnation. Hence it is written: “Cursed is everyone who performs the work of the Lord negligently” (Jer. 48:10).

Therefore it belongs to the pastoral office tirelessly to call back whatever he recognizes as pertaining to the correction of the people—or rather, insofar as it is right to understand it, of his spiritual children—and not, God forbid, through mere negligence to damage another’s hope at his own peril. Rather, whatever concerns the common advantage of salvation must necessarily be provided for through a salutary discourse.

For a religious person it ought to be insufficient merely not to practice or increase the hostility of others by speaking evil, unless he has also tried to extinguish it by speaking well. Behold, we sound the trumpet of our mouth into the ears of human beings [Col. 0042A], and henceforth no one who has been instructed—both by words and by writing—about what he ought to follow will be able to excuse himself by claiming that he was not warned.

What condemnation, and what curse, threatens those who sin against fathers, divine Scripture teaches us. When Ham, the son of Noah, saw his father naked, he did not cover the nakedness of his bodily father but went out and announced it to his brothers; they covered him with a garment. Ham himself, and those born from him, were placed under a curse, while those who covered him merited a great blessing. Much more, then, are those worthy of a greater and more extensive condemnation who try to oppose fathers, rise up against them, or attempt to inflict injury or insult upon them, because [Col. 0042B] whoever resists them also resists God, and whoever inflicts injury or insult upon them does so against God, whose commission they carry out.

“Heaven was appalled at this and shuddered exceedingly,” says the Lord. O intolerable wickedness! O tongue speaking iniquity against God, and mind lifting up its horn on high! And again: “Put a door and a lock upon your tongue, human being. Cease lifting up your horn on high and speaking iniquity against the Lord and your neighbor. How long will you insult the suffering Christ and the brothers?”

These things the aforementioned teacher, instructor, and ruler of us, the prince of the apostles Peter, taught us more familiarly, and he preached them publicly in the Church, giving us an example so that we might act likewise. [Col. 0042C] “Humble yourselves,” he says, “in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you. Do not slander one another, because whoever slanders his brother, or judges his brother, slanders the law and judges the law. But whoever judges the law is not a doer of the law but a judge. There is one lawgiver and judge, who can destroy and save. But who are you to judge your neighbor?” (Jas. 4:10 ff.).

It is not right—and he did not command us—to judge one another, but rather to bring help. “Woe,” he says, “to those who afflict their brothers, and to those who persecute them. But the more you are afflicted, the purer and happier you will become, provided that the affliction itself is endured patiently”; this too the Lord himself taught us. “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice.” And again: “You will be blessed when [Col. 0042D] people hate you,” and “when they persecute you and cast out your name as evil. Rejoice on that day and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. 5:10). Hence he himself also says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself” (Mark 12:30–31).

For, he says, the one who persecutes his brother does not rightly love God, nor does the one who slanders or accuses his neighbor love him, because what a person does not wish to be done to himself, he must never do to another. “Learn,” he says, “my children, wisdom and hold fast to the true faith, and embrace charity, so that you may not fall away. For power has been given to you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High, [Col. 0043A] who will question your deeds and scrutinize your thoughts. Those who have kept justice will be judged justly, and those who have believed what is just will rightly find what they should answer. Always beware of what he has commanded, lest we ever consent to sin and neglect the commandments of our God.”

Establish churches in suitable and useful places, which ought to be consecrated for divine prayers, and in each place appoint priests devoted to God through divine prayers. Everyone ought to venerate them, and no one ought to burden them. Always avoid evil, and for the sake of your souls do not be ashamed to speak the truth. Flee falsehoods and speak the truth from the heart, because suspicion has already caused many to stumble. Always love charity and help your brothers. Those who oppose you will become as though they did not exist [Col. 0043B], and the men who contradict you will perish. Hence the Lord also says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me, and whoever despises me despises the one who sent me” (Luke 10:16).

And again: “Whoever is not against you is for you. For whoever gives you a cup of water to drink in my name, because you belong to Christ, amen, I say to you, he will not lose his reward. And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it is better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea. And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go into the fire of Gehenna, which cannot be extinguished, where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished. And if your foot causes you to stumble [Col. 0043C], cut it off. It is better for you to enter eternal life lame than, having two feet, [Col. 0044A] to be thrown into the unquenchable fire of Gehenna, where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished. But if your eye causes you to stumble, cast it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God one-eyed than, having two eyes, to be thrown into the fire of Gehenna, where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished. For everyone will be salted with fire, and every sacrifice will be salted. Salt is good; but if salt becomes saltless, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:39 ff.).

For whoever among you teaches rightly and lives justly will have glory. But whoever acts otherwise will undoubtedly suffer punishment. Therefore you must always do good, so that you may receive the prize of eternal life. Obey these statements well, therefore, lest anyone believe that these commandments need not be [Col. 0044B] fulfilled and, having neglected the sacred work of the Church, suffer the torments of eternal fire at the judgment of the Lord.

These things, therefore, brother James, I heard from the mouth of Saint Peter as he gave the command. If anyone does not keep these commandments intact, let him be anathema until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. I received these commandments from the holy apostle Peter and have taken care to explain them to you, dearest brother, so that you may command that everything be kept without blemish. Whoever listens to you will be a useful minister of Jesus Christ; but whoever does not listen to you—or rather, to the Lord speaking through you—will receive condemnation for himself.

May Almighty God, dearest brother, guard you by his protection and lead you to the reward of the heavenly homeland with an abundant harvest of souls. May God guard you safe again [Col. 0044C] and again, most reverend brother. Amen.

[Col. 0043]

# THIRD LETTER OF SAINT POPE CLEMENT  
## On the Office of the Priesthood and of Clerics

[Col. 0043C] Clement, bishop of the city of Rome, sends blessing, splendor, and glory, in the grace given to us in Christ Jesus our Lord, to all fellow bishops, priests, deacons, and the remaining clerics, and to all rulers, both greater and lesser, and to all the faithful generally.

Your great love, brothers, and your religious devotion press upon us, since we are obliged to write certain things to you. You, therefore, who enjoy the Lord’s priesthood and have been placed upon the watchtower, ought to know more, so that you may be able to teach fully the peoples subject to you and, with God’s assent, provide them guidance toward the kingdoms of heaven. Hence Truth itself says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables (Luke 8:10),” and so forth.

For this reason I advise each one of you steadfastly to teach the divine words and willingly to lend an ear to God’s word for those who are learning. Since you perform the Lord’s embassy, it is your task to teach the peoples; theirs, however, is to obey you as they would God. But if all the presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and the rest of the clergy, and all the rulers—of both higher and lower rank—and the rest of the peoples, of every tribe and language, do not obey you bishops, they shall be not only disgraced but also exiled from the Lord’s kingdom and from the fellowship of the faithful, and shall be excluded from the thresholds of God’s holy Church. For it is your task to instruct them, and theirs to obey you, so that they may obey the Lord whose embassy you perform, the Lord saying: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me; whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me (Matthew 10:40).” Nothing is more unjust or dishonorable than for children to rebel against their fathers, or for clerics or laypeople to be disobedient or defiant toward their teachers, or disciples toward their masters.

For we know that the first human being fell through disobedience. Therefore we urge everyone to beware of this vice with the utmost care. And because the Lord resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), when he sends you in his place, in the place of the apostles, to preach, he commands you to teach and commands everyone to be faithfully obedient to you. For the earth will not produce its fruits in any other way unless, having been cultivated, it receives seed, and, having been watered, germinates and produces what it is destined to produce.

Thus every person who does not willingly receive God’s word, does not permit it to germinate in his heart, and does not believe at all in his teachers and bishops—who is not well-disposed but rebellious and disobedient—will neither germinate nor produce fruit. He is like that tree of which the Lord says: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matthew 3:19).”

For the first pontiff, Aaron, anointed with the chrism of the composition, was leader of the people. Like a king, he received first-fruits and tribute from the people according to their heads, and, having received by lot the authority to judge the peoples, he judged between the clean and the unclean. But if another person was anointed with that same ointment, by the power thereby received he too became a king, or prophet, or pontiff.

Now if a temporal grace composed by human beings possessed such power, understand how great that ointment must be which was brought forth by the Lord from the shoot of life, since what was made by human beings conferred such outstanding dignities among them. For what in the present age is more glorious than a prophet, more illustrious than a pontiff, or more exalted than a king? Every pontiff anointed with sacred chrism and established in a city, grounded in the holy Scriptures, ought to be exceedingly dear and precious to human beings.

Since he occupies, as it were, Christ’s place, everyone ought to honor him, serve him, and remain obedient to him faithfully for their own salvation, knowing that whether the honor or the injury offered to him redounds upon Christ, and through Christ upon the Lord. Therefore it is necessary to listen to him attentively and receive from him the teaching of faith, but to seek the admonitions of life from the Fathers. From the deacons, however, one should receive the order of discipline.

For this reason I entreat you, my fellow servants and helpers, to learn to care for souls more attentively and to stand on behalf of everyone, especially those who labor in divine worship. Take care of all the churches and provide assistance to their servants; care religiously for widows; rescue orphans with the greatest effort; show mercy to the poor; teach young people chastity. And—to say everything briefly—support one another whenever circumstances require it.

Worship God, who created heaven and earth, and believe in Christ. Love one another and be merciful toward all. Fulfill charity not in word alone, but in action and in material deeds. Do everything within your power, dearest fellow servants, because it is good for each one of you to benefit those who approach the faith of our religion according to his ability. Therefore do not be reluctant, according to the wisdom bestowed upon us through God’s providence, to instruct the ignorant and teach them.

Everyone ought to possess a desire for the teacher of truth and love him as his own eyes, because it is fitting that he should love and teach the people entrusted to him as his own children. This has been bestowed upon him by the heavenly Father. But salvation consists in doing the will of the one whose love and desire they have conceived by God’s gift.

If, therefore, a faithful person wishes to become one and desires to be baptized, once stripped of his former evils, he will thereafter become, through his own deeds, an heir of heavenly blessings. Let the one who wishes approach his priest, give him his name, and hear from him the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. Let him devote himself to frequent fasts and test himself in every respect, so that after completing three months he may be baptized on the feast day.

Each person is to be baptized in flowing waters, with the name of the triune blessedness invoked over him, having first been anointed with oil sanctified by prayer, so that, thus consecrated, he may finally be able to receive a place among the saints.

Let no one, because of the reproach of old age or youth, or because of the nobility of his lineage, neglect to seek from the young and less learned whatever usefulness or salvation may perhaps be found there. For one who lives rebelliously and refuses to learn and do good is shown to be more a member of the devil than of Christ, and is revealed to be unbelieving rather than faithful.

How, then, could it not be pleasing and desirable to everyone that he learn what he does not know and teach what he has learned? For it is entirely certain that neither friendship, nor kinship of lineage, nor royal exaltation ought to be more precious to a human being than truth, because nothing is more precious than the soul.

The Lord, creator of all things, made the human being in his image from the beginning and gave him dominion over the earth, the sea, and the air itself; he also commanded him to seek the truth, as the true Prophet has explained to us and the very order of things teaches. For the human being alone is rational, and it follows that reason should rule irrational things.

At the beginning, while he was still just, he was superior to every vice and to all frailty. But once he sinned and became a slave of sin, he was likewise made liable and subject to frailty. This was written so that human beings might know that, just as through impiety they became capable of suffering, so through piety they can become incapable of suffering—not only incapable of suffering, but also, through even a small faith in God, able to heal the sufferings of others. Thus the true Prophet himself promised, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move (Matthew 17:19).” You yourselves have also received evidence of this saying, and you are not unaware of certain things already accomplished through our teachers, namely the apostles. While we stood by, through their merits demons passed away together with the sufferings they had brought upon human beings, and were driven out.

[Col. 0046D] Since some people suffer while others heal those who suffer, the cause both of suffering and of healing must undoubtedly be understood. It is shown to be nothing other than unbelief in those who suffer, and faith in those who heal. For unbelief, by not believing that the Lord’s judgment will come, grants permission to sin; sin, however, makes a person subject to sufferings.

Faith, believing that God’s judgment will come, restrains people from sin. Those who do not sin are not only free from demons and sufferings; they can also drive out the demons and sufferings of others. From all this, therefore, it is gathered that the origin of all evil descends from ignorance, and that ignorance itself is the mother of all evils. It is begotten by a certain carelessness and laziness.

[Col. 0047A] Negligence, however, nourishes and increases it and roots it in human minds when it is loved. If someone should teach that it must be expelled, it is torn away unwillingly and resentfully, as though from ancient and hereditary dwelling places. Therefore we must labor a little, so that, by the reasoning of knowledge, we may cut away the presumptuous claims of ignorance that resists us, especially those who have been forestalled by certain erroneous opinions. Through these opinions, ignorance has become more deeply rooted in them, as though under the appearance of some kind of knowledge.

For nothing is more serious than for someone to believe and defend that he knows what he does not know, and that what is false is true. Such a person is like someone who, while drunk, thinks himself sober, behaves in every respect as a drunkard, yet still thinks himself sober and wants others to call him so. Thus these people are ignorant of what is true, yet they retain the appearance of some kind of knowledge; they do evil as though it were good and hurry toward destruction as though toward salvation. Therefore, above all, we must hasten toward knowledge of the truth, so that, as though a light had been kindled for us from it, we may drive away the darkness of errors.

[Col. 0047B] Ignorance, as we have said, is a great evil, but because it has no substance, it is easily escaped by those who are zealous. Ignorance is nothing other than failing to know what is advantageous; once you have learned it, ignorance perishes. Knowledge of the truth must therefore be sought in the contest, and no one can assign it except the true Prophet.

This is the way for those who wish to enter life, and the highest road for those proceeding by good works toward the city of salvation. If someone, hearing the speech of the true Prophet, wishes—or does not wish—to receive and embrace its burden, that is, the commandments of life, it lies within his own power, for we possess free choice.

If it were otherwise—if those who heard these things no longer had the power to do anything other than what they had heard—there would be a certain force of nature by which they would not be free to move to another judgment. Or if, again, none of those who heard them received them at all, that too would be a force of nature, compelling one result and leaving no place for the other side. But now, because the mind is free to incline its judgment toward whichever side it wishes and to choose the path it approves, it is clearly established that human beings possess freedom of choice.

Therefore, before someone hears what is advantageous to him, it is certain that he is ignorant; in his ignorance he wills and desires to do what is not advantageous, and for this he is not judged. But once he has heard the causes of his error and received the reasoning of truth, then, if he remains in the errors by which he was previously forestalled, he will rightly be summoned to judgment and pay the penalty, because he has consumed in the mockeries of error the span of this life that he received for living well.

But the one who willingly receives what he hears, and gratefully seeks more attentively the teaching of good things that has been brought to him, and does not cease learning until he knows whether there truly is another age in which rewards have been prepared for the good—once he is certain of this, let him give thanks to God.

If the light of truth has shown itself, from then on let him direct his actions in every good work, certain that a reward has been prepared for him in the future. Let him marvel at everything, be astonished at the errors of other people, and wonder that no one saw the truth placed before their eyes. Rejoicing alone in the riches of wisdom that he has found, let him enjoy them fully and delight in the practice of good works, hastening to reach the future age with a pure heart and a clear conscience, and even to see God, the King of all.

Only ignorance causes us to be deprived of all these things and defrauded of them. For while people are ignorant of how much good knowledge contains, they do not permit the evil of ignorance to be expelled from them. They do not know how great the difference is in this exchange.

Accordingly, this is the advice I give to every learner: willingly lend an ear to God’s word, and listen with love for the Lord’s truth to what we say, so that the mind, having received the best seed, may bring forth joyful fruits through good works. For if, while I teach what pertains to salvation, someone refuses to receive it and, with his mind occupied by perverse opinions, strives to resist, he will have the cause of his destruction not from you but from himself.

He ought to examine what we say by a just judgment and understand that we speak words of truth, so that, having recognized things as they are, he may direct his way in good works and be found a participant in the kingdom of heaven. Let him subject to himself the desires of the flesh and become their master, so that at last he too may become the delightful possession of the ruler of all.

For the one who remains in evil and is a slave of evil cannot become a portion of the good so long as he remains in evil. For, as we have already said, from the beginning God established two kingdoms and gave each human being the power to become part of the kingdom to which he has subjected himself in obedience.

And because it has been determined by the Lord that one human being cannot be a slave of both kingdoms, apply yourselves with every effort to enter the court and the laws of the good king. For this reason, finally, the true Prophet, when he was present with us and saw certain wealthy people negligent toward the worship of the Lord, revealed the truth of this matter in the following way: “No one,” he said, “can serve two masters, and you cannot serve the Lord and mammon (Luke 16:13),” calling wealth *mammon* in their native expression.

This, then, is the true Prophet, because he appeared to us in Judaea, as you have heard. Standing publicly, by a mere command he made the blind see and the deaf hear; he drove out demons, restored health to the sick and life to the dead. Since nothing was impossible for him, he even foresaw human thoughts—something possible for no one except God alone.

He proclaimed the kingdom of God. We believe him concerning everything he said as a true Prophet, drawing the firmness of our faith not only from his words but also from his works. In him are indicated the utterances of the Law which, many generations earlier, had expounded his repentance; and the deeds of Moses, and before him those of the patriarch Jacob, bore throughout a type of him. The time of his coming—that is, the very time in which he came—was likewise foretold by them. Above all, the sacred writings contain the prediction that he was to be awaited by the nations. All these things were fulfilled together in him.

The fact that the Jewish prophet foretold that he would be awaited by the nations confirms true faith in him beyond measure. If he had said that he would be awaited by the Jews, he would not seem to have prophesied anything extraordinary: it would have been natural that the one whose coming had been promised for the salvation of the world should be awaited by his fellow-tribal people and his own nation. That would seem to follow more from the ordinary course of events than from prophetic magnificence.

But when the prophets say that all the hope promised concerning the salvation of the world, the newness of the kingdom to be established through Christ, and everything judged concerning him would be transferred to the nations, prophetic magnificence is confirmed by an utterly incredible outcome of prophecy, not by the ordinary course of events.

For from the beginning the Jews received through the truest tradition that this man would one day appear, through whom all things would be restored. Meditating daily and discerning when his coming would take place, they saw him present and fulfilling the signs and wonders that had been written concerning him. Yet, blinded by envy, they could not recognize him who was present, though they rejoiced in the hope of him while he was absent.

Only the holy apostles, who were chosen by God, understood him, and we, who were chosen afterward through them. This happened by the Lord’s providence, so that knowledge of this good should also be handed on to the nations, and those who had never heard of him or learned of him from the prophets should recognize him, while those who had become vain through daily meditations should remain ignorant.

[Col. 0049C] For now, through you who are present and desire to hear the teaching of his faith and to recognize who he is, how and what sort of coming he has, prophetic truth is fulfilled. For the prophets had foretold that he would be sought by you, who had never heard of him.

Therefore, seeing the prophetic sayings fulfilled in you yourselves, you rightly believe in this one alone, rightly await him, and rightly inquire about him, so that you may not merely await him but, believing, may also obtain the inheritance of his kingdom, according to what he himself said: that each person belongs to the one whose servant he has made himself.

Therefore keep watch, and enroll for yourselves as Lord our Lord and God, who is also Lord of heaven and earth. Reform yourselves according to his image and likeness, as the true Prophet himself teaches, saying: “Be good and merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful (Luke 6:36), who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45).”

Imitate him, then, and fear him. As the commandment is given to human beings: “You shall fear the Lord your God, and you shall serve him alone.” To unbelievers the Lord seems asleep, and he is regarded as absent by those who do not believe that he exists. They do not obey his commandments, and he appears to them to sleep because they are not heard on account of their sins.

Therefore all the faithful, and above all the presbyters, deacons, and the rest of the clergy, must take care to do nothing without the permission of their own bishop. No presbyter is to celebrate Masses in his parish without the bishop’s command; he is not to baptize or do anything without his permission.

Similarly, the rest of the people, both higher and lower, are to do whatever must be done by his permission. They are neither to depart from their parish without his permission nor presume to remain there when arriving in it. Their souls have been entrusted to him. Therefore they ought to do everything according to his counsel and nothing without consulting him.

For all who obey their bishops seem indeed to render some service to God. But those who do not obey them are unquestionably guilty and rejected. Moreover, those who walk in the paths of his justice and commandment and willingly obey their teachers—who are rightly understood as bishops—receive from God the gift of the highest reward.

The blessed Peter, our instructor and ordainer and chief of the apostles, clearly instructed all who heard him concerning these matters, saying:

“Those who speak words of truth and illuminate human souls seem to me to be like the rays of the sun. Once they have gone forth and appeared to the world, they can in no way thereafter be concealed or hidden, since they are not so much seen by human beings as they enable all to see. Hence Truth itself rightly says to the heralds of truth: ‘You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for everyone who is in the house (Matthew 5:14).’”

Therefore, whoever obeys these people offers God, as has been said, a great gift. But whoever resists them or is disobedient does not resist them but the Lord our Savior, whose embassy they perform. For this reason, the first duty of all is to seek God’s justice and his kingdom and to obey his commands: justice, so that we may teach how to act rightly; the kingdom, so that we may know what reward has been appointed for labor and endurance. In that kingdom there is a repayment of eternal blessings for the good, but for those who have acted against his will there is a punishment appropriate to each person’s deeds.

Here, then—that is, while we are placed in the present life—we must recognize God’s will, since here is the place for acting and sacrificing. For it is not permitted to sacrifice or celebrate Masses in other places except those in which one’s own bishop has commanded it, or those governed by a regularly ordained bishop—namely, the city in which he was consecrated.

Otherwise these things are neither to be done nor properly celebrated, as the New and Old Testaments teach us. The apostles received these things from the Lord and handed them on to us. We teach them, and we command you and all those responsible for acting to hold and teach them without reproach. For every matter has its own time and place.

This is the place for works; the future age is the time for rewards. Therefore, lest we be hindered by exchanging the proper order of places and times, let us first seek what God’s justice is, and, as travelers about to set out, let us fill ourselves with good works as with abundant provisions, so that we may be able to reach the Lord’s kingdom as though it were a great city.

God is manifest to those who think rightly through the very works of the world that he makes, using his own creation as testimony. Therefore, since there should be no doubt concerning God, let us now seek only his justice and kingdom.

I therefore persuade you first to seek his justice, so that, traveling by this path and standing upon the way of truth, we may be able to find the true Prophet—not running with the speed of our feet, but with the speed of good works—so that, using him as our guide, we may suffer no error on this road.

For if, following him, we should be found worthy to enter the city to which we desire to reach, we shall already see with our eyes all the things that are sought, having become heirs of them all.

Understand, then, that this life of ours is the road; those who instruct us or perform good works are travelers; the Prophet of whom we speak is the gate; and the city is the kingdom in which the almighty Father dwells. Only those who are pure in heart can see him.

Let the labor of this journey, therefore, not seem difficult to us, because at its end there will be rest. For the true Prophet himself, running through the ages from the beginning of the world, hastens toward rest. He is present with all of us every day, and whenever necessary he appears and corrects us, so that, obeying him, he may lead us to eternal life.

Concerning those who neglect the way of their salvation, who are not yet truly faithful, and who are disobedient or defiant toward his commands and those of his pontiffs, our Lord Jesus Christ, sending his disciples, commanded us, saying that whenever we enter a city or a house we should say: “Peace to this house. And if,” he said, “there is a son of peace there, your peace will come upon him. But if there is not, your peace will return to you. When you leave that house or city, shake off even the dust that has clung to your feet against them. It will be more bearable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city or house (Matthew 10:12 and following).”

He commanded this to be done only after the word of truth had first been preached in the city or house, so that those who received the faith of truth might become sons of peace and sons of the Lord, while those who did not receive it might be reproved as enemies of peace and of the Lord.

Thus we too, following the institutions of our teachers, should offer peace to our hearers, so that the way of salvation may be recognized without any disturbance. But if someone does not receive words of peace and does not yield to the truth, we know that we must wage against him the battle of the word, reproving him more sharply by refuting his ignorance and rebuking his sins.

We therefore necessarily offer peace, so that, if someone is a son of peace, our peace may come upon him; but from one who has made himself alien to peace, our peace will return to us. And again we are commanded that, when we come to a city, we should learn who in it is worthy, so that we may take food with him. How much more, then, is it fitting to know who and what sort of person he is, and formerly what sort he was, to whom the words of immortality are to be entrusted? For we must be careful—very careful—not to “cast our pearls before swine (Matthew 7:6).”

But it is useful to know this man for other reasons as well. If I know that he has been corrected and is blameless in matters concerning which there can be no doubt that they are good—that is, if he is sober, merciful, just, gentle, and humane, qualities which no one doubts are good—then it will seem reasonable that to one who possesses the good of the virtues should also be granted what he lacks in faith and knowledge, and that whatever blemish appears in a life otherwise commendable should be corrected.

But if he remains entangled and defiled by sins that are publicly evident, I ought not to speak to him about more secret and hidden matters of divine knowledge. Rather, I should protest and admonish him, so that he may cease sinning and correct his actions from their vices.

If, however, he forces himself upon us and challenges us to say things that a person acting less rightly ought not to hear, we ought prudently to evade him. For it does not seem useful to give no answer at all, on account of the hearers, lest they perhaps think that we avoid the contest from lack of an answer, and their faith be harmed because they do not understand our purpose.

It will be a great insult and a serious sin for us if we become so foolish that we see one who worships idols being sober while we who worship God refuse to be sober. Let this not occur among us. Rather, let us make every effort so that, if those who err do not commit murder, we do not even become angry; if they do not commit adultery, we do not even desire another man’s wife; if they love their neighbors, we love even our enemies; and if they lend to those who have the means to repay, we also give to those from whom we do not hope to receive.

In every respect, we who hope for the inheritance of the eternal age ought to surpass those who know only the present age. For if their works, compared with ours, should be found similar and equal on the day of judgment, it will be a disgrace to us that we are found equal to them in works for which they are condemned because of ignorance and because they possessed no hope of the future age.

And truly it is a fitting disgrace when we have done nothing more than those who understood less than we did. But if it will be a disgrace for us to be found equal to them in good works, what will happen to us if the future examination finds us inferior and worse than they?

Hear, then, how the true Prophet himself taught us concerning these people.

To those who neglect to hear the words of wisdom he says: “The queen of the South will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, something greater than Solomon is here, and they do not listen (Matthew 12:42).”

But to those who refused to repent of their evil deeds he said: “The men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here (Luke 11:32).”

You see, then, how, by bringing forward as examples those who came from gentile ignorance, he showed those who were instructed from the Law not even to be equal to people who seemed to be situated in error, and thus condemned them by that very comparison.

From all these things the discourse we proposed is confirmed: the testimonies that are observed to some extent even by those who are situated in error must be held by each of us who follow the truth much more purely and attentively in all their individual forms, as we showed above, especially because eternal rewards for observing them have been established among us. For otherwise no one will be able to be saved unless he applies himself to these observances according to his strength.

May God always preserve you, brothers, each one in his own order, within his will, and grant you to please him in all things. Amen.

[Col. 0053]

## FOURTH LETTER OF HOLY POPE CLEMENT

Written to his disciples, who had strayed to some extent through the persuasion of evil people, and to the nations among whom they lived.

[Col. 0053A] Clement, bishop of the city of Rome, to his dearest brothers Julius and Julian and our other fellow members, and to the nations that are around you.

Brothers, all teachers who have been appointed for the salvation of souls and bishops who have been consecrated for winning souls ought to care for everyone and lead those who have gone astray back to the way of truth and the harbor of salvation.

And although it may have happened that you went astray to some extent because of the nations around you, it is nevertheless better to return to the way of truth than to persist longer in that error. Whoever among those who made you go astray, or among those who have not yet heard the word of preaching, you can take with you, take them and lead them back to the way of truth, lest you be found fruitless before the Lord.

For just as neglected land necessarily produces thorns and thistles when its cultivator neglects it, so your mind, through the carelessness of a long period, has germinated many harmful opinions about things and understandings belonging to false knowledge. It is now necessary, therefore, to cultivate the field of your mind with great diligence, so that the word of truth—which is the true and diligent cultivator of the heart—may cultivate it through constant instruction.

It is your task to offer obedience and application, and to cut away unnecessary cares, lest a harmful shoot kill the good seed of the word. For it can happen that brief and constant diligence repairs the negligence of a long time.

The length of each person’s life is uncertain. Therefore we must hasten toward salvation, lest sudden death overtake one who delays. For this reason we must apply ourselves more vigorously, so that, while there is time, the vices gathered from bad habit may be cut away.

You will not be able to do this in any other way than by becoming angry, in a certain sense, against yourselves because of the things you have done uselessly and shamefully. For this is useful, just, and necessary anger: that each person should be indignant at the things in which he has gone astray and acted wrongly, and should accuse himself.

From this indignation a certain fire is kindled within us. Like a fire introduced into barren soil, it consumes and burns out the roots of the worst will and prepares more fertile ground in the heart for the good seed, the word of God.

I think you have sufficient grounds for anger from which this most just fire may grow, if you consider into how many errors the evil of ignorance has led you, how many falls and how many precipices toward sin it has provided, from how many good things it has withdrawn you, and into what evils it has hurled you. Above all, consider that it has made you liable to eternal punishments in the future age.

When the light of truth has shone upon you, is not the fire of the most just indignation kindled within you on account of all these things? Does not a conflagration of anger pleasing to God arise within you, by which every shoot that may have sprung up in the bad soil of desire is consumed and utterly destroyed?

Hence, when the one who sent us came and saw that the whole world had turned toward wickedness, he did not immediately give it peace while it remained in error, lest he confirm it in its evils. Instead, he opposed the ruins of its ignorance with the knowledge of truth, so that, if any should come to their senses and look upon the light of truth, they might rightly grieve that they had been deceived and dragged into the precipices of error, and might conceive the fire of saving anger against their deceptive ignorance.

For this reason he said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were kindled (Luke 12:49).”

There is, then, a certain battle that we must wage in this life. For the word of truth and knowledge necessarily separates people from error and ignorance, just as we often see rotten and dead flesh separated by a blade from the attachment of living limbs.

The recognition of truth accomplishes something of this kind. For the sake of salvation, it is necessary that a son, for example, who has received the word of truth, be separated from unbelieving parents; or, conversely, that a father be separated from his son, or a daughter from her mother.

In this way, among relatives and blood relations—between believers and unbelievers—the battle of knowledge and ignorance, of truth and error, is waged. For this reason the one who sent us said again: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword (Matthew 10:34).”

But if someone says, “How does it seem just for children to be separated from their parents?” (ibid. 35), listen to how: if the parents remain in error, the children will neither benefit them nor be benefited by them, and they will perish together with them. It is therefore just—indeed, entirely just—for the one who wishes to be saved to be separated from the one who does not wish to be saved.

But observe also this: the separation does not arise from those who understand more rightly. They wish to remain together and to benefit these others and teach them better things. Rather, it is a characteristic vice of ignorance that it cannot bear to have the light of truth close at hand when that light refutes it. Therefore this separation arises from the ignorant.

For those who receive knowledge of the truth, because it is full of goodness and understood to have been given by the good God, desire, if possible, to share it with everyone—even with those who hate and persecute them. For they know that the sin of those people is caused by ignorance.

Thus the Teacher himself, when those who did not know him were leading him to the cross, prayed to the Father for his executioners and said: “Father, forgive them their sin, because they do not know what they are doing (Luke 23:34).”

The disciples likewise imitated their teacher. Even when they suffered, they too prayed in the same way for their executioners. If, then, our discipline teaches us to pray even for our executioners and persecutors, how could we not also be believed to endure the persecutions of our parents and relatives, and to pray for their conversion?

Then let us consider more carefully what reason we have for loving our parents. “Because,” he says, “they appear to be the authors of our life.” Our parents, however, are not the authors of our life but its ministers. For they do not provide life, but furnish us with the ministry by which we enter this life; the author of life is one and alone: God. If, then, we wish to love the author of life, let us know that he is the one whom we must love. “But,” he says, “we could not know him, whereas we both know these people and hold them in affection.”

Granted: you could not know who God is. Yet you could very easily know what is not God. For how could it have been hidden from anyone that wood, stone, bronze, or material of this kind is not God? And if, in matters that you could easily discern, you were willing to direct your minds toward examination, it is certain that you were also hindered from recognizing God—not by impossibility, but by the fault of indolence. For if you had wished, from those very useless images you would surely have received a path to understanding.

It is certain that the images were made by means of iron, while iron was fashioned by fire. Fire, however, is extinguished by water; and water is moved by the Spirit. The Spirit, moreover, has his beginning from God. For thus the prophet Moses said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the face of the abyss, and the Spirit of God was over the waters” (Gen. I, 1–2). That Spirit of the Lord, at God’s command, as though he were the very hand of the Creator, separated light from darkness; and afterward, after that invisible heaven, brought forth this visible heaven, so that he might make the upper regions a dwelling place for angels and the lower regions for human beings.

For your sake, at God’s command, the water that was over the face of the earth withdrew, so that the earth might produce fruits for you. He also secretly inserted veins of moisture into it, so that springs and rivers might flow from it for you. For our sake it was commanded to produce living creatures and everything that would serve our use and will.

Do not the winds blow for your sake, so that the earth, conceiving from them, may bring forth fruit for you? Do not rains pour down for your sake, and do the seasons not change in their alternation? Does the sun not rise and set for your sake, and does the moon not undergo its changes? For your sake does the sea not offer its service, so that all things may lie subject to you, ungrateful as you are? Will there not be a just penalty of vengeance on account of all these things, because you alone [12], above all others, remain ignorant of the giver of all these gifts, whom before everything else you ought both to recognize and to venerate?

But even now, by the same means, I am still leading you toward understanding of him. You see that all things are generated from waters; yet water was made in the beginning through the Only-Begotten, and the almighty God is the head of the Only-Begotten. Through him, in the order described above, one reaches the Father. When you have reached him, recognize that this is his will: that through the waters, which were created first, you should be born again.

For whoever has been regenerated through water and filled with good works becomes heir of the one by whom he was regenerated in incorruption. Therefore approach with prepared minds, like children approaching their father, so that your sins may be washed away and it may be shown before the Lord that their sole cause was ignorance. For if, after recognizing these things, you remain in unbelief, the cause of your destruction will now be reckoned to you, and not to ignorance. Nor should you think that, even if you practice all piety and all righteousness but do not receive baptism, you can have hope before the Lord. Rather, you will be worthy of a greater punishment, because you have not rightly performed good works.

Merit is indeed conferred upon a person because of good deeds, but only if they are performed as God commands. God, however, commanded everyone who worships him to be marked with baptism. If you refuse this, obeying your own will more than God’s, you are without doubt opposed and hostile to his will.

But perhaps you will say:

“What does baptism in water contribute to the worship of God?”

First, because what pleased the Lord is fulfilled. Second, because when one is regenerated from the waters and born anew to God, the weakness of the former birth—which was brought about for you through a human being—is cut away, and only then can you attain salvation. Otherwise it is impossible. For the true Prophet testified to us concerning this sacrament, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again from living water, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John III, 3).

Therefore hasten. In these waters there is a certain mercy of his, which from the beginning was borne over them; it recognizes those who are baptized under the designation of the threefold sacrament and snatches them from future punishments, as though offering to God a kind of gift: souls consecrated through baptism.

Therefore flee to these waters, for they alone can extinguish the power of the future fire. Whoever delays approaching them evidently still has within him the idol of unbelief, and is prevented by it from hastening to the waters that confer salvation.

Whether one is righteous or unrighteous, baptism is necessary in every respect: for the righteous, so that perfection may be fulfilled in him and he may be regenerated to God; for the unrighteous, so that forgiveness may be granted for the sins he has committed. All, therefore, must hasten without delay to be born again to God and afterward to be marked by the bishop—that is, to receive the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit—for each person’s end in life is uncertain.

When someone has been regenerated through water and afterward, as mentioned, confirmed by the bishop through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit—for otherwise a Christian can in no way be perfect, nor have a place among the perfect if he has remained not from necessity but through negligence or choice—then, as we have received from the blessed apostle Peter and as the other holy apostles taught at the Lord’s command, he must finally show through good works in himself the likeness of the Father who begot him.

After this, let him recognize that he must honor the Lord. His honor consists in living as he himself wills. He wills each person to live in such a way that he knows neither murder nor adultery; that he shuns hatred and greed; that he rejects and detests anger, pride, and boastfulness; and that he regards envy and all things like it as entirely foreign to himself.

There is also a particular observance of our religion, which is not so much imposed upon people as sought by each person who worships the Lord for the sake of purity. I mean care concerning chastity, of which there are many forms. Let each person first observe this: that he not have intercourse with a menstruating woman, for the law of the Lord considers this detestable. If the law had not warned us about these matters, we would gladly roll about in filth like puppies.

We ought to possess something more than animals, since we are rational human beings capable of heavenly perceptions; and we ought to make it our highest concern to guard the conscience of our heart from every pollution.

It is good and appropriate to purity also to wash the body with water. I call this good, not as though it were the principal thing by which the mind is purified, but because this washing of the flesh follows upon that good. For our Teacher, too, rebuked certain Pharisees and scribes who seemed better than the rest and separated from the common people, calling them hypocrites because they purified only those things that were visible to human beings, while they left their hearts—which God alone sees—polluted and filthy (Matt. XXIII, 25–26).

To some of them, not to all, he said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you cleanse the outside of the cup and dish, while inside they are full of filth. Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside, and what is outside will be clean.”

For truly, if the mind is cleansed by the light of knowledge, once it has become clean and bright, it necessarily also takes care of the person who is outward—that is, of its own flesh—so that the flesh itself may be purified. But where this outward purification of the flesh is neglected, it is certain that no care is being taken over the purity of the mind and the cleanliness of the heart.

Thus it happens that the person who is clean within is undoubtedly also cleansed outwardly. But the person who is cleansed outwardly is not always clean within—namely, when he does these things in order to please human beings.

This form of chastity must also be observed: no one should have intercourse indiscriminately with women merely for the sake of lust, but for the purpose of restoring offspring. Since this observance is found even among certain animals, it is shameful if it is not observed by all rational beings and worshipers of God.

Therefore all have sinned and need God’s help. For this reason, beloved, always pursue love, aspire to better and spiritual things, and help one another, so that you may always be able to please the Lord in all things. Amen.

# THE FIFTH LETTER OF SAINT CLEMENT THE POPE

Concerning the common life, written to his other disciples and sent to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0057]

[Col. 0057C] To the beloved brothers and fellow disciples dwelling in Jerusalem with our most beloved brother James, fellow bishop, Clement, bishop.

The common life, brothers, is necessary for everyone, and especially for those who desire to serve God irreproachably and wish to imitate the life of the apostles and their disciples. The common use of all the things that exist in this world ought to have been shared by all human beings; but through iniquity one person called one thing his own and another person called another thing his own, and thus division arose among mortals.

Indeed, the wisest of the Greeks, knowing that matters stood thus, said that all things ought to be common among friends. Among “all things,” without doubt, wives are included. And just as, he says, air and the brightness of the sun cannot be divided, so neither should the other things that have been given in common to everyone in this world for possession be divided, but they should be held in common.

Therefore the Lord also speaks through the prophet, saying: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. CXXXII, 1), and so forth. Following the custom of this practice, the apostles and their disciples also, as has been said, led a common life with us and with you. Hence, as you well know: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul, and none of them, nor any of us, said that anything of what he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them and to us, and no one among us was in need. All who possessed houses or fields sold them and brought the prices of what they had sold, together with their other possessions, placing them at the feet of the apostles” (Acts IV, 32, 34–35), just as some of you have learned and witnessed among us; “and distribution was made to each according to his need” (ibid., 35).

Ananias, however, an austere man, and his wife Sapphira, who lied to the apostles concerning the price of the fields they had sold, were brought forth dead in our presence, before the sight of all who were standing there, from the presence of the apostles, because of their sin and the lie they had committed (Acts V, 1 and following). The other things that we have learned and witnessed concerning such people are worthy neither of remembrance nor of recounting.

Therefore we command you to beware of these things and instruct you to obey the teachings and examples of the apostles, because those who disregard their commands become not only guilty but also outcasts. These matters must be avoided not only by us but preached to everyone.

It has also been reported that certain people living in your regions oppose sound teachings and, as it seems to them, appear to teach not according to the tradition of the Fathers but according to their own understanding. For, as we have heard, certain people in your regions derive many plausible interpretations from what they read according to human ingenuity. Therefore it must be carefully observed that the law of God, when it is read, should neither be read nor taught according to the understanding of one’s own ingenuity.

There are many words in the divine Scriptures that can be drawn toward the meaning that each person has voluntarily presumed for himself. But this ought not to be done. You should not seek a meaning that is foreign and alien by corrupting the sense from outside, nor should you seek how to confirm that meaning by the authority of the Scriptures. Rather, you should draw the meaning of truth from the Scriptures themselves.

Therefore one ought to learn the understanding of the Scriptures from the person who preserves it according to the truth, as it was handed down to him by his predecessors, so that he too may be able competently to uphold what he has rightly received. When someone has received from the divine Scriptures a complete and firm rule of truth, it will not be absurd if he also contributes something from general education and the liberal studies that he happened to encounter in childhood, in support of the true doctrine—provided, however, that once he has learned the truth, he avoids what is false and fabricated.

The length of life is uncertain even for the young; for the old it is no longer uncertain, since there is no doubt that however much time is thought to remain is brief. Therefore both young and old must be very concerned about conversion and repentance, and must take sufficient care to adorn their souls from this point onward with the most worthy ornaments: the doctrines of truth, the beauty of chastity, the splendor of justice, the brightness of piety, and all the other qualities with which it is fitting for the rational mind to be adorned.

Therefore, giving you counsel, we exhort your chaste prudence not to depart from the apostolic rules, but, leading a common life and understanding the Holy Scriptures, to strive to fulfill what you have vowed to the Lord. And when by continual prayer you have deserved to obtain this, then, without fear of an evil outcome, your vows may be celebrated festively.

May the God of peace be with all of you. Amen.

# THE DECREES OF POPE ANACLETUS BEGIN

Concerning the oppression of bishops, the accusation of bishops, the ordination of archbishops, and primates and patriarchs and their ministers.

(This occurred in the year of Christ 104, during the reign of the emperor Trajan.)

[Col. 0059]

[Col. 0059B] Anacletus, servant of Jesus Christ, serving the Lord in the apostolic see, to all bishops and to all the other faithful who have received with us an equal faith: may grace, peace, and consolation be multiplied for you by the Lord forever.

Blessed is God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy regenerated us to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, preserved in heaven for you, who are guarded by the power of God through faith for the salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.
