In that salvation you will rejoice, although now, if necessary, you are distressed for a little while by various trials, so that the testing of your faith, much more precious than gold—which is tested by fire—may be found genuine (1 Pet. I, 3 and following), provided that you are found approved after having been tested through such tribulations. 13

“Be patient,” beloved, because “patience produces testing, and testing produces hope, while hope does not disappoint” (Rom. V; James I, 3). “Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, enduring patiently until he receives the early and the late rain” (James V, 7). If farmers patiently endure these things for temporal fruits, how much more ought you to be patient for eternal ones?

Be patient, therefore, and strengthen your hearts, so that when Christ the judge comes you may be found joyful and approved. “Do not groan against one another, so that you may not be judged. Behold, the judge stands before the door. Take, beloved, as an example of labor and patience the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, we call blessed those who endured. You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the Lord’s purpose, because the Lord is compassionate and merciful” (ibid., 10–12).

We have heard of your tribulations, brothers, both through our own emissaries and through those of others; we grieve greatly over them and sympathize with you. We are prepared to bring you aid, insofar as he himself grants it—he who was not only afflicted but also suffered for us.

“Do not be surprised, beloved, at the persecutions you endure, as though something strange were happening to you. Rather, rejoice insofar as you share in Christ’s sufferings, so that you may also rejoice and exult at the revelation of his glory. If you are reproached in the name of Christ, you will be blessed, because the Spirit of honor, glory, and virtue of the Lord—that is, his Spirit—rests upon you. Let none of you suffer as a murderer, a thief, a criminal, or one who covets what belongs to others. But if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; rather, let him glorify the Lord in this name, because it is time for judgment to begin with the household of the Lord. And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the gospel of God? And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear?” (1 Pet. IV, 12–18.)

Therefore let those who suffer commend their souls to the faithful Creator in good works, according to the Lord’s will.

For, as the blessed Clement mentioned above, our predecessor, says, the condition of the whole Church is like that of a great ship which carries men from various places and regions across a stormy sea, all desiring to hasten toward the one city of the mighty kingdom.

Let the author of this ship, then, be the almighty God himself; let Christ be its helmsman; then let the bishop perform the office of the pilot; let the presbyter occupy the place of the sailors; let the deacons hold the position of stewards; and let those who catechize be compared with ship-recruiters. Let the multitude of the entire brotherhood be like the passengers.

Let this world itself be regarded as the sea. Let the varieties of winds and whirlwinds be compared with the different temptations; persecutions, tribulations, and dangers shall correspond to the waves. The earthly spirits that blow either from torrents or from valleys represent the words of false prophets, seducers, and teachers of wicked doctrine. Promontories and rugged places represent those who hold worldly power—judges who threaten dangers and deaths.

The double sea, places struck by the twofold tides of deceptive waves, should be compared with those who are doubtful in mind and wavering concerning the truth of the promises, and with those who examine our faith by irrational reasoning. Hypocrites and deceitful people should be regarded as like pirates.

The swift whirlpool, the Tartarean Charybdis, shipwrecks dashed against rocks, and deadly drownings—what else should they be considered except sins?

It remains, therefore, that this ship may safely enter the harbor of the desired city on a prosperous course and pour forth peace to the Lord, so that those who sail may deserve to be heard.

We hear, brothers, that certain people slander and accuse the priests of the Lord, desiring that they be condemned, perhaps not understanding that an injury to priests concerns Christ, whose office they perform. Nor do they heed what the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and our instructor, says: “Therefore, laying aside all malice, all deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and every slander, like newborn infants desire rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow toward salvation” (1 Pet. II, 1), and what the Lord says through the prophet: “Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit” (1 Pet. III, 10), and so forth.

Those who transgress these commands are surely transgressors of the Lord’s law, as well as its despisers and disobedient to his precepts. Hence the blessed apostle James also says: “If you love your neighbors as yourselves, you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors” (James II, 9), and so forth.

And our blessed predecessor Clement, an apostolic man full of the Spirit of the Lord, together with his other holy colleagues, established the following:

The permission to accuse or testify shall be denied to all who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, and the norm of their own law or profession, or the things regularly forbidden. Those who knowingly transgress their own law, violate it, and depart from it shall be called apostates. Every apostate must be rejected before his return; he is not to be received as an accuser of those who act rightly, nor accepted as a witness, because a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.

“But whoever,” as the apostle James says, “keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all. For he who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill.’ Now if you do not commit adultery but do kill, you have become a transgressor of the law. So speak and so act as those who are to be judged by the law of liberty. For judgment will be without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy; mercy triumphs over judgment” (James II, 10).

And the Lord says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn back and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). There are many other sayings of this kind.

“For,” says the Apostle, “none of you lives for himself, and none dies for himself. For whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s. For this reason Christ died and rose again, so that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead. But you—why do you judge your brother? Or you—why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of the Lord. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.’ Therefore each of you shall give an account of himself to God. Let us no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: not to place a stumbling block or a scandal before a brother” (Rom. XIV, 11–13).

For we know that disparagement is very powerful when the disparager is believed to be worthy of faith. Therefore, brothers, the judges and primates of the Church ought not to be weakened by various slanders and accusations; rather, they should be instructed and strengthened by the rules of the apostles and teachers.

Hence it is right that all teachers of the law throughout the Roman world should understand and practice what belongs rightly to the law, and should not confuse the rules of the nascent Church, stain the faith or teaching of the apostles with various doctrines, or harass the brethren.

If everything in this age were avenged, there would be no place for divine judgments. For the person who tries to help the sun with torches labors at a useless expense. Therefore, if anyone thinks that he pleases the Lord by accusing his servants and says that he does this so that they may become better, he labors in vain and is driven more by the goads of envy than of love. The fullness of grace does not need additions, nor does it require any increase through commendation.

Therefore let teachers raise up their consciences. And if at times they are opposed by the uncertain winds of the ages, let them endure evils that should be attributed more to the times than to their merits. For we know that power was given to Satan so that he might sift the servants of Christ, so that whatever could be found of wheat might be brought into the granaries, while whatever was chaff might pass into the fuel of the fires.

To you especially it was said: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII, 32). The sword of the faithless has come among you in order to cut away the decaying limbs of the Church and lead them to heavenly glory. The contest shows whom Christ has as his soldiers; those who deserve triumph are recognized through battles.

We know, however, that many harass teachers in order to destroy them and fulfill the desires of their own will. Nevertheless, teachers must not, insofar as their strength permits, depart from righteous zeal and good intention, knowing that “blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness” (Matt. V, 10).

There is nothing more miserable than a shepherd who glories in the praises of wolves. If he wishes to please them and chooses to be loved by them, this will bring great destruction upon the sheep. No shepherd can please both wolves and flocks of sheep; for a mind bound in earthly prisons loses the memory of its labor.

Just as diligence is found to be the mother of every art in its own work, so negligence is the stepmother of learning. Therefore let no one prejudice another, nor do what he does not wish done to himself. Let no one find a saying about someone else that he does not recognize in that person’s actions.

I recognize that not only my tranquility but also the welfare of my enemies has been shaken by illness and by storms of rumor. Almighty divinity is able to remove the uncertainties of the tempest through the good calm of serenity.

And what else should we do, if “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. II, 21), and the apostles suffered, following his example, and the other fathers likewise, except to follow their footsteps, both their teaching and their example; to endure adversity for Christ; and to carry the cross with the fathers and with the brethren, sharing in their tribulations, so that we may be found true disciples of Christ, who said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX, 23), and so forth?

It is presumption if servants do not follow the benefits granted by their masters.

I therefore think that the service which I am about to render ought to be valued. For what is it that makes the title “son” believed to count for more than service, so that one does not ask what you advance in the balance of love, but what name you attach to the prejudice of the one judging, when among the wise we have called someone offspring in vain unless he displays what he appears to be? But I do not wish, through my own error, to assert the faults of others and thereby be shown to have committed the deed over which I grieve.

“You hate,” says the Lord through the prophet, “[Col. 0063C] all who work iniquity; you will destroy those who speak lies. The man of bloodshed and deceit the Lord abhors; but I, in the abundance of your mercy, will enter your house, and I will worship toward your holy temple in your fear (Ps. V, 7).” Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enchanters; direct my way before your face, for there is no truth in their mouth; their inward parts are treacheries. Their throat is an open grave; they have made their tongue smooth. Condemn them, O God; let them fall from their plans. According to the multitude of their crimes, drive them out, for they have provoked you. And let all who hope in you rejoice; they shall praise your name forever. And you will protect them, and those who love your name shall rejoice in you, for you will bless the righteous. Lord, “[Col. 0063D] you will crown him with the spear of appeasement” (ibid.).

For those who sacrifice to God perfectly ought not to be harassed, but to be supported, consoled, and honored by human beings. When they sacrifice to the Lord, however, they ought not to do this alone, but should bring witnesses with them, so that they may be shown to sacrifice perfectly to the Lord in places consecrated to God. For the authority of divine law says:

“See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place which the Lord your God has chosen.”

A bishop who sacrifices to the Lord should have witnesses with him, as has been stated, and more than another priest. For just as he enjoys a higher rank of honor, so he requires a greater increase of testimony. On more solemn days, therefore, he should have with him either seven, or five, or three deacons—who are called his eyes—and subdeacons, together with the remaining ministers. Clothed in sacred vestments, they should stand before and behind him, while the presbyters stand opposite, to his right and left, with contrite heart, humbled spirit, and bowed face. They should guard him from malicious people and give their assent to his sacrifice. After the consecration has been completed, all who do not wish to be deprived of the thresholds of the Church should receive Communion. Thus the apostles also established it, and the holy Roman Church maintains it.

“Serve,” says the Lord through the prophet David, “in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling (Ps. II, 11)”; worship purely, lest he become angry and you perish from the way. For the one who walks rightly and observes the precepts of his elders does not perish from the way.

Therefore all who serve in the priesthood of the Lord ought to be taught, so that they may instruct others and advance themselves. It is written:

“Those who are learned shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars for everlasting eternities (Dan. XII, 3).”

And elsewhere:

“But the people who know their God shall prevail and act, and those who are learned among the people shall teach very many (Dan. XI, 32).”

Truth itself, moreover, 14 declares and says:

“Blessed is the one who is not scandalized because of me (Luke VII, 23).”

Without doubt, the one who does not teach rightly is scandalized against God, as is the one who scandalizes his bishop or priest. For the impious act impiously, and all the impious do not understand; but the learned shall understand. Therefore all of you should insinuate humility to one another, “because God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (I Pet. V, 5).”

“Do not believe every spirit,” says the apostle John, “[Col. 0064C] but test the spirits, whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world (I John IV, 1).”

The same man also says elsewhere:

“Let what you heard from the beginning remain in you. If what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father. And this is the promise which he himself promised you: eternal life. I have written these things to you concerning those who lead you astray. And let the anointing which you received from him remain in you. You do not need anyone to teach you; but just as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true and is not a lie, and just as it taught you, remain in him. And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not be put to shame by him at his coming. If you know that he is righteous, know also that everyone who practices righteousness has been born from him.

“See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God—and that we are. For this reason the world does not know us, because it did not know him. Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy.

“Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity. And you know that he appeared to take away sins, and there is no sin in him. Everyone who remains in him does not sin; and everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him. Little children, let no one lead you astray. The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous. [Col. 0065A] The one who commits sin is from the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God appeared, to destroy the works of the devil.

“Everyone who has been born from God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born from God. By this the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest. Everyone who is not righteous is not from God, as is the one who does not love his brother. For this is the message which you heard from the beginning: that we should love one another—not like Cain, who was from the evil one and killed his brother. And why did he kill him? Because his works were evil, but his brother’s were righteous.

“Do not marvel, brothers, if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers. The one who does not love remains in death. Everyone [Col. 0065B] who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.

“By this we have come to know the love of God: that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. Whoever has the substance of this world, and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart against him—how does the love of God remain in him? Little children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and in truth.

“By this we know that we are from the truth, and we shall persuade our heart before him; for if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things. Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and whatever we ask we shall receive from him, if we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing before him.

“And this is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he gave us commandment. And the one who keeps his commandments remains in him, and he himself in that person; and by this we know that he remains in us, from the Spirit which he gave us (I John II, 24).”

And just as God the Creator, who created human beings in his own likeness, is love, good, just, patient, gentle, and merciful, together with the other marks of holy virtues that are read of him, so human beings were created to possess love, to be good and just, patient and gentle, pure and merciful. The more each person possesses these virtues within himself, the nearer he is to God and the greater he is, and the more he bears the likeness of his Creator.

But if—God forbid—anyone degenerately strays from this most noble likeness of his Creator through the byways of vices and the separation of crimes, then what is written about him will come to pass:

“Though man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them (Ps. XLVIII, 21).”

What greater honor could a human being have than to be created in the likeness of his Maker and adorned with the same garments of virtue as his Creator? Of him it is written:

“The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty (Ps. XCII, 1),”

that is, he has been adorned with the splendor of every virtue and the beauty of complete goodness. Or what greater disgrace, or more wretched misery, could there be for a human being than to lose this glory of likeness to his Creator and descend to the shapeless and irrational likeness of beasts and animals? [Col. 0066A]

Therefore, let everyone attend more carefully to the excellence of his first creation, recognize within himself the venerable image of the holy Trinity, and strive to possess, through nobility of character, the practice of virtues, and the dignity of merits, the honor of the divine likeness in which he was created. Thus, when he has appeared as he is, he may then appear like the one who wondrously created him in his own likeness in the first Adam and more wondrously restored him in the second.

Every human being, therefore, who has been made in the image of God ought to imitate the one in whose image he was made; he ought to follow the footsteps of the one who made him in his own image. He will not be able to find a better counselor and protector than the one who made him in his own image, who redeemed him with his precious blood, and who did not disdain to become human for his sake. He will certainly find him if, in accordance with the Psalmist’s word, he casts all his hope upon him. For he says:

“Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you; he will never permit the righteous person to waver (Ps. LIV, 23).”

For every person who fails in his own case and hesitates over his own counsels seeks for himself a faithful friend in whose counsel he may trust—he who distrusted his own—and places such confidence in him that he lays bare and discloses to him every secret of his heart.

What is sweeter than to have someone with whom you can speak about everything as with yourself? If such things are done with human beings, how much more ought this to be done with God, who wishes all to be saved and no one to perish? For if we truly believe in God, love him as we ought, love our neighbors as ourselves, and cast all our hope upon him, he himself will rescue and console us. And just as through his angel he sent the prophet Habakkuk with a meal into the lions’ den to the prophet Daniel, and sent Philip, one of the seven deacons, to the eunuch, so he will give us consolation and deliverance.

Pursue these things, beloved, and never harm anyone. You are brothers; love one another, so that you may deserve to become true disciples of God. For the one who infects the rancid hearts of men, spreads malice among human beings, and slanders his brother is a murderer. And whoever takes anything from his father or mother and says that this is not a sin is a participant in murder. [Col. 0066D]

Without doubt, our Father is God, who created us; our mother, however, is the Church, which spiritually regenerated us in baptism. Therefore whoever seizes, takes away, or defrauds Christ’s money and the Church’s is a murderer, and will be reckoned a murderer before the judgment seat of the righteous Judge. The one who steals his neighbor’s money practices iniquity; but the one who takes away the Church’s money or possessions commits sacrilege.

For the holy apostles, by command of the Savior, decreed that the privileges of Churches and priests should remain inviolate and untouched for all time. We confirm the laws of the Church by apostolic authority and remove foreign judgments. Hence, when the Lord speaks of Lot, he says through Moses:

“You entered here,” they say, “as a foreigner; will you now act as a judge? (Gen. XIX, 9).”

Each province ought, according to both ecclesiastical and secular laws, to have its own righteous rather than wicked judges, and not outsiders, unless the authority of this Apostolic See should so decree. Thus whoever has a case may be judged by his own judges, and should not pass over to outsiders, with his case urging him to wander, while despising his own country for the sake of his life. Rather, the matter should be brought before the twelve judges of that province, to whose judgment all the cases of the cities are referred.

If the matter is ecclesiastical, it should be brought before the bishops, with the primate intervening if the case is major; if minor, before the metropolitan. If it is secular, it should be brought before men of the same order, for the Apostle wished the cases of private Christians to be brought more readily before the Churches and settled there by priestly judgment. Every oppressed person may freely, if he wishes, appeal to the judgment of priests; no one may prevent him, but he should be supported and liberated by them.

If difficult cases or more important affairs arise, they should be referred to a higher see. If they cannot easily be discerned or justly settled there, they should be judged jointly and justly, in a manner pleasing to God, before the patriarch or ecclesiastical primate and before the secular patrician, wherever the assembly of the highest authorities has gathered—a meeting which customarily and properly occurs twice each year.

But if more difficult questions arise, or judgments concerning bishops or other leading persons, or more important cases, they should, if an appeal is made, be referred to the Apostolic See, because the apostles established by the command of the Savior that greater and difficult questions should always be referred to the Apostolic See, upon which Christ built the universal Church. He said to blessed Peter, the chief of the apostles:

“You are Peter,” he said, “and upon this rock I will build my Church (Matt. XVI, 18),”

and so forth.

Let our steadfastness, then, brothers, stand against the contentions of those who think contrary things and not the things of God. Our steadfastness will be stronger than a rock, as it is written:

“Do not fear them, nor be terrified by the face of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. What you hear in the ear, proclaim in the light, fearing the one who can kill both soul and body and cast them into Gehenna.”

My brothers, “though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying counsels and every exaltation that raises itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every thought captive to bring it into obedience to Christ (II Cor. X, 3).”

“Finally, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might (Eph. VI, 10),” so that abundant peace and grace may be given to you by God and our Lord Jesus Christ. We embrace and kiss your charity, as though present with you, in the unity of the Spirit, in the bond of peace, and in the charity of Christ.

“Therefore, beloved, while waiting for these things, strive to be found by him immaculate and undefiled, in peace, and regard the patience of our Lord as salvation. As our most beloved Paul also wrote to you, according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters, speaking in them about these matters. In them are certain things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction. You therefore, brothers, knowing this beforehand, guard yourselves, lest you be led astray by the error of the foolish and fall from your own steadfastness. Rather, grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ (II Pet. III, 14).”

“Beloved, remember the words which were foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said to you that in the last time there will be mockers, walking according to their own desires in ungodliness. These are the ones who separate themselves, sensual, not having the Spirit. [Col. 0068C] But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life.

“And indeed rebuke those who have been judged; save others by snatching them from the fire; and on others have mercy in fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh. To him who is able to preserve you without sin and to set you immaculate before the presence of his glory with exultation—to the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, magnificence, dominion, and power, before all ages, now and throughout all ages of ages. Amen (Jude I, 17).”

## ALSO, THE LETTER OF POPE ANACLETUS

On the ordination of archbishops and the other bishops, and of priests. On faith and other matters.

[Col. 0067]

### ANACLETUS, BISHOP, TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN ITALY

Since your charity has shown me the reverence due to the Apostolic See, you have given very much, beloved sons. For although we in some manner hold the reins of the Church in which the holy apostle taught while residing there, nevertheless we confess that we are inferior in honor and holiness; and for this reason we hasten with all our strength to be able to attain the glory of that blessedness.

Therefore we would have responded more fully to your consultations if it had been possible. But, weighed down by the burden of illness and other afflictions, we have not refused to write to you briefly, insofar as the Lord grants, and as we have been instructed by blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, by whom I was also ordained a presbyter, just as you requested.

The ordinations of bishops are to be celebrated by apostolic authority by all the bishops who are in that same province. Coming together, they should conduct a careful examination and celebrate a fast with all in prayer. They should lay hands upon the candidates with the holy Gospels which the candidates are going to preach, praying on the Lord’s Day at the third hour, and anointing their heads with sacred anointing, after the example of the prophets and kings and in the manner of the apostles and Moses. For all sanctification consists in the Holy Spirit, whose invisible power is mingled with the holy chrism. In this manner they should celebrate the solemn ordination.

If all cannot come together, nevertheless they should offer their assent in their prayers, so that in spirit they may not be absent from the ordination itself.

Moreover, blessed James, the first archbishop of Jerusalem, who was called “the Just” and was named the brother of the Lord according to the flesh, was ordained by the apostles Peter, James, and John. They thereby gave a form to their successors, so that no bishop should in any way be ordained by fewer than three bishops, with all the others giving their assent, and so that the ordination should be celebrated by common agreement.

The other priests, however, are to be ordained by their own bishop, with the citizens and the other priests giving their assent; they should celebrate the ordination while fasting. Deacons likewise are to be ordained. For the distribution of the remaining grades, the testimony of three truthful persons, together with the bishop’s examination, may suffice.

The accusation of those about whom you wished to consult us must be made only by suitable and highly approved men who are free from both suspicion and crimes. For the Lord did not wish those who handle his sacred body to be defamed by base, reprobate, and unsuitable persons, nor did he permit them to be calumniated. Rather, he himself drove sinful priests from the temple with his own whip. From this it is clear that the chief priests, that is, bishops, are to be judged by God, not torn apart by human beings or by men of depraved life, but rather supported by faithful people. The Lord himself gave the example when he personally, and not through another, drove the sellers and buyers from the temple, overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of sellers with his own whip, and expelled them from the temple.

And as he says elsewhere:

“God has stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods (Ps. LXXXI, 1).”

And elsewhere:

“I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’ (Ps. LXXXI, 6).”

For, as I think, no one among us is found who would wish his servant to be judged by anyone other than himself. If such a thing were attempted, he would either become angry with great indignation or, rather, seek vengeance upon the offender. If this is done among human beings, what do you think the God of gods and Lord of lords will do, who promised not to defer vengeance upon his servants?

Hence he himself speaks through the prophet, saying:

“God of vengeance, the Lord, God of vengeance has acted freely (Ps. XCIII, 1),”

and so forth.

The Apostle also says:

“Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master (Rom. XIV, 4),”

and again:

“Do not judge one another, but judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling block or a scandal before your brother (Rom. XIV, 13).”

And the Lord says through the prophet:

“Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye (Zech. II, 8).”

For if anyone now begins to attack the eyes of a prince with evil intent, he is plainly judged guilty of treason and is made infamous, or rather is subjected to capital punishment. These things, brothers, must be carefully avoided. What human beings do not wish done to themselves, they ought not to inflict upon the God of gods, lest the Lord perhaps become angry and exact vengeance upon them—even upon those who have not sinned—for the righteous very often perishes on account of the wicked.

The prophet should also be imitated, through whom the Lord says:

“I shall walk in the integrity of my heart in the midst of my house. I shall not set before my eyes a word of Belial. The one who secretly slanders his companion, him I shall destroy.”

Such people must be avoided. Of them Solomon says:

“As he is harmful who casts spears and arrows toward death, so is the man who deceitfully harms his friend and, when he has been discovered, says, ‘I was joking.’ As coals to burning embers and wood to fire, so the angry man stirs up quarrels; the words of a whisperer seem simple, but they reach the innermost parts of the belly (Prov. XXVI, 18).”

And if slanderers of anyone are severely judged and fall into the snare of destruction, much more are those who tear apart, slander, and accuse the aforesaid servants of God, as well as their persecutors, condemned. Unless they correct themselves and undertake fitting penance through worthy satisfaction, they unquestionably go into the abyss and are consumed by avenging flames.

Therefore everyone ought to beware of these things—not only not to do them, but not even to consent to those who do them. For not only those who commit such acts are condemned, but also those who consent to their perpetrators. Concerning such people and those like them, Truth itself says:

“Foxes have dens and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matt. VIII, 20; Luke IX, 58),”

that is, the Lord does not dwell in such people, nor do they remain in him.

And Solomon says:

“The one who digs a pit will fall into it, and the one who rolls a stone will have it return upon him. A deceitful tongue does not love truth, and a slippery mouth works ruin (Prov. XXVI, 27).”

A stone is heavy and sand is burdensome, but the anger of a fool is heavier than both. No one supports a man who slanders the blood of a soul, even if he flees as far as a pit. The one who boasts and enlarges himself stirs up quarrels. The one who hopes in the Lord will be healed. The one who trusts in his own heart is a fool, but the one who walks wisely will himself be saved. The one who presses the breasts forcefully to draw out milk produces butter; the one who blows his nose violently draws blood; and the one who provokes anger produces dissensions.

## The Order of Accusation

Considering these and other dangers, the apostles decreed that the pillars of the holy Church of God—who are rightly called the apostles and their successors—should not easily be disturbed, torn apart, or accused. But if anyone should become hostile to them or to their Churches, or should have a case against them, he should first have recourse to them in a spirit of charity, so that, admonished through familiar conversation, they may heal what ought to be healed and charitably correct what they recognize ought justly to be corrected.

But if anyone should presume to tear them apart, accuse them, or harass them before doing these things, let him be excommunicated and not absolved in any way before he has performed fitting penance through satisfactory reparation, as has already been said. For the injury done to them concerns Christ, whose embassy they fulfill. This is not surprising, because if any one of us entrusted an embassy to one of his servants, and that servant were hindered by someone or despised by one of his subjects, he would immediately become indignant and angry, or would exact such vengeance as he could. He would regard the act as an injury and insult against himself and would return the equivalent, if he could not do so immediately, at a later time.

For if these things occur in the case of human beings, what do you think God will do with those who are his own, concerning whom he has said that not even a hair of their head shall perish? Hence the Lord speaks through the prophet Nahum, saying:

“God is jealous and the Lord is avenging; the Lord is avenging and possesses wrath. The Lord is avenging against his enemies and is angry with his adversaries. Who will stand before his indignation, and who will resist the fury of his anger? His indignation is poured out like fire, and the rocks are dissolved by him. The Lord is good and strengthens in the day of tribulation, and he knows those who hope in him (Nahum I, 2),”

and so forth.

We have already written some of these things to other brothers; they must be repeated as often as they are necessary. The Lord has also reserved for himself the expulsion of the chief priests, as was mentioned above, although he granted their election to good priests and spiritual peoples.

The Apostle commands that their election take place in this manner:

“If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or insubordination (Titus I, 6),”

and so forth.

If a priest is commanded to be chosen as blameless, he is in no way permitted to be accused or calumniated by human beings entangled in crimes, nor by anyone other than those who are themselves blameless and who, by a just election—if necessity requires it, or if they have chosen by their own will to serve the Lord—can become and be ordained blameless priests, and who in every respect are such as priests are commanded to be when chosen.

Moreover, Moses is commanded to choose presbyters. Hence it is said in Proverbs:

“The glory of the old is gray hair.”

This gray hair signifies wisdom, concerning which it is written:

“Gray hair is the prudence of human beings.”

Although we read that men lived nine hundred and more years from Adam to Abraham, no one else was first called presbyter—that is, elder—except Abraham, who is shown to have lived far fewer years. Presbyters, therefore, are not so called because of decrepit old age, but because of wisdom.

The beginning of the priesthood was Aaron’s, although Melchizedek had offered sacrifice first, and after him Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But these men did these things by spontaneous choice, not with priestly authority.

Aaron, however, was the first in the Law to receive the priestly name, and the first to offer victims clothed in the pontifical vestment, at the Lord’s command and according to his word to Moses:

“Take Aaron,” he said, “and his sons, and bring them to the entrance of the tent of testimony. When you have washed the father and his sons with water, you shall clothe Aaron in his garments: a linen tunic, the ephod, and the breastpiece, which you shall fasten with a belt; you shall place the tiara on his head and the holy plate upon the tiara, and you shall pour the oil of anointing upon his head. In this manner he shall be consecrated to the Lord. You shall also bring his sons forward and clothe them in linen tunics, gird Aaron and his sons with belts, and place turbans upon them; and they shall be my priests by a perpetual ordinance (Exod. XXIX, 4).”

In this passage we must understand Aaron, the chief priest, to have been a bishop, while his sons prefigured presbyters. For this was the difference between Aaron, the chief priest, and his sons, who were priests: Aaron received over the tunic the robe, the holy vestment, the golden crown, the tiara, the golden belt, the ephod, and the other items mentioned above; but Aaron’s sons, girded only with linen tunics and wearing turbans, assisted at the Lord’s sacrifice.

In the New Testament, however, after Christ our Lord, the priestly order began from Peter, because the first pontificate in the Church of Christ was given to him, the Lord saying to him:

“You are Peter,” he said, “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XVI, 18).”

He therefore first received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing, and he was the first to bring the people to faith by the grace of God through the power of his preaching. The other apostles received honor and power in equal fellowship with him, and they wished him to be their chief.

At the Lord’s command they were scattered throughout the whole world and preached the Gospel. When they too departed, bishops succeeded them in their place. Their ordination must take place according to the order and manner stated above. Whoever receives them and their words receives the Lord; but whoever despises them despises the one by whom they were sent and whose embassy they fulfill, and he will unquestionably himself be despised by the Lord.

The apostles themselves, seeing that the harvest was abundant and the laborers few, asked the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest. Hence seventy disciples were chosen by them, whose type presbyters bear, and they have been established in their place in the Church. Concerning their ordination and that of the remaining ministers, let what was said above suffice.

Moreover, the fact that a bishop must be ordained not by one but by all, with the agreement or presence of the bishops of his province, and in no case by fewer than three with all the rest consenting, is commanded to be done by the Lord’s institution so that no tyrannical authority might undertake anything against the faith of the one Church and so that the rule or faith of believers might not be confused.

The provinces were divided, for the most part, long before Christ’s coming. Later that division was renewed by the apostles and by blessed Clement, our predecessor. At the head of the provinces—where formerly there had been the chief judges of the secular law and the primary judicial authority, to whom those living in the other cities had recourse when necessity required, when they could not or were not permitted to flee to the imperial courts, as to kings, because of their oppressions or injustices, and whom they appealed to whenever necessary, just as their law commanded—divine and ecclesiastical laws commanded that patriarchs or primates, who hold one form of office although their names differ, should likewise be established in our cities or regions.

Bishops were to have recourse to them if necessary and appeal to them; they alone were to be honored by the title of primate, and no others. The remaining metropolitan cities, which had lesser judges, although they were superior to counts, were to have their own metropolitans, who would justly obey the aforesaid primates, as had formerly been arranged in the secular laws. They were to be honored not by the title of primates, but either of metropolitans or archbishops.

Although each metropolitan city has its own province and ought to have its own metropolitan judges—bishops, just as previously it had secular metropolitan judges—the provinces were nevertheless commanded, as stated above, to have primates both then and now. After the Apostolic See, the most important matters should come before them, so that those who need it may there be relieved and justly restored, and those who are unjustly oppressed may be justly corrected and supported. The cases of bishops and the judgments concerning major affairs should be settled with the greatest justice, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See.

We have received these things from the ancients, from the apostles, and from the holy fathers. We send them to you, as you requested, to be examined and held for future times, and we command that they be preached to the remaining brothers and handed down to all the faithful, lest those who follow become worse through the ignorance of shepherds. The Lord says through the prophet:

“The shepherds themselves have not understood (Isa. LVI, 11),”

and again the Lord detests them, saying:

“And those who hold the law did not know me (Jer. II, 8).”

Truth therefore complains that it is not known by them, and declares that it does not know the leadership of those who do not know, because those who do not know the things of the Lord are certainly not known by the Lord, as Paul bears witness when he says:

“If anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored (I Cor. XIV, 38).”

Hence the Psalmist, not in the spirit of wishing but in the mystery of prophecy, announces:

“Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bend their back (Ps. LXVIII, 24).”

When their eyes have been darkened, therefore, the back is bent, because when those who lead lose the light of knowledge, those who follow are without doubt bent down to carry the burdens of sins.

Here, then, we are somehow placed among the hands of robbers and the teeth of raging wolves. Therefore we must teach others and provide for ourselves, insofar as the Lord grants.

That striker is properly called a teacher who strikes the conscience of the weak with useless speech. Therefore you and all the faithful ought to hold fast to the faithful word that accords with doctrine, so that he may be able to console with sound teaching, refute those who contradict, and strengthen those who live rightly and hold the right faith.

To those, therefore, who say that the Son is inferior because the prophet says, “The Lord will make a word shortened over the whole world,” one must respond with divine testimonies.

## ON BISHOPS, PRIMATES, AND PATRIARCHS, AND THEIR MINISTERS

[Col. 0073]

[Col. 0073C] The “abridged word” that the Lord will make upon the earth does not signify a diminution of the Godhead in the Son of God, but announces the dispensation of the flesh that he assumed. In this dispensation we read that he was made lower not only [by the Father as a son of man; the wording is corrupt], but also below the angels, as the apostle Paul attests: “We see Jesus, who was made for a little while lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death.” And below: “For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: ‘I shall proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I shall praise you (Ps. 21:23).’” And the prophet says: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor (Heb. 2:7).”

And in order to show that the word of God the Father was not abridged in the Son, we approve this sentence from the book of the prophet Isaiah: “Has my word become shortened, or so small that I cannot redeem, or is there no strength in me to deliver?” says the almighty Lord. And again: “Thus says the almighty Lord: Has my hand become shortened, so that I cannot save? Or is it unable to give life to the heart of the humble and the spirit of the contrite?”

And so that the arm of the Father—which is his hand—might be shown to be the Son, he continued, saying: “The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see his salvation (Isa. 52:10).”

For even in the final age this interpretation can fittingly be applied—not without reason. At that time, the Lord, no longer willing to endure from his heavenly court and imperial dwelling the tyranny of the worst demon, raging most cruelly against his creatures, and desiring to unlock the treasure of his immeasurable love, came in an ineffable mystery, assuming flesh for our redemption in the most pure womb of the most chaste Virgin, who knew no intercourse with a man. He came both to destroy by his death the one who held the power of death, and to free, by the power of his might, within that brief and tiny span of time, those whom he had subdued as captives in darkness and the shadow of death.

He was also instructing his disciples concerning this brief time when he urged them beforehand to walk in the light while they still had time. “Little children,” he said, “it is the final hour (1 John 2).” “While you have the light, walk in the light, lest the darkness overtake you (John 12:35).” And in the canonical letters of the Apostles we read: “Little children, it is the final hour, because many false prophets have gone out into this world (1 John 2:18; 4:1).” And the apostle Paul says: “For the time is short (1 Cor. 7:29).” And again: “For the form of this world is passing away (ibid., 31).” And again: “All these things were done for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.”

For the Lord himself shortened the word for us in the very Lord’s Prayer, when, forbidding us excessive speech, he taught us only a few things pertaining to salvation. “When you pray,” he says, “do not speak at length (Matt. 6:7).” And below: “When you pray, say: ‘Our Father who are in heaven (ibid., 9),’” and so forth.

For the prophet did not indicate in this passage that the Son of God had been made lower in the word, since it was he himself who spoke through the prophets in former times, and who now speaks through the apostles and apostolic men in the final age. “I who spoke,” he says, “to my servants the prophets, behold, I am present.” And another prophet says: “As he was from the beginning and remains forever, nothing has been added to him, nor will anything be diminished from him (Sir. 42:21),” because he himself is Lord of his creation.

Behold what kind of abridged word the Lord made throughout the world: not because, as they think, he wished to disclose the Son to human beings as inferior to the Father, but because he announced his final coming.

Therefore, if, as was said above, the sons of Aaron bore the figure of presbyters, and Aaron that of the high priest—that is, the bishop—Moses undoubtedly bore the form of Christ, since he was a likeness of the mediator of the Lord God, Jesus Christ, who is between God and humanity, the true leader of the peoples, the true chief of the priests, and the Lord of pontiffs. To him be honor and glory forever and ever.

[Col. 0076B] Amen.

## THE SECOND LETTER OF THE SAME ANACLETUS

Concerning patriarchs, primates, and the remaining bishops; and that the Roman Church is the hinge and head of all the Churches.

[Col. 0075]

[Col. 0075B] Anacletus, servant of Christ Jesus, established by the Lord in the Apostolic See and ordained presbyter by Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, sends greetings to all bishops and the remaining priests of Christ.

“Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ. Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless in his sight in love, predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, for the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he has favored us in his beloved Son. In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness [Col. 0075C] of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he has made abound in us with all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth, in him. In him we have also been called by lot, predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we may be for the praise of his glory—we who previously hoped in Christ (Eph. 1:3–12).”

Concerning the primates, dearest brothers, about whom some of you have consulted me and requested a decree of apostolic authority—which, although unworthy, we exercise by the Lord’s dispensation—whether they ought to exist or not, we cannot in any way conceal from you what we have thus far learned to have been established by blessed Peter the Apostle, by the other apostles, and by our blessed predecessor and martyr, Saint Clement. Who could refuse the brothers who ask for clarification concerning their doubts or needs?

The order of priests, brothers, is twofold, and, just as the Lord established it, it must not be disturbed by anyone. You know that the apostles were chosen and appointed by the Lord and afterward dispersed through various provinces to preach. When the harvest began to grow, however, and he saw that there were few laborers, he commanded the disciples to choose seventy to assist them. The bishops hold the place of the Lord’s apostles, and the presbyters that of the seventy disciples.

Bishops, however, ought not to be established in castles or small cities. Rather, presbyters are to be ordained and appointed by bishops throughout castles, small cities, and villages, one in each of their respective titles. A bishop must be ordained not by one bishop but by several; and, as has been said, he must not be assigned to a small city, lest the name of bishop be cheapened, but must be titled and designated for a distinguished city. A presbyter, however, is to be placed over any place or church established there, and is to remain in it for the days of his life. No more than these two orders of priests have been bestowed upon us by God, nor did the apostles teach any others.

## CONCERNING THE ORDER OF BISHOPS OR PRIMATES

[Col. 0075]

[Col. 0075D] There is one order of bishops, although there are primates—those who occupy the principal cities—who in some places are also called patriarchs by certain persons. Those who have been established in the metropolis by the blessed apostle Peter, by the command of the Lord, and by our aforesaid predecessor, Saint Clement, or by us, cannot all be primates or patriarchs. Rather, those cities that held primacy in the aforementioned ancient times may enjoy the designation of bishops, patriarchs, or primates; the remaining metropolises, however, must use the names of archbishops or metropolitans, and not of patriarchs or primates. For secular laws likewise contain these distinctions among their rulers.

Other principal cities, whose names we send you written in a certain volume, received from the holy apostles, from blessed Clement, or from us, primate preachers. This most holy Roman and apostolic Church, however, obtained its primacy not from the apostles but from the Lord himself, our Savior, and acquired preeminence of authority over all the Churches and over the whole flock of the Christian people, just as he said to the blessed apostle Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound [Col. 0077B] in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven (Matt. 16:18).”

The fellowship of the most blessed apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, was also added in that same city of Rome. He was crowned together with blessed Peter in glorious death, struggling under the emperor Nero on one day and at one time; and both consecrated the holy Roman Church, placing it before all the other cities throughout the world by their presence and venerable triumph.

And although the prayer of all the saints is continually poured out before the Lord for everyone, the most blessed apostle Paul nevertheless promises the Romans in his own handwriting in these words: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that I continually make mention of you without ceasing in my prayers (Rom. 1:9).”

### Concerning the Roman See

The first see, therefore, by heavenly favor, is that of the Roman Church, which, as has been mentioned, the most blessed Peter and Paul consecrated by their martyrdom. Thus Rome, which previously, through the craft of the evil demon, had been the mother and nurse of every error, after casting off the darkness and abandoning the empty rites of superstition, became, with the rising sun of righteousness, a fertile propagator of the children of God.

### Concerning the Alexandrian See

The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and Evangelist, because he was sent by Peter to Egypt and there first preached the word of truth and received a glorious martyrdom. The venerable Abilius succeeded him.

### Concerning the Antiochene See

The third see is honorably held at Antioch, likewise in the name of blessed Peter the apostle, because he lived there before coming to Rome and appointed Ignatius as bishop. It was there that the name “Christians” first arose for the new people.

As we said above, we have sent you the remaining sees written in a certain volume, avoiding excessive length in this letter. For from that time the blessed Apostles also established among themselves that the bishops of the individual nations should know who among them was first, so that the greater part of their concern might belong to him.

For there was also a certain distinction among the blessed apostles. Although all were apostles, it was granted to Peter by the Lord—and they themselves likewise desired it—that he should preside over all the other apostles and hold the place of Cephas—that is, the head—and the primacy of the apostolate. He handed down this same arrangement to be observed by his successors and by the remaining bishops.

And this was established not only in the New Testament but also in the Old. Hence it is written: “Moses and Aaron among his priests (Ps. 98:6),” that is, they were first among them.

Although this order was established, no one should seek what belongs to himself, but what belongs to another. Hence the blessed apostle Paul says: “Let each of you please his neighbor for good, for edification (Rom. 15:2).”

And just as the Savior himself says to his disciples: “The greater among you shall be your servant (Matt. 23:11),” and so forth.

Although some things have already been said about these matters, nevertheless, repeating them frequently, we admonish you always and in every circumstance to avoid, by everyone, all arrogance of mind and body. The greater each person appears to be, the humbler he should be, just as the Lord our Savior came not to be served but to serve.

And if a brother has been overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct him in a spirit of gentleness. If more difficult matters should arise among you, refer them to the summit of this holy See as to the head, so that they may be settled by apostolic judgment, because the preceding testimonies make clear that the Lord wills this and established it in this way.

This Apostolic See was made by the Lord the hinge and head, and was established by no other. Just as a door is governed by its hinge, so, by the authority of this holy See, all the Churches are governed by the Lord’s disposition.

Those who were enemies yesterday or the day before yesterday cannot be accusers or witnesses, lest, being angry, they desire to cause harm or, having been injured, wish to take revenge. Therefore, the unoffended disposition of accusers and witnesses must be sought, and it must be free from suspicion.

Do not entrust your case to another’s judgment. For it is exceedingly unjust that, neglecting their own affairs, various others should involve themselves in the cases of others, since spiritual care is lacking in no place but extends everywhere that the name of the Lord is preached.

Everyone must strive to ensure that, as is appropriate, there be among you not evil rivalries but devout affections, because all will know that you are true disciples of the Lord if you have love for one another. From every kind of people God deigns to draw many, transferring them from the power of darkness into the kingdom of the Son of his love and making them vessels of mercy out of vessels of wrath.

Therefore, we must strive with the utmost diligence to be fellow workers with God’s grace, because we have been called to this and joined to his familiar conversation, and have been consecrated as priests, so that, with his grace cooperating, we may bring him fruitful sheaves.

For it is necessary that rulers be feared by their subjects and be corrected by them, so that those who do not fear divine judgments may fear to sin through human apprehension. Those who corrupt the life and conduct of teachers are worse than those who plunder the property and estates of others. The former take away things that are outside us, even if they are ours; but those who slander us, corrupt our morals, or take up arms against us deceive us personally. Therefore, they are rightly infamous and deservedly expelled from the Church.

Pastors of the Church are therefore often corrupted on account of the merits of the people, so that those who follow may fall more easily. When the head is languishing, the remaining members of the body are more easily infected, as it is written: “Every head is sick, and every heart is grieving; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, there is no health in it (Isa. 1:5).”

Therefore it is clear that the devil—who, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour—persuades the hearts of the people to bring accusations against or inflict slander upon their teachers and pastors, so that, while the peoples languish or act wickedly, and while the pastors do not hold their reins, they may indulge themselves and fall into the depths.

The harms to morals differ greatly from the harms to temporal possessions, since the latter are outside us, whereas the former are within us. The sentence concerning Ham, the son of Noah, also condemns those who disclose the fault of their teachers or superiors, just as Ham did not cover his father’s nakedness but rather exposed it for mockery.

If a teacher or pastor of the Church should depart from the faith, he must be corrected by the faithful. But because of reprehensible morals he should be tolerated rather than disciplined, because the rulers of the Church are to be judged by God, as the prophet says: “God has stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges the gods (Ps. 82:1).”

Therefore, every faithful person, if he sees or learns that the people are swelling up against their pastor or that the clergy are occupied with slanderers, must strive prudently and with all his strength to uproot and correct this vice. He must not presume to involve himself in any affairs with them if they appear incorrigible, before they have been reconciled with their teacher. For both priests and all the remaining faithful must exercise the greatest care for those who are perishing, so that through their rebuke they may either be corrected from their sins or, if they prove incorrigible, be separated from the Church.

## CONCERNING SUBJECTS WHO ARE FRIENDS WITH THE ENEMIES OF THEIR BISHOPS

[Col. 0079]

[Col. 0079C] The blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, spoke concerning our holy predecessor Clement when he was preaching to the peoples and teaching them how they ought to obey and observe him. Among other things he said:

“If he is an enemy to anyone because of that person’s actions, do not wait for him to tell you, ‘Do not be friends with that person.’ Rather, you ought to observe this prudently, comply with his will without associating with that person, and turn away from the one whom you perceive to be opposed by him. Do not speak with those with whom he does not speak, so that each person who is at fault here, while desiring to retain the friendship of everyone, may hasten to be reconciled with the one who presides over all and, by beginning to obey the commands of the ruler, may return to salvation.

“But if anyone is friendly with those with whom he is not friendly, and speaks with those with whom he does not speak, he is one of those who wish to destroy the Church of God,” and so forth.

From these and very many other instructions, everyone can easily understand how he ought to obey and comply with his superiors, and how he should act toward those with whom they are either friends or enemies.

For if anyone does not observe these precepts, he is an enemy of his own soul and becomes not only infamous but also excommunicated and alienated from the Church, since it is necessary to cut away with the sword those vices that cannot be healed by other remedies.

Let each person refrain from tearing apart or slandering with his tongue, and beware lest he have either a tongue or ears that itch—that is, lest he disparage and slander others, or listen to those who disparage or slander. Let everyone guard his words and know that whoever speaks about others will be judged by his own sentence.

Let every faithful person also beware lest, by disclosing what is done in someone’s house, he cause another household to learn of it. Rather, let him love the households of all Christians as his own. No one willingly reports anything to an unwilling listener. Let each person therefore strive not only to keep his eyes chaste but also his tongue.

But you, dearest ones, who have been placed under the discipline of the Lord, conduct yourselves as true ministers and stewards of his mysteries, so that your ministry may not be censured, lest what is written be fulfilled in you: “As the people are, so is the priest (Isa. 24:2).”

Correct yourselves, your own people, and everyone in such a way that you harm no one, so that you may acquire a good reputation among human beings and deserve to receive from God the reward of recompense in eternal blessedness.

And if anything adverse should happen concerning the unity of the Church, let it be cut off at the root, so that the Church of God and the fruits of its servants may remain unshaken.

“Therefore, dearest ones, while awaiting these things, strive to be found by him immaculate and at peace, and regard the patience of our Lord Jesus Christ as salvation (2 Pet. 3:14).”

“Therefore be prudent and watchful in prayers. Above all, maintain continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins. Be hospitable to one another without murmuring. As each has received grace, administer it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God; if anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies, so that God may be honored in all things through Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen (1 Pet. 4:7).”

## HERE BEGIN THE DECREES OF POPE EVARISTUS

Concerning the ordination of deacons and legitimate marriage, and concerning faith and not injuring or tearing apart bishops.

(He succeeded Anacletus in the year of the Lord 110, under the emperor Trajan.)

[Col. 0081]

[Col. 0081A] Evaristus to all the bishops of the region of Africa, his most beloved brothers.

Dearest brothers, you consulted us concerning what seemed appropriate regarding the matters contained in your writings, what sound reasoning might persuade us of, what had been handed down to us by the blessed apostles, or what remained to be guarded. As you reported, you desired to be instructed by our directives.

Your affection, following the norm of prudent men, preferred to refer the matter to the Apostolic See, as to the head, asking what ought to be guarded concerning doubtful matters rather than presuming upon usurpation.

### Concerning the Ordination of the Seven Deacons

There ought to be seven deacons in each city, according to the constitutions of the apostles. They are like the bishop’s eyes and are to guard the bishop as he preaches, so that he may not in any way be troubled by plotters or harmed by his own people; so that the divine words may not be polluted or despised through slander or plotting; and so that the truth may give forth a spiritual fragrance, while the peace preached by the lips agrees with the disposition of the heart.

### Concerning Legitimate Marriage

We have likewise received and preserved the rule that a wife is to be joined to a husband legitimately. For, as we have received from the Fathers and found handed down by the holy apostles and their successors, no marriage is legitimate unless the wife is sought from those who appear to have authority over the woman and by whom she is guarded; unless she is betrothed by her parents or nearest relatives and given according to the laws; and unless, at the proper time, she is blessed sacerdotally, as is customary, by a priest with prayers and offerings.

She must be guarded and joined by the bridesmen, as custom teaches, sought from her relatives at the appropriate time, given according to the laws, and solemnly received. The couple should devote two or three days to prayers and observe chastity, so that good offspring may be born and may please the Lord in their actions.

For in this way they will please the Lord and beget children who are not illegitimate but legitimate and entitled to inheritance. Therefore, dearest sons, illustrious in accordance with the support of Catholic faith, know that marriages performed in this manner are legitimate.

If they are undertaken otherwise, do not doubt that they are not marriages but rather adulteries, illicit unions, sexual violations, or fornications rather than legitimate marriages, unless personal consent has supported the union and legitimate vows have come to its aid.

For the divine fruit is to observe the divine commandments. No one can doubt that abandoning them constitutes presumption. Why, then, is it considered unworthy that the unity of the Church be preserved? Let us all likewise think and declare the same thing together.

For if unions are presumed upon otherwise, the transgressors themselves certainly destroy themselves, because they deceive themselves.

Send all these writings to be read throughout all the Churches of Africa, and append to them the letters of the perfected which we have added, so that judgment may be made concerning those things that are wickedly praised, if anything of that kind can be proved; that what has been prohibited may be restrained; and that past evils and illicit marriages, if shown to have been committed, may be corrected with appropriate severity.

For the future, let such things be avoided throughout all the Churches, lest the sanctity of the Church, wearied by our negligence, lose the privileges it has acquired through venerable men.

Concerning those by whom you are wearied through plots, and about whom you wished, among other things, to consult us and be instructed by us: some of them suppose that the statement “he alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” was spoken of the Father alone. Strike them, therefore, with apostolic rods and refute them with divine commands.

For the Father alone does not dwell in inaccessible light without the Son, since wherever the Father is, there too the Son must be believed to be, with unquestionable faith. For if the Father alone, without the Son—which it is impious to say—dwells in inaccessible light, the Father must have a dwelling separated from the Son.

But if this is so, how is the same Son said to have been seen by the blessed martyr Stephen standing at the right hand of the Father, if, according to them, the Father alone is said to be contained in the dwelling of light?

Far be this from the understanding of the faithful who cling to Christ in the unity of faith. For just as it does not harm the Son when the Father alone is said to dwell in inaccessible light, so it does not harm the Father when Wisdom, who is the Son, is said alone to circle the vault of heaven.

Therefore, although the Father is invisible and unbegotten in himself, he is shown by the testimony of the Apostle to have been seen in the Son. He is also shown to have remained and rested in the Son, ineffably begotten from himself, with the Son himself speaking through the prophet: “He who begot me rested in my tabernacle (Sir. 24:12).”

And in the Gospel: “The Father who remains in me performs these works (John 14:10).” And: “No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father (John 1:18).”

If the Son was in the bosom of the Father from the beginning, and a good word was uttered from the heart of the Father, how can he not be believed to have dwelt in inaccessible light together with him, existing in the Father’s heart?

Could the Father remain in the Son without any light, or rest in the Son’s tabernacle without that same light, since the Son is the radiance of eternal light and the spotless mirror of the Godhead? Solomon says that he loved this Wisdom above his own salvation and longed always to delight in the hope of her: “Above health and hope,” he says, “I loved her, and I chose to have her for light, because her radiance is inexhaustible.”

Longing anxiously for this light, the prophet David cries out: “Send forth your light and your truth (Ps. 43:3).” And again: “In your light we shall see light (Ps. 36:10).”

In the brightness of this light, therefore, the Son showed himself beforehand on the mountain to three disciples. Terrified by the fear of death and fallen on their faces, they sensed that the end of life was upon them. Demonstrating that this light was in himself, the Son proclaimed it and urged the disciples beforehand to walk in it: “While you have the light,” he said, “walk in the light (John 12:35).”

And again: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of eternal life (John 8:12).” And the Evangelist says: “It was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9).”

If this light, which is promised to believers, is shown to be in the Son and is said to be eternal together with the Eternal One, how can the Son be separated by you from the Father’s inaccessible light?

For if the Son is the true God and eternal life, without doubt he must be believed to dwell together with the Father in this light, which none of us, situated in this mortal body, can in any way behold at present.

But when he appears, then the one who is deemed worthy to be joined to his sight will truly see him as he is—not as Moses and the other prophets saw him through riddles and figures, but, according to the Apostle, will truly behold in the Son the image of the Godhead itself.

For if you wish to investigate this same one—the Son—under the testimony of the prophets, with the serene gaze of the mind that follows after it, you will find that the Son cannot be wholly separated from this light of the Father. Although he alone is said to have lived on earth among human beings, the Father must not be believed to have become alienated from him.

“If we receive human testimony, the testimony of God is greater, because this is the testimony of God, which is greater: that he has testified concerning his Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has God’s testimony within himself. Whoever does not believe in the Son makes him a liar, because he does not believe the testimony that God has given concerning his Son.

“And this is the testimony: God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has eternal life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.

“I write these things to you so that you may know that you have eternal life—you who believe in the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence that we have in him: whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us. And we know that he hears whatever we ask; we know that we have the requests that we ask of him.

“Whoever knows that his brother is committing a sin not leading to death, let him ask, and life will be given to the one whose sin does not lead to death. There is sin leading to death; I do not say that anyone should pray concerning it. Every injustice is sin, and there is sin leading to death.

“We know that everyone born of God does not sin, but God’s generation preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him. We know that we are from God, and that the whole world lies in the evil one. And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and be in his true Son. He is the true God and eternal life (1 John 5:9–20).”

Preach these things, brothers; announce them to everyone. Exhort one another, be perfect, and always rejoice. Pursue peace with all, and the God of peace and love will be with you. To God our Father be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## ALSO, A LETTER OF POPE EVARISTUS

That Christ is the head and bridegroom of the Church, and how priests ought to love their churches and the churches ought to love them.

[Col. 0083]

[Col. 0083C] Evaristus, bishop of the city of Rome, sends greetings in the Lord to all the brothers joined together throughout Egypt.

We ought, brothers, to think and act as one, so that—as we read—it may be shown that we have one heart and one soul. For we know, as we have received from the Fathers, that Christ is the head and that we are his members. He is the bridegroom, and the Church is the bride, whose children we are. Therefore we have one Father in heaven, the Lord.

Priests, however, serve as Christ’s ambassadors in the Church. And just as his bride, that is, the Church, is joined to him, so Churches are joined to bishops, each according to its proper portion. And just as a man ought not to neglect his wife, but ought to love and chastely guard her, so a bishop ought to guard, love, and wisely govern the Church, and all the more [Col. 0083D]. And just as a wife who is under her husband’s authority ought to obey her husband, and love and cherish him, so much rather ought the Church in all things to obey her bishop, and love and cherish him as she ought her own soul, because the former is done carnally, the latter spiritually.

And just as a man ought not to commit adultery against his wife, so neither ought a bishop against his Church: that is, he must not abandon the one to whom he has been consecrated, except through unavoidable necessity or through an apostolic or canonical transfer, and join himself to another for the sake of ambition. And just as a wife is not permitted to abandon her husband and, while he is alive, enter into marriage with another, or commit adultery against him—even if her husband has committed fornication—but, according to the Apostle, must either be reconciled to her husband or remain unmarried, so it is not permitted to a Church to abandon or separate herself from her bishop in order to accept another while he is alive.
