We also forbid foreign proceedings and judgments, because it is unworthy that those who ought to have provincial judges chosen from among themselves should be judged by outsiders. We have cut off every opportunity for criticism from every side. Mindful of heavenly discipline, we extend our right hand to all who fall, raise from the brink of ruin as many as we can, and desire with all our strength to provide the aid of defense.

Certainly, even if the mind is conscious of what is right, the one who becomes a cause of danger to others is worthy of punishment. [Col. 0110B] But whoever persecutes an innocent person or brother by any means drives the blade of death into his own throat, as the divine and blessed herald says:

“Do not disparage, lest you be uprooted; do not accuse, lest you be accused; do not judge, lest you be judged, for by the judgment with which you judge, judgment will be rendered against you.”

No one is believed to hate us if he is not harmed by our report; for the Lord says:

“Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand, and every knowledge or rule divided against itself will not stand.”

Therefore it is necessary that you receive salutary instruction in harmony, while I exhort you to do nothing through contention, but to be of one mind in every effort of devotion and to obey the divine and apostolic constitutions. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Magnus and Camerinus.

## Letter of Pope Hyginus to the Athenians

[Col. 0109]

[Col. 0109C] Pope Hyginus to the Athenians: greetings.

I have great confidence in you, brothers, and much cause for glory because of you. I am filled with consolation and abound in joy amid all our tribulation. For I am troubled whenever I hear concerning you what ought not to be. But I am consoled whenever I learn that those things are being done among you which good Christians ought to fulfill.

“Do not enter into partnership with unbelievers.” Therefore the teacher of the nations speaks, saying:

“What partnership has righteousness with iniquity? What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as the Lord says: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they will be my people’” (II Corinthians VI, 14, 16).

For if God did not spare the angels who sinned, but dragged them down in chains into hell and handed them over to Tartarus to be kept for punishment at the judgment; and if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, the eighth person, a herald of righteousness, bringing the flood upon the world of the ungodly; and if he reduced the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes and condemned them to destruction, making them an example of those who would act impiously—what do you think will happen to the unjust and ungodly who persist in their wickedness?

But he rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the conduct of the wicked, from their outrage; for he was righteous in what he saw and heard, living among those [Col. 0110C] who day after day tormented his righteous soul by their unlawful deeds. God knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unjust for punishment on the day of judgment—especially those who, following the flesh in lust for defilement and scorning condemnation, are bold and self-willed, and do not fear to form sects, blaspheming.

Therefore we cannot receive one who shares another’s error, who does not depart from the path of his own purpose, or one who is disobedient to the commands of the apostolic See; but we permit among the faithful those who believe or obey the commands of the holy Fathers, because there must be a great distinction between the faithful and the unbelievers.

If God did not spare the righteous, brothers, what do you suppose will happen to us sinners? Guard yourselves from every defilement of flesh and body, so that you may be saved on the day of the Lord’s coming.

But let this one thing not be hidden from you, as the Apostle says:

“Dearest ones, one day with the Lord is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day. The Lord is not slow concerning his promises, but patiently waits because of you, not wishing any to perish, but all to return to repentance.”

But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. On that day the heavens will pass away with great force, while the elements will be dissolved by heat. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, through which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will melt in the heat of fire?

But we await new heavens and a new earth according to his promises, in which righteousness dwells.

May the God of all grace, who called you into his eternal [Col. 0112A] glory in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little, himself perfect, confirm, and strengthen you. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Magnus and Camerinus.

## The Decrees of Pope Pius Begin

That Easter should be celebrated on Sunday. (In the year 147, during the reign of Antoninus Verus.)

[Col. 0111]

[Col. 0111B] Pius, archbishop of the apostolic See, to all the churches remaining in the same faith and teaching as we do.

We give thanks to God, brothers, because your faith grows and the charity of each and every one of you toward one another abounds, so that we ourselves glory in you among the churches of God.

Take care, brothers—take care that no one deceive you, walking in a self-imposed humility and worship of angels, dwelling on things he has not seen, vainly inflated by the thought of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its bonds and connections, grows with the growth of the Lord.

Rather, clothe yourselves as God’s chosen, holy and beloved people, with compassion, kindness, humility, modesty, and patience, supporting one another [Col. 0111C] and forgiving one another if anyone has a complaint against another. Just as Christ forgave you, so also should you.

Moreover, we want you to know that the Lord’s Easter is to be celebrated annually on Sunday with solemn observance. In those times Hermes, the teacher of faith and the Scriptures, shone among us. Although we celebrate that same Easter on the aforesaid day, and some people doubted the matter, an angel of the Lord nevertheless appeared to Hermes in the form of a shepherd, to strengthen their souls, and commanded him that Easter be celebrated by all on Sunday at its proper time. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we instruct you also that all must observe the same practice, because we too observe it, and you must not in any way dissent from the head.

Take careful heed, all of you, that no one deceive you through any astrology, philosophy, or empty deceit according to human tradition and the elemental principles of the world, and not according to Christ and the true tradition.

“For in Christ the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power.”

Without doubt, whoever acts against God’s commandments sins, as does whoever gives consent to one who is in error.

He commanded this holy apostolic See to be the head of all the churches, saying to the chief of the apostles, Peter:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever is loosed on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matthew XVI, 18).

For what benefit is it to someone that he is not defiled by another’s error if he gives consent to one who is in error? The sheep must not rebuke their shepherd, nor may the people accuse the bishop, nor may the crowd censure him, because the disciple is not above the teacher, nor the servant above his lord.

Bishops, however, are to be judged by God, who chose them as eyes for himself; they are not to be rebuked, accused, or torn apart by their subjects or by people of corrupt life. The Lord himself gave an example of this when he personally, and not through another, drove the priests who were selling and buying out of the temple, and overturned the tables of the money-changers with his own whip and expelled them from the temple.

And elsewhere he speaks through the prophet, saying:

“God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes among the gods.”

But if anyone turns backward from his own purpose and willingly transgresses the command of the apostolic See, he becomes infamous. Therefore the reproofs of those who are suspect in the true faith must be rejected. Their faith and conduct must first be examined, and only afterward are those who appear irreproachable to be received, not before; for, as the voice of Truth bears witness:

“A good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart, and an evil man brings forth evil things from the evil treasure. For from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”

Therefore each person’s character, reputation, and life must be examined at the outset, because the good are always harassed by the wicked. Although the good are mixed with the wicked in the Church, they are scarcely found to be in agreement, since their thought, will, and action are unlike.

It does a person no good to fast and pray and perform other religious works unless the mind is recalled from wickedness [Col. 0112D] and the tongue is restrained from slander. Hence the prophet says:

“Restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit; turn away from evil and do good.”

No one who does good wishes to harm another by word or deed. How much less should a faithful person come under suspicion of saying or doing what he does not wish to suffer himself! For every suspicion ought rather to be rejected than approved or accepted.

“For charity does not seek what is its own,” but what belongs to others, because the cause of one must not be preferred to that of many.

“Pursue charity; strive for spiritual gifts. Charity is patient and kind. Charity is not jealous, does not act improperly, is not inflated, is not ambitious, does not seek what is its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.”

I always ask you to reject what is worse and perfect what is better, because we have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know [Col. 0114A] what has been given to us by God; and pursue these things without distinction. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Clarus and Severus.

## Letter of Pope Pius Sent to the Italians

[Col. 0113]

[Col. 0113A] Pius, archbishop of the city of Rome, to the Italian brothers: greetings in the Lord.

You know, brothers, that we are God’s cultivated field; therefore we must be his fellow workers, according to the grace that he gave us. If we neglect to be this, there is no doubt that we will be condemned. But if we labor in his service to the best of our ability, become his true fellow workers, and strive to fulfill his will, we will certainly be enriched by him, because, as the Apostle says, the day of the Lord will disclose what each person’s work is like, and fire will test it.

It has been reported to the apostolic See that there are disputes and rivalries among you, and that some people apply estates devoted to divine use to human uses and remove them from the Lord God to whom they were given, so that they may serve their own purposes.

Therefore the insult of every such usurpation must be driven away by all, lest estates dedicated to heavenly mysteries be harassed by certain intruders. If anyone should presume to do so, let him be regarded as a sacrilegious person and judged as such.

We have also heard that those who do this persecute the clergy and the priests of the Lord and defame them, thus adding evil to evil and becoming worse. They do not understand that the Church of the Lord consists in the priests and grows into a temple of God.

Just as the one who devastates the Church of God and strips and invades its estates and offerings becomes sacrilegious, so the one who persecutes its priests is guilty of sacrilege and is judged sacrilegious.

Strive, brothers, for the better spiritual gifts. Do not do such things, nor associate or consent with those who do them, because not only those who do such things are guilty of this crime, but also those who consent to the perpetrators 26. It is not, then, that fornication is a graver sin than sacrilege; rather, just as the sin committed against God is greater than that committed against a human being, so it is graver to commit sacrilege than to fornicate.

Concerning such people the Apostle says:

“And you are inflated, and you did not rather mourn, so that the one who did this deed might be removed from your midst. For I, [Col. 0113D] absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as though present, the one who acted in this way: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled, and my spirit with you, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? Purge out the old leaven, as the Apostle says, so that you may be a new dough, just as you are unleavened. For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, [Col. 0114A] not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

“I wrote to you in my letter,” says the same Apostle, “not to associate with fornicators—not entirely with the fornicators of this world, or with the greedy, or the rapacious, or those who serve idols; otherwise you would have had to leave this world. But now I wrote to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother if he is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or is a slanderer, or a drunkard, or rapacious; with such a person you must not even eat. [Col. 0114B]

“For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Are you not judging those who are inside? God will judge those who are outside. Remove the evil person from among yourselves.

“Does any one of you dare, when he has a case against another, to be judged before the unjust and not before the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we will judge angels, to say nothing of secular affairs? [Col. 0114C]

“If, then, you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are despised in the Church. I say this to your shame: is there no wise person among you who can judge between his brothers? Instead, brother goes to court against brother, and this before unbelievers. Indeed, it is already altogether a fault in you that you have lawsuits among yourselves. Why do you not rather suffer injustice? Why do you not rather endure fraud? Instead, you commit injustice and practice fraud, and this against your brothers.

“Or do you not know that the unjust will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived. Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God. And such were some of you; but you were washed, you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (I Corinthians V, 2–13; VI, 1–11).

[Col. 0114D] For the rest, without prejudice in all things to the apostolic authority, let whatever pertains to the observance of religion be heard in its proper places and by the synods of its own diocese. If any priest or other cleric is disobedient to his bishop, or plots against him, or insults or slanders him, and this can be proved, let him immediately be handed over to the court. Whoever commits an injustice must receive what he has unjustly done.

“Bad company corrupts good morals. Awake to righteousness and do not sin” (I Corinthians XV, 33–34).

Given on the Ides of March, in the consulship of Clarus and Severus, for the fourth time.

## The Decrees of Pope Anicetus Begin

Concerning the ordination of archbishops and other bishops, and concerning appeals by lesser persons to the sees of greater bishops or to the Roman Church. (In the year 164, during the reign of Lucius Antoninus Commodus.)

[Col. 0115]

[Col. 0115A] Anicetus to all the churches established throughout the provinces of Gaul: greetings in the Lord.

It is beyond doubt that God is the author of good works and spiritual endeavors; he stirs the minds of good people and assists their actions. This became clearly evident to us when, despite the great distances between our regions, your hearts were united in one purpose, and the answers you desired were conveyed not by the letter of one person but by the letters of many.

Regarding the ordinations of bishops, about which you wished to consult us, we have already found certain decrees in the ordinations of our holy predecessor Anacletus. For we know that the most blessed James, who was called “the Just” and was also named the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles Peter, James, and John. If so eminent a man was ordained bishop by no fewer than three apostles, it is altogether clear that they, following the form established by the Lord, handed down that a bishop ought to be ordained by no fewer than three bishops.

As the number of bishops increases, however, even more should be assembled unless necessity intervenes. That is, if an archbishop dies and another has been elected for ordination as archbishop, all the bishops of the same province shall assemble at the metropolitan see, so that he may be ordained by all. It is necessary that the man who is to preside over all of them be elected and ordained by all of them. The other provincial bishops, if necessity requires, may, with the consent of the rest, be consecrated by three bishops at the command of the archbishop.

[Col. 0115C]

But it is better if he himself, together with all the others, chooses the man who is worthy and all together consecrate him as bishop. Although this has been granted under the pressure of necessity, nevertheless what was stated and commanded concerning the consecration of an archbishop—that all his suffragan bishops are to ordain him—may in no way be altered. For the man who presides over them must be established by all the bishops over whom he presides.

If anyone presumes otherwise, it is undoubtedly without legal force, because his ordination, having been carried out contrary to this, will be invalid. The archbishop himself, moreover, shall conduct nothing concerning their cases or other common matters, in accordance with the statutes of the apostles, without the counsel of all of them; nor shall they act without him except insofar as the matter concerns their own parishes, since the Most High rejoices in such harmony and glories in his members.

[Col. 0115D]

Let no archbishops be called primates except those who hold the chief cities whose bishops the apostles and their successors established, according to ecclesiastical rule, as patriarchs and primates—unless some people should thereafter be converted to the faith for whom, because of their great number, it is necessary to establish a primate.

[Col. 0116A]

The others who have obtained different metropolitan sees shall be called not primates but metropolitans. If any metropolitan should become arrogant and wish to conduct affairs concerning them or other matters without the presence or counsel of all the bishops of his province, except only those matters pertaining to his own parish, he shall be strictly corrected by all, so that he may not thereafter dare to presume such things.

But if he appears incorrigible and disobedient to them, his contumacy shall be reported to this apostolic see, to which the judgment of all episcopal cases has been commanded to belong, so that punishment may be inflicted upon him and the others may be afraid. If, however, because of excessive distance, an unfavorable time, or the difficulty of the journey, it should be burdensome to bring his case to this see, then the case shall be brought before his primate, and shall be judged by him with the authority of this holy see.

[Col. 0116B]

Likewise, if any bishop regards a metropolitan with suspicion, he shall be heard before the primate of the diocese or before this apostolic see.

“Let the one who is greater among you, according to the Lord’s command, be your servant, and the greater you are in all things, humble yourself.”

Most beloved, do not quarrel among yourselves, and let no one seek to be greater. Rather, in accordance with the Apostle, love one another, “because love is from God, and everyone who loves is born from God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.”

“Feed,” says the chief of the apostles, “the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly according to God, not for the sake of shameful gain but eagerly; not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock from the heart. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory” (I Petr. V, 24).

And according to another apostle: “Brothers, remember the words that were spoken beforehand by the apostles of Jesus Christ, who told you that in the last time there will be mockers, walking according to their desires in ungodliness. These are the ones who separate themselves, sensual, not having the Spirit. But you, beloved, building yourselves up upon your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. And some, indeed, rebuke when judging them; others save, snatching them from the fire. On others have mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh” (Jude 17–23).

[Col. 0116D]

Brothers, prohibit throughout all the churches of your regions that clerics—who ought to be examples of virtue, uprightness, chastity, and dignity to laypeople and the simple, and who ought prudently to present themselves to the less instructed as a sign of a purer life for imitation—wear long hair. Rather, they should shave the top of the head in the shape of a sphere, because just as they ought to be distinguished in their conduct, so also they ought to appear distinguished in their tonsure and in their entire manner of dress.

[Col. 0118A]

We send these things to you, brothers, as you requested, to be observed, and we command that they be observed, “so that at the name of Jesus every knee may bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father,” to whom be honor and dominion forever and ever.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Gallianus and Rufinus.

## The Decrees of Pope Soter Begin

Concerning the faith. (In the year of the Lord 168, during the reign of Antoninus Commodus.)

[Col. 0117]

[Col. 0117B]

SOTER, archbishop of the apostolic see, sends greetings in the Lord to all the Campanians.

You ought to rejoice, brothers, that by the grace granted by God you are called members of the household of the Lord and exercise the dignity of his priesthood. Now I ask you to be willing to labor for the peoples entrusted to you and to strive to bring fruitful sheaves back to the Lord.

For the apostle Paul speaks in this way about the faith, saying: “What he had promised beforehand,” he says, “through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 2).

Likewise, he says to the Galatians: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made subject to the law” (Galatians IV, 4).

And to the Philippians: “Made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Philippians II, 7).

And in the thirtieth psalm: “My strength failed in poverty, and my bones were troubled, and I became a reproach to all my enemies” (Psalm XXX, 11).

Likewise there: “I have been forgotten as one dead from the heart. I have become like a ruined vessel” (ibid., 13).

And in the seventieth: “I have become like a portent to many, but you are a strong helper” (Psalm LXX, 7).

And in the seventy-second: “I have become like a beast of burden before you, yet I am always with you” (Psalm LXXII, 22).

And in the eighty-sixth: “Mother Zion will say: ‘A human being, and a human being, was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her’” (Psalm LXXXVI, 5).

And in the seventy-seventh: “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm LXXVII, 5).

[Col. 0117D]

And in the hundred and eighth: “I became a reproach to them; they saw me and shook their heads” (Psalm CVIII, 15).

And in the hundred and first: “I kept vigil and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Psalm CI, 5).

And in the Gospel: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

Therefore the Son is said to have been made according to the flesh. According to divinity, however, he is nowhere said to have been made by the Father, but to have been begotten. For while the Father speaks, the Son speaks; and when the Son speaks, heavenly testimonies prove that the Father is speaking in him, as the apostle Paul bears witness, saying: “In many parts and in many ways, long ago God spoke to the fathers through the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son.”

And in order to show that this same Son spoke apart from a command of the Father, we produce evidence from the book of the prophet Isaiah:

“This says the Lord: ‘On that day my people shall know that I am the one who was speaking in my servants the prophets, proclaiming the good news of peace; and behold, I am present.’

“Likewise there: ‘I am the Lord who speak righteousness and announce truth.’

“Likewise there: ‘I considered, and I spoke, and I brought forth, and I created and made.’

“And the Apostle: ‘Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?’” (2 Corinthians XIII, 3).

And in the hundred and eighteenth psalm: “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not put to shame” (Psalm CXVIII, 46).

And the Lord himself says in the Gospel to the blind man whom he had enlightened: “You have seen him, and the one who speaks with you is he” (Joan. IX, 36).

And he says to the Samaritan woman: “I am the one who speaks with you” (John IV, 26).

And to the disciples: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John VI, 64).

And to the Father: “I am coming to you, and I speak these things in the world.”

And again he said to the Jews: “I speak to you, and you do not listen. If another comes, you will listen to him.”

And again: “The Lord spoke these things in the treasury while teaching in the temple. And no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come.”

Behold, in all these statements quoted above, the Son is not taught to have spoken at the Father’s command; rather, he exercised his own speech in speaking.

The prophet Isaiah also says: “Thus says the Lord: ‘I made the earth by my understanding, and the human being upon it; I established the heavens with my hand; I commanded all the stars to shine in heaven.’

[Col. 0118D]

“Likewise there: ‘I established all my counsel, and everything that I considered, I myself made.’

“Likewise there: ‘Thus says the Lord, who established heaven and earth, and made and founded it.’

“Likewise there: ‘I am the first, and I am forever; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established the heavens.’

“And in Jeremiah: ‘I made the earth by my great strength and by my uplifted arm.’

“Likewise there: ‘The Lord made the earth by his great power, established the inhabited world in wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens and placed the sound of the waters in heaven.’”

Defend, most beloved, I ask you, the steadfast condition of the Church against malicious people, so that the right hand of Christ may defend you forever.

Given on the Nones of May, in the fourth consulship of Rusticus and Aquilinus.

## Letter of Pope Soter

[Col. 0119]

[Col. 0119A]

To the most beloved holy bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy, Soter the pope.

We are instructed by divine commands and apostolic admonitions to watch over the condition of all the churches with tireless devotion; and if anything anywhere is found deserving of reproach, to restore it quickly from the incompetence of ignorance and the usurpation of presumption.

It has been reported to the apostolic see that consecrated women or nuns among you touch sacred vessels or consecrated cloths and carry incense around the altars. No rightly thinking person doubts that all these practices are full of reproach and disgrace.

Therefore, by the authority of this holy see, we judge that you must cut all these things out completely as quickly as you can, and we command that this plague be swiftly removed, lest it spread more widely throughout all the provinces. For the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians XI, 2).

For the Church is that virgin, the bride of one husband, Christ. She allows herself to be corrupted by no error or dishonorable reproach, so that throughout the whole world there may be for us the integrity of one chaste communion.

Therefore rise up, most beloved, with the Lord, and stand beside him, putting on the weapons of the Spirit against those who attack his faith; and let the spirit of wisdom be tested—that is, let their words be tested to see whether they are from God.

For it is written in Jeremiah: “I have appointed you as a tester among my strong people, and you shall know, act, and test their way” (Jeremiah VI, 27).

[Col. 0119B]

For the vigilance of such a great sacrament of discerning wisdom is greatly necessary to us. It reveals the hidden things of darkness, for the investigation and examination of this matter, because what is concealed and hidden is scarcely grasped, since deceitful wickedness exists in such a way that it cunningly flatters itself with the appearance of piety, so that it may be able to escape the notice of the mind that investigates it.

Knowing this, the blessed Apostle says: “For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ” (2 Corinthians XI, 13).

But it is no wonder if Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light, if his ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness; their end will be according to their works.

The Lord also warns us beforehand about this, saying: “Beware of false prophets who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves; you will know them by their fruits” (Matthew VII, 15–16).

Therefore, with one accord and with your whole heart, first of all make supplication concerning such a question, saying with David: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law; your word is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths” (Psalm CXVIII, 18, 105).

For, as the blessed prophet Daniel says, “wisdom and strength belong to him” (Daniel II, 20). He gives wisdom to the wise, knowledge to those who understand, and discipline. He reveals deep and hidden things, knows what is situated in darkness, and light is with him.

“Because you gave me wisdom and strength, and showed me what I asked of you.”

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourth consulship of Ceticus and Clerus.

## The Decrees of Pope Eleutherius Begin

(In the year of the Lord 177, during the reign of Antoninus Commodus.)

[Col. 0119]

[Col. 0119C]

ELEUTHERIUS, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the churches throughout the provinces of Gaul that serve the Lord.

By the great gift of God’s mercy, the joys of the whole Catholic Church have multiplied, since we have learned that many peoples are hastening to the service of the Lord. For this reason we judged it necessary to instruct you, so that you may not irrationally reject the foods which, as we hear, you avoid.

You know, brothers, that the Lawgiver taught that everything God created was very good; and Truth itself says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth” (Matthew XV, 11).

From this it is clear that one ought not to reject the common foods which God has provided for nourishment to his faithful.

And in the Acts of the Apostles, we read the following concerning clean foods:

[Col. 0119D]

“On the following day, while three household servants were making their journey with Peter and approaching the city [reading uncertain], Peter went up to the upper room to pray, about the sixth hour. And when he was hungry, he wished to taste something. While they were preparing food, a trance came upon him; and he saw heaven opened and a certain vessel descending, like a great linen cloth, lowered by its four corners from heaven to earth. In it were all four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth and birds of heaven. And a voice came to him: ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’

“But Peter said: ‘By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean.’

“And the voice spoke to him again a second time: ‘What God has purified, you must not call common.’

“This happened three times, and immediately the vessel was taken up into heaven” (Act. X, 9, 16).

As for accusations against clerics, about which we have been consulted: because it is difficult to bring all their accusations to the apostolic see, only final judgments concerning bishops shall be brought here and settled by the authority of this holy see, as has already been established by the apostles and their successors with the agreement of many bishops.

Nor may others be appointed over their churches or ordained in them before their affairs have been justly settled here. For although it is permitted to discuss their accusations or charges before provincial bishops, metropolitans, and primates, it is not permitted to settle them otherwise than has been stated above.

[Col. 0120D]

The cases of other clerics, however, may both be discussed and justly settled before provincial bishops, metropolitans, and primates. The judge must nevertheless examine everything thoroughly and investigate the order of events through a complete inquiry, allowing sufficient opportunity for questioning, presenting evidence, and adding further material, so that the proceeding there may be fully confined to the claims of both parties.

Nor should the judge hasten to confront the litigants with his judgment until, after everything has been completed, they have nothing further to present concerning the matter in dispute. The case should be discussed until the truth of the matter is discovered.

He ought to question them frequently, lest something that should properly be added remain inadvertently omitted. Adequate intervals must be granted for investigation, lest anything appear to have been done too hastily by either party, since many things arise through concealment.

[Col. 0121B]

Nevertheless, nothing shall be done without a lawful and suitable accuser. For our Lord Jesus Christ knew that Judas was a thief, but because he was not accused, he was not expelled. Whatever he did among the apostles remained valid by reason of the dignity of his ministry. If secular laws require accusers, how much more do ecclesiastical rules!

For they teach what earthly and human things are, and what ecclesiastical and heavenly things are.

Concerning accusations brought by fellow provincials, it is established as follows: if anyone believes that a particular cleric should be prosecuted for any crimes, he shall pursue his action in the province in which the person being prosecuted resides, and he shall not suppose that the man may be dragged elsewhere or farther away for judgment.

But if the person who has been prosecuted regards the judge as suspect, he may appeal.

[Col. 0121C]

Let the judges of the Church also beware of delivering a judgment in the absence of the person whose case is being discussed, because it will be invalid and will even give grounds for treating the matter as accomplished.

No accusation or word of a traitor shall be heard. For no one can know a debtor more fully than the one who has suffered his injury and wickedness.

[Col. 0122A]

Those who are oppressed must therefore be assisted by everyone in every case. All these matters must be observed with the greatest care.

Nor should the accusation of lesser persons, and even less that of bishops, be readily accepted. The Lord says: “You shall not follow the crowd in doing evil” (Exodus XXIII, 2). And elsewhere: “You shall not receive a false report” (ibid., 1).

And in Chronicles it is written: “The Lord searches all hearts” (1 Chronicles XXVIII, 9), and he knows every thought. A human being sees the face, but God sees the heart.

And elsewhere it is written: “No one may be condemned by human examination whom God has reserved for his own judgment.”

Therefore, brothers, strive through patience to restrain all the weight and circumstances of the adversaries’ evidence, knowing that such people are overturned and condemned by their own mouths because they commit offenses. Those who accuse or harass their brothers do not love them; rather, they neglect them and sin. The Apostle says: “Love of neighbor does no harm” (Romans XIII, 10).

And elsewhere: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?”

For we, humble in heart, are wisely bound together with you by the bond of love, with the Lord as our helper, in matters that are right. While vigorously defending the Catholic religion in all things, we do not neglect to resist the wicked properly. Hence it has been said: “To neglect, when you are able to drive away the perverse, is nothing other than to encourage them; and the person who ceases to oppose an evident crime is not free from the reproach of hidden complicity.”

For this reason the universal Church has been entrusted to you by Christ Jesus, so that you may labor for everyone and not neglect to bring aid to all. A brother who helps his brother will be exalted, and the one who mocks will be scattered.

Therefore always raise up the oppressed and correct the unruly, so that weeds may not be able to choke the Lord’s harvest.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Paternus and Bardua.

## 28. The Decrees of Pope Victor Begin

Concerning Easter and other matters. (In the year of the Lord 189, during the reign of Helvius Pertinax.)

[Col. 0121]

[Col. 0121C]

VICTOR, archbishop of the Roman and universal Church, sends greetings in the Lord to Theophilus the bishop and to all the brothers serving the Lord in Alexandria.

[Col. 0121D]

I have great cause for rejoicing, most beloved brothers, because, as we desire, the light of evangelical clarity has been revealed by God’s grace, the night of pernicious error has already been driven away from the Church for the most part, and the fruit of the stewardship entrusted to us is increasing and being enlarged in the Lord.

Our predecessors already established that the solemnity of holy Easter must be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, and we command that it be solemnly celebrated on that same day, because it is not fitting that the members should differ from the head or act contrary to it.

From the fourteenth moon of the first month through the twenty-first day of that same month, the same festival shall be celebrated. At that time Catholic baptism is also to be celebrated. Nevertheless, if necessity arises or danger of death threatens, gentiles coming to the faith shall be baptized wherever and whenever the need occurs—whether in a river, at sea, or in springs—provided that the confession of Christian belief has been clearly expressed.

Their promises made in baptism must also be observed with the greatest care, so that they may be found faithful and not unbelieving. Those who are marked with the stigma of unbelief are made infamous and are in no way counted among the faithful.

These statutes must not be overthrown by any wickedness or altered by any innovation, because secular causes have one kind of rationale and divine causes another.

We have heard that different judgments are being made among you and that uncertain matters are being judged. Most beloved, let us in no way judge uncertain matters until the Lord comes, who will bring hidden things to light, illuminate the things concealed in darkness, and reveal the purposes of hearts.

For even if things are true, they are not to be believed unless they are established by manifest judgments, unless they are proved by an open judicial decision, unless they are made public according to judicial procedure.

Likewise, it has been reported to the apostolic see that you are judging matters which you are not permitted to settle apart from our authority concerning episcopal cases. It is therefore clear that, from the time of the apostles onward, it was decided that if a bishop accused or judged by bishops of his province has a case, he may freely appeal to and approach the pontiff of the apostolic see. The pontiff shall arrange for the case to be reconsidered either personally or through his representatives.

[Col. 0123B]

While the pontiff conducts the case at a second hearing, no other bishop shall be placed or ordained in his position. For although the bishops of the province may investigate the case of an accused pontiff, they are not permitted to settle it without consulting the Roman pontiff, since it was said by the Lord to the blessed apostle Peter himself and by no other: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”

And elsewhere it is written in the apostolic constitutions: “If anyone thinks that he is being oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the patriarch or primate of the diocese, or before the see of the universal apostolic Church.”

Brothers, such presumption is nothing other than transgressing the boundaries established by the apostles and their successors and violating their decrees. For, as it is written, they are blamed because they presume to judge bishops otherwise than the pope of the apostolic see has decreed.

And who is he who judges the one whom the Lord wished to reserve for judgment by himself and by this holy see?

For the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah:

“Lord God, my helper, therefore I have not been confounded; therefore I have set my face like the hardest rock, and I know that I shall not be confounded. He is near who justifies me. Who will contradict me? Let us stand together. Who is my adversary? Let him approach me. Behold, the Lord God is my helper. Who is the one who will condemn me? Behold, they will all be worn away like a garment; the moth will consume them.

“Which of you fears the Lord and hears the voice of his servant? Who has walked in darkness and has no light? Let him hope in the name of the Lord and rely upon his God.

“Behold, all you who kindle a fire, girded with flames: walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled. This has happened to you from my hand; you shall sleep in sorrows.

“Listen to me, you who follow what is just and seek the Lord. Look to the rock from which you were hewn and to the cavern of the pit from which you were cut. Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you, because I called him alone, blessed him, and multiplied him.

“Therefore the Lord will comfort Zion and will comfort all her ruins. He will make her wilderness like delights and her solitude like the garden of the Lord. Joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise.

“Listen to me, my people, and my tribe, hear me. For a law will go forth from me, and my judgment will rest as a light for the peoples. My righteous one is near; my savior has gone forth, and my arm will judge the peoples. The islands will wait for me and will hope in my arm.

“Lift your eyes to heaven and look down beneath the earth, because the heavens will melt like smoke, the earth will wear away like a garment, and its inhabitants will perish in the same way. But my salvation will be forever, and my justice will not fail.

“Listen to me, you who know what is just, my people, whose law is in their hearts. Do not fear the reproach of human beings or their blasphemies. For as a garment, so the worm will consume them; and as wool, so the moth will devour them. But my salvation will be forever, and my justice from generation to generation” (Isa. L, 7, 21; LI, 1, 2).

Many enticements and many vanities of this world must be resisted, so that the integrity of true love and self-restraint may be attained. For the Lord does not wish anyone to perish but all to be saved.

I am confident that, with the Lord’s help, you will make progress in correcting or defending these matters.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth consulship of Commodus and Gratianus.

## The Letter of the Above-Mentioned to the Africans

Concerning the matters discussed above.

[Col. 0123]

[Col. 0123D]

VICTOR, archbishop of the city of the Roman Church, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Africa.

The restoration of the human race, immutably preordained, always remained in the eternal plan of God; but the order of temporal events to be carried out by our Lord Jesus Christ took its beginning from the disposition of the divine Word.

Therefore, brothers, you ought to be of one mind and mutually provide assistance: you should not differ in right faith or in the divine sacraments, but be harmonious. For although you are few in comparison with the wicked, if you are united, you will easily overcome those who lie in wait for you, with the Lord’s help. But if, God forbid, you are divided, you will not overcome; rather, you will be overcome.

For it has been reported to the apostolic see that some of you wish to harm your brothers and strive for their downfall; likewise, that you differ in the sacraments, and that quarrels and rivalries arise among you on this account.

We command you to turn away from these dissensions, to agree in all these matters, and to provide mutual assistance.

[Col. 0125A]

For if you quickly neglect to do this and do not strive to be reconciled with one another, you may be certain that you will be expelled from communion with the apostolic see and the whole Church.

Nor do you consider, most beloved, how the Lord threatened such people through the prophet Isaiah, saying:

“The Lord spoke this word to them: ‘The earth mourned and faded away; the inhabited world languished and faded away; the height of the people of the earth languished. The earth was polluted by its inhabitants, because they transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, and broke the everlasting covenant.

“‘Therefore a curse will devour the earth, and its inhabitants will sin. For this reason its cultivators will go mad, and few people will be left. The vintage mourned; the vine languished. All who rejoiced in heart groaned. The joy of tambourines ceased; the sound of those who rejoiced rested; the sweetness of the lyre fell silent.

“‘They will not drink wine with song; the drink will be bitter to those who drink it. The city of vanity has been crushed; every house has been closed, with no one entering. There will be a cry over wine in the streets; all joy has been deserted; the joy of the earth has been removed. Solitude has been left in the city, and calamity will oppress the gates.

“‘For these things will be in the midst of the earth and in the midst of the peoples, as when the few olives that remain are shaken from the olive tree, and the grapes after the vintage is finished. These will lift up their voice and praise; when the Lord is glorified, they will whinny from the sea.

“‘For this reason glorify the Lord in teachings, and the name of the Lord God of Israel in the islands of the sea’” (Isa. XXIV, 3, 15).

And the Lord, in the prayer that he taught his disciples to pray, said: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name.”

The name of the Lord is hallowed in good and just people, and it is blasphemed in wicked people. Truth itself says: “If you offer your gift at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift.”

No one, however, may abandon evangelical teaching and yet enjoy priestly honor.

Given on the Kalends of September, in the fourth consulship of Lateranus and Rufinus.

## The Decrees of Pope Zepherinus Begin

(In the year of the Lord 208, during the reign of the emperor Severus.)

[Col. 0125]

[Col. 0125C]

Zepherinus, archbishop of the city of Rome, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Sicily.

We must remember the divine grace toward us, which, through the mercy of its favor, raised us to the dignity of the priesthood for this reason: that, adhering to its commands and stationed as watchmen among its priests, we may prohibit what is unlawful and teach what must be followed.

Just as night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly iniquity does not obscure the minds of the faithful who cling to the firmament of holy Scripture.

Therefore you ought to meditate upon the Scriptures and carefully attend to the divine commands contained in them, lest you appear to be transgressors of God’s law rather than fulfillers of it.

Patriarchs or primates who investigate an accused bishop must not deliver a final sentence before they have been supported by apostolic authority and before the accused has confessed himself guilty or has been convicted by innocent witnesses examined according to ecclesiastical rule.

Such witnesses must not be fewer in number than those disciples whom the Lord commanded to be chosen as assistants to the apostles—that is, seventy-two.

Slanderers must also be rooted out by divine authority. We remove the instigators of enemies from episcopal accusation or testimony. No one of the highest rank may be attacked or destroyed by accusations from lesser persons. In a doubtful matter, a certain sentence must not be pronounced, nor may any judgment be upheld unless it has been conducted according to due order.

No one may be judged in his absence, because both divine and human laws prohibit this.

The accusers of these men must be entirely free from suspicion, because the Lord wished his pillars to stand firmly, not to be shaken by just anyone.

No one shall be bound by a sentence pronounced by a judge who is not his judge, since secular laws likewise command that this be done.

For any accused bishop may, if necessary, choose twelve judges, by whom his case may be justly judged. He shall not be heard, excommunicated, or judged before those judges have themselves been chosen; and after he has been lawfully summoned to the assembly of his bishops, his case shall first be justly heard and reasonably discerned by them.

[Col. 0126C]

The conclusion of his case, however, shall be brought to the apostolic see, so that it may be settled there. It must not be settled beforehand, as was formerly established by the apostles or their successors, before it has been supported by the authority of that see.

Everyone must appeal and hasten to it—especially the oppressed—as to a mother, so that they may be nourished at her breasts, defended by her authority, and relieved from their oppressions, because a mother cannot and must not forget her son.

29 For the judgments of bishops, and the greater causes of the Church, are to be settled with other bishops by the apostolic see and by no other, as the apostles and their holy successors established. For although bishops may pass judgment on others, nevertheless it was said to the blessed apostle Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.” The other privileges likewise that have been granted solely to this holy see are inserted in the decrees of the apostles and their successors, together with many others agreeing with them. For the seventy apostles established these judgments together with many other bishops [Col. 0127A] and decreed that they should be observed.

For it is a sin rashly to judge the hidden things of another’s heart, and it is unjust to condemn on suspicion one whose works appear to be nothing but good, since God alone is judge of those things unknown to human beings. He knows the secrets of the heart, and no one else. Unjust judgments must therefore be avoided by everyone, but especially by the servants of God. A servant of God ought not to quarrel or condemn anyone.

Bishops must be borne by the peoples, the clergy, and the servants of the Lord, so that through the exercise of endurance they may sustain temporal things while hoping for eternal ones. For the merit of virtue is increased when one’s established purpose does not violate religious commitment. We must strive lest any of our brothers be grievously wounded or perish. You ought therefore to come to the aid of the oppressed [Col. 0127B] and free them from the hand of their persecutors, so that with blessed Job you may say:

“‘The blessing of the one who was perishing came upon me, and I consoled the heart of the widow. I clothed myself with justice, and I dressed myself in my judgment as with a garment and a diadem. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and the case that I did not know I investigated most diligently. I crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched the prey from his teeth’ (Job 29:13),” and so forth.

You, therefore, who have been placed by the Lord on the watchtower, must earnestly restrain and repel those who prepare ambushes for their brothers or stir up seditions and scandals against them. It is easy to deceive a human being by words, but not God. Therefore you ought to repel such people and guard yourselves against them, so that, when this kind of darkness has been utterly extinguished, the morning star may shine upon them and joy arise, most holy brothers.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the fourth consulship of Saturninus and Gallicanus. [Col. 0128B]

## The Second Letter of the Same Pope Zephyrinus

[Col. 0127]

[Col. 0127B] Zephyrinus, archbishop of the city of Rome, to his dearest brothers serving the Lord throughout Egypt.

We have received such confidence from the Lord, founder of this holy see and apostolic Church, and from blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, that we labor with tireless devotion for the Church redeemed by the blood of Christ throughout the world, come to the aid of all who serve the Lord, and offer apostolic assistance to all who live piously.

All who wish to live piously in Christ must suffer reproaches from the impious and those unlike themselves, and be despised as foolish and insane, so that they may become better and purer—those who lose temporal goods in order to receive eternal ones. Their contempt and mockery, however, will be turned back upon those who afflict and insult them, when their abundance has passed into poverty and their pride into disgrace.

For it has been reported to the apostolic see through our representatives that certain of our brother bishops are being driven from their churches and proper sees, their possessions being taken from them, and that they are then summoned to judgment naked and stripped of everything. This is entirely unreasonable, since the decrees of the apostles and their successors, the commands of the emperors, and the enactments of the laws forbid precisely this, and the authority of the apostolic see prohibits it.

It was therefore commanded in the ancient statutes that bishops who have been expelled and stripped of their possessions should be received back into their own churches, that all their goods should first be restored to them, and that afterward anyone wishing to accuse them justly should do so at equal risk. They decreed that bishops of sound judgment, assembling in the church where there were witnesses for each of those who appeared oppressed, should be judges. Nor should the bishops be required to answer before all their property and that of their churches had been restored to them completely according to the laws.

Nor is it surprising, brothers, if they persecute you, since they persecuted the true head, Christ our Lord, even unto death. These persecutions must nevertheless be endured patiently, so that you may be recognized as his disciples, for whom you also suffer. Therefore he himself says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5:10). Strengthened by these testimonies, we ought not greatly to fear the reproach of human beings or be overcome by their insults, since the Lord commands us through the prophet Isaiah:

“Listen to me, you who know judgment, my people, in whose hearts is my law. Do not fear the reproach of human beings, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies.”

Considering what is written in the Psalm: “Does God not require these things? For he himself knows the secrets of the heart” (Psalm 43:22), and the thoughts of such people are vain:

“Each one spoke vain things to his neighbor; with deceitful lips and a divided heart they spoke evil. But God will destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things. They said, ‘Our lips are our own; who is our Lord?’” (Psalm 11:3–5).

For if they kept these things in mind, they would by no means rush into such great wickedness. They do not do this according to sound and fatherly teaching, but in order to exercise their vengeance upon the servants of God. For it is written: “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes” (Proverbs 12:15). And again: “There are ways that seem right to a person, but their ends lead to death” (Proverbs 14:12).

We who suffer these things must reserve them for the judgment of God, who will repay each one according to his works. Through his ministers he also thundered, saying: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Romans 12:19).

You, however, come to one another’s aid in right faith, good works, and good will, and let no one withdraw his hand from supporting his brother. For concerning this the Lord says: “Everyone will know that you are my disciples if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Hence he also speaks through the Prophet:

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together as one” (Psalm 132:1).

I speak of a spiritual dwelling and concord that are in God and in the unity of faith—the delightful dwelling which, according to the truth, was more fully adorned in Aaron and in the priests who put on dignity, like ointment upon the head, irrigating the highest understanding and leading it even to the utmost knowledge. In this dwelling the Lord promised blessing and eternal life.

Embracing, therefore, the merit of this prophetic prediction, we have explained the present fraternal passage, seeking nothing and intending to seek nothing of our own, because it is not good to slander those who slander, or, according to the common saying, to knock out one stake with another. Far be this from us; these things are not ours. May the Divinity avert them.

By the just judgment of God, sinners are often given power to persecute his saints, so that those who are helped and guided by the Spirit of God may become more illustrious through the exercise of suffering. For those who persecute, reproach, and slander them, however, there will unquestionably be woe.

Woe, woe to those who slander the servants of God, because their slander concerns him whose ministry they perform and whose office they hold. We pray that the door of restraint—since we wish no one to perish or defile himself with his lips—may be imposed upon their conduct, so that they may neither conceive nor utter from their mouths any harmful word. For the Lord also speaks through the prophet:

“I said: I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue” (Psalm 38:2).

May the almighty Lord, his only-begotten Son, and our Savior Jesus Christ grant you this incentive: that you come to the aid, with whatever strength you possess, of all brothers laboring under whatever troubles, regard their injuries as your own, as is fitting, and offer them the greatest assistance in words and deeds, so that you may be found to be his true disciples, since he commanded those who are brothers to love everyone as themselves.

Conduct the ordinations of presbyters and levites at the proper time and solemnly, with many standing present, and advance to this work men who are approved and learned, so that you may rejoice greatly in their fellowship and assistance.

Constantly place your hearts in the power of God, and proclaim these and all the other divine words to succeeding generations, for “this is our God forever, and he himself will guide us for all ages.”

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Saturninus and Gallicanus.

# The Decrees of Pope Callistus Begin

## On the Fast of the Four Seasons and Other Matters

*(In the year of the Lord 217, during the reign of the emperor Severus.)*

[Col. 0129]

[Col. 0129C] Callistus, archbishop of the catholic Church of the city of Rome, to Benedictus, brother and fellow bishop, greeting in the Lord.

We are bound by the love of brotherhood and compelled by apostolic governance to respond to the consultations of our brothers as the Lord grants, and to instruct them by the authority of the apostolic see.

The fast that you have learned to celebrate among us three times a year we now decree should more appropriately be observed at four seasons, so that, just as the year revolves through four seasons, we too may celebrate a solemn fast four times, in the four seasons of the year. And just as we are filled with grain, wine, and oil to nourish our bodies, so let us be filled with fasting to nourish our souls, according to the words of the prophet Zechariah, who says:

“The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts. Just as I determined to afflict you when your fathers provoked me to anger, and I did not show mercy, so now I have turned and determined in these days to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. Do not fear. These are the words that you shall do: Speak the truth, each one with his neighbor; judge truth and the judgment of peace in your gates; let none of you devise evil in your hearts against his friend; and do not love a false oath. For all these are the things that I hate, says the Lord of hosts.

“And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become for the house of Judah joy and gladness and splendid solemnities. Only love truth and peace, says the Lord of hosts.”

In this, therefore, we must all be of one mind, so that, according to apostolic teaching, we may all say the same thing and there may be no schisms among us. Let us be perfect in the same understanding and in the same knowledge, in whose devoted work we rejoice that your love shares.

For it is not fitting that the members should disagree with the head; rather, according to the testimony of Sacred Scripture, all the members should follow the head. No one doubts that the apostolic Church is the mother of all the churches, and that you must in no way deviate from her rules. And just as the Son came to do the will of the Father, so you must fulfill the will of your mother, which is the Church, whose head, as stated above, is the Roman Church. Therefore, no reason permits anything done without discrimination of justice against this discipline to be considered valid.

No one should accept accusations against a teacher, because children ought not to rebuke fathers, nor servants to wound their masters. All whom teachers instruct are therefore their children. And just as children love their fleshly fathers, so they ought also to love their spiritual fathers.

For the one who does not believe rightly does not live well, nor does the one who rebukes or slanders his fathers. Teachers, therefore, who are also called fathers, are to be borne rather than rebuked, unless they have erred in the right faith.

No one, therefore, should accuse a teacher in writing, nor should he answer anyone except a faithful and legitimate accuser who also leads an irreproachable life and conduct. For it is unworthy that a teacher should answer a foolish, unlearned person who lives reprehensibly, according to his foolishness, as Scripture says: “Do not answer a fool according to his foolishness” (Proverbs 26:4). One who does not believe rightly does not live well.

The faithful person desires no evil. If someone is faithful, let him see that he does not speak falsely or set traps for anyone. A faithful person always acts faithfully, while an unfaithful person craftily lies in wait and strives to destroy those who are faithful and live piously and justly, because like seeks its like.

An unfaithful person is dead in a living body. Against the words of a faithful person, however, the lives of his hearers are protected. A catholic teacher, and especially a priest of the Lord, ought no more to be entangled in error than to be violated by any scheme or desire. For Holy Scripture says:

“Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your will” (Ecclesiasticus 18:30).

One must resist the many allurements of this world and its many vanities, so that the integrity of true continence may be attained. Its first blemish is pride, the beginning of transgression and the source of sin, because the mind, voluntarily greedy, knows neither how to abstain nor how to give its consent to piety.

No one has an enemy among the good except evil itself. It is permitted to exist so that it may either be corrected or serve to exercise the good person.

Whatever is irreproachable, therefore, the catholic Church defends. No emperor or anyone guarding piety may presume to do anything against the divine commands.

An unjust judgment and an unjust decision arranged or carried out by judges through royal fear, royal command, or the command of any bishop or powerful person must have no force. It should not be enough for a religious person merely not to engage in or increase the enmities of others by speaking evil; he must also strive to extinguish them by speaking well.

Humble confession in evil deeds is better than proud boasting in good ones. All who love the blessed life prefer to pursue it in the condition of their tranquility and justice rather than have it interrupted by the avenging punishments of our sins.

For I remember that I preside under the name of that Church whose confession was glorified by the Lord Jesus Christ, and whose faith has always destroyed every error. I understand that I am permitted no other course than to devote all my efforts to the cause in which the salvation of the universal Church is imperiled.

I hope that God’s mercy will be present, so that, with his clemency cooperating, every destructive disease may be removed by him. Whatever can salutarily be done through his inspiration and assistance should be accomplished with praise for your faith and devotion, since nothing can otherwise be secure unless priestly authority defends what belongs to the service of the divine gift.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Antonius and Alexander.

# Letter of Pope Callistus to All the Bishops of Gaul

## On Conspiracies and Other Unlawful Matters, That They Must Not Occur

[Col. 0131]

[Col. 0131C] Callistus to all the beloved bishops established throughout Gaul.

We have learned through the report of many that your love, inflamed by the Holy Spirit, so firmly holds and governs the helm of the Church against assaults that, with God’s authority, it suffers neither shipwreck nor the losses caused by shipwreck.

Rejoicing, therefore, in such evidence, we ask that you permit nothing to be done in those regions against the apostolic statutes. Rather, strengthened by our authority, restrain what is harmful and prohibit what is unlawful.

We have heard that the crimes of conspiracies are flourishing in your regions, and we have been informed that the peoples are conspiring against their bishops. The cunning of this crime is abominable not only among Christians but also among pagans, and it is prohibited by foreign laws.

For this reason, the laws condemn those guilty of this crime—not only those who conspire but also those who consent to them—not only by ecclesiastical law but also by secular law.

Our predecessors, together with a great multitude of bishops, ordered that all who held or occupied priestly rank, or who were clerics, should fall from the honor they used. They ordered the others to be deprived of communion and expelled from the Church, and judged all the men of both orders to be infamous, not only those who acted but also those who consented to them.

For it is just that those who despise divine commands and disobey the injunctions of the fathers should be corrected by more severe punishments, so that others may fear to commit such acts, God may rejoice in brotherhood and concord, and all may take an example of severity and goodness.

For if, God forbid, we neglect ecclesiastical care and vigor, negligence destroys discipline, and the faithful will certainly be harmed.

Such people must not be admitted to accuse anyone, nor can either their voice or that of anathematizers harm or accuse anyone.

No one should receive those excommunicated by priests before a just examination of both parties. No one should share prayer, food, drink, or a kiss with them, nor even say “Hail” to them. For whoever knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or other prohibited matters will himself, according to the institution of the apostles, be subjected to a similar excommunication. Clerics and laypeople who do not wish to suffer the same punishment must therefore abstain from them.

Do not join yourselves to unbelievers or have any participation with them. Those who act in such ways are judged not faithful but unbelieving. Hence the Apostle says: “What partnership has a believer with an unbeliever?” (2 Corinthians 6:15), or “What participation has righteousness with wickedness?”

No one should usurp another’s boundaries, nor should anyone presume to judge or excommunicate another’s parishioner. Such judgment, excommunication, or condemnation will neither be valid nor have any force, since no one is bound or condemned by the sentence of any judge except his own.

Hence the Lord also says: “Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers established” (Proverbs 22:28).

No primate or metropolitan should presume to excommunicate or judge the diocesan church or parish, or anyone from that parish, or to do anything concerning it without that bishop’s counsel or judgment. Rather, he must observe what was established by the apostles, the fathers, and our predecessors, and confirmed by us.

That is, if any metropolitan bishop attempts to act outside his own parish in anything except what belongs solely to that parish, without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province, he will be subject to the danger of losing his rank, and what he has done shall be considered invalid and void.

But whatever it is necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of the provincial co-bishops, their churches and clerics, or the needs of secular persons, must be done with the consent of all the provincial bishops—not with any arrogance of domination, but with the most humble and concordant administration, as the Lord says: “I did not come to be served, but to serve”; and elsewhere: “Whoever has the greater virtue will be your servant,” and so forth.

Likewise, the provincial bishops themselves must act with them in counsel, except insofar as matters pertain to their own parishes, according to the decrees of the holy fathers. Although those fathers preceded us by some interval of time, they nevertheless drew the light of truth and faith from one and the same pure source. Through the same Spirit, their illuminator and guide, they sought the stability of God’s Church and the common benefit of all Christians, so that the holy Trinity might be glorified forever with one mind and one voice, in concord.

No primate, no metropolitan, and no other bishop should enter another’s city or approach a possession that does not belong to him and that is the parish of another bishop, or make any arrangement there concerning anyone’s affairs, unless summoned by the person whose jurisdiction it is known to be. Whatever he arranges, ordains, or judges there, if he wishes to retain the honor of his rank, he does so unlawfully if he has not been summoned. If he presumes to act otherwise, he will be condemned.

And not only he, but also his cooperators and those who consent to him, because just as ordination is prohibited to them, so are judgment and the disposition of other matters. For one who cannot ordain, how will he judge? He certainly will not judge, nor will he be able to judge.

Just as another man’s wife, while her husband is alive, may neither be adulterated by anyone nor judged or disposed of except by her own husband, so the bishop’s wife—that is, unquestionably, his church or parish—may not, while he is alive, be judged, disposed of, or enjoy another’s intercourse, that is, another’s ordination, without his judgment and will.

Hence the Apostle says: “A wife is bound by the law as long as her husband lives; but when her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband.”

Likewise, the bishop’s betrothed—for his Church is called his betrothed wife—is bound to him while he lives. When he has died, she is released, and may marry whomever she wishes, only in the Lord, that is, regularly. If she marries another while he is alive, she will be judged an adulteress. Likewise, if he willingly takes another, he will be considered an adulterer and deprived of communion.

But if he is persecuted in the Church, he must flee to another and associate himself with it, as the Lord says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.” If, however, he must be transferred for the sake of usefulness, he must not do so on his own, but at the invitation of the brothers and by the authority of this holy see—not for ambition, but for usefulness.

The unions of blood relatives are prohibited, since both divine and secular laws forbid them. The divine laws not only expel those who do such things and those born from them, but also call them accursed. Secular laws call such people infamous and exclude them from inheritance.

Following our fathers and adhering to their footsteps, we mark them with infamy and judge them to be infamous, because they are stained with the marks of infamy. Nor should we accept as men or accusers those whom secular laws reject.

For who doubts that human laws which do not conflict with reason and honor should be embraced—especially where they serve the public good, defend the authority of ecclesiastical dignity, or protect it as a support?

We have called those people blood relatives whom the divine laws, and the laws of the emperors, Romans, and Greeks, call blood relatives and admit to inheritance, so that they cannot exclude them. Unions of such persons are neither lawful nor capable of enduring; they must be rejected, and if any have been attempted with rash audacity, they must be dissolved by apostolic authority.

Therefore, anyone who is not lawfully joined, or who is known to have been united without a dowry document and the blessing of a priest, can in no way accuse priests or testify against those lawfully joined. For everyone polluted by the stain of incest is infamous and is not permitted to accuse the persons mentioned above.

Not only must such people be rejected and made infamous, but so must all who consent to them. We judge the same concerning ravishers and those who attack their elders.

Secular laws put such people to death, but, with mercy going before, we receive them into penance under the mark of infamy. We cannot erase the infamy with which they are stained, but we desire to heal their souls through public penance and satisfaction to the Church, because manifest sins must not be cleansed by secret correction.

All who are suspected of right faith must therefore be excluded from accusing priests and those whose faith is beyond doubt, and they must be regarded as doubtful in human testimony. Their voice must therefore be weakened if their faith is doubted, and no credence at all must be given to those who do not know the right faith.

In judgment, therefore, the conduct and faith of both the accuser and the accused must be investigated, because those who are not of upright conduct and faith, whose life is blameworthy, are not permitted to accuse their elders. Nor are those whose faith, life, and freedom are unknown, nor are persons of low standing, admitted to accuse them.

The persons of the accusers must be examined in detail [Col. 0135A]. Without a written document they are difficult to admit; with a written document they must never be admitted, because no one can accuse or be accused through writing. Each person must make his accusation in his own voice and in the presence of the person whom he wishes to accuse, and no accuser is to be believed in the absence of the person whom he wishes to accuse.

Likewise, witnesses must not give testimony through any writing, but, being present, must testify truthfully about what they have seen and know. Nor may they testify concerning other causes or affairs, except those known to have been conducted in their presence.

Accusers who are blood relatives must not testify against outsiders, nor may household members or those arising from the same household do so. If they wish and mutually agree, relatives may testify only among themselves, and not against others.

Nor should suspect accusers [31] or witnesses be admitted, because the affection of kinship, familiarity, and domination ordinarily obstructs the truth. Carnal love, fear, and greed often dull human judgment and distort opinions, so that they consider profit piety and money a reward for prudence.

Let no one speak deceitfully to his neighbor. The mouth of a malicious person is a deep pit; an innocent person, trusting him, easily and quickly falls. But the one who falls rises again, while the evasive person is cast down by his own devices, from which he will never leap out or escape.
