Let each person therefore weigh his words, and let him not say to another what he does not wish said to himself. Hence Sacred Scripture rightly says: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.”

We need time in order to act with greater maturity. We must not rush our counsels and works or corrupt their order. But if someone has fallen in any way, let us not destroy him; let us correct him with brotherly affection, as the blessed Apostle says:

“If a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:1–2).

Moreover, holy David did penance for deadly crimes, yet remained in honor. Blessed Peter also shed very bitter tears when he repented of having denied the Lord, yet he remained an apostle. And the Lord promises sinners through the prophet, saying:

“On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, I will no longer remember any of his iniquities.”

For those who think that priests, after falling, cannot minister to the Lord or enjoy their honors if they have performed worthy penance, thereafter led a good life, and guarded their priesthood suitably, are mistaken.

Those who think this not only err, but also appear to argue and act against the keys entrusted to the Church, concerning which it was said: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18:18). Otherwise this saying is either not the Lord’s or not true.

We, however, unhesitatingly believe that both the priests of the Lord and the other faithful may, after worthy satisfaction, return to their honors, as the Lord testifies through the prophet:

“Will the one who falls not rise again, and will the one who has turned away not return?” (Jeremiah 8:4).

And elsewhere the Lord says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

The prophet David, doing penance, said:

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a willing spirit” (Psalm 50:14).

After his penance he himself taught others and offered sacrifice to God, giving an example to the teachers of the holy Church that, if they fall and perform worthy penance before God, they may do both.

For he taught when he said:

“I will teach the wicked your ways, and sinners will return to you” (ibid., 15).

And he offered sacrifice to God for himself when he said:

“A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (ibid., 19).

Seeing his own crimes cleansed through penance, the prophet did not hesitate, by preaching and offering to the Lord, to heal the crimes of others.

The pouring out of tears therefore moves the soul’s suffering. When satisfaction has been completed, however, the soul is turned away from anger. For whoever does not forgive another—how does he think that he himself will receive help?

Let sins abound, then, and let mercy abound also. For with the Lord there is mercy, and abundant redemption with him. With the Lord there is abundance of all things, because the Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory.

The Apostle says:

“All have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as an expiation through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his justice because of the remission of previous sins, in the forbearance of God, to demonstrate his justice at the present time, so that he himself may be just and the one who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus Christ” (Romans 3:21 and following).

David says:

“Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered.”

A person is therefore cleansed from sin, and the fallen person rises again by the grace of God, remaining in his former office according to the authorities cited above. Let him take care that he sin no more, so that the Gospel sentence may remain in him: “Go, and sin no more.”

Hence the Apostle says:

“Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires. Nor should you present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin; instead, present yourselves as those who are alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of justice to God. For sin will not be condemned in you [as printed, *peccatum enim vobis non damnabitur*], for you are not under the law but under grace.

“What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? By no means. Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey—whether of sin leading to death or of obedience leading to justice?

“But thanks be to God that, although you were servants of sin, you obeyed from the heart the form of teaching to which you were handed over. Having been freed from sin, you became servants of justice—I speak in human terms” (Romans 6:12 and following).

The sin of the one who judges is greater than that of the one who is judged. The Apostle says:

“Do you suppose, O human being, that when you judge those who do such things and do them yourself, you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and forbearance? Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?

“But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will repay each one according to his works: eternal life to those who, by patient continuance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption; but wrath and indignation to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth, yet obey iniquity.

“Tribulation and distress upon every soul of a human being who works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek; but glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works good” (Romans 2:3 and following).

Flee, brothers, not only from holding but also from hearing a judgment that forbids mercy, because mercy is more excellent than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.

We have briefly answered your consultations because your letters found us greatly oppressed and preoccupied with other judgments.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Antonius and Alexander.

# The Decrees of Pope Urban Begin

## On Common Life and the Offering of the Faithful

*(In the year 222, during the reign of the emperor Aurelius Antoninus.)*

[Col. 0137]

[Col. 0137B] Urban, bishop, to all Christians: greeting in the sanctification of the Spirit, in obedience, and in the sprinkling of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

It is fitting, dearest ones, that all Christians imitate the one whose name they have taken. The apostle James says:

“What does it profit, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works?” (James 2:14).

Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you will receive a greater judgment; for we all offend in many things. Whoever among you is wise and disciplined should show his work through good conduct, in the gentleness of wisdom.

We know that you are not unaware that common life has until now flourished among good Christians, and by the grace of God still flourishes, especially among those chosen for the portion of the Lord, that is, among the clergy, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles:

“The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. No one said that any of the things he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them. With great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ, and great grace was upon them all. For no one among them was needy. As many as owned fields or houses sold them, brought the prices of the things they sold, and laid them at the feet of the apostles. They distributed them to each person according to his need.

“Joseph, who was surnamed Barnabas by the apostles—which is translated ‘son of consolation’—a Levite and a Cypriot by birth, having a field, sold it and brought the price and laid it at the feet of the apostles” (Acts 4:32), and so forth.

Seeing, therefore, that the high priests and the others, as well as the Levites and the remaining faithful, could provide greater benefit if they handed over to the churches over which the bishops presided the inheritances and fields that they had previously sold—for from their revenues they could provide much more abundant and better things, both in the present and in future times, to the faithful living a common life than from their sale price—they began to hand over to the principal churches the estates and fields that they had been accustomed to sell, and to live from their revenues.

These properties themselves were, and still are, under the authority of the individual parishes and of the bishops who hold the place of the apostles; and so they must always remain in future times. The bishops and their faithful stewards ought to provide from them all necessities to everyone who wishes to lead a common life, as best they are able, so that no needy person may be found among them. These properties are called the offerings of the faithful, because they are offered to the Lord.

They must not, therefore, be diverted to uses other than ecclesiastical purposes and the needs of the aforesaid Christian brethren or of the needy, because they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sinners, and the patrimony of the poor, and because they have been handed over to the Lord for the accomplishment of the aforesaid work. But if anyone—God forbid—acts otherwise, let him beware lest he receive the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira and become guilty of sacrilege, as those became who defrauded the price of the aforesaid properties. Of them we read in the aforesaid Acts of the Apostles:

> “There was a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife. He sold a field and, with his wife’s knowledge, defrauded part of the price of the field; and bringing a certain portion, he laid it at the apostles’ feet. But Peter said to Ananias: ‘Why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to defraud part of the price of the field? While it remained, did it not remain yours, and after it was sold was it not in your power? Why did you put this matter in your heart? You have not lied to human beings but to God.’ When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard it. The young men rose, removed him, carried him out, and buried him.
>
> “After an interval of about three hours, his wife, not knowing what had happened, entered. Peter answered her: ‘Tell me, did you sell the field for so much?’ She said: ‘Yes, for so much.’ Peter said to her: ‘Why did you agree together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.’ Immediately she fell at his feet and breathed her last. The young men entered, found her dead, carried her out, and buried her beside her husband. And great fear came upon the whole Church and upon all who heard these things” (Acts 5:1 ff.).

These things, brethren, must be carefully avoided and feared, because the properties of the Church, not as private possessions but as common goods offered to the Lord, must be faithfully administered with the greatest fear, and used for no purposes other than those mentioned above. Otherwise those who remove them from the place where they were entrusted will incur the guilt of sacrilege, the punishment and death of Ananias and Sapphira, and—what is worse—become *anathema maranatha*.

Even if they do not fall dead bodily, as Ananias and Sapphira did, nevertheless let the soul—which is more important than the body—fall dead and estranged from the fellowship of the faithful, and let it sink into the depths of the abyss. Therefore all must take care of this and faithfully guard it, driving away the insult of such usurpation, lest estates dedicated to the uses decreed by heaven be harassed by certain intruders.

If anyone does this, after the severity of the deserved punishment that must rightly be inflicted upon sacrilegious persons, let him be condemned to perpetual infamy and delivered to prison, or undergo perpetual deportation into exile, since, according to the Apostle, such a person must be handed over to Satan, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

After these increases and improvements, the churches over which bishops preside grew so greatly, with the Lord’s assistance, and most of them became so abundant in resources, that no one choosing to lead a common life was needy among them, but received all necessities from the bishop and his ministers. Therefore, if in the present or future times anyone arises who attempts to tear this away 32, let him be struck by the condemnation already pronounced.

As for the elevated seats established and prepared in the churches of the bishops like a throne, they show forth the contemplation and the authority to judge, loose, and bind that have been given them by the Lord. Hence the Savior himself says in the Gospel:

> “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18:18).

And elsewhere:

> “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:23).

For this reason, dearest ones, we have set these matters forth, so that you may understand the authority of your bishops, and in them venerate the Lord; that you may love them as your own souls; that you may not associate with those with whom they do not associate; and that you may not receive those whom they have expelled.

The sentence of a bishop is greatly to be feared, even if he binds someone unjustly—although he ought above all to guard against doing so. We exhort and admonish all of you who have embraced Christianity and received the name “Christian” from Christ, not to make your Christianity void in anything, but firmly to keep the pledge that you made to the Lord in baptism, so that you may be found before him not reprobate but worthy.

And whoever has adopted your common life and vowed that he would possess nothing as his own must beware of making his promise void. Rather, let him faithfully keep what he promised to the Lord, so that he may acquire not condemnation but a reward. For it is better not to vow than to fail to fulfill a vow as well as one can. Those who have made a vow and have not fulfilled it, or who have received the faith and ended their lives in evil, are punished more severely than those who ended their lives without a vow, or died without faith, yet performed good works.

For this reason we have received, by the gift of nature and the restoration of a second birth, a rational understanding, so that, according to the Apostle, we may “set our minds more on the things above, not on those upon the earth, because the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.”

What does the wisdom of this age recommend, dearest ones, except seeking what will cause harm, loving what will perish, neglecting what brings salvation, and regarding eternal things as nothing? It commends greed, of which it is said:

> “Greed is the root of all evils.”

This evil has above all the characteristic that, while it thrusts transient things upon a person, it hides eternal things; while it sees things placed outside, it does not look within at what lies hidden inside; and while it seeks what belongs to others, it makes its follower a stranger to himself.

Behold what the wisdom of the age recommends: living in luxury. Hence it is said:

> “The soul that lives in luxury is dead.”

Thus it recommends nourishing the flesh with the softest pleasures, sins, vices, and flames; oppressing the soul with immoderate eating and drinking; shutting out the life of the spirit; and supplying one’s enemy with a sword taken from oneself against oneself.

Behold what the wisdom of the age recommends: that those who have become good should prefer to be evil, and should even strive, through error of mind, to become sinners, without considering that terrible word of God, when sinners will be burned like hay.

All the faithful must receive the Holy Spirit after baptism through the laying on of the hands of bishops, so that they may be found fully Christian. For when the Holy Spirit is poured in, the faithful heart is enlarged for prudence and steadfastness.

From the Holy Spirit we receive the gift of becoming spiritual, because the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God. From the Holy Spirit we receive the ability to discern between good and evil, to love what is just, to reject what is unjust, to resist malice and pride, and to withstand lust, various enticements, and shameful and unworthy desires.

From the Holy Spirit we receive the ability, inflamed by love of life and ardor for glory, to raise our minds from earthly things to what is heavenly and divine.

Given on the Nones of September, that is, on the fifth day of the same month, in the consulship of Antonius and Alexander, for the fourth time.

# THE DECREES OF POPE PONTIAN BEGIN

*(In the year of the Lord 230, during the reign of the emperor Alexander.)*

[Col. 0141]

[Col. 0141A] Pontian, bishop, sends greetings to Felix, subdeacon.

Our heart greatly rejoices with your charity, because you strive with the utmost devotion to fulfill the practice of holy religion and comfort grieving brethren who are abandoned in faith and religion. Therefore we entreat the mercy of our Redeemer, that his grace may assist us in all things and grant us to accomplish in deed what he has allowed us to desire.

In this good work, the benefits of reward increase in proportion as the zeal for labor increases. And because in all these matters the help of divine grace is necessary, we entreat the clemency of almighty God with continual prayers, that he may always grant you both the will and the ability to perform these good works, and direct you along that way with the fruit of good works in which he has testified that he is the Shepherd of shepherds, so that through him, without whom nothing can be done, you may be able to fulfill the good works you have begun.

Concerning the priests of the Lord whom, as we have heard, you assist against the plots of wicked people and whose causes you undertake, know that you please God greatly in this. He chose them for himself to serve him and wished them to be so close to him that through them he would accept even the offerings of others, forgive their sins, and reconcile them to himself. They themselves also consecrate the body of the Lord with their own mouths and distribute it to the peoples.

Of them it is said:

> “Whoever troubles you troubles me, and whoever does you an injury will receive what he has done unjustly.”

And elsewhere:

> “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me. But whoever despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke 10:16).

They must not be attacked but honored. In them also the Lord is honored, whose ambassadors they are.

Therefore, if they should perhaps be brought low by the faithful, they must be raised up and supported. They must not be accused by infamous, criminal, hostile, or sectarian people, nor by people of another religion. If they sin, they should be rebuked by the remaining priests and restrained by the supreme pontiffs, but not accused or expelled by secular persons or by people of evil life.

When we heard that you were grieving over the death of your brother, we were compelled to sorrow greatly. Therefore we ask almighty God to console you with the inspiration of his grace and to protect you by heavenly guardianship from both evil spirits and perverse people.

If, after his death, you are enduring disturbances caused by certain adversaries, do not be surprised that you, who seek to enjoy good things in your own land—that is, in the land of the living—are bearing the evils of human beings in a foreign land. For the life of the penitent is a pilgrimage, and for one who sighs for his homeland, the place of pilgrimage is a torment, even if it appears pleasant.

But for you, who seek your homeland amid the sighs you endure, I also hear the groans of human oppression rising. This happens through the wondrous arrangement of almighty God: while truth calls through love, the penitent world rejects your soul from itself through the tribulations it brings upon you. The mind therefore leaves the love of this age all the more easily as it is driven out while being called.

Accordingly, continue the care of hospitality that you have begun, and labor with the utmost persistence in prayer and tears. Devote yourselves now more generously and abundantly to the almsgiving that you have always loved, so that the fruit of your reward may afterward increase in proportion to the increase here of your zeal for labor.

Furthermore, greeting your goodness with paternal affection, we ask that you not grow weary in the good works you have begun. Let no one be able to turn you away from them, but let all the clerics, servants of God, and Christians who dwell in those regions find in all things the affection of your charity through love of Christ and of Saint Peter, and enjoy your support and assistance in whatever manner may be necessary.

Thus, with all defended and helped by your aid, may we be able to become your debtors in thanksgiving; and may Christ our Lord, and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose causes you labor, repay you with eternal glory, and may blessed Peter the apostle open the gate of that glory.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the fourth consulship of Severus and Quintianus.

# LETTER OF POPE PONTIAN  
## On Brotherly Love and Avoiding Evil

[Col. 0141]

[Col. 0141D] Pontian, bishop, sends greetings to all the bishops of the holy and universal Church who rightly worship the Lord and love divine worship.

> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

These words, dearest ones, belong not to human beings but to angels. They were not conceived by human understanding but announced by angels at the birth of the Savior. From them everyone can undoubtedly understand that peace is given by the Lord not to people of evil will but to people of good will.

Hence the Lord also speaks through the prophet, saying:

> “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart! But my feet were almost moved, my steps nearly slipped, because I was envious of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Psalm 72 and following).

Concerning the good, Truth itself says:

> “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

Those who think evil or harmful things against their brethren are not pure in heart, because the faithful person desires no evil. A faithful person therefore prefers to hear what ought to be heard rather than say what ought not to be said.

And if anyone is faithful, let him beware of speaking evil or laying traps for anyone. By this, then, the sons of God and the sons of the devil are distinguished.

The sons of God always think about and strive to do the things that belong to God; they continually help their brethren and wish to harm no one. The sons of the devil, by contrast, always devise evil and harmful things, because their works are evil.

Concerning them the Lord speaks through the prophet Jeremiah:

> “I will speak my judgments with them concerning all their wickedness” (Jeremiah 1:16).
>
> “Therefore I will still contend in judgment with you, says the Lord, and I will dispute with your children” (Jeremiah 2:9).
>
> “Behold, I will fashion evil against you and devise a plan against you” (Jeremiah 18:11).

These things, brethren, must be greatly feared and avoided by everyone, because whoever is struck by the judgment of God will not escape unpunished.

Therefore each person must take care not to devise or do against a brother what he himself would not wish to suffer. A faithful person must not even come under suspicion, so as to say or do what he does not wish to suffer.

For this reason our predecessors, by apostolic authority, barred as accusers—and we remove and exclude for future times—those who are suspect and hostile, those who readily engage in quarrels, those who do not lead a good life, those whose life is blameworthy, and those who neither hold nor teach the right faith. We do this so that those whom we ought to preserve and save may not easily fall, lest—God forbid—the aforesaid judgment of God come upon both parties, and we perish through their fault.

For it is written:

> “They have appointed you ruler; take care of them, so that you may rejoice because of them and receive the ornament of grace, and obtain a crown and honor with prayer” (Ecclesiasticus 32:1 ff.).

An evil word changes the heart, from which four parts arise: good and evil, life and death; and the tongue continually rules them.

For such reasons, the persons mentioned above must be carefully avoided. Before their opinions have been examined in detail, and before they have been found free of the faults mentioned, they must not be received, because it is a saving sacrifice to heed the commandments and depart from all iniquity. It is pleasing to the Lord to withdraw from iniquity, and praise consists in departing from injustice.

For it is written:

> “Love your neighbor and join yourself to him in faith, because if you reveal his secrets, you will not pursue him afterward. For as a person destroys his friend, so does one who destroys his neighbor’s friendship. And as one who releases a bird from his hand, so are you when you abandon your neighbor and cannot recapture him. Do not pursue him, for he is far away; he has escaped like a doe from a snare, because his soul has been wounded. You will no longer be able to bind him to yourself, and a curse is reconciliation with such a person; for to reveal the secrets of a friend is despair for an unfaithful soul.
>
> “The one who winks with his eye devises evil, and no one will cast him out. 33 In the sight of your eyes he will trample his mouth, and he will marvel at your words. At last he will pervert his mouth and make your words a stumbling block.
>
> “I have hated many things and have not equated myself with him, and the Lord will hate him. Whoever throws a stone upward will have it fall upon his own head, and the wound of the deceitful will divide his injuries. For whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and whoever sets a stone before his neighbor will stumble over it, and whoever lays a snare for another will perish in it.
>
> “The one who devises a most wicked plan will have it roll back upon himself, and he will not know from where it will come upon him. Mockery and reproach will lie in wait for the proud like a lion, and vengeance will do the same. Those who take pleasure in the fall of the just will perish by a snare, and sorrow will consume them before they die. Anger and wrath are both hateful, and the sinful man will be subject to them.
>
> “Whoever wishes to take revenge will find vengeance from the Lord, and he will surely preserve that person’s sins. Forgive your neighbor who has harmed you, and then, when you pray, your sins will be forgiven. Does one person preserve anger against another and seek healing from God? Does he have no mercy on a person like himself, yet pray for his own sins to the Most High? Though he is flesh, he preserves anger and asks God for reconciliation. Who will plead for his offenses?
>
> “Remember the end, and cease from hostility, for decay and death threaten the commandments. Remember the fear of the Most High God, and do not be angry with your neighbor. Remember the covenant of the Most High, and overlook your neighbor’s ignorance.
>
> “Refrain from strife, and you will lessen sins. An angry person kindles strife; a sinful person disturbs friends and introduces enmity among those who live in peace. As fire blazes according to the wood of a forest, so is a person’s anger according to his strength, and according to his wealth he exalts his wrath.
>
> “A hastened quarrel kindles fire, a quarrel pursued in haste pours out blood, and a tongue bearing witness brings death. If you blow upon it, it will burn like fire; if you spit upon it, it will be extinguished. Both proceed from the mouth.
>
> “The whisperer and the double-tongued person are accursed, for they have disturbed many who lived in peace. The third tongue has stirred up many and scattered them from nation to nation. It has destroyed the fortified cities of the rich and dug up the houses of the great; it has overthrown the strength of peoples and dissolved mighty nations.
>
> “The third tongue has driven out married women and deprived them of the fruits of their labors. Whoever watches it will have no rest and will not dwell in peace. The blow of a whip produces a bruise, but the blow of the tongue crushes bones.
>
> “Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not as many as those who have perished through their own tongue. Blessed is the one who is sheltered from an evil tongue, who has not fallen into its anger, who has not drawn its yoke upon himself, and who has not been bound by its chains.
>
> “For its yoke is an iron yoke, and its bond is a bronze bond. Its death is a most wicked death, and the underworld is more useful than it. Its persistence will not endure, but it will possess the ways of the unjust, and its flame will not burn the just.
>
> “Those who abandon God will fall into it; it will blaze against them and will not be extinguished. It will be sent against them like a lion and harm them like a leopard.
>
> “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue. Make doors for your mouth and locks for your ears. Melt your gold and silver, and make a scale for your words; make straight bridles for your mouth. Take care lest you slip with your tongue, fall before enemies lying in wait for you, and your fall be incurable unto death” (Ecclesiasticus 27:18 ff.; 28:1 ff.).

> “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not postpone it from day to day. For his anger will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you. Do not be anxious about unjust riches, for they will profit you nothing on the day of punishment and vengeance.
>
> “Do not toss yourself about in every wind, and do not go along every road. For in this way the sinner is tested by a double tongue. Be firm in the way of the Lord and in the truth of your understanding and knowledge, and let the word of peace and justice accompany you.
>
> “Be gentle in hearing the word, so that you may understand, and give a true answer with wisdom. If you have understanding, answer your neighbor; but if not, let your hand be upon your mouth, lest you be caught in an undisciplined word and be put to shame.
>
> “Honor and glory belong to a sensible speech; the tongue of the imprudent is his own downfall. Do not be called a whisperer, and do not be caught and put to shame by your tongue. For there is shame and repentance for a thief, and the worst disgrace for a double-tongued person. Hatred, hostility, and abuse belong to the whisperer.
>
> “Justify the small and the great alike. Do not become an enemy to your neighbor on account of your friend. For the wicked person will inherit reproach and abuse, and every sinful person is envious and double-tongued.
>
> “Do not exalt yourself in the thought of your soul like a bull, lest your strength be shattered through folly, your leaves be eaten, your fruits be lost, and you be left like a dry tree in the desert. For an evil soul destroys its possessor, gives him over to the joy of his enemies, and leads him into the lot of the wicked” (Ecclesiasticus 5–6).

Dearest ones, strive to raise up the oppressed and always help those in need. Whoever relieves an afflicted brother, rescues one who has been seized, and consoles one who mourns should not doubt that he will receive repayment from the one to whom he has devoted everything, who said:

> “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.”

Therefore strive continually to do good works, so that you may obtain the fruit of good work here and enjoy the grace of God in the future, and thus afterward deserve to enter the hall of the heavenly kingdom.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the fourth consulship of Severus and Quintianus.

# THE DECREES OF POPE ANTERUS BEGIN

*(In the year of the Lord 239, during the reign of the emperor Maximinus.)*

[Col. 0145]

[Col. 0145B] To the most dear brothers, the bishops established throughout the provinces of Baetica and Toledo: Anterus, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

I have always desired, dearest brothers, to hear of the joyful signs of your sincere love and peace, so that letters traveling back and forth might mutually strengthen the indications of your well-being, if the ancient enemy would allow us to remain at peace and free from his attacks.

He is a liar from the beginning, an enemy of truth, the adversary of humankind, whom, in order to deceive, he first deceived himself—a foe of chastity and a teacher of lust. He feeds upon cruelty and is punished by abstinence. He hates fasts while preaching to his servants that they are superfluous, having no hope of future things, struck down by the Apostle’s saying:

> “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Corinthians 15:32).

O unhappy boldness! O cunning of a mind abandoned to despair! He himself encourages hatred and drives away harmony. And because the human mind is easily led toward the worse, wishing rather to walk along the broad road than to cross the path of the narrow way with labor, therefore, beloved brothers, pursue better things and always abandon what is worse.

Do good and avoid evil, so that you may be found truly to be disciples of the Lord.

Concerning the transfer of bishops, about which you wished to consult the holy apostolic see, know that it is permitted when it is done for the common good and because of necessity, but not at anyone’s whim or through domination.

Peter, our holy teacher and prince of the apostles, was transferred from Antioch to Rome for the sake of usefulness, so that he might make greater progress there. Eusebius also was transferred by apostolic authority from a certain small city to Alexandria.

Similarly, Felix was transferred from the city in which he had been ordained to Ephesus by the election of the citizens, on account of the teaching and good life that he possessed, through the common counsel of the bishops, the other priests, and the peoples.

A person does not pass from city to city when he does so according to his own whim or ambition, but when he is transferred for the usefulness or necessity of others, at the exhortation and counsel of those who are superior.

A person is not transferred from a smaller city to a larger one if he does so through ambition or by his own will, but if he has been driven from his own seat by force, compelled by necessity, or transferred and enthroned by others for the usefulness of the place or of the people—not proudly but with humility. For a human being sees the face, but God sees the heart.

The Lord speaks through the prophet:

> “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm 94:11).

Therefore a person who does not change his mind does not change his see; nor does he change his city when he is not transferred of his own accord but by the counsel and election of others.

He does not migrate from city to city who does not leave his own city through greed or willingly, but, as has been said, is either driven from it, compelled by necessity, or transferred to another city through the election and exhortation of priests and peoples.

For just as bishops have the authority to ordain bishops and other priests in accordance with the rules, so, whenever usefulness or necessity demands it, they have the authority, in the manner stated above, both to transfer and to enthrone them.

Since you have requested this, we command that these matters, though perhaps not unknown to you, be observed, lest through the ignorance of some better and more useful things be avoided and less useful things be chosen, as is read in the holy Gospel:

> “Woe to you, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have left the weightier matters of the law—judgment, mercy, and faith. These you ought to have done, without leaving the others undone; blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel.”

They say that what is permitted is not permitted, and that what is not permitted is permitted. Just as Jannes and Mambres resisted the truth, so do these, reprobate in mind, loving pleasure more than God.

They teach that what is permitted is not permitted: namely, that bishops may not move from city to city in the manner stated above. And they teach that what is not permitted is permitted: namely, that mercy should not be shown toward those suffering necessity—that is, that a bishop should not be granted from another city, for the sake of usefulness or necessity, to those who have no bishop and need the sacred episcopal ministry—and they deny that another see should be given to bishops suffering persecution or necessity.

For they contradict sacred Scripture, which testifies that God prefers mercy to judgment. What greater charity or more effective protection of piety could anyone offer another than to drive away from him the darkness of ignorance and the gloom of inexperience, and then refresh him with the nourishment of the teaching of true faith—not for profit, not for ambition, but for instruction and edification?

It is like giving a hand to a maimed person, a foot to a lame person, or an eye to a blind person when someone opens the treasure of wisdom and knowledge to one covered by the darkness of ignorance and kindly reveals the brightness of light and the ways of the Lord.

To both groups—that is, both to those suffering hunger for the word of God and to bishops in need—considerable mercy is shown when, for the common good, they are enthroned in other cities.

Those who deny these things, although they appear to have a form of piety, nevertheless deny its power. For in such a matter I recognize no lineage or pedigree. But if one of the wise, whom the storm of this age has joined through other leaders to the foolish, is stained by participation in crimes, the splendor of the wise person—even if he incurs complicity in crimes—nevertheless does not know how to present himself as a guide to sinners.

There is one cause arising from usefulness and necessity, and another arising from greed, presumption, or personal will. Bishops must not be transferred from city to city on account of greed, presumption, or personal will, but on account of usefulness and necessity.

No one denies this except those of whom it is said:

> “They have erred through drunkenness; they have not known the seer; they have been ignorant of judgment” (Isaiah 28:7).

For if I were compelled, in recounting the past, to disclose what has happened, I would show you that no consolation comes from comparing deeds.

In any event, stand, dearest ones, upon the roads, looking and asking about the ancient paths of the Lord; see which is the good and straight way, walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls.

And, in order to speak according to the words of Wisdom:

> “Love justice, you who judge the earth. Think of the Lord with goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart, because he is found by those who do not test him, and he appears to those who have faith in him.
>
> “For perverse thoughts separate from the Lord, but tested virtue rebukes the foolish, because wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sins.
>
> “For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts without understanding, and it will be rebuked by the iniquity that comes upon it. For the Spirit of wisdom is kindly, and it will not acquit the one who curses with his lips, because God is the witness of his inmost being and the true searcher of his heart, and the hearer of his tongue.
>
> “For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world 34, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice. Therefore the one who speaks unjustly cannot remain hidden, nor will the judgment that rebukes him pass him by.
>
> “For there will be an inquiry into the thoughts of the ungodly, and the hearing of his words will come to the Lord, for the correction of his iniquities, because the ear of zeal hears all things, and the tumult of murmuring will not be hidden.
>
> “Therefore guard yourselves from murmuring, which is of no benefit, and spare your tongue from detraction, because an obscure word will not go away into nothing; the mouth that lies kills the soul.
>
> “Do not be jealous of death through the error of your life, nor acquire destruction through the works of your hands, because God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living.
>
> “For he created all things to exist and wanted the nations of the world to be healable. There is no destructive medicine among them, nor the kingdom of the underworld upon the earth.
>
> “Justice is eternal and immortal, but injustice is the acquisition of death. The ungodly have summoned it by their hands and words; considering it their friend, they have wasted away and made covenants with it, because they are worthy of belonging to it through death.
>
> “For they said within themselves, thinking wrongly: ‘Short and sorrowful is the time of our life, and there is no relief at the end of a person, and no one has been known to return from the underworld. For we have come into being from nothing, and after this we shall be as though we had not been, because our breath is smoke in our nostrils, and speech is a spark for stirring our heart. When it is extinguished, the body will be ashes, and the spirit will be scattered like soft air.
>
> “‘Our life will pass like a trace of a cloud and dissolve like a mist driven away by the rays and heat of the sun. Our name will be forgotten with time, and no one will remember our works; for our time is like a passing shadow, and there is no return from our end, because it has been sealed and no one will return’” (Wisdom 1–2).

Therefore everyone must take care to guard himself with the utmost diligence and provide wisely for himself, so that when the final day and the end of life arrive, he may not pass into everlasting death but into eternal life.

Indeed, the deeds of subjects are judged by us, but ours are judged by God. Yet bishops are sometimes corrupted because of the merit of the people, so that those who follow may fall more easily. When the head languishes, the other members of the body are infected. Those who corrupt the life and conduct of good people are worse than those who seize others’ possessions and estates. Let each person beware lest he have either a prurient tongue or prurient ears—that is, lest he himself disparage others or listen to those who disparage them.

“While sitting,” he says, “you spoke against your brother in detraction, and against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling block,” and so forth. Let each person restrain his tongue from detraction and guard his speech; let them know that all they say about others will be judged according to their own sentence. No one willingly reports anything to an unwilling listener. Let it be the duty of each one, dearly beloved, not only to keep his eyes chaste but also his tongue. Let no other household ever learn through you what is being done in anyone’s home.

Let all possess the simplicity of a dove, so that they do not plot deceit against anyone, and the cunning of a serpent, so that they are not overcome by the snares of others. It is neither fitting for my humility nor within my measure to judge others or to speak anything sinister about the ministers of the churches. Far be it from me to say anything sinister about those who, succeeding to the apostolic rank, consecrate the body of Christ with their sacred mouth; through them we too are Christians, and, possessing the keys of the kingdom of heaven, they judge before the day of judgment.

In the Old Law it is written that whoever did not obey the priests was either stoned by the people after being placed outside the camp, or expiated his contempt with blood, his neck subjected to the sword. Now, however, the disobedient person is cut off by spiritual punishment and, expelled from the Church, is torn apart by the rabid mouth of demons.

For those who possess God as their inheritance ought to serve God without any impediment from the world, so that they may say: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance. O how good and gracious is your spirit, Lord, in all things! You spare all, because all are yours, Lord, lover of souls.” Therefore you correct those who go astray, little by little; you admonish and address them concerning the things in which they sin, so that, abandoning wickedness, they may believe in you, Lord. But you, our God, are gracious and true, patient and ordering all things in mercy. For even if we sin, we are yours, knowing your greatness; and if we do not sin, we know that we are counted among those who are with you. The spirit of those who fear the Lord is sought by him, and they will be blessed in his regard.

Therefore, dearest brothers:

> “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such speech as is good for building up when there is need, so that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice. Be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you. Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant odor.

> “But fornication and every impurity or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or vulgar joking, which is inappropriate, but rather thanksgiving. For know this with understanding: no fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—for greed is the service of idols—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. Therefore do not become partners with them.

> “For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, for the fruit of light consists in every goodness, righteousness, and truth, testing what is pleasing to God. Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, expose them. For it is shameful even to mention the things they do secretly. Everything that is exposed by the light is made manifest, for everything that is made manifest is light. Therefore it says: ‘Rise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.’

> “See carefully, therefore, brothers, how you walk—not as foolish people, but as wise—redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Therefore do not become senseless, but understand what the will of God is. Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord; always giving thanks for everything to God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; submitting to one another in the fear of Christ (Eph. IV, 29–32; V, 1–21).”

Stand firm, therefore, brothers, and hold fast to the traditions of the apostles and of the apostolic see, so that our Lord Jesus Christ, and our Father who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope through grace, may encourage your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word.

Finally, brothers, pray for us, [Col. 0150C] that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, as it is among you, and that we may be delivered from troublesome and evil people. For faith does not belong to everyone. But God is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from evil. Therefore continually set your hearts upon the strength of God, always resist evil people, and declare these things from generation to generation, according to the prophet’s voice, because “this is God, our God forever and ever, and he himself will guide us forever.”

Accordingly, you who have been placed by the Lord upon the watchtower must suppress and drive away with the utmost care those who prepare ambushes for their brothers or stir up seditions and scandals against them. It is easy to deceive a human being by a word, but not the Lord. Therefore you must rebuke such people and turn away from them, so that, when this kind of darkness has been completely extinguished, the morning star may shine upon them and joy arise in their hearts.

We are confident in you, brothers, in the Lord, that you do and will do what we have commanded. For the more abundantly you show your benefits to these people, the greater a return you may expect from the almighty God whom they serve. May almighty God guard you with his protection, grant you to preserve honor and obedience to his command, and may glory and honor be to God the almighty Father, and to his only-begotten Son, our Savior, with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# THE DECREES OF POPE FABIAN BEGIN

*(In the year of the Lord 242, during the reign of Decius.)*

[Col. 0151]

[Col. 0151A] Fabian, to his beloved fellow ministers everywhere in the Catholic Church, greetings in the Lord.

We are admonished by divine commands and apostolic institutions to watch over the state of all the churches with untiring devotion. It follows that you ought to know what is done in the Roman Church in the sacred rite, so that, by following its examples, you may be found to be true sons of the Church that is called your mother.

We therefore have seven deacons in the city of Rome, distributed through the seven regions of the city, as we have received from the fathers. Each week, on Sundays and on the solemn festivals, together with the subdeacons and acolytes and the ministers of the following orders, they observe the ministries entrusted to them and are ready at every hour to perform the divine service and whatever is assigned to them. [Col. 0151B]

Likewise, you should do what is appropriate in each city, so that the divine service may be performed diligently and solemnly, without any delay or negligence.

Finally, we have likewise ordained seven subdeacons to supervise seven notaries, so that they might gather the acts of the martyrs truthfully and in their entirety and disclose them to us for examination. We likewise urge all of you to do this, so that no doubt or question may arise about these matters in the future, “because everything that was written was written for our instruction.” What is truthfully written in our times is directed toward the instruction of those to come.

Therefore we command that these duties be entrusted to the most faithful, lest any deception be found in them from which—God forbid—scandal might arise among the faithful. Hence, with fatherly affection, we ask your charity that the holy Church may now find in all things the devotion of your charity and, wherever necessary, may enjoy the support of your favor. Just as the goodness of your zeal gives us confidence in you, so that we need have no distrust of it in anything, but may rather entrust these matters confidently to you as wise sons of our Church, so, when opportunities for action have been provided, your effectiveness must strive with the greatest effort and, in every possible way, labor earnestly to drive away insults.

We also exhort you, according to the Apostle’s saying, to be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord; and elsewhere:

> “Watch, stand firm in the faith, act courageously, and be strengthened. Let everything you do be done in charity (1 Cor. XVI, 13–14).” [Col. 0151D]

Moreover, we wish you to know that in our times, through the hindrance of our sins and at the urging of the ancient enemy, who always “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour,” Novatus came from Africa, separated Novatian and certain other confessors of Christ from the Church of Christ, [Col. 0152A] and turned them toward a perverse doctrine.

Turn away from them, brothers, and beware of all who hold another faith or doctrine than that which the apostles and their successors held and taught, lest—God forbid—by following him you fall into Satan’s snare and be held in his fetters.

Therefore, with our deepest prayers, we earnestly beseech the charity of your brotherhood to deign to remember our lowliness in your sacred prayers, praying and imploring the Lord of heaven that both we and the holy mother Church of Christ, redeemed by his precious blood, may be freed from the snares of Satan the hunter and from troublesome and evil people; that the word of God may run and be glorified; and that their perverse doctrine, and the doctrine of all who teach perversely, may fall and fail.

We also ask you to strive through your devout prayers to obtain that God and our Lord Jesus Christ[35], who desires all people to be saved and none to perish, may by his great omnipotence turn their hearts back to sound doctrine and the Catholic faith, so that they may repent of the snares of the devil by which they are held captive and may be gathered among the children of mother Church. Remembering your brothers also, have mercy on those whom you can help by your good efforts, so that they may not perish but may be saved by the Lord through your prayers and other works of your goodness.

Act in these matters, therefore, so that you may appear as obedient sons and faithful members of the holy Church of God, and so that you may receive the rewards of your recompense.

These people, and all who neither teach right doctrine [Col. 0152C] nor hold the right faith, cannot rightly accuse anyone who believes correctly, because they are marked with infamy and, by the apostolic sword, have been cut off from the bosom of holy mother Church until their right conduct and return.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, together with all the sons of that same apostolic and universal Church, we establish and decree that all who are suspected in the Catholic faith are not to be admitted to an accusation against those who believe correctly, because suspicions must always be removed. Their accusation is therefore rightly rejected if they are suspected in the right faith, and no credence at all is to be given to those who are ignorant of the faith of the Trinity.

Likewise, we remove all whom the statutes of the holy fathers have anathematized, whether in past or future times, and exclude them from every accusation of the faithful. The faithful must therefore always be distinguished from unbelievers, and the just from the unjust, because unbelievers and malicious people continually harass the faithful by whatever means they can and attempt to destroy them. For this reason they are not to be admitted, but resisted and cast far away, lest they be able to destroy or defame the faithful.

Therefore, dearest brothers, beware of the pit of such people, into which we know that many have fallen; beware of the arrows of such people and of the temptations of the ancient enemy, by which we have seen even close relatives wounded and fall before us. Pay attention to the snares of plotters, by which they habitually strangle acquaintances and comrades. Do not follow such people, but drive them far away.

Be, according to the voice of Truth, “wise as serpents and simple as doves.” See that you do not run or labor in vain, but, supported by one another’s prayers and supplications, strive to do the will of God; and, if those already mentioned prove incorrigible, separate yourselves from them in every way.

Likewise, separate yourselves from all those whom the Apostle mentions, saying that you should not even eat with them, because they too, like the others, are to be rejected and not received before making satisfaction to the Church. Those with whom it is not permitted to eat are plainly shown to be separated from the rest of the brothers until they make satisfaction. Therefore they neither ought nor can be admitted to an accusation against the faithful; rather, they must be excluded from their companionship until the aforesaid satisfaction, lest others become like them or be subjected to their excommunication.

For thus the apostles decreed, saying: “One must not associate with the excommunicated; and if anyone knowingly sings in a house with excommunicated persons while disregarding the rules, or speaks with them, or prays with them, let that person be deprived of communion.” Such people must therefore be avoided in every way and not admitted, because, according to the Apostle, not only those who do such things are condemned, but also those who consent to those who do them.

Thus the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, addressing the people in the *Ordinances of Clement*, among other things said:

> “If this Clement is an enemy to anyone because of his deeds, do not wait for him to tell you, ‘Do not be friends with that person.’ Rather, you must observe this prudently, comply with his will without association, and turn away from the one toward whom you perceive him to be hostile. Nor should you speak with those to whom he does not speak. Thus, whoever is at fault, while wishing to retain the friendship of all of you, should hasten to be reconciled with the one who presides over all, and through this return to salvation when he begins to obey the admonitions of the one in authority.

> “But if anyone is a friend to those with whom he himself does not speak, that person is one of those who wish to destroy the Church of God. Although he may appear to be with you in body, in mind and spirit he is against you. He is a much worse enemy than those who are outside and are openly hostile; for under the appearance of friendship he practices what is hostile, and he scatters and devastates the Church.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, instructing and admonishing you by these apostolic institutions, we urge you to ensure that your charity, now made more certain, strives henceforth to act more diligently and cautiously, lest perverse and faithless people have the opportunity to harm the faithful and benevolent. For the hope of such people and of all the impious is like down carried away by the wind, like thin foam scattered by a storm, like smoke dispersed by the wind, and like the memory of a guest who passes by in a single day.

[Col. 0154B] Dearest brothers, such people must be avoided, turned away, and rejected with the utmost care if they appear harmful, because not only ecclesiastical laws but also the laws of the world do not admit harmful people, but repel them.

Hence it is written: “The mouth of the wicked devours iniquity.” And the Lord speaks through the prophet:

> “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will become perverse; with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the harmful man you will be harmful (Ps. XVII, 26 ff.).”

The Apostle also says:

> “Evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor. XV, 33).”

Therefore, as has been said, evil people must always be avoided, while we must cling to the good and benevolent, so that, as far as we can, we may avoid the danger of negligence. And lest this plague spread more widely, let us cut it off with whatever severity we can, because where there is diligent piety, there is no rash presumption.

Let each one of you, supported by this apostolic instruction, act according to his strength, strive through brotherly love and holy religion to preserve his own conduct, help others mutually in common, remain in charity, and continually cling to the will of God, so that together, praising the Lord, we may always give him tireless thanks.

Farewell in the Lord, dearest brothers, and strive, with the Lord’s help, to fulfill the foregoing as well as you can.

Given on the Kalends of July, in the fourth consulship of Maximian and Africanus.

# THE ABOVE LETTER TO ALL THE BISHOPS

[Col. 0153]

[Col. 0153D] Fabian, bishop of the city of Rome, to all the Eastern bishops and to all the faithful, greetings in the Lord.

Your affection requires the decisions of the apostolic see, which we can neither deny nor ought to deny you. It is clear that our predecessors acted likewise toward the bishops of many regions; and brotherly charity and the duty of obedience compel us, who by the Lord’s favor have been placed in the same see, to do the same.

You must therefore apply care to your concern, so that what has been ordained by the apostles and their successors and instituted under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit may be neglected through no dissimulation or disturbed by any presumption. Just as what reason and usefulness required had to be defined, so what has been defined must not be violated.

In your letters, however, we find among other matters that certain bishops of your region differ from the order both of you and of us, and do not prepare the chrism every year on the Lord’s Supper, but preserve for two or three years a single preparation of the holy chrism. For, as we find in the aforesaid documents, they say that they cannot find balsam every year, and that it is not necessary to prepare chrism every year; rather, while one preparation of chrism remains in abundance, there is no need to make another.

They are mistaken who devise such things, and, thinking in a deranged rather than a sound manner, say these things. On that day, after the Lord Jesus had supped with his disciples and washed their feet, he taught the preparation of chrism, as our predecessors received from the holy apostles and handed down to us. For that washing of our feet signifies baptism, which is completed and confirmed through the anointing of the holy chrism.

Just as the solemnity of that day is celebrated every year, so the preparation of the holy chrism must be carried out every year, renewed from year to year, and handed on to the faithful, because it is newly consecrated each year and must be renewed on the appointed day, while the old chrism must be burned in the holy churches.

We have received this from the holy apostles and their successors, and we command you to maintain it. The holy Roman Church and the Church of Antioch have preserved this practice from the time of the apostles; the Churches of Jerusalem and Ephesus observe it as well. The apostles presided over those churches and taught that the old chrism should be burned, that it should not be used for more than one year, and that thereafter the new chrism should be used rather than the old.

If anyone attempts to oppose these provisions, let him understand that every avenue of indulgence is closed to him by you and by all who understand correctly. For the perverse doctrine of depraved minds, when it makes excessive use of leniency, slips into presumptuous transgression and cannot be rescued unless it is freed through the support and correction of the prudent.

The things that the holy Church does uniformly throughout the world concerning the divine mysteries and those being baptized must not be regarded with idle curiosity, lest we provide an opening for pointless arguments and superstitions. We must not lead the inexperienced minds of the faithful into such matters, for they should be taught rather than mocked.

Good deeds reach us as a source of joy, while things badly done pierce us with the thorns of sorrow. Here, however, we move somehow among the hands of robbers and the teeth of raging wolves, and the subjects and sheep are rebellious. The rage of wolves must be frightened away by the barking of dogs and the shepherd’s staff; wounds that cannot be healed by remedies must be cut away with the knife.

Nor can we remain silent, so that, when we recall some people from unlawful practices, we may be stirred by the impulse of our office. Placed by the Lord upon the watchtower, we must prove the diligence of our vigilance, cutting away what must be restrained and determining what must be observed.

You also wished to consult us, as we find in your aforesaid letters, concerning accusations against priests, which, as we find in those same documents, have become extremely common among you. Moreover, you indicated that many observe that numerous people holding ecclesiastical honors do not live consistently with the words and sacraments they administer to the people.

O wretched people, who, by looking at them, forget Christ—Christ who long before declared that the law of God must be obeyed rather than those who appear worthy of imitation but do not do what they say, and who, while tolerating his betrayer to the end, sent him with the others to preach the Gospel.

The apostles did not have such a practice, nor did they teach that it should be had. Their successors likewise, foreseeing many future matters through the Spirit of God, established provisions concerning such people.

Moreover, as you read in the Acts of the Apostles, at that time there was one heart and one soul among the faithful, and none of them claimed anything as his own; rather, everything was held in common. There was no accusation among them except one arising from familiarity, nor should there ever be one among their imitators or the faithful, since the Lord says: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.” Likewise: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself, and love does no harm to one’s neighbor.”

The apostles themselves and their successors therefore established long ago that those who are suspect, or who were enemies yesterday, the day before yesterday, or some time ago, are not to be admitted as accusers, since they have become suspect; nor are those who do not have good conduct, whose life is blameworthy, or who are uncertain in the right faith.

Likewise, neither are those to be admitted whose faith, life, and freedom are unknown, who are stained by marks of infamy, or entangled in crimes; nor should priests or clerics be accused by those who cannot properly become priests and who do not belong to their order.

For just as priests and the other clerics are excluded from accusations by secular laymen, so those laymen must be excluded and separated from accusations by the clergy. Just as the latter are excluded by the former, so the former must not be admitted by the latter, because, just as the conduct of the priests of the Lord must be set apart from that of the others, so too must their litigation be; for a servant of God ought not to litigate.

[Col. 0156C] Dearest brothers, prohibit such accusations and unjust or harmful rivalries as far as you can, because contention must be avoided above all. For “the righteous man falls seven times a day and rises again,” whereas the wicked fall into evil.

“‘When your enemy falls,’ Solomon says, ‘do not rejoice, and when he is ruined[36], let your heart not exult, lest the Lord see and be displeased and turn away his anger from him. Do not contend with the worst people or envy the wicked, for they have no hope of future things, and the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished. Do not envy evil men or desire to be with them, for their minds meditate robbery and their lips speak deceit.’” Beware of these things, dearest brothers.

Meditate on these matters and provide comfort to the brothers in all things, because by this, as Truth itself says, all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. For if each person’s right and proper order must be preserved in secular affairs, how much more must no confusion be introduced into ecclesiastical disputes! This will be observed if nothing is attributed to power but everything to equity.

Hence it is clear that the bishops of every place must exercise diligent care over all who live under their governance and arrange their affairs and interests with the fear of God. It is therefore exceedingly unjust for anyone else, neglecting his own responsibilities, to interfere in their affairs. Rather, those who ordained them to the priesthood and those by whom they were already ordained ought to regulate their life and judgment with appropriate and orderly governance.

For, as the law says: “Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbor’s boundary”; and all the people said: “Amen.”

God therefore, brothers, appointed you, who exercise the highest priesthood, for this purpose: that you may remove injustices, cut off presumptions, assist those laboring in the priesthood, and not provide an occasion for their reproaches and misfortunes, but bring help to the one who suffers slander and reproach. The person who causes slander or reproach, however, you must cut off, and you must bring help from the Lord to his priests.

The Lord also chose priests for himself, so that they might sacrifice to him and offer offerings to the Lord. He likewise commanded the Levites to be under them in their ministries. Thus he speaks to Moses, saying:

> “Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, the chief of the chiefs of the Levites, shall be over the guardians of the sanctuary of the assembly.”

The Lord spoke these things to Moses:

> “Take the Levites in place of all the firstborn of the sons of Israel, and the cattle of the Levites in place of their cattle; the Levites shall be mine, I am the Lord (Num. III, 34, 44–45).”

If the Lord wished the Levites to be his, how much more did he take priests for himself? Of them he says: “If any outsider approaches, he shall die.”

Everything that belongs to the Lord must be handled carefully and not rashly dispatched. Even among human beings, those who carefully guard and faithfully manage their masters’ affairs, and carefully preserve their masters’ commands without transgressing them, are regarded as faithful. Those who handle their masters’ affairs carelessly and negligently, despise their commands, and do not preserve them as they ought, are regarded as unfaithful.

We have therefore stated these things beforehand so that those who do not know may understand that priests—whom the Lord chose for himself from among all and wished to be his own—must not be treated lightly, torn apart, rashly accused, or rebuked except by their superiors. For the Lord wished to reserve their affairs to himself and to have them avenged by his own judgment.

In these and in the Lord’s other commands, the faithful are recognized and the unfaithful rejected. Such people are to be tolerated by the faithful rather than reproached, like the chaff with the wheat until the final winnowing, and like bad fish with good fish until the separation that will take place on the shore, that is, at the end of the world.

No one whom God has reserved for his own judgment can be condemned by human examination, lest God’s purpose—by which he decreed to save what had perished—be made void. Since his will is not changed, therefore, no one should presume to do what has not been granted to him.

Hence the Apostle says:

> “It is altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather accept being defrauded? (1 Cor. VI, 7).”

Let us return to what the Lord says:

> “If anyone wishes to take your tunic and bring you to court, let him have your cloak as well (Matt. V, 40).”

And elsewhere:

> “From the one who takes away what is yours, do not demand it back (Luke VI, 30).”

There are certain things that would be thought very slight if they were not shown in Scripture to be more serious than people suppose. Who would ever think that a person who says to his brother, “You fool,” is liable to the punishment of Gehenna, unless Truth itself said so?

Those who commit the sins of which the Apostle says, “Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God,” must be very carefully avoided and compelled to correction if they refuse willingly, because they are stained by marks of infamy and will fall into the abyss unless priestly authority comes to their aid.

Likewise, those concerning whom he himself says that one must not even eat with such people must be avoided, because they are marked with infamy until they are healed by priestly authority and restored to the bosom of holy mother Church. Those who are outside us cannot share communion with us.

It is clear that such people are outside us and must remain separated from us, since we may neither eat nor share food with them. Likewise, all persons subjected to any kind of obscenity or vulgarity have become infamous, and all who take up arms against their fathers become infamous.

It is easier to carry sand, salt, and a mass of iron than an imprudent, foolish, or impious person. For the one who is diminished in heart thinks about empty things, and the imprudent and erring person thinks foolish thoughts. Their suspicion has overthrown many and held their senses captive in vanity. A hard heart will fare badly at the end; the one who loves danger will perish in it. A heart entering upon two paths will have no rest, and the perverse heart will stumble in them. A wicked heart will be weighed down by sorrows, and the sinner will add sin to sin.

Considering such matters, the holy apostles and their successors, filled with the Spirit of God, foresaw evil people and took account of the simple. They did not wish accusations against priests to be easy, or perhaps ever possible, lest priests be overthrown or removed by evil people. For if this were easily granted to secular and wicked people, either none or scarcely very few would remain, since it has always been—and still is, and, what is worse, is flourishing excessively—that evil people persecute the good and the carnal harass the spiritual.

Therefore, as stated above, they decreed that priests should not be accused; or, if this could not be avoided, that their accusation should be made exceedingly difficult and should not be attempted by those already specified. Nor should bishops be expelled from their own sees or churches. If this should somehow be attempted, no one should accuse or charge them before their own place and all their property had been restored to them according to the laws. Unless they freely chose otherwise, no one should rebuke them on such grounds.

But after they had been restored, as prescribed above, and all their property had been legally restored to them, they should be granted a substantial period in which to deal with their affairs after arranging and ordering them. Afterwards, if necessary, they should be summoned lawfully to the case; and, if it seemed just, they should answer the accusers’ charges with the support of the brothers.

For no principle permits anything to be brought against them while their goods, or the goods of the Church, or their possessions are temporarily held by rivals or by anyone else; nor can anyone in any way bring any charge, great or small, against them while they lack their churches, property, or authority.

Likewise, it has been established—and, confirming the same statutes, we establish—that if any cleric is hostile or treacherous toward his bishop and wishes to accuse him, or has conspired against him, he shall immediately, before judgment has been examined, be removed from the clergy and handed over to the civil court, which he shall serve all the days of his life; and he shall remain infamous, without any hope of restoration.

No one should ever presume to be both accuser and judge or witness, since in every judgment four persons must always be present: namely, appointed judges, accusers, defenders, and witnesses.

Likewise, establishing this by apostolic authority, we command that the sheep entrusted to their shepherd must not dare to rebuke him unless he has erred in the faith. The deeds of superiors must not be struck down by the sword of the mouth, nor can the disciple be above the teacher, as the voice of Truth says: “The disciple is not above his teacher, nor the servant above his master.”

Pride is hateful before God and human beings, and every iniquity is detestable. God destroys the memory of the proud and leaves the memory of the humble in understanding. The offspring of human beings who fear God will be honored; but the offspring of those who disregard the Lord’s commandments will be dishonored. Among the brothers, their ruler is held in honor, and those who fear the Lord will be in his sight.

“Son,” Solomon says, “preserve your soul in gentleness, and give honor to the one to whom honor is due. Before you inquire, do not reproach anyone; and when you have inquired, rebuke justly. Before you have heard, do not answer a word; and in the midst of elders do not add to your speech.”

The example of Ham, the son of Noah, condemns those who publicly expose the faults of their fathers or presume to accuse or disparage them. Ham did not cover the nakedness of his father Noah but displayed it for mockery. Likewise, those who reverently cover and do not expose what they know their fathers have done wrong are justified by the example of Shem and Japheth.

If a bishop should deviate from the faith, he must first be corrected privately by his subjects. If, however—God forbid—he proves incorrigible, then he must be accused before his primates or before the apostolic see.

For his other actions, however, he is more to be tolerated by his sheep and subjects than accused or publicly disparaged, because when his subjects commit offenses in these matters, they oppose the ordinance of the one who placed them under him, as the Apostle says: “He resists God’s ordinance who resists the authority” [Col. 0160B] (Rom. 13:2). Whoever fears almighty God does not consent in any way to act against the Gospel, the apostles, the prophets, or the institutions of the holy fathers. Priests, therefore, are to be honored, not torn apart or reproached. It is written in Ecclesiasticus:

“Fear God with all your soul, and sanctify his priests; with all your strength love him who made you, and do not abandon his ministers. Honor God with all your soul, and honor the priests, and cleanse yourself with your arms; give them their portion, as it has been commanded you, of the firstfruits and of purification, and cleanse yourself from negligence with a few. Offer the gift of your arms and the sacrifice of sanctification to the Lord, and the first offerings of the holy things; and extend your hand to the poor [Col. 0160C], so that your atonement and blessing may be perfected” (Eccli. 7:31 ff.).

We wish these things to be made known through you, not only to you but to all the brethren, so that, united and of one mind, we may remain in Christ, claiming nothing for ourselves through contention or empty glory, pleasing not human beings but God our Savior, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# LETTER OF POPE FABIAN

[Col. 0159]

[Col. 0159C] Fabian, to his most beloved brother Hilary, bishop.
