We must be mindful of the divine grace toward us, which, through the mercy of its gracious favor, has raised us to the dignity of the priesthood for this purpose: that, clinging to his commandments and established, as it were, in a watchtower of his priests, we may prohibit what is unlawful and teach what ought to be followed. For we have heard that in the western regions where you dwell the devil’s cunning rages against the Christian people and breaks out into manifold deception, so that he oppresses and harasses not only secular laypeople but even the priests of the Lord themselves.

Therefore, placed in great sorrow, we cannot overlook what we ought most severely to correct. Accordingly, suitable treatment must be applied to such wounds, lest an untimely eagerness to heal accomplish nothing against the deadly plague of the head, but, if the disease is treated too slowly, the danger of an illegitimate cure involve both the wounded and those treating them in guilt [Col. 0160C].

For this reason, therefore, we establish and decree that those who are not of good conduct, whose life is blameworthy, or whose faith, life, and liberty are unknown, may not accuse the priests of the Lord, lest persons of low standing be admitted to accuse them. Likewise, those entangled in any crimes, or those under suspicion, shall not have the right to bring accusations against their elders, because a suspicious and hostile voice is accustomed to suppress the truth.

We prohibit by a general apostolic sanction all foreign jurisdictions, while preserving the authority of the Apostolic See in every matter, because it is unworthy that one should be judged by outsiders who ought to have provincial judges chosen from among themselves, unless an appeal has been made. Therefore, if any bishop is accused of definite crimes, he must be heard by all the bishops in the province, since the accused ought not to be heard anywhere [Col. 0161A] except in his own forum.

If anyone believes that a judge is acting against him, let him present an appeal. The appellant must not be harassed by any affliction or injured by imprisonment in custody. Rather, the appellant must be permitted to obtain relief for a corrupted case through the remedy of appeal. It is also permitted to appeal in criminal cases, and the right of appeal must not be denied to one whom a sentence has destined for punishment.

Let the accused state his case before his own judge; but an accused person brought before a judge who is not his own may remain silent if he wishes. And whenever the accused appeal, they shall be granted delays. If, therefore, someone in anger rashly brings a charge against anyone, the insult must not be regarded as an accusation. Instead, after a period has been allowed for reflection, let him declare that he will prove by Scripture what he said in anger, so that, if he should come to his senses and refuse to repeat or write what he said in anger [Col. 0161B], he may not be held as guilty of a crime. Everyone who brings a charge must write that he will prove it.

In truth, a case must always be conducted where the crime was committed. Whoever does not prove what he has charged shall himself suffer the penalty he imposed. It was also decided that if an accused bishop appeals to the Apostolic See, whatever the pontiff of that See has judged shall be established. This rule, however, must be observed entirely in the case of priests, so that no one is bound by a sentence issued by a judge other than his own.

Each of the faithful ought also to come to the aid of those crushed by ruin and of the wretched, so that, through the relief of another’s punishment, they may be able to remove God’s punishment from themselves. For the one who drives away adversity from the afflicted offers prosperity to the Lord; hence it is written: “A brother who helps a brother will be exalted.”

The Church of God ought to exist without stain or wrinkle, and therefore it ought not to be trampled upon or defiled by certain persons, because it is written: “My dove, my perfect one, is one” (Song 6:8). Again, the Lord says to Moses: “There is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock” (Exod. 33:21). What place is there that is not the Lord’s, since all things are contained in him through whom they were created? Yet there is a place with him—namely, the unity of the holy Church—in which one stands upon the rock when the firmness of confession is held humbly.

We admonish you, brother, and all our brothers who govern the Church of Christ, redeemed by his blood, to restrain by whatever means you can all those who are slipping into the precipice by disparaging and persecuting the brethren and the pastors of the Lord in word and deed. Do not permit them to be torn apart on the hook of anger, because it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). Again it is said: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19).

I do not doubt that, with God as your author, you observe all these things. But since an occasion for admonition has arisen, I add myself, as one who admonishes, to your good desires and works, so that what you do without admonition, when I too am added to you as one who admonishes, you may no longer do alone.

Therefore, brothers, you and all the faithful ought to love one another and not disparage or accuse one another. For it is written:

“Love your neighbor and join yourself to him in faith. If you disclose his secrets, do not pursue him afterward. For just as a person who loses his friend is like one who loses the friendship of his neighbor, and just as one who releases a bird from his hand, so you have abandoned your neighbor and will not seize him again. You shall not pursue him, because he is far away; for he has escaped like a wild goat from a snare, because his soul has been wounded. You will no longer be able to bind him up, and reconciliation is accursed. To disclose the secrets of a friend is the despair of an unfaithful soul.

“He who winks with his eye devises evil, and no one will cast him away. In the sight of your eyes he will trample upon his mouth, and he will marvel at your words; but at last he will pervert his mouth and cause scandal through your words. I have heard many things and have not equaled him, and the Lord will hate him.

“He who throws a stone upward has it fall upon his own head, and a treacherous wound divides the wounds of the treacherous. He who digs a pit will fall into it, and he who sets a stone before his neighbor will stumble over it, and he who places a snare for another will perish in it. The one who devises a most evil plan will have it roll back upon himself and will not recognize from where it has come to him.

“Mockery and reproach will lie in wait for the proud like a lion, and vengeance likewise. Those who delight in the downfall of the just will perish by a snare; pain will consume them before they die. Anger and fury are both detestable, and the sinful person will restrain them.

“Whoever wishes to take revenge will find vengeance from God, and he will carefully preserve his sins. Forgive your neighbor who harms you, and then, when you pray, your sins will be forgiven. A person preserves anger against another person and seeks healing from God. He has no mercy on one like himself, yet he pleads for his own sins before the Most High. Though he is flesh, he preserves anger and asks God for reconciliation? Who will plead for his offenses?

“Remember your last things and cease to be hostile. For decay and death threaten in the commandments. Remember the fear of the Lord and do not be angry with your neighbor. Remember the covenant of the Most High and overlook your neighbor’s ignorance.

“Refrain from strife and you will lessen sins, for an angry person kindles strife; and, as a sinner, he will disturb friends and introduce hostility among those who have peace. As the wood of the forest is, so the fire will blaze; and according to a person’s strength will be his anger, and according to his resources so will he exalt his fury. Hasty quarrels kindle fire, and an argument pursued hastily pours out blood; a tongue that bears witness brings death.

“If you blow upon a spark, it will blaze like a fire; and if you spit upon it, it will be extinguished—and both proceed from the mouth. The whisperer and the double-tongued person are accursed, for he has disturbed many who had peace. The third tongue has stirred up many and scattered them from nation to nation. It has destroyed the fortified cities of the wealthy and dug up the houses of the great; it has overthrown the strength of peoples and dissolved strong nations.

“The third tongue has driven out truthful women and deprived them of their labors. Whoever watches over it will have no rest and will not dwell in quiet. The blow of a scourge produces a bruise, but the blow of the tongue crushes bones. Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not as many as those who have perished through their own tongue. Blessed is the one who is protected from an evil tongue, who has not passed into its anger, who has not drawn its yoke upon himself, and who has not been bound by its chains.

“For its yoke is an iron yoke, and its bond is a bronze bond; its death is a most evil death, and hell is preferable and more useful than it. Its persistence will not endure, but it will obtain the ways of the unjust, and its flame will not burn the righteous. Those who abandon God fall into it; it will blaze against them and not be extinguished. It will be sent against them like a lion and injure them like a leopard.

“Fence your ears with thorns and do not listen to an evil tongue; make doors and bars for your mouth and bolts for your ears. Melt your gold [Col. 0163B] and silver, make a balance for your words, and straight bridles for your mouth. Take care lest you slip with your tongue and fall before enemies lying in wait for you, and lest your fall become incurable unto death” (Eccli. 27–28).

Let everyone beware of these things and restrain his tongue from evil, and let his lips not speak deceit.

For the rest, beloved, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might [Col. 0164A]. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and stand perfect in all things.

Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Holy Spirit, which is the word of God.

These things, brother, which we have written to you, we wish to be made known generally to all, so that whatever concerns the others may become known to everyone. May almighty God protect you, brother, and our other brothers dwelling everywhere, unto the end—Jesus Christ our Lord, who has deigned to redeem the whole world and is blessed forever. Amen.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Africanus and Decius for the fourth time.

# THE DECREES OF POPE CORNELIUS BEGIN

On the translation of the bodies of the apostles, and concerning certain heretics.  
(In the year of the Lord 255, while Decius was emperor.)

[Col. 0163]

[Col. 0163C] Cornelius, bishop, to his dearest and most beloved brothers, the sons of the holy Church of God, and to all who serve the Lord in the true faith.

Seeing the goodwill of your charity, because you are lovers of the apostles and hold their faith and teaching, I have resolved, with the Lord as author, to write to you about certain things that it is necessary to know at the present time, and about what has recently been done or is now being done among us in the Roman Church, with the help of the Lord, through the merits of the apostles. For, with charity as our advocate, I believe that you gladly receive the writings of the Apostolic See with fatherly grace, carry out its commands, and rejoice in its progress. Whoever grafts himself into the root of charity neither loses its freshness nor becomes barren of fruits, nor does he lose the effective work of the love that makes fruitful [Col. 0163D].

Charity itself exercises the hearts of the faithful and strengthens their understanding, so that nothing burdensome or difficult is done, but everything undertaken becomes sweet, since it is characteristic of charity to nourish harmony, preserve the commandments, unite what has been separated, set crooked things straight, and strengthen the other virtues with the protection of its perfection.

Therefore I ask you to rejoice with us, because at the request of a certain devout and most noble matron, Lucina, the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul were raised from the Catacombs. First, the body of blessed Paul was quietly raised and placed on the estate of the aforesaid matron, on the Ostian Way, beside the place where he was beheaded. Afterwards, we received the body of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and honorably placed it beside the place where he was crucified, among the bodies of holy bishops, in the temple of Apollo, on the Golden Mount in the Vatican, at Nero’s palace, on the third day before the Kalends of July [Col. 0164C].

We prayed to God and our Lord Jesus Christ that, through the intercession of his holy apostles, he might cleanse the stains of your sins, preserve you in his will throughout the days of your life, and make you steadfast in the fruit of good works.

Rejoice in these things, for the holy apostles themselves also rejoice in your joy. Always praise God, and may he himself be glorified in you. For it is written: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me? I will take up the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:12–13).

Only as much is required from us as we are able to contribute through the service of our ministry. Hence, the more necessary it is for us to persist in urgent preaching, the more we are believed to have been entrusted with a doubled allotment of talents for a perfect undertaking, and the more the assurance of the Lord’s word urges us to receive his rest.

Seeing this, the ancient enemy raised up against us Novatus, an adversary of the true faith and holy teaching [Col. 0165A], who ordained Novatian outside the Church, and in Africa Nicostratus—both heretics, as he himself was. By whatever efforts they could, these men persuaded many to withdraw from the true and Catholic faith and induced them to fall after them into a perverse doctrine hateful to God.

But just as we were deeply saddened by their evasions and crushed by their destruction, so, with the Lord’s help, we have been gladdened by the conduct of others. Almighty God, who mingles joys with sorrows, greatly gladdened us when certain confessors who had formerly been faithful, separating themselves from us and from the true faith at the devil’s instigation, returned to the Catholic Church and the true faith with the presbyter Maximus, and again became faithful confessors as they had been before [Col. 0165B].

Therefore, beloved, we exhort and beseech you through our Lord Jesus Christ to strive, by your exhortations and good efforts, to convert to the Catholic faith and true doctrine both the aforesaid heretics and all whom you know to have apostatized from the true faith and teaching, and persuade them to persist in God’s will.

Hasten not only to bring these people, but also all who have not yet received the true faith, to the Catholic faith, “for neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature,” as the teacher of the nations declares, “will be able to separate us from the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, and from the true faith that is in him” (Rom. 8:38–39).

Therefore do not lose your confidence, which has a great reward (Heb. 10:35). For patience is necessary for us in the struggles against our adversaries, so that, preserving an undefiled faith unto the end, we may receive the promise that he made to those who hasten to compete lawfully. “For yet a very little while, and he who is to come will come and will not delay” (ibid., 37).

Behold, the judge stands before the door, promising joyful crowns to those who submit to sufferings for his sake. But if anyone draws back, my soul will not be pleased with him; rather, he will fall away from the promise because of his denial. We, however, are not children of withdrawal unto destruction, but of faith unto the acquisition of the soul.

Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day against all the enemies of the holy Church and your own. Put on the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace, in all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, being rooted and founded through every prayer and supplication in the comfort of the brethren for Christ Jesus our Lord [Col. 0166B].

And now, brothers, we commend you and all our brothers to the Lord and to the word of his grace, which can perfect us and give us an inheritance with all the saints. May the God of peace and consolation grant you to think the same toward one another, so that you may help one another and not be divided; so that, united, with one mouth and one heart, you may honor him in harmony and in the consolation of the brethren. He is able to strengthen you according to his Gospel, in accordance with the revelation of the eternal mystery—namely, in the perpetual ages in which the gifts of future joys are to be bestowed upon you.

You must also consider most carefully that those who envy the brethren and wish to condemn and destroy them destroy their own doctrines by themselves. For the Lord says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand” (Matt. 12:25); and every knowledge and law divided against itself will not stand. Therefore it is necessary that you receive wholesome exhortations in harmony, doing nothing through contention, but united in every work of devotion, obeying the divine and apostolic constitutions.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of September, in the consulship of Decius and Maximus for the fourth time.

# HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF POPE CORNELIUS ADDRESSED TO THE EASTERN BISHOP

That the priests of the Lord must neither presume to swear nor be compelled to swear.

[Col. 0165]

[Col. 0165D] Cornelius, bishop, to Rufus, fellow bishop, greetings in the Lord.

Your affection, dearest brother, requires that we answer your inquiries from the authority of the Apostolic See. Although we would hasten to do so not at length but briefly, because of certain disturbances which, through the sins that impede us, have come upon us, nevertheless we permit you, in the remaining matters, to search more broadly and investigate according to the institutions of the holy fathers.

For a mind worn down and weighed down by burdens and disturbances cannot accomplish as much good as one that is delighted and freed from oppression. We have not placed these matters before you in order to deny to Your Holiness these or other things that we know to be necessary, but so that what is less available here may be sought more extensively elsewhere.

We have not learned that an oath has hitherto been required from the high priests or from others, except for the true faith; nor have we found that anyone has sworn voluntarily. Therefore the holy Apostle James, prohibiting oaths in the strongest terms, says: “Above all things, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath. Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; no, no,’ so that you may not fall under judgment” (James 5:12).

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not swear falsely, but you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all—neither by heaven, because it is the throne of God, nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet, nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great king; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; no, no.’ Whatever is more than these is from evil” (Matt. 5:33–37)—that is, from the one who demands the oath and from the one who swears.

“These things, dearest brother, the Lord himself prohibits: namely, that one ought not to swear.” All the apostles especially prohibit these things; so do the holy men, our predecessors who presided before us over this holy universal Apostolic Church; and so do the prophets and the other holy teachers scattered throughout the world to preach. If we began to enumerate their examples or insert them in this little document, the hour of the day would end before we finished recording the examples by which they prohibited oaths.

Following these men, we confirm the laws of the holy apostles and their successors and prohibit careless oaths. The Lord himself, therefore, wrote with his own hand on the stone tablets that he gave to Moses: “See that you do not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. 20:7), and what follows [Col. 0167B].

As we briefly mentioned above, we do not know of an oath being offered to bishops, nor should it ever be done, since, as was stated above, we have been commanded by the Lord not to swear: neither by heaven, because it is the throne of God; nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by one’s head, because no one can create a single hair.

Everyone, therefore, standing before God’s altar, must keep the fear of God before his eyes and preserve his own conscience clean for God. Whoever retains this in memory must in no way interrupt it, since “the mouth that lies kills the soul.” The Apostle says: “Speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another” (Eph. 4:25). And elsewhere: “Do not lie to one another” (Col. 3:9).

These are the commandments of the Savior; these are the institutions of the prophets; these are the institutions of the holy Fathers. If anyone treats them as vain, he is the enemy of his own soul, because no one does anything against the prophets, against the apostle, or against the Gospel without danger.

It must also be carefully foreseen that the sheep entrusted to a pastor must not presume to rebuke or accuse him—unless he has deviated from the faith—for such accusations have no force and cannot harm him.

“One thing, beloved,” says the blessed Apostle Peter, “must not escape you: that with the Lord one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day. The Lord is not slow concerning his promises, but deals patiently for your sake, not wishing any to perish but all to return to repentance. The day of the Lord will come like a thief; on that day the heavens will pass away with great violence, and the elements will be dissolved by heat. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness, waiting for and hastening toward the coming of the day of God, through which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will melt in the heat of fire?” (2 Pet. 3:8–12).

But you, beloved, remember, as the Apostle Jude said, the words that were foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said to you that in the last time mockers would come, walking according to their own desires in ungodliness. These are the ones who separate themselves, worldly people, not having the Spirit.

But you, beloved, building yourselves up upon your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. Convict some who are judged; save others by snatching them from the fire; and on others have mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.

Let no priest entrust his case to the judgment of another unless an appeal has been made to the Apostolic See. Rather, let each one have provincial and known judges, unless he fears there the violence of a rash crowd, or has hostile or suspect judges there; for these reasons, he is permitted to appeal and proceed to judges of greater authority and to other provinces.

Therefore, let everything done or judged against absent persons in any matter or place be entirely nullified, because no one condemns an absent person, and no law condemns him. A human being can easily deceive another human being, but not God, before whose eyes all things are naked and open [Col. 0168C]. Hence the prophet says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (1 Cor. 3:20).

A wise person, therefore, is not one who harms; nor does the faithful person wish anything evil or plot snares for anyone.

We exhort and admonish you, brother, to help, strengthen, and console everyone always, as best you can. Prohibit the oaths about which you wished to consult this holy Roman and universal Church, and never harass or harm anyone.

Let Your Holiness make these things known to the remaining brothers, so that all may beware of these evils; and just as they have been generally prohibited by the Lord himself, by the saints and other apostolic men, and by the remaining fathers, so let them be generally observed by all [Col. 0168D].

We always wish your blessedness good health and desire that you advance in sacred virtues, dearest and most beloved brother.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Maximus and Decius for the fourth time.

# HERE BEGIN THE DECREES OF POPE LUCIUS

(In the year of the Lord 258, while Gallus Hostilianus was emperor.)

[Col. 0167]

[Col. 0167D] Lucius, bishop, to all the beloved brothers, all bishops residing in the western regions, both Gaulish and Spanish, greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0168D] We gladly received the letter of your affection that you sent to the See of the blessed Apostle Peter concerning your case, but we were deeply saddened by your afflictions [Col. 0169A]. For you reported that you are persecuted and defamed both by certain persons who do not hold the true faith but are entangled in errors, and by others who imitate them; that your churches are stripped of their endowments and the offerings of the faithful; that your ministers are harassed excessively; and that, as a result, many are departing from you and from the true faith because you are unable to provide them with defense or administer what is necessary.

Do not wonder, brothers, if the malevolent and impious persecute you, since they persecuted Christ himself, our head. Hence you have the Truth itself as your consoler, which says: “If they have called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household!” (Matt. 10:25). Again, consoling us, it says: “If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of this world, and I chose you from the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19).

For the sake of such people, brothers, we exhort you, just as we have established in this holy Church, always to have priests and deacons as witnesses with you. Although one’s own conscience ought to be sufficient, nevertheless, because of the malevolent, according to the Apostle you ought also to have a good testimony from those who are outside.

For we have established in this holy See that two presbyters or three deacons must not leave a bishop in any place, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony. Bishops, therefore, must not be accused or disparaged lightly, because an injury against them concerns Christ, whose place and embassy they fulfill in the Church.

Therefore, for your consolation and that of all who are with you, just as we find was done long ago, it has pleased us to decree that accusations against elders must not be brought by others except by those who bring the charges themselves—provided that they appear worthy and irreproachable, and prove through public records that they are entirely free from suspicion and hostility and lead an irreproachable life of faith and conduct [Col. 0169C].

Therefore it was decided that, from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where there is greater authority, a hearing must not be denied when an appeal has been made.

Likewise, we establish, as we find decreed by the holy apostles and their successors, that if any metropolitan bishop attempts to act outside his own parish in any matter whatsoever, without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province, he shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank, and whatever he has done shall be considered invalid and void.

But whatever it is necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of fellow bishops of the province and their churches, their clergy, and secular persons, or concerning any common matters, shall be done with the consent of all the provincial bishops—not with any display of domination, but through harmonious and most humble administration, as the Lord says: “I did not come to be served, but to serve” (Mark 10:45). And elsewhere: “The one who is greatest among you shall be your servant” (Matt. 23:11), and so forth.

Likewise, the provincial bishops themselves shall conduct everything with his counsel, except insofar as it concerns their own parishes, according to the decrees of the holy fathers, so that with one mind and one voice the holy Trinity may be glorified harmoniously forever.

Likewise, supported by apostolic authority, we command that no metropolitan bishop hear anyone’s cases without the attendance of all the other provincial bishops, because such proceedings will be invalid, and he himself will have to answer for what he has done. Bishops in each province must take care that those later in rank do not place themselves before their predecessors, nor act without consulting them, except insofar as it concerns their own parish. Rather, all must pronounce and determine a harmonious judgment concerning their common affairs, because otherwise the proceedings will have no force and will not be regarded as ecclesiastical.

[Col. 0170B] It would be good, brothers, and very necessary for those who fear God and wish to live piously, if within the Catholic Church no seed of evil or of any disturbance against the priests of the Lord or against those who wish to live justly and piously should arise. But because envy prevails—and what is worse, rises, grows, and extends itself too far in every direction—it is therefore necessary that it be cut away with an ecclesiastical and apostolic sword, lest it be able to harm or destroy the servants of God and the priests of the Lord.

“For the Lord, as it is read in the book of Ecclesiasticus, dishonored the assembly of the wicked, and God destroyed them utterly. God destroyed the seats of proud leaders and made the meek sit in their place. God dried up the roots of proud nations and planted the humble from among those nations. [Col. 0170C] The Lord overturned the lands of the nations and destroyed them to their foundations. He dried up some of them and destroyed them, and caused their memory to cease from the earth. God destroyed the memory of the proud and left the memory of the humble in understanding. Pride was not created for human beings, nor anger for the nation of women. The offspring of human beings who fear God will be honored, but the offspring that transgresses the commandments of the Lord will be dishonored by human beings. In the midst of his brothers their ruler is honored, and those who fear the Lord will be in his sight. The glory of the rich is honor, and of the poor, the fear of God. Do not despise a poor just man, and do not magnify a rich sinful man. Great is the Judge, and powerful in honor, and there is none greater than he who fears [Col. 0170D] God. Free men serve a sensible servant, and a prudent and disciplined man will not murmur when corrected, while the ignorant will not be honored. Do not exalt yourself in carrying out your works, and do not hesitate in a time of distress. Better is one who works and abounds in all things than one who boasts and lacks bread. Son, preserve your soul in gentleness and give it honor according to its merit. Who will justify one who sins against his own soul? And who will honor one who dishonors his own soul? A poor man boasts through his discipline and fear, and there is a man who is honored because of his wealth. He who boasts in poverty—how much more in wealth? And he who boasts in wealth should fear poverty. [Col. 0171A] Wisdom will exalt the head of the humbled man and make him sit in the midst of the great. Do not praise a man for his appearance, nor despise a man for his outward looks. The bee is small among flying creatures, yet its product is the beginning of sweetness. Never boast in clothing, nor exalt yourself on the day of your honor, for the works of the Most High alone are wondrous, and his works are glorious, hidden, and unseen. Many tyrants have sat on a throne, and one beyond expectation has borne the diadem. Many powerful men have been violently oppressed, and the glorious have been delivered into the hands of others. Before you question anyone, do not reproach him; and when you have questioned him, correct him justly. Before you hear, do not answer a word; and in the midst of the elders do not add to your speaking. Do not contend over a matter that does not trouble you, and do not sit in the judgment of sinners. [Col. 0171B] My son, do not let your actions be many; and if you become rich, you will not be free from sin. For if you pursue, you will not apprehend; and if you run ahead, you will not escape. There is a man who labors, hastens, and suffers—an ungodly man—and yet he abounds all the less. There is a man who is weakened and in need of recovery, failing still more in strength and abounding in poverty; and the eye of God looked upon him for good, raised him from his humiliation, and exalted his head, and many marveled at him and honored God. Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from God. God’s gift remains with the just, and its advancement will have success forever. There is one who grows rich by acting sparingly, and this is his portion, according to what he says: ‘I have found rest for myself, and I shall eat of my goods alone’ (Luke XII, 19); yet he does not know that time is passing him by, and he will leave everything to others and die. Stand by your covenant, converse in it, and grow old in the work of your commandments. Do not remain in the works of sinners. But trust in God and remain in your place; for it is easy in the eyes of God suddenly to honor a poor man. God’s blessing hastens as the reward of the just, and by swift honor his progress is justified. Do not say: ‘What need have I, and what good will come to me from this?’ Do not say: ‘I have enough for myself, and what harm could come to me from this?’ On the day of good things do not forget evils, and on the day of evils do not forget good things, for before God it is easy, on the day of death, to repay each according to his ways. The evil of the hour causes great luxury to be forgotten, [Col. 0171D] and at the end of a man comes the uncovering of his deeds. Before death, do not praise anyone, for a man is recognized in his children. Do not bring every person into your house, for there are many snares of the deceitful. For just as the entrails of foul things belch forth, and as a partridge is brought into a cage, and as a doe into a snare, so is the heart of the proud, and so is one who watches for the fall of his neighbor. The plotter turns good into evil and places a blemish upon the chosen. From one spark fire is increased, and from one deceitful man bloodshed is increased. The sinful man, indeed, lies in wait for blood. Beware of the pestilent man: he devises evils, lest perhaps he bring lasting mockery upon you. Admit [Col. 0172A] a foreigner to yourself, and he will overturn you in a whirlwind and estrange you from your own people (Ecclesiasticus X, XI).”

“Such men, dearest ones, must be greatly avoided until they either convert or are cut off by the word of God. But blessed is the one who has not fallen through a word from his mouth and has not been pierced by the grief of sin. Happy is the one who has no sorrow of spirit and does not depart from his hope (Ecclesiasticus XIV, 1–3).” For it is written: “Better is one who fears God than a thousand ungodly men (Ecclesiasticus XVI, 3).”

Not everyone who causes harm is wise. The property of your churches and the offerings of the faithful, which you have reported to be harassed by certain intruders and taken away from you and your churches, are unquestionably a very great sin. Scripture itself bears witness, saying: “Whoever takes [Col. 0172B] anything from his father or mother and says that this is not a sin is a participant in murder.” Our father, therefore, is without doubt God, who created us; and our mother is the Church, which spiritually gave birth to us in baptism. Therefore, whoever takes, defrauds, and steals the money of Christ and of the Church will be judged a murderer in the sight of the just Judge. Hence it is written: “Whoever steals his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but whoever takes money or property belonging to the Church commits sacrilege.”

Thus Judas, who defrauded the money that, by the command of the Savior—whose place bishops hold—was distributed for the uses of the Church, that is, to the poor whom the Church ought to feed, became not merely a thief but a thief and sacrilegious man.

Concerning such men—that is, those who seize, defraud, or [Col. 0172C] take away the resources of the Church—the Lord, threatening them all, speaks through the prophet, saying:

“God, do not keep silent; do not be silent and do not rest, O God, for behold, your enemies have made an uproar, and those who hate you have raised their head. They have dealt wickedly against your people and have taken counsel against your hidden ones. They said, ‘Come, let us destroy them from the nation, and let the memory of the name of Israel cease forever.’ For they conspired in their hearts; together they made a covenant against you. The tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek, Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre. Assyria also joined itself with them; they became an arm for the sons of Lot. Do to them as to Midian, as to Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon. They were crushed at Endor; they became like manure for the earth. [Col. 0172D] Make their leaders like Oreb and Zeeb, like Zebah and Zalmunna, all their princes who said, ‘Let us take possession for ourselves of the beauty of God.’ My God, make them like a wheel, like straw before the face of the wind. As fire burns a forest and as flame consumes mountains, so pursue them in your storm and trouble them in your whirlwind. Fill their faces with disgrace, and they will seek your name, O Lord. Let them be confounded and troubled forever; let them blush and perish, and let them know that you alone—whose name is Lord—are Most High over all the earth.”

[Col. 0173A] The decrees of the prophets, the apostles, their successors, and all the Catholic Fathers forbid such things, and judge such presumptions to be sacrilege. Following their examples, by apostolic authority we expel and condemn with ourselves from the thresholds of holy mother Church all such presumptuous persons, robbers of the Church, and alienators of their property, and we judge them to be sacrilegious. We condemn not only them but also all who consent to them, because not only those who do such things are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those who do them; equal punishment encompasses both the perpetrators and those who consent.

Therefore, brothers, watch and pray; act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord; and, according to the Apostle, let all your actions be done in charity. Do not, because of any disturbance, withdraw from the right faith and the apostolic path, knowing that, according to the Savior’s judgment, blessed are those who suffer persecution [Col. 0173B] for righteousness’ sake (Matthew V, 10).

This is the living tradition of the apostles; this is the true charity that must be preached and especially loved, fostered, and held confidently by all. This holy and apostolic mother of all the Churches—the Church of Christ—which by the grace of almighty God is proved never to have strayed from the path of apostolic tradition, nor to have yielded to be corrupted by heretical novelties, but, just as at its beginning it received the rule of apostolic faith from its founders, the chief apostles of Christ, remains undefiled to the end according to the divine promise of the Lord and Savior himself, who said in his Gospels to the chief of his disciples:

“Peter,” he said, “behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers (Luke XXII, 38, 32).” [Col. 0173C]

Let your excellent prudence therefore consider how good it is to persist in the stewardship entrusted to you [Col. 0174A] and in the right faith, to resist heretics and the rivals of Christ, and never to deviate from the path of truth. For the Lord and Savior of all, whose faith it is, who did not hesitate to die for us and redeemed us with his own blood, who promised that the faith of blessed Peter would not fail and admonished him to strengthen his brothers—this is something which the apostolic pontiffs, my predecessors in my lowliness, are known always to have done confidently before all.

My own littleness, although unequal and very small, nevertheless desires to follow in their footsteps on account of the ministry undertaken by divine favor. For woe will be to us who have undertaken the burden of this ministry if we neglect to preach the truth of our Savior Jesus Christ which the apostles preached. Woe will be to us if by silence we suppress the truth [Col. 0174B] which we are commanded to distribute to the money-changers—that is, to instruct and teach Christian peoples. What will we [40] say at Christ’s own future judgment if we are ashamed to preach the truth of his words? What will become of us when Christ the Lord, our just Judge, strictly demands an account of the souls entrusted to us and of the office we have undertaken?

Therefore, brothers, I exhort, entreat, and admonish your affection to watch with the diligence that you ought and can, so as to investigate heretics and enemies of the holy Church of God, and with whatever severity you are able, according to your strength, to uproot this pest from sound minds, lest it spread more widely. For just as the one who diligently carries out what benefits the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive from God the reward of a worthy recompense, so [Col. 0174C] whoever refuses to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will not be able to excuse himself for the guilt of negligence before the tribunal of the Lord.

Given on the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Gallio and Volusianus IV.

## The Decrees of Pope Stephen Begin

(Year of the Lord 261. Here he destroyed the temple of Mars, while Valerian and Gallienus were ruling, as Rauderus says.)

[Col. 0173]

[Col. 0173C] Stephen, bishop, sends greetings of deepest charity to his beloved brother and familiar friend Hilary.

Although I hope that your affection is devoted to every good work, nevertheless, because you are known to be joined to us by familiarity, so that your diligence may become more effective, it seemed appropriate to us to send these letters of brotherhood to your affection.

We admonish you, dearest one, always to remain in good things and to beware of evil ones; to be constantly with good men of right faith and holy conduct; and to separate yourself from the perverse and from those who plot against their brothers, unless you are converting them and bringing them back to concord. “For, as the Apostle says, evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Corinthians XV, 33).”

Truth itself also says: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you.” The same must be done concerning the foot, because it is better for you to enter the kingdom of heaven one-eyed or lame than, having two eyes, or two hands, or two feet, to be cast into [Col. 0174D] the fiery Gehenna (Matthew V, 29).

And in the book of Ecclesiasticus we find:

“In the prosperity of a man his enemy is hidden, but in his sorrow and misfortune a friend is recognized. An enemy sweetens his lips, but in his heart he lies in wait to overturn you into a pit. Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it. Whoever associates with the proud will put on pride; he takes a burden upon himself who associates with one more honorable than he. Do not be a companion to one richer than you. What fellowship can a kettle have with a pot? When they collide, it will be broken. The rich man will act unjustly and roar, but the poor man, when wronged, will be silent. If you give to him, he will take you up; and if you have nothing, he will abandon you. [Col. 0175A] If you possess anything, he will live with you, and he will empty you, while he himself will not grieve over you. If you are necessary to him, he will trip you; and, smiling, he will give you hope, telling you good things and saying, ‘What need have you?’ He will shame you with his food until he has emptied you twice and three times, and at the end he will mock you. Afterwards, seeing you, he will abandon you and shake his head at you.

Humble yourself before God and await his hand. Take care lest, deceived in your folly, you be humbled. Do not be humble in your own wisdom, lest, humbled, you be led into folly. When summoned by one more powerful, withdraw; for this will cause him to summon you all the more. Do not be insolent, lest you stumble; do not remain far away from him and fall into oblivion. Do not presume to speak with him on equal terms, and do not trust his many words; for by much speech he will test you, and smiling he will question you about your secrets. His harsh spirit will retain your words and will not spare you from malice and bonds. Beware and listen carefully, for you are walking toward your destruction.

When hearing such things, act as though in a dream; watch and remain awake. Love God throughout your whole life and call upon him for your salvation. Every animal loves its kind, and so every person loves one like himself. Every flesh joins itself to flesh of its kind, and every person associates with one like himself. If a wolf ever associates with a lamb, so does a sinner with a just man. What fellowship has a holy man with a dog? Or what good peace has a rich man with a poor man? As a wild ass is the lion’s prey in the wilderness, so the poor are the pasture of the rich. As humility is an abomination to the proud, so the poor man is an execration to the rich.

A rich man who is shaken is supported by friends, but when a humble man falls, he is expelled even by his acquaintances. When a rich man is deceived, he has many helpers; he speaks proudly, and they justify him. A humble man is deceived, and is moreover reproached; he speaks sensibly, and no place is given to him. The rich man speaks, and everyone is silent, and they carry his word up to the clouds. The poor man speaks, and they say, ‘Who is this?’ And if he stumbles, they overthrow him.

Good is the substance in which there is no sin in the conscience; but most evil is poverty in the mouth of the wicked. The heart of a man changes his face, whether for good or for evil. You will scarcely find, and only with difficulty, the mark of a good heart and a good face (Ecclesiasticus XII, 9–15; XIII, 1–32).”

Beware of these things, brother, and do not follow your desires.

But you have consulted the apostolic see about who are infamous or who must not be admitted to ecclesiastical orders. We believe that you know this, and we do not refuse to instruct you by the authority of the apostolic see.

We say that those persons are infamous who are marked with infamy for some fault: that is, all who reject the norm of Christian law and despise ecclesiastical statutes; likewise thieves, sacrilegious persons, and all entangled in capital crimes; violators of tombs; those who willingly violate the statutes of the apostles, their successors, and the other Fathers; and all who arm themselves against the Fathers, who are marked with infamy throughout the whole world.

Likewise, incestuous persons, murderers, perjurers, robbers, sorcerers, poisoners, adulterers, and those fleeing from wars [Col. 0176A]; those who seek to occupy places unworthy of them; those who unjustly remove the property of the Church; those who slander or accuse their brothers without proving their charges; those who provoke the minds of rulers to anger against the innocent; all who have been anathematized or expelled from the Church for their crimes; and all whom ecclesiastical or secular laws declare infamous.

Such persons may not be promoted to sacred orders. Nor may slaves be promoted before lawful emancipation, nor penitents, nor bigamists, nor those who serve in the curia, nor those who are not physically whole, nor those who do not possess a sound mind or understanding, nor those who are disobedient to the decrees of the saints, nor those who are openly insane. None of these should be advanced to the sacred ranks. Neither these, nor freedmen, nor suspect persons, nor those lacking right faith or worthy conduct, can accuse the high priests.

You yourself also do not doubt how obedience and reverence must be shown to superiors by those subject to you. In this matter it is very useful if humility, without compulsion, preserves what the rigor of discipline imposes.

May almighty God, in whose hand all things are, of whom it is written, “There is no wisdom, no prudence, and no counsel against the Lord (Proverbs XXI, 30),” grant that you and yours preserve undefiled the divine institutions and those of the apostolic see, always ascend to better things, beware of worse things from day to day, and pursue and accomplish what is better and pleasing to God.

The ecclesiastical vestments with which the Lord is served [Col. 0176C], and the divine worship which priests and the other ministers of the Church celebrate with all honor and propriety, ought to be sacred and honorable. Since they have been consecrated and dedicated to God and his service, no one should use them for any purposes other than ecclesiastical and worthy duties. Nor should they be touched or carried by others, except by consecrated persons, lest the divine vengeance that struck Belshazzar come upon those who transgress concerning these things and presume such acts, and lest the just scourge of divine vengeance bring them down to the depths.

Make these matters known in the regions where you reside and to all whom you are able, and see that they are observed by apostolic command and authority, because our own people and all those entrusted to us in the holy apostolic and universal Church have professed that they observe these things, both now and in future times.

I have briefly answered your magnificence in this brotherly letter. May your affection join itself to these matters so that, in whatever concerns the condition of the universal Church, nothing is done either doubtfully or sluggishly. Let everything be done with such moderation that neither the claims of benevolence nor those of justice are neglected, but that divine judgment is considered in all things without respect of persons.

In order that this may be preserved by right observance, the integrity of the Catholic faith must first be maintained. And because the way that leads to life is altogether narrow and constricted, let no one deviate from its path either to the left or to the right.

Given on 3 May, in the consulship of Valerian and Gallienus IV.

## Likewise, a Letter of Pope Stephen Concerning Accusations against Priests

[Col. 0177]

[Col. 0177A] Stephen, bishop of the holy apostolic and universal Roman Church, sends greetings in the Lord to all bishops established throughout the various provinces.

We rejoice greatly in the Lord and glory in the gift of his grace, because your faith grows magnificently through good works and is expanded most widely. But we are exceedingly distressed and troubled by your oppression, concerning which the report of the brothers who have come to us has been conveyed with increasing frequency.

You ought not to have been shaken by such great oppressions by those from whom you should have received support, protection, and honor. Therefore, once the evasions of such persons have been removed—evasions by which poisonous malice is accustomed to be revealed and goodness and truth obscured—it is necessary that no small assistance be supplied to you by the faithful and that support be given to you by this apostolic see. [Col. 0177B] By the divine grace of Christ, you deserve to be helped, lest an ill-considered initiative proceed to the disturbance of the whole Church and lest matters that were long ago forbidden by our holy predecessors and the other holy Fathers revive again.

The consideration of our office compels us not to abandon, for the Lord’s sake, those matters that have come to our attention as requiring correction, but to amend them with worthy correction. If secular offices have their proper order and the discipline handed down by our forebears must be preserved, who could tolerate ecclesiastical orders being confused by reckless presumption, matters heard being neglected, and matters requiring correction being postponed without assistance?

[Col. 0177C] For we have heard that you are accused by certain persons, not so much because of your own fault as according to their pleasure, so that they may seize your possessions; and for this reason you are afflicted and shaken so greatly that you are even driven from your own sees, and on such a pretext your churches and possessions are devastated and plundered.

These things, dearest ones, ought not to happen, nor ought they to be repeated. Nevertheless, what is so often usurped must be repeated and prohibited more frequently. For whatever is unjustly done against things consecrated to God and against bishops will be reckoned sacrilege, because they are sacred and must not be violated by anyone.

[Col. 0177D] No bishop who has been stripped of his property or expelled from his own see for any reason may be accused, nor may any crime be brought against him by anyone, before he has been completely restored, before everything taken from him by any means has been restored to him according to law, and before he has been regularly returned to his own see and former status.

All possessions, everything unjustly taken from him, and all revenues must first be entirely restored to the bishop concerned by the primates and the synod, before an accusation is begun, because not only ecclesiastical but also secular laws forbid this from being done otherwise.

Nor should any of them—whether an agent or defender of the bishops or of the Churches—be accused before they have first been approached charitably twice and three times by those who believe themselves injured or wish to correct them for some error, so that they may receive from them either a friendly correction [41] or a just explanation. Whoever presumes to do otherwise must be barred from the thresholds of the church [Col. 0178A] until he has made fitting satisfaction.

We also remove the accusers and accusations that the laws of the world do not admit and that our predecessors prohibited. No foreigner may become either their accuser or their judge. Hence it is written concerning Lot: “You came in as a foreigner; will you also act as a judge? (Genesis XIX, 9).”

No servant or freedman, and no suspect or infamous person, may be an accuser of you. Those who live with your enemies and all laymen must also be rejected, because the attachment of friendship is accustomed to incite the assault of blasphemy. Nor are those to be admitted to your accusation who wish to receive you into their own defamation.

No one who has been anathematized is to be received, nor should anyone believe what is said or written by such persons. [Col. 0178B] I also say that those are anathematized whom bishops have anathematized in their writings or who anathematize the statutes of bishops.

No accusation of anyone is to be accepted in writing, but only by the accuser’s own voice, if the accuser is a lawful and suitable person, and in the presence of the person whom he wishes to accuse; for no absent person can either be accused or accuse.

Nevertheless, no man of the aforesaid order may be accused or required to answer his accusers before he has been regularly summoned by his primate and has been given an opportunity to defend himself and investigate the charges so as to clear away the crimes.

No metropolitan or other bishop is called a primate except one who holds a primary see and whose city the ancient primates judged to be primary. The others who have obtained the remaining metropolitan cities are to be called not primates but either archbishops or metropolitans.

[Col. 0178C] The cities and places over which primates ought to preside were established not in modern times but many ages before the coming of Christ; even the pagans appealed to their primates concerning the most important affairs. In these cities, after Christ’s coming, the apostles and their successors established patriarchs or primates. To them the affairs of bishops are to be referred, with the authority of the apostolic see preserved in all things; and after the apostolic see, the greater cases are to be referred to them.

Although, with the Apostle forbidding it, accusations ought not to be conducted among Christians, nevertheless, if they cannot be prevented, accusations against bishops must be brought by the accusers to the primates mentioned above. Bishops must nevertheless strive to restrain brothers who disagree, directing them more toward peace than toward judgment.

A bishop may not otherwise be heard or judged except in the presence of all the bishops of his province and by all the bishops of his province, because when they are absent, it is neither lawful nor possible.

[Col. 0178D] Which persons are not to be admitted to accuse them has been stated above in part; more fully, both these persons and infamous persons have been enumerated in the letter that we previously sent to Hilary.

[Col. 0179A] The permission to accuse must not extend beyond the boundaries of the province. Every accusation must be heard within the province and decided by the provincial bishops, unless an appeal alone has been made to the apostolic see.

Those accused must also be denied the opportunity to accuse until they have freed themselves from the crime with which they are burdened, because one must not believe the confession of persons entangled in crimes against others unless they have first proved themselves innocent. For the confession of a guilty person against anyone is dangerous and ought not to be admitted.

Family members, those who have confessed voluntarily and are entangled in crimes, and those who were enemies yesterday, the day before, or earlier, must not be admitted. A cleric who has accused his bishop or plotted against him is not to be received, because he has become infamous and must withdraw from his rank or be handed over to the curia for service.

Although laymen may be religious, no layman is ever recorded as having been granted authority to dispose of anything belonging to ecclesiastical property.

[Col. 0179B] We know, dearest ones, that the carnal have always been accustomed to persecute the spiritual, and the malicious to defame and tear apart the benevolent. Therefore the apostles, their successors, and the other holy Fathers did not wish accusations against bishops to be made easy, since, if they were easy, scarcely any bishop—or perhaps none—would now be found.

For bishops are called thrones of God; therefore they ought not to be moved, afflicted, or disturbed. Concerning them the prophet says: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands (Psalm XVIII, 3).”

Those who do not possess good conduct, whose life is blameworthy, or whose faith, life, and freedom are unknown cannot accuse them. First, the persons, faith, life, and conduct of the accusers must always be investigated in detail; afterward, the charges they bring must be examined faithfully. Nothing should be done before the persons, faith, life, and conduct of the accusers have been carefully examined, lest anyone be troubled by another’s envy, hostility, or evil intention.

No one should accept accusations against a teacher, because teachers ought rather to be supported than harmed or defamed. Hence the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ (Galatians VI, 2).”

Charity is not ambitious, does not envy, is not puffed up, and does not seek its own interests but those of Jesus Christ. Whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him. Whoever remains in God wishes to harm no one but desires to help and support everyone, just as the Lord himself came to save all and to give his soul as a ransom for us.

[Col. 0179D] We close the voice of those who would accuse or testify against priests whom we recognize as condemned or dead by human and divine judgment.

Therefore all who persecute the priests of the Lord, whether secretly or openly, must take the greatest care lest they be condemned by the Lord’s commands imposed upon his subjects. Through the prophet Jeremiah the Lord threatens such persons, saying:

“Our iniquities have turned everything aside, and our sins have removed good things from us, because impious men have been found among my people, speaking vain things. They set themselves to destroy men and seized them; like a snare of the fowler full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit (Jeremiah V, 25–27).”

[Col. 0180A] And through David he says:

“Those who devised evils in their heart were engaged in battles all day long. They sharpened their tongues like serpents; the venom of asps is under their lips (Psalm CXXXIX, 3–4).”

And shortly afterward:

“Coals will fall upon them in fire; you will cast them down into pits, and they will not rise. A man of many words will not prosper on the earth; evil will seize the unjust man in destruction. I know that the Lord will execute the cause of the poor and the judgments of the needy (Psalm V, 12–13).”

Again the same writer says: “Let deceitful lips become mute (Psalm XXX, 19).”

And again through Jeremiah he says: “All are judged in blood; each one troubles his neighbor; everyone prepares his hands for evil (Micah VII, 2).”

[Col. 0180B] Foreseeing such people, the Lord commanded the apostles not to allow his servants to be easily torn apart, lest they should perhaps be destroyed or fall into a temptation that they could not endure. For this reason the holy apostles and their successors established the norms of decrees, so that the voice of such persons—which strives more to destroy the innocent and simple than to save them—would not easily be accepted, but that they themselves would be driven far away by these darts and would be unable to destroy the Lord’s disciples according to their wishes and deceptions.

Hence the Lord himself also says: “Shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them (Luke IX, 5).”

And elsewhere Truth itself says concerning such persons: “It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the depth of the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble (Matthew XVIII, 6).”

And the apostle James says: “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has not shown mercy (James II, 13).”

[Col. 0180C] With what face, then, does any sinner hope to obtain forgiveness of his sins from God if he wishes to pardon nothing to a delinquent brother through the duty of piety and clemency? Surely he must consider that he will experience such a God in judgment, when he has been placed before the tribunal of the just Judge, as he himself has shown himself to his brother:

“For with whatever measure we have measured, it will be measured back to us (Mark IV, 24).”

And the apostle and evangelist John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him (1 John III, 15).”

Yet we, dearly beloved sons, exhort you to bear patiently, with the Lord’s assistance, the evils inflicted upon you, and to drive such people far away with these apostolic weapons, lest they be able, in canine fashion, to tear or bite you. Remember also that, according to the Psalmist’s saying, “Man’s days are like grass, and like a flower of the field so he flourishes.” And the Apostle says: “The whole world lies in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19). Therefore we beg you not to fear such people greatly, for they are disgraced and cannot do you much harm, since their voice has been extinguished; for God so hates those who take up arms against their fathers that the attackers of their fathers are branded with disgrace throughout the whole world.

Arm yourselves, therefore, against them with these apostolic supports, and strengthen your hearts with the princely Spirit, so that God, who wished you to be called shepherds of his people, may find you neither negligent nor lukewarm, fleeing when wolves appear, but may always find you, following the example of the good shepherd, courageously defending the sheep together with their mothers, sons, and daughters, and faithfully bringing them back to holy Mother Church. And although the days are evil, do not be foolish, but understand what the will of God is. Therefore be strengthened and stand firm in the faith, acting courageously, and let everything you do be done in charity; and, according to the holy Gospel: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

Remember also the holy apostles and prophets, and remember that, because they labored greatly in the Lord, they attained everlasting rewards. Know also that, according to the Psalmist’s word: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all” [Col. 0181B] (Psalm 7:20).

Therefore, dearly beloved sons, we exhort and beseech you to implore God through the frequent prayers of your devotions, so that, according to the Apostle’s saying, we and you may be delivered from troublesome and wicked people, “for not all possess faith.” Ask also that God and our Lord, who is the refuge of the poor and the hope of the humble, may mercifully rescue his holy Church—redeemed, of course, by his precious blood—and us, who must teach, govern, carry, and protect that same holy Church, from the oppressions and temptations of this wicked age and from all our necessities. Thus may the word of God run its course, and the glorious Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ be glorified; and may his grace not be fruitless in us, [Col. 0181C] lest, God forbid, we appear sterile before God without the fruit of the Gospel and return empty of sons and daughters, and lest, when the Lord comes, we be judged guilty concerning the talent that was hidden. For Satan is always jealous of these things. And therefore he raises up such people against us, who oppress and suffocate us, so that he may seize the Lord’s sheep without us and cause them to fall into the depths, when there are no shepherds to guard and defend them.

You, therefore, labor, pray, and keep watch with all your strength, lest these things happen. Know that we are always prepared, in whatever ways the Lord grants us power, to bring you assistance, although we ourselves have not been spared by the very enemies of God’s holy Church and of us, and although the tribulations of our heart, because of our own distress and yours and that of the sheep entrusted to us, have been greatly enlarged. We also beseech you not to neglect the service entrusted to you by the Lord, but to strive, as the Lord grants you strength, to help all the oppressed, all God’s servants, and, generally, all Christians, so that you may receive an everlasting reward before Christ’s tribunal.

And know that you are continually remembered before God. For just as we sorrowfully learn that you are being troubled by wicked and criminal men, so we continually suffer with you, praying to God for the deliverance and relief of your affliction, which—as it causes us grave anguish—is inflicted upon you day by day by the wicked. Daily prayers are also offered for you before the bodies of the apostles, so that, by the Lord’s help, you may be delivered from troublesome and wicked men, and that the sheep entrusted to you may reach, together with you, the pastures of eternal life forever.

May the almighty Lord, creator of all things, mindful of us, eternally preserve the unity and concord of your love, which is strong and advancing toward the salvation of all peoples. Amen.

Given on the Nones of April, in the fourth consulship of Valerian and Gallicanus.

## 42. THE DECREES OF POPE SIXTUS II BEGIN

*(In the year of the Lord 264, under the emperors Decius and Valerian.)*

[Col. 0181]

[Col. 0181C] Sixtus, bishop, to Gratus, fellow bishop, greetings.

Your letters of affection have made me exceedingly glad and joyful in Christ Jesus [Col. 0181D] our Lord. They clearly show how greatly you love the Catholic faith and how greatly you detest the error of wicked men. For every heresy is exceedingly impious and hostile to evangelical truth; it does not seek to injure merely some portion, but attempts to tear down the very foundations of the Christian religion.

I remember that I preside under the name of that Church whose confession has been glorified by the Lord Jesus Christ, and whose faith has never deceived anyone, but indeed destroys all heresies. I understand, therefore, that I may do nothing other than devote all my efforts to the cause in which the salvation of the universal Church is endangered.

Recognize, dearest son, that the Son of God was not born in time or after time, but was ineffably begotten from the Father’s womb before all times, as God the Father himself says through the prophet: “In the radiance of the holy ones, from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109:3). The prophet Isaiah also clearly expressed this statement to the doubtful and unbelieving, showing that the Son was born ineffably from no other source than the Father: “In his humiliation,” he says, “judgment was taken away from him; who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8.)

And in the Book of Job: “Where will you find the wisdom of God?” he says. “For it is hidden from the eyes of human beings and concealed from the birds of heaven” (Job 28:12). Awaken a little, and if you possess even a small measure of the light of knowledge within yourself, you will discover whose generation the prophet could not declare as occurring in time—or, as you yourself attempt to assert, could not have been generated.

“In the beginning,” says John the Evangelist, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” [Col. 0183A] (John 1:1–3). And again: “He was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (ibid., 9).

Therefore, if you wish to seek a time in the word “was,” you will not find one, since from the moment the Father is, the Son also is, and whatever the Father is, that is also what the Son is. Solomon says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature. I caused unfailing light to rise in heaven, and like a mist I covered the whole earth. I dwell in the highest places, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud. Alone I traversed the circle of heaven and penetrated the depths of the abyss. I stood throughout the whole earth, and I held primacy among the people” (Sirach 24:7–10).

Again, there: “When he prepared the heavens, I was present; and when he set apart his throne. When above the strong winds he made the clouds on high, and when he established the springs beneath the heavens, when he made firm the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things; and I was the one in whom he rejoiced when he rejoiced over the completed world” (Proverbs 8:27–30).

And in Psalm 101: “You, Lord, founded the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 101:26, 29).

There was no age, nor any time, before the Son was born from the Father, since he who established all times by his own power could not be born in time or after time. With these few passages briefly considered, dearest brother, I have answered your consultation.

For the rest, I admonish your affection to strive to convert all whom you know to be in error to the Catholic faith and to the unity of those who believe rightly, and never to depart from the apostolic path. But if they do not listen to you and, God forbid, persist in error, do not delay to make them known to us as soon as you can, so that by apostolic authority they may either quickly be converted to the Church or be separated from the Church.

We have also heard that certain erring men and those who consent with them are harassing you and the other bishops, and that they are drawing some neighboring bishops to themselves for your defamation and condemnation. Therefore, what had long ago been established in this holy see by many bishops has now again been confirmed for your assistance and that of the other brothers: whenever bishops are accused or charged in certain more serious cases, they may freely appeal to the apostolic see and flee to it as to a mother, so that they may be piously supported, defended, and delivered by it, as has always been the case.

The authority of the ancient apostles and their successors, together with the canons, has reserved to its disposition all major ecclesiastical cases and the judgments of bishops, since those bishops are blamed who act toward their brothers otherwise than the pope of that see has chosen should be done. Therefore it has been decreed that a bishop accused or judged by neighboring bishops in any matter may freely appeal to and approach the pontiff of the apostolic see, who shall arrange for his case to be examined either personally or through his representatives. While the pontiff is conducting his case in a renewed judgment, no other person may be placed or ordained in his position as bishop.

For although neighboring bishops may be permitted to investigate the case of an accused bishop, they may not decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff, since the Lord said to the blessed apostle Peter, and not to anyone else: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18:10).

And if anyone believes that he is being oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pope of the universal apostolic Church. For the apostle James says: “Judgment without mercy will be upon the one who has not shown mercy. But mercy triumphs over judgment” (James 2:13).

In everything, therefore, dearest son, guard your heart, as it is written: “With all vigilance guard your heart, for from it life proceeds” (Proverbs 4:23). I have written these brief words as a reminder, but I ask you to pray for me, so that almighty God may deign to guard me from evil spirits and wicked people. For in the pilgrimage of this life [Col. 0184C] evils, and many of them, surround me, so that I may rightly say with the Psalmist: “Your wrath has passed through me, and your terrors have troubled me. They have surrounded me like waters all day long; they have surrounded me together” (Psalm 87:17–18).

May heavenly grace protect us in the cities and you everywhere, for the ancient enemy is not excluded from temptation by earthly places. If he struck down human beings in paradise, what place outside paradise can there be into which he cannot penetrate the minds of human beings? The eyes of the ancient enemy—through whose envy death entered the world—are always watchful, seeking to ensnare human souls. He desires to drag many into perdition with himself by his wickedness, although through his own evil he has fallen from glory into misery.

We must therefore trust solely in the protection of our Creator, to whom we cry from the depths of our heart: “Be for me a God, my protector, and a fortified place, so that you may save me.”

Given on the Kalends of September, in the fourth consulship of Valerian and Decius.

## ALSO, A LETTER OF POPE SIXTUS

[Col. 0183]

[Col. 0183D] Sixtus, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to his most beloved brothers established throughout the provinces of Spain.

By the great gift of God’s mercy, the joys of the entire Catholic Church have been multiplied, since the condition of the Churches flourishes according to the order established by the apostles and their successors. But when we learn that this order is being disturbed by the cunning of the ancient enemy, we are saddened by no small grief.

For this reason, brothers, we exhort, admonish, and earnestly urge you never to depart from the path of apostolic institution or to dissent from the head, but to hold without hesitation the faith and order established by the apostles and apostolic men. For if the columns of some great house collapse, the house itself will afterward not stand. So also you, who are the columns of the Church: if you begin to be shaken, the holy Church—which is governed through you—will waste away and fall. These things, brothers, which I say, are greatly to be feared, carefully weighed, and guarded against lest they occur. For Truth itself said: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be salted?” (Matthew 5:13) and so forth.

Therefore, dearest brothers, I admonish you because I am indebted to you and love you greatly. When I hear good things about you, I rejoice greatly; conversely, when I hear of adversity, I am deeply troubled. Although I am separated from you by long stretches of land, I am nevertheless entirely joined to you in heart. Therefore I trust in every way in your blessedness toward me, because when you love me in return, you are not far from me.

For this reason we give greater thanks to that mustard seed which, from the appearance of a small and despised seed, spread so widely, with branches rising from the same root and extending everywhere, that all the birds of heaven might nest in them.
