And thanks be to that leaven which mixed the whole mass of the human race into unity through three measures of flour, and to that small stone which, cut from the mountain without hands, filled the whole surface of the world. Assuming the nature of our flesh and the form of a servant, it humbly extended itself everywhere, so that, after the whole human race had been brought into unity, it might perfect the entire united body of the Church, while this partial distinction of members might serve the advantage of the whole structure.

Thus we too are not far from you, because in him who is everywhere we are one. Let us therefore give thanks to him who, having abolished enmities in his flesh, made one flock and one fold throughout the whole world under one [Col. 0185C] shepherd. Let us always remember the Preacher of truth, who admonishes you, saying: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3). No one preserves the bond of peace while harassing another or persecuting him in words or deeds.

For this reason, brothers, we have set these matters forth, because we have heard that accusations are being brought among you, and that bishops driven from their sees or stripped of their possessions are being judged. Therefore it has been decreed that if anyone believes he has a personal case against a bishop or against officials of the Church, he should not first approach judges, but should first return to those against whom he has a complaint in the spirit of charity, so that, after being admonished through a private conversation, they may remedy the matters brought forward as grievances. If he acts otherwise, let him be deprived of communion.

From now on, no pontiff may presume to excommunicate or judge a bishop who has been stripped of his possessions or driven from his see, for there is no privilege from which one who has already been stripped can be deprived. No bishop may presume to retain, ordain, or judge another bishop’s parishioner without that bishop’s consent. Just as his ordination will be invalid, so also will his judgment, since we hold that no one is bound by the sentence of any judge except his own. For the one who could not ordain him will in no way be able to judge him.

We command you henceforth to observe these things and to help one another. Know that the brothers whom you unjustly condemned through earthly fear have been justly restored by us. By the authority of blessed Peter and apostolic authority, we order that everything taken from them be returned to them in full, unless you and your princes wish to be separated from our fellowship and from the members of the Church.

For by God’s just judgment, sinners are often given power to persecute his saints, so that those who are helped and led by God’s Spirit may become more illustrious through the exercise of labors. Yet those who do this will in no way escape punishment, because, as the Lord says: “Woe to the one through whom the scandal comes” (Matthew 18:7). And although, according to the Savior’s pronouncement, scandals must come, nevertheless woe to the one through whom they come.

To judge rashly the hidden matters of another’s heart is a sin; and it is unjust to accuse on suspicion one whose works appear to be nothing but good, since God alone is the just judge of things unknown to human beings, and he is the true examiner. Therefore it is written: “Let us not judge uncertain matters until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” [Col. 0186B] (1 Corinthians 4:5).

Even when things are true, they must not be believed unless they are proved by certain indications, unless they are established by manifest judgment, or unless they are made public through judicial procedure. No one, therefore, may be condemned by human examination whom God has reserved for his own judgment. All these matters must be guarded against with the greatest care, lest we appear presumptuous.

Nor is an accusation against bishops to be readily accepted, since the Lord says: “You shall not receive a false report” (Exodus 23:1). And the Apostle says that an accusation against a presbyter must not be received without two or three suitable witnesses. If these precautions must be taken concerning presbyters and other faithful people, how much more concerning bishops?

Once these matters are understood, it is clear that you wish rather to be condemned than to advise your brothers or support them, because honor inflates pride, and what was provided for concord tends toward injury. According to the rules mentioned above, you ought to have reported to us if they had done anything against their order, and to have awaited our response to your consultations. Even if they had committed something serious and intolerable, you ought to have awaited our judgment, so that you would decide nothing beforehand and nothing else except what you knew to be pleasing to us, and so that you would depart from the established rules neither through negligence nor presumption.

Let this kind of presumption cease, suppressed by our authority; let such injuries be avoided. For we can in no way endure such schemes patiently, since it is appropriate that we be diligent guardians of the sanctions of our fathers. It rightly concerns us if we favor error by our silence.

Moreover, our holy predecessors have often established that no one is to be received as anathema upon an accusation brought before us, nor are those to be admitted who refuse to receive us in their complaint or accusation, since we know that the Lord has placed us over them, not them over us. And just as a greater cannot be judged by a lesser, so neither can he be bound by one; for everything great is rare.

Let us bear the burdens of all who are burdened—or rather, blessed Peter the apostle bears them in us, whose legation we exercise and whose rule instructs us, so that, supported by his help, we may now and forever be protected from every adversity.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth consulship of Valerian and Decius.

## THE DECREES OF POPE DIONYSIUS BEGIN

*(In the year of the Lord 266, in the time of Claudius, as Platina says.)*

[Col. 0187]

[Col. 0187A] Dionysius, bishop, sends greetings to Urbanus, prefect.

The highest good is to love those who love us. Conversely, there is no worse evil than for citizens to envy citizens. We give thanks, indeed, to your affection because you receive and assist the faithful of blessed Peter well. Therefore know that you are loved by us and by our people, and that we take no small care for you and yours.

For this reason we exhort your affection not to delay in completing the good work you have begun, since it is not the beginning but the end that is praised. We also exhort you to love and investigate wisdom, so that you may arrange and judge rationally and wisely the matters entrusted to you, as the Lord says through the prophet: “Be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Psalm 2:10).

Therefore fear God and keep his commandments; love him with all your inward being, and your neighbor as yourself. [Col. 0187B] The Most High God created wisdom in the Holy Spirit. He saw, numbered, and measured it, and poured it out upon all his works and upon all flesh. According to his gift he provided it to those who love him.

The fear of the Lord is glory, boasting, joy, and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart and give joy and gladness throughout the length of days. It will be well with the one who fears God at the end, and on the day of his death he will be blessed. The love of God is honorable wisdom. Those to whom it appears in their sight love him in beholding him and in recognizing his great works.

The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. It was conceived with the faithful in the womb; it walks with elect women; it is recognized with the righteous faithful. The fear of the Lord is religious devotion to knowledge; devotion will guard and justify the heart and will give delight and joy. It will be well with the one who fears God, and he will be blessed in the days of its completion.

The fullness of wisdom is to fear God, and its fullness comes from its fruits. It has filled his whole house through generations, and his storehouses with treasures. The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling the heart with peace and the fruit of salvation; and he saw and numbered it.

Both knowledge and understanding are gifts of God. Wisdom will share itself with prudence and exalt those who hold to it. The root of wisdom is to fear God, while its branches are long-lived. In the treasures of wisdom are understanding, knowledge, and devotion; but wisdom is an abomination to sinners.

The fear of the Lord drives away sin, for the one who is without fear cannot be justified. The anger of his indignation is his destruction. The patient person will endure for a time, and afterward there will be a return of delight. Good sense will conceal his words for a time, and the lips of many will declare his understanding.

In the treasures of wisdom is the meaning of discipline; but for the sinner, the worship of God is an abomination. My son, if you desire wisdom, preserve justice, and God will provide it for you. For wisdom and discipline are the fear of the Lord; what pleases him is faith and gentleness, and he will fill his treasuries.

Do not be stubborn or unbelieving toward the fear of the Lord, and do not approach him with a double heart. Do not be a hypocrite before human beings, and do not fall into scandal through your lips. Pay attention to these things, lest you fall, place a stumbling block before your soul, and bring dishonor upon yourself, and God reveal your secrets.

Always contend for faith, brother, for justice, and for the salvation of your soul; act courageously for the assistance of your brothers, so that you may receive recompense from the Lord. For it is written: “My son, preserve the proper time, and avoid evil; for your soul’s sake do not be ashamed to speak the truth” (Sirach 4:23–24).

There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory and grace. Do not accept a person’s face against your own face, nor a lie against your soul. Do not show excessive respect to your neighbor in his misfortune, and do not hold back your word at the time of salvation.

Do not hide your wisdom in its beauty. For wisdom is recognized in the tongue, and understanding, knowledge, and instruction are recognized in words of truth, while strength is recognized in works of justice. Do not contradict the truth in any way, and be ashamed of the falsehood arising from your ignorance.

Do not be ashamed to confess your sins, and do not subject yourself to a human being because of sin. Do not resist the face of the powerful, and do not struggle against the force of the river. Fight for justice for the sake of your soul, and contend for justice even unto death; God will fight your enemies for you and overthrow them courageously.

Do not be hasty with your tongue, useless, or slack in your works. Do not be like a lion in your house, overthrowing your household and oppressing those subject to you. Let your hand not be extended to receive and closed when it is time to give (ibid., 25 and following).

Always supported by these authorities of Scripture, stand upright and do not turn away from the way of truth, so that you may always obtain God’s grace and continually enjoy the friendship of good people. Your mind will depart from love of this age all the more easily in proportion as it is urged while it is being called.

For we desire to see you present and wish at least to converse with you by letter when you are absent. Therefore we hope that blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, may happily bring you to his threshold, so that through your repentance we may deserve to enjoy the grace of almighty God.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the fourth consulship of Aurelian and Bassus.

## LETTER OF POPE DIONYSIUS TO BISHOP SEVERUS

[Col. 0187]

[Col. 0187D] Dionysius, bishop, sends greetings to Severus, bishop.

Long ago and from the beginning, we received such confidence from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that, with the Lord’s assistance, we possess authority to aid the universal Church and to correct and amend by apostolic authority whatever is harmful.

For this reason divine providence established distinct degrees and different orders, so that, while those of lesser rank showed reverence to their superiors and superiors extended love to their inferiors, a single harmonious structure might arise from diversity, and the proper administration of each office might be produced. Indeed, the whole community could not subsist in any other way unless such a great order of distinction preserved it.

Since creation cannot be governed or live in one uniform equality, the example of the heavenly armies instructs us. For it is clear that there are angels and archangels, and that they are not equal, but differ from one another in power and order, as you know. If, therefore, this distinction is established among those who are without sin, what human being would refuse willingly to submit to such an arrangement?

From this, peace and mutual charity embrace one another in turn, and the steadfast sincerity of concord remains in an alternating love pleasing to God. Since each office is then healthfully completed when there is one superior to whom the subordinate may have recourse, concerning the parish churches about which you wished to consult the apostolic see—how they should be guarded throughout the province of Córdoba and distributed among priests—we see nothing better to tell your affection than that you follow what is known to have been recently done by us in the Roman Church.

We gave each individual church to an individual presbyter, and divided among them the parishes and cemeteries. But we established that each should possess his own right, in such a way that no one might invade the boundaries or rights of another’s parish; rather, each should be content with his own boundaries and guard the church and people entrusted to him in such a way that, before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, he might render an account of everything entrusted to him and receive not condemnation but glory for his deeds.

It is also fitting that you, dearest brother, and all the bishops follow this rule, and that you make what has been written to you known to everyone you can, so that this instruction may be general rather than particular.

As for the crimes that you say are being charged against bishops, do not allow them to be brought by others in any way except by those who themselves bring the charges—provided that they prove themselves worthy and irreproachable, and demonstrate through public records that they are entirely free from suspicion and enmity and lead an irreproachable life and conduct.

No one who has confessed something against himself can be believed concerning a crime committed by another, since every confession of such a matter is dangerous and must not be admitted. Similarly, we can neither receive nor ought to receive someone who is an associate of another’s error, who voluntarily departs from the path he has chosen, or who is disobedient to the sacred rules and constitutions of the fathers. Nor do we permit anyone to attack those who believe rightly or obey the sanctions of the holy Fathers. For we consider all those infamous who betray either their own Christian law or willingly set aside apostolic or canonical authority.

Therefore, dearest brother, we command that these things, which we provide out of affection for the priestly name and honor, be observed by you, your subjects, and everyone else; that they be announced and preached to others; and that through them piety may serve usefulness and love may bear fruit.

Let us therefore hasten to benefit those whom we can by rebuking, exhorting, persuading, encouraging, and consoling. Let our tongue be nourishment for the good and a goad for the wicked. Let it blunt the arrogant, calm the angry, sharpen the sluggish, kindle the negligent through exhortation, persuade those who shrink back, soothe the harsh, and console the despairing, so that, since we are called teachers, we may show the way of salvation to those who walk in it.

Let us be vigilant in our watch; let us carefully fortify the entrance against the enemy’s ambushes. And if error should ever lead a lost sheep away from the flocks entrusted to us, let us strive with all our effort to call it back to the Lord’s folds [Col. 0190C], so that from the name of shepherd that we bear we may obtain not punishment but reward.

Since, therefore, the assistance of divine grace is necessary in all these things, let us implore the mercy of almighty God with continual prayers, so that he may grant us both the will and the ability to accomplish them, and may guide us fruitfully along that path of good works in which he testified that he himself is the shepherd of shepherds. Thus, through him, without whom we can do nothing, may we be able to accomplish everything.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the fourth consulship of Claudius and Paternus.

## THE DECREES OF POPE FELIX BEGIN

*(In the years of the Lord 269–274.)* (C)*

[Col. 0189]

[Col. 0189D] Felix, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to Paternus, his most beloved and dear fellow bishop.

Your writings have made me rejoice and exult greatly in the Lord, for they clearly show how greatly you love the Catholic faith and how greatly you detest heretical error. Heresy is exceedingly impious and hostile to evangelical truth; it strives not to injure some portion, but to tear up the very foundations of the Christian religion.

[Col. 0190D] For whoever it seizes, it causes to rush not only into this vice but also into many others; and, at the persuasion of the ancient enemy, they become not only persecutors of the Church but also of its priests. Therefore, with one mind, let us take care to correct and pursue such people, and let us strive to free the Church, its faithful, and the priests of the Lord from their enemy. Our almighty Redeemer will grant strength to charity and justice.

He himself—by whose workmanship the Church, as though in the form of an ark, is constructed with the four sides of the world, joined by a framework of imperishable wood and bound with the bitumen of charity—will grant us who are far apart the unity of his Spirit, so that the Church may not be disturbed by any adversity of spirit or by the swelling of any wave arriving from outside. But just as, under his gracious governance, we must ask that no external wave overtaking us should trouble us, so, dearest brother, we must pray with all our inmost being that, by the right hand of his providence, he may drain away for us the accumulation of our inner bilge-water.

For the adversary, the devil, who rages against the humble and, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking whom he may devour, no longer, as we see, merely circles the sheepfolds, but drives his tooth so forcefully into certain necessary members of the Church that no one can doubt that, unless the provident company of all the shepherds hastens together with the Lord’s unanimous favor, the entire flock—God forbid—will quickly be torn apart.

[Col. 0191A] Therefore, we remove from episcopal accusation both detractors, who must be uprooted by divine authority, and supporters of the enemies. Likewise, so that none of the highest may be attacked or destroyed through accusations brought by the lesser, let no certain sentence be pronounced in a doubtful matter, and let no judgment be upheld unless it has been conducted in due order.

If anyone believes that a cleric should be charged with any crimes, let him pursue his action in the province where the person charged resides, and let him not suppose that the accused should be brought elsewhere or dragged farther away for judgment. If the person charged has judges whom he suspects, however, let him be permitted to appeal to the primates.

The primates, when examining the accused bishop, must not pronounce a sentence of condemnation before, relying on apostolic authority, he either confesses himself guilty or is regularly convicted by innocent witnesses who have been canonically examined. Otherwise we decree the condemnation of bishops to be void and unjust, and therefore subject to reconsideration by a synod, so that assistance may be given to the oppressed by everyone in every case.

Let the judges of the Church beware of pronouncing sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being contested, for it will be void; they too will render an account for their brothers’ proceedings in his presence. The slander of informers, however, and their testimony must not be heard. No one can know a debtor better than the person who has endured his injury and wickedness.

All, therefore, who wish to live devoutly in Christ must necessarily suffer reproaches from the impious and the unlike-minded, and be despised as foolish and insane—those who lose present goods in order to acquire invisible and future ones. Yet the contempt and mockery of such people will rebound upon those who harass them, because their abundance will pass into poverty and their pride into humiliation.

Whatever adversities or evils are inflicted upon the just are not punishment for crime but a testing of virtue. And just as gold becomes better the more it is refined by fire, so the just person, the more he is afflicted—provided he bears the affliction itself patiently—is rendered much purer and brighter before God.

Hence Truth itself says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:10).

[Col. 0191D] Concerning such people the Lord speaks through Isaiah, saying:

“Listen to the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word. Your brothers who hate you and cast you out because of my name have said, ‘Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see your joy’; but they themselves shall be put to shame. A voice from the city, a voice from the temple, a voice of the Lord repaying his enemies. Before she was in labor, she gave birth; before her labor came, she gave birth to a male child. Who has ever heard such a thing, and who has seen anything like it? Will the earth give birth in one day, or will a nation be brought forth all at once, because Zion has been in labor and has given birth to her children? Shall I, who make others give birth, not give birth myself, says the Lord? Shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren, says the Lord your God?

“Rejoice with Jerusalem and exult in her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her, so that you may rise and be filled from the breast of her consolation, so that you may milk and overflow with delights from all her glory. For thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall incline over her like a river of peace and like an overflowing torrent the glory of the nations, which you shall suck. You shall be carried to her breasts, and upon her knees they shall caress you. As a mother caresses someone, so I shall console you, and you shall be consoled in Israel. You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall flourish like grass. The hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, and he shall be indignant against his enemies.

“For behold, the Lord will come in fire, and his chariot will be like a whirlwind, to render his fury in indignation and his rebuke in a flame of fire. For the Lord will judge by fire and by his sword all flesh, and those slain by the Lord shall be many. Those who sanctified themselves and considered themselves clean in the gardens behind the inner door, who ate swine’s flesh, abomination, and the mouse, shall all be consumed together, says the Lord.

“But I know their works and their thoughts. I am coming to gather all nations and tongues, and they shall come and see my glory. I shall place a sign among them, and I shall send from them those who have been saved to the nations, to the sea, to Africa and Lydia, those who hold the bow toward Italy and Greece, to the distant islands, to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory. They shall announce my glory to the nations, and they shall bring all your brothers from every nation as a gift to the Lord, on horses and in chariots, on litters, on mules, and in wagons, to my holy mountain, Jerusalem, says the Lord—as though the children of Israel were bringing an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord.

“And I shall take some of them as priests and Levites, says the Lord. For just as the new heavens and the new earth that I make shall stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your offspring and your name stand. And month after month, and Sabbath after Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before my face, says the Lord. And they shall go out and see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me; their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh unto satiety.”

(Isaiah 66:5–24.)

[Col. 0192D] What else do detractors do but blow into dust and raise up earth into their own eyes? Do they not see even less truth from the place where they blow more intensely with detraction? Nevertheless, dearest brother, such people must be borne with and corrected, because they are blind and guides of the blind.

To these matters, dearest brother, I have briefly responded to your consultations, which we command you and all bishops to observe canonically. Yet we exhort your prudence, brother, to labor with all your strength for the condition of the Church and its priests, to observe in every respect the order of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, and not to permit the decrees of the saints to be violated. Rather, instruct all whom you can, so that you may present fruitful sheaves to the Lord.

Farewell. Given on 5 June, in the fourth consulship of Claudius and Aurelianus, [with] the consuls in office.

# LETTER OF POPE FELIX

[Col. 0193]

[Col. 0193A] Felix, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Gaul.

There can be no doubt that God is the author of good works and spiritual endeavors: he stirs their minds and assists their actions. Therefore, your letters, arising from good zeal and from the integrity of faith and the devotion of your life, made me rejoice; but, for the most part, they also saddened me because of your affliction and distress. I read your sad letters sadly, and I passed through your mournful writings with the grief they deserved, because just as the peace of the churches, the harmony of their priests, and the tranquility of the people bring us heavenly joy when we hear of them, so brotherly affliction troubles and casts us down.

Yet do not be greatly saddened, because Truth itself says: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19)—that is, the lovers of the world.

Whatever these people may say or do against you, always preserve an undiminished faith and maintain a pure conscience, so that spirit and soul may be preserved blameless on the day of the Lord. For your support, brothers, we have summoned more than seventy of our co-bishops, with whom, after treating the following matters canonically, we have decreed what is set out below.

Your letters were read aloud before everyone; they contained, as you know, many complaints and accounts of your oppression. Then the holy synod spoke concerning the decrees dealing with accusations against bishops. These are the provisions that, because of the plots of evil men who rage indiscriminately against the Church and ecclesiastical men, we firmly wish to preserve for all ages from now on.

[Col. 0193C] If a bishop is accused by those accusers who are to be admitted, then, after he has been charitably admonished by them to amend and correct the matter itself, if he refuses to do so, his case must not immediately but then be canonically referred to the highest primates. They must regularly convene a council at a suitable place within that province and at a suitable time—that is, in autumn or summer—so that he may be heard there by all the bishops of the same province.

If he has been regularly summoned and is not prevented from attending by illness or some other serious necessity, he must be present, because no one may be accused beyond the boundaries of his province before a hearing has been requested.

[Col. 0193D] But if he has been stripped of his own property or of that of the Church entrusted to him—or, God forbid, if he has been expelled from his own see, something that must be alien to all the faithful—or if he has been separated from his sheep by some form of detention, then, canonically, before he is restored to his former position with all his privileges and dignity, and before all his possessions that were taken from him through the plots of his enemies have been legally restored, he may neither be summoned nor judged, unless he himself freely chooses to come because of his necessity—though he is not at all to be judged.

No one, therefore, should require him to answer before everything that he had lost through the insinuations of his enemies has been completely restored to his authority by an honorable council in due legal order. The prelate himself must be returned with all honor to his former status; and, after he has freely and securely arranged and ordered his affairs for a considerable time, he must then be summoned according to proper procedure, after four, five, or seven months, as his circumstances permit, and not earlier, to come to a legitimate and canonical council and answer the accusations if it seems just to do so.

[Col. 0194C] For the greatest care must be taken that he not be compelled to answer before all these things have occurred, since contention must always be avoided. No Christian can rightly consider it permissible to deprive a bishop of his episcopate before the outcome of his case has become clear, because such presumption is sacrilege, and the author of such an act is sacrilegious.

If the bishop is ill or some serious necessity prevents him, let him send a representative to the synod on his behalf. Let him not be suspended from communion merely because a charge has been brought against him, unless, having been summoned by letter to state his case before the judgment of the electors on the appointed day, he entirely fails to appear—that is, unless some other urgent necessity has detained him during the period of the aforesaid months or longer, as the case may require.

If both parties come to state their case—for one must not be heard without the other—the court must inquire into the conduct, faith, and reputation of the accusers, and into the purpose for which they are doing this. They must not be admitted for this purpose unless they are men of good conduct and sound faith, namely, men free from every suspicion and distinguished by a good life, who are not infamous.

[Col. 0194D] If the persons of the accusers appear culpable in the judgment of the bishops, they must not be admitted to bring charges unless they wish to assert their own cases, though not criminal or ecclesiastical ones. An infamous person can be neither an agent nor a legal representative.

The accuser must not be heard in the absence of the adversary. Nor will a sentence pronounced by a judge in the absence of the other party have any validity. An absent person cannot be accused or accuse through another, and a related witness must not be admitted.

No one should be brought from one province to another or to the imperial court, except upon the report of the judge to whom an appeal has been made; that is, the plaintiff must always follow the forum of the defendant. If anyone finds that a judge is hostile to him, let him present a verbal appeal, since it must be denied to no one.

We prohibit foreign judgments by general sanction, because it is unworthy that a person should be judged by outsiders when he ought to have judges from his own province, chosen by and from among his fellow provincials.

These provisions, brothers, have been decreed unanimously in synod for your aid and the defense of all our co-bishops, so that if some fools—deceived by the error of diabolical deception—should wish to accuse you, they may repent when they read or hear these things, return to the harmony of unity, and what had previously been directed toward vengeance may pass into glory.

For without doubt there are many who, in the words of the Apostle, “having itching ears, turn away from the truth and turn to fables” (2 Timothy 4:3–4), and proceed to harm good people. The same Apostle says concerning the ignorance of unbelievers: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

Similarly, if these people had perfectly known and loved the Lord, they would never have disturbed his servants or persecuted them in word or deed. But since the same Apostle says, “For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10), why do we persecute, brothers? Why do we disturb the condition of the Church of God and afflict those who ought to serve it?

The martyrs suffered, but their souls were not killed in the suffering of the body, as Truth’s own mouth testifies: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). Here we must recognize that if the souls of martyrs cannot be extinguished by punishments after their bodies have been killed, then neither should the souls of preachers and teachers have been persecuted, disturbed, or turned away from God’s service, since they do not perish together with their bodies.

Such disturbers of the Church not only commit the evils mentioned above but also curse the memorials of the martyrs. Therefore, in the aforesaid synod we established and command you and all the churches to observe and carry out that Masses be celebrated over the memorials of the martyrs, so that their memorials cannot be extinguished by such people or their veneration prohibited.

[Col. 0195D] You, brothers, do not be greatly troubled or distressed; rather, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his glory. In the meantime, hold these decrees, enacted by apostolic authority, as support for you. Know that we are always prepared—even, if necessary, unto death—to accomplish whatever you need, with the Lord’s help.

Those people, however, with God as their author, will perish, while you will stand, provided that your labor is not in vain but full of faith and charity. “Woe,” says the prophet, “to him who gives his companion drink, adding his own gall” (Habakkuk 2:15).

Again, the most wise Solomon says: “He who speaks wicked things cannot remain hidden, nor will the judging condemnation pass him by. For the questioning of the impious will be in their thoughts; the hearing of his words will come to the Lord, and to the correction of his iniquities, because the ear of zeal hears all things, and the tumult of murmuring will not be hidden” (Wisdom 1:8–10).

If they had wished to embrace these things with their own sound understanding, they would not have slipped into a depraved mind. Rather, by taking care to guard their words through fear of God, they would certainly have preserved the pious definition of the holy Fathers without any presumptuous harm, since sacred Scripture says: “Good counsel will preserve you, and sound understanding will guard you.”

For such accusations and detractions do not proceed spiritually from saving fountains toward the attainment of eternal life. Therefore blessed Paul the Apostle, suitably warning us beforehand, says: “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly” (Romans 12:3), persevering in the definition of piety.

Those who pass beyond this have not merely been injured by falling away from their own strengthening; rather, they have left behind in the houses of their folly a memorial of themselves, so that they could not remain hidden in the very things in which they sinned. For glory and dishonor are in speech, and in the speech of the human tongue lies his downfall.

Therefore it is fitting that this display of their censures be inserted into our actions, so that you may no longer suffer such things from those who sow weeds and scandals, but may deserve to rejoice in your offices and doctrines.

[Col. 0196C] Let them therefore be ashamed and hasten to withdraw such blasphemy and the like, if they do not wish to be separated from our priestly college and torn away from the fellowship of the entire Christian people.

Although we could have said and written many further and very necessary things found in the decrees of the apostolic see and established by the apostles and their successors—namely, our predecessors—we have nevertheless thought it better to close the letter with a prayer.

May almighty God, and his only-begotten Son, our Savior Christ Jesus, grant you this encouragement: that you may come to the aid with all your strength of all our brothers and co-bishops who labor under whatever tribulations, and, suffering with them, bear the cross of that same Lord and Savior, so that you may appear before all to be his true disciples. Thus may both you and those who are with you possess here and in the future the better things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him.”

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom, and with whom, glory be to almighty God throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

I wish you health, dearest brothers. Given on 9 August, in the fourth consulship of Claudius and Paternus, [with] the consuls in office.

# ALSO, A LETTER OF THE SAME [POPE] TO BENIGNUS

[Col. 0195]

[Col. 0195D] Felix, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to his dearest brother Benignus, bishop.

[Col. 0196D] We have received the letters of your fraternity, in which you asked me to respond, insofar as the Lord has granted, concerning the teachings of the faith that were held by others in a different manner from what is right and that contain the mysteries of the faith. We did not refuse to answer out of love for your brotherhood.

For doubtful and more important matters have always been accustomed to receive their resolution from this holy see, from the time of the apostles who instructed it by their teachings. Therefore you acted rightly in wishing yourself and the others to be strengthened and instructed by the guidance of this holy see.

Your letters and those of your brothers stated that some say that the Son cannot properly see the Father, because it is written: “For no one has ever seen God” (1 John 4:12). Others fabricate the claim that the Son is therefore less than the Father, because the Father bears witness to him. Others chatter that he is less than the Father because the Father is said to be invisible, whereas the Son is proved to be visible.

[Col. 0197B] These people, ignorant of the authority of the divine Scriptures and of the apostles, manufacture such claims from their own or adulterated understanding and seek to lead astray the hearts of the faithful.

Let us return to the source itself, from which we may demonstrate by clearer testimonies from the writings of the Old and New Testament that the Son has always been able and is able to see the Father. Solomon says: “Wisdom is with you, which knows your works, and was present when you made the world, and knew what was pleasing before your eyes” (Wisdom 9:9).

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27). Again: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father; he has declared him” (John 1:18).

And again he said to the Jews: “You do not know him, but I know him. And if I were to say that I do not know him, I would be like you, a liar” (John 8:55). Likewise there: “He who is from God knows him.” And again: “I know him, because I am from him” (John 7:29).

[Col. 0197C] Behold, we have taught that the Son always sees the Father. How do they assert that he cannot see the Father, in whose bosom he is known to remain?

If you review the divine Scriptures with a clear understanding, you will find not only the Father bearing witness to the Son, but the whole inseparable Trinity testifying together in the Lord himself, who says: “I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John 8:18). Again: “If I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I come from and where I am going” (John 8:14).

And concerning the Holy Spirit: “When the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26). Consider, I ask you, consider: where one power of testimony is revealed, no one is judged either superior or inferior to another.

We have said these things many times already, because the Son is called visible according to the form of a human being, but according to the substance of his deity he is proclaimed invisible, as the Apostle Paul testifies: “O the depth,” he says, “of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Romans 11:33).

And in Isaiah: “To whom do you think him comparable, since he himself is invisible?”

And again the Apostle: “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given among the nations: to evangelize the unsearchable riches of Christ and to enlighten everyone concerning the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages, in which he created all things” (Ephesians 3:8–9).

The same Apostle says: “He is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). And to the Colossians: “I, Paul, a minister, who now rejoice in my sufferings for you and complete what is lacking in the tribulations of Christ in my flesh for his body, which is the Church, of which I have become a minister according to the dispensation of God, for the ministry of Christ, which was hidden from the ages and from generations” (Colossians 1:23–26).

[Col. 0198A] Likewise there: “That their hearts may be consoled in charity, unto all the riches of the fullness of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery that is Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.”

And in Psalm 76: “Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footprints will not be known” (Psalm 76:20).

And in Solomon: “Who will search out the wisdom of God that precedes all things?” (Sirach 1:3.) Likewise there: “The root of wisdom—to whom has it been revealed, and who has known its cunning?” (ibid., 1:6.) Likewise there: “The discipline of wisdom—to whom has it been revealed, and who has understood the multitude of its entrances?” (ibid., 1:7.) Likewise there: “For marvelous are the works of the Most High alone, glorious and hidden, and his works are unseen” (ibid., 11:4).

[Col. 0198B] Behold: just as the Father is invisible, so the Son too is now found to be invisible. How, then, is he judged inferior to the Father by those who say, as you have reported, that he deigned to be seen by us in the flesh?

Do not believe such people, and teach others to turn away from their understanding: “Serve the Lord in fear, and exult in him with trembling. Embrace discipline, lest you perish from the right way.”

This is the living tradition of the apostles; this is the true charity that must be proclaimed, truly loved, cherished, and confidently held by all. This holy and apostolic Church, the mother of all the Churches of Christ, is shown, by the grace of almighty God, never to have gone astray from the path of apostolic tradition, nor to have yielded to be corrupted by heretical innovations. Rather, having received at the beginning the rule of the Christian faith from its founders, the chief apostles of Christ, it remains undefiled to the end, according to the divine promise of the Lord and Savior, who spoke in his Gospels to the chief of his disciples:

[Col. 0198D] “Peter,” he said, “behold, Satan has demanded to sift you as one sifts wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:31–32).

Therefore let your excellent prudence consider how good it is to persevere in the stewardship entrusted to us and in right faith, to resist heretics and rivals of Christ, and never to depart from the path of truth; for all know that the apostolic pontiffs—the predecessors of my humble office—have always confidently done this, trusting in the Lord and Savior of all, whose faithfulness is sure: he did not hesitate to die for us, redeemed us with his own blood, promised that the faith of blessed Peter would not fail, and charged him to strengthen his brothers.

My own humility, though unequal and least of all, nevertheless desires to follow in their footsteps in the ministry entrusted to me by divine condescension. For woe to us who have received the burden of this ministry if we neglect to proclaim the truth of our Savior Jesus Christ, which the apostles preached.

Woe to us if we suppress in silence the truth that we are commanded to distribute to the money-changers—that is, to assist and teach the Christian peoples. What shall we say at Christ’s future judgment if we are ashamed to proclaim the truth of his words? What will become of us when Christ our God, the just Judge, demands a strict account of the souls entrusted to us and of the office we have undertaken?

[Col. 0200A] Therefore, brothers, I exhort, appeal to, and admonish your charity: with all the care you can and ought to exercise, keep watch to seek out heretics and enemies of the holy Church of God, and with whatever severity you can muster, according to your strength, uproot this plague from sound minds, lest it spread more widely.

For just as the person who diligently carries out what contributes to the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive a worthy reward from God, so no one who refuses to protect his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will be able to excuse himself before the tribunal of the Lord for the guilt of negligence.

Given on 5 February, in the fourth consulship of Claudius and Paternus, [with] the consul in office.

# THE DECREES OF POPE EUTYCHIAN BEGIN

*(In the year of the Lord 276, while Aurelian and Tacitus were ruling.)*

[Col. 0199]

[Col. 0199B] Eutychianus, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to his dearest brothers John and all the bishops established throughout the province of Baetica.

The fairness of your request urges us gladly to grant the desire of your brotherhood and to respond briefly to your consultations. Although I know your charity to be devoted to every good work, nevertheless, so that it may become more effective with respect to those who do not understand soundly, we command you how you ought to instruct them concerning the Incarnation of our Savior.

There is therefore one immovable foundation, this one blessed rock of faith confessed by Peter’s mouth: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” It sustains within itself arguments of truth as great as the questions of perversity and the slanders of unbelief that will be raised.

[Col. 0199C] Let the dispensation of the Father’s will therefore stand in the other matters. Thus, breast and body, after the cross, death, and hell, are our salvation.

For the sake of the human race, the Son of God was born of a Virgin, with the Holy Spirit himself serving him in this work and with his own—namely, God’s—power overshadowing her. He fashioned for himself the beginnings and origins of a body and established the beginnings of flesh, so that, having become man from the Virgin, he might receive in himself the nature of flesh; through the fellowship of this union, the body of the entire human race might be sanctified in him. And just as all were established in him through his willingness to be corporeal, so in turn he would be restored to all through that which belongs to him.

The image of the invisible God therefore did not refuse the humiliation of human birth. Through conception, [Col. 0199D] birth, crying, swaddling clothes, and all the humiliations of our nature, he passed. What, then, worthy of the affection shown by such condescension, shall we render in return? Thus the one only-begotten God, whose origin from God cannot be expressed, is inserted into the form of a human body and grows in the womb of the holy Virgin; he who contains all things, within whom and through whom all things exist, is brought forth according to the law [Col. 0200B] of human development. At his voice archangels and angels tremble; heaven and earth and all the elements of this world are dissolved; the cry of infancy is heard.

He who is invisible and incomprehensible, whom sight, perception, and touch cannot circumscribe, is wrapped in swaddling clothes. If anyone recalls these things as unworthy of God, he confesses himself subject to a still greater benefit, since these things correspond so little to God’s majesty. He did not need to become man, through whom man had been made; we needed God to become flesh and dwell among us—that is, by assuming flesh, one might dwell within all flesh. His humility is our nobility; his humiliation is our honor. What he, God, is while abiding in the flesh, that we, renewed from flesh into God, become in turn.

Certainly, the one who does not know Christ Jesus as both true [Col. 0200C] God and true man does not know his own life. It is a matter of the same danger either not to believe that Jesus Christ or the Holy Spirit is God, or to deny that he possesses the flesh of our body.

“Therefore everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:32–33).

The Word made flesh was speaking these words, and Jesus Christ, the Lord of majesty, who was man, was teaching them. He himself was established as mediator for the salvation of the Church, and by that very mystery of mediation between God and human beings he existed as one who was both: himself arising from natures united in one, while in him the reality of each nature remained the same. Yet he lacked neither nature in either one, lest perhaps, by being born, God should cease to be man, [Col. 0200D] and, by remaining God, man should in turn not be God.

This, then, is the true faith of human blessedness: to proclaim God and man, to confess the Word and the flesh, neither to be ignorant that God is man nor to overlook that the flesh is the Word.

The one-only-begotten God, therefore, born as man from the Virgin and destined, in the fullness of time, to bring this man into God in himself, maintained throughout the whole manner of evangelical speech [Col. 0201A] that he should be believed to be the Son of God and proclaimed to be the son of man. In speaking and acting, he showed that, as man, he spoke and did everything that belongs to God; then, as God, everything that belongs to man. Yet in that very speech concerning both kinds, he never spoke except with an indication of his humanity—and also of his deity.

This, then, is the occasion that heretics have for deceiving the simple and ignorant: they falsely claim that the things spoken by him according to man were spoken because of weakness in the divine nature. And because he is one and the same, speaking everything that he speaks about himself, they insist that he spoke everything from the standpoint of divinity.

We certainly do not deny that the whole of the speech which remains his is the speech of his nature. But if Jesus Christ is both man and God, and [Col. 0201B] God is not first God only when he is man, nor, when he is both man and God, is he then not also God, nor, after man in God, is he not whole man and whole God, it is necessary that his mystery be described according to its kind.

When, according to time, you distinguish man from God in him, distinguish also the speech of God and of man. When you confess God and man in time, judge likewise the words of God and of man according to time. But when, from man and God, you again understand the time of the whole man and now the whole God, if what was said was spoken to demonstrate a temporal distinction, fit the words to the time: before man, God was one thing; man and God another; after man and God, the whole man and the whole God are one. Do not confuse [Col. 0201C] the mystery of the dispensation according to times and kinds, since, in accordance with the character of the kinds and natures, there necessarily had to be one sort of speech in the mystery of the man who had not yet been born, another while he was still destined to die, and another concerning the eternal one.

For our sake, therefore, Jesus Christ did all these things. Born as man from our body according to the custom of our nature, he spoke accordingly, yet he did not omit that his own nature is God. For although in birth, suffering, and death he accomplished what belonged to our nature, he nevertheless performed all these realities through the power of his own nature.

Do you see how God and man are proclaimed, so that death is assigned to the man, while the raising of the flesh is assigned to God, yet the one who died is not someone other than the one through whom the dead man rises? Christ died after being stripped of flesh, and again [Col. 0201D] it is the same Christ who, raising Christ from the dead, strips himself of flesh. Recognize the nature of God in the power of the resurrection; acknowledge the dispensation of man in the death. Although both things were accomplished according to their respective natures, remember that it is one Christ Jesus, the one who is both.

These points, therefore, had to be demonstrated by me briefly, so that we might remember that the form of both natures is treated in our Lord Jesus Christ: the one who, while remaining in the form of God, assumed the form of a servant, did not in any way lose his divinity.

Moreover, brothers, we exhort you to admonish them to turn to God. Thus it is written:

“My son, do not delay in turning to God, and do not put it off from day to day. For suddenly his anger will come, and at the time of vengeance [Col. 0202A] he will destroy you. Do not be anxious about unjust riches; they will profit you nothing on the day of reckoning and vengeance. Do not toss yourself about in every wind, and do not go along every path. For every sinner is tested by a double tongue. Stand firm in the way of God and in the truth of your understanding and knowledge, and let the word of peace and righteousness follow you.

Be gentle in hearing the word, so that you may understand, and give your answer with wisdom. If you have understanding, answer your neighbor; but if not, let your hand be upon your mouth, lest you be caught in an undisciplined word and be put to shame. Honor and glory belong to a sensible speech, but the tongue of the imprudent is his downfall. Do not be called a whisperer, and do not let your tongue catch you and bring you to shame. For upon the thief there is shame, repentance, and the worst condemnation; but upon the whisperer [Col. 0202B] there are hatred, enmity, and abuse. Justify the small and the great alike.

Do not become, instead of a friend, an enemy to your neighbor. For the wicked will inherit reproach and insult, and every sinner is envious and double-tongued. Do not exalt yourself in the thought of your soul like a bull, lest your strength be overthrown through folly, your leaves be eaten, your fruits destroyed, and you be left like a dry tree in the wilderness. For a wicked soul destroys what it possesses, gives it over to the joy of the enemy, and leads it into the lot of the ungodly” (Ecclesiasticus 5:8–18; 6:1–4).

With such exhortations, brothers, admonish one another, and always pursue what is good and avoid what is evil. For, according to the blessed Apostle, we must take the greatest care lest the faith and discipline of the Lord be blasphemed. [Col. 0202C] And although certain things must sometimes be tolerated—things which, if the integrity of the others remains intact, are not by themselves able to cause harm—nevertheless those things must be avoided with the greatest care which cannot be admitted without manifest disfigurement. Even if things believed to be understandable on occasion without harm are judged by consideration of circumstances and times, or are condemned by the urgency of expedient provision, how much more must those things not be mutilated which neither necessity nor ecclesiastical usefulness at all compels us to alter?

For this reason, brothers, we have set forth these provisions: the items which, according to the constitution of the apostles and their successors, may not be offered upon the altar are to be carried to the house of the priests, blessed by the priests, and then, once blessed by this simple blessing, received by the people. Only beans and grapes, and the other things which the apostles prescribed, are to be offered upon the altar. [Col. 0202D]

We desire, therefore, dearest brothers, and with our whole heart entreat the almighty Lord in prayer, that he may cause your affection to grow ever more fervent in his love and grant you to remain together in one harmony and in the peace of the Church. We also admonish your fraternity to watch diligently over the souls entrusted to you and to devote yourselves more to the gain of souls than to the advantages of the present life.

In preserving and administering ecclesiastical property, be diligent guardians, so that the Judge who is to come, when he comes to judge, may approve that in every respect you have worthily discharged the office of shepherd entrusted to you. [Col. 0203A] May almighty God guard you with his protection, grant you to preserve by your conduct the honor bestowed upon you by God, help you to lead the souls entrusted to you to the eternal pastures with abundant fruit and worthily present them to him, [Col. 0204A] and deign to place you among his saints and elect.

Given on the second day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Aurelianus and Marcellus for the fourth time.

## Here begins a letter of Pope Eutychianus addressed to all the bishops established throughout Sicily.

[Col. 0203]

[Col. 0203A] 47 To our most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout Sicily, EUTYCHIANUS.

Blessed is God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless in his sight in love. He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, for the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he favored us in his beloved Son.

In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he caused to abound in us in all wisdom and prudence, [Col. 0203B] making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, both those in heaven and those on earth, in him. In him we have also been called by lot, having been predestined according to his purpose, who accomplishes all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we might be for the praise and glory of him in whom we first hoped.

In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation—in him, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of the acquired possession, to the praise of his glory.

Therefore I too, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus Christ and your love for all the saints, do not cease [Col. 0203C] giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, with the eyes of your heart enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his strength which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come.

And he placed all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body and the fullness [Col. 0203D] of him who is fulfilled in all things.

And you, when you were dead in your transgressions and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we too once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and [Col. 0204A] the thoughts, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.

But now, brothers, because God by his grace and free mercy has made us, who were children of wrath, his children, and because we, who were not worthy servants and had no preceding merits, have become his children by his grace, as we have said—in him we cry, “Abba, Father.” Following his example, let us be children of mercy, righteousness, and love, so that with his help we may both be called and truly be sons of God.

“Therefore, according to the Apostle, put away all malice, all deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and every kind of slander, and so forth” (1 Peter 2:1).

Those who do such things are shown to be not sons of God but rather wicked sons, as the same Apostle says:

“The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murder, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5:19–21).

A grave and exceedingly dreadful word, brothers, is what he says: that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. And Truth itself says:

“What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, but suffer the loss of his soul?” (Mark 8:36.)

The things we have set forth are exceedingly serious and must be avoided with the greatest care. For those who are excluded from the kingdom of God are doubtless also denied the Church. Concerning such people, the Lord, announcing in the Gospel the authority of the apostles and their successors, says: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained”—that is, those whom you exclude from the Church, unless they have been reconciled through satisfaction, will also have the door of the heavenly kingdom closed to them. [Col. 0204C]

Therefore, taking precautions against these things and anticipating the minds of fools, by pastoral care, together with all the bishops and the faithful of both orders of the holy Roman and universal Church, we have established that ecclesiastical affairs must not be handled in the same way as secular affairs. For in secular proceedings, once someone has been summoned and has begun to litigate in court, he is not permitted to withdraw before the case has been completed. In ecclesiastical proceedings, however, once the case has been stated, withdrawal is permitted if it is necessary or if the person sees that he is being excessively burdened.

[Col. 0204D] We have both learned and must observe the following order for accusations: if one of the clergy is accused of a crime, he must not immediately be considered guilty merely because he could be accused, lest we make the innocent subject to accusation. Rather, the person who brings the charge must come into court, state the name of the accused, assume and maintain the bond of a written accusation, and undergo the corresponding proceedings, with due consideration nevertheless given to his dignity. [Col. 0205A] [Col. 0205A] Let him know that he has no license to lie, since the correspondence of the penalty demands vengeance upon false accusers.

No heretics, suspected persons, or excommunicated persons, nor murderers, sorcerers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, or those who have committed abduction, given false testimony, or resorted to diviners and magicians, are to be admitted to bring an accusation under any circumstances.

No infamous or sacrilegious person may ever give testimony against a devout Christian in any matter, even if that Christian is of humble or servile status; nor may such a person bring an action or written accusation against a Christian concerning any matter.

Likewise, permission to accuse or testify must be denied to all who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, or the rule of their own law or superior, or prohibitions established by ecclesiastical rule.

Similarly, we forbid ecclesiastical judges to hear cases which are not contained in the laws or which are known to be prohibited. The laws not only of the Church but also of the world command these provisions to be observed.

[Col. 0205B] For accusations against priests must not be made indiscriminately and without restraint. If they were easily admitted, very few priests would be found, since all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution. Yet blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.

Therefore Truth itself says:

“Father, [Col. 0205C] I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world. They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. Now they know that everything you have given me is from you, because the words that you gave me I have given to them, and they received them and truly understood that I came forth from you, and they believed that you sent me.

I pray for them. I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you gave me, because they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I have been glorified in them. Now I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one, as we are.

When I was with them, I kept them in your name. Those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition, so that Scripture might be fulfilled. But now I am coming to you, and I speak these things in the world so that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.

I have given them your word, and the world [Col. 0205D] has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.

Sanctify them in truth. Your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, I also sent them into the world. And for their sake I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth.

I pray not only for them, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you, so that they too may be one in us, and so that the world may believe that you sent me.

And the glory that you gave me, I have given them, so that they may be one, just as we are one. I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected in one, so that the world may know that you sent me and that you [Col. 0206A] loved them as you loved me.

Father, I desire that those whom you gave me may also be with me where I am, so that they may see my glory which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world.

Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me. I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I may be in them” (John 17:6–26).

The Apostle and Evangelist John likewise says in his first letter:

“Dearest ones, let us love one another, because love is from God. Everyone who loves has been born from God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.

In this the love of God was revealed among us: God sent his only-begotten Son into the world so that [Col. 0206B] we might live through him. In this is love—not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an expiation for our sins.

Dearest ones, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us.

In this we know that we remain in him and he in us: that he has given us of his Spirit. And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world.

Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God. And we have known and believed the love which God has for us. God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him. [Col. 0206C]

In this love is perfected with us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world. There is no fear in love; rather, perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. Whoever fears has not been perfected in love.

Therefore, let us love God, because God first loved us. If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must also love his brother.

Everyone who believes [Col. 0206D] that Jesus is the Christ has been born from God, and everyone who loves the one who begot him loves the one who has been born from him. In this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and do his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 4:7–21; 5:1–4).

And through the prophet, the Lord admonishes that his disciples and their successors must not be harmed, saying:

“The angel of the Lord surrounds those who fear him, and he will rescue them. Taste and see that the Lord is good. Blessed is the man who hopes in him. Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for there is no want for those who fear him. Lions suffer want and hunger, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.

Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life and wishes to see [Col. 0207A] good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.

The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their cry. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth. The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and the Lord delivered them from all their tribulations.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, and he will save the crushed in spirit. Many are the evils of the righteous, but the Lord delivered him from them all. The Lord guards all his bones; not one of them will be broken. Wickedness will slay the ungodly, and those who hate the righteous will be condemned.

The Lord redeems the souls of his servants, and he will deliver them.” [Col. 0208A]

Therefore, brothers, place your hearts upon the Lord, and he will nourish you, because he will not allow the righteous to waver forever. But God the Lord will lead our enemies to destruction, according to the prophet’s word:

“Into the pit of destruction, for men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Psalm 54:24).

But always hope in the Lord and have confidence in him, because he will deliver us. For he is blessed from age to age, and there will be no end to his kingdom.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Caro Vero and Carinus for the fourth time.

## Here begin the decrees of Pope Gaius. (A.D. 283–295.)

[Col. 0207]

[Col. 0207B] To his most beloved brother Felix, bishop, GAIUS.

We gladly received the letters sent to us by your charity, filled with the concern of Catholic inquiry. We bless the mercy of our Lord, because he deigns to provide shepherds for his sheep in the farthest regions of the world—shepherds through whom they may abound in saving pastures and be preserved from the predatory violence of the wicked wolf, so that they may not fall into the snares of his deception.

Therefore it is certain that the grace of promised blessedness follows you, since the perfection of heavenly teachings is sought from you with such eager questioning. For it is written:

“Blessed are those who search out his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (Psalm 118:2).

Therefore, dearest brother, as we consider with our whole mind the purpose of your consultation, we are confident that this too proceeds from you: you strive to hold the rule of the Catholic faith by the same footsteps by which you recognize that it was founded in the apostolic see.

Although the sound of the apostles has spread throughout the whole world and their words have extended to the ends of the earth, proving the hearts of your charity faithful to Christ, nevertheless, if anything from these matters has not yet become fully clear in the Church entrusted, with the Lord’s help, to your governance, you return to the same fountain from which that saving stream flowed. That is, because we have embraced you with the charity that is your due, you wished us confidently to confirm by our reply those matters concerning which you said that observance among them was uncertain.

Therefore, greeting your charity in the Lord, we believe that you should be instructed concerning each matter as to what the authority of the apostolic see holds according to Catholic discipline, with certain chapters of the holy rules added.

First, know that pagans and heretics cannot accuse Christians or bring an accusation of infamy against them. Next, no one may ever presume to accuse a bishop before secular judges or other clergy.

If a bishop, priest, deacon, or any member of the clergy is accused before bishops—for elsewhere such an accusation ought not to be received from just anyone, but only from a person whose accusation is properly admissible—whoever undertakes this kind of blameworthy proceeding, whether he is a distinguished man of rank or of any other dignity, must know that he is required to produce proofs.

If anyone brings forward against such persons accusations that cannot be proved, let him understand, by the authority of this sanction, that he will suffer the loss of reputation, so that, through the injury to his honor and the diminution of his standing, he may learn that, at least from now on, it is not permitted to him to lie in wait for another’s modesty with impunity.

For how one is to come to a council; how proceedings are to be conducted concerning those who have been stripped of their possessions or expelled from their own sees; which accusers are to be admitted and which are not; how everything taken from those expelled and dispossessed is to be restored to them according to the laws—for no crime can be brought against them before this has been done; how periods of respite, whether annual or six months, are to be granted to them after full restoration; and how they ought to arrange all their affairs freely and peacefully, without anyone’s serious obstruction, and make use of the councils of their friends and of ecclesiastical fathers—we believe has been sufficiently established by the apostles, their successors, and our predecessors.

On these matters, however, I do not think there is need for further discussion now, unless matters arise which have not yet been made clear. If you do not possess their statutes, send completely trustworthy scribes who, in the presence of faithful witnesses, may record these matters and [report them] to you under formal undertaking.

Moreover, to satisfy your inquiries sufficiently, concerning the word of the Incarnation and of truth: let those who are so blinded and estranged from the light of truth that they deny the truth of the Word of God from the time of the Incarnation show on what grounds they claim the Christian name and how they agree on equal terms with the Gospel of truth. If, through the Virgin’s childbirth, either flesh arose without divinity or divinity without flesh—as it cannot be denied, since the Evangelist says, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1)—so likewise it cannot be denied, as the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims, “God was indeed in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19). But what reconciliation could there be by which God might be reconciled to the human race, if the mediator between God and humanity did not take up the human cause? And in what way would he fulfill the truth of the mediator unless he who, in the form of God, is equal to the Father were also, in the form of a servant, a participant in our condition, so that the bond of death contracted through one transgression might be released by the death of one who alone owed nothing to death?

For the outpouring of Christ’s righteous blood was so rich as a price that, if the whole company of captives believed in their Redeemer, no bonds of the devil would retain them, since, as the Apostle says, “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). And although those born under the sentence of sin received the power to be reborn into righteousness, the gift of freedom was made stronger than the debt of servitude.

What hope, then, do those leave themselves under the protection of this sacrament who deny the truth of human flesh in our Savior? Who is it, as the Apostle says, who “gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians 5:2)? Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true and eternal High Priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh? Although the death of the righteous was precious in the sight of the Lord, the killing of no innocent person was the redemption of the world. The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. From the courage of the faithful arose examples of endurance, not gifts of righteousness. Their deaths were individual deaths, each person’s own; no one paid another’s debt by his own end. The one and only Son of Man, our Lord Jesus Christ, however, truly existed as the spotless Lamb, in whom all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised. Concerning them he himself said, “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).
