For faith that justifies the ungodly and creates the righteous, having been drawn back to participation in his humanity, obtains salvation in him, in whom the human being alone finds himself innocent and, possessing through God’s grace the freedom to glory in his power, is able to do so: he confronted the enemy of the human race in the lowliness of our flesh and grants his victory to those in whose body he triumphed.

Although, therefore, in our one Lord Jesus Christ, true Son of God and true son of humanity, there is one person of the Word and flesh, who inseparably and indivisibly possesses the actions common to both, the qualities of those works must nevertheless be understood. Thus, by contemplating the true faith, we must discern to what the lowliness of the flesh is raised and to what the exaltedness of divinity descends: what the flesh does not do without the Word, and what the Word does not accomplish without the flesh.

Without the power of the Word, the Virgin would neither have conceived nor given birth; and without the truth of the flesh, infancy wrapped in swaddling clothes would not have lain there. Without the power of the Word, the Magi would not have worshiped the child whose appearance was announced by the star; and without the truth of the flesh, the child would not have been ordered to be taken into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution. Without the power of the Word, the voice of the Father sent from heaven would not have said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5); and without the truth of the flesh, John would not have testified, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Without the power of the Word, the restoration of the weak and the giving of life to the dead would not have occurred; and without the truth of the flesh, neither food would have been necessary for one fasting nor sleep for one wearied. Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not have declared himself equal to the Father; and without the truth of the flesh, he would not have said that the Father was greater than he. The catholic faith accepts and defends both, believing, according to the confession of the blessed Apostle Peter, that the one Christ, the Son of God, is both human and the Word.

Although, therefore, from the time when the Word became flesh in the Virgin’s womb there was never any division in either form, and throughout all bodily stages the actions of the entire period belonged to one person, we do not confuse those things which were accomplished inseparably, so to speak, by mixing them together. Rather, we discern what belongs to each form from the character of the works.

Let these hypocrites, then, who refuse to receive the light of truth with blind minds, say in what form Christ, the Lord of majesty, was fastened to the wood of the cross, who lay in the tomb, and, when the stone of the monument had been rolled away, what flesh rose on the third day. And because after his resurrection he rebuked certain disciples who did not believe and refuted the hesitation of those who doubted when he said, “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39), and to the Apostle Thomas, “Put your hand into my side, and see my hands and feet, and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John 20:27)—because by the manifestation of his body he was already destroying the lies of heretics, so that the whole Church of Christ, to be renewed by the teaching of the doctor, might have no doubt that it must believe what the Apostles had received to preach—if heretical blindness does not leave its darkness before so great a light of truth, let it show from where it promises itself hope of eternal life, to which no one can attain except through the mediator between God and humanity, the human being Jesus Christ.

For, as the blessed Apostle Peter says, “There is no other name given among human beings under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). Nor is there redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:6), and who, as the Apostle Paul proclaims:

“Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming in the likeness of human beings and being found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:6–11).

Since, then, there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and in him there is altogether one and the same person of true divinity and true humanity, we understand the exaltation with which God exalted him and granted him the name above every name, as the teacher of the nations said, to belong to that form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glorification.

In the form of God, the Son was equal to the Father; between the Begetter and the Only-Begotten there was no distinction in essence and no difference in majesty. Through the mystery of the Incarnation, nothing had diminished from the Word that could later be restored to him as a gift of the Father. But the form of a servant, through which impassible divinity fulfilled the sacrament of great piety, is human lowliness; raised into the glory of divine piety, it was joined to divinity in such unity from the very conception in the Virgin that neither divine actions occurred without the human nor human actions without God.

[Col. 0211B] Therefore, just as the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, so he who is eternally equal to God is said to have been exalted, because, with the unity of the person remaining inseparable, one and the same person is wholly the son of humanity because of the flesh and wholly the Son of God because of the one divinity he shares with the Father.

Whatever Christ received in time, he received according to his humanity, to which were granted things it did not possess. For according to the power of divinity, the Son possesses without distinction everything the Father possesses; and what he received from the Father in the form of a servant, he himself also bestowed in the form of God. For according to the form of God, he and the Father are one. According to the form of a servant, he did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him; according to the form of a servant, his soul was sorrowful even unto death.

And this same person, as the Apostle proclaims, is both rich and poor: rich because, as the Evangelist says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1); this Word was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. Poor, however, because for our sake the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

What, then, is his self-emptying, and what is his poverty, except the taking of the form of a servant, through which, while the majesty of the Word was revealed, the administration of human redemption was accomplished? For the original bonds of our captivity could not be undone unless there existed a human being of our race whom neither the judgments of nature nor the sentence of sin held captive, and who might erase the deadly bond with his spotless blood. As this had been divinely ordained from the beginning, so it was accomplished in the fullness of time, so that the promise, signified in many ways, might come to the fulfillment long awaited, and what had always been announced by continuous testimonies could not remain in doubt.

The impiety of the heretics reveals that they are involved in great sacrilege when, under the appearance of honoring divinity, they deny the truth of human flesh in Christ, and religiously suppose that one should believe that what saves is not true in our Savior. For, in accordance with the promise extending through all ages, the world has been reconciled to God in Christ, so that unless the Word had deigned to become flesh, no flesh could be saved.

The whole sacrament of Christian faith is disfigured by a great darkness—as the heretics would have it—if the light of truth is thought to have hidden beneath the lie of a phantom. Therefore no Christian should be ashamed of the truth of our body in Christ, since all the Apostles and the disciples of the Apostles, and all the renowned teachers of the churches who deserved to attain the crown of martyrdom or the glory of confession, shone in the light of this faith, proclaiming with harmonious judgments that one person of divinity and flesh must be confessed in the Lord Jesus Christ.

By what likeness of reasoning, by what passage of the divine books, does heretical impiety imagine itself aided when it denies the truth of Christ’s body, although neither the Law has ceased to testify to it, nor the prophets to foretell it, nor the Gospels to teach it, nor Christ himself to display it? Let them search through the entire sequence of the Scriptures for where they may flee from darkness, not for where they may obscure the true light. Throughout all the ages they will find the truth flashing forth, so that from the beginning they may see this great and wondrous sacrament believed, which has been completed at the end.

Since no part of the sacred writings is silent concerning it, it is enough to set forth certain harmonious signs of truth by which the diligence of faith may be directed into the brightest expanse and sincere understanding may see clearly that Christians should not be ashamed, but should glory most steadfastly, in the Son of God who unceasingly professes himself to be the Son of Man, the human being. For, as the blessed Apostle says:

“Great is the sacrament of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16).

Concerning the ordinations of bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the clerics who follow them, we know that the holy Apostles and their successors, especially Anacletus, and also others, have legislated sufficiently. Therefore it is not necessary to repeat these matters now, except where they did not legislate.

We nevertheless establish this and command you and everyone to observe it: those who deserve to be ordained to ecclesiastical orders shall enter them in this manner. If someone is worthy to become a bishop, he shall first be a doorkeeper, then a lector, afterward an exorcist, next be consecrated as an acolyte, then a subdeacon, afterward a deacon, and then a presbyter; thereafter, if he deserves it, he shall be ordained bishop.

The regions shall also be divided among deacons by individual cities, as we have done in this city, wherever the cities are populous. Whatever difficult questions arise in the individual provinces shall always be referred to the apostolic see.

Farewell, brother, and pray for us. Given on the Kalends of March, in the fourth consulship of Diocletian and the consulship of Constantius Verus. [The consular notation is abbreviated in the source: “IV cc. cons.”]

## THE DECREES OF POPE MARCELLINUS BEGIN  
*(In the year of the Lord 295, under the emperor Maximian.)*

[Col. 0213]

[Col. 0213A] Marcellinus, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, sends greetings in the Lord to Salomon, his fellow bishop.

How commendably you are moved on behalf of the truth of the catholic faith, and how diligently you devote the service of a shepherd to the Lord’s flock, is shown by the writings of your fraternity delivered to us by your deacon. In them you have taken care to make known to us what diseases of error have recently arisen in your regions.

For the wording of your letter, the sequence of your memorandum, and the text of your little book declare that certain people, deceived by error, say that the Father is greater than the Son because sacrifice is offered to the Father alone; that the Son has no share in the Father’s work; and that the prophetic statement, “Let the nations know that your name is God; you alone are the Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 82:19), was spoken of the Father alone. They also say that the Son is therefore lesser because, hanging on the cross, he said, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34).

A fitting and appropriate answer must be given to them. For just as we prove that sacrifice was offered to the Father, so also we prove that it was offered to the Son—not only in Christian times but also by priests in ancient times—in various and many ways. The prophet Daniel says:

“There is no place”—the three youths say—“for sacrificing to your name and finding mercy, but may we be received with a contrite soul and a humble spirit. And as with the burnt offerings of rams and bulls and fattened lambs, so may our sacrifice be in your sight today, that it may please you” (Daniel 3:38 ff.).

And so that you may recognize that they confessed themselves to have offered sacrifice to the Son, learn this from the confession of the very king and tyrant who had ordered them to be thrown into the furnace of fire. He declared that he had seen a fourth person joined with the three amid the flames of the blazing furnace:

“Did we not,” he said, “throw three men bound into the furnace?” They answered him, “Certainly, O king.” He said, “Look, I see four men unbound and walking in the midst of the fire, and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of God” (Daniel 3:91–92).

The same Son of God speaks through the prophet, saying, “Kings will offer you gifts” (Psalm 68:30). And to show that he had said this concerning the Son of God, he added:

“The kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring presents, and all kings will worship him; all nations will serve him” (Psalm 72:10–11).

And to demonstrate that all these things indicated above were offered to Christ, the Son of God, we prove that they were fulfilled at his birth, which took place according to the flesh, as the Gospel confirms:

“When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying, ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?’” (Matthew 2:1–2).

And below:

“Entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they worshiped him. Then they opened their treasures and offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh” (Matthew 2:11).

The sacrifice, therefore, which is brought to the sacred altars by Christians is offered not only to God the Father but also to the Son in a common devotion, because neither can the Father be offered without the Son, nor the Son be understood apart from the Father.

That the Father and the Son share a common work is taught in this way: the substance of the first human being is said to have been made by God in the image of God through their common power of operation, as Scripture says, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26). Likewise, there it says, “Let us go down and confuse their language there” (Genesis 11:7; the source prints “Gen. II, 7”). “The Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom from the Lord” (Genesis 19:24). And in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). Likewise, “The works that I do are not mine but those of the Father who sent me” (John 5:36).

All these statements do not display a separate power of the Father and the Son but announce one operation of the divinity. And the one who carries out the Father’s work is not believed to be alien to the Father’s works.

If from the Gospel you had recognized the Son of God as called the Most High, you would never, derogating from the Son, have applied this testimony to God the Father alone, since it is written, “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High” (Luke 1:76). And so that the Son may be believed to have dwelt with the Father indistinguishably in the highest places, this is confirmed by the testimony of Solomon:

“I, Wisdom, dwelt in the highest places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud” (Sirach 24:7).

And in the ninety-second Psalm: “But you are Most High forever, Lord, for behold, your enemies will perish.”

When the devil, lifting himself up in pride, placed his throne in the heights against the throne of his Creator, he dared to utter these words with his impious mouth:

“I will place my seat in the north,” he said; “I will ascend above the stars of heaven; I will sit upon the high mountains, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13–14).

Likewise, in Solomon: “Do not say, ‘I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?’ For the Most High is patient in repaying” (Sirach 5:4).

If you do not wish to lend the hearing of your heart to the divine Scriptures, which teach that the Son is called the Most High, believe at least the devil, who wished to establish a seat for himself against the throne of his Maker.

So that you may recognize that he was not utterly abandoned by the Father—as you suppose—he set down this testimony concerning himself in the Gospel: “The Father who sent me is with me and has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John 8:29).

Accordingly, in view of this surreptitious act [surreptione; the precise reference is uncertain], we command that every care and diligence remain vigilant, and that the faith neither be endangered nor violated. There is now no place for ignorance; no one may use the excuse of former simplicity. One who sins knowingly needs shame, and what was acquired through error must be reformed through knowledge.

Hold fast to these things, brother, and teach them. Would that, for the fuller satisfaction of conversation, the joy of your presence had come to us, so that we might rejoice that we were enjoying both your conversation and your presence, which we have embraced in our earlier writing. Nevertheless, dearest brother, you have demonstrated with what affection you venerate the Christian faith, since you preserve without any transgression of fault those things that belong to the rules of the Fathers and to catholic commands; reject heretical and harmful teaching; hold the catholic and apostolic precepts; and teach and preserve the rules of right faith.

Let us meditate upon these things, dearest brother, and upon the other matters contained in the rules of the Fathers, with undivided reflection upon our lips and in our hearts. As it is written:

“Let us tell them to our children, so that they may meditate upon them in their hearts, sitting in the house, walking on the road, sleeping and rising” (Deuteronomy 6:7),

because “blessed is the one who meditates upon his law in the Lord day and night” (Psalm 1:2).

The Teacher of the nations followed this practice and, instructing his disciple, admonished him: “Meditate on these things; be in them” (1 Timothy 4:15). “You will add the completion; attend to your teaching” [the wording following the citation is textually irregular]. For if we devote ourselves without interruption to instruction in the faith, we are separated from vices, since diligent care for the divine work leaves no room for human error.

If the things mentioned above are held fixed with strong roots, if no one departs from the tradition of the Fathers, questions are steadfastly met, the intention of the perverse is nullified, and the faith and constancy of the good are strengthened.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the consulships of Diocletian and Constantine. [The source’s consular notation is abbreviated: “C. cc. consulibus.”]

## THE SAME LETTER OF POPE MARCELLINUS

[Col. 0215]

[Col. 0215B] To the dearest brothers, all the bishops established throughout the eastern provinces: Marcellinus, bishop.

What is so sweet to one who is concerned as hearing from you those things that I desire? What is so fitting for religious discipline as that priests should preserve among themselves the peace which, in accordance with their office, they must announce to others?

I confess that I received with complete rejoicing your letters, in which you announced to me the peace of the churches and the charity that exists among you. Whatever I could exhort, whatever I could advise, you have voluntarily brought to me. “Confirm, O God, what you have worked in us” (Psalm 68:29). And whatever he commanded to be done for the salvation of souls, may he himself who commanded it accomplish, in the piety by which he redeemed us.

And in response to such good news, we too return the religious service of holy messengers. Whatever we previously reported by letter concerning the Easterners, whom, through the aid of our God, we had summoned back to the unity and body of the Church, we now share with you again through open reports once the matter has become clear.

Soon, in accordance with our edict, an embassy was sent by the Easterners. It hoped for certain things and sought counsel concerning certain things; but we shall summarize what had to be said. Rather, we are sending you the answers we gave in order to inform you, lest either opinion claim for itself or error assume what belongs to a long interval of distance between lands, when it is enough to hold to the truth itself concerning the facts.

As for what concerns the substance of our letter, it would indeed have been proper to set forth your desires more fully. Therefore know that you must abstain from persecuting your brothers and from every dispute, since Scripture says, “The servant of God must not quarrel” (2 Timothy 2:24), nor do any harm. Instead, you must correct all persecutors of the Church and of its servants through your rebukes, as the Apostle testifies: “Reprove, exhort, rebuke” (2 Timothy 4:2).

Whatever disputes arise among Christians must be brought before the Church and settled by ecclesiastical men. A greater cannot be judged by a lesser, nor can bishops bring any prejudice against the pontiff by whom they are proved to have been consecrated. If this is known to have been presumed, it is certainly without force and cannot in any way be regarded as an ecclesiastical statute.

A cleric of any order must not, without the permission of his pontiff, presume to drag anyone before a secular court. Nor may a layperson accuse any cleric. Detraction, accusation, and persecution among Christians must be avoided altogether. For although we are few in comparison with others, if we are united we shall more easily resist our adversaries.

The holy protomartyr Stephen was being stoned, but Jesus was receiving the blows. Therefore each person must take care not to judge or punish anyone unjustly, lest he judge or punish Jesus. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; for with the judgment by which you judge, you will be judged” (Matthew 7:1–2).

Hence the Teacher of the nations also speaks, saying:

“Therefore I say and testify in the Lord: you must no longer walk as the nations walk, in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them because of the blindness of their hearts. They, having become despairing, handed themselves over to indecency, for the practice of every impurity and greed.

“But you did not learn Christ in this way, if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, as truth is in Jesus: that you should put off, according to your former way of life, the old human being, who is corrupted according to the desires of error; that you should be renewed in the spirit of your mind and put on the new human being, who has been created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth.

“Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another. Be angry and do not sin. Do not let the sun go down upon your anger; do not give place to the devil. Let the one who was stealing steal no longer, but rather let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one in need.

“Let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but only whatever is good for the building up required, so that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice.

“Be kind and compassionate toward one another, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you. Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant aroma.

“But let fornication and every impurity or greed not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or vulgar jesting, which does not belong, but rather thanksgiving. For know this with understanding: every fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

“Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience. Therefore do not become their partners. For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light. For the fruit of light is in all goodness, righteousness, and truth, testing what is pleasing to God.

“And do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, reprove them. For the things done in secret by them are shameful even to mention. But everything that is reproved is revealed by the light. For everything that is revealed is light. Therefore he says: ‘Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.’

“See, then, brothers, how carefully you walk—not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God the Father, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 4:17–32; 5:1–21).

For the Catholic Church defends everything that is irreproachable. Therefore it is not permissible for an emperor or for anyone who guards piety to presume anything against the divine commands, or to do anything that conflicts with the evangelical, prophetic, and apostolic rules.

An unjust judgment and an unjust decision arranged by judges through fear of, or at the command of, a king shall have no validity. Nor shall anything stand that has been done against the constitution of evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic teaching, or against that of their successors or the holy Fathers. Whatever has been done by unbelievers or heretics shall cease altogether.

But stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and let all your affairs be done in charity. For this reason, as the Apostle says, “I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner human being, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, rooted and founded in charity, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, depth, and height, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God.”

Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us, to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the sixth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of Maximus. [The source’s consular notation is abbreviated: “IV cc. consul.”]

## THE DECREES OF POPE MARCELLUS BEGIN  
*(In the year of the Lord 304, under Constantius and Galerius.)*

[Col. 0217]

[Col. 0217D] To the dearest brothers, all the bishops established throughout the province of Antioch: Marcellus.

Bearing, according to the Apostle, the concern of all the churches, we must remember the divine grace toward us, which through the mercy of its gracious favor raised us to the height of the priesthood for this purpose: that, adhering to its commands and established as though upon a watchtower of its priests, we may prohibit what is unlawful and teach what must be followed.

Therefore, by letters sent through our deacon Boniface, we admonish you that what is growing wrongly be cut away, wrongs be corrected, good things be pursued, and the examples and statutes of our Fathers be imitated.

We ask you, therefore, brothers, to teach and think nothing other than what you received from the blessed Apostle Peter and from the other Apostles and Fathers. For you were first instructed by him. Therefore you ought not to abandon your own Father and follow others, since he is the head of the whole Church, to whom the Lord said, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18), and so forth.

His see was originally among you; afterward, at the Lord’s command, it was transferred to Rome, over which, with the support of divine grace, we preside today. Nor ought we to deviate from his arrangement, to which, by the ordering of divine grace, all greater ecclesiastical affairs have been commanded to be referred, so that they may be regularly arranged by the see from which they took their beginnings.

If your Antiochene see, which was once the first, yielded to the Roman see, there is no see that is not subject to its authority. To it, as to a head, according to the decrees of the Apostles and their successors, all bishops who wish to do so or who have need must flee and appeal, so that from it they may receive protection and release, from the source from which they received instruction and consecration.

This must by no means be denied to any bishop. Rather, he must be allowed to go freely, without any confinement, excommunication, condemnation, or dispossession. At the same time, inspired by the Lord, they established that no synod should be held without the authority of that same see, and that no bishop summoned on any charges should be heard or judged except in a legitimate synod convened at the proper time by apostolic authority.

For, as was briefly stated above, the judgments of bishops, the affairs of the principal cases, and all doubts must be conducted and concluded by the authority of the apostolic see. All provincial affairs of this holy, universal, and apostolic Church must be reconsidered in judgment if the pontiff of this Church so commands.

Nor may anyone, without prejudice to the Roman Church—to which reverence is owed in every matter—[observe or maintain something: custodire, with the construction apparently defective], leaving behind the priests who, by God’s divine will, govern the Churches in that province, flee to other provinces or seek or undergo the judgment of bishops from other provinces. Instead, once all the bishops of that province have been assembled, the judgment must be concluded by the authority of this see. Nevertheless, as was stated above, it may, if the see wishes, be handled through its vicars, and whatever was done unjustly must be reformed.

Pastoral care therefore admonishes us both to assist the abandoned and to reform everything neglected or wrongly done, so that that fire which the Lord, when he came, sent upon the earth may, stirred by the repeated movement of correction or by repeated meditation, grow hot enough to boil and become so inflamed that it shines.

Often it must be said and done that burgeoning evils ought to be cut away through fraternal charity, so that good things may find the fullest possible room to grow and increase.

“Do not, therefore,” as the Apostle says, “become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you are taking upon yourselves a greater judgment.” For in many things we all offend. If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body. Now if we put bits into horses’ mouths so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look also at ships: although they are large and are driven by strong winds, they are nevertheless steered by a small rudder wherever the impulse of the one guiding them wishes. So also [Col. 0219D] the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts great things. See how great a fire kindles so great a forest! And the tongue is a fire, the whole world of iniquity. The tongue is set among our members; it stains the whole body and sets on fire the course of our birth, being itself set on fire by Gehenna. For every kind of beast, bird, serpent, and other creature is, and has been, tamed by humankind. But no human being can tame the tongue: it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who have been made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing. This ought not to be so, my brothers. Can a spring from the same opening pour forth sweet and bitter water? Can [Col. 0220A] a fig tree, my brothers, produce olives, or a vine figs? So neither can salt water produce sweet water.

Who among us is wise and disciplined? Let him show his works by his good conduct, in the gentleness of wisdom. But if you have bitter zeal and there are contentions in your hearts, do not boast and become liars against the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above; rather, it is earthly, natural, and demonic. For where there is zeal and contention, there are disorder and every evil work. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, compliant, agreeing with what is good, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without partiality and without hypocrisy.

“The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace” (James III, 1 and following).

[Col. 0220B] “Therefore, girding up the loins of your mind, being sober and perfect, hope fully in the grace that is being offered to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. As obedient children, do not be conformed to the former desires of your ignorance, but according to the one who called you, the Holy One, be holy yourselves in all your conduct, because it is written: ‘You shall be holy, because I am holy.’ And if you invoke as Father the one who judges without partiality according to each person’s work, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourn. Know that you were not redeemed from your empty way of life inherited from your fathers with perishable gold or silver, but with the precious blood of the Lamb, as of Jesus Christ, undefiled and spotless, foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world but manifested [Col. 0220C] in the last times for your sake, who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that our faith and hope might be in God. [51] Having purified your souls in obedience to love, love one another earnestly from a sincere heart in fraternal affection. You have been born again, not from perishable seed but from imperishable, through the word of the living and abiding God, because ‘all flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass; the grass withered, and its flower fell, but the word of the Lord remains forever.’ This is the word that was proclaimed to you in the Gospel. Therefore, having put aside all malice, all deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and every kind of slander, like newborn infants desire rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow [Col. 0220D] toward salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet.

“Approaching him, then, as a living stone rejected by human beings but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves also, like living stones, are being built up into spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Therefore Scripture says: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen and precious; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame.’ For you, therefore, there is honor who believe; but for those who do not believe: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,’ and ‘a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense’ to those who stumble at the word and do not believe, to which they were also appointed. But you are a chosen race, [Col. 0221A] a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people acquired as a possession, so that you may proclaim the mighty works of the one who called you from darkness into his marvelous light” (I Peter I, 13–25; 1–9).

Therefore, dearest ones, be prudent and vigilant in prayers. Above all, maintain continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins. Be hospitable to one another without murmuring, each administering [Col. 0222A] the grace he has received to the other, as good stewards of God’s manifold grace. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God. If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies, so that God may be honored in all things through Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen (I Peter IV, 7 and following).

Given on the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Maxentius and Maximus, for the fourth time.

# LETTER OF POPE MARCELLUS TO THE TYRANT MAXENTIUS

[Col. 0221]

[Col. 0221A] Marcellus, bishop of the holy, apostolic, and catholic city of Rome, to Maxentius.

Charity, the teacher of all good things, which seizes nothing belonging to another, does nothing harsh, confused, or factious, and nothing that opposes divine honor, harms one’s own soul, or diminishes the welfare of one’s neighbor—[Col. 0221B] forgetful of itself, seeking not what belongs to it but what belongs to God or to one’s neighbor, envying no one, caring for all, not raging but showing compassion, not seizing but giving, not murmuring but enduring all things with equanimity—if it dwelt perfectly in you, you would restrain your spirit from evil, cease to rage—that is, you would cease persecuting the Church of God and his saints—you would impose a limit upon your tyranny, restrain your fury, attend to humanity, embrace moderation, and strive to enjoy better things.

For charity disciplines hearts and strengthens minds, so that nothing burdensome or difficult is found in what is done, but everything becomes sweet, since it is characteristic of charity to nourish peace, preserve what has been ordered, join together what has been separated, straighten what is crooked, and strengthen the remaining virtues with the protection of its perfection.

Concerning this, therefore, the Apostle admonishes everyone, saying:

[Col. 0221C] “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy in its entirety, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.

“Charity is patient; it is kind. Charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek what belongs to it, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, [Col. 0221D] hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails” (I Corinthians XIII, 1 and following).

Whoever, therefore, plants himself in its root neither withers in verdure nor becomes barren of fruits, because the work of fruitful love does not admit ineffectiveness.

Although charity among the persecutors of the Church of God has now withered, it nevertheless flourishes among those who love the Church and among those who suffer for righteousness. Concerning them Truth itself bears witness, saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness” (Matthew V, 10). And elsewhere: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV, 20).

[Col. 0222A] Rather, we and all the Lord’s priests who are truly his priests have chosen to be persecuted for righteousness and the true faith and to suffer for Christ’s name, rather than to be enriched with many possessions, abound in the greatest honors, and be deprived of the heavenly kingdom. These things are temporal; those are eternal. These are fleeting and pass away in an hour, but those are perpetual and endure without end.

[Col. 0222B] You, therefore, who urge us to abandon divine worship and depart from the true faith: it would be better for you first to make yourself changeable and to exhort everyone to hold fast to the testimonies of the faith and the ministries of divine worship as our fathers, the holy apostles, preached and taught them as they had received them.

For it is the duty of a good ruler and king to restore churches that have been ruined and divided, to build new ones, and to honor and protect God’s priests. Hence we read that the holy apostles and their successors established under divine testimony that persecutions should not occur, that disturbances should not be inflicted, that those laboring in the Lord’s field should not be envied, and that the stewards of the eternal King should not be expelled. Rather, if any have been expelled or stripped of their possessions, everything taken from them by enemies or persecutors must first be [Col. 0222C] restored to them lawfully, and their proper sees, together with everything belonging to them, must be regularly restored. Afterwards, at a suitable time, they must be summoned to a properly convened synod. Before these things have been done, they may not be compelled to answer concerning themselves according to the statutes mentioned above, or to give an account of the charges brought against them if they find themselves oppressed by them.

But once these matters have been properly completed and everything belonging to them has been freely placed at their disposal, then, if it seems just, let them answer their accusers and, if necessary, receive a substantial period of postponement, so that they may investigate the accusations brought against them and not at some time, deceived by fraud, fall while innocent. For no one ought to be judged or condemned before having legitimate accusers present and receiving an opportunity to defend himself and clear the charges.

[Col. 0222D] Thus the prophet says: “Before you know the matter, judge no one” (Ecclesiasticus XI, 7).

In this matter, those who persecute bishops and the other servants of God are not persecuting only them, but also the one whose place they occupy, as it is written: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah II, 8). And elsewhere: “Whoever has caused you grief has caused me grief” (Colossians III, 25); and: “Whoever does wrong will receive what he has done unjustly” (II Corinthians II, 5).

Although “you may kill our bodies, you cannot kill our souls” (Matthew X, 28), nor can you take away the ranks divinely bestowed upon us.

[Col. 0223A] Therefore, although you may gather some bishops, you cannot lawfully hold a synod of bishops without the authority of this holy see. Nor can you condemn any bishop who has appealed to this apostolic see before a definitive sentence has proceeded from here.

For if secular persons use documents of appeal in public courts, how much more may priests do the same, since they are above those persons? Of them it is said: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm LXXXI, 6).

Therefore no bishop, accused of whatever crimes, may be heard or judged except in a legitimate synod, convened at the proper time by apostolic or regular authority, lest an innocent person be condemned or lose communion.

[Col. 0223B] That laypeople, or suspect persons, ought not to accuse bishops, and that accusers coming from an enemy’s household should not be believed, we read was defined by blessed Clement, with the apostles instructing him in this matter; and we confirm the same, since such persons, often inflamed by hatred, strive to disturb those who live and believe rightly.

For this reason, the person, faith, life, conduct, and possible suspicious motives of the accusers must first be carefully investigated; afterwards the accusations must be examined faithfully. Nothing should be done before the life, suspicion, and hatred of those bringing the charges have been investigated.

And if they are not of good conduct, or are laypeople, or manifest enemies, or tainted by hatred, they must by no means be admitted to accuse bishops. This instruction we send to you, who persecute us violently with threats, so that you may guard against these things and cease persecuting those who minister to God. [Col. 0223C] Through their prayers earthly wars are calmed and God is reconciled to sinners.

But if you choose to persecute us further rather than please God, we choose all the more to endure persecution rather than confound ecclesiastical order, encouraged by the very voice of Truth and bearing witness in this way:

“Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew X, 28).

And again:

“If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange can a person give for his soul? For the Son [Col. 0223D] of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to his work” (Matthew XVI, 24 and following).

These are things you must greatly fear and avoid—you who harass and persecute the Church of God and its ministers. Concerning you the Lord speaks threateningly through the prophet:

“A human being, though in honor, did not remain; he was compared with beasts and made equal to them. This is their way, their folly, and afterward those who approve their words will follow it. Like sheep they have been placed in the underworld; death will feed upon them, and the upright will rule over them in the morning. Their form will be destroyed in the underworld, after their dwelling. Yet God will redeem my soul from the hand of the underworld when he takes me up.

“Do not fear when a man becomes rich, when the glory of his house has multiplied; for when he dies he will take nothing with him, nor will [Col. 0224A] his glory descend after him. For in his life he blessed his soul; they will praise you when you have done well for yourself. He will enter to the generation of his fathers; forever he will not see the light. A human being, though in honor, will not be moved; he was compared with beasts and made equal to them” (Psalm XLVIII, 13 and following).

And elsewhere:

“Why do you boast in wickedness, O mighty one? The mercy of God—your tongue devised snares all day, like a sharp razor, working deceit. You loved wickedness more than goodness, falsehood more than speaking righteousness. You loved every devouring word, deceitful tongue.

“But God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and uproot you from your tent, and eradicate you from the land of the living. The righteous will see and fear, and they will laugh at [Col. 0224B] him. Behold the man who did not make God his strength, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and was strengthened in his treacheries.

“But I, like a flourishing olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in God’s mercy forever and ever. I will confess to you forever because of what you have done, and I will await your name, for it is good, in the presence of your saints” (Psalm LI, 3 and following).

All these things have been said to you for your destruction, but to us for encouragement, so that we may not perish.

We write these things to you because we are your debtors, as the Lord says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Romans XII, 20).

And elsewhere Scripture says:

“If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Matthew V, 44).

[Col. 0224C] Supported by these authorities, we desire to bear peacefully the war that you have raised against us, with the Lord’s right hand protecting us and fighting on our behalf, so that, when Christ triumphs, there may be one victory belonging to all true priests, and when the light of truth flashes forth, the sun of error may drive away the darkness together with its authors. For the counsel of God is not in human power.

“For the Lord is just, and all his judgments are just; all his ways are mercy, truth, and judgment” (Tobit III, 2). “In the hand of the Lord is the power of the earth, to whom all iniquity is detestable. In the hand of God is human power, and upon the face of the scribe he will place his honor. God has destroyed the memory of the proud [52] and of those who act unjustly, and he has not abandoned the memory of the humble and [Col. 0224D] good” (Ecclesiasticus X, 4, 7, 5, 21).

Let everyone who rightly worships God know this with certainty: if his life is tested, it will be strengthened; if he is in tribulation, he will be delivered. But if he is under correction, he will come to misery.

Therefore, do not delight in our destruction, because after the storm God brings calm, and after tears and weeping he pours out rejoicing.

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of our fathers, who, when he is angry, will show mercy, and in the time of tribulation forgives sins” (Tobit III, 21, 23). “Great is the Lord forever, and he himself will rule us forever” (Psalm XLVII), for his kingdom remains forever and ever. Amen.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Maxentius and Maximus, for the fourth time.

# THE DECREES OF POPE EUSEBIUS BEGIN  
*(In the year of the Lord 309, in the time of the emperor Constantine.)*

[Col. 0225]

[Col. 0225A] Eusebius to all the most beloved brothers, bishops established throughout the Gallic provinces, beloved by the Lord and God.

I received your letter with great thanksgiving, rejoicing, naturally, at your well-being but greatly saddened by your oppression.

You indicated what ought to be done concerning converts from heresy. Know that we receive those who have been baptized in faith in the holy Trinity through the laying on of hands.

Concerning the accusations against clerics about which you wrote, know that from the time of the apostles it has been observed in this holy city that accusers and accusations which the laws of foreign customs do not admit have been excluded from accusations against clerics.

Similarly, it has until now been observed and established that laypeople do not accuse bishops, because they do not share the same way of life. Indeed, they are exceedingly hostile to them, since their lives and private conduct ought to be removed from the actions of laypeople; nor ought bishops be attacked by those who do not wish to imitate their chastity and dignity, especially since bishops themselves do not wish to receive laypeople in their accusations.

Concerning these bishops, who are, of course, his own cultivators and ministers, the Lord says to laypeople and to all who persecute them: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (I Chronicles XVI, 22). And sacred Scripture itself says: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah II, 8).

Foreseeing such dangers and similar ones, the holy Fathers prohibited laypeople serving in the world from accusing priests. They likewise excluded from the same accusation or evasion slaves and free persons, those subject to public or private censuses, and all persons of infamous status.

For it is not right that carnal persons be permitted to persecute spiritual persons, nor that those entangled in crimes or serving the world defame, tear apart, or bring accusations against bishops. For if the apostles or their successors had permitted this, very few would have remained to serve the Lord in the priestly order.

Therefore we also, following the footsteps of the Fathers, through the Savior, remove from the opportunity to attack another all those persons whom the public laws do not admit to accusation against the servants of God; and no accusations prohibited by the laws of the world are to be heard by ecclesiastical judges.

Consequently, those who do not possess a polished perfection to the utmost degree ought to keep silent about such matters, so that they are neither mutilated nor preferred, and so that those who are suspect either in the Catholic faith or because of enmity are not admitted to bring charges against the aforesaid persons, since infidelity and enmity ordinarily impede professors of the truth.

Nor should those persons be believed or admitted who voluntarily confess the crimes of others. For this reason the truth must be diligently investigated, since the voice freely uttered by such people cannot possess authority. A religious torturer ought to extract it from its hiding places through various torments, so that, while bodies are broken by punishments, what has been done may be investigated faithfully and truthfully.

Therefore, I ask you, first turn your attention to the public laws and then to the judges, who can and wish to speak justly in defense of all.

Will we, whom service to God has made free after the rejection of such things, who either despise or mock the insults, contempt, or abuse of such people, to whom the Apostle’s words concerning servants and men of the common people apply—“Remember that your Lord and theirs is in heaven”—be recalled to these evils of the world? Are we to do what we insist makes another person profane?

Shall what would defile the sight through the ministry of an order and another person’s hand be carried out by our command? Do not preserve this disposition throughout all the Churches, in the manner and nature of rapacious wolves, because after it has stained us, perhaps their bloody investigation will not achieve in these matters the result toward which they strive.

The prophet says to us: “Let us put a ring in their nostrils and a bridle on their lips, and let us lead them back into the right path” (Isaiah XXXVII, 29). For, as the same prophet asserts, those who say “They shall be as though they did not exist” are opposed, and the men who contradict us shall perish.

Without doubt, all the enemies of bishops, and all who take up arms against the Fathers, are infamous, as are those who trample upon the Churches and their priests; those who flee from public battles, despise God’s commands, or are stained by any mark of infamy. In accordance with the institutions of the Fathers, we also remove their permission to attack bishops, because God hates those who persecute the Fathers—invaders of the Fathers, who are branded with infamy throughout the whole world—and therefore they are rightly and regularly rejected.

Now a lengthy admonition is unnecessary. We ought to cover over our hatred toward those who are already ruined, concerning whom nothing remains by which their authors may be condemned. Concerning them the Lord speaks through the prophet, saying:

“Rejecting the word, you hoped in oppression and tumult and relied upon them. Therefore this iniquity shall be for you like a breach” (Isaiah XXX, 12–13).

Again the prophet cries out concerning such persons:

“Draw near here, you children of adultery and fornication. Over whom did you mock? Against whom did you open your mouth wide and put out your tongue? Are you not children of wickedness, a deceitful offspring?” (Isaiah LVII, 3–4).

Let the impious cease to lie through fabricated schemes against the simple, already by fraud.

“Guard your tongue from evil,” says the prophet, “and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their cry. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Psalm XXXIII, 14 and following).

And shortly afterward:

“Wickedness will kill the impious, and those who hate the righteous will be condemned” (ibid., 22).

Although we suffer many things from such people, “let us love one another, dearest ones, because charity is from God.” Everyone who loves is born from God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is charity.

In this the charity of God appeared among us: God sent his only-begotten Son into the world so that we might live through him. In this is charity—not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.

Dearest ones, if God loved us, we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his charity is perfected in us.

By this we know that we remain in him and he in us: because he has given us of his Spirit. We have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world.

Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God. We have recognized and believed the truth that God has in us. God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him.

In this charity is perfected with us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world. There is no fear in charity, but perfect charity casts out fear, because fear has punishment. Whoever fears is not perfected in charity.

Therefore, let us love God, because God first loved us. If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must also love his brother.

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God, and everyone who loves the one who gave birth loves also the one who has been born from him. By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and do his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome, because everything born from God conquers the world.

And this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith. Who is the one who conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

This is the one who came through water and blood: Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is truth. For there are three who give testimony: the Spirit, the blood, and the water; and these three are one.

If we receive human testimony, God’s testimony is greater, because he has testified concerning his Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has God’s testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe the Son makes him a liar, because he does not believe the testimony that God has given concerning his Son.

And this is the testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.

I write these things to you so that you may know that you have eternal life, you who believe in the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence that we have toward him: that whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us. And we know that he hears whatever we ask; we know that we have the requests that we ask of him.

If anyone knows that his brother is committing a sin not leading to death, let him ask, and life will be given to the one whose sin does not lead to death. There is a sin leading to death; I do not say that anyone should pray concerning it. Every iniquity is sin, and there is a sin leading to death.

We know that everyone born from God does not sin, but the generation born of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him. We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.

And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and be in his true Son. This is the true God and eternal life (I John IV, 7–21; V, 1 and following).

Many powerful people have been greatly oppressed because of their evils, and the glorious have been handed over into the hands of others. But God’s blessing hastens as the reward of the righteous and bears fruit in the honor of the good person’s conduct.

Blessed is the person who has not fallen through a word from his mouth and has not been stung by the sorrow of wrongdoing.

Dearest ones, because of that devotion which ought to be shown to you, God’s servants, know that I have graciously received all your proposals as useful to the Catholic faith, so that through their actions both Christian peace may be restored and the error itself may be abolished.

And if anything further concerning such matters or similar ones must be decided, let a report be sent to us quickly, so that, after examining the nature of these matters, our diligence may determine what must be observed.

[Col. 0228D] Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Constans.

# LETTER OF POPE EUSEBIUS TO THE EGYPTIANS

[Col. 0227]

[Col. 0227D] Eusebius, bishop of the Roman and apostolic Church, sends greetings in the Lord to his dearest brothers throughout Alexandria and Egypt, united in the love of Christ, joined by the bond of charity, serving the Lord, and holding the true faith.

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation [Col. 0228D], so that we ourselves may be able to console those who are in every kind of distress, through the encouragement with which we ourselves are encouraged by God. For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through Christ our consolation abounds. Whether we are afflicted for your encouragement and salvation, or whether we exhort you for your encouragement and salvation—which produces endurance of the same sufferings that we also suffer—and our hope for you is firm, knowing that just as you are sharers in the sufferings, so you will also be sharers in the consolation (II Cor. I, 3, [Col. 0229A] and following).”

“‘The old things have passed away, and behold, new things have come to be.’ But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses 53 against them; and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you, on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

“Working together with him, we also exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: ‘At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.’ Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Giving no one any occasion for offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed, but in everything let us present ourselves as God’s ministers: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in imprisonments, in disturbances, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering and gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through favor and low estate, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful, as unknown and yet known, as dying—and behold, we live; as chastened and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.

“Our mouth is open to you, dearest ones; our heart is enlarged. You are not constrained in carnal things, but you are constrained in spiritual things. In return for the same reward—I speak as to children—be enlarged yourselves also. Do not be yoked together with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as the Lord says: ‘I will dwell among them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they will be my people. Therefore come out from their midst and be separated from them, says the Lord, and do not touch what is unclean; and I will receive you. I will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me, says the most good Lord.’

“Since we have these promises, dearest ones, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God (II Cor. V, 17–21; VI, 1–18; VII, 1).”

Correct your error, brothers, and guard yourselves from every stain of error, so that you may be able to offer God a pure gift. Do not persecute the servants of God. Do not defame or accuse bishops, because God has wished to reserve them for his own judgment. For he himself gave an example that he did not wish them to be corrupted or accused by human beings or by men of depraved life, when he himself, and not another, drove the merchants from the temple, overturned the tables of the money-changers with his own whip, and expelled them from the temple. As he says elsewhere: “God stood in the assembly of the gods, but in their midst he judges the gods” (Psalm LXXXI, 1).

Therefore whoever accuses or condemns bishops accuses God’s ordinance, while pursuing spiritual matters less than earthly ones. For the cause of the faith and love on which Christian salvation rests compels me to labor with great anxiety, fearing that the depravity which ought to have been cut off at its beginnings may, with the passage of time, become both more obstinate and more deeply rooted. For it is utterly hostile and unfitting that those who harass bishops or the other true priests by their persecution should be indiscriminately mingled with the name of Catholics, since, by not abandoning the impiety that has already arisen, they condemn themselves through their own depravity. They ought either to be struck down for their faithlessness or released through pardon; for just as it is wholly merciful that the Lord’s charity be restored to the oppressed, so it is just that the authority of one who disturbs everything be cut off.

I am astonished, dearest ones, that you are so quickly moved and transferred from your own judgment, when it is written:

“‘Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your will. If you grant your soul its desires, it will make you a joy to your enemies. Do not take pleasure in crowds, nor in small matters. Their punishment is at hand. Do not be mediocre in contention arising from usury, and you will have nothing in the world. For you will be envious of your own life. A drunken laborer will not become rich, and whoever despises small things will gradually fall. Women cause the wise to apostatize and rebuke the sensible; whoever joins himself to prostitutes will be worthless. Rot and worms will inherit him; he will be raised up as a greater example and his soul will be removed from the number of the living.

“‘Whoever believes quickly is light-hearted and will be diminished, and whoever sins against his own soul will be held accountable. Whoever rejoices in iniquity will be marked out, and whoever hates correction will have his life shortened. Whoever hates loquacity extinguishes wickedness. Whoever sins against his own soul will repent, and whoever delights in wickedness will be marked out.

“‘Do not repeat a wicked and harsh word, and you will not be diminished. Do not disclose your thoughts to friend or enemy; and if you have committed a fault, do not expose it. For he will hear you and watch you, and, as though defending the sin, will hate you; and thus it will always cling to you. Have you heard a word against your neighbor? Let it die within you, trusting that it will not burst you apart—for a fool labors like the groaning of a woman giving birth. An arrow fixed in the thigh of flesh is a word in the heart of a fool.

“‘Reprove a friend, lest perhaps, when he has committed an injustice and does not understand it, he say, “I did not do it”; or, if he did do it, lest he do it again. Reprove your neighbor, lest perhaps he has not spoken; and if he has spoken, lest he repeat it. Reprove a friend, for a fault often occurs, and do not believe every word. There is one who slips with his tongue, but not from his heart. For who is there who has not sinned with his tongue?

“‘Reprove your neighbor before you threaten him, and give place to the fear of the Most High, because all wisdom and knowledge are the fear of God; and in it lies the fear of God, and in all wisdom there is the ordering of the law. There is neither wisdom nor knowledge, nor a good thought, except in it. The prudence of sinners is wickedness, and in it is execration; and he is foolish who is diminished in wisdom.

“‘Better is a person who lacks wisdom and is deficient in understanding yet fears God, than one who abounds in understanding and transgresses the law of the Most High. There is a certain skill, and it is itself wicked; and there is one who utters a reliable word, declaring the truth. There is one who humbles himself wickedly, while his inward parts are full of deceit. And there is a righteous person who submits himself excessively through great humility; and there is a righteous person who inclines his face and pretends not to see what has gone unnoticed. Even if he is prevented from sinning by weakness of strength, if he finds an opportunity to do evil, he will do evil.

“‘A man is known by his appearance, and the sensible person is known by the meeting of his face; the clothing of his body, the smile of his teeth, and a man’s walk disclose what he is. There is a false reproof in the mouth of the insolent, and there is a judgment that is not proved to be good; and there is one who keeps silent, and he is prudent. How much better it is to reprove than to become angry, and not to hinder one who confesses in prayer!

“‘The desire of a eunuch has deprived a young girl of her virginity; so is one who carries out an unjust judgment by force. How good it is, when reproved, to show repentance; for thus you will escape deliberate sin. There is one who keeps silent and is found wise, and there is one who is hateful because he is forward in speaking. There is one who is silent because he lacks the sense to speak, and there is one who keeps silent at the proper time, knowing the suitable moment. A wise person will keep silent until the proper time, but the wanton and imprudent will not observe the time.

“‘Whoever uses many words harms his own soul, and whoever unjustly assumes authority will be hated. There is advancement in evil for an undisciplined man, and there is an invention leading to ruin. There is a gift that is not useful, and there is a gift whose repayment is double; yet because of glory there is diminution, and there is one who will lift his head from humiliation. There is one who buys back much for a small price, and there is one who restores it sevenfold.

“‘The wise person makes himself lovable by his words, but the favors of fools will be poured out; the gift of a fool will not benefit you. For his eyes are sevenfold. He will give little and reproach much, and the opening of his mouth is a fire. Today someone lends at interest, and tomorrow he demands it back; such a person is hateful.

“‘A fool will have no friend, and there will be no glory in his goods. For those who eat his bread are false-tongued; how often and how greatly will they mock him! For he did not distribute what ought to be possessed with sound judgment, nor likewise what ought not to be possessed. A slip of the false tongue is like one falling from a pavement; so the downfall of the wicked will come quickly. An ungrateful person, like a pointless tale in the mouth of the undisciplined, will be continually repeated. From the mouth of a fool the proverb will be rejected, for he does not utter it at the proper time.

“‘There is one who is prevented from sinning by poverty and will be goaded in his leisure. There is one who will lose his soul through shame, and will lose it through an imprudent person; through respect of persons he will lose himself. There is one who, out of shame, makes a promise for a friend, and has gained him as an enemy for nothing.

“‘For a wicked reproach is falsehood in a person, and it will continually be in the mouth of the undisciplined. The persistent praise of a lying man praises the thief; both will inherit destruction. The conduct of men is falsehood without honor, and their shame is with them without interruption’ (Eccli. XVIII, 30–33; XIX, 1–28; XX, 1–28).”

We admonish you, brothers, continually to pursue in the love of Christ what will benefit people toward one another. Likewise, we beseech you in the Lord:

“‘Walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, through all, and in us all.

“‘But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore it says: “When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.” Now, what does “he ascended” mean except that he had first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things.

“‘And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain unity of faith and knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried here and there by every wind of doctrine, through the wickedness of men and through craftiness directed toward the deception of error’ (Eph. IV, 1 and following).”

For it is unjust rashly to judge the hidden things of another’s heart, and it is sinful to condemn on suspicion one whose works alone are seen to be good. Therefore the sheep entrusted to their shepherd ought neither to rebuke him—unless he has departed from the right faith—nor accuse him in any way, because the deeds of shepherds are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, although they may appear rightly subject to correction.

We say these things because in your writings we have found that certain bishops in our regions were accused by their own sheep, some evidently on suspicion and others on definite grounds. For this reason, some were stripped of their possessions and others driven from their own sees. You should know that they can be summoned neither to a provincial synod nor to a general synod, nor judged in any matter, before everything that was taken from them has been legally restored to their authority.

Everything, therefore, must first be legally restored to them, and the churches taken from them must be returned with all their privileges. Afterward, not merely a short period of time but as much time must be granted to them as they appear to have spent dispossessed [Col. 0232D] or expelled, before they are summoned to a synod and heard by all the bishops of their province. For one who has been dispossessed or expelled can neither be summoned to a hearing nor judged, because there is no privilege by which one already stripped bare can be dispossessed.

Hence it was also decreed in ancient times that all possessions, everything taken from a person, and all revenues be restored by the preceptor or primate to the possessor before the case is formally joined. Elsewhere it is written: “The one who suffered violence shall receive everything in the condition in which it had been, and shall securely retain what he possesses.” And elsewhere: “In the synodal decrees of the Fathers and in the edicts of kings it is read that everything is to be restored to bishops who have been dispossessed or expelled, through the penitential ordinance of the bishops, and that they are to be entirely recalled to the places from which they departed, whatever the circumstances of time—whether by deceit, captivity, the power of the great, or by whatever unjust causes they are known to have lost the property of the Church, or their own property or possessions—before their accusation or regular summons to a synod,” and so forth.

It is also decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that whoever invades another’s property shall not escape unpunished, but shall restore everything with increase. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke XIX, 8). And secular law provides: “Whoever steals another’s property shall restore tenfold to the person whose property was taken what has been removed.” And in the divine law it is read: 54 “Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbor’s boundary markers. And all the people shall say, Amen” (Deut. XXVII, 17).

Such acts, therefore, must not be presumed upon without punishment, nor carried out without their own condemnation. Pursue peace, and not another’s loss or injustice, with one another and toward all. But, practicing truth in love, let us grow in every way into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint according to the working proportionate to each member, produces the body’s growth for its building up in love.

Finally, dearest ones, rejoice and be perfected; exhort one another. Be of the same mind; keep peace, and the God of peace and love will be with you. May the Lord guard you now and on the day of eternity. Amen.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, with Constans as consul.

ITEM: LETTER OF POPE EUSEBIUS TO THE BISHOPS OF TUSCIA AND CAMPANIA.

[Col. 0233]

[Col. 0233B] To the dearest brothers, all the bishops established throughout Campania and Tuscia, EUSEBIUS.
