Blessed be the Lord our God, who through his mercy endowed the Roman Church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with the priesthood, and, by the privilege of that same Church, granted us, because of the universal care entrusted to us, the charitable duty of showing a way to those around us, so that we who cling together in the firmness of faith may also be joined in the desired joy of conversation. Thus, while through the ministry of letters we extend ourselves even as far as you, we may stir your hearts toward religious worship through apostolic admonitions, and while we repay the hope of our love as though it were a certain debt, we may show our complete devotion toward God.

Let us therefore join together, dearest brothers, in continual and humble prayers, and, beseeching our God with tears of mouth and heart, let us ask him in unceasing supplication that by institution and deed we may cling to him whose members we desire to be, and never turn aside by a wandering path from that way which is Christ, lest we be justly abandoned by the one whom we impiously leave.

This can come to pass for us through the help of heavenly favor if we observe the apostolic teachings and the commands of the Fathers. For our Lord says: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

And although these words, spoken generally, may suffice either to make us avoid errors or preserve what is Catholic, nevertheless we know that the apostles and their successors established that accusations against teachers are not to be accepted, that foreign judgments are not to be rendered, and that no one is to be bound by the sentence of any judge other than his own.

For Christ is the head of the Church, while the priests are Christ’s vicars, acting as Christ’s ambassadors in the Church. Therefore whatever is done to their injury pertains to Christ, who said: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me. And whoever despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke X, 16).

These things, brothers, are terrifying and must be considered and avoided with the greatest care, both for those who seek to destroy themselves through desire, avarice, or envy—lest they fall into the depths or encounter such evils—and for the persecutors of the Church and its servants, who, though they have eyes, do not see, and though they have ears, do not hear, nor understand what pleases God.

Following the apostolic rule in all things, and proclaiming all its ordinances for the protection of bishops, who are called by God the pillars of the Church, and strengthening the venerable statutes of the Fathers concerning the other true priests, we again establish, together with all the bishops who are with us, as we find was decreed long ago, that murderers, evildoers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, adulterers, incestuous persons, poisoners, suspected persons, criminals, domestics, perjurers, those who have committed abduction, those who have given false testimony, or those who have resorted to sacrilegious persons and diviners, and their like, are in no way to be admitted either as accusers or as witnesses, because they are infamous and rightly to be rejected, since their voice is deadly.

A deadly voice must be forbidden in every matter rather than heard. The danger, therefore, which threatens teachers must always be avoided and shunned with the utmost care, and they must be supported and protected by all, since the Lord says: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 40).

For the first salvation is to preserve the rules of right faith and in no way to deviate from the ordinances of the Fathers. Nor can the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ be disregarded when he says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18). These words are also proved by the results of events, because in the apostolic see the Catholic religion has always been preserved without stain.

Therefore, dearest ones, learn from Holy Scripture to do good and avoid evil, and be instructed in the rules of the Fathers, as it is written:

“‘My son, if you have means, do good to yourself, and offer God worthy offerings. Remember that death does not delay, and the covenant of the underworld, for it has been shown to you. The covenant of this world will die by death. Before your death, do good to your friend, and, stretching out your hand according to your strength, give to the poor. Do not be defrauded of a good day, and let no portion of a good gift pass you by. Do not leave your pains and labors to others. In the distribution of your lot, give and receive; justify your soul. Before your death, practice righteousness, for food cannot be found in the underworld.

“‘All flesh grows old like grass, and like a leaf bearing fruit on a green tree. Some are generated and others are cast down. So it is with the generation of flesh and blood: one ends and another is born. Every corruptible work fails at the end, and the one who performs it will go with it. But every excellent work will be justified, and the one who performs it will be honored in it.

“‘Blessed is the person who remains in wisdom, who meditates in righteousness, and who considers the fear of God with understanding; who contemplates his ways in his heart and is discerning in his hidden matters; who follows after her like an investigator and stands in her ways; who looks through her window and listens at her door; who rests beside her house and fixes a tent peg in her walls. He will establish his shelter by her hands, and gifts will rest in her shelter forever. He will place his children beneath her covering and dwell beneath her branches; he will be protected beneath her branches from the heat and rest in her glory.

“‘Whoever fears the Lord will do this, and whoever is steadfast in righteousness will grasp her. She will meet him like an honored mother and receive him like a woman from virginity. She will feed him with the bread of life and understanding, and give him the water of saving wisdom to drink. She will establish him in her and he will not be shaken; she will hold him fast and he will not be put to shame. She will exalt him among his neighbors, open his mouth in the midst of the assembly, fill him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, and clothe him with a robe of glory. She will store up gladness and exultation for him, and he will inherit an eternal name.

“‘Foolish men will not grasp her, but sensible men will meet her; foolish men will not see her. For she is far from pride and deceit. Lying men will not belong to her, but truthful men will be found in her, and they will have access even to the contemplation of God.

“‘Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, because wisdom is perfected by God. The wisdom of God will stand as praise, and it will abound in the faithful mouth, and the ruler will give it to him.

“‘Do not say, “Through the Lord I have gone astray” [reading uncertain]; do not do what he hates. Do not say, “He has led me astray.” For impious men are not necessary to him. God hates every abomination of error, and it will not be lovable to those who fear him.

“‘God established man from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel. He added his commandments and precepts. If you desire the commandments, they will preserve you, and you will always perform faithful service. He has set before you water and fire; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish. Before man are life and death, good and evil; whatever pleases him will be given to him, for great is the patience of God, and he is mighty in patience, seeing all things without interruption.

“‘The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, and he himself knows every work of man. He commanded no one to act impiously and gave no one room to sin. For he does not desire a multitude of faithless and useless children.

“‘Do not rejoice in impious children if they multiply, nor delight in them if the fear of God is not with them. Do not trust their life and do not look upon their labors. For better is one who fears God than a thousand impious children. It is better to die without children than to leave behind impious children. One sensible person will inhabit a homeland, but three impious persons will abandon it.

“‘My eye has seen many other things, and my ear has heard things stronger than these. In the assembly of sinners fire will blaze; in an unbelieving nation wrath will flare up. The ancient giants, who trusted in their strength and destroyed others, did not pray for their sins. He did not spare their sojourn, but struck them and cursed them because of the pride of their speech. He did not show them mercy, destroying the whole nation and those who exalted themselves in their sins, like the six hundred thousand foot soldiers who gathered in the hardness of their hearts. And if even one had been stiff-necked, it would have been a wonder if he had escaped punishment.

“‘For with him are mercy and wrath; he is mighty to hear prayer and pours out wrath according to his mercy. Thus his correction will judge people according to their works. The sinner will not escape through his robbery, and he will not delay the patience of the one who practices mercy. Every act of mercy will make room for each person according to the merit of his works and according to the understanding of his sojourn.

“‘Do not say, “I shall be hidden from God, and who from the heights will remember me? I shall not be recognized among a great people. For what is my soul in so immense a creation?” Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens, the abyss, the whole earth and all that is in them, will be shaken in his sight; likewise the mountains and hills and the foundations of the earth. When God looks upon these things, they will be shaken with trembling, and in all these things the heart is senseless. Every heart is understood by him, and who understands his ways? And who understands the storm which the eye of man has never seen?

“‘For his works are very many and hidden, but who can recount his works of righteousness, or who can endure them? For the covenant is extensive for some, and the questioning of human beings is at the consummation. Whoever is fainthearted devises evil, and the imprudent and erring person devises foolish things’ (Eccli. XIV, 11–27; XV, 1–22; XVI, 1–23).”

“Therefore, brothers, let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but only such a good word as is suitable for edification and gives grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice. Be kind and merciful to one another, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you.

“Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma. But let fornication and every impurity or greed not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or coarse joking, which is improper, but rather thanksgiving.

“For know this with understanding: every fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—for such a person is a servant of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words. For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of unbelief. Therefore do not become their partners.

“For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light. For the fruit of light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth. Test what is pleasing to God, and do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things they do in secret. But everything that is exposed by the light is made manifest; for everything that is made manifest is light.

“Therefore it says: ‘Rise, sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.’ See carefully, then, brothers, how you walk—not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Therefore do not become imprudent, but understand what the will of the Lord is.

“And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns in your hearts to the Lord, giving thanks always for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ (Eph. IV, 29–32; V, 1–21).”

[Col. 0238A] We command you solemnly to celebrate on the aforesaid calendrical day the feast of the finding of the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was found on the fifth day before the Nones of May while we were recently holding the governance of the holy Roman Church.

Likewise, we command that all heretics who are converted by the grace of God, baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, and holding the rule of the Roman Church, be reconciled through the laying on of hands. The sacrament of the laying on of hands must be held in great veneration; it cannot be performed by others except by the highest priests. Nor is it read or known to have been performed in the time of the apostles by anyone other than the apostles themselves; nor can it ever be performed or ought to be performed by anyone other than those who hold their place, as has already been said. For if it is presumed upon otherwise, it is to be considered invalid and void, and it will never be counted among the ecclesiastical sacraments.

Finally, brothers, rejoice and exult in the Lord, so that, enlightened and strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, with the Lord’s help you may be able to reach and lead your own people to the pastures of eternal life. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit always be with us all. Amen.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, with Constans as consul.

HERE BEGIN THE DECREES OF POPE MELCHIADES. (In the year of the Lord 311, during the reign of Maximinus.)

[Col. 0237]

[Col. 0237C] To the dearest brothers, MARINUS, BENEDICTUS, LEONTIUS, and the other bishops established throughout Spain and in those regions, MELCHIADES.

The words of the apostolic command are that we ought to be without offense among Jews and Gentiles; every Christian guards this with the full strength of his soul. Since this is so, no small danger may remain before God for the one who refuses to extend this even to the faithful. For the Lord’s saying in the Gospel bears witness how those things which, through Christian authors, strike other Christians ought to grieve us who wish no one to perish. For the Savior himself says that “it is better for the one who causes scandal to have one of the little ones plunged into the depths of the sea (Matt. XVIII, 6).” Therefore, let us ask what punishment awaits the one for whom we read that such a penalty is better.

[Col. 0237D] Therefore, dearest brothers, these words must be weighed and guarded with the greatest care, lest eternal things be lost (God forbid) for temporal things, lasting things for things that pass away, and perpetual joys for the most depraved temporal concerns. Hence we beg and implore you: let no one harm another, and let no one be hostile or injurious; rather, according to the Apostle, “Let each bear the burdens of the other, so that he may fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. VI, 2),” and do not judge one another, but, according to the same Apostle, “judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling block or scandal before your brother (Rom. XIV, [Col. 0238C] 13).”

First, always investigate everything diligently, so that you may decide with justice and truth. Condemn no one before a true and just judgment. Judge no one by the arbitrariness of suspicion; first test the matter, and afterward pronounce a charitable sentence. “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another (Luke VI, 31).” Always remember the Lord’s saying, who declares: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned; for with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged (Matt. VII, 1–2).”

Do not judge or condemn bishops without the authority of this see. If you do so, your judgments will be void, and you will be condemned. For this privilege was established for this holy see from the times of the apostles, and it remains unharmed to this [Col. 0238D] day. Therefore, the bishops whom the Lord chose for himself as eyes and wished to be pillars of the Church, to whom he also gave the power of binding and loosing, he reserved for his own judgment; and this privilege he entrusted solely to blessed Peter the key-bearer, as his representative.

Its rightful prerogative therefore grows upon this see, to be inherited and maintained in future times, since there was also a distinction of authority among the blessed apostles. Although the election of all was equal, it was nevertheless granted to blessed Peter that he should preside over the others [Col. 0239A] and prudently arrange the causes and inquiries that came forward as complaints.

We believe that this was ordered in this way by God’s arrangement, so that all those who came afterward would not claim everything for themselves, but that the greater cases—as are those of bishops and of the more important affairs—would always converge upon the one see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that they might receive the conclusion of their judgments from the place where they received the beginning of their establishment, lest they should ever differ from their own head.

But if any one of you should see himself burdened, let him appeal to this see and return here, as has always been the established custom; for we shall willingly sympathize with him and gladly offer whatever assistance the Lord grants. Nor, brothers, should anyone who wishes to share in our communion be hindered or rebuked by anyone, [Col. 0239B] but rather assistance should be given him in coming, since the rebuke administered by many is sufficient for each person, so that, according to the Apostle, “you should rather forgive and comfort him, lest perhaps the one who is in distress be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you,” as he says, “to confirm your love toward him” (II Cor. II, 7).

For we close the mouths of those who accuse priests or testify against them—men whom we know to be dead not by human but by divine words—for the unbelieving man is dead in a living body. Let no faithful person come under suspicion by saying or doing what he does not wish to suffer. If anyone is faithful, let him beware lest he speak falsely or lay traps for anyone. It is easy, therefore, to deceive a human being, but not God. The one who harms is not wise.

The faithful person wishes no evil; in these things we can recognize the faithful and the unfaithful person, in harming and in helping, as Truth itself says: “The good man brings good things forth from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings evil things forth from the evil treasure; for from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matt. XII, 34–35).”

For the Lord speaks on our behalf through the prophet: “Those who judge you, I myself will judge.” And again he said to his servants: “Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies.”

Of such people the prophet also sings, saying: “Not so are the wicked, but like dust which the wind drives away; therefore the wicked will not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous. For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the wicked will perish (Ps. I, 4 and following).”

“Why were the nations disturbed, and why did the peoples meditate on empty things? The kings of the earth rose up, and the rulers joined together against the Lord and against his Christ. Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke away from us. The inhabitant of heaven will laugh, and the Lord will mock them. Then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his fury he will trouble them (Ps. II, 1 and following).”

And elsewhere he said: “The wicked man’s crime is in the midst of his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes (Ps. XIII, 3).”

“For he acted deceitfully against him in his sight, so that he might find iniquity to hate. The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he ceased thinking about doing good. He devises iniquity on his bed; he stands in a way that is not good; he does not reject evil.

“Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your faithfulness reaches to the clouds; your righteousness is like the mountains of God, your judgments are a great abyss. You will save human beings and beasts, Lord. How precious is your mercy, O God! The children of Adam will hope in the shadow of your wings. They will be intoxicated by the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delights. For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light. Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to the upright in heart. Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the wicked move me. There the workers of iniquity have fallen; they have been driven out and could not rise (Ps. XXXV, 2 and following).”

We have heard from certain brothers, against whom you were exceedingly hostile, that quarrels and dissensions exist among you. Therefore we have written these things to you, commanding you [Col. 0240B] to observe them just as the apostolic see commands you to observe them. Hence, when soldiers questioned him, the Lord replied in the Gospel: “Shake no one and accuse no one falsely, but be content with your wages (Luke III, 14).” For the one who unjustly disturbs a person shakes him. Let these words suffice you for the present concerning these matters. But if you require greater things, send with the bearer of this letter, and they will be sent to you.

Regarding the matters about which you asked to be instructed—namely, whether the laying on of bishops’ hands or baptism is the greater sacrament—know that both are great sacraments. And just as one is performed by those of higher rank, that is, by the supreme pontiffs, and cannot be completed by those of lower rank, so it must be venerated and observed with the greater reverence. Yet these two sacraments are so closely joined that they cannot in any way be separated from one another unless death intervenes, and one cannot rightly be completed without the other.

For one, when death intervenes first, can save without the other; the other, however, cannot. Hence it is written: “In those days, says the Lord, I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh (Joel II, 28).” Let us contemplate the supreme riches of God’s goodness. What the laying on of hands grants individually to those being confirmed as newly baptized, the descent of the Holy Spirit then gave universally to the peoples of believers.

But because we say that the laying on of hands and confirmation can confirm one who has already been regenerated in Christ, someone may perhaps ask himself: “What benefit does the mystery of confirmation provide me after the mystery of baptism? Or, as far as I understand, did we not receive the whole gift from the font, if after the font we need the addition of a new kind?”

Do not understand it so, dearest ones. Just as military discipline requires that when the emperor has enrolled someone among the soldiers, he not only mark him as accepted but also equip him with suitable weapons for battle, so in the baptized person that blessing is a fortification. You have given him as a soldier; give him the aid of military service as well.

Does it benefit a parent to grant a great estate to an orphan if he does not also take care to provide a guardian? Thus the Paraclete is guardian, comforter, and protector for those regenerated in Christ. Therefore the divine word says: “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain (Ps. CXXVI, 1).”

Thus the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0241A] who descended upon the waters of baptism in a saving visitation, grants beauty at the font for innocence and, in confirmation, provides increase toward grace, because those who are to live their whole lives in this world must walk amid invisible enemies and dangers. In baptism we are regenerated for life; after baptism we are confirmed for battle. In baptism we are washed; after baptism we are strengthened.

If the benefits of regeneration are sufficient for those who are about to pass immediately onward, the assistance of confirmation is nevertheless necessary for those who are to live. Regeneration by itself saves those who are soon to be received into the blessed peace of the age; confirmation, however, arms and equips those who are reserved for the struggles and battles of this world.

But the person who, after baptism, reaches death undefiled with the innocence he has acquired is confirmed by death, because he cannot sin after death.

If we should also wish to ask what the coming of the Holy Spirit benefited the apostles after Christ’s passion and resurrection, the Lord himself explains it clearly to them: “The things I say to you,” he says, “you cannot bear now; but when that Spirit of truth comes, he himself will teach you all truth (John XVI, 12–13).”

You see that when the Holy Spirit is poured in, the faithful heart is enlarged toward prudence and steadfastness. Thus, before the descent of the Holy Spirit, the apostles are terrified even to the point of denial; after his visitation, they are armed even to martyrdom, scorning their lives. Accordingly, through Christ we are redeemed, but through the Holy Spirit we are enlightened, built up, instructed, equipped, and perfected by the gift of spiritual wisdom, so that we may hear that voice of the Holy Spirit:

“I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you will walk (Ps. XXXI, 8).”

From the Holy Spirit we receive the power to become spiritual, because “the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (I Cor. II, 14).” From the Holy Spirit we receive the ability to discern good from evil, to love what is just, and to reject what is unjust; to resist malice and pride; and to withstand luxury, various enticements, and shameful and unworthy desires.

From the Holy Spirit we receive love of life and ardor for glory, so that, kindled by God, we may raise our minds from earthly things to those above and to divine things.

Therefore no one ought to observe a fast on the Lord’s day or on the fifth day of the week, so that a true and not a false distinction may be maintained between the fast of Christians and that of Gentiles, between true believers and unbelievers and heretics. Hence it is written: “What partnership has Christ with Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? What participation does righteousness have with iniquity?” (II Cor. VI, 15.) And again: “Do not enter into a yoke with unbelievers (ibid. 14).”

“Finally, brothers, see that no one deceives you with empty words, nor through philosophy and empty deceit according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; because in Christ dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power. In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away of the body of flesh, in the circumcision of Christ; for you were buried with him in baptism, in which you also rose through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.

“And you, when you were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made alive together with him, forgiving you all trespasses, wiping out the record of debt that stood against you, which was contrary to us; he removed it from our midst, fastening it to the cross. He stripped principalities and powers and led them forth openly, triumphing over them in himself.

“Therefore let no one judge you concerning food or drink, or concerning a festival, a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of future things, but the body is Christ’s. Let no one deceive you, wishing to do so through humility and the worship of angels, entering into things he has not seen, walking vainly, puffed up by the sense of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its bonds and connections, grows toward an increase of faith.

“If you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though you were living in the world, do you make decrees: ‘Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle’? These things all perish through use, according to the commands and teachings of human beings. Such practices have indeed an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, but they do not spare the body, nor do they possess any honor for the satisfaction of the flesh.

“Therefore, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with [Col. 0242C] him in glory.

“Therefore put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols. Because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. You too once walked in these things when you lived among them.

“But now lay aside all anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and shameful speech from your mouth. Do not lie to one another; strip off the old person with his deeds, and put on the new person, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him. There is neither Jew nor Gentile, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all.

“Therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, put on a heart of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another if anyone has a complaint against another. Just as Christ forgave you, so also do you. Above all these things, have love, which is the bond of perfection.

“And let the peace of Christ prevail in your hearts; in it you were also called in one body. And be grateful. Let the word of God dwell abundantly in you, in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing yourselves with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God.

“Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father through him [Col. 0243A] (Col. II, 8–23; III, 1–17).”

Dearest ones, do not grow weary of doing good. But if there should be anyone who does not obey the apostolic words, take note of him and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother. [Col. 0244A] May the God of peace grant you to think the same thing toward one another and toward all, and may he himself always be with you in every place. Amen.

Given on the Kalends of March, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Volusianus and Rufinus.

## CONCERNING THE PRIMITIVE CHURCH AND THE COUNCIL OF NICAEA

[Col. 0243]

[Col. 0243A] No one who reads the divine Scriptures is unaware that, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, when the disciples were gathered together with the multitude of believers, among whom there was one heart and one soul, those who sold their estates and possessions brought the proceeds, and distribution was made to each according to what each one needed (Acts IV, 32 and following).

For the apostles foresaw the future Church among the Gentiles, especially because the Lord had foretold to them: “Go into the whole world, preaching the gospel (Mark XVI, 15).” Since they were to be expelled from Judaea, they knew that they would be scattered among the Gentiles and that the Church would be gathered from an unformed people.

For this reason they did not acquire estates in Judaea, but only the proceeds, in order to support the needy. But when the Church grew amid the storms and adversities of the world, it reached such a point that not only the Gentiles but also the Roman princes, who held the monarchy of almost the whole world, hastened to the faith of Christ and to the sacraments of baptism.

The most religious man, Constantine, [Col. 0243C] the first, openly received the faith of truth and granted permission throughout the whole world, to those living under his rule, not only to become Christians but also to build churches; he likewise decreed that estates should be granted.

Finally, the same prince established immense gifts and the construction of the temple of the first see, that of the blessed prince of the apostles, to such an extent that he abandoned the imperial seat which the Roman princes had possessed and granted it for the benefit of blessed Peter and his bishops.

When the same man was presiding at the holy synod gathered at Nicaea and saw that a complaint brought by certain people was being presented before him, he said: “You can be judged by no one, because you are reserved for the judgment of God alone; for you are called gods. Therefore you cannot be judged by human beings.”

From that time onward, [Col. 0233D] the most religious men consecrated to the Lord not only the possessions and estates they had owned, but also themselves, building basilicas on their own lands in honor of the saints and martyrs, throughout cities and in countless monasteries where assemblies of those serving the Lord might gather.

Finally, kings, governors, and magistrates not only granted this permission but also gave from their own resources throughout all the kingdoms of the earth, so that the needy, who possessed nothing in the world, might be fed; so that the churches of God might be built and restored; and so that supplies might be provided to those who rightly served God and his Church and to his servants, so that they might be free from want. By receiving these things, they could, according to the Apostle’s exhortations, “make prayers, petitions, supplications, and thanksgivings for all people, for kings and for all who are in high positions, so that they may lead a quiet and peaceful life. And this is good and acceptable before God (I Tim. II, 1 and following).”

Therefore the teacher of the Gentiles, upon whom “the care of all the churches rests (II Cor. II, 28),” and who “appointed bishops to govern the Church of God through the Holy Spirit (Acts XX, 26),” protests. To them he says: “Feed the flock of God that is among you, watching over it not under compulsion but willingly according to God, not for the sake of shameful gain but voluntarily (I Pet. V, 2).”

For when he says, “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs (II Tim. II, 4),” the holy canons clearly show and expressly prohibit what secular affairs are: namely, that certain people who appear to have been chosen for the clergy should, for the sake of shameful profits, become administrators of other people’s possessions and take secular business under their care, making light of the Lord’s ministry while going about the houses of secular people and, out of greed for estates, [Col. 0244C] assuming responsibility for them.

The holy synod decreed that henceforth no cleric should lease estates or involve himself in secular business, except on behalf of wards and orphans, or if perhaps the bishop of the city should order him to have responsibility for ecclesiastical affairs. For it is plainly evident that some affairs are secular and others ecclesiastical.

Was not Moses living in the world when he frequently “entered and left the tabernacle, being rapt within in contemplation (Exod. XXXIII, 8),” while outside he was pressed by the affairs of the infirm, considering God’s mysteries within and bearing the burdens of those in the flesh outside?

The priests in the Church ought to enact his type: when they go outside to attend to detestable affairs for the needs of their subjects, they should return inwardly to themselves through contemplation of the commandments, like Paul, “who was admitted into heavenly secrets (II Cor. XII, 4),” yet through the depths of his condescension examined the dwelling-place of those in the flesh.

Thus Jacob also saw angels ascending and descending (Gen. XXVIII, 12), because the rulers of the Church not only seek what is above through contemplation of God, but also descend in compassion to its members below.

And when priests imitate the deeds of these men, guard themselves, bear the burdens of their subjects, and appear to be such as that distinguished preacher describes—“those who use this world as though they did not use it, those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, and those who buy as though they did not possess (I Cor. VII, 30)”—

## EDICT OF THE LORD EMPEROR CONSTANTINE

[Col. 0245]

[Col. 0245A] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the emperor Caesar Flavius Constantine, faithful in Christ Jesus, our Savior, Lord, and God, one of the same holy Trinity, gentle, beneficent, Alemannic, Gothic, Sarmatian, Germanic, Britannic, unique, pious, fortunate, victorious and triumphant, ever august, to the most holy and most blessed Father Silvester, bishop and pope of the city of Rome, and to all his successors, the pontiffs who will sit upon the see of blessed Peter until the end of the age, and also to all the most reverend and God-beloved Catholic bishops subject throughout the entire world to that same most holy Roman Church through this imperial constitution of ours, both those now established and all those established in future times:

Grace, peace, love, joy, long-suffering, and mercy from God the almighty Father, and from Jesus Christ his Son, and from the Holy Spirit, be with you all.

Those things which our Savior and Redeemer, our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the Most High Father, through his holy apostles Peter and Paul, with the intervention of our Father Silvester, supreme pontiff and universal pope, graciously deigned to accomplish, our most gentle serenity has undertaken to disseminate in a clear account, through the document of this imperial establishment of ours, for the knowledge of all peoples throughout the whole world.

First, we present with inward confession of heart, for the instruction of all your minds, the faith which we have been taught by the aforesaid most blessed Father and our advocate, Silvester, the universal pontiff, and then we proclaim the mercy of God poured out upon you.

We wish you to know that, as we indicated through our earlier sacred pragmatic ordinance, we have withdrawn from the worship of idols, from mute and deaf images made by hand, from diabolical compositions, and from all the pomps of Satan, and have attained the complete faith of Christians, which is true light and everlasting life. We believe, according to what that nurturing supreme Father and our teacher, Silvester the pontiff, instructed us, in God the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible.

And in Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, our Lord, through whom all things were created. And [Col. 0245D] in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life to every creature. We confess this Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that in the perfect Trinity there may be both the fullness of divinity and the unity of power: the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and the three are one in Jesus Christ. Thus there are three forms, but one power.

For God, wise from the beginning and forever, brought forth from himself the Word, through whom the ages were always to be generated. And when by that single Word of his wisdom he formed the whole creation from nothing, everything was with him, arranged by his mysterious design. Therefore, after perfecting the heavenly powers and all the materials of the earth, by the pious command of his wisdom he first fashioned humankind from the mud of the earth in his own image and likeness [Col. 0246A] and placed the human being in this paradise of delight.

The ancient serpent, the hostile and envious devil, through the most bitter taste of the forbidden tree, made him an exile from those same joys (Gen. I, II). After his expulsion, the devil did not cease to extend his poisonous darts in many ways, so that, by drawing the human race away from the way of truth, he might persuade it to serve the worship of idols—that is, the creature—and not the Creator, so that through those whom he wished to entangle in his snares he might make them burn with him in everlasting punishment.

But our God, taking pity on his creation, sent his holy prophets, through whom he announced the light of the life to come, namely, the coming of his Son, the Lord [Col. 0246B] God and our Savior Jesus Christ. He sent that same only-begotten Son, the Word of wisdom. Descending from heaven for our salvation, born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John I, 14).” He did not lose what he had been, but began to be what he had not been.

We understand him, as our Father Silvester, the supreme pontiff, proclaims, as perfect God and perfect man: as God, performing miracles; as man, enduring human sufferings. Thus we understand the Word as man and the Word as God, so that we have no doubt that he was true God and true man.

Having chosen twelve apostles, he shone forth in miracles before them and before an innumerable multitude of people. We confess that the same Lord Jesus Christ fulfilled the Law [Col. 0246C] and the prophets, suffered and was crucified according to the Scriptures, rose from the dead on the third day, was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

For this is our faith, Catholic and orthodox, delivered to us by our most blessed Father Silvester, the supreme pontiff.

Therefore we exhort every people and the various nations of the Gentiles to hold, honor, and proclaim this faith, and in the name of the holy Trinity most suitably to obtain grace, and to worship our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout infinite ages.

Our most blessed universal Father, Silvester the pontiff, proclaims that he is to be adored with a devoted heart. For our Lord himself, taking pity on me, a sinner, sent his holy apostles to visit us, shed upon us the light of his splendor, and brought me from darkness to the true light and knowledge. Rejoice with me in this.

For when a severe and loathsome leprosy had invaded all the flesh of my body, and the care of many physicians who came together had been applied, yet we had obtained salvation through the care of none of them, the priests of the Capitol came saying that a basin should be made for me in the Capitol and filled with innocent blood, and that I could be cleansed in that heated place.

And in accordance with their words, when a great number of innocent children had been gathered and the sacrilegious pagan priests were about to slaughter them and fill the basin with their blood, our serenity saw the tears of their mothers, immediately recoiled from the crime, took pity on them, and ordered their own sons to be restored to them. We provided vehicles and granted gifts, and sent them rejoicing back to their homes.

After these things had taken place, during the silence of the night, when the time for sleep had come, the holy apostles Peter and Paul appeared, saying to me:

“Because you have put an end to crimes and recoiled from the shedding of innocent blood, we have been sent by Christ the Lord, our God, to give you counsel for recovering your health. Hear our instructions, therefore, and do whatever we indicate to you.

“Silvester, the bishop of this [Col. 0247B] city, fleeing your persecutions, is sheltering with his clerics in caves among the rocks on Mount Soracte. When you have brought him to you, he himself will show you a pool of mercy. When he has immersed you in it three times, all this illness of leprosy will depart from you.

“When this has happened, repay this favor to your Savior: by your command, let churches be restored throughout the whole world. Purify yourself in this matter also, so that, having abandoned every superstition of idols, you may worship and honor the living and true God, who alone exists and is true, and thus attain his will.”

Therefore, rising from sleep, I immediately carried out what I had been instructed by the holy apostles. I summoned that distinguished and magnificent Father and our illuminator, Silvester, the universal pope, and recounted to him all the words commanded me by the holy [Col. 0247C] apostles.

We asked him who these gods, Peter and Paul, were. But he replied that they were not truly called gods, but apostles of our Savior, the Lord God Jesus Christ.

Again we began to ask the same most blessed pope whether he possessed likenesses depicting these apostles, so that from the painting we might recognize that they were the ones whom the revelation had made known. Then that venerable Father ordered the images of the same apostles to be brought by his deacon.

When I looked at them and recognized in those images the faces of the men whom I had seen represented in my dream, I confessed with a great shout before all my satraps that they were the ones whom I had seen in my dream.

At this, that most blessed Father Silvester, [Col. 0247D] bishop of the city of Rome, imposed upon us a period of penance within our Lateran palace, in a single hair shirt, so that by vigils, fasts, tears, and prayers we might obtain from our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior forgiveness for everything we had impiously done and unjustly ordered. Then, led by the laying-on of the hands of the clergy, I came to the very bishop. There, renouncing Satan, his pomp and works, and all idols fashioned by human hands, I openly professed before all the people that I believed in God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of things visible and invisible, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, by his own free will. [Col. 0248A] After the font had been blessed, its water purified me there by a triple immersion, the water of salvation. When I had been placed in the bosom of the font, I saw with my own eyes a hand descending from heaven and touching me. From this, recognize that I arose cleansed from every foulness of leprosy; and when I had been lifted from the venerable font, he clothed me in white garments and bestowed upon me the sealing of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit through the anointing of the blessed chrism. He traced the sign of the holy cross upon my forehead, saying: “God marks you with the seal of his faith; in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in the sealing of faith.” All the clergy replied, “Amen.” And the bishop added: “Peace be with you.”

Therefore, on the first day after receiving the mystery of holy baptism and after my body had been healed from the foulness of leprosy, I recognized that there is no other God except the Father, the Son, [Col. 0248B] and the Holy Spirit, whom Pope Silvester, blessed, proclaims: the Trinity in unity, and unity in Trinity. For all the gods of the nations whom I had hitherto worshiped are proved to be demons, works fashioned by human hands. Indeed, that same venerable Father most clearly declared to us how great a power our Savior had bestowed upon his blessed apostle Peter in heaven and on earth. Finding him faithful in his interrogation, he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18).”

Give heed, you powerful, and attend with the ear of your heart to what the good Master and Lord added to his disciple, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven (ibid., 19).” It is exceedingly wondrous and glorious to bind and loose on earth, and for what is bound and loosed to be so in heaven as well. When I recognized these things as blessed Silvester preached them, and found myself restored to perfect health through the benefits of that blessed Peter, we judged it useful, together with all our satraps, the entire senate, my nobles, and the whole Roman people subject to the glory of the empire, that just as he appears to have been appointed the vicar of the Son of God on earth, so also the pontiffs who exercise the authority of that prince of the apostles should, by our imperial clemency, appear to have received from us and our empire a power greater than an earthly one. We chose that the prince of the apostles himself, or his vicars, should be firm patrons for us before God; and just as our power is earthly and imperial, so we decreed that his most holy Roman Church should be reverently honored, and that the most sacred see of blessed Peter should be gloriously exalted above both our empire and our earthly throne.

Granting it power, dignity, strength, and imperial honor, we decree and establish that it should hold authority both over the four principal sees—Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople, and Jerusalem—and also over all the Churches of God throughout the entire world. The pontiff who at any time presides over that most holy Roman Church shall be higher and chief among all the priests of the whole world; and by his judgment whatever arrangements are made for the worship of God or for securing the faith of Christians [Col. 0249A] shall be determined. For it is just that the holy law should hold the primacy there where our Savior, the institutor of the holy laws, commanded blessed Peter to possess the chair of the apostolate; where, bearing the cross’s gallows, he drank the cup of blessed death and appeared as an imitator of his Master and Lord.

There let the nations bend their necks in confession of Christ’s name, where their teacher, the blessed apostle Paul, was crowned with martyrdom for Christ, his neck outstretched. There, to the end, let them seek the teacher where the holy teacher’s body rests; and there, prostrate and humbled, let them serve the office of the heavenly King, God our Savior Jesus Christ, where the proud served the rule of an earthly king.

Meanwhile, we wish all the peoples of every race and nation to know that we have constructed within our Lateran palace a church for our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, from its foundations, together with a baptistery. You should know that we carried twelve baskets of earth from its foundations upon our own shoulders, according to the number of the twelve apostles. We decree that this most holy Church be called, worshiped, venerated, and proclaimed the head and summit of all the Churches throughout the world, just as we have established in our other imperial decrees.

We have therefore built churches for the blessed Peter and Paul, the chief apostles, and enriched them with gold and silver. There, having deposited their most sacred bodies with great honor, we constructed their shrines from electrum, which no force of the elements can overcome; and we placed a cross of the purest gold and most precious gems upon each of their shrines, fastening them with golden nails. For the provision of lamps we granted them estates and landed possessions, enriched them with various goods, and by our sacred imperial command granted them, both in the East and in the West, and also in the northern and southern regions—namely, in Judaea, Greece, Asia, Thrace, Africa, and Italy, as well as on various islands—through our generosity, on the express condition that everything be administered through the hands of our most blessed Father Silvester the pontiff and his successors.

Let every people and the nations of the whole world rejoice with us. We exhort all of you to render with us immense thanks to our God and Savior Jesus Christ, for which that same God, in heaven above and on earth below, visiting us through his holy apostles, made us worthy to receive the sacrament of holy baptism and of bodily health. For this reason we grant to those holy apostles, my lords, the most blessed Peter and Paul, and through them also to our blessed Father Silvester, supreme pontiff and pope of the universal city of Rome, and to all his successors, the pontiffs who shall sit in the see of blessed Peter until the end of the world, and at the present time we grant to them the Lateran palace of our empire, which is preferred and pre-eminent among all palaces throughout the world.

We further grant the diadem, namely, the crown of our head, together with the pallium or mitre, the Phrygian cap, and also the shoulder covering, namely, the band that customarily surrounds the imperial neck; likewise the purple cloak, the scarlet tunic, and all imperial garments; also the dignity of the imperial commanders of cavalry. We grant as well the imperial scepters, all the standards and banners, various imperial ornaments, and the entire procession of the imperial eminence and the glory of our power.

58. For the most reverend men, the clergy of various orders serving that most holy Roman Church, we decree that they shall possess the eminence, distinction, power, and pre-eminence with which our most extensive senate appears to be adorned—that is, that they shall be made patricians and consuls, and shall also be proclaimed and adorned with the other imperial dignities [Col. 0250B]. And just as the imperial soldiery is adorned, so we decree that the clergy of the holy Roman Church be adorned. Just as imperial power is distinguished by the various offices of chamberlains, namely, doorkeepers and all the guards, so we wish the holy Roman Church to be decorated.

And so that pontifical splendor may shine forth most magnificently, we decree also that the clergy of that holy Roman Church decorate their horses with saddlecloths and linen coverings—that is, with the whitest color—and ride them in this manner. Just as our senate uses footwear with udones, that is, footwear made splendid with white linen, so that heavenly and earthly things alike may be adorned to the praise of God.

Above all, however, we grant permission to our most holy Father Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, [Col. 0250C] and pope, and to all the most blessed pontiffs who shall succeed him and come in perpetual times, for the honor and glory of Christ our God, in that great catholic and apostolic Church of God, to raise to the clergy and number among the religious clergy whomever, according to our judgment, he may wish to clericalize by his own deliberate decision, without anyone among all men presuming to act arrogantly.

We have therefore decreed this also: that our venerable Father Silvester, supreme pontiff, and all his successors, the pontiffs, shall use the diadem—that is, the crown which we granted to him from our head—made of the purest gold and precious gems, and shall wear it upon their heads to the praise of God and in honor of blessed Peter. But that most blessed pope did not permit himself to use that golden crown above the clerical crown which he wears for the glory of blessed Peter. We placed upon his most sacred head, with our own hands, the Phrygian cap, shining with white brilliance and signifying the Lord’s resurrection. Holding the bridle of his horse, we performed for him, in reverence for blessed Peter, the office of groom. We establish that all his successors shall use that Phrygian cap individually in processions, in imitation of our empire.

Therefore, so that the pontifical summit may not be diminished but rather be adorned more greatly than the dignity and glorious power of an earthly empire, behold: both our palace, as was said above, and the city of Rome, and all the provinces, places, and cities of Italy and of the western regions, we grant and leave to you, our most blessed pontiff Silvester, universal pope, and decree by this our divine imperial authority and pragmatic constitution that they be administered under the firm imperial judgment and power of your pontifical successors, and that they remain granted to the right of the holy Roman Church.

Therefore we have deemed it fitting that our empire and the power of our kingdom be transferred and moved to the eastern regions, and that in the province of Byzantium, in a most suitable place, a city be built in our name and our empire established there. For where the principate of the priests and the head of the Christian religion has been constituted by the heavenly Emperor, it is not right that an earthly emperor should possess power there.

All these things which we have established and confirmed through this sacred imperial decree and through our other divine decrees, we decree shall remain inviolate and unshaken until the end of the world. Therefore, before the living God, who commanded us to reign, and before his terrible [Col. 0251B] judgment, we adjure, by this our imperial constitution, all our successors, emperors, all nobles, satraps, the most extensive senate, and the whole people throughout the world subject to our empire, now and in all future times, that none of them shall in any way be permitted to oppose, violate, or in any respect overturn those things which have been granted by our imperial sanction to the most holy Roman Church and to all its pontiffs.

But if anyone—which we do not believe—should prove to be a violator or despiser of this, let him be bound under eternal condemnations, and let him experience the holy princes of God, the apostles Peter and Paul, as his adversaries in the present and future life; and, burned in the lower hell with the devil, let him perish with all the impious.

Strengthening the document of this our imperial decree with our own hands, we placed it upon the venerable body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. There, promising the same apostle that we would preserve everything inviolate and leave it as a command to our successors, the emperors, with the assent of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, we hand it over to our Father Silvester, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and to all his pontifical successors, to be possessed perpetually and prosperously. And [Col. 0252B] the imperial subscription: “May divinity preserve you for many years, most holy and blessed Fathers.” Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of April, under our lord Flavius Constantine Augustus, for the fourth time consul, and Gallicanus, for the fourth time consul, most illustrious men.

## At what time the Council of Nicaea took place

[Col. 0251]

[Col. 0251B] The canons of the general councils began in the time of Constantine. For in the preceding years, while persecution raged, no opportunity was given for instructing the peoples, except through what proceeded from the Roman see. Hence Christianity was divided into various heresies, because bishops were not permitted to assemble together until the time of the aforesaid emperor. He himself granted Christians the freedom to gather. Under him also the holy Fathers, assembling at the Council of Nicaea from the whole world, handed down, in accordance with the evangelical and apostolic faith, the creed that came after the apostles.

## Preface to the Council of Nicaea

[Col. 0251]

[Col. 0251C] Under the most blessed Silvanus, bishop of the apostolic see in the city of Rome, and under Constantine Augustus and Licinius Caesar, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Paulinus and Julianus, in the 336th year from Alexander, in the month of July, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, the catholic faith was set forth at Nicaea in Bithynia because of the heresies that had arisen. The most holy and most reverend Roman Church embraces and venerates this faith, since the 318 Fathers, through Victor and Vincent, the most religious presbyters of the Roman see, brought it forth under God’s inspiration to block the poisons of Arius. For certain regulations were also appended, which the aforementioned Church, recognizing them, confirmed.

All Catholics should certainly know that the holy Roman Church has not been placed first by any synodical decrees, but obtained its primacy through the evangelical voice of the Lord and our Savior, when he said to the blessed apostle Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven (Matthew 16:18–19).”

The fellowship of the most blessed apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, was also added in that same city of Rome. He was crowned in glorious death, struggling together with Peter on the same day and at the same time under the emperor Nero, and both together consecrated the holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord and placed it before all the other cities throughout the world by their power and venerable triumph.

Although the prayer of all the saints is continually poured out before the Lord on behalf of everyone, the most blessed apostle Paul nevertheless promises the Romans in his own handwriting, saying: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I make mention of you always in my prayers (Romans 1:9–10).”

The first see, therefore, by heavenly favor, is that of the Roman Church, which the most blessed Peter and Paul dedicated by their martyrdom. The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist, because he was the first to preach the word of truth in Egypt, sent there by Peter, and received a glorious martyrdom. The venerable Abilius succeeded him.

The third honorable see is held at Antioch, belonging to the same blessed apostle Peter, because he lived there before coming to Rome and appointed Ignatius bishop there; and there the first name of the Christian people arose. The bishop of Jerusalem is also regarded by everyone as honorable, out of reverence for so great a place. Especially because there the most blessed James, who was called the Just and was also named the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained bishop by the apostles Peter, James, and John.

Therefore, according to the definition of the ancient Fathers, the first see is not said to be in Jerusalem, lest perhaps unbelievers or ignorant people should think that the see of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is in heaven, is on earth. For his see is heaven, while the earth is the footstool of his feet, since he is the one through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1:3): “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory for ever and ever. Amen (Romans 11:36).”

At Ephesus, however, the most blessed John, apostle and evangelist, wrote the Gospel by divine inspiration and rested there long after the Lord’s resurrection and ascension into heaven. For this reason the bishop of Ephesus, in memory of so great an apostle and evangelist, holds a more honorable see than the other metropolitan bishops in synods.

But since we must discuss the Council of Nicaea, what was the reason that, after the glorious preaching of the apostles—which had wondrously spread throughout the whole earth—so many bishops were gathered under Constantine Augustus? The tenth book of Rufinus, which is joined to the nine books of Ecclesiastical History published by the most learned man Eusebius of Caesarea, must necessarily be brought forward here, so that the brief account which he wrote at its beginning concerning the perversity of Arius may be recalled. For there is no doubt that the 318 most holy Fathers were assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia from the entire eastern world so that, with Christ’s help, the impious doctrine of Arius might be utterly condemned and, through salutary providence, that which ought to be observed in the holy catholic Church might be established.

Again, from the tenth book of Rufinus:

When, after Achillas, who had succeeded Peter in martyrdom, Alexander had assumed the priesthood at Alexandria, and peace and relief from persecutions had come to us, while the glory of the Churches rejoiced in the merits of the confessors, the prosperity of our affairs was disturbed by domestic conflict. For a certain presbyter at Alexandria named Arius, a man religious more in appearance and bearing than in virtue, but shamefully eager for glory, praise, and novelty, began to put forward perverse claims concerning the faith of Christ and to proclaim what he had discovered by an artful process of inquiry. For he attempted to cut off and separate the Son from the eternal and ineffable substance or nature of God the Father. This matter disturbed many people in the Church and drove them away from the sweet tranquility of mind.

But although Alexander, [Col. 0254A] the bishop, naturally gentle and peaceful, continually sought through admonitions to recall Arius from his perverse undertaking and impious assertions, the matter nevertheless did not proceed according to his wishes. Since Arius had infected many with a kind of contagion of his pestilential assertion and had spread it throughout the cities not only of Alexandria but also of other provinces, Alexander, believing that it would be destructive to ignore such things, informed many of his fellow priests of the matter. The question became known to the laity. The report reached the ears of the devout ruler, who took the greatest care and diligence over our affairs. Then, following the judgment of the priests, he summoned an episcopal council at the city of Nicaea. There, with 318 bishops seated, he ordered Arius to be present and commanded them to judge his propositions and questions.

But I do not think the emperor’s admirable action at that council should be passed over in silence. For when bishops had gathered from almost every place and, as commonly happens, had brought before one another quarrels arising from various causes, individual bishops frequently approached him, petitions were presented, accusations were brought forward, and they devoted their attention more to these matters than to the business for which they had come. Seeing that the principal matter was being frustrated by such quarrels, he appointed a fixed day on which each bishop who seemed to have any complaint would present it. When he had taken his seat, he received the petitions from each of them. Holding them all together in the fold of his robe, and not disclosing what they contained, he said to the bishops:

“God appointed you priests and gave you power to judge even us. And therefore we are rightly judged by you, but you cannot be judged by human beings. For this reason, await among yourselves the judgment of God alone, so that all your quarrels, whatever they may be, may be reserved for that divine examination. For you have been given to us by God as gods. It is not fitting that a human being should judge gods, but only he of whom it is written: ‘God stands in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes among the gods (Psalm 81:1).’ Therefore, setting these matters aside, examine the other questions that concern the faith of God without any contention of spirit.”

After saying this, he ordered all the petitions of complaint to be burned, so that the hatred and reproach of the priests would not become known to him.

But when, for many days, the question of the faith was debated in the council of bishops, and some held differing opinions and strongly supported Arius’s undertakings, [Col. 0254D] there were nevertheless more who cursed his impious project. Since a great number of the priests at that council were confessors, they all opposed Arius’s innovations. Men skilled in disputation favored him and, for that reason, opposed the simplicity of the faith.

How powerful the simplicity of faith is, we learn even from what happened there. For when, at the urging of the devout emperor, the priests of God had assembled from the whole world, philosophers and dialecticians, very noble and highly renowned, also gathered, moved by curiosity. Among them, one distinguished in the art of dialectic engaged each day in a strenuous contest with our bishops, men who likewise possessed no mean training in dialectic. [Col. 0255A] It became a great spectacle for the learned and literate men who gathered to listen.

Yet no one could in any way confute or constrain the philosopher. With such skill in speaking did he meet the questions put to him that whenever he was thought to have been most tightly constrained, he slipped away like a slippery snake. But to show that God’s kingdom “does not consist in speech but in power (1 Corinthians 4:20),” one of the confessors, a man of the simplest nature who knew nothing except “Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2),” was among the other bishops and listeners.

When he saw the philosopher insulting our men and boasting of his clever art of disputation, he asked everyone to grant him an opportunity to speak briefly with the philosopher. Then our men, who knew only the man’s simplicity and lack of education in speech, became afraid and suffered a kind of embarrassment, lest holy simplicity should be made a laughingstock before clever men.

The elder nevertheless persisted, and began his speech in this way:

“In the name of Jesus Christ, philosopher, hear what is true. There is one God who made heaven and earth, who gave a spirit to the human being whom he had formed from the clay of the earth, who created by the power of his Word all things that are seen, and established them by the sanctification of his Spirit. This Word and Wisdom, whom we call the Son, taking pity on human errors, was born from a Virgin; through the suffering of death he freed us from everlasting death; through his resurrection he bestowed eternal life upon us; and we await him as the one who will come to judge all that we have done. Do you believe that these things are so, philosopher?”

The philosopher, as though he had never learned any speech of contradiction, was so stupefied by the power of the words that he could answer nothing but this: that it seemed to him to be so, and that nothing else was true except what the elder had said.

Then the elder said: “If you have believed that it is so, rise and follow me to the Lord’s house, and receive the seal of this faith.”

And so the philosopher became a Christian and at last rejoiced that he had been defeated.

At that council there was also Paphnutius, a man of God and bishop of Egypt, in whom grace was present with such power that signs were performed through him no less than formerly through the apostles. At that time Spyridion, the distinguished bishop of Cyprus, was also held in high regard. Thus, even in those times, many such men shone forth in the Churches of the Lord, and very many of them were present at that council.

Meanwhile, the assembly was conducted day after day. They did not readily or rashly dare to establish matters of such importance. Arius was frequently summoned to the council, his assertions were examined through continuous discussion, and they sought, with the utmost deliberation, what they ought to hold and establish against them.

After a long and extensive debate, however, everyone agreed, and as though with one mouth and one heart it was decreed that “Omousion” should be written—that is, that the Son should be confessed to be of the same substance as the Father. This was pronounced as the firmest judgment of all.

At that time only seventeen are said to have existed who preferred the faith of Arius, affirming that the Son of God was created externally from things that did not exist, and had not been begotten from the very divinity of the Father. The judgment of the priestly council was reported to Constantine. He venerated it as though it had been issued by God. If anyone attempted to oppose it, as though acting against divine decrees, he declared that he would send him into exile.

The preface ends.

## The chapters of the Council of Nicaea begin

[Col. 0255]

[Col. 0255C] 1. Concerning eunuchs who mutilate themselves.  
2. Concerning those who immediately seek the clergy after baptism.  
3. Concerning women admitted into clerics’ households.  
4. How bishops ought to be ordained.  
5. Concerning excommunicated clerics or laypeople.  
6. Concerning the primacy of metropolitan bishops.  
7. Concerning the honor of the bishop of Jerusalem.  
8. Concerning the Novatians.  
9. Concerning presbyters appointed without examination.  
10. Concerning clerics ordained after falling away.  
11. Concerning those who have fallen voluntarily, and how they ought to do penance.  
12. Concerning the excommunicated who depart from the world.  
13. Concerning fallen catechumens.  
14. Concerning deacons: that they should not give the body of Christ to presbyters or receive communion before presbyters.  
15. Concerning clerics who rashly withdraw from the Church.  
16. Concerning presbyters, deacons, or clerics who transfer to other cities.  
17. Concerning clerics belonging to another bishop: that they are not to be ordained by another in his own church without the consent of their own bishop.  
18. Concerning clerics who accept interest or increase.  
19. Concerning the rebaptism of the Paulianists and Cataphrygians.  
20. Concerning Sundays and Pentecost, that on those days we should pray standing.

## The canons of the Council of Nicaea begin

What was enacted under the emperor Constantine, in the consulship of the brothers Paulinus and Julianus, in the year 363, on the third day before the Kalends of July.

[Col. 0255]

[Col. 0255D] When this holy and great council had assembled at the city of Nicaea in the province of Bithynia, the following decrees were established by them, translated from Greek into the Latin language.

[Col. 0256D] I. If anyone has been mutilated during illness, or has been cut by physicians, or has been castrated by barbarians, it has been decided that he may remain in the clergy. But if anyone, while healthy, mutilates himself, even if he is already in the clergy, he must cease from the clergy, and thereafter no one of this kind ought to be ordained. These provisions have been established concerning those who have desired such things or have dared to mutilate themselves. Likewise, if some have been mutilated by barbarians or by their masters and are of a reputable life, the ecclesiastical rule admits such men into the clergy.

II. Since many things have been done contrary to the rule, whether through necessity or for whatever reason, so that people recently coming from a pagan life, newly catechized or instructed, immediately proceeded to spiritual baptism and, as soon as they had been baptized, were advanced even to the episcopate or presbyterate, it has rightly seemed good that nothing of this kind should henceforth occur. For a catechumen needs time, and after baptism requires much testing.

There is indeed an evident apostolic command which says: “Not a novice, lest, being puffed up, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil (1 Timothy 3:6).” If, as time passes, he commits some sin and is convicted by two or three witnesses, one who is such must cease from the clergy. But if anyone acts contrary to these provisions, he will endanger his clerical status as one acting against the decrees of the holy council.

III. The holy synod has altogether forbidden a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any cleric whatsoever to keep with him a woman from outside, unless she happens to be his mother, sister, grandmother, paternal aunt, or maternal aunt. For only in these persons and those similar to them is every suspicion arising from women removed. Anyone who acts otherwise endangers his position in the clergy.

[Col. 0257C] IV. A bishop ought to be ordained by all the bishops in his province, if this can be done. But if this is difficult, either because of urgent necessity or because of the length of the journey, at least three bishops must assemble together, while also securing in writing the consent of the others who are absent; and in this way they shall perform the ordination. The authority or confirmation shall belong, in each province, to the metropolitan bishop.

V. Let this decision be observed: those who are excommunicated by some shall not be received into communion by others. It must also be investigated whether they may have been excommunicated by their bishop because of some anger, dispute, or other disturbance.

Therefore, so that these matters may be examined by a worthy investigation, it has rightly seemed good that twice each year, in every province, a council of bishops should be held. They shall assemble together from the common province and examine such questions, so that those who have deservedly incurred the offense of their bishops on account of their faults may likewise rightly be regarded as excommunicated by the others, until the council as a whole or their own bishop sees fit to issue a more lenient judgment concerning them.

One council shall be held before the days of Lent, so that, after all disputes—if there are any—have been cut off, a pure solemn offering may be presented to God. The second shall be held around the time of autumn.

VI. Let the ancient custom remain in Egypt, Libya, [Col. 0258A] and the Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these regions, since a similar custom also belongs to the Roman bishop. Likewise, at Antioch and in the other provinces, let each Church retain its proper honor.

In every respect it is clear that if anyone has been ordained contrary to the will and knowledge of the metropolitan bishop, the great and holy council has judged that he ought not to be a bishop. But if, after the common consent of all has been reasonably established according to ecclesiastical rule, two or three, driven by hostility, oppose it through contention, let the decision of the greater number of priests prevail.

VII. Since an ancient custom and an old tradition have prevailed that honor be given to Aelia, that is, to the bishop of Jerusalem, [Col. 0258B] let him consequently possess honor, while the proper dignity of the metropolitan city nevertheless remains.

VIII. If some from among the Novatians wish to come to the catholic Church, it has pleased the holy council that they be ordained and remain in the clergy. Above all, they must make this confession, which ought to be required according to Scripture: they must profess that, by common agreement, they will observe the statutes of the catholic Church—that is, that they will enter into communion both with those who may have entered a second marriage and with those who fell during the time of persecution, although a manner and period of penance have been assigned to such fallen persons—so that in all things they follow what is observed in the catholic Church.
