And wherever such men themselves are found—whether in villages or in cities—serving as clerics ordained by Catholics, let them likewise remain in the clergy, each in his own order. But if a bishop or presbyter of the catholic Church is present to whom some of these people come, it is certain that the Catholic bishop shall retain his dignity, and likewise the presbyters and deacons shall retain theirs.

As for those who come from them: if one of them happens to be a bishop, he shall possess the dignity of the priesthood, unless the Catholic bishop should choose to grant him also the honor of the episcopal title. If this is not pleasing, the bishop shall find him a place so that he may be a co-bishop in the parish or a presbyter in the clergy; and two bishops must not appear to exist in one city. He must in every respect be seen to remain in the clergy.

[Col. 0258D] IX. If some have been promoted as presbyters without examination and, after being examined, have confessed their sins, and after their confession men have rashly laid hands upon them contrary to the rule, the ecclesiastical order does not admit them. For in all things the Church defends what is irreproachable.

X. Whoever among those who have fallen has been ordained through ignorance, or through disregard of those who ordained him, this does not prejudice the ecclesiastical rule; but when the matter has been discovered, they shall be deposed.

XI. It pleased the holy synod, although they are unworthy of mercy, nevertheless to show them some measure of humanity. Therefore, if any are sincerely repentant, let them remain among the penitents for three years. If they are nevertheless faithful, let them spend seven further years among the penitents; for two years, however, let them participate with the people in prayer alone, without offering. But if some, having been called by God’s grace, first demonstrated their faith by laying aside the military belt, and afterward returned to their own vomit, so that they both offered money and sought to return again to military service, let these remain among the penitents for ten years, after the first three years being among the hearers. Above all, let this be observed by everyone: that their disposition and the fruit of their repentance be examined. For whoever, persevering with all fear and tears and in good works, demonstrates the character of his life not by words alone but by deed and truth, when the appointed time has also been completed by them, and they have already begun to participate in prayers, may even receive more humane consideration from the bishop. But those who have treated their fall indifferently and think it sufficient for them that they have entered the Church shall in every way complete the appointed periods.

II. Concerning those who depart from the body, the rule of the ancient law shall also now be observed, so that, if someone should depart from the body, he is not deprived of the necessary provision for his journey. But if some desperate person survives after receiving communion, let him be among those who participate in prayer alone. In the case of all who depart from the body, however, the bishop shall exercise care and judgment in giving them communion.

XIII. Concerning catechumens who have fallen, this holy and great council decreed that they should remain for three years merely among those hearing the word; afterward, let them pray with the catechumens.

XIV. It has come to the holy council’s attention that in certain places and cities deacons give the sacraments to presbyters. Neither rule nor custom has handed this down: those who do not have authority to offer the sacrifice are not to give the body of Christ to those who offer it. It has also become known that deacons receive the sacraments even before bishops.

All these practices must be abolished, and deacons are to receive holy communion in due order from the bishop or presbyter, after the presbyters. If neither bishop nor presbyter is present, they themselves may bring it forth and eat it. Nor is it permitted for deacons to sit among the presbyters. If anyone does not wish to be satisfied with these provisions, after this definition he shall cease to be a deacon.

XV. Because of the many disturbances and frequent tumultuous uprisings that are accustomed to occur, it was decided that this custom, which is contrary to the rule, must everywhere be cut off, wherever it exists: namely, that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon should pass from one city to another. If anyone thereafter attempts to do such a thing contrary to the statutes of this holy council, every such attempt shall be nullified, and he shall be restored to his own Church, in which he was ordained.

XVI. If any, having no fear of God before their eyes and observing none of the ecclesiastical statutes, withdraw from their Church—whether presbyters, deacons, or persons placed in any ecclesiastical order—they must not be received into another Church. Rather, they must be compelled by every necessity to return to their own Church. If they persist, they must be excommunicated.

XVII. If anyone dares to ordain in his own Church someone who belongs to another, without the consent of the bishop from whom that cleric has withdrawn, such ordination shall be invalid.

XVIII. Since many clerics, pursuing shameful profits out of avarice, have forgotten the divine commandment which says, “Who has not given his money at interest,” and, lending at one hundred percent, demand usury, this holy council decrees that, if anyone is found after this definition to accept interest, or to pursue shameful profits from any such business, or even to lend measures of grain at sixfold repayment, anyone who attempts such a thing for gain shall be cast out of the clergy and regarded as excluded from the ecclesiastical order.

XIX. If anyone takes refuge in the Catholic Church from the Paulianists or Cataphrygians, it has been decreed that they must be rebaptized. If any of them were clerics, then, provided they are found blameless and irreproachable, after being rebaptized they shall again be ordained by the bishop of the Catholic Church. But if, upon examination, they are found unfit, they must be deposed. The same procedure shall likewise be observed concerning deacons and all who are found in that clergy. We have also mentioned the deaconesses found among them, who have received no laying-on of hands at all; they are to be regarded entirely as laywomen. Likewise, deaconesses who are not included in the Catholic canon are to be assigned to the same status, that is, as laywomen and as though unconsecrated.

XX. Since there are certain people who kneel for prayer on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, it has therefore been decreed by the holy synod that, since a harmonious and fitting custom is to be observed in all churches, we should offer our vows to the Lord while standing for prayer.

## Creed of the same Council of Nicaea

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator of things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, that is, of one substance with the Father (which the Greeks call *homoousion*), through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth. For us human beings and for our salvation he descended from heaven, was incarnate and became human, suffered, died, and rose again on the third day; he ascended into heaven and will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was when he was not,” and, “Before he was born he did not exist,” and that he was made from things that did not exist, or from some substance or nature, and who say that the Son of God is mutable and changeable, the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes and condemns. This is the faith expounded by the Fathers, first against the blasphemous Arius, who said that the Son of God was a creature, and against every heresy: that of Sabellius, Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Mani, Valentinus, Marcion, and absolutely every heresy that may have arisen against the Catholic and apostolic Church. All three hundred and eighteen bishops assembled at Nicaea condemned them.

## The Faith of Gregory the Greater

One God, the beginning and Father of the living Word, of existing Wisdom, of Power, and of his own image; the perfect begetter of the Perfect; and one Lord from one, the Father of the only-begotten Son; and one Lord from one, God from God, the form of the Father’s substance, the image of God, God the Word of the world, and maker of the whole substance, Wisdom containing all things that exist; the true Son from the true Father, invisible from the invisible, incorruptible from the incorruptible, immortal from the immortal, and everlasting from the everlasting; and one Holy Spirit, perfect, perfect life, the holiness of those who live, and the fountain of holiness, and minister of edification, through whom God is in and over all believers, and the Son is through all.

A Trinity of perfect glory and everlasting kingship, indivisible and inalienable. Therefore there is nothing created, servile, or enslaved in the Trinity; nothing adventitious or introduced later, as something that previously did not exist and entered last. For the Son does not at any time cease to be with the Father, nor the Holy Spirit with the Son; rather, this same Trinity is always immutable and unchangeable.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF ANCYRA BEGIN

[Col. 0261]

[Col. 0261B] 1. Concerning presbyters who lapsed during the persecution. 2. Concerning deacons who sacrificed. 3. Concerning clerics or laypeople whose hands others placed, under compulsion, upon idol sacrifices. 4. Concerning those who dined in idols’ temples, as above. 5. Concerning those who, through fear, performed pagan rites. 6. Concerning those who ate in places dedicated to idols. 7. Concerning those who frequently sacrificed to idols. 8. Concerning those who were compelled to use idols in sacrificing. 9. Concerning those who gave others occasion to sacrifice. 10. Concerning deacons. 11. Concerning betrothed girls corrupted by others. [Col. 0262B] 12. Concerning those who sacrificed to idols before baptism. 13. Concerning co-bishops. 14. Concerning presbyters who abstain from meat. 15. That presbyters must not sell ecclesiastical rights. 16. Concerning those who have lived irrationally. 17. Concerning those who have lived like dumb animals. 18. Concerning bishops who, once ordained, are not received. 19. Concerning those who profess virginity. 20. Concerning adulterers. 21. Concerning women who fornicate and kill their offspring. 22. Concerning those who commit intentional homicide. 23. Concerning those who live like pagans. 24. Concerning the man who violated his bride’s sister.

## 61. THE COUNCIL OF ANCYRA BEGINS (In the year of the Lord 600)

[Col. 0261]

[Col. 0261C] These canons, or rules, actually precede those of Nicaea, but the Nicene canons are written first because of the authority of the great and holy council held at Nicaea.

The following assembled in the aforesaid synod at the city of Ancyra: Marcellus of Ancyra, Agricolaus of Caesarea, Lupus of Tarsus, Vitalius of Antioch, Basil of Amasia, Philadelphus of Juliopolis, Testulus of Nicomedia, Heraclius of Zela, Peter of Iconium, Munecius of Laodicea, Pergianus of Antioch in Pisidia, and Narcissus of Nerodias.

### CHAPTER I

Presbyters who sacrificed and afterward entered the contest again—if they did this sincerely and not by preparing some pretext for themselves, so that they might appear to be arrested again or subjected to tortures as unwilling persons; if, therefore, they struggled sincerely and not by agreement or for display, but themselves offered sacrifice—it was decided that they should retain the honor of their own seat, but that they may neither offer, address the people, nor perform any priestly functions.

[Col. 0262C]

### II

Likewise, deacons who sacrificed but afterward resisted again must be deprived of their honor and must cease from every sacred ministry, so that they neither offer bread nor the cup nor make proclamations. Unless, perhaps, some bishops, aware of their labor, humility, and gentleness, should wish to grant them something more or take something away; the authority in these matters shall therefore rest with the bishops themselves.

### III

Those who, fleeing through fear of persecution, were captured, or were handed over by relatives or members of their household, and either lost their own possessions, endured tortures, or were even confined in prisons, yet proclaimed themselves Christians—and, while the violence continued, were brought to the point that their hands were seized and forcibly dragged onto sacrifices, while they themselves persevered in the faith and cried out that they were Christians—if they show that they bitterly bear what happened against their will and under compulsion by others, and if by a humble manner of life they demonstrate their grief at having been unwillingly forced, these are not to be barred from communion as though guilty.

But if some have already barred them from communion, either for the sake of a more diligent investigation or through someone’s ignorance, they ought to be received immediately. This provision must be observed both concerning clerics and concerning all laypeople. As for laypeople who have fallen into a similar necessity, it was decided that they should be admitted to ordination as though they had committed no sin, especially if a commendable life supports their case.

### IV

Concerning those who were compelled to sacrifice and, in addition, dined in the temples of idols: if any of them were brought to the temples in more elegant dress, and there, after changing into more costly clothing, became participants in the meal, indiscriminately consuming everything that had been set before them as offerings to idols, it was decided that they should be placed among the hearers for one year, perform penance for three further years, participate in prayer alone for two years of that three-year period, and be reconciled to the sacraments in the third year.

### V

Those who went up to the temples in mourning garments and, reclining among the others, ate while weeping, if they complete three years of penance, shall be received into communion without offering—that is, they themselves shall not offer the oblation. But if, after being brought to the temples, they did not eat, let them remain in penance for two years. In the third year they shall communicate, but without offering, as stated; in the fourth year they shall receive full restoration.

The bishop must have authority to consider the sins of each of them and, according to what he sees of their conduct, assign the standard and rule of their way of life—that is, acting with humanity, he may shorten the period for someone according to his manner of life, or add a longer period wherever he judges correction necessary. The former and later life of all these persons must be examined, and priestly humanity must accordingly be applied to them with discretion.

### VI

Concerning those who yielded merely to threats, or were deterred by the surrender of their possessions or the punishment of transportation, and sacrificed, and who have not yet repented or converted, but now—that is, at the time of this synod—have presented themselves, forming the intention of conversion: it was decided that they should be received among the hearers until the great day, perform penance for three years, then communicate for two further years without offering, and thus, when six years have been completed, attain full restoration.

If any were admitted to penance before this council, the beginning of the prescribed six-year period shall be reckoned for them from that time. If any danger of death should befall one of them, whether through illness or some other cause, communion must not be denied them as provision for their journey.

### VII

Concerning those who attended the banquets of pagans on their festival days in remote places belonging to them, and nevertheless brought and ate their own food there: it was decided that after two years of penance they should be received. Whether they are to be received with the offering or admitted only to communion, however, each bishop shall examine their life and weigh the matter after considering both their past and present conduct.

### VIII

Those who sacrificed a second or third time under compulsion shall submit themselves to penance for four years; for two further years they shall communicate without offering, and in the seventh year they shall receive full restoration to communion.

### IX

All who not only deviated from the Lord’s faith but also attacked others, persuaded their brethren, and became guilty of persuasion shall be kept among the catechumens for three years; for another six years they shall receive the status of penitents; in another year, that is, the tenth, they shall receive communion without offering, so that, when the ten years have been completed, they may enjoy full restoration. During this entire period, their life and conduct must also be considered.

### X

Concerning deacons: whoever, when being ordained, protested during the ordination itself, saying that he wished to have a wife and could not remain continent, may remain in the ministry if afterward he enters marriage, because the bishop granted him permission. Those who kept silent, however, and accepted the laying-on of hands while professing continence, must cease from the ministry if afterward they enter marriage.

### XI

Concerning betrothed girls who afterward were corrupted by others: it was decided that they should be rescued and returned to those to whom they had been betrothed, even if it is established that they lost the flower of their chastity at the hands of their abductors.

### XII

Those who sacrificed to idols before baptism and afterward received baptism may be promoted to the order, as having been cleansed from every crime by the sanctification of the saving bath.

### XIII

Deputy bishops—whom the Greeks call *coepiscopi*—may not ordain either presbyters or deacons. Nor may presbyters of a city command anything without the bishop’s instruction, or do anything in any parish without his written authority.

### XIV

Concerning presbyters or deacons who are in the clergy and abstain from meat: it was decided that they must not despise meat as unclean, but touch it. Those who wish to abstain may have the authority to do so, provided that, when meat is cooked with vegetables, they do not judge the vegetables polluted as though by meat, but eat such food even while abstaining from meat.

If they judge meat so unclean and abominable that they consider even vegetables cooked with meat inedible, they must cease both from their ministry and from their order, as refusing to accept this rule. If anyone does not obey the admonitions of this rule but considers meat, as stated, unclean and abominable, he must cease from his order.

### XV

If presbyters sell ecclesiastical property while there is no bishop, it was decided that, after the contract has been rescinded, the property must be restored to ecclesiastical ownership. It shall be for the bishop to judge whether the stipulated price ought to be accepted, since it often happens that the proceeds of the property sold must be repaid in a larger amount than the price received.

### XVI

In this title the Greek words are: *Περι τῶν ἀλογῶς διαγόντῶν καὶ διαγόνται*, which we can render as “concerning those who have lived or are living irrationally.” The sense of this sentence may be twofold, as is inferred from what follows: either concerning those who have mixed sexually with animals, or concerning those who, in the manner of beasts, have committed incest with close blood-relatives.

Therefore, whoever committed such a crime before his twentieth year shall, after completing fifteen years in penance, begin to participate in prayer alone. Let him then remain for another five years in communion consisting only of prayer. After the twentieth year, let him be received into communion with the offering; but his conduct during the time of penance must also be examined, and he shall receive treatment according to this humanity.

If anyone has persisted more obstinately in this abuse, let him undertake a longer period for this crime, namely twenty years of penance. Those who, after reaching the age of twenty, and having wives, have fallen into this crime shall, after completing twenty-five years of penance, be admitted to communion in prayers; after remaining in that communion of prayers for another five years, they shall receive full communion with prayer.

But if any, while having wives and being over fifty years of age, have fallen into this crime, let them be granted communion only at the end of their life.

### XVII

The same persons—not only those made leprous by this sort of crime, but also those who infect others with this disease—it was decided should pray among those tossed about by the storm, whom we understand as the possessed.

### XVIII

If bishops are not received by their own diocese in which they had been designated, they must be compelled by judicial decree to return to it. If they wish to occupy other Churches and use force against the bishops whom they find there, stirring up seditions against them, they must be separated. If they wish to reside as presbyters in the church where they had previously been presbyters, they must not be deprived of their own dignity.

But if they are also found to stir up seditions there against the bishops established in that place, they must be separated and, nevertheless, deprived of the dignity of the presbyterate.

### XIX

All women who have violated a promise of virginity, disregarding their profession, must be counted among the *digami*, that is, those who have passed to a second marriage. We forbid virgin girls who wish to live as sisters with certain men to remain in their company.

### XX

If anyone has committed adultery, after completing seven years in penance, let him be restored to full standing according to his former rank.

### XXI

Concerning women who fornicate and kill their offspring, and also those who act so that what has been conceived in the womb is expelled: whereas the ancient definition removes them from the Church until the end of their life, we now define more humanely that they be assigned a period of ten years’ penance.

### XXII

Those who commit voluntary homicide shall continually submit themselves to penance. Toward the end of life, however, they shall be considered worthy of communion.

Those who commit homicide not voluntarily but accidentally were, according to the former rule, joined to communion after seven years of penance, according to the established stages. This more humane definition assigns a period of five years.

### XXIII

Those who observe omens, auspices, dreams, or any divinations according to pagan custom, or who introduce such people into their houses to inquire into matters by magical arts, or who purify houses by such rites, shall, after confessing, perform five years of penance according to the ancient established rules.

### XXIV

If someone who has a fiancée perhaps violates her sister and becomes attached to her as though she were his own and the woman whom he ought to marry, but afterward, having deceived her, marries the betrothed woman, and the woman who suffered the violation perhaps takes her own life, all who were aware of this act shall be reduced to ten years of penance according to the established canons.

The Council of Ancyra ends.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF NEOCAESAREA BEGIN

[Col. 0265]

[Col. 0265D] 1. That presbyters must not marry. 2. That a woman may not marry two brothers. 3. Concerning those who have entered into many marriages. 4. Concerning unconsummated desire. 5. Concerning sinful catechumens. 6. Concerning the baptism of pregnant women. 7. That presbyters must not pray at second marriages. 8. That the husband of an adulterous wife must not become a cleric. [Col. 0266D] 9. Concerning presbyters overtaken by bodily sin. 10. Concerning deacons overtaken by bodily sin. 11. That a presbyter under thirty years of age must not be ordained. 12. Concerning those baptized in illness. 13. Concerning presbyters from another region. 14. Concerning the seven deacons.

# THE COUNCIL OF NEOCAESAREA BEGINS

[Col. 0267]

[Col. 0267A] These canons are second to those set forth at Ancyra and Caesarea, but are found to precede the Nicene canons.

The following assembled in the aforesaid synod at the city of Neocaesarea: Vitalis, Germanus, Sedus, Hystrius, Lupus, Gerontius, Salamnus, Leontius, Saint Basil, Valentinus, Stephanus, Gregory, Longinus, Narcissus, Decasius, Leontius, Heraclius, and Alipius. From them the rules written below were issued.

### CHAPTER I

If a presbyter marries, he must be deposed from his order. If he has fornicated or committed adultery, he must be expelled from the Church and reduced to penance among the laity.

### II

If a woman marries two brothers, she shall be expelled until the day of her death. Nevertheless, out of humanity, she ought to be reconciled to the sacraments at the end of her life, provided that, if she recovers, she be admitted to penance after the marriage has been dissolved. If a woman dies while living in such a union, the penance of the surviving partner will be difficult; this judgment applies equally to men and women.

### III

Concerning those who frequently marry, whether men who repeatedly take wives or women who repeatedly marry: the period prescribed for them is clear, but their conduct and faith may shorten the period.

### IV

If someone desires a woman, and even has the desire for intercourse with her, but the act does not follow, it is clear that he has been freed by divine grace.

### V

A catechumen—that is, a hearer—who enters the church and stands with the catechumens, if he is seen to sin, shall hear the word while kneeling, so that he may abstain from the sin he has committed. If he persists in it, he must be expelled entirely.

### VI

Concerning pregnant women: they ought to be baptized whenever they wish. Nothing in this sacrament is shared between the woman who is about to give birth and the one who will be born from her womb, because each person’s freedom of choice is declared in that confession.

### VII

A presbyter must not attend the banquet of secular marriages, especially since penance is prescribed for second marriages. What presbyter would consent to such marriages on account of the banquet?

[Col. 0268A]

### VIII

If it is proved that someone’s wife committed adultery while he was a layman, he cannot be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry. If she committed adultery after he had already entered the clergy, he must dismiss her after granting her a divorce. If he wishes to retain her companionship, he cannot enjoy the ministry he has received.

### IX

Anyone who has committed a bodily sin and was afterward ordained presbyter, if he confesses that he sinned before his ordination, shall not offer, but may remain in the other offices because of the usefulness of his zeal. For many have judged that other sins also result in deprivation of ordination. But if he has not confessed these matters and cannot be manifestly convicted by anyone, authority concerning him must be entrusted to himself.

### X

Likewise, if a deacon has become entangled in the same double guilt, he shall restrain himself from the ministry.

### XI

A presbyter must not be ordained before the age of thirty, even if his life is commendable; he must be kept until the appointed time. For the Lord was baptized in his thirtieth year and then preached.

### XII

If someone is baptized while suffering from illness, he must not be ordained presbyter. His faith was not voluntary but arose from necessity—unless afterward his zeal and faith prove commendable, or a shortage of men makes it necessary.

### XIII

Presbyters who are not from the same region cannot offer in a church when the bishops or presbyters of the city are present, nor give sanctified bread, nor present the cup. If the priests of the city are absent and the visiting presbyters have been invited to give the prayer, they alone may give it.

Deputy bishops—whom the Greeks call *coepiscopi*—were established after the example of the seventy elders. But, as fellow priests, because of the care and zeal they show toward the poor, they may offer and shall be held in honor.

### XIV

There must be seven deacons according to the rule, even if the city is large. The authority of the rule is this, as the Book of Acts of the Apostles also indicates.

The Council of Neocaesarea ends; it took place in the year of the Lord 314, in Pontus Polemoniacus.

# [COUNCIL OF GANGRA]

[Col. 0267]

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF GANGRA BEGIN

[Col. 0267D] 1. Concerning those who condemn marriage. 2. Concerning those who condemn people who eat meat. 3. That a slave must not despise his master on religious grounds. 4. Concerning the offering of a married presbyter. 5. That the Church’s prayers must not be despised. 6. That people must not assemble outside the Church. [Col. 0268D] 7. Concerning giving fruits in the Church and nowhere else. 8. Concerning what is contributed for the use of the poor. 9. That one devoted to virginity must not curse marriage. 10. Concerning those who are proud on account of virginity. 11. That the brothers’ love-feast must not be despised. 12. Concerning the continent and the use of passions. [Col. 0269A] 13. That a woman must not assume men’s clothing for the sake of continence. 14. That one who condemns marriage must not leave her husband. 15. That no one must neglect his children for the sake of continence. [Col. 0270A] 16. That children must not despise their parents on religious grounds. 17. That a woman may not shave her head. 18. That one must not fast on the Lord’s Day. 19. That the common fasts must not be dissolved. 20. That communion must be received in the basilicas of the martyrs.

# THE COUNCIL OF GANGRA BEGINS (In the year of the Lord 333, in Paphlagonia)

[Col. 0269]

[Col. 0269A] To the honorable lords and fellow priests, the bishops established in Armenia: Eusebius, Alpius, Philetus, Eulalius, Pappus, Basil, Bithynicus, Heratius, [Col. 0269B] Ipatius, Bassus, Eugenius, Gregory, Elianus, Pressius, and Eugenius, who assembled in the Council of Gangra: greetings in the Lord.

Since the holy synod of bishops assembled in the Church of Gangra to investigate certain ecclesiastical and necessary matters and to discern what had been done concerning Eustathius, it found many improper things being done by those who followed that same Eustathius. It therefore necessarily decreed that everything wrongly committed by him should be openly abolished before all.

For it was demonstrated that these people accused marriage and taught that no one living in the married state had hope before God. Consequently, many women were deceived and, abandoning their own husbands, while men were deprived of their wives, [Col. 0269C] dissolved the marital bond while professing continence; when they were unable to maintain it, they committed adultery.

They were also found teaching dissension and separation in the Lord’s churches—that is, that ecclesiastical traditions and the things done in churches should be despised—and, establishing private gatherings, presuming to celebrate everything in imitation of what is done in the house of God. They also rejected ordinary clothing and assumed new and unusual garments.

They claimed for themselves the firstfruits of produce and the offerings that the institution of the ancients assigned to the churches—that is, according to their own doctrinal system, as though these should be offered to them as holy persons and distributed among themselves. Slaves who withdrew from their masters, adopting this unusual religious appearance, despised their masters under the pretext of their religion.

Women likewise, contrary to custom and to the adornment proper to their sex, sought to justify themselves by believing that they had assumed men’s dress; and many of them, on religious grounds, completely cut off the hair that was their natural adornment. They asserted that the fasts preached in the Church should be despised.

Some also regarded certain foods, especially meat, as unlawful. They persuaded people that prayers ought not even to be celebrated in the houses of married persons, to such an extent that they forbade them to be held and decreed that no one should participate in offerings made in houses.

They say that presbyters who have contracted marriages ought to be despised, and that no one should touch the sacraments consecrated by them. They despise the places of the holy martyrs and the basilicas, and criticize all who gather there and celebrate the sacraments. They say that wealthy believers who do not renounce everything they possess have no hope before the Lord.

They also established many other things that no one can enumerate, each of them according to his own judgment. For each one of them departed from the ecclesiastical canon through such an institution, presuming to make laws for himself. Nor do they share one common and unified judgment. Each, as it seems and pleases him, strives to accuse the Church—as though there were no ruler—either adding to or diminishing the decrees.

For this reason, then, this council was convened and held in the Church of Gangra, to set forth these canons, by which the aforesaid persons are shown to be outside the Church. If they condemn through repentance all these things that they have wrongly believed, so that the teachings they improperly issued may be accepted as repudiated by them, the synod judged that each of the matters they ought to condemn should be explained to them.

But if anyone refuses what has been established today, he shall be rejected as a heretic, anathematized, and condemned. He shall be not only excommunicated but also expelled from the Church as an outcast, until he begs pardon from the bishops and determines, concerning all that has been found and exposed among them, which of these matters he has accepted and must observe.

### CHAPTER I

If anyone condemns marriage and regards a faithful and religious woman sleeping with her husband as abominable, or even condemns her on the grounds that married people cannot enter the kingdom of God, let him be anathema.

### II

If anyone believes that a person who eats meat, with faith and religious observance, apart from blood, meat sacrificed to an idol, and strangled meat, must be condemned as one without hope because he eats it, let him be anathema.

### III

If anyone teaches another man’s slave, on religious grounds, that he ought to despise his master and abandon his service, and does not instead teach him to serve his master in good faith and with all due honor, let him be anathema.

### IV

If anyone makes a distinction against a married presbyter, as though he ought not to offer because of his marriage, and for that reason abstains from his offering, let him be anathema.

### V

If anyone teaches that the house of God ought to be despised, together with the gatherings held in it, let him be anathema.

### VI

If anyone privately gathers people outside the Church and despises ecclesiastical sanctions, wishing to appropriate the things belonging to the Church in another manner, with a presbyter not approved in accordance with the bishop’s decree, and conducts the Church among them without the bishop’s counsel, let him be anathema.

### VII

If anyone wishes to receive or give outside the Church the offerings of fruits or firstfruits owed to the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, and does not think that these things should rather be done with that person’s counsel, let him be anathema.

### VIII

If anyone gives or receives offerings of fruits apart from the bishop or the person appointed by him to dispense mercy to the poor, both the giver and the receiver shall be anathema.

### IX

If anyone who has professed virginity or continence judges marriage abominable, and does not do so merely because the good of continence and virginity is a holy vocation, let him be anathema.

X. If anyone, having professed virginity for the Lord, arrogantly censures those living in marriage, let him be anathema.

XI. If anyone considers those who practice the agape—a communal meal—to be contemptible, and, because of the Lord’s honor, refuses to share in the gathering of poor brothers, treating their invitations and what is done as worthless, let him be anathema.

XII. If any man thinks that, for one devoted to the holy purpose—that is, continence—it is appropriate to wear a cloak as though he would thereby possess righteousness, and reproaches or judges others who reverently wear the birrus and other ordinary clothing in common use, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0271C] XIII. If any woman, judging it useful for her purpose to wear men’s clothing, changes herself into a man’s attire, let her be anathema.

XIV. If any woman wishes to leave her husband, dissolving the marital bond and condemning marriage, let her be anathema.

XV. If anyone abandons his own children, does not nourish them, and does not provide what piety requires, but under the pretext of continence considers them deserving of neglect, let him be anathema.

XVI. If any children abandon their especially faithful parents on the pretext of divine worship, judging this to be right, and do not rather render their parents the honor due to them, so as to venerate in them precisely the fact that they are faithful, let them be anathema.

[Col. 0271D] XVII. If any woman, judging that it accords with religious devotion, cuts off her hair, which God gave her as a covering and as a reminder of her subjection, as though thereby dissolving the law of subjection, let her be anathema.

[Col. 0272A] XVIII. If anyone, judging this to be appropriate, fasts on Sunday in contempt of that day, let him be anathema.

XIX. If anyone among those devoted to the purpose of continence grows proud beyond bodily necessity, and considers the common fasts of the entire Church contemptible, claiming in his own knowledge a perfect rationale, let him be anathema.

XX. If anyone, through pride and considering himself perfect, either accuses the assemblies held in various places and in the basilicas of the holy martyrs, or even believes that the offerings celebrated there ought to be scorned, and that the memorials of the saints ought to be held in contempt, let him be anathema.

XXI. We have written these things not to cut off those who, according to the Scriptures, choose the holy purpose of continence in the Church of God, but those who assume its distinctive dress and are lifted up in pride against those who live more simply. We also condemn those who exalt themselves against the Scriptures and the ecclesiastical canons and introduce new precepts.

We admire virginity with humility; we declare continence, joined with chastity and religious devotion, to be most acceptable to God; and we commend with approval the renunciation of secular affairs and activities when undertaken with humility. We honor the bond of marriage, which endures in accordance with chastity; we do not reject the wealthy when accompanied by justice and good works; and we do not condemn frugality with humble clothing. Likewise, apart from care for the body, we praise unstained adornment.

But we do not accept loose and dissolute comportment in dress. We honor the houses of God and receive the assemblies held in them as holy and beneficial, without confining ownership to private houses. We honor every place built in the name of God, and accept the gathering held in the church for the common benefit. We bless the good works performed according to one’s ability for poor brothers, in accordance with ecclesiastical traditions, and we desire that everything consistent with apostolic traditions and the precepts of the holy Scriptures be done in the Church.

[Col. 0272D] The Council of Gangra ends.

BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF SARDICA.

[Col. 0271]

[Col. 0271D] 1. That a bishop ought not to be transferred to another city. 2. That a bishop ought not to pass from one province to another unless he has been invited. 3. Concerning two bishops of one province who are in dispute with each other. 4. Concerning a bishop who has been judged. 5. Concerning bishops deposed by a synod. 6. Concerning the matters above. [Col. 0272D] 7. Concerning accused bishops. 8. That bishops should not indiscriminately go to the imperial court. 9. Concerning the matters above. 10. Concerning the matters above. 11. Concerning the matters above. 12. Concerning the matters above. 13. That no bishop should be ordained from among the laity. 14. That a bishop should not remain in another province. [Col. 0273A] 15. Concerning bishops who possess property in another province. 16. Concerning the excommunication of clerics. 17. That clerics, if they have been unjustly excommunicated, may approach neighboring bishops. 18. That a bishop may not ordain another bishop’s cleric in his own church. [Col. 0274A] 19. Concerning the matters above. 20. That foreign clerics should not be received at Thessalonica. 21. Clerics who have suffered violence or persecution, if they go to another city, are not to be forbidden to remain there as long as they are unable to return.

64 BEGIN THE COUNCIL OF SARDICA OF THREE HUNDRED BISHOPS. (In the year of the Lord 351, in Thrace.)

[Col. 0273]

[Col. 0273A] In the sixth year of the Emperor Constantine, during the consulship of Leontius and Sallustius, in the year 371 of the era, the Synod of Sardica was assembled. There all the Arian bishops throughout the East were condemned: when summoned to the council, they refused to attend, conscious of their guilt. At this council, among other matters, the following regulations were established for ecclesiastical discipline.

CHAPTER I. Bishop Hosius said: A bad custom no less than a pernicious corruption must be utterly eradicated, so that no bishop may be permitted to pass from his own city to another city. The reason why they attempt to do this is clear, since no bishop has ever been found in this matter to pass from a larger city to a smaller one. Hence it is evident that they are inflamed by greed and serve ambition, so that they may exercise domination.

If, therefore, it pleases everyone that this kind of destruction be punished more severely, and that such a person not even have lay communion, all replied: It pleases us. If, however, some such rash person should arise and perhaps offer the excuse that he had received letters from the people, although it is clear that a few people without sincere faith could have been corrupted by reward and payment to shout in the Church and appear to request that very man as bishop, we condemn these frauds as needing to be removed altogether, so that such a person may not receive even lay communion to the end of his life. If this pleases all of you, establish it.

All replied: It pleases us.

II. Bishop Hosius said: Let this also be established: a bishop must not pass from his own province to another province in which there are bishops, unless perhaps he has been invited by the brothers, lest we seem to close the door of charity.

III. Bishop Hosius said: Provision must also be made that, if in some province a bishop should happen to have a dispute with another bishop, neither of the two should summon bishops from another province to judge the case.

IV. Bishop Hosius said: If a bishop has been judged in some case and thinks that he has a good cause, so that the judgment may be reopened, if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the holy Apostle Peter. Let a letter be written either by those who examined the case or by other bishops who reside in the province near the Roman bishop. If he judges that the case ought to be reheard, let it be recalled and let him appoint judges. But if he determines that the case is such that what has been done should not be reopened, whatever the Roman bishop decrees shall be confirmed. If, therefore, this pleases everyone, let it be established.

The synod replied: It pleases us.

V. Bishop Gaudentius said: If it pleases you, this should be added to the sentence you have pronounced with complete holiness: when a bishop has been deposed, and he appeals to the judgment of those bishops who reside in neighboring places and declares that his case ought to be heard in the city of Rome, another bishop must absolutely not be ordained to the same see after the appeal of the one who is considered deposed, unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.

VI. Bishop Hosius said: If it should happen that in one province containing many bishops only one bishop remains, and through negligence he refuses to ordain a bishop, while the people summon bishops from a neighboring province, they must first approach the bishop who resides in that same province and show him that the people are asking for a ruler, and that it is right for those bishops themselves to come and ordain a bishop together with him.

But if, after being summoned by letter, he remains silent, dissimulates, and gives no answer, then the people must be satisfied: bishops are to come from neighboring provinces and ordain a bishop. Permission to ordain a bishop must not, however, be granted indiscriminately. For if suddenly some village, or a small city for which one presbyter is sufficient, wishes to have a bishop ordained for it, so that the name of bishop and the authority of the highest dignity may be cheapened, those invited from another province ought not to make him a bishop, except in cities that have had bishops, or in a city so populous, or a place so deserving, that it merits having a bishop.

The synod replied: It pleases us.

VII. Bishop Hosius said: It has also pleased us that, if a bishop has been accused, and all the assembled bishops of that region have judged and expelled him from his rank, then, if the one who appears to have been deposed appeals and flees to the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church and wishes to be heard, the Roman bishop, if he considers renewal of the examination just, should deign to write to the bishops in a neighboring and adjoining province, so that they themselves may carefully investigate everything and determine everything according to the truth of the faith.

If the one who requests that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his entreaty, so that he sends presbyters from his own side, it shall be in the Roman bishop’s power to decide what he wishes and what he judges appropriate. If he decrees that they should be sent to judge in the presence of the bishops, they shall also possess the authority of the person by whom they were sent; this shall be at his discretion. But if he believes that the provincial bishops are sufficient to bring the case to an end, he shall do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.

VIII. Bishop Hosius said: The excessive frequency of our importunities and our unjust petitions have caused us not to possess as much favor or confidence as we should, since certain bishops—especially the Africans—do not cease going to the imperial court. As we have learned, they scorn and disregard the salutary counsels of our most holy brother and fellow bishop.

They bring to the imperial court not only many different cases that will not benefit the Church, instead of doing what is customary and proper—providing aid to the poor, widows, or orphans—but also request secular dignities and administrative offices for various people. This depravity has long stirred up not only murmuring but also scandals.

It is honorable for a bishop to offer his intercession to those who are oppressed by some unjust force, or if a widow is afflicted, or an orphan despoiled—provided, nevertheless, that all these matters have a just cause and petition. If this therefore pleases you, dearest brothers, decree that bishops may not approach the imperial court unless they have been invited or summoned by letters of the most religious emperor.

Since, however, it often happens that those who suffer injustice, and those who, because of their sins, are condemned to exile or to the islands, or certainly receive any other sentence, flee to the mercy of the Church, assistance must therefore be given to them, and forgiveness must unquestionably be sought for them through the Church. If this pleases you, let it be established.

All replied: It pleases us, and let it be established.

IX. Bishop Hosius said: Your prudence must also consider this. Since you have decreed that bishops should not incur the reproach of misconduct by going to the imperial court, anyone who has or receives any of the petitions mentioned above should send it through his deacon, because the person of the minister will not be subject to envy and will be able to return more quickly with whatever he has obtained.

It also seems appropriate that everyone who has a petition should send it to our brothers and fellow bishops who reside in the chief city—that is, in the metropolitan city—and that they should send it through their deacons, providing letters of recommendation in the same manner to our brothers and fellow bishops who at that time reside in those regions and cities in which the fortunate and blessed Augustus governs the state.

If any bishop has friends at court through whom he wishes to obtain something that is nevertheless honorable, he should not be forbidden to ask them through his deacon and to inform those whom he knows can, through kindly intercession, assist him in his absence.

But whoever comes to Rome should, as has been said, deliver the petitions he has to our most holy brother and fellow bishop of the Roman Church, so that he may first examine whether they are honorable and just, and may take care and responsibility for having them conveyed to the imperial court.

All replied: It pleases us.

[Col. 0276A] X. Bishop Aliphius said: If they undertake the hardships of travel on behalf of orphans and widows, or of people who are suffering and have just causes, they will have some reasonable justification. But when they seek things that cannot be free from everyone’s envy and criticism, it is not necessary for them to go to the imperial court.

XI. Bishop Gaudentius said: The measures you have wisely provided, appropriate to sound judgment and pleasing both to God and to human beings, can retain their force only if fear is joined to this decision. We ourselves know that, very often, because of the imprudence of a few, the sacred and religious name of the priesthood has been criticized.

If, therefore, anyone appears to prefer ambition to God, contrary to the judgment of all, he must know that, once the reasons have been given, he will lose his honor and dignity. This can be learned and discovered if each of us who is stationed at the checkpoint, when he sees a bishop passing through, investigates his journey, examines his reasons, and learns where he is going.

If he discovers that the bishop is going to the imperial court, he should inquire about the matter stated above, lest the man perhaps have been invited and thus be permitted to go. But if, as your holiness mentioned above, he has attempted to go to the imperial court because of desires and ambitions, his letters must neither be signed nor he himself received into communion.

If this pleases you, it must be confirmed by the judgment of all.

All replied: This is honorable and the decree pleases us.

[Col. 0276C] XII. Bishop Hosius said: Moderation is also necessary, dearest brothers, lest some who do not yet know what has been decreed in the synod suddenly arrive at the cities situated along the route. The bishop of that city must admonish and instruct him; from that place the man must send a deacon, while he himself, having been admonished, must return to his own parish.

XIII. Bishop Hosius said: I think you must consider most carefully that, if a wealthy man, a legal scholar from the forum, or someone from an administrative office is sought for the episcopate, he is not to be ordained until he has first served in the office of reader and in the ministries of deacon and presbyter.

He should thus ascend through each rank, if he is worthy, to the summit of the episcopate. Through these promotions, which necessarily require a considerable period of time, it is possible to test what his faith, moderation, seriousness, and modesty are like. If he is worthy, once tested, let him be honored with the divine priesthood.

For it is neither fitting nor permitted by the discipline of reason that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who is a neophyte should be ordained rashly and lightly, especially since the most blessed Apostle, the teacher of the nations, appears to have announced and forbidden that this should happen. Rather, those should be ordained whose lives have been examined over a long period and whose merits have been proved.

All replied that these provisions pleased them.

XIV. Bishop Hosius said: You must also establish this: when a bishop comes from one city to another, or from his own province to another province, and serves ambition more than devotion, so that he wishes to reside for a long time in a foreign city, and it happens that the bishop of that city is not so well instructed or learned, while the newcomer begins to despise him and frequently preaches in order to dishonor and disfigure his reputation, [65] it may happen that the newcomer does not hesitate to abandon the church assigned to him and transfer to another.

Therefore set a definite period, because it is inhuman not to receive a bishop, while it is harmful for him to remain too long. Provision must therefore be made that this does not happen.

I remember that at an earlier council our brothers established that, if a layman in the city where he lives did not hold the assembly of communion for three Sundays—that is, for three weeks—he should be deprived of communion. If such provisions have been made concerning laymen, how much more is it neither permitted nor fitting for a bishop to be absent from his church for so long, even if he has a very serious necessity or an exceptionally difficult reason, lest he distress the people.

All replied that this pleased them.

XV. Bishop Hosius said: Since nothing ought to be omitted, there are certain brothers and fellow bishops of ours who do not reside in the city in which they appear to have been established as bishops. Alternatively, they are known to have only a small property there, while possessing suitable estates elsewhere, or they have the concerns of relatives whom they indulge.

They should therefore be permitted to visit their possessions and arrange or manage the produce of their labor. After three Sundays—that is, after three weeks—if it is necessary for them to remain, they should stay preferably on their own estates. If there is a nearby city in which there is a presbyter, so that they may not appear to be without a church on Sunday, they should go there, so that their domestic affairs do not suffer loss through their absence.

By coming frequently to another city in which there is a bishop, they should not incur suspicion of ostentation and ambition.

All replied that this pleased them.

XVI. Bishop Hosius said: If this also pleases everyone, then, whether a deacon, presbyter, or any cleric has been deprived of communion by his own bishop and has gone to another bishop, if the bishop to whom he has fled knows that he was expelled by his own bishop, he ought not to grant him communion. If he does so, let him know that he will have to give an account of the matter when the bishops have been convened.

All replied: This provision will preserve peace and safeguard harmony.

XVII. Bishop Hosius said: I must not remain silent about what still troubles me. If some bishop should happen to be irascible—as he ought not to be—and should quickly or harshly become angry with his presbyter or deacon, and wish to expel him from the church, provision must be made lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion.

Therefore, let the one who has been expelled have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and examined more carefully, since a hearing ought not to be denied to one who requests it. Let the bishop who expelled him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept that the matter be examined, so that his judgment may either be confirmed by the majority or corrected.

Nevertheless, before everything has been carefully and faithfully examined, no other person should presume to receive into communion or associate with communion anyone who has been separated from communion.

If those who have assembled to hear the case observe arrogance and pride in the clerics, it is not fitting that a bishop should suffer insult or abuse. They should correct them with sterner words, so that they obey the bishop when he gives honorable commands. For just as the bishop ought to show the clerics sincere love and charity, so likewise the ministers ought to offer their bishop unstained obedience.

XVIII. Bishop Januarius said: Let your holiness also establish this: no bishop may solicit the ecclesiastical minister of another bishop’s city in order to ordain that cleric in his own diocese, because discord commonly arises from such disputes. Therefore let the judgment of all forbid anyone to dare to do this.

XIX. Bishop Hosius said: We have all also established this: if anyone from another parish wishes to ordain another’s minister without the consent and without the will of that bishop, his ordination shall not be valid. Whoever usurps this authority must be admonished and corrected by our brothers and fellow bishops.

XX. Bishop Cletitius said: You are not unaware of how great and important the city of Thessalonica is. Presbyters and deacons often come there from other regions, and they are not content to remain or reside there for a short time; alternatively, they are compelled to return to their own places only after long intervals.

All replied: The periods established concerning bishops must also be observed with regard to these men.

XXI. Bishop Hosius said: At the suggestion of our brother and fellow bishop Olympius, this also has pleased us: if anyone has suffered violence and has been unjustly driven out for the sake of discipline, or in defense of the Catholic faith, or while confessing the truth, and, fleeing danger as an innocent person, has come to another city, he must not be forbidden to remain there for as long as he is unable either to return or to obtain a remedy for his injury.

For it is harsh not to receive one who is suffering persecution. Generous benevolence and kindness must also be shown to him.

BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF ANTIOCH.

[Col. 0277]

[Col. 0277D] 1. That Easter may not be celebrated at a different time or celebrated together with the Jews. 2. That the communion of the Church may not be despised, nor communion be shared with the excommunicated. [Col. 0278D] 3. That a cleric who migrates to another church may not remain there. 4. That a bishop or any cleric who has been deposed may not exercise ministry. [Col. 0279A] 5. That clerics may not gather separately after despising their bishop. 6. Concerning the excommunicated. 7. That no foreigner may be received without the bishops. 8. That letters be issued only by a fellow bishop. 9. Concerning metropolitan bishops. 10. Concerning fellow bishops. 11. Concerning those bishops or clerics who go to the emperor without letters from the bishops. 12. Concerning deposed bishops or clerics. 13. That bishops may not ordain clerics in another province. 14. Concerning accused bishops. 15. Concerning the matters above. 16. Concerning vacant sees. [Col. 0280A] 17. Concerning bishops who, after receiving the laying on of hands, do not agree to undertake the ministry. 18. Concerning the matters above. 19. That no bishop may be ordained without the counsel of the metropolitan bishop. 20. That a synod be held twice a year. 21. That a bishop ought not to pass from one diocese to another. 22. That a bishop ought not to intrude into another’s city. 23. That a bishop may not appoint his own successor. 24. Concerning ecclesiastical and episcopal property. 25. That a bishop has authority to dispose of ecclesiastical property.

BEGIN THE COUNCIL OF ANTIOCH.

[Col. 0279]

[Col. 0279B] The holy and most peaceful synod, assembled as one, sends greetings in the Lord to the unanimous holy bishops and fellow priests throughout the individual provinces.

The grace and truth of Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior, visiting the holy Church of Antioch and joining it together through the harmony of the most peaceful spirit, has accomplished many things and others besides. In every respect, however, through the prompting of the holy and peaceful Spirit, it has also accomplished this: that the matters which, after extensive consideration and judgment, appeared rightly established should be brought to your knowledge together with all of us, the bishops gathered here at Antioch from different provinces.

We trust in the grace of the Lord and in the Holy Spirit of peace that you will join with us as though you had been gathered into one power, striving with us in prayer and being strengthened all the more by the presence of the Holy Spirit. If you consent to the very decisions that have been defined and strengthen by your agreement those matters that appeared right, you will seal them with the assent of the Holy Spirit.

The ecclesiastical canons established in advance are those written below, promulgated by the bishops listed here: Eusebius, Archelaus, Aeneas, Macedonius, Nicetas, Esicius, Bassus, Antiochus, Jacobus, Moses, Agaphius, Peter, Mocinius, Alexander, Narcissus, Etherius, Patricius, Siricius, Magnus, Paul, Eustachius, Manicius, Peter, Paul, Theurus, Municius, Aliphius, Peter, Tarcodunantus, Anatholius, Theodorus, Alius, Theurus, and Sirion.

From the provinces of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, Arabia, and Mesopotamia, they established these provisions written below.

[Col. 0279D] CHAPTER I. All who dare to dissolve the rule of the holy and great Council of Nicaea, held in the presence of the most God-loving Emperor Constantine, concerning the holy and saving feast of Easter of our Savior, must be excommunicated and cast out from the Church, especially if they persist out of a spirit of contention in overturning what has been most rightly established.

These statements concern laypeople. But if any of those who preside over the Church—that is, a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—after this definition and this fixed rule should dare, for the subversion of the people and the disturbance of the Churches, to gather separately and wish to celebrate Easter with the Jews, the holy synod will judge him already alien from the Church, as one guilty not only of his own sin but also as having become a corrupter and subverter of others whose minds have been led astray.

The synod commands not only that such a person be deposed from the priesthood and ministry, but also that those who dare to associate with him after his condemnation be deposed. Those who have been deposed must also be deprived of the external honor they had earned through the holy canon and the priesthood of God.

II. All who enter the Church of God and hear the holy Scriptures, but do not join the people in prayer, and who, because of some personal discipline, reject the holy reception of the Lord’s sacrament, must be cast out of the church until, after confessing, they show the fruits of repentance and, having made their supplication, deserve to be received once pardon has been granted.

It is not permitted to share communion with the excommunicated, nor to enter houses with them and pray with them, since those who belong to the Church participate in prayer. Nor may one who has been excommunicated by one church be received into another church.

If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or even anyone enrolled among the clergy is discovered to be sharing communion with the excommunicated, he too must be deprived of communion, as one who confuses the rules of the Church.

III. If any presbyter, deacon, or any cleric thinks that he ought to abandon his own church and transfer to another, and there gradually attempts to remain permanently in the place to which he has migrated, he must not exercise ministry, especially if his own bishop has urged him to return.

If, after being recalled by his bishop, he does not obey but persists in disobedience, he must be deposed from his office altogether and must never retain hope of restoration. If another bishop receives someone deposed for this fault, he too will deserve punishment from the common synod, as one who dissolves ecclesiastical rights.

IV. If a bishop has been deposed by a synod, or a presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, and presumes to undertake anything pertaining to the priesthood or the sacred mystery, he is no longer permitted to do so; nor may he have hope of restoration in another synod or any opportunity to make a defense. All who communicate with him must also be cast out of the Church, especially if, after learning that a sentence had been pronounced against him, they have stubbornly continued to communicate with him.

66 V. If any presbyter or deacon, despising his bishop, separates himself from the Church and dares to set up a private altar for himself among the people he has gathered, and nevertheless remains disobedient even when his bishop exhorts him and recalls him once and again, he must be deposed by every means and must not hope ever to obtain healing or regain his proper honor. If he also persists, disturbing the entire Church outside, he must be corrected as a seditious person.

VI. If anyone has been excommunicated by his own bishop, he must not first be received by others unless he has either been received by his own bishop or appears before a council convened by the bishops and gives an account. If he satisfies the synod, we establish that he is to be received under a different sentence. This rule is likewise to be observed concerning laypeople, presbyters, deacons, and all who belong to the clergy.

VII. No foreign cleric is to be received without a *formata*—which the Greeks call an epistle.

VIII. Nor may a presbyter presume to send *formatae*, that is, canonical letters, to distant regions, except simple letters to neighboring bishops. But bishops' vicars, whom the Greeks call fellow bishops, may issue *formatae*.

IX. In each province, every bishop ought to know that the metropolitan bishop, who presides, has undertaken the care and oversight of the entire province. Therefore those who have cases should go to the metropolitan city.

Accordingly, it has pleased us that he should surpass the others in honor, and that the remaining bishops should do nothing beyond what belongs to each church in its own diocese without the metropolitan bishop, in accordance with the ancient canon of our fathers.

Each bishop ought to have authority over his own diocese, so that he may rule and govern it with the respect appropriate to each person and exercise care over the entire region subject to his city. Thus he may also ordain presbyters and deacons by a sound judgment and deliberate with moderation and gravity concerning the individual cases of that region.

Beyond this, however, he is permitted to do nothing without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop; nor may the metropolitan undertake anything without the counsel of the other priests.

X. The fellow bishops who have received the laying on of hands from bishops and have been consecrated as bishops shall nevertheless, it has pleased the holy synod, retain their proper limits, govern the neighboring cities assigned to them, and be content with the care and governance they have received.

They may appoint readers, subdeacons, and exorcists, who need receive permission only for these ranks. But they must not dare to ordain a presbyter or deacon without the knowledge of the bishop of the city or church adjacent to which they are situated, whether that means the city itself or the region over which they are recognized as presiding.

If anyone dares to violate these decisions, he must be deposed and deprived of the dignity with which he is endowed. A fellow bishop, however, must be ordained by the bishop of the city or place to which he is adjacent.

XI. If any bishop, presbyter, or indeed anyone established under ecclesiastical rule goes to the emperor without the counsel or letters of the bishops within the province, especially those of the metropolitan, he must be repudiated and expelled, deprived not only of communion but also of his own dignity, as one troublesome and importunate to imperial ears and acting contrary to ecclesiastical regulations.

If necessity compels him to go to the emperor concerning some matter, he must go with the deliberation and counsel of the metropolitan bishop of that province, with the knowledge of the other bishops in the same province, and with their letters.

XII. If a presbyter or deacon deposed by his own bishop, or any bishop deprived of office by a synod, presumes to trouble imperial ears, he must instead turn to a greater synod of bishops, present in their council the just claims he thinks he possesses, and await from them whatever judgment is pronounced concerning him.

If, overcome by weakness of spirit, he refuses to do this and becomes importunate with the emperor, he shall receive no pardon, no opportunity to make that defense of his, and no hope of recovering his rank in the future.

XIII. No bishop may dare to pass from one province to another to ordain anyone for the churches or admit anyone to sacred ministry, nor may he bring other bishops there, unless he has gone after being requested by letter—not only by the metropolitan but also by all the bishops of that province who are with him.

If he arrives disorderly, without being invited, and presumes either to ordain anyone or to usurp any acts belonging to that church, which in no way pertain to him, everything he has done shall be void and empty. He himself, however, must answer for the fitting consequences of this undisciplined and irrational undertaking, as one deposed by the holy synod and already condemned for such presumption.

XIV. If anyone is accused in the judgment of the bishops concerning criminal charges, and it happens that the bishops of the province who have assembled hold differing opinions—some declaring him innocent and others guilty—then, to remove such controversy, it has pleased the holy synod that the metropolitan bishop of another neighboring province be summoned, together with several other bishops.

After sitting together, they shall settle whatever questions arise, so that the judgment promulgated by the bishops of one province may be firm.

XV. If a bishop criminally accused has received one unanimous judgment from all the bishops within the province, he may not be judged further by others. The unanimous judgment pronounced by all must remain against him as a fitting, firm, and valid sentence.

### XVI

If a bishop without a see comes upon a vacant church and thinks that he may seize and occupy it precipitously without a plenary synod, he must be expelled, even if the people whom he has plundered wish to retain him as their bishop. A plenary synod is one at which the metropolitan bishop is also present.

[Col. 0283B] XVII. If a bishop, after receiving the laying-on of hands and being appointed to preside over a people, does not undertake the priestly ministry or consent to take possession of the church in which he was ordained, he must be excluded from communion until he is compelled to consent to accept the people assigned to him, or until the province’s plenary synod makes some decision concerning him.

XVIII. If an ordained bishop does not go to the parish for which he was ordained—not through his own fault, but perhaps because of opposition from the people—he must retain the honor he has received and exercise the priesthood, provided that he causes no trouble to the church in which he had been established. He must await the province’s plenary synod until a decision is made concerning what is appropriate for him.

XIX. A bishop must not be ordained without the counsel and presence of the metropolitan bishop; it would be preferable for the bishops of the entire province to assemble. If this cannot be done, those who are unable to be present must indicate their consent concerning him in letters of their own; only then, after the concordant judgment of the majority, whether expressed by presence or by letters, may he be ordained. If it is done otherwise than has been established, such an ordination shall have no validity. But if the ordination is celebrated according to the prescribed rules and some object because of their own private and domestic quarrels, the judgment of the majority shall prevail over them.

XX. For ecclesiastical matters and for resolving disputes that arise, it has seemed sufficient that a council of bishops be held twice each year in each province. Once, after the third week of the Paschal festival, so that it may be completed in the following fourth week—that is, at mid-Pentecost. The provincial bishops are to be summoned by those who live in the cities, that is, in the metropolitan cities. The second council is to be held on the Ides of October, which among the Greeks is found to be the tenth month, Hyperberetaeus. At these councils, presbyters and deacons must also be present, as well as all who consider themselves injured and who await the synodical judgment. No one may hold councils privately without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishops, to whom jurisdiction over all matters is known to have been granted.

XXI. A bishop must not pass from one diocese to another, whether he intrudes on his own initiative, is forcibly drawn by the people, or is even persuaded to do so by bishops. He must remain in the church of God which he received by lot from the beginning and must not migrate elsewhere, in accordance with the rule formerly established by the Fathers on this matter.

XXII. A bishop must not invade another province that is demonstrably not subject to him, nor enter a region known not to belong to his care in order to ordain anyone; nor may he appoint presbyters or deacons belonging to other bishops, unless perhaps with the consent and testimony of the bishop of the region concerned. If anyone should wish to do such a thing, the ordination shall be invalid, and he shall be censured by the synod for what he has wrongly usurped. For if he is unable to ordain, he must under no circumstances presume to judge another’s parishioner.

XXIII. A bishop must not appoint another as his future successor, even when he is thought to be near death. If anything of this kind has been done, the ordination shall be invalid. He must observe the ecclesiastical constitutions, which provide that a bishop cannot be appointed otherwise than through the counsel and consent of those bishops alone who, after the death of the predecessor, have authority to advance the one who is worthy.

[Col. 0284C] XXIV. Whatever possessions belong to the Church must be administered and distributed with every care and in the good faith owed to God, who provides for and judges all things, and under the judgment and authority of the bishop, to whom the souls of the entire people appear to have been entrusted. The things belonging to the Church must be made known, with the knowledge of the presbyters and deacons who are around him, so that they may not be ignorant and so that none of those who belong to the Church may be kept unaware of anything. Thus, if the bishop should depart this life, the ecclesiastical possessions will be manifest and known, lest they be lost and perish. Nor should the bishop’s private property be attacked by anyone as though, because of its association with ecclesiastical property, it were liable to seizure. For it is just and acceptable to God and to human beings that the bishop’s private possessions be left to those whom he himself has designated, while those belonging to the Church are reserved for the Church. In this way neither will the Church suffer any loss, nor will the bishop be proscribed on account of ecclesiastical possessions, nor will matters belonging to him be brought against him, nor will his memory after death be burdened with any curses.

67 XXV. A bishop must have authority over ecclesiastical possessions, so that he may distribute them to all who are in need with complete fear and reverence of God. He himself may also receive from them and use what he requires, if indeed he requires it, either for his necessary expenses or for the brothers who stay with him for the sake of hospitality, so that they may not be deprived through want in any respect, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Having daily food and bodily clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8). But if he is not content with or satisfied by these things, and transfers ecclesiastical possessions or any of the Church’s resources to his own needs, or gathers the produce of ecclesiastical lands for himself without the knowledge of the presbyters, and grants control of such things to his household, relatives, brothers, or their children, so that through their secret management ecclesiastical interests appear to be harmed, he must render an account of this offense before the metropolitan of the province.

If a bishop, or the presbyters who are with him, is accused in this way—namely, that they are said to appropriate to themselves what belongs to the Church, whether lands or any other ecclesiastical possessions, while the poor are oppressed by need and poverty, and that as a result not only the Church’s accounts but also its administrators are subjected to increased blame and reproach—he must receive the correction he deserves, with the holy synod also taking cognizance of the matter.

Eusebius was present and wrote down all that had been established. Theodorus, Nicetas, Macedonius, Anatolius, Marcodunanetus, Atherius, Narcissus, Eustachius, Esichius, Manicius, Paulus, and the others, whose names are already given above in Greek, consented and subscribed.

The Council of Antioch ends here.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF LAODICEA BEGIN

[Col. 0285]

[Col. 0285B] 1. On bigamists. 2. On those who fall into various sins. 3. On neophytes not to be promoted to the priesthood. 4. Clerics must not be ordained in the presence of catechumens. 5. Clerics may not take interest or “sixfold” profit. 6. Heretics who remain in heresy must not enter the church. 7. On Novatians and Quartodecimans. 8. On Cataphrygians coming to the Church. 9. Catholics must not enter places called the martyria of heretics. 10. A Catholic woman must not be joined in marriage to a heretic. 11. On the Church’s catechumens.

[Col. 0285C] 12. On bishops to be ordained with the counsel of the metropolitan and neighboring bishops. 13. The people may not choose altar ministers. 14.
