Holy offerings must not be sent to other parishes as blessings during the Paschal festival. 15. On psalmists. 16. The holy Gospel is to be read on Saturdays. 17. Psalms must not be confused by being joined together indiscriminately. 18. On daily prayers. 19. On the order of the prayers of catechumens and the faithful, and on communion. 20. On the discipline and conduct of clerics. 21. On the ministry of subdeacons. 22. Ministers must not use the orarium. 23. Readers and psalmists must not use the orarium and read in that manner. 24. Readers and psalmists must not enter taverns. 25. Ministers may not give bread or bless the cup. 26. On exorcists. 27. Clerics or laypeople invited to the agape must not carry away portions. 28. Reclining couches must not be set up or an agape held in churches. 29. Christians must not observe the Sabbath as Jews do.

[Col. 0286B] 30. No Christian may bathe with women. 31. On avoiding marriages with heretics. 32. Blessings must not be received from heretics. 33. One must not pray with heretics or schismatics. 34. No one must go to false martyrs. 35. Christians must not abandon the church and gather at corner assemblies. 36. Clerics may not be magicians or enchanters, or make amulets. 37. Festal gifts sent by heretics or Jews must not be received. 38. Unleavened bread must not be received from Jews. 39. Festivals must not be celebrated with pagans. 40. Bishops summoned to synod must not show contempt. 41. No cleric or layperson may travel without the bishops. 42. No cleric may travel or receive a letter of commendation without his bishop’s order. 43. Ministers must not leave the doors. 44. No one may be received for baptism during the two weeks of Lent. 45. A woman must not enter the altar. 46. Those to be baptized must learn and recite the creed. 47. On those baptized in sickness. 48. The baptized must be anointed after baptism. 49. During Lent, offerings are to be made only on Saturday and Sunday. 50. The Thursday of the week of the greater fast may not be exempted from fasting. 51. During Lent, the birthdays of martyrs are to be celebrated only on Saturday and Sunday. 52. Weddings may not be celebrated during Lent. 53. Christians going to weddings may not sing or dance. 54. Altar ministers and any other persons may not attend spectacles presented at weddings or in theaters.

[Col. 0287A] 55. A cleric or Christian layperson must not celebrate banquets from associations. 56. Presbyters must not enter before the bishop or sit on tribunals. 57. Bishops must not be ordained in villages or rural districts, nor may presbyters do anything without the bishop’s command or counsel.

[Col. 0288A] 58. Offerings must not be made by bishops or presbyters in private houses. 59. Psalms composed by ignorant persons must not be sung in church, nor may books that are not canonical be read.

## THE COUNCIL OF LAODICEA BEGINS

[Col. 0287]

[Col. 0287A] The holy synod, which assembled at Laodicea of Phrygia Pacatiana from various provinces of Asia, set forth ecclesiastical rules, as written below.

### Chapter I

On the requirement, according to the ecclesiastical canon, that those who have been freely and lawfully joined in a second marriage and have not engaged in secret sexual relations should devote a short period to prayers and fasts, and that communion should be restored to them according to mercy.

### II

Those who fall into various sins and demonstrate, through prayer, confession, and repentance for their evils, a complete conversion of life are to be assigned a period of repentance according to the nature of the sin, because of God’s mercy and goodness. Those who are such are therefore to be recalled and admitted to communion.

### III

A neophyte must not be promoted to the priestly order.

### IV

The laying-on of hands for those being ordained must not take place in the presence of catechumens.

[Col. 0287C] V. Ministers of the altar and those established in the priestly order may not lend at interest or receive interest or profits called “sixfold.”

VI. Heretics who remain in heresy must not be granted entry into the house of God.

VII. Novatians, and likewise Quartodecimans—whom the Greeks call *Thesserescedecatires*, that is, those who celebrate Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the first month—and their faithful catechumens must not be received until they condemn every heresy in which they were held. Above all, those who are now called faithful among them must first be fully instructed in the creed; then it is appropriate that, after being anointed with holy chrism, they should share in the divine sacrament.

VIII. Those who convert from the heresy called [Col. 0287D] the Cataphrygian heresy, who consider themselves established in the clergy, even if they are said to be prominent, must be carefully catechized and baptized by the bishops and presbyters of the Catholic Church.

IX. Catholics must not enter cemeteries or places called the martyria of heretics for the sake of prayer or to seek healing. Those who have gone there, if they are faithful, must be excluded from communion and subjected to repentance for a certain period; but those who repent and confess that they have erred must be received.

X. Women whom the Greeks call *presbyterae*, but whom you call widows, elder single-husband women, or *matricuriae*, must not be established in the Church as though they were ordained officials.

[Col. 0288A] XI. Those who belong to the Church must not indiscriminately join their own children in marriage with heretics.

XII. A bishop must not be appointed to rule a church apart from the judgment of the metropolitan and neighboring bishops, nor may anyone be chosen except those whose life, long beforehand, has commended them as tested and reputable. They must likewise have been proved in the speech of faith and in right conduct through their manner of life.

XIII. On the principle that the people must not be granted the choice of those who are to be assigned to the ministry of the altar.

XIV. Holy offerings must not be sent to other parishes as blessings during the Paschal festival.

XV. No one may sing in church except the canonical singers, those regularly appointed who ascend the pulpit and read from a book.

[Col. 0288C] XVI. We decree that the Gospels are to be read on Saturdays together with the other Scriptures.

XVII. During processions, different verses and meanings from the book must not be joined together into a single song. Rather, the reading of each individual psalm must be carried out in an orderly manner.

68 XVIII. Supplications and prayers must always be celebrated at the ninth hour and at evening.

XIX. The bishop must first celebrate separately the prayer of the catechumens, after they have prostrated themselves. When they have departed, those who are undergoing repentance shall also pray. After the laying-on of hands, when these too have withdrawn, the faithful must then pray. Three prayers are to be made for them: the first in silence, and the second and third aloud. Only then are they to give the kiss of peace. After the presbyters have given peace to the bishop, the laity are also to give it, and then the offering is to be presented. Only altar ministers may enter the altar and communicate there.

XX. A deacon must not sit before a presbyter, but must sit at the presbyter’s command. Likewise, the deacon is to be honored by the lower ministers and by all the clerics.

XXI. Subdeacons must not have permission to enter the *secretarium* or *sacrarium*—which the Greeks call the *diaconicon*—or to touch the Lord’s vessels.

[Col. 0289A] XXII. A minister must not use an orarium or leave the doors.

XXIII. Readers and psalmists must not use an orarium and read or sing in that manner.

XXIV. Clerics serving from the presbyterate down to the diaconate, and thereafter all the ecclesiastical orders down to ministers, readers, psalmists, exorcists, doorkeepers, and even those who have adopted a life of continence, must not enter taverns.

XXV. A deacon must not give bread or bless the cup.

XXVI. Therefore, those who have not yet been advanced by the bishops must not perform exorcisms, either in churches or within houses.

[Col. 0289B] XXVII. Altar ministers or any ecclesiastics invited to an agape must not carry away portions, because of the dishonor that on this account might be attributed to the ecclesiastical order.

XXVIII. An agape must not be held in basilicas or churches, nor may people eat inside or set up reclining couches.

XXIX. Christians must not Judaize and cease work on the Sabbath, but must work on that day, giving precedence to the Lord’s Day. If they wish, they may rest as Christians. But if they are found Judaizing, let them be anathema.

XXX. Altar ministers, clerics of any kind, those practicing continence, and indeed every Christian must not share baths with women. For among the Gentiles this is the first reproach.

XXXI. One must not contract marriages with heretics, nor give sons or daughters to them, but rather receive them, provided that they profess that they will become Christians and Catholics.

XXXII. One must not receive blessings from heretics, since they are curses rather than blessings.

XXXIII. One must not pray with heretics or schismatics.

XXXIV. A Christian must not abandon the martyrs of Christ and go to false martyrs, for these are alien to God. Whoever wishes to go there, let him be anathema.

XXXV. Christians must not abandon the Church of God and go off to corners to form assemblies of detestable idolatry, all of which are forbidden. Whoever is found secretly devoting himself to this idolatry, let him be anathema, because, abandoning our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, he has approached idols.

XXXVI. Altar ministers and clerics must not be magicians or enchanters, nor make what are called *phylacteria*, which are great bonds of souls. We have ordered that those who use such things be expelled from the Church.

XXXVII. One must not accept from Jews or heretics the holiday gifts that are sent, nor celebrate holidays with them.

XXXVIII. One must not receive unleavened bread from Jews or share in their impieties.

XXXIX. One must not celebrate festivals with pagans or have fellowship in their impieties.

XL. Bishops summoned to synod must not show contempt, but must go and either teach or be taught what is useful for the correction of the Church and of the others. If a bishop treats this with contempt, he appears to have accused himself, unless perhaps he is unable to go because of illness.

XLI. An altar minister or even a layperson must not depart anywhere without canonical letters, that is, a *formata*.

[Col. 0290B] XLII. An altar minister or any cleric must not depart on a journey without the bishop’s command.

XLIII. Ministers—that is, doorkeepers—must not be absent from the doors, even for a short time, in order to devote themselves to prayer.

XLIV. No one may be received for baptism after the second week of Lent.

XLV. Women must not enter the altar.

XLVI. Those to be baptized must learn the creed and recite it on the Thursday of the final week to either the bishop or the presbyter.

XLVII. Those who received baptism while ill, once they have recovered, must be taught the creed, so that they may know with what gift they have been deemed worthy.

[Col. 0290C] XLVIII. Those who have been baptized must receive the most holy chrism after baptism and become participants in the heavenly kingdom.

XLIX. During Lent, bread must be offered only on Saturday and Sunday.

L. During Lent, on the Thursday of the final week, the fast must not be broken and the whole of Lent dishonored. Rather, they must fast throughout all the days and use foods suitable for abstinence, that is, drier foods.

LI. During Lent, the birthdays of the martyrs must not be celebrated; their commemoration is to be made only on Saturday and Sunday.

LII. During Lent, neither weddings nor any birthdays or festival celebrations may be held.

[Col. 0290D] LIII. Christians going to weddings must neither dance nor perform dances; it is appropriate for Christians to dine or eat chastely.

LIV. Altar ministers or any clerics must not attend spectacles presented either at weddings or on the stage. They must rise from the banquet and depart before the theatrical performers enter.

LV. Altar ministers, clerics of any kind, and even Christian laypeople must not celebrate banquets from the associations that the common people call *commissalia*.

LVI. Presbyters must not enter the church before the bishop’s entrance or sit on tribunals, [Col. 0291A] but must enter with the bishop, unless perhaps the bishop is ill or it is established that he is absent for the convenience of a journey.

LVII. Bishops must not be ordained in villages and rural districts; instead, visitors—that is, those who travel around—are to be appointed. Concerning those who were ordained before this, we decree that they are to do nothing without the knowledge of the bishop of the city. Likewise, presbyters must do nothing without the bishop’s command and counsel.

LVIII. Offerings must not be made in private houses by bishops or presbyters.

LIX. Psalms composed by ignorant persons and popular psalms must not be recited in churches, nor may books outside the canon be read, except the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments alone. The books that ought to be read and received as authoritative are these:

Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, [Col. 0292A] Joshua son of Nun, Judges, Ruth, the four books of Kings, the two books of Chronicles, Ezra, the Book of Psalms, numbering 150, the Proverbs of Solomon, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Job, Esther, the twelve books of the Prophets—that is, Hosea and Amos, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi—Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel.

Of the New Testament: the Gospel according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, according to John; the Acts of the Apostles; seven canonical Epistles: one of James; two of Peter, 1 and 2; three of John, 1, 2, and 3; one of Jude; and fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul: to the Romans; to the Corinthians, 1 and 2; to the Galatians; to the Ephesians; one to the Philippians; one to the Colossians; two to the Thessalonians, 1 and [Col. 0292B] 2; two to Timothy, 1 and 2; to Titus; to Philemon; and to the Hebrews.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF CONSTANTINOPLE BEGIN

[Col. 0291]

[Col. 0291B] 1. The faith of the 318 Fathers is to be preserved. 2. Bishops are to govern their own dioceses and not enter others. 3. Bishops who have not been invited must not go beyond their own diocese. [Col. 0292B] 4. On churches established among barbarian peoples. 5. On the honor of the bishop of Constantinople. 6. On Maximus the Cynic philosopher. 7. On the creed established at Constantinople.

## THE COUNCIL OF CONSTANTINOPLE BEGINS

Held by 150 bishops under Theodosius the Great, in the consulship of Siagrius and Eucherius, in the year 419 of the era, against Macedonius.

[Col. 0291]

[Col. 0291C] 69 These rules or definitions were set forth by the 150 bishops who assembled at Constantinople when the blessed Nectarius was ordained bishop, after Maximus the Cynic had been condemned. Their names and provinces are contained in the Greek text.

### Chapter I

The faith of the 318 Fathers who assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia must not be despised; rather, it must remain ratified. Every heresy must be anathematized, especially that of the Eunomians—or rather the Anomians, who in Latin are called “without law”—and of the Arians or Eudoxians, the offspring of the Arians, as well as the Pneumatomachi, that is, those who fight against the Holy Spirit, and the Sabellians, Marcellians, Photinians, and Apollinarians.

[Col. 0291D] II. Bishops who are outside their diocese must not approach churches outside their boundaries, nor confuse or intermingle churches contrary to the established rules. The bishops of Alexandria alone are to have care of the whole of the East, while preserving the primatial honors of the Church of Antioch that are contained in the rules of the Council of Nicaea. Likewise, the bishops of the Asian diocese are to govern the matters in Asia and those belonging only to the Asian diocese. The bishops of Pontus are to have care only of the Pontic diocese, and those of Thrace only of Thrace itself.

III. Bishops who have not been invited must not go beyond their diocese to ordain anyone or to arrange any ecclesiastical matters, while preserving the rule written above concerning each diocese. For it is clear that, in every province, the provincial synod must administer and govern all things, according to what was defined at Nicaea.

IV. The churches of God established among barbarian peoples must be governed and administered according to the custom known to have been maintained by the Fathers.

V. The bishop of the city of Constantinople must have the primatial honor after the bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome.

VI. Because of the teaching of his complete indiscipline, which arose at Constantinople, it was decreed that Maximus must not be considered, or even have been, a bishop; nor may those ordained by him possess any clerical rank. Everything done concerning him or by him is revoked as invalid.

### The Creed of the Same Council of Constantinople

VII. We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, those in heaven and those on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down from heaven, and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and became human from the Virgin Mary; he suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, and rose again on the third day; he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father; from there he will come in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

We believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets; in one catholic and apostolic Church; we confess one baptism for the remission of sins; we await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

The names of the 150: Sectarius of Constantinople; Timothy of Alexandria; Dorotheus of Corinth; Cyril of Jerusalem; Calasius of Caesarea; Macer of Hiericontis; Dionysius of Diospolis; Priscianus of Nicopolis; Saturninus of Sebaste; Auxentius of Ascalon; Elianus of Ranea; Zenon of Tyre; Paulus of Sidon; Deisius of Ptolemais; Philippus of Damascus; Varachus of Peneacles; Timothy; Basilides; Abbibo; Mochinius of Araclea; and the others.

[Col. 0294B] The end.

## THE SYNOD OF EPHESUS BEGINS

[Col. 0293]

[Col. 0293B] THE FIRST SYNOD OF EPHESUS begins, of two hundred bishops, held against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who asserted that a mere human being had been born from the holy Virgin Mary, making one person of the flesh and another of the Godhead. He did not understand Christ as one in the Word of God and in the flesh, but preached separately and distinctly one Son of God and another son of man. This synod met during the consulship of Theodosius the Younger for the thirteenth time and Valentinian for the third time, in the year 468 of the era. The most blessed Cyril, formerly bishop of Alexandria, presided over the synod and, together with the entire council, sent these synodical decrees to the same Nestorius.

## LETTER OF THE COUNCIL OF EPHESUS TO NESTORIUS

[Col. 0293]

[Col. 0293B] To the religious and God-beloved fellow priest NESTORIUS, CYRIL, and whoever else is with the synod at Ephesus.

[Col. 0293C] Since our Savior plainly declares, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37), what will become of us, who are asked by your religious profession to love you above Christ, the Savior of all? For what benefit will this bring us on the day of judgment, or what defense will we be able to find because of our prolonged silence concerning the blasphemies you have uttered against him? If you were harming only yourself by teaching or holding such views, our concern would be less. But since you have scandalized the whole Church and mixed among the peoples the ferment of an unprecedented perversity and a new heresy, not only among those present there but also among those established everywhere, for the books of your explanations have been circulated throughout the world, what further reason or speech of excuse can suffice for our silence?

Or when would it not be necessary to remember Christ the Lord saying: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword; for I have come to separate a man against his father and a daughter against her mother” (ibid., 34)? For when the faith is harmed, reverence for parents is despised as useless and dangerous, love toward children and brothers is avoided, and finally pious men choose death even over life itself, so that they may obtain a better resurrection, as it is written (Heb. 11:35).

Behold, therefore, we address you for the third time in these synodical writings, together with the holy synod assembled in the great city of Rome under the presidency of our most holy and reverend Father and fellow priest, Coelestine, [Col. 0294C] bishop. We advise you to abstain from such perverse doctrines, which you are known both to hold and to teach. Receive instead the right faith handed down from the beginning to the churches through the most blessed apostles and evangelists, who saw these things with their own eyes and are shown to have been ministers of the Word.

If your religious profession delays doing this, then, in accordance with the time limit prescribed in the letter of our most holy and reverend fellow priest, Coelestine, bishop of the Roman Church, know that you will have no share with us, nor will you possess a place or fellowship with the priests and bishops of God. For it is not lawful for not only churches, thus troubled and scandalized among the peoples, and the most correct faith, violated and scattered, to be ruined, but also for the flock which you ought to have guarded—if indeed you had been, along with us, a lover of right doctrine, piously following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers.

We therefore receive into our communion all those whom your religious office removed from communion on account of the faith, or deposed from their order, whether laypeople or clerics. For it is not just that those who know how to hold right opinions should be oppressed by your decrees. They also acted wisely in resisting you while doing you good; you took care to signify this very thing in the letter that you sent to the bishop of the great city of Rome, our holy fellow bishop Coelestine.

Nor is it sufficient merely for your religious office to confess the creed that was expounded at that time through the gift of the Holy Spirit by the venerable and great council assembled at Nicaea.

You did not understand this creed or interpret it correctly—indeed, you interpreted it perversely—even though you pronounced the same words aloud. But it is also necessary for you to confess under oath that you anathematize your polluted and profane doctrines, and that you hold and teach what all of us—bishops, teachers, and leaders of the peoples throughout East and West—believe and teach.

The Church gave its assent to the letters sent from Alexandria to your religious office, both the holy synod assembled at Rome and all of us, as letters correctly and irreproachably written. To these we added our own statements concerning what must be believed and taught, and what it is appropriate to avoid. For this is the faith of the Catholic Church, to which all orthodox bishops throughout East and West give their assent.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father as the Only-Begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of one substance with the Father—through whom all things were made in heaven and on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation descended from heaven. And he was incarnate and, having become human, suffered; and rising on the third day, he ascended into heaven, [Col. 0295C] from there to come to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and “Before he was begotten he was not,” and “Because he was made from things that did not exist,” or who say that he is from another substance or essence, or that the Son of God is mutable or changeable, the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

Following, therefore, the confessions of all the holy Fathers, which they uttered with the Holy Spirit speaking through them, adhering with equal steps to the intention present in their understanding, and walking along the royal road, we confess that the Only-Begotten Word of God, begotten from the very essence of the Father, true God from true God, light from light, through whom all things were made, whether in heaven or on earth, for the sake of our salvation, descended and graciously humbled himself to the point of self-emptying; and, having been begotten and become human—that is, having received flesh from the holy Virgin and made it his own—he endured our birth from the womb, proceeding from a woman as a human being, yet not casting aside what he was.

For although he came to be in the assumption of flesh and blood, nevertheless he also remained what he was: God by nature and in truth. We do not, therefore, say that the flesh was changed into the nature of the Godhead, nor that the inseparable essence of the Word of God, accompanying the flesh, was changed into the substance of flesh.

For he is unalterable and immutable, always remaining the same according to the Scriptures. Yet he was seen as a little child, placed in a cradle and established in the lap of his virgin mother, while as God he filled the whole creation and remained undivided with his Father. For what is divine is known without quantity and without bulk, and is contained by no boundaries.

Confessing the Word of God according to subsistence, we worship one Son and Lord, Jesus Christ, not setting him apart and defining a human being and God as joined to one another by a union of dignity and authority—for this is merely a novelty of expression and nothing else. Nor do we name separately as Christ the Word of God who is from God, and separately as another Christ him who was born from a woman; rather, we recognize one and the same Christ, the Word of God the Father together with his own flesh.

For then also, according to us, he was anointed, although he himself bestowed the Spirit upon those worthy, and not according to measure, as the blessed evangelist John affirmed. Nor do we say that the Word of God dwelt as in an ordinary human being who was born from the holy Virgin, or that Christ the human being should be believed to possess God as an inhabitant.

Although the Word dwelt among us and it was said that “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily in Christ,” nevertheless we understand the Word who became flesh not as one is said to dwell in the saints. Nor will we attempt to define that such a habitation occurred in him. Rather, being one according to nature and not utterly changed into flesh, he made for himself a habitation of the kind that the soul of a human being is also believed to have in its own body.

Therefore Christ and Lord is one, not as though by some kind of conjunction there were a unity of dignity [Col. 0296C] and authority belonging to a human being in relation to God. For equality of dignity alone cannot unite a nature. Thus Peter and John are equal to one another in dignity, on account of which they are shown to be apostles and holy disciples; nevertheless the two are not one.

Nor do we understand the manner of their union as an association or connection, for that is insufficient for natural unity, nor according to an effect of participation. Even we, who cling to the Lord, are one spirit with him; indeed, we avoid the name “conjunction” as unsuitable to signify the mystery of unity.

Nor do we assert that the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ, lest we once again more plainly divide into two the one Christ, the Son and Lord, and fall again into the crime of sacrilege by making God and Lord for him.

For, as we said above, the Word of God, united to flesh according to substance, is indeed God of all and ruler of the universe. Yet he is neither servant nor Lord to himself, since it is foolish, or rather impious, to think or say this.

Although he calls God his Father, since he is God and is from his substance, nevertheless we in no way fail to recognize that, while remaining God, he also became human, assuming under God the law proper to human nature. How, then, could he be God or Lord to himself? Accordingly, insofar as he is human, in keeping with what suitably corresponds to the measure of his self-emptying, he chose to be under God and to be with us.

We also take care not to say of Christ that he was made subject to the law, although he himself promulgated the law and existed as God and lawgiver. Because of the one who assumes, I honor the one assumed; and because of the invisible one, I worship the visible one.

But it is dreadful even to say this: “The one who is assumed is called God together with the one who assumes.” For whoever says this again divides the one Christ into two, setting the human being apart on one side and God likewise on the other. He plainly denies the unity according to which one is not worshiped together with another, nor is one called God together with another; rather, one Christ Jesus, the Only-Begotten Son of God, is understood and is to be honored with one service together with his own flesh.

We also confess that the very one who was begotten from God the Father, the Only-Begotten Son, is God, although according to his own nature he was without suffering. Nevertheless, for us, according to the Scriptures, he was struck or suffered in the flesh, and, while in the crucified body of his own flesh, he referred the suffering to himself without suffering in his own nature.

By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone, handing over his own body, although he himself is naturally life and the resurrection of the dead. For, in order by ineffable power to destroy death, and so that the Firstborn, God, might first become from the dead in his own flesh—although according to his own nature he was exempt from death—“the first fruits of those who sleep” (1 Cor. XV, 20), and might make a way for human nature to return to incorruption, by the grace of God, as was said above, he tasted death for human beings; and, rising on the third day, he stripped the underworld.

Therefore, although it is said that the resurrection of the dead occurred through a human being, we understand that the Word who is from God became human, and that through him the dominion of death was destroyed.

He will come at the appointed times, as the one Son and Lord in the glory of the Father, “to judge the world with equity” (Ps. IX, 9), as Scripture bears witness.

We necessarily add this as well. Proclaiming, as we do, the death according to the flesh of the Only-Begotten Son of God, that is, of Jesus Christ, and likewise confessing his resurrection and ascension into heaven, we celebrate in the churches the bloodless service of sacrifice.

Thus we also approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, who is the Redeemer of us all—not as though we were receiving ordinary flesh, God forbid, nor as sanctified men joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, or as possessing a divine habitation, but as receiving flesh truly life-giving and made the very flesh of the Word himself.

For since he exists naturally as life, being God, and was united to the flesh as his own, he confessed it to be life-giving. Therefore, although he says to us, “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood” (John VI, 54), we must not regard it as the flesh of one ordinary human being among us. For how could the flesh of a human being be life-giving according to its nature? Rather, we must regard it as truly made his own—the flesh of him who for our sake became and was called the Son of Man.

We do not divide the sayings that the Savior uttered in the Gospels between two substances or persons. For the one Christ is not twofold, nor is he God alone, although he is recognized as having come together from two different and diverse realities into an undivided unity, just as a human being also consists of soul and body: one is not two, but rather is composed of both.

Accordingly, observing that human and divine sayings alike were spoken by one Christ, we think rightly. When, speaking with the highest dignity about two things, he says of himself, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9), and, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30), we understand his divine and ineffable nature, according to which he is one with his Father because of the one and same substance, “being the image and imprint of his glory” (Heb. I, 3).

But when, in no way ignorant of the measure of human nature, he addresses the Jews, saying, “You are seeking to kill me” (John VII, 20), a human being who spoke the truth to them, we recognize him no less as the true God who is in the likeness and equality of the Father, also within the measures of his humanity.

If it is necessarily believed that he who exists as God by nature became flesh—or rather, a human being endowed with a rational soul—why should anyone be ashamed of any of his sayings if he uttered them as befit a human being? And if he rejects words appropriate to a human being, what compelled him, according to us, to become human? But when he mercifully and willingly humbled himself for our sake, for what reason would he have avoided words worthy of examination?

We therefore ascribe everything said by him in the Gospel to one person, to the one substance of the Word, that is, of the incarnate Word, because one is the Lord Jesus Christ.

As it is written, the Apostle called him “the high priest of our confession” (Heb. III, 1), as one who offers to God and the Father the confession of our faith, which is continually offered by us to God the Father himself. Again, we say that he himself is by nature the Only-Begotten Son from God, and we assign the name and office of priesthood to no other human being besides him.

For he became “the mediator between God and human beings” (1 Tim. II, 5), and the reconciler, offering himself to God and the Father for us “as a fragrant offering” (Eph. V, 2). Therefore he said:

“Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; burnt offerings for sin did not please you; but you prepared a body for me. Then I said: Behold, I come. In the heading of the book it is written of me, to do your will, O God” (Heb. X, 5 ff.).

For he offered his own body, not for himself but for us, as a fragrant offering. For what offering or sacrifice would he, existing as God and free from every sin, need for himself? If all have sinned and lack the glory of God (Rom. III, 23), human nature, having become more prone to excess through mutability, was sick with sins. But he was not so. Therefore we need his glory.

Why should there now be any further doubt that the true Lamb was sacrificed for us? Whoever says that he offered himself both for himself and for us will in no way escape the charge of impiety, since he committed absolutely no offense and made no sin at all. What offering, then, would he need when there was no crime of his own? For whom, if it were necessary, would he offer an offering suitably sufficient?

Concerning the Spirit also, when he says, “He will glorify me” (John XVI, 14), we rightly understand this and confess one Christ, Lord and Son, not as though he needed glory from another, but as having received glory from the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit is his and is neither better nor superior to him.

But because, while performing human works, he used the power of his own Spirit to demonstrate his divinity, he is said to be glorified by him, just as one’s own power or discipline glorifies each person.

Although his Spirit exists in its own substance, and its personal property is understood according to the fact that it is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless it is not alien to him. For it is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is the truth; hence the Spirit proceeds from him as likewise from God the Father.

Indeed, this same Spirit, accomplishing glorious miracles through the hands of the holy apostles, glorified the Lord Jesus Christ after he had ascended into heaven. For Christ, believed to exist as God by nature, performed mighty works through his Spirit; therefore he said, “He will take from what is mine and declare it to you” (ibid.).

The same Spirit is by no means said to be wise or powerful through participation in another, because he is perfect in every respect and is entirely in need of no good. He is believed to be the Spirit of the Father’s power and wisdom, that is, of the Son; and therefore he is shown to be power and wisdom in reality and in subsistent being.

Since, therefore, the holy Virgin bodily bore God united to flesh according to subsistence, we confess her to be the Mother of God—not because the nature of the Word received from the flesh the beginning of its existence, for “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God, and the Word was with God” (John I, 1), and he himself, the creator of the ages and of the universe, was coeternal with the Father—but because, as we said above, uniting human nature to himself according to subsistence, he endured birth from the bodily womb itself.

This was not because, according to his nature, he necessarily needed the birth that took place in the final times of the ages, but so that he might bless the first fruits of our substance. And when she had given birth as a woman to God united to flesh, that curse which had been uttered against the whole human race would cease, and she would no longer consign our bodies to death.

By dissolving also what had been said, “In sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. III, 16), he showed true what the prophet had foretold in the words, “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. XV, 34). And again, “God has wiped away every tear from every face” (Rev. VII, 17).

For this reason we say that, in the economy of salvation, he also blessed those very marriages when he was invited with the holy apostles at Cana of Galilee (John II, 1).

We have been taught to think this way by the holy apostles and evangelists, by all divinely inspired Scripture, and also by the confessions of the blessed Fathers, founded upon the truth. It is fitting that your Reverence should agree with all these things and consent without any deceit. The things that it is necessary for your Reverence to anathematize are appended to this letter.

### Chapter I

If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is truly God, and therefore does not confess the holy Virgin to be the Mother of God—for according to the flesh she bore the Word of God made flesh, according to what is written, “The Word became flesh”—let him be anathema.

### II

If anyone does not confess that the Word of God the Father was united according to substance to the flesh, and that the same one is one Christ with his own flesh, namely, God and human being at the same time, let him be anathema.

### III

If anyone divides the substances in the one Christ after the union, joining them only by a connection according to the dignity of the flesh, or even according to authority and power, and not rather by the coming together that occurred through natural unity, let him be anathema.

### IV

If anyone divides between two persons or subsistences the sayings contained in the apostolic and evangelical writings, or those spoken about Christ by the saints or by Christ himself, and applies some of them as belonging specifically to a human being understood apart from the Word of God, while assigning others as appropriate to God alone, to the Word of God the Father, let him be anathema.

### V

If anyone dares to say that Christ the human being is *theophoros*, that is, “God-bearing,” rather than confessing him to be truly God, as Son by nature according to the fact that the Word became flesh and likewise shared, as we do, in flesh and blood, let him be anathema.

### VI

If anyone says that the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ, and does not rather confess that the same one is God and human being at the same time because the Word became flesh according to the Scriptures, let him be anathema.

### VII

If anyone says that Jesus as a human being was helped by the working of the Word of God, and attributes the glory of the Only-Begotten as though it existed on account of him, let him be anathema.

### VIII

If anyone dares to say that the human being who was assumed should be worshiped together with the Word of God, glorified together with him, and called God together with him as one person with another—for the added syllable “co-” compels this meaning—and does not rather worship Emmanuel with one supplication and render him one glorification, according to the fact that the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.

### IX

If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Holy Spirit as one who used an alien power through him and received from him the ability to prevail against unclean spirits and to perform divine signs before human beings, and does not rather confess that his own Spirit was the one through whom he fulfilled the divine signs, let him be anathema.

### X

Holy Scripture records that Christ became the High Priest and Apostle of our confession. For he offered himself for us “as a fragrant offering” to God and the Father.

Therefore, if anyone says that our High Priest and Apostle was not the very Word of God when he became flesh and human, according to us human beings, but as though he were another human being specifically distinct from him, or if anyone says that he offered himself as an offering for himself and not rather for us alone—for he who knew no sin at all had no need of an offering—let him be anathema.

### XI

If anyone does not confess that the Lord’s flesh is life-giving and the very flesh of the Word of God the Father, but regards it as belonging to another joined to him by dignity, or as though it possessed a divine habitation, and does not rather confess that it is life-giving because it was made the flesh of the Word who is able to give life, let him be anathema.

### XII

If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, and tasted death in the flesh, becoming the Firstborn from the dead, insofar as he is life and, as God, the giver of life, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0301B] ### XIII

The great and holy synod therefore says that the one who is naturally begotten from God the Father, the Only-Begotten Son, God from true God, light from light, through whom and with whom the Father made all things, descended, became incarnate and human, suffered, rose on the third day, and ascended again into heaven.

We must follow these words; it is fitting that we obey these doctrines, considering what it means for the Word of God to become incarnate and human.

For we do not say that the nature of God was changed or altered, but rather that the Word united to himself flesh endowed with a rational soul, and that the Word became human substantially, ineffably and incomprehensibly, and was also called the Son of Man—not by naked will alone, nor by the assumption of a person alone, but because different natures came together into one.

Nevertheless, one Christ and Son came from both, without the diversity of the natures being emptied or removed through their conjunction; rather, divinity and humanity together made for us one God, Christ, and Son through that mysterious and ineffable union.

Thus he who was begotten from the Father before all ages was also carnally produced from a woman. This was not because his divine nature took its beginning from the holy Virgin, nor because he himself needed to be born a second time after the birth he had from the Father.

For it is foolish and senseless to say that he who is coeternal with the Father before all ages needed a second generation in order to begin to exist. Rather, because for our salvation he united human nature to himself and proceeded from a woman, he is therefore said to have been born according to the flesh.

For a common human being was not first born from the holy Virgin and only then did the Word dwell in him. Rather, in the very womb and virginal uterus he united flesh to himself and endured a carnal generation, making the birth of his flesh his own birth.

Thus we said that he suffered and rose again—not because the Word of God suffered in his own nature, or received blows, nails, piercings, or other wounds, for God is incorporeal and beyond suffering, but because that body which was made his own endured these things.

Therefore he is said to have suffered all these things for us, for God, who could not suffer, was in that body which suffered.

In the same way we understand his death. The Word of God is naturally immortal and incorruptible, life and life-giver; but because his own body, by the grace of God, in the words of Paul, “tasted death for everyone” (Heb. II, 9), he himself is therefore said to have suffered death for us.

This does not mean that he himself experienced death insofar as his nature is concerned—for it is madness either to think or to say this—but that, as we said, his true flesh tasted death. Likewise, when his flesh rose again, we speak of his resurrection—not because it had fallen into corruption, God forbid, but because his body rose.

Thus we confess one Christ and Lord, not worshiping a human being together with the Word as though some appearance of division were introduced, but worshiping one and the same, because his body is not alien to the Word, with whom he himself also sits at the right hand of the Father.

Nor do we say this as though two sons were sitting there, but one together with the flesh through unity. For if we wish to understand the union that occurred according to substance as though it were a union with something subject to suffering, or as though it were somehow inadequate or dishonorable, we shall fall into saying that there are two sons.

It is necessary to distinguish and say that a human being existed separately, honored only by the title of Son, and again that the Word who is from God, existing in the human being, was truly the Son of God. But we must not distinguish the one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons.

For this does not assist the sound reasoning of faith, even if some speak of some kind of union of persons. Scripture does not say that the Word of God assumed a human person for himself, but that he became flesh.

This means that the Word of God had, as we do, a beginning consisting of flesh and blood, made our body properly his own, and proceeded as a human being from a woman, without casting aside or laying down his divinity so as to lose the generation he had from the Father. Rather, even in the assumption of flesh he remained God, as he was.

This, therefore, is what the reasoning of right faith proclaims. We find that the holy Fathers held this understanding; therefore they did not hesitate to call the holy Virgin *theotochon*—“God-bearer” or “Mother of God”—not because the nature and divinity of the Word took their beginning from the holy Virgin, but because from her was born that holy body, endowed with a rational soul, to which the Word of God was substantially united and is said to have been born according to the flesh.

I write these things to you out of love in Christ, appealing to you as a brother and calling God and his chosen angels to witness, so that you may think and teach these things together with us, so that the peace of the Churches may be preserved and the indissoluble bond of concord and charity may remain among the priests.

# The Council of Chalcedon

Of six hundred and thirty bishops, during the consulship of Valentinian VI and Ahinus, in the year 469 of the era (A.D. 454), against Eutyches and Dioscorus.

[Col. 0303]

[Col. 0303A] In the consulship of the most pious and Christ-loving Flavius Marcianus, perpetual Augustus, on the Ides of October, a synod was held in the city of Chalcedon, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, by decree of the synods and of the most faithful emperors Valentinian and Marcian.

They assembled in the church of the holy and triumphant martyr Euphemia: the most glorious princes, namely the most magnificent and glorious master of the soldiers, former prefect and former consul, the patrician Anatolius; the most magnificent and glorious prefect of the sacred praetorium, Palladius; the most magnificent prefect of the city, Tatianus; the most magnificent and glorious master of the divine office, Vincemalus; the most magnificent and glorious master, Martialis; and the most glorious and magnificent count of the domestics, Sporacius; and the great count of the private estates, Genetholius.

Also present from the glorious senate were the most magnificent and glorious former prefect of the praetorium, six times former ordinary consul and patrician Florentius; the most magnificent and glorious former ordinary consul and patrician senator; the most magnificent and glorious master, former ordinary consul and patrician Nomo; the most magnificent and glorious former prefect and former ordinary consul and patrician Protogenius; the most magnificent and glorious master, former prefect Zoilus; the great and glorious former prefect of the city, Apollonius; and the most magnificent former provost of the city, Artaxerxes.

The council of the whole world, according to the divine command, was assembled in the city of Chalcedon: namely, the bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius, the presbyter Boniface, the legates of the venerable and holy archbishop of ancient Rome, Leo; and the holy Anatolius, most magnificent archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, together with the remaining most holy and reverend six hundred and thirty bishops.

Behold, when all had arrived before the railings of the holy altar with the magnificent and distinguished senate, and when the most pious emperor Marcian had also arrived in the aforesaid most holy basilica, the most pious and faithful queen, the beautiful Augusta, inflamed with divine zeal and the fervor of faith, addressed the holy synod as follows:

“When by election we were advanced from the secrecy of God to the kingship amid such great public responsibilities, we imposed upon ourselves no duty more strictly than that of making the right and true faith of Christians, which rests upon holiness and reverence, manifest and unquestioned to all.

“For it is evident that, through greed or empty ambition, those who in earlier times held and taught various opinions to the people according to what pleased them, rather than according to what was fitting and what the truth or the teaching of the Fathers required, led many into error.

“Therefore we hasten to bring the holy synod to this perfection, and we have judged it necessary to impose this labor upon you, so that every dark error may be wiped away and, according to the way in which the divinity itself wished to make itself manifest to human beings, as the teaching of the Fathers has demonstrated, our faith—which is pure and holy—may enter the souls of all and shine with the light of its own truth.

“From now on let no one dare to discuss the birth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ in any way other than that which the apostolic teaching of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers is known to have handed down in agreement with this doctrine, as the letters of the most holy Pope Leo, who governs the apostolic throne, testify to Flavian of holy memory, formerly bishop of the royal city of Constantinople.

“We have devised this synod, following the example of the emperor Constantine, to confirm the faith, not to establish a new authority. Thus, in the future, the multitude of the people will not be found dissenting after being drawn into corrupt institutions. For the simplicity of some has easily been deceived by inventions—or, as we have said until now, by speeches—since disagreements and heresies have plainly been displayed through the corrupt teachings of various people.

[72] “We must therefore apply every effort to unite the people, who think alike because of the true and holy doctrine, to one right Church. Therefore let your Reverence hasten, with harmonious minds, to set forth the true and catholic faith according to the teaching of the Fathers, so that, just as the true faith became known to human beings from the Council of Nicaea up to the present time after error was cut away, so now also, through this holy synod, the mist that—as we said above—appears to have arisen in those few years from the corruption and greed of certain people may be removed, and what has been established may always be preserved.

“It will belong to divine providence to preserve forever and most firmly what we piously wish to accomplish.”

After the king had spoken these words, all the bishops cried out:

“To Marcian, the new Constantine: Many years to the king! Many years to the queen! Many years to the Orthodox! May the reign of Marcian, the Christ-loving emperor, endure forever, worthy lover of the orthodox faith and of Christ. Let envy be far from us.”

After this, Aetius, archdeacon of Constantinople, New Rome, and chief of the notaries, said:

“By the command of heavenly grace and through the divine zeal of your serenity, most pious emperors, to whom every kingdom has been granted by God, this holy and great synod of the whole world has been assembled around your decree.

“After the summons of very many people over many days and through divine diligence, it has driven away every discord that previously arose against our right and inviolable catholic faith through the word of truth, banishing every innovation, as the acts set down in writing demonstrate throughout the ages to come.

“It has established a simple definition fortified by the power of the divine Scriptures, preserving within it the judgment of the holy and most blessed Fathers, for the true knowledge of sincere readers and for the long-lasting crown of your empire.

“I have it in my hands, and, if it pleases your serenity, I shall read it in full.”

The most pious and faithful emperor said: “Read it.”

Aetius the archdeacon read:

“The holy, great and venerable synod, which by the grace of God was assembled in the city of Chalcedon, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, in the holy basilica of the triumphant martyr Euphemia, by decree of the most pious emperors Valentinian and Marcian Augustus, has established the matters set forth below.

“Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, strengthening his own disciples in the recognition of the faith, said: ‘I give you my peace; I leave you my peace’ (John XIV, 27), so that no disagreement in faith might arise among neighbors, but that the proclamation of the truth might be displayed equally.

“But because the Evil One does not cease to insert his weeds among the very seeds of piety and always to devise something new against the truth, our Lord, wishing as usual to provide for the human race, raised up this most pious and faithful emperor to zeal. He summoned the leaders of the priests from every direction to himself so that, with the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ cooperating, he might remove every plague of falsehood from the sheep of Christ and refresh them with the shoots of truth.

“By common decree, therefore, we reject the foreign sects of error, renew the right faith of the Fathers, and preach to all the confession of the three hundred and eighteen. As associates of these, we also assign to this most pious title the one hundred and fifty bishops who assembled at Constantinople, since they too subscribed to the same faith.

“We therefore establish the order, preserving all the formulas of faith, including the holy synod held at Ephesus, whose leaders were Celestine of the city of Rome, of venerable memory, and Cyril, priest of the Church of Alexandria.

“Thus the exposition of the right and blameless faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea under Constantine, the pious emperor of blessed memory, shall shine forth; and there shall also be contained the decree of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers in the city of Constantinople, issued for the destruction of the sects then sprouting up and for the confirmation of our own catholic and apostolic faith.”

## Creed of the Council of Nicaea

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, Only-Begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance with the Father—through whom all things were made, those in heaven and those on earth; who for us and for our salvation descended and was incarnate.

Having become human, he suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and “Before he was begotten he was not,” and “Because he was made from things that did not exist,” or who say that he is from another subsistence or substance, or that the Son of God is mutable, the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

And this is likewise the creed of the one hundred and fifty Fathers:

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Only-Begotten, begotten from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance with the Father—through whom all things were made; who for us and for our salvation descended; and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; and became human, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father. He will come again to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets.

One catholic and apostolic Church.

We confess one baptism for the remission of all sins.

We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come.

Amen.

The most careful and salutary creed of divine grace would indeed suffice for the fullest knowledge and confirmation of piety: for it teaches a perfect doctrine concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and makes manifest the Lord’s incarnation to those who faithfully receive it. But since those who strive to destroy the proclamation of truth give birth to certain novelties of their own heresy—some daring to corrupt the mystery of the divine dispensation accomplished for our sake, and denying that voice of the divine Father addressed to the Virgin; others introducing mixture and confusion, senselessly composing one nature of flesh and divinity, and thus monstrously proclaiming the divine nature of the Only-Begotten to be passible—therefore, wishing to exclude every contrivance they might set against the truth, the holy and great universal synod, teaching this proclamation as immovable, decreed above all that the undefiled faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers should remain intact.

And on account of those who oppose the Holy Spirit, it confirms the doctrine concerning the substance of the Holy Spirit handed down somewhat later by the one hundred and fifty Fathers who assembled in the city of Constantinople. They too made this doctrine known to everyone—not by adding anything lacking in the earlier statements, but by making more fully manifest the understanding concerning the Spirit, in opposition to those who strive, through testimonies from the Scriptures, to diminish His lordship and divinity. [Col. 0307A]

For the sake, moreover, of those who attempt to corrupt the mystery of the dispensation and unwisely proclaim that the one born from the holy Virgin Mary was merely a man, it received the synodical letters of the most blessed Cyril, formerly priest of the Alexandrian Church, both the one addressed to Nestorius and those addressed to the others throughout the East, which agreed with and supported it: these were received both for the refutation of Nestorian madness and for the instruction of those who, in religious zeal, desire the meaning of the salutary creed.

Alongside these it also clearly appended the letter of the holy and most blessed archbishop of the first see, Leo, written to Flavian, archbishop of holy memory, for the destruction of Eutyches’ wickedness. This letter, agreeing with the confession of the great Peter, constitutes a common and coherent combat against those who do not glorify rightly, in confirmation of the Catholic faith. For it rejects from the council of priests those who attempt to divide the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation into two sons, and those who dare to assert that the divinity of the Only-Begotten Son is passible. It opposes those who argue for mixture or confusion in Christ’s two natures. It casts far away those who madly assert that the form of a servant which He assumed from us is heavenly or derives from some other substance. And it anathematizes those who deliriously assert that the Lord had two natures before the union but invent one nature after the union.

In agreement with the holy Fathers, with one harmonious voice we likewise teach that we confess one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same perfect God in divinity, and truly the same man, consisting of a rational soul and a body; according to divinity, of one nature with the Father; according to humanity, the same of one nature with us, like us in every respect except sin. Before the ages He was born from the Father according to divinity; in these last days the same, for us and for our salvation, was made man.

This one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, Only-Begotten, is to be recognized in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. The distinction of the natures is in no way abolished because of the union; rather, the property of each nature is preserved, and the two come together in one person and one state. He is not to be divided or separated into two persons, but is one and the same Only-Begotten Son, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ, just as the prophets taught concerning Him from the beginning, and as He Himself instructed us and handed down to us in the creed. [Col. 0308B]

Having thus ordered all these matters on every side with the utmost precision and diligence, the holy and universal synod decreed that no one might profess, write, teach, or state any other faith or anything otherwise. Whoever dares to set forth another faith, produce or teach another creed, for those wishing to turn to knowledge of the truth—whether from the Gentiles, the Jews, or any heretics whatsoever—if they are bishops or clerics, they are to be foreign to the episcopate and the clergy respectively. If they are monks or laymen, they are to be anathematized.

## Chapters of the Same Council of Chalcedon

[Col. 0307C]

1. On preserving the canons of each council.  
2. That clerics or monks ought not to undertake secular estates or lawsuits.  
3. That bishops or anyone from the clergy ought not to be ordained for money.  
4. On the honor appropriate to monks, and that none of them should attempt to disturb ecclesiastical or secular affairs, or receive another’s slave without the knowledge of his master.  
5. That a bishop or anyone from the clergy may not pass from one city to another.  
6. That no one should be ordained without a definite ecclesiastical appointment.  
7. On clerics and monks who do not remain in their chosen vocation. [Col. 0307D]  
8. On clerics serving in parishes, monasteries, and martyr-shrines that exist under the authority of the bishop of each city.  
9. That clerics ought not, bypassing their bishop, to resort to secular courts.  
10. That clerics may not serve in two churches.  
11. That a letter should be given to the poor, while persons of higher standing should be certified by letters of recommendation. [Col. 0308C]  
12. That a province should in no way be divided between two metropolitans.  
13. That foreign clerics ought not to serve without letters of recommendation.  
14. That a cleric may not take a wife from another sect, unless she promises that she will come to the true faith.  
15. On women deacons, that none may be ordained unless they are forty years old.  
16. On monks or maidens dedicated to God: that they may not enter marriage.  
17. On churches in parishes held or restored by a bishop in cities for thirty years.  
18. On the conspiracy of clerics, which the Greeks call *fratrea* [a brotherhood or faction]. [Col. 0308D]  
19. That councils should be held twice a year in each province.  
20. That clerics may scarcely transfer to another city, except those who have lost their own cities through persecution.  
21. On the accusers of bishops or clerics, what sort of persons should be admitted to bring an accusation.  
22. That clerics may not seize property belonging to their bishop after his death. [Col. 0309A]  
23. On excommunicating clerics and monks who come to the royal city against the will of their bishop.  
24. That monasteries once consecrated may not be turned into secular lodging houses. [Col. 0310A]  
25. That after a bishop’s death the ordination of another bishop ought not to be delayed.  
26. On having stewards—that is, administrators—in each church.  
27. On those who abduct women for themselves.

## The Decrees of the Council of Chalcedon Begin

*(A.D. 454, in Asia.)*

[Col. 0309]

[Col. 0309B]

We decree that the rules issued by the holy Fathers in each synod up to the present shall retain their proper force.

### II

If any bishop, having accepted money, performs an ordination and reduces the priceless grace to a price, and ordains for money a bishop, a co-bishop, a presbyter, a deacon, or anyone else numbered among the clergy; or if, having accepted money, he ordains a steward—that is, a defender or *paramonarius*—then whoever has undertaken such a thing, if he is convicted, shall himself incur the penalty attached to his rank. The person so ordained shall receive no benefit from such commerce and disgraceful appointment, but shall be excluded both from the dignity and from the office which he entered through money. The person who appeared as intermediary in such shameful and unlawful dealings, if he is a cleric, shall likewise leave his own rank. If he is a layman or monk, let him be anathema.

### III

It has come to the holy synod that certain persons numbered among the clergy, for the sake of shameful profit, undertake leases of large estates and secular lawsuits; they separate themselves through negligence from the sacred ministries, but hasten to the houses of secular persons and, out of greed, take charge of their property. Therefore the holy and great synod decreed that henceforth no one among them—that is, neither a bishop, cleric, nor monk—may lease estates or involve himself in secular administration, except those who are compelled by law to undertake the guardianship of minors or unavoidable forms of care; or one to whom the bishop of the city himself has entrusted the administration of ecclesiastical property, or the care of orphans, defenseless widows, or persons who most especially require ecclesiastical assistance, for fear of God.

Whoever transgresses these statutes shall be subject to ecclesiastical correction.

### IV

Those who truly and purely choose the solitary life are worthy of fitting honor. Since, however, certain monks wearing the habit indiscriminately commend themselves throughout the cities and monasteries on their own presumption, it has been decided that no one may build or establish monasteries or a house of prayer without the knowledge of the bishop of that city.

Those who are in monasteries throughout the individual cities or estates must be subject to the bishop, devote themselves to quiet, and observe fasts and prayers, remaining in the places where they once devoted themselves to God. They must neither participate in ecclesiastical affairs nor undertake any secular business, and must not leave their monasteries unless perhaps they are ordered to do so by the bishop of that city because of urgent necessities.

No slave is to be received into a monastery to become a monk with the others without the knowledge of his own master. We decree that anyone who acts contrary to these provisions is to be excluded from communion, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed. It is therefore fitting that the bishop of the city provide the monasteries with the necessary care and oversight.

### V

On account of those bishops or clerics who pass from city to city, it has been decided that the definitions issued by the holy Fathers shall retain their proper force. [Col. 0310C]

### VI

No one is to be ordained presbyter or deacon without a definite appointment, nor is anyone to be placed in an ecclesiastical order unless the one being ordained is openly entitled to exercise that ordination in the church of the city or estate, in a martyr-shrine, or in a monastery.

Concerning those who are ordained without a definite appointment, the holy synod decreed that the laying-on of hands shall be void and that such an act shall have no force, to the injury of the person who ordained him. [Col. 0310D]

### VII

Those who have once been enrolled among the clergy, or assigned to monasteries, are forbidden to enter military service or secular offices. Those who have dared to do this and have preferred not to repent of their action and return to the same vocation which they had previously chosen before God are to be anathematized.

### VIII

Clerics established in parishes, monasteries, or martyr-shrines are to be under the authority of the bishop who is in the city, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, and they must not presumptuously withdraw from their bishop.

Those who dare in any way to overturn this arrangement, or who refuse to submit to their own bishop, if they are clerics, shall be subject to the condemnations of the canons according to the rank of the persons involved. If they are monks or laymen, they shall be deprived of communion.

### IX

If a cleric has a dispute with another cleric, he must not leave his bishop and resort to secular courts. The dispute must first be brought before his own bishop; or, if the bishop himself is involved in the judgment, the case must be heard by arbitrators chosen by both parties.

Whoever acts contrary to this shall be subject to the corrections prescribed by the canons. If a cleric has a case against his own bishop or another bishop, he shall bring his complaint before the synod of the province. If a bishop or cleric has a dispute with the metropolitan bishop of that province, he shall go to the primate of that diocese, or at least to the see of the royal city of Constantinople, so that the matter may there be investigated. [Col. 0311A]

### X

A cleric may not be ordained in the churches of two cities, but only in the church in which he was ordained at the beginning and to which he belonged before his flight. If, because of a desire for empty glory, he happens to flee afterward to a larger church, he must unquestionably be recalled to the church in which he was ordained from the beginning, and there alone may he serve.

If someone has already been transferred from one church to another, he shall have nothing in common with the former church, whether with the martyr-shrines established under that church, its parishes, its hospices, or their affairs.

Those who dare, after the ordination of this great and universal synod, to do what has been prohibited shall fall from their own rank. [Col. 0311B]

### XI

We decree that all poor and needy persons who require ecclesiastical assistance, when they travel with a letter of verification—a letter of peace, as such letters are called ecclesiastical—are to be commended only by such a letter, and not by letters of recommendation. For the letters which we call letters of recommendation ought properly to be given only to those who are distinguished in their work, so that they alone may receive them. [Col. 0311C]

### XII

It has come to our attention that certain persons, seeking power contrary to ecclesiastical order, divide one province into two by an imperial administrative instrument, so that two metropolitan bishops are found in the same single province.

Therefore the holy synod decrees that no bishop henceforth attempt anything of this kind. Those who attempt such a thing shall fall from their own rank.

If any cities have previously been honored with the title of metropolitan by imperial administrative authority, they shall enjoy the name alone; and the bishop who governs its church shall retain the privilege belonging by right to the metropolitan bishop. [Col. 0311D]

### XIII

A foreign cleric or reader may nowhere serve outside his own city without letters of recommendation from his own bishop.

### XIV

Since in certain provinces psalmists and readers are permitted to take wives, the holy synod decrees that none of them may in any way take a wife from another sect.

If anyone has already entered such a marriage and has children from it, and if those children have already been baptized among heretics, he must offer them to the holy Catholic Church, so that they may participate there in communion.

Those who have not yet been baptized may under no circumstances be baptized in a heretical church, nor may they be joined in marriage to a heretic, Jew, or pagan, unless the prospective spouse promises, when joined to an orthodox bride, that he will come to the orthodox faith.

Whoever violates this definition of the holy synod shall be subject to the condemnations of the rules. [Col. 0312A]

### XV

A deaconess must not be ordained before the age of forty, and this only after careful examination. If she receives ordination and observes the ministry for any length of time, but afterward gives herself to marriage, thereby doing injury to the grace of God, let her be anathema, together with the man who joined her in that marriage.

### XVI

If a virgin has dedicated herself to God, or likewise a monk, they may not enter marriage. If they are found doing so, they shall remain excommunicated. We decree, however, that mercy may be shown toward them if the bishop of the place judges that this should be done.

### XVII

In every rural church, parish, or estate, the churches are to remain fixed under those bishops who hold them, especially those who have governed them without violence for thirty years.

If a dispute concerning them has arisen or arises within the thirty-year period, those who claim to have been wronged may bring the matter before the synod of the province. If anyone believes that he is being oppressed by his own metropolitan, he may bring the case before the primate of the diocese or before the see of Constantinople, as has been stated.

If any city has been restored by imperial authority, or is restored in the future, its ecclesiastical parochial organization shall henceforth follow the civil and public arrangements. [Col. 0312B]

### XVIII

The crime of plots and conspiracies, which among the Greeks is called *fratrea* [a brotherhood or faction], is expressly prohibited even by the public laws. It is all the more fitting that it be rejected and forbidden from occurring in the holy Church of God.

If clerics or monks are found swearing conspiratorial oaths, or forming brotherhoods or factions against their bishops or other clerics, they shall altogether fall from their own rank. [Col. 0312C]

### XIX

It has come to our ears that the councils of bishops established in the provinces are scarcely being held. From this it is evident that many ecclesiastical matters requiring correction are being neglected.

Therefore the holy synod decrees, in accordance with the rules of the Fathers, that the bishops of each province assemble twice a year, so that each matter that has arisen may be corrected.

If the appointed bishops refuse to assemble in their cities, when they are in good bodily health and free from all other urgent and unavoidable business, they may be corrected by admonitions of fraternal love. [Col. 0312D]

### XX

As we have already decreed, clerics established in their own churches may not be ordained in the churches of another city, but must remain in the church in which they were originally deemed worthy to serve. The exception is those who have lost their own cities and have migrated to other churches out of necessity.

If any bishop, after this definition, receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, the holy synod has decided that both the one who received him and the one who was received shall remain excommunicated until that cleric returns to his own church.

[Col. 0313A]

### XXI

Clerics or laymen who accuse a bishop or clerics must not be rashly or indiscriminately admitted to bring an accusation unless their reputation has first been investigated.

### XXII

Clerics may not, after the death of their bishop, seize property belonging to him, as has already been established by the preceding rules. If they do so, they must know that they place their own rank in danger.

### XXIII

It has come to the ears of the holy synod that certain clerics and monks, having received no assignment from their own bishop—and sometimes even having been excommunicated by him—come to the royal city of Constantinople. Remaining there for long periods, they disturb the peace of the Church and corrupt the households of various persons.

The holy synod decrees that the defender of the holy Church of Constantinople shall first warn them to leave the royal city. If they persist wickedly in the same intention, the defender himself shall expel them even against their will, so that they may return to their own places. [Col. 0313B]

### XXIV
