Monasteries once consecrated are to remain perpetual, under the judgment of their bishop; and we decree that the property belonging to them is to be preserved for the monasteries themselves. They may no longer be turned into secular dwellings.

Those who permit this to happen shall be subject to the condemnations established by the canons.

### XXV

Since, as has been reported to us, certain metropolitans neglect the flock entrusted to them and delay ordaining bishops, it has pleased the holy synod that the ordinations of bishops be carried out within three months, unless perhaps an unavoidable necessity compels the time of ordination to be extended.

If any bishop fails to observe this, he must be subject to ecclesiastical condemnation. It has also been decided that the revenues of the church left vacant are to be preserved intact with the steward of that church. [Col. 0313C]

### XXVI

Since, as has come to our attention, in certain churches bishops administer ecclesiastical property without a steward, it has been decided that every church possessing a bishop must have a steward from its own clergy. He is to administer the church’s property with the bishop’s authorization, so that the administration of ecclesiastical property may not be without testimony, its assets consequently be scattered, and reproach be brought upon the priestly dignity.

If anyone fails to observe this, he shall be subject to the divine rules. [Col. 0313D]

### XXVII

The holy synod decrees that those who abduct women for themselves, and those who have assisted them, if they are clerics, shall fall from their own rank. If they are laymen, let them be anathema.

## Subscription of the Bishops

Paschasius, bishop of the city of Lilybaeum, acting in the place of the most blessed Bishop Leo, subscribed with his definition.

Lucentius, bishop of the city of Ausculum, that is, acting in the place of the most holy Bishop Leo, subscribed with his definition.

Boniface, presbyter of the city of Rome, acting in the place of the Apostolic See, subscribed with his definition.

Anatolius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, New Rome, subscribed with his definition.

Juvenculus, bishop of Jerusalem, subscribed with his definition.

Maximus, bishop of Antioch, subscribed with his definition.

Quintilius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, subscribed with his definition.

Palafindus, bishop of Heraclea in Macedonia, acting in the place of the most holy man Anastasius, subscribed with his definition.

Stephen, bishop of Ephesus, subscribed with his definition.

Lucianus, bishop of Byze, acting in the place of the most holy Bishop Cyriacus of Heraclea in Thrace, subscribed with his definition.

Eusebius, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, subscribed with his definition.

Diogenes, bishop of Cyrrhus, subscribed with his definition.

Peter, bishop of Corinth, subscribed with his definition.

Florus, bishop of Sardis, subscribed with his definition.

Eunomius, bishop of Nicomedia, subscribed with his definition.

Anastasius, bishop of Nicaea, subscribed with his definition.

Eleutherius, bishop of Chalcedon, subscribed with his definition.

All the remaining bishops, six hundred and thirty in number, subscribed with their definition. [Col. 0314B]

After it had been read aloud, the most pious emperor said to the holy council:

“Let the holy council state whether the definition that has now been read was issued with the agreement of all the bishops.”

All the most reverend bishops replied:

“We all believe thus: one faith, one judgment. Let us all act in complete agreement. We have all subscribed in agreement. We are all orthodox. This is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of the apostles; this is the faith of those who believe rightly; this is the faith that saves the whole world.

“Long life to Marcian, the new Constantine, the new Paul, the new David, the most pious emperor, lord Augustus.”

After these words the most pious and faithful emperor said to the holy synod:

“The venerable Catholic faith has been made manifest by the holy and universal synod according to the exposition of the Fathers. And if we have imposed labor upon your reverence and caused you offense, we give the greatest thanks to God Almighty, our Savior, because the discord of many who were wandering concerning the faith has been cut off, and we have all now come together into one and the same faith, hoping that through your prayers a celebrated and better portion than all others may be granted by God.”

The holy synod again cried out:

“These things are worthy of your imperial rule; these things belong properly to your imperial rule. This correction of your imperial rule is worthy of Christ and worthy of the faith of the empire. Therefore the whole world is brought to peace.”

After these words the most pious [Col. 0314D] and faithful emperor said to the holy synod:

“Let your tranquility confirm that the venerable Catholic faith of the holy and venerable synod, according to the exposition of the Fathers, is manifest, lawful, and fitting, so that every future occasion for dispute concerning its faith may be removed.

“Therefore, if any civilian, soldier, or cleric publicly gathers a crowd and creates an uproar under the pretext of arranging matters, then, if he is a civilian, let him be expelled as a condemned person from the royal city; if he is a soldier or cleric, he shall suffer the loss of his rank and shall also be subject to other penalties.”

## Edict of the Emperor Marcian Confirming the Council of Chalcedon

The emperors Valentinian and Marcian, Augusti, to all peoples. [Col. 0315A]

At last what we desired with our most earnest prayers and efforts has come to pass: controversy has been removed from the orthodox law of Christians; at last remedies for culpable error have been found; and the divergent opinion of the peoples has come together in one agreement and harmony.

From all the provinces the most religious priests came to Chalcedon in accordance with our commands, and by a clear definition taught what must be observed in religion. Profane controversy has therefore now departed. For he is truly impious and sacrilegious who, after the judgment of so many priests, leaves anything further to be considered according to his own opinion.

It is the height of folly to seek an artificial light in the midst of clear daylight. Whoever, after the truth has been found, investigates anything further is seeking falsehood. Therefore no cleric, soldier, or person of any other condition shall henceforth attempt publicly to discuss the Christian faith, which has been definitively settled, before an assembled audience, seeking from this an occasion for tumult and treachery.

Such a person does injury to the judgment of the most religious synod if he attempts to reopen and publicly debate matters once correctly judged and settled. For the matters now established concerning the Christian faith are known to have been defined in accordance with the apostolic expositions and the institutions of the holy Fathers—three hundred and eighteen and one hundred and thirty.

There will be no lack of punishment for those who despise this law, since they not only oppose a faith rightly composed, but also profane the venerable mysteries through such disputation, as do Jews and pagans.

Therefore, if the offender is a cleric who has dared publicly to discuss religion, he shall be removed from the fellowship of the clergy. If he is a soldier, he shall be stripped of his military belt. All others guilty of this offense shall be expelled from this most holy city with judicial severity and shall also be subjected to the appropriate punishments.

For it is evident that the beginnings and fuel of heretical madness are nourished when certain persons publicly argue and dispute. Therefore they must preserve everything established by the holy Council of Chalcedon, and must thereafter raise no doubts.

Having thus been warned by this edict of our sincerity, resist profane voices and cease henceforth from disputing about divine matters, which is unlawful. For we believe that this sin will not only be punished by divine judgment, but will also be restrained by the authority of the laws and judges.

Published at Constantinople on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, during the consulship of Patricius.

## The Sacred Sanction of the Augusti Valentinian and Marcian Begins, Issued after the Council of Chalcedon for Its Confirmation and the Condemnation of Heretics

[Col. 0315D]

The emperors VALENTINIAN and MARCIAN, Augusti, to PALLADIUS, prefect of the praetorium.

Thanks must always be referred and rendered to the divine power, which neither permits the authors of heresy, though hidden, to remain concealed nor allows them to endure unpunished. It has full power to expose one of these evils and, in warding off the other, furnishes the rest with an example.

That God cares for human actions, and especially for reverence toward religion, has recently become evident in the confirmation of the Catholic faith: He neither neglected to expose Eutyches, a follower of criminal doctrines, whose wickedness had long remained hidden, nor, once the crime had been revealed, allowed him to escape punishment for his crime.

Thus condemned by divine and human judgments, he received the synodical decree as he deserved: guilty before God, whom he had injured, and guilty before human beings, whom he had attempted to deceive.

Very recently the innumerable and most blessed bishops from throughout the world assembled at Chalcedon and, together with the synod, expelled the wicked inventions of the aforementioned Eutyches, just as the definitions of the holy ancestors had been established—whether at Nicaea by the three hundred and eighteen, or later in this noble city by the one hundred and fifty bishops, or at Ephesus, when the error of Nestorius was excluded, under the presidency of Celestine of the city of Rome and Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria. [Col. 0316B]

Therefore we have judged and continue to judge that the matters defined according to the ancient discipline by the venerable Council of Chalcedon must be observed in every respect, in that faith by which we worship God. For it is entirely fitting that the definitions of priests who worship God with pure minds, which have preceded us as sacred safeguards for the orthodox faith according to the rules of the Fathers, be preserved together with veneration.

Since it belongs to the care of the ruler to crush every evil at its beginnings and to cut out the disease of serpents through the medicine of the laws, by this law we decree that those deceived by the error of Eutyches, following the example of the Apollinarians whom Eutyches followed—and whom the venerable rules of the Fathers, that is, the ecclesiastical canons and the most sacred enactments of the divine emperors, condemn—may create or designate no bishop, no presbyter, and no clerics whatsoever.

Eutyches himself is to be entirely deprived of the title of presbyter, which he used unworthily and from which he has been stripped. If any persons should dare, contrary to our definitions, to create bishops, presbyters, or other clerics from among them, we order that both those who are created and those who create or presume to do so shall be subject to the loss of all their property and to the danger of perpetual exile.

We order that none of them have permission to gather monks or build monasteries. Any places in which they should at some time dare to assemble are to be confiscated, provided that they assembled with the knowledge of the owner of the place. If they assembled without the owner’s knowledge, we decree that the lessees of the place, after being beaten with clubs, shall undergo deportation.

Furthermore, we do not permit them to receive anything from anyone’s will, nor to be left anything by testament by persons belonging to the same error. We do not allow them to serve in the army, except perhaps in the palace guard or the frontier forces.

If anyone is found serving outside these designated military units, either because his perversity in religion was not known or because he came to this error after acquiring his military belt, then, once released from military service, he shall receive this fruit of his infidelity: he shall be deprived of the fellowship of the nobles and of the palace, and may reside nowhere except in the village or city in which he was born.

If any of them were born in this noble city—which it is impious even to believe—they shall be excluded from this venerable city, from the most sacred imperial retinue, and from every metropolitan city.

We establish this generally concerning all who have been or are polluted by this calamity of defilement.

As for those who were previously clerics of the orthodox faith, and certain monks who provided Eutyches with lodging—which must not be called a monastery, since it contained enemies of religion—who have persisted in such madness that, abandoning the venerable worship of religion embodied in the Chalcedonian synodical decree, which priests from nearly the whole united world established, they followed the ill-starred assertion of Eutyches and, abandoning the true light, believed that darkness ought to be chosen:

We order that they be held subject to all the punishments established by the preceding laws against heretics, or rather that they be expelled beyond Roman soil, just as the preceding most religious enactments decreed concerning the Manichaeans, lest innocent or weak minds be deceived by their poisonous frauds and criminal inventions. [Col. 0317B]

Moreover, we have learned that they lied about certain matters to the insult of religion and the discrediting of the venerable synodical definition. Having written books and volumes of documents, they fabricated many things that openly revealed their madness against the true faith. Therefore we order that wherever writings of this kind are found, they be burned in the fire.

Those who, out of a desire to follow them, listen to anyone speaking such wickedness shall be restrained by a fine of ten pounds of gold.

Those who have written such things, or have handed them to others to read, whether with the intention of teaching or of learning, shall, we decree, be punished by deportation. This disastrous heresy must be destroyed, as was previously provided in the edicts of our Serenity.

We also remove from everyone the capacity by which those who attempt to teach unlawful things may be subjected to the ultimate penalty. In this way the material for error will be removed, if the sinner has neither a teacher nor a hearer.

Therefore, dearest and most beloved Palladius, let your illustrious and magnificent authority make known through published edicts everything we have ordered, so that the governors of the provinces and their officials, as well as the defenders of the cities, may know that we decree that the holy and true faith is to be guarded with holy purpose.

If they neglect this or permit it to be violated, they shall be struck with a fine of ten pounds of gold as betrayers of religion and the laws, and they shall also suffer the consequences in their assessment.

Given at Constantinople on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, during the consulship of Aspiratus and his announced colleague.

## Another Edict of the Emperor Marcian against the Same Heretics

[Col. 0317D]

The emperor MARCIAN, Augustus, to PALLADIUS, the prefect.

Although it has already been provided and defined by the most sacred constitution of My Clemency that severity must be exercised against those who, following the heretical perversity of Eutyches or Apollinaris, have deviated from religion and the Catholic faith, nevertheless the citizens and inhabitants of the city of Alexandria have been infected with such poisons of Apollinaris that it has been necessary now to decree again by a repeated law what We previously sanctioned.

Therefore, whoever, whether in this sacred city, in the city of Alexandria, throughout the Egyptian diocese, or in various other provinces, follows the profane perversity of Eutyches and does not believe as the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers taught when they founded the Catholic holy faith in the city of Nicaea, or as the one hundred and fifty other venerable bishops who later assembled in this noble city of Constantinople believed—just as Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril of holy memory, bishops of the city of Alexandria, believed—whom also the Council of Ephesus, presided over by Cyril of blessed memory, followed in its entirety, when the error of Nestorius was expelled, and whom the venerable Council of Chalcedon recently followed, with the earlier councils of priests agreeing in every respect, removing nothing from the most holy Creed and adding nothing to it, but condemning the deadly doctrines of Eutyches: let them know that they are heretics. For Apollinaris’s most criminal sect was followed by Eutyches and Dioscorus.

Accordingly, let all who follow the perversity of Apollinaris or Eutyches know that they will be punished by the penalties which the deified emperors of earlier times enacted against the Apollinarists, or which Our Serenity later enacted against the Eutychianists.

Therefore, whether they are Apollinarists—that is, Eutychianists—in this noble city, in the city of Alexandria, or within Egypt, although their designation differs, their heresy is nevertheless united, and their name is different but their sacrilege the same, and whether they do not believe as the aforementioned venerable men believed, or do not communicate with the most reverend Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, who holds the orthodox faith, in accordance with the constitutions of the deified emperors of earlier times promulgated concerning the Apollinarists, they shall not have the power to make a will, nor shall they acquire anything left to them in anyone’s will; nor shall they obtain anything from any gift. If anything should come to them through generosity, or should be conferred upon them by the will of a living or dying person, it shall immediately be assigned to Our treasury. They themselves shall not be able to give anything from their property to anyone.

Nor shall they be permitted to create or maintain bishops, presbyters, or other clerics for them. Let both Eutychianists and Apollinarists who dare to confer upon anyone the name of bishop, presbyter, or cleric, and those who attempt to retain the ecclesiastical name conferred upon them, know that they will be punished with exile and the loss of their property.

Those who had been clerics of the churches of this Catholic Rome or monks of the orthodox faith, but, having abandoned the worship of God, followed the heresy of Apollinaris or Eutyches, or shall follow it hereafter, We order to be subject to all the penalties established either by earlier laws against heretics, and also to be expelled beyond the soil of the Roman Empire itself.

Furthermore, no Apollinarist or Eutychianist shall build churches or monasteries for themselves, hold synaxes or gatherings, or allow members of this most deadly sect to assemble in anyone’s house, estate, monastery, or any other place belonging to another.

If they do so, and it is established, God willing, that this has been done, then the house or estate in which they assembled shall be joined to the treasury; the monastery, however, We order to be assigned to the orthodox Church of that city in whose territory it is located.

But if, without the owner’s knowledge, though with the knowledge of the person responsible for managing the house, or of the tenant, steward, or manager of the estate, forbidden conventicles should meet, then the tenant, steward, manager, or author of the gathering—or whoever has received them into a house, estate, or monastery, or has permitted unlawful parasynaxes and assemblies to be held—shall, if persons of low and abject condition, be publicly beaten with rods, both as punishment for themselves and as an example to others. If they are persons of respectable status, they shall be compelled to pay ten pounds of gold into Our treasury.

Furthermore, We order that no Apollinarist or Eutychianist aspire to any military service except service in the cohortal or frontier forces. If any act contrary to this, they shall be deprived of the belt of an honorable man and of association with the palace, and they shall not reside in any city, village, or district except that in which they were born.

If any were born in this noble city, they shall be expelled both from the most sacred imperial service and from every metropolitan city throughout the province.

Moreover, no Eutychianist or Apollinarist shall have the power publicly or privately to summon assemblies, or to assert the perversity of the criminal doctrine.

Nor shall anyone be permitted to dictate, write, read aloud, or publish anything against the venerable Council of Chalcedon. Let no one dare to possess books of this kind. If they are found involved in these offenses, let them be condemned to perpetual deportation. Those who, from a desire to learn, listen to disputants concerning the ill-omened heresy shall suffer a loss of ten pounds of gold, which shall be assigned to Our treasury.

All papers and books that contain the deadly doctrine of Eutyches shall be burned.

Therefore, dearest Father, let Your Illustrious Authority cause the provisions decreed by this most sacred constitution in this noble city and in the various provinces, especially in the city of Alexandria and throughout the entire Egyptian diocese, to be made known to everyone by edicts customarily posted, so that the severity We have established may immediately be exercised against those found guilty. Let the governors of the provinces and their apparitors know that, if they neglect the law which We have decreed must be guarded with the utmost religious observance, or permit it to be violated through any rash act, they shall be compelled to pay a fine of ten pounds of gold into Our treasury and shall moreover suffer danger to their reputation. We have likewise chosen that the provisions concerning pagans, which shall have equal force throughout the Roman Empire, be enforced with the greatest urgency against those who are established to celebrate profane rites.

Given on the Kalends of August, at Constantinople, in the eighth consulship of the Deified [Emperor] and the fourth of Anthemius. [The following notation is uncertain in the transmitted text: “CC. concess.”]

## Bishop Atticus: How a Formata Letter Is Made

[Col. 0319]

[Col. 0319B] No one who has even slight knowledge of the Greek language is unaware that the elements of the alphabet also express numbers. Therefore, lest any fraud of falsification be rashly attempted in the preparation of canonical letters, which Latin usage calls *formatae*, the three hundred and eighteen Fathers assembled at Nicaea most beneficially devised and established the following rule: that *formatae* letters should have this method of calculation or reckoning.

The first Greek letters of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are to be taken into the reckoning, namely Π, Υ, Α. These letters signify respectively the numbers eighty, four hundred, and one.

The first letter of the apostle Peter—that is, the letter which signifies the number eighty—is also to be taken; likewise, the first letter of the person who wrote the letter, the second letter of the person to whom it is written, the third letter of the recipient, the fourth letter of the city from which it is written, and the number of the current indiction. All these Greek letters, which, as we have said, express numbers, are then added together, and whatever total is obtained is to be used to identify the letter. The person who receives it must examine this with every caution and verify it explicitly. In addition, he must separately add to the letter the number ninety and the number nine, which according to the Greek letters signify [their respective numerical values].

Farewell in the Lord.

Thus far the Councils of the Greeks.

# 76. The Latin Councils Follow, the First of Which Is Carthaginian

[Col. 0319]

## The Chapters of the First Council of Carthage Begin

[Col. 0319D]

1. That baptism received in the Trinity is not to be repeated.  
2. Concerning the tombs and honor of the martyrs.  
3. That clerics and women dedicated to holiness shall not live with unrelated men or women.  
4. That they shall not reside with widows or other unrelated persons.  
5. That clerics or laymen shall not be ordained in another person’s church.  
6. That clerics shall not undertake secular business or management.  
7. That clerics or laymen shall not communicate in another church under letters from their own bishop.  
8. That clerics entangled in other people’s affairs shall not be ordained before rendering an account.  
9. That laymen shall not appoint clerics as their agents or accountants.  
10. That one bishop shall not usurp the congregations or boundaries of another bishop.  
11. Concerning contumacious clerics and the number of presbyters and deacons who are to judge.  
12. That agreements made between bishops shall be observed.  
13. That clerics shall not lend money at interest.  
14. That laymen who despise the canons shall be excommunicated, while clerics shall be deprived of their honor.

## The First Council of Carthage Begins

[Col. 0321]

[Col. 0321A] When Bishop Gratus had taken his seat at the Council of Carthage together with his colleagues, and those who had assembled at Carthage from the various African provinces—Felix of Baiana, Fortunatianus of Rampta, Crescens of Baia, Vindicianus of Lacubai, Abundantius of Hadrumetum, Priatus of Begesilta, Gaudentius of Turretalis, Patricius of Sinca, Quietus of Utica, Romulus of Theveste, and the others whose signatures are included—Bishop Gratus said:

“We give thanks to almighty God and to Christ Jesus, who has brought an end to wicked schisms and looked upon His Church, so that He might raise all her scattered members into her embrace. He commanded the most religious Emperor Constantius to undertake the cause of unity and to send the servants of God, Paul and Macarius, ministers of this holy work.

“Therefore, gathered by God’s will for unity, so that we may hold councils throughout the various provinces, and so that the whole province of Africa might come today by God’s grace to the council at Carthage, let the necessary topics be discussed, with you considering them together with my humble self. We must keep in mind the divine commandments and the teaching of the divine Scriptures, and, contemplating the time of unity, define each matter in such a way that Carthage does not weaken the force of the law, while we nevertheless establish nothing excessively harsh at a time of unity.”

### Chapter I

“Therefore, if it pleases you, let us first consider the matter of rebaptization. I ask Your Holiness to express the judgment of your minds concerning one who has descended into the water, been questioned concerning the Trinity according to the faith of the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles, and confessed a good conscience toward God concerning the resurrection of Jesus Christ: is he permitted to be questioned again in the same faith and immersed again in water?”

All the bishops said: “Far be it, far be it.”

“We decree that rebaptizations are unlawful and entirely foreign to sincere faith and Catholic discipline.”

Bishop Gratus said:

“Great blessedness has been granted in our time by God the Father through the Lord Christ, so that religious minds may be instructed in ecclesiastical discipline, and so that hearers, receiving the correct rule that pleases God, may obtain the rewards of many good things, so that God may be honored in them in all things and for all things.

“The necessary matter of rebaptization has been examined, in which the madness of schism lay more deeply concealed. With the force of the law moderated, and with authority, the faith has been preserved.

“Nevertheless, I intend to commend this point to your wisest minds. Although your prudence has been instructed by God and deserves to receive abundant gifts from above in peace and unity, I too am one of you and bear equal concern with you. For the sake of ecclesiastical order, I shall take care to commend this matter.”

### II

[Col. 0322B] “Let no profane person defame the dignity of the martyrs, nor let them reduce the bodies which have been committed to burial solely for the sake of ecclesiastical remembrance, so that they may not call the names of martyrs—without due reason or at the proper time when the martyrs’ festivals are celebrated—those who have been driven headlong by madness or separated by some other form of sin. If anyone, to the injury of the martyrs, associates madmen with their glory, let it be decreed that, if they are laymen, they be brought to repentance. If they are clerics, then, after admonition and investigation, let them be deprived of their honor.”

All said: “Your Holiness has rightly established this; the same has also been decreed in individual councils.”

### III

Bishop Gratus said:

“And this above all, if it seems good to Your Affection, must be guarded: pastoral care, so far as regular prudence ought and can do so, must give warning that no one who abstains from carnal relations may live together with unrelated persons. Opportunities for sins must be cut off, and all suspicions removed by which the devil’s cunning, under the pretext of charity and affection, is accustomed to entangle souls that are unwary or ignorant.

“Therefore, no man and no woman devoted to holiness and virginity ought, to the blasphemy of the Church, to live under one roof with unrelated persons. If it pleases you—”

All said:

“Those who do not wish to marry and choose the better portion of chastity must avoid this. They must not only refrain from living together, but must not even allow anyone access to them. Thus the law commands, and Your Holiness commends this, as has been established in the individual councils.”

Bishop Gratus said:

“Persuasion sometimes restrains the prudent from sins, whereas fear of this kind ought to constrain the imprudent when they reject sound counsel and a salutary command. Therefore, if they are laymen, and, after admonition, they despise it, let them be separated from communion.”

All said: “It pleases us.”

### IV

Bishop Gratus said:

“Although there are countless matters written into the law that advance discipline, and each of us, by continual discussion and frequent admonition concerning every individual case, can invite the people to advance in discipline, nevertheless some of them must be brought forward by us and established in the council because of the blasphemies involved.

“If it seems good to you, let the same law and judgment also apply to those who live with widows and are not related to them by any kinship.”

All said:

“Let the same law and judgment remain concerning widowers and widows.”

### V

Bishop Primatus of Begesilta said:

“I commend to Your Holiness that you establish that no one may receive a foreign cleric without letters from his bishop, nor retain him with himself; nor may a layman usurp someone from another bishop’s congregation and ordain him without the knowledge of the bishop whose congregation he belongs to.”

Bishop Gratus said:

“This observance preserves peace. For I also remember that it was established at the most holy Council of Sardica that no one should usurp a man belonging to another’s congregation; but if he should perhaps be needed, he should ask his colleague and receive him with his consent.”

### VI

Bishop Nicasius of Culustis said:

“I believe that my proposal will please Your Holiness and that you will disapprove of this: those who serve God and are attached to the clergy should not engage in the business, administration, or management of households.”

Bishop Gratus said:

“The statutes of the apostles also say that no one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in secular affairs. Therefore, let them either be clerics without the management of households, or managers without clerical office.”

All said:

“Let us observe this.”

### VII

Bishop Casianus of Usula said:

“Let Your Gravity establish that no cleric or layman may communicate in another’s congregation without letters from his own bishop.”

Bishop Gratus said:

“Unless this is observed, communion will become indiscriminate. If someone is received with letters, harmony is preserved between the bishops, and no subtle person, fleeing the communion of one, secretly approaches another.”

All said:

“You provide for everyone and consult for both clergy and laity.”

### VIII

Bishop Magnus of Astuaga said:

“What does Your Affection think? Should managers and agents, even those who are guardians of orphans in their own right, be ordained?”

Bishop Gratus said:

“If, after all matters have been laid aside and accounts rendered, their conduct in life has been approved in every respect, they ought, if requested, to be honored with clerical office and praise. For if someone is ordained without due consideration before being released from business or official responsibilities, the Church is disgraced.”

All said:

“Your Holiness has rightly established everything; therefore this is also our judgment.”

### IX

Bishop Metus of Canusium said:

“It has rightly been established that those answerable for other people’s business shall not be ordained. Nevertheless, once released, they must give thanks and refrain from injuring the clergy; nor shall they be permitted to choose our clerics as storekeepers or accountants.”

Bishop Gratus said:

“No one doubts that all persons—whether masters, managers, or anyone else in authority—when they have heard the most salutary regulations of the council and have learned that provision has been made for them and no obstacle imposed, must restrain their own injury toward our clerics.

“But if, contrary to the imperial constitution, they should think that our clerics ought to be harassed, then, provided that ecclesiastical defense does not mock us, public shame will be exacted.”

All said:

“Such most salutary declarations ought to have been granted by so great a council.”

### X

Bishop Felix of Baia said:

“No one ought to injure his colleague, for many overstep their own boundaries and usurp those belonging to others against their will.”

Bishop Gratus said:

“No one doubts that the desire for greed is the root of all evils. Therefore it must be prohibited that anyone usurp another’s boundaries, overstep his fellow bishop, or usurp another’s congregations without that bishop’s request, because all the other evils arise from this.”

All said:

“It pleases us, it pleases us.”

### XI

Bishop Elpidophorus of Cuicul said:

“Let Your Holiness establish that clerics who are proud or contumacious be restrained, so that those who inflict injuries upon their superiors may be afraid.”

Bishop Gratus said:

“It is clear that one who despises humility does not belong to God but to the devil, who is the inventor and leader of pride. Therefore, if anyone becomes arrogant or insulting toward an older man, or has any case to bring, let him be heard by three neighboring bishops if he is a deacon, by six if he is a presbyter, and by twelve fellow priests if he is a bishop.”

The bishops all said:

“Contempt for contumacy and pride must be broken in every case; but the case must be heard according to the persons involved by the prescribed number.”

### XII

Bishop Antigonus of Matira said:

“I suffer a grave injury, and I believe that Your Holiness grieves over my insult and counts it as a common injury. When Optantius presented himself, he had my agreement, and it was divided, so that he might entice the souls of ignorant people against discipline, against the evangelical tradition, and against the peace that had been approved.

“For if they thought that this could happen to them, surely no one would ever have sinned against a brother. Therefore, let him either obtain the firmness of the agreement he made, or, if he does not restrain himself, let him experience ecclesiastical discipline.”

All said:

“Let peace be preserved; let agreements be observed.”

### XIII

Bishop Abundantius of Hadrumetum said:

“It was established in our council that clerics may not lend money at interest. Let the view of Your Holiness and of this council be indicated by the present decision.”

Bishop Gratus said:

“New proposals, whether obscure or concealed under a general category, will receive their form after examination by us. But concerning matters which divine Scripture has clearly decreed, judgment must not be delayed; rather, it must be carried out. Therefore, what is condemned in laymen ought much more to be condemned beforehand in clerics.”

All said:

“No one acts against the prophets or against the Gospels without danger.”

### XIV

Bishop Gratus said:

“In accordance with the statutes of the council and the judgment of my humility, I propose that we bring all matters to a conclusion. Let all the designated and arranged topics retain their judgments.

“I believe that you remember that, in many councils of our fathers, rash innovation was condemned and the impiety of rebaptization was punished. I believe that these matters have now also received their conclusion in our council.

“As for the remaining matters, whether deeds or words, which have been set out above or recorded in other councils and are found to accord with the law, it is our duty to observe them. If anyone transgresses or corrupts the statutes, or thinks them worthy of being disregarded, then, if he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if he is a cleric, let him be deprived of his honor.”

All said:

“It pleases us, it pleases us.”

[Col. 0326A] Bishop Gratus said:

“It remains now for you to confirm by your subscriptions all the decisions of us all that have been written with your agreement.”

All said:

“The writings of this council testify that we have agreed, and our agreement will be declared by our subscriptions.”

And they subscribed.

## The Chapters of the Second Council of Carthage Begin

[Col. 0325]

[Col. 0325A]

1. That the Trinity be both believed and preached.  
2. That chastity be observed by deacons and priests.  
3. That the preparation of chrism, the consecration of girls, and the reconciliation of penitents not be performed by presbyters.  
4. That a presbyter reconcile a penitent when ordered by his bishop.  
5. That a diocese which has never had a bishop shall not have one.  
6. That those entangled in crimes shall not accuse clerics.  
7. That whoever receives a person excommunicated by another shall be excommunicated.  
8. That if an excommunicated presbyter presumes to offer the sacrifice, he shall be anathematized.  
9. That if a presbyter celebrates rites without consulting his bishop, he shall be deprived of his honor.  
10. How many are to judge a priest and a deacon.  
11. That no one presume to take over another’s parish.  
12. That no bishop be ordained without consulting the metropolitan.  
13. That whoever comes in the council against his profession and subscription shall be deposed.

## The Second Council of Carthage Begins

Held in the year 428 of the era.

[Col. 0325]

[Col. 0325B] In the consulship of the most glorious Emperor Valentinian Augustus for the fourth time and of Theodosius, men of illustrious rank, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, at Carthage, in the Basilica of Perpetua, which had been restored, when Bishop Genedius had taken his seat together with Victor of Adrianum, another Victor of Pupinianum, and his other fellow bishops from various provinces, Bishop Genedius said:

### Chapter I

“I give thanks to almighty God, who permitted you, in accordance with the common resolution reached in the praetorium, to come to Carthage for the faith and benefit of the Church, according to the tenor of my letter of request, although not all of you have come. Nevertheless, because charity persuades all things, those who are absent in body may be regarded as joined with us in spirit.

“Therefore, by God’s favor, since you are present, the ecclesiastical faith handed down by us must first be confessed in this glorious assembly by a common profession. From this point the ecclesiastical order of each matter must be constructed and strengthened with the agreement of all, so that the minds of the brothers and fellow bishops recently promoted may be strengthened concerning the matters to be proposed.

“As we have received from the Fathers by certain determination, we retain within our bosoms the Trinity consecrated there—the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which, as we have learned, is understood to possess no division. Let us instruct God’s peoples as we have learned.”

All the bishops said:

“Certainly. Thus we received it; thus we hold it, following the apostolic faith.”

### II

Bishop Aurelius said:

“When, in the previous council, the regulation of continence and chastity was being discussed, these three orders were bound to chastity by a certain written enactment through their consecrations. I mean bishops, presbyters, and deacons. It was agreed that they should be continent, as befits the most holy bishops and priests of God, and likewise deacons and those who serve the divine sacraments, so that they may be able to obtain simply from God whatever they ask, and so that we may observe what the apostles taught and antiquity itself preserved.”

All the bishops said:

“It pleases all that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and those who handle the sacraments, as guardians of chastity, abstain even from their wives.”

All said:

“It pleases us, and that chastity be guarded in all things and by all who serve at the altar.”

### III

Bishop Fortunatus said:

“If Your Holiness orders it, I make this proposal, for I remember that it was established in the previous council that chrism, the reconciliation of penitents, and the consecration of girls should not be performed by presbyters. If anyone should arise who does this, what ought to be decreed concerning him?”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“Your Dignity has heard the proposal of our brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus. What do you say concerning these matters?”

All the bishops said:

“The preparation of chrism and the consecration of girls shall not be performed by presbyters, nor shall a presbyter be permitted to reconcile anyone at a public Mass. This pleases all.”

### IV

Bishop Aurelius said:

“If anyone is in danger and asks to be reconciled to the divine altars, then, if the bishop is absent, the presbyter must consult the bishop and, by his command, reconcile the person in danger. We must confirm this provision by salutary counsel.”

All the bishops said:

“It pleases us that Your Holiness has deemed it necessary to instruct us in this matter by salutary counsel.”

### V

Bishop Felix of Selemsela said:

“If it also pleases Your Holiness, I suggest that dioceses which have never received bishops should not have them, and that a diocese which once had a bishop should have its own. If, as time passes and faith in God increases, the people multiply and desire to have their own ruler, then, with the will of the person in whose authority the diocese is established, let it have a bishop. Let Your Holiness determine what ought to be done according to this proposal.”

Bishop Genedius said:

“If it pleases you, let the proposal of our brother and fellow bishop Felix be confirmed by all.”

All the bishops said:

“It pleases us.”

### VI

[Col. 0327B] Bishop Numidius of Massila said:

“Furthermore, there are many men of bad conduct who think that their elders or bishops should be dragged indiscriminately and randomly into accusation. Should such persons be admitted so easily or not?”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“Therefore, let it please Your Affection that a person entangled in any crimes have no right to bring an accusation against his elders.”

All the bishops said:

“If he is a criminal, let him not be admitted. This pleases all.”

### VII

Bishop Felix of Selemsela said:

“I also commend this matter to Your Holiness. Those who are expelled from the Church for their crimes and dare to go to the imperial court, or rush to public courts, or perhaps disturb the thresholds of the Catholic Church—if a bishop or cleric of any congregation receives them without consent, what is your judgment concerning them?”

Bishop Epigonius of the regions of Bullis said:

“If a bishop who holds Catholic communion rashly receives such men as they proceed with empty flatteries, let him know that he is rightly corrupted or condemned together with them.”

Bishop Genedius said:

“Therefore our brothers and fellow bishops make a proper proposal: if those who have deservedly been expelled from the Church for their crimes are received into communion by any bishop, presbyter, or cleric, that person too shall be held liable to the same crime as they, because they have fled the regular judgment of their own bishop.”

All the bishops said:

“This pleases all.”

### VIII

[Col. 0327C] Aliphius, bishop and legate of the Church of Tagasta in the province of Numidia, said:

“This also must not be omitted: if a presbyter, having been corrected or excommunicated by his bishop, should, puffed up with arrogance or pride, think that sacrifices ought to be offered to the Lord separately, or believe that another altar should be erected and something done against ecclesiastical faith and discipline, he must not escape unpunished.”

Valentinus, bishop of the first see of the province of Numidia, said:

“What our brother Aliphius has set out is necessarily consistent with ecclesiastical discipline and faith. Therefore, announce to Your Affection what you think should follow from it: if a presbyter, puffed up against his bishop, creates a schism, let him be anathema.”

All the bishops said:

“If a presbyter has been excommunicated or corrected by his superior, it is appropriate for him to complain to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and he may be reconciled to his own bishop through them.

“If he does not do this, but, puffed up with pride—which God forbid—decides that he must separate himself from communion with his bishop, and, creating a schism with some others, offers sacrifice to God separately, let him be regarded as anathematized, deprived of his office, and deprived of his place. Furthermore, let him be driven far from the city and congregation in which he was, lest he deceive either the ignorant or those living simply by a serpentine fraud.

“For, according to the Apostle, the Church is one, the faith is one, and baptism is one. If he has no just complaint against his bishop, an investigation must be made.”

### IX

Bishop Numidius of Massila said:

“In certain places there are presbyters who, either through simple ignorance or through bold dissimulation, celebrate rites in many households while the bishop is present and without consulting him. Your Holiness recognizes that this is inconsistent with discipline.”

Bishop Genedius said:

“We do not delay in giving a fitting response to the worthy proposal of our brother and fellow bishop.”

All the bishops said:

“Any presbyter who wishes to celebrate rites in any place without consulting his bishop acts against his own honor.”

### X

Bishop Felix of Selemsela said:

“I add this also, in accordance with the statutes of the ancient councils: if any bishop—which we do not suppose—should incur some offense and be in such great need that he cannot assemble many people, lest he remain under accusation, let him be heard by twelve bishops, by six presbyters, and by three deacons together with his own bishop.”

Bishop Genedius said:

“What does Your Holiness say to this?”

All the bishops said:

“We must preserve the statutes of the ancients.”

### XI

Bishop Victor of Abzirida said:

“Ecclesiastical discipline must be strengthened, so that no bishop may harass the congregations or diocese of another through his importunity. How is one who attempts to do this to be restrained?”

Bishop Genedius said:

“Both the holy law prohibits this and Truth itself declares that no one ought to covet what belongs to another. Therefore, mark in your own words what pleases all of you.”

All the bishops said:

“It pleases us, in accordance with the authority of the divine law and the holy Gospel, that none of us transgress another’s boundaries.”

### XII

Bishop Numidius of Massila said:

“Some bishops, by a kind of usurpation, think that, after disregarding the primate of a province, they may ordain a bishop according to the desire of the people without letters being sent to them from the first see, and without later receiving such letters. What does Your Holiness establish concerning this?”

Bishop Genedius said:

“Since the honor which ought to be preserved for each person is common to all, it is fitting that you pronounce the same judgment to our brotherhood.”

All the bishops said:

“It pleases all that no one presume so readily, without consulting the primate of any province, to ordain a bishop anywhere with many bishops, without his command, as has been said. But if necessity arises, three bishops, wherever they may be, must ordain a bishop by command of the primate.”

### XIII

Bishop Genedius said:

“Therefore, let everything established by your most glorious assembly be observed by all.”

All the bishops said:

“It pleases us that they be observed by everyone.”

Bishop Genedius said:

“If—which we do not suppose—any of these provisions should be violated by anyone, what do you decree should be done?”

All the bishops said:

“Whoever acts against his own profession or subscription shall himself separate from this assembly.”

Bishop Genedius said:

“Let us rejoice in our Lord, who has granted that, for the preservation of the Catholic Church, we have decided by salutary counsel that all these things must be observed. Therefore, we must confirm by our own subscriptions what has been said by all.”

All the bishops said:

“Let it be done, let it be done.”

And they subscribed.

## The Chapters of the Third Council of Carthage Begin

[Col. 0329]

[Col. 0329A] 1. That bishops of the same province should inquire of their primate concerning the date of Easter. 2. That a council be held every year. 3. That, before being ordained, a bishop should know the canon. [Col. 0329B] 4. That levites and virgins should not be consecrated before the age of twenty-five. 5. That the sacrament should not be given to catechumens. 6. That baptism or the Eucharist should not be given to the dead. 7. Where and within what period an accused bishop should be examined. 8. Concerning presbyters and deacons: how many bishops should hear them. 9. That clerics should not appeal to public courts. 10. If anyone appeals from some ecclesiastical judges to other judges, whether ecclesiastical or of greater authority, it should not prejudice the earlier judges if they have issued differing [Col. 0329C] judgments. 11. That the sons of clerics should not attend spectacles. 12. That unbelievers should not be joined in marriage to the children of clerics. 13. That clerics should not transfer anything from their possessions to unbelievers. 14. That clerics should not allow their children to leave their authority unless they have been tested in age and conduct. 15. That clerics should not be contractors or merchants. 16. That clerics should not be usurers. 17. That foreign women should not live with clerics.

[Col. 0329D] 18. That clerics should not be ordained unless all those who live with them are believers. 19. That when clerics reach puberty they should profess either marriage or chastity. 20. That one bishop should not usurp another’s congregations. 21. That no bishop should dare to retain or ordain another bishop’s cleric. 22. That no cleric should be ordained unless he has been found worthy. 23. Concerning prayers and intercessions. 24. That only bread and the chalice should be offered in the sacrifice. 25. That clerics or continent persons should not have solitary access to widows or virgins.

[Col. 0330A] 26. That the bishop of the first see should not be called “chief of the priests.” 27. That clerics should not enter taverns. 28. That a bishop should not travel a considerable distance without a *formata* from the metropolitan. [Col. 0330B] 29. That the Mass should be celebrated by people who are fasting. 30. That no one should hold a banquet in the church. 31. That penitents should be assigned penance according to the measure of their sins. 32. That a presbyter should not reconcile penitents except by the bishop’s order or in his absence. 33. Concerning the guardianship of sacred virgins. 34. Concerning sick persons being baptized when they can no longer speak. 35. That penance should not be denied to converts who were apostates or actors. 36. That a presbyter should not prepare chrism. 37. That clerics should not remain in another city without necessity.

[Col. 0330C] 38. That the transfer of bishops should not be permitted. 39. That two bishops should not presume to ordain a bishop. 40. That when a bishop is elected, if he has opponents, five priests should assemble. 41. That each year the bishops who assemble in council should also be informed by their primate concerning the celebration of Easter. 42. That a congregation which is always subject to a bishop in his diocese should not receive another bishop. 43. That those who, despising their own congregation, refuse to come to the council should lose both their congregation and their honor.

[Col. 0330D] 44. That no bishop should presume to ordain another’s cleric for himself. 45. That a bishop who has several clerics should give one to a bishop who is requested to ordain one and is in need. 46. That a bishop who has been appointed in a diocese should retain only the congregation in which he was ordained. 47. That nothing except the canonical Scriptures should be read in the church under the name of divine Scripture. 48. Concerning those baptized by the Donatists. 49. That what anyone acquires while occupying an ecclesiastical rank should be transferred to the Church. 50. That the acts of the council should be confirmed by the bishops’ subscriptions.

# The Third Council of Carthage Begins

Held by ninety-seven bishops, in the year 435 of the era.

[Col. 0331]

[Col. 0331A] In the consulship of the most illustrious men Caesarius and Atticus, on the Kalends of September, at Carthage, in the secretarium of the restored basilica, when Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat together with his fellow bishops, with the deacons also standing by, the following matters were established and defined by the present council.

## Chapter I

It was therefore decided at the outset, because an error often tends to arise, that all the bishops of the African provinces should take care to receive the determination of the Easter observance from the Church of Carthage.

## II

Likewise it was decided that, because ecclesiastical matters which often grow harmful to the congregations are neglected, a council should be summoned each year. To it, all the provinces that have primatial sees should send two or five bishops chosen from their councils, so that they may be less subject to envy and less burdensome in expense to their hosts, and so that, once the assembly has been gathered, its authority may be complete. From Tripoli, however, because of the scarcity of bishops, one bishop should come.

## III

It was likewise decided that, when bishops or clerics have been ordained, the decrees of the councils should first be impressed upon their ears by those who ordained them, lest they regret having done anything contrary to the council’s statutes.

## IV

It was likewise decided that before the age of twenty-five neither deacons should be ordained nor virgins consecrated, and that readers should not greet the people.

## V

It was likewise decided that during the most solemn days of Easter the sacrament should not be given to catechumens, except the customary salt; for if the faithful do not alter the sacraments during those days, [Col. 0331C] neither ought catechumens to alter them.

## VI

It was likewise decided that the Eucharist should not be given to the bodies of the dead, for the Lord said: “Take and eat.” But corpses can neither take nor eat. Care must also be taken lest the weakness of the brethren believe that the dead can be baptized, since it is not lawful for the Eucharist to be given to them either.

## VII

Bishop Aurelius said: Whoever of the bishops is accused, let the accuser bring the case before the primate of that province. Let the person against whom the charge is brought not be suspended from communion unless, having been summoned by letter to state his case on the appointed day before the chosen judges, he fails to appear at all—that is, within the period of one month from the day on which it is established that he received the letter. If, however, he proves some genuine reasons of necessity [Col. 0331D] by which it is clear that he was unable to appear, he shall have a full opportunity to state his case within the following month. Nevertheless, after the second month he shall not communicate until he has been cleared.

But if he does not wish to appear at the universal annual council, or if his case is concluded there, he shall be judged to have pronounced upon himself the sentence of his own condemnation. During the period in which he does not communicate, he shall not communicate in his own church or parish either. His accuser, however, if he has never been absent during the days appointed for hearing the case, shall not be removed from communion. But if he has at any time been absent, withdrawing himself, then, once the bishop has been restored to communion, the accuser shall be removed from communion, though in such a way that he too is not deprived of the opportunity to pursue the case if he proves that he wished to appear but was unable to do so.

It was further decided that when he has begun to act before the judgment of the bishops, if the accuser’s person is culpable, he should not be admitted to bring an accusation unless he wishes to assert his own cases, but not ecclesiastical ones.

## VIII

If presbyters or deacons are accused, their own bishop, together with the proper number of colleagues from neighboring places whom the accused requested from that same body, should be joined to them: that is, six bishops besides himself in the case of a presbyter, and three in the case of a deacon. They should examine their cases, while the same procedure concerning days, delays, removal from communion, and examination of [79] persons is observed between the accusers and the accused. The cases of the remaining clerics may be heard and concluded by the bishop of the place alone.

## IX

Concerning the various orders serving the Church: if anyone becomes involved in a criminal case and rejects ecclesiastical judgment, he ought to suffer the consequences. The sons of priests should not attend secular spectacles.

It was likewise decided that whoever among the bishops, presbyters, deacons, or clerics, when a charge has been brought against him in the Church or a civil case has been initiated, wishes—having abandoned ecclesiastical judgment—to be cleared in the public courts, shall lose his position, even if a judgment has been pronounced in his favor. This applies in a criminal action. In a civil case, he shall lose what he has won if he wishes to retain his position, since, if he hesitates to choose judges for himself from the fellowship of the Church and considers the Church’s fellowship worthless, he thinks ill of the whole Church when he seeks help from secular judgment, although the Apostle commands that the cases of private persons also be brought to the Church and decided there.

## X

It was also decided that, when an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where greater authority exists, it should not prejudice those whose judgment has been annulled if they cannot be convicted of having judged with hostile intent, or of having been corrupted by some greed or favor. Certainly, if the judges were chosen by agreement of the parties, it should not be permitted to appeal even from a smaller number than the number established.

## XI

The sons of priests or clerics should not stage secular spectacles, nor should they watch them, although all laypeople too are prohibited from attending spectacles. For this has always been forbidden to all Christians: they should not go where there is blasphemy.

## XII

It was likewise decided that the sons or daughters of bishops, or of any clerics, should not be joined in marriage to pagans, heretics, [Col. 0333A] or schismatics.

## XIII

Bishops or clerics should not transfer anything from their possessions by gifts to those who are not Catholic Christians, even if they are relatives.

## XIV

Bishops or clerics should not allow their sons to leave their authority by emancipation unless they are confident concerning their conduct and age, so that they may already be capable of bearing responsibility for their own sins.

## XV

It was likewise decided that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or clerics should not be contractors or agents, nor should they seek their livelihood through any disgraceful profit or dishonorable business, because they ought to remember that it is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.”

## XVI

No cleric should receive more than he has lent. If he lent money, he should receive money; if a specific object, he should receive that same kind of object in the amount he gave; and whatever else he gave, he should receive the same amount in return.

## XVII

Foreign women should not live with any clerics at all, except mothers, grandmothers, maternal aunts, paternal aunts, sisters, and the daughters of brothers or sisters; also, any women from the household who, because of domestic necessity, were already living with them before they were ordained; or, if their sons took wives after their parents had been ordained, women whom necessity required them to bring from elsewhere because they had no servants in the household whom they could marry.

## XVIII

Bishops, presbyters, and deacons should not be ordained before they have made all those in their household Catholic Christians.

## XIX

It was decided that when readers reach the age of puberty they should be compelled either to take wives or to profess continence.

## XX

It was decided that no bishop should usurp another’s congregations, and that no bishop should overstep his colleague in the diocese.

## XXI

No one should dare to retain or promote in the Church entrusted to him another’s cleric without that cleric’s bishop’s permission. The designation “clerics” includes readers, psalmists, and doorkeepers.

[Col. 0333D] ## XXII

No one should be ordained a cleric who has not been tested, either by examination by the bishops or by the testimony of the people.

## XXIII

No one should name a father for a son or a son for a father in the prayers; when one stands at the altar, the prayer should always be directed to the Father. And whatever prayers anyone writes for himself, he should not use them until he has first submitted those compositions to the brethren for instruction.

## XXIV

In the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood, nothing more should be offered than the Lord himself handed down—that is, bread and wine mixed with water. Nothing more should be offered in the sacrifices than what comes from grapes and grain.

[Col. 0334A] ## XXV

Clerics or continent persons should not approach widows or virgins except at the command or with the permission of the bishops and presbyters. They should not do this alone, but with clerics or with those whom the bishop or presbyter directs. Nor should bishops or presbyters have solitary access to such women, unless either clerics or some respectable Christians are present.

## XXVI

The bishop of the first see should not be called “chief of the priests,” “high priest,” or anything of that kind, but only “bishop of the first see.”

## XXVII

Clerics should not enter taverns to eat or drink, unless compelled by the necessity of travel.

[Col. 0334B] ## XXVIII

It was likewise decided that bishops should not travel across the sea unless they have consulted the bishop of the first see or the primate of whatever province it is, so that they may especially obtain from that bishop a *formata* or letter of recommendation.

## XXIX

The sacraments of the altar should be celebrated only by people who are fasting, except on the one annual day on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated. If a commendation must be made at midday for some of the dead, whether bishops or others, it should be done only with prayers if those who are to perform it have already eaten.

## XXX

No bishops or clerics should hold banquets in the church, unless perhaps travelers are refreshed there because of the necessity of lodging. The people too should be prohibited from such banquets as far as possible.

[Col. 0334C] ## XXXI

For penitents, the bishops should determine the periods of penance according to the differences among their sins.

## XXXII

A presbyter should not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, except when necessity compels him to do so in the bishop’s absence. In the case of any penitent whose crime is public and most widely known, and has disturbed the whole Church, hands should be laid upon him before the apse.

## XXXIII

If sacred virgins are deprived of the parents by whom they were guarded, they should, through the bishop’s provision—or, when the bishop is absent, through that of the presbyter—be entrusted to a monastery of virgins or to more serious-minded women [Col. 0334D], so that, living together, they may guard one another and not damage the Church’s reputation by wandering about indiscriminately.

## XXXIV

Sick persons should be baptized if they cannot answer for themselves, provided that their own people have testified to their will. The same procedure should be followed with penitents.

## XXXV

Grace or reconciliation should not be denied to actors, stage performers, and certain persons of this kind, or to apostates who have converted or returned to the Lord.

## XXXVI

A presbyter should not consecrate virgins without consulting the bishop, and should never prepare chrism.

[Col. 0335A] ## XXXVII

Clerics should not remain in another city unless the bishops or presbyters of the places have determined that their reasons are just.

## XXXVIII

We report the mandate given to us, which also appears to have been established in the plenary council at Capua: rebaptisms, reordinations, or transfers of bishops should not be permitted.

For Cresconius, bishop of the village of Regiensis, abandoned his own congregation and invaded the Church of Tiburnum. Even to this day, although admonished according to the established ruling to leave the congregation he had invaded, he has refused to do so. We have heard that the statutes which had been pronounced were indeed confirmed. We therefore ask, in accordance with the mandate given to us, that you deign to grant us the assurance that, when necessity itself requires it, we may approach the governor of the province against him according to the statutes of the most glorious emperors, so that the man who refused to comply with your mild admonition and to correct what was unlawful may immediately be excluded by judicial authority.

Bishop Aurelius said: If, while the form of discipline is preserved, your assembly has been reluctant to withdraw with greater moderation because of your charity, this desire will not be considered offensive, since the assembly has also been convened by judicial authority because of his contempt and obstinacy.

The bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: This pleases everyone.

All the bishops said: It is just; it pleases us.

## XXXIX

The bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: We have also been given this mandate: because two of our neighboring brothers in Numidia presumed to ordain a bishop, declare that ordinations may be carried out only by twelve bishops.

Bishop Aurelius said: The ancient form shall be preserved, so that no fewer than three who have been sent by the metropolitan to ordain a bishop shall suffice. This is because barbarian peoples seem perhaps to lie between Tripoli and Arguze. In Tripoli, as is reported, there are only five bishops, and perhaps two of that number may be occupied by some necessity. It is difficult for all of any number to be able to attend. Should this very circumstance become an impediment to ecclesiastical utility?

Moreover, in this Church your holiness has graciously been willing to convene frequently, and we have almost every Sunday persons to be ordained. Shall I frequently be able to summon twelve, or ten, or even fewer bishops? It is easy for me to add two neighboring bishops to my own small number. Therefore your charity sees with me that this cannot be observed.

## XL

This too must be established: when we assemble to choose a bishop, if some opposition arises—for such things have happened among us—the three should not presume to clear the man who has been ordained. Instead, two or three should be summoned to bring the number up to that mentioned above, and the matter should be examined in the same congregation for which the man is to be ordained. First the character of those who object should be investigated, and finally the accusations themselves should be examined. Once he has been cleared in public view, only then should he be ordained.

If this accords with the mind of your holiness, let it be strengthened by the response of your dignity.

All the bishops said: It pleases us greatly.

## XLI

The bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: Since it is known that certain matters have been discussed concerning the council, we add that we have also been given a mandate concerning the day of Easter: we are always to be instructed by the Church of Carthage, as stated above, and not within an excessively short period of time.

Bishop Aurelius said: If it seems right to your holiness—since we remember that we promised earlier that we would assemble each year for discussion—when we have gathered together, the holy day of Easter will then be made public through the envoys who were at the council.

The bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: From this present assembly we ask that you deign to inform our province by letter concerning this day.

Bishop Aurelius said: It must be done.

## XLII

Bishop Epigonius said: In many councils this has been established by the priestly assembly: congregations held in dioceses by bishops, which have never had bishops of their own, should receive their own rulers—that is, bishops—only with the consent of the bishop under whom they are held.

But because some, having acquired a certain domination, shrink from the fellowship of their brothers, or, once elevated, claim tyrannical domination for themselves as though in a fortress; because many foolish presbyters raise their necks against their bishops, or win the congregation over to themselves by banquets, so that through evil and unlawful persuasion they want the same men to appoint rulers for them; and because we recognize this as the distinguished intention of your mind, religious brother Aurelius, since you have often resisted such requests by refusing to concern yourself with them, I say that, because of their evil thoughts and perversely contrived councils, that congregation which has always been subject to a diocese and has never had its own bishop should not receive a ruler.

Therefore, if this proposal of mine pleases the entire holy council, let it be confirmed.

Bishop Aurelius said: I do not oppose the proposal of our brother and fellow priest; I confess that I have done this and will continue to do so.

## XLIII

This concerns those who have been in agreement—not only concerning the Church of Carthage, but concerning the entire priestly fellowship.

For there are many who conspire with their own congregations, which they deceive, as has been said, scratching their ears in order to seduce men of vicious life; or who, puffed up and separated from this fellowship, think that they should cling to their own congregation. Sometimes, when summoned, they refuse and delay coming to the council, perhaps fearing that their crimes may be exposed.

I say that, if it pleases you, not only should their dioceses no longer be preserved for them, but action should also be taken in every way against their own Church, which has been ill-disposed toward them, so that they may be rejected by public authority and removed from the principal sees themselves. For the one who has adhered to all his brothers and to the entire council ought to possess not only his own rights intact but also his dioceses. But those who think that their own congregations are sufficient for themselves, despising brotherly love, should lose not only their dioceses but, as I have said, even their own sees by public authority, as rebels.

The bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: The supreme care of your holiness has accorded with the minds of each one of us, and I think that, by the response of everyone, what you have deigned to propose should be approved.

All the bishops said: It pleases us; it pleases us.

## XLIV

Bishop Epigonius said: In many councils this has been established, and it has now again been confirmed by your prudence, dearest brothers: no bishop should seize for himself another’s cleric against the will of the one whose cleric he is.

I speak of Julianus, who is ungrateful for the benefits of God bestowed upon him through my humble person. He has proved so rash and audacious that the man who was baptized by me when he was a very needy boy, who had been commended to me by that same man, and who had been nourished and raised by me for many years—the man who, as I have said, was baptized in my church by my humble hand and had begun to serve as a reader in the diocese of Appaba, indeed had read there for nearly two years—this same Julianus, I do not know through what contempt for my humility, seized and claimed without consulting me, saying that he was virtually a fellow citizen of his own place, Nazareth. He even ordained him a deacon.

Let this be made clear to you, most blessed brothers: if this license is not permitted, such shamelessness must be restrained, and he should not join anyone’s communion.

Bishop Numidius said: If Julianus appears to have done this without requesting or consulting your dignity, we all judge that it was done unjustly and unworthily. Therefore, unless Julianus corrects his error and, with satisfaction, returns to your congregation the same cleric whom he dared to ordain, he will be separated from us by his obstinacy and will face judgment for acting against the statutes of the council.

Bishop Epigonius said: Our brother and colleague Victor, a father by age and most senior in promotion, a praiseworthy man, wishes this petition to be made general for all.

## XLV

Bishop Aurelius said: Hear my statement, brothers. It sometimes happens that churches lacking superiors request either bishops or presbyters. Yet, remembering the statutes, I follow this practice: I approach the bishop concerned and impress upon him that his cleric has been requested by some church. Perhaps today they did not resist; but it may happen that they resist when they are requested by me in this matter, since you know that, by God’s favor, I bear responsibility for many churches and for the ordination of their ministers.

It is therefore just that I approach any fellow priest with two or three witnesses from our fellowship. But if he proves unwilling, what does your charity judge should be done? For, as you know, brothers, by the favor of God I bear the care of all the Churches.

Bishop Numidius said: This has always been the privilege of this see: it could choose from wherever it wished and, once the assembly had settled on a person, ordain a bishop according to the desire of whatever Church was concerned.

Bishop Epigonius said: Kindness keeps authority in reserve. You presume too little, brother; and because you show yourself good and merciful to everyone, you have this within your discretion. It is enough that the person of each bishop be satisfied at the first consultation. But if he should judge that something must be claimed for this see, you must support all the Churches.

Therefore we do not give you authority, but we also assign it to you: you may always retain whomever you wish, so that you may appoint as superiors over congregations or churches those who have been requested, and from wherever you wish.

Bishop Posthumianus said: Further, if someone has only one cleric, should that one presbyter himself be taken away from him?

Bishop Aurelius said: There can be one bishop, through whom, by divine favor, many presbyters can be appointed; but it is difficult to find one bishop who can be appointed. Therefore, if someone has a presbytery necessary for the episcopate, and, as you said, brother, has only one, he should also give that one for promotion.

Bishop Posthumianus said: Then if another has an abundance of clerics, should another congregation come to my aid?

Bishop Aurelius said: Certainly. Just as you have aided another church, that one who has more clerics will be persuaded to give you one for ordination.

## XLVI

The bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: We have heard it established that dioceses should not be entitled to receive a bishop except with the consent of the one under whom they were constituted. But in our province, when some persons in a diocese have perhaps been ordained bishops with the permission of the bishop under whose authority they had been constituted, they also claim the dioceses for themselves. This must be corrected and henceforth prohibited by the judgment of your charity.

Bishop Epigonius said: What was fitting has been preserved for each bishop: no diocese should be taken from the mass of dioceses as though it had had its own bishop, unless the bishop himself had given his consent to its being granted. It is enough if he has consented that the same granted diocese should have only its own bishop and should not claim the other dioceses for itself—dioceses which, having been taken out from the bundle of many, alone deserved the honor of receiving an apostolate.

Bishop Aurelius said: I have no doubt that it pleases your charity that the one who, with the consent of the bishop, held the principal church in a diocese should retain only that same congregation in which he was ordained.

## XLVII

It was likewise decided that nothing except the canonical Scriptures should be read in the church under the name of divine Scripture.

The canonical Scriptures are these: first, Genesis; second, Exodus; third, Leviticus; fourth, Numbers; fifth, Deuteronomy; sixth, Joshua son of Nun; seventh, Judges; eighth, Ruth; ninth, four books of Kings; two books of Chronicles; one book of Job; the Davidic Psalter; five books of Solomon; the twelve books of the prophets; Isaiah; Jeremiah; Ezekiel; Daniel; Tobit; Judith; Esther; two books of Ezra; two books of Maccabees.
