Of the New Testament there are twenty-seven: four books of the Gospels; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, including one to the Hebrews; two Epistles of the Apostle Peter; three of the Apostle John; one of the Apostle Jude; one of James; and one book of the Apocalypse of John—which together are twenty-seven.

This should also be made known to our brother and fellow priest Boniface, or to the other bishops of those regions, for confirmation of this canon, because we received from the fathers that these books were to be read in the church. It is also permitted to read the passions of the martyrs when their annual feast days are celebrated.

## XLVIII

It was decided that we should consult our brothers and fellow priests Siricius and Simplicianus concerning only the infants baptized among them, lest, when they have been converted to the Church of God with a salutary purpose, the error of their parents prevent them from being advanced to ministers of the sacred altar for something they themselves did not do.

At this point the bishops Honoratus and Urbanus, envoys of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis, said: Some time ago, when we were presenting written submissions before your holiness, we were delayed on the consideration that our brothers might arrive as envoys from Numidia. But since they have not come, although they were awaited for many days, [Col. 0339B] we ought not postpone any longer what our fellow bishops have charged us with. Therefore, brothers, willingly receive our petition.

We have heard concerning the faith that was dealt with at Nicaea; and also concerning the prohibition of offering sacrifices after eating, so that they may be offered by those who are fasting. This was confirmed both then and now.

## XLIX

It was decided that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or any clerics who are ordained while possessing nothing, and who during the time of their episcopate or clerical office acquire fields or any estates in their own name, should be held guilty of invading divine property, unless, after being admonished, they transfer those very possessions to the Church.

If something comes to them personally through someone’s generosity or through inheritance from relatives, they should dispose of it in a manner consistent with their profession. But if they deviate backward from their profession, they should be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, like reprobates.

## L

Bishop Aurelius said: Since I therefore judge that everything has been discussed, if all these matters have agreed with your mind, strengthen them all by your statement.

All the bishops said: These things have pleased us all, and we confirm them by our subscription.

And they subscribed:

[Col. 0340B] Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have agreed to this decree and, having reread it, have subscribed.

Epigonius, bishop of the region of Bulla, have subscribed.

Augustine, bishop of the congregation of Hippo, have subscribed.

Likewise all the bishops, forty-four in number, subscribed.

The Council of Carthage is concluded.

[81] The Chapters of the Fourth Council of Carthage Begin.

## THE FOURTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE BEGINS

Held by 214 bishops, in the era 436.

[Column 0341]

[Column 0341D] In the consulship of Augustus Honorius for the fourth time and Eutychianus, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, when Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat at a universal council in Carthage, in the secretariat, together with all his fellow priests, it pleased all who were present in that holy synod to establish the following matters, necessary to canonical discipline concerning ecclesiastical orders. At the beginning it was established what sort of person ought to be ordained bishop.

[Column 0342D] **Chapter I.** When a bishop is to be ordained, he must first be examined as to whether he is naturally prudent, teachable, moderate in conduct, chaste in life, sober, always careful in his own affairs, humble, approachable, merciful, learned, instructed in the law of the Lord, prudent in understanding the Scriptures, and trained in ecclesiastical doctrines. Above all, it must be determined whether he asserts the articles of faith with unequivocal words—that is, affirming that the Father, the Son, [Column 0343A] and the Holy Spirit are one God—and proclaims the entire deity of the Trinity to be of one essence, consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent; whether he declares each individual person in the Trinity to be fully God, and all three persons to be one God; whether he believes that the divine incarnation took place not in the Father or in the Holy Spirit but in the Son alone, so that he who was the Son of God the Father in divinity himself became the son of a human mother in humanity: true God from the Father, true man from his mother, possessing flesh from his mother’s womb and at the same time a rational human soul. In him the two natures—that is, God and man—are one person, one Son, one Christ, one Lord, creator and author of all that exists, Lord and ruler, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, of all creatures; [Column 0343B] that he truly suffered the passion of the flesh, truly died the death of his own body, and rose again through the true restoration of his flesh and the true recovery of his soul, in which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

He must also be asked whether he believes that the New and Old Testaments—that is, the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles—have one and the same author and Lord; whether the devil became evil not by nature but by choice; whether he believes in the resurrection of this flesh that we bear, and not of another; whether he believes that judgment will come and that each person will receive either punishments or rewards for what he has done in the flesh; whether he does not prohibit marriage; whether he does not condemn second marriages; whether he does not blame the eating of meat; whether he communes with penitents who have been reconciled; whether in baptism all sins are forgiven, both original sin contracted and those committed voluntarily; and whether no one is saved outside the Catholic Church.

When he has been examined and found fully instructed in all these matters, then, with the consent of the clergy and laity and the assembly of all the bishops of the province, especially the metropolitan, he is to be ordained bishop with due authority or presence. Having received the episcopate in the name of Christ, he must submit not to his own pleasure or impulses but to these definitions of the Fathers. Thereafter it is determined how ecclesiastical offices are to be ordered.

82 **II.** When a bishop is ordained, two bishops shall place and hold the book of the Gospels over his head [Column 0343D] and neck, and while one pours the blessing over him, all the other bishops who are present shall touch his head with their hands.

**III.** When a presbyter is ordained, while the bishop blesses him and holds his hand over his head, all the presbyters who are present shall likewise hold their hands, alongside the bishop’s hand, over his head.

**IV.** When a deacon is ordained, only the bishop who blesses him shall place his hand upon his head, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to ministry.

**V.** When a subdeacon is ordained, since he alone has not received the laying on of hands, he shall receive from the bishop’s hand an empty paten and an empty chalice, and from the hand of the archdeacon a water jug, water, a cloth, and a towel.

[Column 0344A] **VI.** When an acolyte is ordained, he shall indeed be instructed by the bishop how he ought to conduct himself in his office, but he shall receive from the archdeacon a candle-holder with a candle, so that he may know that he is assigned to lighting the lamps of the Church. He shall also receive an empty water jug for supplying wine for the Eucharist of the blood of Christ.

**VII.** When an exorcist is ordained, he shall receive from the bishop’s hand a booklet in which the exorcisms are written, while the bishop says to him: “Receive this, commit it to memory, and have the power to lay hands upon a possessed person, whether baptized or a catechumen.”

**VIII.** When a lector is ordained, the bishop shall speak about him to the people, indicating his faith, life, and character. After this, in the sight of the people, he shall hand him the book from which he is to read, saying to him: “Receive this, and be a lector of the word of God; if you faithfully and usefully fulfill this office, you will have a share with those who have ministered the word of God.”

**IX.** When a doorkeeper is ordained, after he has been instructed by the archdeacon how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God, at the archdeacon’s prompting the bishop shall hand him the keys of the church from the altar, saying: “Act as though you will have to render an account to the Lord for the things that are locked away by these keys.”

**X.** A psalmist—that is, a cantor—may undertake the office of singing by the presbyter’s sole command, without the bishop’s knowledge. The presbyter shall say to him: “See that you believe in your heart what you sing with your mouth, and prove by your works what you believe in your heart.”

**XI.** When a consecrated virgin is offered to the bishop for her consecration, she shall be presented in such clothing as she will always use, suitable to her profession, her consecrated status, and the religious life she has undertaken.

**XII.** Widows or consecrated women who are chosen for the ministry of baptizing women shall be instructed for this office, so that they may teach inexperienced and rustic women, in suitable and sound language, at the time when they are to be baptized: how they should answer the questions of the baptizer and how they should live after receiving baptism.

**XIII.** When a bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by a priest, they shall be presented by their parents or by the bridesmen. After they have received the blessing, they shall remain virgins that same night out of reverence for the blessing itself.

**XIV.** A bishop is to have a small lodging not far from the church.

**XV.** A bishop is to have humble furnishings, a simple table, and poor food, and is to seek the authority of his dignity through faith and the merits of his life.

**XVI.** A bishop is not to read the books of pagans, but may read those of heretics when necessity and circumstances require.

**XVII.** A bishop is to administer the care of widows, orphans, and strangers not personally but through the archdeacon or archpresbyter.

**XVIII.** A bishop is not to undertake the guardianship of wills.

**XIX.** A bishop is not to litigate, unless provoked, over transitory matters.

[Column 0345A] **XX.** A bishop is not to take upon himself any care of household affairs, but is to devote himself solely to reading, prayer, and the word of preaching.

**XXI.** A bishop is not to be prevented from going to the synod except by sufficiently serious necessity; nevertheless, he must send a representative in his own person, intending to accept, without compromising the truth of the faith, whatever the sacred synod determines.

**XXII.** A bishop is not to ordain clerics without the council of his clergy, and must seek the assent, approval, and testimony of the citizens.

**XXIII.** A bishop is not to hear anyone’s case without the presence of his clergy; otherwise the bishop’s sentence will be invalid unless confirmed by the presence of the clergy.

**XXIV.** If, while a priest is speaking in the church, anyone leaves the assembly, let him be excommunicated.

**XXV.** If bishops are at odds, let the synod reconcile them, if the fear of God does not do so.

**XXVI.** Bishops must strive to urge brothers who are at odds, whether clerics or laymen, toward peace rather than judgment.

**XXVII.** A bishop is not to move ambitiously from an obscure place to a distinguished one. Nor is any cleric of a lower order to be transferred, unless the usefulness of the Church requires it and the bishops receive a decree concerning him, presented by the clergy and laity, before the synod; nevertheless, another bishop is to be appointed in his place. Priests of a lower rank, however, or other clerics may, with the permission of their own bishops, move to other churches.

[Column 0345C] **XXVIII.** An unjust condemnation of bishops is to be considered invalid and therefore reconsidered by the synod.

**XXIX.** If a bishop brings a charge against a cleric or layman, the matter is to be brought before the synod for proof.

**XXX.** Let the judges of the Church beware of issuing a sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being disputed, because it will be invalid; indeed, they will have to answer in the synod for the case as though it had been settled.

**XXXI.** A bishop is to use property as entrusted to him, not as his own.

**XXXII.** A bishop’s donation, sale, or exchange of Church property without the approval and subscription of the clergy shall be invalid.

**XXXIII.** If bishops or presbyters come to the church of another bishop in order to visit that church, they are to be received according to their rank and invited both to speak and to consecrate the offering.

[Column 0345D] **XXXIV.** Wherever a bishop is seated, he is not to allow a presbyter to remain standing.

**XXXV.** In church, a bishop is to sit in a higher seat among the presbyters; within the house, however, he is to recognize that he is a colleague of the presbyters.

**XXXVI.** Presbyters who govern churches throughout the dioceses are to request chrism not from just any bishops but from their own, and not through a junior cleric, but every year, either themselves or through the person who keeps the sacristy, before the solemnity of Easter.

**XXXVII.** A deacon is to recognize that he is the presbyter’s minister, just as he is the bishop’s minister.

[Column 0346A] **XXXVIII.** When a presbyter is present, a deacon may distribute the Eucharist of the body of Christ to the people, if necessity requires it and he has been ordered to do so.

**XXXIX.** A deacon is to sit wherever the presbyter orders him.

**XL.** A deacon is to speak when questioned in the assembly of presbyters.

**XLI.** A deacon is to wear the alb only during the offering or the reading.

**XLII.** A cleric who perseveres in his office amid temptations is to be advanced in rank.

**XLIII.** A Catholic Christian who suffers tribulations for the Catholic faith is to be honored by the priests with every honor; food is also to be supplied to him by the deacon.

[Column 0346B] **XLIV.** A cleric is neither to grow his hair long nor shave his beard.

**XLV.** A cleric is to demonstrate his profession both in clothing and in conduct; therefore he is not to seek elegance in garments or footwear.

**XLVI.** A cleric is not to live with unrelated women.

**XLVII.** A cleric is not to walk through streets and passageways except for a definite and very great necessity of his office.

**XLVIII.** A cleric who wanders about in the markets or forum without intending to buy something is to be degraded from his office.

**XLIX.** A cleric who is absent from vigils without bodily weakness is to be deprived of his allowances and excommunicated.

[Column 0346C] **L.** A cleric who withdraws from his office amid temptations or acts negligently is to be removed from his office.

**LI.** A cleric, however well educated in the word of God, is to seek his livelihood through a craft.

**LII.** A cleric is to provide himself with food and clothing through a craft or agriculture, provided that this does not impair his office.

**LIII.** All clerics who are physically able to work are to learn both crafts and letters.

83 **LIV.** A cleric who envies the progress of his brothers is not to be promoted as long as he remains in this fault.

**LV.** A bishop is to excommunicate those who accuse their brothers; if they correct the fault, he is to admit them to communion but not to the clergy.

[Column 0346D] **LVI.** A cleric who is caught devoting himself to flattery and treachery is to be degraded from his office.

**LVII.** A cleric who uses abusive language—especially if he is a priest—is to be compelled to ask pardon; if he refuses, he is to be degraded and is never to be restored to office without making satisfaction.

**LVIII.** No one is to accept the testimony of a cleric who litigates frequently and is quick to bring legal actions without a serious examination.

**LIX.** A bishop is to bring clerics who are at odds into agreement either by reason or by authority; the synod is to condemn the disobedient after hearing the case.

**LX.** A vulgar cleric who jokes with obscene words is to be withdrawn from office.

[Column 0347A] **LXI.** A cleric who swears by created things is to be rebuked for the offense; if he persists in the fault, he is to be excommunicated.

**LXII.** A cleric who sings during meals is to be restrained with the severity of the sentence stated above.

**LXIII.** A cleric who breaks the fast during an appointed fast without unavoidable necessity is to be regarded as inferior.

**LXIV.** A person who deliberately fasts on the Lord’s Day is not to be believed to be Catholic.

**LXV.** The solemnity of Easter is to be celebrated on one day and at one time.

**LXVI.** A cleric who considers the bishop’s strictness toward him unjust is to appeal to the synod.

**LXVII.** Seditious persons are never to be ordained clerics, nor usurers, nor those who avenge their own injuries.

[Column 0347B] **LXVIII.** No cleric is to be ordained from among penitents, however good he may be.

**LXIX.** If this has happened through the bishop’s ignorance, the man is to be deposed from the clergy, because at the time of his ordination he did not disclose that he had been a penitent. But if the bishop knowingly ordains such a person, he himself is to be deprived of the power of ordaining only within his episcopate. A bishop is subject to the same sentence if he knowingly ordains a cleric who has had a widow, a divorced woman, or a second wife.

**LXX.** A cleric is equally to avoid both the banquets and the associations of heretics or schismatics.

**LXXI.** A gathering of heretics is not a church but an assembly.

[Column 0347C] **LXXII.** One is neither to pray nor to sing psalms with heretics.

**LXXIII.** Whoever communes or prays with an excommunicated person, whether cleric or layman, is to be excommunicated.

**LXXIV.** A priest is to impose the laws of penance upon one who asks for penance, without regard to the person.

**LXXV.** More negligent penitents are to be reconciled later.

**LXXVI.** If a person asks for penance while ill, and, when the priest has been summoned and comes to him, he becomes speechless under the pressure of illness or is overcome by delirium, those who heard him are to give testimony, and he is to receive penance. If he is believed to be immediately dying, he is to be reconciled by the laying on of hands, and the Eucharist is to be poured into his mouth. If he survives, he is to be informed by the witnesses mentioned above that his request has been fulfilled, and he is to be subjected to the established laws of penance, since the priest who imposed the penance will have tested him for a long time [the concluding reading is syntactically uncertain].

[Column 0347D] **LXXVII.** Penitents who are ill are to receive the viaticum.

**LXXVIII.** Penitents who, while ill, have received the Eucharistic viaticum are not to consider themselves absolved without the laying on of hands if they survive.

**LXXIX.** If penitents who diligently carry out the laws of penance die by accident on a journey or at sea, where no assistance can be given them, their memory is to be commended through prayers and offerings.

[Column 0348A] **LXXX.** Throughout the time of fasting, priests are to lay hands upon those who ask for it.

**LXXXI.** Penitents are to carry out and bury the dead of the Church.

**LXXXII.** Even when they come on days of remission, they are to kneel.

**LXXXIII.** The poor and the elderly of the Church are to be honored more than others.

**LXXXIV.** A bishop is not to prevent anyone from entering the church and hearing the word of God, whether pagan, heretic, or Jew, up to the Mass of the catechumens.

**LXXXV.** Those who are to be baptized are to give their names and, after a long period of abstinence from wine and meat, together with the laying on of hands and frequent examination, are to receive baptism.

[Column 0348B] **LXXXVI.** Neophytes are for some time to abstain from richer banquets, spectacles, and marital relations.

**LXXXVII.** A Catholic who brings his case—whether just or unjust—before the judgment of a judge of another faith is to be excommunicated.

**LXXXVIII.** Anyone who neglects the solemn assembly of the church on a solemn day and goes to spectacles is to be excommunicated.

**LXXXIX.** A person who serves omens or incantations is to be separated from the assembly of the Church; likewise one who adheres to Jewish superstitions or festivals.

**XC.** Every day the exorcist is to lay hands upon the possessed.

**XCI.** The possessed are to sweep the floors of the houses of God.

[Column 0348C] **XCII.** For the possessed who sit in the house of God, daily food is to be supplied by the exorcists at the appropriate time.

**XCIII.** The offerings of brothers who are at odds are not to be received either in the sacristy or in the treasury.

**XCIV.** The gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be rejected by the priests.

**XCV.** Those who either deny the offerings of the dead to the churches or return them reluctantly are to be excommunicated as murderers of the needy.

**XCVI.** In court it must be investigated what sort of conduct and faith belong both to the accuser and to the accused.

**XCVII.** The person who is to be placed over religious women is to be tested by the bishop of the place.

**XCVIII.** A layman is not to presume to teach in the presence of clerics unless they themselves ask him to do so.

[Column 0348D] **XCIX.** A woman, however learned and holy, is not to presume to teach men in the assembly.

**C.** A woman is not to presume to baptize.

**CI.** Young widows who are physically weak are to be supported at the expense of the Church to which they belong as widows.

**CII.** It is counted as guilt against the bishop or the presbyter in charge of the parish if, for the sake of supporting their present life, younger widows or consecrated women are subjected to the familiar associations of certain persons.

**CIII.** Widows who are supported by an allowance from the Church must be so constantly engaged in God’s work that they assist the Church both by their merits and by their prayers.

**CIV.** Just as the good of chastity is a reward, so it must be guarded with even greater observance and injunction, so that if any widows—however young they may still be, and though left by a husband when they had reached mature age—have devoted themselves to the Lord, laid aside secular clothing, and appeared in religious dress under the testimony of the bishop and the Church, but afterward have passed over to secular marriages, they will, according to the Apostle, have condemnation, because they dared to nullify the pledge of chastity that they had vowed to the Lord. Such persons, therefore, are to remain without communion with Christians and are not even to share meals with Christians. For if adulterous wives are liable to guilt before their husbands, how much more will widows who have changed their religious way of life be marked with the crime of adultery [Column 0350A] if they corrupt by lustful pleasure the devotion that they voluntarily offered to God and pass over to a second marriage? Even if, when violence suddenly occurs, they are seized by someone and afterward consent, through the pleasure of lust, to remain married to the robber or violent man, they are to be held liable under the condemnation stated above. The Apostle says of such women: “When they have become wanton, they wish to marry, bearing condemnation because they have nullified their first pledge.”

Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have subscribed. Donatianus of Taleprensis, of the first see, have subscribed. Augustine, of Hippo Regius, have subscribed. Likewise all the bishops subscribed.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIFTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE BEGIN

[Column 0349]

[Column 0349B] 1. Concerning not summoning clerics to give testimony. 2. Concerning clerics condemned for their own crime, that they not be defended by anyone. 3. Concerning priests and Levites, that they abstain from their wives. 4. Concerning not alienating Church property without the counsel of the metropolitan bishop. 5. That no bishop, having left his see, should reside elsewhere in his diocese. 6. Concerning those who know themselves to have been baptized without any testimony, that they should be baptized; the same is to be done concerning the consecration of churches. 7. Concerning the time of Easter and of the council. 8. Concerning administrators, that they should not retain the see of a deceased bishop for long, but provide a priest within a year. 9. Concerning requesting a defender of the churches from the ruler. 10. That bishops should attend on the day of the council. 11. That hands should not be laid upon fallen priests as upon lay penitents. 12. Concerning excommunicated clerics, how long they may be permitted to assert their innocence. 13. Concerning clerics or monks ordained by another bishop. 14. Concerning basilicas dedicated without the relics of martyrs. 15. Concerning the destruction of idol shrines.

84 ## THE FIFTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE BEGINS

Held by seventy-four bishops, in the era 438.

[Column 0349]

[Column 0349C] After the consulship, it was decided that on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the restored basilica, the following provisions should be established, when Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat together with his bishops, with deacons standing by. These matters were established which were defined in the council that follows.

**Chapter I.** At the outset it must be established that if someone should wish to bring any case in a church under the apostolic law imposed upon churches, and perhaps the withdrawal of the clergy should displease one party, it is not permissible to summon as a witness a cleric who was a legal representative or was present, nor may any ecclesiastical person be summoned to give testimony.

**II.** It must also be established that if a cleric of any rank has been condemned by the judgment of bishops for any crime, he may not be defended either by the churches over which he presided or by anyone else, under penalty of loss of money and honor; and we decree that neither age nor sex is to provide an excuse.

**III.** Because reports had been made of the incontinence of certain clerics even toward their own wives, it was decided that bishops, presbyters, and deacons, according to their own statutes, should also abstain from their wives; if they do not, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office. Other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this, but the practice is to be observed according to the custom of each church.

**IV.** It was also decided that no one should sell Church property. But if some necessity compels this, it must be reported to the primate of the province, so that he may determine, together with the prescribed number of bishops, whether it ought to be done. If such great necessity presses upon the Church that it cannot consult beforehand, at least afterward the seller must show due diligence, notify the neighboring bishops of the matter beforehand, and refer these necessities of the Church to the council. If he does not do so, the seller is to be held liable before the council.

**V.** It was decided that no one should have permission, after leaving the principal see, to transfer himself to any church established in the diocese, or, while remaining in his own property longer than appropriate, to neglect the care or regular attendance of his own see.

**VI.** It was decided concerning infants that whenever completely certain witnesses cannot be found who testify without doubt that they have been baptized, and the infants themselves, because of their age, are not able to answer without hesitation concerning the sacraments given to them, they are to be baptized, lest this uncertainty deprive them of the cleansing of the sacraments. Our brothers, the envoys of the Moors, consulted us about this, because they redeem many such infants from the barbarians. The same is to be done concerning churches whenever there is doubt about their consecration: they are to be consecrated without any hesitation.

**VII.** It was decided that the venerable day of Easter should be announced to everyone by a written subscription; the day of the council is to be kept on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November. It is also to be written to the primates of each and every province that, whenever they convene a council in their own provinces, they should not interfere with this date.

**VIII.** It was likewise established that no administrator may retain the see to which he has been appointed through the efforts or uprisings of any people, but must take care to provide them with a bishop within a year. If he has neglected this after the year has elapsed, another administrator is to be assigned.

**IX.** It is to be requested from all the emperors, on account of the distress of the poor, whose troubles weary the Church without respite, that defenders be appointed for them against the power of the rich, with provision made by the bishops.

**X.** It was likewise decided that whenever a council is to be convened, bishops who are hindered neither by age, illness, nor another more serious necessity should attend suitably. The primates of their provinces are to be notified so that all the bishops may be divided into two or three groups, and from each group as many as have been chosen are to attend the day of the council with the greatest urgency in turn. If they cannot attend, they are to sign their excuses in the official notice; or, if some necessity should perhaps arise suddenly after the arrival of the official notice, unless they give an account of the reason for their impediment to their own primate, they are to be excluded from communion with the Church.

**XI.** It has likewise been confirmed that if presbyters or deacons are ever convicted of a more serious offense for which they must be removed from ministry, hands are not to be laid upon them either as penitents or as faithful laymen, nor is it ever to be permitted that those who have been rebaptized be promoted to the rank of the clergy.

**XII.** It has again been established that whenever clerics have been convicted and confessed of some crime, whether out of consideration for those whose shame is being spared, or because of the disgrace to the Church, or because of the insolent attacks of heretics and pagans, if they should wish to appear in their own case and assert their innocence, they must do so within one year of their excommunication. But if they refuse to clear their case within the year, their case is not to be heard thereafter at all.

**XIII.** It was likewise decided that if anyone wishes to promote to the clergy someone belonging to another monastery, or to appoint someone as superior of a monastery in his own monastery, the bishop who does this is to be separated from communion with the others and remain content with communion with his own people; and that person is not to continue either as a cleric or as superior.

**XIV.** It was likewise decided that altars established here and there through fields or along roads as memorials of martyrs, in which no body or relics of martyrs are proved to have been buried, are to be overturned, if possible, by the bishops who preside over those places. If popular disturbances prevent this, the people are nevertheless to be warned not to frequent those places, so that those who think rightly may not be held there by any superstition. In general, no memorial of martyrs is to be accepted as credible unless there is a body or certain relics, or unless the origin of some dwelling, possession, or martyrdom is handed down with completely reliable provenance. For altars that are established everywhere through dreams and empty so-called revelations of various people are to be rejected in every way.

**XV.** It was likewise decided that a request be made of the most glorious emperors that the remaining traces [of idolatry] be utterly destroyed not only in statues but also in every kind of place, grove, or tree. Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have subscribed to the statutes set forth above in our council. Likewise seventy-two bishops subscribed.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE SIXTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE BEGIN

[Column 0351]

[Column 0351D] 1. Address of the holy Bishop Aurelius to the synod. 2. Response of Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, concerning matters established in the Church partly by canon and partly by custom. 3. Concerning the reading of the memorandum of the Roman pope. 4. Response of Bishop Alypius concerning the search for authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea. 5. Where Bishop Faustinus said that the synod should notify the Roman pope concerning the investigation of the truth of the Nicene synod. 6. 7. Concerning the sentence of the Council of Sardica, read at the request of Bishop Novatus. 8. Where Bishop Augustine, together with the synod, promises to preserve the Council of Nicaea. [Column 0352D] 9. Where Bishop Faustinus requests that the Roman pope be written to concerning the uncertainty of the chapter that was read. 10. Where the synod decreed that copies of the Council of Nicaea should rather be sought from the Eastern bishops. 11. Profession of the faith of the Council of Nicaea. 12. Rescript of the bishops of Rome, Alexandria, and Constantinople, together with the copies of the Council of Nicaea established for the African synod. 13. Letter of the African bishop to Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome. 14. Letter of the African council to Celestine, bishop of the city of Rome.

84 ## THE SIXTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE BEGINS

Conducted by 217 bishops, in the era 457.

[Column 0353]

[Col. 0353A] At this council it was enacted that the Council of Nicaea should be requested from the Eastern bishops. Present at the council’s proceedings were the delegation of the Roman Church—Faustinus the bishop, and the presbyters Philip and Asellus. After the consulship of the most glorious emperors, Honorius, for the twelfth time, and Theodosius, for the eighth time, the Augusti, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, these acts were written at Carthage in the secretariat of the Basilica of Faustus, when Aurelius the pope was present together with Valentinus, bishop of the first see of Numidia; Faustinus of the Church of Potentia, the first see of the Italian province of Picenum, legate of the Roman Church; and also legates of the various African provinces, namely the two Numidias, Byzacena, Mauretania Sitifensis, and Mauretania Caesariensis, as well as Tripolitania; and Vincentius of Culisita, Fortunatianus, and the other bishops of the province of Proconsular Africa, two hundred and seventeen in number, together with Philip and Asellus, presbyters of the Roman Church. When Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat, with the deacons standing by, he said:

**CHAPTER I.** After the appointed day of the council, as you remember, most blessed brothers, many requests were made by our brothers who were waiting and who have now arrived as legates at this present synod. These matters must necessarily be joined to the acts. For this reason we give thanks to our Lord for the assembly of so great a gathering. It remains that both the copies of the Council of Nicaea that we now possess and that were established by the Fathers, and also what our predecessors here established while confirming the same council, as well as what was beneficially ordered according to its form throughout all the clerical ranks, from the highest to the lowest, should be brought forward [Col. 0353C]. The whole council said, “Let them be brought forward.” Daniel the notary read out the profession of faith and the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, which are as follows.

**II.** When Bishop Faustinus of the congregation of Potentia, in the Italian province of Picenum, legate of the Roman Church, had read them, he said:

Some matters have been entrusted to us by the Apostolic See in writing, and some also by oral instruction, to be reconsidered with Your Beatitude, as we also recalled in the earlier proceedings. These concern the Nicene canons: that they be preserved, together with their constitution and custom, since some matters are maintained by ordinance and canon, while others have been confirmed by custom. Let us therefore, if it pleases Your Beatitude, discuss these matters, and afterward the other matters that have been enacted or begun will be confirmed by being inserted into the acts, so that you may be able to report them to the Apostolic See in your replies, and so that it may clearly appear before the venerable pope that you instructed us. Although the chapters of the proceedings have already been inserted into the acts, we must nevertheless deal with these matters themselves, as was said above, and determine what pleases Your Beatitude. Let the memorandum therefore be brought forward, so that Your Beatitude may know what it contains and may give a specific response.

[Col. 0353D]

**III.** Bishop Aurelius said:

Let the memorandum be brought forward which our brothers and fellow priests recently cited in the proceedings [Col. 0354A], and let the other matters that have been enacted or that are to be enacted follow.

Daniel the notary read the memorandum addressed to Brother Faustinus and to the sons, the presbyters Philip and Asellus.

Bishop Zosimus said:

The matters entrusted to you are not hidden from you. Carry them all out as though they were ours—or rather, because our presence is there in you, as though they were ours—especially since you can also regard this as our instruction. We have inscribed in this memorandum the words of the canons for greater certainty. For thus they said, most beloved brothers, in the Council of Nicaea when they were determining the matter of episcopal appeals:

“It has been decided that if a bishop has been accused, and the assembled bishops of his own region have judged him and deposed him from his rank, and the bishop is seen to have appealed and has taken refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, and has wished to be heard and has considered it just that the examination be renewed, let him write to those bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may diligently investigate everything and decide according to the fidelity of truth. But if the one who requests that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his entreaty to send a presbyter from his side, it will be within the power of the Roman bishop to determine what he wishes and considers appropriate. If he decides that persons should be sent to judge in the presence of the bishops, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, that decision will be at his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, let him do what he judges by his most wise counsel.”

[Col. 0354C]

**IV.** When this had been read, Bishop Alippius of Tagaste, legate of the province of Numidia, said:

We have already replied concerning this matter in earlier letters of our council, and we profess that we will observe what was established in the Council of Nicaea. This alone troubles me: when we examined the Greek copies of this Council of Nicaea, we found these provisions there not at all, for some reason unknown to me. Therefore we ask Your Reverence, holy Pope Aurelius, since it is said that this authentic Council of Nicaea is in the city of Constantinople, to be so kind as to send certain persons with letters from Your Holiness—not only to that holy brother of ours, the bishop of Constantinople, but also to the venerable priests, the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch—so that they may send this council to us under the guarantee of their letters [Col. 0354D]. In this way every subsequent ambiguity may be removed, since we have not found these provisions at all, as Brother Faustinus reported.

Nevertheless, we profess that we shall observe them for the time being, as I said earlier, until complete copies arrive. The venerable bishop of the Roman Church, Boniface, should also be asked by our letters to be so kind as to send certain persons to the aforesaid churches, who may produce the same copies of the aforementioned Council of Nicaea in accordance with his written instructions. For the present, however, let the copies of the aforementioned Council of Nicaea that we possess be joined to these acts [Col. 0355A].

**V.** Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, said:

Nor does Your Holiness prejudice the Roman Church, whether concerning this chapter or others, because our brother and fellow bishop Alippius has seen fit to say that the canons are uncertain. But be so kind as to write these very matters to our holy and most blessed pope, so that he, while seeking the complete canons, may discuss all the decrees together with Your Holiness. It is sufficient that the most blessed bishop of the city of Rome himself investigate the matter, just as Your Holiness is discussing it here, so that no contention may appear to arise between the churches, but rather so that you may deliberate in fraternal charity, with him replying as to what ought preferably to be observed.

[Col. 0355B]

Bishop Aurelius said:

In addition to what we have promised must be included in the acts, it is necessary that we also set out fully, in a letter from our humble self, each matter we are discussing for our holy brother and fellow priest Boniface. Therefore, if it pleases everyone, let us learn our statement from the mouth of all.

The whole council said: “It pleases us.”

**VI–VII.** Novatus, legate of Mauretania Sitifensis, said:

We now remember that the memorandum just read also contains a provision concerning presbyters and deacons, specifying how they ought to be heard by their own bishops or by neighboring bishops; yet we have not read this at all in the Council of Nicaea. Therefore let Your Holiness order that this very passage be read to us.

Bishop Aurelius said:

Let the requested passage, as well as this matter, be read at the proper place.

Daniel the notary read:

“Concerning the appeals of clerics—that is, of the lower rank—the synod’s definite response remains. We believe that what you are going to do concerning this matter should be inserted. It was stated as follows from the Council of Sardica.”

Bishop Hosius said:

I must not conceal what still causes concern. If a bishop happens to become angry—which ought not to happen—and quickly or harshly grows incensed against his presbyter or deacon and wishes to expel him from the Church, care must be taken lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. The expelled man shall have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that they may hear his case and examine it carefully, for a hearing ought not to be denied to one who makes a request. That bishop, whether he expelled him justly or unjustly, should patiently accept either that the case be examined, or that his judgment be proven correct or corrected, and so forth.

[Col. 0355D]

**VIII.** When this had been read, Augustine, legate of the province of Numidia from the Church of Hippo Regius, said:

We also profess that we shall observe this, subject to a more careful investigation of the Council of Nicaea.

Bishop Aurelius said:

If this also pleases all of you in your charity, confirm it by your response.

The whole council said:

Everything established in the Council of Nicaea pleases us all.

Jocundus, legate of the province of Byzacena from the Church of Suffetula, said:

No one can in any way violate what was established in the Council of Nicaea.

**IX.** Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, said:

I believe that some matters have been confirmed, and that some ought to be confirmed, according to the profession of both the holy Alippius and our brother Jocundus, since the canons themselves have now come into question. Therefore, if it pleases you and Your Beatitude, let Your Holiness write to the holy and venerable Bishop Boniface of the Roman Church, so that he too may deliberate on what the holy Augustine has seen fit to establish—whether this too should be granted or passed over in silence—that is, concerning appeals of those of lower rank. If this chapter has again come into question, it is just that the bishop of the most blessed Roman See should be informed, provided that this can be found among the approved canons.

[Col. 0356A]

**X.** Bishop Aurelius said:

You do not allow us to have read aloud and inserted into the acts not only the copies of the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, concerning which we recently informed Your Charity, but also what our predecessors here beneficially formulated according to the norm of that same council, and what we have now ordered.

The whole council said:

The copies of the faith and the decrees of the Council of Nicaea that were brought to our council by Cecilian, bishop and predecessor of Your Holiness, of blessed memory, who was present there, as well as what the Fathers established here while following those copies, and what we now establish by common deliberation, shall remain inserted in these ecclesiastical acts. As was said above, may Your Beatitude be so kind as to write to the venerable bishops of the churches of Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople, so that they may send the most authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea under the guarantee of their letters. Thus the clear truth will establish whether those chapters which our present brother and fellow bishop Faustinus, together with the fellow presbyters Philip and Asellus, brought with them in the memorandum—or which we found there—are confirmed by us, or, if they are not found, we shall discuss the matter in the assembled synod at a later time.

[Col. 0356C]

Daniel the notary read the profession of faith and the decrees of the Council of Nicaea in the African council.

### The Nicene Creed

**XI.** We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father as the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father (which the Greeks call *homoousion*), through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. For us human beings and for our salvation he descended, was incarnate from the Holy Spirit, and became human; he suffered, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead, and we believe in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and, “Before he was begotten he did not exist,” and who say that he was made from things that did not exist, or is of another substance or nature, and who call the Son of God mutable and changeable—these the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

### Letter of the African Council to Pope Boniface

**XII.** To the most blessed and honorable lord and brother, BONIFACE [Col. 0357A], AURELIUS, VALENTINUS, of the first see of the province of Numidia, and the others who were present, two hundred and seventeen in number, from the entire council of Africa.

Since it pleased God that our humility should reply to Your Reverence concerning the matters transacted with you by our holy brothers, our fellow bishop Faustinus and the fellow presbyters Philip and Asellus, as well as by Bishop Zosimus of blessed memory, from whom they brought us instructions and letters, and since by divine providence you have been established in his place, with the Christian cause prospering happily, we ought briefly to make known those matters that were settled by the agreement of both sides—not those contained in the lengthy volumes of the proceedings, in which, while preserving charity, we nevertheless remained engaged in the labor of a not insignificant dispute. We deliberated in the acts on the matters now relevant to the case, although he too, if he were still alive, would more gladly accept what he saw settled more peacefully.

The presbyter Apiarius, whose ordination, excommunication, and summons had given rise to the dispute, was not only the object of our anger, but also caused no small scandal to the entire African Church through all his offenses. After asking pardon, he was restored to communion. Our former fellow bishop, Urbanus of Sicca, corrected without hesitation whatever in his conduct appeared to require correction. But because the peace and tranquility of the Church had to be safeguarded not only for the present but also for the future, since many such cases had preceded this one and it was necessary to prevent similar or even graver cases thereafter, it pleased us that Apiarius should be removed from the Church of Sicca, while retaining the honor of his rank as presbyter, and that, after receiving a letter of authorization, he should exercise the office of presbyter wherever else he wished and was able. We granted this to him without difficulty when he himself requested it by letter.

Before this case was closed with that outcome, among the other matters we had discussed for a long time, the request itself required us to ask our brothers, the fellow bishop Faustinus and the fellow presbyters Philip and Asellus, in the ecclesiastical proceedings, to disclose whatever had been entrusted to them to conduct with us. They pursued some matters orally without any written document; but when we pressed them especially to produce the memorandum contained in their letters, they brought it forward. It was read to us and cited in the proceedings that they were to carry back to you. In it, four matters were entrusted to them for action with us [Col. 0357D]:

First, concerning appeals by bishops to the priest of the Roman Church.

Second, that bishops should not sail rashly to the imperial court.

Third, concerning the cases of presbyters and deacons before neighboring bishops if they had been excommunicated by their own bishops lightly or culpably.

Fourth, concerning the excommunication or summons to Rome of Bishop Urbanus, unless he corrected those matters that appeared to require correction.

Of all these matters, concerning the first and third—that is, that bishops should be permitted to appeal to Rome, and that the complaints of clerics should be settled before the bishops of their own provinces—we already took care to inform the same Bishop Zosimus, of venerable memory, in a letter sent to him the previous year. We asked that he allow us to observe these provisions for a short time without any injury to him, until the decrees of the Council of Nicaea had been investigated. Now we ask Your Holiness to cause us to observe them in the same manner as they were enacted or established by the Fathers at Nicaea, and to cause the provisions they brought in the memorandum to be put into practice there among you, namely:

If a bishop has been accused, and the assembled bishops of his region have judged him and deposed him from his rank, and he is seen to have appealed and has taken refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, and has wished to be heard and has considered it just that the examination be renewed, let him write diligently to those bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may investigate everything carefully and decide according to the fidelity of truth. But if the one who requests that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his entreaty to send a presbyter from his side, it will be within the power of the bishop to determine whom he wishes to send and what he considers appropriate. If he decides that persons should be sent to judge in the presence of the bishops, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, that decision will be at his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he will do what he judges by his most wise counsel.

If a bishop becomes angry—which ought not to happen—and quickly or harshly grows incensed against his presbyter or deacon and wishes to expel him from the Church, care must be taken lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. The expelled man shall have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and examined more carefully; for a hearing ought not to be denied to one who makes a request. The bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, should patiently accept that the matter be examined, so that his judgment may either be proven correct or corrected.

These provisions have indeed been inserted into the proceedings pending the arrival of the most authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea. If the matters that the brothers sent from the Apostolic See cited among us were contained in the memorandum according to its proper order, and if they were observed among you in Italy, we would in no way be compelled to recall or tolerate such provisions, or to endure what is intolerable. But, with the mercy of the Lord our God assisting us, we trust that, with Your Holiness presiding over the Roman Church, we shall no longer suffer this kind of treatment. The provisions that ought to be observed toward us should be maintained, even without our arguing the matter, with the fraternal charity that you yourself recognize must be preserved according to the wisdom and justice that the Most High has granted you—unless the canons of the Council of Nicaea are otherwise.

Although we have read very many books, nowhere in the Latin copies have we read in the Council of Nicaea what was sent to me in the aforementioned memorandum. Since we have been able to find these provisions in no Greek copy here, we desire all the more that they be brought from the Eastern Churches, where it is said that the same decrees can also be found in authentic form. For this reason we earnestly beseech Your Reverence to write also to the priests of those regions, namely of the Churches of Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople, and, if it should also please Your Holiness, to any others, so that the same canons established by the Fathers at the city of Nicaea may come to us from there. With the Lord’s help, you would thereby confer this benefit especially upon all the Western Churches.

For who could doubt that the copies of the Council held at Nicaea in Greece are the most authentic, since copies brought from and compared with various places and distinguished Greek Churches agree with one another? Until this is done, we profess that we shall observe, for the sake of verification, the provisions cited for us in the aforementioned memorandum concerning appeals by bishops to the priest of the Roman Church and the settlement of clerical cases before the bishops of their own provinces. We trust that Your Beatitude will assist us in this according to God’s will.

As for the other matters enacted or confirmed in our synod, since the aforementioned brothers of ours, the fellow bishop Faustinus and the presbyters Philip and Asellus, are carrying them with them, if Your Holiness is willing, let them make them known to you.

In another hand:

May our Lord preserve you for many years for us, most blessed brother. Amen.

Aurelius, bishop of Carthage; Alippius; Augustine; Possidius; Marinus; and the other bishops, two hundred and fourteen in number, subscribed.

**XIII.** The replies to the African council of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, begin here. He sent authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea translated from Greek by the presbyter Innocentius. These, together with the letter concerning the Council of Nicaea, were sent through the aforementioned presbyter Innocentius and Marcellus, subdeacon of the Church of Carthage, to the holy Boniface, bishop of the Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December.

To the honorable lords, holy brothers and fellow bishops AURELIUS and VALENTINUS, and to the entire holy congregation assembled in the council at Carthage, CYRIL sends greetings in the Lord and his love.

I received with great joy the letter of Your Reverence, full of complaint, through our son Innocentius the presbyter. In it you ask us to send to Your Charity, from the archive of our Church, the most authentic copies of the authentic council established and confirmed by the holy Fathers at the city of Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia, under our profession of faith. Therefore, honorable lords and brothers, with health preceding, I considered it necessary to send to Your Charity, through the bearer of this letter, our son Innocentius the presbyter, the most trustworthy copies of the authentic council held in the city of Nicaea in Bithynia. You will also find this if you investigate the ecclesiastical history.

Concerning Easter, as you wrote, we inform you that we shall celebrate it on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May in the coming indiction.

In another hand:

May God our Lord preserve your holy congregation, which is our desire, most beloved brothers.

### Letter of Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople, to the Same

To the holy and deservedly most blessed lords, brothers and fellow bishops Aurelius, Valentinus, and the other most beloved men established in the synod held at Carthage, Atticus the bishop.

Through our son Marcellus, our subdeacon, I received your letter of affection with every expression of thanksgiving, giving thanks to the Lord that I have been deemed worthy to enjoy the blessing of so many brothers, most blessed lords and brothers.

You wrote asking me to send, under guarantee, the most authentic canons established by the Fathers at the city of Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia. Who is there who would deny his brothers the common faith or the decrees confirmed by the Fathers? Therefore, through the same son of mine, Marcellus our subdeacon, who was in great haste, I have sent the complete canons, as they were established by the Fathers in the city of Nicaea, just as you ordered. I ask that your holy congregation order many prayers to be offered for me.

In another hand:

May our Lord preserve Your Holiness, which is our desire, most holy brothers.

The copies of the Council of Nicaea sent to the African council by the aforementioned pontiffs begin here, after the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius XII and Theodosius VII, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December.

### CREED

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator of things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, our Lord, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not created, of the same substance as the Father, through whom all things were made, heavenly and earthly. For us human beings and for our salvation he descended, was incarnate, became human, suffered, and rose again on the third day. He ascended into heaven and will come from there to judge the living and the dead, and we believe in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and who say that he was made from nothing, or that he is from another substance or essence, or who say that the Son of God is mutable or changeable—the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

To this creed of faith are also appended copies of the decrees of the same Council of Nicaea, translated from Greek into Latin by Teilon and Thearistus of Constantinople.

The chapters of the same Council of Nicaea begin here.

1. Concerning eunuchs who mutilate themselves.  
2. Concerning those who, after baptism, are promoted from the gentiles to the clerical order.  
3. Concerning those who live together with women.  
4. Concerning the ordination of bishops.  
5. Concerning the excommunicated.  
6. Concerning the privileges belonging to certain cities.  
7. Concerning the bishop of Aelia, that is, of Jerusalem.  
8. Concerning those called Cathari, that is, the Pure.  
9. Concerning those promoted to the priesthood without examination.  
10. Concerning those who have lapsed and have been ordained in ignorance.  
11. Concerning those who denied the faith and are retained in their places.  
12. Concerning those who renounce the world and have returned again to it.  
13. Concerning those who request communion at the point of death.  
14. Concerning lapsed catechumens.  
15. Concerning clerics, that they should not transfer from one city to another.  
16. Concerning those who did not remain in the churches in which they had been advanced.  
17. Concerning clerics who receive interest.  
18. Concerning the privileges of presbyters.  
19. Concerning those who come to the Church from Paul of Samosata.  
20. Concerning kneeling.  
21. Concerning observance of the Council of Nicaea, so that no further variation may arise in the churches.

**CHAPTER 1.** If anyone has been castrated by physicians because of illness, or has been mutilated by barbarians, let him remain in the clergy. But if anyone, while healthy, has mutilated himself, he must abstain even if he is already in the clergy, and thereafter no one of this sort is to be promoted. Just as it is clear that this statement concerns those who devise such a thing and dare to mutilate themselves, so the canon admits to the clergy those who are found otherwise worthy but have been castrated by barbarians or by their masters.

[Col. 0361B]

**2.** Since many things have been done, either from necessity or because people were compelled by other circumstances, contrary to ecclesiastical canon—for example, people newly coming to the faith from a pagan life, instructed as catechumens for only a short time, being immediately led to the spiritual washing and, as soon as they had been baptized, promoted to the episcopate or presbyterate—it has been decided that nothing of this kind is to be done thereafter. For the one being instructed as a catechumen needs time, and after baptism a fuller examination is also necessary. The apostolic Scripture clearly says: “Not a novice, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil.”

If, as time proceeds, some sin of the mind is discovered in such a person and he is convicted by two or three witnesses, let him cease from the clergy. But if anyone acts contrary to this, as though setting himself against the great council, he will place himself in danger concerning the clergy.

**3.** The holy council has altogether prohibited a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all belonging to the clergy from keeping with him a woman introduced into his household, unless she is his mother or sister, or one of those persons alone who are beyond every suspicion.

**4.** A bishop ought, above all, to be ordained by all the bishops within the province. If this is difficult, either because of urgent necessity or because of the length of the journey, then in every case three bishops shall meet together, with the absent bishops consenting and giving their assent in writing; only then shall the laying on of hands take place. Confirmation of what has been done must be given by the metropolitan of each bishop’s own province.

**5.** Concerning those who are excommunicated, whether they belong to the clergy or to the body of the laity: let the judgment of the bishops prevail throughout the individual provinces, so that those rejected by some are not received by others, according to the canons. It must also be investigated whether the bishops have excommunicated them out of faintheartedness, obstinacy, or some other annoyance. Therefore, so that this may be investigated more appropriately, it has been judged good that twice each year councils be held in every province, with all the bishops assembling together, so that such questions may be investigated.

Thus, those who have manifestly offended a bishop may reasonably be considered excommunicated by all for as long as it pleases either the common assembly or the bishop to issue a more lenient judgment concerning them. Let the councils be held once before the forty days preceding Easter, so that, every faintheartedness having been removed, a pure offering may be presented to God; and the second around the time of autumn.

[Col. 0362A]

**6.** Let the ancient privileges of those in Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis prevail, so that the bishop of Alexandria exercises care over all of them, since a similar custom also belongs to the bishop of the city of Rome. Likewise, in the region of Antioch and in the other provinces, let their own privileges be preserved for the metropolitan churches.

This, however, is entirely clear: if anyone is made a bishop contrary to the judgment of the metropolitan, the great council has determined that he ought not to be a bishop. But if, after a common decision of all has been made and reasonably approved according to ecclesiastical canon, two or three oppose it because of their own private enmities, the decision of the majority shall prevail.

**7.** Let the ancient custom of Jerusalem be preserved, so that the bishop of Aelia may be honored and possess the rank of honor, while the dignity of the metropolitan of that province is nevertheless preserved.

**8.** If any of those called Cathari should at some time come to the catholic Church, it has been decided that, if they have been ordained, they should remain in the clergy, as was also decided by the great synod. Above all, however, they must make this profession in writing: that they agree with and follow the doctrines of the catholic and apostolic Church. This includes communicating with those who have married twice and with those who fell during the persecution, for whom a period and a definite day have also been established; and they must follow in all matters what has been approved by the bishop or presbyter of the catholic Church.

Wherever all of them—whether in villages or in cities—are found joined together, those who are ordained and found in the clergy shall remain in the same rank. But whenever they come over to a bishop or presbyter of the catholic Church, it is clear that the bishop of the Church shall possess the dignity of bishop. The one called a bishop among them shall have the honor of a presbyter, unless it should please the Catholic bishop to allow him to enjoy the title of honor. If this does not please him, he shall provide him with a place either as a chorepiscopus [country bishop] or among the presbyters, so that he may clearly remain entirely within the clergy, and so that there may not be two bishops in one city.

**9.** If some have been promoted as bishops or presbyters without examination, or, when examined, have confessed the sins they committed, or if they are convicted by others, and, despite their confession, men moved contrary to the canon have laid hands upon them, the canon does not accept such persons but rejects them. For the catholic Church defends what is irreproachable.

**10.** Whoever has been ordained from among the lapsed through the ignorance or concealment of those who ordained him—this does not prejudice the ecclesiastical canon; once they are recognized, they are deposed.

**11.** Concerning those who transgressed without necessity, without the loss of their property, without danger, or without anything of that sort, as occurred under the tyranny of Licinius: although they are unworthy, the holy council has decided nevertheless to show them humanity. Therefore, as many as sincerely repent shall remain three years among those who hear [instruction].

[Col. 0363A]

The faithful who have lapsed shall submit for seven years; for two years they shall communicate with the people in prayers without an offering.

**12.** Whoever was called by grace and initially demonstrated good works, then laid aside the military belt, but afterward returned to his own vomit, so that some even give money and seek to recover military service through favors, shall submit for ten years after the three-year period of hearing.

In all these cases, however, it is necessary to examine the intention and the form of repentance. Those who demonstrate their conversion not by pretense but through fear, tears, perseverance, and good works shall, after completing the prescribed period of hearing, rightly communicate in prayers. Afterward, the bishop may consider showing them greater humanity. But those who have acted indiscriminately and have thought that their entrance alone was sufficient for conversion must complete the entire prescribed period.

**13.** Concerning those departing from the body, let the ancient and canonical law now also be preserved, so that those expected to die may not be deprived of the final assistance. But if someone who was considered beyond hope, after receiving communion and partaking of the offering, should recover, let him remain among those who communicate only in prayers. In general, whenever a dying person asks for the grace of communion, the bishop should reasonably grant him the offering.

**14.** Concerning lapsed catechumens, it has been decided, as also by the great synod, that they shall hear instruction for only three years and afterward pray with the catechumens.

**15.** Because of the great disturbance and seditions that occur, it has been decided that the custom admitted in some regions contrary to the canon must be removed entirely, so that no bishop, presbyter, or deacon may be transferred from one city to another. If anyone attempts to do anything of this kind after the definition of the holy and great council, or offers himself for such a transaction, the scheme shall be annulled, and he shall be restored to the church in which he was ordained as bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

**16.** Those who readily thrust themselves into dangers, who do not keep the fear of God before their eyes, and who do not know the ecclesiastical canon, and who leave their church—whether presbyters, deacons, or anyone established in the canon—must in no way be received by another church. Every compulsion should instead be imposed upon them so that they return to their own parishes. The obstinate must be excommunicated.

But if anyone, acting with reckless audacity, should seize someone belonging to another church and ordain him in his own church, without the consent of the bishop from whom the cleric established in the canon departed, such a laying on of hands shall be invalid.

**17.** Since many who are established in the canon pursue greed and shameful profit, forgetting the sacred Scripture that says, “Who has not given his money at interest,” and, when they lend, demand hundredths (*centesimae*) from others, the holy and great council has justly decreed that if anyone, after this definition, is found receiving interest [Col. 0364A], or devising anything else for the sake of shameful profit, he shall be rejected from the clergy and shall be excluded from the canon.

18. It has come to the attention of the holy and great council that in certain places or cities deacons distribute the grace of holy communion to presbyters, although neither canon nor custom has handed this down: those who do not have the power to offer should not distribute the body of Christ to those who do offer it. It has also become known that certain deacons receive the Eucharist before the bishops. Let all these practices therefore be abolished, and let deacons remain in their own order, knowing that they are ministers of the bishops but are inferior to presbyters. Let them receive the Eucharist in due order after the presbyters, with either the bishop or the presbyter giving it to them; nor may they sit among the presbyters. [Col. 0364B] If this is done, it is shown to be contrary to canon and contrary to order. If anyone refuses to obey, let him cease from the diaconate after this definition.

19. Concerning the Paulianists who come over to the Catholic Church, the following definition has been issued: they are to be rebaptized altogether. If any of them previously belonged to the clergy, then, provided they have been without reproach and blame, they are to be ordained by the bishop of the Catholic Church after baptism; but if examination finds them less suitable, they are to be deposed. The same procedure is to be observed concerning deacons and, in general, concerning those who are enrolled in the canon. We also remember the deaconesses who are of the same kind, since they do not receive any laying-on of hands: they are to be counted altogether among the laywomen. [Col. 0364C]

20. Since there are some who kneel on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, the holy and great synod has decided that everyone, in every place, must pray to God standing, harmoniously and unanimously.

21. Since the holy council has handed down and duly arranged everything so that the peace and faith of the Churches may be preserved as one and the same in the regions of East and West, we necessarily believe that these ecclesiastical statutes should be inserted here.

**Here ends the copy of the Council of Nicaea.**

## Letter of the African Council to Coelestine

**XIV.** To our most beloved and honored father, the Lord Coelestine: Aurelius, Palestinus, Antonius, Tutus, servant [Col. 0364D] of God, Terentius, Fortunatus, Martianus, Januarius, Optatus, Celticius, Donatus, Theasius, Vincentius, Fortunatianus, and the rest who were present at the universal African Council of Carthage.

If, just as your Holiness informed us by letter sent through our fellow presbyter Leo that you had rejoiced at the arrival of Apiarius, we could likewise send you this written account of his purification with joy, surely both our own and your present happiness would be more certain, and those things that had previously taken place—both concerning the hearing and concerning what had been heard—would not appear so hastily and prematurely undertaken.

When our holy brother and fellow bishop Faustinus arrived among us, we convened a council. We believed that he had been sent with Apiarius for this reason: just as Apiarius had previously been restored to the presbyterate through Faustinus’s efforts, so now, with Faustinus laboring on his behalf, he might be cleared of the many crimes alleged against him by the Thabracenians. Yet the examination conducted by our council found such great and monstrous offenses alleged against him by the Thabracenians that it showed the aforesaid man to have offered advocacy rather than judgment, and the service of a defender rather than the justice of an adjudicator.

For, first, consider how greatly he opposed the whole assembly by bringing forward various injuries, as though asserting the privileges of the Roman Church and wishing us to receive into communion a man whom your Holiness, believing that he had appealed, had restored to communion, although he could not prove the matter. This, however, was by no means permissible, as you will more clearly recognize from reading the proceedings. Nevertheless, after a most laborious three-day hearing, while we were distressingly investigating the various charges brought against him, as well as the delays of our fellow bishop Faustinus and the evasions of Apiarius himself—by which he was attempting to conceal his unspeakable disgrace—the just Judge, God, strong, patient, and long-suffering, cut the matter short with great efficiency.

For his most foul and putrid obstinacy was crushed: by his shameless denial he had wished to bury so great a mass of bloody filth. But when our God stirred his conscience and revealed to human beings the hidden things that He had already condemned in Apiarius’s heart as in a dung-pit of crimes, the crafty denier suddenly burst into a confession of all the charges. At last, concerning all the unbelievable disgraces, he convicted himself voluntarily and turned into lamentation even the hope we had held and desired—that he might be cleansed of such shameful stains. Our sorrow was mitigated by only one consolation: his confession both freed us from the labor of a lengthier investigation and provided some kind of remedy for his wounds, even if, while alive and with his conscience resisting, he had been led to make that confession, Lord Brother.

After offering the duty of the greeting owed to you, we earnestly beg you henceforth not to admit too readily those who come from here to your ears, nor to wish any longer to receive into communion those whom we have excommunicated. Your Reverence can easily perceive that this too was defined by the Council of Nicaea. For even if provision there appears to have been made concerning lower-ranking clerics or laymen, how much more did it wish this to be observed concerning bishops? Let not bishops suspended from communion in their own province appear to be rashly, hastily, prematurely, or improperly restored to communion by your Holiness. May your Holiness also repel, as is worthy of you, the improper appeals of presbyters and other clerics of lower rank. No definition of the Fathers has deprived the African Church of this right; and the Nicene decrees have plainly entrusted both clerics of lower rank and the bishops themselves to their metropolitan bishops. [Col. 0365D]

For they wisely and justly saw that whatever matters arise in the places where they originate should be settled there, and that the grace of the Spirit would not be lacking to any prudent administrator, so that equity might be wisely discerned and steadfastly upheld by Christ’s priests. Above all, everyone has been granted the right, if offended by the judgment of those who examined the case, to appeal to the councils of his own province or even to a universal council. Unless, perhaps, someone believes that our God can inspire justice in a single examiner while denying it to the innumerable priests assembled in the Council of Nicaea; or how can that overseas judgment be valid when the necessary witnesses could not be brought to it, either because of the weakness of old age or because of many other intervening obstacles? [Col. 0366B]

For we have found no synod of the Fathers establishing that certain persons should be sent as though from the side of your Holiness. As for what you previously transmitted through our fellow bishop Faustinus as though it came from the Council of Nicaea, we could find nothing of that sort in the more authentic councils accepted as Nicene, which were sent from the holy Cyril, our fellow bishop of the Alexandrian Church, and from the venerable Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, from the authentic records. These documents had also previously been transmitted by us to Boniface, bishop of venerable memory and our predecessor, through the presbyter Innocent and the subdeacon Marcellus, by whom they had been sent to us. [Col. 0366C]
