Do not send your clerical agents to anyone who asks, and do not grant them authority, lest we appear to be introducing into Christ’s Church the notorious pomp of the world, whereas the Church displays the light of simplicity and humility to those who desire to see the day of the Lord.

As for our brother Faustinus, we are confident that the integrity and moderation of your Holiness, while preserving fraternal charity, will not permit Apiarius—now sorrowfully removed from Christ’s Church because of his unspeakable wickedness—to be tolerated any longer in Africa.

And in another hand: May our Lord preserve your Holiness, Lord Brother, praying for us through a long age. [Col. 0366D]

# The Chapters of the Seventh Council of Carthage Begin

[Col. 0365]

[Col. 0365D] 1. That the excommunicated are not to be admitted to the accusation of clerics. 2. The persons to whom the accusation of clerics is forbidden. 3. That those who have not proved the first charge brought against them are not to be admitted to the remaining charges. [Col. 0366D] 4. The persons forbidden to give testimony against clerics. 5. Concerning one whom someone presumes to excommunicate on his sole testimony.

# The Seventh Council of Carthage Begins, with Thirty-Eight Bishops

[Col. 0365]

[Col. 0365D] After the consulship of the most glorious emperors, Honorius III and Theodosius VIII, Augusti, on the third day before the Kalends of July, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the Restored Basilica, when Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat together with [Col. 0367A] Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church for the Potentine church of the Italian province of Picenum; Vincentius Culusianus; Fortunatianus of Naples; Maurianus of Uzippara; Adeodatus of Simidic; Pentadius of Carpis; Rufinianus of Muzua; Praetextatus of Sicilibba; Quodvultdeus of Vescera; Candidus of Abiritum; Gallonianus of Utica, legates of the province of Numidia and of the Proconsular province; Alippius of Thagaste; Augustine of Hippo Regius; and Possidius of Calama, legates of the province of Numidia; Maximianus of Aquae Regiae; Jocundus of Suffetula; and Hilarinus of Horreocelos, legates of the province of Byzacena; Novatus of Sitifis and Leo of Opta, legates of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis; Nivellus of Rusurium, Laurentius of Icosium, and Numerianus of Nusgumium, legates of the province of Mauretania Caesariensis; with the deacons chosen by all the judges of the council standing by, and [Col. 0367B] after certain matters had been completed, many bishops complained that they could not endure the delays involved in completing the remaining business and were hastening to their own churches, the whole council decided that men should be selected from each of the provinces to remain for the sake of the other business to be completed. Accordingly, those were present whose subscriptions testify that they had attended.

**Chapter I.** Since the decrees of earlier councils have already established which persons are to be admitted to the accusation of clerics and which persons are not to be admitted, we therefore define that no one is properly to be admitted to an accusation who, after having been excommunicated, still remains under that excommunication, whether he is [Col. 0367C] a cleric or a layman, if he wishes to accuse.

**II.** It was likewise decided that no slaves or personal freedmen are to be admitted to an accusation, nor anyone whom the public laws do not admit to the accusation of public crimes. This includes all persons stained by the marks of infamy—that is, actors and persons subject to disgraceful occupations—as well as heretics, pagans, and Jews. Nevertheless, for all those to whom the right of accusation is denied, permission to bring an accusation in their own cases must not be denied.

[Col. 0368A] **III.** It was likewise decided that whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by accusers, if the accuser is unwilling to prove one of those charges, the one with which he dealt first, he is not to be admitted to the others.

**IV.** Witnesses who are not to be admitted to give testimony are those who are not ordered to be admitted to an accusation, as well as those whom the accuser himself produces from his own household. No one under fourteen years of age is to be admitted as a witness.

**V.** It was likewise decided that if a bishop says that someone confessed a particular crime to him alone, and that person denies it, the bishop must not regard it as an insult to himself that his sole testimony is not believed. If he says that, because of a scruple concerning his own conscience, he does not wish to communicate with the denier, then, for as long as his bishop does not communicate with the excommunicated person, no other bishops are to communicate with that bishop, so that a bishop may take greater care not to say against anyone what he cannot prove by other evidence.

And they subscribed: Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage; Faustinus of Potentina in the province of Picenum; Alippius of Thagaste, legate of the province of Numidia; Augustine of Hippo Regius, legate of the province of Numidia; Possidius, bishop of Calama, legate of the province of Numidia; Novatus of Sitifis, legate of the same province; Leo of Opta, legate of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis; Mauritianus of Uzippara; Rufianus of Muzua; Quodvultdeus of Vescera; Candidus of Abiritum Germanicianum; Gallonianus of Utica; Jocundus of Suffetula, legate of the province of Byzacena; Hilarinus of Horreocelos, [Col. 0368C] legate of the province of Byzacena; Maximianus of Suffetula, legate of the province of Byzacena; Maximianus of Aquae Regiae, legate of the province of Byzacena; Nivellus of Rusurium, legate of the province of Caesariensis; Laurentius of Icosium, legate of the province of Caesariensis; Numerianus of Nusgumium, legate of the province of Caesariensis; Philippus, presbyter of the Roman Church; and Asellus, presbyter and legate of the Roman Church.

# The Chapters of the Council of Milevis Begin

[Col. 0367]

[Col. 0367C] 1. Against the Pelagians, who say that Adam could also have died without sin. [Col. 0367D] 2. That, according to the testimony of the Apostle, even infants who have not yet committed any sin are truly baptized for the remission of sins. 3. That God’s grace not only forgives sins but also helps people not to commit them. 4. That by God’s grace we know what we ought to do and love doing it. 5. That God’s grace enables the law to be fulfilled, rather than—as Pelagius says—making it possible to fulfill it more easily, though with greater difficulty, as if without God’s grace it could nevertheless be fulfilled. 6. That, according to the judgment of John the Evangelist, no one can be without sin. 7. That every righteous person must say not only for others but also for himself: “Forgive us our debts.” [Col. 0368C] 8. That the saints truly say: “Forgive us our debts.” [Col. 0368D] 9. That a general council ought to be convened for common matters of the Church, but a special council of each province for private matters. 10. That the metropolitan is to subscribe and dispatch the letters summoning a council. 11. That whatever is decreed in a council concerning heretics and unbelievers is to be enforced by the ruler. 12. That prayers and collects are not to be recited unless they have been approved in a council. 13. That later bishops are not to be preferred to earlier ones, nor are they to presume to do anything without consulting their primates. 14. That bishops are to have letters from their ordainers recording the time of their consecration. [Col. 0369A] 87 15. That wherever someone first reads, there he is to remain as a cleric. 16. That agents or advocates are to be requested from the ruler for the affairs of the churches. 17. That neither a man dismissed from his marriage nor a woman dismissed from hers is to marry another. 18. Concerning those who do not communicate in their own province: they are not to communicate elsewhere. 19. Concerning clerics who have completed either a secular judgment before the ruler or a synodal proceeding. 20. That no one is to travel to the imperial court without an official credential, and how such credentials are to be made. [Col. 0370A] 21. Concerning bishops who seized what they could have reclaimed, bypassing a synod. 22. Concerning clerics who complain about the judgments of their bishops. 23. Concerning those who have received penance from heretics. 24. Concerning bishops negligent toward heretics. 25. The foregoing. 26. Concerning virgins who, under the pressure of necessity, are veiled before the age of twenty-five. 27. Concerning bishops who, after the proceedings of the Council of Carthage, were detained in order to complete the remaining business.

# The Council of Milevis Begins

[Col. 0369]

[Col. 0369B] In the consulship of the most glorious emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Augusti, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the city of Milevis, in the secretariat of the basilica, when Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, had taken his seat in the universal council, with deacons standing by, Bishop Aurelius said:

Since the holy Church is one body and the head of all its members is one, it has come about, by the Lord’s will and with his help for our weakness, that we should come together here, invited by love and brotherhood. Therefore I ask your Charity—since this must be believed—that our coming to you is neither superfluous nor displeasing to all. For this reason, let certain matters concerning the faith, especially the present Pelagian controversy, first be discussed in this most holy assembly; then let other matters follow, including some that are necessary for ecclesiastical discipline. [Col. 0369C]

**Chapter I.** All the bishops who were present at this holy synod therefore decided to establish the following. Whoever says that the first human being, Adam, was made mortal in such a way that whether he sinned or did not sin he would die in the body—that is, depart from the body—not because of the merit of sin but by the necessity of nature, let him be anathema.

**II.** It was likewise decided that whoever denies that newborn infants are to be baptized, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but derive nothing from Adam’s original sin that is cleansed through the bath of regeneration—so that consequently the baptismal formula “for the remission of sins” is understood in their case as not true but false—let him be anathema. For the Apostle’s statement, “Through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned,” must not be understood in any other way than the way in which the Catholic Church, spread throughout the world, has always understood it. Indeed, because of this rule of faith, even infants who have not yet been able to commit any sins in themselves are truly baptized for the remission of sins, so that through regeneration what they have acquired through generation may be cleansed in them. [Col. 0369D]

**III.** It was likewise decided that whoever says that the grace of God by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord is effective only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also as help to prevent sins from being committed, let him be anathema. [Col. 0370B]

**IV.** Whoever says that the same grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord helps us not to sin only because through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to seek and what we ought to avoid, but that through it we are not enabled to love and to be capable of doing what we have recognized must be done, let him be anathema.

For the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” It is exceedingly impious to believe that we have the grace of Christ for that which puffs us up, but not for that which builds us up, since both are gifts of God: knowing what we ought to do and loving in order to do it, so that, when love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up. Just as it is written of God, “who teaches human beings knowledge,” so it is also written:

**V.** It was likewise decided that whoever says that the reason we are given the grace of justification (love is from God) is so that we may more easily fulfill by grace what we are commanded to do through free choice—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily—let him be anathema. For the Lord was speaking about the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do it with greater difficulty,” but said, “Without me you can do nothing.” [Col. 0370D]

**VI.** It was likewise decided concerning what the holy Apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” Whoever thinks this must be understood in such a way that, out of humility, we ought to say that we have sin, not because this is true, let him be anathema.

The Apostle continues and adds: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” It is sufficiently clear here that this is said not only humbly but also truthfully. The Apostle could have said, “If we say that we have no sin, we exalt ourselves, and humility is not in us.” But when he says, “We deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” he clearly shows that the person who says he has no sin is not speaking the truth but falsely. [Col. 0371A]

**VII.** It was likewise decided that whoever says that the saints say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts,” not for themselves, because this petition is no longer necessary for them, but for the sinners among their own people; and that therefore each saint does not say, “Forgive me my debts,” but “Forgive us our debts,” so that the righteous person is understood to ask this for others rather than for himself, let him be anathema.

For the apostle James was holy and righteous when he said, “In many things we all offend.” Why was “all” added, unless this statement was meant to apply universally? Likewise in the Psalm where it is written, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight”; and in the prayer of the wisest Solomon, “There is no human being who does not sin”; and in the Book of Job, “He seals up the hand of every human being, so that every person may know his own weakness.”

Thus holy and righteous Daniel, when he said in his prayer in the plural, “We have sinned, we have acted wickedly,” and the other things that he confesses there truthfully and humbly—lest it be thought, as some hold, that he was speaking not of his own sins but rather of the sins of his people—later said: “When I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord our God.” He did not say “our sins,” but spoke of his people’s sins and his own, because, like a prophet, he foresaw those who would understand this so badly. [Col. 0371C]

**VIII.** It was likewise decided that whoever wishes the very words of the Lord’s Prayer, when we say “Forgive us our debts,” to be spoken by the saints in such a way that they say them humbly but not truthfully, let him be anathema.

Who could tolerate someone praying and lying not to human beings but to the Lord himself—saying with his lips that he wishes his debts to be forgiven while saying in his heart that he has no debts to be forgiven?

Thus far concerning the faith against the Pelagians; now the ecclesiastical regulations are addressed.

**IX.** It was decided that there should no longer be an annual obligation that wearies the brethren. Rather, whenever a common matter requires it—that is, whenever letters from every part of Africa concerning a council have been delivered to this see—a synod is to be assembled in whatever province opportunity recommends. Matters that are not common are to be judged in their own provinces. [Col. 0371D]

**X.** It was also decided that Your Holiness alone should subscribe all the letters of all the bishops that are issued from the council.

**XI.** It was also decided concerning heretics, pagans, and their superstitions that the legates sent from this glorious council should obtain from the most glorious emperors whatever useful measures they determine.

**XII.** It was also decided that prayers, collects, or Masses that have been approved in the council—whether prefaces, commendations, or laying-on-of-hands prayers—are to be celebrated by all. No others at all are to be said in the Church except those that have been discussed by more prudent persons or approved in a synod, lest something contrary to the faith should have been composed through ignorance or insufficient care. [Col. 0372A]

**XIII.** Bishop Palentinus said: If the goodness of your patience permits, I will pursue the matters that are necessary for ecclesiastical discipline. We know that ecclesiastical discipline has remained inviolable in this way: no brother has ever dared to put himself before his predecessors, but the legitimate offices have always rendered to those who came before them what those who followed could reasonably receive. Let Your Holiness strengthen this order more firmly through your own statements.

Bishop Aurelius said: It would not have been fitting for us to repeat these matters unless perhaps the thoughtlessness of certain people had sharpened our minds to establish them. But this is also the common concern that our brother and fellow bishop has brought forward: each of us must recognize the order assigned to him by God, and those who come later must defer to those who came earlier, nor presume to do anything without consulting them. Therefore those who think that something may be presumed upon while disregarding their superiors must properly be restrained by the whole council.

All the bishops said: This order has been observed by the Fathers and by our predecessors, and, with God’s favor, it will be observed by us, while preserving also the right of primacy of Numidia and Mauretania.

**XIV.** It was then decided that all who are thereafter ordained by bishops are to receive from their ordainers letters subscribed by their own hand, stating the consulship and the day, so that no dispute may arise concerning those who are later or earlier. [Col. 0372C]

**XV.** It was likewise decided that whoever has read even once in one church is not to be retained for the clerical order by another church.

**XVI.** It was further decided that agents are to be assisted in all just requests. It was also decided that the most glorious emperors should be asked to order the judges to provide the scholastic advocates requested by them, who are active in, or hold office in, the defense of ecclesiastical cases, so that, following the custom of the priests of the province—that is, those who have undertaken the defense of the churches—they may have authority, whenever the affairs of the churches require it, either to resist those who deceitfully mislead or intrude, or to enter the judges’ secretariats to present what is necessary. [Col. 0372D]

**XVII.** It was decided, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, that neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband is to marry another person. They are to remain as they are or be reconciled to one another. If they refuse, they are to be brought to penance. In this matter, a law of the emperor is to be requested and promulgated.

**XVIII.** It was decided that whoever, while not communicating in his own province, secretly goes to other provinces or overseas regions to receive communion is to suffer the loss of communion or of his clerical office.

**XIX.** It was decided that whoever asks the emperor to review public judgments made by bishops is to be deprived of his proper rank. If, however, he asks the emperor for an episcopal judgment, this is not to harm him. [Col. 0373A]

**XX.** It was decided that any cleric who wishes, because of his own necessity, to go somewhere to the imperial court is to receive an official credential from his bishop. If he wishes to travel without such a credential, he is to be removed from communion. If an unexpected necessity arises somewhere requiring him to go to the imperial court, he is to explain that necessity to the bishop of the place and carry with him a written statement from that bishop.

The credentials issued by primates or by any bishops to their own clerics are to bear the date of Easter. If the date of Easter for that year is still uncertain, the preceding date of Easter is to be added, in the manner customarily written after the consulship in public records.

**XXI.** It was likewise decided that whenever bishops reclaim churches or communities that they consider to belong to their see, they are to proceed by presenting their cases before bishops acting as judges. If they invade a church held by someone else, whether the communities wish it or not, their case is to suffer damage. Anyone who has already done this, if the dispute has not yet been settled among the bishops but is still being contested, is to withdraw if it is established that he invaded the church after bypassing ecclesiastical judgments.

No one is to flatter himself because he has obtained letters from a primate authorizing him to retain the church. Whether he has such letters or not, he must approach the person holding it and receive his letters, so that it may be evident that he has held peacefully the church belonging to him. If the other party raises any question, the matter is to be settled through episcopal judges, whether the primates assign them or the parties themselves, by mutual agreement, choose neighboring bishops. [Col. 0373C]

**XXII.** It was likewise decided that if presbyters, deacons, or other lower clerics have cases and complain about the judgments of their bishops, neighboring bishops are to hear them and settle whatever exists between them, being appointed by agreement with their own bishops.

If they think they ought to appeal from those bishops as well, they are not to appeal except to African councils or to the primates of their own provinces. Anyone who thinks of appealing overseas is not to be received into communion by anyone within Africa.

**XXIII.** It was decided that whenever someone converted from the heretics says that he received penance among them, each Catholic bishop is to inquire where and for what reason he received penance from those same heretics. When he has established this with reliable evidence, he is to determine the period of penance or reconciliation according to the nature of the sin, as seems appropriate to that Catholic bishop. [Col. 0373D]

**XXIV.** It was likewise decided that whenever bishops neglect to win for Catholic unity the places belonging to their sees, diligent neighboring bishops are to summon them, so that they may not delay doing what is required. If they have not done so within six months from the day of the summons, then the places may belong to whoever is able to win them.

This is subject to the following condition: if the person to whom the places appeared to belong can prove that the heretics had deliberately chosen his negligence, so that they might remain there with impunity, and had forestalled his diligence in order to avoid his more careful administration, then, when the episcopal judges have learned this, they may restore the places to the see.

If the bishops between whom the case is being disputed belong to different provinces, the primate of the province in which the disputed place lies is to appoint the judges. If, by common agreement, neighboring judges are chosen, either two or three are to be appointed. If three are chosen, the decision is to follow either the judgment of all or that of two. No appeal is permitted from judges chosen by common agreement. Whoever is proved, through contumacy, to be unwilling to obey the judges is, once this has been established before the bishop of the first see, to be the subject of letters ordering that none of the bishops communicate with him until he obeys. [Col. 0374A]

**XXV.** If a bishop in a principal see is negligent toward the heretics, he is to be summoned by diligent neighboring bishops, and his negligence is to be demonstrated to him, so that he cannot excuse himself. If, within six months from the day on which he is summoned, an executor is available in his province and he has not taken care to convert the heretics to Catholic unity, no one is to communicate with him until he fulfills the obligation.

If the agent has not come to the places, this is not to be charged against the bishop. But if he is proved to have lied about their communion by saying that people were in communion when, as he knew, they were not, he is also to lose his episcopate.

**XXVI.** It was likewise decided that if any bishop, because of the danger threatening a virgin’s chastity—when a powerful suitor or some abductor is feared, or when she has been troubled by some dangerous fear of death—veils a virgin, whether at the request of her parents or of those responsible for her care, or whether he has veiled her before she reaches twenty-five years of age, this is not to be held against him under the council’s decree concerning that number of years. [Col. 0374C]

**XXVII.** It was likewise decided that, so that all the bishops assembled for the council would not be detained longer, the whole council should choose three judges from each province. The following were chosen: from the province of Carthage, Vincentius, Fortunatianus, and Clarus; from the province of Numidia, Alippius, Augustine, and Restitutus; from the province of Byzacena, together with the venerable old man Domitianus the primate, Cresconius, Jocundus, and Melianus; from Mauretania Sitifensis, Severianus, Asiaticus, and Donatus; and from the province of Tripolitania, Plautius, who, according to custom, was sent as the sole legate.

All these, together with the venerable old man Aurelius, are to investigate everything. The whole council requested that he subscribe both all the proceedings that had already been completed and the bishops themselves, and they subscribed.

Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage: I have agreed to and subscribed this decree after it was read.

Donatianus of Telepte, of the first see: I have subscribed.

Augustine of Hippo Regius: I have subscribed.

All the bishops likewise subscribed.

**Thus far the councils of Africa.**

# The Councils of Gaul Follow

[Col. 0375]

# The Chapters of the Council of Arles Begin

[Col. 0375A] 1. That Easter is celebrated on one day and at one time. 2. That each person remains where he is ordained. 3. That those who lay down their arms in peacetime are excommunicated. 4. That charioteers are excommunicated while they are driving. 5. That those who assemble in theaters are excommunicated. 6. That those converted in illness receive the laying-on of hands. 7. Concerning governors: that they communicate with the knowledge of their bishop. 8. That those converted from heresy are baptized in the Trinity. 9. That those who carry letters from confessors receive other letters. 10. That the man whose wife has committed adultery is not to take another wife. [Col. 0375B] 11. That faithful women who have joined themselves to pagans are excommunicated. 12. That clerics who lend at interest are excommunicated. [Col. 0376A] 13. That betrayers of their brothers, or of vessels, or of the Scriptures, are deposed with flogging. 14. That false accusers of their brothers are excommunicated until death. 15. That Levites are not to offer. 16. That penitents communicate where they received their burden of penance. 17. That no bishop trample upon another bishop. 18. That a deacon do nothing without his presbyter. 19. That presbyters do nothing without the knowledge of their bishops. 20. That a place for offering the sacrifice be given to a visiting bishop. 21. That no bishop be ordained without three bishops. [Col. 0376B] 22. That a cleric who transfers elsewhere is excommunicated. 23. That apostates who return late are not received except through worthy penance.

# The First Council of Arles Begins, Held in the Time of the Emperor Constantine

[Col. 0375]

[Col. 0375C] To the Lord and most holy Bishop Sylvester: the assembly of bishops who were gathered at the town of Arles sends greeting. We communicate charitably what we have decided in common council, so that everyone may know what they ought to observe in the future.

**Chapter I.** Concerning the observance of the Lord’s Pasch: it is to be observed throughout the whole world on one day and at one time, and, according to custom, you are to send letters to everyone.

**II.** Concerning those who have been ordained as ministers in any places: let them remain in those places.

**III.** Concerning those who lay down their arms in peacetime: it was decided that they are to abstain from communion.

IV. Concerning charioteers who are faithful: it was decided that, for as long as they drive, they shall be separated from communion.

V. Concerning theatrical performers: it was likewise decided that they, for as long as they perform, shall be separated from communion. [Col. 0375D]

VI. Concerning those who wish to believe while suffering illness: it was decided that hands ought to be laid upon them.

89 VII. Concerning governors who are faithful and advance to the governorship: it was decided that, when they have been promoted, they shall receive ecclesiastical letters of communion, but in such a way that, wherever they exercise office, the bishop of that place shall care for them. When they begin to act with public authority, only then shall they be excluded from communion. [Col. 0376C] The same shall be done with those who wish to administer public affairs.

VIII. Concerning the Arians, who follow their own law and rebaptize: it was decided that they should be rebaptized. If some from this heresy come to the Church, the priests of our faith shall question them concerning the Creed; and if they find that they were baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, only hands shall be laid upon them, so that they may receive the Holy Spirit. But if, when questioned, they do not confess this Trinity, they shall not be baptized.

IX. Concerning those who bring letters from confessors: it was decided that, once those letters have been taken from them, they shall receive other letters of communion.

X. Concerning those who discover that their wives have committed adultery, when these men are themselves young and faithful and are forbidden to marry: it was decided that, insofar as possible, counsel should be given to them not to take other wives while their own wives are living, even if adulterous. [Col. 0376D]

XI. Concerning faithful girls who join themselves to pagans: it was decided that they should be separated from communion for some time.

XII. Concerning ministers who lend at interest: it was decided that they should abstain from communion according to the divinely given rule.

XIII. Concerning those who are said to have handed over the sacred Scriptures, or the vessels of the Lord, or the names of their brothers: [Col. 0377A] it was decided by us that whoever among them has been exposed in public records, or by plain testimony, shall be removed from the clerical order. For if the same men are discovered to have ordained anyone, and if the case against those who ordained them is sustained, nevertheless their ordination shall not stand, since there are many who appear to fight against ecclesiastical rule and think that they ought to be admitted to an accusation through purchased witnesses. Such witnesses are not to be admitted at all unless, as we said above, they prove through public records that they are free from every suspicion.

XIV. Concerning those who falsely accuse their brothers: it was decided that they shall not communicate until death, but that a false witness, according to Scripture, must not be left unpunished.

[Col. 0377B] XV. Concerning deacons whom we have learned to offer in many places: it was decided that this must by no means be done.

XVI. Concerning those who are separated from communion for their offense: it was decided that, wherever they were excluded, they shall receive communion in that same place.

XVII. No bishop shall trample upon another bishop.

[Col. 0378A] XVIII. Concerning urban deacons: they shall presume nothing on their own, but honor shall be reserved for presbyters.

XIX. Presbyters shall do nothing without the knowledge of their bishops.

XX. A place for a visiting bishop to perform satisfaction shall be provided.

XXI. Concerning those who claim for themselves the right that only they should ordain a bishop: it was decided that no one shall presume this unless he has taken seven other bishops with him; but if they cannot obtain seven, they shall not dare to ordain without three brothers.

XXII. Concerning presbyters or deacons who are accustomed to leave the places in which they were ordained and transfer themselves elsewhere: it was decided that they shall minister in the places to which they were assigned. Those who, abandoning their own places, [Col. 0378B] wish to transfer themselves to another place shall be deposed.

XXIII. Concerning those who apostatize and, before presenting themselves to the Church, do not even seek to perform penance, but afterward, seized by illness, ask for communion: it was decided that communion must not be given to them unless they have confessed and performed worthy fruits of penance.

The First Council of Arles ends.

# Chapters of the Second Council of Arles Begin

[Col. 0377]

[Col. 0377B] 1. On not ordaining neophyte clerics. 2. How married men are to be advanced to the priesthood. [Col. 0377C] 3. No cleric or deacon shall have an unrelated woman in his service. 4. No cleric shall admit a girl into his storeroom or private quarters. 5. When a bishop is ordained with the consent of the metropolitan, three bishops shall ordain him. 6. Concerning a bishop who has been ordained without the metropolitan’s consent. 7. Concerning those who mutilate themselves. 8. Concerning those who receive excommunicated persons from another bishop. 9. Novatians shall not be admitted to communion. 10. Concerning those who lapsed during the persecution. [Col. 0377D] 11. Concerning those who, overcome by punishments, were compelled to sacrifice. 12. Concerning those who died while doing penance. [Col. 0378B] 13. No one shall abandon his own church for any necessity. [Col. 0378C] 14. A cleric shall not accept interest. 15. A deacon shall not sit in the presence of a presbyter or distribute the Eucharist. 16. Photinians and Paulianists shall be baptized. 17. Heretics who have been baptized in the Trinity shall be received with chrism and the laying on of hands. 18. The synod shall be convened at the metropolitan’s discretion. 19. No bishop may be absent from the synod or depart before the synod has been completed. 20. Concerning faithful charioteers and theatrical performers. 21. If someone marries after receiving penance. 22. Penance shall be given to married persons with their consent. 23. Concerning priests who have not destroyed idolatry. [Col. 0378D] 24. Concerning accusers of their brothers. 25. Concerning apostates, if they do not return.

The chapters end.

# The Second Council of Arles Begins

The names of the authors of this same council.

[Col. 0377]

[Col. 0377D] From Sicily: Sixtus, bishop of Syracuse, and Florus, deacon. From the province of Campania: Prothus, bishop of the city, and Agrippa, and Tutus, deacon. From the province of Apulia: Pardus, bishop, and Crescens, deacon. From the province of Damultum: Theodorus, bishop, and Agathon, deacon. From the city of Rome, whom Bishop Sylvester sent: Claudianus and Abitus, presbyters, and Eugenius and Quiriacus, deacons. From the province of Italy: Orosius, bishop, and Nazareus, lector, from the city of Arelas in the province of Vienne; Martinus, bishop, Salanias, presbyter, Nicetus Afer, Ursinus, and Petrus, deacons, from the same province of Vienne. [Col. 0379A] Verus, bishop, and Bedas, exorcist, from the city of Vaison; Dammas, bishop, and Victor, exorcist, from the city of Orange; Laustinus, presbyter, from the gate; Innocentius, deacon, and Agapius, exorcist, from the province of Gaul, city of Reims; Ibethanius, bishop, and Prigenius, deacon, from the city of Rouen; Avidamus, bishop, and Nicetius, deacon, from the city of Augusta; Idonupetius, bishop, Amandus, presbyter, and Filomatis, deacon, from the city of Helvidon; Votius, bishop, and Pitulius, exorcist, from the city of Cologne; Maternus, bishop, and Maurinus, deacon, from the province of Aquitaine, city of Vagalia; Genialis, bishop, from the city of Bordeaux; Orientalis, bishop, and Flavius, deacon, from the city of Verus; Artius, bishop, and Felix, exorcist, from the city of Toulouse; Martinus, [Col. 0379B] bishop, and Leontius, deacon, from the province of Bithynia; Eburius, bishop, from the city of Culnia; Adelsius, from the city of Rome; Liberius, bishop, and Flonetius, deacon, from the city of Baetica; Sabinus, presbyter, from the city of Tarragona; Probatus, presbyter, and Castorius, deacon, from the city of Zaragoza; Clementinus, presbyter, and Rovinus, exorcist, from the city of the Tebestigenians; Trimanus, presbyter, and Victor, deacon, from the province of Caesarian Mauretania; Fortunatus, bishop, and Deuterius, deacon, from the province of Sardinia; Quintus, bishop, and Admonius, presbyter, from the province of Africa; Cecilianus, presbyter, and Sperantius, deacon, from the city of Onina; Lampadius, bishop, from the city of Utica; Victor, bishop, from the city of Beneventum; Anastasius, bishop, from the city of Turbistum; [Col. 0379C] Faustus, bishop, from the city of Cocofeltum; Surgentius, bishop, from Numidia; Victor, bishop, from the city of the Virenses; Vitalis, bishop, from the port of the city of Rome; Gregorius, bishop, from Centumcellae; Epitatus, bishop, from the city of Ostia; and Leontius and Macharius, presbyters.

I. A neophyte must not be ordained to the office of deacon or priest.

II. No one may be admitted to the priesthood while bound by marriage, unless a change of life has been promised.

III. If any cleric of the rank of deacon presumes to have in his service a woman other than his grandmother, mother, sister, daughter, niece, or a wife who has converted with him, he shall be considered excluded from communion; and the woman likewise shall be punished if she refuses to separate from him.

IV. No deacon, presbyter, or bishop shall admit into the privacy of a storeroom a girl, whether freeborn or enslaved.

V. No bishop shall presume to ordain a bishop without the metropolitan’s permission, nor shall a metropolitan bishop do so without three bishops of the same province. The other bishops of the province shall be notified by letter so that they may indicate their consent in their reply. But if there is some disagreement between the parties, the metropolitan shall consent to the election according to the greater number.

VI. Above all, let it be clear that one who has been established as bishop without the metropolitan’s knowledge ought not, according to the Great Synod, to be considered a bishop. [Col. 0380A]

VII. If anyone, unable to resist carnal vice, mutilates himself, he cannot attain the clergy.

VIII. If anyone, after the prohibition, presumes to receive an excommunicated person belonging to another bishop, whether cleric or layman, let him know that he has made himself guilty of a breach of brotherhood and will have to render an account before the council. 90

IX. A Novatian must not be received into communion unless, having undertaken penance, he condemns his former error of unbelief.

X. Concerning those who lapsed during the persecution: if they voluntarily denied the faith, the Council of Nicaea established the following concerning them: they shall spend five years among the catechumens and two among those excluded from communion, so that they do not presume to receive communion while among the penitents. [Col. 0380B] Nevertheless, it shall lie within the power or discretion of the bishop, if he sees that they grieve their error from the heart and perform penance, to receive them humanely into communion in their own church, should he wish to do so.

XI. But if some, overcome by distress and the burden of persecution, were compelled to deny the faith and sacrifice, they shall be suspended from communion for two years among the catechumens and three years among the penitents.

XII. Concerning those who died while doing penance: it was decided that no one should be dismissed without communion; rather, because he honored penance, his offering shall be received.

XIII. No cleric of any rank—neither deacon, presbyter, nor bishop—shall, for any reason whatsoever, abandon his own church. [Col. 0380C] Instead, he shall either be excommunicated outright or compelled to return. If, during the period of his residence, someone lives in another church against the will of his own bishop and is ordained a cleric by the bishop of that place, such ordination shall be considered invalid.

XIV. If a cleric has lent money at interest, or wishes to be a tenant of another’s property, or conducts any kind of commerce for the sake of shameful profit, he shall be deposed from the clergy and considered excluded from communion.

XV. In the secretariat, deacons may not sit among presbyters, nor may they presume to distribute the body of Christ in the presence of a presbyter. If they do so, they shall withdraw from the office of the diaconate.

XVI. Photinians or Paulianists ought to be baptized according to the decrees of the Fathers. [Col. 0380D]

XVII. As for Bonosians coming from the same error—who, like the Arians, are plainly baptized in the Trinity—it is sufficient, once they have been questioned and confessed our faith with all their heart, to receive them into the Church with chrism and the laying on of hands.

XVIII. The synod shall be convened at the discretion of the bishop of Arles. We read that in the time of Saint Martin a council and assembly were held in that city from all parts of the world. If anyone who has been notified is absent because of illness, he shall send a representative in his place.

XIX. But if anyone neglects to attend, or thinks that he should leave the gathering of the brothers before the council is dissolved, let him recognize that he is excluded from the communion of the brothers. He may not be received unless he has been absolved at the following synod. [Col. 0381A]

XX. Concerning faithful charioteers and theatrical performers: it was decided that, for as long as they perform their occupations, they shall be separated from communion.

XXI. Penitent women who, after the death of their husband, presume to marry others, or who enter into a suspect or forbidden relationship with an outsider, shall be barred from the thresholds of the Church together with that man. It was decided that the same rule should be observed concerning a man placed under penance.

XXII. Penance shall be given to married persons only with their consent.

XXIII. If, in the territory of any priest, unbelievers light torches or venerate trees, springs, or stones, and he neglects to uproot these practices, let him recognize that he is guilty of sacrilege. The lord who ordained him, [Col. 0381B] if, after being admonished, he refuses to correct the matter, shall be deprived of communion. [Col. 0382A]

XXIV. Concerning those convicted of bringing false capital charges against their brothers: it was decided that they shall not communicate until death, as the Great Synod previously established, unless they repent with worthy satisfaction.

XXV. If some, after making a holy profession of religion, apostatize and return to the world, and afterward do not seek the remedies of penance, they shall absolutely not receive communion without penance. We also command that they not be admitted to the clerical office; and whoever he may be, after penance he shall not presume to resume secular dress. If he presumes to do so, he shall be considered excluded from the Church.

The Second Council of Arles ends.

# Chapters of the Third Council of Arles Begin

[Col. 0381]

[Col. 0381B] 1. A deacon shall not be ordained before the age of twenty-five, nor a priest before the age of thirty. 2. Bigamists, penitents, and husbands of repudiated women shall not be advanced to the priesthood. [Col. 0382B] 3. A layman shall not be ordained before a year of conversion has elapsed. 4. Whoever endeavors to defend another’s cleric shall be deprived of communion.

# The Third Council of Arles Begins

Of twenty-four bishops, in the year 461 of the era.

[Col. 0381]

[Col. 0381C] In the consulship of the Augusti Martianus and Opilio and of Vincomalus, on the eighth day before the Ides of July, when, by God’s will, the priests of the Lord had assembled in the city of Arles for the dedication of the basilica of Saint Mary, it seemed appropriate and reasonable to them that, first considering with the utmost care the canons to be observed and how the ecclesiastical rule was to be maintained by themselves, they should establish the matter through a salutary decree.

I. Since it is recognized that the regulations of the ancient Fathers concerning the ordination of clerics have not been observed in their entirety, as is fitting, lest the priests of the Lord be wearied by the importunate and disorderly petitions of various persons and be compelled to transgress commands so often issued, they determine among themselves that the following shall be observed: no bishop shall presume to ordain a deacon before he has completed twenty-five years. No layman shall receive the dignity of the episcopate or the honor of the presbyterate before the completion of the previously specified year of conversion or before thirty years of age. [Col. 0381D]

II. No one shall dare to ordain a penitent, a bigamist, or the husband of a widow to the aforesaid honors. Although nearly all the canons already contain these provisions, it was nevertheless necessary—lest importunity or an unjust suggestion from petitioners, as we have already said, creep upon any priest—that the priests of the Lord should now impose a stricter rule upon themselves. Therefore, whoever from this day forward presumes to ordain a cleric contrary to the provisions stated above shall not presume to celebrate Mass for a full year from the day on which this was established against him. If anyone refuses to observe this and, acting against the decision of the brothers, presumes to celebrate Mass, let him know that he is alienated from the charity of all the brothers, since it is right that one who scorns to observe what the holy Fathers salutarily established should feel the severity of ecclesiastical discipline. [Col. 0382C]

III. Although the ancient Fathers prescribed longer periods to be observed for laymen, nevertheless, because the number of churches is increasing, it is necessary for us—without prejudice, however, to the ancient canons—to establish the following: no metropolitan shall confer the dignity of the episcopate upon any layman, nor shall the other bishops presume to confer the honor of the presbyterate or diaconate unless a full year of conversion has first been completed.

IV. If any cleric, evading the rule of ecclesiastical discipline, should wander away, whoever receives him and does not reconcile him with his own bishop, but instead presumes to defend him, shall be deprived of communion. [Col. 0382D]

Caesarius, bishop, in the name of Christ: I have reread and subscribed this definition of my holy brothers and myself.

Contumeliosus, bishop: I consented and subscribed.

Filiargius, bishop: I subscribed.

Pretaxatus, bishop: I subscribed.

Maximus, bishop: I subscribed.

Julianus, bishop: I subscribed.

Florentius, bishop: I subscribed.

Likewise Cyprianus, bishop: I subscribed.

Coelestinus, bishop: I subscribed.

Proitianus, bishop: I subscribed.

Eucherius, bishop: I subscribed.

Catafronius, presbyter, sent by my lords Bishops Agricius and Severus: I subscribed.

I, Desiderius, presbyter, sent by my lord Bishop Joannes: I consented and subscribed.

Leontius, presbyter, sent by my lord Bishop Constantinus: I subscribed.

I, Metherius, sent by my lord Bishop Gallianus: I consented and subscribed.

# Chapters of the Council of Valence Begin

[Col. 0383]

[Col. 0383A] 1. Concerning bigamists not being consecrated. 2. If a consecrated woman marries or commits adultery, she shall be assigned to penance. 3. Concerning those who, after one and holy washing, have defiled themselves either with profane sacrifices to demons or with an incestuous washing. [Col. 0384A] 4. If priests or Levites confess any crime concerning themselves, they shall be deposed.

# The Council of Valence Begins

Of thirty bishops, in the year 413 of the era, under the emperors Gratian and Valentinian, in the consulship of Gratian for the third time and Quintinus.

[Col. 0383]

[Col. 0383B] To our most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Gaul and the five provinces: Fegadius, Emerius, Florentius, Artemius, Emilianus, Britto, Justus, Eufodius, Rodamius, Evortius, Cretus, Concordius, Constantinus, Paulus, Anterius, Felix, Neuterius, Urbanus, Simplicius, and Vincentius, bishops, send greetings in the Lord.

Once everything at Valence had been settled and, in God’s name, the matters that had begun the dispute had been placed in a better condition, a useful and religious proposal of certain Fathers was reconsidered concerning matters which, on account of the Church’s holiness, we can neither accept nor, because of custom, condemn altogether. For the seed of this kind of vice has taken root throughout all the churches to such an extent that access to complete remedies is not easy—certainly not without embarrassment to those to whom the matter pertains, since it produces among the brothers a residual cause of hatred. 91 By a measured decision, therefore, a course of caution was maintained that would both remove scandals and preserve the holiness of the Church.

I. It is therefore fitting that, after this synod—which, though late, comes to the aid of such unlawful situations—no one should be able to ordain bigamists or men who have had wives as clerics; nor should inquiry be made as to whether these men were polluted by this unhappy condition through an initial association with the divine sacraments or through pagan practices.

II. Concerning girls who have vowed themselves to God: if they have voluntarily turned to earthly marriage, we have decreed that the following must be observed: they are not to be immediately received as penitents; and, once penance has been imposed, communion shall be deferred for them unless they have fully made satisfaction to God, insofar as the case requires. [Col. 0383D]

III. Concerning those who, after one holy washing, have polluted themselves either with profane sacrifices to demons or with incestuous washing, we have said that this form of censure must be maintained: in accordance with the Council of Nicaea, some avenue of satisfaction must not be denied them, lest the door of consolation be closed to the unhappy through despair over their tears. They are to perform penance until the day of death, yet not without hope of remission—which they must fully hope to receive from the one who alone possesses its abundance and is so rich in mercy that no one should despair. For God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living. [Col. 0384B]

IV. Nor did we consider it foreign to the usefulness of the Church to write the following, brothers, so that you might know that anyone who, while under ordination to the diaconate, presbyterate, or episcopate, says that he has been polluted by a mortal crime must be removed from the aforesaid orders, whether he is guilty because of a true confession or because of a falsehood. For one who has declared himself to be the cause of his own death cannot be absolved, since he becomes a greater murderer. May divine mercy preserve you forever, most beloved brothers.

The same council’s letter.

To our most beloved brothers, the clergy and people of the church of Fréjus: Fegadius, Emerius, Florentius, Artemius, Emilianus, Britto, Justus, Eufodius, Rodamius, Evortius, Constantius, Paulus, Cretus, Concordius, Anterius, Neuterius, Nicecius, Urbanus, Felix, Simplicius, and Vincentius, bishops, send greetings in the Lord.

Although Benedict our brother has proposed matters concerning the person of the most holy man which are worthy of a prudent and Christian man, and although he has announced what all of you have earnestly requested for the honor of the priesthood, nevertheless, because the synod had already ruled that such ordinations, which cannot take place without scandal, must be excluded, we could not grant to one what was denied to the others. Although we do not fail to recognize that many, out of shame, and some, because of the honor of receiving the priesthood—and, in order to reject the honor, falsely representing as signs of holiness the things that cause them fear—have said such things about themselves, nevertheless, [Col. 0384D] since the judgment of almost everyone is inclined toward what is worse, and material for disputes against the priests of God is thereby sought, the synod decided that, whatever anyone had said about himself, whether true or false, the testimony that he confirmed concerning himself should be believed. Therefore, it was decreed that they must immediately be removed from the rank which ought to be free from every scandal. May divine mercy protect you forever.

The Council of Valence ends.

# Chapters of the Council of Laurinum Begin

[Col. 0383]

[Col. 0383D] 1. Whoever proves that his city was a metropolis shall hold the primacy. [Col. 0384D] 2. Bishops who act contrary to the statutes shall be deprived of their honor. 3. Concerning laymen who bring charges against clerics. [Col. 0385A] 4. Concerning clerics who are excommunicated by their bishop on account of a fault. 5. Concerning those who wish to separate themselves from heretics, so that they may be received by the Catholic Church. [Col. 0386A] 6. One cleric shall not promote another’s cleric, nor receive one who has been deposed. 7. Concerning those who have been ordained contrary to a prohibition, or have fathered children while holding office.

# The Council of Turin Begins

[Col. 0385]

[Col. 0385A] To our most beloved brothers, established throughout Gaul and the five provinces: the holy synod that assembled in the city of Turin.

When, at the request of the provinces of Gaul, we priests had assembled in the city of Turin and, with the Lord as hearer and mediator, had taken our seats in the church of that city, after hearing the arguments of the bishops—namely, those who had been brought to judgment—the following form of judgment proceeded concerning the individual cases: since few observed the canonical statutes, a useful remedy had to be applied to the contentions of the many.

I. Since the holy Proculus, bishop of the city of Marseille, was the first of all to say that, as metropolitan, he ought to preside over the churches that appeared to be situated in the Second Province of Narbonensis, and that the ordinations of the chief priests in that province ought to be carried out by him, asserting that those churches had either belonged to him or that the bishops in those same churches had been ordained by him, while, on the other hand, the bishops of that region defended another position and contended that a priest from another province ought not to preside over them, the holy synod judged the matter with a view to peace and concord. It decided that precedence should be granted not so much to his city, which is situated in another province and whose size we entirely failed to ascertain, as to his position as a father among his sons, unless that honor were especially withheld.

For it seemed fitting that, although they were not held together by the unity of a province, they should nevertheless be bound together by affection born of piety. This arrangement shall be observed for him alone during the days of his life: in the churches of the Second Province of Narbonensis, wherever it is established that his parishes or his disciples were ordained, he shall have the dignity of primacy.

The parties are also to observe the following, of which he is reminded—not superfluously, though not without usefulness: Proculus himself, as a pious father, shall honor his fellow priests as sons; and the priests of the aforesaid province, as good sons, shall regard him as a parent. They shall show one another affection in charity, fulfilling what the blessed Apostle says: “Anticipating one another in honor; not being wise in lofty matters, but consenting to the humble.”

Furthermore, concerning the bishops of the cities of Arles and Vienne, who were disputing before us over the honor of primacy, the holy synod decreed that whichever of them proves that his city is a metropolis shall obtain the primacy throughout the entire province and shall possess the authority to regulate ordinations according to the canons. Certainly, in order to preserve the bond of peace, this council decreed the following more useful arrangement: if it pleases the bishops of the aforesaid cities, each of them shall secure for himself the cities nearest to him among the provinces and shall visit those churches which are established to be the largest in relation to his own towns, so that, mindful of unanimity and concord, neither may disturb the other by usurping for himself what is closer to the other. [Col. 0385D–0386A]

II. It was therefore decided that the discipline which the holy synod decreed concerning the bishops Octavus, Ursio, Remigius, and Triferus should be endured. They had been summoned for censure on account of a certain usurpation concerning the ordination of priests. Up to this point, it appears that this had been granted them for the following reason: they had been warned that henceforth they should attempt no such usurpation, since they had defended themselves in this matter with the excuse that they had not previously been summoned.

Accordingly, the synod judged that, if anyone from now on acts contrary to the statutes of the Fathers, the person ordained shall know that he is to be deprived of the honor of the priesthood, while the one who ordained him shall know that he is to retain no authority in ordinations or councils. This sentence shall prevail not only against the bishops mentioned above, but against all who, deceived by a similar error, have carried out such ordinations.

III. Concerning Palladius, a layman who had brought a serious charge against the presbyter Spano, and concerning whom Bishop Triferus testified that he had investigated the causes of the same charge, the authority of the council decreed that Palladius should remain under the same sentence by which he had been punished by the priest Triferus at the time of the investigation. The council reserved this act of humanity for him: Triferus himself shall have the power to remit the sentence whenever he wishes.

[Col. 0386C] IV. The holy synod also made a ruling concerning the presbyter Exuperantius, who had agreed to many grave acts against his holy bishop Triferus and had provoked him with repeated insults, so that he had committed several acts against ecclesiastical discipline. For this reason he had been deprived by him of the Lord’s communion. His restoration shall lie within the discretion of the one in whose power his deposition lay: that is, he shall receive the grace of communion when Exuperantius has either made satisfaction or Bishop Triferus has judged it appropriate. [Col. 0386D]

V. The holy synod further decreed that, since the bishops of Gaul who are in communion with Felix have sent legates, anyone who wishes to separate himself from Felix’s communion shall be received into the fellowship of holy peace, in accordance with the letters formerly issued by Ambrose, bishop of venerable memory, or by the priest of the Roman Church, which were read to the penitent legates in the council.

VI. Nor must the following be omitted: the judgment of the synod decreed that, according to the statutes of the canons, no one shall take possession of another’s church, nor dare to ordain someone in another rank for his own church, nor receive into communion one who has been deposed.

VII. The authority of the synod has decreed that those who have been ordained contrary to a prohibition, or who have fathered children while in the ministry, shall not be permitted to advance to the higher orders. [Col. 0388A] May our Lord preserve you unharmed for a very long age, most beloved brothers.

# Chapters of the Council of Riez Begin

[Col. 0387]

[Col. 0387A] 1. Perverse ordainers shall no longer take part in any ordinations. 2. A bishop ordained by two bishops may at some point not be a bishop. 3. Concerning heretical and schismatic bishops: what must be observed if they come to the Catholic faith. [Col. 0388A] 4. A bishop shall both bless and confirm a neophyte. 5. When a bishop buries a bishop, he shall take charge of that bishop’s church. 6. Without the metropolitan’s letters and consent, no one shall approach a church left without a bishop.

# The Council of Riez Begins

[Col. 0387]

[Col. 0387B] Under the emperors Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian, in the consulship of Theodosius for the seventh time and Festus, when, by the will of the Lord, we had assembled at the church of Riez and were seeking a remedy for the transgression that had occurred at the church of Embrun, it was clear that, with the holy canons of the Church and the revered constitutions of the Fathers neglected in every respect, an invalid semblance of ordination had been rashly attempted by two men meeting together without the presence of three bishops, without letters from the bishops of the province, and without the authority of the metropolitan. The grief arising from this rash lapse and from the disruption of the church itself remained for a long time in the hearts of all during their deliberations.

First, because—not a desire for vengeance but a desire for remedy, by the Lord’s command, had wholly taken root in the hearts of all through priestly counsel—each speech made it clear, with evident piety, that just as the invalid acts that had been attempted ought to be annulled, so charity might absolve those who had attempted them, even though censure compelled their exposure. This was especially so because those who had fallen into such perversity had, from the very day of their first lapse, offered prayers everywhere, as penitents imputing their fault either to themselves or to ignorance. For even if it were thought forgivable for a priest not to know priestly statutes, that was nevertheless lighter than if he openly admitted, with shameless lips, that he had trampled upon them.

I. Accordingly, concerning those who had usurped such disordered and unstable powers, it was decided that, through an act of mercy and charity, they should be received into communion and affection, but in such a way that they would know that, according to the recent and most salutary decree of the Council of Turin, for the remainder of their lives they would henceforth take part in no ordinations and in no ordinary councils, since no salutary decision could be expected from men who had furnished the church of Embrun with examples of such great abuse and such detestable conduct.

It seemed especially necessary to deliberate carefully because the church had suffered more severely from being without a legitimate priest for four months out of two years. [Col. 0388B] The innocent cleric, as was proved, had been harassed by the insolence and varied disturbance of certain men. He had recently endured, even from priests and ministers, threats, quarrels, and the most bitter violence, culminating in a destructive killing; the matter could not be postponed. It was necessary to take account of the good and of discipline, lest, by delay, they appear to flatter the wishes of the obstinate and disorderly—men whose conspiracies, insofar as they could be detected, ought to have been punished by ecclesiastical censure in the past and subjected to it in the future.

Therefore, we too judged that the ordination which the canons declare invalid must be annulled: the presence of three bishops had been omitted, letters from the bishops of the province had not been sought, and the will of the metropolitan had also been disregarded. Nothing at all had been shown that could make him a bishop.

[Col. 0388C] II. Therefore, by the will of the Lord, once the one who had been wrongly appointed bishop had been removed, it was decided that the brothers’ appointment should be made in full accordance with ecclesiastical tradition. But since this holy synod exercised not only discipline but also mercy, the following circumstances also came before it: in recent days he had presented himself to that church as a herdsman amid much insolence from flatterers; yet it was also brought forward that he had departed before the admonition, that some priests had encouraged him in this very matter, and that he had returned to a private household. He had sent letters to the clergy themselves, in which he renounced his desire for the episcopate that he acknowledged he had obtained; he had authority in his own name, and he confirmed by protest that the very thing which was firmly and unquestionably established would already at that time be disordered and invalid.

The judgment therefore inclined rather in the direction of showing greater support to the young man, once instructed in the fear of the Lord, because he had sometimes sensed what was sound amid the most vicious conduct, than of yielding in any respect to youthful impulses. Accordingly, setting aside the matters at his entry which, without any possibility of excuse, clearly associated him with guilt, the priests of the Lord who were present at this council preferred to pass over him as though innocent and free from condemnation.

### III

Therefore, just as the Council of Nicaea was able, in the case of receiving certain schismatics, to establish for each person within his own territories, so this present assembly also decrees that the same arrangement must be observed by all: namely, that any of the brethren to whom councils prescribe some such act of charity may be permitted to cede one church from among his parish churches, in which they may be supported either under the title of chorepiscopus, as the same canon says, or, as they call it, by foreign communion.

It is therefore first decreed that this shall be permitted in every province except Alpina Maritima. If he should enter any part of that province, as an instigator of evil and one intolerant of peace, he shall be subject to the condemnation which he had provoked against himself. But if anyone should communicate with him while he transgresses any of these established provisions, let him be excluded from communion with all. Furthermore, he shall exercise his office nowhere except in public, lest any layman be assigned to him who is ennobled by the appearance or rank of a curia or city.

It is added that he must never presume to offer in cities in the absence of the bishops, nor ordain even the lowest cleric; nor may he ordain in that same church, however small, which has been assigned to him. Nor may any bishop, whether already established or later appointed, yield to him in his beginnings, as though out of respect for his age. Nor may he anywhere usurp anything belonging to episcopal duties, except in the church which he has obtained through someone’s compassion. There he is permitted only to confirm neophytes and to offer before the presbyters.

If anyone, having been moved in this manner by another’s charity, should at any time change his residence, he shall not receive a place of repose in another church otherwise than he had received in the former church which he had renounced. Nor shall he ever hold the governance of two churches. Even in the church which yields to him, its ministers must be ordained by the bishop of the city.

Since mention has been made of ministers, and since some men were found to have been rashly advanced in the clergy despite being excommunicated, it has been decreed that those who were so appointed must be deposed. But those against whom no stain of conduct has prejudiced their case are, according to what seemed right to the priest of Ebredunum when the matter was being settled, either to be retained in the ministry of their own church or transferred to him wherever he had resided. They are to receive permission from the people to give blessings by authority of this constitution, as was defined above [Col. 0389D], and to confirm neophytes in one and the same church.

In castles and villages, wherever they may come, they shall be permitted to do before the presbyters everything that is prescribed in cities.

### IV. That presbyters may bless the faithful privately

It seemed right, in order to bring these interminable disputes to a definite conclusion, to open to the presbyter the power of blessing, according to the desire of the faithful, among families, in the countryside, and in private houses. It appears that some provinces already possess this practice; it has also seemed right that it be granted in the parishes of the churches, though more in the rural districts than in the cities.

In the church in which he has been ordained, he shall also have the right to consecrate a virgin, just as he has the right to confirm a neophyte. In all things, as a testimony of great indulgence, he must always conduct himself as inferior to the bishop and superior to the presbyter. He shall live in the fear of the Lord, supported by the commands and prayers of all the saints; he shall honor his bishop, serve God, give thanks for the synod’s benevolence toward him, and always confess that he is unworthy of the concessions granted to him and unequal to them.

### V

All the priests who had assembled jointly judged that they must guard against scandals of this kind. Therefore, by a firm decree, it was decided that henceforth the following should be observed: no one should approach a church that had lost its bishop unless the bishop of a neighboring church came at the time of the funeral rites. He must nevertheless immediately exercise the strictest care over that church, so that, before an ordination, nothing might be permitted that could subvert the clergy through discord and novelty.

Accordingly, whenever such an event occurs, the neighboring bishops are entrusted with the inspection, description, and review of the affairs of the neighboring churches.

### VI

All these matters are to be carried out from the time of the funeral rites until the seventh day after the deceased’s death. Thereafter, the metropolitan’s instruction having been reported to the church, the deceased is to be buried together with all the holy bishops. No one should approach a church that has lost its chief priest unless invited by letters of the metropolitan [Col. 0390C], lest he be deceived by the people and appear to have wished to suffer violence.

I, Hilary, bishop, in accordance with what pleased all the holy bishops who subscribed with me, have subscribed these definitions to the statutes of the Fathers, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and Festus for the fourth time.

I, Severian, bishop, was present at this definition and subscribed on the day and in the consulship stated above.

I, Audentius, bishop, was present at the decrees, on the day and in the consulship stated above.

I, Julius, bishop, was present at the decrees and subscribed on the day and in the consulship stated above.

I, Achadius, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed on the day and in the consulship stated above.

I, Auspicius, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed on the day and in the consulship stated above.

I, Severinus [Col. 0390D], bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed.

I, Valerius, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed.

I, Neuterius, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed.

I, Asclepius, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed.

I, Theodore, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed.

I, Vincentius, presbyter, ordained by the bishop of Constantiniana, was present in his place and subscribed.

## The Chapters of the Council of Orange Begin

[Col. 0389]

[Col. 0389D]

1. That no minister depart without chrism.

2. Concerning heretics who convert when in danger of death.

[Col. 0390D]

3. Concerning penitents who depart this life.

4. Concerning clerics who desire penance.

[Col. 0391A]

5. Concerning those who flee to a church, that they not be handed over.

6. That no one seize the slaves of clerics who flee to a church.

7. Concerning freedmen who have been entrusted to the church, that they not be oppressed.

8. Concerning those who presume to ordain another’s cleric.

9. Concerning those who ordain citizens of another community.

10. Concerning bishops who have built a basilica on an estate and in another’s diocese.

11. Concerning bishops who receive another’s excommunicated person.

12. Concerning those who suddenly become mute, who may receive both baptism and penance.

[Col. 0391B]

13. Concerning those who become mentally deranged.

14. Concerning the baptized possessed.

15. That provision be made for the possessed and catechumens concerning baptism.

16. That the possessed not be promoted to the clergy.

[Col. 0392A]

17. That the presentation of the sacrament be consecrated as one.

18. That catechumens not hear the Gospels.

19. That catechumens not approach the baptisteries.

20. That catechumens not receive the blessing with the faithful.

21. That two bishops not make a bishop.

22. That married clerics not become deacons unless they profess continence.

23. Concerning those found incontinent after receiving the diaconate.

24. Concerning those found incontinent before they were ordained.

25. Concerning proven men if they contract a second marriage.

26. Concerning women deacons, who are not to be ordained.

27. Concerning women who have professed widowhood before the bishop.

[Col. 0392B]

28. Concerning those who have professed chastity, if they violate their profession.

29. That no bishop leave the council without consent or refuse to attend the council.

## The Council of Orange Begins

In the time of the younger Theodosius and Cyrus as consuls, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the church of Justiniana.

[Col. 0391]

### Chapter I

No minister who has received the office of baptizing ought to go anywhere without chrism, because it has been agreed among us that a person is chrismated once in baptism. Concerning one who, for whatever necessity, was not chrismated in baptism, the priest shall be reminded at the confirmation. For among us there is only one blessing of chrism itself. I do not say this prejudicially, but so that re-chrismation may be regarded as necessary.

### II

It has pleased us that heretics who are in danger of death, if they desire to become Catholics, may be signed with chrism and blessing by presbyters when a bishop is absent.

### III

Those who depart this life after receiving penance are, we decree, to be admitted to communion without the imposition of the hand of reconciliation [Col. 0391D]. This is sufficient consolation for the dying, according to the definitions of the Fathers, who appropriately called such communion viaticum. If they survive, however, let them remain in the order of penitents, so that, after demonstrating the necessary fruits of penance, they may receive legitimate communion with the imposition of the hand of reconciliation.

### IV

Penance is not to be denied to clerics who desire it.

### V

Those who have fled to a church ought not to be handed over, but should be defended through reverence for the holy place and through intercession.

### VI

If anyone thinks that the slaves of clerics should be seized on behalf of his own slaves who have fled to a church, let him be struck throughout all the churches with the strictest condemnation.

### VII

If anyone attempts to force persons manumitted in the church and commended to the Church by testament into slavery, service, or the condition of tenant-farmers [Col. 0392C], he shall be restrained by ecclesiastical punishment.

### VIII

If anyone thinks that a cleric residing elsewhere should be ordained, he must first determine that the man will live with him; nor may he presume to ordain him without consulting the bishop with whom he previously lived, since it was not without cause that he remained for so long unordained by another.

### IX

But if anyone ordains citizens of another community or persons residing elsewhere, so that they may not be accused of being irregular in any respect, let them either recall those men to themselves or command them to live with the persons with whom they had been residing.

### X

If any bishop intends to build a church in the territory of another city—whether because of the affairs of his estate, ecclesiastical utility, or any other convenience—and permission to build has been granted (for it is impious to prohibit this), he must not presume to perform the dedication. The dedication is entirely reserved to the bishop in whose territory the church rises.

The bishop who built it is nevertheless granted this privilege: he may ordain whatever clerics he wishes to see serving in his own property, provided that he is willing to allow the bishop of the city in whose territory the church lies to retain them if they have already been ordained.

All governance of that church shall belong to the bishop in whose city’s territory the church has arisen. If any layperson builds a church and thinks that someone other than the bishop in whose territory he builds should be invited, both the person whom he wishes to favor against the constitution and discipline, and all the bishops invited to such a dedication, shall abstain from the assembly. If anyone transgresses, he shall be called to account; if anyone transgresses, let him recognize the canonical order.

### XI

It has pleased us that the bishop who, after being warned that someone has been excommunicated, presumes to communicate with him without that person’s reconciliation with the one who excommunicated him, should incur guilt [Col. 0393A]. If reconciliation should intervene, all questions concerning the injustice or iniquity of the recent excommunication are to be reserved for the next synod.

### XII

A person who suddenly becomes mute may be baptized or receive penance, as has been established, if he has testimony of his former will in the words of others, or of his present will in his own gesture.

### XIII

Whatever acts of piety are appropriate are to be bestowed upon those who are mentally deranged.

### XIV
