Baptized persons who are possessed, if they take care concerning their purification, submit themselves to the care of the clergy, and obey their admonitions, are in every respect to communicate in the power of the sacrament—either to be protected from the attacks of the demons [Col. 0393B] by which they are afflicted, or to be cleansed, since their life is already shown to be more purified.

### XV

As necessity demands or opportunity permits, provision is to be made concerning baptism.

### XVI

The possessed are not only not to be admitted to any clerical order; those who have already been ordained are also to be removed from the office imposed upon them.

### XVII

We have judged that the mingling of the Eucharist is to be consecrated simultaneously.

### XVIII

It has pleased us that the Gospel not be read in the church to catechumens.

### XIX

Catechumens are sometimes to be admitted, even during the private prayers.

### XX

Catechumens are to be separated and instructed, so that, if they return and the faithful offer them separately to be signed or blessed, this may be done [Col. 0393C].

### XXI

If two men presume to ordain a bishop in your provinces, it has pleased us to decree concerning such presumptuous persons that, wherever it happens that two bishops make an unwilling man a bishop, after the instigators have been condemned, the man who suffered this action shall be substituted in one of their churches, provided his life is suitable; and the other shall likewise be ordained in the place of the one who was deposed. If two men have done this voluntarily, the man who was made bishop shall also be condemned, so that the ancient institutions may be observed with greater caution.

### XXII

It was further decided that henceforth married men are not to be ordained deacons, except those who have first confessed chastity with the purpose of conversion.

### XXIII

If anyone is found to be incontinent with his wife after receiving the Levitical blessing [Col. 0393D], he shall be removed from office.

### XXIV

Concerning those who fell into this same conduct before they were ordained, the judgment of the Council of Turin is to be followed, by which they are ordered not to be promoted further.

### XXV

Concerning suitable and proven men who are attached to the clergy: if the circumstances of life should bring them into a second marriage, they are not to receive anything beyond the subdiaconate or ecclesiastical dignities.

### XXVI

Women deacons are under no circumstances to be ordained. Those who already exist are to submit their heads to the blessing bestowed upon the people [Col. 0394A].

### XXVII

A woman who has made a profession before the bishop, in the secretarium, to preserve widowhood must not violate the widow’s garment imposed by the presbyter. The man who rejects her, or the woman who abandons such a profession, is rightly to be condemned.

### XXVIII

Those who abandon a professed chastity are to be regarded as violators of their pledge, and all are to be counseled through legitimate penance.

### XXIX

We wish and decree that these matters which we have subscribed, together with the agreement of those who gave their consent, shall henceforth be valid and shall be observed among us and among our people. We do not overlook those who avoid attending the synod, whether personally, through their consent, or by sending substitutes in their place, so that it may become known what opinion should be held of those who despise the statutes of the Fathers.

This is not because the circumstances of the times make it difficult for us to assemble at a holy synod. We add that, if hereafter we wish to convene assemblies, in similar circumstances, for ecclesiastical well-being and remedies among pagans, we shall establish that no assembly may be dissolved without announcement of the other assembly.

Therefore, in the following year, if it is granted by the permission of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us hold an assembly in the territory of Orange on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November. It is announced so far in advance that there may be neither freedom for excuses nor compulsion of invitation.

We ourselves shall be reminded of the day and place. Let each of us bring copies and report what has been established by us. We leave to the care of our most blessed brother Hilary those who were absent, having sent copies to them for their admonition.

If, after all this, human frailty should intervene—if any bishop should fall into illness, weakness, or dullness of understanding, or should lose the use of speech—he must not permit presbyters to carry out in his presence those acts that are performed only by bishops. Rather, he should appoint a bishop for whatever must be done in the church.

I, Hilary, bishop, subscribed.

I, Claudius, bishop, subscribed.

I, Constantine, bishop, subscribed.

I, Audentius, bishop, subscribed.

I, Egrestius, bishop, subscribed.

I, Julian, bishop, subscribed.

[Col. 0394D]

I, Auspicius, bishop, subscribed.

I, Maximus, bishop, subscribed.

I, Theuderius, bishop, subscribed.

I, Eucherius, bishop, subscribed.

Awaiting the assent of my fellow provincial holy priests mentioned above, I, Nectarius, subscribed.

Justus, bishop, subscribed.

Augustalis, bishop, subscribed.

Ingenius, bishop, subscribed.

Salonius, bishop, subscribed.

I, the substitute, subscribed and confirmed on behalf of my father, the bishop Claudius.

## The Chapters of the Council of Valence Begin

[Col. 0393]

[Col. 0393D]

1. That Gallic bishops not be investigated in Gaul.

[Col. 0394D]

2. Concerning penitents who suddenly die, that their offerings be received.

[Col. 0395A]

3. That no one receive another bishop’s chrism, but only that of his own bishop.

4. That those who retain the offerings of the dead be excommunicated.

5. That whoever does not submit to the judgment of his bishop appeal to the synod.

6. That an excommunicated person humble himself so that he may be reconciled quickly.

[Col. 0396A]

7. That accusers not be heard in minor matters, but that they be examined in serious crimes. [The printed text reads “94” here.]

8. That a bishop rebuke another’s cleric when he sins.

9. That whoever finds an exposed child notify the church.

10. That whoever demands the return of a child contrary to the established procedure be regarded as a murderer.

## The Council of Valence Begins

Era 480.

[Col. 0395]

[Col. 0395B]

The constitutions of the synod were discussed in the city of Valence, at the church of the bishop Urbicus of the Catholic Church, in the time of the younger Theodosius and Dioscorus as consul, on the day of the Ides of November.

### Chapter I

It pleased us that bishops coming from the Gallic provinces into Gaul should not be investigated, but that it should be sufficient if no one had forbidden them communion. For among people who live near one another and are almost mutually known, the reputable do not so much need testimony as the depraved need denunciation and accusation.

### II

When persons who have received penance, living in a good course of life with a satisfactory contrition, are unexpectedly overtaken without communion by death in the fields or on journeys, their offering is to be received, and their funerals and subsequent commemoration are to be pursued with ecclesiastical affection [Col. 0395C].

For it is unlawful to exclude from the saving mysteries the commemoration of those who, striving toward those same mysteries with faithful devotion, regard themselves as guilty for a longer period, judge themselves unworthy of the mysteries of salvation, and desire to be restored in a more purified condition—for those who are overtaken before receiving the viaticum of the sacraments, and to whom perhaps the priest would not have thought the fullest reconciliation should be denied.

### III

In each territory, presbyters or ministers are to request chrism annually from their bishops as the solemnity of Easter approaches—not from whichever neighboring bishops they please, but from their own bishops. It is not to be carried by just any ecclesiastical person, but, if some necessity or the ministers’ occupation requires it, by a subdeacon, because it is dishonorable to entrust what is highest to inferiors.

It is best that the person who will use it in administering it should himself receive it. If something prevents this, then at least the person whose office it is to arrange the sacrarium and receive the sacraments should receive it.

### IV

Those who retain the offerings of the dead and delay handing them over to the churches are to be expelled from the church as unbelievers. For it is certain that this aggravation of divine mercy reaches the point of destroying faith: the faithful who depart this life are deprived of the fullness of their vows, and the poor of the consolation of nourishment and necessary support.

Such men are to be regarded as killers of the needy and as people who do not believe in God’s judgment. Hence one of the Fathers inserted in his writings the fitting saying: “To take anything from a friend is theft; to defraud the church is sacrilege.”

[Col. 0396B]

### V

If anyone does not submit to the judgment of a bishop, let him appeal to the synod.

### VI

Useful passages from a letter of Saint Clement, which are necessary for the churches in the present time, are to be brought forward honorably and received with reverence by all the faithful, especially by clerics. Among these passages, what particularly pleased us, on account of its venerable antiquity, we strengthen by the present statutes. The blessed martyr mentioned above recalls it from the constitution of the most blessed Peter, saying:

“Some things you yourselves ought also to understand, if there are matters which he himself, because of the plots of wicked men, cannot state more clearly and openly. For example, he is an enemy to someone because of that person’s actions. You must not wait for him to say to you, ‘Do not be friends with that man’; rather, you ought prudently to observe this and obey the will of the one who has charge of the church, even without being admonished. You should turn away from the person whom you perceive to be opposed to him, and neither speak with those with whom he does not speak. Thus each person who is at fault, while desiring to restore the favor of all of you toward himself, will hasten more quickly to be reconciled with the one who presides over all. In this way he may return to salvation when he begins to obey the admonitions of the one who presides.”

And the other matters which in what follows identify the friends of those who are enemies of the truth.

Let the clergy therefore know that henceforth they will be held liable, and let the faithful people know that they will be held culpable, if anyone is counted among the wicked in this vice and is recognized as a subverter of discipline.

### VII

It further pleased us to restrain, where it exists in your orders, the freedom to accuse when it is exercised frivolously [Col. 0396D]. If a bishop judges that someone should be abstained from as a humiliation and correction of a brother, and others rise to plead for him, let the rest comply with the brother concerned, after correction and warning have been applied.

But if he thinks that someone should be condemned for a crime, let the matter be examined as though by an accuser, if he knows how. For it is right that matters proved to one person should be proved to all.

### VIII

If a bishop knows himself to be aware of another’s cleric’s wrongdoing, he must say nothing for as long as he cannot prove it. Instead, he should work with the bishop through private corrections to bring the cleric to contrition.

But if the person who has been corrected becomes more stubborn, presents himself publicly for communion, and the bishop is unable to produce proof when rebuking the man whom he judges guilty, the cleric, though uncondemned by those who know nothing of the matter, is nevertheless to be ordered to withdraw for a time, in view of the greater authority of the bishop [Col. 0397A]. Meanwhile, until the matter can be proved, he shall remain in communion with all except the bishop who judges him guilty.

### IX

Concerning exposed children: a general complaint has arisen that they are no longer exposed to mercy but to dogs, and that human compassion, although miserable, hesitates to collect them for fear of accusations, contrary to the commands of mercy.

According to the statutes of the most faithful, pious, and august emperors, whoever collects an exposed child must notify the church and record the notification [Col. 0398A]. Likewise, on the Lord’s Day, the minister must announce from the altar that an exposed child has been collected by the church.

Within ten days from the day of exposure, the child may be reclaimed. If anyone proves that he recognized the child, he must repay the collector, according to his ability, for the mercy shown during those ten days; alternatively, with God’s favor, he may possess the child permanently if he wishes.

### X

If any person who exposed a child collected according to this procedure should later appear as a claimant or accuser, he is to be regarded as a murderer.

## The Chapters of the Council of Agde Begin

[Col. 0397]

[Col. 0397B]

1. Concerning bigamous clerics, that they not minister.

2. Concerning contumacious clerics and those slow to perform their office.

3. Concerning bishops who excommunicate either innocent people or people for very minor causes.

4. Concerning those who defraud the church of their own offerings or those of their relatives.

5. If a cleric commits theft from the church.

6. If anything is left to a bishop by anyone.

7. How bishops are to possess the property of the church, and how the church’s slaves are to be manumitted by a bishop.

8. Concerning clerics who flee to secular authorities.

9. Concerning presbyters and deacons who return to conjugal intercourse.

[Col. 0397C]

10. That no cleric live with unrelated women.

11. That no cleric admit a woman into the storeroom or private chamber.

12. That every Saturday in Lent be observed as a fast.

13. That the Creed be preached to the candidates eight days before Easter.

14. That the altar be both blessed and anointed.

15. How adults and how minors are to receive penance.

16. At what age deacons are to be ordained.

17. At what age bishops and presbyters are to be consecrated.

18. At what times laypeople ought to receive communion.

[Col. 0397D]

19. At what age nuns are to be veiled.

20. Concerning clerics who grow their hair long.

21. That the greater solemnities be celebrated in the cities.

22. That a presbyter or cleric not be permitted to sell or give away church property.

23. That a junior cleric not be placed over a senior.

24. Concerning exposed children who are found.

25. Concerning laymen who abandon their wives.

26. That if a cleric voluntarily causes damage to the church, he both make satisfaction and be excommunicated.

[Col. 0398B]

27. That no one establish a monastery of monks without consulting the bishop.

28. That a monastery of girls be established far from monks.

29. Concerning freedmen, that they be protected by the church in time of need.

30. That prayers be said after the antiphons.

31. Concerning those who, because of hatred, do not return to peace.

32. That a cleric not go to a secular judge without consulting the bishop.

33. If a bishop who has no heirs does not make the church over which he presided his heir.

34. Concerning Jews who wish to convert, how they are to be received.

[Col. 0398C]

35. If a bishop, warned by the metropolitan concerning a synod or episcopal ordination, delays coming.

36. That clerical stipends be distributed according to merit.

37. Concerning murderers and false witnesses.

38. That a cleric or monk not depart without a letter from his bishop, and concerning monks and abbots.

39. That clerics avoid wedding feasts.

40. That Christians not partake of Jewish banquets.

41. That clerics avoid drunkenness.

42. Concerning fortune-tellers and augurs, that they be separated from the church.

43. That no cleric be ordained from among penitents, and that a presbyter not erect an altar.

[Col. 0398D]

44. That a presbyter not presume to give a blessing to the people or to a penitent in the church.

45. That a bishop dispose of something insignificant without the consent of the clerics, if necessity requires.

46. That a bishop be permitted to sell fugitive slaves of the church.

47. That the people not presume to leave before the Mass has been completed.

48. Concerning the church’s own or acquired property.

49. Concerning the non-alienation of church property by anyone, and concerning freedmen.

50. Concerning clerics who incur a capital crime.

51. Concerning a bishop’s testament.

[Col. 0399A]

52. Concerning clerics who depart without letters from their bishop. [The printed text includes “95” here.]

53. Concerning parish presbyters who dispose of church property.

54. Concerning those same presbyters, that whatever they buy they acquire in the name of the church.

55. That priests and Levites not use dogs for hunting or hawks.

56. Concerning sales which abbots presume to make.

57. That one abbot not be placed over two monasteries.

58. That no monastery be established without the bishop’s knowledge.

59. Concerning church property supplied for use, that it not be defended by prescription.

[Col. 0399B]

60. Concerning those who have fallen from the Catholic faith into heresy.

[Col. 0400A]

61. Concerning incestuous marriages.

62. Concerning those who kill their slaves without a judge.

63. Concerning laypeople who do not come to the city on the greater solemnities.

64. Concerning clerics who are absent from the church’s office on solemn days.

65. Concerning Levites, that they not sit without the presbyter’s command.

66. Concerning ministers, that they not enter the secretarium.

67. That Catholics not enter into marriages with heretics.

68. Concerning Levites and clerics, that they not be magicians or enchanters.

69. Concerning seditious clerics.

[Col. 0400B]

70. Concerning clerics who are buffoons or performers.

71. That a synod be convened every year.

## The Council of Agde Begins

On the third day before the Ides of September, in the consulship of Massalus.

[Col. 0399]

[Col. 0399B]

When we had assembled in the city of Agde in the name of God and had taken our seats in the basilica of Saint Andrew, intending to discuss the discipline and ordinances of clerics and bishops, as well as the interests of the churches [Col. 0399C], it pleased us first that the canons and statutes of the Fathers should be read in order.

### Chapter I

It pleased us concerning bigamists or husbands in a second marriage—although the statutes of the Fathers have decreed otherwise—that those who have been ordained up to this time should, by indulgence, retain only the title of presbyter or deacon. They must not presume to exercise the office of consecrating as presbyters or of ministering as such deacons.

### II

Contumacious clerics are to be corrected by the bishops according to what the order of their dignity permits. If any, carried away by the pride of their former rank, should perhaps disdain communion, neglect to attend the church, or fail to perform their office, let foreign communion be granted to them, so that when penance has corrected them, they may be restored by written decision to their rank and dignity in the register [Col. 0399D].

### III

If bishops, setting aside priestly moderation, presume to excommunicate innocent persons or those culpable only of very minor causes, or perhaps refuse to receive those hastening toward grace, they are to be warned by letters from the neighboring bishops of any province.

If they refuse to show mercy, communion shall be denied them for a time by the other bishops, until the synod, lest perhaps, because of the sin of the excommunicator, the excommunicated should be overtaken by death after a long period.

### IV

Clerics or laypeople who persist in retaining offerings of parents, whether gifts or left by testament, or who think that what they themselves have donated to churches or monasteries should be taken away, are, as the holy synod has decreed, to be excluded from the church as killers of the poor until they return what they have retained.

[Col. 0400B]

### V

If a cleric commits theft from the church, let foreign communion be granted to him.

### VI

Concerning bishops established in the highest priesthood: whatever is left or donated to them by outsiders, whether together with the church or separately, is to be counted among the church’s resources, not as their own property but as something left to the church. For the donor is understood to offer it for the redemption of his soul, not for the benefit of the priest.

It is just that, just as the priest has what has been left to the church, so the church should have what is left to the priest. Certainly, whatever is perhaps left by a trust either to the priest or to the church for the future benefit of someone else, the church may neither count among its own resources nor retain.

### VII

As the ancient authority of the canons commanded, bishops are to possess the church’s small estates and slaves, or its vessels used in ministry, as entrusted to faithful stewardship, with the church’s rights preserved in their entirety [Col. 0400D]. That is, they must not presume either to sell them or to alienate through any contract the property from which the poor live.

If necessity compels the disposal of anything for the church’s necessity, usefulness, or benefit—whether by usufruct or indirect sale—the reason why it must be sold is first to be proved before two or three provincial or neighboring bishops. After episcopal examination, the sale that has been made is to be confirmed by their signatures. Otherwise, the sale or transaction shall have no validity.

If a bishop should grant freedom to any church slaves who have deserved well, it has pleased us that the freedom granted by his successors be preserved, together with whatever the manumitter conferred upon them in their liberty. We nevertheless order that this be limited to twenty solidi in the form of a small plot of land, a small vineyard, or a modest lodging [Col. 0401A]. Whatever more has been given is to be reclaimed for the church after the death of the manumitter.

We permit less useful church servants to be assigned for the use of strangers or clerics, with the church’s rights preserved.

### VIII

It also pleased us that, if a cleric, abandoning his office because of disciplinary pressure, should perhaps flee to a secular authority, and the person to whom he appeals should offer him the protection of defense, that person is to be expelled from communion with the church together with the cleric.

### IX

It also pleased us that, if presbyters or married deacons wish to return to the bed of their wives, the ordinance of Pope Innocent or the authority of Bishop Siricius be preserved.

If that formula of ecclesiastical life, and likewise of the discipline which came from Bishop Siricius to the provinces, is not shown to have reached certain people, pardon is granted to them on account of their ignorance, provided that henceforth they begin entirely to abstain and retain the rank in which they are found, without being permitted to rise to higher ranks. Their benefit is that they do not lose the position which they retain.

But if any are found to have known the way of life sent by Bishop Saint Siricius and nevertheless not immediately to have cast aside the desires of lust, they must be removed in every way, because, after learning the admonition, they judged pleasure preferable to obedience.

### X

For the safeguarding of life and reputation, we prescribe by a special ordinance that no cleric become attached to an unrelated woman through any association or familiarity. Not only must an unrelated woman not enter his house, but he himself may not have the power to frequent an unrelated woman.

He may live freely only with his mother, sister, daughter, or granddaughter, if he has or wishes to have such relatives. Concerning these relationships, it is impious to suspect anything other than what nature has established.

### XI

It has pleased us that female servants or freedwomen be removed from the office of cellarer, private service, and the same residence in which the cleric lives.

### XII

It also pleased us that all churches, except on Sundays during Lent, fast even on Saturday, with priestly prayer and the warning of discipline.

### XIII

It also pleased us that the Creed be preached publicly in the church by all churches on one day, namely eight days before the Sunday of the Resurrection [Col. 0401D], to the candidates for baptism.

### XIV

It pleased us that altars be consecrated not only by anointing with chrism but also by a priestly blessing.

XV. At the time when penitents seek penance, they are to receive from the priest the imposition of hands and sackcloth upon the head, as has been established everywhere. But if they do not cut their hair or change their clothing, they are to be rejected, and unless they do penance worthily, they are not to be received. Penance is also not to be readily assigned to the young, because of the frailty of their age; nevertheless, the viaticum is not to be denied to anyone at the point of death.

XVI. A bishop is absolutely not to entrust the blessing of the diaconate to anyone under twenty-five years of age. If, however, married young men agree to be ordained, the consent of their wives is likewise to be sought, so that, with their marital chamber set apart and religious commitment first undertaken, they may be ordained after they have been converted together.

XVII. No metropolitan is to presume to ordain a presbyter or bishop before the age of thirty—that is, before he has reached the age of a fully mature man—lest, on account of age, they be blamed for some error, as has happened more than once.

XVIII. Laypeople who do not receive communion at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, or Pentecost are not to be regarded as Catholics or counted among Catholics.

XIX. Women dedicated to religious life, however approved their life and conduct may be, are not to be veiled before their fortieth year of age.

XX. Clerics who grow their hair long are to be forcibly shorn by the archdeacon, even against their will. They are likewise not permitted to wear or possess clothing or footwear except what is appropriate to their religious status.

XXI. If anyone wishes to have an oratory in the countryside, outside the parishes in which the regular and lawful assembly is held, we permit him, on the other feast days, to hold Masses there because of the fatigue of the household, according to the proper order. But on Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, and any other days that are especially observed as feasts, they are to hold services only in cities or parishes. If any clerics wish to celebrate or hold services in oratories on the feasts mentioned above without the order or permission of the bishop, they are to be expelled from communion.

XXII. Although it is superfluous to define again a matter already known and prohibited by ancient canons, nevertheless, so that greed or dishonesty may be more easily restrained, we establish what all the canons command: that the citizens, or diocesan presbyters and clerics, while preserving the rights of the Church, may possess Church property—as the bishops have permitted—but must absolutely not presume to sell or give it away. If they do so, both the sale itself is to be invalid and, from whatever personal resources they possess, they are to make the Church whole and be deprived of communion.

XXIII. No one is to place a later bishop before an earlier one, even when the bishops’ life is beyond reproach, unless perhaps, carried away by pride, he refuses to fulfill what the bishop has ordered for the needs of the Church. If, however, he is unable to perform or discharge the office of archdeacon because of a simpler nature, he is to retain the title of his own position, while the bishop is to place before him in the Church’s order the person whom he has chosen.

XXIV. Regarding exposed children who have been found, the provision already established long ago by the holy synod is to be observed.

XXV. If laypeople abandon or have abandoned the marital union because of a serious fault, without presenting any credible grounds for their disagreement, and leave their marriages in order to presume upon either illicit or other people’s unions, then, if before stating the causes of their disagreement before the provincial bishops they have rejected their wives before judgment has been rendered against them, they are to be excluded from the communion of the Church and from the holy assembly of the people, because they have stained faith and marriage.

XXVI. If any cleric presumes, with blameworthy and punishable obstinacy, to suppress, deny, or perhaps hand over to adversaries documents by which the Church’s possession is secured, he is to restore from his own resources whatever loss has been inflicted upon the Church through the absence of the documents, and is to be deprived of communion. Those also who, having been wickedly solicited to the Church’s detriment, have accepted anything from the betrayers are to be held under the preceding sentence.

XXVII. No one is to presume to begin or establish a new monastery of monks without the bishop’s permission or approval. Wandering monks are not to be ordained to the clerical office, either in cities or in parishes, unless their abbot has given them a testimonial. No abbot is to presume to receive or retain a monk who transfers to another monastery without the permission or consent of his own abbot; wherever he may be, he is to be recalled to his abbot by the authority of the canons. If it should be necessary for a cleric to be ordained from among the monks, the bishop is to presume to do so with the abbot’s consent and will.

XXVIII. Monasteries of women are to be located farther away from monasteries of monks, both because of the snares of the devil and because of human slander.

XXIX. The Church is to protect freedmen lawfully emancipated by their masters, if necessity requires it. If anyone, before a hearing, presumes either to seize or despoil such a person, he is to be expelled from the Church.

[Col. 0403C] XXX. Since it is fitting that the order of the Church be observed equally by all, care must be taken that everywhere, as is done, after the antiphons, the collects be said in order by bishops or presbyters, and that morning and evening hymns be sung every day. At the conclusion of the morning or evening Masses, little chapters from the Psalms are also to be recited after the hymns, and in the evening the people are to be dismissed by the bishop with a collected prayer and a blessing.

XXXI. It was also resolved that, as is often done, whenever people have become divided from one another through hatred or a prolonged dispute and cannot be recalled to peace by sustained effort, they are first to be rebuked by the priests of the city. If they then refuse, with destructive intent, to lay aside their enmities, they are to be expelled from the Church’s assembly by the most just excommunication.

XXXII. A cleric is not to presume to bring anyone before a secular judge without the bishop’s permission. If he himself is summoned, he is neither to answer nor bring a claim, nor is he to dare to present a criminal case in a secular court. If, however, any layperson attempts, through calumny, to harass the Church or the clergy, and is defeated, he is to be restrained from the thresholds of the Church and from communion with Catholics, provided that he has done worthy penance.

XXXIII. If a bishop who has no sons or grandsons has left the Church as his sole heir, anything he has spent, alienated, or given away from the Church’s property, except for the Church’s business or necessity, is to be regarded as invalid.

[Col. 0404A] XXXIV. Jews—whose perfidy frequently returns to its vomit—if they wish to come to the Catholic law, are to enter through the threshold of the Church among the catechumens for eight months. If they are then known to have come with a pure faith, only at that point are they to merit the grace of baptism. If, however, they encounter the danger of illness during the prescribed period and are judged to be near death, they are to be baptized.

XXXV. If a metropolitan bishop sends letters to the bishops of his province inviting them to the ordination of the supreme pontiff or to a synod, they are not to delay attending on the appointed day, setting aside everything except serious bodily illness or a royal command. If they fail to appear, then, as the ancient authority of the canons commands, they are to be deprived of the affection of their brothers and of communion with the Church until the next synod.

XXXVI. All clerics who faithfully and diligently serve the Church are to receive from the priests the stipends owed for their holy labors, according to the merit or arrangement of their service.

XXXVII. Accordingly, we have judged that homicides and false witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion unless they have washed away their crimes through the satisfaction of penance.

XXXVIII. Clerics are not to wander without letters of recommendation and permission from their bishop. The same rule is to be observed for monks; if verbal rebuke does not correct them, we decree that they are also to be restrained by beatings. It is likewise to be observed regarding monks that they may not leave the community for solitary cells unless, after proven labors have been completed, or because of the necessity of illness, the abbot relaxes the stricter rule. Even then, this is to be done only in such a way that, while remaining within the same monastery enclosure and still under the abbot’s authority, they are permitted to have separate cells. Individual abbots are likewise not permitted to have different cells or several monasteries, except that, because of an enemy invasion, they may establish a refuge within the walls.

XXXIX. Presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and all subsequent clerical orders, who are not permitted to take wives, are also to avoid the banquets of other people’s weddings. They are not to join gatherings where love songs are sung and shameful or obscene bodily movements are displayed through choruses and dances, lest hearing and sight, assigned to the sacred mysteries, be polluted by contact with disgraceful spectacles and words.

XL. Henceforth all clerics and laypeople are to avoid the banquets of Jews, and no one is to receive them at a banquet. Since Jews do not share common foods with Christians, it is unworthy and sacrilegious for Christians to eat their food, when they judge the foods that we eat—with the Apostle’s permission—to be unclean. It would be as though Christians became inferior to Jews if we consumed what they set before us while they despised what is offered by us.

XLI. Above all, clerics must avoid drunkenness, which is the fuel and nurse of every vice. Therefore, when it has been established that someone was drunk, we decree that, according to the order of things, he is either to be removed from communion for thirty days or subjected to corporal punishment.

XLII. And lest it perhaps appear that we have omitted what most especially attacks the faith of the Catholic religion: some clerics and laypeople devote themselves to omens and, under the name of a fictitious religion, profess the art of divination through what they call “the lots of the saints,” or permit divination by examining any writings whatsoever. Any cleric or layperson discovered either consulting or teaching such things is to be regarded as outside the Church.

XLIII. Regarding penitents, it was resolved that the judgment established by our holy Fathers in synod be observed: no one from among them is to be ordained a cleric. Those who have already been ordained through ignorance are to occupy the position either of bigamists or of men in a second marriage; nor is a presbyter to presume to minister to deacons or to consecrate the altar.

XLIV. A presbyter is absolutely not permitted to pour a blessing over the people in the church or to bless a penitent in the church.

XLV. If necessity requires it, a bishop has the power, without the counsel of his brothers, to sell off small plots of land or small vineyards that are of little use to the Church or are situated far away.

XLVI. Fugitives who abandon their homes or households are to have those homes or households sold, even if they are later recalled or if they have deserved such treatment.

XLVII. We specifically command that laypeople remain for the whole of Sunday Mass, so that the people do not presume to leave before the priest’s blessing. If they do so, they are to be publicly disgraced by the bishop.

XLVIII. Whatever belongs to the bishop’s own property, whether inherited or acquired, and whatever the bishop possesses from his personal resources, he may leave to his heirs if he wishes. Whatever, however, comes from the provision of his Church—whether lands, crops, or offerings—we have judged must all be reserved by right to the Church.

XLIX. Deacons or presbyters established in a parish are not to dare to exchange, sell, or give away anything from the Church’s property entrusted to them, since it is known to be consecrated to God. Priests likewise are not to presume to alienate anything from the Church’s property entrusted to them, as was stated above. If they are convicted of doing so in council and deposed from their honor, they are to restore from their own property another amount equal to what they appear to have presumed to take. If anyone, under any circumstances, presumes to alienate something from the Church’s property, he may retain it only if he first contributes from his own property to the Church an amount equal to what he appears to have taken. We nevertheless command that freedmen whom priests or deacons wish to make from the Church entrusted to them continue to perform the Church’s work. If they disdain to do so, it was resolved that they return to their former service.

L. If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon commits a capital crime, falsifies a document, or gives false testimony, he is to be deposed from the honor of his office, confined in a monastery, and there receive only lay communion for as long as he lives.

[Col. 0406A] LI. If a bishop, after making a will, bequeaths something belonging to ecclesiastical property, the bequest is not valid unless he makes up the amount from property belonging to his own right.

LII. No one is to give communion to a presbyter, deacon, or cleric who travels without letters from his bishop.

LIII. Whatever a parish presbyter has alienated from property belonging to ecclesiastical right is to be regarded as null and void, both for the seller and for the purchaser, and for the person who sold it at auction.

LIV. While a presbyter holds a diocese, he is to draw up a document assigning to the Church whatever he has purchased, or else withdraw from the administration of the Church he holds.

LV. Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are not permitted to keep dogs for hunting or hawks. If anyone of these ranks is discovered to have this intention, the bishop is to suspend himself from communion for three months, the presbyter is to abstain for two months, and the deacon is to cease from every office and from communion.

LVI. In the sales that abbots presume to make, this rule is to be observed: whatever is sold without the bishop’s knowledge is to be recalled to the bishop’s authority. An abbot is not permitted to manumit slaves given to monks, for we consider it unjust that, while monks perform daily rural labor, their slaves should enjoy the leisure of freedom.

LVII. We forbid one abbot to preside over two monasteries.

[Col. 0406C] LVIII. We prohibit the establishment of new cells or small communities of monks without the bishop’s knowledge.

LIX. Whatever clerics may have possessed for any length of time from the Church’s remuneration is not to be claimed as their own property by prescription of time, provided that it is clear that the property belonged to the Church. Thus bishops are not to appear to have had to make lengthy or merely requested administrations when they were ordained, nor are they to be able to transfer resources long retained into the right of their own property.

LX. Regarding the lapsed—that is, those who were baptized in the Catholic faith but afterward passed into heresy through blameworthy apostasy—antiquity established great difficulty in returning. We, shortening the number of years, impose upon them two years of penance under the following observance: after the prescribed two years, in the third year they are to fast without relaxation and diligently attend the church. They are to observe the humility of standing and praying in the place of penitents, so that when the catechumens are instructed to leave, they too are to depart. If they are willing to observe this, the discipline may be relaxed at the appointed time and they may be admitted to the altar. If they consider the requirement difficult or harsh, they must fulfill the regulations established by the earlier canons.

LXI. We reserve absolutely no forgiveness for incestuous unions, unless they have healed the adultery by separation. Those involved in incest are not to be counted under any name of marriage; indeed, it is grievous even to identify them. We judge such a case to exist when someone pollutes by carnal union his brother’s widow, who had previously been almost like a sister; when a brother takes his full sister as a wife; when someone marries his stepmother; when someone joins himself to his cousin; when someone has intercourse with the widow or daughter of his uncle; when a father has intercourse with his daughter or stepdaughter; or when anyone pollutes by intercourse, or takes as a wife, a woman related to him by blood or one whom a blood relative has had as a concubine. We do not doubt that all such persons were incestuous in former times and are incestuous under this constitution, and we command that they remain and pray among the catechumens until they have made legitimate satisfaction. We now prohibit these unions in such a way, however, that we do not dissolve what has been established up to this time. Those whose illicit union is forbidden will nevertheless have the freedom to enter into a better marriage.

[Col. 0407B] LXII. If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of the judge, he is to expiate the guilt of bloodshed through excommunication or two years of penance.

LXIII. Citizens who neglect to attend with the bishops on the feasts of the principal solemnities—that is, Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, or Pentecost—although they ought to know that they are placed in the cities in order to receive communion or a blessing, are to be deprived of communion with the Church for three years.

LXIV. If anyone established among the clergy is absent from his church on the solemn days—that is, the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Easter, or Pentecost—because he is pursuing private profit rather than fulfilling his service, it is fitting that he be suspended from communion for three years. Likewise, if a deacon or presbyter is absent from his church for three weeks, he is to incur this condemnation.

[Col. 0408A] LXV. Since a deacon ought not to sit in the presence of a presbyter, he is to sit only at the presbyter’s command. The deacon is likewise to be honored by the lower ministers and by all clerics.

LXVI. Since it is not proper for anyone to have the liberty to enter the sacristy, which the Greeks call the *diakonikon* (διακονικόν), among the consecrated ministers, or to touch the Lord’s vessels.

LXVII. Since it is not proper to mix marriages with all heretics, or to give sons or daughters to them, but rather to receive them from them—provided, however, that they profess that they will become Christians and Catholics.

LXVIII. Since ministers of the altar or clerics ought not to be magicians or enchanters, or perform the practices they describe, namely, amulets (*phylacteria*), which are great bonds of souls, we have commanded that those who use such things be expelled from the Church.

LXIX. Rioters are never to be ordained as clerics, nor are usurers or those who avenge their own injuries.

LXX. A cleric who is buffoonish and makes jokes with shameful words is to be withdrawn from office.

LXXI. It was also resolved that, according to the regulations of the Fathers, a synod should be assembled every year. Since we dismiss the assembly in peace, we give thanks to God, praying for his mercy, so that for many years we may be able to carry out these same things in the Lord’s honor. I, Caesarius, bishop in the name of Christ, in accordance with what all my fellow bishops wrote together with me, following the regulations of the Fathers and assenting to these definitions, have subscribed on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. The others likewise subscribed.

The Council of Agde ends here.

THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF ORLÉANS BEGIN.

[Col. 0407]

[Col. 0407C] 1. Concerning homicides, adulterers, and thieves, if they flee to the church.  
2. Concerning robbers who flee to the church.  
3. Concerning slaves, if they flee to the church.  
4. Concerning one who demands something from a bishop, so that he is not deprived of the Church for making that claim.  
5. If a bishop makes another person’s slave a cleric.  
6. If a deacon or presbyter commits a capital crime.  
7. Concerning those who have violated their penance.  
8. If a presbyter or deacon has suspended himself from the Eucharist on account of some guilt.  
9. If the wife left by a presbyter or deacon joins herself to another man.  
10. Concerning what is offered at the altar.  
11. Concerning what the faithful offer in parish churches.  
12. That the bishop protect the poor and the sick.  
13. That basilicas remain under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are located.  
14. Concerning incestuous unions, so that they may be excommunicated.  
15. That abbots be under the authority of bishops, and concerning wandering monks.  
16. That monks not use prayer-cloths or belts.  
17. If a monk takes a wife.  
18. That a monk not construct cells without the permission of the bishop or abbot.  
19. If a bishop grants small plots of land to anyone for cultivation, they are to be held without prejudice to the Church’s rights.  
20. That Lent be observed before Easter.  
21. That no citizen celebrate the greater feasts in the countryside.  
22. That no one among the people presume to leave before Mass is completed and the blessing has been received.  
23. That litanies be celebrated before the Ascension of the Lord.  
24. Concerning clerics who disdain to come to the service.  
25. Concerning familiarity with strange women.  
26. Concerning religious or laypeople who attend to divinations.  
27. That a bishop ought not to be absent from the church on Sunday.

THE COUNCIL OF ORLÉANS OF THIRTY BISHOPS BEGINS.

[Col. 0409]

[Col. 0409A] When, by God’s authorship, a council of the highest bishops had been assembled in the city of Orléans, it pleased all by common deliberation that what they had established in words should also be strengthened by the testimony of Scripture.

CHAPTER I. We establish that the following is to be observed, as the ecclesiastical canons have decreed and Roman law has established: it is wholly unlawful to drag defendants from the atria of the church or from the bishop’s house. Nor may they be handed over to another person unless, after oaths have been given upon the Gospels, they are guaranteed against death, bodily harm, and every kind of punishment. Thus, the person to whom the accused is liable must reach an agreement with him concerning satisfaction. If he is convicted of violating his oath, as guilty of perjury he is to be separated not only from communion with the Church and all clerics, but also from the banquets of Catholics. If the person to whom he is liable refuses to settle the matter through negotiation, and the accused leaves the church out of fear, the Church’s clerics are not to pursue him.

II. Concerning robbers, we have judged that the following must be established: if a robber flees to the church with the woman he has abducted, and it is established that the woman herself suffered violence, she is immediately to be freed from the robber’s power. The robber, once granted immunity from death or punishment, is either to be subjected to servitude or is to have the free opportunity to redeem himself. If it is established that the abducted woman has a father and that the girl consented to the robber, she is to be returned, free from punishment, to her father’s authority, while the robber is to be held liable to the father for satisfaction of a superior condition.

[Col. 0409C] III. If a slave who has fled to the church on account of any offense receives from his master an oath concerning the offense committed, he is immediately to be compelled to return to his master’s service. If, after being handed over to his master under oath, he is proven to have endured any punishment for the same offense from which he had been excused, then, for contempt of the Church and violation of faith, he is to be regarded as outside communion and the banquets of Catholics. If, however, a slave, defended by the Church on account of his offense, has received from the Church, at the clerics’ insistence, an oath guaranteeing immunity, then, if he refuses to leave, the master is permitted to seize him.

IV. If anyone believes that he has something to reclaim from his bishop, from the Church, or from his own right, and makes no accusation of insult or crime, he may not be removed from communion with the Church merely because of the dispute.

V. If, while the master is absent or unaware, a bishop knowingly ordains another man’s slave as a deacon or presbyter, and the slave remains in the clerical office, the bishop is to compensate the master with double satisfaction. If, however, the bishop did not know that he was a slave, those who gave testimony or petitioned for his ordination are likewise to be held liable for restitution.

[Col. 0410A] VI. If deacons or presbyters commit a capital crime, they are to be expelled at once both from office and from communion.

VII. Concerning those who, after undertaking penance, forget the religious commitment they professed and relapse into secular life: it was resolved that they are to be suspended from communion and separated from the banquets of all Catholics. If, after the prohibition, anyone presumes to eat with them, he too is to be deprived of communion.

VIII. If a deacon or presbyter, on account of his guilt, has withdrawn himself from communion at the altar under a penitent’s profession, then, if others are absent and a case of definite necessity arises, he is nevertheless permitted to baptize one who requests baptism.

IX. If the widow left by a presbyter or deacon joins herself in a second marriage to any man, they are either to be separated after correction, or, if they persist in their criminal intention, punished with equal excommunication.

X. Rereading the ancient canons, we believe that the earlier statutes must be renewed: of what is brought to the altar as an offering of faith, the bishop is to claim half, while the clergy are to receive the other half for distribution among themselves according to their ranks, whether it comes from estates or from every kind of revenue that remains under the bishop’s authority.

XI. Regarding what any of the faithful offer to parish churches in lands, vineyards, slaves, or personal property, the statutes of the ancient canons are to be observed, and everything is to remain under the bishop’s authority. Of what is brought to the altar, however, one third is to be faithfully delivered to the bishops.

[Col. 0410C] XII. The bishop is to distribute food and clothing to the poor and to the sick who, because of weakness, cannot work with their own hands, to the extent that his means permit.

XIII. It was resolved, according to the rule of the earlier canons, that all basilicas constructed in various places, or constructed daily, are to remain under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated.

XIV. A surviving brother is not to ascend into the bed of his deceased brother, nor may anyone dare to join himself to the sister of his deceased wife. Those who do so are to be struck by ecclesiastical discipline.

[Col. 0410D] XV. Abbots, because of the humility of their religious status, are to remain under the authority of the bishops. If they do anything outside the rule, they are to be corrected by the bishops, whom they are to meet once a year at the place the bishop chooses, after receiving a summons. Monks, however, are to be subject to their abbots in all obedience and devotion. If anyone proves disobedient through defiance, presumes to wander through various places, or possesses anything as private property, the abbots are to take away everything he has acquired, according to the rule, for the benefit of the monastery. Those who have wandered are to be recalled under guard wherever they are found, with the bishop’s assistance, as fugitives. The abbot is to understand that he will be held guilty if he has not pronounced regular discipline against such persons, or if he has received another abbot’s monk.

XVI. A monk is not permitted to have a prayer-cloth or belts in the monastery.

XVII. If afterward he is joined to a wife, as guilty of so great an apostasy he is never to receive an office in an ecclesiastical rank.

XVIII. No monk, after abandoning the monastery’s community under the impulse of ambition and vanity, is to presume to build a cell without the bishop’s permission or his abbot’s will.

[Col. 0411B] XIX. If a bishop, out of consideration for human kindness, grants small slaves, vineyards, or plots of land to clerics or monks for cultivation or temporary possession, then, even if long periods of years are shown to have passed, no secular legal document that prejudices the Church is to be imposed, and the Church is not to suffer any disadvantage.

XX. It is decreed for all priests that before the solemnity of Easter, not the fiftieth day but the fortieth is to be observed—that is, Lent rather than a period of fifty days.

XXI. No citizen is permitted to celebrate the solemnities of Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, or Lent in the countryside, except one whom illness is proved to have confined there.

[Col. 0412A] XXII. When the people assemble in God’s name to celebrate Masses, they are not to depart before the solemnity of the Mass has been completed and, where no bishop is present, they have received the priest’s blessing.

XXIII. It was resolved that the Rogation ceremonies—that is, the litanies—be celebrated before the Ascension of the Lord, with the previously announced three-day fast being ended on the solemnity of the Lord’s Passion. During those three days, male and female slaves are to be released from work, so that the whole people may assemble more fully. Throughout those three days, everyone is to abstain and use the foods of Lent.

XXIV. Clerics who disdain to be present for the holy service are to receive ecclesiastical discipline according to the bishop’s judgment.

[Col. 0412B] XXV. Regarding familiarity with strange women, both bishops and presbyters and deacons are to observe the statutes of the earlier canons.

XXVI. If any cleric, monk, or layperson believes that divination or omens should be observed, or thinks that the lots falsely claimed to be those of the saints should be consulted and disclosed to anyone, he is to be expelled from communion with the Church together with those who believe in such things.

XXVII. Unless prevented by illness, a bishop ought not to be absent on Sunday from the church nearest to him. The others who subscribed with me, thirty-three in number, likewise agreed.

Here end the councils of Gaul.

THE COUNCILS OF SPAIN FOLLOW.

THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF ELVIRA BEGIN.

[Col. 0411]

[Col. 0411C] 1. Concerning those who sacrifice to idols after baptism.  
2. Concerning pagan priests who sacrifice after baptism.  
3. Concerning the same, if they have given only a gift to idols.  
4. Concerning the same, if they are still catechumens and sacrifice, and when they are to be baptized.  
5. If a mistress kills her maidservant out of jealousy.  
6. If anyone kills a person while serving in the military.  
7. Concerning penitents for adultery, if they sin again.  
8. Concerning women who leave adulterous husbands and marry others.  
9. Concerning women who leave their husbands and marry others.  
10. Concerning the widow of a catechumen, if she marries another man.  
11. Concerning the widow of a catechumen, if she becomes seriously ill.  
12. Concerning women who practice pandering.  
13. Concerning virgins consecrated to God, if they commit adultery.  
14. Concerning unmarried virgins, if they commit adultery.  
15. Concerning the marriage of those who come from paganism.  
16. Concerning believing girls, so that they are not joined to unbelievers.  
17. Concerning those who join their daughters to pagan priests.  
18. Concerning priests and ministers, if they commit adultery.  
19. Concerning clerics who pursue business or markets.  
20. Concerning clerics and laypeople who practice usury.  
21. Concerning those who come late to church.  
22. Concerning Catholics who pass into heresy, if they do not return.  
23. Concerning the times of fasting.  
24. Concerning those baptized abroad, so that they do not enter the clergy.  
25. Concerning the communicatory letters of confessors.  
26. That there be a fast every Saturday.  
27. That clerics not have a strange woman in their house.  
28. Concerning the offerings of those who do not receive communion.  
29. Concerning how the possessed are to be treated.  
30. Concerning those who commit adultery after baptism, so that they do not even become subdeacons.  
31. Concerning adolescents who commit adultery after baptism.  
32. Concerning excommunicated presbyters, so that they may give communion in necessity.  
33. Concerning bishops and ministers, so that they abstain from their wives.  
34. That candles not be lit in cemeteries.  
35. That women not keep vigil in cemeteries.  
36. That paintings not be made in churches.  
37. Concerning the baptism of the possessed.  
38. That, in necessity, the faithful also baptize.  
39. That the faithful not receive anything that has been used in idolatry.  
40. That masters prohibit their slaves from worshiping idols.  
41. Concerning those who come to the faith, how they are to be baptized.  
42. Concerning the celebration of Pentecost.  
43. Concerning pagan prostitutes, if they convert.  
44. Concerning catechumens who do not attend church.  
45. Concerning the length of penance for the faithful if they apostatize.  
46. Concerning one who has a wife, if he commits adultery repeatedly.  
47. Concerning those to be baptized, so that clerics receive nothing.  
48. Concerning the crops of the faithful, so that they are not blessed by Jews.  
49. Concerning Christians who eat with Jews.  
50. Concerning heretics, so that they are not promoted to the clergy.  
51. Concerning those who place defamatory writings in the church.  
52. Concerning bishops who give communion to another person’s excommunicate.  
53. Concerning parents who break the faith of betrothals.  
54. Concerning pagan priests who no longer sacrifice.  
55. Concerning magistrates and those in positions of authority.  
56. Concerning those who give clothing for the adornment of pomp.  
57. Concerning those who carry communicatory letters.  
58. Concerning the faithful, so that they do not ascend to the Capitol for the purpose of sacrificing.  
59. Concerning those who are killed while destroying idols.  
60. Concerning those who are joined to two sisters.  
61. Concerning augurs and pantomimes, if they convert.  
62. Concerning wives who kill children born of adultery.  
63. Concerning women who commit adultery with other men until death.  
64. Concerning the adulterous wives of clerics.  
65. Concerning those who marry their stepdaughters.  
66. Concerning the marriage of a female catechumen.  
67. Concerning an adulterous female catechumen who kills her child.  
68. Concerning married men who afterward fall into adultery.  
69. Concerning women who commit adultery with the knowledge of their husbands.  
70. Concerning the corrupters of boys.  
71. Concerning adulterous widows, if they afterward marry the same husband.  
72. Concerning informers.  
73. Concerning false witnesses.  
74. Concerning those who accuse priests but do not prove the accusation.  
75. Concerning deacons, if they are proved to have sinned before receiving their rank.  
76. Concerning baptized people who die before they have been confirmed.  
77. Concerning married believers, if they commit adultery with a Jewish woman or a pagan.  
78. Concerning those who play board games.  
79. Concerning freedmen.  
80. Concerning women’s letters.

THE COUNCIL OF ELVIRA OF NINETEEN BISHOPS, IN THE TIME OF CONSTANTINE, BEGINS.

[Col. 0413]

[Col. 0413D] When the holy and religious bishops had assembled in the church at Elvira—namely, Felix, bishop of Aquitania; Conscius, bishop of Córdoba; Savinus, bishop of Seville; Camerinus, bishop of Tacita; Sinagius, bishop of Pegrensis; Secundinus, bishop of Catalensis; Pardius, bishop of Mentasa; Flavianus, bishop of Elvira; Catonus, bishop of Corsica; Liberius, bishop of Mérida; Valerius, bishop of Zaragoza; Decentius, bishop of León; Melantius, bishop of Toledo; Januarius, bishop of Siblaria; Vincentius, bishop of Ossoloba; Quintianus, bishop of Elbora; Successus, bishop of Elicroca; Euticianus, bishop of Basti; and Patricius, bishop of Málaga—with thirty-six presbyters also seated, deacons standing by, and the whole people present, all the bishops said:

### Chapter I

It was decreed that anyone who, after the faith of saving baptism, [Col. 0414D] at an adult age should enter a temple of an idol in order to worship an idol and commit the crime, should not be admitted to communion even at the end of life.

### II

As for the flamines who, after the faith of the washing and regeneration, should sacrifice, since they have doubled their crimes by adding homicide, or tripled their offense by adding adultery, it was decreed that they should not be admitted to communion even at the end of life.

### III

Likewise, as for flamines who did not sacrifice but merely gave a gift, since they abstained from the deadly sacrifices, it was decreed that communion should be granted to them at the end of life, provided that they had performed the prescribed penance. Likewise, if they should commit adultery after penance, it was decreed that communion should no longer be given to them, lest they appear to have made a mockery of the Lord’s communion.

### IV

Likewise, if flamines are catechumens and have abstained from sacrifices, it was decreed that after three years they ought to be admitted to baptism.

### [Col. 0415A] V

If a woman, inflamed by the fury of jealousy, should beat her maidservant with whips so that she dies in agony within three days, since it is uncertain whether she killed her intentionally or accidentally: if intentionally, after seven years; if accidentally, after five years, once the prescribed penance has been performed, it was decreed that she be admitted to communion. But if she becomes ill during the prescribed period, she is to receive communion.

### VI

If anyone should kill another by magic, since he could not accomplish the crime without idolatry, communion is not to be granted to him even at the end of life.

### VII

If any believer, after falling into adultery and completing the prescribed period of penance, should again commit fornication, it was decreed that he should not have communion even at the end of life.

### [Col. 0415B] VIII

Likewise, women who, without any prior cause, have abandoned their husbands and joined themselves to other men are not to receive communion even at the end of life.

### IX

Likewise, a believing woman who has abandoned an adulterous husband who was a believer and has married another man is to be forbidden to marry. But if she does marry, she is not to receive communion until the man whom she abandoned has departed from this world, unless illness compels communion to be given sooner.

### X

If the woman whom a catechumen has abandoned marries another man, she may be admitted to the washing of the font. The same is to be observed concerning female catechumens. But if a woman is married by a man who has abandoned an innocent wife, and she knows that he abandoned his wife without cause, it was decreed that communion is to be given to such a woman at the end of life.

### [Col. 0415C] XI

If a female catechumen should become seriously ill within the five-year period, it was decreed that baptism, which ought not to be denied, should be added for her.

### XII

If a father, relative, or any believing woman should practice procuring, since she has sold another person’s body—or rather her own—it was decreed that she should not receive communion even at the end of life.

### XIII

If virgins who have dedicated themselves to God should lose their agreement to preserve virginity and should serve lust, not understanding what they have lost, it was decreed that communion should not be given to them even at the end. But if they should repent of themselves, because they had fallen through bodily weakness, and such women should perform penance throughout the remainder of their lives and abstain from intercourse, since they seem rather to have fallen through weakness, it was decreed that at the end they ought to receive communion.

### [Col. 0415D] XIV

If virgins who have not preserved their virginity should marry and remain married to the very men who violated them, since they have violated only the marriage bond, they ought to be reconciled after one year without penance. But if they have relations with other men, since they have committed adultery, it was decreed that they should be admitted to communion after five years, once the prescribed penance has been performed.

### XV

Because of the abundance of young women, Christian virgins are by no means to be given in marriage to pagans, lest an age swelling in its flower be dissolved in adultery of the soul.

### XVI

It was decreed that Catholic girls should not be given to heretics who are estranged from the Catholic Church, nor to Jews, nor to heretics, since no fellowship can exist between a believer and an unbeliever. If parents act contrary to the prohibition, it was decreed that they abstain for five years.

### [Col. 0416A] XVII

If anyone should join his daughters in marriage to priests of idols, it was decreed that communion should not be given to him even at the end of life.

### XVIII

If bishops, presbyters, or deacons, while serving in the ministry, are discovered to have committed adultery, it was decreed that, both because of the scandal and because of the abominable crime, they ought not to receive communion even at the end of life.

### XIX

Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are not to leave their places for the sake of conducting business, nor, traveling through the provinces, are they to pursue profitable markets. [Col. 0416B] Certainly, in order to acquire food for themselves, let them send a son, freedman, hired servant, friend, or anyone else; and if they wish to conduct business, let them do so within the province.

### XX

If any member of the clergy should devote himself to receiving interest, it was decreed that he be degraded and excluded from communion. If a layman is also proved to have received interest and, when corrected, promises that he will cease and will no longer exact it, it was decreed that he be granted pardon. But if he persists in that iniquity, let him know that he is to be expelled from the Church.

### XXI

If anyone residing in a city should fail to enter the church for three Sundays, he is to be excluded for a short time, so that he may be seen to have been corrected.

### XXII

If anyone should pass from the Catholic Church to heresy and then return again to the Church, it was decreed that penance should not be denied him, since he has recognized his sin. He is to perform penance for ten years, after which communion ought to be granted to him. But if children have been led away, since they did not sin through their own fault, they are to be received without delay.

### [Col. 0416C] XXIII

It was decreed that a fast, in addition to the regular abstinences, be celebrated each month, except during the days of the two months of July and August, on account of the weakness associated with them.

### XXIV

All who have been baptized abroad, since their manner of life is not sufficiently known, are not to be promoted to the clergy in foreign provinces.

### XXV

Anyone who brings letters of confessors with the confessor’s name removed, since under the glory of this name they partly unsettle the simple, is to be given letters of communion.

### [Col. 0416D] XXVI

It was decreed that the error be corrected, so that every Saturday we celebrate a fast in addition to the established observance.

### 100 XXVII

A bishop or any other cleric is to have with him only either a sister or a virgin dedicated to God; he is not to have an unrelated woman with him at all.

### XXVIII

It was decreed that a bishop ought not to accept gifts from one who does not share in communion.

### XXIX

The name of a possessed person who is driven by a wandering spirit is neither to be recited at the altar with the offering nor is he to be permitted to minister in the church with his own hand.

### [Col. 0417A] XXX

A subdeacon is not to be ordained if he committed adultery in his youth, since thereafter he is not to be promoted by appointment to a higher rank. But if some have already been ordained, they are to be removed.

### XXXI

Young men who have committed adultery after the faith of the saving washing, once they have married wives and performed the prescribed penance, were decreed to be admitted to communion.

### XXXII

If anyone, through a serious fall, should fall into the ruin of death, it was decreed that he ought not to perform penance without consulting the bishop, but should rather perform it before the bishop, though under the compulsion of illness. It is not for presbyters or deacons to grant communion to such persons unless the bishop has ordered them to do so.

### [Col. 0417B] XXXIII

It was decreed to prohibit entirely bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons serving in the ministry from having sexual relations with their wives and from begetting children. Whoever does this is to be expelled from the honor of the clergy.

### XXXIV

It was decreed that candles not be lit in the cemetery during the day, for the spirits of the saints are not to be disturbed. Those who do not observe this are to be excluded from communion with the Church.

### XXXV

It was decreed that women be forbidden to keep vigil in the cemetery, since they often secretly commit crimes under the pretext of prayer.

### XXXVI

It was decreed that there ought not to be paintings in the church, lest what is worshiped or adored be depicted on the walls.

### [Col. 0417C] XXXVII

Those who are tormented by unclean spirits, if they are found at the point of death, are to be baptized. But if they are believers, communion is to be given to them. It is also to be prohibited that they light lamps publicly; if they wish to act against the prohibition, they are to abstain from communion.

### XXXVIII

Those travelling abroad by sea, or where there is no church nearby: a believer whose baptism is intact and who is not a bigamist may baptize a catechumen in the emergency of illness, provided that, if the latter survives, he brings him to the bishop so that he may be perfected through the laying on of hands.

If pagans, during illness, should desire that hands be laid upon them, and their life has been honorable in some respect, it was decreed that hands be laid upon them and that they become Christians.

### [Col. 0417D] XXXIX

It was decreed to prohibit landowners, when they receive their accounts, from bringing in as accepted anything that has been given to an idol. But if they act after the prohibition, they are to be kept from communion for a period of five years.

### XL

It was decreed that believers be admonished to prevent, as far as they can, idols from being kept in their homes. But if they fear the violence of their servants, let them at least keep themselves pure. If they do not do so, they are to be regarded as outsiders to the Church.

### XLI

Those who first approach the faith, if their conduct has been good, were decreed to be admitted to the grace of baptism within two years, unless an emergency compelled by illness should require it, whether to help a companion in danger or one requesting grace.

### [Col. 0418A] XLII

It was decreed that a corrupt practice be corrected according to the authority of Scripture, so that we all celebrate Pentecost. Whoever does not do this is to be marked as having introduced a new heresy.

### XLIII

A woman who was once a prostitute and later had a husband, if she subsequently comes to the faith, was decreed to be received without delay.

### XLIV

If anyone has remained a catechumen for an indefinite period and has never entered the church, but someone from the clergy has known that he wished to be a Christian, or faithful witnesses have existed, it was decreed that baptism not be denied him, since he appears to have sinned in the old person.

### [Col. 0418B] XLV

If a believing apostate has not entered the church for an indefinite period, but has at some point returned and has not been an idolater, it was decreed that he receive communion after ten years.

### XLVI

If a believer who has a wife has committed adultery not once but repeatedly, he is to be confronted at the point of death. If he promises that he will cease, communion is to be given him. If, having recovered, he again commits adultery, it was decreed that he should no longer partake of the communion of peace.

### XLVII

It was decreed that the practice be corrected whereby those who are baptized put coins into a shell, lest the priest appear to sell for a price what he received freely; nor are their feet to be washed by priests or clerics.

### [Col. 0418C] XLVIII

It was decreed that landowners be admonished not to allow their produce, which they receive from God, to be blessed by Jews with thanksgiving, lest they make our blessing weak and ineffective. If anyone presumes to do this after the prohibition, he is to be expelled entirely from the Church.

### XLIX

If any cleric or believer should eat with Jews, it was decreed that he abstain from communion, so that he may be corrected.

### L

No one from any heresy who comes to us as a believer is to be promoted to the clergy; and if any have previously been ordained, they are without doubt to be deposed.

### LI

If anyone is found to place defamatory pamphlets in the church, let him be anathematized.

### [Col. 0418D] LII

It was decreed by all that anyone receive communion from the bishop by whom he had been excluded for some offense. But if any bishop should presume to admit him while the bishop from whom he had been deprived of communion is still entirely unaware or has not consented, let him know that he will have to answer for such matters among the brethren, at the peril of his own status.

### LIII

If parents should break the faith of their betrothals during the three-year period, they are to abstain from communion. If, however, the betrothed man or woman has been discovered in a serious crime, the parents will be excused. But if they have polluted themselves by consenting to the same fault, the preceding judgment is to remain in force.

### LIV

Priests who merely wear the crown of those who sacrifice, but neither sacrifice nor provide anything from their own resources to idols, were decreed to receive communion after two years.

### [Col. 0419A] LV

It was decreed that a magistrate, during the year in which he holds the duumvirate, be prohibited from withdrawing from the church.

### LVI

Matrons or their husbands are not to give their garments for secular display and pomp; if they do so, they are to abstain for three years.

### LVII

It was decreed that everywhere, and especially in the place where the bishop of the principal see has been established, those who issue letters of communion be questioned as to whether they have everything in proper order and confirm it by their testimony.

### LVIII

It is to be prohibited that any Christian or pagan ascend to the Capitolium for the purpose of sacrificing or observing the sacrifice. If he does so, he is to be held liable for the same crime; if he is a believer, he is to be received after ten years, once the prescribed penance has been performed.

### [Col. 0419B] LIX

If anyone breaks idols and is killed on the spot, since this is not written in the Gospel and is nowhere found to have been done by the apostles, it was decreed that he not be admitted among the martyrs.

### LX

If anyone, after his wife’s death, marries her sister, and she is herself a believer, it was decreed that he abstain from communion for five years, unless perhaps the necessity of illness compels peace to be granted sooner.

### LXI

If a soothsayer or pantomime should wish to believe, it was decreed that he first renounce his arts and only then be received, in such a way that he does not return to them thereafter. If they attempt to act contrary to the prohibition, they are to be expelled from the Church.

### [Col. 0419C] LXII

If a woman, while her husband is absent, conceives through adultery and then kills the child after the crime, it was decreed that communion not be given to her even at the end of life, since she has doubled her crime.

### LXIII

If a woman remains adulterous with another man until the end of her life, it was decreed that communion not be given to her even at the end. But if she abandons him, she is to be received into communion after ten years, once the prescribed penance has been performed.

### LXIV

If the wife of any cleric has committed adultery, and her husband knows that she is committing adultery but does not immediately cast her out, he is not to receive communion even at the end of life, lest those who ought to be examples of good conduct appear to be producing instruction in crime.

### LXV

If anyone marries his stepdaughter, since this is incest, it was decreed that communion not be given to him even at the end of life.

### [Col. 0419D] LXVI

It is to be prohibited that any believing woman or catechumen keep either comic actors or stage performers. Any woman who does this is to be excluded from communion.

### LXVII
