If a female catechumen conceives through adultery and kills the child conceived, it was decreed that she be baptized at the end of life.

### LXVIII

If anyone who has a wife should fall once, it was decreed that he ought to perform penance for five years and then be reconciled, unless necessity compels communion to be given before the time. The same is to be observed concerning women.

### [Col. 0420A] LXIX

If a wife has committed adultery with her husband’s knowledge, it was decreed that communion not be given to her even at the end of life. But if she abandons him, she is to receive communion after ten years, if he knowingly retained her as an adulteress in his house for any period of time.

### 101 LXX

Communion is not to be given even at the end of life to those who violate boys.

### LXXI

If a widow commits adultery and afterward has the same man as her husband, it was decreed that, after five years and the completion of the prescribed penance, she be reconciled through communion. If she marries another man and abandons him, communion is not to be given to her even at the end of life. Or if the man she married is a believer, she is not to receive communion unless after ten years and the completion of the prescribed penance, unless illness compels communion to be given sooner.

### [Col. 0420B] LXXII

If an informer is a believer and, through his denunciation, someone has been proscribed or killed, it was decreed that he not receive communion even at the end of life. If the case is lighter, he may receive communion within five years. If he is a catechumen, he is to be admitted to baptism after five years.

### LXXIII

A false witness is to abstain in proportion to the crime. If what he alleged did not involve death, and if he proves that he kept silent for a long time, he is to abstain for two years. But if he does not prove it in an assembly of clerics, it was decreed that he abstain for five years.

### LXXIV

If anyone should attack a bishop, presbyter, or deacon with false accusations and be unable to prove them, communion is not to be given to him even at the end of life.

### [Col. 0420C] LXXV

If anyone has allowed himself to be ordained a deacon and is afterward discovered to have committed a capital crime at some earlier time, if he voluntarily confesses, it was decreed that, after performing the prescribed penance, he receive communion after three years. But if someone else exposes him, he ought, after five years and the completion of the prescribed penance, to receive lay communion.

### LXXVI

If a deacon governing a congregation without a bishop or presbyter should baptize anyone, the bishop ought to complete them through a blessing. But if he should depart from this world before that happens, he may be considered righteous according to the faith in which each person believed.

### LXXVII

If a believer who has a wife commits adultery with a Jewess or a pagan woman, he is to be excluded from communion. [Col. 0420D] But if someone else exposes him, he may, after five years and the completion of the prescribed penance, be joined to the Lord’s communion.

### LXXVIII

If a believer plays at dice—that is, at the board—it was decreed that he abstain; and if, having been corrected, he ceases, he may be reconciled to communion after one year.

### LXXIX

It is to be prohibited that freedmen whose patrons are still in the world be promoted to the clergy.

### LXXX

Women are not to dare to write privately, without mentioning their husbands’ names, to laymen who are believers, nor to receive letters of peace written solely in their own name from anyone.

The Council of Eliberitanum ends.

# The Chapters of the Council of Tarraco Begin

### [Col. 0421]

1. That they should also go to their nearest relatives with the testimony of a cleric.  
2. That clerics not be permitted to make a practice of buying more cheaply or selling more dearly.  
3. That a cleric receive as much as he has advanced.  
4. That no bishop or subordinate cleric presume to judge cases on Sunday.  
5. That whoever has not been ordained bishop in the metropolitan city present himself to the metropolitan after two months.  
6. That a bishop who, having been summoned by the metropolitan, does not come to the synod be excommunicated.  
7. That the diocesan clerics observe weekly rotations and that all assemble together on Saturday.  
8. That bishops visit the diocese each year and receive no more than a third part of the parishes.  
9. Concerning clerics and doorkeepers who associate with adulterous women: that they be prohibited from doing so.  
10. That no bishop accept gifts for judgments.  
11. That a monk sent anywhere presume not to perform clerical ministry, nor become a businessman.  
12. That if a bishop dies intestate, the clerics make an inventory of his possessions and no one take anything from them.  
13. That a bishop admonish the diocesan presbyters, and summon certain laymen by letters.

# The Council of Tarraco Begins

The council of ten bishops, in the forty-fourth year of the era.

### [Col. 0421]

### [Col. 0421B]

In the name of Christ, a synod was held at Tarraco in the sixth year of King Theodoric, during the consulship of Peter, on the eighth day before the Ides of November. The ancient Fathers appear to have judged concerning those matters which, whether left to them in their own time or handed down to them, they certainly confirmed by the testimony of their own actions. Following their example, we too decided that the things which are not being done should be observed, that past practices should be maintained without ambiguity, and that present practices should be made firm through this observance. Therefore, when we had assembled together in the city of Tarraco, founded with the greatest care as a metropolitan city, we wrote down the following titles to be observed.

### Chapter I

Concerning those to whom, because of urgent care, permission is given to have proximity: they are to sustain their needs with such caution that the benefits of piety necessary for them are provided from a greater distance. When clerics enter to visit them, they are to return after the greeting and are not to remain there. Those, however, who do not go to visit them are to take with them a person already proven by faith and action as a witness of their consolation. If any cleric disregards these decrees, he is to be deprived of the dignity of his place. But if he is a religious or monk, he is to be shut up in a monastic cell and devote himself to penitential lamentation; there, under singular affliction, he is to receive bread and water as food according to the abbot’s order.

### II

It has been confirmed by the statutes of the canons that whoever wishes to be in the clergy must not practice buying cheaply or selling dearly. Certainly, if he wishes to engage in this, he is to be restrained from the clergy.

### III

If a cleric has advanced a solidus in a time of need, [Col. 0421D] he is to receive in return wine or grain of the kind which, at the appointed time, has been decreed to be sold for the purpose of trade. But if he did not possess the necessary commodity, he is to receive back exactly what he gave, without any increase.

### [Col. 0422B] IV

No bishop, presbyter, or cleric is to presume, on Sunday, to judge the matter of any case, except only to perform the solemn rites appointed for God. On the other days, with the proper persons present, they may judge what is just, except in criminal cases.

### V

If anyone has not been ordained bishop in the metropolitan city, but afterward, having received the blessing through letters of the metropolitan, has attained the honor of bishop, we have decreed that it is best that, at the appointed time—that is, when two months have been completed—he present himself before his metropolitan, so that, instructed by his ecclesiastical admonitions, he may more fully recognize what he ought to observe. If by chance he neglects to fulfill this, he is to be rebuked and corrected by the brethren in synod. And if he has been prevented from fulfilling it by some illness, he is to ensure that he indicates this to the metropolitan in a letter.

### VI

If any bishop, summoned by the metropolitan to the synod, refuses to come without some serious bodily necessity intervening, then, as the judgments of the Fathers have decreed, he is to be deprived of the communion of charity of all the bishops until the next council.

### VII

Concerning diocesan churches and the clergy, it was decreed that the presbyters or deacons established there should observe weekly rotations with the clerics: that is, the presbyter should serve for one week, after which the deacon should succeed him for an equal period. This condition is to be observed: the entire clergy is to be ready by Saturday evening, so that the solemnity may more easily be celebrated on Sunday with everyone present. They are nevertheless to celebrate vespers and matins on every day, because, when the clergy ceased doing so, we discovered—the worst situation—that even the lights were not being provided in the basilicas. If any, through the fault of negligence, are unwilling to fulfill these things, let them know that, according to the statutes of the canons and in proportion to their rank, they are to be subjected to canonical discipline.

### [Col. 0423A] VIII

Experience as our teacher has shown us that many diocesan churches have been abandoned. For this reason we decreed by this constitution that the order of ancient custom be maintained, that the dioceses be visited annually by the bishop, and that, if any basilica should be found abandoned, it be ordered to be restored under his direction, since we know that it was established by ancient tradition that bishops receive a third part of all revenues.

### IX

If any lector wishes to associate or remain attached to the company of an adulterous woman, let him either abandon the adulteress or be regarded as an outsider to the clergy. The lust of doorkeepers is to be punished by a similar judgment.

### X

We have also decreed that it be observed that no priest or cleric presume, in the manner of secular judges, to accept gifts for services of advocacy, except perhaps free offerings presented in churches, which do not appear to have been accepted because of a gift but to have been brought as a contribution of devotion. If he is proved to accept solicited payments, like an exactor of interest or a possessor of usury, let him know that, according to the statutes of the Fathers, he is to be degraded.

### XI

We prohibit monks who leave the monastery from presuming to perform any ecclesiastical ministry outside, except perhaps by command of the abbot. Likewise, none of them—that is, none of the monks—is to be an undertaker or agent in secular business, except for whatever the monastery’s needs require, with the abbot nevertheless commanding him, while the constitution of the Gallican canons concerning these matters is observed above all.

### XII

If a bishop should die intestate anywhere, after his death the presbyters and deacons are to make a faithful inventory of his possessions, from the smallest to the greatest—that is, of his utensils and all his furnishings. If anyone is then convicted either of having presumed to take something or of having secretly carried something away, he is to restore everything according to the law concerning theft.

### XIII

Letters of this kind are to be sent in separate directions by the metropolitan, so that they summon not only the presbyters of the cathedral churches but also the diocesan clergy to the council, and so that they bring with them some of the secular sons of the Church.

John, bishop of the city of Tarraco, in the name of Christ, have subscribed to the constitutions written by us.  
Paul, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed, and my fellow bishop has subscribed.  
Fortunianus, I have subscribed.  
Agricius, I have subscribed.  
Orontius, I have subscribed.  
Vincentius, I have subscribed.  
Ursus, I have subscribed.  
Emidius, I have subscribed.  
Nibridius, I have subscribed.

# The Chapters of the Council of Gerunda Begin

### [Col. 0423]

1. That each province maintain one order in its liturgical office.  
2. That litanies be celebrated after Pentecost, from Thursday through Saturday.  
3. Concerning the celebration of a second series of litanies on the Kalends of November.  
4. That baptism be given only at Easter and Pentecost, except to those who are ill.  
5. That an infant one day old be baptized if in danger.  
6. That those ordained without wives not have unrelated women in their homes.  
7. That laymen who have married a widow or a divorced woman not be admitted to the clergy.  
8. Concerning those who do not receive public penance but only the viaticum, so that they may be promoted to the clergy.  
9. That the Lord’s Prayer be said at the evening and morning hours on every day.

# The Council of Gerunda Begins

In the seventh year of King Theodoric, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, during the consulship of Agapetus III.

### [Col. 0423]

### Chapter I

The ordering of the Mass is to be conducted in the name of God throughout the entire province of Tarraco as it is conducted in the metropolitan church. Both the order of the Mass itself and the custom of singing and ministering are to be maintained.

### II

When the solemnity of Pentecost has been completed, abstinence is to be observed during the following week, from Thursday through Saturday—that is, for these three days.

### III

Likewise, a second litany is to be held on the Kalends of November, with this condition observed: if a Sunday occurs during those days, it is to begin in another week on Thursday, according to the observance of the preceding abstinence, and it is to end when Mass has been celebrated on Saturday evening. During these days, however, we have decreed that abstinence be made from meat and wine.

### [Col. 0424D] IV

Concerning the baptism of catechumens, it was decreed that they come to be baptized at the solemnity of Easter or Pentecost. At the other solemnities, only the sick are to be baptized; baptism is not to be denied to them at any time.

### V

Concerning infants born prematurely, it was decreed that if they are weak, as commonly happens, and do not seek their mother’s milk, they are to be baptized even on the same day on which they were born, if they are brought forward.

### VI

Concerning those who are ordained without wives but have households: if they have a father living with them as a witness of their way of life, their property is not to be administered by any person of the female sex. Instead, they are to arrange their household through a boy or a friend, unless they have a mother or sister in the household, so that, according to the statutes of the earlier canons, their property may be administered through those women.

### [Col. 0425A] VII

If any layman, after his wife, has had relations with another woman of any status, he is not to be admitted to the clergy under any circumstances.

### VIII

But if someone, overcome by the weakness of illness, has received through communion the blessing of penance—which we designate as the viaticum—and afterward, recovering his health, has not publicly submitted himself in the church to the headship of penance, he may be admitted to the clergy provided that he is not held liable for prohibited vices.

### IX

It has always been decreed that this be observed on every day: after matins and vespers, the priest is to recite the Lord’s Prayer.

John, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed.  
Fortunianus, bishop, have subscribed.  
Paul, bishop, have subscribed.  
Agricius, bishop, have subscribed.  
Emidius, bishop, have subscribed.  
Nibridius, bishop, have subscribed.  
Orontius, bishop, have subscribed.

The Council of Gerunda ends.

# The Chapters of the Council of Caesaraugusta Begin

### [Col. 0425]

1. That believing women be separated from the assemblies of male clerics.  
2. That anyone who receives the Eucharist in the church and does not consume it there be anathematized.  
3. That no one fast on Sundays and that no one absent himself from the church during the days of Lent.  
4. That no one withdraw from the church during the three weeks before Epiphany.  
5. That those deprived of communion by their own bishops not be received by others.  
6. That a cleric who wishes to become a monk because of luxury be excommunicated.  
7. That no one assume for himself the title of teacher unless it has been granted to him.  
8. That consecrated virgins not be veiled before the age of forty.

# The Council of Caesaraugusta Begins

Of twelve bishops.

### [Col. 0425]

### [Col. 0425C]

On the fourth day before the Nones of October, when the bishops Siradius, Delphinus, Raticius, Ampelius, Augentius, Lucius, Italius, Splendinius, Valerius, Simposius, Catterius, and Italius were seated in the secretariat at Caesaraugusta, all said: “Let the judgments be read.” Bishop Lucius read.

### Chapter I

All women faithful to the Catholic Church are to be separated from the reading and assemblies of unrelated men, so that others do not come to the women who are reading, whether to teach or to learn, since the Apostle also commands this. All the bishops said that those who do not observe this judgment of the council would be anathema.

### II

He likewise read: If anyone is proved not to have consumed in the church the grace of the Eucharist that he received, let him be anathema forever. All the bishops said: “It is approved.”

### III

He likewise read: Let no one fast on Sunday because of the season, persuasion, or deception; let the faithful not be absent from the churches during the days of Lent, nor dwell in the hiding places of bedrooms or mountains, those who persist in suspicion. Instead, let them observe the example and command of the priests, and let them not gather at other places for any reason involving assemblies. All the bishops said: “Let whoever commits this be anathema.”

### [Col. 0426C] IV

For twenty-one days—that is, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January until the day of Epiphany, which is the eighth day before the Ides of January—no one is permitted on any of these consecutive days to be absent from the church and remain at home, sit at a country estate, go to the mountains, or walk barefoot; instead, everyone is to assemble at the church. Whoever among those admitted does not observe this is to be anathema forever. All the bishops said: “Let him be anathema.”

### V

It was likewise said that those who have been separated from the Church by the discipline or judgment of a bishop are not to be received by other bishops. If they knowingly do this, they are not to have communion. All the bishops said: “Whoever commits this is not to have the communion of the bishops.”

### VI

He likewise read: If any cleric should voluntarily withdraw from his office because of luxury and an arrogant presumption of vanity, and should prefer to appear as a monk observing the law rather than as a cleric, he is to be expelled from the Church in such a way that he is not received unless, after pleading and earnestly entreating for a very long time, he has made satisfaction. All the bishops said: “Let it be done so.”

### VII

It was likewise read: Let no one assume for himself the title of teacher except those persons to whom it has been granted, according to what is written. All the bishops said: “It is approved.”

### VIII

It was likewise read: Virgins who have vowed themselves to God are not to be veiled unless they have reached the proven age of forty, as confirmed by the priest. All the bishops said: “It is approved.”

# The Chapters of the Council of Ilerda Begin

### [Col. 0425]

1. Concerning those who serve at the altar: that they abstain from human blood.  
2. Concerning those who procure abortions or kill their children after birth.  
3. Concerning monks: that they be ordained clerics with the abbot’s consent, and that when they are offered to the monastery they not be taken away; and concerning basilicas built by laymen.  
4. Concerning incestuous persons: that as long as they remain in the crime they be counted among the catechumens.  
5. Concerning those who serve at the altar, if they suddenly fall into bodily weakness.  
6. Concerning the person who inflicts sexual violation on a penitent widow or a religious virgin.  
7. Concerning those who bind themselves by an oath not to return to peace.  
8. If a cleric should take a servant or pupil away from the church: that he perform penance.  
9. Concerning those who have been rebaptized: how much penance they are to perform.  
10. Concerning those who, although ordered by the bishop to leave, refuse to depart from the church after their guilt has been remitted.  
11. Concerning clerics who rush into mutual killing.  
12. Concerning those ordained contrary to the canons: that they be deposed.  
13. Concerning Catholics who have handed over their children to the baptism of heretics.  
14. Concerning Catholics: that they not associate with the rebaptized.  
15. That clerics not live with unrelated women.  
16. When a priest dies, what is to be observed concerning the church’s possessions.

# The Council of Ilerda Begins

Held in the twelfth year of King Theodoric, on the eighth day before the Ides of August.

### [Col. 0427]

[Col. 0427A] **CHAPTER I.** Concerning those clerics who have been placed under necessity during sieges: it has been decreed that those who minister at the altar, administer the body and blood of Christ, or [Col. 0427B] handle the sacred vessels assigned to the service, must abstain from all human blood, even that of an enemy. If they should become involved in this, they are to be deprived for two years both of office and of communion, so that during those two years they may, according to the strength the Lord grants, atone through vigils, fasts, prayers, and almsgiving; only then are they to be restored to office 103 or to communion. This is nevertheless to be done on the condition that they not thereafter be promoted to more important offices. If they prove negligent regarding their salvation for an indefinite period, the priest retains the authority to prolong the time of their penance.

**II.** Those, however, who have attempted to kill fetuses wrongly conceived through adultery, or children already born, or who have destroyed them in their mothers’ wombs by means of potions, whether adulterers or adulteresses, are to be admitted to communion after the course of seven years, but on the condition that throughout the whole of their lives they persist in tears and humility. If they are clerics, they may not recover the ministry of their office; nevertheless, from the time they receive communion, they may participate in the choir of those singing the psalms, with its privileges. Only at the point of death, if they have mourned their crimes throughout their entire lives, are they to be granted communion.

[Col. 0427C] **III.** Concerning monks, it has seemed good that the decree known to have been established by the Synod of Agde be observed, with this addition only: when a bishop has judged certain men suitable for promotion to clerical office for the benefit of the Church, they must be ordained with the consent of the abbot. Whatever is offered from the property belonging to the monastery is not, in any way, to be touched by the bishops under diocesan law. If any layman wishes a basilica built by him to be consecrated, he must by no means attempt to remove it from diocesan jurisdiction under the pretext of its belonging to a monastery where no community is gathered and where no rule has been established by the bishop.

[Col. 0427D] **IV.** Concerning those who defile themselves with incestuous pollution: [Col. 0428A] it has seemed good that, for as long as they persist in that detestable and illicit union of the flesh, [Col. 0428B] they be admitted in the church only as far as the Masses of the catechumens; nor should they, together with those catechumens, take any food with Christians, as the Apostle commanded.

[Col. 0428B] **V.** If any of those who serve at God’s altar should suddenly fall through the weakness of the flesh, and, with the Lord looking favorably upon them, should perform worthy penance, offering to God the sacrifice of a contrite heart with the body mortified, it shall remain within the authority of the bishop either not to suspend the genuinely afflicted for long, or to separate the negligent from the body of the Church for a longer period. This is nevertheless to be done in such a way that, when they recover their places in the offices, they cannot thereafter be promoted to higher offices. If they should once again return like dogs to their vomit, they are not only to lose the dignity of their office but also are not to receive holy communion except at the point of death.

[Col. 0428C] **VI.** Whoever has violated a penitent widow or a religious virgin is to be separated from the communion and fellowship of Christians if he refuses to withdraw from her. If, however, the woman who suffered the assault returns to holy religion, the sentence of excommunication is to remain against him alone until he publicly performs penance.

**VII.** Whoever has bound himself by an oath not to return in any way to peace with someone with whom he is in dispute is to be separated for one year from communion in the blood and body of the Lord on account of perjury. He is to free himself from his guilt through almsgiving, tears, and as many fasts as he is able to undertake; but he must hasten quickly toward charity, which covers a multitude of sins.

**VIII.** No cleric shall dare to drag away, or presume to scourge, his servant or disciple who has fled for refuge to a church. If he does so, he is to be separated from the position to which he failed to show honor until he performs worthy penance.

[Col. 0428D] **IX.** Concerning those who, through apostasy, have been rebaptized after falling away without any necessity or compulsion: it has seemed good [Col. 0429A] that the decrees of the Nicene Synod known to have been enacted concerning apostates be observed in their case—that is, that they pray for seven years among the catechumens and for two years among the Catholics, and afterward, through the moderation and mercy of the bishop, communicate with the faithful in the offering of the Eucharist.

**X.** Whoever, when ordered by a priest to leave the church for any offense, contemptuously refuses to do so is to be admitted to pardon more slowly because of the offense of disobedience.

**XI.** If any clerics break out into mutual slaughter, the bishop is to exact stricter punishment from them in proportion to the dignity of their offices and the insult committed in such an excess.

**XII.** Those who until now have indiscriminately ordained clerics contrary to the decrees of the canons: may the Lord, or holy ecclesiastical charity, forgive them. But from now on, if they persist in such a practice, the canonical decree established concerning their persons is to be observed—namely, that they dare not ordain anyone thereafter—and those who are ordained henceforth are to be deposed. Those who have so far been ordained in this manner are never to be promoted.

[Col. 0429B] **XIII.** If a Catholic offers his children to be baptized in heresy, his offering is in no way to be received in the church.

**XIV.** Religious faithful are not to share food with those who have been rebaptized.

**XV.** Although the holy Fathers, in their ancient admonitions, have entirely commanded that familiarity with foreign women be avoided by the churches, it has nevertheless now seemed good to us that, if anyone is found to have such familiarity and, after a first and second warning, neglects to correct himself, he be deprived of the dignity of his office for as long as he persists in the offense. If, with God’s help, he corrects himself, he is to be restored to the sacred ministry.

[Col. 0429C] **XVI.** Although ancient canonical authority has not been silent concerning this matter, which we decree by a salutary ordinance, but has expressly commanded that, when the bishop of any church dies, no one should rush at will to seize the property he left behind or ransack the house, the priest who is present at the time of the funeral ought to secure with careful vigilance everything pertaining to its usefulness and preservation, [Col. 0430A] nevertheless, because this sanction—what is worse—is known to be violated by many clerics, so that, without the priest’s command and with every strictness of discipline set aside, they savagely invade and strip away whatever is found in the bishop’s house, we have therefore now judged that this constitution of our decree is to be guarded among us with disciplinary force.

When a bishop has died, or even while he is still in his final illness, no cleric—whatever his order, office, or rank—shall presume to take anything from the house, or attempt to seize anything recognized as belonging to the useful equipment of the house, whether movable or immovable property of the Church. He shall suppress, remove, or conceal nothing by theft or deceit. Rather, the person entrusted with the house, together with those subject to him and with the advice of one or two most faithful men, must preserve everything until a successor is appointed to the bishopric, [Col. 0430B] or provide the clerics found in the house with their customary sustenance.

The bishop appointed as successor shall arrange the affairs of the see, just as God has commanded, so that he may use them with those whom he knows to have faithfully obeyed the discipline and charity of his predecessor. If thereafter any cleric of whatever order, as stated above, is proved to have taken anything from the entire property on any pretext, or perhaps to have acquired something through deceit, he is to be condemned as guilty of sacrilege under a prolonged anathema; scarcely even a foreign communion is to be granted him. For it is harsh that those who are known to have labored in the service of the Lord with the bishop of the chief see should be in any way tormented or despised by men known to have been squatters upon and wanderers through their possessions.

[Col. 0430C] Sergius, bishop, in the name of Christ, have reread and subscribed these constitutions, according as, with God’s inspiration, they pleased us together with our brothers. Justus, in the name of Christ, have subscribed. John, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed. Peter, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed. Marulius, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed. Taurus, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed. Febrorius, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed. Gratus, bishop, sent by my lord Stephen the bishop, was present at these constitutions and have subscribed.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF VALENCE BEGIN

[Col. 0429]

[Col. 0429D] 1. That the Gospel be read after the Apostle.  
2. That, when a bishop has died, no one presume to seize anything belonging to him or to the church.  
3. That the relatives of a dying bishop take nothing of his property without the knowledge of the metropolitan and the bishops of the province.  
[Col. 0430D] 4. Concerning the funeral of a dying bishop and how he is to be buried.  
5. Concerning wandering and disobedient clerics.  
6. That no one ordain another’s cleric, and that no one be a cleric who does not promise the place to which he has been assigned.

# THE COUNCIL OF VALENCE BEGINS

Of six bishops; held in the year 533, in the fifteenth year of King Theodoric.

[Col. 0429]

[Col. 0429D] **CHAPTER I.** In the fifteenth year of King Theodoric, on the second day before the Nones of December, when the Council of Valence had assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and we were considering ecclesiastical rules while rereading the ancient canons, among other matters we judged that the following should be observed: the holy Gospels are to be read before the presentation of the gifts, during the Mass of the catechumens, after the Apostle, in the appointed order of readings, so that the saving commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ and the priest’s sermons may be heard not only by the faithful but also by catechumens and penitents and by all those who are on the other side. For we clearly know that, after hearing the preaching of bishops, some have been drawn to the faith.

**II.** It also seemed good that, when a bishop is summoned from this world at the Lord’s command, the clerics keep their grasping hands entirely away from all furnishings, or whatever exists in the house of the church or of the bishop—books, valuables, implements, small vessels, crops, flocks, animals, or absolutely any other thing—and seize nothing in the manner of thieves. If, despite the authority of the canons, they should seize anything, they are to be compelled, under the strict enforcement of the metropolitan or of all the priests of the province, to restore everything to its former condition, so that nothing necessary may be lost to the bishop or future administrator.

So that this may be observed with greater confidence while justice is maintained, according to the decrees of the Synod of Riez, when a bishop departs from the body, the bishop nearest to him is to approach him. After the customary funeral rites have been celebrated, he must immediately exercise the strictest care over that church, so that, before the future bishop is ordained, nothing may be permitted to the remaining clerics for subversion or plunder. Thus, after everything has been examined, a more certain inspection and a most faithful inventory 104, if possible, are to be completed within the octave of the deceased bishop under the supervision of the bishop presently in charge. [Col. 0431C]

Thereafter, the matter, having been properly investigated, is to be reported to the metropolitan’s notice, so that by his election a person may be appointed to administer the affairs of the church’s household who will distribute the customary stipends to the clerics and, if there should perhaps be a delay in ordaining the bishop, be able at suitable times to give the metropolitan an account of the property entrusted to him. Thus, under this salutary constitution, the clerics, fully content with their stipends, will not plunder the labors of the deceased bishop, and the future bishop will not enter a church emptied of its household with sorrow, but will rather be able to rejoice himself in what his predecessor left behind and to distribute it to others.

**III.** In the same way, notice is to be given to the parents and relatives of the deceased bishop, if he died intestate, so that they do not attempt to take possession of anything belonging to the deceased without the knowledge of the metropolitan or of the priests of the province. Otherwise, they might seize along with hereditary property something belonging to the church or mixed with it. They are to wait until the future bishop is ordained, or, if the matter should take a long time, they are to have recourse, as stated, to the metropolitan’s arrangement.

If any cleric or layman, despising the fear of God, should attempt with wicked intent to act against these holy synodal decrees, he is to be deprived both of communion and of fellowship [Col. 0432A] with the Church. For it is harsh that he should approach the one he was not afraid to strip, unless, seized by a better spirit, he ceases from his presumption and recovers forgiveness. If, however, anyone reasonably and modestly claims what is legally owed to him, neither the property nor the account is to be denied him without any penalty by the metropolitan or by the person whom he appoints.

These provisions bind all who, whether in the past or in the future, have seized and plundered church property or the property of a bishop.

**IV.** We also decree with prudent counsel that, because the funeral rites of holy bishops are often delayed through the absence of the bishop entrusted with them, so that the venerable remains of the bishop, when buried too late, are subjected to every kind of indignity, the bishop who is customarily invited to come after the death of his brother for his burial should not delay visiting him when informed that he is ill and still alive. He may thus either rejoice more fully in the priest’s recovery, or at least consult with his brother concerning the administration of his household and put his approved wishes into effect. When the bishop is departing from this world, the visiting bishop is to offer God the sacrifice presented for his commendation and then, with the greatest care, consign him to burial; nor is he to delay fulfilling the canonical provisions established above.

If, as often happens, a bishop dies suddenly and the neighboring priests are unable to arrive from a distance, the lifeless body of the priest is to remain for only one day and its accompanying night. It is not to be kept without the attendance of brothers and religious persons or the watch of those singing psalms. The priests are to place it with every care in a separate place, but it is not immediately to be buried; rather, it is to be honorably entrusted there until a bishop summoned from wherever necessary can arrive without delay and solemnly bury it himself, as is fitting. In this way an occasion for indignity will be removed and the ancient custom concerning the burial of priests will be observed.

**V.** It also seemed good that a wandering and unstable cleric, even if established in the ministry of a deacon or the office of a presbyter, who does not obey the commands of the bishop by whom he was ordained—namely, that he carry out his appointed ministry assiduously in the church assigned to him for as long as he persists in the offense—be deprived both of communion and of honor.

**VI.** No one, contrary to the decrees of the canons, shall dare to ordain another’s cleric without the consent of his bishop. Nor shall any bishop ordain anyone who has not first promised to remain attached to a particular place. By this means no one is to be permitted to deviate with impunity from ecclesiastical rule or discipline.

Celsivus, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed. Setabius, bishop, have subscribed. Benagius, bishop, have subscribed. Ampelius, bishop, have subscribed. Sallustius, archdeacon and vicar of my lord Marcellus the bishop, have subscribed.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGIN

[Col. 0431]

[Col. 0431D] 1. Concerning presbyters and deacons who father children after ordination.  
[Col. 0432D] 2. That a penitent, if necessity compels it, may become a lector or doorkeeper.  
[Col. 0433A] 3. Concerning those who marry widows, that they not become deacons.  
4. That a subdeacon who, after his wife’s death, marries another woman become a doorkeeper.  
5. That a cleric of any order who comes late to church be deposed.  
6. That a religious girl not have the familiarity of men in her house.  
7. That a cleric whose wife has sinned have authority, short of killing her, to discipline her, and not eat with her.  
8. Concerning one who has served as a soldier after baptism, that he not be permitted to the diaconate.  
9. That no professed woman or widow, when the priest is absent, perform priestly or lamp-lighting services in her house.  
[Col. 0433B] 10. That no one make a cleric of a person bound to another without the consent of his master or patron.  
11. That if a powerful man strips anyone of his property and does not return it when warned by the bishop, he be excommunicated.  
[Col. 0434A] 12. That no cleric leave his bishop and transfer himself to another.  
13. Concerning those who enter the church but do not communicate, that they be excommunicated.  
14. Concerning one who receives the Eucharist but does not consume it, that he be rejected as a sacrilegious person.  
15. Concerning those excommunicated by priests, that no one approach them.  
16. That a consecrated woman who commits adultery perform penance for ten years; if she marries, she is not to be admitted to penance unless her husband has died.  
17. That a man who has a wife, if he has a concubine, not communicate.  
18. If the widow of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon takes a husband.  
[Col. 0434B] 19. If the religious daughter of a priest or deacon sins, that she communicate only at the end of life.  
20. That no one except a bishop prepare chrism.  
21. Concerning the rules of the Catholic faith against the Priscillianists.

# THE FIRST COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGINS

Of eighteen bishops; held in the time of Honorius and Arcadius, while Stilicho was consul.

[Col. 0433]

[Col. 0433B] The bishops assembled in the church at Toledo: Patronus, Marcellus, Alitianus, Aphrodisius, Jocundus, Olympius, Severus, Astutius, Hilary, Lampadius, Eustochius, Exuperantius, Serenus, Florus, Leporius, Aurelianus, Lampiodus, Gallia, and Lucentius. This assembly was held in the town of Celenis. These are those who, in other proceedings, delivered a written judgment against the followers of Priscillian and the heresy he had established. With the presbyters seated, the deacons standing, and the others who were present gathered for the council, Patronus the bishop said:

“Since each of us has begun to do different things in our churches, and from this so many scandals have arisen that they have reached the point of schism, let us, if it pleases you, decide by common counsel what all bishops are to follow in ordaining clerics. For my part, I am pleased that what was first established by the Council of Nicaea be observed perpetually and that no departure be made from it.”

All the bishops said: “This pleases us, provided that, if anyone, after learning the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea, presumes to do anything other than what has been established and does not think that the decree must be persevered in, he be considered excommunicated unless he corrects his error through the admonition of his brothers.”

**CHAPTER I.** It has seemed good that deacons, whether upright, chaste, and of continent life, even if they have wives, be appointed to the ministry, but on this condition: if any have lived incontinent with their wives even before the prohibition established by the bishops who preceded us, they are not to be advanced to the honor of the presbyterate. If any presbyters have fathered children before the prohibition, they are not to be admitted from the presbyterate to the episcopate.

**II.** It has likewise seemed good that penitents not be admitted to the clergy, except only that, if necessity or practical use requires it, they may be assigned among the doorkeepers or among the lectors, but they are not to read the Gospels or the Apostle. If any were ordained deacons before this decree, they are to be counted among the subdeacons, but they are not to lay hands on anyone or touch sacred objects.

By “penitent” we mean one who, after baptism, having undertaken public penance for homicide or for various grave crimes and sins, has been reconciled to the altar under divine counsel.

**III.** The holy synod likewise decrees that, if a faithful lector takes another man’s widow as his wife, he is to hold no higher office but is always to remain a lector, or perhaps a subdeacon.

**IV.** If a subdeacon, after his wife has died, takes another wife, he is to be removed from the office to which he was ordained and counted among the doorkeepers or lectors, but he is not to read the Gospel or the Apostle, so that one who has served the church may not appear to serve in public offices. If he takes a third wife—which ought not even to be mentioned—he is to abstain for two years and afterward, having been reconciled through penance, communicate among the laity.

**V.** If a presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, or any cleric assigned to the church is not within the city, or in the place where the church is located, whether in fortified settlements, villages, or estates, and does not come to the church or to the daily sacrifice, he is not to be regarded as a cleric, unless, having been disciplined, he wishes to obtain pardon from the bishop through satisfaction.

**VI.** A girl dedicated to God is not to have familiarity with a confessor or with any layman unrelated to her by blood, nor is she to go alone to a banquet, except where there is an assembly of elders, honorable men, or honorable widows—where any confessor may honorably attend the meal in the presence and with the testimony of many witnesses. [Col. 0435A] She is not at all to be admitted into the houses of lectors or seen by them, unless she is their sister by blood or their half-sister through the same mother.

**VII.** It has seemed good that, if the wives of any clerics sin, lest they have still greater license to sin, their husbands receive authority—short of killing them—to guard them and bind them within their house, compelling them to salutary, not deadly, fasts. The poor clerics are to assist one another if they do not have servants. They are not to eat with those wives who have sinned, unless the women return after undertaking penance in the fear of God.

**VIII.** If anyone has served as a soldier after baptism and has taken the military cloak or belt for the killing of the faithful, even if he has committed no serious offense, he is not to receive the dignity of the diaconate if he has been admitted to the clergy.

**IX.** No professed woman or widow, when the bishop or presbyter is absent, is to perform antiphons 105 in her house with her confessor or servant. The lamp-service, however, is not to be read anywhere except in a church; or, if it is read in an estate, it is to be read in the presence of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

**X.** Clerics who are bound either through an arrangement or by belonging to a household are not to be ordained unless they are of approved life and the consent of their patron has been obtained.

**XI.** If any powerful person strips a cleric, a poorer person, or a religious person of his property, and the bishop orders him to come before him to be heard but he refuses, written notices are immediately to circulate among all the bishops of the province and among all whom they are able to reach, so that the offender is considered excommunicated until he obeys and restores what belongs to another.

**XII.** No cleric is to have the freedom to leave his own bishop and communicate with another, except perhaps with one whom another bishop willingly receives when he has departed from a heretical schism and returned to the Catholic faith. If any Catholics depart and are found, openly or secretly, in communion with those who are either excommunicated or already condemned by a sentence, they are to share, even in condemnation, the fellowship of those to whom they have chosen to go.

**XIII.** Those who enter the church and are observed never to communicate are to be admonished. If they do not communicate, they are to undertake penance; if they do communicate, they are not to abstain continually. If they fail to do so, they are to be subjected to abstinence.

**XIV.** If anyone does not consume the Eucharist received from a priest, he is to be driven away as a sacrilegious person.

**XV.** If a layman is placed under abstention, no one is to approach his house, whether cleric or religious person. Likewise, if a cleric is placed under abstention, clerics are to avoid him. If anyone is discovered speaking or dining with him, he too is to be subjected to abstention. This provision concerns the clerics who belong to his bishop and all who have been warned about the person under abstention, whether layman or cleric.

**XVI.** A consecrated woman who sins is not to be received into the church unless she has ceased from sinning. If she ceases and performs suitable penance, she is to receive communion after ten years. Before she is admitted into the church for prayer, she is not to attend the banquet of any Christian woman. If she is admitted, the woman who received her is also to be considered absent from communion; the corrupter is likewise to be bound by an equal penalty. A woman who takes a husband is not to be admitted to penance unless, while her husband is still alive, she begins to live chastely, or unless she does so after his death.

**XVII.** If a faithful man who has a wife keeps a concubine, he is not to communicate. A man who does not have a wife but keeps a concubine in place of a wife is not to be excluded from communion, provided that he is content with the union of one woman only, whether wife or concubine, whichever he prefers. If he lives otherwise, he is to be expelled until he ceases and returns to penance.

[Col. 0436B] **XVIII.** If the widow of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon takes a husband, no cleric or religious woman is to dine with her, and she is never to communicate; only at the point of death is the sacrament to come to her aid.

**XIX.** If the daughter of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon is a consecrated woman, sins, and takes a husband, and her father or mother receives her back with affection, they are to be considered excluded from communion; the father is to know that he must give an account of the matter at the council. The woman is not to be admitted to communion unless, after her husband’s death, she has performed penance. If, while he is alive, she withdraws from him and performs penance, she is in no way to receive communion except when she is at the point of death.

**XX.** Although it is observed almost everywhere that no one prepares chrism without a bishop, nevertheless, because in certain places or provinces presbyters are said to prepare chrism, it has seemed good that from this day no one except a bishop prepare chrism and send it throughout the diocese. Thus, from each church, deacons or subdeacons are to be sent to the bishop before Easter Day, so that they may bring in due time the chrism prepared by the bishop and sent for Easter.

It is clear that the bishop may prepare chrism at any time. Without the knowledge of the bishop, however, presbyters are absolutely not to presume to do anything. It has also been established that a deacon is not to chrism, but that a presbyter may do so in the bishop’s absence, though not in his presence unless instructed by him. The archdeacon is always to remember to bring this constitution to the attention of the bishops, whether present or absent, so that the bishops observe it and the presbyters do not abandon it.

Patronus, bishop, have subscribed. Marcellus, bishop, have subscribed. Aphrodisius, bishop, have subscribed. Alicianus, bishop, have subscribed. Olympius, bishop, have subscribed. Asterius, bishop, have subscribed. Lampadius, bishop, have subscribed. Serenus, bishop, have subscribed. Jocundus, bishop, have subscribed. Severus, bishop, have subscribed. Leonas, bishop, have subscribed. Hilary, bishop, have subscribed. Florus, bishop, have subscribed. Leporius, bishop, have subscribed. Aurelianus, bishop, have subscribed. Eustochius, bishop, have subscribed. Lampadius, bishop, have subscribed. Exuperantius, bishop, have subscribed.

**XXI.** The bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica, at the command of Pope Leo, composed a rule of faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillianists, and sent it to Balconius, bishop of Galicia. They themselves also established the twenty chapters of canons written above in the Council of Toledo.

## Statement of the Faith of the Same Council

We believe in one true God, the almighty Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, maker of visible things, through whom all things were made in heaven and on earth: one God, and one Trinity of the divine substance.

The Father is not the Son himself, but has a Son who is not the Father. The Son is not the Father, but the Son of God, possessing the nature of the Father. The Spirit is also the Paraclete, who is neither the Father himself nor the Son, but proceeds from the Father and the Son. [Col. 0437B]

The Father, therefore, is unbegotten; the Son is begotten; the Paraclete is not begotten but proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Father is he whose voice was heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5). The Son is he who said: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world from God” (John 16:28). The Paraclete is the Spirit of whom the Son said: “Unless I go away to the Father, the Paraclete will not come” (John 16:7).

We believe this Trinity, distinct in persons but indivisible, undifferentiated, and one in substance, power, authority, and majesty; and besides it we believe that there is no divine nature, whether of an angel, spirit, or any power that is considered God.

We therefore believe that this Son of God, God born from the Father before every beginning whatever, sanctified the womb of the virgin Mary and assumed from her a true human being generated without the seed of a man. Thus two natures—that is, divinity and flesh—came together entirely in one person, namely our Lord Jesus Christ. His body was not imaginary or that of some phantom, but solid and real; he hungered, thirsted, suffered, wept, and endured every injury to the body.

Finally, he was crucified by the Jews, buried, and rose again on the third day. He afterward lived among his disciples and, on the fortieth day after the resurrection, ascended into heaven. We call this Son of Man also the Son of God, and the Son of God also the Son of Man. We believe that there will be a resurrection of human flesh, but that the human soul is not of the divine substance or of God the Father; it is a creature created by the will of God.

[Col. 0437D] If anyone says or believes that this world was not made by almighty God, together with all its ordered structures, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that the same person is the Son and the Father, or the Paraclete, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that God the Father is the same person as the Son or the Paraclete, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that the Paraclete is either the Father or the Son, let him be anathema.

If anyone believes or says that the Son of God assumed flesh without a soul, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that Christ is unbegotten, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that divinity is begotten, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that Christ’s divinity was changeable or capable of suffering, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that there is one God of the ancient Law and another of the Gospels, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that the world was made by another God and not by the one of whom it is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that human bodies do not rise after death, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that the human soul is a portion of God or is God’s substance, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that writings other than those which the Catholic Church receives are to be held authoritative or venerated, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that there is one nature in Christ, that of divinity and flesh, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that there is something that can show itself to exist outside the divine Trinity, let him be anathema.

If anyone thinks that astrology or the mathematical arts are to be believed, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that human marriages which are permitted according to divine law are detestable, let him be anathema.

If anyone says or believes that the flesh of birds or cattle given for food is not merely to be avoided as a discipline for human beings, but is to be cursed, let him be anathema.

If anyone follows or professes the sect of Priscillian in error, so as to do anything contrary to the See of Saint Peter in saving baptism, let him be anathema.

The rule of the Catholic faith against the Priscillianists is complete. Patronus, bishop, have subscribed. Marcellianus, bishop, have subscribed. Afridius, bishop, have subscribed. The holy bishops and the others who were present at the council.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGIN

[Col. 0437]

[Col. 0437D] 1. Concerning those whom their parents from infancy devoted to the clerical office, if they later wish to marry.  
2. Concerning the cleric who transfers to another church, and the person who receives him.  
[Col. 0438D] 3. That no one from the rank of subdeacon upward have a foreign woman.  
4. That whatever clerics have held from the property of the church return to the church after their death.  
5. Concerning those who unite themselves to their nearest relatives, that they be separated from the communion of Christ.

# THE SECOND COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGINS

Held in Era 565, in the fifth year of King Amalaric.

[Col. 0439]

[Col. 0439A] Since, by the will of the Lord, we had assembled in the city of Toledo in the presence of the holy bishops, and there was discussion of the institutions of the holy Fathers and the decrees of the canons, when we had come together it seemed good to us that, if anything had not been mentioned in the ancient canons, it should be established through salutary deliberation and careful consideration. Whatever had been neglected in the earlier canons should regain the renewed disciplinary force of the ordinance, so that, while we devote the zeal of religious observance to those matters which have been decreed in councils but until now abandoned through the abuse of time, and which pertain to the worship of the faith, we may more easily obtain the mercy of God.

### Chapter I. Concerning those whom their parents, from the earliest years of infancy, placed in the clerical order or monastic life

[Col. 0439B] We likewise decree that the following be observed: as soon as they have been tonsured or entrusted to the ministry of the chosen, they are to be instructed by their superior in the church’s household, under the bishop’s supervision. But when they have completed their eighteenth year, their desire concerning the pursuit of marriage is to be examined by the bishop in the presence of the entire clergy and congregation. If, by God’s inspiration, they prefer the grace of chastity and answer that they will preserve their vow of continence without the necessity of marriage, they are to be placed, as seekers of the narrowest way, under the Lord’s gentle yoke; and, after their profession has been tested, they are to receive the ministry of the subdeaconate beginning at the age of twenty.

But if they complete their twenty-fifth year without blame and without offense, they are to be promoted to the office of the diaconate, [Col. 0439C] provided that the bishop finds them capable of fulfilling it with understanding. They must nevertheless be warned not at any time to forget their pledge and return thereafter to earthly marriages or illicit sexual unions. If they should do so, they are to be regarded by the Church as outsiders guilty of sacrilege.

As for those whom, at the time of questioning, their own desire persuades to wish to marry, we cannot withdraw the judgment granted by the bishops. Thus, when they have entered marriage at a mature age, if they promise by mutual agreement that they will renounce the works of the flesh, they may aspire to the sacred orders.

### II

Likewise, it seemed good to guard against anyone among those formed by such an education presuming, under any compelling circumstance, to leave his own church and transfer to another. [Col. 0439D] If a bishop should perhaps presume to receive him without the knowledge of his own priest, let him know that he is guilty before the whole brotherhood. For it is harsh that one should presume to receive and claim the man whom another, through rustic judgment and the offense of infancy, has stripped away.

### III

Moreover, we have decreed by a special ordinance what the ancient councils also did not leave unmentioned in all their canons: no cleric from the rank of subdeacon and above is to keep, within the fellowship of his household, any woman—whether freeborn, freedwoman, or slave. [Col. 0440A] If he has women in such service, he is to entrust them to his mother, sister, or another female relative, and whatever he has produced with his own hands is to be handed over to his lawful master.

Or, if there is no memory of kinship, accommodation in another adjoining household is to be sought, so that in every way no opportunity is allowed for a woman to enter the cleric’s house, from which some injury might bring a charge against the reputation of the innocent. Henceforth, after this warning has been given, whoever wishes to enjoy the company of any such woman must know that he will not only be removed from the clerical office or expelled from the church doors, but also deprived of communion with all Catholic clerics and laypeople, with absolutely no consolation even of conversation being left to him, so that the rust of this evil custom, once scraped away, may not be able to spread among posterity through the poison of its root. [Col. 0440B]

### IV

If any cleric is proved to have made for himself small fields or vineyards on church lands for the support of his life, he may possess them until the day of his death. After his departure from this life, however, he is to restore his right to the holy Church, in accordance with the provisions of the earlier canons. He is not to leave them by testamentary right to any heir or prospective heir, unless perhaps the bishop wishes to grant them to someone for services rendered and for the benefit of the Church.

### V

We also wisely decree that the following be guarded against: no member of the faithful is to desire to join himself in marriage to a blood relative, so far as he recognizes the lines of kinship through the succession of his lineage. [Col. 0440C] For it is written: “No man shall approach his nearest blood relation, to uncover his nakedness”; nor is the sentence without its stated consequence, for shortly afterward it adds and says: “The person who does any of these abominations shall be cut off from among his people.”

Therefore, if anyone should become a transgressor of this decree and presume to violate what is forbidden, let him recognize that he must suffer a sentence all the more severe insofar as he does not deny that the person to whom he chose to join himself is closer to him in the line of origin. He is likewise to be separated from the body of Christ and from the fellowship of the brotherhood for a period of excommunication all the longer insofar as he has been polluted by the contagion of nearer blood.

We who have subscribed to this ordinance solemnly promise, with irrefragable authority, that we will observe it. [Col. 0440D] But if anyone should presume to oppose this salutary ordinance—whether ours or that of those who are now absent from the holy synod from this province—or should negligently fail to fulfill it diligently, once convicted he is to be regarded for a time as an outsider to all fraternal charity.

In accordance with the decrees of the earlier canons, we declare that a council is to be held, if the Lord wills, at the church of our brother Bishop Montanus. Accordingly, we decree that our brother and fellow bishop Montanus, who is in the metropolitan city, is to send letters to our fellow provincial priests of the Lord, at the approaching time, summoning them to assemble in synod. [Col. 0441A]

Now, therefore, in the name of the Lord, these matters having been concluded which came before us for consultation, we give thanks to almighty God. Then, seeking divine mercy for our glorious lord King Amalric, we ask that, throughout the countless territories of his kingdom, he grant us the freedom to carry out what pertains to the worship of the faith.

Montanus, bishop, in the name of Christ: I have assented to these constitutions, reread them, and subscribed them on the day and in the year stated above.

Pancarius, bishop: I have assented to these constitutions, reread them, and subscribed them.

Canonius, bishop: I have subscribed.

Paul, bishop: I have subscribed.

Domitianus, bishop: I have subscribed.

Marracinus, bishop: I have subscribed.

Nibridius, bishop: I have subscribed.

Justus, in the name of Christ bishop of the Catholic Church of Urgell: I reread, approved, and subscribed this constitution of my fellow priests, held in the city of Toledo, when I arrived after some time had passed, without prejudice to the authority of the ancient canons.

## The Third Council of Toledo begins

In which the heresy of Arius is condemned in Spain.

[Col. 0441]

[Col. 0441B] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fourth year, during the reign of the most glorious and most pious, and most faithful to God, our lord King Reccared, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the era 627. This holy synod was held in the holy royal city of Toledo by the bishops of all Spain and Galicia who are listed below.

### Chapter I

Since the same most glorious prince had ordered all the bishops of his realm to assemble together because of the sincerity of his faith, so that they might rejoice in the Lord over his conversion and over the renewal of the Gothic people, and might give thanks to divine favor for so great a gift, the most holy prince addressed the venerable council as follows:

“I do not think it is unknown to you, most reverend priests, [Col. 0441C] that I summoned you into the presence of our serenity in order to restore the form of ecclesiastical discipline. Since, as time passed, the threatening heresy had prevented synodal affairs from being conducted throughout the whole Catholic Church, God—who was pleased through us to remove the obstacle of that same heresy—admonished us to restore ecclesiastical practice in the customary manner.

“Therefore, let it be a joy to you if, by God’s regard and through our glory, the canonical custom is brought back to its ancestral bounds. First, however, I jointly admonish and exhort you to devote yourselves to fasts, vigils, and prayers, so that the canonical order which long and lasting forgetfulness had withdrawn from priestly minds—an order which our age admits that it does not know—may by divine gift once again be disclosed to you.”

After this, while the entire council gave thanks to God and the most religious prince and acclaimed him with praises, a three-day fast was proclaimed. But when, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, the priests of God were present in one assembly, and each priest, after the prayer had been offered, had taken his seat in the appropriate place, behold, the serene prince appeared in their midst and joined himself with the priests of God in prayer. Filled with divine inspiration, he began to speak as follows:

“I do not believe that it is hidden from your holiness how long Spain had labored in the error of the Arians, nor that only a few days had passed after the death of our father when your blessedness learned that we had been joined to the holy Catholic faith. We believe that you experienced, in general, great and eternal joy. Therefore, venerable fathers, [Col. 0442B] we have gathered you here to conduct this synod, so that you yourselves may offer eternal thanks to the Lord for all those who have recently come to Christ.

“Whatever it was necessary for us to undertake in words before your priesthood concerning the faith and hope that we possess, we have written and presented in this volume. Let it be read aloud in your midst, and, having been examined in synodal judgment, let it shine throughout all succeeding time as the glorious testimony of our faith.”

The volume of the holy faith was then received by all the priests of God, when the king offered it, and, as the notary proclaimed it, it was read aloud in a clear voice.

### II

Although almighty God has granted us to undertake divine worship for the welfare of the peoples of our kingdom, and has entrusted the governance of not a few nations to the care of our kingship, we nevertheless remember that we are constrained by the condition of mortals. Nor can we otherwise merit the happiness of future blessedness unless we account ourselves devoted to the worship of the true faith and please our Creator with the confession of salvation that is worthy of him.

For this reason, the more we are exalted by royal glory over our subjects, the more watchful we ought to be in those matters which come from God, whether to increase our hope or to care for the peoples entrusted to us by God. Otherwise, what can we offer to divine omnipotence in return for so many bestowals of benefits, when everything belongs to him and he has no need of any of our goods, except that we believe in him with complete devotion just as he wished to make himself known through the sacred Scriptures and commanded us to believe?

That is, we are to confess that there is a Father who begot from his own substance a Son who is equal and coeternal with him. Yet the Son is not himself both begotten and unbegotten: the person who begot is one, the Father; the person who was begotten is another, the Son. Nevertheless, both subsist in the divinity as one substance: the Father is the one from whom the Son exists, while he himself exists from no other.

The Son has a Father, yet, without beginning or diminution, he subsists in that divinity in which he is coequal and coeternal with the Father. The Holy Spirit also must be confessed and proclaimed by us to be from the Father and to proceed from the Son, and to be of one substance with the Father and the Son. He is the third person in the Trinity, yet he shares with the Father and the Son the essence of divinity.

For this holy Trinity is one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. By his goodness the created nature of humanity was indeed made good; yet, through the form of human condition assumed by the Son, we are restored from a condemned race to our original blessedness. And just as the sign of true salvation is to perceive the Trinity in unity and unity in the Trinity, so the judgment will be complete if we hold the same belief within the universal Church and preserve apostolic unity, established upon the apostolic foundation.

You, priests of God, must nevertheless remember the many afflictions that the Catholic Church has endured throughout Spain up to this time from the opposing party: the Catholics steadfastly held and defended the unity of their faith, while the heretics, with more obstinate hostility, strove for their own faithlessness. As the matter itself makes clear, the Lord stirred up one inflamed by the fervor of faith [Col. 0443B] so that, once the obstinacy of unbelief had been driven away and the fury of discord removed, I might recall to the knowledge of the faith and to fellowship with the Catholic Church the people who, under the name of religion, had been serving error.

For the entire illustrious Gothic nation is present—a people distinguished by the courage of nearly all nations. Although, through the depravity of its teachers, it had until now been separated from the faith or from the unity of the Catholic Church, it now, with complete agreement, participates in the communion of that Church which receives the multitude of diverse nations into its maternal bosom and nourishes them at the breasts of charity. Of this the prophet’s song says: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matthew 21:13) “for all nations.”

Nor does the conversion of the Goths alone add to the fullness of our reward. Indeed, we also brought back to the origin of truth, through our zeal, the innumerable multitude of the Suevic people, whom we had subjected to our kingdom with heavenly protection, though they had been led into heresy by another’s judgment.

Therefore, most holy fathers, I offer these most noble peoples, who through us have been brought into the Lord’s gains of grace, as a holy and acceptable sacrifice to the eternal God through your hands. I shall have an unfading crown, or joy in the reward of the just, if these peoples, who through our diligence have hastened to the unity of the Church, remain founded and established in that same unity.

For just as, by divine providence, it was our care to draw these peoples into the unity of Christ and the Church, so let it be your teachability to instruct them in Catholic doctrines, so that, instructed in the complete knowledge of the truth, they may know to reject entirely their destructive errors, retain the path of the true faith in charity, and embrace the communion of the Catholic Church with more eager desire.

Moreover, just as I confidently believe that it is easy to attain pardon for a people so illustrious that until now it did not know and had gone astray, so I do not doubt that it is more serious if, after recognizing the truth, it holds it with a doubtful heart and—God forbid—turns its eyes away from the manifest light.

Therefore I recognized that it was greatly necessary for your blessedness to assemble together, holding fast to the Lord’s sentence in which he says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” I believe that the blessed divinity of the Holy Trinity is present at this holy council. [Col. 0444A] Therefore, as though before the sight of God, I have set forth in your midst the faith that I profess, fully conscious of the sentence that says: “I have not hidden your mercy from the great congregation.”

I have also heard the apostle Paul instructing his disciple Timothy: “Fight the good fight of faith; take hold of eternal life, to which you were called, having confessed the good confession before many witnesses” (1 Timothy 6:12). For true is the sentence of our Redeemer from the Gospel, in which he says that “whoever confesses me before men, I will confess before the Father,” and that “whoever denies me, I will deny” (Matthew 10:33).

It is expedient for us to profess with our mouth what we believe in our heart, according to the heavenly command which says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

Therefore, just as I anathematize Arius, with all his doctrines and accomplices, who asserted that the only-begotten Son of God was degenerate from the substance of the Father, denied that he was begotten by the Father, and said that he had been created from nothing, and just as I anathematize all the counsels of the wicked which they instituted against the holy Council of Nicaea, so, to the honor and praise of God, I observe the holy faith of the Council of Nicaea and honor what the holy episcopal synod of 318 bishops wrote against that same plague, Arius, in defense of the right faith.

I therefore embrace and hold the faith of the 150 bishops assembled at Constantinople, who slew Macedonius, who diminished the substance of the Holy Spirit and separated it from the unity and essence of the Father and the Son, with the sword of truth.

I likewise believe and honor the faith of the First Synod of Ephesus, which was issued against Nestorius and his teaching. Similarly, I reverently receive with the Catholic Church the faith of the Council of Chalcedon, which it set forth with complete holiness and learning against Eutyches and Dioscorus.

I also observe with equal veneration the councils of all venerable orthodox priests which do not differ in purity of faith from the four synods written above.

Let your reverence therefore hasten to attach this faith of ours to the canonical records, so that the faith which the bishops, the religious, and the leaders of our people have believed in the Catholic Church may be carefully read. Let it, renewed and strengthened by its written text and by their subscriptions, be preserved for future times as a testimony before God and all the faithful.

The peoples whom we strike with royal power in God’s name, and who, having abandoned their ancient error, have received the Paraclete—the Holy Spirit—within God’s Church through the anointing of the most holy chrism or through the laying on of hands, confess him to be one and equal with the Father and the Son. These peoples have been gathered by God’s gift into the bosom of the holy Catholic Church.

But if any of them should refuse to believe this confession and our holy profession, let them receive the wrath of God with an eternal anathema, so that their destruction may be a joy to the faithful and an example to unbelievers.

In agreement with this confession of mine, with the constitutions of the holy Scriptures and councils, I have subscribed with complete sincerity of heart, as a testimony before God.

[Col. 0445A] **The Faith of the Council of Nicaea**

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us and for our salvation descended and was incarnate, became man, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead.

And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was when he was not,” and “Before he was born he was not,” and who say that he was made from things that did not exist, or that the Son of God is of another substance or subsistence, and is mutable and changeable, the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

**The Creed of the 150 Fathers of the Council of Constantinople**

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible.

And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. [Col. 0445C]

For us and for our salvation he descended, and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; he became man, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. He will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom shall have no end.

And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is to be worshiped and glorified together, who spoke through the prophets.

One Catholic and apostolic Church.

We confess one baptism for the remission of sins. We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

**Likewise, the Treatise of the Council of Chalcedon**

[Col. 0445D]

This cautious and salutary symbol of divine grace would indeed have been sufficient for the fullest recognition and confirmation of piety. For it teaches a perfect doctrine concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and faithfully manifests the Lord’s incarnation to those who receive it.
