But since those who strive to destroy the proclamation of truth give birth to certain innovations of their own heresy—some daring to corrupt the divine dispensation carried out for us and denying to the Virgin the utterance concerning virgin birth; others introducing mixtures of confusions and senselessly composing one nature of flesh and divinity, monstrously proclaiming through such confusion that the divine nature of the only-begotten is passible—therefore the holy and great universal synod, wishing to exclude every device set against the truth, teaches and establishes the ancient proclamation as immovable, and above all decrees that the undefiled faith of the 318 holy fathers remain intact.

And because of those who oppose the Holy Spirit, it confirms the teaching concerning the substance of the Holy Spirit handed down by the 150 fathers who met somewhat later in the city of Constantinople. They also made this known to everyone—not because anything had been lacking in what preceded, but by adding their understanding concerning the Holy Spirit against those who strive to deprive him of the dominion of deity, and by manifesting it more fully through the testimonies of Scripture.

For those who attempt to corrupt the mystery of the dispensation and shamelessly proclaim that the one born from the holy Virgin was a mere man, it recalls the synodical letters of the most blessed Cyril, formerly priest of the Church of Alexandria, written both to Nestorius and to the others throughout the East, appropriate and concordant with one another: some for the refutation of Nestorian madness, others for interpreting the understanding of those who receive the salutary symbol with religious zeal.

Along with these, we also remember the letter of the holy and most blessed Leo, archbishop of the first see, written to Flavian, to destroy Eutyches’ wickedness completely. It agrees with the confession of the great Peter and, as a common document against those who do not glorify correctly, it clearly adds confirmation of the Catholic religion.

It curses those who strive to divide the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation into two sons; it rejects those who argue for a mixture or confusion of Christ’s two natures; it casts far away those who, in their madness, assert that the form he assumed for us was heavenly or of some other substance; and it anathematizes those who fabricate two natures before the union but one after the union.

Therefore, agreeing with the holy fathers, we are likewise taught, with harmonious voice, to confess one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same perfect God, truly God, in unity; the same true God and man, consisting of a rational soul and a body; according to divinity, of one nature with the Father; according to humanity, the same of one nature with us, like us in all things except sin; begotten from the Father before the ages according to divinity; and in these last days, for us and for our salvation, the same born from Mary the virgin, Mother of God, according to humanity.

We confess one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, only-begotten, recognized in two natures without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation. The distinction of the natures is in no way removed because of the union; rather, the property of each nature is preserved, and the two come together in one person and one state of being. He is not to be divided or separated into two persons, but is one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, only-begotten, true God, Jesus Christ, just as the prophets taught us concerning him from the beginning and he himself instructed us, and as the symbol of the fathers handed down to us.

Having ordered these matters with every subtlety and diligence, the holy and universal synod decreed that no one may produce, write, believe, separate, or teach any other faith.

But if any should dare either to arrange another faith, or to produce or hand down another creed to those wishing to turn to the knowledge of the truth, whether from the gentiles, the Jews, or any heretics whatsoever—if they are bishops or clerics, we decree that the bishops be strangers to the episcopate and the clerics to the clergy. [Col. 0447A] If they are monks, laypeople, or clerics, let them be struck with anathema.

I, King Reccared, holding this holy faith and confession, which the Catholic Church throughout the whole world confesses as one, in my heart and confirming it with my mouth, have subscribed with my right hand, God protecting me.

I, Badda, glorious queen, have believed and received this faith; with my own hand and with all my heart I have subscribed.

Then the entire council acclaimed the praises of God and the favor of the prince:

“Glory to God the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, whose care it is to provide peace and unity for the holy Catholic Church.

“Glory to our Lord Jesus Christ, who gathered the Catholic Church from all nations at the price of his blood.

“Glory to our Lord Jesus Christ, who joined so illustrious a people to the unity of the true faith and established one flock and one shepherd.

“To whom does an eternal reward from God belong, if not to the truly Catholic King Reccared? To whom does an eternal crown from God belong, if not to the truly orthodox King Reccared? To whom do present and eternal glory belong, if not to the lover of God, King Reccared?

“He is the gatherer of new peoples into the Church; he truly deserves apostolic reward, for he has fulfilled an apostolic office. Let him be beloved by God and by all, who has glorified God so wondrously on earth, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit forever and ever.”

**Likewise, the confession of faith of the bishops, presbyters, and leaders of the Gothic people who subscribed below**

At the command and order of the entire venerable council, one of the Catholic bishops addressed the bishops, religious clerics, and elders converted from the Arian heresy, beginning with these words:

“We are compelled by the care of our office and by the admonition of the most faithful and glorious prince carefully to inquire of your charity what you condemn in the heresy and what you believe within the holy Catholic Church. For, as the Psalmist says, we speak with the Lord beginning in confession.

“It is best, and fitting for your salvation, to confess openly what you believe and, in the hearing of all, to anathematize what you have rejected. Then you will be able most rightly to become participants in the faith of the Gospel and the apostolic see, if you begin that same Catholic faith with a Catholic confession and strengthen it by your own subscription.

“And just as you are already known to God in conscience for your good confession, so you should also signify to your neighbors that you are members of Christ’s body. Then our lowliness will never suspect anything doubtful or unfaithful concerning your brotherhood, once it has become clear that you condemn the plague of Arian faithlessness with all its doctrines, rules, offices, communion, and books, and that, stripped of the contagion of the detestable heresy, you have been renewed within God’s Church, as it were in the splendid garment of the brightness of the true faith.”

Then all the bishops, together with their clerics, and the leaders of the Gothic people said with common agreement:

“Although we have already done what your fatherhood and brotherhood wish to hear from us, and what you ask us to do, at the time of our conversion, when on this day we followed our glorious lord King Reccared and passed over to the Church and anathematized the Arian faithlessness with all its superstitions, casting them away together, nevertheless we are now eager not only to perform most readily these same things that you request, in the charity and devotion which we remember that we owe to God and to the holy Catholic Church, but also to do whatever else you discern to be fitting for the faith and persuade us to undertake in charity.

“For the love of the right faith once brought us into this devotion to the faith, so that we shall hold whatever your brotherhood reveals to us more truly, and confess it with an unrestricted profession.

“Therefore, whoever desires still to hold the faith and communion that came from Arius and was retained down to us, and does not condemn it with the full intention of his heart, let him be anathema.

“Whoever denies that the Son of God, the Lord Jesus, was begotten without beginning from the substance of the Father, and that he is equal to the Father or consubstantial with him, let him be anathema.

“Whoever does not believe in the Holy Spirit or does not believe that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, and does not say that he is coeternal and coessential with the Father and the Son, let him be anathema.

“Whoever does not distinguish the persons in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and does not acknowledge the substance of one divinity, let him be anathema.

“Whoever asserts that the Son of God, our Lord Jesus, and the Holy Spirit are, according to divinity, lesser than the Father, separates them by degrees, or says that they are creatures, let him be anathema.

“Whoever does not believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance, omnipotence, and eternity, let him be anathema.

“Whoever says that the Son does not know what God the Father knows, let him be anathema.

“Whoever assigns a beginning to the Son of God and to the Holy Spirit, let him be anathema.

“Whoever dares to profess that the Son of God, according to his divinity, is visible or passible, let him be anathema.

“Whoever does not believe that the Holy Spirit is, like the Father and the Son, true God almighty, let him be anathema.

“Whoever holds the Catholic faith and communion anywhere other than in the Church which holds and likewise honors the decrees of the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon, let him be anathema.

“Whoever separates or divides the Father and the Son in honor, glory, or divinity, let him be anathema.

“Whoever does not believe that the Son and the Holy Spirit, together with the Father, are to be glorified and honored, [Col. 0449A] let him be anathema.

“Whoever does not say, ‘Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,’ let him be anathema.

“Whoever believes or has believed that the sacrilege of rebaptism is a good work, and practices it, let him be anathema.

“Whoever possesses the detestable booklet issued by us in the twelfth year of King Leovigild, in which the Romans’ conversion to the Arian heresy is contained, and in which glory is given to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit, and in which our wrongly established teachings are contained, let him be anathema forever.”

For we confess that we were converted from the Arian heresy to the Catholic Church with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind. Let no one doubt that we and our successors erred in the Arian heresy and have now learned the evangelical and apostolic faith within the Catholic Church.

Therefore, the holy faith which our most religious lord disclosed in the midst of the council and subscribed with his own hand—we also hold, confess, and receive it. We permit it to be preached and taught among the peoples.

This is the true faith, which, because the whole Church holds it throughout the entire world, is believed and recognized to be Catholic. Whoever does not approve, or should not approve, this faith, let him be anathema—*maranatha* (“Our Lord, come”)—at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Whoever rejects the faith of the Council of Nicaea and of the 150 bishops of Constantinople, and does not affirm it to be true, let him be anathema.

Whoever does not hold the faith of the First Synod of Ephesus and of Chalcedon, and does not delight in them, let him be anathema.

Whoever does not receive the councils of all orthodox bishops that agree with the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, let him be anathema.

Therefore, with their anathema, we subscribe with our own hands this condemnation of the faithlessness of Arian communion and of all the councils that fostered the Arian heresy.

As for the constitutions of the holy councils of Nicaea, Ephesus, Constantinople, and Chalcedon, which we heard with the greatest gratitude, we have approved by our agreement that they are true, and we have subscribed them with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind. We judge that nothing can be clearer for the knowledge of truth than the authority contained in the councils named above.

Concerning the Trinity and the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, nothing more true or clearer has ever been or can ever be demonstrated by these councils. [Col. 0449D] Concerning the mystery of the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God for the salvation of the human race—by which the true assumption of human nature without the contagion of sin, and the fullness of the divinity remaining incorrupt within him, are proved—these councils make sufficiently clear the truth to be believed by us without any doubt: neither nature is destroyed, and one person of our Lord Jesus Christ exists from both.

If anyone should ever attempt to corrupt, alter, or pervert this holy faith, or should wish to separate or withdraw himself from that same faith or Catholic communion—which, by God’s mercy, we have recently attained—let him be eternally liable before God and the whole world to the charge of faithlessness.

But may the holy Catholic Church flourish most peacefully throughout the whole world and excel in the holiness and power of its teaching.

If there are any within it who have entered into communion with it, they will hear, placed at the right hand of the Father: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

But if any have departed from it, undermined its faith, and rejected its communion, they will hear from the divine mouth on the day of judgment: “Depart from me, accursed ones; I do not know you. Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Therefore, let whatever is condemned through this Catholic faith be condemned in heaven and on earth, and let whatever is accepted through this faith be accepted in heaven and on earth, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belongs glory forever and ever.

**The Creed of the 318 Fathers of the Council of Nicaea**

[Col. 0450B]

We believe in one Lord God, the almighty Father, creator of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousios* with the Father, that is, of the same substance as the Father; through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. He, for us and for our salvation, descended and was incarnate, was made man, suffered, and rose again on the third day; he ascended into heaven and from there will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit [Col. 0450C].

But the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes those who say that “there was when he was not,” or that “before he was born he was not,” or that he was made from things that did not exist, or that he exists from another substance or subsistence, or who say that the Son of God is changeable or alterable.

## Creed of the 150 Fathers of the Council of Constantinople

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousios* with the Father, that is, of the same substance as the Father [Col. 0450D]. Through him all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. For our salvation he descended and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, was made man, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, and rose again on the third day. He ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead. His kingdom will have no end.

And in the Lord, the life-giving Spirit, proceeding from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is to be worshiped and glorified, who spoke through the prophets; in one, catholic, and apostolic Church. I confess one baptism for the remission of sins. We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

## Treatise of the Council of Chalcedon. Subscription of the Bishops

[Col. 0451A]

This most careful symbol of divine grace, as stated above, would indeed have sufficed for the fullest recognition and confirmation of piety. Anastasius, bishop in the name of Christ, anathematizing the heresy of the Arian doctrine condemned above, have subscribed with my own hand, with all my heart, to this holy catholic faith which I believed when I came into the catholic Church.

Murila, bishop in the name of Christ, anathematizing the heresy of the Arian doctrine, as above.

Vuiligiscus, bishop in the name of Christ: anathema.

Sumnila, bishop in the name of Christ: anathema.

Cardingus, bishop in the name of Christ, bishop of the city of Tui: anathema.

Beccila, bishop in the name of Christ, bishop of the city of Lugo [Col. 0451B]: anathema.

Arbitrus, bishop in the name of Christ, bishop of the city of Porto: anathema.

Eruiscius, bishop in the name of Christ, bishop of the city of Ourense: anathema.

Likewise the remaining 109 presbyters and deacons converted from the Arian heresy subscribed.

The mark of Gussinus, an illustrious and distinguished man.

I, Fonsa, an illustrious man, anathematizing, have subscribed.

I, Afrila, an illustrious man, anathematizing, have subscribed.

I, Abila, an illustrious man, anathematizing, have subscribed.

I, Flavi, an illustrious man, have subscribed.

Likewise all the elders of the Goths subscribed.

After the confession and subscription of all the bishops and of the elders of the entire Gothic people, our most glorious lord Reccared the king addressed the priests of God as follows, for the simultaneous preparation and confirmation of the practices of ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 0451C]:

“Royal care ought to be extended and directed to such a degree that it is clearly capable of comprehending the full measure of age and knowledge. For just as royal power stands forth more gloriously in human affairs, so its foresight ought also to be greater in looking after the welfare of its fellow provincials.

“Now, most blessed priests, we do not devote our diligence only to those matters by which the peoples placed under our rule may be governed and live in the greatest peace; with Christ’s help we also extend ourselves to consider heavenly things, and we strive not to be ignorant of what makes peoples faithful.

“Moreover, if all human strength must be exerted to set limits to human conduct and to restrain the fury of the insolent by royal power; if we ought to provide assistance for the cultivation of quiet and peace [Col. 0451D], then much more care must be applied to desire and contemplate divine things, to yearn for what is lofty, and, after drawing peoples back from error, to show them the truth of serene light.

“For this is how one acts who intends to be rewarded many times by God. This is how one listens who increases what has been entrusted to him, when he is told: ‘Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return.’

“Therefore, since your blessedness has now reviewed in full the form of our faith and confession, and since the faith and confession both of the priests and of our nobles have likewise become evident to your holiness, our authority has decided, humbly beseeching God, to institute the following as necessary for the firmness of the catholic faith: for the strengthening of the recent conversion of our people [Col. 0452A], all the churches of Spain and Galicia shall observe this rule: at every time of sacrifice, before the communion of the body and blood of Christ, they shall unanimously recite aloud the most sacred creed of faith, according to the custom of the eastern regions. Thus the people may first confess what belief they hold, and then, with hearts purified by faith, present themselves to receive the body and blood of Christ.

“For while this decree is perpetually preserved in the Church of God, the faith of the faithful is strengthened through care, and the faithlessness of unbelievers, stirred by what is repeatedly recited, recognizes what the catholic Church holds and believes.

“Therefore, among all the chapters which your holiness must still add to the ecclesiastical regulations, propose this, out of reverence for and firmness of the holy faith: that which our serenity, instructed by God, has decreed concerning the recitation of the creed. For the future, however, with your clemency in agreement, settle the prevention of insolent conduct by stricter judgments; prohibit by firm discipline what ought not to be done, and establish immovably what ought to be done.”

## The Chapters of the Same Council Begin

1. That the statutes of councils and the decrees of the Roman bishops be observed.

2. That the creed be recited in all churches on Sunday.

3. That no one alienate church property except in case of necessity.

4. That a bishop be permitted to make one of the churches of his parish a monastery [Col. 0452C].

5. That priests and Levites not live with their wives.

6. That a church slave manumitted by a bishop never depart from the church’s patrimony, and that the freedmen of others be defended by the bishop.

7. That the divine Scriptures be read at the bishop’s table.

8. That clerics from the fisc’s household not be given away by the prince.

9. That the churches of the Arians remain under the catholic bishop in whose diocese they are located.

10. That no one inflict violence upon widows on account of chastity, and that a woman not marry a man against her will.

11. That a powerful person do penance.

12. Concerning those who seek penance: if the person is a man, he is first to be tonsured; if a woman, she is first to change her clothing [Col. 0452D].

13. That clerics who seek secular judges be excommunicated.

14. Concerning the Jews.

15. That fiscal slaves who build a church provide it with an endowment.

16. That bishops, together with judges, destroy idols, and that masters prohibit idolatry to their slaves.

17. That bishops, together with judges, correct those who kill their children with stricter discipline.

18. That a synod be held once a year, with judges and fiscal officials present.

19. That the church and its possessions belong to the bishop’s administration [Col. 0453A].

20. That a bishop not impose forced labor or levies in his diocese.

21. That judges not compel clerics or church slaves to perform their forced labor.

22. That the bodies of religious persons be escorted only with psalm-singing.

23. That *ballimathiae* [probably dances] be prohibited at the feasts of the saints.

# THE DECREES OF THE COUNCIL BEGIN

## Chapter I

After the condemnation of the Arian heresy and the exposition of the holy catholic faith, this holy council decrees:

Because in some churches throughout Spain the canonical order has been neglected, whether through the pressure of heresy or of paganism, while permission to transgress abounded and the choice of discipline was denied [Col. 0453B], while every excess was defended by the patronage of heresy and the abundance of an evil age kept the rigor of discipline far away, now that peace has been restored to Christ’s Church through mercy, let what the authority of the ancient canons prohibits be forbidden again as discipline rises, and let everything that it commands be carried out. Let the enactments of all councils, together with the synodical letters of the holy Roman bishops, remain in force.

Henceforth no unworthy person shall aspire to ecclesiastical honors contrary to the statutes of the canons. Nothing shall be done contrary to what the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, decreed ought not to be done; and whoever presumes to do so shall be restrained by the severity of the earlier canons.

## II

Out of reverence for and exaltation of the most holy and undefiled faith of Christ, and for the strengthening [Col. 0453C] and support of the feeble minds of human beings—which often tend to stray from the way of truth, partly through the fault of ignorance, since we are naturally born darkened from the very beginning of life, and partly because they have been corrupted by an unhappy upbringing, so that they sometimes disdain, at great cost to the soul, what right reason advises, natural instinct teaches, and the purity of truth urges us to follow—

the rational soul, that noble creation of God and outstanding work of the most holy Trinity, bearing within itself traces of its Creator and therefore bound to be raised through true understanding toward love of its Creator, is instead enveloped in the darkness of ignorance and turned toward the depravity of heresy. It abandons the true worship of its Creator and serves foreign gods.

Therefore, to confront these evils, so that the cloud of error may be driven far away, the splendor of the truth and of the one faith may shine forth [Col. 0453D], and the beauty of purity and of the unfailing way may be implanted in human minds—through which the whole affection of the soul may be raised toward its God, and, seized by desire for him, the mind may turn the sharpness of its eyes through prudent inquiry wholly toward the inextinguishable light of truth, which is God, without whose attainment the mind does nothing but grow blind, stray, and be driven away from the goal of happiness—

the synod, with the counsel of the most pious and glorious King Reccared, decrees that throughout all the churches of Spain and Galicia, according to the form of the eastern churches and of the Council of Constantinople—that is, the creed of the 150 bishops—be recited, and that it be proclaimed aloud before the Lord’s Prayer is said, so that the true faith may be manifest and have its testimony, and so that the hearts of the people, purified by faith, may approach to partake beforehand of the body and blood of Christ [Col. 0454A].

## III

This holy synod grants no bishop permission to alienate church property, since this is also prohibited by the more ancient canons. If, however, they give something that does not burden the church’s welfare, for the support of monks or of churches belonging to their parish, let it remain valid. They are permitted, while preserving the rights of the Church, to provide for the needs of pilgrims, clerics, and the poor whatever they are able to provide at the time.

## IV

If a bishop wishes to dedicate one of the parish churches under his authority as a monastery, so that a community of monks may live there according to the rule, he shall have permission to do so with the consent of his council [Col. 0454B]. If he also gives that place something from the church’s possessions for their sustenance, provided that it causes no detriment to the church, the gift shall remain secure. The holy council gives its consent to the establishment of this good work.

## V

The holy council has learned that bishops, presbyters, and deacons who have come from heresy are still joined to wives through carnal desire. Therefore, so that this may not happen in the future, it is decreed, as is also contained in the earlier canons, that they may not live in a lustful association. Rather, while the marriage bond between them remains, they shall have a common concern for the good, but shall not live under one roof. Or, if virtue permits, he shall arrange for his wife to live in another house, so that chastity may have a good testimony before God and human beings [Col. 0454C].

If anyone, after this agreement, chooses to live obscenely with his wife, he shall not even be permitted to remain a lector. Those who have always lived under ecclesiastical canon, if, contrary to the commands of the ancients, they keep women in their cells whose presence could generate suspicion of disgrace, shall indeed be disciplined canonically; but the women’s property shall be sold by the bishops, and the proceeds themselves distributed to the poor.

## VI

Concerning freedmen, the holy synod decrees that if any presbyters or deacons have been made free by bishops according to the manner in which the ancient canons grant permission, they shall be free; nevertheless, both they as clerics and those born from them shall not depart from the church’s protection. Those also who have been handed over to freedom by others and entrusted to churches shall be gathered under the bishop’s protection. The bishop shall ask the prince that they not be given to anyone [Col. 0454D].

## VII

Out of reverence for God and the priests, the entire holy synod decrees that, since idle tales are often introduced during meals, a reading from the divine Scriptures shall be included at every priestly banquet. Through this, souls are built up toward goodness and unnecessary stories are prevented.

## VIII

At the command and with the consent of the Lord Reccared, the priestly council decrees that no one dare seek from the prince clerics from the fisc’s household as gifts. Rather, they shall regularly render to the Church of God, to which they are bound for as long as they live, the tribute owed in respect of their own persons.

## IX

By decree of this council it is established that the churches [Col. 0455A] which were formerly in the Arian heresy but are now catholic shall belong, together with their possessions, to those bishops to whom the parishes in which those churches are founded appear to belong.

## X

For the prudent advancement of chastity, which ought especially to benefit from the council’s exhortation, and with the consent of our glorious lord King Reccared, this holy council affirms that widows who wish to do so shall maintain chastity, and that no widow shall be compelled to enter marriage. If, however, before professing continence, they choose to marry, they may marry those whom they freely choose to have as husbands. The same condition shall apply to virgins: they shall not be compelled to take husbands against the will of their parents or their own will.

If anyone impedes the resolve to chastity of a widow or virgin, he shall be considered excluded from holy communion and from the thresholds of the church [Col. 0455B].

## XI

Because we have learned that in certain churches of Spain people do penance for their sins not according to the canon but in a most shameful manner, and that whenever they wish to sin they demand reconciliation from the priests again and again, the holy council decrees, to restrain so execrable a presumption, that penance be given according to the form of the ancient canons.

That is, the person who repents of his deed shall first be suspended from communion and placed among the other penitents, frequently returning for the laying on of hands. Once the period of satisfaction has been completed, the priest, as his pastoral judgment approves, shall restore him to communion [Col. 0455C]. Those who relapse into their former vices either during the period of penance or after reconciliation shall be condemned according to the severity of the earlier canons.

## XII

Whoever, healthy or ill, asks a bishop or presbyter for penance: the bishop and presbyter shall observe this above all—that if the person is a man, whether healthy or ill, he first tonsures him or makes him change his clothing for sackcloth and ashes, and then gives him penance.

If the person is a woman, he shall not accept her for penance unless she has first been veiled or has changed her clothing. For often, when laymen carelessly give penance to women, they relapse after receiving penance into deeds that must again be mourned.

## XIII

A long-standing presumption has opened the way to illicit attempts to such an extent that clerics drag their fellow clerics before public courts after abandoning their own bishop [Col. 0455D]. Therefore we decree that no one presume to do this in the future. If anyone presumes to do so, he shall lose the case and be excluded from communion.

## XIV

Our assembly has ordered that this be inserted among the canons: Jews may not have Christian wives or concubines, nor purchase a Christian slave for their own use. The children born from such a union must be taken to baptism.

No public offices shall be assigned to them by which they might be given an opportunity to inflict punishment upon Christians. If any Christians have been defiled by them with the rite of Judaism, or even circumcised, they shall return to freedom and to the Christian religion without repayment of the price [Col. 0456A].

## XV

If any of the fisc’s slaves should happen to build churches and endow them from their poverty, the bishop shall arrange for these churches to be confirmed by royal authority through his petition.

## XVI

Since throughout almost all Spain and Galicia the sacrilege of idolatry has become widespread, the holy synod, with the consent of the most glorious prince, has ordained that every priest in his own place, together with the judge, diligently investigate this sacrilege throughout the territory and not delay in eradicating whatever is found. All who gather for such an error shall be restrained without distinction by whatever punishment they can impose.

If they neglect this, they shall know that both of them will incur the danger of excommunication [Col. 0456B]. If any masters neglect to root out this evil from their property and refuse to prohibit their household from it, they too shall be expelled from communion by the bishop.

## XVII

When many complaints were being brought to the ears of the holy council, among other matters an act of such cruelty was reported that the ears of faithful priests could not endure it: in certain parts of Spain, parents, eager for fornication and alien to piety, kill their own children.

If they are weary of having numerous children, they ought first to restrain themselves from fornication; for since marriages are joined for the propagation of offspring, those who kill their own children show that they took wives not for children but for lust, and are held guilty of both parricide and fornication [Col. 0456C].

This abomination was therefore brought to the attention of our glorious lord King Reccared, whose glory deigned to command the judges of those regions to work diligently with the priest to remove so great a crime and, having exercised severity, to prohibit it.

Accordingly, the holy synod also addresses the priests of those places where the enormity of this crime is committed, commanding them to investigate the same crime more carefully together with the judge and to prohibit it by stricter discipline, without capital punishment.

## XVIII

This holy and universal synod decrees that, while the authority of the earlier canons remains—which ordered councils to be convened twice a year—the bishops, because of the length of the journey and the poverty of the churches of Spain, shall assemble once a year at a place chosen by the metropolitan [Col. 0456D].

The judges of the regions, or the administrators of the fiscal estates, shall, by decree of our lord, meet together with the council of the priests in the autumn, on the day of the Kalends of November, so that they may learn how piously, justly, and humanely they ought to deal with the peoples. They must not oppress them with unjust taxes and excessive exactions, but rather, moved by compassion, defend them from burdens, as is fitting for good protectors of the people. Nor should they burden either private persons or the fisc with forced labor or unnecessary works.

According to the king’s admonition, the bishops are observers of how the judges deal with the people, so that they may correct them after warning them, or make their insolence known to the ears of the princes [Col. 0457A]. If they cannot correct those who have been admonished, they shall suspend them both from the church and from communion. The priest and the elders shall deliberate what the judges ought to provide in the provinces at their own detriment if they do not come to the council.

The council shall not be dissolved until they have first chosen the place where, at the appropriate time, they shall assemble again for the council. Thus the metropolitan bishop will no longer need to send letters to convene the council if, at the preceding council, the time and place have been announced to everyone.

## XIX

Certain people, contrary to all authority, demand that the churches they have built be consecrated in such a way that they consider the endowment they have given to the same church not to belong to the bishop’s administration [Col. 0457B]. What has been done in this manner in the past shall be corrected, and it shall be prohibited from happening in the future. Everything shall belong to the bishop’s administration and authority according to the ancient constitution.

## XX

Because we have learned that bishops do not serve their parishes in a priestly manner but serve them cruelly, and since it is written, “Be examples to the flock, not as those who lord it over the clergy,” and since they inflict exactions or damages upon their dioceses, we therefore decree that, except for what the ancient constitutions command bishops to have from their parishes, everything else that has hitherto been presumed shall be denied them.

That is, neither presbyters nor deacons shall be wearied by forced labor, nor shall they be burdened in any way by judges, lest we appear in the Church of God to be exactors rather than bishops of God [Col. 0457C].

Those clerics, both local and diocesan, who recognize that they are being burdened by the bishop shall not delay in bringing their complaints to the metropolitan, so that the metropolitan may not delay in restraining such presumptions.

## XXI

We grieve that the slaves of churches, and the slaves of bishops or of all clerics, are being wearied by judges or public officials through various forced labors. For this reason the entire council, moved by piety, has asked our most glorious lord to prohibit such attempts in the future. The slaves of the aforementioned offices shall instead work in their service or for the Church.

If any judge or official wishes to occupy a cleric, or a cleric’s or church’s slave, in public or private business, he shall be excluded from ecclesiastical communion, which he obstructs [Col. 0457D].

## XXII

Those who depart from this life through the divine calling are to be carried to their graves only with psalms and the voices of those singing psalms. We entirely prohibit the funeral lament which is commonly sung for the dead, as well as beating one’s own breast or the breasts of relatives or members of the church.

It is sufficient that, in the hope of the resurrection, the service of divine songs be offered to the bodies of Christians. For the holy Apostle forbids us to mourn the dead, saying: “But concerning those who are asleep, I do not want you to grieve, as do the others who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4:12).

And the Lord did not weep for the dead Lazarus, but wept over the afflictions of this life when he raised him again. If a bishop can prohibit all Christians from doing this, let him not delay in doing so [Col. 0458A]. We judge that it ought not to be done in any other way for religious Christians. For in this manner the bodies of deceased Christians ought to be buried throughout the entire world.

## XXIII

The custom which the common people are accustomed to practice during the solemnities of the saints is irreligious. The people, who ought to attend to the divine offices, spend their time in shameful greetings, singing not only evil songs but also making noise during the offices of religious persons.

The holy council entrusts to the care of the priests and judges that this be driven out of all Spain.

# Edict of the King Confirming the Council

The most glorious Lord King Reccared to all who remain under the rule of our authority:

Divine truth, making us lovers of itself, has principally inspired our royal senses [Col. 0458B], so that, for the restoration of the faith and of ecclesiastical discipline, we ordered all the bishops of Spain to be presented before our majesty.

After careful and prudent deliberation, both concerning matters pertaining to the faith and those relating to the correction of morals, everything has been arranged with mature judgment and the gravity of understanding.

Therefore our authority commands all people belonging to our kingdom: if anything has been defined in this holy council held in the city of Toledo, happily in the fourth year of our reign, no one may despise it and no one may presume to pass it over.

The chapters which have pleased our royal judgment, are consistent with discipline, and have been written in the present synod shall be observed and remain in full authority by everyone, whether clerics or any others. These are:

Concerning the observance of the earlier canons;

Concerning the creed being recited by the people in the church;

Concerning bishops, that they may not alienate church property;

That a bishop may make one of the churches of his parish a monastery;

That bishops, presbyters, and deacons converted from heresy may no longer associate with wives;

That those who have always been catholic may not live in their cells with unrelated women;

That freedmen made free by bishops or by others and entrusted to churches must remain free;

That a reading must be read at all priests’ tables;

That no one may ever presume to take clerics from the households of our fisc, and that any such gift, if received, shall remain void [Col. 0458D];

Concerning churches transferred from heresy, that they belong to the bishops in whose parishes they are located;

Concerning widows, that those who wish shall maintain continence, while those who choose to marry may marry whomever they wish;

Likewise concerning virgins; that penitents must do penance according to the manner of the ancient canons;

That those who wish to do penance must first be tonsured or change their clothing;

That Jews may not take Christian women as wives or concubines, or purchase Christian slaves;

That Jews may not perform public offices;

That it must remain firm that if our fisc’s slaves build churches and endow them from their own property, this shall stand;

That the worship of idols must be investigated and eradicated by priests and judges;

That anyone who kills his son must be disciplined by priests or judges [Col. 0459A];

That once a year priests, judges, and administrators of our patrimony must assemble for the council;

That the affairs of all churches must belong to the bishop’s administration;

That priests must act moderately in their parishes;

That the slaves of the church or of clerics must not be wearied by any forced labor by our officials;

That the bodies of religious persons are to be carried to their graves only with hymns and songs;

That *ballimathiae* [probably dances] and shameful songs are to be prohibited at the solemnities of the saints.

All these ecclesiastical constitutions, which we have briefly and summarily touched upon, just as they are contained more fully in the canon, we decree shall remain with perpetual stability.

If, therefore, any cleric or layperson refuses to be an obedient observer of these sanctions, resisting the statutes of his superiors with a proud face, then, if he is a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric, he shall be subject to excommunication by the entire council.

If he is a layperson of the more honorable class, he shall lose half of his possessions, which shall benefit the rights of the fisc. If he is a person of a lower station, he shall be deprived of his property and assigned to exile.

I, Flavius Reccared the king, confirming this decision which we defined together with the holy synod, have subscribed.

Mausona, in the name of Christ, metropolitan bishop of the catholic Church of Mérida, and the bishops of the province of Lusitania: I have subscribed with my own hand to these constitutions, at which I was present in the city of Toledo.

Likewise the other bishops subscribed.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE FOURTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGIN

[Col. 0459]

[Col. 0459B] 1. On prayer and the confession of faith preached in the holy Church of God. 2. Almost nothing has driven discipline and good order farther from the Church of Christ than the disorderly diversity of the liturgy. 3. On the procedure according to which the holy synod is to be held in the name of God. 4. How variation in the celebration of Easter has arisen in Spain. 5. On the sacrament of baptism. 6. We have learned that in some churches, on the Friday of the Lord’s Passion, the service is not celebrated when the doors of the basilicas are closed. 7. Some break their fast at the ninth hour on the day of that same Passion.

[Col. 0459C] 8. The lamp and candle are not blessed during the vigils in certain churches, and they ask why we bless them. 9. Some priests throughout Spain are found who recite the Lord’s Prayer, which our Savior taught and commanded, not daily but only on Sunday. 10. That the priests of Spain chant the Alleluia during the days of Lent. 11. That in certain churches of Spain the Laudes are chanted after the Apostle. 12. Also concerning the hymns that are to be sung. 13. Also concerning the hymn of the three boys, in which every creature of heaven and earth praises God together. 14. That at the end of the psalms one should say not, as some have done, “Glory to the Father,” but “Honor and glory to the Father.” 15. There are some who do not say the Gloria at the end of the responsories. 16. Concerning the book of the Apocalypse: that it is to be accepted, and when it is to be read. 17. That certain priests, improperly, communicate immediately after the Lord’s Prayer has been said and afterward give the blessing to the people. 18. That a pernicious custom must by no means be retained.

[Col. 0460B] 19. That in the Old Law the Levites are commanded to be ordained from the age of twenty-five. 20. That the priests of God must be irreproachable. 21. That we ought to have a pure conscience before God and an excellent reputation among human beings. 22. That, as bishops are, so presbyters and Levites should maintain both their manner of life and the testimony of their life, in merits as well as in name. 23. That every age from adolescence is inclined toward evil. 24. That ignorance of errors must especially be avoided among the priests of God. 25. Concerning parish priests: when they are ordained, they ought to receive an official document from their own priest.

[Col. 0460C] 26. When priests or deacons are appointed to parishes, they ought to make a profession to their bishop. 27. If a bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon has been deposed from his rank and is found innocent at a second synod, how he is to be received. 28. If a bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone from the clerical order is discovered consulting magicians, haruspices, diviners, augurs, or those who cast lots, what is to be done with them. 29. Priests in districts bordering the enemy, on account of those who have received permission from royal authority, are to be cleared in synod.

[Col. 0460D] 30. That princes often entrust their affairs to priests against persons liable to charges of treason. 31. That bishops should not doubt that God has imposed upon them the responsibility of protecting and defending the people. 32. That avarice, the root of all evils, possesses the minds of certain priests. 33. That any bishop who has possessed another bishop’s diocese for thirty years without any objection is to retain it.

[Col. 0461A] 34. That just as thirty years’ possession removes another’s diocese, so it does not remove the assembly of the territory. 35. That bishops ought to visit all their dioceses and parishes every year. 36. What is to be done if bishops, with anyone’s assistance, provide something from ecclesiastical revenues. 37. Priests must provide the comfort of life to those in need, especially to those to whom a return of kindness is owed. 38. Some deacons break out into such great arrogance that they place themselves before priests. 39. If it is not permitted for bishops, nor for priests, to wear two stoles, how much less for deacons, who are their ministers.

[Col. 0461B] 40. That all clerics and lectors, like the Levites and priests, should have the upper part of their head tonsured, leaving only a circular crown below. 41. That foreign women must not live with clerics. 42. Concerning clerics who, without having a lawful marriage, seek the forbidden companionship of foreign women or their own female servants. 43. Concerning clerics who have married without consulting their bishop. 44. Concerning clerics who willingly took up arms in any sedition. 45. If a cleric is discovered demolishing tombs. 46. Concerning the command of our lord King Sisenand.

[Col. 0461C] 47. On choosing stewards. 48. On the profession of a monk: whatever has been professed is to be maintained. 49. Concerning clerics who desire the monastic way of life. 50. What right bishops ought to have in monasteries. 51. Concerning monks who, on leaving the monastery, not only return to the world but also take wives. 52. Concerning religious persons of their own region who are counted neither among clerics nor among monks. 53. Concerning those who receive penance when in danger.

[Col. 0461D] 54. Concerning laymen who, after receiving penance, have had their hair tonsured and then, lapsing again, have become laymen. [Col. 0462A] 55. That there are two kinds of widows: secular women and consecrated women. 56. Concerning the Jews: that they must not be forced to believe by violence. 57. Concerning the greed of a bishop, priest, deacon, or cleric who gives assistance to Jews against the Christian faith. 58. Concerning the apostasy of those who were formerly admitted to the Christian faith. 59. Concerning the sons and daughters of Jews: that they must no longer be entangled in their parents’ errors. 60. Concerning baptized Jews, if afterward they have apostatized from Christ. 61. Concerning evil associations: that they corrupt even the good. 62. Concerning Jews who have Christian women as wives.

[Col. 0462B] 63. One who has been impious toward God cannot be faithful toward human beings. 64. By command of the Lord and of the most excellent King Sisenand, Jews, or those descended from Jews, are under no circumstances to seek public offices. 65. That Jews may not possess Christian slaves. 66. Concerning those who give nothing from their possessions to Christ’s poor. 67. Concerning bishops who wish to manumit a slave belonging to the Church without retaining the Church’s protection. 68. That priests who either leave their own possessions to the Church or, possessing nothing, acquire estates for their churches may, if they wish, make some of the Church’s servants freedmen.

[Col. 0462C] 69. Concerning the Church’s freedmen: because their patroness never dies, they must never depart from her protection. 70. Concerning the Church’s freedmen who depart from that protection. 71. Concerning freedmen who have been manumitted by anyone and entrusted to the Church’s protection. 72. That those who receive freedom from their masters in such a way that the patron retains no service over them may be received into the clergy. 73. That it is permitted to appoint priests or deacons from the Church’s servants throughout the parishes.

[Col. 0462D] 74. Concerning the institutions and decrees of the ecclesiastical order that pertain to the discipline of certain persons.

## THE FOURTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGINS.

[Col. 0461]

[Col. 0461D] [p. 112] CHAPTER I. In the third year of the reign of our most glorious lord, Prince Sisenand, on the Nones of December, in the era 681, when, moved by zeal for the love of Christ and by the diligence of the most religious King Sisenand of Spain and Galicia, we priests had assembled in the city of Toledo in the name of the Lord, so that, prompted by his commands and orders, we might deliberate concerning certain matters of ecclesiastical discipline, we first gave thanks to our Savior, Almighty God. Afterward we gave thanks to the aforementioned most excellent and glorious ruler, whose devotion toward God is so great that he remains concerned not only with human affairs but also with divine matters.

For while the whole assembly of us was already present in the basilica of the most blessed and holy martyr Leocadia, he entered with the most magnificent and noble men, in keeping with the merit of his faith. First he prostrated himself on the ground before the priests of God and, with tears and groans, asked that the Lord be entreated on his behalf. Then, in a devout address, he exhorted the synod to remember the decrees of our fathers and to apply itself to confirming ecclesiastical rights among us, and to correcting those practices which, having come into use through negligence, had claimed for themselves license and usurpation contrary to ecclesiastical custom.

Rejoicing, therefore, at such exhortations of his, it became necessary, in accordance with his wish and ours, to deliberate concerning matters appropriate both to the divine sacraments, which are celebrated in the churches of Spain in diverse and unlawful ways, and to those practices that are known to have been wrongly usurped in matters of conduct.

And since we are holding a general council, it is fitting that the first words of our speech should concern God, so that, after the confession of faith, the subsequent aims of our work may be established as upon the firmest foundation. As we have received from the holy Fathers, we confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be of one deity and substance, believing a Trinity in the diversity of persons and proclaiming unity in divinity. We neither confuse the persons nor separate the substance.

We say that the Father was made by no one and begotten by no one; we affirm that the Son was not made by the Father but begotten. We confess that the Holy Spirit was neither created nor begotten but proceeds from the Father and the Son.

We confess that the Lord Jesus Christ himself, the Son of God and Creator of all things, was begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages and descended from the Father in the last times for the redemption of the world, while never ceasing to be with the Father.

For he was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the glorious holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and was born from her: the same one Lord Jesus Christ, one within the holy Trinity, perfect in soul and flesh. Without sin he assumed humanity, remaining what he was and assuming what he was not; equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity, possessing in one person the properties of two natures.

For there are two natures in him, God and human being. Yet there are not two sons, but [the OCR reads “two gods”]; rather, the same one person endured suffering in both natures, and death for our salvation, not in the power of divinity but in the weakness of humanity.

He descended to the underworld to rescue the saints who were being held there; and, having conquered the dominion of death, he rose again. Taken up into heaven, he will come in the future for the judgment of the living and the dead.

Cleansed by his death and blood, we have obtained the forgiveness of sins. We are to be raised by him on the last day, and in the flesh in which we now live and in the form in which the same Lord rose, we shall receive from him—some, according to the merits of their righteousness, eternal life; others, according to their sins, the sentence of eternal punishment.

This is the faith of the Catholic Church. We preserve and hold this confession; whoever guards it most firmly will have perpetual salvation.

### II

After the confession of the true faith that is preached in the holy Church of God, it pleased all of us priests who are united in the unity of the Catholic faith that we should undertake nothing further that is diverse or discordant in ecclesiastical sacraments, lest any difference among us appear to the uninitiated or the worldly to display the error of schism, and lest the variation among churches become a scandal to many.

Therefore one order of praying and psalm-singing is to be preserved by us throughout Spain and Galicia; one manner in the solemn celebrations of Mass; one in the evening services. There must no longer be a diversity of ecclesiastical custom among us, because we are held together by one faith and one kingdom. For the ancient Fathers also decreed that each province should maintain the same custom in singing the psalms and in administering the rites.

### III

Almost nothing has driven discipline and good order farther from the Church of Christ than the negligence of priests who, disregarding the canons, neglect to hold a synod for the correction of ecclesiastical customs. Therefore we have universally determined that, since the difficulty of the times does not permit a council to be held twice a year in accordance with the ancient decrees of the Fathers, it should at least be held once by us.

Nevertheless, if the matter concerns the faith, or any other common and general ecclesiastical matter, a synod of all Spain and Galicia is to be convened. If, however, the discussion concerns neither the faith nor the common welfare of the Church but the council is particular, it is to be conducted as the metropolitan of each province determines.

All those who are known to have causes against bishops, judges, powerful persons, or anyone else in authority are to come together at the same council. Whatever is found, through synodal examination, to have been wrongly usurped by anyone is to be restored most justly to those who possess the rights, through the intervention of the royal executor. Thus, for compelling judges or secular persons to attend the synod, an executor is to be requested from the prince at the metropolitan’s initiative.

The synod is to be assembled on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June in whatever province, because of the spring season, when the earth is clothed with grass and fresh pasture is available.

At the first hour of the day, before sunrise, everyone is to be expelled from the church. After all the doors have been closed, doorkeepers are to sit at the one entrance through which the priests must enter. All the bishops are to assemble and enter together, then sit according to the dates of their ordination.

[Col. 0464D] After all the bishops have entered and taken their seats, the priests whom the matter requires are to be summoned to enter. No deacon is to intrude among them. After these, suitable deacons whom the order of proceedings requires to be present are to enter. The bishops’ seats are to form a circle; the priests are to sit behind them, and the deacons are to stand in their presence. Then the laymen whom the council has selected as worthy to take part are to enter.

The notaries whom the proceedings require for reading or recording are also to enter, and the doors are to be closed. While the priests sit in prolonged silence, directing their hearts only toward God, the archdeacon is to say, “Pray.” Immediately all are to prostrate themselves on the ground. While they pray for a long time in silence, with tears and groans, one of the senior bishops is to rise and openly pour forth a prayer to the Lord, while all the others still lie on the ground.

When the prayer has ended and all have answered, “Amen,” the deacon is again to say, “Rise.” Immediately all are to stand, and, with complete fear and discipline, both bishops and priests are to sit down.

When all have thus taken their places in silence, the deacon, dressed in a white garment, is to bring forward the book of canons in the midst and announce the chapters concerning the conduct of councils.

When the titles have been completed, the metropolitan bishop is to address the council, saying: “Behold, most holy priests, the decisions of the ancient Fathers from the canons concerning the celebration of a council have been read. Therefore, if any matter moves anyone, let him bring it forward before his brothers.”

Then, if anyone brings before the priestly hearing any complaint whatsoever that proceeds against the canon, no other chapter is to be taken up until the matter first proposed has been settled.

Moreover, if any priest, deacon, cleric, or layman among those standing outside thinks that the council should be appealed to concerning any matter, let him report his case to the archdeacon of the metropolitan church, and the archdeacon is to announce it to the council. Permission is then to be granted to that person both to enter and to present his case.

No bishop is to withdraw from the common assembly before the appointed hour of general withdrawal arrives. No one is to dare to dissolve the council until everything has been determined, so that whatever is concluded by common deliberation may be written down by the hands of each of the bishops.

For God is to be believed to be present at the council of his priests when, with all tumult cast aside, ecclesiastical affairs are settled carefully and peacefully.

### IV

In Spain there is usually variation in the proclamation of the Easter solemnity, for the differing observance of the Easter calendars sometimes produces error. Therefore it was decided that three months before Epiphany the metropolitan priests should consult one another through books, so that, instructed by common knowledge, they may announce to their fellow provincials the day of Christ’s resurrection as one to be celebrated at the same time.

### V

Concerning the sacrament of baptism: because in Spain some priests perform three immersions and others one, this is regarded by some as schism, and the unity of the faith appears to be divided. For when different parties act in contrary ways in baptizing, some contend that those baptized by the others have not been baptized.

Therefore, concerning what is to be determined by us amid this diversity in the sacrament, let us be instructed by the precepts of the Apostolic See, following not our own but our fathers’ institution.

Gregory, of blessed memory, bishop of the Roman Church, who not only enlightened the regions of Italy but also taught churches far away through his doctrine, was asked by the most holy Bishop Leander of Spain what ought preferably to be followed in this Spanish diversity. Among other things, he replied as follows:

“Concerning the threefold immersion in baptism, nothing truer can be answered than what you yourselves have perceived: that, in one faith, a different custom does no harm to the holy Church. We immerse three times to signify the mystery of the three-day burial, so that, when the child is brought up from the waters for the third time, the resurrection after three days may be expressed.

“But if anyone should think that this is done also in veneration of the highest Trinity, neither does it create any obstacle to immersing the one being baptized once in the water. For since there is one substance in three subsistences, the child may be immersed in baptism either three times or once: in the three immersions the Trinity of persons can be signified, and in one immersion the singularity of the divinity.

“But because until now the child was immersed three times in baptism by heretics, I do not think that this should be done among you, lest, while they count the immersions, they divide the divinity; and while they continue to do what they did, they boast that they have followed our custom.”

Therefore, since a man of such authority has given an account of both practices performed in holy baptism, and since both are considered irreproachable in the holy Church of God, yet in order to avoid the scandal of schism or the practice of heretical doctrine, let us maintain the single immersion in baptism, lest those among us who immerse three times appear to approve the assertion of the heretics while following their custom.

And lest anyone perhaps doubt the mystery of this single sacrament, let him see in it the death and resurrection of Christ. Immersion in the waters is like a descent into the underworld, and rising again from the waters is a resurrection.

Let him likewise see in it the unity of the divinity and the Trinity of persons: unity, when we immerse once; Trinity, when we baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The mystery of this singular baptism is also made clear by examples from the holy Scriptures, as the Apostle Paul testifies: “I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1).

The Red Sea signifies baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood. Through it the people of God passed once beneath the pillar of fire and cloud, although the whole Trinity was present there, with the pillar of fire and cloud preceding the people. In the fire the Father is signified, in the pillar the Son, and in the cloud the Holy Spirit. [p. 113]

The people of God likewise passed once through the waters of the Jordan with the ark. This signifies the single immersion of baptism, through whose sacrament the Church is washed and, through baptism, enters from the labors of this faith into the land of the heavenly promise as through the Jordan.

### VI

We have learned that in certain churches, on the Friday of the Lord’s Passion, the service is not celebrated when the doors of the basilicas are closed, nor is the Lord’s Passion preached to the people, although our Savior himself commanded his apostles, saying: “Preach my passion, death, and resurrection to everyone.”

Therefore on that day it is necessary to preach the mystery of the cross—which he himself wished to be proclaimed to all—and to have the whole people await the forgiveness of sins in a loud voice, so that, cleansed by the contrition of repentance, we may deserve to receive the venerable feast of the Lord’s resurrection with our sins forgiven and partake, cleansed from sin, of the sacrament of his body and blood.

### VII

Some break their fast at the ninth hour on the day of the Lord’s Passion, and sit down to banquets. Although on that same day the sun itself grew pale in darkness and withdrew its light, and the elements themselves, thrown into turmoil, displayed the sorrow of the whole world, they pollute the fast of so great a day and devote themselves to feasting.

And because the universal Church spends that entire day in mourning and abstinence on account of the Lord’s Passion, whoever on that day, except children, the elderly, and the sick, completes his fast before the prayers of absolution have been performed is to be excluded from Easter joy and is not to receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, since he did not honor the day of his Passion through abstinence.

### VIII

In certain churches the lamp and candle are not blessed during the vigils, and they ask why we bless them. Because of the glorious mystery of that night, we solemnly bless these things, so that we may receive, through the blessing of sanctified light, the mystery of Christ’s holy resurrection, which comes as an object of desire during that night.

And because this observance is commended in churches throughout many lands and regions of Spain, it is fitting, for the unity of peace, that it be preserved in the churches of Galicia. No one who despises this will go unpunished; rather, he will be subject to the rules of the Fathers.

### IX

Some priests in Spain are found who recite the Lord’s Prayer, which the Savior taught and commanded, not daily but only on Sunday.

Since the Apostle taught us to pray without ceasing, and Christ commanded how we should pray, saying, “When you pray, say: ‘Our Father who are in heaven’” (Matthew 6:9), how can that which is commanded to be said without ceasing not be said daily?

Indeed, this prayer must be said daily to such an extent that it bears this very title. It is called the daily prayer, as the holy Fathers named it; this is also found among teachers renowned for their distinguished learning.

Saint Cyprian says: “Thus, in the Lord’s Prayer, we ask that our bread—that is, Christ—be given to us daily, so that we who remain and live in Christ may not withdraw from his sanctification and body.”

Saint Hilary says: “‘Give us this day our daily bread’ (Matthew 6:11). What does God desire so much as that Christ, who is the bread of life and the bread from heaven, should dwell in us daily? And because it is the daily prayer, we pray daily that it may be given.”

Saint Augustine says: “For daily and lesser sins, without which this life is not lived, the daily prayer of the faithful makes satisfaction. For those who have been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit are the ones who say: ‘Our Father who are in heaven.’ This daily prayer therefore wipes away the small daily sins; it wipes away even those sins from which the life of the faithful, though crimes have been committed, turns away through repentance and is changed for the better.”

Therefore, just as Christ commanded, so the Apostle instructed; and just as the ecclesiastical teachers established, since we sin daily in thought or word, so daily we ought to pour forth this prayer in the presence of God.

Whoever, therefore, among the priests or subordinate clerics omits this Lord’s Prayer daily, whether in public or private worship, out of arrogance, is to be judged and deprived of the honor of his rank.

### X

Likewise, we have learned that certain priests of Spain chant the Alleluia during the days of Lent, except in the final week of Pascha. Henceforth we prohibit this, decreeing that throughout all the aforementioned days of Lent—since it is not a time of joy but of mourning—the Alleluia is not to be chanted.

At that time it is necessary to persist in tears and fasts, to clothe the body in sackcloth and ashes, to humble the spirit with grief, and to turn joy into sadness until the time of Christ’s resurrection arrives, when it is proper to remain in gladness and change sorrow into joy.

The agreement of the universal Church has established this throughout all parts of the world. It must therefore be preserved by all of us throughout the provinces of Spain and Galicia.

At other times also, namely on the Kalends of January, when pagan error is practiced, the Alleluia is not to be chanted at all. During those days, as during the other forty days, abstinence is to be observed from all meat except fish and vegetables, and some do not even drink wine.

If, therefore, any bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone from the clerical order is found to judge his own discretion preferable to this decree, he is to be compelled to lose the office of his rank and be deprived of communion at that Easter.

### XI

In certain churches of Spain the Laudes are also chanted after the Apostle and before the Gospel is preached, although it is commanded that after the Apostle not the Laudes but the Gospel be announced. It is presumptuous to place before those things that ought to follow.

For this reason the Laudes follow the Gospel: because of the glory of Christ, which is preached through that Gospel to all nations.

Henceforth this order is to be maintained by priests; those who disturb it are to incur the punishment of excommunication.

### XII

We also have the example of the Savior and the apostles concerning the singing of hymns. The Lord himself is reported to have sung a hymn, as Matthew testifies: “And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 26:30). The Apostle Paul also wrote to the Ephesians: “Be filled with the Spirit, speaking in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Ephesians 5:19).

Since some hymns are known to have been composed through human effort in praise of God and of the apostles and in celebration of the triumphs of the martyrs, such as those produced by the most blessed teachers Hilary and Ambrose, certain people nevertheless specifically reject them because they do not derive from the writings of the holy canons or from apostolic tradition.

Let them therefore also reject that hymn composed by human beings which we say daily in public and private worship at the end of all the psalms:

“Glory and honor to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.”

The hymn that the angels sang at the birth of Christ in the flesh is likewise:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

The remaining words that follow there were composed by ecclesiastical teachers. Therefore they too must not be sung in churches, because they are not found in the books of the holy Scriptures.

Masses, petitions, prayers, commendations, and laying on of hands are composed; if none of these is sung in the Church, all ecclesiastical services are left vacant.

The Apostle exhorts and instructs Timothy to do these things, saying: “Therefore, first of all I urge that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:1).

Therefore, just as no one rejects prayers, so no one among us should henceforth reject hymns composed in praise of God. Let them be celebrated in the same manner in Galicia and Spain. Those who dare to reject hymns are to be punished by excommunication.

### XIII

Certain priests neglect to sing the hymn of the three boys, in which every creature of heaven and earth praises God together, and which the Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, celebrates, during the Masses of Sundays and on the solemnities of the martyrs.

Therefore the holy council has decreed that throughout all the churches of Spain and Gaul the same hymn be sung publicly at every solemn celebration of Mass. Those who violate the ancient custom concerning this hymn and our decree are to lose communion.

### XIV

At the end of the psalms, one is to say not, as some have done until now, “Glory to the Father,” but “Glory and honor to the Father,” as the prophet David says: “Give to the Lord glory and honor” (Psalm 95:7), and the Evangelist John says: “A host said, ‘Honor and glory to our God who sits upon the throne’” (Revelation 5:13).

Accordingly, these two expressions ought to be said on earth just as they resound in heaven. We therefore impose this observance upon all ecclesiastical persons; whoever neglects it will suffer the loss of communion.

### XV

There are some who do not say the Gloria at the end of the responsories, and consequently it sometimes sounds unsuitable. The distinction is this: in joyful pieces the Gloria is to follow; in more sorrowful ones, the beginning is to be repeated.

### XVI

The authority of many councils and the synodal decrees of the holy Roman bishops declare the book of the Apocalypse to belong to the Evangelist John and have established that it is to be received among the divine books.

Since there are many who do not accept its authority and disdain preaching it in the Church of God, anyone who henceforth either does not accept it or does not preach it in the Church from Easter to Pentecost is to receive the sentence of excommunication.

### XVII

Some priests communicate immediately after the Lord’s Prayer has been said and afterward give the blessing to the people. Henceforth we prohibit this. After the Lord’s Prayer, the blessing is to be given to the people, and only then is the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood to be received.

The order is to be as follows: priests and Levites are to communicate before the altar, the clergy in the choir, and the people outside the choir.

### XVIII

A pernicious custom must by no means be accepted when, passing beyond the decrees of the Fathers, it disturbs the whole order of the Church: some seek priestly offices through canvassing; others assume the episcopate by offering gifts; and some, entangled in crimes or devoted to secular military service, have reached the honor of the highest and sacred order though unworthy of it.

Concerning their exclusion and removal, it would indeed have been necessary to establish a rule. But, lest the greatest disorder arise in the Church, we believe it necessary, without revisiting what has been omitted, to insert the following rule concerning those who are not to be promoted to the priesthood:

Those who have been detected in any crime; those stained by a mark of infamy; those who have confessed, through public penance, to having committed ancient crimes; those who have fallen into heresy; those known to have been baptized or rebaptized in heresy; those who have castrated themselves, or who are naturally defective in their limbs or are known to lack something through mutilation; those who have had relations with a second wife, or have entered into numerous marriages; those who have married a widow or a woman abandoned by her husband; those who have been husbands of corrupted women; those who have kept concubines or prostitutes; those subject to servile status; those who are unknown; those who are neophytes or laymen [p. 114]; those devoted to secular military service; those bound by obligations to a municipal curia; those ignorant of letters; those who have not yet reached thirty years of age; those who have not advanced through the ecclesiastical degrees; those who seek office through canvassing; those who strive to obtain office through gifts; and those chosen for the priesthood by their predecessors.

Nor henceforth is that man to be a priest whom neither the clergy nor the people of his own city have elected, or whose election has not been sought by the authority of the metropolitan or by the consent of the priests of the province.

Therefore, whoever is henceforth proposed for the priestly order, examined concerning the matters listed above, and found free from all of them, and who, upon examination, has proved to possess an honorable life and sound teaching, is to be consecrated priest on Sunday, in accordance with synodal or decretal regulations, with the consent of all the clergy and citizens, by all the bishops of the province or at least by three of them. The others who are absent are to signify their agreement by letters, with particular regard to the authority or presence of the one established in the metropolitan city.

A bishop of the province is to be consecrated wherever the metropolitan chooses. The metropolitan, however, is to be consecrated only in the metropolitan city, with the bishops of the province assembled there.

If anyone henceforth attempts, contrary to the prohibitions of the canons stated above, to aspire unworthily to the priestly rank, he will be subject, together with those who ordained him, to the danger of losing the honor he has obtained.

### XIX

In the Old Law, from the age of twenty-five, Levites were commanded to serve in the tabernacle; the holy Fathers followed this authority in the canons.
