We, forgetful of both the divine law and the decrees of the councils, make infants and boys Levites before the lawful age and before the experience of life. Therefore, so that this may no longer be done by us, we are admonished by the judgments of the divine law and the canons: Levites are to be consecrated at the age of twenty-five, and priests are to be ordained at thirty, so that they may first be tested according to the commandment and then minister, possessing no crime.

### XX

All who have been placed in the priesthood of God must be irreproachable, as the Apostle testifies: “A bishop must be irreproachable” (1 Timothy 3:2).

Therefore priests ought to be blameless and undefiled. They must not be polluted by any contagion of fornication; rather, living chastely, they must present themselves pure for the celebration of the sacraments.

Let us therefore abstain from every evil deed and remain free from every defilement of the flesh, so that, pure in body and cleansed in mind, we may approach the sacrifice of Christ worthily and beseech God for the offenses of all.

### XXI

Although we ought to have a pure conscience before God, it is nevertheless fitting that we also preserve an excellent reputation among human beings, so that, in accordance with the apostolic precept, we may possess a testimony of holy life not only before God but also before human beings. For some priests have hitherto created no small scandal by not maintaining a good reputation in their manner of life. Therefore, so that every shameful occasion for suspicion may henceforth be excluded, and so that no opportunity for secular people to slander may be given, bishops ought to have in their own residence the testimony of reputable persons concerning their conduct and life, so that they may please God through good conduct and the Church through the good reputation of all.

### XXII

It has likewise seemed good that, just as bishops do, priests and levites whom infirmity or the burden of age perhaps does not allow to remain in their own residence should have witnesses of their life in their cells, and should maintain their life in merit as well as in name.

### XXIII

Every age is inclined toward evil from adolescence onward, for nothing is more uncertain than the life of adolescents. For this reason it ought to be established that, if there are boys or adolescents in the clergy, they should all reside together in a single chamber of the atrium, so that they may spend the years of their slippery age not in luxury but in ecclesiastical disciplines, with a most reputable elder appointed whom they may have both as a teacher of discipline and as a witness of their life.

If any of them are orphans, let them be fostered under sacerdotal guardianship, so that their life may remain untouched by crimes and their property safe from the injury of wicked persons. Those who resist these precepts, however, shall be assigned to monasteries, so that their wandering and proud spirits may be restrained by a stricter rule.

### XXIV

Ignorance, the mother of all errors, must especially be avoided by the priests of God, who have undertaken the duty of teaching the people. For the Apostle Paul frequently admonishes priests to read the holy Scriptures, saying to Timothy: “Attend to reading and exhortation” (1 Tim. 4:13). They should know that they must always remain teachers in these matters.

Therefore priests should meditate upon the holy Scriptures and the canons, so that all their work may consist in divine preaching and instruction, and so that they may edify everyone both through knowledge of the faith and through the works of discipline.

### XXV

When priests are ordained in parishes, they should receive from their own priest an official booklet, so that they may succeed to the churches assigned to them with proper instruction and not, through ignorance, offend even in the divine sacraments. Thus, whenever they come either to the litanies or to the council, they may render an account to the bishop of how they celebrate or baptize in the office entrusted to them.

### XXVI

When priests or deacons are appointed throughout the parishes, they ought first to make a profession before their bishop that they will live chastely and devoutly in the fear of God. Once he has bound them by such a profession, they should preserve holy discipline.

### XXVII

If a bishop, priest, or deacon who has been unjustly expelled from his rank is found innocent in a holy synod, he cannot be what he was unless he receives back the ranks he lost from the hand of the bishops before the altar: if he is a bishop, the stole, ring, and staff; if a priest, the stole and paten; if a deacon, the stole and alb; if a subdeacon, the paten and chalice. Likewise, let the other ranks receive, upon their restoration, what they had received when they were ordained.

### XXVIII

If a bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone from the clerical order is found to have consulted magicians, haruspices, diviners, augurs, or sortilege-practitioners, or those who profess any such art, or anyone practicing something similar, he shall be deposed from the honor of his dignity and be committed to the custody of a monastery. There, devoted to perpetual penance, he shall atone for the sacrilegious crime he has committed.

### XXIX

Priests living near the enemies, except those who have received permission from the lofty authority of the royal power, must not presume secretly to receive or send any stranger carrying a mandate. Whoever is discovered or denounced and convicted shall be punished with a fitting penalty before the council after being reported to the prince.

### XXX

Princes often entrust their affairs to priests concerning various persons liable to a charge against the majesty. Since priests have been chosen by Christ for the ministry of salvation, they may consent to become judges for kings only where clemency toward punishment is promised by oath, not where a sentence involving danger is being prepared.

If, therefore, any priest, contrary to this common resolution, acts as an examiner in the dangers of others, he becomes guilty before Christ of shed blood, and before the Church he shall lose his own rank.

### XXXI

Bishops should have no doubt that God has imposed upon them the care of protecting and defending the people. Therefore, when they see judges and powerful persons oppressing the poor, they should first rebuke them through sacerdotal admonition. If they refuse to be corrected, the bishops should report their insolence to the ears of the king, so that royal power may restrain from wrongdoing those whom sacerdotal admonition does not bend toward justice.

If any bishop neglects this, he shall be liable before the council.

### XXXII

Avarice is the root of all evils, and its thirst also possesses the minds of priests. Many of the faithful, out of love for Christ and the martyrs, build basilicas in the parishes of bishops and give holy offerings. The priests take these away and convert them to their own uses. Hence the worshippers of holy things grow scarce, because they lose their stipends; hence the ruins of collapsing basilicas are not repaired, because everything is taken away by sacerdotal avarice.

For this reason, the present council has decreed that bishops should govern their dioceses in such a way that they presume to take nothing away from their rights, but, in accordance with the authority of earlier councils, should receive one third both of the offerings and of the tributes and crops. If they presume to take anything more from them, it shall be restored through the council, at the appeal of the founders themselves or, if those founders have already departed from this world, of their relatives.

Let the founders of basilicas therefore know that they have no power over the things they confer upon those same churches. Rather, in accordance with the regulations of the canons, just as the church belongs to the bishop’s administration, so too does its endowment.

### XXXIII

If any bishop has possessed another bishop’s diocese for thirty years without any objection, then, since according to the force of the law the diocese appears to belong to him, an action for reclaiming it must not be admitted against him. This applies only within a single parish; outside it, it is not permitted in any way, lest, while a diocese is being defended, the boundaries of the provinces become confused.

### XXXIV

Just as thirty years’ possession removes an alien diocese, so it does not remove the jurisdiction of a territory. Therefore basilicas that are newly founded undoubtedly belong to the bishop in whose territorial district they are shown to be.

### XXXV

A bishop ought to visit all his dioceses and parishes each year, to inquire what each basilica needs for its repair. If he himself is unable to fulfill this duty because he is held by illness or entangled in other occupations, he should send reputable priests or deacons who will investigate the revenues of the basilicas, their repairs, and the life of those who minister in them.

### XXXVI

Whenever bishops, with the assistance of anyone, provide some ecclesiastical benefit and promise any advantage in return for it, they ought to fulfill the payment of what was promised, so that the matter may be brought before the provincial council and their agreement confirmed, because, as Paul says: “The laborer is worthy of his wage” (1 Tim. 5:18).

### XXXVII

Priests must provide the support of life to those in need, and especially to those to whom a reciprocal obligation is owed. Therefore, if any of the faithful have contributed something from their possessions to the Church out of personal devotion, and if they themselves or their children should later be reduced to poverty, they should receive from that same church assistance for their livelihood for as long as necessary.

For if ecclesiastical property is generously distributed, solely out of regard for religion, to clerics, monks, pilgrims, or anyone enduring some necessity, how much more ought provision to be made for those to whom a just repayment is owed!

### XXXVIII

Some deacons rise to such arrogance that they place themselves before priests and presume to stand first themselves, while the priests are positioned in the second choir. Therefore, so that they may recognize priests as superior to themselves, both groups should stand in either choir.

### XXXIX

If it is not even lawful for a bishop or priest to wear two stoles, much less is it lawful for a deacon, who is their minister. Therefore the levite ought to wear one stole on his left shoulder, because of which he prays—that is, preaches. He ought to keep his right side free, so that he may move more readily to the sacerdotal ministry.

Henceforth, therefore, let levites beware of using a double stole. Let them wear only one, plain and pure, without any colors or ornament of gold [*auro*; the source reads *a tyro*].

### XL

All clerics and readers, like levites and priests, should have the entire upper part of the head shaved, leaving below only a circular crown. They should not follow the practice that readers in the regions of Gallaecia are still seen to observe: like laymen, with long hair, they shave only a small circle at the crown of the head.

For this custom has hitherto belonged to heretics in the Spains. Therefore, in order to remove scandal from the churches, this sign of disgrace must be taken away, and there should be one tonsure, or one form of appearance, as is the custom of all Spain. Whoever does not observe this shall be guilty against the Catholic faith.

### XLI

No extraneous woman may live with clerics, except a mother, sister, daughter, or paternal aunt; in the case of these persons, the bond of nature permits no crime to be suspected. This was also decreed by the constitution of the ancient Fathers.

### XLII

Some clerics who do not have a lawful marriage seek the forbidden companionship of foreign women or of their own female servants. Therefore, those women who are joined in this manner to clerics shall be removed and sold by the bishop, while those whom they have infected with their lust shall, for the time being, be confined for penance.

### XLIII

Clerics who have taken wives without the counsel of their bishop, or who have taken into marriage a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute, must be separated by their own bishop.

### XLIV

Clerics who, in any sedition, are found either wishing to take up arms or having taken them up shall, after losing the rank of their order, be handed over to a monastery for penance.

### XLV

If any cleric is discovered demolishing tombs, since this crime is punished by the public laws with blood as sacrilege, one exposed in such a crime ought, according to the canons, to be removed from the clerical order and assigned to three years of penance.

### XLVI

At the command of our lord and most excellent King Sisenand, the holy council has decreed that all freeborn clerics, on account of the duty of religion, shall be exempt from every public levy and labor, so that they may serve God freely and not be drawn away from ecclesiastical duties by any of the aforesaid necessities.

### XLVII

Those whom the Greeks call *oikonomoi*—that is, those who manage ecclesiastical property in place of bishops—as the holy Synod of Chalcedon established, all bishops ought to appoint from their own clergy to govern the churches. Whoever henceforth disregards this shall be liable under the authority of that same great council.

### XLVIII

A monk is made either by parental devotion or by his own profession. Whichever of these has bound him shall hold him bound. Accordingly, we close the way for such persons to return to the world and forbid all return to secular life.

### XLIX

Clerics who seek the monastic way because they desire to follow a better life should freely be granted entry by the bishop into monasteries. Their purpose should not be obstructed when they strive to pass over to the desire for contemplation.

### L

It has been reported to the present council that monks are being enslaved to servile labor by episcopal command, and that the rights of monasteries are being usurped through illicit presumption contrary to the regulations of the canons, so that the monastery almost becomes a possession, and the illustrious portion of Christ is reduced to emptiness and servitude.

Therefore we admonish those who preside over churches not to presume to do such things any longer. Priests should claim for themselves in a monastery only what the canons prescribe: namely, to admonish abbots to holy conduct, to establish other offices, and to correct acts committed outside the rule.

If they presume to do anything among monks that the canons forbid, or attempt to usurp any part of the monastery’s property, the sentence of excommunication will not be lacking against those who thereafter do not withdraw from unlawful acts.

### LI

Some monks, when they leave the monastery, not only return to the world but also take wives. Therefore, they must be recalled to the same monastery from which they departed and assigned to penance; there they must lament their crimes, in the place from which they departed.

### LII

Religious persons of the local region who are counted neither among the clerics nor among the monks, as well as those who wander through various places, shall have their licence restrained by the bishops in whose jurisdiction they are known to reside, so that they may be assigned either to the clergy or to a monastery, except those released by their own bishop on account of illness.

### LIII

If persons who are in danger receive penance without confessing any manifest crimes, but merely proclaiming that they are sinners, then, if they recover, they may even attain ecclesiastical ranks through the integrity of their conduct.

Those, however, who receive penance in such a way that they publicly confess to having committed some mortal sin can in no way attain the clergy or ecclesiastical honors, because they have marked themselves by their own confession.

### LIV

Whenever secular persons, upon receiving penance, have had their hair tonsured and then, transgressing again, have become laymen, they shall be seized by their own bishop and recalled to the penance from which they withdrew.

If some are irrevocable in their apostasy and do not return after being admonished, they shall be condemned before the Church as true apostates by a sentence of anathema.

The same shall apply to those who were tonsured by their parents, or who, after losing their parents, voluntarily devoted themselves to religion, but later assumed secular dress. Once seized by a priest, they shall be recalled to the religious way of life after first doing penance.

If they cannot be converted, they shall be subjected, as apostates, to the sentence of anathema. The same rule shall also be observed with widows, consecrated virgins, and women doing penance who have assumed the habit of religious women and later either changed their clothing or entered into marriage.

### LV

There are two kinds of widows: secular and religious. Secular widows are those who, while still intending to marry, have not laid aside secular dress. Religious widows are those who, having already changed their secular dress, have appeared in religious attire before a priest and the Church.

If these enter into marriage, according to the Apostle they will not be without condemnation, because, after first vowing themselves to God, they have afterward abandoned their purpose of chastity.

### LVI

Concerning the Jews, the holy synod has commanded that henceforth no one be compelled by force to believe. For God has mercy on whomever he wishes, and hardens whomever he wishes. Such persons are not to be saved unwillingly, but willingly, so that the order of justice may remain unimpaired.

For just as a human being perished by obeying the serpent through the will of his own free choice, so, when God’s grace calls, each person is saved by the conversion of his own mind through believing. Therefore they are to be persuaded to convert, not driven to it by force, but by the free choice of the will.

Those, however, who were formerly compelled to become Christians, as happened in the time of the most devout prince Sisebut, since it is already established that they have been joined to the divine sacraments, have received the grace of baptism, have been anointed with chrism, and have become participants in the body and blood of the Lord, must be compelled to hold even the faith that they received under force or necessity, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed and the faith they received be regarded as worthless and contemptible.

### LVII

So great is the greed of certain people that some, desiring it, “have even wandered from the faith” (as the Apostle says) “because of it” (1 Tim. 6:10). For up to now many priests and laymen, accepting gifts from Jews, have fostered their perfidy by their patronage. They are not undeservedly known to be of the body of Antichrist, because they act against Christ.

Therefore, if henceforth any bishop, cleric, or layman provides them assistance against the Christian faith, whether by gift or favor, he shall be regarded as profane and sacrilegious, anathematized, and excluded from the Catholic Church, because he is worthy to be separated from the body of Christ who becomes a patron to the enemies of Christ.

### LVIII

Many who were formerly brought to the Christian faith from Judaism are now known to have blasphemed Christ, not only by practicing Jewish rites but also by presuming to perform abominable circumcisions.

After consultation with our most devout and religious lord, King Sisenand, this holy council has decreed concerning such transgressors that, corrected by pontifical authority, they shall be recalled to the practice of Christian doctrine, so that sacerdotal discipline may restrain those whom their own will does not reform.

Those whom they circumcise, if they are their children, shall be separated from the companionship of their parents; if they are slaves, they shall be given their freedom in reparation for the injury done to their bodies.

### LIX

We decree that the sons and daughters of Jews be separated from their parents’ company, lest they be further entangled in their parents’ errors, and assigned either to monasteries, to Christian men, or to women who fear God. Under their way of life they shall learn the practice of the faith and, properly instructed, make progress both in conduct and in faith.

### LX

If baptized Jews afterward transgress against Christ and are condemned to any punishment, their faithful children ought not to be excluded from their possessions, because it is written: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18:20).

### LXI

The company of the wicked often corrupts even the good, and all the more those who are inclined toward vices. Therefore, let there henceforth be no fellowship between Jews who have been converted to the Christian faith and those who still remain in the ancient rite, lest they be subverted by sharing in their company.

Accordingly, if any of those who have been baptized do not henceforth avoid the company of unbelievers, the baptized shall be given to Christians, and the unbelievers shall be assigned to public beatings.

### LXII

Jews who have Christian women as wives shall be admonished by the bishop of that city that, if they wish to remain with them, they must become Christians. If, after being admonished, they refuse, they shall be separated, because an unbeliever cannot remain in the union of one who has already been transferred to the Christian faith.

The children born from such unions shall follow the faith and status of their mother. Likewise, those born from unbelieving women and faithful Christian men shall follow the Christian religion, not Jewish superstition.

### LXIII

No one can be faithful toward human beings who has been unfaithful toward God. Therefore, Jews who were formerly made Christians but have now transgressed against the faith of Christ must not be admitted to give testimony, even though they proclaim themselves to be Christians. For just as they are suspect in the faith of Christ, so they are considered doubtful in human testimony.

The testimony of those who are taught to be false in faith must therefore be invalidated, and no credence must be given to those who have cast away from themselves faith in the truth.

### LXIV

At the command of our lord and most excellent King Sisenand, the holy council has decreed that Jews, or those descended from Jews, must in no way seek public offices, because under this pretext they injure Christians. Therefore the provincial judges, together with their priests, must suspend the offices fraudulently obtained by such persons and must not permit them to exercise public offices.

If anyone permits this, excommunication shall be pronounced against him as against a sacrilegious person, and the one who has insinuated himself into office shall be assigned to public beatings.

### LXV

By decree of the most glorious prince, this holy council has determined that Jews may not purchase Christian slaves, Christian female slaves, or acquire them through anyone’s gift. For it is impious that members of Christ should serve the ministers of Antichrist.

If Jews henceforth presume to possess Christian male or female slaves, those slaves shall be removed from their dominion and receive freedom from the prince.

### LXVI

If those who distribute nothing from their possessions to the poor of Christ will be condemned in the future by the voice of the eternal Judge, how much more will those be condemned who take away from the poor what they did not give?

Therefore, let bishops who have contributed nothing of their own to the Church of Christ fear this divine judgment, and let them not presume to make freedmen from the Church’s households to their own condemnation. For it is impious that one who has not contributed his own property to the Church should inflict harm and attempt to alienate the Church’s rights.

A successor-bishop shall therefore recall such freedmen to the rights of the Church without any opposition, because it was not equity but wrongdoing that freed them.

### LXVII

If a bishop wishes to manumit a slave belonging to the Church without retaining the Church’s protection, he must offer before the council of the church over which he presides two slaves of equal merit and peculium, with the priests subscribing to the exchange, so that the settlement of the exchange may be found valid and just.

For then he will be able to grant free manumission without the Church’s protection, when he has already acquired for his own right the person whom he intends to hand over to freedom.

Such a freedman, however, shall be denied the right to accuse or testify against the Church to whose jurisdiction he belonged. If he presumes to do so, it is decreed that, while the exchange remains in force, he shall be recalled into his owner's private slavery, against the Church which he attempts to harm.

### LXVIII

The consensus of the entire council has determined that priests who either leave their own possessions to the Church or, possessing nothing, acquire some estates or households for their churches may manumit certain members of that same church’s household, in proportion to the property contributed, as the ancient canons have decreed.

They must remain freeborn, together with their peculium and descendants, under the protection of the Church, carrying out the duties imposed upon them as far as they are able.

### LXIX

Freedmen of the Church, because their patroness never dies, must never depart from the protection of that same Church, nor may their descendants do so, as the earlier canons have decreed.

And lest their freedom fail to extend to their future offspring, and lest that posterity, resisting by natural free status, withdraw itself from the Church’s protection, it is necessary that both these freedmen and those descended from them make a profession before their bishop. Through it they shall acknowledge that, having been made freedmen from the Church’s household, they must not abandon its protection but, according to their ability, offer service and obedience.

### LXX

Freedmen of the Church who, leaving its protection, have attached themselves to various persons shall, if they refuse to return after being admonished, have their manumission declared void, because through the contempt of disobedience they are held liable for an act of ingratitude.

### LXXI

Freedmen of the Church who have been manumitted by anyone and entrusted to the Church’s protection shall, as the regulations of the ancient Fathers established, be protected by sacerdotal defense from the insolence of anyone, whether in the condition of freedom or in the peculium they are known to possess,

### LXXII

Those who receive freedom from their masters in such a way that the patron retains no service from them should, if they are without crime, be admitted to the clerical order, because they are known to have been released by direct manumission.

Those, however, who have been manumitted while retaining an obligation of service must in no way be promoted to the ecclesiastical order, because they remain subject to the service of their patrons, lest their masters, whenever they wish, turn clerics into slaves.

### LXXIII

It is permitted to appoint priests and deacons from the Church’s households throughout the parishes, provided that uprightness of life and integrity of conduct commend them. The condition, however, is that they first be manumitted and receive the freedom of their status, and only afterward advance to ecclesiastical honors.

For it is irreligious that those who assume the dignity of the sacred order should remain bound to slavery.

Whatever is granted to such persons through freedom, or given to them by succession, or conferred upon them through any advantage, they may not transfer any part of it to outsiders. After their death, everything must belong to the church by which they were manumitted.

Like the other freedmen of the Church, these too are denied access to accusing or testifying against the Church. If they aspire to do so, they shall lose not only the benefit of freedom but also the rank of honor that they obtained not through the dignity of their nature but in a time of necessity.

LXXIV. After certain regulations of ecclesiastical order or decrees concerning the discipline of some persons, this is the final judgment which we, all priests, must issue: for the strength of our kings and the stability of the Gothic people, we must deliver, under God as judge, a final pontifical decree.

For among many peoples—as is reported—there exists such great treachery of mind that they disdain to keep the faith promised by oath to their kings; they feign with their mouths the profession of an oath while retaining in their hearts the impiety of treachery. They swear to their kings, yet violate the faith they promise, and they do not fear that book of God’s judgment by which a curse and many threats of punishment are brought upon those who swear falsely in God’s name. What hope, then, will such peoples have when laboring against their enemies? What faith can thereafter be trusted with other nations in peace, after a treaty has been violated? What rights among enemies will remain secure through a stable pledge, when they do not preserve the faith sworn to their own kings? For who is so mad as to cut off his own head with his own hand? Those men, as is evident, forgetful of their own salvation, kill themselves with their own hands by turning their strength against themselves and their own kings.

And since the Lord says, “Do not touch my anointed ones” (1 Chronicles 16:22), and David says, “Who has stretched out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and remained innocent?” (1 Samuel 26:9), they neither fear committing perjury nor hesitate to bring destruction upon their kings. Faith in a pact is given even to enemies, and it is not violated. If faith is maintained in war, how much more must it be preserved in other matters! It is sacrilege if peoples violate the faith promised to their kings, because the treaty is thereby transgressed not only against them but also against God, in whose name the promise itself is made.

For this reason the heavenly anger has changed many kingdoms of the earth, so that, on account of the impiety of their faith and conduct, one was separated from another. Therefore we too must beware of the cause of such peoples, lest we likewise be struck by a sudden calamity and punished with a cruel penalty. For if God did not spare the angels who transgressed against him, who through disobedience lost their heavenly dwelling—and therefore he says through Isaiah, “My sword is intoxicated in heaven” (Isaiah 34:5)—how much more must we fear the destruction of our salvation, lest we perish when the same wrath is raging through our infidelity!

If, then, we wish to avoid divine anger and desire to move his severity toward clemency, let us preserve toward God the worship and fear of religion, and let us guard toward our rulers the faith and pledge which we have promised. Let there not be among us, as among certain peoples, the impious subtlety of infidelity, the treachery of a deceitful mind, the crime of perjury, or the wicked schemes of conspiracies. Let no one seize the kingdom through presumption; let no one stir up mutual seditions among citizens; let no one plot the destruction of kings. Rather, when a ruler has died in peace, let the leading men of the people, together with the priests, establish the successor to the kingdom by common counsel, so that, while concord in unity is preserved among us, no division of country or people may be stirred up through violent ambition.

But if this admonition does not correct our minds and does not lead our hearts at all toward the common salvation, hear our judgment. Therefore, whoever among us or among all the peoples of Spain, by any conspiracy or design, violates the oath of faith which he has promised for the condition of the country and Gothic people or for the preservation of the king’s safety; or touches the king with murderous intent; or strips him of royal power; or usurps the height of kingship through tyrannical presumption—let him be anathema in the sight of God the Father and the angels, and let him be made an outsider from the Catholic Church which he has profaned by perjury, and alien from every assembly of Christians, together with all his accomplices in impiety, because it is right that one punishment should hold liable those whom the same error has found entangled.

This we repeat a second time, saying: Whoever from now on, whether among us or among all the peoples of Spain, by any negotiation or design, violates the oath of his faith which he has promised for the condition of the country and Gothic people or for the preservation of the king’s safety; or touches the king with murderous intent; or strips him of royal power; or usurps the height of kingship through tyrannical presumption—let him be anathema in the sight of Christ and his apostles, and let him be made an outsider from the Catholic Church which he has profaned by perjury, alien from every fellowship of Christians, and condemned at God’s future judgment. Let him be held together with his accomplices, since it is right that those who associate with such men should themselves be held liable by sharing in their condemnation.

This also we proclaim a third time, saying: Whoever from now on, whether among us or among all the peoples of Spain, by any plan or design, violates the oath of his faith which he has promised for his own salvation, for the condition of the Gothic people, or for the security of royal power; or touches the king with murderous intent; or strips him of royal power; or usurps the height of kingship through tyrannical presumption—let him be anathema in the sight of the Holy Spirit and the martyrs of Christ, and let him be made an outsider from the Catholic Church which he has profaned by perjury, alien from every communion of Christians. Let him have no share among the righteous, but let him, together with those who strive after the same conspiracy, be condemned with the devil and his angels to everlasting punishments, so that an equal punishment of destruction may bind together those whom wicked fellowship joins in ruin.

Therefore, if this pleases all of you who are present, confirm this judgment, repeated for the third time, by the consent of your voices.

The whole clergy and people said: “Those who presume against this our definition—anathema maranatha, that is, let them be destruction at the coming of the Lord—and let them and their associates have a share with Judas Iscariot. Amen.”

Therefore we ourselves, and all the priests, admonish the holy Church of Christ and the people that this dreadful judgment, so often repeated, may condemn none of us in the present or eternal judgment. Rather, by guarding the faith promised to our most glorious lord, King Sisenand, and serving him with sincere devotion, may we not only call forth in ourselves the clemency of divine mercy, but also deserve to receive the favor of the aforementioned ruler.¹¹⁷

We also humbly beseech you, present king, and the future rulers of succeeding generations, to rule with justice and piety the peoples entrusted to you by God, being moderate and gentle toward your subjects, and to repay with good reciprocity Christ the giver who has appointed you over us, reigning in humility of heart with zeal for good action. Let none of you, acting alone, strike a captive or a guilty person with a sentence; rather, with public consent and together with the governors, let the guilt of offenders be revealed through manifest judgment, while you preserve gentleness toward those who have offended, so that you may prevail over them more by mercy than by severity. Thus, while all these things are preserved by you with pious moderation, with God as their author, may kings rejoice in their peoples, peoples in their kings, and God in both.

We likewise promulgate this judgment concerning future kings: if any of them, contrary to reverence for the laws, exercises power over the peoples with proud domination and arrogance, in disgraceful acts, crime, or most savage greed, let him be condemned by Christ the Lord’s sentence of anathema, and let him suffer separation from God and judgment because he presumed to act wickedly and to lead the kingdom to destruction.

Concerning Simithilan, who, fearing his own crimes, deprived himself of the kingdom and stripped himself of the insignia of power, we have decreed, with the counsel of the people, that neither him nor his wife, on account of the evils they committed, nor their children shall ever be joined to our unity; nor shall we ever promote them to the honors from which they were cast down on account of their iniquity. Just as they are regarded as outsiders from the height of the kingdom, so also let them remain strangers to possession of the goods which they had increased from the resources of the wretched, except for what they obtained through the mercy of our most merciful ruler.

Likewise, concerning Geillan, the brother of the aforementioned Simithilan by both blood and crime, who proved stable neither in the faith of brotherhood nor in preserving the faith promised to our glorious lord, it has pleased us that he, together with his wife, as was done previously, be separated from the fellowship of the people and from our association, and that he not be restored to the possessions in which they had grown through iniquity, except for what they may have obtained through the mercy of the most clement ruler, whose favor enriches the good with the rewards of gifts and does not exclude the wicked from his beneficence.

But glory and honor belong to our almighty God, in whose name we have assembled. After this, peace, salvation, and long life be granted to our most pious and Christ-loving lord, King Sisenand, whose devotion summoned us to this salutary decree. May grace strengthen his kingdom, and may the grace of the supreme God protect him and the Gothic people in the Catholic faith, in years and merits, until his final old age. After the glory of his present kingdom, may he pass into the eternal kingdom, so that he may reign without end—he who rules happily in this world—through the one who is King of kings and Lord of lords, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.

Since, therefore, the matters set forth above have been defined, with the most religious ruler giving his assent, it was subsequently agreed, with nothing standing in the way, that none of our number should violate what has been established, but that everything should be preserved by salutary counsel. And because these things contribute to the advancement of the Church and to the salvation of our souls, we confirm them also by our own subscription, so that they may endure.

I, Isidore, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Seville, having established these things in the name of Christ, have subscribed. Likewise the other bishops subscribed, forty in number.

## The Chapters of the Fifth Council of Toledo Begin

Held in the era 584, in the first year of Chintilla.

[Col. 0481]

[Col. 0481D] 1. On the establishment of new litanies.  
2. On the safeguarding of the kings’ welfare and the defense of the offspring of absent rulers.  
[Col. 0482D] 3. On the rejection of persons who are forbidden to attain the kingdom.  
4. On those who flatter themselves with hope while the king is still alive.  
[Col. 0483A] 5. On those who presume to curse rulers.  
6. That the faithful of kings should not be deprived by royal successors of their property-rights as recompense for their service.  
7. That, at the celebration of every council, the synod held at Toledo in the time of Sisenand should, by a clear proclamation of the voice, be made known to all for its safeguarding.  
[Col. 0484A] 8. On the indulgence preserved by rulers for offenders.  
9. On the favor granted to rulers by the acclamation of the council.

## The Fifth Council of Toledo Begins

[Col. 0483]

[Col. 0483A] At the city of Toledo, we, priests of the Lord from various provinces of Spain, seated together in the one kiss of peace in the basilica of the holy martyr Leocadia, offer thanksgiving to almighty God for his great mercy, by whose will we have come together in this harmony. We also offer prayers for the beginning of the reign of our glorious ruler, King Chintilla, for whose steadfast safety and happiness we implore heavenly clemency. He entered the midst of our assembly with the nobles and elders of the palace, humbly commended himself to the prayers of all, and by holy exhortation compelled his faithful to do likewise. By divine inspiration he put forward this institution, which we enact at his command and by our decree.

### Chapter I

Namely, throughout the whole kingdom granted by God, this special and proper religious observance shall be maintained at all times: beginning on the day of the Ides of December, a litany shall be performed everywhere for three days in annual succession, and pardon for sins shall be sought with tears. If a Sunday intervenes, it shall be celebrated in the following week. For, since the abundance of iniquity causes evil to be spread everywhere and to commit new crimes, this new custom also shall arise, able to serve as our purification before the eyes of almighty God.

### II

We must provide with the greatest vigilance and with deep religious care that the evils which are continually reported to be perpetrated may be eradicated through watchful ecclesiastical discipline. For it was not written in vain: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser.” Therefore, since the burden of sins has grown heavier, experience teaches us that punishment repeatedly brings about what we ought above all to avoid. This is also preserved when we do not violate through presumption what we have promised by the divine sacraments. Accordingly, what is often found to be transgressed must be restrained.

But so that successors may not outstrip their predecessors, nor those who follow envy their superiors, and so that everything may remain quiet and peaceful, this judgment, considered jointly in the council, is issued: preserve whatever has been provided and written by the universal and great synod concerning the safety and welfare of rulers.

Let these additions also be observed: namely, that toward every authority of our ruler, King Chintilla, affection be maintained with all kindness and all firmness, and that a reasonable means of defense be provided, so that those matters justly arranged—or even suitably secured by the provision of parents or by lawful ownership—may not be unjustly defrauded by anyone, nor may any person be given an unlawful pretext for injuring them, nor may they in any way be harassed in any matter through disregard of affection. For such license makes rulers suspicious of their subjects and subjects greedy for the goods of rulers.

Therefore, lest the foregoing be disregarded, and so that greed, the root of all evils, may be removed, we call upon all who are present and absent, and even those who will come in future times, before God and his angels: if anyone proves reckless and contemptuous of this admonition, and by any argument attempts maliciously to harass or in any way injure them, let him be anathema in the assembly of all Christians and condemned by heavenly judgment; let him be reproachable to all Catholics and abominable to the holy angels appointed to God’s service; let him be lost in this age and condemned in the future, because he refused to give his consent to so upright a provision.

### III

For inexperienced new customs a new remedy ought to be found. Therefore, since the minds of certain people are thoughtless and unable to contain themselves—people whom neither ancestry ennobles nor virtue adorns, and who everywhere suppose that they may freely reach the heights of royal majesty—we offer the judgment of all of us, invoking God in this matter: if anyone has conceived such plans, whom neither the election of all has raised up nor the nobility of the Gothic people draws to this summit, let him be deprived of the fellowship of Catholics and condemned by divine anathema.

### IV

Since it is plainly both hostile to religion and harmful to human beings to think unlawfully about the future, to seek the downfall of rulers, and to provide for oneself in advance, although it is written, “It is not for you to know the moments or times which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7), we decree by this judgment that whoever is found to have pursued such plans, and, while the ruler is alive, to have looked toward another in hope of a future kingdom or to have drawn others to himself for that reason, shall be expelled from the assembly of Catholics with a sentence of excommunication.

### V

For the pestilential conduct of men, we also decree, after salutary deliberation, that no one heap curses upon a ruler. For it is written by the lawgiver: “You shall not curse the ruler of your people” (Exodus 22:28). If anyone does so, let him be punished by ecclesiastical excommunication. For if revilers will not possess the kingdom of God, how much more must such a person be expelled from the Church, since he is found to be a violator of the divine sentence?

[Col. 0485A] ### VI

With similar foresight, our judgment is issued concerning the faithful of kings: whoever outlives a ruler shall suffer no loss in possessions lawfully granted or acquired through the ruler’s generosity. For if the minds of the faithful are freely and unjustly disturbed, no one will wish to offer loyal and faithful service, while everything is wavering in uncertainty and they fear the prospect of future danger. Rather, the ruler’s piety ought to provide assistance for their safety and possessions. Others are encouraged to faith by examples, when the faithful are not deprived of their reward.

### VII

Because of the readiness of wicked minds and the forgetfulness of memory, this most sacred synod establishes that in every council of the bishops of Spain, the decree of the universal council which was established for the safety of our rulers must, after all the proceedings, be proclaimed aloud in the synod. Thus, by being frequently repeated to their ears, the minds which are terrified by the persistence of the wicked may be corrected; for such minds are led toward transgression by forgetfulness and carelessness.

[Col. 0486A] ### VIII

In all the matters set forth above, we reserve to the ruler the power of granting indulgence for the faults of offenders, so that, according to the measure of his goodness, wherever he perceives improvement in their minds, he may grant pardon for their offenses.

### IX

Bringing all these matters to an end and giving them strength by our subscription, we render glory and praise to almighty Lord God, insofar as mortal strength permits. After this, we give thanks to our excellent and most glorious ruler, King Chintilla, whose ardor of faith, zeal for good intention, and harmony of unanimity and charity have been granted to us.¹¹⁸ May the Lord give him triumph over his enemies and joy in blessedness; may he guard him with continual protection and fortify him with the safest vigilance of his good will, whose kingdom remains for ages of ages.

I, Eugenius, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Toledo and of the province of Carthage, have subscribed, assenting to all these matters along with the others. Likewise the other bishops subscribed, twenty in number.

## The Chapters of the Sixth Council of Toledo Begin

[Col. 0485]

[Col. 0485B] 1. On the fullness of the Catholic faith.  
2. On the observance of the litanies.  
3. On safeguarding the faith of the Jews.  
4. On the condemnation of clerics who obtain ecclesiastical orders through money.  
[Col. 0485C] 5. On the stipends of clerics, so that they may not be alienated from the rights of the churches.  
6. On sacred men and women who transgress their sacred profession.  
7. On penitents who transgress.  
8. That certain penitents be restored to their former communities.  
9. On professed persons and the obedience of the Church’s freedmen.  
10. On the offspring of the Church’s freedmen, so that they may not be permitted to depart from the Church even by formal declaration.  
[Col. 0486B] 11. That no one be condemned in a lawful accusation.  
12. On those who flee to enemies.  
13. On the honor due to the leading men of the palace.  
14. On the remuneration granted to the faithful of kings.  
[Col. 0486C] 15. That ecclesiastical property lawfully granted by anyone remain securely and permanently theirs.  
16. On the safety of the royal offspring and the affection to be shown toward them.  
17. On those who, while the king is alive, provide for a kingdom for themselves or others, and on persons forbidden to approach the kingdom.  
18. On safeguarding the lives of rulers and the defense which succeeding kings must provide for those who came before them.  
19. On the thanksgiving offered to God and the ruler in the fellowship of the council.

## The Sixth Council of Toledo Begins

[Col. 0485]

[Col. 0485D] When we, the bishops of Spain and Galicia, had assembled in response to the salutary exhortations of the orthodox and glorious ruler, King Chintilla, without hindrance in the praetorium of Toledo, seated in the church of the holy martyr Leocadia, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the first year of the aforementioned ruler and triumphator in Christ, in the era 680, we established the following.

### Chapter I

When, first, so many acts of grace had been accomplished in us by almighty God for the crown of the brethren, nothing better or more salutary entered the minds of all than that, following the custom of the universal synod, after the solemn prayer had been completed, we should recount with our tongues what we had inwardly pondered in our minds and pour forth from our mouths what we believed in our hearts, with the heavenly judgment assisting, which says: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Psalm 44:2); and, according to the prophet, “The Lord has made his word brief upon the earth.”

Therefore, from the abundance of our hearts let there be a confession of the voice, so that the tongue, acting as interpreter, may pour forth outwardly in confession the faith which the mind of all bears inwardly.

Accordingly, we believe and profess the most holy and almighty Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God alone, not solitary; of one essence, power, authority, and majesty, and of one nature; distinct in distinguishable persons, yet essentially undivided in the substance of the Godhead; creator of all creatures.

The Father is unbegotten and uncreated, the fountain and origin of the whole Godhead. The Son was begotten from the Father timelessly, before every creature, without beginning—not a creature. For the Father never existed without the Son, nor did the Son ever exist without the Father. Yet the Son is God from God the Father, not the Father God from God the Son. He is the Son of the Father and God from the Father, in all things coequal with the Father, true God from true God.

The Holy Spirit is truly neither begotten nor created, but proceeds from the Father and the Son; he is the Spirit of both. Accordingly, the Father and the Son are substantially one, and the one Spirit proceeds from both. In this Trinity the unity of substance is so great that it lacks plurality and retains equality. He is no less in each individual person than in all together, nor greater in all than in the individual persons.

Of these three persons of the Godhead, we confess that only the Son came forth from the Father’s secret counsel and hidden mystery for the redemption of the human race and for the cancellation of the debts of sin which we incurred originally through Adam’s disobedience and through our own free will, and assumed a sinless human being from the holy ever-virgin Mary. Thus the same Son of God the Father would be the Son of man: perfect God and perfect man, so that perfect man and God might be one Christ, one person in two natures, lest a quaternity be added to the Trinity if Christ had a double person.

Therefore, his person is believed to be separable from the Father and the Holy Spirit, but his nature from the humanity assumed; the same person exists as one with that human being, while in nature he is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit. As we have said, from two natures and one person there is one Lord Jesus Christ: in the form of Godhead equal to the Father, in the form of a servant less than the Father.

For this is his voice in the psalm: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Psalm 21:11). Born from God without a mother, born from a virgin without a father, he alone is “the Word made flesh and dwelling among us” (John 1:14).

Although the whole Trinity cooperated in the formation of the humanity assumed, since the works of the Trinity are inseparable, only the Son nevertheless assumed humanity in the singularity of his person, not in the unity of the divine nature—that is, what is proper to the Son, not what is common to the Trinity. For if one person had fashioned the humanity born and another the Godhead, the whole Trinity would have assumed a body, since it is established that the nature of the Trinity is one, though not its person.

This Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, sent by the Father, assuming what he was not and not losing what he was—inviolable by what belonged to him, mortal by what belonged to us—came into this world to save sinners and justify believers. Performing miracles, he was handed over on account of our offenses; he died for our expiation; he rose for our justification. By his bruising we have been healed, by his death we have been reconciled to God the Father, and by his resurrection we have been raised again.

We also await him coming at the end of the ages, when in his most just judgment he will repay the righteous with rewards and the wicked with punishments at the resurrection of all.

We believe also that the Catholic Church, without spot or wrinkle, is his body, and that it will possess the kingdom with its head, almighty Christ Jesus, after this corruptible nature has put on incorruption and this mortal nature immortality, so that God may be all in all. By this faith hearts are purified; by this faith heresies are uprooted. In this faith the whole Church, already joined to the heavenly kingdom, thereafter glories in the present age. For salvation is not found in another faith, “nor is there any other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

### II

Receiving with great reverence and veneration the devotion of our most religious ruler and the decree of our fellow priests, established in the first year of his reign and now celebrated annually throughout his whole kingdom, and which it has pleased us to confirm by our own assertion, we therefore decree by the authority of the universal council that the days of the litanies instituted in the aforementioned synod shall be observed each year with every solemnity at the time when they were ordered to be celebrated. Thus, for the sins in which we have until now been jointly entangled, there may be expiation for us before the eyes of almighty God.

### III

The unyielding treachery of the Jews now seems at last to have been bent by heavenly mercy and power. For this is evident: under the inspiration of the supreme God, the most excellent and Christian ruler, inflamed with the ardor of faith, has chosen, together with the priests of his kingdom, to eradicate their transgressions and superstitions completely. He does not permit anyone who is not Catholic to dwell in his kingdom. For this fervor of faith we give thanks to the almighty Lord of heaven, because he has created so illustrious a soul and filled it with his wisdom. May he also grant him long life in the present age and eternal glory in the future.

We must, however, decide with provident care and highly vigilant diligence that the heat of his faith and our labor may not at some time grow cold and melt away among our successors. Therefore, with heart and mouth in harmony with him, we promulgate a judgment pleasing to God. Together with the agreement and deliberation of his noble and illustrious men, we decree that whoever in succeeding times receives the summit of the kingdom shall not ascend the royal throne until, among the other conditions of his oath, he has promised that he will not permit them to violate this Catholic faith, and that he will in no way, by favoring their treachery, through neglect, or enticed by greed, provide a path to the precipice of infidelity and transgression. Rather, what has been diligently secured in our time must remain unimpaired in the future.

After he has assumed the government of the kingdom according to the order prescribed above, if he himself proves to be a violator of this promise, let him be anathema maranatha in the sight of God and become food for eternal fire. At the same time, let all priests or other Christians who have become involved with him through fear be struck with the same condemnation.

For we decree the present matters in such a way as also to confirm what was written concerning the Jews in the universal synod of the past, since we establish that the necessary precautions which could be written for their salvation are contained in those decrees. Therefore we judge that what was then decreed shall remain valid.

### IV

Although we know that the shoots of depravity, often springing up, have very frequently been condemned at first with just severity, nevertheless, since they are seen to flourish again with repeated roots, we decree that they be cut off from the root with the sharper force of justice.

Accordingly, whoever, as an imitator of Simon, proves to be a follower of the simoniacal heresy, seeking to obtain the ranks of ecclesiastical orders not by the dignity of his conduct but by the expenditure of gifts, and gaining them through offerings—although neither the order of reason nor any dignity of conduct commends him—shall in no way be permitted to attain the heights of the sacred orders. If he has attained them, he shall be deprived of communion and condemned, together with those who ordained him, by the loss of his own goods.

### V

It often happens that the passage of a long time opposes proof of original ownership. Therefore, making provision, we decree that any cleric who receives a stipend from the property of any bishop’s church through generosity must write a declaration under the name of a precarious grant. He must not inflict prejudice upon the church through a prolonged claim, and whatever he has received for use he must work beneficially, so that property belonging to divine right may not appear to be neglected on any pretext and so that clerics may receive support from the church which they serve. If any of them refuses to do this, he will appear to deprive himself of his stipend.

### VI

The course toward pleasure is easy, and nature imitates vices. Therefore, whoever, whether man or woman, has once voluntarily assumed the religious habit; or if a man devoted to the Church, or a woman, has been or is assigned to a monastery of girls—if either sex violates the profession, that person must be compelled unwillingly to return to the appointed way: the man must be tonsured, and the girl must return to the monastery.

If they wish to remain deserters under any protection, let them be regarded by priestly judgment as exiles from the assembly of Christians, so that no place of communion may exist for them. Widows who desert their profession or habit shall likewise be condemned by the foregoing judgment, as the universal synod has already decreed.

¹¹⁹

### VII

Although earlier councils have never been silent concerning so great a crime, reason nevertheless demands that matters repeated through frequent transgression be condemned by frequent judgment. Human perversity has become so great that those whom the profession of penitence, under a religious habit, leads or has led to the hand of the priest for the forgiveness of sins are again recalled by revived wickedness to the filth of their former life.

For this reason the holy synod decrees that if any freeborn persons of either sex have lived under a religious habit in the name of a penitent, but thereafter grow their hair or assume secular clothing and return to what they had abandoned, they must be seized by the bishop of the city in whose territory they have been converted and, against their will, again subjected in monasteries to the laws of penance.

If this proves difficult because of the power of some person, then, as the decrees of the ancient canons have established, they shall be held excommunicated and condemned by anathema until they return to the order they abandoned. The same applies to those who, after communion has been forbidden, communicate with them.

The priest to whom they are known to belong, if through any gift, favor, or negligence he does not wish to admonish them—either to receive them when they return or to expel them from the Church when they persist in contempt—shall be punished by the same judgment until he publishes his decision concerning their correction or condemnation.

### VIII

There is an ancient and most holy judgment of the Father, Pope Leo: if someone who is in the age of adolescence, fearing the danger of death, has come to the remedy of penance, and, if married, happens to be incontinent, let him return to his former marriage so that he may not afterward fall into adultery, until with the maturity of time he can attain the state of continence.

We decree the same equally concerning women as concerning men—not indeed as a general canonical command, but as an indulgence granted by us on account of human frailty—with this proviso: if the person who is not bound by the laws of penance dies before the one who had returned by mutual agreement to continence from the state in question, the survivor may not again return to the embrace of a spouse.

But if the life of the person who did not receive the blessing of the penitent’s condition continues, the other may marry if unable to remain continent and may once more enjoy the companionship of a spouse. We make clear that this has been decreed equally for both sexes, with the condition that in all these matters the priest’s decision be awaited, so that, according to what he observes to be suitable for the person’s age, he may impose the rule either of release from or strictness in continence.

### IX

The passage of time often makes the condition of one’s origin unknown. Therefore, it was already decreed in a canon of the preceding universal council that the freedmen of the Church must make their profession, declaring that they belong to the households of the Church and will never abandon the Church’s service.

We add this also concerning them: whenever a priest has completed the course of his life and departed from this life, as soon as his successor arrives, all the Church’s freedmen and those descended from them must themselves publicly display their documents before the bishop who has been installed, and renew their profession in the sight of the Church, so that they may retain the force of their status and the Church may not be deprived of their obedience.

But if, within the year following the ordination of the new bishop, they neglect to display the documents of their freedom or refuse to renew their professions, those documents shall remain void and empty, and they shall be restored to their origin as perpetual slaves.

### X

For it is fitting that those whose parents received the title of freedom from the households of the Church should be nourished within the church to which they owe obedience, for the sake of instruction. It is contempt for their patrons if, while those patrons are neglected, the offspring of the manumitted are given to others for upbringing.

Therefore we decree that they be kept by the bishop in the service of instruction without prejudice to their status, so that they may render the service they owe and suffer no diminution of their freedom. Those who attempt to act otherwise than our judgment has decreed, we order the bishops to bring back to this arrangement against their will.

But if their parents should perhaps refuse to give them to their own bishops and adopt other patrons for themselves, let them be struck by the law applicable to ungrateful freedmen.

### XI

It is fitting that the life of an innocent person be stained by no harm inflicted by an accuser. Therefore, whoever is accused by anyone shall not be handed over to punishment before the accuser has been brought forward and the judgment of the laws and canons has been investigated. But if the person is found unworthy to bring an accusation, judgment shall not be rendered on the basis of that accusation.

### XII

The audacity of depraved minds often seeks refuge with enemies, either because of the malice of their thoughts or on account of their offenses. Therefore, whoever has committed such offenses and, seeking to defend himself, appeals to adversaries and brings loss of property upon his homeland or his people [Col. 0491B] shall, after being brought back by the authority of the king and the people, be excommunicated and confined, and subjected to the laws of a more distant penance. But if, remembering his evil beforehand, he himself should flee to the Church, the priests’ intercession and reverence for the place shall ensure that royal mercy toward him is preserved, together with justice.

### XIII

Those who, by precedence of dignity and reverence, or by favor earned through merit, are held in honor at the palace shall in every respect receive modest honor from their juniors. The juniors, in turn, shall be embraced by their seniors with an affection of love and instructed by the example of usefulness.

### XIV

To deprive the faithful of their reward is not only inhuman but also unjust. Therefore, since the merit of fidelity in both divine and human affairs is not to be regarded with ingratitude [Col. 0491C], it seems fitting that by priestly judgment we should provide for the king’s faithful subjects. Accordingly, as the holy council decreed in the first year of our most serene prince, all the faithful who have obeyed the prince’s wishes or commands through obedience and sincere service, and who have devoted their entire purpose to guarding his safety, shall not be unjustly deprived by the successors of the kingdom either of their dignity or of their former possessions. Rather, they shall now be regulated according to the discretion of each prince’s benefit, just as he recognizes them to be necessary for the homeland. His benevolence shall be distributed to them in such a way that, in other matters, the power of his great favor may be shown, so that they may enjoy freely all the things they have justly acquired, whether to leave them to their descendants or to bestow them upon whomever their will shall determine.

[Col. 0491D] But if anyone should prove disloyal in the royal administration or useless in matters entrusted to him, while our most pious lord, King Chintillan, is still alive, the regulation of such a matter shall remain within his merciful power, to be established at his own will. For it is impious to call into question the power of one to whom the governance of all things has plainly been entrusted by divine judgment. But if, after his death, anyone should be found to have been disloyal to his life, let him lose whatever he possessed among the property acquired through his generosity, that property being confiscated and distributed to the faithful.

### XV

Since it is evident that we have provided the best support for those who serve princes worthily and render them faithful obedience, when we decree that things justly acquired from princes shall remain undivided in their possession [Col. 0492A], it is especially equitable that we provide timely care for the property of the Churches of God. Accordingly, whatever property has been or shall be justly granted to the Churches of God by princes, or whatever has been or shall be fairly bestowed upon them by any other person under any title, we order to remain in their possession with firm stability, so that it can in no circumstance or at no time be taken away.

For it is fitting that, just as we have judged the faithful services of human beings not to be met with ingratitude, so gifts bestowed upon the churches—which are the proper sustenance of the poor—should remain undisturbed, as recompense for the injury suffered by those who offer them.

### XVI

Just as the insolence of wicked kings is always hateful and detestable to their subjects, so the prudent usefulness of good kings becomes beloved among the peoples. Therefore [Col. 0492B], what Christian could endure, or see such a Christian erring, who attempted to strip the royal offspring or descendants of their possessions or deprive them of their dignities?

To prevent this, now that a general judgment concerning the sons of the prince is being issued, we establish suitable decrees concerning the present descendants of the most excellent King Chintillan: the entire kingdom shall preserve, with regard to all his descendants, what the synod held in this church in the preceding year decreed. That is, his sons shall be shown benevolent and steadfast affection, and wherever circumstances require, they shall be granted proper means of defense, so that through any cunning plot they may not be deprived of possessions justly acquired, of dignities secured by their parents, of gifts from princes, of expenditures made on their behalf, or even of property owed to them by right. Nor shall anyone be provided with an opportunity or pretext for injuring them [Col. 0492C], because it is fitting that, since we enjoy security under his rule, we should grant peace by conciliar decree to his descendants.

Finally, our prince’s benefits toward us are so great that it would take too long to recount them individually. Through God’s agency he has given us peace; he has, as it were, brought love back from captivity; through his help we are at peace; through his generosity we have been enriched; by the medicine of his goodness he has both spared the guilty and raised up the upright. If we wished to respond to him with worthy benefits, we would not possess such abundant resources of virtue as could match such great goodwill.

### XVII

Although a judgment concerning this matter was promulgated in the preceding council, held in the first year of our glorious prince, it is nevertheless pleasing to repeat what must be preserved [Col. 0492D]. Therefore, while the king remains alive, no layman of any dignity, nor anyone consecrated to the rank of bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor anyone devoted to any other clerical office, shall designate a future king for himself by any action or deliberation against the welfare—and certainly against the will—of the living king. No one shall, through flattery or persuasion in pursuit of that hope, draw others to himself, nor shall he himself consent to another.

For Christians ought to regard it as wicked and utterly detestable to look ahead to unlawful arrangements for a future time and to dispose of the future while ignorant of their own life. If anyone has already contemplated such wicked things with anyone else, let him know that priestly moderation grants him this indulgence, if he asks pardon, namely, that he should promptly endeavor to make the matter public to the ears of the present prince [Col. 0493A]. But if he conceals it and refuses to disclose the schemes of his deliberation, let him be punished with the worst anathema.

When the king has died, no one shall assume the kingdom through tyrannical presumption. No one tonsured under the guise of religion, disgracefully shaven, descended from a servile origin, or belonging to a foreign people shall be raised to the summit of the kingdom unless he is advanced on account of worthy birth and character. Whoever violates this most holy command shall be condemned by perpetual anathema.

### XVIII

Although provision for the safety of our princes is already known to have been made in the preceding universal synod, we wish to repeat what was rightly decreed and to strengthen salutary ordinances with due authority. Therefore, before God and the entire order of angels, before the choirs of prophets and apostles and of all the martyrs, before the whole Catholic Church and the assembly of Christians, we testify:

Let no one plot the destruction of the king; let no one attack the prince’s life; let no one deprive him of the reins of the kingdom; let no one usurp the summit of the kingdom through tyrannical presumption; let no one by any contrivance join himself to the hand of conspirators acting against him.

If any of our people should rashly presume any of these things, struck by divine anathema, let him be condemned and held over to eternal judgment without any place of remedy. But the one who has succeeded to his throne [120], if he wishes to be cleansed from so great a sacrilege, shall avenge that king’s death as though it were his own father’s.

For the aid of his defense, let the strength of the entire kingdom of the Goths consent. But if, through negligence and lesser zeal, anyone should refuse to avenge so deadly a crime, let all such persons, by our judgment, be a reproach to the other nations.

### XIX

With all these matters duly arranged and considered through prolonged consultation, we return blessing, glory, and honor to the invisible Father, author of all lights, and implore the help of his aid in preserving them, so that he may grant strength to our constitutions and make human weakness effective for this arrangement—that is, salutary—so that he may not judge it transgressive.

Therefore, with all the authority of the ancient canons, we confirm everything written above by our subscription [Col. 0494B]. We give thanks to our most Christian and most glorious prince, Chintillan, through whose zeal and insistence we have been summoned and gathered. His approved will has proved a religious ordinance, until the Lord grants that excellent prince a lasting triumph in the present age and an eternal kingdom among the just, and until he himself, blessed through blessed years, enjoys prolonged happiness and is everywhere fortified by the protection of the divine right hand.

I, Silva, although unworthy, bishop of the Church of Narbonne, have subscribed to these constitutions issued by us. Likewise, the other bishops subscribed, thirty-seven in number.
