[Col. 0493]

[Col. 0493B]  
1. Concerning fugitive and perfidious clerics and laymen.  
2. Concerning the illness of serving clerics.  
3. Concerning the funeral rites of a dying bishop.  
[Col. 0494B]  
4. Concerning the exactions of the churches of the province of Galicia.  
5. Concerning dishonorable recluses and vagrants.  
6. Concerning neighboring bishops who are to reside in the royal city.

## THE SEVENTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGINS

Thirty bishops, in the sixth year of King Chindaswinth, in the era 680, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.

[Col. 0493]

### CHAPTER I

Since, in the name of the holy Trinity, an assembly had been convened in the city of Toledo for certain ecclesiastical disciplines, through both our devotion and the zeal of our most serene king and lover of Christ, Chindaswinth, it seemed appropriate, through mutual consultation, to decree what, as we trust, will prove highly beneficial for careful preservation by both the present and future generations. Indeed, whatever is judged useful for ecclesiastical conduct or for the public welfare—without which we do not live in peace—must always be provided for with the greatest care.

For although constitutions of the canons already exist and could suffice for every correction, if anyone would willingly attend to them, nevertheless the brightness of their light shines more fully the more diligently and frequently they are handled [Col. 0493D]. It contributes greatly to the correction of many if established matters are recalled to memory through fraternal consultation, and if those things are also added that seem to be lacking or that are judged altogether appropriate to establish [Col. 0494C].

Who does not know how many unlawful acts have hitherto been perpetrated by tyrants and fugitives who transferred themselves to foreign regions, and how often their abominable arrogance has been practiced—acts that brought diminution upon the homeland and imposed unceasing labor upon the Gothic army? If this had been done by the madness of laymen, it might perhaps sometimes seem tolerable to us. Yet what is much more astonishing—and worse—is that men dedicated to so great a religion are sometimes carried headlong into this presumption, so that it would bring no slight confusion upon us if a matter which both secular law and ecclesiastical discipline require to be corrected were allowed in any way to remain.

Therefore, by unanimous judgment, it has now pleased us to define that whoever, established in the clerical order from the highest rank to the lowest, transfers himself for any reason into the territory of a foreign people, so that from there he appears arrogantly to seek either his return or anything else, or so that under this pretext he has arranged or in any way carried out something that could harm or might be done against the Gothic people, the homeland, or the kingdom—and likewise anyone found to be privy to such matters, and known to provide them either counsel or assistance, whether concerning the seeking of flight to a foreign people, the persistence in the evils they had begun, or any injury they might inflict after their flight upon the Gothic people, the homeland, or the prince, while persevering in the same depravity—whoever is recognized to have done this shall unquestionably be deprived of every degree of his honor, so that another shall immediately and perpetually receive the place in which he had served, to govern it.

The transgressor himself, placed under penance, if he properly repents of the evil he committed and continues to repent until the day of his death, shall receive communion only at the very end of his life, and not before the time of his end has arrived. If any priest should consent to communicate with him even at the command of the prince, he shall become a participant in that crime, be anathematized forever, and be condemned by the same sentence as the one with whom he communicated. For no priest ought, by the prince’s power, to give assent in a matter by which he might appear to incur perjury.

Or, God forbid, if a prince who is a transgressor of the Catholic faith should arise, a priest must in no way be compelled by the prince’s favor or terror to return from the light of right belief to darkness. For we must never nullify the foregoing chapters either through the commands or the threats of princes. We know that almost all the priests of Spain, all the nobles, judges, and other men of palace office have sworn, and that it has now been decreed by law, that no fugitive or perfidious person who, acting against the Gothic people, the homeland, or the king, is found to have transferred himself into the fellowship of another people shall in any way be restored to the entirety of his property—unless perhaps the princes should wish to grant such persons some act of humanity. Even then, however, the prince shall have the power to grant him no more than a twentieth part of the property from which the king chooses to give.

But because the presumption of an unstable and sometimes depraved mind occasionally elevates many clerics so that, abandoning the seriousness of their order and forgetting the oath they had promised to keep toward the reigning prince, they rashly consent to the election of another, this license ought to be wholly abolished and entirely eradicated from our fellowship. Thus, if any layman should at some time, while within the borders of the Gothic homeland, arrogantly attempt to seize the summit of the kingdom, and any cleric should provide him assistance or favor, and through the success of that offense the one who appears to be acting arrogantly should manage to attain the same ambition for the kingdom, then from that day or time onward the same bishop or cleric of whatever order who became involved in such a crime shall remain excommunicated forever.

Nevertheless, if, because of the wickedness of the prince to whom he gave wrongful consent, he could not be suspended from communion through the efforts of the priests, then, if he survives beyond that king’s death, he shall be subject to the foregoing correction of anathema; and no one shall consent that the grace of communion be bestowed on him except at the final end of his life—provided that he is shown to have repented lawfully.

In the meantime, reason has persuaded us to decree by synodal constitution that any layman who, in violation of the prohibited chapters, should be found henceforth guilty of acting against the people, the homeland, or royal authority by going into foreign regions or providing assistance to such persons shall not only, as has been said, be deprived of ownership of all his property, but shall also be condemned to perpetual excommunication. Communion shall never be granted to him except at the final moment of his death, unless the remedy of communion for him—or for those whom we discussed above—has been obtained from the prince through the priests’ petition [Col. 0496B].

For if anyone is found wickedly to speak in insult or defamation of the prince, or to plot or give consent for the king’s death or the seizure of his property, we indeed judge him worthy of such excommunication. Whether communion should ever afterward be granted to him, however, we leave to the prince’s mercy to decide, since it is undoubtedly within his power to temper the faults of his subjects by a judgment of mercy and justice.

We admonish the most merciful princes and, by the ineffable sacrament of the divine name, unanimously and earnestly beseech them not, at any time, to suspend through any rash act the sentence of this excommunication against perfidious clerics or laymen who transfer themselves to foreign regions or give their consent, unless a just priestly petition has been made where necessary. For the interests of the realm will be better served if the form of our constitution is preserved.

Let any king henceforth who believes that the censure of this canon ought to be violated in any respect, or permits it to be violated, become an accursed anathema and, as a transgressor of the Catholic faith, remain forever guilty before the Lord.

### II

Nothing shall be presumed through the audacity of rashness against the statute of the order, nor shall those things which are held in the highest veneration be undone by even the slightest touch of presumption, since these arrangements were ordered for the sole purpose that they should not be recognized as interrupted or that nature should not be deprived of the strength of health through the onset of illness [Col. 0496D].

Human care therefore provides not only for bodily weakness but also ensures attentive concern for the sacred mysteries of God. Accordingly, we have judged it appropriate that, when the holy mysteries are consecrated by priests during the time of the Mass, if an occurrence of illness should prevent completion of the begun mystery of consecration, it shall be lawful for a bishop or another presbyter to carry out the consecration and complete the office that has been begun.

For nothing else is suitable to complete the mysteries already initiated except the completed blessing of either the priest who began or the one who follows, since they cannot be regarded as perfected unless they are completed according to the order of perfection. Since we are all one in Christ, diversity creates nothing contrary where the unity of faith manifests the effectiveness of a favorable outcome. Let all the clergy of every order recognize that this provision also applies indivisibly to them. As stated above, others may willingly succeed those who preceded them for the sake of completion, but what is provided because of bodily weakness must not be turned into the ruin of presumption.

No one shall celebrate Mass after taking even the smallest amount of food or drink. No minister or priest, once he has begun an incomplete office, shall presume to abandon it without an evident onset of illness. Whoever presumes to violate these provisions shall incur the sentence of excommunication.

### III

Things appropriate to propriety often fail to be fulfilled through the negligence of certain persons. Since it is therefore known, from the canons and the tradition of ancient custom, what dignity is to be preserved in the funeral rites of a dying bishop [Col. 0497B], we add only this: if any priest, after being summoned according to the statutes of the Council of Valence to come for the burial of the body of a deceased bishop, should delay through sluggishness, then, if the clergy of the dying bishop appeal to the synod or to the metropolitan bishop, he shall have absolutely no permission for the space of one year either to celebrate Mass or to receive communion.

Presbyters and other clerics who hold a position of greater honor in the same church whose priest has died, but who are found slow to give all necessary attention to the funeral rites either of one already dead or of a bishop who is immediately about to die, or who are shown to neglect this through any disturbance of mind, shall be assigned to penance in monasteries for the entire period of one year.

### IV

Among the other matters which it was appropriate for us to settle by common consent, it was also necessary to examine most carefully the complaints of the parish priests of the province of Galicia, which necessity, as we have learned, finally compelled them to bring into public inquiry against the rapacity of their bishops.

For the bishops there, as clear investigation has revealed, burdened the parish churches with indiscriminate administration. Since they frequently exceeded proper limits in their exactions, they are shown to have brought certain basilicas almost to the point of demanding their last resources. Therefore, lest what has clearly been presumed disorderly up to now occur again, no bishop of the province shall expect to receive by annual levy more than two solidi from each diocese or each church, in accordance with the Council of Braga. The basilicas of monasteries, however, are exempt from this payment.

When a bishop visits a diocese, he shall not be burdensome to anyone through excessive numbers, nor shall he ever exceed the number of five attendants, or have permission to remain more than one day at any single basilica. Any of these bishops who presumes to act otherwise than we have decreed shall unquestionably be subject to the correction of the canons, as a transgressor of synodal constitutions and a corrupter of the edict of the ancient Fathers.

### V

We observe that certain people, ignorant of or forgetful of the traditions of the Fathers [Col. 0498A], have fallen into such great negligence that, through their detestable practice, things that were lawfully established are almost revealed as forgotten. When the unlearned desire to teach, what else do they show except that they are afflicted by the error of ignorance? And because, relying on a backward course, they put forward presumption before the discipline of teaching, it is clear that they do not seek the grace of profound humility but serve the demand of corruption.

Therefore, while justly decreeing such matters with severity, we make this distinction by appropriate judgment: those whom an ambition for a secluded holy life keeps enclosed in their own cells, and whom both the merits of that same holy purpose aid and integrity adorns, are protected by God’s help and our favor.

But those whom laziness, rather than knowledge of wisdom, has driven into such a purpose, and whom no dignity of life adorns—but whom, worse still, ignorance disgraces and detestable conduct disturbs [Col. 0498B]—we decree must be expelled from the cells and places in which they are either reported to wander or are held enclosed. They shall be assigned in every respect to monasteries by the bishops or by the superiors of the monasteries from whose community they came or near which they reside.

There, while studying the teachings of the holy order, they shall first be able to learn what was established by the Fathers, so that afterward they may teach what they have acquired through holy meditation. Only then, if they have become fruitful in doctrine and holy work, shall they proceed toward the highest virtue, imbued through the practice of holy intention.

Henceforth, whoever decides to enter this holy way of life shall not again be permitted to attain it by any other route, nor shall he be able to achieve it beforehand unless, first trained in monasteries and more fully instructed according to the holy rules of the monasteries, he has been able to earn both the dignity of honorable life and knowledge of holy doctrine [Col. 0498C].

But those whom such extreme madness has seized that they are recognized as wandering in fixed places and dishonorable through depravity of conduct, possessing absolutely neither stability of residence nor integrity of mind, any priest or minister who finds them wandering shall either, if they are nearby, assign them to the Fathers of the monasteries for correction, or, if that is difficult, entrust them to the authority of those who can instruct them for the sake of restoring their integrity.

### VI

It has also pleased us that, out of reverence for the prince and honor for the royal seat and for the metropolitan of that city, and for the consolation of the neighboring bishops of the city of Toledo who have received the admonition of that bishop, they should reside in the same city during the individual months of the year, except during the harvest and vintage holidays [Col. 0498D].

We unanimously offer thanks to immortal God and to the glorious prince Chindaswinth, on whose account we have come together in holy devotion to this city. With a welcome effort, we earnestly ask that the affection of faith and peace of the holy Catholic Church may always be increased, and that the aforementioned prince may, together with the prosperity of his present kingdom, also be granted future rewards of joy—through him who, as one God in the Trinity, lives and is glorified forever and ever.

Horontius, metropolitan bishop of the holy Emeritan Church, have subscribed, defining these enactments in the name of Christ. Likewise, the other bishops subscribed, thirty-eight in number.

3. Concerning incontinent bishops.  
4. Concerning incontinent presbyters and deacons, and women who join themselves to such men.  
5. Concerning incontinent deacons.  
[Col. 0500A]

## THE EIGHTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGINS

Held in the era 651, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0499]

[Col. 0499A] In the fifth year of the orthodox and glorious King Recceswinth, preeminent in the true dignity of clemency [Col. 0499B], when, by divine ordinance and at the most serene command of that same prince, all of us had been summoned to gather in the basilica of the holy apostles for the sacred assembly of the synod, at last the long-desired day of joy, eagerly hoped for and welcome, arrived. It was received with a more eager longing of our hearts insofar as it had been sought by the panting inward parts as a remedy for salvation.

When, according to custom, each member of our order had taken his appointed seat and the expectation of a peaceful outcome awaited the course of events, the most serene prince appeared, filled with pious religion and glorious with the highest title of praise. Presenting himself as inclined toward our assembly, he stood before us and, like a son, exhorted us with sweet words to commend him to the almighty Lord in our prayers [Col. 0499C]. He gave thanks to the God of hosts that, fulfilling the decree of his command, we had been gathered together into one council.

But when we recognized the humility of his soul and saw the height of so exalted a glory inclined toward us, we were inflamed with such great joy of exultation that we gladly and reverently returned to him the thanks and honor due to him. Yet just as the sublime order of humility had exalted the prince, so the examples of the most sacred prince’s character instructed us in the exercises of the highest virtue and in the form of our religion.

Then, after praises had been offered to God for the outcome of mutual unity, he addressed us with great tranquility and said:

“Although the supreme Author of all things raised me to the throne of the kingdom during the reign of my lord, of divine memory, my father, and made me a participant in his glory by granting me a share in it [Col. 0499D], now that he has attained eternal rest among the dwelling places, the divine power has wholly subjected to me the rights of complete rule that he left transferred to me. Since the welfare of those who are governed is the welfare of the head, and the happiness of peoples is nothing other than the gentleness of princes, I have gladly resolved, with you present before me, to disclose openly by decree the deliberations of my wishes, and to present, with sincere display, decrees suited to my purposes.

“But since an eager heart pours itself into the crossroads of promises, lest it submit to the burdens of delay, wearied by sluggishness, I have compressed a lengthy speech into the brevity of a summary. What I could have spread abroad in an assembly through extended words, I have decided to offer in its entirety, enclosed in this volume, to your reverend holiness [Col. 0500B]. With earnest prayer I exhort you to attend closely to whatever is written there, examine it with discerning zeal, and whatever proves pleasing to God, let it be reported to us through the sacred oracle of your mouths.”

Then, having received the volume offered to us, we acclaimed our thanks to the Lord:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

After the joy of this blessed exultation and the hymn of heavenly glory, we blessed the same sacred prince. When the volume had been opened, we found the following composed within it [Col. 0500C]:

“In the name of the Lord, Flavius Recceswinth, king, to the most reverend Fathers sitting in this holy synod, the holy bishops.

“Gratefully holding the solid rule of my faith as an admirable gift, recognizing it as fully instructed, and prostrating before its honor the diadem of glory with humility of heart, rejoicing in that saying which declares that all the kings of the earth serve and obey God, I come before you, reverend Fathers, raised to an even higher honor of veneration. I call upon your devotion to the favor of your gentleness, and, bowing before the fearful signs of almighty God as a testimony to your vision of me, I return abundant thanks to him with a joyful heart, because in the clemency of his will he has deemed it worthy, at the command of our lofty authority, to lead you into the desired assembly of this holy congregation [Col. 0500D].

“I trust that the reward of his grace will be present both for me and for you throughout the sequence of present times and the length of future ages, since by your concord in assembling you demonstrate a unanimous and religious affection, and you will be able clearly to recognize how pious is the purpose of my policy in governing peoples.

“Now, since a preliminary admonition cannot contain the excess of a lengthy discourse, retain in the sequence of this volume and learn fully what I know concerning the holy faith, which I have recognized as having descended from heaven to me through the mouths of the holy apostles and the frequent gatherings of the Fathers, and also what I have resolved to make known concerning the matters that are to follow, for the sake of which I judged this assembly of the congregation ought to be brought together [Col. 0501A].

“Learn fully what has been set down in writing there, and let the gravity of your blessedness bring forth and mercifully apply an effective outcome to all that the authority of our majesty has impressed upon the tenor of this volume, just as the serenity of our clemency has entrusted its fulfillment to you.”

Therefore, beginning the opening of my address with a definition of the holy faith, and intending to state the remaining matters that must be pursued in the future, as though I were building upon the firmness of a rock, and undertaking from God the construction of my work, I shall set forth what follows with greater strength insofar as I have placed the firmest matters first with greater propriety. First, therefore, let your Reverence bear in mind what it does not doubt: that I possess fully, know truly, and hold most firmly the true, holy, and sincere rule of the orthodox faith, from a pure heart and a good conscience; that I embrace, venerate, and love it just as holy apostolic tradition teaches it, just as the holy Synod of Nicaea established it, just as the assembly of the holy Fathers at Constantinople defined it, just as the unity of the first gathering at Ephesus affirmed it, and just as the definition of the Council of Chalcedon set it forth.

I preserve this faith with the faithful, invite unbelievers to salvation through it, govern subject peoples according to it, commend it for observance to my own nations, proclaim it among foreign peoples, so that, glorifying God through it, I may attain among mortals the blessedness of the supreme Divinity, and may receive from Him a glorious inheritance in the land of the living. Behold, most reverend Fathers, how much your Honor has judged that I have explained, as far as the truth of the holy faith is concerned, the titles of my confession with my whole soul. Now I consider it especially appropriate to join to the fellowship of this same true faith the endeavors of holy action toward which we are striving, lest we possess it either dead and without works or, while the dignity of its fullness remains unrecognized, dishonorably fall away from it—for Scripture does not remain silent about certain people who say that they know God but deny Him.

Therefore, so that we may possess this faith more fully, founded upon that stone “which some builders rejected, yet which was made by the Lord into the cornerstone and is marvelous in our eyes” (Psalm 117:22–23), and so that we may be more fittingly adorned with its insignia, attend to the fruit of what work and the increase of what activity we wish to associate with and attach to the endeavors of this holy faith. Thus, when we recall the times gone by, we remember that you and the whole people swore that any person, of whatever rank or honor, who was discovered to have contemplated or carried out anything harmful against the assassination of the king and the destruction of the Gothic people and homeland, having been punished by the severity of an irrevocable sentence, should nowhere deserve the remedy of pardon or receive any support whatsoever from leniency.

But now, since this is judged grave and burdensome, since this sentence is seen to resist acts of compassion with serious opposition, and since the affirmation of condemnation is thus retained in full, so that no access whatever may remain for the mercy which, as the Apostle proclaims, is useful for all things (1 Timothy 4:8), I entrust these matters to your sacred judgments to be examined and resolved by your decisions, so that, with divine compassion inspiring you, it may be yours to regulate the measure of both dangers in such a way that neither the condition of the oath holds the guilty bound nor the vengeance of impiety makes us inhuman. Thus may the pattern of your judgment instruct us, so that we do not keep subject peoples submissive either in profanations or contaminated by the bonds of impiety.

After this address concerning the dispute, we likewise append the causes of the matters that follow, asking you to attend with similar concentration.

We decree, bearing witness by the coequal, coeternal, and inseparable Trinity of the supreme Divinity, and by the sacrament of that mystery which true faith throughout the world proclaims: that the Son of God was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary for the salvation of the world; and by the coming of that same Jesus Christ, Son of God and our Lord, by which the impious are to be destroyed and by which His kingdom will glorify the saints—that whatever matters may arise from hearings concerning anyone’s complaints, once disclosed, should be concluded in the judgments of the laws with justice and vigor, mercifully and in harmony with the moderation of the most just compassion.

With the consent of our Serenity, you are to arrange only those things that accord with sincere justice and the sufficiency of the matters at issue, whether certain canons appear distorted, excessive, or improperly introduced; bring whatever is obscure in the canons and turned into doubt back into the light of clear understanding; and strive to establish all assemblies of the various orders and the condition of every matter brought before you in such a way that, agreeing most justly, piously, and temperately with the rules of our ancestors, it may come about both that I, who long for the fruits of good endeavors, may attain a share among the blessed, and that you, who fulfill God’s will and do not despise me in my supplication, may be received by the religion of eternal blessedness and be granted to cling forever to the vision of God’s delight.

You illustrious men also, whom the primacy of your offices in the palace has obtained for this holy synod, whom distinguished nobility has honored, and whom experience has required to govern the common people—whom I embrace as partners in government, faithful in adversity, and energetic in prosperity—through whom justice fulfills the laws, compassion fulfills the law, and moderation of equity restrains the severity of the law against justice: I adjure and beseech you, by all that wondrous and sole sacrament of the one sacred faith, and by the venerable holy assembly of all the holy Fathers by whom I adjure you, to direct your minds according to the most just pattern of all truth and discernment.

Whatever you recognize as close to innocence, near to justice, not alien to piety, or pleasing to God alone, deign to accomplish promptly, modestly, and with your whole attention, so that your mental gaze may turn nowhere away from the agreement of the Fathers present and of the holy men. Know that, insofar as you fulfill these sober wishes of mine, you show yourselves beloved by God; and insofar as I strengthen the decrees of our decisions by displaying favor, I show that I, together with you and with the Lord, am pleasing.

To all of you collectively, to the ministers fit for divine worship, and to the rulers of the royal court bound by an adjuration in the name of God, I add the true and pure promise of my consent: whatever you choose, with common agreement, to decree or fulfill as close to justice and piety and to salutary discernment, I shall complete with God’s favor and, by the authority of the ruler, fortify and defend against every sort of contentious complaint.

[Note: Thus it should be read: “and, by the authority of the ruler, fortify and defend against every sort of contentious complaint.” With the foregoing, etc.]

After these foregoing matters, which the rule of truth proved to concern those of the household of faith, the zeal of your Blessedness’s assembly for that same faith still asks something else. Following the traditions, I affirm a cause not foreign to your dignity; although Christ urges me to win it, He nevertheless does not doubt that it is hostile to Him until He obtains what He ardently desires. I denounce, namely, the life and customs of the Jews, whose contagion alone I know to have polluted the land of my rule.

For although almighty God has utterly uprooted all heresies from this region, this one disgrace of sacrilege is recognized to remain: either it must be corrected by the zeal of our devotion or destroyed by the vengeance of His punishment. Among them I see some retaining, through an ancient error of tradition, the rights of unbelief; others, cleansed by the washing of holy baptism, have fallen back again into the error of apostasy, so that the blasphemy uttered by them is found more detestable than that of those who are not yet known to have been purified by the water of sacred rebirth.

For this reason, in the struggle of good intention and for the gain of true faith, I entreat your Blessedness’s Reverence, and by the terms of the dread oath mentioned above I solemnly charge you, without any favor and without any partial acceptance of persons among them, to order that concerning these people a judgment be given which is ardently and most truly pleasing to God and to my faith, in whatever pertains to the true faith and true honor of the Lord and my Redeemer Jesus Christ. Thus, just as divine mercy has granted me the kingdom of the faithful, among whom it recognizes that faith, so may it also grant me the gain of the unbelievers, among whom I may rejoice that the good of His will is accomplished and that they have entered His venerable kingdom.

Given on the day of the Kalends of January, in the fifth year, happily, of the glory of our reign. In the name of the Lord, I, Flavius Reccesiunthus, king, have subscribed with my own hand this deliberation of my faith and good will.

## CHAPTER I

When the entire page had been reread or completed, after we had glorified God for hearing the principal matter of the faith and for the affection of His good will, we immediately turned our attention to conducting the remaining cases and began their proceedings. At the beginning of the first account, the subject of the true faith came before us. We began by speaking of it first, so that from it we might take the beginning of firmness—from the same source where we took the beginning of sacred birth—so that, with the firm judgment of holy affirmations placed first, whatever should subsequently arise in the conduct of the cases might more firmly support the sequence of the decrees.

Therefore, we both profess with the full strength of our soul and proclaim with acclamation that we hold one true profession and one true rule of the sacred faith; and with complete deliberation we continually preach it to all, so that they may receive and retain it, just as it is taught as having been shown by the holy Apostles, proved as having been explained by the orthodox Fathers who followed, and truly and holily confirmed in those sacred synodal acts in which the insane error of Arius and Eutyches is detected and uprooted from its foundations, just as finally we profess and recite it with united voice in the solemn celebrations of the sacred Masses.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible.

And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages: God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. For us and for our salvation He descended and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; He became man and suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, and rose again on the third day. He ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead; His kingdom will have no end.

We believe also in the Holy Spirit, the giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets.

And in one catholic and apostolic Church.

We confess one baptism for the remission of sins.

We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come.

Amen.

The rule of this holy faith does not now receive a fuller exposition, because it is abundantly known to have been explained by the sacred teachers, and because the business of the imminent cases draws us toward other matters to be conducted.

## II

At the occurrence of the second discussion, a matter presented itself, both easy and serious. A debate was raised concerning refugees and traitors, and it was investigated with considerable effort whether the sentence against those condemned might be moderated. But when the series of the conditions was recalled to our hearing—conditions to which, after not many years had passed, the devastation of war had compelled us to swear because of their destitution—we found such a severe obligation contained in them that the knot of their offenses seemed not so much to have prohibited transgressions as to have closed the very entrails of compassion.

For there was present on both sides that which stirred fear: lest the holy name be profaned, and lest the exercise of mercy perish. The thing that caused fear was not far removed from profanation of God’s name, while what the prohibition of compassion sought to prevent was also present.

And while the sentences pronounced seemed to oppose one another through the alternating danger of the two possibilities, we, caught between them, were endangered on the divided path of the disputing parties, uncertain by which route the judgment should hasten toward resolution. But when the difficulty of the dispute confronted the steps of our argument and cast us from the road, at last, abandoning the danger of haste, amid the crash of sobs and showers of tears, we turned both our words and our praying hearts to God, who is the fountain of compassion:

“Breathe upon us, Holy Spirit, and lead us into the harbor of Your will” (Psalm 106:30), calming the waves of our ignorance. For behold, the shoals of dangers rise on the shore of our course, and with the obstacles of shipwreck confronting us on every side, we cannot discern, with attentive consideration, where we should spread the sails of our debate. But breathe upon us, Holy Spirit, and by Your gift grant us to know what You command, and by Your command enable us to fulfill what You order, so that by illuminating You may make clear what we do not know, and by assisting You may complete what we fear to undertake.

Let us therefore rest in You, and, casting aside the fears of wandering waves, command us to arrange the commerce of peace. Let us begin those things which may both contribute to the glory of Your omnipotence and, with Your assent, be granted for human salvation.

Not many years ago, when the rebellious faction of certain refusers frequently brought devastation upon the lands through its tumultuous sedition and inflicted scandals upon the peoples together with destruction, to such an extent that they led away bands of captives and laid waste churches—churches so shaken by that plague that no effort could restore them—it was exacted from us, more by the force of arising necessity than by considered judgment, that we should swear the harshest oaths against them and those very like them, together with almost the entire people.

That we swore by invoking the divine name is shown by the condition of the oath; and the authority of sacred Scripture insists that it cannot be dissolved. For it is written in Exodus (20:7): “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not hold innocent the one who takes the name of his God in vain.”

Likewise in Leviticus (19:12): “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God. I am the Lord.”

But that the severity of the pressures imposed can and ought to be relaxed is indicated both by the harshness of these bonds and laments and by the commands of the same divine authority. For, according to the Old Translation, the Lord rebukes and condemns certain people through Isaiah with a grave reproach, saying:

“Woe to the sons of desertion, says the Lord. You made a plan, but not through me, and an agreement, but not through my Spirit, adding sin upon sin” (Isaiah 30:1).

Likewise in Jeremiah:

“Our iniquities have turned everything away, and our sins have removed good things from us, because the impious have been found among my people. Speaking vain things, they made plans to scatter men and seized them; like a snare full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit” (Jeremiah 5:25ff.).

And through Micah:

“Woe is me, my soul, for the faithful person has perished from the land, and there is no one upright among human beings. All are judged in blood; each one oppresses his neighbor; all prepare their hands for evil.”

Concerning beneficence—which is so much more pleasing in the eyes of God as it is found to be more immediate—Isaiah instructs us, saying:

“Dissolve the bonds of wickedness; release the burdens that oppress” (Isaiah 58:6).

Paul also, the vessel of election, says:

“Piety is useful for all things” (1 Timothy 4:8).

And James:

“Judgment without mercy will be rendered to the one who has not shown mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment” (James 2:13).

John likewise:

“Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (1 John 3:15).

And Truth Himself says:

“Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44).

And again:

“Forgive, and you will be forgiven. But if you do not forgive, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6:12ff.).

Behold, these are the commands of the Lord’s order, supported on every side by the firmest guarantee. Therefore, because they have been established by the utterance of the divine mouth, they will remain fixed forever by eternal law.

What then? Shall we say that oaths of justice and oaths of peace oppose one another, when it is written: “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have embraced one another” (Psalm 84:11)?

But because the course of controversies spreads itself through contention, if we have declared that the assertion of one party cannot be fulfilled, why should the insistence of the other party suffer loss? And because the keeping of an oath does not moderate the vengeance to be feared, should the atrocity of impiety therefore produce a detestable death? Far be it.

For if, in public sacred proceedings—may God avert it—someone were to allege that an unlawful or evil condition had been established which compelled him either to murder a father’s soul or to commit violation against a most sacred virgin, would it not be more tolerable to cast away the promises of a foolish pledge than, by keeping useless promises, to fulfill a measure of crimes deserving horror? If that were so, how could observance of a single command be believed to be the fountain of compassion if it brought forth thorns of vengeance? Or what kind of observance of sacred law would that be which committed sacrileges against righteousness? What kind of injustice would it seem to be if, from the safeguard of one command, a savage brutality of killing were to arise?

But we do not now argue in such a way that, once the divisions of controversy have been stirred up, we ourselves become involved in contentious struggles. There is true peace in both of the things we say, because the Holy Spirit regulates our journey and course so that no deviation may exclude us from the proper arrangement.

Therefore, with full voice, fuller faith, and fullest intention, we proclaim—and together proclaim and desire throughout the whole community of the holy Church—that the name of the one and supreme Divinity must never be invoked in any profanation, profaned by no improper perjury, and never touched by any contact with deceit.

For if, as Truth bears witness, swearing is altogether forbidden in order to avoid the profanation of perjury, when it is said, “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; no, no. Whatever is more than this is from evil” (Matthew 5:37), how will it be unpunished voluntarily to have profaned a name of such glory, when the faith established in it is recognized to have perished?

Or how will treaties of peace be bound among disputes between nations if the agreements of oaths are not preserved intact under the sanction of the oath? Indeed, everything that enters into treaties of peace stands more firmly when the intervention of an oath strengthens it; and everything that reconciles the minds of friends endures more securely when the bonds of an oath bind them. Everything, too, that a witness confirms is established more truly when the addition of an oath affirms it; and if the official records fail, the mere declaration of an oath reveals the faith of the innocent.

Thus, so that the divine will might be disclosed to human minds—what God wished, lest fragile uncertainty hold as doubtful what the promise of inviolable truth expressed—He speaks through Isaiah, saying:

“I am the Lord, and there is no other; by myself I have sworn” (Isaiah 45:23).

If, therefore, vows sworn under the limit of such an institution must be observed, who, being alien to truth, would decide that they should be violated detestably? The life-giving commands of sacred authority will therefore stand, and must in no way be rashly violated through empty profanation.

Yet lest the oaths that have been given appear to have so completely closed our hearts against compassion that our souls can conceive no indulgence born of a merciful affection, while maintaining the contracts of the oath we open the bosom of mercy. We judge all those things pleasing to God to be objects of compassion, so that neither the safeguard of the oath may hold us guilty nor inhumanity make us detestable.

Each person ought certainly to meet the ruin of the afflicted with whatever assistance he can provide, and by relieving another’s punishment remove God’s punishment from himself. For the person who drives adversity away from the afflicted offers prosperity to the Lord.

Thus Job, instructed by the experience of suffering, remembering the patience of his own suffering as he showed patience toward those who suffered, and weaving together a catalogue of his virtues, adds among other things:

“The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow” (Job 29:13).

And shortly afterward:

“I once wept over the one who was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor” (Job 30:25).

Hence Solomon also says:

“Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction” (Proverbs 24:11).

Instructed by these decrees of sacred authority, it is clear that we have not profaned the holy name, since the principle of our declaration in no way indicates that it is to be profaned. Rather, with the inward parts of indulgence opened, although those condemned by the profession of their own mouths scarcely deserve to be absolved, according to what is written, “Your blood is upon your head, for your mouth has spoken against you” (3 Kings 2:37), and again, “By your mouth you will be condemned, and by your mouth you will be justified” (Matthew 12:37), nevertheless, out of regard for compassion, we open a way to spare them and extend mercy.

We are compelled especially to temper the harsh and bloody sentence of this promise by the following consideration: although these two evils must be avoided with the greatest caution, if the necessity of danger compels us to moderate one of them, we ought to undo the one known to bind us with the lesser bond. Let us investigate with the acumen of piety which of these is lighter and which heavier.

For when we are compelled to perjure ourselves, we offend the Creator, but we stain only ourselves. When, however, we fulfill harmful promises, we both proudly despise God’s commands, harm our neighbors with impious cruelty, and slaughter ourselves with an even crueler sword. In the former case we are struck by a twofold weapon of guilt; in the latter we are slaughtered three times over.

It remains, therefore, that our judgment proceed in the direction where the way of mercy has opened. This mercy is shown to be so acceptable to the Lord that He now desires it more than venerable sacrifices, as He Himself says:

“I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13).

With this permission to show indulgence granted, we place the exercise of compassion in the power of the glorious prince, so that, because God has opened to him the way of mercy, he too may not refuse remedies of compassion. Let these be moderated by princely discernment in such a way that mercy is granted to those people to some extent, while the nation and homeland nowhere suffer through them any danger or loss. It is enough that the matter be tempered under the protection of this compassion.

As for whatever oaths have been exacted or may hereafter be exacted for the safety of royal power and the protection of the people and homeland, we decree that they must be observed indissolubly with every care and vigilance, entirely released from the religious obligation of mutilation of limbs and the sentence of death.

But lest the crafty wickedness of depraved minds at some time lead us into the guilt of perjury, or claim that this sentence proceeds from the rule of the holy faith, we have taken care to attach to this discussion both the oracles of divine authority and the assertions of the Fathers who preceded us.

For although the words of the immutable God are most firm, nevertheless His oaths and His repentance are frequently read of, concealed within the sacred mysteries. To swear, in God’s case, means in no way to overturn what He has established of Himself; to repent means to alter, when He wills, those same established things.

Thus He says through Jeremiah:

“Suddenly I shall speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot it, destroy it, and annihilate it. If that nation repents of its evil concerning which I have spoken against it, I too will repent of the evil which I had thought to do to it” (Jeremiah 18:7–8).

And through Ezekiel:

“If I say to the righteous man that he shall live, and he turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses shall be forgotten, and in the iniquity that he has committed he shall die. But if I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezekiel 18:24ff.).

If, therefore, our conversion changes the divine sentence in this way, why should the abundant tears of the wretched, or such oppression, not moderate so harsh a vengeance through compassion? For this reason, punishment is often suspended against the Israelite people, and the destruction of the Ninevites is calmed by a change in the divine sentence.

The distinguished author Ambrose, renowned for the title of illustrious praises, speaks of this matter in the first book of *On Duties*:

“It is also sometimes contrary to duty to keep a pledged oath, as in the case of Herod, who swore that he would give the daughter of Herodias whatever she requested and granted her the death of John, lest he deny his promise” (Mark 6:22ff.). “For what shall I say about Jephthah? He sacrificed his daughter, who first met him as he returned victorious, in order to fulfill the vow he had made that whatever first came out to meet him, he would offer to God” (Judges 11:34ff.). It would have been better to promise nothing of that kind than to fulfill a promise through parricide.

Likewise, in the third book:

“First, therefore, the affection ought to be sincere, and each person should speak plainly; he should possess his own vessel in holiness and not deceive his brother through a trick of words. Let him promise nothing dishonorable; and if he has promised it, it is more tolerable not to fulfill the promise than to do what is shameful. Often many bind themselves by the sacrament of an oath, and although they themselves recognize that the thing ought not to have been promised, nevertheless, out of regard for the oath, they do what they promised, as we have written above concerning Herod, who shamefully promised a reward to the dancing girl and cruelly paid it. It is shameful that a kingdom should be promised for a dance; it is cruel that death should be given under the declared religious obligation of an oath. How much more tolerable would such perjury have been than the oath?”

And, discussing Jephthah briefly:

“Wretched is the necessity that is resolved by parricide. It is better not to fulfill a vow than to fulfill what the one to whom the promise is made would not wish to be fulfilled.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, not all promises are always to be fulfilled. Finally, God Himself, as Scripture indicates, frequently changes His sentence.”

The most holy man Augustine, cautious through the keenness of his investigation, outstanding in the art of discovery, flowing in his abundance of argument, graceful in the flower of eloquence, and fruitful in the yield of wisdom, says the following in his own utterances:

“There are altogether two kinds of lies in which there is not great guilt, yet which are not without guilt: when we joke, or when we lie about a promise. The first, in joking, is not especially harmful, because it does not deceive; the person to whom it is said knows that it was said as a joke. The second is lesser because it retains some benevolence.”

The same author says:

“Let truth not take away mercy, nor mercy impede truth. For if, on account of truth, or as though on account of rigid truth, you have forgotten mercy, you will not walk in the way of the Lord, in which mercy and truth have met one another” (Psalm 39:12).

Blessed Pope Gregory, also worthy of honor for the merits of his life and deservedly preferred in nearly all ethical assertions, says the following in his *Moral Books*:

“Since, therefore, this Behemoth is bound in ways so inexplicable that a mind often brought into doubt is bound more tightly by the very thing by which it strives to free itself from guilt, it is rightly said: ‘The sinews of his testicles are intertwined.’ For the arguments of his machinations, the more they are loosened so that they may release, the more they are entangled so that they may hold.

“Yet there is something that can usefully be done to destroy such wiles: when the mind is bound by a lesser and a greater sin, if no way of escape is open without sin, the lesser sins should always be chosen. For one who is enclosed by the circuit of walls so that he cannot escape rushes toward flight where the shorter wall is found.”

Isidore also—our own age’s teacher, the latest glory of the Catholic Church, last in age among those who preceded him but not inferior in doctrine, and, what is greater, the most learned of the ages that have now come to an end, worthy to be named with reverence—writes in the second book of his *Sentences* concerning such a matter:

“An oath that is wrongly and carelessly promised should not be preserved, as when someone promises an adulteress perpetual fidelity to remain with her. For it is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to remain in the disgrace of fornication.”

Likewise, in the *Synonyms*:

“In evil promises, rescind your pledge; in a shameful vow, change your decision. What you vowed carelessly is an impious promise when it is fulfilled through crime.”

Let this brief sampling from the sacred pages and the principal authors suffice. Anyone who seeks these matters by reading more attentively will be able to collect very much more. But those for whom these things are not sufficient should at least take this material in shameful silence, since the Vessel of Election desires to be accursed from Christ for the sake of his brothers rather than to persist in cruel wrongdoing.

## III

In the third address of our reasoning, we mourned that, contrary to the earlier admonitions of the Fathers, the vows of those who came later have become most destructive. For the more frequently the former forbade harmful things, the more zealously the latter do not cease to perpetrate what was forbidden.

Thus, by opposition, what ought to have been utterly extinguished does not cease to attack, and what could have withered after being cut down by so many decrees grows green again, like the head of the Lernaean monster, as the stories relate, which grows back after being severed.

Finally—and this must be said with great sorrow—very many are found wishing to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit through the transaction of a gift, while the one who bestows the reward grants it so that the recipient may receive the sublime height of the episcopal order, forgetting Peter’s words to Simon:

“May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed through money” (Acts 8:20).

Therefore, because this is an evil that is nevertheless customary, and because it is frequently known to have been cut down by the sword of our ancestors, we too apply the remaining red-hot iron to this cancerous wound. We decree absolutely that whoever henceforth is discovered to have offered any reward in order to receive the dignity of the priesthood shall know that from that moment he is condemned under the disgrace of anathema and excluded from participation in the body and blood of Christ, since it is clear that he has committed the detestable crime against Christ.

If anyone should come forward to accuse the person who obtained this order through acceptance of gifts, let that person both be deprived of the rank of honor he received and be confined in a monastery under perpetual penance. Those who accepted gifts for this purpose, if they are clerics, shall be punished by loss of honor; but if they are laymen, they shall be condemned by perpetual anathema.

## IV

At the occurrence of the fourth assembly, the fall from the summit of episcopal dignity confronted us, since we were compelled first to weep and then to make arrangements according to due order. For since Christ, according to the mystery of the flesh He assumed, has deigned to be the head of His Church, it is rightly understood that the activity of bishops is carried out in His members as though by the eyes.

They themselves govern and arrange the subject multitudes of the peoples from the height of their more elevated rank. Therefore, the more they become leaders, the more they ought to shine forth with the light of their merits. Accordingly, all bishops, among the other ornaments of virtue, ought to strive especially for purity of the flesh, so that by this their hearers may desire purity, since their teachers are not disfigured by impurity.

Thus, if henceforth bishops are discovered to have polluted themselves through detestable crimes with women of any kind and to have maintained intimate familiarity with them, they shall know that they will be punished by the irrevocable sentence of the Fathers: namely, they shall be deprived both of the dignity of their place and of their order.

## V

Through the impulse of the fifth action, it came to the sacred hearing of the entire council that certain priests and ministers, forgetting the constitutions of their ancestors and predecessors, were being defiled by the impure association and detestable contagion either of wives or of women of any kind. With the worst obstinacy of heart, they opposed both the sacred writings and the rules of the Fathers, not even considering with the slightest pause what is written:

“Be holy, because I also am holy, says the Lord” (Leviticus 11:44).

And the Apostolic command:

“Put to death your members that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:5), that is, fornication and impurity, evil desire, and greed—vices whose power in evil is so much more persistent that they require a correspondingly harsher response through decrees.

Therefore, once such crimes have been discovered, the holy council specifically decrees that all bishops should diligently ensure that the same matter is investigated in their own dioceses. When they have been able to discover the truth of it, they shall bind and restrain all concerned by a suitable safeguard, so that they never again commit such abominations.

The women who have been so shamefully associated with them, whether free or enslaved, shall be separated from them in every way—or sold—in such a manner that every avenue by which they might return to their partners in crime is thereafter denied to them. If the men cannot be restrained at all, they shall be assigned to monasteries until the end of their lives and remain entirely subject to monastic discipline.

VI. At the sixth point under discussion, the marked statement of certain men conscious of wrongdoing was brought to light. For it was reported to us that certain subdeacons, after attaining the rank of the sacred [Col. 0511D] order, are defiled not only by carnal impurity—although it is written, “Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52)—but also, which is unspeakable, are joined to wives, asserting that this is permitted to them because they do not know that they have received a blessing from the pontiff. Therefore, with every veil of excuse torn away, we order that the following be observed: when these same subdeacons are ordained, they shall receive from the bishop a blessing together with the vessels of ministry, just as ancient tradition is reported to preserve this practice in certain Churches and sacred custom is recognized to support it, with every impurity and association with women wholly removed from them. If thereafter they are wounded by this offense, they shall immediately be confined in monasteries under the burdens of penance until the end of their lives.

[Col. 0512A] VII. With the approach of the seventh assertion, there came before our assembly both an immodest proceeding and a base and detestable presumption. For we know that certain men, whether because of pressing circumstances or fear of dangers, received from bishops the offices of ecclesiastical dignities. And since, when these offices were imposed upon them, they testified that they had not wished this to be done to them, they therefore attempt to reject it and return to their former marriages and ways of life, wickedly dissolving the laws of heaven while eagerly gaping after the allurements of the world.

Accordingly, we must recognize that the summit of episcopal eminence has rightly been judged highest among all sacred offices, since it entrusted to the other priests the functions to be exercised by them—namely, the consecration of God’s temples, the blessing of chrism, and the restoration [Col. 0512B] of the sacred orders—which remain otherwise established for as long as they are conferred with the highest authority, because they are singularly performed by bishops to the same degree that they are reserved for that supreme dignity to carry out. How, then, can one who has received these things upon himself reject them from himself, when he knows that they can be conferred by no one other than pontiffs alone, by whom neither what has been bound can be loosed nor what has been loosed be bound again by anyone?

For the Truth says to Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). What is known to have become sacred through the authority both of divine command and of apostolic tradition can never be profaned. But just as the holy chrism that has been conferred and the honor of the altar cannot be torn away, so also the sacred dignity of offices, which is considered equal and allied to these, once received under whatever circumstance, shall remain altogether unshaken.

[Col. 0512C] To eradicate from the roots the useless argument of this crafty contrivance, they claimed that they had reasonably refused to have it imposed upon them on the ground that the immeasurable gift of holy baptism is always bestowed, and often not only upon those unwilling but even—what is more—upon those unaware, yet no one is at all permitted to profane it. If it is objected here also that the person proved to have received this gift was not yet capable of reason, let them understand fully from this that, if adults do not go unpunished for abandoning what children receive either unknowingly or unwillingly, how much less is it fitting to violate what is known to have come about through the hidden dispensation of God, in order to escape death or the danger of punishments? [Col. 0512D]

Let the shameless favors of such desires therefore withdraw without embarrassment. Although they unwillingly received what they did not deserve to have, let them nevertheless willingly retain the heavenly merit which they attained by unwillingly accepting it through the circumstances of earthly necessity, so that they may desire to love good things as unwillingly as they are seen voluntarily to attack them.

But if, after this perpetual decree of regulation, anyone does not sincerely adhere to sacred worship, casts away from himself the grace he received, returns to marriage, and attempts to resume the customs of the world—or if it is established that he has returned to them—he shall immediately be deprived of every dignity of ecclesiastical order. As an apostate from the threshold of the holy Church and from the fellowship of the faithful, he shall be held wholly excluded and shall be shut up under penance within the enclosure of a monastery for as long as he lives.

[Col. 0513A] VIII. We have found certain men devoted to divine offices to be filled with such profound dullness of ignorance, and so unacquainted with letters and discipline, that they are not proved to be adequately instructed even in the orders in which they are engaged in their daily duties. Therefore it is carefully established and decreed that henceforth no one of whatever ecclesiastical dignity shall receive a rank who does not know the entire Psalter, or the complete supplement of the customary canticles and hymns, and the rite of baptizing.

Those who already hold the honor of a dignity but are afflicted by the blindness of this ignorance shall either voluntarily undertake the resolve to learn what is necessary in full, or be compelled by their superiors, unwillingly if need be, to perform the duties of a reader. For it is absurd that those who are to teach the rest, both the simpler people and the laity, and who ought to be for them a kind of mirror of discipline and life, should be promoted to any rank or dignity while they are ignorant of God’s law and are not distinguished even by a moderate knowledge of letters. [Col. 0513B]

Therefore let no one come to handle the sacred mysteries of God unwashed and blinded by the darkness of ignorance; only one whom innocence of conduct and the brilliance of learning make illustrious shall approach. Otherwise, the vengeance of God and of his Church will in the future threaten both those who ordain and those who are ordained.

IX. At the prompting of the ninth intention, the dreadful gluttony of voracious men was exposed. Since it is not restrained by the bridle of frugality, it is shown to oppose religion, for Scripture says: “Whoever despises small things will gradually [Col. 0513C] fall” (Ecclus. 19:1). Those men rage with such shameless greed that they appear to despise heavenly and almost supreme things.

Moreover, the forty days of Lent—which are reckoned as the tenth part of the whole year and are consecrated to the Lord in the offering of fasting, and during which the most salutary condition of the human race is purified, while a person who is to believe in this religion is brought from the four parts of the world, formed from the four elements, and suitably afflicted four times ten because of the transgression of the Decalogue—those who rashly despise all this and do not restrain the greed of their appetites, and, worse still, profane the Paschal feasts by consuming forbidden foods, are therefore forbidden to do so with such severity that whoever, without unavoidable necessity, physical frailty, evident illness, or even the incapacity of age, presumes to eat meat during the days of Lent shall be not only guilty with respect to the Lord’s resurrection but also excluded from the holy communion of that day. This shall be added to his punishment: throughout the remainder of that year he shall abstain from every eating of meat, because he forgot the discipline of abstinence during the sacred days. [Col. 0513D]

Those, however, whom age bends, illness weakens, or necessity constrains shall not presume to violate what has been forbidden until they receive permission from a priest.

[Col. 0514A] X. With the assent expressed at the tenth conference, and in response to troublesome actions which a shrewd investigation of piety would have opposed, it was decreed that not so much the freedom to govern well as gentleness itself had proved to be under attack. We have seen clearly, as we think, that the decree of that glorious ruler and of this holy synod has been sufficiently contradicted.

For through both definitions the Holy Spirit breathed upon the hearts of mortals, so that by the life-giving breath of his words he might thereafter burn away every rage of minds that wickedly desire. Those definitions accomplished this: since the incomprehensible nature of divine piety joined itself to the condition of mortals in the mystery of the union of persons for the redemption of humankind, we too, as members of this Head, must uproot and cut away entirely, with an equal fire, sword, and every [Col. 0514B] instrument, both the evil of unbelief and desire, which “is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10), and avarice, “which is idolatrous service” (Eph. 5:5).

From now on, therefore, rulers are to be appointed to the glory of the kingdom in such a way that, whether in the royal city or in the place where the ruler has died, they are chosen with the complete consent of the chief pontiffs and the greater officers of the palace—not by an external gathering, a conspiracy of a few, or the tumultuous sedition of rustic crowds. They shall be defenders of the Catholic faith, defending it as well as the Jewish unbelief that now threatens and the injury of all heresies. They shall be judges in their actions and modest in their lives. In administering resources they shall be more sparing than lavish, so that they neither exact nor seek to exact from their subjects obligations contracted by written instruments or definitions of any kind. In things acquired by obligation they shall be most gracious, not looking to the rights of their own advantage but consulting the interests of their country and people. [Col. 0514C]

Of the resources gathered by them, they shall claim for themselves only those portions that the true authority of the ruler has prescribed. Whatever they leave in an unordered condition shall pass by inheritance to their own successors, and whatever was most justly acquired before the kingdom shall be taken by their children or heirs according to the right of proximity. In the succession or gift of relatives, even if such things have been left without order, they shall often benefit either the children first, or the heirs and relatives.

Thus, in all their actions, ways, and possessions, the authority of private law shall have such force that it will remain perpetually unshaken, and no one shall receive the summit of the kingdom before declaring by the terms of an oath that he will fulfill that law in every respect. We decree, moreover, showing reverence for this law and episcopal decree not only in the future but also in the present, that whoever chooses to be a detractor rather than a venerator of that decree and law, whether religious or lay, shall not only be punished by ecclesiastical excommunication but also deprived of the dignity of his order. [Col. 0514D]

[Col. 0515A] XI. In the eleventh article of the occasion, we gave perpetual confirmation to the universal decrees, knowing that God always relieves the distress of the oppressed through many forms of opposition to judgment. Just as, when the wickedness of men demands it, he permits the hardships of vengeance to be exercised, so, when he wills, he relieves the burdens of oppression.

For this reason, the decrees of the preceding Fathers rightly judged that a synodal assembly should be held in order to uproot contention and quarrels over judgments, so that extended disputes over differing judgments might have their end there, where the Holy Spirit has gathered together the universal assembly. Therefore, so that any future succession may not be able to disturb anything with impunity and the general body may remain secure, we unanimously and firmly decree that whatever has been or shall be written by definition of universal authority concerning matters of faith and ecclesiastical affairs—whether in past acts, present constitutions, or future decrees—no one henceforth dare contradict, no one presume to alter, and no one strive not to fulfill.

For if anyone, from religious motives, should prove disobedient to these provisions, or a whisperer, or indeed a mutilator, or envious, rather than an agent of the same provisions, let him mourn, punished by the loss both of his honor and of sacred communion. When a holy synod is being held, or something is peacefully defined among the pontiffs, if a smaller number should happen to dissent through ignorance or contention, let them either withdraw with the disgrace of confusion after being admonished by the assembly of the majority, or suffer the sentence of an annual excommunication. [Col. 0515B]

XII. The proposal of the twelfth question, together with the supplication of the most sacred ruler, became clear to our assembly as a matter requiring the most pious condemnation because of the Jews’ abominable and unspeakable unbelief. For this reason we judged that it should be placed at the end of the judgments. We lament that this same people, brought back through the merit of its offense according to the pronouncements of divine sanction, which had placed it at the head, is [Col. 0515C] now at the tail.

But because Christ died for them just as he did for us, according to what he himself said: “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished, of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24), we deemed it necessary to devote the utmost care to them, for those for whom he “did not disdain to lay down his own soul” (John 10:15). This was also most devoutly approved by the ruler’s clemency, which prefers that the summit of his kingdom be made firm by God if it acquires the bands of those who are perishing for the Catholic faith, considering it unworthy that an orthodox ruler should command sacrilegious people and be polluted by the fellowship of unbelievers.

Nothing else is defined concerning them according to our judgment except that the decrees of the Council of Toledo, which was assembled in the time of King Sisenand of blessed memory, be carried out fully by us and by our successors. [Col. 0515D] Whoever wishes to dissent from the judgment of that synod shall know that he will be condemned as a true sacrilegious person.

May the inseparable name of the Trinity, just as by wondrous inspiration it illumined our undertaking at its beginning, so bring it to completion and conclude it with a sublime consummation, so that our having unfolded it may be in him from whom our beginning came to us.

Therefore we give glory and honor to that holy and indivisible Trinity, which enabled us both to say these things and to fulfill in itself what has been said; it restored the remedies of the ages at the end of the world and loosed the bonds of fetters.

[Col. 0516A] May salvation and blessing from the Lord of hosts be given to the most serene Reccesiunthus, glorious ruler. From all of us together, may there be thanksgiving and the fullness of reverence for that most merciful ruler, the grateful giver of good things, to whom God in his kindness has brought the earnestness of our vows so that they might be fulfilled; whose most pious ordering has removed the destructive forces of oppression; under whose reign justice gains strength and every prosperity overflows. May the Lord grant him, after the times of the present age, a long-lasting crown among all the saints as his reward.

We all commend this series of decrees, flowing as a fountain of what is just, of right faith, piety, and justice, before God and his angels, to all the orthodox both now and in the future, earnestly entreating them both to fulfill it reverently and to defend it kindly against its rivals.

But upon those who despise it may the fearful vengeance of divine severity come; while upon those who observe everything may perpetual peace and everlasting glory, flowing forth abundantly, come.

By the force and authority of this judgment, we decree that the series of our decree which we issued in the name of our most serene lord, King Reccesiunthus, concerning the possessions acquired under any title by his father of blessed memory, shall remain wholly valid. [Col. 0516B] Finally, we confirm with equal strength the law which that most merciful ruler issued concerning the detestable and dreadful greed of rulers, and we decree by the same judgment that it be observed in every way for future times.

And so that these provisions may not be abandoned through the silence or forgetfulness of time, we have decreed that both be joined to this constitution of ours. We commend them to the memory of all in such a way that they may in no respect remain separated from all the rules established above.

[Col. 0516C] As for the other judgments of our decrees, which are known to have been enacted by this holy synod, if anyone should perhaps attempt to tear them down, or recklessly neglect to fulfill them, or at any time wish to violate them, let him be anathema by the judgment of almighty God.

To our God alone be glory forever and ever. Amen.

**Subscription of fifty-nine bishops. Decree of the universal council issued in the name of the ruler.**

To restore solidity to what was broken and to make what had been struck down rise again is both an increase [Col. 0516D] of this reward and the fullness of completed perfection. For if the care of equals and neighbors is sufficient to oppose the weight of a ruin that brings collision, how much greater will be the guilt incurred by the danger of the negligence described above, if they do not use whatever power they possess to raise up, from the common burden, the peoples entrusted to them?

We must therefore hasten to rescue the crowds of those who have been struck down from the ruins of their collisions, so that from this point onward the detestable oppression may no longer possess the strength to do harm, and every person who has been crushed may know that the remedies of holy sanction have been granted to him.

[Col. 0517A] When, therefore, as time passed, the oppressive power of harsh condemnation raised itself up, and the domination of the wicked over subject peoples did not restore the laws of governance but brought the destruction of vengeance, we saw that the condition of the subjects was not strengthened according to the proper order of a ruler but cast down by the weight of power.

[Col. 0517B] For kings contracted their lofty heights in the two-fronted conflict of the one who stirs things up: either the severe law raged in punishments, or a voluntary law offered favor in plunder. From this, hope did not sustain their sorrowful hearts through a gift; rather, endurance tormented them in their destruction.

Therefore, now that restoration is at hand, not reason alone compels us to proceed, but the very disturbance of affairs also urges us, so that, after deliberation by all our minds, that concordant judgment may remain which both properly puts an end to illicit ventures and provides a legally grounded safeguard for the peoples who must be saved.

For we have seen certain kings, after they had attained the glory of the kingdom, accumulate royal profit for themselves by weakening the strength of the peoples. Forgetting that they were called kings, they turn defense into devastation and avoid driving devastation away by means of defense. They add to this the more serious fault that they do not assign the things they appear to acquire to the honor or glory of the kingdom, but prefer to merge them into their own right, as though they had decided that these things should be transmitted as a debt to the posterity of their children.

For this reason they attempt to draw into the bosom of private property those things which, it is clear, they received solely because they had attained the height of rule; and they place in the cave of their own right what was acquired, as is clear, for the benefit of the people. For could the arrivals of the peoples or the revenue of their possessions have come to them unless they had been raised to the heights of glory? Or could they have been enriched by the accumulation of possessions from their equals unless they had been able to rise to the glorious summit through their subjects? [Col. 0517C]

The memory of the entire common people, subject to the principal head, reveals everything to him. With attentive regard to the command owed to him, they look to him for the remedy of their affairs, to whom they offer revenue, sometimes as a favor and sometimes as a debt.

[126] The orthodox royal eminence therefore proves that all these things are owed to it from the moment it recognizes itself as king, and on that account justly defends what has been acquired for itself and no other. Hence it does not doubt that these things are owed not to the person but to the power.

Eternal laws make the king; it is not the person, since the king’s status is not established by personal mediocrity but by the honor of eminence.
