Therefore let what is owed to honor serve honor, and let what kings accumulate be left to the kingdom, so that, because the glory of the kingdom adorns them, they too may not diminish but adorn the glory of the kingdom.

[Col. 0517D] Henceforth let duly established kings possess, in governing, just judgments; in sparing, ready hearts; in acquiring, frugal efforts; and in preserving, sincere purposes. Let them retain the glory of the kingdom with happiness in proportion as they preserve the laws of governance and gentleness and direct them with equity, the promised reward of their dominion.

Lest this be thought to have emerged merely from the tinder of reason, it is appropriate to reveal it through the clearest form of action, so that the integrity of truth may find us suitable defenders from the point at which the quality of our conduct has always preserved itself.

[Col. 0518A] For behold, we have found and lament that many men from the middling and greater ranks of our people have fallen up to the present. When their ruins are recognized, we can consider nothing other than the judgments of the divine promise. The spoils of their houses, the wealth of their powers, and their estates have been so utterly emptied that they are found to have been transferred neither for the usefulness of the treasury nor as a saving remedy for the offices of the palace.

When the sequence of this matter is considered from both sides together—since those judged by the sentence of judgments were struck down, and no one rose up to enrich himself in their goods in their place—it is almost reckoned that discipline was not maintained in due order among the people but that failure was introduced, with this greater loss to salvation added: the entire abundance of the rulers’ property had enclosed in its own bosom both what the force of judicial judgments had withdrawn from the judgments and what any kind of income had worn away through the order of dissipation. [Col. 0518B]

Thus, once only the ruler’s belly had been filled, all the limbs of the entire people, emptied by its death, would languish. Hence it happened that neither the lesser could obtain support nor the greater dignity. For while the force of the sole power occupied the greatest things, the condition of the whole people defended not even its smallest rights.

[Col. 0518C] Therefore, together with the entire office of the palace and with the assembly of the greater and lesser, we all—pontiffs, priests, and all who serve in sacred orders—decree and desire by unanimous definition that every acquisition amassed, in all living and immovable things and in all things capable of being moved, whether in body or appearance, form or kind, which King Cindasiunthus of glorious memory is found to have made in any manner from the day on which he is known to have ascended to the kingdom, shall pass into the perpetual power and be assigned in perpetuity to the right of our most serene and merciful lord, the ruler Reccesiunthus.

These possessions are not to be held by parental succession but possessed through royal assumption, so that each person may receive what is justly due to him, and the ruler’s will may exercise itself over whatever possessions he chooses for the remedies of his subjects. The sole exceptions are those things which the aforesaid ruler Cindasiunthus of blessed memory is seen to have possessed before the kingdom, either from his own property or from things acquired with complete justice.

In all these things, let there be free division and possession in the fullest peace among his sons together with our glorious lord King Reccesiunthus. [Col. 0518D] But those things which the aforesaid ruler is seen to have conferred or left to his sons, or to anyone else, from just revenues shall remain unshaken in their right. This truth concerning the matter is preserved: since the goodwill of our lord King Reccesiunthus determines to restore to each person what is most justly due to him, let no one bring an accusation of seizure or demand damages, except for those possessions which it is established that his father of glorious memory held improperly.

**Law issued in the same council under the rule of the glorious ruler.**

In the name of the Lord. Flavius Reccesiunthus, king.

Earthly eminence and exalted rank are then shown to seek what is lofty most beneficially, when they are seen to profit the salvation of those nearby through pious compassion. Thus it usually happens that a person gains more benefit from the salvation of another than he advances through his own humility.

[Col. 0519A] For when the salvation of many is considered among many, the sum of greater profit is achieved. But when private advantage is sought, it is not enough to acquire the reward of a single benefit. Thus, too, the salvation of governing peoples consists precisely in this: it does not enclose its boundaries within private will but defends the limits of the whole community by the common law of piety.

Therefore, lest a salutary order seem to be obtained more by imperial words than by agreements, we turn away from the claim of eminence toward the petitions of suppliants, with a tranquil and attentive gaze, so that salutary compassion may derive its benefit from the place where the peoples have obtained the fulfillment of their petitions.

[Col. 0519B] Since, then, over the course of preceding times, the immoderate greed of rulers had spread itself headlong over the plunder of peoples and had increased the property revenue of rulers through the lamentable misery of their subjects, at last, through the affection of heavenly regard, it was divinely inspired in us that, since we had granted reverence to subject kings, we should also place a restraint of moderation upon the excesses of rulers.

Therefore, with sincere deliberation in gentleness, for ourselves and for all the future successors of our glory, with God’s help we establish a law and promulgate a decree of royal observance: no king, through any impulses of his own agitation or by any faction, shall so extort, or arrange to have extorted, documents concerning any possessions owed to another that anyone might be proved to have obtained ownership of possessions not owed to him unjustly and violently.

[Col. 0519C] But if, by the most welcome free will of anyone, he receives something from another’s possessions, or gains something through an evident transfer, the condition of the voluntary transfer shall be expressly recorded in the same document. Through it either the ruler’s oppression or the fraud of the person making the transfer may be exposed with complete clarity. If it becomes clear that the document was exacted from an unwilling person, then either the ruler’s wickedness shall repent and annul what it wrongly constructed, or, after his death, the possessions themselves shall without delay be restored to the person from whom the document was exacted or to his heirs.

Those possessions, however, which, with every argument of seizure removed, passed directly into the ruler’s power through mere desire, shall remain there permanently by right; and whatever the same ruler wishes to arrange concerning those possessions shall be subject to his own discretion.

[Col. 0519D] But so that sincerity of truth may strengthen the whole conduct of this matter, whenever documents concerning any possessions exist in the ruler’s name, the persons whom the ruler chooses shall diligently investigate whether they know of any indication, in any manner whatsoever, either of the ruler’s coercion or of fraud on the part of the person who made the document. Thus either the document’s sequence shall remain duly executed, or, if invalidly made, shall vanish. [Col. 0520A]

The same judgment shall also be observed concerning lands, vineyards, and slaves, if the agreement was made in any manner before witnesses without the text of a document.

Concerning all possessions acquired by rulers from the time of King Simitillanus up to the present, and concerning those that may thereafter be acquired, whatever a ruler has left or may leave in an unordered condition, if they are shown to have been acquired for the sake of the royal summit, we decree that they belong solely to the successor of the kingdom, with this power granted to him: he shall be free to will whatever he chooses to do with them.

[Col. 0520B] But concerning those possessions that came to the ruler either from the property of his parents or through the succession of any of his nearest relatives, the rights of inheritance shall be open to that ruler and, if he has no sons, to his legitimate heirs, just as they are known to have been open by law or by paternal grant to others.

If it becomes clear that anything from the possessions of any parents or relatives came into his right not only by succession but also through any gift or any contract, then, if these possessions happen to be left in an unordered condition, the entire acquisition shall belong not to the successor of the kingdom but specifically to the sons or heirs of the person who acquired it.

For concerning those possessions which the same ruler is known to have held before the kingdom, either from his own property or from a most just acquisition, the power either to do whatever he wishes shall remain by irrevocable order, or full succession shall be open to his sons. If he has no sons, his legitimate heirs may enter by hereditary right upon whatever he has left in an unordered condition.

[Col. 0520C] This law shall be observed only in the affairs of rulers, and shall remain perpetually valid in such a way that no one shall ascend the royal throne before promising by the bond of an oath that he will fulfill this law in every respect.

But whoever is shown to have acquired the heights of the kingdom either through tumultuous crowds or through a public scheme contrived by hidden authority shall immediately, together with all who consented to such wickedness, become anathema and lose the fellowship of Christians. He shall be struck down by so severe a vengeance that every worshiper of the divine order who presumes to communicate with him shall perish under a similar condemnation and waste away in punishment.

[Col. 0520D] For if anyone from the office of the palace, out of ill will, should wish to tear apart the text of this law by attacking or disparaging it, or should at any time be discovered speaking against it—whether silently insulting or openly resisting it—by annulling it, he shall immediately be stripped of all associations and offices of palatine dignity, lose half of all his possessions, and, reduced to the place assigned to him, remain excluded from the fellowship of the entire palace. A religious person who falls into this offense shall likewise suffer the loss of half his property.

**HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE NINTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO.**

[Col. 0519]

[Col. 0519D]

1. That bishops take nothing from the property of the Church, and how the nearest relative of the founder of a church is to exercise care.

2. That founders of churches, for as long as they live, have care of them, and that they themselves choose the ministers who will serve there.

3. If it is said that something is given from the property of the Church as a payment, let the reason for the payment be investigated.

[Col. 0521A]

4. That an equal division be made of acquired possessions between the Church and the heirs of the priest.

5. If a bishop establishes a monastery or enriches a parish church, let him contribute a fourth part of the Church’s possessions.

6. That the bishop confer the third part of ecclesiastical possessions owed to him upon whomever he chooses.

7. That the heirs of a deceased priest not presume to take possession of his property outside the established order.

8. That in documents which priests or ministers have unjustly made, the number of years be reckoned after their death.

9. How much benefit a bishop may take from a church whose priest he has buried.

10. Concerning the condemnation of children proved to have been born from priests and ministers.

[Col. 0522A]

11. That bishops should grant freedom to enslaved clerics.

12. That after the death of a priest, the period of years should be reckoned during which freedom was granted to slaves.

13. That those born from the Church’s freedmen and from free persons not withdraw from service to the Church.

14. If the Church’s freedmen do not wish to return to it, let all their property be assigned to the right of the Church.

15. Concerning the service and discipline of the Church’s freedmen.

16. That a Church freedman may not transfer any of his property to another.

17. That baptized Jews celebrate the feast days with the bishops.

[127] **HERE BEGINS THE NINTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO.** Held in the era 663, in the third year of the reign of King Reccesiunthus, on the Kalends of November, by seventeen bishops.

[Col. 0521]

[Col. 0521A]

By the decree of canonical definition, after the Kalends of November, in the city of Toledo, for the holding of a council, we had been gathered together with the Lord’s favor in the basilica of holy Mary ever-Virgin, in the [Col. 0521B] seventh year of the glorious ruler Reccesiunthus. We decreed by common decision that the chapters which had by no means been inserted in the ancient canons should be promulgated by an equal judgment and joined to the ancient rules, to remain in perpetual continuity and to be preserved with every reverence.

But since one who does not first chastise himself by the rigor of justice cannot rightly judge his subjects, it seemed suitable and expedient to us first to impose a limit upon our own excesses and thus correct the errors of our subjects. For the beginnings of judgments are then better ordered when judgment is arranged beforehand, since the form of judgment is more completely fulfilled when equity in judging is placed before the beginnings of the affairs.

Therefore the beginning of equity must be made by judges, so that the completed pleading of the law may more clearly establish its boundary.

[Col. 0521C] **CHAPTER I**

Every quantity of ecclesiastical property grants a remedy of pardon to the person who gives it, but properly prepares harm for the person who defrauds. Therefore, no priest or minister shall take anything from the possessions of the Church that the faithful bestow in any place whatsoever, or attach it to his own right or to the city of his see.

For just as the devotion of each person gratefully offers a vow to God, so it has determined that the fullness of those vows should be preserved in the place where they are held as though deposited. If they are frustrated, however, the ruin of the defrauder threatens. [Col. 0521D]

But so that there may be stronger security in this matter, it shall be lawful for the worthy sons, grandsons, and more honorable relatives of the person who built or enriched the church to exercise this diligence with good intention: if they foresee that a priest or minister is defrauding anything from the possessions bestowed, they shall either restrain him through an honorable agreement of admonition or report to the bishop or judge that the matter must be corrected.

[Col. 0522A] If the bishop attempts to do such things, they shall take care to disclose them to his metropolitan. [Col. 0522B] But if the metropolitan does such things, they shall not delay making them known to the ears of the king.

Nevertheless, the heirs themselves shall not be permitted to assert power over these possessions as though they were their own right, nor to introduce robbery, fraud, or any violence; they shall apply themselves only to a salutary concern, either so that harmful conduct may result in no injury at all, or so that a salutary penalty, in whole or in part, may be imposed.

If anyone thereafter wishes to violate these warnings, he shall restore what he wrongly seized with shame and shall bear the sentence of annual excommunication.

## II.

Since it is often customary to extort even what is not owed by entreaty and supplication, and in a manner by force through the pain of distress, how much more should things sought both in due legal order and in compassionate concern be granted without obstruction? Since, therefore, it is commonly recognized that parish churches or holy monasteries sometimes fall into such dreadful ruin through the insolence or negligence of certain bishops that the sorrow of those who built them becomes greater than the joy with which their labor had arisen in establishing them, we decree with pious compassion that, for as long as the founders of those churches remain alive, they shall be permitted to maintain vigilant care and exercise special solicitude over those places. The founders themselves shall also present suitable rectors to the bishops for ordination in those basilicas. But if such men cannot be found by them, then the bishop of the place shall, with their consent, institute as ministers those whom he has judged pleasing to God and suitable for sacred worship. If, however, while those founders remain alive, a bishop presumes to appoint rectors there, he shall know both that his appointment is invalid and that, to his own disgrace, others whom the founders themselves have chosen as worthy shall be ordained in their place.

## III.

If priests or ministers grant anything from church property to anyone under the pretext of a lease or other payment, they shall state the purpose of the document clearly, so that either the transaction may be known to have been lawfully concluded or the improper fraud concealed within it may become apparent. Otherwise, any document thereafter drawn up for this transaction shall have no validity.

## IV.

Priests, or whatever persons they may be to whom the administration of ecclesiastical property has been entrusted, shall ensure that whatever they purchase during the period of their administration—if they possess little or nothing of their own, or only property of slight value—is documented in the name of the church over whose instruments and charters they preside. For it is not fitting that a church, which raises up an outsider, should make him rich through another’s property while he retains a fraud against its own.

Those who are known to possess an increase of their own property shall, from everything they are seen to have acquired after the day of their ordination, whether or not any documents have been drawn up, have their own property and the church’s property compared and balanced. If the quantities of the two are equal, the acquisition shall belong by equal right to the church and to the heirs of the deceased. But if either portion has grown larger through the greater accumulation of its own property, it shall receive the larger share in the division.

No one of the priests or ministers mentioned above who, for his own advantage, friendship, payment, or by any other means, has earned the right to claim something from anyone—whether through a written document or otherwise—shall be able to count it among ecclesiastical property. Rather, whatever they wish to do with it shall remain subject to their own discretion, since, if after their death it should perhaps remain disordered, the church over which he presided or in which he served as minister shall claim it permanently for itself. [The final wording is textually uncertain.]

## V.

To provide wisely for what is good is both regarded as a support for the present life and understood to promise the reward of eternal recompense. Therefore, if any bishop should wish to build a monastery in his diocese and enrich it with property belonging to the church over which he presides, he shall not give more than a fiftieth part of that property. In this way, while the fairness of moderation is preserved, he will provide an appropriate support to the recipient without inflicting serious loss on the one from whom he takes.

A church that is not ordered according to monastic rules, or that he has not wished to enlarge through his own charters, may receive there no more than a hundredth part of the revenues of the church over which he presides. This precaution must nevertheless be observed: he may take only one of the two forms of remuneration that he prefers.

## VI.

Although the previous enactments have made it very well known what portion of the property of parish churches is to be assigned to the bishop, we have nevertheless thought it appropriate to decree that, if a bishop should decide to give the third that he knows is likewise owed to him from that property either to the church whose property it is evidently shown to be, or to another church to which he has chosen to assign it, this shall be permitted and his decision shall possess irrevocable force.

## VII.

The relatives of a deceased bishop shall presume to take nothing from his property without the knowledge of the metropolitan. If the deceased was himself a metropolitan, his successors shall be subject to his decision or to a council, so that permission to enter indiscriminately upon an inheritance may not be granted concerning church property, lest either the full accounting be disregarded or fraud be found to have been committed.

If those who are established to have died were presbyters or deacons, their heirs shall not be permitted to enter upon their property without the acknowledgment of their bishop. Whoever is thereafter found to have transgressed shall, for the property he has seized without awaiting the proper procedure, be subject to the penalty of the law for unlawful invasion.

## VIII.

If a priest or minister, while appearing to administer the governance of churches, is discovered to have diverted something from church property contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, the reckoning shall begin not from the day on which he decreed such things in writing, but from the day on which, at his death, he left them settled. For the life of one who judges invalidly shall in no way be counted as extending over the three-year period; for the status of contracts did not take its beginning from the origin of equity.

## IX.

Many, while greedily desiring what they ought not to take, either fail to perform the work of mercy suitably or mix wrongful losses into that very mercy. Therefore, lest the work of mercy should henceforth be execrably corrupted, we decree by common decision that, when a bishop happens to die, the bishop who comes to bury his body, after listing all the treasures and ornaments, shall, if the deceased’s church is wealthy, attempt to take no more than one pound of gold, apart from the church’s ornaments and with the consent of those who offer it.

But if the church is poorer in property, he may lawfully take half a pound for himself. Even this would not be permitted by any rational principle were it not that antiquity, out of regard for the injury of the priest who deserved it, had preserved this practice as permissible.

Moreover, the person who made the inventory shall take care to send to the metropolitan a brief account of the listed property, prepared in good faith. The metropolitan, however, shall presume to take absolutely nothing from the same church of the deceased, but shall provide only the salutary care that belongs to him.

## X.

Although many decrees of the Fathers concerning the incontinence of the clerical order have hitherto been issued, and correction of their morals has in no way been brought about, they have prolonged the judgment of those who condemn their offenses to such an extent that punishment was imposed not only on the authors of the crimes but also on the offspring of the condemned.

Therefore, if henceforth anyone from a bishop down to a subdeacon, while holding ecclesiastical rank, should beget children from a detestable union either with a slave woman or with a freeborn woman, those from whom such children are proved to have been begotten shall indeed be condemned by canonical judgment. But the offspring, polluted by another’s wrongdoing, shall not only never receive their parents’ inheritance; they shall also remain in perpetual servitude to the church whose priest or minister’s disgrace gave them birth.

## XI.

Those who are summoned from the church’s households by their bishops to serve in the clergy must receive the gift of freedom; and only if they become distinguished by the merits of an honorable life shall they thereafter undertake higher offices. But those whom an incorrigible offense has defiled shall be bound in the chain of perpetual servitude according to their condition.

## XII.

If a priest wishes to grant freedom to the slaves of the church, the period of years shall not be reckoned from the day on which the document was drawn up, but from the time when it is more certainly established that the person who drew up the document has died.

## XIII.

We often see the paternal church behaving toward the excesses of the church’s freedmen, and we are compelled to grieve under a twofold burden: on the one hand, because the authority of the proud man resisting the freedom granted to him is despised; on the other, because the freedom of the arrogant man is forced to fall back into a condition of servitude.

Although many different enactments of the Fathers have already been issued concerning this matter, we have nevertheless perceived that a certain completion suited to the fullness of the case must still be added. Therefore, just as the venerable sanction of the laws has judged, so the nobility of the entire stock has allowed to be preserved: no foreign mixture should stain what one’s own nobility has adorned.

Accordingly, by a general judgment, all freedmen and freedwomen of the churches, together with their offspring, are forbidden henceforth, on account of marriage, to join themselves either to freeborn Romans or to Goths. If this should ever be found to have occurred, the offspring born from such a mixture shall never attain the right to the dignity owed to them, nor shall they ever be free from the services of the church through whose benefaction they are known to have obtained the gift of freedom.

## XIV.

If anyone from among the freedmen of the church or their descendants should, contrary to the earliest and more recent regulations of the Fathers, be joined either to Goths or to freeborn Romans, neither they nor their offspring shall be permitted to withdraw from the church’s protection. They must be compelled to return to the services owed. If they refuse to return, whatever either their parents or they themselves have obtained from the church, or are seen to have acquired under its protection, shall, at the insistence of the bishop, be restored to the authority of their own church.

## XV.

The freedmen of the church and their descendants shall provide ready and sincere services to the same basilica from which they earned the favor of freedom. For just as useful freeborn persons will give in this service according to their ability, so useless freeborn persons will suffer in the correction of their offenses.

## XVI.

The freedmen of the church and their descendants may not transfer to the ownership of outsiders, by any transaction whatsoever, anything they are known to possess by right of the church. If they should perhaps wish to sell any of it, they shall appropriately offer it for purchase to the priest of that church, and may either dispose of the prices of those goods as they please or retain them. For we in no way permit the property-value of their goods to pass into the ownership of another party.

They shall, however, have completely open access to sell or donate whatever they wish to their own children or relatives who have been subjected to the service or protection of that same church.

## XVII.

We decree that baptized Jews, wherever they may reside for a fixed period, shall nevertheless celebrate with the chief priests of God, in cities and public gatherings, both the principal feasts consecrated in the sequence of the New Testament and those days which they formerly considered solemn according to the sanction of the old law. In this way the bishop may approve their conduct and faith, and truth may preserve them.

Whoever violates this edict shall, as the bishop permits, be subjected either to flogging or to abstinence.

When all that had been brought forward for fraternal deliberation according to the rule of honorable conduct had been completed, we give thanks to the immortal Lord alone, by whose wondrous disposition we have deserved to be united in this assembly of the holy congregation, so that our common gathering might display prosperity and our common union establish concord.

We beseech his abundant mercy to grant such happiness in the present life to our most serene Lord and beloved Christ, the glorious prince Reccesiunth, that after long years he may bestow upon him the glory of angelic blessedness; and that he may make us so glad in that same happiness that he may raise us, rewarded, to the land of the living.

Thereafter, holding most beneficially to the order of antiquity, after your fraternity has learned the reckoning of the Paschal feast, know that in the coming year you are to assemble in this city, with the Lord’s favor, on the day of the Kalends of November, for the holding of a council, so that in a similar deliberation we may either decree what we foresee to be suitable or rejoice in an assembly devoted solely to peace.

This holy council was completed on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the seventh fortunate year of the reign of our most serene and clement lord, King Reccesiunth, in the year 667 of the era.

# The Chapters of the Tenth Council of Toledo Begin

1. Concerning the celebration of the Lord’s Annunciation.  
2. Concerning those who conspired against the prince.  
3. Concerning bishops who appoint their relatives or supporters over monasteries or churches.  
4. Concerning the profession and habit of widowed nuns.  
5. Concerning female religious who have abandoned their commitment.  
6. Concerning those who, at a young age and in the presence of their parents, have assumed the religious habit, and whether parents may hand their children over to religion up to the age of four.

# The Tenth Council of Toledo Begins

In the year 668 of the era, the eighth year of King Reccesiunth’s reign.

Divine grace bestowed spiritual rejoicing upon us when it granted that we should meet together in the pursuit of the desired works of peace and the frequent practice of salutary discipline. Therefore, after we had assembled both in unity of mind and in the gathering at this place, giving thanks to the invisible God and to the glorious lord of all things, King Reccesiunth, by whose most holy wish, while the tradition of holy fatherhood was preserved, we were able to unite in a sacred assembly, we establish by unanimous definition that the rules appended below shall remain fixed as eternal law.

## Chapter I. Concerning the Celebration of the Feast of the Divine Mother

Although nothing contrary to the integrity of the faith arises from diversity, and no variation tears apart the unity of Catholic discipline, nevertheless there are matters which, unless preserved in unity of time, both produce disagreement within undivided unity and cannot remain consistent with the unity of the sacraments.

For this reason we celebrate the Paschal feast on one day and at one time, lest we fall into Jewish error. For this reason, unless we await the coming of the Holy Spirit after the Lord’s resurrection at the appointed time and after the defined number of days, we cannot be filled with the gift of that same Spirit; for if it lacks the fullness of the number, it may also lack the sacramental mystery.

For this reason, the sacred feast of the Lord’s birth, when the Word clearly came forth from the Virgin’s womb made flesh, both follows the course of time without doubt and represents the particular significance of the day. If, therefore, the days of the birth and death of this incarnate Word are held to be so fixed and certain that they are celebrated without variation throughout the whole world by every church in concord, why should the feast of his glorious mother not likewise be observed everywhere on one and the same day and with the same honor?

Indeed, it is found that in many parts of Spain the feast of this holy Virgin is not celebrated on one single day throughout all the cycles of the years. For where does the diversity of times lead people when they are shown not to maintain uniformity in celebration?

Since, therefore, on the day when the angel is found to have announced to the Virgin the conception of the Word in words and to have bestowed it through miracles, the feast cannot suitably be celebrated because Lent or the Paschal feast may sometimes coincide with it—and, as has been provided by the rule of antiquity, nothing concerning the solemnities of the saints ought to be celebrated during those times—it is not appropriate, according to the very incarnation of the Word, for that event to be proclaimed in celebrations when it is known that, after the death of the flesh, it was raised by the glory of the resurrection.

Therefore, by a special constitution, it is decreed that the day of his mother shall also be held as most solemn and distinguished before the eighth day on which the Lord was born. For it is fitting that the honors correspond: just as the dignity of the Son’s birth is followed by the succeeding days, so the sacred solemnity of the mother’s feast should be followed by the same number of days.

For what is the feast of the mother except the incarnation of the Word? Its feast must be solemn in the same manner as the feast of the birth of that Word. This institution is also seen to be established without lacking the example of a fitting custom known to be observed in various parts of the world.

Accordingly, since this custom is recognized in many churches distant from us both in space and in lands, henceforth, so that every doubt may be removed, the solemnity of the Lord’s mother shall be celebrated absolutely on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, and the birth of her Son, our Savior, shall be solemnly observed everywhere on the eighth day before those same Kalends, as is customary.

## II.

The harmful impulse of frequent disturbances may indeed be disregarded with the dignified gravity appropriate to its magnitude. But because honorable vigilance hastens to restrain what repeated practice does not take care to avoid, and because both certain decrees of our fathers and legal enactments have provided that no one should attempt to deliberate against the safety of the princes, the people, or his own country, we now specifically set forth this one rule for observance:

If anyone among the religious—from a bishop down to the lowest rank of the clergy or of monks—is found, through profane will, to have violated the general oaths sworn for the safety of the king, the people, or the fatherland, he shall immediately be deprived of his own dignity and excluded from his place and honor. Only this concession of mercy shall be reserved: the ruling power shall possess the right and permission to decide whether he may retain his place, his honor, or both.

## III.

Let this be received with the hearing of complete reverence, for it is not without reason that a harsh matter is compelled to be eradicated by this harsher censure. We have learned that certain bishops are so forgetful of the command of the Prince of the Apostles—“Feed the flock that is among you, not under compulsion but willingly, and do not lord it over the clergy, but become an example to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2)—that they often appoint as prelate over certain monasteries and parish churches either persons of their own blood or participants in their favor.

In this way they provide them with dishonorable advantages, so that either they may be given what a just order would have required to be given to the bishop himself, or what the violence of an appointed collector might be able to seize.

Accordingly, it is suitably pleasing to all that such conduct be rescinded at present and not be undertaken thereafter. Whoever among the bishops should henceforth attempt to commend such profits either to relatives by blood or to persons bound to him by favor shall have both the ruin of his wicked presumption and whatever has been commanded declared invalid. The one who made the appointment shall be subjected to a year’s excommunication, and whatever may have been taken shall be restored twofold by the one who took it.

## IV.

Through the Spirit of the Lord we may rightly say with the holy Apostle, “You are not ignorant of Satan’s cunning” (2 Corinthians 2:11), because we are driven and set ablaze by “zeal for the house of God” (John 2:17).

We see that destruction has grown strong through such extensive efforts at fraud that some regard the original constitution of the Fathers as something to be mocked and suppose that the new intention of the judges should be suppressed. For certain widows are found covering themselves with various excuses to such an extent that they flatter themselves that they are not bound by the full religious institution of the Fathers.

Therefore, while the ancient rules remain inviolable, this is added by the pronouncement of a new sanction: a widow who wishes to maintain the commitment of holy religion shall make a written profession to the priest or minister to whom she has gone, or who happens to have come to her. It shall be marked either by her sign or by her subscription, and shall state that she wishes henceforth to preserve this religious commitment perpetually and without violation.

Then, after receiving from the priest or minister suitable religious clothing, whether resting in a bed or residing in any place whatsoever, she shall use that clothing without hesitation. The garment shall not be conspicuous for a different color or a different style, but shall be religious and beyond suspicion, free from variations of color and differences of form, so that without any suspicion of transgression it may remain suitable solely for the practice of holy religion and appropriate to her sex as a testimony of her probity.

Moreover, so that nothing may thereafter be called into doubt, from the beginning of her assumption of religion she shall cover her head with a purple or black-colored veil. Thus, while she bears there the sign of demonstrable holiness, where no observer’s sight can be deceived, she shall never attempt the cunning of detestable presumption.

## V.

All women who are proved to have previously been clothed in the religious habit shall have no excuse, and no objection shall be effective in opposition, even if they wish to conceal themselves beneath various and crafty arguments of deceit. Rather, the most sacred sanction of discipline shall hold them bound and subject.

They shall indeed be admonished by the authority of the priest to return voluntarily. If they refuse to return at the priest’s urging, they shall be brought back to religious observance and, once confined in monasteries, shall be struck with an appropriate sentence of excommunication.

The same procedure shall also remain in force in the condemnation of those who had not received any religious garment from a priest, but who themselves either put on such clothing or remained for a long time in a habit which observers believed to be religious. If they are shown, before the Church, a priest, or even five competent witnesses, to have worn it with definite signs or testimony, all such women—whether coming for the first time to religion or resuming a renewed conversion after transgression—shall, as stated above, cover their heads with a veil and draw up a written and confirmed profession by which they shall henceforth not be permitted to fall back into the audacity of violation.

Those among all these women who are found to have given their mind or clothing over to transgression shall receive a sentence of excommunication. After changing their habit again in monasteries, they shall remain confined under the hardships of severe penance until they close their final day.

## VI. Concerning Those Who at a Young Age Assumed the Religious Habit in the Presence of Their Parents

The effects of undisciplined conduct have sometimes caused the honorable decree of the constitution to be changed, when what is held indissoluble by the authority of the sanction is thought to be dissoluble. Therefore, whatever is evidently encountered from uncertainty must be rejected, so that nothing may remain thereafter that wavers in doubt.

Accordingly, if, at any immature age, either one or both parents have given children of either sex the tonsure of religion or the clothing proper to religion, and if they did not immediately renounce it when they saw that their children had received it—whether because the children were unwilling or unaware—but instead permitted those children to retain such things openly, either in their presence or before the Church and in public assembly, those children shall never at any time be permitted to return to secular clothing.

Once it has been established that they at some time possessed the tonsure or religious clothing, they shall immediately be restored to religious observance and habit and compelled to serve under the strict enforcement of this discipline.

Parents shall have permission to hand their children over to religion only up to the children’s tenth year of age. After that, whether it is with the parents’ consent or a solitary vow of the children’s own devotion, the children shall be permitted to assume the religious life.

Whoever is discovered to have committed a transgression, whether by removing the tonsure or by assuming secular clothing, shall receive the censure of excommunication and shall remain attached to religion forever.

With the assistance of divine mercy and the continuing religious will of the most glorious prince Reccesiunth, these witnesses having been most fittingly bound together and joined in peace, from the whole depth of our hearts we give glory and honor to the one eternal and immortal God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. By his gift we acknowledge that it has been granted to us, for the condition of his Church, both to direct its care and to arrange by the competence of sacred government the laws appropriate to it.

From him we ask and desire that he extend the life of the most sacred prince through a length of happy days and cause him perpetually to flourish in safety with every adornment of glory. May he also grant us to govern with equity the authority over his Church that we have received, to administer it with vigilance, and to preserve it in peace, so that after enduring the trials of this world we may be able to reach the heavenly kingdoms.

Amen.

I, Eugenius, unworthy metropolitan bishop of the see of Toledo, have subscribed these statutes of our definitions. Likewise, the other bishops subscribed, sixteen in number.

# Decree Concerning Bishop Potamius

We might have taken up the melodious flute in a song of fraternal joy, because divine mercy had summoned our assembly to pursuits of concord, and we had gathered to avoid sadness, since through the customary practice of discipline we seemed to be renewing the rules of the Fathers. But instead we take up a grievous rattle in place of a cymbal and sing a funeral instead of a song. Groaning with Jeremiah’s tears, we say: “The joy of our heart has been dissolved; our chorus has been turned into mourning.”

Therefore we behold woe before us, because we see that the crown of our head has fallen, when something so noble has collapsed into weakness—something that had stood so excellent in lofty holiness.

For while we were peacefully discussing ecclesiastical rules, a letter of confused confession and a subscription to be erased was brought before our assembly. Bishop Potamius of the Church of Braga had written it in articles concerning his own actions. When it was opened, sorrowful contrition, through tears rather than words, reviewed what the page to be obliterated and the letters to be erased revealed.

Then, after the bishops of God had been gathered alone and in secret, we had the aforementioned bishop brought before us. Addressing him with sobs more than with words, we produced the document that disclosed his disgrace and our confusion. After receiving it and examining it, when we asked whether the statement concerned his own work and was written by his own hand, he immediately asserted that the act was his, the words were his mouth’s, and the authority of the writing was from his own fingers. He confirmed this as he reread it there.

Again, invoking him under oath by the divine name, we earnestly adjured him to state truthfully whether he was willingly speaking a lie about himself or was being pressured by someone’s violence and, terrified, was recounting such things.

Then, in a mournful voice, with eyes wet from weeping and amid the clamor of sobs, under oath by the name of the one God, he cried out that he was confessing these evils about himself truthfully and that no violence was weighing upon him to make this confession. He further stated that he had voluntarily abandoned the governance of his church for nearly nine months and had shut himself up in a kind of prison to perform penance for the offense he had committed.

It was then learned through his truthful confession that he had been defiled by contact with a woman.

Although the antiquity of the Fathers decrees through the sacred rules that he should be removed from honor, we, preserving the laws of mercy, did not take away the title of honor that he had already taken away from himself by confessing his crime. Instead, by firm authority we decreed that he should devote himself to the duties and hardships of perpetual penance. We judged it better that he should travel through the harsh solitude of penance and eventually reach a dwelling of refreshment than, left to the freedom of his own will, be cast headlong into eternal damnation.

Then, by the common election of all of us, we appointed the venerable Fructuosus, bishop of the Church of Dunil, to hold the governance of the Church of Braga. He is to assume the care of the whole metropolitan province of Galicia, of all its bishops and peoples and assemblies, and of all the souls belonging to the Church of Braga, and is to order and preserve them in such a way that he may glorify our Lord through the uprightness of his work and provide us with joy through the safety of his Church.

Since it is appropriate to look ahead to the future, lest some disturbance of litigation arise within the condition of peace, our vigilance has taken care to attach to this decree the judgment of the Fathers, which condemns the aforementioned Bishop Potamius according to justice.

## From the Council of Valencia, Title 4

Nor did we consider it foreign to the usefulness of the Church to write this, brothers, so that you might know that whoever under the order of deacon, presbyter, or bishop says that he has been polluted by a mortal crime must be removed from the offices mentioned above, whether he is convicted by a true confession or by a falsehood of deceit.

For such a person cannot be absolved in these matters if he says of himself what would be punished if said of others, since everyone who becomes the cause of his own death is a greater murderer.

Many other judgments could indeed have been attached to this decree, ordering that the aforementioned Bishop Potamius be removed with the severest authority. But we preferred to include this one judgment from among them, lest, if we had repeated decrees of total condemnation, we should appear to be authors of an exceedingly severe punishment.

This decree was made on the day of the Kalends of December, in the eighth fortunate year of the reign of the most glorious lord, King Reccesiunth.

I, Eugenius, unworthy metropolitan bishop of the see of Toledo, have subscribed this decree of our judgment. Likewise, the other bishops subscribed, seventeen in number.

# Testamentary Decree

We have seen that what is just is discovered through deliberations, confirmed by the experience of those who judge, and found more fully authoritative according to the statutes of the supreme judgment.

Therefore, directing the intention of our mind and the efforts of our speech together toward the matter brought before us for hearing, the assembly of the holy council received directly from our glorious lord King Reccesiunth, through the illustrious man Vuamban, the testament of the holy Bishop Martin of the Church of Braga, of glorious memory, who is also seen to have built the monastery of Dunil. It was presented so that, once opened, what that blessed man had decreed might be revealed to our examination.

After the testament had been reread in the presence of all, we discovered that it had been formally sent to us by the aforementioned prince, because the same holy man of glorious memory had decreed that, as kings succeeded one another in order, his own constitution should remain entrusted to them for completion.

Thereafter, the testament of Ricimirus, bishop of the aforementioned Church of Dunil, was brought before us, concerning which he had decreed that his property should be settled by a truthful examination. After it was reread, we learned that this author had issued various provisions concerning it, among which he attempted to bind one firmly by the act of relegation: he assigned the collection of taxes and the prices of crops to be distributed annually to the poor without any reduction, leaving nothing without deliberation that could in some generous manner serve the uses of the Church.

Then, according to the testimony of the father of the Church of Dunil, it was added that Bishop Ricimirus had ordered, at his death, all kinds of goods and all the property of every type and material that he had found inside the house of that Church for domestic use and at the time of his ordination, as well as whatever he himself had been able to have made and brought in through the work of craftsmen of either sex belonging to the Church’s households, and whatever he appeared to have acquired through his own profession, to be distributed entirely to the poor.

He had also ordered certain people from the households of that Church to be made free, and is found to have given them, together with all the other persons belonging to him, more than fifty slaves of both sexes.

When these losses had become known, and because all the household’s internal resources had been given away so indiscriminately that nothing seemed to remain for the Church’s restoration, while there was no pressing circumstance of the poor’s need that demanded that everything be distributed so completely and exhaustively, and because nothing was shown to have been given in accordance with canonical sanction on behalf of those freedmen, nor was anything found to have been left in compensation to the Church for the slaves and other goods given to those same freedmen, and because he had even relegated his own property in the name of the poor in such a way that no benefit from it could reach ecclesiastical use, we were led, both by consideration of reason and by the wording of the sanctions of the Fathers, to bring the terms of the testament—not entirely to invalidate it—under a certain reasonable and authoritative moderation.

That is, because the ecclesiastical property is recognized to be burdened by the losses of such great expenditures made by the aforementioned Bishop Ricimirus, all his property that he left assigned to the name of the poor shall serve the Church of Dunil with full authority until the whole loss that it suffered in the household’s equipment can be more clearly repaired.

Then, once the restitution of the loss has been completed, the terms of the testament shall be observed as they were decreed. As for the freedmen made from the Church’s households, and the property and everything else known to have been bestowed either upon them or upon their people among the slaves and other persons, we leave the whole matter to be arranged at the discretion of our venerable brother Fructuosus, bishop of the Church.

Since the evident order of the Fathers invalidates these arrangements, his moderation shall bring them toward mercy, so that neither the measure exceeds the paternal rule nor severity extinguishes compassion. According to the merits of those who serve, he may either withdraw or grant the rewards of freedom and the gifts of property.

Issued on the day of the Kalends of December, in the seventh fortunate year of the reign of our most glorious lord, King Reccesiunth.

I, Eugenius, unworthy metropolitan bishop of the see of Toledo, have subscribed this decree of our judgment. Likewise, the other bishops subscribed, ten in number.

# The Chapters of the Eleventh Council of Toledo Begin
[Col. 0533B] 1. That the council not be disturbed by tumult. 2. That the metropolitan must not cease instructing those of neighboring districts. 3. That diversity of rites not be maintained within one province. 4. Concerning discord among priests. 5. Concerning the restraint of priests’ excesses. 6. That priests must not inflict mutilations of limbs in any ecclesiastical household, nor pass judgment on anything punishable by death. 7. What discretion the rulers of churches ought to exercise, lest through undisciplined correction they incur the charge of homicide. 8. That no reward be accepted for the divine sacraments.

[Col. 0533C] 9. What must be observed if anyone becomes a bishop through payment, and by what sentence he is to be punished if he is discovered to have been ordained to the office he received through money.

[Col. 0534B] 10. That all bishops and rulers of churches, at the time when they are to be ordained, promise under security that they must live with complete justice. 11. Concerning the clarification of the ancient canon which commands that if anyone does not consume the Eucharist received from a priest, he be driven away as a sacrilegious person. 12. That a penitent at the point of death not be deprived of divine reconciliation, and that the offering of a penitent who dies without having been reconciled nevertheless be received by the Church. 13. Concerning priests who, when afflicted, appear to fall. 14. That those who sing and sacrifice to the Lord always have established places of support behind them. 15. Concerning the establishment of a fixed time at which the council is to be held.

[Col. 0534C] 16. Concerning the giving of thanks for the completion of the council.

# The Eleventh Council of Toledo Begins

Held in the era 713, in the thirteenth year of King Wamba, on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

[Col. 0533]

[Col. 0533C] In the name of the holy Trinity, when the priests of the province of Carthage had gathered together in the city of Toledo, in the seat of blessed Mary, the Virgin Mother of the Lord, in the fourth year of the most excellent and religious ruler Wamba, on the seventh day before the Ides of November, there came upon us an occasion of votive joy and a day of greatly desired thanksgiving. On it we were granted both to behold together and to lament what tears we owe to the Lord for past events.

Until now we had been unstable amid the filth of the declining age, because the long succession of times, deprived of the light of councils, was removing vices less than it was implanting ignorance, the mother of all errors, in idle minds. Until now, grunting boars had ravaged the flourishing vineyard of the Lord. The deceitful contrivance of heretics had attempted to defile and pollute the bride of Christ, whom he had reconciled through the outpouring of his most precious blood; to divide the Lord’s seamless garment; to tear apart the unity of faith; and to remove the supports of charity, since it obstinately wished to cling to its own judgment and profaned the purity of sacred Scripture through its understanding distorted by perversity.

Moreover, the guardians of God’s holy Church also wound it. Although, because of the excellence of their dignity, they ought to summon others through imitation of their virtue to observe charity and unity, like salt that has lost its savor they provide material for scandal rather than edification. Hence, those who observed these things could see how the cauldron of Babylonian confusion, once kindled, at one time turned the seasons away from councils and at another entangled the priests of the Lord in dissolute morals. For they followed the impulses of the purple-clad prostitute, since there was no discipline in ecclesiastical assemblies and no one to correct the factions of those who were going astray, while the divine word was held in hatred.

And because there was no command for the bishops to assemble, the monstrous life of the worse grew. At last, however, divine clemency, grieving over the destruction of the work of its own hands and bringing back what had been led astray, wishing to establish his holy host (*Sabaoth*) with new shoots and fresh plants, substituted diligence for negligence, introduced discipline in place of ignorance, skill in place of sluggishness, unity in place of schism, and granted the bond of true peace in place of weeds. In place of things that fall away, it infused desires for heavenly things; it urged us to pursue honorable things instead of disgraceful ones; and it raised us from earthly and lowly things to sublime ones.

From the height of heaven, it looked upon us—dying rather than living in this valley of tears, wandering in this vast sea of dangers without a helmsman or rudder, battered here and there by the waves of storms through precipices, struggling continually in the battle-line of evils, surrounded by a thousand perils, where an exceedingly cunning enemy lies in wait, equipped with a thousand arts of doing harm—and presented itself as meeting our harsh condition and our salvation, preparing for our age the mind of a religious ruler, at once devout and instructed.

Through the pious intention of his provident care, the light of councils shone forth again, and mutual charity stirred one another to correct and instruct our morals. The glorious ruler’s exhortation granted us the opportunity to assemble, and suitable discipline was prepared for correction. Thus, after a long passage of time—after eighteen years, that is, of passing years—we who had deserved to be gathered into one assembly might deserve to receive spiritual healing.

For this number is not foreign to salvation. Thus, in the Gospel, “that woman who had been bent over for eighteen years” (Luke 13:11 and following), who bore the figure of the whole human race, was granted the former health of salvation under the sacramental significance of this number.

[Col. 0535C] Therefore, while the condition of our order remained bent over for years, because no decision of councils united us and no assembly of the ecclesiastical order gathered us together, at last, summoned by the command of the divine will and by the order of the religious ruler, we came together in the city of Toledo. When we had been seated in our appointed places in the church of the blessed Virgin Mary, among the other matters arranged below in an orderly sequence of chapters, we began our discussion nowhere else than with the purity of faith.

Since this is always the first way of salvation for those being initiated into the blessed life, it was fitting that it should also precede our decrees. Therefore, embracing the secrets of sacred instruction contained in the records of the holy councils—namely, those of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—through which the false assemblies of heretics are destroyed from their roots and the norm of the Catholic faith is declared, we determined by common and reciprocal judgment that we should endeavor to recite this very rule of our faith to one another alternately and individually.

Whatever, within three days, came to each of us from the memory of what we had seen in reading concerning such questions was to be noted in a simple style, with every sober brevity. Nevertheless, the account of this mystery itself was to be pure and clear, beginning first from its head and proceeding to its remaining members, containing no lines of obscurity and no rules of unfamiliar expression. Its sole purity was to be the clarity of its words, so that a simple exchange might, by its own power of awakening understanding, convey the meaning of the words more clearly than an exposition drawn from dense reading.

For indeed it is fitting that the priests of God should know the mystery of so great a matter in such a way that they are not carried away by the surface of unfamiliar words, but are found instructed by sound understanding, so that, especially in discussing the secrets of this holy Trinity, clarity rather than eloquence may make them discerning.

They had been drawn to this by the gift of divine grace, so that the promise of our reciprocal definition might be shown in action. Accordingly, what the tongue of the presiding metropolitan uttered on the first day, the voice of all of us repeated individually and collectively on the third day. This, then, is the tenor of our faith, which flowed abundantly from its head and shone forth gloriously, approved by its members.

[Col. 0536B] We confess and believe that the holy and ineffable Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is naturally one God, of one substance, of one nature, and likewise of one majesty and power. We profess that the Father is neither begotten nor created, but unbegotten. For he derives his origin from no one; from him the Son received birth and the Holy Spirit procession. He himself, therefore, is the fountain and origin of the whole divinity.

The Father, by the ineffable essence of his substance, ineffably begot the Son; yet he did not beget anything other than what he himself is: God from God, light from light. From him, therefore, is all “fatherhood in heaven and on earth” (Ephesians 3:15).

We confess that the Son was born from the substance of the Father before the ages, without beginning, and yet was not made, because neither did the Father ever exist without the Son, nor the Son without the Father. Yet the Father is not from the Son in the same way that the Son is from the Father, because the Father did not receive generation from the Son, but the Son from the Father.

The Son is therefore God from the Father; the Father, however, is God, but not from the Son. The Son is the Father’s Son and God from the Father, yet in all things equal to God the Father, because he neither began at any time to be born nor ceased to be so.

He is also believed to be of one substance with the Father; for this reason he is called *homoousios* with the Father, that is, “of the same substance as the Father.” For *homos* in Greek means “one,” while *ousia* means “substance.” Joined together, the two sound as “one substance.” The Son is not to be believed to have been begotten or born from nothing, nor from any other substance, but from the Father’s womb—that is, from his substance. He is eternal, although he is Son.

If the Father always existed, he always had the Son whose Father he was. For this reason we confess that the Son was born from the Father without beginning. Nor, because he was begotten from the Father, do we call this same Son of God a small portion of a divided nature. Rather, we assert that the perfect Father begot the perfect Son, without diminution and without defect. For it belongs only to divinity not to have an unequal Son.

Hence the Son of God is Son by nature, not by choice. God the Father is not to be believed to have begotten him either by will or by necessity, because no necessity falls upon God, nor does will precede wisdom.

We believe that the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the Trinity, is one God, equal with God the Father and the Son, of one substance and likewise of one nature. Yet he is neither begotten nor created, but proceeds from both and is the Spirit of both.

This Holy Spirit is believed to be neither unbegotten nor begotten, lest, if we call him unbegotten, we should speak of two fathers, or, if begotten, appear to proclaim two sons. Nevertheless, he is called not the Spirit of the Father alone or of the Son alone, but at once the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.

For he does not proceed from the Father into the Son, or from the Son toward the sanctification of creation; rather, he is shown to have proceeded from both at once, since he is recognized as the charity—or holiness—of both.

This Holy Spirit is believed to have been sent by both, just as the Son is; yet he is not regarded as lesser than the Father and the Son, just as the Son, because of the flesh he assumed, testifies that he is lesser than the Father and the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0537B] This is the account handed down concerning the holy Trinity. It must be called and believed not “threefold,” but “Trinity.” Nor can it rightly be said that in one God there is a Trinity; rather, there is one God who is Trinity.

In the relative names of the persons, the Father is referred to the Son, the Son to the Father, and the Holy Spirit to both. Although three persons are thus named relatively, one natural substance is nevertheless believed. Just as we do not proclaim three substances along with three persons, so we proclaim one substance and three persons.

For what the Father is, he is not in relation to himself but to the Son; and what the Son is, he is not in relation to himself but to the Father. Similarly, the Holy Spirit is referred not to himself but relatively to the Father and the Son, in that he is proclaimed the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.

Again, when we say “God,” the word is not spoken in relation to something else, as “Father” is spoken in relation to the Son, or “Son” in relation to the Father, or “Holy Spirit” in relation to the Father and the Son. Rather, “God” is spoken specifically in relation to himself.

For if we are questioned about each individual person, we must confess God. Thus the Father is individually called God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God; yet there are not three gods, but one God.

Likewise, the Father is individually called almighty, the Son almighty, and the Holy Spirit almighty; yet there are not three almighty beings, but one Almighty, just as one light and one beginning are proclaimed.

Therefore each person individually is confessed and believed to be one God. They have one undivided and equal divinity, majesty, and power, which is neither diminished in the individual persons nor increased in the three. For there is nothing less when each person is individually called God, nor anything more when all three persons are named together.

This holy Trinity, therefore, which is one and true God, neither departs from number nor is comprehended by number. Number is perceived in the relation of the persons; but in the substance of the divinity, what has been enumerated cannot be comprehended.

Thus the only thing that number indicates is that they exist in relation to one another; and in this number they are without number, because they exist in themselves. For one natural name so properly belongs to this holy Trinity that in the three persons it cannot become plural.

For this reason we believe that the following has been said in the sacred writings: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number” (Psalm 146:5).

[Col. 0538A] Nor, because we have said that these are three persons in one God, may we therefore say that the Father is the same as the Son, or that the Son is the one who is the Father, or that he who is the Holy Spirit is the Father and the Son. For he who is the Father is not himself the Son or the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, the Father is the same as the Son in nature, the Son the same as the Father in nature, and the Father and the Son the same as the Holy Spirit in nature—that is, one God. When we say that the Father is not the same person as the Son, this refers to the distinction of persons. When, however, we say that the Father is the same in nature as the Son, and the Son the same in nature as the Father, and the Holy Spirit the same in nature as the Father and the Son, this is shown to pertain to the nature or substance by which God is God.

They are one in substance; we distinguish the persons but do not separate the divinity. We therefore acknowledge the Trinity in the distinction of persons and profess unity because of the nature or substance.

These three are therefore one in nature, not one person. Nevertheless, these three persons must in no way be regarded as separable, since none is believed ever to have existed or acted before another, after another, or without another.

They are found to be inseparable both in what they are and in what they do. For we believe that there was no interval of time between the Father who begets, the Son who is begotten, and the Holy Spirit who proceeds: the begetter never preceded the begotten, the begotten was never absent from the begetter, and the proceeding Spirit never appeared later than the Father or the Son.

For this reason this Trinity is believed and proclaimed by us to be inseparable and without confusion. These three persons are therefore so called, according to the definition of the Fathers, that they may be recognized. For if we attend to what Holy Scripture says about Wisdom—“she is the splendor of eternal light”—then, just as we see splendor inseparably adhere to light, so we confess that the Son cannot be separated from the Father.

We therefore neither confuse these three persons of one and inseparable nature nor in any way proclaim them separable. The Trinity itself has deigned clearly to show this to us: even in everything in which it wished the persons to be recognized individually, it does not permit one to be understood without the other.

For the Father is not known without the Son, nor is the Son found without the Father. The very relation of the personal name forbids the persons to be separated. Although it does not name them together, it indicates them together. No one can hear any one of these names without being compelled to understand the other also.

Although these three are one and the one is three, each person nevertheless retains his own property. The Father possesses eternity without birth; the Son, eternity with birth; and the Holy Spirit, procession without birth.

Of these three persons, we believe that only the person of the Son, for the liberation of the human race, assumed a true human being without sin from holy and immaculate Mary the Virgin. From her he was begotten through a new order and a new birth, because the invisible one in divinity is shown visible in the flesh.

His birth was new because her untouched virginity knew no intercourse with a man, yet, made fruitful through the Holy Spirit, supplied the material of the flesh. The Virgin’s childbirth can be grasped neither by reasoning nor by example, for it will be unique.

Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit must not be believed to be the Father of the Son because Mary conceived when she was overshadowed by that same Holy Spirit, lest we appear to assert two fathers of the Son—which it is certainly impious to say.

In this wondrous conception, “Wisdom built herself a house” (Proverbs 9:1). “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Yet the Word itself was not so converted and changed into flesh that it ceased to be God when it willed to be human. Thus the Word of God is not merely there, but also everything belonging to humanity; and the whole is called God because of God and human because of the human being.

In this Son of God we believe there are two natures, one divine and the other human. He united them in himself in such a way that neither divinity can ever be separated from humanity nor humanity from divinity. Hence he is perfect God and perfect man in the unity of person.

Yet, because we have said that there are two natures in the Son, we do not confess that there are two persons in him, lest—God forbid—a quaternity appear to be added to the Trinity. God the Word did not receive the person of a human being, but its nature; and the eternal person of divinity received the temporal substance of flesh.

Likewise, we believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance. Yet we do not say that the Virgin Mary gave birth to the unity of this Trinity, but only to the Son, who alone assumed our nature in the unity of his person.

The incarnation of this Son of God must nevertheless be believed to have been accomplished by the whole Trinity, because the works of the Trinity are inseparable. The Son alone, however, took the form of a servant in the singularity of his person, not in the unity of the divine nature; he took what is proper to the Son, not what is common to the Trinity.

That form was joined to him for the unity of person, so that the Son of God and the Son of man would be one Christ.

Likewise, this same Christ exists in these two natures with three substances: that of the Word, which is to be referred to the essence of God alone, and those of body and soul, which pertain to a true human being. He therefore possesses in himself the twofold substance of his divinity and our humanity.

Yet, in that he was born from God the Father without beginning, he is understood only as born, not made or predestined. In that, however, he was made and born from the Virgin Mary, he must be believed both made and predestined.

Both births are wondrous: from the Father before the ages he was begotten without a mother, and at the end of the ages he was born from a mother without a father. Yet, insofar as he was created as a human being, he is the Son of Mary his mother.

Likewise, insofar as he is God, he is equal to the Father; insofar as he is human, he is less than the Father. He must also be believed both greater and less than himself. In the form of God, the Son himself is greater than himself because of the humanity he assumed, since divinity is greater. In the form of a servant he is less than himself, that is, in his humanity, which is regarded as less than divinity.

For just as, through the flesh he assumed, he is regarded as less not only than the Father but also than himself, so, according to the divinity by which he is equal to the Father, both he and the Father are greater than the human being whom the person of the Son alone assumed.

Again, when it is asked whether the Son can be both equal to and less than the Holy Spirit, just as he is now believed to be equal to and now less than the Father, we answer: according to the form of God, he is equal both to the Father and to the Holy Spirit; according to the form of a servant, he is less both than the Father and than the Holy Spirit.

For neither the Holy Spirit nor God the Father, but only the person of the Son, assumed flesh; through it he is believed to be less than those two persons.

This Son is believed to be a person distinct and separable from God the Father and the Holy Spirit, but from the human being he assumed he is distinguished by nature.

With the human being he exists as one person; with the Father and the Holy Spirit, according to the nature of his divinity, he is the Son. Nevertheless, the Son must be believed to have been sent not only by the Father but also by the Holy Spirit, according to what is said through the prophet: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 6).

He is also understood to have been sent by himself, because the will and operation of the whole Trinity are recognized as inseparable.

He who before the ages was called the Only-Begotten was temporally called the Firstborn because of the flesh he assumed, in which he took the form of a human being. According to the truth of the Gospel, he is believed to have died without sin. He alone endured that passion for us—while preserving his divinity—for our offenses, was condemned to death, and received the true death of the flesh upon the cross.

On the third day he rose from the tomb, raised by his own power. Following this example of our Head, we confess in true faith the resurrection of the flesh of all the dead—not in air or in some other flesh, as certain deluded people believe we shall rise, but in this flesh in which we live, stand, and move.

After completing the example of this holy resurrection, our Lord and Savior returned by ascending to the paternal throne, from which he never departed according to his divinity. There, seated at the right hand of the Father, he is awaited at the end of the ages as judge of all the living and the dead.

From there he will come with all the saints to render judgment, giving each person the due of his own reward, according to what each has done while placed in the body, whether good or evil.

We believe that the Catholic Church, purchased at the price of his blood, will reign with him forever. Within her bosom we are established, and we believe in one baptism; we confess the remission of all sins; under this faith we also truly believe in the resurrection of the dead and await the joys of the age to come.

This alone must be prayed and requested by us: that, when the Son has completed and finished the judgment and handed over the kingdom to God the Father, he may make us participants in his kingdom, so that through this faith by which we cling to him, we may reign with him without end.

This is the faith of our confession, set forth in which the doctrine of all heretics is destroyed, by which the hearts of all the faithful are cleansed, and by which one approaches God gloriously. Having refreshed ourselves with its most holy savor through the continuous effort of our recitations during a three-day fast, we proceeded on the following day to the matters set down below for decision.

## Chapter I

The priests of the Lord, seated in the place of blessing, must neither make a disturbance with indiscriminate voices nor be troubled by any tumult. They must not be driven by empty tales or laughter, nor—what is worse—pour forth tumultuous voices in obstinate disputes.

“For if anyone,” as the Apostle says, “thinks that he is religious, not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, his religion is vain” (James 1:26).

Justice loses its due observance when silence is lost, and a crowd of noisy voices confuses judgment, as the prophet says: “The observance of justice will be silence” (Isaiah 32:17).

Whatever is done before the consultations of those who are seated, or is brought forward by the party presenting a case, must therefore be expressed with such gentle wording that contentious voices neither disturb the understanding of those listening nor weaken the strength of the judges through tumult.

Whoever in the assembly of the council believes that the foregoing rules may be violated, and disturbs the council contrary to these prohibitions, whether by tumult, insults, or laughter, shall, according to the command of divine law—“Drive out the scoffer, and strife will depart with him”—be removed with every disgrace from the confession of faith and withdraw from the common assembly; he shall also undergo a sentence of excommunication for three days.

## Chapter II
