The higher the position someone occupies at the summit of rank, the more necessary it is that he precede others in the grace of his merits, so that, in presiding over individuals, he may be distinguished by an eminent holiness. He must have on his lips the sword of truth and in his actions the effectiveness of light, so that, in accordance with Paul, he may be able “to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it” (Titus 1:9).

We must carefully consider the next degree of our order and the manner of the governance we have undertaken, so that those who have assumed the office of preaching may not be deprived by any cares of divine reading. For the minds of certain bishops are so shut off from the grace of reading by bodily indolence that the mute herald finds nothing to offer to the flocks entrusted to him by way of doctrine.

The greater ones must therefore always insist that those whom they protect under their governance not be allowed to perish from hunger for the word of God. Just as metropolitan bishops must watch over their suffragans and others devoted to ecclesiastical orders, so suffragans must watch over the religious persons entrusted to them, so that the ignorance of such people may be imbued with instruction in divine law.

Thus every superior, seeking his subjects with unceasing concern, should either joyfully recognize their progress or instruct their ignorance without arrogance.

It therefore pleased us to define specifically concerning such matters, in accordance with the institutions of the Council of Toledo, that they should either willingly undertake the necessary intention of learning thoroughly or be compelled, against their will, by their superiors to undertake exercises in reading.

## Chapter III

Concerning those who, contrary to the Apostle’s will, “are carried about by every wind of doctrine” (Ephesians 4:14), this holy council decrees that, compelled by the authority of the metropolitan see, the citizens and rulers of the churches of each province shall maintain one and the same manner of psalm-singing that they have learned to be established in the metropolitan see. They must not allow themselves to be separated from the metropolitan see by any diversity of order or office.

For it is just that everyone should receive the rules of instruction from the place from which he received the consecration of his honor, so that, in accordance with the decrees of the Fathers, the see that is the mother of each person’s sacerdotal dignity may also be the teacher of ecclesiastical order.

Abbots may retain the offices granted to them, which they are to fulfill regularly according to the will of their bishop. But they may not celebrate the other public offices—that is, Vespers, Matins, or Mass—in a manner different from that of the principal church.

Whoever proves to be a violator of these decrees shall be deprived of communion for six months and shall remain under the metropolitan’s supervision, subject to the discipline of penance and correction. In this way he shall both wash away with tears the guilt of his past transgression before him and diligently learn the necessary doctrine concerning the offices.

Under this rule, therefore, the metropolitan must not only bind all the bishops and priests of the province, but the other bishops also must compel the rulers of the churches subject to them to obey these institutions.

## Chapter IV

Just as everyone who loves his brother is from God (1 John 4:7), so everyone who hates his neighbor is from the devil (1 John 3:17). For it is by love alone that it is discerned from whom someone is begotten, as John says:

“By this the children of God and the children of the devil are revealed: everyone who does not do righteousness is not from God, nor does he love his brother” (1 John 2:29).

“For this is the message that you heard from the beginning: that we should love one another.” And shortly afterward:

“Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him” (1 John 3:15).

Behold, he is reasonably declared to be a murderer who separates himself from brotherly fellowship. Even if he does not move his hand to kill, nevertheless, because he is harshly disposed toward killing, he is already held by God to be a murderer. The other lives, while this one is already shown to be his killer.

Since the blessed Apostle Paul agrees with these commandments in sound preaching, saying, “Do not let the sun go down upon your anger, and do not give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27), reports have reached us that certain priests have allowed their discord to grow into such obstinacy that not only does the setting sun fail to recall them from anger, but not even the passage of many years inclines them toward the good of charity. Indeed, in their hearts Christ, the sun of righteousness, has set, so that they can scarcely return to the light of charity.

We have therefore judged that the offerings of these and similar dissenting brothers must in no way be received, in accordance with the definition of the ancient canon. Concerning the persons of those who are in discord, however, we decree specifically that, before true reconciliation has united them, neither may dare approach the Lord’s altar or receive the grace of holy communion. Instead, they shall compensate through penance for twice the period during which they served discord.

If one of them, while the other shows contempt, hastens to make satisfaction in charity, then from the time when he is shown to have hurried toward reconciliation he shall be regarded within the Church as a peacemaker. Nevertheless, the preceding sentence remains in force, so that the time he spent in anger must be paid back twofold in penitential satisfaction.

## Chapter V

The lives of prelates must not be disturbed by any excesses, for it is exceedingly unworthy that those who are called the thrones of God should be shaken by a slight impulse, and that those who ought to be the path of justice should themselves become a breeding ground for strife and plunder.

How, then, will such men be “blameless,” as the Apostle says (1 Timothy 5:7), when they not only do blameworthy things but rather commit deadly and accursed acts?

Reports have indeed reached us concerning certain priests: setting aside all the dignity of the priestly order, they anticipate the judgment of those hearing cases with fury, and, through the excessive impulse of dishonorable agitation, refuse to hear judgments, although they ought to have endured judgments of equity.

While they flatter themselves on the height of their honor, they refuse to exercise patience. Those who ought to preserve the position of truth without wavering suddenly change their religious purpose and, in headlong fury, anticipate judgment. Thus, in a matter in which they ought to have endured the assembly of judgment, they act through usurpation in a way that brings confusion upon their presumption.

Such men are either to be punished alike by loss of property and excommunication, or, with the settlement of property matters omitted, are to be corrected by the sole satisfaction of penance.

Those who are supported by the resources of their own property, or who are known already to have transferred their property in advance into the name of the Church, if they themselves, through their subjects, or through anyone else seize another’s property or commit any act of presumption or killing—whether against fiscal property or against property belonging to anyone whatsoever—must make restitution, according to the law of the most excellent ruler, for what they have seized or wrongfully claimed.

For the excess contrary to religion that they dishonorably committed before judgment, they are to be punished by two weeks of excommunication.

Those who appear to possess no property of their own must be treated with great discretion, so that they neither redeem unlawful ventures with the resources of the churches nor remain wholly exempt from punishment. For it is not just that the churches over which priests preside should suffer loss because of their wrongful acts, or that satisfaction for such excesses should be demanded from the churches, since the Church instructs her servants not toward litigation but toward honorable conduct.

Concerning such men, therefore, it pleased us to decree that those who possess no property of their own, but have been found to have committed usurpation anywhere or to have inflicted killing or any act of presumption upon any persons, must not, through any bending of their status, be subjected to the servitude of men. Rather, according to the degree of presumption of which each such person has been guilty, he shall be subjected to the laws of penance.

That is, if someone is convicted of presumption involving a sum of ten solidi, he shall cleanse himself through twenty days of penitential satisfaction. Whether he has committed an excess involving a smaller or a larger sum, he shall always repay it through a similar twofold satisfaction of penance.

We remit to the secular courts the ecclesiastical slaves who are known to have committed such excesses, so that they may be heard according to the secular laws.

Let this suffice concerning general excess. Proceeding, moreover, to the order of particular cases, we decree:

If any bishop dishonors the wife, daughter, granddaughter, or any woman related to a magnate by whatever degree, through any deceit or adulterous artifice, he shall lose the rank of his own honor and undergo a perpetual sentence of excommunication under exile and banishment. Nevertheless, toward the end of his life he is to be assisted by the remedy of communion.

The same sentence shall also be deserved by those who knowingly commit homicide, or who appear to have inflicted anything through killing or any injury whatsoever upon palace officials, noble persons, or any women or girls of distinguished rank.

Accordingly, in accordance with the provisions of the secular laws, they ought either to receive retaliation in kind, or a surrender of their persons, or proscription.

## VI

Those to whom the sacraments of the Lord are entrusted may not exercise judgment involving bloodshed. Therefore such excesses must be strictly prohibited, lest, driven by the impulses of indiscriminate presumption, they presume either to pass judgment on their own authority in matters punishable by death, or themselves inflict mutilations upon any persons, or order them to be inflicted. If any one of them, forgetful of these precepts, does such a thing either against members of his own church or against any persons whatsoever, let him be deprived both of the honor of the order granted to him and of his position, and let him be kept confined in a prison of perpetual condemnation. Nevertheless, communion is not to be denied him when he is departing this life, for the sake of the Lord’s mercy, “who does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live” (Ezek. 33:11).

## VII

Since, according to the decree of ancient institution, benevolence ought to be employed more than severity toward those who are to be corrected, exhortation more than agitation, and charity more than power, it has been reported to us that certain of the brethren, pursuing their subjects more out of the spite of hatred than from a desire for correction, while pretending to apply spiritual correction to them, suddenly inflict indiscriminate death, when they cast them out without a hearing and punish them with unlawful judgments under the pretext of penance.

Therefore, from now on, let it not be permitted to perverse wills to pretend what they feign. Whenever any one of their subjects must be corrected, the matter should either be dealt with publicly by priestly discipline, or, if the rulers prefer another course, the testimony of two or three spiritual brothers should be specially brought forward; both the nature of the crime should be established and the measure of the penance imposed. If, however, he is found deserving of exile or confinement, or if some other particular penalty is decreed, the measure of the penance which the priest has imposed upon the transgressor before three brothers must be recorded by the special handwritten subscription of the person who pronounced the sentence.

Thus it will happen that transgressors will not suffer the destruction of their lives without testimony, nor will rulers be ashamed to accuse themselves concerning the temptations of any persons.

## VIII

Whatever is granted through the bestowal of invisible grace must never be sold outright for profit or for any rewards, since the Lord says: “You have received freely; give freely” (Matt. 10:8), and so forth. Henceforth, anyone established in ecclesiastical order who accepts any prices or rewards—unless voluntarily offered for such ambition—for baptizing and signing the faithful, for the bestowal of chrism, or for promotions in rank [Col. 0545A].

If such a thing is perpetrated by subjects with the knowledge of the bishop of the place, that bishop shall be subjected to excommunication for two months, because he concealed the evil that he knew of and did not apply the necessary correction. But if any one of his subordinates, without his knowledge, thinks that he should accept something under any of the aforesaid headings, then, if he is a priest, he shall be punished by three months’ excommunication; if a deacon, by four months. A subdeacon or cleric serving these desires must be punished both with a suitable penalty and with the due excommunication.

## IX

Many judgments of the Fathers have been issued concerning this matter, namely, that no one should suppose that the priceless grace of the Holy Spirit can be acquired through gifts or presents. But—what must be said with profound grief—the more this has been prohibited by the frequent commands of decrees, the more it is recognized as repeatedly practiced among us through fraud. Those who strive to purchase the grace of their ordination with such a price anticipate the time of their promotion by means of a gift, or, after receiving the honor, pay the reward of their promises with the apparatus of shameful gain.

Therefore, so that the opportunity for these and similar devices may henceforth be cut off, this holy synod has determined that whenever anyone approaches the altar of the Lord to receive the summit of the episcopate, he must be bound by an oath that, for the consecration of the honor being conferred upon him, he has neither given nor will ever arrange to give any person any bestowal of a reward. Thus either, being free from this contagion, he will receive consecration to the prelacy, or, when this crime has been publicly disclosed, he will be openly stripped of it before the Church and will not attain the honor which he sought to purchase.

Those, however, who are subsequently shown to have been ordained to the prelacy through a reward, we judge must be separated from the Church as heretical simoniacs (*haeresimoniachos*), under defined laws of penance: that is, they are to be banished into exile for two years, restrained by worthy satisfaction or by a sentence of excommunication, and are to strive through tears to seek and restore the rank of honor which they bought with rewards. If worthy satisfaction finds them during the period of their penance, they are to be restored not only to communion but also to their position and to all the duties of the order from which they had been separated. [Col. 0545D]

## X

Although all who are devoted to the sacred orders are bound by the canonical rules, it is nevertheless expedient that they promise the vows of their commitment under a formal guarantee, as ecclesiastical discipline approves for advancement in rank. For what a person promises individually is usually feared more than what is concluded by a general pledge.

Therefore it has pleased this holy council that anyone who is about to enter ecclesiastical ranks should not receive the consecration of honor until he has promised in a written declaration acceptable to him that, while preserving the Catholic faith with sincere devotion of heart, he will live justly and piously; that in none of his works will he contradict the canonical rules; and that each person will render in every respect the honor and reverent obedience due to whoever is set over him, according to the decree of blessed Pope Leo:

> Whoever knows that he has been placed over some persons should not be troubled that someone has been placed over him; but the obedience which he requires, he too must render.

Nevertheless, the penalty customary according to ecclesiastical practice, and prescribed for such matters, must be imposed and paid by those who become transgressors.

## XI

Since nothing in the divine canon ought to be confused, doubtful, or indiscriminate in the decisions of our assembly, the canon of the First Council of Toledo was reread. It commands that if anyone does not consume the Eucharist received from a priest, he should be driven away as a sacrilegious person. No distinction concerning intention was added, although a faithful person may faithfully receive what physical necessity does not naturally allow him to swallow.

Human weakness is often so burdened at the very end of life and weighed down by such a burden of dryness that it cannot be refreshed by any intake of food, but can scarcely be sustained by the grace of the drink taken. We have also seen this at the death of many who, desiring the viaticum of communion with all the longing of their prayers, rejected the Eucharist given to them by the priest—not because they did this through unbelief, but because, on account of drinking from the Lord’s chalice, they were unable to swallow the Eucharist delivered to them.

Such persons, therefore, are not to be separated from the body of the Church if they did these things not through unbelief but through necessity, especially when no suspicion of false faith is held concerning them. It has therefore pleased us to determine that this should neither harm the faithful nor remain unpunished in the unbeliever.

Accordingly, if any faithful person, compelled by some unavoidable illness, rejects the Eucharist he has received, he shall not be subjected to any ecclesiastical condemnation. Likewise, no punitive judgment shall rebuke those who do such things during infancy or while placed in any form of mental derangement, when they appear unaware of what they have done.

But whoever, whether among the faithful or the unbelieving, casts away the Lord’s body without the unavoidable illness mentioned above shall, if faithful, be deprived of communion perpetually; if unbelieving, he shall both be subjected to scourging and banished into perpetual exile. If any of these persons laments such an excess with worthy satisfaction of penance, he may be restored to his former communion after five years.

## XII

A person who undertakes penance in the danger of death must not be kept long from the grace of reconciliation. If, pressed by the imminent danger of death, he receives penance through the imposition of hands, reconciliation must immediately be granted to him, lest the sick man depart from human affairs before receiving the gift of reconciliation. Otherwise, those who survive might in some way seem to be condemned to perpetual sorrow, if death’s nature were to carry away from the present life someone who had been cut off from the members of the Church and had certainly not merited reconciliation.

Therefore, according to the decree of Pope Leo, for those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger, customarily implore the protection of penance and reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied, because in the mercy of God we can impose neither measures nor fixed times. [Col. 0547A]

As for those who, after receiving penance, depart this life before they are reconciled, although differing instructions concerning this matter are found, we have nevertheless approved the opinion of those who, in considerable number, have decided more humanely concerning such persons: that their memory should be commended in the churches and that an offering for their offense should be received by the priests.

## XIII

It has rightly been defined by the rules of our predecessors that those ensnared by demons or other afflictions may not handle sacred ministries. With the assent of reason to this command, we collectively determine that none of those who, while on the ground, are struck down by demons, or are violently overcome in any manner by attacks of possession, may dare to minister at sacred altars or, without examination, thrust themselves into the divine sacraments.

This does not apply to those who, afflicted by various bodily ailments, are nevertheless shown to have been cast down on the ground by such attacks. Even these, however, are to be suspended from the office, order, and position of their ministry until, after the passage of one year, they are found by the bishop’s discernment to be free from demonic attacks.

## XIV

Let each person also heed that warning of the divine oracle where it is written: “Woe to the solitary, for when he falls he has no one to raise him up” (Eccli. 4:10).

We must be extremely fearful and vigilant lest, during those hours and at those times when psalmody is offered to the Lord or sacrifice is celebrated, a harmful seizure or some bodily illness overtake anyone who is engaged alone in the divine offices, causing his body suddenly to collapse or confusing his mind through derangement or terror. Therefore, taking precautions against such dangers, we have judged it necessary to establish that wherever the time, place, or availability of the clergy permits, whoever is singing to God and offering sacrifice should have behind him the assistance of a nearby companion. Thus, if the one who has approached to perform the offices is disturbed by any accident or is struck down upon the ground, he will always have behind him someone who can fearlessly perform his duty in his place.

## XV

After everything that has been promulgated in this council for the correction of our order had been completed, it pleased us to determine that, obedient to the institutions of our fathers, every year we should come with devoted zeal to celebrate the council in the metropolitan see, at the time fixed by the prince or the metropolitan. We must not absent ourselves on any pretext that may be offered; rather, on the appointed day when judgment has been determined, all the bishops of the province must assemble in the metropolitan see, and the council must be celebrated with God presiding.

Any bishop who, apart from unavoidable cause or necessity, absents himself from the council to be held shall be punished by excommunication for one full year. If thereafter one year passes without his attending the celebration of the council, he shall remain subject to the judgment of the common censure of all the bishops of the province of Carthage Superior—that is, if no authority of the prince, illness, or unavoidable cause prevents him, but he fails to assemble for the celebration of the council solely at his own will.

## XVI

To these constitutions of ours, which we have judged necessary to enact, we have added the final subscription of our own hand, rendering glory and honor to our immortal God and Lord. He makes us joyful through the gathering of mutual vision; he has opened our mouth in confession of his praise; and he has also completed the decrees of this council of ours with propriety.

After this, we rendered thanks to our religious Lord and beloved prince, our king Vuamba, through whose zeal we have been assembled. As a new restorer of ecclesiastical discipline in our age, he has appeared not only intending to restore the neglected order of councils but also establishing that they should be celebrated through annual returns. By the yearly correction of morals, he gladly brings us together at the appointed time, in accordance with the prophet’s oracle: “What is broken I will bind up, and what is cast away I will bring back” (Ezek. 34:4).

May the Lord therefore grant that, for the sake of his devotion to this sacred concern, the same prince may pass through the course of his present life in peace and, after many years, reach him in peace with his sins forgiven. May he thus lead a happy life and, happy together with all over whom he rules, reach Christ without confusion. Since through him the crown of our order is restored for the better, may he receive the crown of the future kingdom, reigning from now on with Christ in the land of the living, for ever and ever. Amen.

Seventeen bishops attended this council. I, Quiricus, metropolitan bishop of the royal city, have subscribed these synodal proceedings determined by us. The other seventeen bishops likewise subscribed.

# THE TWELFTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGINS

Held in the era 719, in the first year of King Eringius, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

[Col. 0547]

[Col. 0547D] When, by the glorious command of the aforementioned prince, we had been gathered into one assembly and had taken our appointed seats in the basilica of the holy apostles, the same most merciful prince appeared before us. Full of humanity and conspicuous for the clear devotion of his piety, he presented himself humbly and devoutly to our assembly. First, he entrusted himself to the assistance of all the priests’ prayers; then he offered abundant thanks to almighty God for the gathering of the entire council, because, by being present together, they had fulfilled the desire of his glorious command and brought about the renewal of the joys of mutual vision. Then he addressed the whole council as follows:

“It is beyond doubt, most holy Fathers, that the excellent assistance of councils comes to the aid of a falling world if what must be corrected is carried out with diligent zeal. Therefore, I do not think it is unknown to your paternity through what afflictions we are perishing as the days succeed one another. For we are firmly convinced that, because of contempt for the divine commandments, the earth endures the ruin of oppression, as the Lord says through the prophet: ‘Therefore the earth shall mourn, and everyone who dwells in it shall grow weak’ (Jer. 4:28).

“Therefore, since you are shown to be the mouth of our Savior and Lord, salvation ought to obtain its benefit through you, through whom it has received the sacrament of regeneration. Through the diligence of your graciousness, may the earth be cleansed of every contagion and freed from the plague of weakness, and may it be made fruitful in the increase of every good thing.

“Now, whatever suitable reason permits me still to say, and whatever is fitting to relate to your ears, either the interruption of the written headings withdraws from memory or the weariness of a lengthy speech cuts short. Behold, therefore, read through the matters of my devotion, briefly gathered and written down in this volume, to be recognized; when read, examine them; when examined, determine them through polished and discerning judgments of the headings. Thus the pure and God-pleasing discernment of your decisions may endure, adorning the beginnings of our kingdom with the exhortation of justice and restraining the terrors of the peoples with the proper severity of judgment. For it is written: ‘Justice exalts a nation, but sin makes peoples miserable’ (Prov. 14:34).”

Then, having received this volume from the glorious prince as such a wholesome invitation, we returned abundant thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ and again blessed the glorious prince. After that most serene prince had departed, we found the following written in the aforesaid volume.

## Address of King Eringius to the Council

In the name of the Lord, Flavius Eringius, king.

To the most holy Fathers sitting in this sacred synod:

Most reverend Fathers, if fathers and honorable priests of the heavenly ministries truly hold the solidity of holy faith and embrace it with sincere devotion of heart, I call upon the strongest testimony of your paternity as an aid to our salvation. We believe that, with God as its maker, we have undertaken the kingdom for the salvation of the land and the raising up of the peoples; may we therefore be assisted by the councils of your holiness.

Although the beginnings of our elevation are surely not unknown to your assembly through reputable report—namely, by what clear arrangement of divine judgments I ascended the throne of ruling and received the sacred anointing of the kingdom—you will now be able to know this more fully from the written account and to make it public through the judgments of your promulgation. Just as your holy assembly has learned that the beginnings of our kingdom were divinely ordered, so may it offer comfort through prayers concerning them and impart the nourishment of wholesome counsels. Thus, just as I now hold the kingdom as pleasing through your assent, may I enjoy its consecration through the definitions of your blessings, so that this gathering of your order may in some way appear to renew our imperial authority.

Therefore, since the Lord commanded in the Gospel, saying, “Amen I say to you: If two of you agree on earth about anything whatsoever they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18:19), I have come to the venerable assembly of your paternity with an outpouring of tears, so that the land may be cleansed of the contagion of wickedness through the zeal of your governance.

Rise, I beg you, rise! Untie the knots of the guilty; correct the shameful conduct of transgressors; awaken the discipline of zeal against the treacherous; extinguish the sharpness of the proud; come to the aid of the burdens of the oppressed; and, above all, eradicate from the roots the plague of the Jews, which is continually breaking out anew into madness.

Examine also, with every integrity of judgment, the laws that have recently been promulgated against the perfidy of those same Jews for the sake of vain glory. Both add an unshaken force of continuity to those laws and promulgate, gathered into a single body, the judgments established for the excesses of those same perfidious people. For we must take great care lest the many rules of the ancient canons promulgated against their errors make us liable for their offenses, if the construction of those canons is allowed to pass away during the time of our kingdom.

Above all, this must be feared: God forbid that, during the time of our serenity, that clear ordinance of faith should cease, by which the Lord of blessed memory and our predecessor, King Sisebut, bound all his successors under the perpetual penalty of a curse—namely, that any king who permitted a Christian slave to serve and attend upon a Jew would be condemned, and so forth.

After this, I also submit for correction to your God-pleasing judgment the matter that the command of our predecessor, sanctioned by promulgated law, established: that anyone who did not go forth on military campaign or who fled from the army should be irrevocably deprived of the testimony of his rank.

Since this severe institution has not been applied throughout all the regions of Spain, it has subjected nearly half the people to perpetual disrepute. In certain small villages, territories, or districts, the inhabitants of those places have been degraded through [an uncertain reading: *portis*] of this infamy; and because they have no permission to testify to the truth, the judgment appears to have perished altogether. Thus the land is worn down by a twofold evil, deprived both of the law and of the assistance by which truth may be discovered.

Although the mildness of our glory intends to temper this law, your paternity’s judgment nevertheless most devoutly desires that those who had lost the title of their rank through that mark of infamy be clothed again with the clear testimony of their former nobility.

Now, with mercy going before you, arrange these matters in such a way that neither our glory applies the ministry of cruelty nor the severe command presses the land beneath the prolonged yoke of infamy. I also generally ask that whatever in the laws of our glory appears absurd or contrary to justice be corrected by the judgment of your humanity.

As for the other causes and matters that ought to be shaped by a new institution, write them out under headings of judgments to be examined. Since the religious governors of the provinces and the leaders of the most distinguished orders throughout Spain are present and will learn beforehand the judgments of your promulgation, let them exercise those judgments over the broad territories entrusted to them with unerring diligence, in proportion as they have received in person the clear institutions of our mouth.

I appeal collectively to all of you: to you, most holy Fathers, and to you, illustrious men of the royal court, whom our highness has chosen to attend this holy council. I appeal to you by the divine testimony given to us and by the dreadful day of future judgment, that without respect of persons or favoritism, without any scruple of malicious contention or desire to overturn the truth, you examine with sound consideration of language whatever is brought before your minds for hearing, and approve it with the soundest judgment.

Thus, after the causes have first been deliberated, may the discerning integrity of our order establish the headings. In this way, when love of equity has made us eager to expedite the matters, the effectiveness of just works may also join us eternally to God. Then, rejoicing in your good actions, may I both gain the benefit of the present life and enjoy with you the everlasting joys of the heavenly dwellings.

Given at Toledo, on the fifth day before the Ides of January, happily in the first year of the reign of our serenity and tranquility, in the name of God.

## Subscription

In the name of the Lord, Flavius Eringius, king.

The great welfare of our people, nation, and kingdom is ensured if these synodal decrees and proceedings, enacted according to the devout zeal of our piety, are confirmed by the strong authority of our unshakable law. Thus, what was decreed by the most serene command of our highness and written out in headings for the venerable Fathers and the illustrious elders of our palace may be defended from its adversaries by the edict of this present law of ours.

This is the very definition of the canons, noted under the following order of headings.

## The chapters of the same council begin

1. On the acknowledged and confirmed elevation of the principal dignity in the name of the Holy Trinity.

2. On those who receive penance with their consent.

3. On the reception of the guilty, or their communion within the Church.

4. That where there is no bishop, no bishop should ever be ordained.

5. On the most shameful custom of certain priests who do not communicate after offering sacrifices to God. [Col. 0551D]

6. On the power of a general synod granted to the bishop of Toledo, so that a bishop of another province may be ordained in the royal city with the connivance of the princes.

7. On the testimony received from persons who, through the law enacted concerning military promotion, had lost the right to testify.

8. On those who leave their wives after divorce has intervened.

9. On the confirmation of the laws promulgated against Jewish wickedness, and on the prescribed order of the headings of those laws, which are enumerated in the same canon.

10. On those who flee for refuge to a church.

11. On the worshipers of idols.

12. On the fixed time appointed at which the council must be celebrated.

13. Conclusion of the definitions, in which thanks are given to God and prayer is offered for the prince.

# THE DECREES OF THE TWELFTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGIN

On the first day of the synodal opening, when all the bishops and elders of the palace were seated, the first discussion concerned the Holy Trinity. It was not a matter defined in the novel style of an imposed demand, but one disclosed in simpler words so as to reveal itself to sluggish minds, with a reading always placed first, which the following exposition would unfold.

We believe and teach together, concerning the same purity of holy faith, whatever evangelical and apostolic tradition has sanctioned, whatever the holy Council of Nicaea established, whatever the assembled gathering of the Fathers at Constantinople promulgated, and whatever the definition of the assembly at Ephesus taught, as we have received it expounded and handed down to us in the testimony of many Catholic Fathers, and as we also proclaim it in the solemn celebrations of the Mass with clear voices of confession.

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, creator of visible and invisible things; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages: God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *omousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth.

For us and for our salvation he descended, and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and became man. He suffered under Pontius Pilate and was buried; on the third day he rose again; he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

We believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, [135] who spoke through the prophets.

One Catholic and apostolic Church. We confess one baptism for the remission of sins. We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

## CHAPTER I

After the peaceful efforts of this holy discussion of the faith, there first presented itself for recognition to our minds that knowledge of the Savior which bound the hearts of all with such ardor of love that this same knowledge itself sprang forth to be fully recognized in the assembly of the general council.

For the evident testimony of the Scriptures teaches under what peace and order the most serene prince Eringius ascended to the summit of the kingdom and received the power of ruling through sacred anointing. In these Scriptures the acceptance of Vuamba’s penance is also recognized, as is the transfer of the honor of the kingdom to the name of our present prince.

When Vuamba was held by the unavoidable event of necessity, he immediately assumed the proper religious observance and the venerable sign of sacred tonsure. Then, through a written declaration of his decision, he designated this illustrious lord of ours, Eringius, to reign after him and to be anointed with priestly blessing.

We saw and together clearly observed, with the light of mutual vision shining before us, the documents of this aforementioned order: the record strengthened by the hand of the elders of the palace, before whom the former prince acquired both the observance of religion and the venerable sign of sacred tonsure; the document issued by that same prince, in which he desired that our glorious lord Eringius become king after him; and another instruction of the aforesaid man, issued in the name of our honorable and most holy brother Julian, bishop of the see of Toledo, in which he both separated him and instructed him to anoint our aforesaid lord Eringius as king with every diligence and to ensure that the celebration of his anointing be carried out with every diligence.

In that document the subscription of the same prince Vuamba was also clear to us, and all the evident confirmation of those documents plainly manifested itself. When all these matters had been approved and embraced, it seemed entirely fitting to our assembly that the confirmation of all our written documents should be added to the aforesaid declarations, so that he who had been foreknown to reign in hidden judgments before the appointed time might now, in the manifest time, be consecrated by the definitions of all the priests in general.

Therefore, the people’s hand, released from every bond of the oath by which it had been bound to the aforementioned man Vuamba while he still held the kingdom, must follow this one most serene prince who remains, Eringius, with the service of grateful obedience. It must follow freely the man whom divine judgment chose beforehand for the kingdom, whom the former prince established as his successor, and, above all, whom the affection of the entire people selected.

With these matters known and foreknown, service must therefore be rendered to the God of heaven and to our aforesaid prince, King Eringius; he must be obeyed with devout loyalty and served with the readiest will; and whatever benefits his safety and whatever he judges beneficial to his people and his homeland must be pursued with zeal.

Henceforth, no one will be free from the sentence of anathema or secure from divine vengeance if he raises his voice against his safety, incites slaughter, or seeks any form of retaliation to harm him.

## II

Often those whom the Lord’s mercy assists even when they are willing appear ungrateful for God’s benefits and abuse the grace of the giver, through which they could have obtained absolution from their crime. They frequently attack what they ought to honor and reject, through profane objections, the gift of granted grace which they ought to embrace with their utmost prayers.

For we have often seen many who were in a state of health and desired the final fruit of penance subsequently betray the natural duty of speech and understanding through the excess of illness, so that they appeared to have no concern for their salvation and were not recognized as yearning with any desire for their former devotion.

Yet, moved by fraternal compassion for their condition, the brotherhood received such persons’ necessities in faith, so that the final viaticum might be granted to them and they might not appear to pass from the world without the fruit of penance.

If, perhaps, through the Lord’s regard, they are restored to their former health, they then employ empty safeguards and detestable objections to drive from themselves the venerable sign of tonsure and cast off the religious habit. They assert most foolishly that they are not bound under this vow by any rules of ecclesiastical discipline because they neither asked for penance themselves nor received it with their consent.

Their shamelessness, disgracefully forgetful of the divine goodness that called them to so venerable and fruitful a sacrament, and their obstinate insolence would never say such things if they remembered how they had come to life through the grace of the most holy washing. For the life of infants is subject to original sin, and because of their age they are judged capable of no faculty of discerning or desiring; unless they receive the sacrament of baptism through the pledge of the faithful, they can seek it neither with any understanding nor through any exercise of discernment.

Therefore, just as baptism is received in faith alone, without any resistance, on behalf of little children who do not know it, so they who have received the gift of penance without knowing it must observe it, even though others attack it as a violation.

If anyone, having received penance in any manner, violates this synodal institution, he shall be struck as a true transgressor by the rules of the Fathers.

In establishing this, we do not absolve priests so that they may dare indiscriminately and freely to extend the gift of penance to those who are not penitents. Rather, we bind those who have received penance in whatever manner, so that they may not return thereafter to the military belt.

But priests who, without consent and without penance, have given penance with rash presumption, and who cannot prove that they were invited to do so by the exhortation, gestures, or any other clear signs of the person receiving penance, shall be subjected to a sentence of excommunication for one year.

## III

We have seen, and we have wept, that certain persons from among the guilty who had been received into the favor of princes were excluded from the fellowship of the priests. This produces a disgraceful evil, because the prince’s license, where he more freely arranges to be absolved, binds others; and those whom he appears to receive into his own communion he appears to separate from the communion and peace of the Church, so that those who dine with him are deprived of the priests’ communion alone.

Therefore, since the remission of such persons—those who act against the law, the people, or the homeland—is punished solely by royal authority according to the definitions of the ancient canons, no priestly communion shall henceforth withhold itself from them, against whose royal authority they are known to have sinned. Rather, those whom royal power has either received into the favor of its kindness or made participants at its table must also be received by the assembly of priests and peoples into ecclesiastical communion, so that what the prince’s piety accepts should not be foreign to the priests of God.

### IV

To oppose recklessly the institutions of our predecessors, to tear down the decrees of the holy Fathers, and with unbridled desire to resist the enactments of one’s superiors contrary to the most holy teaching of the Apostle—what else is this than to break “the bond of fellowship in Christ” (1 John 1:3) and, by the license of usurped presumption, to disrupt the order of the Church?

Accordingly, while our venerable and most holy brother Stephen, bishop of the see of Mérida, was proceeding, a matter arising from a recent act of presumption and usurpation was brought before us for consideration. It deserved to be overthrown by our common judgment in proportion to the audacity of the wrongdoing by which it was known to have been committed.

For he said that he had been compelled by royal violence to establish a new episcopal dignity in the monastery of a small village, where the venerable body of the most holy confessor Pinevius rests with due honor. Thus, yielding through indiscriminate and overly ready assent to the unjust commands of King Wamba, he introduced a new and unjust appointment to a pontifical see there, where canonical legislation absolutely forbids such a thing.

The aforesaid man, therefore, having prostrated himself on the ground and seeking healing through the medicine of our instruction, asked that pardon be granted him. He also requested that our judgment determine what ought principally to be done concerning the person who had been ordained there.

But we knew truthfully—and indeed we knew it together—that the aforesaid prince, acting on a counsel of fickleness, had not only ordered that a bishop be established in the aforesaid place, but had also persisted in his customary obstinacy to such an extent that he ordained a bishop in the Praetorian church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul in the suburb of Toledo, and similarly did so in other villages and small settlements.

Therefore, because of such an insolent license of uprooting, we ordered that what the canonical institutions prescribe concerning this matter be brought forward. The following texts were then read in due order.

First, from Paul’s Epistle to his disciple Titus, where he commanded that bishops be appointed throughout the cities.

Next, from the Council of Nicaea, title eight, where among other things it is prescribed that two bishops must not be seen to exist in one city.

Next, from the Council of Laodicea, title fifty-seven, where it says: “Bishops ought not to be ordained in villages and small settlements,” and so forth.

Next, from the Second Council of Africa, title five, where Felix, bishop of Selemsela, said:

“Even if this has seemed good to your holiness, I submit that dioceses which have never had bishops should not have them, while a diocese which once had a bishop should have its own bishop. According to this proposal of your holiness, the matter must be assessed as to what ought to be done.”

Bishop Genedius said: “If the submission of our brother and fellow bishop Felix is acceptable, let it be confirmed by all.”

All the bishops said: “It is acceptable.”

Next, from the Third Council of Africa, title forty-two, where it says that a people which has always belonged to a diocese must not receive another bishop.

Bishop Epigonius said among other things:

“I say that a people which has always belonged to a diocese and has never had its own bishop ought not to receive a ruler. Therefore, if this statement of mine pleases the entire most holy assembly, let it be confirmed.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“I do not oppose the proposal of our brother and fellow priest, but I profess that I have done this and will continue to do so.”

Next, from the Council of Sardica, where among other things it is prescribed:

“License must not be granted indiscriminately. For if some village or small city, for which one presbyter is sufficient, should suddenly wish a bishop to be ordained for itself, so that the name and authority of bishop may be cheapened, those invited from another province ought not to make a bishop for it where there had previously been none.”

Concerning also the judgment against those who carry out such ordinations, and against those who are ordained contrary to these canonical institutions, from the Council of Tauris, in the title where it says:

“It has also pleased us that a record of the proceedings be written down for perpetual discipline: what the holy synod decreed concerning the eighth [case], Ursio Remigius, bishop of Adrepha, who was summoned, apparently through envy, over a certain usurpation in the ordination of priests.” [The transmitted wording is uncertain.] It seemed that this had been granted to them in such a way that, having been warned by this authority for the future, they would attempt to usurp nothing, since they defended themselves from this charge with the excuse that they had not previously been summoned.”

Therefore the synod judged that, if anyone thereafter acted against the institutions of the predecessors, he should know that the man ordained would be deprived of the honor of the priesthood, while the man who ordained him would not retain authority either in ordinations or in councils.

This sentence will prevail not only concerning the aforementioned bishop, but also concerning all who, deceived by a similar error, have carried out such ordinations.

Accordingly, setting the effect of a pious work against these strongest regulations, we have chosen by common definition that henceforth no episcopal see remain in the aforementioned small village, and that no bishop be established there in the future.

Nevertheless, Convildus, who appears to have been instituted there as bishop contrary to the decrees of the predecessors, shall not be punished by any canonical sentence to his condemnation, because he was ordained not through ambition but through the compulsion of the prince.

Therefore, we grant him this remedy of humility: that he be transferred to the see of any bishop who has died. The aforesaid place, however, shall henceforth remain under monastic governance and shall no longer enjoy an episcopal privilege, nor shall it in any way remain subject to the rule of an abbot, as it has been until now.

Now, establishing a general edict for the future: if anyone attempts to violate these canonical prohibitions by choosing and making a bishop in places where there has never been a bishop, let him be anathema in the sight of almighty God. Moreover, both the ordainer and the ordained shall lose the rank of their order, because he has dared to tear down not only the decrees of the ancient Fathers but also the apostolic institutions.

### V

It has been reported to us that some priests do not receive the grace of holy communion as many times as sacrifices appear to be offered in one day. Rather, if they offer several sacrifices to God in one day, they abstain from communion at all the offerings and receive the grace of holy communion only at the offering of the final sacrifice—as though one ought not to participate in that true and singular sacrifice as many times as the immolation of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ has taken place.

For the Apostle says: “Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?” (1 Corinthians 10:18.)

It is certain that those who sacrifice but do not eat are guilty with respect to the Lord’s sacraments.

Therefore, whoever among the priests thereafter approaches the divine altar to offer a sacrifice and abstains from communion shall know that he has been excluded for one year from the very grace of communion from which he improperly deprived himself.

For what kind of sacrifice will that be in which even the one offering the sacrifice is not known to participate?

Therefore, it must be observed in every way that whenever the celebrant immolates the body and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord upon the altar, he should likewise present himself as a participant in the reception of Christ’s body and blood.

### VI

It also seemed necessary for us to determine by mutual deliberation that in certain cities, when their own bishops have died and the ordination of a successor is long delayed, no small offense against the divine offices is created. The movement of messengers is hindered by the distance of the roads, so that either the death of the deceased prelate cannot be reported to the king’s ears, or the free choice of a successor to the dead bishop cannot be awaited from the prince.

Such matters often create difficulty for our order through the report concerning them, and they impose an injurious necessity upon the royal authority when it awaits our advice concerning the substitution of bishops.

Therefore it has pleased all the bishops of Spain and Galicia, without prejudice to the privilege of each province, that henceforth it be lawful for the bishop of Toledo to appoint as prelates in any provinces those whom the royal authority has chosen and whom the aforesaid bishop of Toledo has judged worthy, over the preceding sees, and to choose successors for deceased bishops.

This provision shall apply on the condition that whoever is ordained shall, within three months after his ordination, come to present himself before his own metropolitan, so that, instructed by his authority and discipline, he may properly hold the governance of the see entrusted to him.

But if, through negligence or neglect, anyone exceeds the limits of the appointed time and is unable to present himself before the sight of his metropolitan, he shall know that he is excommunicated in every respect, unless he proves that he was prevented by royal command.

It has likewise pleased us that this formula of definition be observed concerning the other rulers of the churches just as it is concerning bishops.

### VII

All discipline ought to rebuke those subject to it in such a way that it does not seem to take away hope of pardon, nor impose the yoke of correction completely, but always apply the remedy of moderation.

Therefore, since the mildness of our lord, Prince Ering, has determined to temper that law enacted by Lord Wamba the prince, which is recorded concerning treason, this holy council has necessarily defined, with the consent of our glorious and most devout prince Ering, our lord, that those who have lost the dignity of giving testimony under the earlier law may, once the testimony of their former dignity has been restored, pursue the cases belonging to their lawful action.

They shall equally recover the title of solid nobility, and shall obtain permission to testify lawfully concerning whatever they wish from the past; no judges shall prohibit or restrain them.

We add this provision: if they wish to testify concerning past matters and were rejected solely on account of this matter, they may now seek by their testimony what they could have sought in the past, provided that it is clear that, when they were called to give testimony concerning past matters and were rejected under the institutions of the aforesaid law, they then had no other mark of crime, or that thirty years had elapsed when they were brought forward to testify; in that case they shall plainly convict those who rejected them.

### VIII

The Lord’s command is that, except in the case of fornication, a wife must not be dismissed by her husband.

Therefore, whoever dismisses his wife for any reason other than the aforesaid criminal fault, because he has chosen to separate what God joined together, shall remain deprived of ecclesiastical communion and alienated from the assembly of all Christians for as long as he does not sincerely embrace and cherish the companionship of the wife he abandoned.

This shall apply in such a way, however, that those who, after having been admonished once, twice, and three times by a priest to correct themselves, refuse to return to their wives’ beds shall, by their own deserts, separate themselves from the office of palatine dignity. Moreover, as long as they remain in their fault, they shall lose the testimony of noble dignity, because they have delivered their own flesh to the sword of discord.

### IX

Concerning the detestable treachery of the Jews, we have read, with vigilant attention of mind, the laws newly entrusted by the glorious prince under distinct titles, and we have approved their institutions with the strict weight of seriousness.

Accordingly, the following laws, issued with the judgment of due reason and approved by synodal dignity, shall henceforth be upheld in irrevocable judicial order against their offenses:

The laws promulgated concerning the observance of the ancient ceremonies of the Jews and their transgressions, and concerning their renewed confirmation.

Likewise, concerning blasphemers of the holy Trinity.

Likewise, that Jews must not withdraw themselves, their children, or their servants from the grace of baptism.

Likewise, that Jews must not celebrate Passover in their customary manner, practice circumcision of the flesh, or turn any Christian away from faith in Christ.

Likewise, that Jews must not presume to celebrate Sabbaths or the other festivals of their rite in their customary manner.

Likewise, that every Jew abstain from work on Sundays and on the days specified above.

Likewise, that Jews must not distinguish foods according to their custom.

Likewise, that Jews must not contract marriages through kinship of their blood, and that they must not dare to marry without the blessing of a priest.

Likewise, that Jews must not dare to insult our religion and defend their own sect, nor, fleeing from the faith, transfer themselves elsewhere.

And that no one may receive those who flee from the faith.

Likewise, that no Christian receive from Jews any gift contrary to the faith of Christ.

Likewise, that Jews must not dare to read books which the Christian faith rejects.

Likewise, that Christian slaves must not serve Jews or remain attached to them.

Likewise, concerning a Jew who professes himself to be a Christian and for that reason does not wish to dismiss from himself a Christian slave.

Likewise, the profession of the Jews: how each person who comes to the faith must write out a record of his profession.

Likewise, the conditions of the Jews which those who come from among them to the faith and submit their professions must swear.

Likewise, concerning Christian slaves belonging to Jews who have not revealed themselves as Christians, and concerning those who expose them.

Likewise, that Jews must not, after receiving authority from anyone, attack, punish, or constrain any Christian outside the royal ordinance.

Likewise, that if slaves of Jews, not yet converted, flee to the grace of Christ, they shall be granted liberty.

Likewise, that Jews must not, for administrative purposes, reduce a Christian household into the order of stewards and agents; and concerning the penalties of those who order such things to be done.

Likewise, a Jew coming from other provinces or territories belonging to the dominion of our king must not delay presenting himself to the bishop or priest of the place, so that he may know what he ought to observe in every respect.

Likewise, that gatherings of Jews must take place before the bishop on the appointed days.

Likewise, that whoever has a Jew accompanying him must not dare to retain him with himself when the priest demands it.

Likewise, that the entire responsibility for constraining Jews belongs solely to priests.

Likewise, concerning the penalties of priests or judges who delay fulfilling the institutions of the laws against Jews.

Likewise, that judges must not presume to judge anything concerning the offenses of the treacherous without the cooperation of the priests.

Likewise, that bishops shall then be regarded as free from penalties when they have sent their priests to correct matters which the bishops themselves had not corrected.

Likewise, concerning the power of showing mercy preserved for princes toward those who have truly converted to the faith of Christ.

Likewise, that all bishops give the Jews belonging to them a booklet concerning the errors published against them, and that they deposit their professions and conditions in the church archives.

The promulgation of all these laws, just as it has been approved by synodal judgment, shall likewise be enforced thereafter by the general definition of all of us against their offenses.

### X

For those who seek the church out of any fear or terror, this holy council, with the equal consent of our most glorious lord Ering, the king, has defined that no one may dare to drag away those fleeing to the church or remaining there, or inflict any harm, damage, or plunder upon those residing in the holy place.

Rather, those who seek the church shall have every right to proceed thirty paces from the doors of the church. Within these thirty paces, the reverence due to each church shall be protected around its entire circuit.

This shall apply on the condition that those who flee to it do not depart in any way into houses outside or far separated from the church. Instead, proceeding within this number of thirty paces without taking refuge in outside houses, they shall obtain access so that they may go out to the proper places for the needs of nature.

Nor shall those who have entrusted themselves to be defended within the Lord’s enclosure be held back by any circumstance of necessity.

But if anyone attempts to violate this decree, he shall be subject both to ecclesiastical excommunication and to the sentence of royal severity.

As for those who have fled to the church, if, in accordance with the institutions of the ancient canons, those who demand them back have furnished the sacred pledge, and if the priest of that church has not removed them from the church by its doors or by flight, then, should such a case arise, a judgment concerning such priests must be sought, or a sentence of damages imposed upon them according to the choice of the prince.

### XI

The Lord’s commands are these:

“You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or of what is in the waters under the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them” (Exodus 20:4–5).

Likewise:

“Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be killed, except to the Lord alone” (Exodus 22:20).

Likewise:

“Whether man or woman, if they do evil in the sight of the Lord their God and transgress his covenant, going and serving foreign gods and worshiping them, or the sun and the moon and the whole host of heaven—which I have not commanded—and this is reported to you, and after inquiry you investigate carefully and discover that it is true, and that this abomination has been committed in Israel, you shall bring the man or woman who committed this most wicked deed to the gates of the city, and they shall be stoned with stones” (Deuteronomy 17:2 and following).

We set forth these commands of the Lord not for the purpose of vengeance but to terrify offenders. We warn the worshipers of idols, the venerators of stones, those who kindle torches, and those who adorn springs, so that they may recognize that they voluntarily subject themselves to death, since they appear to sacrifice to the devil. For the devil is called by the name of death, as it is written concerning him: “His name was Death.”

Accordingly, every sacrilege of idolatry, or whatever it may be that is contrary to the holy faith, in which foolish people, held captive by diabolical worship, serve such practices, must be discovered through the diligence of a priest or judge. The sacrileges must be uprooted and, once exterminated, cut off.

Those who run toward such an error shall be restrained with blows and, loaded with chains, handed over to their masters, provided that their masters promise under oath that they will guard them so carefully that it will no longer be lawful for them to commit such wickedness.

But if their masters do not wish to receive such offenders under their responsibility, they shall be presented by those who restrained them before the royal presence, so that the prince may exercise authority and free power of rule over such persons.

The masters, however, who refuse to punish the errors of such slaves after they have been reported to them shall both incur a sentence of excommunication and know that they have lost the rights over that slave whom they refused to restrain.

If freeborn persons become involved in these errors, they shall likewise be struck with perpetual excommunication and punished by a stricter exile.

### XII

It has pleased this holy council that, in accordance with the institutions of the canons of the earlier bishops of the individual provinces, they shall gather every year in each province on the Kalends of November to celebrate a council.

Whoever delays coming on the aforesaid Kalends of November for the celebration of the synod shall duly be subject to excommunication.

### XIII

Having set forth all these synodal proceedings and brought them to an honorable conclusion of decrees, we attach perpetual strength to them through the subscription of our hands, giving glory and honor for them to the immortal God and Lord, by whose inspiration both the judgment of our determination prevailed and the integrity of the cases reached an honorable conclusion.

Therefore we ask the ineffable name of the holy Trinity and the glorious majesty of its immeasurable power to grant our serene lord and most beloved prince Ering, lover of Christ, by whose command we have deserved to be summoned to this gathering, to rule mercifully, to reign successfully, to receive the fruit of mercy, to obtain the reward of God’s justice, and to win a trophy through devotion.

May he here always appear as an unconquered victor over his enemies, and after the long courses of this world may he reach, with all his own, the eternal kingdom to be crowned there, by the favor of God and of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

This holy council was confirmed on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the first fortunate year of the reign of our most serene lord Ering, king, in the era 718.
