With all these synodal proceedings, decrees, and agreements, we have shown the due reverence of honor and hasten to attach to them the manifest force of our authority.

Therefore, from the present day and time—namely, from the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the first year of our reign—no one shall dare to despise these synodal constitutions set forth above, nor shall anyone pass them over. No one shall dare to tear apart the rights of these constitutions, and no violator shall overturn these decrees.

Let no unlawful actor or despiser withdraw their force from these institutions. Rather, throughout all the provinces of our kingdom, these canonical institutions, enacted in the times of our glory, shall prevail with the height of their due authority and shall be held with an inviolable judicial force.

If anyone despises these institutions, let him know that he will be condemned by the sentence against those who despise them: namely, that, according to the will of our glory, he shall withdraw excommunicated from our assembly, and in addition shall lose a tenth part of his property, to be joined to the treasury.

If he has no property from which he can pay the aforesaid composition, he shall, without any further disgrace to him, be beaten with fifty blows, so that he may always remain infamous.

This law was issued in confirmation of the Council of Toledo on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the fortunate first year of the reign of our glory.

In the name of the Lord, Flavius Ering, king, I have subscribed this edict of our law promulgated in confirmation of this council.

## THE THIRTEENTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO BEGINS

Held in the era 721, in the fourth year of the reign of King Ering.

[Col. 0561]

[Col. 0561D] Through the impulse of unblemished charity, restored to one another’s sight by alternating visits and gathered together by God the Creator into one assembly in the church, namely, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, in the fourth year of the reign of the most serene prince Ering, on the second day before the Nones of November, in the era 721, when each of us had taken his appointed seat, the same prince appeared, supported by the full ardor of faith and adorned with the grace of humility.

Commending to the synod the wishes of his deliberation and earnestly asking that it pray to God on his behalf, he addressed the council with this particular exhortation: that matters appropriate to ecclesiastical discipline and suitable for correcting morals be established with evident sanctions for our region.

Then he entrusted to the synodal assembly, for confirmation, the devout wishes of his clemency by which he determined that assistance should be given to the unfortunate. He offered the holy bishops a written volume, pleading and solemnly charging them that whatever had been gathered there through the more elegant scattering of the pen should be arranged by the synodal authority under its titles.

Then we gave glory to God for the volume received from the prince and blessed the same glorious prince.

After the prince had completed the action of his wishes, he departed from the council’s assembly with its favor. After the royal presence had withdrawn, we found the following written in the statement of that volume.

### In the name of the Lord, Flavius Ering, king, to the most holy Fathers sitting in this holy synod

Behold, most holy bishops, to be cultivated through religious devotion and most zealous followers of divine worship: before the reverence of your assembly I humbly and devoutly prostrate myself.

I stand leaning forward in attendance and readily give my assent. First, I offer an abundance of thanks to the Father of lights for the gathering of your assembly; then I entrust the aims of my wishes to your judgments for resolution.

For it is not lawful for anyone to act without a council, even if the work is good, since God has nevertheless permitted many good things to be done with the counsel of good men.

Therefore, that I may conclude with a brief exhortation, I indicate to the understanding of your fatherhood the wishes by which I delight to put remedies of mercy into practice. But so that these may not escape memory through forgetfulness, and so that an interval of care may not withdraw them from my own report, receive them recorded in the folding of this volume.

As I turn its pages, I must first make known my wish to spare the unfortunate: we are attempting to restore to the embrace of our fellowship a part of our body torn away by tyranny.

For in the past, during the time of our predecessor of blessed memory, King Wamba, a sentence of punishment was imposed upon those who profaned the fatherland and who once assumed tyranny with Paul. By a universal judicial edict they lost the right of testimony and were deprived of their own property. All this is known to your holiness.

Nevertheless, we have resolved both to receive them again into the fellowship of our association and to divest them of such property as it is lawful to divest them of.

We also wish to establish a measure of the most just inquiry concerning the accused, so that, whether among the religious or among the lay people, anyone who has been attacked by another’s zeal of accusation may not be suppressed by secret frauds or acts of violence, nor forcibly restrained by a hidden declaration. Rather, he must be judged in the common examination of all, so that, according to the substance of his public declaration, the guilty may receive the appropriate penalties of condemnation, while the innocent, proved so by the judgment of all, may be brought into the light.

What shall I now say concerning the exactions of fiscal taxes, whose repayments have increased into such great heaps of debts that, if they are ordered to be exacted in full, the condition of the peoples will be utterly overturned, and in the collapse of their ruin they will feel the final destruction of their own land’s downfall?

Therefore, preferring to lavish the remedies of mercy not only upon private persons but also upon fiscal slaves, our glory has abundantly determined that all tax exactions outstanding against them from former times, up to the first year, shall be remitted by our clemency. Our authority has chosen to consign this remission to our holy assembly.

I shall add and speak of something else that is always dreadful to our wishes and detestable to our minds. The condition of ignobility among freedmen or slaves, being treated as equal to the status of our people, degrades that status.

For this reason it pleases our mind and our glory that, except for fiscal slaves or freedmen, once the license of this evil presumption has been removed, no one who is a slave or freedman from the servitude of anyone whatsoever shall pass into palatine offices.

If he does so, he must know without doubt that he is to be returned to serve in the condition from which he took his origin or from which he received the title of freedman.

Having presented these statements of my wishes, I ask that you provide the strong assistance of your fatherhood.

For it is clearer than light that whatever the sacred assembly of bishops determines must be observed, and through the gift of the Holy Spirit is entirely fixed for eternity.

Therefore I appeal to and adjure all of your fatherhood, and the nobility of the exalted men who, from their service in the royal court, have been selected to sit with us in this holy synod. By that ineffable sacrament I charge you: whoever brings before you a matter to be judged or reconsidered, ensure that both what has been said by us and whatever else has entered your hearing are resolved by the common strength of justice and the moderation of mercy.

Thus, subject with all reverence to the regulations of the preceding Fathers, the sentence of your complete unanimity may proceed from no source other than truth.

Accordingly, apply the solid instrument of deliberation most readily to the matters set forth above. Also discuss whatever else is necessary for carrying out the disciplines of ecclesiastical rule and resolving disputes, and carefully write down what has been resolved in a more devout form.

In this way, while you spread saving doctrine among the peoples, may you gain Christ the Lord by increasing the fruit of justice, so that, while you preach and fulfill what is pleasing to divine eyes and beneficial to us, we may always be able to act accordingly.

May there be for both parents in this world ineffable joy from the profit of souls, and in the future an unshaken reward from attaining eternity.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of November, in the fortunate fourth year of the reign of our glory, in the name of God, at Toledo.

After the beginning of the volume containing the necessary institutions had been read before everyone, our discourse first began with the faith of the holy Trinity. We jointly professed and believed what the Gospels transmit and the apostolic decrees establish concerning this holy Trinity, just as the Council of Nicaea expounded this mystery of faith, as the definition of Constantinople decreed it, and as the clear teaching of the first assembly of Ephesus and of Chalcedon established it.

This accords also with the elaborated confession of the most holy Creed, which is openly proclaimed in the solemn celebrations of the Mass by the voice of all the faithful.

## The Faith of the Council of Nicaea

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth.

For us and for our salvation he descended and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; he was made man, suffered under Pontius Pilate, and was buried. On the third day he rose again. He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

We believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father, who spoke through the prophets.

One catholic and apostolic Church.

I confess one baptism for the remission of sins. We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

After setting forth the written form of this holy faith, we constructed the structure of what follows as though upon the most solid rock, so that whatever has been built permanently upon the foundation of true faith may endure with unshaken firmness.

Therefore, we have issued by common agreement all these judgments which, at the prince’s exhortation, we received for construction. We also judge that they must be observed with the eternal force of reverence.

## THE FIRST COUNCIL OF BRAGA BEGINS

Era 569, in the third year of the reign of King Ariamir, on the Kalends of May.

[Col. 0565B] In the third year of King Ariamir, on the Kalends of May, when the bishops of the province of Galicia—Lucretius, Andrew, Martin, Cottus, Hilderic, Lucetius, Timothy, and Maliosus—had assembled, at the command of the aforesaid most glorious King Ariamir, in the metropolitan church of that same province, with the bishops seated together, the presbyters present, the ministers standing by, and the entire clergy in attendance, Lucretius, bishop of the aforementioned metropolitan church, said:

“Most holy brothers, it has long been our desire, in accordance with the institutions of the venerable canons and the decrees of Catholic and apostolic discipline, that a priestly assembly should be held among us, because such a gathering not only accords with ecclesiastical rules and orders but also always establishes a steadfast harmony of fraternal charity, while priests gathered together in the name of the Lord seek from one another, in salutary discussion, those things which, according to apostolic teaching, preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

“Now, therefore, since our most glorious and most pious son has, with the Lord’s favor, usefully commended to us the desired day of this [Col. 0565D] assembly, let us first discuss the state of the faith, as was said above. For although the contagion of the Priscillianist heresy was long ago detected and condemned in the provinces of Spain, nevertheless, lest anyone still be infected by some pestilence of that error through ignorance or through deception by certain apocryphal writings, let it be declared more plainly to ignorant people, especially those who, situated at the extremity and farthest boundaries of this province, have acquired little or almost no knowledge of sound instruction.

“I believe that your blessed fraternity knows that, at the time when the poisons of the most impious Priscillianist sect were spreading through the regions, the most blessed Pope Leo of the city of Rome, who was almost the fortieth successor of the Apostle Peter, sent his writings through Turpius, notary of his see, to the synod of Galicia against the impious sect of the Priscillianist heresy. The bishops of Tarragona and Carthage, as well as those of Lusitania and Baetica, also held a council among themselves, composing a rule of faith against the Priscillianist heresy together with certain chapters, and sent it to Baleonius, then bishop of this Church of Braga. Since we have here before us a copy of that prescribed faith together with its chapters, let it be read for the instruction of the ignorant, if this pleases your reverence.”

All the bishops said: “The reading of these chapters is exceedingly necessary, so that, while the ancient institutions of the saints are disclosed to the simpler members, the fabrications of the Priscillianist heresy—long ago abhorred by the see of the blessed Apostle Peter and condemned—may be recognized.”

The copy of the faith, together with its chapters, was read; these have not been inserted in full into these proceedings, lest they make them too lengthy. After the reading of the chapters—although the necessary reading has thus been reviewed—let what is execrable be declared even more clearly and simply by setting out the chapters as well, so that the less educated may understand, and so that, once the sentence of anathema has been pronounced, the fabrications of Priscillian’s error may be condemned. Thus, if any cleric, monk, or layman is discovered still to hold or defend anything of this kind, he shall be cut off immediately from the body of the Catholic Church as a truly rotten member, lest the stain of his association or depravity, through the mixture of such people, be reckoned as a reproach against right-believing orthodox Christians.

The chapters proposed and reread against the Priscillianist heresy contain the following:

**I.** If anyone does not confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as three persons of one substance, power, and authority, as the Catholic and apostolic Church teaches, but says that there is only one solitary person, so that he himself is the Father who is the Son and is also the Spirit, the Paraclete, as Sabellius and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**II.** If anyone introduces outside the holy Trinity certain evil names of divinity—I do not know what—saying that divinity itself is a trinity, as the Gnostics and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**III.** If anyone says that the Son of God, our Lord, did not exist before he was born of the Virgin, as Paul of Samosata, Photinus, and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**IV.** If anyone does not truly honor Christ’s birth according to the flesh, but only pretends to honor it, fasting on that day or on the Lord’s Day because he does not believe that Christ exists in human nature, as Cerdon, Marcion, Manichaeus, and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**V.** If anyone believes that human souls or angels came into being from God’s substance, as Manichaeus and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**VI.** If anyone says that human souls first sinned in a heavenly dwelling and were therefore cast down into human bodies on earth, as Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**VII.** If anyone says that the devil was not previously a good angel made by God, nor that his nature was God’s workmanship, but says that he emerged from darkness, has no author of his own, and is himself the principle and substance of evil, as Manichaeus and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**VIII.** If anyone believes that the devil made certain unclean creatures and that the devil himself, by his own authority, produces thunder, lightning, storms, and droughts, as Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**IX.** If anyone believes that souls and human bodies are bound by a fatal sign, as the pagans and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**X.** If anyone believes that the twelve signs—that is, the stars which mathematicians are accustomed to observe—are distributed among the individual members of the soul or body, and says that they are assigned the names of the patriarchs, as Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**XI.** If anyone condemns human marriages and shudders at the procreation of those being born, as Manichaeus and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**XII.** If anyone says that the formation of the human body is a fabrication of the devil, and says that conceptions in the wombs of mothers are produced by the works of demons, and for this reason does not believe in the resurrection of the flesh, as Manichaeus and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**XIII.** If anyone says that the creation of all flesh is not God’s workmanship but that of evil angels, as Manichaeus and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**XIV.** If anyone considers unclean the meats which God gave for human use, and abstains from them not for the affliction of his body but because he considers them unclean, so that he does not even taste cooked vegetables prepared with meat, as Manichaeus and Priscillian taught, let him be anathema.

**XV.** If any member of the clergy, apart from his mother, sister, or women joined to him by close blood relationship, keeps other women with him as though they were adopted relatives and lives with them, as the sect of Priscillian taught, let him be anathema.

**XVI.** If anyone on the Thursday of Holy Week, which is called the Lord’s Supper, does not hold the liturgy in the churches at the proper hour after the ninth hour while fasting, but, following the sect of Priscillian, celebrates its feast from the third hour by breaking the fast through Masses for the dead, let him be anathema.

**139 XVII.** If anyone reads the Scriptures which Priscillian corrupted according to his own error, or the treatises of Dictinius, which Dictinius himself wrote before his conversion, or writings which he fabricated under the names of patriarchs, prophets, and apostles and in conformity with his own error, and follows or defends their impious fabrications, let him be anathema.

**XVIII.** After these chapters had been proposed and reread, Bishop Lucretius said:

“Since those things which Catholics abhor and condemn have now been declared more clearly and openly even to the ignorant, I consider it necessary, if this seems good to your fraternity, that the institutions of the holy Fathers should next be made known to us through a review of the ancient canons, and that at least some of them—if not all—which pertain to the instruction of clerical discipline should be reread.”

All the bishops said: “This decree is pleasing, and it is appropriate that those who perhaps through negligence have allowed ecclesiastical constitutions to be obliterated should hear the rule of the holy canons and observe it.”

After the canons both of general synods and of local synods had been reread from the book before the council, Bishop Lucretius said:

“From this very reading of the canons your holy fraternity may recognize that not only in general councils but also in local ones priests gathered together established by common agreement those things which accorded with ecclesiastical order, and provided for each matter according to its requirements, following the saying of apostolic teaching: ‘Test what is good and hold fast to it.’ Therefore, if it pleases your charity, since there are certain ecclesiastical observances which, especially at the extremity of this province, are carried out—not, God forbid, through contention, but rather, as we have said, through negligence or ignorance—let us establish certain chapters among ourselves, so that practices which are not held by us in one manner may be brought altogether to one form?”

All the bishops said:

“We judge it necessary and exceedingly useful that those things which among each of us are retained through varied and disorderly custom should, by God’s grace, be celebrated among us with united and harmonious observance. Therefore, whatever it may be, great or small, which we see being varied, let it be brought, as has been said, to one form by chapters reasonably established, especially since we also possess instruction from the Apostolic See concerning certain definite matters—an instruction which your predecessor of venerable memory, Profuturus, once received from the very chair of the blessed Peter in response to his questions.”

Bishop Lucretius said:

“Your fraternity has rightly recalled the authority of the Apostolic See. Although it became known at the same time as it was sent, nevertheless, for the firmness of its testimony and the instruction of many, if this pleases your unanimity, let it be read before everyone, since it is here before us.”

All the bishops said: “Since mention has been made of this authority, it is right that its teaching should be heard by those standing here.”

The authority of the Apostolic See addressed to a certain Bishop Profuturus was reread; it has not been inserted in full into these proceedings because of its length. After it had been read, Bishop Lucretius said:

“It is now more evident that apostolic teaching assists us. Therefore, as your fraternity has said, if anything is varied among some through ignorance, let it be bound to one form by a harmonious rule and by the chapters prescribed among us.”

The chapters containing the following were proposed:

**XIX.** It pleased everyone by common agreement that one and the same order of psalmody should be maintained at the morning and evening offices, and that different private customs of monasteries should not be mixed with ecclesiastical rules.

**XX.** It likewise pleased everyone that, during the vigils and liturgies of solemn days, the same readings, and not different ones, should be read in the church by all.

**XXI.** It likewise pleased everyone that bishops and presbyters should not greet the people differently, but in one manner, saying, “The Lord be with you,” as is read in the Book of Ruth; and that the people should answer, “And with your spirit,” as the whole East retains it as handed down by the apostles themselves, and not as the Priscillianist heresy altered it.

**XXII.** It likewise pleased everyone that the Masses should be celebrated by all according to the same order in which Profuturus, formerly bishop of this metropolitan church, received the written instruction from the authority of the Apostolic See itself.

**XXIII.** It likewise pleased everyone that no one should omit the order of baptism which the metropolitan Church of Braga previously observed, and which the aforesaid Bishop Profuturus received in writing as having been sent to him by the see of the blessed Apostle Peter, to remove the doubts of certain people.

**XXIV.** It likewise pleased everyone that, while the primacy of the metropolitan bishop is preserved, the other bishops should yield one another places of seating according to the time of their ordination.

**XXV.** It likewise pleased everyone that ecclesiastical property should be divided into three equal portions: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, and the third for the repair or lighting of the church. The administrator of the fourth part, whether archpresbyter or archdeacon, shall render an account to the bishop.

**XXVI.** It likewise pleased everyone that no bishop should presume to ordain another bishop’s cleric, as the ancient canons also forbid, unless perhaps he has received the cleric’s sealed written authorization.

**XXVII.** It likewise pleased everyone that, since in some churches of this province deacons use oraria concealed beneath their tunics [Col. 0570A], so that they appear to differ in nothing from subdeacons, from now on they should wear their oraria over their shoulders, as is proper.

**XXVIII.** It likewise pleased everyone that no one from among the lectors should be permitted to carry the sacred vessels of the altar, but only those who have been ordained subdeacons by the bishop.

**XXIX.** It likewise pleased everyone that lectors ordained in the church while wearing secular dress should not sing psalms, nor let their hair fall in the manner of pagans.

**XXX.** It likewise pleased everyone that nothing composed poetically from the Old Testament should be sung in the church, as the holy canons also command.

**XXXI.** It likewise pleased everyone that laymen or women should not be permitted to enter the sanctuary in order to receive Communion, but only clergy, as the ancient canons also established.

**XXXII.** It likewise pleased everyone that all members of the clergy who do not eat meat should, to remove suspicion of the Priscillianist heresy, nevertheless be compelled to taste cooked vegetables prepared with meat. If they refuse, then, according to what the holy Fathers established long ago concerning such people, they must, because of suspicion of heresy, be entirely removed from office after being excommunicated.

**XXXIII.** It likewise pleased everyone that, if people are excommunicated for heresy or for some crime, no one should presume to communicate with them, as the ancient statutes of the canons also contain. Whoever disregards this voluntarily makes himself an outsider to communion.

**XXXIV.** It likewise pleased everyone that, if people bring death upon themselves by the sword, poison, a precipice, hanging, or any other form of violence, no commemoration of them should be made in the offering, nor should their corpses be escorted to burial with psalms; for many people usurp this for themselves through ignorance. It was likewise decided that the same should be done regarding those who are punished for their crimes.

**XXXV.** It likewise pleased everyone that catechumens who die without receiving the baptism of redemption should similarly receive neither commemoration in the offering nor the ministry of psalmody, for this too has been usurped through ignorance.

**XXXVI.** It likewise pleased everyone that the bodies of the dead should in no way be buried in the basilica of the saints, but, if necessary, burial outside, beside the wall of the basilica, should not be regarded with such abhorrence. For if cities to this day retain this most firm privilege—that the body of any dead person may in no way be buried within the circuit of their walls—how much more ought the reverence due to the venerable martyrs to preserve it?

**XXXVII.** It likewise pleased everyone that, if any presbyter after this prohibition dares to bless the chrism or consecrate a church or altar, he should be removed from his office. The ancient canons also forbid this.

**XXXVIII.** It likewise pleased everyone that no layman should advance to the priesthood unless he has first learned ecclesiastical discipline for an entire year in the office of lector or in the diaconate, and then, instructed through each grade, come to the priesthood. For it is exceedingly blameworthy that someone who has not yet learned should already presume to teach, especially since this too has been prohibited by the ancient institutions of the Fathers.

[Col. 0571A] **XXXIX.** It likewise pleased everyone that whatever is offered from the contributions of the faithful, or during the festivals of the martyrs, or in commemoration of the dead, should be faithfully collected by one of the clergy and, at an appointed time, distributed among all the clergy either once or twice a year. For considerable discord arises from this very inequality, so that each person should receive in his own week whatever has been offered.

**XL.** It likewise pleased everyone that no one should dare to disregard the commands of the ancient canons, as they were recited in the council. If anyone obstinately transgresses these commands, he must be degraded from his office.

After the chapters had been reread, Bishop Lucretius said:

“Since, with the Lord’s help, we have by unanimous discussion decreed those things which concern the weakness of the Catholic and orthodox faith and those which pertain to the office of ecclesiastical order, as was appropriate, it remains now that each of us should diligently teach and instruct his own diocese in all these things which, by God’s grace, have been salutarily established.

“If any one of us, after learning the institutions of this council, finds in his parishes a cleric or monk resisting this sound teaching, or perceives that some error of the Priscillianist sect still lies hidden there, and does not immediately cast that person out of the church as excommunicated and anathematized—so that no faithful person may presume either to eat with such a person or to communicate with him—let him know that whoever receives such a person is liable to fraternal excommunication and, beyond doubt, guilty before the divine judgment.”

All the bishops said:

“Whatever has been decreed by us in united agreement through God’s grace must be observed with vigilant care. In order that these decisions may possess the firmness of an established constitution, let each person subscribe these proceedings with his own hand.”

The subscriptions of the bishops then followed:

“I, Lucretius, bishop, have subscribed.”

“I, Andrew, [Col. 0572B] bishop, have subscribed.”

“I, Martius, bishop, have subscribed.”

“I, Cottus, bishop, have subscribed.”

“I, Hilderic, bishop, have subscribed.”

“I, Lucentius, bishop, have subscribed.”

“I, Timothy, bishop, have subscribed.”

“I, Maliosus, bishop, have subscribed.”

**140. THE SECOND COUNCIL OF BRAGA BEGINS.**

[Col. 0571]

[Col. 0571B] In the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year 610 of the era, in the second year of King Ariamir, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, when the bishops of the province of Galicia, from both the synod of Braga and that of Lugo, had assembled with their metropolitans by command of the aforesaid most glorious king in the metropolitan church of Braga—that is, Martin, Nitigis, Remisol, Andrew, Lucentius, Adoricus, Victimer, Sardinarius, Viator, Avila, Polemus, Mailoc—while the bishops were seated together and the entire clergy was present, Martin, bishop of the Church of Braga, said:

“I believe, most holy Fathers, that this has come about through God’s inspiration: through the arrangement of our most glorious son the king, we have come together from both councils into one, so that we might rejoice not only in seeing one another but also discuss together those matters which pertain to ecclesiastical order and discipline. For it is written in the Gospel, the Lord saying: ‘Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them’ (Matthew 18:20).”

Nitigis, bishop of the Church of Lugo, said:

“Nothing else can be believed except that those things which pertain to the benefit of our souls ought both to be begun and completed through divine inspiration.”

And therefore, being unanimous and thinking the same thing in the Lord, they desired to recognize whatever pertained to their instruction when it was brought before them.

Bishop Martin said:

“We believe that your blessedness remembers that, when the council of bishops was first gathered in the Church of Braga, after many things had been established to strengthen the harmony of the faith, we also confirmed certain matters containing the discipline of the rules of the holy canons. So that their usefulness may be recalled more clearly, let your letter itself be reread in your presence, if this pleases you.”

All the bishops said: “It is entirely fitting that it be recited in the hearing of everyone who is present here.”

The chapters of the preceding council were therefore recited; they have been inserted in these proceedings so as not to make them too lengthy. Bishop Martin said:

“Let these matters which have now been recited—those which at that time seemed to us varied, doubtful, or disordered—be ordered, with God’s help, and receive their own immovable firmness. But those matters which did not then come to mind, or which it was burdensome to introduce in such quantity into that first council, now seem necessarily to be brought to the attention of our holy charity, with particular attention given to them, so that, tested by spiritual examination, they may be purified.

“For the holy Fathers, our predecessors, either gathered general synods from everywhere for the unity of right faith—as at Nicaea, against Arius, three hundred and eighteen; at Constantinople, against Macedonius, one hundred and fifty; at Ephesus, against Nestorius, two hundred; and at Chalcedon, against Eutyches, six hundred and thirty—or certainly gathered particular synods throughout their provinces, each in his own region, to cut away disputes or correct the negligence of certain people. According as the outcome of faults or any kind of excess required, they wrote, with God’s Spirit mediating among them, separate divine judgments of the canons, which we ought to reread and observe.

“And since, by the assistance of Christ’s grace, there is no uncertainty in this province concerning the unity and correctness of the faith, we must now act more particularly, so that, if anything perhaps blameworthy is found among us through ignorance or negligence concerning apostolic discipline, we may return to the testimonies of the holy Scriptures or the institutions of the ancient canons and, with common agreement of mind, correct whatever is displeasing by reasonable judgment.

“First, if it pleases you, in rereading the commands of the blessed Apostle Peter which he clearly wrote in his letter as a rule for priests, let us hasten without hesitation to correct whatever appears not to be done according to the same standard in which the chief of the apostles instructed us. Otherwise, while we preach to others, we might ourselves be found rejected and condemned by that divine utterance which says: ‘But you hate discipline and cast my words behind you’ (Psalm 49:17).”

All the bishops said:

“We desire that the letter of the Apostle Peter just mentioned be brought to the place where priests ought to hear it.”

Then, when the book had been brought, the following was recited from that same letter:

“Elders, I appeal to my fellow elder: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, overseeing it not under compulsion but willingly according to the Lord, not for the sake of shameful profit but willingly, not lording it over the clergy but becoming an example to the flock from the heart, so that when the chief Shepherd appears you may receive the unfading crown of glory.”

After these words had been reread, all the bishops said:

“Having learned what has been recited from the letter of the blessed Apostle Peter, we desire, with the assistance of God’s grace, to obey the divine commands and in all things to imitate the pattern of the apostolic letter which has been read to us, lest perhaps, walking disorderly in some matters, we be condemned by the divine judgment—which God forbid. Rather, following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers, may we deserve to share in their rest and, with them, receive that unfading crown of glory which has been promised.

“Therefore we all ask your charity together to append to these proceedings a brief account of all these matters, arranged under individual chapters, together with the manner in which they ought to be corrected. When these have been carefully reread and clearly brought to the knowledge of all of us, let each person subscribe with his own hand for their correction and confirmation, so that these decrees may benefit not only us but also our successors toward the perfection of episcopal office.”

**CHAPTER I.** It pleased all the bishops, and they agreed, that in each church and throughout their dioceses the bishops should first examine the clergy concerning how they observe the order of baptism and how they perform the offices of the Mass in the church. If they find that these things are being done correctly, let them give thanks to God; if not, they must teach the ignorant.

“In every way also command this, as the ancient canons order: twenty days before baptism, the catechumens should assemble for the purification of exorcism. During these twenty days all the catechumens should be specially taught the Creed: ‘I believe in God the Father almighty.’

“After the bishops have examined and instructed their clergy in these matters, let them summon the people of that church on another day and teach them to flee the errors of idols and various crimes—that is, murder, adultery, perjury, false testimony, and the other deadly sins—and not to do to another what they do not wish done to themselves. Let them also teach them to believe in the resurrection of all human beings and in the day of judgment, on which each person will receive according to his works. After this, the bishop should depart from that church and go to another.”

**II.** It pleased everyone that no bishop traveling through his dioceses should take anything from the churches beyond the honor due to his chair, namely, two solidi, nor demand a third part of any offering of the people in parish churches. Rather, a third part should be retained there for the lighting or repair of the church, and an account of it should be rendered to the bishop each year. For if the bishop takes that third part, he has taken away the church’s light and sacred roofs.

“Likewise, parish clergy should not be compelled to serve bishops in certain tasks in the manner of slaves, because it is written: ‘Nor as domineering over the clergy.’”

**III.** It pleased everyone that bishops should accept no gifts for the ordination of clergy, but, as it is written, what they receive freely from God’s generous gift, they should give freely. The grace of God and the laying on of hands must not be sold for any price, because the ancient definition of the Fathers established this concerning ecclesiastical ordinations, saying: “Let the giver and the receiver be anathema.”

“Since some people, burdened by many crimes and unworthy to minister at the holy altar, obtain this position not through the testimony of good deeds but through an outpouring of gifts, clergy must therefore be ordained not through the favor of gifts but first through careful examination and then through the testimony of many.”

**IV.** It pleased everyone that, since the small quantity of balsam blessed for the sacrament of baptism is supplied to the churches and they customarily demand three tremisses from each person for it, nothing further should be demanded. Otherwise, what is consecrated for the salvation of souls through the invocation of the Holy Spirit might be sold by us, so that we might be damnably sold in the same way that Simon Magus wished to purchase God’s gift with money.

**V.** It pleased everyone that whenever bishops are invited by one of the faithful to consecrate churches, they should not demand a gift from the founder as though it were owed. If the founder himself offers something from his own vow, it should not be refused. But if poverty or necessity restrains him, nothing should be demanded from him.

“Nevertheless, each bishop should remember not to dedicate a church until he has first received confirmation, by a deed of gift, of the endowment of the basilica and the provision for its service. For it is no slight act of recklessness to consecrate a church without lights or without substantial support for those who are to serve there, as though a private house were being consecrated as a church.”

**VI.** It pleased everyone that, if anyone builds a basilica not out of devotion to the faith but out of greedy desire for profit, whatever is collected there from the offering of the people should be divided equally with the clergy, since he founded the basilica on his own land for the sake of profit—a practice said still to occur in certain places.

“From now on this must be observed: no bishop should consent to so abominable an intention, nor dare to consecrate a basilica founded not for the protection of the saints but rather under a tributary condition.”

[Col. 0575A] **VII.** It pleased everyone that each bishop should command throughout his churches that, if those who present their infants for baptism voluntarily offer anything as their vow, it should be accepted from them. But if, through the necessity of poverty, they have nothing to offer, no pledge should be taken from them by force by the clergy.

“Many poor people, fearing this, hold back their children from baptism and perhaps delay it. If they depart this life without the grace of baptism, their destruction must be demanded from those whose seizure of their property they feared and because of which they withdrew from the grace of baptism.”

**VIII.** It pleased everyone that, if anyone accuses a member of the clergy of fornication, two or three witnesses should be required from him, according to the command of the Apostle Paul. If he cannot prove, through the witnesses presented, that what he has said is true, the accuser should receive the excommunication of the accused.

**IX.** It pleased everyone that, before all matters had been arranged in the council of priests, the following should be observed: the metropolitan bishop should announce on which calendar day and on which lunar date the Easter of the coming year ought to be observed. The other bishops and the remaining clergy should note this in a brief document, and each bishop should announce it in his own church on the coming day of the Lord’s Nativity, with the people present, after the reading of the Gospel.

“At its beginning, neighboring churches should gather together for three days, walking through the basilicas of the saints with psalms and celebrating litanies. On the third day, after Masses have been celebrated at the ninth or tenth hour, the people should be dismissed and instructed to observe the fasts of Lent. In the middle of Lent, they should present the infants who are to be baptized twenty days later for the purification of exorcism.”

**141. X.** It pleased everyone that, because of the folly of a recently presumed error—or, rather, because we have learned that some presbyters remain corrupted by the stench of the ancient Priscillianist heresy—they persist in the audacity of this presumption and dare to consecrate Masses for the dead even after drinking wine or taking food.

“Therefore, by the warning of this plainly established judgment, let the following be observed: if, after this decree of ours, any presbyter is found in this madness again—that is, if, not fasting, but after taking any food whatsoever, he consecrates an offering on the altar—he shall immediately be deprived of his office and deposed by his own bishop.”

After these matters had been enacted, it pleased everyone, for the confirmation of their observance, that each person should subscribe with his own hand to this decision, so that if anyone transgressed the limit of any of these chapters and wished to return to disorderly customs, he might be struck by the excommunication of the entire council and know that the true sentence concerning the degradation of his order threatened him.

“Martin, bishop of the metropolitan Church of Braga, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Remisol, bishop of the Church of Beses, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Lucentius, bishop of the Church of Coimbra, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Adoricus, bishop of the Church of Idanha, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Sardinarius, bishop of the Church of Lamego, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Viator, bishop of the Church of Magnataria, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Alitigitis, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Lugo, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Andrew, bishop of the Church of Ourense, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Anila, bishop of the Church of Tui, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Pulensus, bishop of the Church of Astorga, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Mailoc, bishop of the Church of Britonia, have subscribed these proceedings.”

“Victimer, bishop of the Church of Ourense, have subscribed.”

**THE PREFACE OF SAINT MARTIN, BISHOP OF BRAGA, TO THE BOOK OF CHAPTERS COLLECTED FROM THE GREEK SYNODS BEGINS.**

[Col. 0575]

[Col. 0575C] To my most blessed lord and brother in Christ, Bishop Nigesus, worthy to be received with the honour of the Apostolic See, and to the entire Council of the Church of Lugo: Martin, bishop.

The canons established in the eastern regions by the ancient Fathers were first written in the Greek language and later, as time went on, translated into Latin. Since it is difficult to transfer something simply from one language into another, and since it also happens that over such long periods scribes, whether failing to understand or falling asleep, omit many things, certain passages in the canons consequently appear obscure to simpler people.

Therefore I thought it appropriate to restore, with every care, both what the translators expressed obscurely and what the scribes altered, in a simpler and more corrected form. I observed this principle first: that those matters which concern bishops or the entire clergy should be written together in one section, and likewise those which concern laypeople should be gathered together in one place, so that anyone wishing to learn about a particular chapter may find it more quickly.

[Col. 0578A]

57. On neither fasting nor kneeling on the Lord’s Day.  
58. On tasting meat and not declaring it accursed.  
59. That priests and clerics may not attend spectacles.  
60. That priests and clerics may not make incantatory and harmful bindings.  
61. That they may not hold banquets from collected contributions.  
62. On usury and profits from business.  
63. On clerics who do not assemble for matins or vespers.  
64. That clerics may not be absent from church on the Lord’s Day.  
65. That clerics may not dine before the third hour.  
66. On cutting clerics’ hair and maintaining proper dress.  
67. That poetic psalms may not be recited in church, nor apocryphal books read.  
68. That Masses may not be held over the monuments of the dead.

The chapters concerning the laity follow.

[Col. 0578B]

69. That Christians may not carry meals to the monuments.  
70. That Catholic clerics or laymen may not receive *eulogiae* from heretics, or pray with them and with schismatics.  
71. That Christians may not observe various practices.

[Col. 0578C]

72. That Christians may not retain pagan traditions.  
73. That it is not permitted to observe the moon or the courses of the stars.  
74. That it is not permitted to observe the Kalends.  
75. That it is not permitted to gather medicinal herbs with any ritual observance.  
76. That Christian women may not observe anything superstitious in their weaving.  
77. On adulteries.  
78. On fornicating women and those who cause abortions.  
79. On voluntary and involuntary homicide.  
80. On a woman who has married two brothers, and a man who has had two sisters.

[Col. 0578D]

81. On those who have repeatedly married.  
82. On those who have intercourse with animals.  
83. On those who persist in sins until the end of life and ask for Communion at the point of death.  
84. On those who enter the church but abstain from the sacrament out of lust.  
85. On the excommunicated.

[CANONS.]

[Col. 0577]

**I.** The people may not make the election of those who are being advanced to the priesthood; rather, it is the judgment of the bishops that they themselves test the one to be ordained, whether he has been instructed in speech, faith, and life.

**II.** A bishop ought above all to be appointed by the whole council. But if this is difficult either because of necessity or because of the length of the journey, three are to be gathered from all the bishops, and the signatures of all, whether present or absent, are to be obtained; only then is the ordination to take place. Throughout every province, authority in this matter belongs to the metropolitan bishop.

**III.** A bishop must not be ordained without the counsel and presence of the metropolitan bishop. All the priests in the province ought to be present, and he must summon them by his letter. If all attend, so much the better. But if this is difficult, the greater number must assemble. Those who do not come are to make their presence known by letters; then, with the consent of all expressed, the bishop’s ordination must be carried out. If anything is done otherwise than we have established, we decree that such an ordination has no force. But if the bishop’s ordination has been carried out according to the canons, and someone maliciously objects in any respect, the consent of the majority shall prevail.

**IV.** In each province the bishops ought to acknowledge the metropolitan bishop, who is to assume responsibility for the primacy. The other bishops are to do nothing without him, according to what is contained in the canon established long ago by our fathers. Therefore the metropolitan bishop himself 142 must not presumptuously undertake anything without the counsel of the others.

**V.** If anyone is found to have participated in ambition—whether a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—he must not move from a lesser city to a greater. If anyone obstinately acts against these decrees of the great council, the action is to be wholly annulled, and he is to be restored to his own church, in which he had previously been appointed bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

**VI.** A bishop may not move from his own parish to another, nor enter one on his own initiative, whether invited or compelled by another bishop. He must remain in the place where he was ordained by God, and in the church that fell to his lot, according to the ordinance of the ancient canons.

**VII.** If a bishop comes from one province to another without having been requested in writing by the metropolitan bishop or by those who are with him, and presumptuously intrudes, undertaking the ordination and appointment of clerics who do not belong to him, all that he has established is void and empty. He himself is to be excommunicated with due rebuke and excluded from the holy council.

**VIII.** A bishop may not appoint another as his successor before the end of his life. If anyone attempts to usurp this right, such an appointment shall be invalid. It must be done only with the council and judgment of the bishops who, after the predecessor’s death, have the authority to choose a worthy man.

**IX.** If a bishop, while a church is vacant and without a bishop, slips in and, without the council of the whole order, forces his way upon the people—even if the people whom he has deceived desire him—he must be regarded as alien to the church. By a complete and perfect council we mean one in which the metropolitan bishop is present.

**X.** If someone ordained through popular contention, or for some reason other than his own fault, does not go to the parish assigned to him, he may retain only the rank of the priesthood, but must presume nothing concerning the property of the church in which he has gathered; he must submit to whatever the holy council decides concerning him.

[Col. 0580A]

**XI.** If an ordained bishop is unwilling to exercise the priesthood and refuses to go to the church entrusted to him, he ought to be excommunicated. If he despises it because he was compelled, the holy council shall determine what it wishes concerning him.

**XII.** If an ordained bishop does not wish to accept the parish to which he was appointed, but wishes to be ordained elsewhere, and uses force and incites rebellions against those who ordained him, he must be removed from his honor. If he wishes to remain in his former presbyteral rank, he is not to be prevented from retaining the grade he held. If he resists, he is also to be deposed from the honor of the presbyterate.

**XIII.** If a bishop is judged in certain disputes and sees that the bishops in the province disagree in judgment—some appearing to justify the one being judged, others to condemn him—the holy council has decided, to resolve this disagreement, that another metropolitan bishop from a neighboring province is to be summoned, so that through him whatever accords with the correct canon may be confirmed.

**XIV.** If a bishop, compelled by no ecclesiastical necessity, sells anything belonging to the Church without the knowledge of the clergy, or where there happens to be no presbyter, he must be compelled to restore the things themselves to his own church. He is to be deposed by the judgment of the bishops after being heard and, as one guilty of theft or robbery, deprived of his honor.

**XV.** The things belonging to the Church ought to be preserved with common diligence, a good conscience, and faith in God, who sees and judges all things; they must be administered with the judgment and authority of the bishop, to whom the whole people and congregation of souls have been entrusted. What belongs to the Church must be openly known to the presbyter and deacon who are with the bishops, so that all of them may know what is the Church’s property. Thus, if a bishop should depart this life, none of the things belonging to the Church can remain hidden from them, and they cannot in any way be diminished or destroyed. Nor should the bishop’s own property be harassed on account of the Church’s property.

It is worthy and just before God and human beings that the bishop leave his own possessions to whomever he wishes, while what belongs to the Church is preserved for that same Church, so that neither the Church suffers loss nor the bishop is proscribed among his own people on account of ecclesiastical property; nor, after his death, should those belonging to him fall into lawsuits, nor should he himself appear to incur a curse.

**XVI.** The bishop is to have authority over the Church’s property, so that he may distribute it to those in need with all reverence and fear of God. He ought also to share what is necessary if he himself or the brothers who are with him should lack anything, so that they suffer no want, according to the Apostle’s saying: “We are content with food and clothing.”

But if a bishop wishes to appropriate ecclesiastical property for his own purposes, and corrupts the Church’s lands and the produce of its fields without the counsel of the presbyters or deacons, or gives brothers, sons, or any relatives power to cause the Church’s property secretly to be harmed through them, he must be answerable to the council. Likewise, if a bishop, or the presbyters or deacons with him, are accused because they gather into their own pockets what comes from the Church’s income or any ecclesiastical activity, defraud the poor, and wear them down with hunger, they must be corrected according to what the holy council has decreed.

**XVII.** If a presbyter or deacon is found to have sold anything belonging to the Church’s ministries, since he has committed sacrilege, it has been decided that he is not to be counted among the ecclesiastical order. Nevertheless, he is to be left to the bishop’s judgment, whether he is worthy or unworthy to be restored to his rank, because many times what has been polluted from the sacred altar itself has been left to the bishop’s authority.

[Col. 0581B]

**XVIII.** For ecclesiastical concerns and the resolution of disputes, it has rightly been decided that a council be held twice each year in every province. The metropolitan bishop is to summon all the provincial bishops, and all the presbyters and deacons are to attend the council, so that the cases of those who believe themselves injured may be examined in the council and brought to a just judgment. If bishops, presbyters, or deacons are clearly found guilty of an offense, they are to be excommunicated according to the case, until it is decided by common consent what sentence should be passed concerning them. No bishop may hold councils on his own authority, except those to whom metropolitan sees have been entrusted.

**XIX.** A bishop summoned to the council must not despise it, but must go and teach what concerns the benefit of the Church and the others, if he knows it, or be taught, if he does not know it. If he refuses to go, except on account of illness, he shall be guilty before the council of the brethren.

**XX.** If anyone has not completed thirty years of age, he may in no way be ordained presbyter, even if he is very worthy, because the Lord himself was baptized in his thirtieth year and then began to teach. Therefore the one who is to be ordained must be preserved until this lawful age.

**XXI.** If someone has had his natural organs cut off by physicians because of illness, and likewise those who have been castrated by barbarians or foolish masters, if they appear worthy in character, this canon permits them to be advanced to the clerical office. But if someone, being healthy, not through the discipline of religion and abstinence but by cutting off the body fashioned by God, castrates himself, believing that he can thereby amputate carnal desires, we decree that he is not to be admitted to any clerical office. If he has already been advanced to the clergy, he is to be prohibited from his ministry and deposed.

**XXII.** Whoever has been baptized after reaching the lawful age may not immediately be advanced to an ecclesiastical order, because he must first be taught how he may teach and be tested for a considerable time after baptism, so that he comes to the clergy after having been well tested, according to the Apostle’s command: “Not a neophyte, lest, being puffed up with pride, he fall into judgment and the devil’s snare” (1 Tim. 3:6).

If, as time passes, he is overcome by some grave sin through the testimony of two or three persons, he must be deposed from his rank and cease from the clergy. If anyone presumes to act against the rule, let him be cast out of the clergy as an opponent of the great council.

[Col. 0582A]

**XXIII.** A penitent may be assigned among the doorkeepers, or first among the lectors, only if necessity or custom requires it, so that he may read the Gospels or the Apostle. If he has already been ordained, he is to be counted among the subdeacons, but he may neither lay hands nor touch the sacred things.

By “penitent” we mean one who, after baptism, has been reconciled to the divine altar after carrying out public penance under sackcloth for homicide, various crimes, or very grave sins.

**XXIV.** If presbyters or deacons have been ordained without any examination, or, when examined, have confessed their criminal sins, or have been exposed by others after ordination, they are to be expelled from the clergy. The same rule is to be observed concerning the whole clerical order, for the holy Catholic Church defends what is irreproachable.

**XXV.** If a presbyter sinned before ordination and, after ordination, confessed the sin into which he had previously fallen, he may not offer the sacrifice, but, out of reverence, may bear the name of presbyter. If he did not confess it himself but was publicly convicted by another, he may not retain even the right to bear the name of presbyter.

The same is to be observed concerning deacons: if the deacon himself confesses, he is to receive the rank of subdeacon.

**XXVI.** If anyone marries a widow or a woman dismissed by another man, he is not to be admitted to the clergy; if he slips in, he is to be deposed. Likewise, if after baptism he has been involved in homicide—whether by deed, command, counsel, or consent—and has entered the clergy through some subterfuge, he is to be deposed and receive Communion at the end of his life.

**XXVII.** If a presbyter or deacon commits fornication or adultery, he is to be expelled and do penance.

**XXVIII.** If a layman’s wife is discovered in adultery, such a man is in no way to be brought into ecclesiastical ministry. If the wife of a cleric commits adultery after his ordination, he must dismiss her 143. If he wishes to remain with her, he is to be excluded from the ministry.

**XXIX.** If the widow of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon takes another husband, no cleric and no religious woman is to eat with her; no one is ever to communicate with her. Only the sacrament is to assist her when she is dying.

**XXX.** Concerning the daughter of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon: if she has been dedicated to God and takes a husband, and her father or mother receives her affectionately, they are to be held apart from Communion. The father must know that he will have to give an account of the matter before the council. The woman is not to be admitted to Communion unless, after her husband’s death, she has done penance. But if she leaves him while he is alive and repents, she is to receive Communion when she is failing at the end of her life.

[Col. 0583A]

**XXXI.** A dedicated woman who sins is not to be received into the Church unless she ceases to sin, and, after ceasing, performs suitable penance for ten years and receives Communion. Before she is admitted into the Church, she may not approach prayer or the banquet of any Christian woman. If she is admitted, the woman who received her is also to be regarded as excluded, and the corrupter is to be bound by an equal penalty.

A woman who has taken a husband is not to be admitted to penance unless she has lived chastely while that husband is still alive, or after he has departed this life.

**XXXII.** No bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all from the clergy may have permission to introduce into his household an adopted woman, as though in the place of a daughter, sister, or mother, except perhaps his father’s or mother’s sister, and only those persons who are free from every evil suspicion.

Likewise, we prohibit religious women from intimacy and association with unrelated laymen, namely those who are neither subject to the fear of God nor maintain the discipline of continence.

**XXXIII.** If a presbyter, deacon, or anyone from the clergy, being under condemnation, leaves his own church, he is in no way to be received by another church, but must be compelled in every way to return to his own church. If he persists in pride and refuses to return, he is to be excommunicated and expelled.

If a bishop dares to ordain him in his own church without the consent of the bishop whom he abandoned, his ordination is to be considered void.

**XXXIV.** If a presbyter, deacon, or anyone from the clergy abandons his own church, goes to another church, and remains there for a long time, he must never minister in the clergy. If his bishop admonishes him to return to his own parish and he refuses, he is to be deposed from his office where he is, so that he may never return to his former rank, because of the sin of dissolution.

If another bishop receives him while aware of his guilt, that bishop is not to be admitted to the common council without rebuke, so that he may no longer violate the ecclesiastical canon.

**XXXV.** If an excommunicated bishop, presbyter, or deacon complains in the council that he was unjustly condemned, he is to return to the council of the greater bishops and, awaiting their inquiry and judgment, set before them whatever just causes he believes he has. But if he despises this and wishes to trouble the ears of princes by importunately appealing to the palace, he can obtain no pardon and will have no hope of future reconciliation.

[Col. 0583D]

**XXXVI.** If a bishop, or a presbyter or deacon belonging to a bishop, falls into the opinion of some heresy and is excommunicated for this reason, no bishop may receive him into communion unless he first satisfies everyone at the common council by presenting a written statement of his faith. The same decree is to apply to faithful laymen if they have been accused of holding some heretical opinion.

**XXXVII.** If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon has been excommunicated at a council by his bishop, and after excommunication presumes to make an offering, or perform the morning or evening sacrifice, as though exercising his former office, he may neither hope for reconciliation at another council nor ever be reconciled.

Those who have communicated with him are likewise all to be rejected from the Church, especially those who knew that he had been deposed. If he persists in disturbing and inciting the Church through an external power, he must be compelled by the whole people, as a seditious person.

[Col. 0584B]

**XXXVIII.** A presbyter ought not to become a guest at a second marriage. If he attends a second marriage, he must ask for penance. How can that man be a presbyter who attends such a marriage for the sake of the banquet?

**XXXIX.** If a deacon who is being chosen declares, concerning the taking of a wife, that he cannot remain chaste, he is not to be ordained. If he keeps silent at his ordination, is ordained, and later desires marriage, he is to be excluded from the ministry and released from the clergy.

**XL.** A deacon may not sit before a presbyter unless by the presbyter’s command.

**XLI.** No one may touch the Lord’s vessels in the sacristy except a subdeacon or acolyte.

[Col. 0584C]

**XLII.** A woman may not enter the sacristy.

**XLIII.** If a lector takes another man’s widow as his wife, he is to remain in the status of lector; or, if necessity requires, he may become a deacon, but nothing higher. The same applies if he has had two wives.

**XLIV.** If a subdeacon takes a second wife, he is to be counted among the lectors or doorkeepers, and may not read the Apostle.

**XLV.** No one may chant or read from the ambo except those ordained lectors by the bishop.

**XLVI.** If someone is bound by a servile tax, by some condition, or by the patronage of anyone, he is not to be ordained a cleric unless he has a proven life and the patron’s consent has been given.

**XLVII.** If anyone teaches another person’s slave, on religious grounds, to despise his master and withdraw from his service, he is to be severely rebuked in every respect.

**XLVIII.** Martyrs’ festivals may not be celebrated during Lent. Offerings may be made for their commemoration only on Saturday and Sunday. Nor is it permitted to celebrate festivals or weddings during Lent.

**XLIX.** No one may be received for baptism two weeks before Easter, but three weeks beforehand. During those days, those who are to be baptized must learn the Creed and, on the Thursday of the final week, recite it to the bishop or presbyter.

[Col. 0585A]

**L.** It is not permitted to break the fast on the Thursday of the final week or to dishonor the whole of Lent, but, abstaining sincerely, the whole of Lent must be completed.

**LI.** At all times the bishop may prepare the chrism and send it throughout his dioceses, provided that, in order to convey the chrism, a deacon or subdeacon from each church is sent to the bishop before Easter Day.

**LII.** A presbyter may not sign the infants in the presence of the bishop unless the bishop has specifically commanded him to do so.

**LIII.** A presbyter may not enter the baptistery before the bishop, but only with the bishop, unless the bishop is absent or ill.

[Col. 0585B]

**LIV.** If a pregnant woman wishes to receive the grace of baptism, she may do so whenever she wishes. For the mother does not share anything in this matter with the child who is born, since each person’s own will is shown in confession.

**LV.** Nothing else ought to be offered in the sanctuary except bread, wine, and water, which are blessed as a representation of Christ. For, while he hung upon the cross, blood and water flowed from his body; these three are one in Christ Jesus. This is the sacrifice and offering of God for a pleasing fragrance.

**LVI.** Presbyters from outside the city may not offer or minister among the people in the presence of the bishop or the city’s presbyters, unless those persons are absent.

[Col. 0585C]

**LVII.** If a presbyter, having received public penance from a priest, or because of some necessity, fasts on the Lord’s Day for a certain religious purpose, like the Manichaeans, let him be anathema.

Likewise, because the ancient canon holds what was handed down by the apostles, it has been decided that on every Sunday and on all the days of Easter until Pentecost, they are not to prostrate themselves in humble prayer, but are to perform the duty of prayer before the Lord with upright faces, because on these days we celebrate the joy of the Lord’s resurrection.

**LVIII.** If anyone abstains not for the sake of abstinence but out of abhorrence for foods, the holy council has decided that he should first taste them; and, if he then wishes to abstain, let him abstain. But if he rejects them, refusing even to taste cooked vegetables with meat, he is disobedient, has not removed the suspicion of heresy from himself, and is to be deposed from the clerical order.

[Col. 0585D]

**LIX.** Priests and clerics may not watch any spectacles at weddings or banquets; before the spectacles begin, they must rise and withdraw.

**LX.** Clerics may not be enchanters or make bindings, which are the binding of souls. If anyone does these things, he is to be expelled from the Church.

**LXI.** Priests and clerics, and likewise religious laymen, may not hold banquets from collected contributions.

**LXII.** If anyone, forgetting the fear of the Lord and the Holy Scripture, which says, “He has not given his money at usury” (Ps. 14:5), lends at interest after this decree of the holy council has been made known, and demands the hundredth (centesima), or seeks shameful profit from any business, acquiring an increase by buying or selling wine, grain, or any other thing, he is to be deposed from his rank 144 and regarded as excluded from the clergy.

[Col. 0586A]

**LXIII.** If a presbyter, deacon, or cleric assigned to a church is within the city, or in any place where there is a church, and does not assemble at the church for the daily psalmody and sacrifice at the morning or evening hours, he is to be deposed from the clergy if, after being disciplined, he refuses to obtain pardon from the bishop through satisfaction.

**LXIV.** No cleric may be absent from church on the Lord’s Day. He must attend the solemnities of the Mass and the fast.

**LXV.** Clerics and religious laymen ought not to enter banquets before the sacred third hour of the day. Clerics may never eat without first reciting a hymn, and after eating they must give thanks to God the Creator.

**LXVI.** Clerics ought not to grow their hair and minister in that fashion. They must have their heads shorn, their ears uncovered, and, following Aaron, wear a full-length garment, so that their dress may be orderly.

**LXVII.** Composed and popular psalms must not be recited in church, nor books outside the canon read, but only the canonical books of the New and Old Testament.

[Col. 0586C]

**LXVIII.** Unlearned clerics must not presumptuously carry the mysteries into the field over monuments, or distribute the sacraments there. Rather, an offering for the dead is to be made either in the church or in the basilica where the relics of the martyrs have been placed.

The canons concerning the laity follow.

**LXIX.** Christians may not carry meals to the tombs of the dead and sacrifice to the dead.

**LXX.** Laymen and clerics may not receive *eulogiae* from heretics, since they are curses rather than blessings. Nor may anyone pray either with heretics or with schismatics.

**LXXI.** If anyone, following pagan custom, brings diviners and sorcerers into his house, supposedly to drive out evil, discover magical practices, or perform pagan purifications, he must do penance for five years.

[Col. 0586D]

**LXXII.** Christians may not retain pagan traditions.

**LXXIII.** Christians may not observe or worship the elements, the course of the moon or stars, or the empty deception of signs when building a house, planting crops or trees, or arranging marriages. For it is written: “Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God” (Col. 3:17).

**LXXIV.** It is not permitted to celebrate the day of the Kalends and devote oneself to pagan idleness, nor to gird houses with laurel or the greenery of trees. All such observance is thoroughly pagan.

[Col. 0587A]

**LXXV.** When gathering medicinal herbs, it is not permitted to attend to any observances or incantations, except only with the divine Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, so that only God, the Creator and Lord of all, may be honored.

**LXXVI.** Christian women may not observe any vain practice in their weaving, but must invoke God as their helper, who has given them the wisdom to weave.

**LXXVII.** If anyone’s wife commits adultery, or a man attacks another man’s wife, he must do penance for seven years.

**LXXVIII.** If a woman commits fornication and kills the child born from it, or strives to cause an abortion and kill what has been conceived, or works to prevent conception—whether from adultery or from a lawful marriage—the earlier canons decreed that such women receive Communion only at death. We, however, out of mercy, judge that such women, and those complicit in their crimes, are to do penance for ten years.

[Col. 0587B]

**LXXIX.** If anyone commits voluntary homicide, he must remain perpetually at the door of the Catholic Church and receive Communion at the end of his life. If he commits homicide not voluntarily but by some accident, the earlier canon ordered seven years of penance, while the second commanded five.

**LXXX.** If a woman has married two brothers, or a man has married two sisters, they must abstain from Communion until death. At death, if they receive Communion and recover from their illness, they must do full penance for the appointed period.

[Col. 0587C]

**LXXXI.** If anyone has been joined in many marriages, he must do penance; but the conversion and faith of the penitent shorten the time.

**LXXXII.** If anyone sins through intercourse with any animal, he must remain in humility at the church door for fifteen years. After these years, he is to be received into the communion of prayer for another five years and do penance, and thus receive the grace of the sacrament. Others are to be questioned about what kind of life he led during his penance, and then he may obtain the mercy of Communion.

But if, after twenty years of age and while having a wife, anyone falls into this sin, he must remain in humility for twenty-five years and, for five years, participate only in prayers; afterward he may receive the sacrament. If anyone exceeds this measure, he may obtain the sacrament at the point of death. Such persons ought to pray among those possessed by demons.

[Col. 0588A]

**LXXXIII.** If anyone, departing from the body, asks for the final and necessary viaticum of Communion, it must not be denied him. But if, having been in despair, he recovers after receiving Communion, he is to participate only in prayer. He must not receive the sacrament until he has completed the appointed period in purity.

Therefore, those who are at the point of death and desire to receive the sacrament ought to receive it with the bishop’s consideration and examination.

**LXXXIV.** If anyone enters the church of God and hears the holy Scriptures, but turns away from Communion with the sacrament because of his lust, and avoids the established rule of discipline in observing the mysteries, we decree that such a person is to be expelled from the Catholic Church until he does penance and displays the fruit of his penance, so that, having received Communion, he may merit pardon.

[Col. 0588C]

**LXXXV.** It is not permitted to communicate with the excommunicated, nor to enter their houses and pray with them, nor to separate oneself with them in another church. If a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any ecclesiastical person communicates with an excommunicated person, as one who disturbs the whole ecclesiastical discipline, he is to be excommunicated.

Here ends the book of excerpts of Saint Martin, bishop of Bracara, from the synods of the East.

THE THIRD COUNCIL OF BRACARA BEGINS, held in the fourth year of King Wamba, in the era 613.

[Col. 0587]

[Col. 0587D] Having been suitably assembled in the city of Braga by the divine Spirit, and intending to discuss those things that are done within the Church through perverse action, we have gathered together, with the assistance of him who says, “Wherever two or three have been gathered in my name, there I shall be in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20). Rising up with one mind and with equal zeal for devotion, let us uproot errors that have been badly established. For when synodal action had gathered us into one body, after we had taken our appointed seats, we first began to discuss the sacrament of the holy faith—namely, lest through the vanity of disputants or the ignorance of the simple anything belonging to error should be held in this sacrament of faith. When, therefore, we all examined ourselves in the true faith as in a mirror and found ourselves unharmed, since in this matter [Col. 0588D] no storm of schismatic error had wearied any of us, but true and simple apostolic preaching had shown us competent in this sacrament, we offered thanks to almighty God because we had prefaced this rule of our faith by recalling it in the very words and formulations in which we know it to have been declared at the assembly of the Council of Nicaea.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages: God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—[Col. 0589A] through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth; who for us and for our salvation came down. And he was incarnate from the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will come again to judge the living and the dead. His kingdom shall have no end. We also believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets.
