And in one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church. We confess one baptism for the forgiveness of sins. We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

[Col. 0589B] After this sacrament of the holy faith, a manifest and various error was reported in the assembly of us all—an error that ought to be beaten back by as rigorous a discipline as the perversity by which it is shown to have been introduced. For some are reported to offer milk instead of wine in the Lord’s sacrifices; they also believe that the Eucharist soaked in wine should be presented to the people [Col. 0590A] as the completion of communion; and, worse than all these things, some priests set food before themselves in the Lord’s vessels and presume to eat from them. Some priests have also been reported to dare to say Mass without the prayer of supplication, omitting the customary ecclesiastical order; and, on the festivals of martyrs, to place relics around their necks and believe that in their little chairs they should be carried by no others than deacons dressed in white. It has also been reported that many priests live with women without witnesses, and that some of them subject their honored brothers to indiscriminate beatings. Likewise, some, seized by the greed of Simon, release those whom they are about to ordain [145] under a guarantee that, after they have been ordained, they will accept from them the money they promised. It has also been reported that they wear down the Church’s household through their own labors, causing loss to the Lord’s property. We believe that all these matters should be set out under distinct headings, so that they may not appear to have been presented confusedly.

## The Chapters Begin

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589B] 1. That, after all superstitious opinions have been rejected, only bread and wine mixed with water should be offered in the sacrifice.  
2. That vessels consecrated to the Lord should not serve human uses.  
3. That a priest should not dare to celebrate Mass without the *orarium*.  
4. That priests, or anyone from the clergy, should not live with any women without witnesses.  
[Col. 0590B] 5. Concerning the condemned presumption of certain bishops who, proceeding to the church on the festivals of martyrs, carry relics hung around their necks and are borne by deacons in little chairs.  
6. Concerning the dignity of honored persons and discipline.  
7. That no one should be sold through a promise of gifts, under the pretext of conferring honor.  
8. That the administrators of the Church should not be more diligent in working their own property than in attending to ecclesiastical rights.

## The Canons Begin

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589C] **Chapter I.** Since every crime and sin is blotted out by sacrifices offered to God, what will thereafter be given to the Lord for the expiation of offenses when an error is committed in the very offering of the sacrifice? For we have heard that some, held by schismatic ambition and acting contrary to divine ordinances and apostolic institutions, consecrate milk instead of wine in the divine sacrifices; others present the dipped Eucharist to the people as the completion of communion; [Col. 0589D] and some even offer in the sacrament of the Lord’s chalice wine that has not been pressed, but communicate the people only with what has been offered. How contrary this is to evangelical and apostolic teaching, and how opposed to ecclesiastical custom, is easily proved from the very source of truth from which the ordered mysteries of the sacraments proceeded.

When the teacher of truth commended the true sacrifice of our salvation to his disciples, we know that he commended to them not milk, but only bread and the chalice under this sacrament. For the evangelical Truth says: “Jesus took bread and the chalice, and, blessing it, gave it to his disciples” (Mark 14:22). Therefore let milk cease to be offered in the sacrifice, since the manifest and evident example of the evangelical Truth has shone forth, allowing nothing else to be offered besides bread and wine.

But as for the practice of giving the people the dipped Eucharist as the completion of communion, this too receives no supporting testimony from the Gospel, where he commended his body and blood to the apostles, for the giving of the bread is remembered separately and the giving of the chalice separately. We do not read that Christ gave dipped bread to anyone else except that one disciple whom the dipped morsel of the teacher revealed as a traitor—not that it demonstrated the institution of this sacrament. As for communicating the people with pressed grape-clusters—that is, with grains of grapes—this is altogether very confused. For the Lord’s chalice, as a certain teacher explains, ought to be offered mixed with wine and water, because we understand the people to be signified by the water, while the blood of Christ is shown by the wine.

Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the chalice, the people are united to Christ, and the people of believers are joined and attached to him in whom they have believed. This union and joining of water and wine is so mixed in the Lord’s chalice that the union cannot be separated. For if someone offers wine alone, the blood of Christ begins to exist without us; but if there is water alone, the people begin to exist without Christ. Therefore, when a grape-cluster alone is offered, in which only the efficacy of wine is represented, the sacrament of our salvation is neglected, which is signified through [Col. 0591A] the water.

The Lord’s chalice cannot be water alone or wine alone unless both are mixed with one another. And therefore, since many and various judgments of our predecessors have already flowed from this matter—men whose religious devotion toward God has both explained the manifold effects of these sacraments and set forth their most truthful institutions—all such error and presumption must henceforth cease, lest the disordered structure of the perverse weaken the established order of truth. Therefore, from now on, no one may offer anything else in the divine sacrifices except, in accordance with the judgment of the ancient councils, bread alone and a chalice mixed with wine and water. Whoever thereafter acts otherwise than has been commanded shall cease from offering the sacrifice until, corrected through the lawful satisfaction of penitence, he returns to the rank of his office [Col. 0591B] that he lost.

**II.** Every care and every effort must be taken lest those who appear to hold positions of governance appear to inflict insult upon the heavenly sacraments. For we have been informed of something judged terrifying to hear and detestable to see: some priests, rushing headlong in sacrilegious recklessness, take the Lord’s vessels for their own uses and set food in them for themselves to eat. We lament this evil in astonishment, and in lamenting it we are astonished—that human recklessness should prepare a meal for itself where it is known that the Holy Spirit has been invoked; that a person should take and gorge himself on the eating of meat where he appears to have celebrated divine mysteries; and that in those vessels in which he commanded sacraments to be offered for the expiation of sins, he should fulfill the purpose of his mockery.

Therefore, by the decree concerning this presumption, any person who knowingly transfers divine vessels or implements to his own uses, or eats from them, or chooses to take a drink from them, shall incur the penalty of his rank or office. If he is a layman, however, he shall be condemned to perpetual excommunication; if he is a religious person, he shall be removed from office. Under this same sentence of condemnation those also shall be held liable who knowingly transfer ecclesiastical ornaments, any other garments, or utensils to their own uses, or believe that they should be given or sold to others.

**III.** Since we know that ancient ecclesiastical institution established that every priest, when ordained, should be surrounded by the *orarium* across both shoulders—so that he who is commanded to stand undisturbed amid prosperity and adversity may always appear enclosed on both shoulders by the ornament of the virtues—why does he not assume, at the time of the sacrifice, what there is no doubt he received in the sacrament? Accordingly, it is fitting for all of us that what each person received at the consecration of his dignity he should retain also in the offering or reception of his salvation. Thus, when a priest approaches the solemn rites of Mass, whether he is about to offer the sacrifice to God himself or to receive the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, he must approach only after being surrounded by the *orarium* across both shoulders, just as he is recognized to have been consecrated at the time of his ordination. From one and the same *orarium* he shall press it against his neck and both shoulders and form the sign of the cross upon his breast [Col. 0592A]. If anyone acts otherwise, he shall be subject to the appropriate excommunication.

**IV.** Although the ancient institution of the canons has issued extensive and numerous disciplines and regulations concerning such presumption, nevertheless, desiring for the sake of brevity to remove every opportunity for fornication, we decree with complete authority that this must be observed: no priest, nor anyone from the clergy, may presume secretly to associate with any women without honest and suitable testimony, except for his mother alone. This applies not only to foreign women but also to sisters and female relatives, lest, through the permission given to sisters or female relatives, any man who is otherwise free should become more familiar with them for the perpetration of crime. The transgressor of this command [Col. 0592B] shall know that he is subject to the laws of penitence for six months.

**V.** It is indeed a good thing for priests to handle the divine mysteries, but great care must be taken lest anyone twist this to the use of his own depravity, when he ought to please God alone through a good conscience. For it is written: “Woe to those who do the work of the Lord deceitfully and negligently” (Jeremiah 48:10).

When the detestable presumption of certain bishops was brought before our assembly for judgment, we learned that some bishops, when they were about to proceed to the church on the solemn festivals of martyrs, placed relics around their necks so that they might swell with the glory of greater pomp before men—as though they themselves were the ark of the relics—and that Levites dressed in white carried them in little chairs. This detestable presumption must be abolished in every respect, lest, under the appearance of holiness, simulated vanity alone prevail if the reverence owed to each order does not recognize its proper measure.

Therefore the ancient and solemn custom shall be maintained in this matter: on every festival day, the ark of the Lord with its relics shall be carried on the shoulders not by bishops but by Levites, whom we know were commanded to bear this same burden under the Old Law. If a bishop chooses to carry relics himself, he shall not be carried by deacons in a little chair. Rather, proceeding on foot together with the people, he shall carry the holy relics of God to the assemblies of the holy churches. Whoever knowingly delays fulfilling these regulations shall cease from offering the sacrifice for as long as he remains in fault.

[Col. 0592D] **VI.** Since the blessed Apostle commands that one should rebuke, entreat, and admonish with all patience, we know that certain brothers, contrary to this teaching, rage against honored persons with beatings as severe as those that could be deserved by robbers. Therefore those who have already merited ecclesiastical rank—namely, priests, abbots, and Levites—should not, except for grave and mortal faults, be subjected to any beatings. It is not fitting that every superior should indiscriminately subject his honored members to blows and pain, according to his own will and pleasure. For while he strikes his subjects’ members carelessly, he may also deprive himself of the reverence that his subjects owe him, in accordance with what a certain wise man said: “One corrected gently shows reverence to the one correcting him; but through the harshness of excessive reprimand, he accepts neither correction nor salvation.”

Therefore, if anyone, puffed up by the authority he has received, believes that the aforementioned honored subjects should be beaten out of mere malice, contrary to what has been said, he shall, according to the measure of the blows he has inflicted, undergo both excommunication and a sentence of exile.

**VII.** Since it is not fitting that the gift of the Holy Spirit be purchased with money, although diverse disciplines concerning this remain from the ancient canons, nevertheless, because what is continually presumed must be struck back more frequently, we establish the form of this new regulation. Whoever, in order to confer any clerical rank on someone, has accepted any gift or promise of a gift before that person is ordained, or has presumed to receive payment for this same purpose after he has been ordained—whether the giver or the recipient—shall, in accordance with the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon, incur the penalty of his rank.

**VIII.** It is not fitting for the administrators of the Church to be energetic in their own affairs and negligent in ecclesiastical matters. For it is reported as the opinion of some that certain priests so exhaust the Church’s households through their own labors that they increase the prosperity of their private property while causing loss to the Lord’s property. Therefore whoever, through such neglect, delays attending to divine matters must be compelled by a special decree. If he has thereby increased his own gain through his labors from the Church’s property or revenues, and through this has shown neglect toward ecclesiastical matters or caused their diminution or loss, he must restore to the Church whatever he diminished, from whose property and support he is proved to have increased his own maintenance by his labors.

But if he has spent something for the benefit of the Church or its possessions, or has incurred some loss or destruction, and this can be proved, the whole amount shall be restored to him from the property of that Church for whose benefit he is proved to have spent it. [146]

We therefore offer thanks to the Almighty. After this, may there be peace, salvation, and long duration for our most devout and Christ-loving lord, King Wamban, whose devotion summoned us to this salutary decree. We ask divine mercy that the glory of Christ may strengthen his kingdom until the extremity of old age, through him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and is glorified as God in the Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

Leodigius, bishop, have subscribed in the name of Christ.  
Julianus, bishop, have subscribed in the name of Christ.  
Genitivus, bishop of the Church of Tudensis, have subscribed in the name of Christ.  
Froaricus, by God’s command, bishop of the Church of Portugalensis, have subscribed.  
Beia, bishop of the Church of Brittaniensis, have subscribed in the name of Christ.  
Isidorus, bishop of the Church of Asturensis, have subscribed.  
Alarius, bishop of the Church of Auresina, have subscribed.  
Rectogerus, bishop of the Church of Lucensis, have subscribed.  
Hidulphus, also called Felix, bishop of the Church of Hiriensis, have subscribed.

The Third Council of Braga ends.

## The Chapters of the First Council of Seville Begin

[Col. 0593]

1. Concerning the letter sent from the Council of Seville to Bishop Pegasius.  
2. Concerning the Church’s slaves transferred by the bishop to his relatives.  
3. Concerning clerics who cohabit with women.

## The First Council of Seville Begins

[Col. 0593]

[Col. 0593C] To the holy lord and most reverend and beloved brother PEGASIUS, bishop, whom we honor: Leander, John, Agapius, Stephen, Basil, Celatus, Fintitius, and Peter, bishops, who are present together in the one city of Seville. We greet your Holiness with the devotion of charity and pray the Lord, who graciously allows us to rejoice in one another’s salvation and in seeing one another, to preserve you happily for a long time.

**Chapter I.** While we were sitting together in the Church of Holy Jerusalem at Seville, your deacons presented to us a brief register of the Church’s slaves whom your predecessor, the bishop Gaudentius of holy memory, appeared to have freed. We not only reread in it those whom he had freed there, but also found recorded those whom he had given from the Church’s household to his relatives [Col. 0593D].

For this reason we consulted the provisions of the canons, asking whether such freedom or transaction could be valid. We found it stated in a canon that if a bishop leaves his own property to someone other than his sons and grandsons, and not to his own Church, whatever he has given, sold, or transferred in any way from the Church’s property is to be considered void.

Therefore, if your Church does not possess the property of your predecessor, Bishop Gaudentius, those whom he made free have not been lawfully released. But if his property serves as compensation for your Church, let them remain entirely free. For, as was stated above, if he did not make provision from his own property, he ought not to have suffered such a loss.

Accordingly, with one accord we all declare—thinking more humanely than severely—that those who are known to have been freed under such a condition should remain as dependents under the right of the Church, and should leave their property not to other persons but only to their sons. Their sons and grandsons likewise, together with their property, shall remain as dependents under the right of the Church and shall not be permitted to transfer anything from it to an outsider [Col. 0594D]. If any of them should die without an heir, his property shall benefit the holy Church.

**II.** As for those slaves whom the aforementioned bishop removed from the right of the Church and gave to his relatives, if he did not compensate that Church with equivalent property of his own, your Church shall receive them without any opposition [Col. 0595A]. This rule shall be observed not only by your Church—that is, the Church of Astigi—but also by all those who throughout the province of Baetica have, under such a condition or arrangement, passed from the right of the Church. They shall all be subject to the same judgment.

For it is harsh and irreligious that a bishop who lives on ecclesiastical stipends, and does not contribute his own property to the Church’s profit, should deprive the Church’s right of the offerings of others.

**III.** Among other matters, know that we have established the following for removing the stains of clerics. Certain bishops, failing to observe the recent edict and decree of the Council of Toledo, have been insufficiently attentive to those subject to them. It has therefore seemed good that, if priests, deacons, or clerics do not, after admonition by their priest, remove from themselves the companionship of foreign women or the familiarity of female servants [Col. 0595B], secular judges, with the will and permission of the bishop, may seize those women and appropriate them as their own profit. Thus, when the priest is unable to suppress this vice, judicial authority may restrain it. The judges must nevertheless give the bishops an oath that they will not restore the women to the clerics by any device. If they do restore them, the judges themselves shall be struck by a sentence of excommunication.

As for those women, once they have been separated from the clerics by the priest according to the earlier canons, their price shall be distributed to those in need. We have subscribed these regulations with our own hands and sent them to Your Holiness on the second day before the Nones of November, in the fifth year of our glorious lord Reccared, king, in the era 628.

Leander, bishop of the holy Church of Seville, have confirmed and subscribed this constitution.  
John, bishop of the Church of Agabra, have confirmed and subscribed this constitution.  
Agapius, bishop of the holy Church of Corduba, have confirmed and subscribed this constitution.  
Stephen, bishop of Elibera, have confirmed and subscribed this constitution.  
Basil, [Col. 0596B] bishop of Elipa, have confirmed and subscribed this constitution.  
Celatus, bishop of Tucci, have confirmed and subscribed this constitution.  
Peter, bishop of Alberia, have confirmed and subscribed this constitution.

## The Chapters of the Second Council of Seville Begin

[Col. 0595]

[Col. 0595B] 1. Concerning the complaints of Theodulf of the Church of Malaga against the other bishops regarding certain parishes.  
2. Concerning the complaints of Bishops Fulgentius and Honorius regarding certain parishes. [Col. 0595C]  
3. Concerning clerical deserters, that they should be restored to their bishops.  
4. That bigamists should not be promoted to the priesthood or diaconate.  
5. That priests should not presume to ordain a deacon or priest.  
6. That priests or deacons should not be deposed by a single bishop. [Col. 0596B]  
7. Concerning what corepiscopi are forbidden to do in ecclesiastical sacraments.  
8. Concerning proud freedmen of the Church, that they should be recalled to service. [Col. 0596C]  
9. Concerning stewards, that they should not be appointed from the laity.  
10. That monasteries should not be torn apart.  
11. Concerning monasteries of virgins, that they should be protected by monks.  
12. Concerning a certain bishop of the Acephali.  
13. Concerning the two natures and one person in Christ.

## The Second Council of Seville Begins

Held in the era 659, in the time of King Sisebut.

[Col. 0595]

[Col. 0595C] In the name of our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ: Isidore, Bisinnus, Rufinus, Fulgentius, Cambra, Fidentius, Theodulf, and Honorius, bishops, who have gathered together in the city of Seville on certain ecclesiastical matters. As we were sitting together [Col. 0595D] in the secretariat of the most holy Church of Holy Jerusalem at Seville, illustrious men were present: Sisibutus, administrator of public affairs, and Sualane, administrator of fiscal affairs, while the most religious assembly of the clergy stood by.

**Chapter I.** At the first session, a petition was presented to us by Theodulf, bishop of the Church of Malaga. He asserted that the ancient parish of that city had been cut off during the danger of a military invasion and that part of it had been retained by the Churches of Astigi, Celeber, and Agabra. It therefore seemed good that every parish which anyone could prove his Church to have held under its ancient jurisdiction before the military invasion should be restored to it by privilege.

For just as, under worldly law, the ancient possession is restored by right of return to those whom barbarian severity has carried away into captivity under the necessity of captivity, so the Church shall recover the parish that it formerly held, together with its property, whether it is possessed by other Churches or has been transferred into the possession of anyone else. A limitation based on the passage of time shall not be raised where the necessity of invasion intervened.

**II.** A dispute arose between our aforementioned brothers Fulgentius, bishop of Fastigi, and Honorius, bishop of Corduba, concerning the parish of a certain basilica. One of them asserted that it belonged to Celtica, the other that it belonged to Reginum. Since the matter of the boundary had until now been claimed by both sides, although its long-standing retention conferred no legal prejudice on either party, we did not wish our judgment between them to be called into further doubt.

Accordingly, after canons had been produced, the synodal decrees were read aloud. Their authority teaches that greed must be restrained so that no one may usurp another’s boundaries. It therefore seemed good that surveyors should be sent between the opposing parties. If an ancient boundary, marked by old signs, should show that the basilica lies within the diocese of the possessor, its ownership shall remain permanently with the Church whose right it is to retain it [Col. 0597A].

But if a lawful boundary does not enclose that basilica, and nevertheless a claim based on long possession is proved, the appeal of the bishop reclaiming it shall not prevail, because the thirty-year objection imposes silence upon him. This is commanded both by the edicts of secular rulers and by the authority of the decrees of Roman bishops. If, however, within the thirty-year period the basilica is found to have been unjustly retained beyond another’s boundaries, it shall without delay be restored to the right of the bishop reclaiming it.

**III.** In the third ruling, a petition was presented to us by our most reverend brother Cambra, bishop of Italica, concerning a certain cleric named Passandus. From the beginning of his childhood he had been dedicated to the worship of his own Church, but he had transferred himself to the Church of Corduba. We determined that, unless anything were brought forward against him, he should be restored to his own bishop without delay.

For worldly law concerning agricultural tenants states that wherever a person has begun to be, there he should remain. Likewise, the decree of the canons commands this concerning clerics who labor in the field of the Church: they must remain where they began to be. Therefore, if a cleric deprived of the ministries of his own Church transfers to another, at the compulsion of the priest to whom he has fled, he must be returned to the Church in which he formerly lived.

Whoever receives him and does not immediately choose, without any attempt at an exception, to send him back to his own Church shall know that he is deprived of communion for as long as he delays restoring him. The cleric who has deserted shall be stripped of the belt of his honor and ordination and, for a certain period, confined in a monastery; afterward he may be recalled to the ministry of the ecclesiastical order. For permission to wander in such ways cannot be abolished unless, for the correction of discipline, a penalty has followed.

**IV.** At the fourth session we were informed that certain recent ordinations at the Church of Astigi had been illicit, so that some husbands of widows had been consecrated to the ministry of Levites. They should properly be recalled from the rank they received as invalid, and those who are found to have been instituted contrary to divine and ecclesiastical law should not be advanced any further to the ministry of the diaconate.

**V.** In the fifth judgment, the deacons of Agabra brought to the attention of our examination a report concerning certain clerics of that Church [Col. 0597D]. While one was being consecrated to the priesthood and two to the ministry of Levites, their bishop, who is said to have been suffering from pain in his eyes, is reported to have laid his hand upon them only, and a certain priest gave them the blessing contrary to ecclesiastical order.

Although he could have been accused and condemned by the present judgment because of the audacity of so great a presumption, he had already been overtaken by the summons of death and was no longer living. Since he has been left to divine judgment, he cannot be accused by human judgment. But those who remain, and who received from him not the title of consecration but a mark of disgrace, must not be allowed to claim such usurpation as a license for themselves. We therefore decree that, having been deposed from the rank of the priestly or levitical order that they perversely obtained [Col. 0598A], they shall be rejected by an equitable judgment. Such men have rightly been judged fit for removal, because they were found to have been improperly appointed.

**VI.** At the sixth session we discovered that Fragitanus, a priest of the Church of Corduba, had formerly been unjustly expelled by his bishop and condemned to exile though innocent. We restored him to his order and, in opposition to such presumption, decreed anew that, according to the decree of the ancient fathers, none of us may dare, without examination by a council, to depose any priest or deacon.

For many condemn people who have not been examined by tyrannical power rather than by canonical authority. Just as they raise some to high position through the favor of partiality, so they humble others, moved by hatred and envy, and condemn them on the light breath of opinion [Col. 0598B], even though they do not approve their alleged crime.

A bishop alone may grant honor to priests and ministers, but he cannot alone take it away. For if those who in the world have obtained the honor of freedom from their masters are not returned to the bond of slavery unless they have been publicly accused before praetors in a tribunal, how much more must those who have been consecrated to the divine altars and adorned with ecclesiastical honor be protected? For the sake of sin they may be condemned neither by one person nor by the judgment of one person be stripped of the privileges of their honor. They must be presented to synodal judgment, where the canon concerning them shall be defined.

**VII.** At the seventh examination it was reported to us that the once most revered Agapius, bishop of the city of Corduba, had frequently sent corepiscopi or priests—who, according to the canons, are one and the same for this purpose—to erect altars and consecrate basilicas in the absence of the bishop. It is not surprising that a man ignorant of ecclesiastical discipline and immediately transferred from secular military service to priestly ministry should have issued such a command.

Therefore, lest such permission be usurped by us again, it was necessary to establish by common judgment that, just as it is unlawful for a priest or corepiscopus to consecrate an altar, so it is unlawful for him to establish one. Aaron alone erected the altar and himself anointed it, because he was certainly the high priest of God, as it is written concerning him: “Moses and Aaron among his priests” (Psalm 98:6). Therefore priests, who bear the figure of the sons of Aaron, should not presume to carry out what was commanded only to the chief priests, whose type Moses and Aaron represented.

Although priests share with bishops in the administration of many ministries, they must know that certain things are forbidden to them by the authority of the Old Law and others by newer ecclesiastical regulations: the consecration of priests, deacons, and virgins; the establishment, blessing, or anointing of an altar; the giving of the Spirit through the laying on of hands to baptized believers or to converts from heresy; the making of chrism; and the signing of the foreheads of the baptized with chrism.

Nor may they publicly reconcile a penitent at Mass, even if the person is penitent; nor may they send letters of recommendation to anyone. All these things are unlawful for priests or corepiscopi because they do not possess the summit of the episcopate, which the authority of the canons commands to belong to bishops alone [Col. 0599A], so that through this both the distinction of ranks and the eminence of the dignity of the chief priest might be demonstrated.

Nor is it lawful for them, in the presence of a bishop, to enter the baptistery, or, while the bishop is present, to baptize or sign an infant; nor to reconcile a penitent without the command of their bishop; nor to celebrate the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood in his presence; nor, when he is present, to teach, bless, or greet the people; nor, of course, to exhort the congregation. All these things are known to have been forbidden to them by the Apostolic See.

**VIII.** The eighth discussion concerned a certain Helisaeus from the household of the Church of Agabra. His bishop had granted him freedom, but immediately after obtaining freedom he leapt into the disease of disobedience. In his pride [Col. 0599B], he not only wished to injure the safety of that bishop through evil practices, but, forgetful of the Church that had been his patron, he also condemned it.

Against this ungrateful man the authority of the canons and laws is rightly directed: punished by the loss of an undeserved freedom, he is to be recalled to the bond of slavery. For the status of such people, who strive to bring down their bishop or patron Church rather than preserve them, ought to fall rather than be maintained, so that a harmful freedom may become a salutary servitude and those who have learned to be proud in acquired freedom may learn obedience in subjection.

**IX.** At the ninth session we learned that certain members of our college, contrary to ecclesiastical custom, had appointed laymen as stewards over divine affairs. Accordingly, after considering the matter together, we choose that each of us should appoint a steward from his own clergy, in accordance with the decrees of the fathers of Chalcedon [Col. 0599C].

For it is unbecoming that a layman should be the bishop’s deputy and that secular persons should judge in the Church. In one and the same office, the profession should not be different—a matter also prohibited in the divine Law, where Moses says: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” (Deuteronomy 22:10), that is, you shall not join people of different professions in one office.

Therefore we too ought to obey the divine books and the commands of the holy Fathers, establishing that those who are associated with bishops in the administration of the Church should not differ either in profession or in dress. Those whose pursuits and vows are different cannot cohere or be joined together. If, from now on, any bishop chooses to have an ecclesiastical matter administered through a lay procurator, or believes that it may be governed without a steward’s testimony, he shall indeed, as a despiser of the canons and a defrauder of ecclesiastical property, be judged guilty by Christ concerning the goods of the poor, and shall also remain liable to the council.

### X

[Col. 0600A]

In the tenth action, at the request of the fathers of the monasteries, we decreed by common agreement that the monasteries recently founded in the province of Baetica, like those which are ancient, should remain firmly established with immovable and unshaken stability. But if any one of us, or of the priests who succeed us, should attempt either to strip any monastery by force of greed, or to tear it down through some pretended fraud, or to dissolve it—far be this from us—let him remain under anathema and be excluded from the kingdom of God. Let no good of faith or work benefit him for salvation, since he has destroyed the path of so great and salutary a way of life. Moreover, let all the bishops of the province of Baetica, assembled together, suspend that sacrilegious destroyer of his own assembly from communion, and restore the monastery that has been torn down together with its possessions, so that what one man has impiously overthrown, all may rebuild.

### XI

[Cols. 0600B–0600C]

In the eleventh action, by common agreement we decreed that the monasteries of virgins in the province of Baetica should be governed under the administration and protection of monks. For we then provide what is salutary for virgins dedicated to Christ when we choose for them spiritual fathers, by whose governance they may be protected and by whose teachings they may be built up. Nevertheless, this precaution concerning the monks must be maintained: removed from familiarity with the virgins, they must not be permitted to approach even the vestibule freely. Nor shall the abbot, or the man placed in charge, be permitted to speak with the virgins of Christ about anything pertaining to the formation of morals except through the woman who presides over them; nor should they frequently speak even with her alone, but only in the presence of two or three sisters, so that the visits may be rare and the conversation altogether brief.

For far be it from us to wish monks—something that it is itself unlawful even to say—to be familiar with the virgins of Christ. Rather, in accordance with what the commands of the rules and canons admonish, we assign them as their governors while keeping them far apart and separated. We decree, however, that one of the most proven monks be chosen, whose responsibility shall be to attend to their rural or urban estates, construct buildings, and provide whatever else is necessary for the monastery, so that the women devoted to Christ, concerned only for the benefit of their souls, may serve solely in divine worship and holy works.

Certainly, the man proposed by the abbot must be approved by the judgment of his bishop. As for clothing, let the virgins have it made by those from whom they expect protection, and from those same persons let them again—as has been said—receive the fruits of their labor and the assistance of their administration. But if any of the monks should despise this arrangement or neglect it through any kind of sluggish laxity, let them know that their recklessness and arrogance must be punished by the penalty of excommunication.

### XII

[Cols. 0600D–0601A]

In the twelfth action, a certain man of the Acephali heresy, Syrian by nationality, entered our presence, claiming—as he himself asserted—to be a bishop. He denied the distinct property of the two natures in Christ and maintained that the divinity was passible. When the confusion of so great an error had become evident to our understanding, we produced for him testimonies concerning the incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ and recited the judgments of the holy Fathers. We then invited him, with priestly moderation and every form of exhortation, to return to the rectitude of the true faith.

For a long time, through many and prolonged disputes, he stubbornly resisted these saving admonitions. At last, instructed by divine grace, he renounced his own heresy before all who were standing present and confessed the two natures and one person in our one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, believing that the nature of the divinity is impassible and that he assumed the weaknesses of suffering and the cross in his humanity alone.

Thus converted and received, he publicly produced a confession of the faith he had embraced, together with an affirmation of it, and appeared cleansed of all his errors. Rejoicing at such an outcome, we gave thanks to Christ, because divine grace had brought him back from the depravity of heresy to the rectitude of the faith. We desire that, remaining in the faith of Christ, he may be preserved in it purely and most devoutly.

### XIII

[Cols. 0601A–0606A]

In the thirteenth proceeding, we thought it necessary to give a brief account for the refutation of those same heretics who, in their delirium, confuse the two natures of Christ after the union and assert in him a passible substance of divinity. Against their blasphemies, we must demonstrate the distinct property of the two natures in the one person of Christ and show that his passion took place in the assumption of humanity alone. Thus, if any foolish persons have been deceived by the error of this opinion, they may come to their senses when they read these things and firmly hold the truth of the right faith.

For without doubt there are many who, according to the Apostle’s saying, “having itching ears, turn away their hearing from the truth and turn instead to myths.” Therefore, as the immaculate faith and the holy Church of God teach, we confess that our Lord Jesus Christ was born timelessly from God the Father, and temporally was brought forth as a man from the womb of the glorious virgin Mary. For this reason, existing in one person, he has two natures: the divinity in which he was begotten before the ages, and the humanity in which he was brought forth in the last days. In the one he exists according to the form of God, in the other according to the form of a servant; in the one he remains equal to the Father, in the other, without sin, like our condition; in the one inviolate, in the other passible; in the one, from which he could not die, in the other, in which he accepted death.

The distinction of these two natures must first be drawn from the writings of the Law, then from the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic writings, and set before the pagans, so that what we assert may be confirmed not by arguments but by examples from Scripture.

The Law demonstrates both natures in the one and same person of our Savior in this way. It shows the divine nature when the Lord says to Moses: “Behold, I send my angel, who will go before you; observe him and hear his voice” (Exod. 23:20), “because my name is in him.” It shows the human nature when the same Lord says to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. 22:18), that is, in the flesh of Christ, which descended from the lineage of Abraham.

Prophecy in the Psalms displays both natures under the one and same person of Christ in this way: the divine, according to the words, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3); the human, according to these words: “A man was born in her, and he himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5). Again, the divine, according to: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44:2); the human, according to: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44:8).

Prophecy in Proverbs likewise declares both natures in the one and same person of Christ: the divine, according to the words, “Before the hills he begot me” (Job 15:7); the human, according to: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (Prov. 8:22). Again, the divine, according to: “The abysses were not yet, and I was already conceived” (Prov. 8:24); the human, according to: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. 24:3), namely, the temple of his body, in which the Son of God was to dwell, when the Word became flesh.

Prophecy in Isaiah demonstrates both natures under the one and same person of Christ in this way: the divine nature, according to: “Shall I, who make others give birth, myself not give birth? says the Lord” (Isa. 66:9); the human nature, according to: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14). Again, the divinity, according to: “Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise together” (Isa. 45:8). Elsewhere, the humanity, according to: “A little one is born for us” (Isa. 9:6); the divinity, according to: “A son is given to us” (ibid.).

For the little one who was born pertains to Christ’s assumed human nature, because he was made man; but the son who was given pertains to the divinity, because he is the Son of God. And to show that in both natures there is one person, that of the little one born and the son given, he added: “His name shall be called Angel of great counsel, Mighty God, Prince of the age to come” (Isa. 9:6).

In the Gospel also, in the one and same Christ, the divine nature is signified by: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3); the human nature by: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6:38).

The Apostle Paul likewise expresses the nature of divinity in the one and same Christ when he says: “He is the firstborn of all creation; he is before all, and all things consist in him” (Col. 1:17). He declares the nature of humanity when he says: “He is the head of the body, the Church” (Col. 1:18), and elsewhere: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6).

By saying, “although he was in the form of God,” he shows in him the nature of divine majesty; by adding, “he took the form of a servant,” he signifies the nature of humanity. Again: “Although he was rich, he became poor” (2 Cor. 8:9), so that by his poverty we might become rich. Where he says, “although he was rich,” the glory of the divine nature is revealed; where he adds, “he became poor,” the submission of human weakness and the assumption of the condition of a servant are demonstrated.

Likewise, at the very beginning of the apostolic Creed, the distinction of the two natures is shown in the one and same Christ: the divinity from the Father, when it says, “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, and in Christ Jesus his only Son, our Lord”; the humanity from his mother, when it adds, “born of the Holy Spirit from the womb of the virgin Mary.”

Behold, from both Testaments there are two natures in Christ, one of divinity and the other of humanity. These two together made one person, because there is one and the same mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

Now, concerning the passion of this same Savior and our Lord Jesus Christ, which he endured in his humanity alone and not in his divinity, the authority of the Law and the prophets, as stated above, as well as the preaching of the Gospels and the Apostles, must be brought forward.

The Law speaks of the passion of Christ’s body in this way: “He will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Gen. 49:11). What is the garment here, and what is the robe, except the flesh of Christ adorned with the blood of his passion? For this flesh alone endured the insults of the cross; the majesty of the divine nature felt no injury.

The prophet likewise asserts in the Psalms that Christ’s passion occurred in the flesh alone: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21:17). Here injury is understood not of the divinity but only of the body. By the indication of the limbs, flesh alone is declared to have been hung upon and fastened to the wood by nails, just as it is also read in Jeremiah: “Come, let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. 11:19), that is, the cross into his body.

For the divinity could not be suspended from wood; only the humanity was fastened to and hung upon the cross. Elsewhere, the endurance of death suffered by his flesh is shown when it is said: “My flesh will rest in hope” (Ps. 15:9), since in Christ the flesh alone, having died through the frailty of mortality, awaited the hope of its resurrection and, as he adds, was to be received without corruption: “Nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Acts 2:27).

Solomon, preaching in the Song of Songs concerning the passion of Christ’s flesh, says: “My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers with a drop” (Song 5:5). Here it is specifically shown that only the flesh of Christ was pierced through the hands and fingers by the stake, just as it is read in Psalm 118: “Fasten my flesh with the nails of your fear” (Ps. 118:120).

Isaiah foretold that Christ, in the humanity that appeared, would suffer the injury of the passion in this way: “A man,” he says, “in affliction and knowing how to bear weakness; truly, he himself bore our infirmities” (Isa. 53:4). Who is “he himself” except, unmistakably, the man? For the nature of God could not suffer or fail in him; rather, the man bore in him the passion and death, in whom death itself has its condition.

When he said that he would come from Edom, with garments stained from Bozrah, he added: “Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” (Isa. 63:2). What did he wish to show by the garment and clothing red like that of those treading the winepress, except the passion of Christ’s flesh alone, stained with the blood of the cross? Hence, in the very passion Christ is clothed in a scarlet cloak, so that the image of blood might be demonstrated only in the flesh.

Jeremiah likewise speaks of Christ offering his body in the passion: “I was not rebellious,” he says, “nor did I contradict; I gave my body to those who struck me” (Isa. 50:6). He did not say “the divinity,” which does not know how to endure passion. Again: “I gave my back to scourges and my cheeks to those who struck” (ibid.). This too refers to the suffering of the flesh, not to an injury of the divinity.

And Zechariah says: “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10). Whom else could this mean without doubt except the man whom the Jews crucified and whom they will see judging in the flesh?

Behold, this has been proclaimed from the Law and the prophets. The truth of this faith is so powerful that neither tyrants have been able to confuse it by their cruelty, nor the deceitful trickery of heretics to overthrow it, nor the false pretense of hypocrites to diminish it.

Let us pass from there to the Gospels. There let us seek Christ, the Son of God, to have borne the weaknesses of suffering and the injury of the cross in the flesh alone. He himself says to his disciples: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again” (Luke 18:31, 33).

All of this, spoken of Christ according to the man, pertains not to the substance of the divinity but to the nature of the flesh. This is also taught in what follows, when the Jews say to Christ: “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” (John 2:18). And Jesus said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). He said this about the temple of his body.

Likewise, in his passion, when he rebuked the betrayer and said: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48), whom does the betrayer signify that he was handing over except the man whom they also seized? It was not the divinity, which they were unable to recognize because of their blindness and unbelief.

The blessed Apostle Paul likewise asserts that Christ endured the cross in the man alone: “As a man,” he says, “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. 2:8). He therefore said “as a man,” so that by the designation “man” the distinction of the passible nature might be indicated. Confirming this elsewhere, he says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me? He is not weak toward you, but powerful among you. For although he was crucified from weakness, he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:3–4).

Christ therefore suffered and died, but from our weakness; he lives, however, impassible and immortal, from his own power, which is so great that it neither receives passion nor admits death into itself.

The Apostle Peter also, chief of the Apostles, proclaims that Christ’s punishment was completed in the body alone: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; by whose wound we have been healed” (1 Pet. 2:24). Shortly afterward: “Since Christ therefore suffered in the flesh…”

Therefore, if Christ suffered in the flesh, he was crucified not according to God but according to man. It has become perfectly clear that what the Son of God suffered and that he died belonged only to the body, not to the divinity.

For these things are alien to him, as the prophet testifies concerning him: “The eternal God, the Lord, who created the ends of the earth, will not labor and will not grow weak” (Isa. 40:28); and in the Psalm: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:28). For humanity alone bore all the weaknesses in Christ.

The flesh had the cries of an infant, not the divinity. The flesh was wrapped in swaddling clothes, not the divinity. The flesh received food. The flesh passed through the changes of the ages. For the fact that he became weary, that he hungered, that he slept, that he wept, that he was sorrowful when approaching the passion, and finally that he endured the passion itself and the condition of death—all this pertains to the weakness of humanity, not to the incomprehensible substance of divinity.

For there is one Christ, God and man, flesh and Word. From that by which he is God, he has immortality; from that by which he is man, he endured passion; from that by which he is flesh, he died; from that by which he is Word, he is eternal.

For the divinity cannot be passible in him who is equal in nature to the power of the Father’s glory. Hence the Father is dishonored when the nature of divinity is believed to be passible in the Son. If the substance of the Father and the Son is one, then, just as the Father is immortal, so also is the Son immortal. “I and the Father are one.” Just as there is no death in the Father, so there is no death in the Son of God. And if it is true that “all that the Father has is mine,” then the Father’s immortality is shared with the Son.

When the Apostle says concerning the ignorance of unbelievers, “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8), this does not mean that the Lord of glory was crucified as though the nature of divinity were passible. Rather, because Christ is one in both natures, the Lord of glory is said to have suffered according to the assumed form of man.

Conversely, there is this statement: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.” He could not have descended from heaven except as the Son of God alone, before that same one became the Son of Man.

Because of the unity of the person, therefore, things that are proper to God are also referred in Christ to the man, and things that belong to man are ascribed to the divinity. Thus, when he is said to suffer and die, this is proper not to the divinity but to the flesh. Nevertheless, because of the unity of the person, the same God is proclaimed to have been born of the virgin, to have suffered, and to have died—but through the weakness of our flesh, not through the power of his divinity.

When the same Apostle says: “For if we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:10), the Son of God is said to have died in the same way that martyrs are said to have suffered and died, although their souls were not killed in the suffering of the body, as the Word of Truth testifies: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

Here it must be understood that if the souls of martyrs cannot be extinguished by punishments when their bodies have been killed, how could God, who is the creator of souls, have suffered the destruction of death through the cross of the flesh?

This is also declared more clearly elsewhere, when the same Son of God says: “I have authority to lay down my soul, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:17). If the divinity itself had died, I ask who restored his soul. It is therefore foolish to apply the passion of the cross to the divine nature; it belongs only to what is created and human.

The flesh alone felt the destruction of the cross; the flesh alone endured the lance; from it alone flowed blood and water; it alone died; it alone was placed in the tomb; it alone was raised on the third day; it was also glorified and ascended into heaven. In it he will come to judge in the glory of the Father, judging the living and the dead.

After producing the testimonies of the New and Old Testaments in which the two natures of Christ were revealed as subsisting in one person, and in which his passion appeared to have been completed in the man alone, it was then necessary to append the judgments of the holy Fathers who shone with great glory in sacred writings. Thus their tradition also makes perfectly clear that our Lord Jesus Christ subsists from two natures and one person, and that he accepted death and passion in the flesh alone.

[Cols. 0606A–0609B]

Saint Hilary, in his exposition of the Epistle to Timothy, speaks as follows:

“For when Scripture says ‘the man Christ,’ and when it says ‘Christ died,’ and when it says ‘the Word became flesh,’ the statement must not be stripped of its proper explanations by the fraudulent interpretation of the reader. Where it says ‘the man Christ,’ the mediator of God and human beings comes first: from God, man; both one, and mediator between man and God, confessing in himself both natures. Where it says ‘Christ died,’ the one who rose again and who is at the right hand of God is being designated. In his death there is the weakness of our flesh; in his resurrection, his power; in the agreement of God, his dignity.”

Saint Ambrose likewise asserts in his exposition of the Gospel according to Luke:

“For Christ ascended not his own cross but ours, and that death was not the death of the divinity but of the man.”

A little later he says:

“For Christ is all, and in Christ all, and Christ in each. Yet the flesh dies so that it may rise again.”

In the same book, explaining other passages, he says:

“‘My soul is sorrowful’; and elsewhere: ‘Now my soul is greatly troubled.’ It is not, therefore, the one who assumes that is troubled, but what is assumed. The soul is subject to sufferings, while the divinity is free; for the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. It is not he himself who is sorrowful, but the soul. Wisdom is not sorrowful, nor the divine substance, but the soul. He assumed my body; he did not deceive me, so that one thing might be and another appear.”

Saint Athanasius, in the treatise that he wrote on the birth of Christ, says:

“Let our faith, therefore, most beloved brothers, consist in this, and let our whole salvation and life rest upon this: that we believe that God the Son of God was first begotten invisibly by God the Father before all ages; then that he was born from the virgin Mary according to man; that according to this man he suffered, died, was buried, rose from the dead, and ascended into heaven.”

The same author, in his exposition of the faith, says:

“The Word is born from the virgin Mary, receiving an animal body; but the Word was not confined by the flesh, rather he was in the flesh and above the flesh. And just as he is the foreknower of God, so he is the power of God and the truth of God. He suffered in human flesh, but the Word of God is impassible. In the passion, the man dies so that he might give life to the first-formed human being who had fallen through disobedience.”

Saint Gregory, writing to Cledonius, says:

“For there are two natures in Christ, God and man, but not two Sons, nor two gods.”

The same author, in a sermon on the Son, says:

“I admonish you in one brief chapter: ascribe the higher things to the divinity and to that nature which is shown to be superior to sufferings and to the body; but attribute the lower things to human nature, which was assumed from the portion of our weakness.”

Again, in the fourth book against Eunomius:

“And lest anyone apply the passion of the cross to the incorruptible nature of the divinity, he corrects such an error more clearly elsewhere, calling the mediator himself of God and human beings both man and God, so that, when two things are said of one, what is fitting for each may be understood. With respect to God there is impassibility; with respect to humanity, the dispensation of suffering.”

Saint Basil, likewise, writes in the fourth book against Eunomius:

“What does ‘The Lord created me’ mean, and ‘Before all the hills he begot me’? Here, what he says ‘begot’ must be understood of the Son of God; but what he says ‘created’ refers to that part in which he is in the form of a servant, so that he might show both natures in one person.”

Saint Cyril says in his first letter to Succensus:

“Therefore, as far as understanding and faith are concerned, and as far as the eyes of the soul are concerned, we say that the Only-Begotten, in the manner in which he was incarnate, consists of two natures; but we confess one Son and Christ, the Lord God, the incarnate Word and the man who was made.”

Again, in his second letter to the same Succensus, he says:

“Since Christ the Son is one alone, the same one is both God and man, perfect in divinity and likewise perfect in humanity. We do not say that the Only-Begotten Son of God, insofar as he is understood and exists as God, suffered in his own nature, but that the earthly nature suffered. For it is necessary to preserve both truths concerning the one true Son: that he did not suffer according to his divinity, yet that the same one is said to have suffered according to his humanity, for his flesh itself suffered.”

Again, in his exposition of Leviticus:

“Consider once more the whole mystery of our Savior in these matters, and the purification that takes place through holy baptism. For two birds are commanded to be taken, living and clean, so that through the birds you may understand the heavenly man together with God, divided according to reason into two natures, each receiving what is appropriate to it.”

Saint Augustine likewise says:

“For in that assumption neither of the two was converted and changed into the other. The divinity was not changed into a creature, nor did the creature receive any increase of divinity by being changed into the divinity. Far be it from us to suppose that the ineffable and incomprehensible fullness can receive increase. Therefore each nature of the Son of God remains, and there is one person.”

Again, in his work against Maximus:

“If, then, you attend to the distinctions of the natures, the Son of God descended from heaven, while the Son of Man was crucified. If you attend to the unity of the person, the Son descended from heaven, and the Son was crucified on earth.”

In the following passage he says:

“Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day. Where does he rise except in that which was able to fall? Where did he rise except in that in which he died? Seek death in the Word: it could never have existed there. Seek death in the flesh: plainly, it was there, and it was there because the death was real.”

A little later:

“Why are you surprised? Certainly Christ is life. Seek dead life: neither the soul died, nor did the Word die. The flesh alone died. Why? So that death might die in it.”

The same author, in his exposition of the Gospel of John:

“Who, then, is the one through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? The same Christ, but in the form of a servant.”

The blessed Leo, bishop of the apostolic see, likewise says in his letter to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople:

“Therefore, with the property of each nature preserved and the two coming together into one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by strength, mortality by eternity. And, in order to discharge the debt of our condition, the inviolate nature was united to a passible nature, so that the one and same mediator of God and human beings, Christ Jesus, could both die by virtue of one nature and could not die by virtue of the other.”

“Thus, in the complete and perfect nature of a true human being, true God was born: wholly in what was his own, wholly in what was ours.”

A little later:

“The one who, remaining in the form of God, made man was himself made man in the form of a servant. Each nature retains its own property without defect. Just as the form of a servant does not take away the form of God, so the form of God does not diminish the form of a servant.”

Again, shortly afterward:

“For each form acts, in communion with the other, according to what is proper to it: the Word doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines with miracles; the other submits to injuries. And just as the Word does not depart from equality with the Father’s glory, so the flesh does not abandon the nature of our race.”

Saint Fulgentius, in the book that he wrote on the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, says among other things:

“I therefore tell you, in accordance with the tradition of the holy Fathers, that we confess our Lord Jesus Christ to be one person or substance in two unmixed natures, that is, in divinity and humanity.”

Later he says:

“If anyone therefore refuses, or hesitates, to believe or proclaim that in our Lord Jesus Christ there are either two natures or one person; or if anyone refuses to confess that he is the same God and man—that is, the Word truly incarnate and truly born from the virgin Mary for our salvation—he is found and shown to be outside the Catholic faith, as one ungratefully resisting the sacrament of human redemption.”

A little later:

“The Word became flesh: one from both and in both, that is, in the human and divine nature, persisting altogether gloriously from the beginning. Thus, whether anyone removes Christ’s humanity from his divinity or takes away divinity from his humanity, he dissolves Christ by sacrilegious unbelief and blasphemous teaching.”

Again, shortly afterward:

“Christ suffered for us in the flesh, he who alone was born from God the Father, the impassible God. We therefore truly believe that Christ himself, the Son of God, tasted death for us in the flesh, while the immortality of his divinity remained intact.”

Again:

“For there is not one God and another man, but the same one Christ is God and man. Therefore the same God Christ who accepted his death in the flesh is also the same man Christ who destroyed his death through the divinity. The same Christ, the Son of God, who could not die in his divinity, died in the flesh, which immortal God assumed as mortal. And therefore Christ the Son of God, having died in the flesh, rose again, because when he died in the flesh he did not lose the immortality of his divinity.

“Thus, after his resurrection, just as he truly demonstrated the solidity of his flesh in the real scars and in the real eating of fish and honey, so, entering while the doors were closed, he showed in himself the true power of eternal divinity. In this way it was recognized both that Christ’s weakness in dying was natural to him and that majesty was likewise naturally present in the one who died.”

These teachings, which both divine Scripture and the eloquence of the holy Fathers have taught, we have briefly inserted into our decrees and set forth, demonstrating the twofold nature of flesh and divinity in the one person of our Lord and Savior, and also that the same one suffered in the nature belonging to the body but did not suffer in the nature belonging to the divinity.

[Cols. 0609B–0610A]

Therefore, with one accord, we appended our individual subscriptions to the definition as its confirmation.

I, Isidore, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Spalis, have subscribed.

I, Bisinus, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Liberitania, have subscribed.

I, Rufinus, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Asidona, have subscribed.

I, Cambra, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Italica, have subscribed.

I, Fidentius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Tucci, have subscribed.

I, Theodulphus, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Córdoba, have subscribed.

I, Honorius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Málaga, have subscribed.

You have here, diligent reader, up to this point—under the authorship of Isidore of Spalis—the order that those who decide to celebrate a council ought to observe; likewise, the canons of the Apostles, as well as the decrees of thirty pontiffs, from Clement namely to Sylvester; and finally, the acts of fifty-two councils.

### 150

[Col. 0610B]

With the councils of the holy Fathers arranged up to this point, there follow the decrees of the Roman bishops, the constitutions of the prelates of the aforesaid apostolic see, which concern the rule of faith or ecclesiastical discipline and have been collected in this book with diligent care. Thus, the decrees of each pontiff, insofar as we have found them, are prefaced by their proper titles under the sequence of each one’s letter, in the same manner in which the canons of the ancient Fathers were arranged through our effort above, so that the diligence of the reader may more easily understand them when he attends to their division into separate chapters.

## HERE BEGIN EXCERPTS FROM THE DECREES OF SAINT SYLVESTER, POPE

[Column 0609]

[Col. 0609B] In the time of Saint Sylvester, pope, and Constantine, the most devout Augustus, a great council was held at Nicaea in Bithynia. Three hundred and eighteen Catholic bishops were duly assembled there at the summons of the same Pope Sylvester; they set forth the complete, Catholic, undefiled faith and condemned Arius, Photinus, Sabellius, and their followers.

At that same time, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, the day on which the great council mentioned above was assembled at Nicaea, after the pope’s summons had been canonically issued, he himself convened in the city of Rome, together with the council of the aforesaid Augustus Constantine, two hundred and fifty-eight bishops. He again condemned both Callistus and Arius, as well as Photinus and Sabellius, and decreed that a penitent Arian presbyter was not to be received unless the bishop of that place reconciled him and, through the imposition of episcopal hands, confirmed him with sacred chrism by the grace of the Holy Spirit—a grace that cannot be given by heretics.

With the agreement and subscription of all, it was also decreed that no layman should dare bring a charge against a cleric; that a presbyter should not bring any accusation against a bishop, a deacon against a presbyter, a subdeacon against a deacon, an acolyte against a subdeacon, an exorcist against an acolyte, a lector against an exorcist, or a doorkeeper against a lector; and that a bishop should not be condemned except by seventy-two [persons]. Nor should the supreme bishop be judged by anyone, since it is written: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Matt. 10:24).

A cardinal presbyter should not be condemned without forty-four witnesses; a cardinal deacon established in the city of Rome should not be condemned without twenty-six; and a subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, lector, or doorkeeper should not be condemned except, as it is written, by seven witnesses.

The witnesses and accusers, moreover, must be free from every disgrace, have wives and children, and be entirely professing Christ. No one should accept the testimony of a layman against a cleric. No one should presume to examine any cleric publicly except in the church. No cleric, whether deacon or presbyter, should enter a court for any cause, nor presume to plead a case before a judge wearing the military belt, since every court is so called from bloodshed and the sacrifice of idols. If any cleric accusing another cleric should enter a court, let him receive anathema.

Among other matters, the aforesaid council unanimously decreed that no one should presume to celebrate the altar sacrifice on silk or dyed cloth, but only on pure linen consecrated by the bishop—linen produced and woven from the earth—for our Lord Jesus Christ’s body was buried in a clean linen shroud.

If anyone desired to serve or advance in the church, he was first to be a doorkeeper, then a lector, and afterward an exorcist, for the periods established by the bishop; then an acolyte for five years, a subdeacon for five years, a guardian of the martyrs for five years, a deacon for five years, and a presbyter for three years. He was to be tested in every respect, so that he might even have a good reputation among those outside; he was to be the husband of one wife, who nevertheless had to have been blessed by a priest. If he was proved worthy, and the votes of the people and clergy concurred canonically, he was to be consecrated by the bishops. Thereafter neither the clergy nor the people should disturb him, because bishops, who are called the thrones of God, must not be torn apart. Concerning them blessed Paul the apostle says:

“Do not rebuke an elder, but appeal to him as to a father” (1 Tim. 5:1).

For we read that the Lord himself said: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Matt. 10:24). This means that no one should claim for himself, to the injury of teachers, the authority to teach, nor by any scheme disparage or defame the Lord’s disciples—that is, the successors of the apostles—for an injury done to teachers concerns Christ, in whose place they serve as ambassadors. How greatly those who presume to do this grieve the Lord, the Savior himself declares in the Gospel, saying:

“It would be better for the one who causes one of these little ones to stumble to be plunged into the depths of the sea, with a millstone hung around his neck” (Matt. 18:6).

If such a punishment is promised to those who cause the Lord’s disciples to stumble, it must be carefully considered what will befall them in the future, and how much danger may remain before the Lord for those who refuse to render these services to his ministers. They will be able to prove this only if they fear God—those who do not fear to practice such things—and if, having imposed upon themselves an evil silence, they henceforth guard themselves from such conduct. For it does a person no good to perform other good deeds unless his mind is recalled from iniquity and his tongue restrained from slander.

Therefore the Prophet says:

“Restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit; turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:14).

No one who does good wishes to harm another by word or deed, and so forth.

At this council, by the unanimous agreement of all, it was decreed that no presbyter should presume to celebrate Mass except in places consecrated by the bishop who thereafter wished him to share in his priesthood.

Moved by pious compassion, this most holy pope, in response to synodal petitions and through apostolic authority, recalled to communion many who had been excommunicated by other bishops and expelled by tyrants, and restored them to the churches in which they had formerly been instituted, after satisfaction had been made. He received them after their purification, providing an example for the future of rescuing priests from the hands of their persecutors.

He also decreed that no person from overseas should be received among us into the clerical order in any manner unless he had been designated by the signed letters of five bishops.

## THE DECREES OF POPE MARCUS BEGIN.

[Col. 0611]

### Letter of the Egyptian Bishops to Pope Marcus concerning Copies of the Council of Nicaea, since the Arians had Burned Their Copies

[Col. 0611B]

To the holy lord Marcus, worthy of veneration as the summit of the apostolic dignity, pope of the holy Roman and apostolic see and of the universal Church: Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt.

We do not doubt that you have learned how much and how grievous a persecution we suffer daily from the heretics, especially the Arians, and how intensely we are persecuted by them, so that life itself has become burdensome to us. For, suddenly and unexpectedly, they recently rushed upon us; and while we were fleeing, in accordance with the Lord’s command, which says, “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10:23), they were unable to seize us because we withdrew to avoid the slaughter of the people. But they plundered everything we possessed, devastating it so completely that they left us neither books nor ecclesiastical clothing, nor other ornaments, nor any remaining utensils.

They burned our books down to the last, leaving not even one iota, and especially burned the Nicene council, through which the clergy and people were instructed—and had already been instructed—in the true faith, doing this as an insult to us and to all Christians. Therefore we beg you, most blessed Father, since we do not doubt that complete copies of the Council of Nicaea are preserved with you, to send us, under secure guarantee, those copies that belonged to your predecessor Sylvester, of holy memory.

For when we attended the aforesaid council with Alexander, of blessed memory and worthy of God, our pontiff—that is, the bishop of the great city of Alexandria—in the office of deacons, as witnesses to our repentance, the seventy chapters mentioned below were sent to the aforesaid Pope Sylvester through the blessed men Victor and Vincent, presbyters and representatives of the apostolic see, with a guarantee attached.

When we asked, eighty chapters were treated in the aforesaid council: forty were issued by the Greeks in the Greek language, and forty by the Latins, likewise issued in the Latin language. But it seemed good to the three hundred and eighteen Fathers assembled in that holy council, filled with the Holy Spirit—especially to the aforementioned Alexander and the representatives of the apostolic see—that ten chapters should be joined together and inserted in other suitable places, and that, in the pattern of the sixty disciples and of the languages of the whole world, sixty chapters should be made of so great and excellent a council. These would instruct the whole Christian world, so that all who lived under the priestly and Christian name might be governed by one faith and one priestly and clerical rule, and no one might disagree with his head.

Now, as has been said, the enemies of God’s holy Church, especially the Arians, by whom we are daily attacked, crushed, and oppressed, have burned the aforementioned seventy chapters of the Council of Nicaea. I had brought them from the aforesaid council, after they had been produced there by the command of my lord Alexander and by the decree of all the bishops; I had also read and copied them before everyone. We desire that, through the authority of the Church of your holy see, which is the mother and head of all the Churches, we may receive them through the present envoys, for the correction and restoration of the orthodox faithful.

We truly know that the heart of your apostolate is so inflamed by the grace of the Holy Spirit that you come to the aid of all the oppressed—how much more, then, to us, who, although of a lowly order, are nevertheless yours and obedient to you, together with all those entrusted to us, and are so now and always wish to remain so.

Therefore it is fitting and necessary that you provide us, without delay, with these things that we ask, and with whatever else you recognize as necessary according to the wisdom that the Most High has granted you, so that the filth of such great misery may be wiped from the minds of the faithful. May a wound driven into the body be healed, as it were, by the salutary remedy sought amid such great misery. Thus, relying on divine assistance and strengthened by your authority and aid, may we be able to escape the evasions of our adversaries and, with an unashamed face, stand before the eternal Judge, unshaken by anyone’s deceit, and be worthy to hear Christ’s voice:

“Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25:23).

And the subscription:

May the Lord preserve your holy apostolate, which prays for us, for many years.

### Reply of Pope Marcus concerning the Sending of the Chapters of the Council of Nicaea to Athanasius and all the Bishops of Egypt

[Col. 0613B]
