To the venerable lords and brothers Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt: Marcus, bishop of the holy Roman and apostolic see and of the universal Church.

I grieve, brothers, and am greatly distressed over your affliction, but I am exceedingly consoled that, though shaken by the wind, you are not a reed, but remain steadfast in faith amid every struggle with storms and whirlwinds. After reading the letter of your fraternity, we recognized the strength of your constancy, which we had known in former times, and we rejoice with you because you vigilantly pursue pastoral care in order to guard the flock, lest the wolves who have entered under the appearance of sheep tear apart the suppliants with bestial savagery. They did not enter so that they might advance through correction, but in order to corrupt what is sound.

Therefore I admonish and exhort your love to strive, with the assistance of divine grace, to bring to completion the good work you have begun, as the voice of truth admonishes:

“Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end” (Matt. 24:13).

For whence does blessed perseverance arise except from the virtue of patience? In accordance with the Apostle, all who desire to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution. This is not to be understood only as persecution carried out against Christian devotion by sword, fire, or any sort of punishment, even though the savagery of persecution may supply all these things. Rather, the dissimilarity of conduct, the obstinacy of the disobedient, and the darts of malicious tongues are among the conflicts by which the common members are continually struck; no portion of the godly is free from such conflict.

Thus they are not free either from dangers or from ease, neither from labor nor from rest. These things, and all the growth of worthy endeavors, together with perseverance in them to the end and the increase of good will, must always be attributed to the grace of Christ, so that God may be perfectly praised at every time in all that we do.

Concerning the true chapters of the Council of Nicaea, which you indicate by your letter that we attended, we made careful inquiries of our own men who attended it together with you. Just as your letter attested, they explained the entire order to us, and testified that your letter was wholly truthful. We did this not because we suspected anything sinister on your part, but so that we, you, and they might thereafter hold one judgment without any hesitation, and so that the holy Roman Church—which has always remained undefiled and, by the Lord’s providence and with the help of the blessed apostle Peter, will remain so in the future—might stand firm and immovable at all times, without any assault by heretics.

When this had been carefully done, we searched the sacred treasury of our apostolic see and found unharmed the same seventy chapters that, as you reported, had been sent to my predecessor Sylvester, of holy memory. We did not send you those very copies, because of the authority and subscription of so many Fathers and of that great council. Instead, we arranged to write back to you through your representatives copies containing similar material, the same number, the same words, and the same subscription, and to send them under definite guarantee and confirmation.

Who would dare refuse such things to his brothers? Through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the Lord has taught us that these matters are not to be neglected by us, but faithfully practiced and distributed, entrusted, and taught to our brothers. This is the living tradition of the apostles; this is true charity, which must be proclaimed and especially loved, cherished, and held confidently by all. This is the holy and apostolic mother Church of all the Churches of Christ, which by the grace of almighty God is proved never to have strayed from the path of apostolic tradition, nor to have yielded to be corrupted by the novelties of heretics. Rather, having received from her founders, the chief apostles of Christ, the rule of the Christian faith at her beginning, she remains undefiled to the very end, according to the divine promise of the Lord and Savior himself, who said in his Gospel to the prince of his disciples:

“Simon,” he said, “behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have returned, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:31).

Therefore let your eminent prudence consider how good it is to persevere in the stewardship entrusted to you, in the right faith, and in resisting heretics and Christ’s rivals, never turning aside from the path of truth. For the Lord and Savior of all, whose faith this is, did not hesitate to die for us and redeemed us with his own blood. He promised that the faith of the blessed Peter would not fail and instructed him to strengthen his brothers. Everyone knows that the apostolic pontiffs who preceded my insignificance have always done this confidently; and although my littleness is unequal and weak, it nevertheless desires, in the ministry entrusted to it by divine favor, to follow in their footsteps.

Woe to us who have received the burden of this ministry if we neglect to preach the truth of our Savior Jesus Christ, which the apostles proclaimed. Woe to us if we suppress the truth in silence, when we are commanded to distribute it to the moneychangers—that is, to instruct and teach the Christian peoples. What shall we say at Christ’s future judgment if we are ashamed to preach the truth of his word? What will become of us when Christ our God, the just Judge, strictly demands an account of the souls entrusted to us and of the office we have received?

Therefore, brothers, I exhort, beseech, and admonish your love to remain vigilant with the diligence you ought and can exercise, in order to seek out the heretics and enemies of God’s holy Church and, with such severity as you are able, to uproot this plague from their minds, lest it spread more widely. For just as the one who diligently carries out what benefits the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive a worthy reward from God, so no one who refuses to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will be able to excuse himself before the Lord’s tribunal for the guilt of negligence.

Given on the twentieth day before the Kalends of November, during the consulship of the most illustrious men Nepotianus and Secundus.

## THE DECREES OF POPE JULIUS BEGIN.

### The Roman Synod Held by Pope Julius and the Other Orthodox Bishops Begins

In the name of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, while the Augusti Constantius and Constans were reigning, in the fourth year, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the sixth indiction, with the holy and most blessed Julius, pope of the apostolic see of the city of Rome, presiding, the sacred and venerable Gospels having been placed before them in the Church of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ called Constantinian, and with the venerable men sitting there and hearing together with him—Benedict, bishop of Aquileia; Rufus, bishop of Carthage; Agapitus, bishop of the church of Ravenna; Julius, bishop of Milan; Lucian, bishop of Mauriana; and the others with them, one hundred and sixteen bishops in all—the aforementioned most holy Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, said:

It is necessary, most blessed brothers, for the holy synod of God and the apostolic synod, assembled here harmoniously and unanimously in the ancient and venerable city of Rome by the will of God and by the grace of the undivided communion of the Holy Spirit, for the sacred confirmation and correction of our faith and of the undefiled discipline of Christians, as you know, to reflect and for all of us to teach together according to the nature of the supreme God and the wisdom of the Father, the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. The voice of Truth bears witness to every person who desires a human and divine nature in him:

“Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me and my words, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:33).

Therefore we ought first to set forth the faith confirmed by the three hundred and eighteen Fathers at the Council of Nicaea, and afterward faithfully discuss whatever is necessary.

Everyone answered with one voice:

For this purpose we have assembled: after this first matter, to do what accords with the will of God; to begin from the foundation, Christ Jesus; and, addressing anew the oppression of our brothers, to labor on their behalf. For while they are grievously afflicted, we cannot breathe freely or rest; while the members are tormented, the rest of the body can have neither peace nor quiet. This, then, is the faith treated by the universal Council of Nicaea.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, was incarnate, and was made human; who suffered. He rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead.

And we believe in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” or, “He was not before he was made,” or, “He was made from things that did not exist,” or who say that he exists from another substance or essence, or that he is created, or that the Son of God is changeable—the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes such persons. This faith the venerable three hundred and eighteen acknowledged and confirmed; agreeing unanimously, they set it forth clearly in writing.

For our Lord, sending his disciples to preach, said:

“Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

Concerning these things we affirm that this is what we hold and believe, and that we have held and believed this from the beginning. We will persevere in this faith even unto death, anathematizing every godless heresy. We testify before almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ, with truth, that we have held all these things in our heart and soul from the time when we came to know ourselves, and that we now hold and confess them.

These matters having thus been stated at the outset, the unbegotten nature of the Father is distinct; but it must be proclaimed that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, since the Son of God has no equality in any respect with created things, but is wholly like the Father who begot him. He is not from any other substance or essence, but from the Father, before all things.

For the impious and wicked, godless doctrines of Arius and those who agreed with him were carefully examined, and, by the present decree of all, it pleased the council to anathematize his impious sect, together with the wicked and godless words and names he used when blaspheming the Son of God, saying that he was from things that did not exist and, again, that there was a time when he did not exist.

How could he have existed, or how could he again not have existed? They also said that the Son of God was capable of malice and virtue according to free choice, calling him a creature and a work.

The holy and universal council therefore anathematized all these foolish, childish, and blasphemous claims, and did not give even a hearing to the impious sect, to its fear, or to the understanding of its wicked opinions.

You have already heard what outcome all the things done concerning him had, and you will hear more; nor should we perhaps seem to be speaking against a man who bears deserved reproaches for his offense. Those who divide the Son from the Father in substance and divinity, and alienate the Word from the Father, ought to be separated from the Catholic Church and regarded as strangers to the Christian name.

Therefore let them be anathema to us and to all, because they appear to have trafficked in the Word of truth. For the apostolic command says: “If anyone announces to you anything beyond what you received, let him be anathema.”

Declare, therefore, that no one is to communicate with them. There is no fellowship between light and darkness; drive them far away from everyone, for there is no concord between Christ and Belial.

Guard yourselves, dearest brothers, so that you neither write to them nor receive their writings. Strive also, dearest brothers and fellow ministers, as though present in spirit, to consent to our council and to establish by your subscription that one harmony be preserved everywhere by all our fellow ministers.

But we renounce and cast far beyond the boundaries of the Catholic Church those who do not affirm that Christ is God, but say: “He is not true God, because he is the Son; yet he is not truly the Son, lest he be both begotten and unbegotten.” For they claim to understand “begotten” in this way, because they said: “What is begotten has been made.”

And although Christ existed before the ages, they gave him a beginning and an end—something that does not belong to time, but which he possesses before the ages.

Let us pray together for ourselves and for all the other oppressed brothers, that they may be rescued unharmed and preserved undefiled; and may the things that have pleased God remain firm through our Lord Jesus Christ, accomplished according to the good will of God and the Father in the Holy Spirit, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

The consubstantial Trinity is eternal.

Given on the Kalends of November, in the fourth consulship of Felicianus and Maximianus.

### Admonitory Letter of Pope Julius to the Eastern Bishops concerning the Affairs of Athanasius and the Excesses Committed against the Roman Church

To all the venerable brothers, the Eastern bishops: Julius.

It would have been fitting for you, brothers, to instruct others in ecclesiastical disciplines, and not to accuse those who contrive such things, since John the Baptist says: “You shall shake down no one, and you shall bring no false accusation” (Luke 3:14), and so forth. The Apostle Paul also instructs us concerning this matter, saying: “Brothers, if anyone is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Gal. 6:1), and so forth. Elsewhere the Apostle Peter says:

“Be all of one mind in prayer, compassionate, loving the brotherhood, merciful, modest, humble, not returning evil for evil or insult for insult, but, on the contrary, blessing, because you were called to this, so that you may inherit a blessing. For whoever desires to love life and to see good days, let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good, let him seek peace [Col. 0618A] and pursue it, because the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (1 Pet. 3:8–12).

What could be worse, brothers, than that the priests of the Lord—152 who ought to be free from every defilement of evil and from injury to all Christians—should, even more, pursue brothers and fellow bishops, whom they ought to protect and assist against ambushes and whom they ought above all to cherish and love, seeking to drive them out and deprive them of communion? Do you not remember the wisdom that says: “For perverse thoughts separate people from God” (Prov. 15:26)? If perverse thoughts separate people from God, how much more do wicked deeds? What is more wicked than that anyone should attempt to turn away from, persecute, or destroy those of whom the Lord says: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” [Col. 0618B] (Zech. 2:8)?

Proven virtue, however, bears, protects, and consoles the oppressed and instructs the foolish. God is the witness of the human heart, the true examiner of every individual conscience, and the hearer of every tongue. The spirit of the Lord has filled the world, “and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice.” Elsewhere the same apostle says:

“God is love. In this the love of God was revealed among us: God sent his only-begotten Son into the world so that we might live through him. This is love—not that we loved God, but that he first loved us and sent his Son as an expiation for our sins. Beloved, if God loved us, we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us. In this we know that we remain in him and he in us: because he has given us of his Spirit. And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God. And we have come to know and believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him. In this love is perfected—not that we loved God, but that he first loved us, because as he is, so are we in this world. There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and whoever fears is not perfected in love. Let us therefore love God, because God first loved us. If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God: ‘Whoever loves God must also love his brother’” (1 John 4:9–21).

Wisdom itself also says:

“The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge, but the mouth of fools boils over with folly. In every place the eyes of the Lord contemplate the good and the evil. A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but the undisciplined one crushes the spirit. The house of the righteous is very strong, but in the fruits of the wicked there is disturbance. The lips of the wise spread knowledge, [Col. 0619A] but the heart of fools is unlike it. The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to the Lord, but the vows of the righteous are pleasing. Whoever follows righteousness is directed by the Lord” (Prov. 15:2–9).

Again, elsewhere:

“The lips of the righteous consider what is pleasing, but the mouth of the wicked speaks perverse things” (Prov. 10:32). “The simplicity of the righteous will guide them, but the treachery of the perverse will destroy them. The righteousness of the upright will deliver them, and the wicked will be caught in their own traps. The righteous will be delivered from distress, and the wicked will be handed over in his place. The deceiver with his mouth tricks his friend, but the righteous will be delivered by knowledge. In the prosperity of the righteous the city will be exalted, and in the destruction of the wicked there will be praise. By the blessing of the righteous the city will be exalted” (Prov. 11:3, 5, 6, 8, 11).

Nor do you consider, you who do not cease persecuting brothers, what the most patient Job says among other things:

“The ear that heard me blessed me, and the eye that saw me bore witness to me, because I had delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I consoled the widow’s heart. I clothed myself with justice and covered myself with it as with a garment, and with judgment as with a diadem. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and the case that I did not know I investigated most carefully. I crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched the prey from his teeth” (Job 29:11–17).

A little later he says:

“If I denied the poor what they desired, and made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it—because from my infancy compassion grew up with me, and from my mother’s womb it came forth with me” (Job 31:16–18).

[Col. 0619C] For if anyone considers everything with a right eye, he will hasten not to harm his brothers but to deliver them, because nothing is worse than citizens envying citizens, brothers laying ambushes for brothers, or bringing false accusations.

Desiring to resist such ambushes, therefore, the holy Fathers convened a general synod at Nicaea, wishing to correct the life of those dwelling in the Church. Although many institutions of the holy Fathers had already long been written down, they established laws which we call sacred canons. In these, many provisions necessary for the condition of the holy Church of God and for the strengthening of its pillars—that is, the bishops who bear it upon their own shoulders—were decreed, and injuries against them were prohibited. Thus, if any clerics should attempt such things or presume to harm them, they are to be cast down from their own rank; if they are monks or laypeople, they are to be anathematized.

Armed with these examples, therefore, and inspired by almighty God, we have judged that we ought to extinguish by apostolic authority this flame of discord that has been kindled, and not permit it to continue devouring human souls. Accordingly, together with all subject to the apostolic see, we decree that henceforth no Christian shall presume to perpetrate such things or rashly harm bishops, since the Teacher of the Gentiles also prohibits the same, saying: “Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father” (1 Tim. 5:1), and so forth. Without doubt it is good and desirable for all who fear God to restrain dissensions and quarrels, [Col. 0620A] to assist brothers, and not to envy one another but to help one another.

Hear, I say, of the synod already held in the city of Nicaea, to which I myself also duly rendered the service of my conscience, wishing nothing other than to establish concord for all and to rebuke and remove throughout this quarrelsomeness of those who lay ambushes. Foreseeing these ambushes and unlawful disputes, the holy Fathers unanimously decreed in the aforementioned synod of Nicaea that no bishop, unless summoned by apostolic authority in a lawful synod at the proper time, should be heard concerning certain accusations—that is, judged or condemned. If anyone should presume otherwise, what they have done is to be nullified, and shall in no way be considered ecclesiastical.

The rights and judgments of the first see concerning the summoning of general synods and the judgments of bishops were granted to that church by a singular privilege through evangelical, apostolic, and canonical institutions. For the greater cases have always been ordered by many authorities to be referred to the apostolic see, and in no way can a greater be judged by a lesser. That see is greater and pre-eminent over all churches, having obtained its singular primacy not only through the decrees of the holy Fathers’ canons but also through the voice of our Lord and Savior:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” and so forth.

And:

“Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 16:18–19).

Moreover, it had long before been decreed by the holy apostles and their successors in the aforementioned ancient [Col. 0620C] statutes—which the holy and universal apostolic Church still upholds—that councils should not be held, nor a bishop condemned, without the judgment of the Roman pontiff, since they wished the holy Roman Church to be the primate of all churches.

And just as the blessed Apostle Peter was first among all the apostles, so also this Church, consecrated in his name, by the Lord’s institution is the primatial head of the others. To it, as to the summit, all the greater cases of the churches and judgments of bishops should have recourse, and from it they should receive their judgment according to due process. Nothing concerning these matters ought to be decreed outside the Roman pontiff, so that no one may act so arrogantly or according to his own desire and private judgment—as a metropolitan used to do—without consulting the Roman pontiff, whether by overthrowing the greater cases of the Church or by condemning bishops. Rather, through the common council of the bishops of the holy Roman see and through harmonious action, they should arrange whatever must be done in zeal for Christ, think rightly with one accord, and fulfill what they have determined, not by disagreeing among themselves but by doing what pleases God.

It was also unanimously established in the aforementioned synod of Nicaea that accusers and accusations which the laws of the world do not admit should be wholly removed from priestly injury. “Behold,” says the Prophet, “how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together as one!” (Ps. 132:1). Those do not dwell together as one who withdraw themselves from the support of their brothers or prepare ambushes for them.

You will not permit yourselves, brothers, [Col. 0621A] to be burdened by another’s sin, because we fear to say what is necessary—namely, lest the religion of someone be destroyed and indignation be provoked. Keep before your eyes, and reverently behold with the full attention of your minds, the glory of blessed Peter, together with him the common crowns of all the apostles, and all the palms of the martyrs who suffered not for the destruction but for the strengthening of their brothers and for the truth in Christ.

We, therefore, who wish both to be called and to be the Lord’s disciples, ought to bear Christ’s cross and suffer with our brothers, not persecute them. We beg you: withdraw your actions and thoughts from such injuries, if you do not wish to incur the punishment upon yourselves, for the one who prepares a pit for his brother deserves retaliation.

And know that henceforth we will not tolerate this pattern: that matters belonging particularly to this holy see—such as the judgments of bishops and the greater cases of the Church, as was stated a little above—should be seized without consulting us, at the peril of our position. But if anyone from this day forward should presume to condemn someone or drive him from his own see without the judgment of this holy see, let him know that he is irrecoverably condemned and will be deprived forever of his own honor. Those who have been expelled or condemned without the judgment of this see, know that by the authority of this holy see they are to receive their former communion and be restored to their own sees.

For these rights were first granted to this holy see from the time of the apostles, and afterward, in the aforementioned synod of Nicaea, because of the attacks of wicked people and the persecutions and schemes of heretics [Col. 0621C] lying in wait for their brothers, they were unanimously strengthened by all. Thus individuals would take greater care not to dare to perpetrate such things, and would restrain themselves—if not for God’s sake and love of their brothers, then at least through fear and shame—because of human reproach, their own disgrace, and canonical punishment, so that these things might be suppressed in silence, with all excess of usurpation cut off.

No one ought to presume to claim what does not appear to have been granted to him. You could in no way have fallen into this fault if you had taken the law of complete observance from the place from which you receive the consecration of your honor, and if the see of the blessed Apostle Peter, which is the mother of your priestly dignity, had been the teacher of ecclesiastical order for you.

Therefore, just as the things rightly and piously done by us greatly rejoice us, so the things wrongly done grieve us exceedingly. After experiencing so many cases of this kind, it is necessary that we look ahead anxiously and guard against them more carefully, so that the things established by the apostles and their successors may be neglected through no indolence, violated through no dissension, and disturbed through no quarrel.

For just as in one body we have many members, and all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another. The connection of the whole body creates one health and one beauty. This connection of the whole body requires unanimity, but above all it demands concord [Col. 0622A] among priests. Although they do not possess a common dignity, they do possess a common order, since among the most blessed apostles there was a certain distinction of authority within the likeness of honor. Though the election of all was equal, to one nevertheless was given the position of precedence over the others.

From this pattern arose a distinction among bishops, and by a great ordinance provision was made lest everyone claim everything for himself. Instead, in each province there were to be individual bishops whose judgment would hold first place among the brothers. Again, certain bishops established in the greater cities were to assume greater care, through whom the concern of the universal Church would flow together to the one see of Peter, and nothing anywhere would disagree with its head.

Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over some people should not resent that someone has been placed over him, but should himself render the obedience that he demands.

Do not therefore go astray, my dearest brothers, nor be led away by various and foreign teachings. You possess the institutions of the apostles and apostolic men, and their canons: make use of them, surround yourselves with them, delight in them, arm yourselves with them, so that, relying upon them, you may be able to stand firm against the arrows of your enemies. It is most unworthy for any bishop or member of a subordinate order to reject the rule which he sees the see of blessed Peter both following and teaching.

It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree with itself in this observance, which derives its authority from the place where the Lord established the primacy of the entire Church. Scripture says: “Set in order love in me” (Song 2:4), and again: “Let everything be done in order.”

Again, as the Psalmist proclaims:

“Encircle Zion and embrace her; recount it in her towers. Set your hearts upon her strength, so that you may recount it to the next generation, because this is God, our Lord forever, and he himself will rule us for ever” (Ps. 47:13–15).

In consideration of our office, we are not permitted to dissemble or to remain silent, since the zeal of the Christian religion rests more heavily upon us than upon all others, lest through silence we should appear either to favor or to consent to the injuries done to our brothers.

Given on the Kalends of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Felicianus and Maximianus.

## Letter of the Easterners to Pope Julius, complaining that he had received Athanasius and the others whom they had condemned

To the most blessed and honorable Lord, Father Julius, venerable bishop of the apostolic see, Eusebius, Theognius, Theodorus, and Berinthus, together with the remaining brothers and our fellow bishops assembled at Antioch.

Although we know that the Roman Church is generous toward all, exercises apostolic care, and always remains a mother of piety—even though preachers of piety came to it from the East—we would nevertheless wish you to agree with us: that those whom we suspended from communion should be suspended by you, and that those whom we confirm in the episcopal order should be confirmed by you. We should not be treated as second in rank, since apostles who preached doctrine came from these regions to you.

For we did not oppose your decisions, although we could have done so, when Novatian was expelled from the Roman Church. For, to speak according to common usage, everyone who wishes to withdraw from a friend seeks enmity. Nor can one be free from guilt who receives into communion someone excommunicated by another without the permission of the one by whom he was deprived of communion, since the canons command that an excommunicated person not be received by others while those by whom he is known to have been deprived of communion are alive.

Nor do you inflict an insult upon us only in these matters, but also in this: that you dissolve our councils and do not allow them to stand as valid. For the following men were condemned by us, and especially by the bishops of the entire East: Athanasius of Alexandria, Paul of Constantinople, Marcellus [Col. 0623B] of Ancyra, Asclepas of Gaza, and Lucian of Adrianople, on account of specific crimes with which they have been charged among us. Through the pages of this letter we will not fail to make everything known to your holiness in a precise account.

Once you have learned these things, if you choose to assent to our decisions rather than to their schemes, and to confirm in the place of the condemned those bishops who have been appointed, we wish to have peace and communion with you. But if you act otherwise, and judge that you should assent to them more than to us, we will hold contrary assemblies. Henceforth we neither wish to assemble with you, obey you, nor favor you or yours. Instead, we will strive to act on our own according to whatever we judge better.

For there is no one of mature age in this part of the world who does not know the schemes of the aforementioned seducers. On their account many evils have been committed, many councils held in different and difficult times, many seditions and plots undertaken, many insults inflicted upon us, and many other things which it would take too long to enumerate.

For if you choose to support them, it is clear that you wish to destroy us, rather than cherish us as a father cherishes his sons. Both their citizens and their priests say and affirm that you wish to support these men, who are murderers, destroyers of sacred temples, violators of virgins, burners of sacred books, defrauders of sacred vessels and other sacred ministries, neglecters of offices, faithless toward the emperors, traitors to their people and homeland, and producers of the greatest discord among priests, because they introduced the word “consubstantial,” which is not found written in the teaching of the faith.

Why is it necessary to enumerate more, when on their account such a great slaughter of people was perpetrated, known to us and to all the inhabitants of this region, that more than a thousand people were struck down? To favor such men—what else is it than to consent to their crimes? Yet sacred Scripture forbids this, saying: “Not only those who do such things are guilty, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. 1:32).

You ought to oppose such men with all your strength, lest you become involved in their sins, and you should not accept their excommunication. Drive such men far from you, lest, because of the contentiousness of such people, weak souls and ignorant peoples perish in sacrilegious dissension.

It is therefore necessary for you to resist the wicked firmly. If you neglect to overthrow the perverse, it is clear that you are protecting their error. Nor is the one free from the suspicion of secret association who ceases openly to oppose crimes.

It is fitting for you to sharpen your tongues in order to rebuke their arrogance and to drive them away from you like poisonous men, lest you or those belonging to you be wounded in any way by their poison.

Our complaints against them that have been brought forward are therefore sufficient, since time will fail us, as the Apostle says: “If we wished to bring forward all the complaints of those who speak against them, especially since what has been said above is sufficient for us.” Nor is it necessary for you to publicize their evils again, since they reveal themselves by themselves. Above all, all the Easterners stand as witnesses to their evils; as it is written, every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses—how much more so amid the multitude of so many priests, peoples, abbots, and monks, whose voices, in writing and without writing, cry out daily against their depravity.

We, for our part, waited for them for a long time with great patience, “so that they might produce grapes, but they instead produced wild grapes” (Isa. 5:2). You therefore ought not henceforth to neglect or delay dealing with such men, lest—God forbid—you become subject to the crimes mentioned above by irrationally installing them as bishops. For unless they are quickly corrected, they are, as the blessed Apostle declares, “storing up wrath for themselves according to their hardness and unrepentant heart on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2:5–6).

They must be corrected, lest through temporal pleasure, lies, and their own fabrications, while you give them your assent, they lose the eternal rewards which they could obtain through true repentance.

We do not bring these charges only against Athanasius and his followers, but also because he acted contrary to the rule we had decreed. He did not receive the priesthood by a decree of the common council of bishops; rather, by arrogating the Church to himself, he had entered it and taken his seat, although it had long before been decreed that no one should be restored by a smaller number than the number by which he had been deposed.

Furthermore, although a crowd arose upon his arrival and many people were killed in the ensuing sedition, and although these things were not carried out only by him and on his account, it is also said that certain people beaten by the aforementioned Athanasius were handed over to the judges [OCR: *jndicibus*, probably *judicibus*]. These and countless other things were shamelessly perpetrated by him and his followers. You have associated them in communion, although we have heard that they were excommunicated, acting contrary to the rule and insulting all the Easterners.

After offering the aforesaid duty of due greeting out of honor for blessed Peter, we ask you henceforth not to admit so readily those coming from here to your ears, nor to be willing any longer to receive into communion those excommunicated by us, lest you be found transgressors of the canons. Rather, preserving fraternal charity, do not in the future tolerate this error at all. May the Lord preserve your apostolate, which prays for us, for a longer age, most blessed Father. Amen.

## Reply of Pope Julius against the Easterners on behalf of Athanasius and the others

Julius, bishop of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, to Eusebius, Theognius, Theodorus, Berinthus, and the other Eastern bishops.

It would have been fitting for you to speak respectfully, not mockingly, against the holy Roman and apostolic Church, since our Lord Jesus Christ himself addressed it suitably, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:18).

For by a singular privilege it has been granted the power to open and close [Col. 0625B] the gates of the heavenly kingdom to whomever it wishes. Since you did not hesitate to disparage what was sanctified by the Lord’s mouth and exalted from above, it is no wonder that you do not cease to inflict injuries upon your brothers. Hence the things tumultuously and stormily decreed in your council can no longer be concealed in silence.

It is evident that truth was overwhelmed by tumultuous indiscipline, since, without consideration, you claim that what pleases God is determined by the quarrels you have against your neighbors, and you insist that your resolutions cannot be avoided. But divine providence will be required, so that, once the contrary has been openly exposed, it may be explained, and whatever you did there when assembled—whether out of favor, hatred, or causes of enmity—may be utterly rejected.

Therefore, I wish all of you to hasten with all speed to the reverence of this [Col. 0625C] holy see, so that you may yourselves demonstrate the integrity of what was done before us. For I do not think you doubt that Athanasius, a teacher of sacred law, has been proved by us and by the synod of Nicaea to be a worshiper of the true faith. After Alexander, that remarkable old man who had overthrown the blasphemies of Arius, died, Athanasius received the episcopate of the Alexandrian Church five months after the Council of Nicaea.

Against him and his followers you wove many lies and composed naked slanders as though they were true accusations. You declared to us that he was the cause and source of many evils, and you indicated in your writings that he was a disturber not only throughout Egypt but also throughout Palestine, Phoenicia, and the neighboring peoples.

For this reason, following ecclesiastical rule, we summoned you to Rome in due form for judgment on the appointed day—not within a narrow space of time, so that no excuse might find a place—by letters and by messengers. After accepting the summons, they came on the appointed day; but you delayed coming, lest you be caught in your own lies and your slander be exposed.

Nor were you content with these schemes alone. Seeing the sheep abandoned by their shepherds, you placed wolves over them in the shepherds’ place. It would therefore have been fitting for you to come to the regular summons, so that you might give a true account of these and your other presumptions. Truth would have come forward if falsehood displeased you.

No one doubts that the guilty avoids judgment in the same way that the innocent seeks it in order to be acquitted. Nor is the one free from suspicion who disparages another with accusations of having spoken falsely, while he himself, summoned to judgment in order to prove what he alleged, delays coming.

I would have wished you rather to come to the aforementioned canonical summons, so that before the universal council you might give an account of why you convened a synod at Antioch to overthrow the condition of the churches and of the brothers, and to destroy the great Council of Nicaea; or why, without consulting us, you summoned bishops to it, although neither the greatest bishop of Jerusalem came nor our delegation was present.

For the canons of the synod of Nicaea command that no council be held in any way without the judgment of the Roman pontiff, nor bishops condemned. Why, moreover, did you place other adulterous men in the place of the aforementioned brothers [Col. 0626B] before the case had been canonically examined before us or our messengers and had reached a proper conclusion?

Those who came regularly to the aforementioned summons, seeing you withdraw from the accusations described above, report many tearful and painful things against you. They accuse you and say that they suffered many unbearable things at your hands. You, however, refused to come, while they persisted in the truth and protested against your accusations. The bishops of Egypt also testify in letters sent to us that everything those who contrived these things against Athanasius and his followers have alleged is false, being entirely the product of the blasphemous schemes of the Arians.

From such fabrications it is clear that they are blameless and you are guilty. For if you were confident in your true innocence, you would in no way have withdrawn from the canonical summons just mentioned, which was not announced suddenly but with ample time. You would have hastened to come without delay, with every excuse removed, and to give an account of your causes.

When these things had taken place, I wrote to you and to all who had assembled at Antioch against the apostolic and canonical rule without consulting us. First I rebuked you for the insults in your letters; then I rebuked you for summoning Athanasius and his followers to your council, since the canons command that nothing be decreed outside the Roman pontiff. These and greater ecclesiastical matters have been specially entrusted to him, as has already been stated, both by the Lord himself and by the brothers of all councils everywhere, through a special privilege.

But you refused and, although summoned so many times to the council, did not wish to attend. Since they also persisted in their protest and just cause, and since we recognized your crimes and examined the justice of their case, finding all of them in agreement with the Council of Nicaea and obedient to our apostolic commands, it seemed right to us and to the entire council that we, instructed by divine precepts and apostolic admonitions, must watch tirelessly and actively over the condition of all churches. If anything anywhere is found liable to reproach, we must promptly recall it from ignorance and inexperience or from presumptuous usurpation.

Having thus considered and distinguished these matters, as those who bear care for all, and out of regard for the dignity of our own see, we received them into communion [Col. 0627A] and, by the authority of this holy see, restored to each of them, together with his possessions, his own church. For, by the Lord’s institution and through the holy apostles and their successors, who have strengthened this authority in each council, this has always been permitted to this holy see because of the ambushes of wicked people, and, with the Lord’s help, it will be permitted forever.

Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over others should not be troubled that someone has been placed over him, but should himself freely render the moderation that he demands from others.

I write to you, therefore, in rebuke, because you did not deal rightly with blameless men. You deprived them of communion and drove them from their churches, although their cases had not been examined by us, inflicting an injury upon ecclesiastical discipline and failing to observe the decree of the Council of Nicaea. You did not fear to act so indisciplinately.

Since you previously refused to come when summoned, we now summon you again in due form by letters and messengers for a fixed day, namely the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, so that we may show before you that we pronounced a just judgment against them and that henceforth we will not tolerate such things.

For it is decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that one who invades another’s property shall not escape unpunished but shall restore it with increase. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). The law likewise declares: “Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbor’s boundary markers,” and all the people shall say, “Amen” (Deut. 27:17).

I therefore marvel that you should be so bold and act so shamelessly, and that you should invade the boundaries and rights of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. For, as was proved a little above, it belonged to his jurisdiction that no one should, without the authority of his holy see, either hold councils, summon bishops to a synod, or condemn them. You did not fear to violate all these provisions.

What else, then, is such presumption but a transgression of the decrees of the apostles and their successors, and a failure to fear receiving the curse described above and prescribed in the law—a curse which all the people confirmed with one mouth and a concordant response by saying “Amen,” that is, “Let it be”?

For, as I think, bound by such cords of transgression, you avoided our examination lest your crimes be exposed, and delayed coming to the summons mentioned above. It is plainly evident that those who, after being summoned so many times, delay coming without an unavoidable reason and do not make use of the opportunity to clear themselves are confessing their own crime.

For if you were confident in what you had said, you would not have delayed proving it face to face. Foreseeing such ambushers, the holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea established laws which we call canons, so that the good would not easily be condemned by the wicked.

We have judged it unnecessary to insert any of their judgments here, so that our letter might be strengthened by the authority of such great Fathers, and so that all the Eastern bishops and those of the other regions, hearing these things, might not fall into so great a pit, lest they receive the condemnation decreed by the Fathers.

The following chapters from the aforementioned Council of Nicaea follow: XVIII, XIX, XXI, XXIII, XXVI, XXVII, XXVIII, XXXIII, XLI, and V, [Col. 0628A] VII, and IX, as well as LI, LII, LIII, LIV, LV, LVII, LVIII, LIX, LX, LXI, LXIII, and LXVI.

That all bishops who are accused or charged in certain more serious cases may, whenever necessary, freely appeal to the apostolic see and flee to it as to a mother, so that they may be piously supported, defended, and delivered by it, as has always been the case. The ancient authority of the apostles, their successors, and the canons has reserved to it all the greater ecclesiastical cases and the judgments of bishops.

Since bishops are censured if they have acted toward their brethren otherwise than the pope of that same see has approved, it has been decreed that a bishop accused or judged by the provincials in any case may freely appeal and [Col. 0628B] approach the pontiff of the apostolic see, who either personally or through his vicars shall arrange for the case to be reconsidered. While the pontiff is conducting the retrial of his case, no one else may be appointed or ordained in his place. For although the bishops of the province may investigate the pontiff’s case, they are not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff, since the Lord said to the blessed apostle Peter, and not to anyone else: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19).

If anyone thinks that he is being oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese, or before the pope of the universal apostolic Church.

[Col. 0628C]

We unanimously exclude accusers and accusations that the laws of the secular world do not admit; nor should impiety be committed in a rigorous examination, since the sentence of judgment in an election should be just.

No bishop shall presume to retain, ordain, or judge another bishop’s parishioner without that bishop’s consent, saving in all things the authority of the apostolic see. For just as his ordination will be invalid, so also will his judgment, since we hold that no one is bound by the sentence of any judge other than his own. For whoever could not ordain him cannot in any way judge him.

If anyone believes that he has a personal case against a bishop or against officers of the Church, let him not first approach the judges, but let him first appeal to them in a spirit of charity, so that, admonished by familiar conversation, they may remedy the matters brought forward in complaint. If he acts otherwise, let him be deprived of communion.

[Col. 0628D]

No pontiff shall henceforth presume to excommunicate or judge a bishop who has been stripped of his possessions or expelled by him, for there is no privilege from which one who has already been stripped bare can be stripped. In the same manner we decree that no credence be given to an accuser who, in the absence of his adversary, brings forward a case before both parties have been heard; nor should accusers or witnesses who are not competent be admitted.

It has been decreed that, if an accused or condemned bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff, whatever he himself justly judges shall be established. We also hold all who take up arms against the Fathers to be infamous, and we judge that those who associate with enemies are not to be admitted either to accusation or to testimony.

[Col. 0629A]

It has been decreed that, whenever clergy are accused, the person, faith, life, and conduct of the slanderers must first be examined. For faith ought to precede all a person’s actions: one who is doubtful is unfaithful, and no credence at all should be given to those who do not know the faith of truth or lead a life of upright conduct, since such people readily and indiscriminately attack and accuse those who live rightly and devoutly. Therefore their suspicion must first be examined and corrected, and credence must not be given to suspicious accusers who emerge from the household of enemies.

Those churches alone are to be called metropolitan or primatial which were formerly primatial and, after Christ’s coming, merited primacy by apostolic and synodal authority. The others, however, are not to be called primatial but metropolitan; and their bishops shall bear the title either of metropolitans or of archbishops, not of primates.

We hold all who violate either their own Christian law or set aside canonical authority to be infamous, saving in all things the privilege of the Roman Church. No metropolitan shall hear anyone’s cases without the insistence of all the other bishops of the province, for his proceedings will be invalid; indeed, by doing so he will give cause for a synodal charge against himself.

[Col. 0629C]

We cannot receive one associated with the errors of others, or one who has departed from the path of his own profession, or one disobedient to the sacred canons; nor do we permit those who rightly believe or obey the decrees of the holy Fathers to be attacked.

We prohibit foreign judgments by general decree, since it is unworthy that one who ought to have provincial judges chosen by himself should be judged by outsiders.

Saving the authority of the apostolic Church, no bishop shall be summoned to judgment outside his own province. Once summoned, he himself shall be heard canonically, at a synodal time and in a place suitable for all, by all the bishops of the province, who must pronounce upon him a concordant and canonical sentence. For if this has been granted to lesser persons, both clergy and laity, how much more ought it to be observed in the case of bishops. If he regards the metropolitan or judges as suspect, or perceives them to be hostile, let him be judged before the primates of the diocese or before the pontiffs of the Roman see.

[Col. 0629D]

No one may be believed, on the basis of his own confession, concerning another person’s crime, since his profession regarding himself and every other matter is dangerous and ought not to be admitted against anyone.

No pontiff shall ever presume to judge uncertain matters. For even if they are true, they are not to be believed unless they are established by manifest evidence, unless they are proved by an open judgment, and unless they are made public according to judicial procedure.

Accusations against persons of higher rank must not be made through others, but only by those who bring the charges themselves—provided that they appear worthy and irreproachable, have demonstrated by public records that they are free from every suspicion and enmity, and lead a life of irreproachable faith and conduct.

[Col. 0630A]

A synod of the province may be reconsidered through vicars of the bishop of the city of Rome, if he himself so decrees.

It has been decreed that, whenever an appeal is made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges whose authority is greater, a hearing must not be denied. If a metropolitan bishop attempts to do anything without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of the province, except in matters belonging solely to his own parish, he shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank; and whatever he has done shall be held invalid and void. But whatever it is necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of the provincial bishops, their churches and clergy, and secular necessities must be undertaken with the full consent of the provincial pontiffs—not with any arrogance of domination, but with the most humble and harmonious administration, as the Lord says: “I did not come to be served, but to serve” (Mark 10:45); and elsewhere: “The one who is greater among you shall be 155 your servant” (Matt. 23:11), and so forth. Likewise, the provincial bishops themselves shall act with his counsel, except in matters belonging to their own parishes, in accordance with the constitutions of the holy Fathers, so that the holy Trinity may be glorified harmoniously with one voice and one mind forever.

[Col. 0630B]

Let the judges of the Church beware lest they pronounce sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being heard. For the sentence will be invalid, and they will also have to render an account in synod for their action; and, like the slander of a betrayer, their voice shall not afterward be heard. For no one can know a debtor better than the one who suffers his injury and wickedness.

[Col. 0630C]

If anyone believes that a cleric should be accused concerning any crimes, let him bring his action in the province in which that cleric resides, and let the accuser not think that he should be dragged elsewhere or farther away for judgment. If the person accused regards the judges as suspect, he may appeal. The primates, when examining an accused bishop, must not pronounce a sentence of condemnation before they are supported by apostolic authority, unless the accused himself confesses, or is regularly convicted by innocent witnesses examined canonically.

An unjust condemnation of bishops is invalid [Col. 0630D] and must therefore be reconsidered by synod, so that assistance may be given to the oppressed in every case. We exclude from episcopal accusation detractors, whom divine authority commands to be uprooted, and supporters of enemies. Likewise, no person of higher rank is to be attacked or destroyed by accusations from inferiors; no sentence is to be given in a doubtful matter; and no judgment is to stand unless it has been conducted in due order.

We do not insert more concerning these matters here, lest we seem to empty out or cheapen the aforementioned synod, or lest the length of the letter produce weariness for its readers and hearers. If anyone wishes to know more extensive and fuller details concerning these matters, he will be able to find them in the sacred archive of the church of our see, together with what we have stated above.

[Col. 0631A]

The divinity itself bears witness that I have spoken the truth. As for the reception of the see, priesthood, and honor, concerning which you said that Athanasius had been received without a conciliar decree, we do not find the matter to be as you falsely alleged. Rather, by the counsel and decree of certain bishops he recovered the priesthood that he had unjustly lost and took his seat again.

What you wrote—that he could not be restored by a smaller number of bishops than the number by which he had been deposed—is not so. Nor is this a rule of the bishops of the orthodox holy Church; it is a rule of the Arian associates. Indeed, this invention was devised and constructed for the destruction of orthodox bishops. For, as truthful witnesses have reported to us, when you were assembled at Antioch for the condemnation of the faith concerning consubstantiality, you produced this rule out of hatred for the aforementioned Athanasius. It has no force, nor can it have any, since that council was not conducted by orthodox bishops, nor was a legation of the Roman Church present, although the canons require councils to be held without its authority. No council is, or ever will be, valid unless it has been supported by the authority of that Church.

[Col. 0631B]

Therefore, you do not act rightly in reproaching Athanasius for his flight, since the Lord himself gave us this command: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10:23). The Lord himself also gave us an example when “the Pharisees took counsel against him, that they might kill him. But Jesus, knowing this, departed from there” (Matt. 12:14–15). Elsewhere: “[Col. 0631C] The Jews took up stones to throw at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple” (John 8:59); and, “passing through the midst of them, he went away” (Luke 4:30). Thus he departed. The disciples also withdrew because of fear of the Jews, concealing themselves; and Paul, when sought by the ruler of the people at Damascus, was lowered from the wall in a basket and escaped the hands of his pursuer. Many others, innumerable holy men, are likewise read to have fled, both in the Old Testament and in the New.

If, then, you reproach those who flee for fleeing, you should rather be ashamed to persecute and cease to lie in wait; then those who are fleeing will immediately cease. For whether you kill them—their death continually cries out against you—or impose further exiles upon them, everywhere you are known to send forth the memory of your evil against yourselves, while they profit through their suffering.

[Col. 0631D]

Therefore the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28).

We have known many who were unjustly deposed by the worst intrigues. Therefore, with the assistance of the supreme Apostle, I must take the greatest care—I, to whom the care of the universal Church has been entrusted in the place of the prince of the apostles—that such things not happen again. For this reason the aforementioned privileges have been granted especially to this holy see: concerning the convening of councils, the judgments and restorations of bishops, and other matters, so that all the oppressed may receive help from it, the unjustly condemned may receive restoration, and such acts may neither be attempted by the wicked without punishment nor carried out without condemnation.

[Col. 0632A]

You therefore did not act rightly in slandering the aforementioned brethren, since the Lord says: “You shall not slander your neighbor, nor oppress him by force” (Luke 19:13). You did not act rightly in celebrating a council without consulting us, summoning them to the council, and presuming to condemn them, although the canons, as stated above, command that none of these things be done without the authority of this holy see. You did not act rightly in delaying to come when regularly summoned by us to the council. You did not act rightly in refusing to come and give an account concerning them, so that your sentence against them might either be proved right or shown to be wrong, nor did you send a reasonable explanation for your refusal.

When all these matters have been weighed, it is clear that you are guilty, while they remain innocent; that you have been rightly excommunicated, while they have been justly freed.

[Col. 0632B]

The Lord did not wish his ministers to be treated so lightly as you treat them, or condemned by you, but—as has been stated—either to be reserved for this see to which they have been entrusted, or for his own judgment. For he says: “Whoever grieves you grieves me; whoever does you an injury shall receive what he has done unjustly” (Col. 3:15).

The Gospel sufficiently explains what punishment awaits those who scandalize the Lord’s disciples, where it speaks of those who scandalize the disciples. That they are not to be condemned by you, but either by this holy see, as stated above, or reserved for him, he himself clearly demonstrates by the example of the sinful priests whose place bishops now hold in the holy Church. [Col. 0632C]

He himself, not another, drove the buyers and sellers from the temple and overturned the money-changers’ tables with his own whip; he himself expelled them from the temple.

Elsewhere he says: “God stands in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges among the gods” (Ps. 81:1), and other things of this kind. The same Lord also says elsewhere: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned” (Luke 6:37). “For with the judgment you judge, you shall be judged.”

Therefore no one should presume, as you do, to vomit forth his own iniquity so rashly. Rather, the one who judges all things must investigate carefully and examine the order of events through a full inquiry. He must not presume to judge in any way concerning matters that have not been granted to him. The patience of questioning, presenting, and adding evidence must not be denied to the accused, so that the action of the parties may be fully limited there.

[Col. 0632D]

His sentence should first meet the claims of the litigants, unless, after everything has been completed there, they have nothing further to propose in the dispute. No one ought to be judged or condemned before he has his accusers present and has been given sufficient opportunity to defend himself and clear the charges.

Likewise, it was decreed in the aforesaid synod that permission to accuse must not extend beyond the boundaries of the province, unless an appeal has been made to this apostolic see. To it all who wish must come freely and without any impediment, bringing their cases against others.

Likewise, the aforementioned synod decreed that the following must not be accepted as accusers: the suspect, the infamous, the criminal, the troublesome, the slanderer, the related party, the wicked, or those who litigate readily, but only persons free from every suspicion. For the Lord wished his pillars to stand firmly and not be shaken by certain persons.

[Col. 0633A]

Likewise, the aforementioned synod decreed that no one should be bound by a sentence pronounced by a judge who is not his own. The judges must be no others than those chosen by the person who is hindered, or those whom this holy see, with his consent, or its primates, acting by the authority of this holy see, have delegated.

From these and the other provisions established both in this holy see and by the apostles and their successors, you granted nothing to the aforementioned bishops. Instead, by using force against them and condemning them unjustly, as mentioned above, you expelled some while they were absent. This is hostile to every Christian religion.

[Col. 0633B]

It is evident in these matters that you have preserved neither the Lord’s rights for the Lord nor the rights of this holy mother and apostolic Church, which—as prescribed above—wished them to be reserved for its judgment or for the judgment of this see, so that they would not be condemned or expelled by men as wicked as you are.

In all these matters it is hidden from no sensible person that you are fools and transgressors of the Gospels and the canons. Nor were you satisfied with this transgression of yours: after first expelling them and stripping them of their possessions, you as it were summoned and condemned them, although no one can be regularly summoned or judged before he has been regularly restored and all his possessions have been fully returned to him according to law.

[Col. 0633C]

For it has been unanimously decreed by all in the holy synod already mentioned, and confirmed by apostolic authority, that if any bishop has been stripped of his possessions and brought under accusation, the holy order of pontiffs must first contend for this purpose: all that he lost through the representations of his enemies must first be legally restored to his authority by an honorable council; the prelate must first be regularly restored to his former status; and only then, once he has arranged and ordered his affairs, may he come at the appointed time to the case and, if it seems just, answer the charges of the accusers.

Why, then, have you transgressed the boundaries of the Fathers by judging and condemning those whom you ought not to have judged? Why did you judge those whom you had not regularly established as subject to judgment?

[Col. 0634A]

You did not observe what is written in the Book of Kings: “Not as man sees does God see, because man sees the face, but God sees the heart.” And in Chronicles: “God searches all hearts and knows every intention” (1 Chron. 28:9). Elsewhere it is written: “One whom God has reserved for his own judgment cannot be condemned by human examination.”

All these matters must be guarded against with the greatest care, and the accusation of bishops must not easily be received, since the Lord says: “You shall not receive a false report.” The Apostle also says that an accusation against a presbyter is not to be received without two or three suitable witnesses. If these precautions must be taken concerning presbyters and other faithful persons, how much more concerning bishops.

Once these matters are understood, it is clear that you wish rather to dominate than to advise your brethren or support them, since honor puffs up toward pride, and what was foreseen for concord tends toward harm.

[Col. 0634B]

You ought, in accordance with the rules stated above, if they had done anything against their order, to have informed us and awaited what we would write in response to your consultations. Even if they had committed something grave and intolerable, you ought to have awaited our judgment, and you ought to have discerned nothing beforehand or otherwise than what you knew would please us. Thus you should have departed from the established rules neither through negligence nor through presumption.

Let this kind of presumption, now restrained by our authority, cease; let such injuries be avoided. We can by no means patiently endure such intrigues, since it is fitting that we be diligent guardians of the sanctions of the Fathers. The matter rightly concerns us, if we favor error by silence.

Moreover, it was established in the aforesaid holy Council of Nicaea that no one under anathema is to be received in an accusation brought before us, nor those who do not wish to receive us in their complaint or accusation, since we know that we have been set over them by the Lord, not they over us. And just as a greater person cannot be judged by a lesser, so neither can he be bound by one; for everything great is rare.

[Col. 0634C]

Let us bear the burdens of all who are oppressed—or rather, the blessed apostle Peter bears them in us, whose office we discharge and whose rule instructs us—so that, strengthened by his help, we may now and forever be protected from every adversity.

Given on the Kalends of November, during the consulship of Felician and Maximian.

# THE DECREES OF POPE LIBERIUS BEGIN

[Col. 0633]

## Letter of Athanasius and the Egyptian Bishops to the Same Pope, Concerning the Oppressions of the Arians

[Col. 0633D]

To the most blessed Lord and honorable holy father, Pope LIBERIUS: ANASTASIUS and all the bishops of Egypt.

Assembled together synodically at Alexandria, we know that the rights of your most blessed fatherhood are 156 manifest before God, since the whole earth has been filled with the cultivation of true faith through apostolic preaching and teaching. Yet, through the instruction of the divine utterances and your exhortatory admonition, the orthodox Church of Christ, founded upon apostolic institution and most firmly strengthened by the faithful of [Col. 0634D] earlier times, is built up. To it all the most blessed apostles, endowed with an equal share of honor and power, led the hosts of the peoples, bringing men, by divine commands and admonitions, piously and holily from darkness to light, from falling to the true faith, and from death to life, as members of the race predestined by God.

Your fraternity, worthy of honor because it follows the merits of those holy apostles and more fully fulfills their examples, adorns the Church of God by the integrity of its conduct and the holiness of its actions. Its sacred faith, flourishing in Christian morality, continually works and advances through episcopal zeal in the things it has commanded to be pleasing to God, preserving the commandments of the divine law.

For, as the Apostle says, those who hear the law are not righteous before God, but those who do the law will be justified.

[Col. 0635A]

We desire to meditate upon these matters and to preach what we have received from your holy see through the preaching of the apostles and their successors, as well as what we know to have been confirmed at the Council of Nicaea. We desire to repel the blasphemies of the Arians and of the other heretics. Yet every day we are persecuted by them, handed over to condemnation, and destined for death.

Therefore we ask that we be helped by your exhortations, both through you and through your representatives, so that, while they increase and we diminish, the true faith may not be destroyed and their heresy may not grow beyond our faith. For we fear that, when iniquity has abounded, the charity of many may grow cold.

For this reason, a great reward and praise of your sacred teaching is reserved for you both with God and with all the faithful, if these matters are made known through your authority. Below we set forth the faith that we received from the holy Fathers, hold, and teach, so that, if anyone reports to you—whether by accusation, whispered allegation, or written slander—that we believe or teach otherwise, you may clearly recognize from this that we believe and teach as follows.

[Col. 0635B]

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, [Col. 0635C] true God from true God; begotten, not made; *omousion* (*homoousion*)—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth.

For us human beings and for our salvation he came down from heaven, was incarnate and became human, suffered, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead.

And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and, “Before he was begotten he was not,” and who say that he was made from things that did not subsist, or from another substance or essence; or who say that the Son of God is *trepton*—that is, capable of conversion and change—the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

This venerable faith was acknowledged and embraced by the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, who explained it in writing with one voice and unanimous agreement.

[Col. 0635D]

But now, as you know, such things are rising up against this faith as ought not to arise. Come, therefore, beloved brethren, and with God let us descend to an examination—that is, an inquiry—into their words. Let us confound, by the truest demonstration, their tongues raised there against knowledge of the only-begotten Son of God; and, because they speak iniquity against the height of his humanity, let us “break their bonds” (Ps. 2:3) by the spiritual sword, which is the word of God, and “cast their yoke from us” (ibid.) by defeating their profane understanding.

“Then the Lord himself will laugh at them and [Col. 0636A] mock them; then he will speak to them in his anger and trouble them in his wrath” (Ps. 2:4–5), saying according to the blessed Jeremiah:

“Those prophets prophesy falsely in my name; I did not send them, I did not command them, nor did I speak to them. They prophesy to you a false vision, divination, fraud, and the deceit of their heart. Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who prophesy falsely in my name: They shall be cast out upon the roads of Jerusalem” (Jer. 14:14–16).

They shall be “a trampling underfoot of all who confess me piously,” and no one shall bury them.

No one can conceal himself through certain fabricated deceptions, just as Adam, the ancient transgressor of the commandment, could not conceal himself with fig leaves. He was shamelessly stripped by his own tongue. “His lips are a snare for the strong man”; he is captured by his own words, and the recompense of his hands’ work—and the rebuke of his impiety—will be given to him.

“I will rebuke you,” he says, “and set you before your face, because you wickedly thought that I was like you” (Ps. 50:21).

[Col. 0636B]

Therefore, as the Lord says to Gideon, let us bring them down to the water of true discernment and test them there by regular examination, seeing them fall together headlong through the manifestation of their perverse understanding. Let us determine whether they are wise among themselves while ignorant of the knowledge of the divine word. For, claiming to be wise, they became fools and changed the glory of the catholic Church through their own novelty and will, or by introducing heretical turmoil through things illicitly undertaken in its defense.

Let us appropriately retain what is well said to us in Jesus son of Sirach: “Fight for the truth unto death, and the Lord will fight for you” (Sir. 4:33).

For this reason the universal Church has been entrusted to you in Christ Jesus, so that you may labor for everyone and not neglect to bring aid to all. For while the strong man armed guards his courtyard, everything that he possesses is in peace.

Therefore, since such great necessity presses, restrain the hostile by your supreme authority and raise up the oppressed, so that, with the Lord’s help and without grievous difficulty, we may be worthy to sacrifice to him gladly and unharmed at all times.

And the subscription:

May the eternal divinity preserve you for many years, most holy father of the Fathers. Amen.

## Liberius’ Reply to the Same

[Col. 0636D]

To his most beloved son ATHANASIUS and to all the bishops of Egypt assembled together and rightly believing concerning the faith of the Trinity: Pope LIBERIUS.

Long ago and from the beginning we received such confidence from the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that we possess authority to defend the right faith on behalf of the universal Church, so that no one may disturb the order of the holy Church to the injury of those who rightly believe without endangering his own honor.

We had your letter, which was addressed to us, read aloud in our presence. We understood the tribulations and persecutions that you suffer for the right faith. Concerning these, we too sympathize with you, and we are prepared to labor for you as a father for his sons.

In the same letter we found the faith of the Council of Nicaea to be right, and for it we rendered abundant thanks to God. For its sake we are prepared not only to endure persecutions and sufferings with you, but also, if necessary, we do not refuse to die for Christ’s name, insofar as our weakness permits.

[Col. 0637A]

Therefore, as we read, the aforementioned holy Council of Nicaea defined that no one is permitted to produce, write, compose, hold, or teach another faith, nor to think or express anything in matters of faith that could oppose the rules of these Fathers.

But if anyone presumes to compose another faith, or to present, teach, or hand down another creed to those wishing to turn to the way of truth from any heresy, whether from the Jews or from the pagans, [Col. 0637B] and wishing to become Christians—if such persons are bishops or clergy, the bishops shall be removed from the episcopate and the clergy from the clergy. If they are monks or laypeople, they shall be struck with anathema.
