For the blessed Apostle declares: “If anyone competes, he is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). The Lord says again: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13).

Since sacred contests have been set before us for the defense of the catholic Church, and great salvation is hoped for from the God who gives every good thing, let not our hands, beloved brethren, grow weak through any occasion of sluggish negligence. Rather, let us be made strong through the Lord’s grace and the power of his might, for he made our feet like those of his own and established our understanding more firmly upon the heights of his supreme humanity for the sake of our salvation, especially since we have so great a cloud of holy witnesses laid upon us.

[Col. 0637C]

Therefore, laying aside every burden and the novelty of our adversaries that surrounds us, let us run with patience, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who, in the task set before us for his sake, grants us the spirit of his truth to speak in us and restrains the great things of faith through the teaching of the holy Fathers, whom the adversaries daily slander.

For it is written in the prophets: “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Zion’s sake I will not rest, until her righteous one goes forth like brightness and her savior is kindled like a lamp” (Isa. 62:1).

Indeed, the catholic Church, which is the true Zion and the city of Christ, the king of heaven, has been attacked for so many years by those who oppose the words of faith—people who neither fear God nor revere human beings. They persist in vain against the devout and canonical teachings concerning this matter, although they had been summoned by such numerous written and unwritten testimonies to correct their own position and bury their heresy, as was also demonstrated more clearly through the earlier inquiry, both by letters and by the representations of most reverend priests and venerable abbots.

The Apostle warns us that we must avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction, knowing that such a person is subverted and sins, condemned by his own judgment.

[Col. 0638A]

Therefore we must by no means remain silent or rest any longer, lest we be judged wicked for embracing a peace hateful to God. For it is written: “I was jealous among sinners, seeing the peace of sinners.” It may also be said of us: “My priests despised my law and polluted my sanctuaries; they did not distinguish between the holy and the profane, nor did they understand the difference between the polluted and the clean.”

Rather, we must rise up in God and stand promptly for him, putting on the weapons of the Spirit against those who rage against his faith, so that we may wisely test the spirits—that is, their words, whether they are from God.

For it is written in Jeremiah: “I have appointed you as a tested and strong examiner among my people; you shall know and test their way” (Jer. 6:27).

[Col. 0638B]

We need great vigilance and such searching of divine wisdom as reveals the hidden things of darkness for the investigation and examination of this matter. For deceitful wickedness lies concealed and hidden in a certain way and is scarcely grasped, because it cunningly flatters itself with piety so that it may escape the mind of those who investigate.

Knowing this, the blessed Apostle says: “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ” (2 Cor. 11:13). But this is not surprising, since Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. Therefore it is not surprising if his ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness, whose end will be according to their works.

The Lord also warns us in this matter, saying: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves; you will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:15–16).

[Col. 0638C]

Therefore, with one heart, let us first of all offer a prayer concerning this question and say with David: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118:18); “your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:18).

For wisdom, as the blessed prophet Daniel says, belongs to him, as does strength; “he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who understand discipline. He reveals deep and hidden things, he knows what is established in darkness, and light is with him” (Dan. 2:20–22).

Since you have given me wisdom and strength, he says, and have shown me what I asked of you, let us diligently attend to the divine works described for each person whose novelty has brought him under accusation, as they are served up from our venerable archive and presented to us in due order.

[Col. 0638D]

Thus those who presume to transgress these matters shall first be subject to the terrible judgment of almighty God; then they shall also fear whatever royal indignation may follow. Through it, if they are bishops or clergy, they shall in every way be removed from their priestly office or from the order of the clergy. If they are monks, they shall be separated and removed from their places. If they possess rank, a military belt, or military service, they shall be stripped of these. If they are private persons, then, if they are noble, they shall suffer proscription of their property.

[Col. 0639A]

But if they are of low status, they shall not only be scourged in the 157 body but also punished by perpetual exile, so that all, restrained by fear of God and revering the punishments threatened against them, may preserve the immovable and undisturbed peace of the holy Churches of God.

[Col. 0640A]

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourth consulship of Asclepius and Deodatus. Grace from Jesus Christ our Lord; peace be with you. Amen. Thanks be to God.

# THE DECREES OF POPE FELIX BEGIN

[Col. 0639]

## Letter of the Egyptian bishops to the same [pope] concerning the attacks of the Arians

[Col. 0639A]

To the most blessed Lord and venerable holy father FELIX, pope of the holy Apostolic See of the city of Rome: ATHANASIUS and all the bishops of the Egyptians, Thebaids, and Libyans, gathered by the grace of God in the holy Alexandrian synod.

We respectfully bring to the attention of your holy apostolate that you deign, according to your customary practice, to take care of us, in keeping with your most prudent wisdom, which is clearer than light to all. For your Beatitude, moved by the apostolic compassion of your heart because of our tribulation, has urged us all to assemble together for the protection of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, and to deliberate unanimously concerning our canonical [Col. 0639B] oppression. We say, compassionately, together with the blessed apostle Paul: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Cor. 11:29), striving lest any of the rational sheep entrusted to us should be seized by beasts.

Therefore, most blessed father, since our predecessors and we ourselves have always drawn help from your holy Apostolic See, and since we have recognized that you care for us, we earnestly seek that foremost and supreme Apostolic See, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, so that we may receive help from the place from which our predecessors received their ordinations, doctrines, and relief. To it also, as to a mother, we flee for refuge, that we may be nourished at her breasts, since a mother cannot forget her infant. Thus [Col. 0639C] do not forget us, who have been entrusted to you, since our enemies have involved us in no slight troubles and daily contrive to afflict and seize us; they threaten to bind us with iron unless we consent to their errors. We presume to do nothing of this kind without your counsel, since the canons command that, apart from the Roman pontiff, we must decide nothing concerning greater causes.

Therefore, returning to the appointed goal and hastening toward the prize, we implore the help of your Apostolic See. For, as we believe, God has not despised the prayers of his servants offered to him with tears; rather, for this reason he has established you and your apostolic predecessors as pontiffs at the summit of authority and has commanded them to care for all the churches: so that you may come to our aid and, protecting us, not neglect to free us from our enemies—you to whom every judgment concerning bishops has been entrusted. For we know that at the great Council of Nicaea, consisting of three hundred and eighteen bishops, it was unanimously confirmed that councils must not be held without the judgment of the Roman pontiff, nor bishops [Col. 0640A] condemned. Yet these and many other necessary synodical decisions have been burned and taken away by the heretics who daily attack us and strive to destroy us, so that they may seize us more easily.

Taking advantage of this opportunity, and setting aside every canonical and apostolic authority, they drive us out by force from our own sees without consulting you. They invade the sheep entrusted to us by Christ the Lord through apostolic grace, deprive us of our rank, and—what is worst and contrary to all Christian law—strive to accomplish their purpose.

Therefore, as has always been the custom of your holy See, come to the aid of those in danger, strengthen the oppressed, extend your hand to those in tribulation, forbid such acts, and impose laws, so that the apostolic [Col. 0640B] teaching which is in God may quickly bring our case to judgment and victory, and, with Peter the prince of the apostles supporting us, may free us from the dangers that threaten.

For we know that it was generally decreed in the aforesaid Council of Nicaea that no one should rashly and indiscriminately tear apart or accuse bishops, nor should anyone who is not of the right faith, of good life, or of reputable conduct presume to defame them. Rather, if anyone has a case against bishops or leaders of the Church, he should first approach them with charity and gentleness, so that he may properly heal from them the wound at issue; or, if the accuser has acted otherwise, he himself should be excommunicated.

But if he is unable to obtain from them any proper remedy, then he should first approach the highest primates, and they must summon them canonically at a suitable time. [Col. 0640C] If those persons have been stripped of their possessions, expelled from their own sees, exiled, oppressed, or unjustly treated, they must first be rescued and canonically restored, and everything taken from them must be returned to them in full according to the law. For before this has been done, as was established in the aforementioned council, they can neither be canonically summoned nor compelled by anyone, since even the laws of the world do not permit such things to be done—how much less the laws of the Church?

Likewise, it was defined unanimously by the aforesaid Fathers that if any bishop has the metropolitan, his fellow provincials, or the judges under suspicion, he should appeal to your holy Roman See, to which the power of binding and loosing has been specially granted by the Lord himself as a privilege above others. That See, established by God as a firmament, firm and immovable, has been constituted by the Lord Jesus Christ as the clearest model of all ecclesiastical titles. It is the sacred summit on which all are turned, sustained, and lifted up; and just as Christians are renewed in Christ, and Peter in the rock—that is, in Christ—so are the churches renewed.

[Col. 0641A]

You are, as the divine word truly bears witness, Peter, and upon your foundation the columns of the churches—that is, the bishops, who must support the Church and carry it upon their own shoulders—have been established for you. To you he entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and he proclaimed with authority the power to bind and loose what is on earth and what is in heaven.

Nevertheless, as the overthrower of profane heresies, assailants, and all persecutors, you stand as prince, teacher, and head of all orthodox doctrine and immaculate faith. Therefore, father, do not despise the piety and good intention of your fathers; and just as those fathers and our predecessors freed many from oppressions and difficulties, so may you deign to free us.

[Col. 0641B]

For it has always been permitted to your holy and Apostolic See, by the authority of its power, to restore those unjustly condemned or excommunicated, to return all their possessions to them, and to punish by apostolic privilege those who condemned or excommunicated them, as we know was done both in our own times and in earlier times.

Moreover, the primates themselves, who ought to undertake the causes of bishops and of the highest ecclesiastical affairs, were enumerated in the aforementioned Council of Nicaea, so that no dispute might arise from this in the future.

O most holy father, cut off the blasphemies of the fathers, the boasting of empty talkers, and the attacks of those who plot against us and our brothers, oppressing us and wishing to destroy us. We flee to you as to our head, so that, supported by your help, we may be freed and, with the Lord’s assistance, rescue the sheep of Christ entrusted to you and to us from the mouths of wolves [Col. 0641C] before they are swallowed.

For it is not lawful to despise the prayers of suppliants offered to the Apostolic See, whether in writing or without writing. Rather, as is fitting and as is the privilege of your See, let both they and we be canonically summoned, and let us contend before you concerning our charges with complete integrity, just as our predecessors did before your predecessors, and as the canonical institutions teach in the aforesaid holy synod. Like grain separated by the winnowing fan of canonical examination, may we, standing together in the common assembly, receive full purification and share in the mature and nourishing doctrines of the Catholic Church, which strengthen the human heart, and in the instruction of the fathers.

For it was established by ancient rules that whatever might be undertaken, even in distant or remote [Col. 0641D] provinces, concerning complaints or accusations against bishops, must not first be handled or accepted until a decision had been issued for the information of your life-giving See; that decision would either weaken or confirm the case, and from that source they would take their standard from which the churches took the beginning of their preaching, lest the columns of the churches be overthrown indiscriminately by plotters.

For it is certain that the decrees of the Fathers have assigned to your same holy See, in honor of the most blessed Peter, a special reverence from God for investigating and determining matters which ought carefully and justly to be examined by that apostolic summit of the bishops. Its concern has always been, and remains, both to condemn what is evil and to approve what deserves praise.

[Col. 0642A]

Therefore, rendering the humblest obedience to your apostolic eminence, as the Lord commanded and the decrees of the holy Fathers established, we report with tears what we cannot keep silent without a groaning of the heart. For we are persecuted to such an extent by the persecutors of the holy Church of God and by our enemies that we are more weary of living than of dying.

Accordingly, above all we confess that our heart has been wounded so deeply that we long for that prophetic lament, saying: “Who will give water to our head and a fountain of tears to our eyes, so that, sitting down, we may weep day and night?” (Jer. 9:1).

For behold, the Church of God is being seriously disturbed, its columns are being fiercely attacked, and evil men strive to remove them. The voices and groans of Christians and bishops resound far and wide; innovations arise, [Col. 0642B] calumnies increase, persecution rages, and the destruction of peoples takes place. It is your duty to extend your hand to us, because we have been entrusted to you; it is your duty to defend and free us; and it is our duty to seek help from you and obey your commands.

Because of our excessive grief and groaning, we are unable adequately to recall and report to you all the things that press upon and harass us. Therefore we beseech your life-giving apostolate to restore the law promulgated in the aforementioned Council of Nicaea, although it has been suppressed by the aforesaid plotters and other evil men so that they may more easily ensnare bishops and ministers of God through their corruption. Inform us and all our brothers, by the authority of your holy See, of whatever you recognize as necessary, so that, supported by your authority and with the Lord’s help, we may escape unharmed from the plots of [Col. 0642C] evil men.

For it is not the task of sheep to foresee the plots of wolves, but of shepherds. We know that the pontiffs of your See—first the apostles, and then their successors—have always made you responsible for the care of the universal Church, and especially for the bishops, who are called the eyes of the Lord because of their contemplation and vigilance. You must continually consider our revelation and our law, as it is written: “Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1:2).

This meditation is not perceived merely through reading the figures of the letters; rather, through the grace of Christ overflowing in you, it is recognized as firmly planted in your conscience and in no way departing from your heart: the sacred law of Christ, God and Lord. As the prophet says in the psalm: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment; the law of his God is in his heart” (Ps. 36:30). It is written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God in your hidden mind, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of the heart of flesh, as the letter of the most blessed apostle Paul sent to the Corinthians teaches us.

[Col. 0642D]

Having stated these things, we make known to your God-pleasing fatherhood that, on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth indiction, our humility, with divine grace preceding us by its gift as he commanded, received consecration and the stole of pontifical honor in the holy Roman Church through your holy and God-worthy prayers.

[Col. 0643A]

In this dignity, we ask that we may be governed by the Almighty Most High and freed from every evil, so that, through the protecting help of Christ the Lord our God, we may possess not merely the name of priesthood but also its merit. We commend ourselves to your holy and God-pleasing prayers, asking that, strengthened by your prayers poured out to God on our behalf and instructed by good teachings, we may be made worthy, together with all the Christian people entrusted to us, to be protected unharmed by divine strength.

For the greeting of your holy and venerable fatherhood, we have sent in our place our blessed and humble brother, your bishop, together with Alexander the presbyter and Crispinus the deacon, your servants. We ask that they be returned to us quickly by your Beatitude, so that, strengthened by your exhortations [Col. 0643B] and instructed by your rules, with our enemies restrained, we may prudently return, comforted, to our own churches before winter, God willing.

For it is your duty, most holy father, carefully to oppose by canonical discipline those who resist ecclesiastical order and those who plot against their brothers, and not to permit anyone to say anew what the authority of the venerable Fathers has in no way decreed.

We, humble in heart and, with the Lord’s help, wise in what is right, are bound to you by one bond of charity, vigorously defending the true faith and Catholic religion in all things. Therefore we must strive all the more diligently to resist wicked Catholics, lest, overcome by sluggish negligence, we be held liable for the guilt of silence and be judged as though we were lending support, while [Col. 0643C] we neglect to repel what is hostile to the Catholic faith.

Hence it has been said: “To neglect, when you are able to disturb the wicked, is nothing other than to encourage them; and the one who ceases to oppose an evident crime is not free from the suspicion of secret complicity.” It is clear, most holy teacher, that the cunning of serpents, without simplicity, is poisonous, while the deceitful trickery of enemies is manifest.

Come to the aid, we ask, of the oppressed; free us from the hand of our persecutors, so that, together with blessed Job, you may sing:

“The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I consoled the heart of the widow. I clothed myself with justice and covered myself with it as with a garment, and with judgment as with a diadem. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and the case that I did not know I investigated most diligently. I crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched [Col. 0643D] the prey from their teeth” (Job 29:13–17),

and the rest.

For we, whose greatest care you are expected to have—that is, all bishops—must above all deserve your judgment and must not be devoured by others. Rightly, therefore, the cause of the Lord concerns us priests if we favor error by our silence.

Let such persons indeed be corrected, and let them not be free to make judgments according to their own will. Let innovation cease to harass antiquity; let disturbance cease to trouble the peace of the churches. For, so that all metropolitans and other bishops might not be able to exercise their hatred or vengeance against other bishops, the primates were expressly designated in the Council of Nicaea, so that they might hear and judge the other bishops and so that no fraud could intrude into the judgment of bishops.

[Col. 0644A]

Therefore, you who by God’s grace have been placed upon the highest watchtower must watch and restrain those who raise seditions and scandals against their brothers. For this reason we beseech you not to despise the afflictions and tearful prayers offered by our humility and by all the priests and peoples of the orthodox East. Rather, holding fast the word of life as lights for the whole world, extinguish the darkness introduced by the most wicked plotters, which in our own times has grown insolently.

Then, once such darkness has been completely extinguished, may Lucifer shine upon us through you, most holy father, together with the dogmas and the definition that bring joy to all, which the glorious holy Fathers of the Church are known to have proclaimed with the utmost devotion as a firm inheritance of eternal life; and the subscription.

[Col. 0644B]

May the Lord preserve you unharmed and pleasing to God, most holy father of fathers, praying for us, forever. Amen.

## Reply of Pope Felix to the same persons
To the most reverend and beloved brothers Athanasius and all the bishops of the Egyptians, Thebaids, and Libyans assembled in the holy Alexandrian synod, Felix, bishop of the blessed city of Rome and of the universal Church, and the holy synod gathered in the city of Rome, greetings in the Lord.

We gladly received your sacred synodal letter, composed through the grace of the Holy Spirit and with devotion pleasing to God, through the favor of your sanctity, which is honored by God. We ordered it to be read aloud word by word in the synod and commanded everyone attentively to gather its words [Col. 0644C]. While we hoped and desired to rejoice over them, our lyre was turned into mourning, our song into lamentation, and all the joy of the entire synod was changed into sorrow, because it was not fitting that those who daily consecrate the body of Christ with their own mouths should suffer such persecution. For our God, providing salvation for the human race, commanded that persecutions not occur, that disturbances not be inflicted, that those laboring in the Lord’s field not be envied, and that the stewards of the great King not be harassed or expelled.

“Rest,” says the holy and great Council of Nicaea, “and do not persecute those who serve God perfectly, who preserve the commandments of the Most High God with sincere devotion, and who are subject to our laws, because it is neither fitting nor permitted by order that the wicked and carnal should persecute the spiritual.” [Col. 0644D] For everyone who resists another—now by distorting, now by concealing the truth—lies against the person with whom he contends; and whoever is hostile to someone acts in every respect like an enemy and, moreover, strives to speak against him.

We warn you, brothers, that you must stand watch, so that, insofar as you can and the Lord grants assistance, you may resist such persons with our apostolic authority and yours. Let none of you withdraw from helping his brother, but let each provide assistance according to his strength. For although you are few, if you are united in mind, you will in no way be overcome, with justice supporting you and the Lord also bringing aid, because “a threefold cord is not easily broken.”

If human law comes to the aid of secular offices, how much more ought divine and catholic law to support ecclesiastical offices and, above all, the priests of the Lord [Col. 0645A]? For the divine word says concerning bishops: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zech. II, 8). And if secular persons are examined in many ways under human law, with investigations and adjournments of many months granted to them so that they may not be unjustly condemned, how much more ample periods must be granted to bishops, who are closer to God and have been placed over others in the heavenly service, which must be weighed with greater care, so that they may not be burdened or oppressed by certain persons or condemned suddenly.

Let us therefore begin, with the help of God and of the holy apostle Peter, through whom the apostolate and episcopate began their origin in Christ. For many causes have often arisen which in some cases were not causes but crimes [Col. 0645B], because, as we have discovered, they were imposed upon brothers more through iniquity than through charity.

So that henceforth care may be taken that such things do not occur, let us set forth certain chapters established by the holy fathers, both in the Council of Nicaea and in this See. Fortified by these, our brothers and fellow bishops may, with the Lord’s help, escape the snares of their enemies. And insofar as the Lord grants ability, let us imitate the concise form of so many great matters with fewer words; let us briefly review what we have found in the volume of your letter, and, as you request, set forth certain other matters necessary for the present time.

It has been decreed by synodal ordinances that no one may accuse a bishop before secular judges, but only before the highest primates. If anyone has a case against a bishop, he must not first approach other bishops [Col. 0645C] to accuse him before he has privately made his complaint known to him and received from him either a just correction or a reasonable explanation. The Truth itself instructs us:

“If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone; if he does not listen to you, take with you two or three others; and if he does not listen to you, tell it to the Church” (Matt. XVIII, 15–17)—that is, accuse him publicly, and not before that, and so forth.

If anyone afterward chooses to accuse a bishop, he must state his case before the highest primates of the bishops, not before secular persons. They should recall the parties to peace rather than judgment, so that charity may be preserved in all things and by all.

If the primates cannot privately reconcile the accusers with the bishops, then, at the proper time, they must canonically summon them to a canonically convened synod, not within an unduly short period [Col. 0645D], and not before informing them in writing of the charges brought against them, so that they may arrive prepared to answer.

For if they have been expelled by force or fear, or stripped of their property, they can neither be canonically summoned to a synod nor required to answer their adversaries before they have been canonically restored and all their property has been legally returned to them.

If any bishop has been stripped of his property or expelled from his church by force or fear—a thing hostile to every Christian name—it is proper and fitting that the bishops’ resolve should always yield at the outset, so that everything taken away may be legally restored to his authority, and that the bishop be restored first [Col. 0646A]. Only afterward, not immediately but after a long period and extended intervals, when his property has been placed under his authority and prepared for his needs, should he come at the appointed time to the hearing and, if it seems just, answer his accusers.

No infamous or sacrilegious person may give testimony in any matter against a religious Christian, however humble or servile that person may be; nor may such a person bring a Christian to trial over any matter, whether by formal accusation, legal action, or indictment.

If a bishop has been lawfully accused and, according to the procedure stated above, canonically summoned to a council, he must go without any fear. If he cannot go himself, he must send a representative to the synod.

No cases are to be heard by ecclesiastical judges that are not contained in the laws or that are known to be prohibited.

If anyone refuses to accept any other procedure and insists on accusing a bishop, he must proceed according to the form stated above, since otherwise the accusation cannot be valid. First, the accuser must canonically bring the case of the accused before the primates. The accused must not be deprived of communion unless, after being canonically summoned to the judgment of the chosen judges, he delays coming for three, six, or more months in order to give an account of himself [Col. 0646B]. If he can prove that he did not refuse but was unable to come, this will do him no harm.

But the man who has been driven from his see by force or fear, or stripped of his property, must not be summoned to a synod until everything has been restored to him according to the laws. He must remain peacefully and with full authority in his own see, disposing of everything, for as long as he had appeared, while expelled or stripped, to have lacked his property.

When he comes to the judgment, if [Col. 0646C] he wishes and necessity requires it, adjournments established by the fathers must be granted to him without hindrance. Judges chosen by him must also be assigned, so that he may select a suitable place—either the place from which the accused is himself, or, if he fears the violence of some rash crowd elsewhere—in which he can, without fear, have his witnesses with him if necessity demands, and bring his canonical case to a conclusion without hindrance, since many things commonly arise through clandestine intrigue.

Permission to testify or accuse must be denied to those who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, the rule of their own law or profession, or matters regularly prohibited.

Detraction becomes exceedingly powerful when the detractor is believed. Therefore a primate must not be undermined by various disparagements and accusations [Col. 0646D], but rather strengthened by the rules of the fathers. He must not presume lightly or indiscriminately to accept accusations, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “You shall not receive a false report.” He must first examine the suspicion and the case, or the intention with which the accuser acts, and only afterward accept it, because the profession of truth is often obstructed—and harm inflicted upon brothers—by relationship, hostility, fear, affection, hatred, and desire.

The persons who bring accusations must be such that their faith, conduct, and life are demonstrably upright and without reproach, and that they are entirely free from suspicion. For this too, in your presence, as you well know, was defined by everyone in the Council of Nicaea, because of the attacks of wicked men, although many such provisions have been erased by the plots of evil persons [Col. 0647A].

The primates shall be those, and no others, who were established in the Council of Nicaea. The others who occupy metropolitan sees are called archbishops, not primates—without prejudice in anything to the dignity of the Apostolic See, which was granted to it by the Lord himself and afterward strengthened by the holy men of earlier times.

In every accusation of bishops, the life, character, and conduct of the accusers must always first be investigated in detail. Only afterward should the matters alleged be faithfully examined, since nothing ought to be done before the credibility of the accusers has first been ascertained.

The character, life, and actions of the persons involved must be examined, because the life of the innocent must not be torn apart by the destruction caused by wicked or scheming men. Indeed, good people are very often scattered by evil persons who never cease to disparage others through their own calamities. Therefore the greatest care must be taken that such things do not happen [Col. 0647B].

No slave, no freedman, no unfaithful person, no one entangled in crimes, no slanderer, no one devoted to hostility, no habitual litigant, no one quick to accuse or disparage, no infamous person, and no one whom the public laws do not admit to the accusation of public crimes may be permitted to accuse bishops. For I cannot see why the sacerdotal order ought to receive accusers or accusations that the laws of the secular world do not accept, since these matters were also prohibited in the Council of Nicaea. Such persons ought rather to be judged by these men, not these men by them; and the Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one.”

Heretics, by whom we are grievously oppressed, and excommunicated persons—murderers, sorcerers, thieves, sacrilegious persons [Col. 0647C], robbers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, those who have given false testimony, and those who have resorted to diviners and magicians—must in no way be admitted either to accusation or to testimony. Nor should ecclesiastical cases be conducted in the same manner as secular ones.

For in secular matters, once someone has been summoned according to the laws and has begun to contend in court, he may not withdraw before the case has been completed. In ecclesiastical matters, however, a person may withdraw after the case has been stated, if necessity requires it or if he sees that he is being overburdened.

Whenever a bishop is accused of definite crimes, if the accusers are such as ought to be accepted justly and canonically, they must all be heard canonically in a lawful synod convened at the proper time, with all the bishops of the provinces present. But if the accusers are not legitimate, the bishop must not be wearied [Col. 0647D], because priests ought to be free for sacrifice, not litigation. Nor should those who are called the thrones of God be disturbed by the plots of wicked men; they should serve Christ the Lord freely.

The bishops of a province, together with their metropolitan, may indeed jointly conduct the cases of the bishops of their province. Nevertheless, as was established in the synod mentioned above, they may not decide them without the authority of the Roman pontiff. If some presume to act otherwise, those who have done so must bear the penalty of their presumption; and those whom they have wrongly excommunicated or condemned must be released and restored by the authority of this holy See and by the power of our blessed teacher and key-bearer Peter.

[Col. 0648A] For the Lord himself says: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed on earth and in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19).

Whenever bishops think that they are being overburdened by their fellow provincial bishops or by their metropolitan, or whenever they regard them with suspicion, they must immediately appeal to the Roman See. They must be allowed to go there freely, without any detention or seizure of their property. Once they have appealed to the Roman Church, the mother spoken of above, or have requested to be heard by it, no one may presume to excommunicate them, seize their sees, take away their property, or inflict any force upon them before their case has been concluded by the authority of the Roman pontiff.

If anyone presumes to act otherwise, his action will be nothing and will have no force.

For we do not presume this improperly. It was established in the Council of Nicaea, and our predecessors acted properly in accordance with it. You know this, Athanasius, because when you, Paul of Constantinople, Asclepius of Gaza, and Lucian of Adrianople [Col. 0648B] were condemned by the eastern bishops without consulting our predecessor of holy memory, Julius, and fled to him as to the head of the whole world—as has always been permitted to this holy See—he, having learned of their wickedness and your justice, received you into communion. Concerned for all of you, and because of the dignity of his own See, he wrote to the easterners, restoring each of you to your churches and reproving them because they had not dealt rightly, expelling innocent men from their churches and failing entirely to preserve the decree of the Council of Nicaea.

He ordered certain of them to appear before him on a fixed day so that they might give a definite account of such presumptuous actions [Col. 0648C], and so that he might show in their presence that he had issued a just decree against them. He also warned them that their brothers would not suffer such things thereafter, and that unless they ceased from such presumptuous actions, they would be removed from their own ranks.

By this privilege of this holy See, you and your brothers received your own churches, together with everything belonging to them. These and many other examples make it clear that no bishop who has appealed to this holy See or chosen it as his defender ought to be condemned or stripped of his property until he has learned the judgment issued concerning him by our apostolic authority—that is, by the authority of Peter, prince of the apostles. For Christ Jesus alone entrusted this power to this holy See, that is, to the Apostolic See, since the aforesaid prince of the apostles alone, on behalf of all, was entrusted with and merited receiving from Christ God, the King of kings, the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

Concerning the adjournments of bishops, about which you consulted us, we find that the fathers established differing rules. Some ordered a year or six months to be granted, in order to repel the schemes of inexperienced persons, prepare their answers, confirm witnesses, seek councils of bishops and friends, and make other preparations. Others prescribed a year, with which many agree; I have found no provision of less than six months, since such adjournments have been granted even to laypersons, and therefore much more to the priests of the Lord.

Our predecessors and the other holy fathers were also often forbidden [Col. 0649A] to allow anyone to bring detraction against the priests of the Lord—how much more accusations not arising from the root of charity.

“Rest,” they say, “and do not persecute those who serve God perfectly, whose prayers calm earthly wars and drive away the attacks of angels who have departed from God, and who, through the constancy of their prayers, put to shame all demons who have been corrupted.”

Adjournments must not be granted for a short period but for a long interval, so that the accused may prepare himself, meet with all the communicants in the provinces, prepare witnesses, and fully arm himself against his attackers. Judges and accusers must be persons entirely free from suspicion and desirous of delivering their judgment from the root of charity.

Having set forth these matters both legally and canonically [Col. 0649B], we ask also that all Christians rejoice in reverence, with spiritual affection intervening, and with the fear of the Lord, through which human offense is removed and the building up of the churches is proposed to everyone, so that all may labor more for the edification of their brothers than for their condemnation. For the Lord says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII, 31).

We have already provided a rule, and have learned that our predecessors provided one, namely, that anyone who recognizes himself to be a Christian should preserve what is known to have been declared by the apostles. The Apostle Paul says: “If anyone announces to you anything besides what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. I, 9).

For Christ, the Son of God and our Lord [Col. 0649C], granted the human race complete salvation through his own suffering, in order to free us. And if God loved us so greatly that he did not spare even his own Son but delivered him up for us all in order to free us, why do we not love our brothers, or why do we rashly judge them, when the Apostle mentioned above says: “Let us not judge one another, but rather judge this: that you do not place a stumbling block or scandal before your brother” (Rom. XIV, 13)?

For if those who love their brothers are born of God and see God, what then will become of those who persecute them and seek to condemn them by disparaging, plotting against, accusing, and harassing them? If the former are children of God, without doubt the latter are children of the devil, who always “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V, 8) [Col. 0649D], and so persecute their brothers that they may destroy them.

Those who refuse to help their brothers acquire a greater burden of sins and become liable for the deprivation of fraternal support. “Woe,” says the prophet, “to him who gives his companion drink, pouring in his own gall” (Hab. II, 15).

And again the wisest Solomon says: “For the one who speaks wickedly cannot remain hidden; judgment will not pass him by when it reproves him” (Wis. I, 8). Thus there will be an inquiry into the thoughts of the impious, and the hearing of his words will reach God for the correction of his iniquities, because the ear of jealousy hears everything, and the tumult of those who murmur will not be hidden.

If they had wished to embrace these things, they would not have slipped away from their own sound understanding into a depraved mind [Col. 0650A]. Rather, by the fear of God they would have guarded themselves against their words and preserved the pious definition of the holy fathers without any presumptuous harm, since the sacred word says: “Good counsel will preserve you, and sound understanding will guard you.”

Such accusations and disparagements do not proceed spiritually from life-giving springs toward the pursuit of eternal life. Therefore blessed Paul appropriately admonishes us, saying: “We must not think more highly than we ought to think, but think with sober judgment” (Rom. XII, 3).

Those who pass by the definition of piety are not merely injured by falling away from their own strength, but have also left mankind a memorial of their folly, so that they could not remain hidden from those against whom they sinned; for glory and disgrace are in human speech, and a person's tongue is his downfall.

Therefore it is fitting that this demonstration be joined to the rebuke of those persons through our actions, so that you may no longer suffer such things from those who sow weeds and scandals, but may deserve to rejoice in your offices and doctrines [Col. 0650B].

Let them therefore be ashamed and hasten to withdraw such things and similar blasphemies, if they do not wish to be separated from our priestly fellowship and torn away from the society of the entire Christian people.

Although we could have said and written much more about these matters and about many things of the greatest necessity that are found established in the decrees of the Apostolic See and by the apostles and their successors—our predecessors—it nevertheless seemed better to us to close the letter with a prayer.

May almighty God, and his only-begotten Son and our Savior Jesus Christ, grant you this encouragement: that you may [Col. 0650C] come to the aid with all your strength of all our brothers and fellow bishops who are laboring under whatever tribulations, and, suffering with them, carry the cross of that same Lord and Savior, so that you may appear before everyone as his true disciples. May both you and those who are with you possess here and in the future the better things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9), through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory belongs to God the almighty Father, forever and ever. Amen.

I wish you well, most beloved brothers. Given on the Ides of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Agarius and Julianus.

## On the Oppression of the Arians

[Col. 0650D]

Felix, pope of the holy universal Church and, by the grace of God, bishop of the catholic and apostolic Church of the city of Rome, together with our holy council of the most reverend priests who have assembled here with us for the confirmation of the most pious doctrines of the catholic Church and the relief of our oppressed brothers and fellow bishops—namely, those who hold the right faith of the Council of Nicaea and do not harass their brothers—to all our spiritual brothers and to the rest consecrated to the Lord in the priestly fellowship, and to the entire fullness of the catholic Church: may grace and peace be multiplied to you in the strengthening and communion of the Holy Spirit, so that, advancing in him from glory to glory, we may “proclaim the mighty deeds of him who called us out of darkness into his marvelous light” (I Pet. II, 9), “with whom there is no change or shadow due to alteration” (James I, 17).

We exhort you, brothers, to bear persecutions and tribulations patiently, so that you may be found to be sons of him whom you call daily your Father in heaven, and in him conquer all things, just as he conquered all things for us. He “did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32).

It is fitting for those who imitate God to imitate God in every word and deed. Therefore we must say what the Lord himself testified about himself: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

Those who persecute you and us have come, because they cannot persecute you without us: we are members of one God [Col. 0651A] [Col. 0651B], and through his sanctification we retain one priesthood. They found nothing of their own in us, because whatever we are, we are by the grace of God, although for this reason they have irrationally attempted to slander us, as enemies are accustomed to do, hastening thereby to conceal their own madness, so that through falsehood they might be able to overshadow the truth.

“I wrote to you,” says the Apostle, “through many tears, not so that you would be grieved, but so that you might know the abundant love I have for you.” For it is not good to disparage those who disparage us, lest, provoked by the things written, we should fail in the contest of insult.

We must not fear the reproach of human beings at all, nor be overcome by their taunts, since the Lord commands this through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, in whose hearts is my law: do not fear the reproach of human beings, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies” (Isa. LI, 7) [Col. 0651C].

We must also consider what is written in the Psalm: “Will God not seek these things? For he knows the secrets of the heart” (Ps. XLIII, 22), and the thoughts of such people, since they are empty. “Everyone has spoken vanity to his neighbor; deceitful lips have spoken from the heart and from the heart they have spoken evil. The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue. They said: ‘Our lips are our own; who is our lord?’” (Ps. XI, 3–5.)

If they kept these things in memory, they would not rush into such great iniquity. They do not act according to worthy and paternal teaching, but so that they may exercise their vengeance upon the servants of God. For it is written: “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes,” and, “There are ways that seem right to a person, but their end leads to death.”

We who suffer this must leave the matter to the Judge, who will repay each person according to his works, and who also thundered through his ministers, saying: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. XII, 19).

You, however, assist one another in right faith and with pure and good will. Let no one withdraw his hand from supporting his brother, for the Lord says concerning this: “Everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII, 35).

Therefore he speaks through the prophet, saying: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII, 1) [Col. 0652A].

I speak of a spiritual dwelling and of the harmony that is in God, and of the unity of faith that is delightful according to the truth of this dwelling. This dwelling was more fully adorned in Aaron and in those who wore the priestly dignity, like oil upon the head, watering the principal understanding and leading it onward to the very end of knowledge. In this dwelling the Lord promised blessing and eternal life.

Embracing the merit of this prophetic prediction, we have interpreted the present fraternal expression, seeking neither now nor hereafter anything for ourselves because of charity. For it is not good to disparage those who disparage us, or, according to the common saying, to drive out one stake with another. Far be it from us. These things are not ours; therefore may the Divinity avert them.

Our habits have not been taught to overcome in this way, but through patient endurance and a spirit of humility. For just as, to speak prophetically, black cumin is not purified through harshness, so the peaceful fruit of understanding is not drawn out through severity. For this reason we have endured the blows of words, so that little by little we might be able to imitate him who deigned to humble himself for us, and through this wound avoid the words of his final vengeance.

Let us therefore hear and agree with the Church’s preacher, who cries out in a clear voice through the tongue of the Spirit: “Let everything among you be done in charity” (I Cor. XVI, 14).

Thus, whether we seek something, or merely speak, or are merely heard, let charity intervene; let there be some skill for composing concord and joining together what is good.

For, as we seek God, we must examine the intentions of our mind in a spirit of uprightness and dwell peacefully in the temple—in him who spoke through the prophet, for God's sake: “Seek by seeking, and dwell with me” (Isa. XXI, 12) [Col. 0652C].

God has made us a mirror for his people. Those who have been appointed by God to attain the priesthood must therefore advance toward one another in the humility of their minds, so that those who look to us may be built up for the better, rather than—as it pains me to say—have the path of their feet shaken by our discord.

Let us judge ourselves toward concord, let us think as one in charity, and let us honor humility, through which the height of the spirit is usually grasped.

If until now we have preferred silence concerning words to loquacity, we have considered this good, lest, by responding in turn to your letters, we kindle the fuel of injury and be judged faint-hearted by him who has proclaimed that all things must be directed toward charity [Col. 0652D].

“We prayed that a door of restraint be placed around our lips” (Ps. CXL, 3), so that we might conceive a word for utterance rather than a word that must be sounded aloud. Yet this too is a gift from the Lord: “I became like a person who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth” (Ps. XXXVII, 15).

But because there is a time for speaking and a time for silence, I cover the word and suitably close the door through silence, praying: “Lord, open my lips” (Ps. L, 17), “and I shall answer those who reproach me with a word” (Ps. CXVIII, 42) [Col. 0653A]. Although we have been silent, we will not always remain silent, when the Lord opens for us the keys of speech.

Therefore, when the representatives of your blessed fraternity had been sent to us, after many discordant discussions had taken place between us concerning ecclesiastical inquiry, they finally reached this point: they admonished and urged us to interpret the meaning of the will of our one true God and to send such an interpretation to your most sacred reverence.

We accepted the admonition of the aforesaid venerable men, given with a good conscience. We also recognized that we are ready to give satisfaction, as the summit of the apostolate teaches, to anyone who asks for a word concerning the hope that is in us, according to the fear of God, tempering gentleness with sound knowledge. Concerning this particular inquiry, therefore, we set forth our mind in these words, avoiding and guarding against superfluous verbal exercises and disputes, because of the weariness they cause and their inappropriateness to the present time [Col. 0654A].

We understand and proclaim nothing at all other than what we have heard and learned from the holy, universal, and great apostles and their successors, and what our fathers have explained to us; and, hearing it, we have proclaimed it while striving toward the heavenly calling.

Our concern is that peace be established. For those who are in the contest of piety, there is one glory, and the intercessor receives the crown. We have been made manifest before God, who judges all things and approves them.

We do not stand in a quarrelsome manner; we do not look toward contradiction, nor do we embrace empty favor. Rather, in the word of God, we are known to have made resolutions concerning this inquiry, confessing that the Lord God of peace has preserved among us unity and affection, to the glory of his most benevolent majesty.

We, and those who are with us, give abundant greetings in Christ to the entire fraternity existing with your blessedness [Col. 0654B].

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Philemon and Atticus.

## Letter of Pope Liberius

That no one should abandon his Church during persecutions while he is able to remain.

[Col. 0653]

[Col. 0653B] To the most holy and God-loving lords, all the bishops: LIBERIUS, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

Nothing can stand for long except by the grace of God. Moreover, the devil’s wickedness, a contemptible evil full of deadly poison, sows destruction; he “goes about above and below, seeking whom he may devour (I Pet. V, 8).” Therefore we must watch and be sober for prayers, draw near to God, and, with the Lord’s help, reject the foolish snares of men insofar as the Lord grants us power; we must follow the fathers and not transgress the boundaries of the fathers—not so that we may abandon our churches while we are at some point able to persevere in them and hurry to others, nor neglect the peoples entrusted to us in order to seek greater quiet than labor on their behalf, for whom we ought even to lay down our lives. Although many persecute us and desire to tear Christ’s sheep apart, they “appear outwardly like sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves, whom we recognize by their fruits (Matt. VII, 15–16).”

These people at first indeed seem to be from among us, but they are not from us; for if they had been from us, they would certainly have remained with us. But when they have vomited forth their impiety, breaking out in the deceit that is within them and seizing the weaker, they drag along with them to destruction those who have untrained understanding of the divine utterances. They overturn those whom it is necessary to forewarn so that they may beware, lest, seduced by their malice, they be severed from their own firmness. “For they sharpen their tongues like serpents, according to the prophet’s voice: the poison of asps is under their lips (Ps. CXXIX, 4).”

Nor should you be reluctant to labor through temporal sufferings for Christ’s name; rather, let the rewards of the future recompense persuade you to endure the afflictions of this age.

[Col. 0654B] For it is written: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I shall receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord (Ps. [Col. 0654C] CXV, 12).”

Only as much is demanded from us as we can contribute through the service of our ministry. Therefore it is all the more necessary for us to persist in urgent preaching, the more we are believed to have been entrusted with a doubled allocation of talents in a perfected enterprise, and the more the Lord’s declaration urges us to receive his rest.

For it has been reported to us that, because of past labors and persecutions, some of you are abandoning the peoples assigned and entrusted to you by God; and that in the future you intend to abandon still more of those churches which you ought to protect. You neglect to labor for the sheep entrusted to you, hasten to devote yourselves to the quiet of monasteries, choose release from episcopal labors, and prefer to spend your life in silence and leisure rather than remain in the duties entrusted to you.

[Col. 0654D] For the Lord says: “Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end (Matt. XXIV, 13).” What is blessed perseverance, then, except the virtue of patience? According to apostolic preaching, all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution. Therefore, dearest brothers, do not let the bitterness of afflictions constrain you to withdraw from the devout purpose of your minds.

Consider how much our Creator, Lord, and Redeemer endured for our absolution and liberation, and to what insults he handed himself over, so that he might free us from the bonds of the devil’s power. Therefore take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock in which “the Holy Spirit appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God (Acts XX, 28),” which he acquired with his own [Col. 0655A] blood, so that no one may deceive or seduce you through subtle speech, causing you to abandon the peoples entrusted to you and surrender yourselves to quiet because of the reproach of evil men, so that you alone may be saved while leaving your children orphaned.

For the Holy Spirit most clearly says through the Apostle “that in the last times some will depart from the faith and charity, attending to seducing spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose conscience has been branded (I Tim. IV, 1–2).”

For this reason we exhort your charity, after the example of him who was willing to suffer for us, to remain ready in all things for his service, and in no way to withdraw from the care entrusted to you, but to persevere bravely with all your strength in the duties committed to you, to the very end.

[Col. 0655B] For blessed is the one who perseveres to the end; it is not the beginning that is praised, but the end. “Let no one deceive you with empty words. For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience (Eph. V, 6).”

Therefore do not become participants in their doctrines, nor share in their fruitless words; rather, rebuke them. For they are a gathering of transgressors, and they have stretched out their tongue like a bow of falsehood and not of truth. What is written has been fulfilled in them: “They have gone from evil to evil, and they have not known me,” says the Lord. For they will not speak the truth; they have trained their tongue, as persecutors of the churches and their priests, to speak falsehood, so that they might act impiously. “They labored, and they refused to know me (Jer. IX, 6),” says the Lord.

“Stand therefore, beloved, upon the ways, and see; inquire about the ancient paths of the Lord, and see which is the good way of the holy fathers, and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls (Matt. XI, 29).”

But if you suffer for Christ, you will be blessed. Do not fear their fear, nor be troubled; rather, sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. He himself says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna. Are not two sparrows sold for an as? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father. Even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Therefore do not fear: you are worth more than many sparrows (Matt. X, 28–31).”

Remember, then, brothers, him who endured such opposition from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary and fail in your minds; for you have not yet resisted sin to the point of blood.

[Col. 0655D]

We are confident concerning you, dearest brothers, of things better and nearer to salvation: that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither powers, neither present things nor future things, neither strength nor height nor depth, nor any other creature, as the teacher of the nations teaches, will be able to separate us from the love of our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. VIII, 38–39), and from the right faith that is in him.

[Col. 0656A] Therefore do not cast away your confidence, which has a great reward. Patience is necessary for us in our struggles against adversaries, so that, preserving an undefiled faith to the end, we may receive the promise that he promised to those who hasten to contend lawfully (Heb. X, 35–36).

“Yet a very little while, 161 and the one who is to come will come, and will not delay (Heb. X, 37).” “For behold, the judge stands before the door (Jas. V, 9),” promising crowns joyfully to those who submit to sufferings for his sake. But if anyone withdraws, his soul will not be pleased with him, and he will fall from [Col. 0656B] the promise because of denial. But we are not children of withdrawal, leading to perdition, but of faith, leading to the gaining of the soul.

“Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day against all the enemies of God’s holy Church and your own; and put on the breastplate of righteousness, with your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one. And receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, rooted and founded through every prayer and supplication in the consolation of the brothers, through Christ Jesus our Lord (Eph. VI, 13–14).”

“But even now, brothers, we commend you all to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to perfect you and give you an inheritance among [Col. 0656C] all the saints (Acts XX, 32).”

“May the God of peace and love grant you to think the same toward one another (Rom. XV, 5),” so that you may assist one another and not be divided; so that, with one mind, one mouth, and one heart, we may honor him in concord and in the consolation of the brothers. He is able to strengthen us according to his Gospel, in accordance with the revelation of the eternal mystery, throughout the ages in which the gifts of future joys are to be bestowed upon you.

You must also consider most carefully that those who envy their brothers and desire to condemn or destroy them destroy their own doctrines by themselves. For the Lord says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand (Matt. XII, 25),” and every knowledge and law divided against itself will not stand.

Therefore it is necessary that you receive these saving exhortations harmoniously, doing nothing through contention, but unanimously obeying the divine and apostolic constitutions with every effort of devotion. In no respect should you permit the decrees of the provident canons to be violated, so that both the ordinances of the Nicene canons and those decreed carefully and beneficially by us or by our predecessors may remain undefiled in the future.

## THE DECREES OF POPE DAMASUS BEGIN.

[Col. 0655]

His letter to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch.

[Col. 0655D]

I. That he assumed a complete human being without sin.

[Col. 0656D]

II. That Christ is one: begotten from the Father before the ages and born from the Virgin in time.

To his dearest brother PAULINUS: DAMASUS.

[Col. 0657A] Through my son Vitalis I had sent you a letter, leaving everything to your will and judgment; and through the presbyter Peter I had indicated that I had been moved to some extent by certain matters concerning the stage of his completion. Therefore, so that no scruple might remain with you, lest your prudent caution, perhaps wishing to unite with the Church, should delay the faith, we sent our statement both to you, who are joined to his faith and communion, and to those who, by subscribing to it, wished through you to be joined to us and to you, dearest brother.

Accordingly, if my aforementioned son Vitalis and those who are with him wish to be joined to you, he must first subscribe, in that undertaking of faith, to what was confirmed at Nicaea by the devout will of the fathers.

I. Then, since no one can apply medicine to future wounds, the heresy must be eradicated which is said later to have sprouted in the East. That is, it must be confessed that the Son of Wisdom, the Word of God, assumed a human body, soul, and sense—in other words, the complete Adam and, to speak more explicitly, our entire old human being, without sin.

For just as, when we confess that he assumed a human body, we do not immediately add to him the human passions of vices, so also, when we say that he assumed both a human soul and sense, we do not immediately say that he was subject to the sin of human thoughts.

II. But if anyone says that the Word took the place of the human sense in the Lord’s flesh, the Catholic Church anathematizes him. It likewise anathematizes those who confess two sons in the Savior—that is, one before the incarnation and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin. Rather, all who wish to subscribe to this letter must confess the same Son of God both before and afterward.

This is to be understood, however, in such a way that, if they have already subscribed both to the ecclesiastical canons, which you know very well, and to the Nicene faith, you ought to receive them without any ambiguity. Not because we could not propose these very things that we have written to those who are returning to communion, but so that our agreement may provide you with a free example in receiving them.

## Roman Synod under Pope Damasus

After the Council of Nicaea, another council was subsequently assembled in the city of Rome. At it the Catholic bishops added a statement concerning the Holy Spirit, because afterward this error grew up, so that certain people dared, with sacrilegious speech, to say that the Holy Spirit had been made through the Son.

Therefore we anathematize all who do not proclaim with complete freedom that he is of one power and substance with the Father and the Son. We also anathematize those who follow the error of Sabellius, saying that the Father is the same as the Son. We anathematize Arius and Eunomius, who, with equal impiety though differing in speech, assert that the Son and the Holy Spirit are creatures. We anathematize the Macedonians, who, coming from the stock of Arius, changed not their perfidy but their name. We anathematize Photinus, who renews the heresy of Ebion and confesses the Lord Jesus Christ as existing only from Mary the Virgin.

[Col. 0658A] We anathematize those who assert two sons, one before the ages and the other after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin. We anathematize those who say that the Word of God was active in human flesh in place of a rational and intelligible human soul, though the Son himself is the Word of God, and that he was in his body in place of a rational and intelligible soul, but that he assumed and saved our soul—that is, a rational and intelligible soul—without sin.

We anathematize those who contend that the true Son of God will, through extension or collection, be separated from the Father and have a substantive existence and an end. If anyone does not say that the Father has always existed, the Son has always existed, and the Holy Spirit has always existed, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Son was born from the Father—that is, from the Father’s divine substance—let him be anathema. If anyone [Col. 0658B] does not say that the Lord’s Word is the Son, God from God, almighty, and equal to the Father, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that, while established in the flesh, the Son of God, when he was on earth, was not in heaven with the Father, let him be anathema. If anyone says that in the passion of the cross the Son of God, who is God, endured suffering, and not the flesh with the soul that he had assumed, “in the form of a servant which he had taken for himself, as Scripture says (Phil. II, 7),” let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that, in the flesh “which Christ assumed, he sits at the right hand of the Father, and in that flesh he will come to judge the living and the dead (II Tim. IV, 1),” let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is truly and properly from the Father, just as the Son is from the divine substance, and that he is true God, let him be anathema. If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is almighty, knows all things, and is everywhere, just as the Father and the Son are, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a creature, or was made by the Son, let him be anathema. If anyone does not say that the Father made all things through the Son and the Holy Spirit—that is, visible and invisible things—let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one divinity, one power, one glory, one dominion, one kingdom, one will, and one truth, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the three persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are truly equal, always commanding all things, containing visible and invisible things, almighty, judging all things, giving life to all things, making all things, and saving all things, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is to be worshiped by every creature, just as the Son and the Father are, let him be anathema. If anyone thinks rightly about the Father and the Son but does not hold a right belief about the Holy Spirit, he is a heretic.

## Letter of Pope Damasus to the presbyter Jerome

DAMASUS, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to his brother and fellow presbyter HIERONYMUS.

When many volumes of books had been placed at my disposal, it happened that I realized in haste that the Book of Psalms had also been entrusted to my consideration. I therefore thought that I should refresh the memory of my capacity, dearest brother and ever a priest in Christ. I ask you, according to the seventy interpreters and presbyters—that is, Matthias, Tholomaeus, Muchius [Col. 0659A] Cassius, Dithronius the brother, Simon, and the others—to send us, insofar as your knowledge permits, whatever traces you can find of the Seventy.

I also ask your charity that, just as you learned from your rector, the co-bishop Alexander, your fraternity may delight in directing to us the Greek psalmody. For among us there is such an investigation into simplicity that on the Lord’s Day only one epistle of the Apostle is read and one Gospel passage is recited; the custom of psalm-singing is not observed, nor is the beauty of hymns known in our mouths.

Therefore, through our brother and fellow presbyter Boniface, I ask that your fraternity may be pleased to disclose these traces to us. Sent on the fifth day before the Kalends of November through Boniface, presbyter of Jerome.

## Jerome the presbyter’s reply to Pope Damasus, in which he recommends singing “Glory to the Father” and “Alleluia” at the end of the psalms in the Roman Church

[Col. 0659B]

To the most blessed Pope DAMASUS of the apostolic see of the city of Rome: HIERONYMUS.

As a suppliant, I have read the letters of your apostolate requesting that, according to the simplicity of the Seventy Interpreters, I hasten to interpret the canons and the psalm-writer, for the sake of the Romans’ weariness, so that where obscurity obstructs, the meaning may be expressed more clearly in both Greek and Latin.

Your client therefore begs that this voice of those singing the psalms may be sung day and night in your Roman see, and that the order of your apostolate should command it to be joined to the end of every psalm, whether at the morning or evening hours: “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,” and the rest.

[Col. 0659C] Command that this song of praise be joined to every psalm, so that the faith of the 318 bishops of the Council of Nicaea may be declared in your mouths with equal fellowship. Wherever God and man are sung in an honorable voice, let “Alleluia” always be attached to all the psalms, so that at night it may be answered communally in every place.

In the Church, however, let it conclude the period from the Resurrection until holy Pentecost; during the interval between the days, let it be sung for you alone on the fiftieth day, because of the novelty of holy Easter, in Aleph, which in Greek is called the prologue and in Latin the preface.

## Letter of Stephen, archbishop, and the three councils of Africa to Pope Damasus, concerning the privilege of the Roman see

[Col. 0659D]

To the most blessed Lord, exalted to the apostolic summit, the holy Father of fathers, Pope DAMASUS, supreme pontiff of all prelates: STEPHANUS, archbishop of the council of Mauretania, and all the bishops of the three councils of the African province.

We make known to your blessedness that certain brothers situated near our borders are casting, or attempting to cast, certain of our brothers—namely, venerable bishops—from their proper rank without consulting you. Yet the decrees of all the fathers reserve to your see the judgments concerning bishops and the conclusion of the highest ecclesiastical matters, with every decision, out of reverence for the investigation of divine affairs, which we ought to observe with all care and diligence.

They ought especially to be examined by that apostolic summit of prelates whose ancient concern it is both to condemn evils and to reveal what deserves praise. For it was established by ancient regulations that whatever of this kind might be done in provinces, even remote or far distant, must not first be handled or accepted unless it had been brought to the knowledge of your nourishing see, so that it might be confirmed by its authority according to what had been pronounced, and so forth—many other matters of this kind and similar matters that have been established concerning them.

If this was done unlawfully, hasten, as has always been the custom of your see, to intervene, and stand firmly against them, fighting as a father for his sons, as it is well said by Jesus son of Sirach: “Fight for the truth unto death, and the Lord God will fight for you always (Eccli. IV, 33).” “For it is not good to accept the person of the impious, so as to turn aside from the truth of judgment (Prov. XVIII, 5).”

[Col. 0660A] But if these actions are not unlawful, most blessed Father, let such license be openly available to all of us; or, if it is permissible to summon or condemn these men, or even clerics of lower rank, without their having been canonically summoned at the legitimate time, without legitimate accusers or true and innocent witnesses, without their having been manifestly convicted canonically or having always confessed, and without their first having been restored to their sees and their property, then let this be made clear.

For we read that they cannot canonically be summoned to a synod before they have long held and governed their sees, with their strength fully recovered and everything legally restored to them; nor can they be compelled to come to a synod unless they wish to do so voluntarily.

May God, the creator of all things, preserve your long-lived apostolate for the stability of the holy Churches and of the orthodox faith. May he preserve you as the good shepherd who lays down your life spiritually for the sheep, drives away ravenous wolves with the pastoral staff, and brings aid to all the oppressed. This is what we always desire you to do for these men and for everyone, most holy pope.

Subscription in another hand. Pray for us, dearest Father.

## Replies of Pope Damasus to the same persons

DAMASUS, servant of the servants of God and, by his grace, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, to STEPHEN, archbishop of the council of Mauretania, and to all the bishops of the African province.

Having read the letters of your fraternity, I first give thanks that I have been deemed worthy to enjoy the blessing of so many brothers; then I give thanks that I have found you concerned for your brothers and carrying the Lord’s cross with them, he who says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me (Matt. XVI, 24),” together with the other passages that pertain to this in the same manner.

Therefore, when your blessedness, moved by apostolic compassion, exhorted us in the present consultation concerning the acts appropriately undertaken to provide, by apostolic authority, protection for the brothers and aid against their injuries—and when it is clear that you compassionately say with the Apostle, “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burned? (II Cor. XI, 29)”—you are striving lest anyone among those entrusted to you be torn apart or captured by savage beasts.

For this reason, in accordance with your prudent admonition, and more especially according to the Lord’s divine command, we who have received episcopal ministry over his household—that is, over the universal Catholic Church—must watch carefully so that no one, without our knowledge and counsel, may be condemned from among his sacred ministers, namely, the apostolic men, the successors of the apostles, and their ministers.

[Col. 0661A] You know, dearest brothers, that the apostolic see has been established as the firmament, fixed and immovable, and as the brightest title of its priests—that is, of all bishops—and as the summit of the Churches. For, as the divine Word truly declares: “You are Peter, and upon your firmament the pillars of the Churches, understood as bishops, have been established; and to you I have entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and I have proclaimed to you the power to bind and loose the things that are in heaven and the things that are on earth.”

You are, as prince and teacher of orthodox and undefiled faith, the profaner of impious men and of my members, especially of my disciples; in whose place we today perform, by the grace of God, the embassy for Christ, and all the prelates of this holy see have acted, act, and will act in his place.
