Therefore I would not have commanded all the things that you have reported to be unlawful unless I knew that you were so fully instructed that you did not doubt that everything about which you consult us is unlawful.

It is permissible for metropolitans, together with all their comprovincial bishops, so that none of them is absent and all agree concerning each individual matter, to investigate bishops and the causes of the highest ecclesiastical affairs. But it is entirely impermissible for them to decide those matters, conclude the principal ecclesiastical causes, or condemn bishops without the authority of this holy see. All must appeal to it, if necessary, and be supported by its aid.

For, as you know, it is not Catholic to hold a synod without its authority. Nor can a bishop be definitively condemned in a legitimate synod, convened at the proper time by apostolic summons; nor are any councils ever read as having been ratified unless they were supported by apostolic authority.

[Col. 0661D] The accusers of bishops and the witnesses concerning whom you have asked must be entirely free from infamy, suspicion, and manifest blemish, and must be fully instructed in the true faith. They must be of the sort whom divine authority commands to be chosen for the priesthood, since priests, as ancient authority teaches, cannot be accused or testified against by persons who ought not, and cannot, be advanced to that same honor.

According to the canonical decrees of the fathers, the one who is accused must be summoned to the synod at a suitable and canonical interval, both by his personal presence and through writings and envoys. For unless he has been canonically summoned at the proper time and through canonical procedure, even if he comes to the assembly by some other arrangement, he is in no way to answer his plotters unless he wishes to do so voluntarily. For the laws of the world do not permit this to be done; how much less do the divine laws?

Concerning those who have been deposed and stripped of their property, I can report nothing more truthful to you than what the most holy fathers have defined and our predecessors have strengthened by apostolic authority.

[Col. 0662A] The holy canons have decreed that bishops who have been expelled and stripped of their property must first be restored to their own Churches and have everything legally returned to them. Only afterward, if anyone wishes to accuse them, may he do so at equal risk. The canons have established that judges should be men who think rightly and desire justice; that the bishops should first be given time—indeed, a long time—to recover their strength and enjoy their property with full authority; and that they should meet in the Church with prudent friends and servants of God offering wise counsel, where witnesses to each individual matter would be present concerning those who appear to have been oppressed.

For we know that unarmed men cannot properly fight against armed men. Likewise, those who have been expelled or stripped of their goods cannot properly litigate against those who remain in their rank and enjoy their friends and possessions.

Nor do the laws of the world permit this to be done to secular persons. Rather, they order that those who have first been expelled, oppressed, or stripped of their property be restored with everything of theirs, and afterward, at the proper time, be summoned to court, as their law provides. They do not permit an appellant to be prevented by any imprisonment. For, as you know, earthly matters teach heavenly matters in part.

Accusers and accusations that the laws of the world do not admit must in no way be admitted in these cases, because the Catholic Church defends everything that is irreproachable.

It is fitting for the priests of the Lord to handle the cases of their brothers piously and attend to them with reverence, arranging their judgments concerning sacrifices, and carrying out everything not with insolent or tyrannical domination, as is reported concerning certain men, but with charity for God and fraternal love.

No one should presume to inflict upon another what he does not want done to himself, according to the Lord’s word; and “with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.”

We must always hold to the things that we have commanded through the preaching of the apostles and the instruction of the fathers, lest we appear either to forge something new or to aim at the harm of our brothers, but rather “bear one another’s burdens, so that, according to the Apostle, we may fulfill the law of the Lord (Gal. VI, 2).”

[Col. 0662C] A suitable time must be foreseen, for the case of every accused person should be brought forward most properly in the midst of the assembly, so that they may recognize its gravity and the agreement of the matter, which must not be produced contrary to the decrees of the fathers or the confession of synods. Let everyone attend to it in an orderly manner, so that they may answer it rationally in every respect and clearly demonstrate that they desire justice.

No one, however, should be brought forward in person; rather, accusers and accused should be heard on equal terms, according to what the order of the proceedings requires. Accusers and judges must not be the same persons. There must be accusers in their own capacity, judges in their own capacity, witnesses in their own capacity, and accused persons in their own capacity—each properly in his own order.

For an inscription of the accusation must always be made first, so that the slanderer may receive the corresponding penalty. No one should be judged or condemned before the inscription, since the laws of the world also maintain these same provisions. In all these matters, true equity must always be observed, so that through the truth of the proceedings they may obtain the reward due to accusation, judgment, and testimony.

For it is written: “Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord (Prov. XII, 22),” and “a false witness who speaks lies and sows scandals and quarrels among brothers (Prov. VI, 19).” He himself admonishes and says: “You shall not slander your neighbor, nor oppress him by force; you shall not do what is unjust, nor judge unjustly; you shall not favor the person of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful; judge your neighbor justly (Lev. XIX, 18 and following),” and “what you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another (Tob. IX, 16),” and other passages.

[Col. 0663A] Above all, we must heed the apostolic command to take heed to ourselves and to the flock “in which the Holy Spirit placed us as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired through his own blood (Acts XX, 28).”

It is also fitting to take heed of wolves and of evil workers, who act perversely and speak hostile words, always seeking to disparage the Lord’s disciples and defame them. You and all the priests of the Lord must correct such people with the greatest zeal, for there is no worse evil than for citizens to envy citizens and for priests or clerics to plot against priests or bishops.

The voice of Truth also bears witness: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye (Zech. II, 8).” And again: “Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones, it would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were drowned in the depths of the sea (Matt. XVIII, 6).” And again: “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized because of me (Luke VII, 23).”

Without doubt, the one who scandalizes God is the one who scandalizes his bishop or priest. There are many other passages of this kind which are not inserted here, lest the letter become too lengthy.

You must also admonish and instruct the aforementioned neighboring brothers to withdraw from such actions, and to correct promptly what they have done unlawfully against the appointed brothers; and those whom they have injured without consulting us, they must heal and reconcile promptly through full satisfaction, if they do not wish to accept the censure of the apostolic see.

For if anything had arisen either among them or against them, they ought to have awaited our examination, so that by our authority—as the privilege has always been granted to this see—they might either be condemned or strengthened by our assistance.

Nor ought they, according to their own pleasure, to invade our rights without the disposition and command of the apostolic see.

[Col. 0663D] Henceforth all priests who do not wish to be excluded from priestly honor by the censure of the apostolic rock—upon which Christ, as was said above, built the universal Church, to which the highest judgments concerning bishops and the causes of greater persons have been reserved and entrusted alone, as was mentioned somewhat earlier—must abstain from such actions.

For accused bishops in criminal cases must be granted an adjournment of six months, or longer if necessary. No one trained in secular disciplines is unaware that this is permitted even to laymen; how much more must it be permitted to priests, who are unquestionably superior to them?

It is also established in the decrees of the holy Fathers that it is not canonical to judge or condemn any priest before the accused has his accusers, canonically examined, present and receives an opportunity to defend himself—that is, ecclesiastical time for clearing the charges, and so forth. Nor may an accusation for initial examination be brought outside its own province without an apostolic injunction, whose authority must be respected in every case, since the ancient rule of the Fathers also teaches this, and imperial statutes agree with it. “The examination of crimes,” they say, “must be conducted where the crime was committed.” For elsewhere the accused in a criminal matter is forbidden to be heard, and elsewhere this is prescribed in the canons. “Whatever cases have arisen must be concluded in their own places,” and other such provisions and those resembling them, with apostolic authority preserved in all respects, so that nothing in these matters is settled before it is known to be pleasing to that authority—for all ought to be supported by it, and if anything serious and intolerable should befall them, its judgment must always be awaited.

Nor should anyone rashly or driven by the impulse of his own thought—as we have often learned has happened—presume to disparage or accuse any priest, because an injury against them pertains to Christ, in whose place he serves as ambassador for the people redeemed by Christ’s blood. Their cases, because they are God’s cases, must be reserved for the judgment of him who can kill the body and cast the soul into Gehenna (Matthew 10:28), who says, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Ephesians 10:30). Before him conscience is naked, and hidden things are not concealed from him.

Everyone must also be instructed that, through us, Christ has thundered to them that it is not for sheep to anticipate the attacks of wolves, but for the shepherd (John 10:12–13). Therefore blessed Paul the Apostle warns “that judgment should not rashly and lightly be presumed concerning those matters about which no one can judge more truly or better than God” (1 Corinthians 4:5). “But you,” he says, “why do you judge your brother, or why do you despise him? For we shall all stand before the tribunal. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.’ Thus each of us shall give an account of himself to God” (Romans 14:10).

Therefore no one should arrogate to himself rashly the authority to do anything in this matter except what pertains to concord, lest the unity of the Church be thereby scattered. Let no one lightly consent to the disparagement, judgment, or condemnation of the brethren, and especially of priests, who are nearer to God and who, with their own mouth, consecrate the body of Christ; “for on this account the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience” (Ephesians 5:6), who persecute Christ in his members. “Do not, brothers—do not become their partners” (ibid. 7), nor share in the sins of such men or in their fruitless words. Rather, rebuke the assemblies of such persons, who strive to stretch out their tongues against the brethren as though they were a bow. Therefore defend the brethren, and warn everyone to arm themselves against the persecutors of the brethren.

“But we are confident concerning you of better things, and things nearer to salvation” (Hebrews 6:9), because “neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither pressing things nor things to come, neither powers, neither height nor depth, nor any other creature,” as the Teacher of the nations teaches, “will be able to separate us from the love of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 8:38–39), which is perfected above all in priests and in his other members. Therefore do not cast away your confidence, which has a great reward.

For behold, the judge stands before the door, joyfully promising crowns to those who bring aid to the brethren for his sake, assist the oppressed, and labor together in charity. But if anyone withdraws, he will not please God; rather, he falls, because he did not raise up the one who was falling, but withered away. Let us not be agents of withdrawal into oppression, but helpers in the acquisition and strengthening of the brethren.

Therefore “take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist all who presume in this way; put on the breastplate of righteousness, and let your feet be shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, with all prayer and supplication” (Ephesians 6:13 and following), “rooted and founded” (Ephesians 3:17), so that you may all say the same thing, and so that there may be no schisms among you dividing the body of the Church, which is good and whole, through twisted innovations.

Therefore the Apostle warns us no longer to judge one another rashly (Romans 14:13). A person judges rashly if he condemns a bishop without the authority of the apostolic see, although, as was briefly stated above, this particular privilege has been specially reserved to it. “But judge this rather,” he says, “that you do not place a stumbling block or scandal before your brother” (ibid. 14).

It is plainly evident to all, through these and countless other testimonies of the decrees, that a bishop must not be condemned, even if his opinion is investigated, until the judgment from the mouth of our apostolic authority—that is, of the Prince of the Apostles—is known. He alone, above all others, was entrusted with this, and he merited receiving from Christ God, the King of kings, the keys of the kingdom of heaven: to open it to the faithful and well-disposed who believe in our same Lord, and to close it against unbelievers and ill-disposed persons, against his own priests, and against the attackers or offenders of the holy Church redeemed by his precious blood.

This is what he has also required us to do—not because anything new is now being commanded, but so that what, through the negligence of some, is knowingly or carelessly transgressed may henceforth be observed by all, and so that those things established by apostolic and patristic tradition may always be held under the fear of unshakable authority.

For it is written in the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians and to Timothy, with the Apostle admonishing: “Stand firm and hold fast to your traditions which you have learned, whether by word or by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:14). Likewise, elsewhere through the prophet: “I waited,” as blessed Isaiah thundered, “that they should do judgment, but they committed iniquity and not justice, bringing disturbance upon all the devout” (Isaiah 5:7). They must also know that “the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things. Although they are ignorant of the riches of God’s goodness, forbearance, and patience, they do not know that God’s kindness leads them to repentance; but according to their hardness and impenitent heart they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each according to his works” (Romans 2:5–6).

Elsewhere it is written: “I am the Lord your God. You shall not commit iniquity”; “In judgment you shall not show partiality to a person” (Matthew 22:16); “Nor shall you be awed by the face of the powerful” (Leviticus 19:15); “You shall turn away from every iniquitous word”; “You shall not attack or kill the innocent and the just” (Daniel 13:53).

Without doubt, the person commits iniquity in judgment who claims for himself what he is not permitted to claim. Therefore no one should presume to usurp, without consulting this holy see, the things granted to it—unless he wishes to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor as a contemptuous person.

Thus negligence must be driven away, but in such a manner that the guilty are not strengthened, and that good men may resist the wicked and those who plot against the brethren, lest, overcome by the torpor of negligence, they be held liable for their silence. Whoever can oppose and disturb the perverse but does not do so is nothing other than a supporter of their impiety. Nor is the person free from the suspicion of secret partnership who ceases to oppose an open crime.

Be perfect and whole, then, established in the same understanding and in the same knowledge, so that, directing your ways by it, you may steadfastly confront all oppressors, because the Lord is entrusted to you. When you approach him, he is the living stone rejected by human beings and, because of the impiety of such people, chosen and honored by God; upon him “you, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to him as a fragrant offering” (1 Peter 2:5).

It is a very pleasing sacrifice to the Lord to assist the oppressed, and all the more those of whom he says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me,” and so forth (Luke 10:16). The person offers the Lord a favorable sacrifice who drives adversity away from the afflicted and oppressed.

But now, brothers, “we commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to perfect you and give you an inheritance among all the sanctified” (Acts 20:32). “May the God of peace and consolation grant you to think the same thing toward one another and always in him and in all things, so that with one mind and one mouth and one heart you may honor him” (Romans 14:5–6), in concord and in aid of the brethren—him “who is able to strengthen and console all according to his Gospel and according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal times” (Romans 16:25), but made manifest through the Holy Scriptures and the teachings of the orthodox Fathers, according to the command of the eternal God, “for obedience to the faith made known to us in all things” (Romans 1:5)—to the only wise God, our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, are glory, honor, dominion, and power forever and ever. Amen (Romans 14:27).

May the Lord keep you safe and unharmed always, most beloved brothers.

Issued on 8 November, in the fourth consulship of Flavianus and Stilicho.

## That all who think wrongly about the Son of God and the Holy Spirit, and about the unity of the Trinity, are like the Jews; and concerning the unity of the Trinity

If anyone permits God the Father, God the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be called “gods” and not God, despite the one divinity and power which we believe and know to belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; if, by excluding either the Son or the Holy Spirit, he thinks that God the Father alone should be called or believed to be the one God, we anathematize him—indeed, as the text says, even in relation to all Jews. For the name “gods” has been placed and bestowed by God upon angels and upon all the saints. But concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of their one and equal divinity, the name not of gods but of God is shown and indicated to us, as we believe. For we baptize only in the Son and the Holy Spirit, and not in the names of archangels or angels, as heretics, Jews, or foolish pagans do.

This, therefore, is the salvation of Christians: that, believing in the Trinity—that is, in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—as the true and only divinity, we believe without doubt in the one power, majesty, and substance of that same deity.

Blessed Isaiah also says: “For the sake of Zion I will not be silent, and for the sake of Jerusalem I will not rest, until her righteous one goes forth like brightness and her Savior is kindled like a lamp” (Isaiah 62:1).

Indeed, the Catholic Church, which truly stands as Zion, the city of Christ, the King of heaven, has for so many years been attacked by adversaries of the word of faith, “who neither fear God nor respect human beings” (Luke 18:2). Although pious and canonical teachings concerning this matter had been brought forward in vain, they had been summoned by contrary and weighty testimonies, both written and unwritten, to correct their own error and bury their heresy, as was shown more clearly in the preceding inquiry, both through the petitions and through the representations of the most revered priests and venerable abbots.

The Apostle bears witness to us that “a heretical person, after the first and second admonition, must be avoided” (Titus 3:10), since we know that such a person is subverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment. Therefore we must by no means remain silent or rest any longer, lest we in some way be judged wicked for embracing a peace hateful to God.

For it is written: “I was jealous when I saw the prosperity of sinners” (Psalm 72:3). And it may also be said of us: “My priests have despised my law and profaned my sanctuaries; they have made no distinction between the holy and the profane, and they have not understood the difference between the polluted and the clean” (Ezekiel 23:38). Rather, we must rise with God and promptly stand firm, putting on the weapons of the Spirit against those who act maliciously against his faith, so that we may test the spirits wisely—that is, their words—to see whether they are from God.

For it is written in Jeremiah: “I have appointed you as a strong tester among my people, and you shall know and test their way” (Jeremiah 6:27).

Great vigilance is therefore necessary for us, together with such a measure of the divine wisdom of discernment as reveals the hidden things of darkness, in order to investigate and scrutinize this matter. For malicious deceit lies hidden and concealed in a certain way and is scarcely apprehended, because it cunningly flatters itself with the appearance of piety, so that it may escape the mind of those who investigate it. Knowing this, blessed the Apostle says: “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness; their end will be according to their works” (2 Corinthians 2:13–14).

The Lord also warns and arms us in this matter, saying: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:15).

Therefore, with one accord and with our whole heart, let us first bring supplication concerning this question, saying with David: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118:18). “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths” (ibid. 105). For, as blessed Daniel the prophet says: “His are wisdom and strength; he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who possess understanding. He reveals deep and hidden things, and he knows what is established in darkness, and light is with him; for you gave me wisdom and strength and showed me what I asked of you” (Daniel 2:20–24).

With divine assistance, let us give careful and methodical attention to the written submissions of each person accused in connection with the fabrication of novelty, brought forth in due order from the venerable archive at our command.

## Concerning chorepiscopi: what they are the same as, and whether they are something or nothing

To our venerable brothers and lords, Prosper, bishop of the first see of Numidia; Leo, Reparatus, Alexander, Benedictus, Rufus; and all the other orthodox bishops everywhere who stand firm in the right, holy, and apostolic faith: Damasus.

Although, dearest brothers, the decrees of the Fathers are known to you, we cannot help admiring your diligence concerning the institutions of the ancients, since you do not cease to refer to us, as to the head—as has always been customary—everything that may admit of some doubt, so that you may receive answers from the source from which you received your formation and the rule of right living. Accordingly, we recall that you are not forgetful of the canons, which also command this very action—not because anything is lacking in your knowledge of ecclesiastical discipline, but so that, supported by the authority of the apostolic see, you may deviate in nothing from its rules.

Therefore, concerning the chorepiscopi, about whom you consult us as to what their ministry is, what they may do, what authority they possess, and whether they may be created at all—for we have heard that they have already been prohibited—and concerning what should be done with those who are found already ordained, we can give you no answer more certain than the decree that we found to have been issued long ago by our predecessors: nothing whatever should be reserved for their pardon except deprivation of the sacred ministry which they unlawfully assumed, since they had been prohibited both by this holy see and by the bishops of the whole world.

Their institution, therefore, is exceedingly unlawful, exceedingly perverse. For their presumption of anything from the highest priestly ministry lacks every authority, is found contrary to the sacred canons, and tends through arrogant and superfluous elevation toward the disturbance of the whole Church. Whatever they have done in the aforesaid ministry of the highest priesthood is empty and vain.

That these men are the same as presbyters is sufficiently shown by the fact that they were originally instituted according to the pattern and example of the seventy disciples. But because, thanks be to God, they are now not necessary, as they were in the primitive Church because of the service they were required to render to the poor; and because they presumed to do unlawful things, so that what they did was not valid; and because many, having fallen into security, were thereby defrauded and deprived of ecclesiastical ministry, they have therefore been removed from pontifical offices both by this holy see—as we mentioned above—and by all the bishops of the whole world.

For, as was reported to us, certain bishops, for the sake of their own ease, do not fear to entrust their congregations to them, so that they may perform unlawful and prohibited acts—that is, they usurp for themselves those things that belong only to bishops—while the bishops themselves languish in their own ease and neglect the care entrusted to them by God. Yet the Lord says: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, calls them by name, knows his own, and his own know him” (John 10:2–11). And again: “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father, and I lay down my life for my sheep” (ibid. 11).

You know well what he says about the hired man: “He sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees; and the wolf seizes and scatters the sheep” (ibid. 12), and so forth.

Because of such men the care of the Church is neglected, her condition is disturbed, and therefore they have been prohibited—so much so that, if any of them are found, they are to fall from their own rank.

Those bishops who presume such things for themselves seem to me like prostitutes who, as soon as they give birth to their children, hand them over to other nurses to be raised, so that they may more quickly satisfy their own lust. So these men hand over their children—that is, the peoples entrusted to them—to others to raise, so that they may satisfy their own desires: that is, so that they may devote themselves at will to secular concerns and do more freely whatever each of them sees fit. Because of such conduct souls are neglected, sheep perish, illnesses increase, heresies and schisms arise, churches are destroyed, priests are corrupted, and other evils follow.

The Lord did not teach this, nor did the apostles establish it. Rather, those who undertake the care should themselves carry it out, and they themselves should present their own sheaves to the Lord. For he diligently sought the lost sheep himself, found it himself, and carried it back on his own shoulders; he taught us to do the same.

If he himself showed such care for all, if he himself taught, cared for, healed, and carried it back on his own shoulders, and loved it so greatly that, enduring many injuries, many insults, and many sufferings for us, he handed over his own life—what will we wretched and sluggish people say, who neglect to devote care even to the sheep entrusted to us and hand them over to others to lead?

These things must be corrected, brothers. For whoever labors more receives the greater reward.

We know that there are no more than two orders among the Lord’s disciples: that of the twelve apostles and that of the seventy disciples. From where this third order has arisen, we utterly do not know, and what lacks reason must be eradicated.

That these men are not bishops is evident to everyone, since they have been ordained by fewer than three bishops. For, as you know well, the holy Fathers prohibited that those ordained by one or two bishops should even be called bishops. If they do not have the name, how will they have the office? Whatever they have done among bishops, or concerning matters belonging only to bishops, must necessarily—as was already stated above—be declared invalid, because those who do not possess something cannot possibly give it.

Especially since no one among the seventy disciples, whose likeness these men represented in the Church before they were prohibited, is read to have assumed anything of what belonged specially to the apostles and their successors. Nor, in the law of the Lord which is read to have been dictated by the Lord himself to Moses, did the sons of Aaron presume anything of what had been specially granted to the high priests, namely Moses and Aaron.

No one doubts that Moses and Aaron alone, at the Lord’s command, erected the altar in God’s tabernacle; alone anointed; alone instituted priests through sacred anointing; and alone performed the other things belonging to the high priesthood, concerning which the divine writings speak sufficiently, since they were the Lord’s high priests, as it is written of them: “Moses and Aaron among his priests” (Psalm 98:6).

So now, because the shadow of the law has passed and the light of the Gospel shines manifestly upon us by God’s grace, those who bear the form of the seventy disciples—and whose type was represented by the sons of Aaron—must presume nothing of those things belonging to the high priests, that is, to bishops, whose figure Moses and Aaron bore, just as those sons of Aaron touched nothing of the ministry of the high priesthood.

For the canon sufficiently shows that, before the aforesaid prohibition, the chorepiscopi had been instituted according to the pattern of the seventy. It says: “The chorepiscopi also appear to be according to the example and pattern of the seventy,” and so forth.

Nor does this seem to us something that should be passed over: elsewhere it is expressly stated in the canons, “Those who are called chorepiscopi in villages and estates, although they have received the imposition of the hands of bishops and have been consecrated as bishops,” and so forth.

I do not consider it irrelevant that it says “although they have received the imposition of the hands of bishops,” since the word *episcoporum* (“of bishops”) contains a plural number and among grammarians is a plural genitive. Let it be granted, then, that at that time they were ordained not by one but by several bishops; for it would in no way have said *episcoporum* if the ordination of such men had been performed by one person, since *episcoporum* is expressed in the plural.

But when it said *chorepiscopus*, it certainly intended a village bishop to be understood. And if he is a village bishop, what is he doing in a city, when it is altogether forbidden for there to be two bishops in one city? And if he is in a village or in a place where bishops had not previously existed—although it is forbidden for a bishop to be created even in a small city, village, or fortified town, and altogether in any place where bishops had not previously existed, lest the authority and name of bishop be cheapened—what, I ask, will they be?

Behold: neither does the place agree with the ordination, nor the ordination with the place. For if they received the imposition of the hands of bishops and were consecrated as bishops, where were they consecrated—to a village, since *chora* means “village” among the Greeks? And how could they be consecrated for a village if it is not permitted even in a fortified town or a small city? I ask you to bring this forth. If you cannot bring it forth—for I know that by reason or by full authority you cannot do so—put your finger to your mouth and do not doubt that they lack every authority.

Three things, clearly, invalidate their action or institution.

First, they are accustomed to be ordained by one bishop; in this their ordination disagrees with the canons, which command that they be instituted through the hands of bishops.

Second, if they were ordained by several bishops, it remains that they were appointed either in a village, a fortified town, or a small city, or altogether not in the place where bishops ought lawfully to be created; or they were appointed where bishops had not previously existed, lest the authority and name of bishop be cheapened; or they were appointed in a city together with another bishop, although, as stated above, two bishops ought not to exist in one city.

Third, they may have been instituted independently, as we have heard concerning certain men. All these things entirely lack episcopal authority.

There remains also the fact that their order has no authority in the divine writings. For, as was stated, there are only two primary orders in the Church: that of the apostles and that of the seventy disciples.

If, then, they are not bishops—for they cannot be bishops for the reasons stated above—and if they do not wish to be called presbyters because they aspire to be something greater and attempt to do more than the seventy disciples would have done, according to whose pattern, as we briefly mentioned above, these men were instituted by certain fools—“seeking their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21)—before they were prohibited, and presume to do unlawful and forbidden things; and if they do not wish to be called what they are, I ask you to state plainly what they are. For either they are something or they are nothing.

It is plainly evident that they are not bishops. And if they are not bishops, while they disdain to be presbyters, what will they be? Either they will be something altogether, or nothing; for nothing can exist unless it has a source from which it comes. If it has no source or origin, it possesses no authority and cannot properly stand, because it is empty and must be destroyed and fall, since it is nothing and will be reckoned as nothing.

But if they are none of the things we mentioned above, then necessarily they are nothing of those things that belong to priests. Therefore they must not be counted in the priestly register, except only—as we first stated—that, out of mercy toward those who are willing to bear this humbly, no longer aspire to more, and confirm the same in writing with their own hand beneath it, this alone may be granted to them: that they have a place among priests, remain content with the ministry of presbyters, and participate only in the Lord’s table.

Those, however, who wish to aspire to more must not retain even this privilege of being priests, but must be wholly deprived of ecclesiastical honor.

They are not permitted to consecrate priests, deacons, or subdeacons; to consecrate virgins; to erect, anoint, or consecrate an altar; to dedicate churches; to prepare chrism; to mark the foreheads of the baptized with chrism; publicly to reconcile any penitent at Mass; to send formal letters; to bless the people; to enter the baptistery or the sacristy before the bishop; to baptize or sign a child in the bishop’s presence; to reconcile a penitent without the command of his own bishop; to celebrate the sacred sacrament of the body and blood of Christ in the bishop’s presence unless the bishop commands it; to teach or greet the people while he is present; or to exhort the congregation.

You have been taught all these things by the preceding and by other constitutions of the Fathers and sacred canons as belonging to bishops alone. If necessary, they can be fully taught and instructed for the benefit of some who know less [or: *minus*, “less”—a marginal or textual indication], so that by this both the distinction of ranks and the summit of dignity belonging to the highest bishops may be demonstrated.

The same provisions must also be observed concerning presbyters: they must do nothing without the command of their own bishop, because what is rare appears also to be more beautiful. And if the name of bishops is cheapened, the whole order of the Church is disturbed.

There is therefore a threefold guilt in this matter: first, that they do what is prohibited; second, that the sacred ministry is polluted by the disgrace of such association; and third, that the rights of bishops are dissolved insofar as concerns the rashness of unlawful usurpation.

[Col. 0672C] But that it belongs exclusively to the apostles and their successors to confer the Holy Spirit, the book of the Acts of the Apostles teaches—especially since none of the seventy disciples, whose figure these men bear in the Church, is recorded to have conferred the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, as has been said. Therefore, since these practices are wholly without reason, let no one henceforth usurp them or consent to them—no priest, that is, who does not wish to be separated from our sacerdotal college [165]. Nor should what is being extinguished by us, and has already been extinguished, as stated, by our predecessors and by the remaining bishops of the whole world, be sown among anyone through dark roots. Rather, whatever is known to have grown up wickedly must be torn out by the roots, lest any weeds corrupt the Lord’s harvest.

Thus the priests of the Lord will produce abundant fruit, if those things that customarily destroy the growing crop are cut away by the roots. Let that presumption cease which so many judges have prohibited and condemned. Nor should the chief priests imitate harlot women, who, driven by the pleasure mentioned above, give their infants to others to nourish; rather, let them themselves nourish them for their own Lord, themselves return the fruit with interest, and present fruitful sheaves with glory. For if the Lord touched and cleansed lepers among the other cares of his sheep, why do we disdain to do the same? Or why do we ourselves, who have undertaken the pastoral office, hand them over to others to be nourished? Especially since the Lord said to Peter, our teacher: “If you love me, feed my sheep,” and many other things of this kind (John [Col. 0673A] XXI, 17).

For the blessing which the aforesaid chorepiscopi gave by the laying on of hands before their prohibition seems to us rather to inflict a wound than to bring salvation. And since they possessed the summit of the episcopate, how could they give what they did not possess, since there was nothing for the giver himself to receive? Or who among human beings, though we speak in human fashion, can give what he does not have? Especially since, because they were not bishops, they could not give what belongs exclusively to bishops. Therefore, they wounded all the more those whom they touched through the laying on of hands, when by some blessing they gave what had not been conferred upon them.

For this reason, whatever they presumed to exercise from the aforesaid episcopal ministries was invalid, and they accomplished nothing for those whom they touched; rather, according to the prophet, they conferred “a curse instead of a blessing, if it is proper to say so” (Jer. XLIV, 8). Consequently, through that unlawful laying on of hands, as we briefly indicated above, the head of the person who seemed to have received something was wounded. And where a wound has been inflicted, medicine must necessarily be applied so that the implanted blemish may be healed. That is, whatever has been performed or conferred unlawfully and is not at all approved must be repeated, if it is to be regarded as complete.

For I cannot discover how one who received honor from someone who did not lawfully possess the power to give it could retain that honor. Since he who did not possess episcopal honor could not grant episcopal rights, neither could they claim for themselves what they had not been capable of receiving, because the very obstacle had stood in their way.

Therefore, claiming for ourselves in particular the care of this matter, we earnestly ask for mercy, so that whatever offenses may perhaps have been committed in these matters may be corrected, that such things may no longer be permitted to occur, and that no excuse may arise from ignorance. For just as the condition of the Churches, established and adorned by a salutary arrangement, brings us joy, so we are deeply saddened whenever we learn that anything has been presumed or committed against the decrees of the canons or ecclesiastical discipline.

If we do not cut these things away with the vigilance we ought to show, we cannot excuse those who wish us to be watchmen, if we do not, as far as we are able, preserve pure from such unlawful superstitions the Church entrusted to us universally. For we are not otherwise one flock and one shepherd unless, as the Apostle teaches, we all say the same thing: “Let us be perfect in the same understanding and in the same wisdom” (I Cor. I, 10).

Nor shall we otherwise be true disciples of the Lord unless each of us hastens, according to his strength, to uproot the root of bitterness that grows upward—as, you assert, this practice now does—so that it cannot harm anyone by causing the episcopal ministry to become contemptible through the negligence of those priests who have been appointed by him to uproot evil and plant what is better. Let each one strive to eradicate it according to his ability, and let him who must render an account to the eternal Judge for his sheep strive to cherish and educate them.

If we desire to be the Lord’s disciples, let us imitate his footsteps, so that it may be said of us: “I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and I call them by name, and my sheep know me,” and the rest (John [Col. 0674A] X, 11).

And again, instructed by the command of the Lord’s voice through which the most blessed apostle Peter was imbued by a threefold repetition with a mystical injunction, let the one who loves Christ diligently love and carefully feed Christ’s sheep. For we are constrained by love and reverence toward the holy see over which, through the abundance of divine grace, we preside, so that, as far as we can, we may avoid the danger of so great a superstition, which, as stated above, is supported by no authority. Otherwise the love of our blessed teacher and chief apostle—by which he testified that he was a lover of God—will be found empty in us. For everyone who feeds the Lord’s flock negligently is shown not to love the supreme Shepherd, nor to wish to become the disciple of one whose example he neglects to imitate. Indeed, greater grace will surely be acquired if the shepherd’s diligence offers the Lord profit from the sheep entrusted to him.

We also remember that blessed Jacob, who had served for a long time for his wives, said: “For twenty years I was with you. Your sheep and goats were not barren; I did not eat the rams of your flock, nor did I show you what had been taken by a wild beast. I bore every loss; whatever was lost by theft you demanded from me. By day and by night I was burned by heat and frost; sleep fled from my eyes” (Gen. XXXI, 38–39).

If, then, the man who fed Laban’s sheep labored and kept watch, with how much labor and with how many vigils must the one who feeds God’s sheep devote himself? But in all these matters may he himself instruct us who gave his life for his sheep, and may he help us so that, concerning those entrusted to us, he may grant us to carry back to eternal joys abundant fruit and overflowing measure.

And may such love for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, inflame you that, in his sheepfold—to which all creatures have been entrusted—you may hasten, with the greatest desire and through your holy endeavors, to restore all who have wandered in this way and presumed upon what is unlawful and forbidden, so that the souls redeemed by Christ’s precious blood may not perish through their deception.

For it remains that these men did not enter through the door at all, because they had no door through which they could enter. For, as has been said, if they are not bishops yet aspire to be more than presbyters, through what door will they enter? Since only these two orders are read to exist in the Church, no further door to any pastoral office lies open through which a shepherd may enter.

Hear, brothers, not me, but Truth itself speaking: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold of all through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John X, 1), and the rest. And since the outstanding preacher also says: “No one can lay another foundation except that which has been laid” (I Cor. III, 11), and since only the aforesaid two foundations are found to have been laid in the Church, whatever else is found to have been laid upon them cannot stand in any way. Therefore it must be uprooted, together with all its foundations, actions, and roots, so that it may no longer be able to grow or sprout.

Let the oft-repeated statement not, therefore, produce disgust in you, brothers, because there is the greatest necessity for that which, as we have learned, you repeatedly and unlawfully usurp to be prohibited again and again. For Truth, when repeatedly assailed, shines forth more brightly like a light; and whatever is repeatedly admonished against is being excessively practiced.

Much has already been said about these matters by our predecessors, by whom they were condemned and prohibited, just as they now are by us. Therefore, repeating our warning, we admonish everyone to avoid such things and to abstain from such persons, lest they become, together with them, alienated from the sacerdotal ministry as rebels. We shall be able to establish this only if you strive to eradicate such men rather than favor them. Then complaint about this matter will cease in the future, because whatever is repeatedly usurped after being forbidden is done out of a desire to insult.

We command that all these decretal rulings and the constitutions of all our predecessors, promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be observed by you, by all bishops, and generally by all priests. If anyone transgresses them, let him know that forgiveness will henceforth be denied him. For truth would prevail if falsehood were displeasing; and rightly the matter concerns us, who ought to hold the supreme helm of the Church, if we favor error by silence.

Given on the Kalends of June, in the fourth consulship of Libo and Theodosius.

### Likewise, concerning priests who migrate from their own churches to other churches

As for those priests who have migrated from their own churches to others, we hold them separated from our communion for as long as it takes them to return to the cities in which they were first established. For if, while one man was migrating elsewhere, another was ordained in the place of the living man, let the one who abandoned his city remain deprived of the dignity of the priesthood for as long as his successor rests in the Lord.

### Likewise, a letter of Damasus and of the bishops who had gathered to him in the city of Rome from Italy and Gaul

Damasus and the other bishops assembled at Rome send greetings in the Lord to their most beloved brothers, the bishops established in Illyricum.

We believe that your holy faith, founded upon the instruction of the apostles, maintains and expounds to all peoples that which in no way departs from the constitutions of the Fathers, through whom it is right that the others be instructed. But from the report of the Gauls and of certain venerable brothers, we have learned that some favor heresies. Bishops must not merely avoid this evil; they must also resist the actions of those deceived by perverse interpretations through ignorance or simplicity.

It is therefore not fitting that the faith be shaken by varied teachings; rather, we must labor in accordance with the judgments of our Fathers. It is clear, therefore, that Auxentius of Milan was especially condemned in this matter. Hence it is right that throughout the Roman world the teachers of the law should understand the things belonging to the law and not stain the faith with varied doctrines.

Accordingly, when the wickedness of the heretics first began to sprout—and even now the blasphemy of the Arians is plainly sprouting—our Fathers, the three hundred and eighteen chosen men, after deliberation in the city of Nicaea, established this strongest wall against the weapons of the devil. By this remedy deadly poisons were driven away, so that the Father, the Son, and likewise the Holy Spirit are to be believed to possess one divinity, one power, one greatness, and one essence or substance.

They judged those who thought otherwise to be strangers to our communion. Some attempted to corrupt and violate this salutary boundary and venerable decision with other ideas. But from the very beginning the matter was brought back to the point that those same men who had been compelled at Ariminum to revoke or reconsider their position confessed that they had been deceived by another stratagem, or at least that they had not understood that their position was contrary to the judgment established by the Fathers at Nicaea.

Nor could any prejudice have been created by the number assembled at Ariminum, since it is established that neither the Roman bishop—whose decision they ought above all to have awaited—nor Vincent, who had guarded the episcopate inviolate for so many years, nor others had given their consent to such things. This is especially true since those very men who seemed to have departed through that assembly later, adopting better counsel, testified that these things displeased them.

Your soundness of judgment therefore perceives that this one faith, founded at Nicaea upon the authority of the apostles, must be preserved with perpetual firmness. At the same time, the Easterners who acknowledge themselves to be Catholics do this with us, and the Westerners likewise glory in it.

We believe that those who are failing in this effort must not long remain in our communion; the name of bishop must be taken away from them, so that their peoples, freed from error, may recover their breath. For those held in the snare of deception cannot in any way correct the people from deception.

Let your judgment also agree with all the priests of God; we have judged you to be steadfast and firm in this charity. If, then, we are to believe rightly together with you, gladden us with reciprocal letters of your charity.

Farewell, most beloved brothers.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, in the fourth consulship of Siricius and Ardabur.

### Likewise, a letter of Damasus to the bishops of Italy

Damasus, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy.

[Col. 0676D] Most beloved, because of the love belonging to our college I had wished all the priests of the Lord, as in the primitive Church, to be “one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32), to persevere in one devotion, and for no priest to be corrupted by favor or fear of secular persons, or in any way to depart from the path of truth.

But since many things occur that can be corrected, the mercy of God surpasses the sins of those who offend; therefore punishment is suspended so that correction may have its place.

For it has been reported to the apostolic see that you receive written accusations against brothers without a legitimate accuser. By apostolic authority we henceforth prohibit this from being done throughout the whole world. We ask you without delay to correct what has recently been done, and never to examine the case of those accused through their writings beforehand, unless they have been canonically summoned to a synod through the institution of formal complaints, so that the person present may truthfully recognize and understand, in the presence of the person accusing him, what is alleged against him.

This is well expressed through the wisdom of Solomon: “Before you examine, do not reprove; understand first, and then rebuke. Before you hear, do not answer” (Eccli. XI, 7–8).

Although the examination of opposing parties is entirely appropriate, nevertheless those appointed to investigate according to God must preserve the proper order in examining those who have been brought before them, so that, with the work cooperating with us, we may discover the truth and confess God, who says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” [Col. 0677B] (Matt. XVIII, 20).

Our Lord Jesus Christ knew that Judas was a thief, but since he was not accused in his presence, he was not expelled. Nor should you in any way do what he did not wish to do. The laws of the world require accusers to be present, not absent through written statements.

Hence the canonical constitutions of the Fathers proclaim, not once but very often, that neither accusations nor any testimony can be presented in writing, and that no one may give testimony concerning other matters except those known to have occurred in his presence.

Likewise, anyone who chooses to accuse another must accuse him in person and while present, not through someone else, though a written statement may first be submitted. No one at all should ever be judged before he has legitimate accusers present and has been granted an opportunity to defend himself and clear away the charges.

Care must also be taken that no one insinuate himself in such a way as to accomplish more quickly what is not permitted.

May almighty God, as you observe these things, all the divine commands, and the apostolic precepts, protect you in all your actions by the extension of his heavenly arm, and lead you, with abundant fruit of souls, to the reward of the heavenly homeland. Amen.

Given on the third day before the Ides of April, in the fourth consulship of Siricius and Ardabur.

## HERE BEGIN THE DECREES OF POPE SIRICIUS

[Col. 0677]

[Col. 0677B] 1. Concerning Arians who have become Catholics, that they are not to be baptized.  
2. That baptism is not to be celebrated except at Easter and Pentecost.  
3. Concerning apostates, that they are to be separated from the Church.  
[Col. 0677C] 4. That it is not permitted to marry another man’s betrothed.  
5. Concerning those who have not at all kept the penance they accepted.  
6. Concerning monks and virgins who do not maintain their commitment.  
7. Concerning incontinent ministers.  
8. What sort of men should attain the clerical office.  
9. Concerning those who, already advanced in age, turn to the sacred service.  
10. Concerning clerics who marry a second time, that they are to be deposed.  
11. Concerning women who may live with clerics.  
[Col. 0677D] 12. Concerning the promotion of monks to the clergy.  
13. That clerics are to receive penance through the laying on of priests’ hands.  
14. Concerning penitents, bigamists, and husbands of widows, that they are not to be admitted to the clerical order.

### The letter of Pope Siricius to Cumerius, bishop of Tarragona, begins

Siricius sends greetings to Cumerius, bishop of Tarragona.

The report of your fraternity, addressed to our predecessor of holy memory, Damasus, has found me already established in his see, because the Lord so ordained. When we read it carefully in the gathering of the brothers, we found as many matters deserving reproach and correction as we would have wished to find deserving praise.

And because it was necessary for us to enter upon the labors and cares of the one whom, by God’s grace, we have succeeded in honor, after first providing, as was appropriate, an indication of my advancement, we do not refuse to give a fitting answer to each of your consultations, insofar as the Lord has deigned to inspire us. For, in consideration of our office, we are not free to dissemble or remain silent—we upon whom, above all, zeal for the whole Christian religion rests.

We bear the burdens of all who are burdened; indeed, blessed Peter the apostle bears these burdens in us, as we trust, protecting and guarding us as heirs of his administration in all things.

### Chapter I

At the very beginning of your letter you indicated that many baptized by the impious Arians are hastening to the Catholic faith, and that some of our brothers wish to baptize them again. This is not permitted, since the Apostle forbids it, the canons oppose it, and the general decrees sent to the provinces by my predecessor Liberius, of venerable memory, after the annulled Council of Ariminum prohibit it.

As has been established in the synod, we admit Novatians and other heretics to the Catholic assembly through the invocation alone of the sevenfold Spirit and the laying on of the bishop’s hand. The entire East and West also observe this practice. After this, you too must not depart from that path, if you do not wish to be separated by synodal judgment from our college.

### II

Next follows an intolerable and correctable confusion concerning all the times at which baptism may be administered, according to each person’s preference. Our fellow priests presume this—something we say with indignation—not on the authority of any reason, but through mere rashness, so that countless peoples, as you report, obtain the mystery of baptism indiscriminately and freely on the festivals of Christ’s birth and manifestation, and likewise on those of the apostles and martyrs.

Among us and among all the Churches, however, the Lord’s Easter, together with its Pentecost, claims this privilege especially for itself. On these days alone throughout the year it is appropriate to confer the general sacraments of baptism upon those coming to the faith—only upon those chosen who have given their names forty days or more beforehand and have been purified through exorcisms, daily prayers, and fasts—so that the apostolic command may be fulfilled: “When the old leaven has been purged, let the dough become new” (I Cor. V, 7).

Therefore, just as we say that the sacred reverence due to Easter must in no way be diminished, so we wish the sacred water of baptism to come with all speed to infants who, because of their age, are not yet able to speak, and to those for whom it is needed in any emergency. Otherwise it may lead to the destruction of our souls if, when the saving font is denied to those who desire it, someone departs from this world and loses the kingdom and life.

Whoever encounters the danger of shipwreck, an enemy attack, the uncertainty of siege, or the desperation of any bodily illness, and asks to be helped by the single aid of faith, let him receive, at that very moment when he asks, the rewards of the regeneration he seeks.

Let enough error in this matter have occurred up to now. From this point let all priests observe the rule stated above—those who do not wish to be torn away from the firmness of the apostolic rock upon which Christ built the universal Church.

### III

It has also been reported that certain Christians are passing into apostasy—a thing forbidden even to mention—and have been profaned by the worship of idols and the pollution of sacrifices. We command that they be cut off from the body and blood of Christ, by which they were formerly redeemed through birth. If, after coming to their senses, they should at some time turn to lamentation, they are to perform penance for as long as they live, and at the end of their life the grace of reconciliation is to be granted them, since the Lord says: “We do not desire the death of sinners, but that they should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII, 32).

### IV

In response to the inquiry concerning the prohibition of marriage—whether one man may take in marriage a girl betrothed to another—we absolutely forbid this from happening. For among the faithful, the blessing which the priest imposes upon a bride is like a kind of sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.

### V

You have not improperly judged that the apostolic see should be consulted concerning those who, after performing penance, return like dogs and pigs to their former vomit and wallowing, and have again sought the military belt, frivolous pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden sexual relations.

The children born after absolution have caused them to forfeit the continence they had professed. Since they now have no refuge in which to perform penance, we have decided that they are to be joined to the faithful within the church only in prayer, and, although they do not deserve it, are to attend the sacred celebrations of the mysteries. They are, however, to be excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table, so that, corrected at least by this strictness, they may chastise their own errors within themselves and provide an example to others, so that others may be drawn away from obscene desires.

Nevertheless, since they fell through the weakness of the flesh, we wish them to be aided by the grace of communion as a viaticum when they begin to depart to the Lord. We judge that the same rule is to be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves to such pollutions.

### VI

Furthermore, you declare that certain monks and nuns, having cast aside their commitment to holiness, have sunk into such great wantonness that at first they secretly united themselves in unlawful and sacrilegious contamination under the pretext of monasteries. Later, driven into the abyss by despair of conscience, they openly produced children from their unlawful embraces—something condemned both by public laws and by ecclesiastical rights.

We therefore command that these shameless and detestable persons be expelled from the company of monasteries and from the assemblies of the Churches, so that, confined in their own prisons and mourning such a great offense in continual lamentation, they may be purified in the cleansing fire of repentance, and so that, even at death, indulgence may be granted them through the grace of communion, out of regard for mercy alone.

### VII

Let us now come to the most sacred orders of clerics, which, as your charity has informed us, we find trampled upon and thrown into confusion throughout your provinces, to the injury of venerable religion. We must therefore say with the voice of Jeremiah: “Who will give water to my head, or a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep for this people day and night?” (Jer. XIX, 1.)

If the blessed prophet said that he could not have enough tears to mourn the sins of the people, how greatly must we be struck with sorrow when we are compelled to lament the crimes of those who belong to our own body? For, according to blessed Paul, “daily urgency and concern for all the Churches continually rests upon us. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (II Cor. XI, 28–29).

For we have learned that very many priests of Christ and Levites, after long periods in their consecration, have fathered offspring both by their own wives and through shameful intercourse, and defend their crime by this presumption: that in the Old Testament priests and ministers are said to have been granted the ability to beget children.

Let whoever he is who follows lust and teaches vice answer me: if he thinks that in the law of Moses the reins of lust were freely loosened by our God for the sacred orders, why does he warn those to whom the Holy of Holies was entrusted, saying: “Be holy, because I also am holy, the Lord your God” (Lev. II, 44)? Why were priests also ordered to live far from their homes in the temple during the year of their service? Obviously this was so that they could not even have sexual relations with their wives, and so that, shining with integrity of conscience, they might offer a gift acceptable to God.

After their period of service had been completed, the use of a wife was permitted to them solely for the sake of succession, because no one except someone from the tribe of Levi had been commanded to be admitted to the ministry of God. Hence, when the Lord Jesus had illumined us by his coming, he declares in the Gospel that he came “to fulfill the law, not to abolish it” (Matt. V, 17).

Therefore he wished the Church, whose bridegroom is beautiful in appearance, to shine with the splendor of chastity, so that on the day of judgment, when he comes again, he may find her “without stain or wrinkle,” as he established through the Apostle (Eph. V, 27).

All priests and Levites are bound by an unbreakable law to dedicate our hearts and bodies to sobriety and chastity from the day of our ordination, so that in all things we may please our God through the sacrifices we offer daily. “Those who are in the flesh,” says the Chosen Vessel, “cannot please God; but you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. VIII, 8–9).

And where can the Spirit of God dwell, unless in holy bodies, as we read?

Since some of those about whom we speak, as your Holiness has reported, lament that they fell through ignorance, we say that mercy is not to be denied them on this condition: that, without any increase of honor, they remain for as long as they live in the office in which they were discovered, provided that thereafter they strive to show themselves continent.

But those who rely upon the excuse of an unlawful privilege and assert that this was granted to them by the old law are to know that, by the authority of the apostolic see, they have been removed from every ecclesiastical honor which they have unworthily used. They can never again handle the venerable mysteries from which they deprived themselves while they yearned after obscene desires.

Since present examples warn us to take precautions for the future, if any bishop, presbyter, or deacon—something we do not desire—is henceforth found to be such, let him understand that every avenue of indulgence has now been closed to him by us, because wounds that have not responded to soothing remedies must be cut out with the sword.

### VIII

We have also learned that men of untested character, some of whom have had numerous marriages, freely and without examination aspire to the aforesaid dignities, according to each person’s preference. We attribute this not so much to those who reach these offices through immoderate ambition as especially to the metropolitan bishops, who, by conniving at forbidden attempts, disregard, insofar as they are able, the commands of our God.

To say nothing of what we suspect more deeply, where is the command established by our God through the law given by Moses, which says: “Let my priests marry only once”? And elsewhere: “Let a priest take a virgin as his wife, not a widow, not a divorced woman, and not a prostitute” (Lev. XXI, 14).

Following this, the Apostle, who changed from persecutor into preacher, commanded that both priest and deacon “should be the husband of one wife” (I Tim. III, 2, 12). All these provisions are despised by the bishops of your regions as though they had rather been established in opposition to them.

Since we must not neglect such usurpations, lest the just voice of the indignant Lord rebuke us—“You saw a thief, and you ran with him, and you set your portion with adulterers” (Ps. XLIX, 18)—we decree by a general pronouncement what all the Churches are henceforth to follow and what they are to avoid.

Therefore, whoever has vowed himself to the service of the Church ought to be baptized in childhood, before the years of puberty, and joined to the ministry of the readers. From the beginning of adolescence until his thirtieth year, if he has lived commendably, he is to be content with one wife only—the wife whom, as a virgin, he received through the common blessing of the priest—and is to be an acolyte and subdeacon. Then, after he has first proved himself worthy through continence, he may advance to the rank of deacon.

If he has lived honorably and ministered suitably for more than five years, let him attain the presbyterate. Thereafter, after ten years, he may attain the episcopal chair, provided that during these periods the integrity of his life and faith has been approved.

### IX

But whoever, already advanced in age, is prompted by a way of life directed toward a better purpose and hastens to pass from the laity into the sacred service will obtain the fruit of his desire only if, at the time of his baptism, he is immediately enrolled among the readers or exorcists, provided it is established that he has had, or has, one wife, and that he received her as a virgin.

After he has been initiated, upon completion of two years he is to become an acolyte and subdeacon for another five-year period, and thus advance to the diaconate, if he is judged worthy after these periods of service. Thereafter, as time advances, he may be admitted to the presbyterate or episcopate if the election of the clergy and people calls him to it.

### X

Any cleric who marries either a widow or, certainly, a second wife is immediately to be stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical dignity. Only lay communion is to be granted to him, and he will be able to retain even that only if thereafter he commits nothing by which he may lose it.

### XI

We do not permit any women to live in the houses of clerics except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely for reasons of necessary relationship.

### XII

We both desire and command that monks whose seriousness of conduct and holy formation in life and faith commend them be attached to the offices of clerics. Those who are worthy while under thirty years of age are to be promoted through the individual grades, as time advances, and thus reach the insignia of the diaconate or presbyterate through consecration at a mature age. They are not to leap directly to the summit of the episcopate unless the periods we prescribed above for each dignity have been observed in their case as well.

### XIII

It was also fitting for us to provide that, just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layman may ever attain the honor of the clergy. For although they may have been cleansed from the contagion of every sin, those who were formerly vessels of vices ought not to receive the instruments for administering the sacraments.

### XIV

Since in all these matters that have come under reproach the sole excuse offered is ignorance, which meanwhile we must mercifully forgive out of regard for compassion alone, whoever is a penitent, whoever is a bigamist, and whoever is the husband of a widow, if he has improperly and incompetently slipped into the sacred service, is to understand that forgiveness has been granted him by us on this condition: he must count it a great benefit if, with every hope of promotion taken away, he remains in perpetual stability in the order in which he is found.

Henceforth, let the chief bishops of all the provinces know that if they should presume to admit any such person to the sacred orders, an appropriate judgment will be issued by the apostolic see both concerning their own status and that of those whom they have promoted contrary to the canons and to our prohibitions.

### Siricius’ Exhortation to Cimerius
We have explained, as I believe, dearest brother, everything that was arranged in response to the complaint, and to each of the individual cases about which you reported to the Roman Church, as to the head of your body, through our son, the presbyter Bassianus, we have given sufficient answers, insofar as I judge. Now we urge your fraternal spirit more and more to observe the canons and to hold fast to the decretal regulations, so that you may have what we have written in reply to your inquiries conveyed to the knowledge of all our fellow bishops—not only those established in your diocese, but also to all the Carthaginians, Baeticans, Lusitanians, and Gauls, as well as those who border on your provinces on either side—so that what has been established by us in a salutary arrangement may be sent under the cover of your letters.

And although no priest of the Lord is free to be ignorant of the statutes of the apostolic see or of the venerable definitions of the canons, it may nevertheless be especially useful and honorable for your devotion, in view of the antiquity of your priesthood, if what has been written to you in general terms under your particular name is, through your unanimous diligence, conveyed to the knowledge of all our brethren. Thus both what has been salutarily established by us—not inconsiderately, but prudently, with the utmost caution and deliberation—may remain inviolate, and access may be closed to every excuse in the future, an access which can no longer be open to anyone before us.

Given on the third day before the Ides of February, in the fourth consulship of Arcadius and Bauto.

## On the condemnation of the heretic Jovinianus and his letter

Dearest brothers, I would always wish to announce to the sincerity of your love and peace occasions for joy, so that, as letters passed between us, signs of good health might mutually strengthen us—if the ancient enemy would allow us to remain undisturbed and free from his attacks.

Since he was a liar from the beginning, an enemy of truth, the envious foe of humankind—having first deceived himself in order to deceive the human being—an enemy of chastity and a teacher of lust, he feeds on cruelties and is punished by abstinence; he hates fasts, with his ministers proclaiming them superfluous; and, having no hope concerning the future, he is struck by the apostle’s sentence: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isaiah 22:13).

O unhappy boldness! O desperate cunning of the mind! A speech hitherto unknown among heretics had already begun to spread within the Church like a cancer, so that, seizing the breast, it might hurl the whole person into death. And unless the Lord of Hosts had broken the snare he had prepared, the spectacle and public display of so great an evil would have dragged many simple hearts into ruin, because the human mind is easily led toward the worse side, preferring to walk along the broad road rather than laboriously travel the narrow way.

For this reason, dearest ones, it was entirely necessary to entrust to your awareness what has taken place here, lest through the ignorance of any priest the Church be defiled by the contagion of the worst men who are entering it under a religious name, as it is written, the Lord saying: “Many come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; you will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:15).

These are the men who subtly boast of being Christians, so that, walking under the veil of a pious name and entering the house of prayer, they may pour forth a serpentine disputation, “to shoot in the dark at those upright in heart” (Psalm 10:3), and, turning them away from catholic truth, lead them with a devilish mouth into the madness of their own teaching and defraud the simplicity of the sheep.

Indeed, from apostolic times until now we have learned about and tested the wickedness of many heresies. But never have such dogs wearied the mystery of the Church with their barking as these sudden enemies of the faith, who, bursting forth with a doctrine of perfidy that had [168] sprouted, revealed by the fruits of their words whose disciples they were.

For while other heretics have proposed to themselves individual classes of questions, badly understood, in order to tear apart and mutilate the divine ordinances, these men, “not having a wedding garment” (Matthew 22:12), wound Catholics, perverting, as I have said, the continence of the New and Old Testament, interpreting it in a devilish spirit. Through seductive and fabricated speech they have already begun to ravage some Christians and associate them with their madness. Keeping within themselves the poison of their wickedness, they rashly revealed their blasphemies publicly in writing as though they were chosen men, and, driven by the fury of a desperate mind, published them indiscriminately in the frenzy of the gentiles.

But a document, honored by faithful Christian men, excellent in birth and distinguished in religion, suddenly appears to have been brought to my humility, so that, once exposed by priestly judgment, doctrines contrary to the divine law might be erased by spiritual sentence.

We have certainly not disdainfully received the vows of marriage, at which we were present under the veil; but we honor virgins devoted to God with greater distinction. When the presbyteral council had been held, it became clear that their teaching was contrary to our doctrine—that is, to Christian law.

Therefore, following the apostolic command, because they were proclaiming something other than what we had received, it is established that all our people—the presbyters, the deacons, and the whole clergy—formed one judgment: Jovinianus, Ausentius, Genialis, Geminator, Felix, Plotinus, Martianus, Januarius, and Ingeniosus, who were found to be promoters of a new heresy and blasphemy, were condemned forever by divine sentence and by our judgment, and were to remain outside the Church.

Trusting that your holiness will preserve this decision, I have sent these writings through my brothers and fellow presbyters, Crescentius, Leopardus, and Alexander, who may fulfill their religious duty to the faith with a spirit burning with zeal.

## Likewise, a letter of Pope Siricius to all the orthodox

1. That no unworthy man should be made a bishop.  
2. That the priesthood should not be given to unknown men.
