3. That neophytes or laymen should not become priests.

## Chapter I. Pope Siricius to the orthodox throughout the various provinces

As we consider, dearest brothers, the fear of divine judgment and the fact that after this life each person will receive according to what he has done, it has not been permissible to remain silent about what is liable to complaint; necessity compelled us to speak, as the prophet says: “Raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58:1).

And since the care of all the churches has been entrusted to me, if I remain silent, I shall hear the Lord saying: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your traditions” (Matthew 15:6). For what else is it to reject the commandment of God than to take excessive delight in establishing new things by private judgment and human counsel?

It has therefore been brought to the attention of the apostolic see that people presume to act against the ecclesiastical canon, introducing certain new observances of their own even though earlier generations arranged matters so that they should not be violated by so much as a light whisper; and, neglecting the foundation, they wish to build upon sand, while the Lord says: “You shall not pass beyond the boundaries your fathers established” (Numbers 20:17).

The holy apostle, preacher of the New and Old Testament, in whom Christ spoke, likewise admonishes us: “Stand firm and hold fast to your traditions which you learned, whether by word or by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:14).

For this reason your sincerity sees how much care and diligent attention priests ought to exercise in the sacred mysteries and in your ordinations. Finally, he says to Timothy: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5:22). This is recalled so that, after examination, moral integrity, and ecclesiastical labor, the one called forward may be more worthy to receive the supreme priesthood: approved by judgment, not accepted through favor; received on the basis of truth, not personal influence; exercising the apostolic order, not acting through precipitous will.

Concerning this, dearest ones, letters have come to your sincerity with the agreement of many brothers and fellow priests, so that the ecclesiastical canon established at Nicaea, confirmed by your subscription, might remain firmly founded according to its proper authority. Men of the kind whom apostolic authority commands should be permitted to enter the ecclesiastical order—not, I say, men who once boasted of being bound by the belt of secular military service.

After they have celebrated with worldly pomp, desired to serve in public affairs, or undertaken the cares of the world, such men, having obtained the assistance of some person and being supported by the favor of relatives, are frequently brought to my attention as men who might become bishops, although by tradition and evangelical discipline they cannot be bishops.

How often has this been declared in statutes and with all the force of authority! Yet nothing of this kind could be selected unless reason compelled it. Even those who must be ordained should come from far away, so that they may be able to be approved as worthy both by the judgment of the people and by ours.

### II

The unlawfulness of this cannot be sufficiently estimated: they are unwilling to assist with provisions passing strangers—whether they merely pretend to be monks or actually are what they call themselves—whose life and baptism we cannot know and whose faith is unknown and untested to us; instead, they hasten immediately either to make them deacons or to ordain them presbyters, or, what is more serious, they do not fear to appoint them bishops.

Among such men, money is more readily given to a passerby than priesthood to an unknown man. From this they are lifted up into pride; from this they quickly fall into perfidy, because, as wanderers throughout the ecclesiastical world, they are not asserted to have learned the true faith.

### III

Certainly this also must not be passed over: what necessity once or twice introduced among heretics is presumed, contrary to apostolic commands, to be lawful as though it were a rule—namely, to ordain a neophyte or a layman who has performed no ecclesiastical office, without due consideration, either as presbyter or as deacon, as though they were better than the apostles and dared to alter their command.

A man who has not learned is compelled to teach. Thus no suitable member of the clergy is found, neither among the deacons nor among the other clerics is anyone considered worthy of the priesthood; instead, a layman is requested for the commendation of the church.

I warn and proclaim that this must not happen again, so that, since we possess one faith, we may also share one judgment in tradition, showing ourselves unanimous, concordant, and peaceful in Christ, and maintaining charity in the apostolic observances.

Through the Father, the only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit, and through the one divinity in the Trinity, I call upon you to ensure that our catholic faith and discipline remain in these matters. Let no one think that earthly ordinations are being carried out, since the priesthood is heavenly, so that the glory of this dignity may remain with the faithful and that, from this point onward, they may have nothing for which they can be accused before the tribunal of Christ.

## The Council of Thelë begins concerning the matter of Pope Siricius

After the consulship of the most glorious Honorius for the eleventh time and of Constantius for the second time, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, a council having assembled in the church of the Apostles of the people of Thelë, the blessed Father Donatianus, bishop of the first see and of the city of Thelepte, having taken his seat, with Januarius, Felix the second, Cyrinus, Victor, Secundianus, Geta, Eunomius, Maximianus, Donatus, Cresconius, Jucundus, Sopatus, Restutus, Julianus, Maximinus, Romanus, Tertiolus, Micilus, Maximus, Donatianus, Basilius, Papinianus, Januarius, Porphyrius, likewise Porphyrius, Donatus, Julianus, Tutus, Fortunius, Quintianus, Capio, and the remaining bishops sitting with him; and also Vincentius and Fortunatianus, legates of the proconsular province sent to the council at Byzantium, and others.

Vincentius and Fortunatus said:

“Even when we were at Thusdrum, as your memory recalls together with me, and had delivered letters of blessed memory, Siricius, bishop of the apostolic see, reading from them one document of our brother Bishop Lato, our present report indicates that both should now be read; grant that they be read.”

The bishops said:

“Let the letters of Siricius, of venerable memory, be read, so that we may know what their text contains.”

When they had been handed over, Privatus the notary said:

“Copy of the letter of instruction of the bishop of the city of Rome.”

## Likewise, a letter of Pope Siricius

To our dearest brothers and fellow bishops throughout Africa, Siricius.

Although many brothers had assembled together at the relics of the holy apostle Peter, through whom the beginning of the apostleship and episcopate in Christ was established, and although it had seemed good, on account of the many matters arising—some of which were not merely matters but crimes—that thereafter each person in the Church should take responsibility for such care, just as the apostle Paul teaches: “To present to God a Church without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27), so that our conscience might not appear contaminated by the breath of any diseased sheep, it was decided, upon better counsel, especially for the sake of those who could not be present on account of bodily illness or the weakness of advanced age.

So that a permanent form of this kind might be maintained, it seemed good to issue such a letter—not one imposing any new commands, but one expressing our desire that those things neglected through the indolence and laziness of some be observed, since they have nevertheless been established by apostolic and patristic constitution. It is written: “Stand firm and hold fast to our traditions, whether by word or by letter” (1 Thessalonians 2:14).

Certainly this ought to shake your minds more forcefully, dearest brothers: that we may come securely into God’s presence free from every stain of this world. For we shall not be free from it merely because we preside over peoples, since it is written: “From the one to whom much has been entrusted, more will be required” (Luke 12:48).

Therefore, since we are compelled to render an account not only for ourselves but also for the people entrusted to us, we must teach the people divine discipline and humility. For some have arisen who, despising the statutes of their predecessors, have violated the Church’s chastity through presumption, following the will of the people and fearing not the judgment of God.

Therefore, lest we appear to connive at such men in silence and give them our consent, and thus incur the punishments of Gehenna, the Lord says: “You saw a thief and ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49:18). These are the matters which, from now on, all catholic bishops ought to guard with regard to divine judgment.

First, no one should dare to ordain without the knowledge of the apostolic see—that is, of the primate. A judgment is sound when it is reached by the decision of many, so that one bishop may not presume to ordain another, lest, through arrogance, the benefit appear to have been conferred secretly. For this is established as having been defined at the Synod of Nicaea.

Likewise, if anyone, after the remission of sins, has worn the belt of secular military service, he must not be admitted to the clergy.

That a cleric must not take a woman—that is, a widow—as his wife.

That one who, while a layman, has married a widow must not be admitted to the clergy.

That no one should usurp the right to ordain a cleric from another church, and that another church should not admit a cleric who has been rejected.

That those coming from the Novatians or Montenses should be received by the laying on of hands, except those whom they rebaptize.

Moreover, we advise what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: that priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives, because ministers engaged in the ministry are occupied with daily necessities. For Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying: “Abstain, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Corinthians 7:5).

If abstinence is commanded to lay people so that they may be heard when they pray, how much more must a priest at every moment be ready, secure in the purity of cleanliness, lest he be required either to offer the sacrifice or to baptize? If he has been defiled by carnal desire, what will he do? Will he make excuses? With what modesty, with what state of mind, will he presume to act? With what conscience, with what merit, does such a man believe that he will be heard, when it has been said: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus 1:15)?

For this reason I exhort, admonish, and beseech you: let this reproach be removed, which even the gentiles may rightly accuse. Perhaps someone thinks this is justified because Scripture says, “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2). He did not say this of one remaining in the desire to beget, but with a view to future continence; for neither did he exclude the unmarried, he who says: “I wish that all people were as I myself am” (1 Corinthians 7:7). And he declares more openly: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh; you are in the Spirit” (Romans 8:8–9).

Therefore, brothers, if all these things are observed by everyone with full vigilance, ambition will cease, dissension will be quieted, heresies and schisms will not arise, the devil will find no opportunity to rage, unanimity will remain, and iniquity, separated from us, will be trampled down. Charity will burn with spiritual fervor, and the peace proclaimed by the lips will agree with the will.

This is the peace of our God and Savior, which, near the time of his passion, he commanded to be preserved and left to us by right as an inheritance, saying: “I give you peace; I leave you peace” (John 14:27). And the apostle says: “Let us remain of one mind, having one understanding in Christ, claiming nothing for ourselves through rivalry or empty glory, and pleasing not human beings but our God and Savior” (Philippians 2:2–3).

If we faithfully wish to obey all these commands, the Lord will guard our bodies and our souls on the day when he will repay each person according to his works. But if anyone, puffed up in the mind of his flesh, wishes to wander from this rule, let him know that he will be excluded from our communion and will suffer the punishments of Gehenna.

Moreover, mercy must be exercised together with judgment. For one ought to extend a hand to those who are slipping, so that they do not drag into ruin those who are running along with them.

Given at Rome, in a council of eighty bishops, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, after the consulship of the emperors Arcadius and Bauto, consul for the fourth time.

## Likewise, the bishops’ reply to the same Siricius

To our most beloved lord and brother Siricius, Ambrosius, Sabinus, Bassianus, and the others.

We have recognized in your letter the vigilance of a good shepherd: you carefully guard the gate entrusted to you and, with devoted concern, protect Christ’s fold, worthy to be heard and followed by the Lord’s sheep. Because you know Christ’s little sheep, you easily detect the wolves and, like a prudent shepherd, rush to meet them, lest by the bites and savage howling of their perfidy they scatter the Lord’s fold. We praise this, most beloved lord and brother, and celebrate it with our whole affection.

Nor are we surprised that the Lord’s flock recoiled from the madness of wolves in whom it did not recognize Christ’s voice. For it is a savage howl to preserve no grace of virginity, no order of chastity; to wish to confuse everything indiscriminately; to abolish the various ranks; and to introduce a kind of poverty into the rewards of merits, as though Christ granted only one crown and not many abundant titles of reward.

These men pretend not to give themselves to marriage. But what praise can there be for marriage if there is no glory of virginity? We do not, of course, deny that marriage has been sanctified by Christ, since the divine voice says: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), and one spirit. But what we were born as comes before what we have become, and the mystery of the divine work is far more excellent than the remedy of human weakness.

A good wife is rightly praised, but a devout virgin is preferred as better, since the Lord says: “He who joins his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not join her does better” (1 Corinthians 7:38).

The one thinks about the things of God, the other about the things of the world. The one is bound by marital bonds, the other is free from bonds. The one is under the law, the other under grace.

Marriage is good, through which offspring for the continuation of the human race has been produced; but virginity is better, through which the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom has been acquired and the succession of heavenly merits discovered. Through a woman, care entered the world; through a Virgin, salvation came.

Finally, Christ chose virginity as a special gift for himself, displayed the gift of integrity, and represented in himself what he had chosen in his mother.

What madness possessed those accursed barkers that they said Christ could not be born from a virgin, while asserting that virgins could remain virgins after giving birth to human beings from a woman? Christ therefore grants to others what, according to their claim, he could not grant to himself. Yet he assumed flesh and thus became human so that he might redeem humanity and recall it from death.

At the same time, he came with a divine gift, as it were, so that, just as he had said, “Behold, I make all things new” (Revelation 21:5), he might be born from the immaculate Virgin, and, as it is written, might be believed to be God with us (Isaiah 7:14).

But they are exposed as saying, in their perverse course: “The Virgin conceived, but the Virgin did not give birth.” Thus the Virgin could conceive but could not give birth, although conception always precedes and birth follows.

But if the teachings of priests are not believed, let the oracles of Christ be believed; let the instructions of the angels be believed, who said: “For no word is impossible with God” (Luke 1:37); let the apostles’ creed be believed, which the Roman Church has always kept and preserved undefiled.

Mary heard the angel’s voice. When she had earlier asked, “How will this happen?” (Luke 1:34), she was not questioning in disbelief concerning the birth; afterward she replied: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).

This is the Virgin who conceived in the womb; the Virgin who gave birth to a son. For it is written: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall give birth to a son” (Isaiah 7:14). It did not say merely that the Virgin would conceive, but also that the Virgin would give birth.

What is that outer gate toward the east which remains closed, and through which, he says, no one passed, but only the God of Israel passed through it (Ezekiel 44:1–2)? Is this not Mary, through whom the Redeemer entered this world?

This is the gate of righteousness, as he himself said: “Allow us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). This is the gate, Mary, of whom it is written: Because the Lord passed through it, it shall remain closed after the birth, because she both conceived as a virgin and gave birth as a virgin.

What is so incredible if Mary gave birth contrary to the ordinary course of natural origin and remained a virgin, when, contrary to the course of nature, “the sea saw and fled, and the streams of the Jordan turned back to their source” (Psalm 114:3)?

It therefore does not exceed faith that a Virgin gave birth, when we read that the rock poured forth water and that the wave of the sea became solid like a wall. It does not exceed faith that a human being came forth from a Virgin, when a rock gushed forth a flowing spring, iron floated upon the waters, and a human being walked upon the waters.

Therefore, if a wave carried a human being, could a Virgin not give birth to a human being? But what human being? The one of whom we read: “The Lord sends them a man who will save them, and the Lord will be known to the Egyptians” (Isaiah 19:20–21).

In the Old Testament, therefore, the staff of the Hebrews led the army through the sea. In the New Testament, the Virgin was chosen for salvation in the palace of the heavenly King.

Why should we add the praises of widowhood when, in the Gospel, after the Virgin’s celebrated birth, the widow Anna is introduced, who had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity, and had been a widow for eighty-four years? “She did not depart from the temple, serving with fasts and prayers night and day” (Luke 2:36–37).

Widowhood, which is accustomed to observe fasts, is rightly despised by these men, who grieve that they have at some time been worn down by such practices. They seek to drive away the labor of abstinence through daily banquets and the habit of luxury; they do nothing more rightly than condemn themselves with their own mouths. Yet they fear that God may count that fast against them.

Let them choose what they wish. If they have ever fasted, let them show repentance for their good deed. If never, let them themselves confess their intemperance and luxury. For this reason they say that Paul was a teacher of luxury.

But who is the teacher of sobriety, if that man was a teacher of luxury who chastised his body and brought it into servitude (1 Corinthians 9:27), and who declared that through many fasts he had rendered to Christ the observance he owed—not to praise himself and his own deeds, but to teach us what we should follow?

Did he teach luxury when he said: “Why, as though you were living in this world, do you submit to decrees: ‘Do not touch, do not handle, do not taste,’ all of which are destined for corruption”? Did he teach luxury when he said that one must live not in indulgence of the body, not in any honor that serves the satisfaction and care of the flesh, not in the desires of error, but in the spirit by which we are renewed?

If what the apostle said is insufficient, let them hear the prophet saying: “I covered my soul in fasting” (Psalm 69:10). Therefore, whoever does not fast is uncovered and naked, exposed to the wound.

Finally, if Adam had clothed himself in fasting, he would not have been made naked. Nineveh freed itself from death through fasting (Jonah 3:5–9), and the Lord himself says: “This kind does not go out except through prayer and fasting” (Matthew 17:20).

But why say more before the teacher and instructor, when those men have already received the fitting price of their perfidy—those who came here so that no place would remain in which they were not condemned, and who truly proved themselves Manichaeans by refusing to believe that he had come from the Virgin?

What is this madness of the new Jews, almost their equal, if they do not believe that he came and do not believe that he assumed flesh? Then he appeared in a phantom, was crucified in a phantom, and is our Redeemer in truth.

He is a Manichaean who denies the truth, who denies Christ’s flesh. Therefore there is no forgiveness of sins for them, but only the impiety of the Manichaeans, which even the most merciful emperor has cursed, and from which all who have seen them have fled as from a kind of contagion.

The brothers and our fellow presbyters Crescentius, Leopardus, and Alexander, serving with a holy spirit, are witnesses of this: they left them, condemned by the execration of all, as fugitives from the city of Milan.

Therefore know that Jovinianus, Ausentius, Germinator, Felix, Plotinus, Genialis, Martianus, Januarius, and Ingenius, whom your holiness condemned, have likewise been condemned among us according to your judgment.

May our almighty God preserve you safe and flourishing, most beloved lord and brother.

Likewise, the subscription:

“I, Bishop Eventius, greet your holiness in the Lord, and have subscribed to this church.”

Bishop Maximus, Bishop Felix, Bishop Bazianus, Bishop Theodolus—at the command of the Lord Bishop Germinianus, who was himself present—Presbyter Aprus, Bishop Eutasius, Bishop Constantius, and Bishop Eustasius: they all subscribed in due order.

# The Decrees of Pope Anastasius Begin

[Column 0691]

## Anastasius, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops of the Germanic and Burgundian regions

Your devotion, dearest ones, requires that we respond, by the authority of the apostolic see, to the inquiries you have submitted, and, although not at length but concisely, we would hasten to do so on account of certain other occupations.

Nevertheless, if it should again be necessary, because of these or other occupations, to send to the head of the Church, do not hesitate to do so in a spirit of charity, since we regard your petitions as welcome both now and then.

You report that certain priests sit in church when the Gospels are being read, and hear the words of the Lord and Savior not while standing but while seated, claiming that they received this practice from the tradition of their ancestors. We command, by apostolic authority, that you allow this to happen no longer. Rather, while the holy Gospels are being recited in church, priests and all the others, not sitting but standing reverently bowed in the presence of the Gospel, should listen attentively to the words of the Lord and worship faithfully.

Likewise, do not receive into the honor of the clergy foreigners from overseas, about whom you have consulted us, unless they are identified by letters from five bishops or more, because many things commonly occur through underhanded means. Therefore these matters must be guarded against with the greatest care.

As for the Manichaeans whom we found in the city of Rome and their followers, do not receive them, communicate with them, or have any participation with them before they turn to the true faith. Nor should the seeds of their evil growth, which we extinguish in the city, be sown or allowed to sprout among you with the worst of roots.

Our investigation found many of them, as well as followers of their impiety and their teachers; vigilance exposed them, and authority and discipline restrained them. Those whom we could correct, we corrected. We compelled them publicly in the Church, by profession and by their own signatures, to condemn the Manichaean with his preaching and teachings. Thus, after they confessed, we raised them from the abyss of their impiety by granting them penance.

Some, however, had plunged themselves so deeply that no remedy capable of helping them could provide assistance. Subjected to the laws according to the enactments of Christian rulers, they were sent by public judges into perpetual exile, lest they pollute the holy flock with their contagion. Everything profane or shameful that they possessed, both in their writings and in their secret traditions, we displayed clearly before the eyes of the Christian people, so that the people might know what to reject or avoid.

Indeed, the very man who was said to be their bishop, when detained by us, exposed the shameful things he maintained in his mysteries, as the sequence of the official proceedings will be able to teach you. For your instruction we have also sent those proceedings themselves; once you have read them, you will be able to know everything we discovered.

And because we learned that some of those whom a more severe guilt prevented from being absolved had fled, we have sent this letter to your devotion, so that, once your holiness has been made more certain of the facts, it may act more diligently and cautiously, lest men of Manichaean perversity find among your peoples an opportunity to injure them and teachers of this sacrilege.

For we cannot govern those entrusted to us in any other way than by pursuing these perverse and lost teachers with zeal for the Lord’s faith and cutting them away, with whatever severity we can, from the minds of those influenced by them, lest this plague spread more widely.

Therefore I exhort, beseech, and admonish your devotion to remain vigilant with the concern you ought to have and can exercise, investigating them lest they find anywhere an opportunity to conceal themselves.

These men, brothers, must be guarded against with great care, lest they be able to contaminate the Lord’s flock with the perversities they can spread. Some of them appear as sheep by their clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; according to the voice of Truth, we must recognize them by their fruits (Matthew 7:20).

When they begin to assume impiety, what is hidden within them is revealed, and every deception becomes manifest to all.

There are also men weak in faith who thirst for the divine readings; these men hurl them along with themselves into destruction. For they disperse and disparage the teachings of the Fathers and abandon the holy Scriptures to their own ruin. As has been said, we must provide for such men and guard carefully against them, lest some, occupied with their wickedness, fall from their steadfastness.

I greet you, brothers, and all the churches that share good understanding with you. I also ask that, as you are now doing, you address us more frequently by letter and more often gladden us concerning your faith, good intention, and welfare, so that we may share a common joy and serve the Lord faithfully with equal devotion.

Given on the Nones of October, in the fourth consulship of Arcadius and Bauto.

## Letter of Pope Anastasius addressed to the most noble man Nerianus

To his most beloved brother Nerianus, Anastasius.

Much in all your letters, which display your faith and goodness, gives me cause for joy: namely, that you show such zeal in the practice of religion and strive to assist the Lord’s priests in your regions [Col. 0694A]. Therefore I give thanks to the Lord, who urges you to this, and I pray that he may make you persevere in good works. Yet in prosperity as well as adversity we ought greatly to praise God and “humble ourselves beneath his mighty hand, so that in due time he may comfort and exalt you in your tribulation, as the blessed apostle Peter says” (I Pet. V, 6).

We have heard that your fraternity has been afflicted by the loss of your parents. This caused us such profound sorrow that, since charity has made us one out of two, our heart felt your tribulations in a special way. Yet amid this grief I was greatly consoled when I considered your holiness, because it is fitting both to bear sadness patiently and not to prolong your mourning over the death of your people [Col. 0694B]. Nevertheless, lest any further affliction remain in your mind, I urge you to rest from grief. It is unfitting to be overcome by weariness and sorrow on account of those whom we must believe to have reached true life through death.

Perhaps those who do not know of another life, who do not trust that there is a passage from this world to something better, have a legitimate excuse for prolonged grief. But we who know this, who believe and teach it, ought not to grieve excessively for the dead, lest what appears to others to be a form of piety become for us rather a fault. For it is, in a certain sense, a kind of distrust contrary to what every preacher who loves righteousness seeks, as the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope” [Col. 0694C] (I Thess. IV, 12).

With this reasoning, therefore, dearest brother, before our eyes, we must strive not to be distressed by the dead, provided that we show affection to the living, for whom piety may be useful and love fruitful. Lay aside your sorrow, then, dearest one, and take up the spiritual fruit of joy for the benefit of the holy Church of God and the advancement of his servants. Strive to illumine whatever span of your life there may be with eternal and divine duties, so that he who has made you distinguished may render you more glorious to himself throughout the ages of ages.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and Palladius for the fourth time.

# THE DECREES OF POPE INNOCENT BEGIN. (C)

[Col. 0693]

## The chapters of Pope Innocent begin.

[Col. 0693D]

1. On giving the kiss of peace after the sacred mysteries have been completed.  
2. On not reciting names to the priest before the prayer.  
3. That the baptized should not be signed except by a bishop.  
4. That fasting should properly be observed every Saturday.  
5. On the leavened bread sent only to the priests of the city.  
6. On baptized persons possessed by an evil spirit.  
7. On penitents.  
8. On the Epistle of Saint James the Apostle, in which prayer for the sick is commanded.

## [LETTER]

**INNOCENT, to DECENTIUS, bishop of Gubbio, greetings.**

[Col. 0694D] If the priests of the Lord wished to preserve intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed apostles, there would be no diversity or variation in those rites and consecrations. But since each person considers that what seems right to him, rather than what has been handed down, must be observed, different practices appear to be maintained or celebrated in different places and churches. As a result, scandal arises among the people: because they do not know that ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, they think either that their churches do not agree with one another or that contradiction has been introduced by the apostles—or, more precisely, by apostolic men.

For who could be unaware, or fail to notice, that what was handed down by Peter, the chief of the apostles, to the Roman Church and has been preserved down to the present must be observed by all [Col. 0695A], and that nothing should be superimposed or introduced which either lacks authority or appears to have been taken from elsewhere as an example? Especially since it is clear that throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one founded churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Let them read, if they can, that in these provinces any other apostle is found or is reported to have taught. If they cannot, because this is found nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves, since there is no doubt that they received their beginning from it. Otherwise, while pursuing foreign assertions, they may appear to omit the source of their institutions.

There is no doubt that your Dilection has often come to the city and met with us in church [Col. 0695B], and has learned what custom we observe in consecrating the mysteries and in our other sacred rites. I would have considered this sufficient for the instruction or reform of your church, if I had been certain that your predecessors had observed anything less or differently. But since you said that we should be consulted about certain matters, we have answered—not because we think that you are ignorant of anything, but so that with greater authority you may instruct your people, or admonish those who have strayed from the institutions of the Roman Church, or not delay in identifying them, so that we may know who introduces innovations or thinks that the custom of a church other than the Roman should be observed.

### I. The kiss of peace

You report that some command the people to exchange the peace before the mysteries have been completed, or exchange it among themselves as priests [Col. 0695C]. Yet peace must be proclaimed after all the things that I ought not to disclose have been completed. Through it, it is shown that the people have given their assent to everything performed within the mysteries and celebrated in the church; and when everything is finished, this is demonstrated by the sign of the peace that brings it to its conclusion.

### II. The recitation of names

As for reciting names before the priest offers his prayers and commends in his prayer the offerings of those whose names are to be recited, you yourself recognize through your prudence how superfluous this is. You mention the name of one whose offerings you have not yet offered to God, although nothing is unknown to him. The offerings must first be commended, and then the names of those persons must be announced, so that they may be named amid the sacred mysteries, not among the other things that we place first, [Col. 0695D] by which we open the way for the prayers that will follow in the mysteries themselves.

### III. The signing of infants

It is clear that infants may not be signed by anyone other than a bishop. For although priests are priests, they do not possess the fullness of the episcopate. It belongs to bishops alone either to sign them or to impart the Spirit the Paraclete. This is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by that passage in the Acts of the Apostles which states that Peter and John were sent to impart the Holy Spirit to those who had already been baptized.

When priests baptize, whether without a bishop or in the bishop’s presence, they may anoint the baptized with chrism that has been consecrated by the bishop; but they may not sign the forehead with the same oil [Col. 0696A], which belongs to bishops alone when they impart the Spirit the Paraclete. I cannot state the words, lest I seem to disclose more than to answer the consultation.

### IV. Saturday fasting

The clearest reasoning shows that one must fast on Saturday. For if we celebrate the Lord’s Day because of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ—not only at Easter but also by repeating an image of that day in each weekly cycle—and if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s passion, we must not omit Saturday, which seems to lie between the sorrow and joy of that period.

It is certain that the apostles remained in sadness and mourning for two days and hid themselves because of fear of the Jews [Col. 0696B]. There is no doubt that they fasted during those two days to such an extent that the tradition of the Church holds that the sacraments are not celebrated at all during this two-day period. This pattern must be maintained in each week because the commemoration of that day is always to be celebrated.

If they think that one should fast only once, on a single Saturday, then the Lord’s Day and Friday should likewise be celebrated only once, at Easter. But if the image of the Lord’s Day and Friday is to be renewed each week, it is foolish to observe the custom of the two-day period while omitting Saturday, since it has the same cause as Friday—namely, the day on which the Lord suffered and was also among the dead, so that, rising on the third day, he might restore joy after the preceding two-day sorrow.

Therefore we do not deny that one must fast on Friday [Col. 0696C], but we say that this must also be done on Saturday, because both days imposed sadness upon the apostles and upon those who followed Christ. On the Lord’s Day they were gladdened and wished that day not only to be most festive but also to be observed throughout all the weeks.

### V. The leavened bread

As for the leavened bread that we send on the Lord’s Day to the titular churches, you have consulted us unnecessarily, since all your churches are located within the city. Their priests cannot meet with us on that day because of the people entrusted to them; therefore they receive from us, through the acolytes, the bread that we have prepared, so that they may not consider themselves separated from our communion, especially on that day.

I do not think this should be done in the outlying parishes, because the sacraments do not have to be carried a long distance [Col. 0696D], nor do we send them to different cemeteries where priests have been established, so that those priests may possess both the right and the permission to prepare them.

### VI. Baptized persons seized by an evil spirit

Your Dilection has asked whether baptized persons who are afterward seized by a demon, some defect, or an intervening sin may or should be signed by a priest or deacon. This is not permitted unless the bishop has ordered it. Hands must absolutely not be laid upon them unless the bishop has given authority for this to be done. It belongs to the bishop to order that hands be laid upon them by a priest or by other clerics.

For how could this be done without great difficulty, so that a possessed person living far away could be brought to the bishop [Col. 0697A], when, if such an event occurred to him on the journey, he might neither be easily carried to the bishop nor easily taken back home?

### VII. Penitents

Regarding penitents—whether they are doing penance for more serious offenses or for lesser ones—the custom of the Roman Church shows that, if no illness intervenes, they are to be released from penance on the Thursday before Easter.

The priest must judge the weight of the offenses [Col. 0697B], paying attention to the penitent’s confession and to the sobs and tears of the one who is correcting himself, and ordering his release when he sees that adequate satisfaction has been made. If someone falls ill and reaches the point of death, he must be released before Easter, so that he does not depart from this world without communion.

### VIII. Anointing the sick

Since your Dilection wished to consult us about this matter as about the others, my son Caelestinus the deacon added in his letter that your Dilection had cited what is written in the Epistle of the Apostle James:

“Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the priests, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James V, 14–15).

There is no doubt that this should be understood and received concerning sick believers, who may be anointed with the holy oil of chrism. This oil, prepared by the bishop, may be used not only by priests but by all Christians, for anointing themselves or their own people in a time of need.

But we see that the addition is superfluous if it is meant to create doubt about the bishop, since it is beyond doubt that this is permitted to priests. Priests are mentioned for this reason: bishops, being occupied with other duties, cannot visit all the sick. If afterward a bishop considers someone worthy of his visit, he can without hesitation bless and touch him with chrism, since he is the one who prepares the chrism itself.

But this cannot be poured upon penitents [Col. 0697C], because it is a kind of sacrament. For when the other sacraments are denied to them, how can it be thought that one kind may be granted?

These matters, therefore, dearest brother, which your Dilection wished us to explain, we have answered as best we could, so that your church may be able to observe and preserve the Roman custom from which it derives its origin. As for the remaining matters, which it was not lawful to put in writing, when you are present we shall be able to state them in answer to your questions.

It will also belong to the power of the Lord to arrange that you properly instruct both your church and our clerics who serve under your episcopate in divine duties, and that you provide others with a model which they ought to imitate.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time, Palladius for the fourth time, and CC [uncertain reading], as consuls.

# The chapters of the same pope addressed to Bishop Victoricus begin.

1. That bishops are not to be ordained without the knowledge of the metropolitan.  
2. That those who received the belt of secular military service after baptism must not be admitted to the clerical order.  
3. That cases involving clerics which are not justly settled in the province should be determined by the apostolic see.  
[Col. 0698A]
4. Concerning clerics: that they marry virgins and not take a second wife.  
5. That if a layman marries a widow, he must not become a cleric.  
6. That one who has married a second wife must not be a cleric.  
7. That no bishop may presume to ordain another bishop’s cleric.  
8. That those coming from the Novatians or Montanists are not to be rebaptized.  
9. That priests and Levites must not have relations with women.  
10. That if a monk becomes a cleric, he must preserve his chosen way of life.  
11. That no one from the municipal governing class should become a cleric, because of the entertainments which he is compelled to provide and which were invented by the devil. [Col. 0698B]  
12. Concerning consecrated virgins, if they fall and marry publicly.  
13. Concerning virgins who are not veiled, if they go astray.

## [LETTER]

**INNOCENT, to VICTORICUS, bishop of Rouen, greetings.**

Although, dearest brother, because of the merit and honor of the priesthood in which you greatly excel, all the rules for ecclesiastical living and teaching are known to you, and although there seems to be nothing from the sacred readings that you have not gathered, nevertheless, since you earnestly requested the norm and authority of the Roman Church, I have willingly complied with your desire and sent with my letter teachings concerning the conduct of life and disciplines of approved morals. Through them, the peoples of your region [Col. 0698C] may learn by what principles and rules the life of Christians in every profession should be governed, and what discipline is observed in the churches of the city of Rome.

It will be your Dilection’s task to present this book of rules diligently, as a teacher and admonisher, to the neighboring peoples and to our fellow priests who preside over their own churches in those regions, so that they may both recognize our practices and shape, through diligent instruction, the conduct of those who flock to the faith. They will either learn their own purpose from this suitable instruction of ours or, if anything is still lacking, will easily supply it by good imitation.

Let us begin, therefore, with the help of God and of the holy apostle of God, Peter, through whom both the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ received their beginning. Since many matters have often arisen [Col. 0698D] which in some cases were not merely matters but crimes, every priest must henceforth be concerned to exercise such care in his church as the blessed apostle Paul teaches, presenting a church to God that does not have “spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V, 27), lest our conscience be polluted and defiled by the breath of any diseased sheep.

For the sake of those who, whether through ignorance or negligence, do not observe ecclesiastical discipline and presume many things that must not be presumed, you rightly requested that in those regions the form maintained by the Roman Church should be observed—not because any new commands are being imposed, but because we desire that what some have neglected through negligence should be observed by all. These rules, however, have been established by apostolic [Col. 0699A] and patristic tradition.

For it is written in the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians and in the letter to Timothy, with the Apostle Paul giving instruction: “Stand firm and hold to the traditions that we handed on to you, whether by word or by letter” (II Thess. II, 14).

This ought certainly to stir your mind more forcefully, so that you may be found before God free from every stain of this world and secure. “For from the one to whom much has been entrusted, more will be required” (Luke XII, 48). Therefore, since we are compelled to render an account not only for ourselves but also for the people of Christ, we must sanctify and instruct the people through the discipline of God.

You assert that certain men have existed who, not observing the statutes of their forefathers, violate the chastity of the Church through their presumption, pursuing the favor of the people and not fearing God’s judgment [Col. 0699B]. Therefore, lest our silence make us seem to consent to them—since the Lord says through the prophet, “You saw a thief and ran with him” (Ps. XLIX, 18)—these are the matters that, in view of divine judgment, every Catholic bishop should henceforth take care to observe.

### I. The ordination of bishops

First, no one should dare to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan. A judgment is sound when it is confirmed by the opinions of many; and one bishop must not presume to ordain a bishop, lest the benefit appear to have been conferred secretly. The Council of Nicaea also established and defined this.

### II. Military service after baptism

It also established and defined that if anyone, after the remission of sins, has taken up the belt of secular military service [Col. 0699C], he must absolutely not be admitted to the clerical order.

### III. Ecclesiastical cases

If any cases or disputes arise among clerics or among laymen, whether of higher or lower rank, it has been decided, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea, that judgment should be concluded when all the bishops of that province have assembled. No one may, without prejudice to the Roman Church—to which reverence is owed and must be preserved in every case—abandon the priests who by divine will govern the churches of God in that province, rush to other provinces, or first seek the judgment of bishops from other provinces.

If anyone should presume to do this, he must be removed from the clerical office and judged by all to be guilty of injury. If more serious cases are brought forward, they are to be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment, as the council decreed and as venerable custom requires.

### IV. Clerics and widows

[Col. 0699D] A cleric must not marry a widow, because it is written: “The priest shall take a virgin as wife, not a widow, nor one cast out” (Ezek. XLIV, 22). Anyone who strives to attain the priesthood through his own labor and upright life must take care lest, obstructed by this disqualification, he be unable to reach it.

### V. A layman who marries a widow

If anyone, even though a layman, marries a widow, whether before or after baptism, he must not be admitted to the clergy. He is considered excluded by the same fault: in baptism crimes are forgiven, but the marriage to a wife already taken is not annulled.

### VI. Second marriages

[Col. 0700A] A man who has married a second wife must not become a cleric, because it is written: “The husband of one wife” (I Tim. III, 2); and again: “Let my priests marry once”; and elsewhere: “Let my priests not marry again.”

No one should think that, if a man took a wife before baptism and, after she departed from this world, married another and claimed that the first marriage had been dismissed in baptism, this is permitted. He is far from the rule. In baptism sins are forgiven; the number of wives taken is not abolished.

A wife is taken in accordance with the commandment of the law, to such an extent that when the human parents of the race were joined in paradise, they were blessed by the Lord himself, and Solomon says: “A wife is prepared for a man by God” (Prov. XIX, 14). The practice of the Church itself demonstrates that all priests must also preserve this form.

It is extremely absurd to believe that a wife taken before baptism [Col. 0700B] is not counted after baptism, since the blessing imposed by the priest upon those marrying is taught not to have supplied material for wrongdoing but to have preserved the form of the law established by God from ancient times. If a wife taken before baptism is not to be counted, then children born before baptism are not to be regarded as children either.

### VII. Clerics from another church

No one may presume to ordain or judge a cleric from another church unless that cleric’s bishop, having been earnestly petitioned, wishes to grant permission. The Council of Nicaea also appears to contain this rule. A cleric rejected by his own church must not be received by another church.

### VIII. Novatians and Montanists

Those coming from the Novatians or Montanists are to be received [Col. 0700C] by the laying on of hands alone, because although they were baptized by heretics, they were baptized in the name of Christ. This excludes those who, after going over from us to them, were perhaps rebaptized. If such people repent, reflect upon their ruin, and wish to return, they must be admitted only after a long satisfaction of penance.

### IX. Priests and Levites

The Church must observe what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: priests and Levites must not have relations with their wives, because they are occupied with the necessities of their daily ministry. For it is written: “Be holy, because I also am holy, the Lord your God” (Lev. XI, 44).

In ancient times, priests of God [Col. 0700D] did not leave the temple during the year of their service, as we read concerning Zechariah, nor did they visit their homes at all. The use of a wife had been permitted to them for the sake of the succession of offspring, because no one from another tribe, and no one except from the seed of Aaron, was commanded to approach the priesthood.

How much more, then, should these priests and Levites preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry exists without succession? Not a day passes on which they are free either from the divine sacrifices or from the duty of baptism.

For if the blessed apostle Paul wrote to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain from one another for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (I Cor. VII, 5)—and he certainly commanded this to laypeople—then priests, whose continual duty is both to pray and to offer sacrifice, must much more always abstain from such relations.

If someone has been polluted by carnal desire, with what shame will he presume to offer sacrifice [Col. 0701A], or with what conscience or merit believe that he will be heard? For it is said: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the polluted and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus I, 15).

Perhaps he thinks this is permitted because it is written: “The husband of one wife.” But this does not refer to someone who remains in the desire to beget children; it refers to future continence. He did not exclude those who were physically intact, for he says: “I wish that all were as I myself am” (I Cor. VII, 7). He explains this more clearly when he says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; but you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom. VIII, 8–9).

### X. Monks who become clerics

Monks who have spent a long time in monasteries and afterward enter the clerical order must not depart from their former way of life. Either, as they were in the monastery, they must not abandon what they have long observed after being placed in a higher [Col. 0701B] rank; or, if one who has been corrupted is afterward baptized and, while remaining in the monastery, wishes to enter the clerical order, he may not have a wife at all, since one who has already been corrupted cannot be blessed with a bride.

This form is observed among clerics. The ancient rule especially holds that anyone who, after being corrupted, was baptized and wished to become a cleric must promise not to marry a wife at all.

### XI. Curials and public officials as clerics

Moreover, some of our brothers frequently strive to make clerics of men occupied with municipal or other public offices. Later, when the emperor orders that they be recalled, this brings greater sorrow than the appointment had brought joy.

It is clear that such men, even in those offices, provide entertainments [Col. 0701C] which were certainly invented by the devil; they either preside over the arrangements of games and public spectacles or perhaps take part in them. Let the concern and sorrow of our brothers, which we have often expressed in the presence of the emperor while repeatedly pleading for these men, serve as an example. You yourself, when present with us, learned of this.

Not only did great pressure arise to restore lower clerics from the municipal governing class, but the same pressure concerned men who had already been placed in the priesthood.

### XII. Consecrated virgins who marry

Those who marry Christ spiritually and are veiled by a priest [Col. 0701D], if they afterward marry or are corrupted, publicly or secretly, must not be admitted to perform penance unless the person to whom they joined themselves has died.

For if this rule is observed concerning human beings—“Any woman who, while her husband is alive, marries another is called an adulteress” (Rom. VII, 3)—and permission to perform penance is not granted to her unless one of them has died, how much more must it be observed concerning a woman who had first joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterward chose to pass over to human marriage!

### XIII. Unveiled virgins who marry

Those women who, although not yet covered with the sacred veil, have always professed their intention to remain committed to a virginal purpose [Col. 0702A], must, if they marry, perform penance for a considerable time, even though they were not veiled, because their pledge was held by the Lord.

If among human beings a contract made in good faith is ordinarily dissolved for no reason, how much more will this promise, which they made with God, be unable to be dissolved without punishment?

For if the Apostle Paul said that those who departed from their commitment to widowhood “have condemnation because they have rejected their first faith” (I Tim. V, 12), how much more does this apply to virgins who have in no way preserved faith with their earlier promise!

Therefore, dearest brother, if this rule is guarded by all God’s priests with complete vigilance, ambition will cease, dissension will come to rest, heresies and schisms will not arise, and the devil will find no opportunity to rage. Unity will remain, iniquity will be conquered and trampled down, truth will burn with spiritual fervor, and the peace proclaimed by the lips will agree with the will of the heart.

The Apostle’s command will be fulfilled: “Let us remain united, thinking one thing in Christ, claiming nothing for ourselves through rivalry or empty glory” (Phil. II, 2–3). We shall please not human beings but our God and Savior [Col. 0702B], “to whom are honor and glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen” (Rom. XVI, 27).

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus and Aristo.

# The same pope’s letter to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse

1. On the innocence of priests and Levites.  
2. On those who, after baptism, have devoted themselves continually to the pleasures of sexual incontinence and ask for penance at the end of life.  
3. On secular administrators or judges.  
4. That men must not associate with adulterous wives.  
5. That those who draft petitions or accusations are to be held immune. [Col. 0702C]  
6. That those who, after a divorce, have joined themselves to other spouses are shown to be adulterers.  
7. Which books are received into the canon.

**INNOCENT, to EXUPERIUS, bishop of Toulouse, greetings.**

When you consulted me, dearest brother, about what I thought should be observed concerning each of the cases proposed, I replied, insofar as my understanding allowed, with what seemed appropriate: what should be followed, what a teachable judgment persuaded, what the authority of Scripture showed, or what the established sequence of events demonstrated.

Your Dilection, following the practice of prudent men, preferred to refer to the apostolic see what should be observed in doubtful matters rather than, through presumptuous usurpation, to determine for yourself what seemed right in each case [Col. 0702D]. Why should we think it more shameful to learn something than to be completely ignorant?

I myself also gain teachability through discussion, since, after examining the reasons, I am compelled to answer what has been proposed. Thus the person who is asked to teach always learns something. Let each question therefore be presented, and I shall append the answer.

### I. Incontinent priests and Levites

You asked what should be observed concerning those who, placed in the ministry of the diaconate or in the office of the priesthood, have been shown by the children they generated to be or to have been incontinent.

Concerning these matters there is both the discipline of the divine laws and the clear admonitions of Siricius, bishop of blessed memory. They state that those placed in such offices who are incontinent must be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor [Col. 0703A] and must not be admitted to a ministry which ought to be fulfilled through continence alone.

There is a very ancient authority of the sacred law, preserved from the beginning: priests were commanded to reside in the temple during the year of their service, so that, serving at the sacred offerings, they might claim the divine mysteries as pure and cleansed from every stain. It was not lawful to admit to the sacrifices those who engaged in carnal relations even with their wives, because it is written: “Be holy, because I also am holy, the Lord your God” (Lev. XI, 44).

The use of a wife had been permitted to them for the sake of the succession of offspring [Col. 0703B], because no one from another tribe, and no one except from the seed of Aaron, was commanded to approach the priesthood. How much more, then, should these priests and Levites preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry exists without succession?

Not a day passes on which they are free either from the divine sacrifices or from the duty of baptism. For if the blessed apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain from one another for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (I Cor. VII, 5)—and he certainly commanded this to laypeople—then priests, whose continual duty is both to pray and to offer sacrifice, must always abstain from such relations.

If someone has been polluted by carnal desire, with what shame will he presume to offer sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit believe that he will be heard, when it is said: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the polluted and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus I, 15)?

Perhaps he thinks this is permitted because it is written [Col. 0703C]: “The husband of one wife” (I Tim. III, 2). But this does not refer to someone who remains in the desire to beget children; it refers to future continence. He did not exclude those who were physically intact, for he says: “I wish that all were as I myself am” (I Cor. VII, 7). He explains this more clearly when he says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; but you are no longer in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom. VIII, 8–9).

He said this of one who has children but does not beget them; yet that is plainly a different and distinct proposition. If anyone is not shown to have received that form of ecclesiastical life and discipline which was transmitted from Bishop Siricius to the provinces, forgiveness will be granted to those who were ignorant of it, provided that from then on they begin entirely to abstain. They may retain the rank in which they are found, but they may not rise to higher offices. They should nevertheless regard it as a benefit that they do not lose the position they currently hold.

But if some are discovered to have known the form of life transmitted by Siricius [Col. 0703D] and nevertheless did not immediately abandon their lustful desires, they must in every way be removed, because, after recognizing the admonition, they judged pleasure preferable.

### II. Penitence at the end of life

It was also asked what should be observed concerning those who, after baptism, have devoted themselves throughout their lives to the pleasures of incontinence and, at the very end of life, request both penance and restoration to communion.

The earlier practice was stricter; the later one, with mercy intervening, is more lenient. For the earlier custom held that penance should be granted but communion denied. Since persecutions were frequent in those times [Col. 0704A], and the easy granting of communion to those seeking reconciliation did not recall people from falling, communion was rightly denied while penance was granted, so that everything would not be refused. The circumstances of the time made the remission more severe.

But after our Lord restored peace to his churches and terror had been driven away, it was decided to give communion to those departing this life. This was done because of the Lord’s mercy, and so that we might not appear to follow the harshness and severity of the Novatian heretics, who deny forgiveness, rather than provide the viaticum for those about to depart.

Communion is therefore granted together with final penance, so that such people, with the permission of our Savior, may at least in their final moments be rescued from eternal destruction.

### III. Secular administrators and judges

It was also asked about those who, after baptism, served as administrators [Col. 0704B] and either exercised torture alone or even pronounced capital sentences. The elders established no ruling about them.

They remembered that these powers had been granted by God, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of the guilty, and that the minister of God had been appointed as an avenger in such matters. How, then, could they have condemned an act which they saw had been permitted by God as its author?

Therefore, concerning these men, let us maintain the practice preserved until now, so that we may not appear either to overturn discipline or to act against the authority of the Lord. Their deeds themselves, however, will be retained when they are called to render an account.

### IV. Men and adulterous wives

It was desired to know why men who are in communion do not associate with adulterous wives [Col. 0704C], while, conversely, wives appear to remain in the company of adulterous husbands.

In this matter the Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes. But women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and hidden sins do not receive punishment. Men, however, are accustomed more freely to report adulterous wives to priests.

Therefore communion is denied to women once their crime has been exposed, whereas, because the offense of men remains hidden, no one is readily excluded on the basis of suspicion alone. He will certainly be removed if his disgrace is uncovered. Since the cause is therefore the same, the administration of punishment sometimes ceases when proof is lacking.

V. You also wished to inquire whether, after the regeneration of baptism, those who dictate petitions are permitted to ask rulers for someone’s death or blood on account of guilt [Col. 0704D]. Rulers, however, never grant such a request without investigation; instead, they always refer the matters or crimes themselves to judges, so that punishment may be imposed after the case has been examined. When the matter has been delegated to the investigator, either acquittal or condemnation is issued according to the character of the case; and while the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the petitioner remains immune.

VI. Your Dilection also inquired about those who, after a divorce had intervened, joined themselves to another marriage; it is evident that they are adulterers on both sides. Those, however, who, while their wife is still alive—although the marriage may appear to have been dissolved—hasten to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers, to such an extent that even the persons joined to them appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery” (Mark 10:11). Likewise: “And whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery” (Matthew 5:32). Therefore all such persons are to be excluded from the communion of the faithful.

Nothing of this kind can be established concerning their parents or relatives unless they are discovered to have been instigators of the illicit union.

VII. A brief appendix shows which books are received in the canon of the Holy Scriptures. These, then, are the matters about which you wished to be instructed by an oral reply:

The five books of Moses—that is, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy; likewise Joshua son of Nun, Judges, and the four books of Kings; also Ruth; the sixteen books of the Prophets; the five books of Solomon; the Psalter; and, among the historical books, one book of Job, one of Esther, one of Judith, two of Maccabees, two of Ezra, and two of Chronicles.

Likewise, in the New Testament: the four books of the Gospels; fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul; four Epistles of John; two Epistles of Peter; the Epistle of Jude; the Epistle of James; the Acts of the Apostles; and the Apocalypse of John.

As for the remaining writings attributed to Matthias, or to James the Less, or to Peter and John, which were written by a certain Leutius, or those attributed to Andrew, written by the philosophers Nexocharydes and Leonidas, or those attributed to Thomas, and any others of this kind, one should know that they are not merely to be disregarded [Col. 0705C], but are also to be condemned.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Stilicho and Anthemius.

## Letter of Innocent to Felix, Bishop of Nuceria

1. A cleric who voluntarily amputates any part of his body cannot be a cleric; one who does so unwillingly may be.  
2. Bigamists cannot be admitted to the clergy.  
3. Those who come from the laity are not to be promoted to the clergy.  
4. Which laymen may become clerics; here a concubine is expressly prohibited.  
5. Concerning the periods of service to be spent in the clergy.

### Innocent to Felix, Bishop of Nuceria [Col. 0705D]

We cannot be surprised that Your Dilection follows the institutions of our predecessors and refers to us, as to the head and summit of the episcopate, everything that may admit of some doubt, so that the apostolic see, having been consulted, may pronounce from these doubtful matters what ought certainly to be done. We gladly accept this, and approve Your Dilection as mindful of the canons.

You therefore wrote that, through the fervor of faith with which you are endowed and through love for the holy people, you had either restored the churches of God or built new ones, but that among those whom you appointed clerics there were some mutilated and some twice-married. We were astonished that a prudent man should have wished to consult us about matters that are clearly known to everyone by reason. Thus we are not speaking to you as though you were ignorant, but we say that, perhaps occupied with other matters, you have forgotten this one [Col. 0706A].

I. Whoever voluntarily cuts off part of any finger from himself is not admitted to the clergy by the canons. But if this happens to someone accidentally while he is attending to agricultural work, or if, while doing something else, he strikes himself involuntarily, the canons command that such men may become clerics; and if they are found already in the clergy, they are not expelled. For in the former cases the will is judged, since a person has dared to apply iron to himself; in the latter, the accident has earned pardon.

II. There should have been no consultation concerning the twice-married, since the apostle’s clear reading says that a man admitted to the priesthood or the clergy must be “the husband of one wife” [Col. 0706B], provided that he took her as a virgin. If she had had a husband previously, however, even if he had died, and she was afterward joined to a cleric, the cleric who took her cannot be a cleric, because the law prescribes that a priest may not have as his wife “a widow or one cast off.”

III. Your Religiousness consulted us concerning laymen whom the canons forbid to be ordained. It is certainly true that the ecclesiastical rules contain this provision, but it has not been defined in such a way that it applies to all laymen without distinction. Clerics are not born but made. Rather, categories have been specified of those who cannot reach the clergy: if a believer has served in the army; if a believer has practiced law—that is, has acted as an advocate; or if a believer has administered public affairs.

Concerning members of the municipal council, the reason is clear: even if men of this kind are found who ought to become clerics, they are often summoned back to the council, and they must therefore be avoided because of the trouble that frequently comes to the Church through them [Col. 0706C].

IV. Laymen who were baptized while having wives, and who thereafter conducted themselves in such a way that their reputation in no respect falters—whether they have remained attached to clerics or have adhered to monasteries from the time of their baptism—are not to be excluded from the clerical order, provided that they have not known a concubine or mistress and have remained vigilant in all their works [Col. 0706D].

V. This is to be understood with the proviso that the periods established by our predecessors are observed for them. No one should quickly become a lector, quickly an acolyte, quickly a deacon, or quickly a priest. If they remain for a long time in the lesser offices and both their life and their service are approved, they may afterward come to the priesthood after completing the merits of their periods of service; they must not seize prematurely what an approved life deserves to receive.

Since it has been shown by a firm definition who ought to be admitted and who ought to be rejected, from among all those whom Your Dignity sees not to be subject to rejection you should choose those whom you will make clerics. For if we wish to grant no favor or benefit to anyone, we can find men whose appointment will bring us neither danger nor shame.

## Concerning those who have fathered children while in the presbyterate, so that they may be removed from office

### Innocent to Maximus and Severus, bishops, through Britius

The rule of the ecclesiastical canons ought to be unknown to no priest, since it is sufficiently disgraceful for a bishop not to know these things—especially when religious laymen know them and consider them necessary to observe. The enclosed text of the petition shows what sort of complaint our son Maximilianus, an imperial agent, recently brought forward.

Led by zeal for faith and discipline, he does not tolerate the Church’s being polluted by unworthy presbyters whom he asserts to have fathered children while in the presbyterate. I would explain that this is not permitted if I did not know that Your Prudence possesses knowledge of the whole law. Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the contents of the enclosed petition, you shall order those accused of having committed such acts to be brought forward publicly. After the accusations brought against the presbyters have been investigated, if they are convicted, they are to be removed from the priestly office, because those who are not holy cannot handle holy things; they must also be made strangers to the ministry that they have polluted by living unlawfully [Col. 0707B].

We are astonished that bishops conceal such conduct, so that they appear either to connive at it or to judge that they do not know it to be unlawful.

## That no penitent may be admitted to the clergy

### Innocent to Agapitus, Macedonius, and Maurianus, bishops in Apulia

Reports from various persons and highly trustworthy submissions have stated that many things contrary to the ecclesiastical canons and the decrees of our predecessors are being usurped in the province. These abuses could easily be cut away if bishops were not found to be their authors [Col. 0707C]. While they try to grant favor to friends or to those who serve them, they violate religion and corrupt the orders. Thus it happens that certain unworthy men receive ecclesiastical honors and are admitted to the clergy—men who would not deserve to hold a worthy place even among the laity.

This is demonstrated in the petition recently submitted to us: a certain Modestus, entangled in many crimes and said also to have performed penance for them, was not merely made a cleric, although this is forbidden, but was even advanced to the summit of the episcopate, although the canons established at Nicaea exclude penitents even from the lowest clerical offices. Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the contents of the petition, order him to be presented; and if he is truly found to be such as the petition asserts [Col. 0707D], remove him not only from ambition for office but also from the clerical office.

## Concerning Bubalius and Taurianus, condemned by the provincial bishops, whose sentence the apostolic see undertook to reconsider

### Innocent to Rufus, Gerontius, Sophronius, Flavianus, Macedonius, Prosdotius, and Oristeus, bishops established throughout Macedonia

The delay of our fellow bishops Maximianus and Eumenius—or rather, the pressure of the circumstances—caused you to renew your complaint concerning Bubalius and Taurianus, and caused us once again to rise against men utterly ruined. But, as best I can, I shall make a brief summary of such great evils and briefly review what I have seen in the volume of our letters [Col. 0708A].

It ought not to have seemed burdensome to your most devout minds that anyone’s judgment should be reconsidered, because truth, when repeatedly tested, shines more brightly in the light, while a crime recalled for judgment is condemned more gravely and without reprieve. For it is a divine fruit, dearest brothers, that justice should often be examined.

Yet I see what has disturbed your minds: on many occasions Bubalius, caught in deceptions, produced copies of forged letters as though they had come from us, while, given the man’s habitual conduct, nothing he brought forward now appeared sufficiently worthy of trust. But let every murmur about such a matter now cease, and let the very breathings of the convicted devil himself be suppressed.

We have appended to these letters the earlier letters that we sent through the bishops mentioned above. In them the judgment of our minds has been set out so fully that, when you reread them, you will find nothing ambiguous and nothing further to seek in this case [Col. 0708B]. Send this little page of ours to the bishops who trust you, so that they may reread it carefully and know fully what has been pronounced concerning Bubalius, Taurianus, and the others. Those who deserve admonition should learn to avoid such men, lest they associate with them.

## Concerning the invasion of another bishop’s parish

### Innocent to Florentius, Bishop of Tibur

Divine Scripture cries out not once but repeatedly that the boundaries established by our predecessors must not be moved, because it is unlawful for one person to invade what another has always possessed. Our brother and fellow bishop Ursus asserts that Your Goodness has done this [Col. 0708C].

He has complained with sorrow that you invaded the parish of Nomentum, or Facilis, which by ancient right belonged to his diocese, and celebrated the divine mysteries there while he was unaware. If this is true, know that you have incurred no light offense. Therefore, if you wish to avoid the odium of so great an usurpation, you should abstain after being admonished by this letter of ours.

But if you believe that something supports your case in justice, you must come after the holy days of Easter, with everything intact and remaining in its former condition, so that you may respond to the claims mentioned above and, with the relevant documents brought forward publicly, we may investigate what antiquity or truth establishes.

## Concerning a man whose wife returned from captivity, so that he should receive her after repudiating the other woman whom he had married

### Innocent to Probus [Col. 0708D]

The upheaval of the barbarian storm brought an incident before the authority of the law. A marriage properly established between Fortunius and Ursa would have suffered a blemish through the incursion of captivity, had the sacred ordinances of religion not provided a remedy.

While the aforementioned woman Ursa was being held in captivity, the said Fortunius is known to have entered another marriage with Restituta. But Ursa, by the favor of the Lord, returned and came to him. Without anyone expressing doubt, she proved that she was the wife of the man mentioned above.
