Therefore, illustrious lord and deservedly honored son, with the support of the Catholic faith we have determined that the marriage first founded by divine grace was the true marriage, and that the union with the second woman, while the first survived and had not been expelled by divorce, could in no way be legitimate.

## A familiar letter to the holy priests of God, Aurelius of Carthage and Augustine of Hippo

### Innocent to Aurelius and Augustine, bishops [Col. 0709A]

The return of Germanus, my most beloved fellow presbyter, ought not to have been devoid of our service to you. For it seems natural and fitting to us to greet those most dear to us through those who are dear to us. We therefore wish you, our beloved brothers, joy in the Lord, and we ask you to offer equal prayers to the Lord on our behalf, because, as you well know, through shared and reciprocal prayers we accomplish more than through solitary or private ones.

## Concerning the date of Easter, to the same Aurelius

### Innocent to Aurelius [Col. 0709B]

The service of our charity is not interrupted by any interval, even if no letters are carried between us. Spiritual grace lives reciprocally in our hearts and nourishes our love, while the priestly fellowship itself fosters it.

Therefore take care, as is fitting, that the unity of the Church be guarded. Let us all alike think and declare the same thing, dearest brother. I have therefore written these letters concerning the date of Easter in the other—that is, the coming—year.

Since on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April the full moon is reckoned as the sixteenth day—not anything less—and since on the fourth day before those same Kalends it will be the twenty-third day, I judged that the Paschal feast should be celebrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends mentioned above, because we know that Easter has never previously been celebrated on the twenty-third day of the moon.

I have explained and declared the substance of my opinion [Col. 0709C]. It will now be for Your Prudence, my brother and associate, together with our unanimous fellow priests, to reconsider this matter in a most devout synod. If nothing conflicts with our arrangement, write back to us fully and openly, so that we may in due time write back and reserve the date of Easter that has been determined, as is customary.

Although I know that you will most gladly receive our fellow presbyter the archdeacon in your customary manner, I nevertheless ask, as an additional favor, whether you would be willing to have him among your own.

## That no one be made bishop contrary to the order of the canons

### Innocent to his dearest brother Aurelius

Your Fraternity knows well with what indignity and distress the Church, and especially a bishop, may be mistreated; and I cannot find words adequate to such grief when hands are easily laid on men and the supreme priest is chosen carelessly [Col. 0709D].

Behold, a public complaint has arisen, making it always necessary that reverence common to all should tremble. Thus clerics nourished and honored within ecclesiastical teaching are rejected from Christ’s altars, while outsiders are promoted, as though it were unlawful to reach primacy through the proper order.

For when men entangled in worldly bonds, whether in conduct or morals, are abruptly admitted to so great a priestly fellowship, those from whom the choice ought to have been made appear to be despised, while those who break in outside the order are improperly admitted rather than chosen. How miserable it is when one is made a teacher who was never a disciple [Col. 0710A]—when one is made the supreme priest who never served a priest in that rank.

Reread the letters of the prefects and see what things are falsely or truthfully recorded in writing concerning exalted powers. We ourselves have certainly destroyed the reverence owed to holiness—I mean we ourselves—by making supreme priests out of what is treated as something utterly worthless, so that it is now beginning to be condemned in public declarations as though it were something harmful.

Dearest brother, I wish you to send these writings for reading throughout all the African churches, and to attach to them the letters of the prefects that we have enclosed. Let counsel and judgment be given concerning the things that are unjustly praised, so that past evils, if proved to have been committed, may be restrained with due severity, and so that in the future care may be taken lest the holiness of the Church, wearied by our negligence, lose the privileges that it has obtained through venerable men [Col. 0710B].

May God keep you safe. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of June, in the consulship of Julius IV and Palladius V.

## To Juliana, a noblewoman

It is sufficiently evident to everyone that you are a singular member of your Church and that the greatness of your religious devotion is held in the highest reverence by us. At the very summit of nobility, you offer the Church a devotion far nobler still; with a joy more radiant in your knowledge of Christ, you obey his commands; and you exult in faith rather than boast of the splendor of so great a lineage.

It is the mark of supreme virtue to conquer the glory of the flesh, and it is a great grace of Christ to surpass nobility through character, illustrious lady and daughter, deservedly honored. Therefore, dearest daughter, being certain of this, strive to illumine whatever span of this life remains with eternal and divine duties, so that he who has made you distinguished may render you more illustrious for himself throughout the ages [Col. 0710C].

## Concerning the Church of Antioch

### Innocent to Boniface, presbyter

The Church of Antioch, which the blessed apostle Peter honored by his presence before he came to the city of Rome, did not long permit itself, as though a sister Church, to remain alienated from the Roman Church. For when it sent legates, it asked for and obtained peace in such a way that the Evagrian clergy were received into their orders and places with the ordination they had received from Memoratus left unimpaired. It also gathered and united the clerics and laypeople of John of holy memory.

My brother Alexander, bishop of that city, promised that if anyone should later come to them either from us or from elsewhere, he would receive him without controversy and would recite the name of the aforementioned bishop among the bishops at rest [Col. 0710D].

Know, dearest brother, that we have given our consent to this matter and received them into our own heart, lest members who had sought healing from the unity of the body should long be regarded as alienated from it. My son, the deacon Paul, bearer of this letter, will be able to recount to Your Dilection everything that was done in due order, so that you may share our common joy and inform those who customarily intervene on behalf of Atticus.

## To Alexander, Bishop of Antioch, concerning peace

### Innocent to Alexander, bishop

You will learn, by reviewing the acts themselves, how welcome, pious, and necessary was the delegation sent to us by Your Holiness, dearest brother [Col. 0711A]. For our fellow presbyter Cassianus wished this little document of our friendship to be written, through your fellow presbyter Paul, the deacon Nicholas, and Peter the subdeacon, our sons, as the first fruits of our peace.

I therefore greet your fraternity in Christ, which is dear to me, and the entire Church that shares your good judgment. I ask you, as you do us, to address us more frequently by letter and to gladden us more often with news of your well-being. For, as I trust, the Lord will grant us to make up for the losses of all the past time through the most loving conversation of letters.

## Concerning Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople

### Innocent to Maximianus, bishop [Col. 0711B]

We are astonished at Your Prudence, which asks us to write to Atticus, bishop of the city of Constantinople, both through your own petition and through the written submission appended below, although you have not produced any letters sent by him either to you or to your synod. You judge that something should be granted to one who has not asked for it, although you see that what was granted to petitioners was granted only after investigation.

Communion that has been suspended is restored to one who demonstrates that the causes for which it occurred have now been removed and who declares that the conditions of peace have been fulfilled. But Atticus, as I have already said, has not wished either before you or before us to say or demonstrate, by sending any of his people, that this has been accomplished, as our brother and fellow bishop Alexander of the Church of Antioch did through a worthy embassy and proved [Col. 0711C].

You were present and graciously took part in all these matters, and you learned how I examined, point by point, all the earlier writings of our most blessed former bishop John concerning this case, writings that showed him with complete clarity that everything which ought to have been done at Antioch had been completed.

Having embraced their peace, we gave it our faith and, by a broad path, showed to all the same thing that you await: if only they should at some time demonstrate that, in their own place, they too have done or completed what has been examined and fulfilled, and should solemnly ask through an embassy that communion be restored to them, as these men did.

We therefore await both the declaration of the aforementioned man concerning the fulfillment of all the conditions that we specified at different times and his request for communion, so that we may rightly restore it to one who both asks for it and proves himself worthy of it, dearest brother [Col. 0711D]. For you received long ago our fullest letters concerning all these matters addressed to the holy synod of our brothers.

## To Alexander, Bishop of Antioch, concerning peace

The favor of the apostolic see has shone upon us with the great splendor of peace, and it has poured such light and joy upon the faithful that, while giving the greatest praises to God, we acknowledge that we owe him still greater ones. We have been gladdened by God all the more because, after examining every aspect of the actions of Your Fraternity, we learned that everything had been conducted with such piety and patience that we praised the Lord in all things [Col. 0712A].

We see that this success was granted to your labors because, being a lover of peace with all your strength, you sought it, found it, and held it with the greatest charity—especially toward those who had once been counted under the name of the bishops Paulinus and Evagrius.

I have received the fulfillment of my highest prayers: the cleansing of the ancient stain has been prolonged into your time and through your merits. I also judged that those of the same name who had earned the distinction of the clergy in Italy should retain the grace of the quiet settlement already received.

Since our fellow presbyter Cassianus thought that it would be pleasing to Your Dignity if, by my advice, they were regarded as belonging to the clerical order in your city, I have gladly decided, out of regard for your goodwill and because of the promises of the aforementioned man, that they be numbered among the other priests and ministers who are in the city [Col. 0712B], dearest brother.

Furthermore, I learned that the bishops Helpidius and Papo recovered their churches without dispute. I investigated the acts with great care, as the appended documents testify, to determine whether every condition had been satisfied in the case of John, that blessed priest truly worthy of God.

When the statement of the legates acknowledged, point by point, that everything had been completed as desired, I gave thanks to God and received your Church into communion in such a way as to proclaim that the disciples of the apostolic see were the first to open to the others the way of peace. In this peace the kindness of the Lord Christ will embrace and strengthen both you and us so firmly that henceforth we shall be struck neither by the slightest irritation nor by the shame of any minor dispute.

As for the writings of Bishop Atticus, since they were submitted together with yours, we accepted them so that the man who had once been suspended by us would not be rejected through injury to you. Nevertheless, as you will kindly take care to reread in full what we established in the acts concerning what must be observed in his case, if he should ask to be wholly united with your holy counsels and actions, let the favor of communion and letters be extended to that old man through your goodwill and our judgment [Col. 0712C].

Twenty bishops signed. Twenty-four from Italy.

## Letter of the same Innocent to Alexander, bishop

1. That the first see of blessed Peter is said to have been at Antioch.  
2. That, according to the emperor’s enactments, there ought not to be two metropolitan bishops.  
3. That the clerics of the Arians are not to be received into their offices, although the Church confirms their baptism, which is acknowledged to be Catholic.

### Chapter I. Innocent to Alexander, bishop

Both the burden and the honor imposed upon us by Your Fraternity have introduced matters requiring necessary discussion, so that we may be able to respond to your letter or memorandum as the grace of the Holy Spirit grants.

Accordingly, when we review the authority of the Council of Nicaea—which sets forth the mind of all the bishops throughout the world—we recognize what it judged concerning the Church of Antioch as necessary for all the faithful, not to say for all priests, to observe. We recognize that this Church was established over its stated diocese, not over some other province [Col. 0713A].

From this we understand that this distinction was granted not so much because of the magnificence of the city as because it is shown to have been the first see of the first apostle. There the Christian religion received its name; there it deserved to host the most celebrated gathering of the apostles; and it would not yield to the see of the city of Rome except that Rome received its distinction from what Peter merited in passing, while Antioch rejoices in what it received and completed within itself.

Therefore, dearest brother, we judge that just as you ordain the metropolitans by your singular authority, so you should not permit the other bishops to be appointed without your permission and knowledge. In this matter you will rightly observe the following practice: arrange by letters that those who are far away be ordained by those who now ordain them solely at their own discretion; but if you judge them to be nearby, establish that they should come to receive the laying on of hands from Your Grace [Col. 0713B]. For those whose care chiefly awaits you ought especially to receive your judgment.

II. You ask whether, when provinces have been divided by imperial decision so that there are two metropolises, two metropolitan bishops ought to be appointed. It has not truly seemed right that the Church of God should be altered according to the shifting needs of worldly affairs or be subjected to honors or divisions that the emperor has determined for the execution of his own concerns.

Therefore metropolitan bishops ought to be appointed according to the former arrangement of the provinces. You state that the Cypriots, once harassed by the power of Arian impiety, did not observe the canons of Nicaea in ordaining bishops for themselves and have continued to presume to ordain according to their own discretion, consulting no one.

For this reason we urge them to take care to think in accordance with the Catholic faith of the canons and to share one mind with the other provinces, so that it may be evident that they too, like all the Churches, are governed by the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0713C].

III. As for the Arians and the other destructive groups, whose laypeople converted to the Lord we receive under the appearance of penance and through the laying on of hands for the sanctification of the Holy Spirit: it does not seem that their clerics should be received into the dignity of their fellow priesthood or of any ministry.

We permit only their baptism to be valid—baptism which is performed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. We do not think that they possess the Holy Spirit through that baptism and those rites, because, when the founders of their sects departed from the Catholic faith, they lost the perfection of the Spirit that they had received.

For they cannot bestow the Spirit’s fullness, which operates especially in ordinations; through the treachery of their impiety, or rather, I should say, through their lack of faith, they have lost it. How can we regard as worthy of Christ’s honors the profane priests of those whose laypeople, being imperfect, as I have said, we receive under the appearance of penance in order to obtain the grace of the Holy Spirit?

Therefore let Your Seriousness bring these matters to the attention of your fellow bishops, either through a synod if you can, or by having them read aloud, so that the things about which you yourself so necessarily inquired and to which we have responded so explicitly may be observed by the common agreement and zeal of all.

## To Atticus, Bishop of Beroea, concerning John, the holy Bishop of Constantinople

### Innocent to Atticus

We have judged it a cause for rejoicing to learn from your letters of your Fraternity’s joy over the reception of the clerics and peoples of the bishops Paulinus and Evagrius, and over the restoration of our fellow bishops Helpidius and Papo. We have also seen that, with every contemptuous attitude set aside, you have taken care—although late—to revive the grace of the peace that was received.

For this reason we have sent these letters to your unanimity, to be delivered to the excellent brother and our fellow bishop Alexander. If every hostility and every rivalry concerning both the name of John, the holy and admirable bishop, and all those who share his communion have departed from your mind, receive these letters of our fellowship, dearest brother—provided that before our beloved mediator Alexander, in your own words, you acknowledge as a communicant everything confirmed by these acts [Col. 0714B].

For just as this cause of unanimity and charity is venerable to us, so our concern remains fixed upon it, lest anything distorted or unfinished be found to remain in anyone.

## Letter of Pope Innocent to Laurentius, Bishop of Syme

1. That the Bonosians are to be compared with the Jews.  
2. Concerning the reception of clerics whom Bonosus is known to have ordained before his condemnation.

### Chapter I. Innocent to Laurentius, Bishop of Syme

For a long time we were astonished, after reading Your Dilection’s letters, that the heretics of Photinus, who follow poisonous teachings, are not only present in your territory but publicly prepare meeting places for themselves on the estates of certain persons [Col. 0714C]. In almost the entire world they have chosen nowhere to live in such numbers as among you.

Marcus, the former author of their wicked doctrine, who was long ago expelled from the city, has been driven by such audacity that he claims the first place among them. But so that they may no longer have the opportunity to run wild and drag simple people and country folk with them into the hell to which they are destined, action has been taken against them by defenders of our Church, enabling them to expel them.

They deny that Christ God was begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages. Therefore, together with the Jews, who denied and continue to deny his divinity, they are to share in condemnation.

It is your duty, dearest brother, to carry out without slackness what has been commanded, lest you lose the people entrusted to you through negligence and begin to render an account to God for those who have been lost [Col. 0714D].

II. Innocent to Martianus, Bishop of Naissus

In an earlier period, if I remember correctly, I recall that I sent letters both to Your Dilection and to our fellow bishops Rufus and the others concerning the clerics of Naissus—those who claimed that, before the condemnation of Bonosus, they had been ordained by him as presbyters and deacons. We stated that if, having abandoned and condemned his error, they wished to be joined to the Church, they should be willingly received, lest perhaps those who were worthy of recovering salvation should perish in the same error.

But now, as I am staying in the city of Ravenna because of the many needs of the Roman people [Col. 0715A], Germanus, who claims to be a presbyter, and Lupentinus, who says that he is a deacon, came as though entrusted with an embassy from many such men. They eagerly expressed their personal grievances through repeated petitions, asserting that they retained the churches situated in the parishes of Your Dilection but had been unable to obtain your communion.

The reason, they said, was that a certain Rusticius had received the presbyterate through a second ordination. This has become a serious obstacle, whether because those men grieve that he is retaining a man in the Church, or because he believes that he himself ought to sin against others in the same way that he recognizes sin to have been committed against himself.

Although my letters on this matter, mentioned above, contain a fuller treatment, we have nevertheless now thought it necessary to admonish Your Fraternity as well: if it is truly established that certain men ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation later wished, or now wish, to return, we judge that they must be received [Col. 0715B].

This is especially so because the aforementioned men assert that they were ordained at such an earlier time that Cornelius, the bishop of Syme of holy memory, as well as our brother Nicetas and several others, were present when the honors that they say they hold were increased.

Therefore, dearest brother, if their assertion deserves credence as true, you must not hesitate to receive those whom he permitted for so long to retain the churches entrusted to them.

## Letter of the same Innocent to the bishops of Macedonia

1. If a priest or any member of the clergy marries a widow or a woman who has been dismissed, he is to lose his office [Col. 0715C].  
2. If a catechumen has a wife and, after her death, takes another woman after baptism, he cannot be a cleric.  
3. Clerics ordained by heretics are not to be admitted.  
4. In ordinations, crimes and vices are not rightly believed to be removed.  
5. Those ordained by the heretic Bonosus were received for this reason: so that scandal might not remain in the Church.  
6. In the Church, the sin of the people commonly remains to a great extent.  
7. Something was concealed from the apostolic see, and it changed its judgment for the better when it rescinded the condemnation of Photinus [Col. 0715D].

### Innocent to Rufus and Eusebius, and to the other bishops of Macedonia, and to the deacons: greeting in the Lord
Great joy filled me when, after the dangers of the whole world, so to speak, Vitalis, archdeacon and bearer of your letter, sent from those regions all the way to us, arrived. When we had seen him, we immediately, as was proper, inquired about your condition. But when we learned that you were prospering as desired, we gave abundant thanks to our God, who deigns both to protect his servants, serving at his altars, in adversity and to govern them in prosperity.

After he had delivered the letters, I ordered them to be read immediately. In them I foresaw that many things had been set down which would cause astonishment in our minds [Col. 0716A] and would make us considerably wonder whether we should think otherwise, or whether those matters really had been written as they sounded. When I had them read repeatedly, I perceived that an injury was being done to the apostolic see, to which a report had been sent as to the head of the churches, yet whose judgment was still being held in doubt. Therefore, concerning matters about which I remember having written some time ago, your repeated inquiry now compels me to go over the same ground again, with fuller and clearer explanations.

### I

I have learned that those who are said to have taken widows as wives were not merely made clerics, but even advanced to the insignia of the highest priesthood—something which everyone knows to be contrary to the commands of the law. For when Moses the lawgiver proclaims: “Let the priest take a virgin as his wife,” and, lest anything should be thought ambiguous in this command, he added, “not a widow, nor one who has been divorced” (Ezek. 44:22).

Against this command, supported by divine authority, no defense based on another injunction is offered except your custom, which, as you yourselves confess, was established out of ignorance—to put it more gently—not from apostolic tradition and sound reasoning. But let your affection know that all of us who govern the churches throughout East and West utterly refuse to admit such men, or even to assign them the lowest place in the ecclesiastical order; and, if any are found, we remove them.

### II

Next, it is maintained that a man should not be called a bigamist if, while a catechumen, he had and lost a wife, and afterward acquired another after baptism; rather, the latter is to be regarded as the first wife joined to the new man, because that marriage, having occurred before baptism, was washed away along with the other sins.

But since this is said of one wife, surely if, while still in the old man, he had had three wives, the woman who was fourth after baptism would be his wife. On this interpretation, she who had been taken in the fourth place would likewise be called a virgin. Who, I ask, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command, which says: “A priest must be made the husband of one wife” (Tit. 1:6)?

But it is objected that in baptism everything done in the old man was washed away. Tell me, speaking with your leave: are only sins forgiven in baptism, or also those other things which are accomplished according to the Lord’s commands and God’s institutions? Is taking a wife a sin, or is it not a sin? If it is a sin, then—with the pardon already requested—the one who joined them and blessed them would be responsible for their committing sin in paradise. But if it is not a sin, since what God has joined cannot rightly be called a sin, and Solomon added, “For a wife is prepared for a man by God” (Prov. 19:14), how can anyone believe that what Scripture records as completed by God’s authority was forgiven among sins?

What is to be said about the children of such men? Are they not to be admitted to a share in the inheritance because they were born from a woman who had been his wife before baptism? Are they to be called, then, natural children or bastards, because, as you seem to think, no marriage is legitimate except one contracted after baptism?

When the Lord was asked by the Jews whether it was lawful to divorce a wife (Matt. 19:3), and explained that this should not be done, he added: “Therefore, what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6). And lest anyone think that he was speaking only about those women taken after baptism, let them remember that he was questioned about this by Jews and that his answer was given to Jews.

I ask, and ask anxiously: if the one and same woman is the wife of a man who first received her as a catechumen, afterward became a believer, and had children by her while he was a catechumen, and later had other children while he was a believer, are the children to be called brothers, or are those born first to have no share, after their father’s death, in the division of the inheritance because spiritual rebirth is believed to have taken away from them the name of children?

Since it is absurd to think and judge in this way, what reason is there for defending this evil and proclaiming it with empty opinion rather than supporting it by some authority, when what the law commanded, what God joined, and what the law joined cannot be counted among sins? Suppose a catechumen devoted himself to virtue, pursued humility, maintained patience, gave alms, rescued those condemned to death by whatever means, abhorred adultery, and preserved chastity. I ask whether, after he became a believer, he loses these things because baptism is thought to remove everything done by the old man.

Let us consider the Gentile Cornelius, who through his prayers and almsgiving saw an angel by revelation, and Peter himself. Were these things taken away from him through baptism—the very things because of which baptism appeared to be granted to him? If this is believed, believe me: there is considerable error. Whatever has been done well and preserved according to the commands of the law cannot perish for those who have done it.

Therefore, the union of marriage, because it is completed by God’s command, cannot be called a sin. And if it is not a sin, it must not in any way be dissolved among sins. It follows that the designation of the earlier wife cannot be abolished, since it was not remitted as a sin, having been completed according to God’s will.

### III

We have come to the third question, which because of its difficulty requires a longer discussion. We say that those ordained by heretics have the source of their wound in that laying on of hands. Where a wound has been inflicted, a remedy must be applied through which health can be restored. But the health that follows a wound cannot exist without a scar; and where the remedy of penance is necessary, there the honor of ordination cannot have a place.

For if, as it is written, “Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Num. 19:22), how can what is conferred by such a person customarily receive cleanliness and purity?

But the opposite is asserted: that one who has lost honor cannot give honor, nor has the recipient received anything, because there was nothing in the giver that he could receive. We agree, and it is true: certainly one who did not possess something could not give it. But he did give the condemnation that he possessed through a wrongful laying on of hands; and I cannot discover how one who has become a participant in the condemned man should receive honor.

### IV

It is said, however, that the true and just blessing of a legitimate priest removes every fault that had been introduced by a corrupt person. If that is so, then let sacrilegious men, adulterers, and those guilty of every crime be admitted to orders, since the crimes or faults are thought to be removed by the blessing of ordination. Let there be no place for penance, because ordination can accomplish what prolonged satisfaction ordinarily accomplishes.

But the law of our Church is to grant those coming from heretics—provided that they were baptized there—only lay communion through the laying on of hands, and not to appoint any of them, even to the least clerical office.

### V

But those who passed from the Catholic faith to heresy—whom it is proper to receive only after penance—not only do not perform penance among you, but are even loaded with honor.

The chief deliberation of our former brother Anysius and the other priests was this: those whom Bonosus had ordained should remain ordained, lest they remain with him and a serious scandal arise. We have, I think, overcome the ambiguity. It is therefore clear that what was established as a remedy and necessity of the time did not exist originally, and that there were ancient rules, handed down by the apostles or apostolic men, which the Roman Church preserves and commands to be preserved by those who have judged that it should be obeyed.

But the necessity of the time urgently required this to be done. Therefore, when the necessity has ceased, what necessity discovered as a remedy must also cease, since what was pressing must likewise come to an end. One thing is the legitimate order; another is the usurpation which present circumstances compel.

But the canons established at Nicaea permitted this to be done in the case of the Novatians. The canon first instituted by the Fathers must be set forth, so that we may understand both what was meant by them and how they understood that command:

“Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, the Pure, and who at some time come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great synod that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy.”

We may say that this command concerns only these Novatians and does not apply to clerics of other heresies. For if they had defined this concerning everyone, they would have added that those returning from the Novatians and other heretics should be received into their own order.

If that were so, then what was said especially about the Paulianists could also be confirmed: those coming from them are commanded to be baptized. When they command, in speaking of the Paulianists, that all who return from heretics should be baptized, are all who return from heretics to be baptized on this model? Since no one dares to do this, reason itself shows that the command concerns only the people in question.

Finally, those properly baptized by the evangelist Philip are completed by Peter and John through the laying on of hands alone. But those whom the Apostle Paul found baptized with John’s baptism he asked, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit?” When they replied, “We have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit,” he ordered them to be baptized (Acts 19:2–6).

You therefore see that those who were rightly baptized cannot repeat that gift, whereas those who were washed only with water must necessarily be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Thus it is read with clear demonstration that the command was given only concerning the Novatians.

The evident reason shows why this was distinguished in the case of these two heresies: the Paulianists do not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and no question concerning the unity of divine power—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—has ever arisen among them. Therefore, after all the others had been separated out, this one group alone was selected as the group to which this concession could be granted, because there was no fault in its sacrament of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But if someone who has passed from the Catholic faith to heresy, or who, having been a believer, returns from apostasy and repents, wishes to return, can he be admitted to the clergy by the same reasoning, when his offense can be abolished only through prolonged penance? Do the canons themselves, by their authority, permit him to become a cleric even after penance?

It is therefore clear that those who passed from the Catholic Church to the condemned Bonosus, and endured this—or desired to be ordained by him—ought not to have received the dignity of ecclesiastical ordination. By abandoning the judgment of all the churches in communion with one another, they judged that their spiritual unity should be pursued in Bonosus.

Yet it is clear that many were compelled by force, dragged against their will, and ordained by him while resisting. Let anyone who believes this answer me: if he was not present after Bonosus’s ordination, if he did not participate in his communion, and if he immediately departed from his most wicked assembly and returned to the Church, such a person may have some color of excuse.

But those who returned to the Church after a year or a month—we understand that these were men who knew they could not be admitted to ordination in the Catholic Church because of their vices, and therefore went to one who indiscriminately and without any examination carried out unlawful ordinations, believing that through this arrangement they could obtain a place in the Catholic Church, of which they had previously despaired.

Now, concerning what remains, I ask you to state your judgment more openly: what do you think of the man who returned after a month or more, confident that he had been ordained a presbyter by Bonosus, if he performed no sacraments, distributed none to the people, and celebrated no Masses according to custom?

In short, those who received nothing from Bonosus are guilty of usurping a dignity: they claimed for themselves the authority to perform sacred rites and supposed that what had not been granted to them by any regular procedure belonged to them.

### VI

Let your affection therefore recognize that such matters have proceeded this far, and understand that what necessity—according to your own account—commanded was not to be presumed upon against churches already established in peace. But, as often happens, whenever a people or crowd commits an offense, because punishment cannot be exacted against everyone on account of their number, much is ordinarily allowed to pass.

I therefore say that the earlier matters should be left to God’s judgment, while for the future the greatest vigilance must be exercised.

### VII

I now come to the greatest matter, as though to a kind of foundational theme, and I shall review the judgments of our predecessors concerning what causes me anxiety and difficulty. Concerning that matter, something had previously been established in one way or another, as you yourselves also remember—indeed, something more serious.

But since you assert that this was secretly taken from this see by false rumor and extracted through intrigues, and since the matter has returned to a state favorable to salvation, after the condemnation we now, in the apostolic manner, grant you this concession, insofar as you press for it. We judge that it would be harsher than all other measures not to agree with such strong assertions of yours and with men so good and dear.

Therefore, dearest brothers, in accordance with your approval, judgment, and request, have Bishop Photinus. It is lawful to establish matters as you ask; receive our judgment, changed for the better, as having been brought to fulfillment by our effort or testimony.

Likewise, do not expect Eustachius, whom I have very often approved, to be stripped of the dignity of the diaconate. I gladly hear that you are concerned for his salvation, but I do not gladly admit that anything should be done against his head. To the one to whom you extend your hand, I extend mine with you. To the one to whom I extend mine, extend yours with me.

For this apostolic kindness was declared to the Corinthians: that the good should always follow without distinction a judgment led and restored in one spirit (2 Cor. 4:13).

For, I confess, this matter first commends the deacon Eustachius to me: he has neither said anything against the faith nor admitted anyone who spoke against it, and I have never learned that he committed any crime deserving death, whether one ever alleged or invented.

Since he is sound in these matters, if in some way he does not possess agreeable habits, he should be regarded as one who is less loved for the time being, not as an enemy to be handed over perpetually to the devil.

I know that amid those conflicts and storms he held a different opinion from the efforts of many—I do not say what sort of efforts—and although the matters and calamities themselves have now been corrected, the reform of the subdeacons Dizonianus and Syriacus has still not been able to revive among you.

I ask you to restrain the minds of those who, as you see, are stirred by unjust rivalries against him and the aforesaid men, so that he, remaining whole among us and restored among you together with his associates, may deserve genuine peace and provident charity.

Therefore, let charity come before all of you and before each one individually, and let it rejoice forever in the Lord, bound together with you by those bonds which Christ can never in any way dissolve.

## To the synod established in the city of Toulouse

1. Concerning the reproach of the Spaniards, who irregularly appoint clerics.  
2. That advocates, curials, and those devoted to secular military service are not to be admitted to the clergy.  
3. That whoever has been ordained as such is to be deposed together with his ordainers [Col. 0720D].  
4. Concerning the commemoration of the Council of Nicaea, at which the matters stated above were prohibited.  
5. What sort of men are to be chosen for the clerical order.  
6. That a man who had a wife before baptism and another after baptism is not to become a cleric.

### I

INNOCENTIUS to all the bishops assembled in the synod at Toulouse, his dearest brothers, greetings in the Lord.

While concern about the schisms caused by the dissension of the churches often, and excessively, kept me anxious—for rumor declares that this evil is advancing day by day through the Spanish provinces by way of separation—the necessary time has arisen when such correction can no longer be deferred and suitable medicine must be provided.

For concerning the ordinations which we know the Spanish bishops to celebrate through the fault of a wicked custom [Col. 0721A], something ought to have been established according to the tradition of our predecessors, unless we had considered that we would stir up many disturbances in the churches. We therefore criticize their conduct in such a way that, because of the number of those who must be corrected, we do not call into question what has been done in any manner, but rather leave it to God’s judgment.

### II

How many have we discovered to have been brought into the priesthood from among those who, after receiving the grace of baptism, practiced in the law courts and adopted the stubbornness of litigation! Rufinus and Gregory are said to be among their number.

How many have come from military service—men who, while obeying authorities, necessarily carried out severe commands! How many from the curial class—men who, while obeying the authorities, did what was commanded of them! How many who had entertained the people with amusements and public spectacles have reached the honor of the highest priesthood!

No one among all these ought even to have reached membership in the clerical order. If we ordered each case to be examined individually, we would seem, through our zeal for correction, to be indicating not insignificant disturbances or scandals in the Spanish provinces which we desire to heal. For this reason we think these matters should rather be allowed to pass.

But so that similar things may not be committed in the future, your maturity must take care that at least now a necessary end be imposed on such usurpation, namely, by establishing that whoever has been ordained in this way shall be deposed together with his ordainers.

### III

After this, if anyone attempts to enter either the ecclesiastical order or the priesthood itself against the forms of the canons [Col. 0721C], he shall be deprived, together with his ordainers, of the order and honor in which he is found.

Although the Nicene regulations are known to you, dearest brothers, and although they prescribe how the orders are to be conferred, I nevertheless thought that a portion concerning ordinations should be inserted, so that we may know that ordinations are to be celebrated according to it in the future, and that free discretion to interpret it otherwise may not be left.

Let the prohibited matters first be arranged.

### IV

No one who has served in the army after baptism is to be admitted to the clerical order; nor those who have practiced law after receiving baptism; nor those who, after receiving the grace of God, have administered public affairs [Col. 0721D].

Nor may anyone from the curial class enter the ecclesiastical order if, after baptism, he has been crowned with military honors, held what is called a priesthood, or conducted public spectacles.

For it is also necessary to guard against worldly entanglements, lest those who have been curials should at some time be reclaimed by their own curiae, as we frequently see happen.

All these matters, rationally prohibited, must be guarded against by every possible means.

### V

The clear rule declares what sort of men are to be chosen for the clerical order: those who were baptized from early childhood and joined to the office of lector; or, if they are older, those who, after receiving the grace of God, immediately devoted themselves to the ecclesiastical orders.

And if they have had wives, it must be asked whether they had a virgin as wife, since it is written in the Old Testament: “Let the priest take a virgin as his wife”; and elsewhere: “Let my priests marry only once.”

Nor should men who have had two wives be admitted, because the Apostle Paul says: “The husband of one wife” (Tit. 1:6).

### VI

Nor should the objection be admitted which some raise in defense of their wicked error, asserting that everything is forgiven before baptism. They do not understand that only sins are forgiven in baptism, nor that the number of wives is abolished.

For if, as it is written, “A wife is prepared for a man by God” (Prov. 19:14), and “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6), and if the very founders of the human race were blessed by God at their origin, how can these completed realities be thought capable of being forgiven?

If, according to those who think this way, the claim is true, then all righteousness performed by catechumens before baptism must be taken away through baptism. Let no one therefore think or admit anything of this kind against the apostles, but let him understand faithfully the phrase “the husband of one wife,” whether it is understood of a man before baptism or after baptism.

For if a wife taken before baptism is not counted, then the children born from her ought not to be counted among the children either. Your wisdom will better judge how absurd and alien this is.

Therefore no one may interpret the divine Scriptures otherwise than sound reason permits, lest, while some prepare unlawful remedies for themselves as excuses, they be judged to have broken the law and overturned the regulations. Rather, those things must be held which the sequence of the divine Scriptures contains [Col. 0722C] and which the priests have established with useful reasoning.

Farewell, dearest brothers.

## Letter of the Council of Carthage to Saint Pope Innocent

To the most blessed and most honored lord and brother, Pope Innocent: Aurelius, Numidius, Rusticianus, Fidentius, Evagrius, Antonius, Palatinus Adeodatus, Vincentius, Publianus, Theasius, Tutus, Pannonius, Victor, Restitutus, another Restitutus, Rusticus, Fortunatianus, Ampelius, Avinius, Felix, Donatianus Adeotatus, Octavius, Serotinus, Majorinus, Porturianus, Crispolis, Victor, another Victor, Leutius, Marinus, Fructuosus, Faustinianus, Quodvultdeus, Candorius, Maximus, Magarius, Rusticus, Rufinianus, Proculus, Thomas, Januarius, Octavianus, Praetextatus, Sixtus, Quodvultdeus, Pentadius, Cyprianus, Servilius, Pelagius, Marcellus, Venantius, Dydimus, Saturninus, Bazecenus, Germanianus, Germamenus, Juventius, Majorinus, Juventius, Candidus, Cyprianus, and Emilianus, Romanus, Africanus, and Marcellinus, who were present at the council of the Church of Carthage.

When, according to custom, we had solemnly come to the Church of Carthage and a synod had been assembled from among us for various reasons, our fellow presbyter Orosius gave us a letter from our holy brothers and fellow priests Averothis and Lazarus, the text of which we have decided should be appended here.

After these letters had been read, we all recognized Pelagius and Coelestius as the authors of a wholly wicked error, to be anathematized by everyone. Accordingly, we asked that what had been discussed here at the Church of Carthage five years earlier concerning Coelestius’s name be reread.

When it had been recited—as your holiness will be able to observe from what follows—although it was clear that a judgment had been rendered and that, at that time, this wound appeared to have been cut away from the Church by episcopal judgment, we nevertheless, after common deliberation, judged that the authors of such a persuasion must themselves also be anathematized unless they openly anathematize it, even though the same Coelestius is said afterward to have reached the presbyterate. In this way, if the health of those authors could not be secured, at least the health of those who have been deceived by them or may be deceived by them could be provided once they know the judgment pronounced against them.

We have therefore thought it necessary, lord brother, to inform your holy charity of what has been done, so that the authority of the apostolic see may be added to the decisions of our modest assembly, both for safeguarding the salvation of many and for correcting the perversity of some.

For these men strive by their damnable disputations not to defend free will, but rather to exalt it in sacrilegious pride, leaving no place for the grace of God by which we are Christians. By that grace the very freedom of our will is truly made free, when it is liberated from condemnation to carnal desires, as the Lord says: “If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

Faith obtains this help—the faith that is in Christ Jesus [Col. 0723C] our Lord.

But these men assert—as we have learned from brothers who have read their books—that God’s grace is to be understood as consisting in the fact that he instituted and created human nature in such a way that, through its own will, it can fulfill God’s law, whether that law was written naturally in the heart or given in written form. They also say that the same law belongs to grace because God gave it to human beings as an aid.

But they entirely refuse to recognize the grace by which, as has been said, we are Christians, of which the Apostle is the preacher when he says:

“I delight in the law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:22–25).

They do not dare openly to oppose this teaching. But what else are they doing when, among animal human beings who do not perceive the things of God’s Spirit, they continually try to persuade people that human nature alone is sufficient to carry out and complete righteousness and fulfill God’s commands? They do not attend to what is written: “The Spirit helps our weakness” (Rom. 8:26); and, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of the grace of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16); and, “We are one body in Christ Jesus, individually members of one another” (Rom. 12:5); “Gifts differing according to the grace that has been given to us” (Rom. 12:6); and, “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty; rather, I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10); and, “I give thanks to God, who gave us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 15:57); and, “We are not capable of thinking anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5); and, “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may belong to God and not come from us” (2 Cor. 4:7); together with innumerable other passages from all the Scriptures, which would fill a volume if we wished to collect them.

We are afraid that, by recalling these matters to you, we may seem improperly to be reminding you of a time when you proclaimed greater grace from the apostolic see. But we do so because, in that respect in which each of us is weaker, whoever among us is thought to be more attentive in preaching the word of God everywhere suffers these men to rise against us with greater boldness.

Therefore, if Pelagius has appeared to your veneration to have been justly acquitted on all counts by the episcopal proceedings said to have been conducted in the East, nevertheless the error itself and the impiety—which now have many scattered advocates in different places—must also be anathematized by the authority of the apostolic see.

Let your holiness consider, and share with us in pastoral compassion, how pestilential and destructive to Christ’s sheep is what necessarily follows from their sacrilegious disputations: that we ought not to pray not to enter into temptation, although the Lord admonished his disciples to do so and placed this request in the prayer he taught (Matt. 6:13); nor to pray that our faith may not fail, although he himself testified that he prayed this for the Apostle Peter (Luke 22:32).

For if these matters are placed within the power of the capacity of nature and of the will, who would not see that they are asked of the Lord in vain and prayed for deceitfully, since in prayer we request what the already-created nature possesses through sufficient powers? In that case the Lord Jesus Christ should not have said, “Watch and pray” (Mark 14:38), but only, “Watch, so that you do not enter into temptation.” Nor should he have said to the most blessed Peter, the first of the apostles, “I have prayed for you,” but rather, “I warn you, or command and instruct you, so that your faith may not fail.”

Their contempt also contradicts our blessings, so that we appear to say over the people in vain whatever we ask from the Lord: that they may please him by living rightly and piously, or whatever the Apostle prays for believers when he says:

“I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant us, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit” (Eph. 3:14–16).

If, then, in blessing the people, we wish to say, “Lord, grant him strength to be strengthened through your Spirit,” their disputation contradicts us, asserting that free will is denied if we ask God for what lies within our power. For, they say, if we wish to be strengthened by virtue, we can do so through the capacity of nature—not through the mercy that we now receive, but through that which we received when we were created.

They also deny that infants should be baptized for the salvation given through Christ the Savior, as though by their deadly teaching they were killing them eternally. They promise that even if they are not baptized they will possess eternal life, and that they do not belong among those of whom the Lord says: “For the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Matt. 18:11).

“For,” they say, “they were not lost, and there is nothing in them to be saved or redeemed at so great a price, because nothing in them has been corrupted or is held captive under the power of the devil; nor is it read that blood was shed for them for the remission of sins.”

Although they say that through the baptism of Christ the redemption even of infants takes place, Coelestius himself confessed this in his little book at the Church of Carthage.

But many of those who are said to be or to have been their disciples do not cease, with whatever cunning they can, to affirm these evils by which they attempt to overturn the foundations of the Christian faith. Thus, even if Pelagius and Coelestius have been corrected—or say that they never held these views—and deny that any writings produced against them are theirs, there is no way to convict them of falsehood.

Nevertheless, whoever in general teaches and asserts that human nature is sufficient for overcoming sins and carrying out God’s commands, and who in this way is found to oppose the grace of God, which is made especially evident through the prayers of the saints, and whoever denies that infants are liberated from perdition through the baptism of Christ and receive eternal salvation—let him be anathema.

As for whatever other charges may be brought against them, I do not doubt that your veneration, when it has examined the episcopal proceedings said to have been conducted in the East concerning this same matter, will indicate the judgment by which we may all rejoice in God’s mercy.

Pray for us, most blessed lord pope.

## Reply of Pope Innocent to the Council of Carthage

INNOCENTIUS to Aurelius, to all the holy bishops, and to the others who were present at the council of Carthage, his beloved brothers of the Church, greetings in the Lord.

In investigating these matters—which it is fitting that priests should handle with every care, especially in a true, just, and catholic council—while preserving the precedents of ancient tradition and mindful of ecclesiastical discipline, you strengthen the vigor of our religion no less [Col. 0725D] now in your deliberations than earlier when you pronounced judgment. You approve referring the matter to our decision, knowing what is owed to the Apostolic See (since all of us placed in this position desire to follow the apostle), from whom the episcopate itself and the whole authority of this title have arisen. Following him, we take care both to condemn such evils as must now be condemned and to approve what deserves praise; or rather, you do not judge that what the institutions of the Fathers have guarded with priestly duty should be trampled upon.

Those institutions were established not by human but by divine judgment: whatever was being done, even in provinces separated and remote from one another, was not to be brought to completion before it had come to the knowledge of that See, so that the judgment [Col. 0726A] might be confirmed by the authority of the whole See, as it ought to be. From there the other Churches were to draw, as though from their native spring, waters that proceeded everywhere; and these, flowing through the various regions of the entire world from an uncorrupted source, would determine what must be commanded, whom they must cleanse, and whom the water worthy of clean bodies should avoid, as though they had been soiled in uncleanable mud.

I therefore rejoice, dearest brothers, that you have sent letters to us through our brother and fellow bishop Julius. While you are caring for the Churches over which you preside, you demonstrate your concern for the benefit of all; and you ask that what is beneficial to all the Churches throughout the whole world be decided jointly, so that Churches made steadfast by their own rules may not be able to seek, from that which guards against them, a judgment justly confirmed by decretal decisions. Those men, instructed—or rather destroyed—by perverse subtleties of language, disputing under the appearance of the catholic faith, breathe out a pestilential poison and seek to overturn the entire discipline of true doctrine, corrupting the hearts of right-thinking people toward what is worse. [Col. 0726B]

It must therefore be healed quickly, lest this execrable disease penetrate more deeply into people’s minds. When a physician sees some illness in an earthly body, he considers it a great proof of his skill if, through his prompt intervention, someone who was thought beyond hope escapes; or when he sees a festering wound behind him, he applies poultices and other remedies by which the wound that has arisen may be covered. If, however, it cannot be healed while remaining, lest it infect the rest of the body with its corruption, he cuts away with the knife what was harmful, preserving and leaving untouched whatever remains sound. [Col. 0726C]

What has crept in like a wound upon an otherwise pure and healthy body must therefore be cut away, lest, when it is cleansed too slowly, the drainage of this evil settle afterward in the very inward parts of punishment, from which it cannot be drawn out. For what sound judgment can we afterward form of those minds that think, because they are good, that something is owed to them, and do not consider the One whose grace they receive daily? Indeed, those who are such receive no grace from God, because they trust that, without him, they can attain as much as those who scarcely deserve even what they ask of him and receive.

What could be so unjust, so barbarous, so ignorant of the whole of religion, so hostile to Christian minds as to deny that you owe to him whatever you obtain through daily grace, when you yourself confess that you owe to him the fact that you were born? Will you therefore be more capable, in providing for yourself, than the One who made you exist? [Col. 0726D] And if you think you owe him the fact that you live, how can you not think you owe him the manner in which you live, since you obtain his daily grace? And when you deny that we need divine assistance, as though we were made perfect entirely by our own ability, how do you not call assistance upon us, since we can also be such by ourselves?

For anyone who denies God’s assistance—I should like to ask what he is saying: whether he claims that we do not deserve it, or that God cannot provide it, or that there is nothing for which each person ought to ask for it. God’s ability to do this is attested by the works themselves. We cannot deny that we need daily assistance. Whether we are living well, we invoke it so that we may conquer more excellently and more holily; or whether, thinking wrongly, we are turned away from good things, we need his assistance all the more, so that we may return to the right path. [Col. 0727A]

Could anything appear more deadly, more precipitous toward a fall, more exposed to every danger than this: if, thinking that what we received when we were born—the freedom of the will—can alone suffice for us, we should seek nothing further from the Lord? That is, forgetting our Creator, we should deny his power in order to display ourselves as free, as though he no longer had anything he could give—he who made you free at your birth. We do not know that, unless grace is summoned and descends upon us through great prayers, we cannot in any way attempt to overcome the errors of earthly defilement and the worldly body, since it is not free choice but God’s assistance alone that can make us equal to resisting them. [Col. 0727B]

For if he cries out that he needs divine assistance, though he would not seek it worthily—if free choice were more beneficial to anyone—indeed, though he is a blessed man already chosen by the Lord and has done nothing, nevertheless he thus entreats the Lord:

“Be my helper; do not abandon me, nor despise me, O God my Savior” (Psalm 26:9).

We claim free choice for ourselves; he asks the Lord as his helper. We say that what we were born with can suffice for us; he implores God not to abandon him. Do we not, I ask, plainly say that we should pray, when that supremely blessed man, as we said above, longs not to be despised? Those who affirm the former must necessarily be refuted by the latter. David should be accused of ignorance of prayer and of his own nature if, although he knows that the Lord is his helper within his nature and an unfailing helper, even that unfailing help is not enough for him, but he immediately longs in prayers that the Lord never despise him. [Col. 0727C] Throughout the whole body of the Psalter he proclaims and cries out for this.

If David knew this to be so great that he said it continually, and confessed it to be so necessary that he taught it, how can Pelagius and Coelestius, setting aside every response found in the Psalms and rejecting such teaching, trust that they can persuade anyone that we neither ought to seek nor need God’s assistance, when all the saints testify that they can do nothing without it?

For long ago that perverse man, through free choice, while using his goods without due thought, fell into the depths of transgression and, submerged there, found no way by which he could rise afterward. Deceived by his freedom forever, he would have remained crushed beneath the ruin of this fall unless Christ’s coming had raised him up through his grace. Through the cleansing of the new birth, Christ washed away every former fault by the laver of baptism; and, strengthening his condition so that he might proceed more rightly and securely, he nevertheless did not deny him his grace for the future. [Col. 0727D]

For whoever redeemed a human being from his former sins, knowing [179] that he could sin again, preserved many remedies for his restoration, so that he might correct him even afterward. He provides those daily remedies; unless we rely and trust upon them, we shall in no way be able to conquer human errors. For it is necessary that, by the help of the One through whom we conquered, we should again be conquered if he does not assist us. [Col. 0728A]

I could say more, were it not clear that you have said everything. Therefore, anyone who appears to agree with the opinion that we do not need divine assistance declares himself an enemy of the catholic faith and ungrateful for God’s benefit. Nor are such people worthy of our communion, which they have polluted by preaching in this way. Following these teachings of their own accord, they have fled farther from true religion.

Since the whole of our profession consists in this, and since in our daily prayers we do nothing except seek how we may obtain God’s mercy, how can we endure such boasts? What error so blinds their hearts, I ask, that, if they themselves feel no grace from God because they are neither worthy nor deserving of it, they do not consider that divine grace is bestowed daily upon each of the others? [Col. 0728B]

All such people are worthy of blindness, since they have not even left themselves the belief that they can be called away from their errors by divine assistance. By denying God’s help, they have taken it away entirely not from others but from themselves. They must therefore be removed farther away and kept far from the inward parts of the Church, lest an incurable error, after occupying many people for too long, grow stronger.

For if they remain for a long time under this impunity, they must lead many minds into their perversity and deceive the innocent—or rather, the uninstructed—who do not follow the catholic faith. They would think those people right-thinking whom they still see remaining in the Church. Let the incurable wound therefore be separated from the healthy body; once the breath of the raging disease has been removed, let what is sound remain more cautiously preserved, and let the purer flock be cleansed from the contagion of this evil herd. [Col. 0728C]

Let the perfection of the whole body remain unimpaired. We have learned that you follow and maintain it in this judgment against them, and together with you we preserve it with equal agreement. If, however, they should ever call upon the assistance of God within themselves—the assistance they have denied until now—and recognize that his work is needed as their help, so that they may be freed from this stain into which they fell by the crookedness of their hearts; if, as though dragged into the light from foul darkness, they remove and reject all the things by which their entire vision was defiled and darkened so that it could not see the truth; if they condemn what they have held until now, and, at last applying their minds to sound arguments, are corrected to some degree from this stain, let them entrust and submit themselves to true counsels for healing.

If they do this, it will lie within the power of the bishops to assist them to some extent and to provide a certain care for such wounds—a care that the Church ordinarily does not deny to those who have fallen when they repent—so that they may be brought back from their precipices within the Lord’s fold. Otherwise, remaining outside and excluded from the faith’s present and so great protection, they will be exposed to every danger, to be devoured and tormented by the teeth of wolves, against which they cannot resist by the perverse teaching with which they have provoked them upon themselves. [Col. 0728D]

Your admonitions, together with the sufficiently abundant examples of our law, have therefore provided an adequate answer. We say that nothing remains for us to say, since it is clear that you omitted nothing and suppressed nothing by which those men have been refuted and shown to be thoroughly convicted. For this reason we set forth no testimonies ourselves: the full report is already filled with them, and it is sufficiently clear [Col. 0729A] that you, most learned priests, have said everything. Nor is it fitting to believe that you omitted anything capable of settling the case.

And in another hand:

Fare well, brothers.

## Letter of the Council of Milevis to Pope Innocent

To the most blessed lord, deservedly venerable and honored in Christ, Pope Innocent: Silvanus the elder, Valentinus, Aurelius, Donatus, Restitutus, Lucianus, Alippius, Augustine, Placentius, Severus, Fortunatus, Possidius, Novatus, Secundus, Maurentius Leo, Faustinianus, Cresconius, Lucius, Honorius, Adeodatus, Processus, Secundus, Felix, Asiaticus, Rufinus, Faustinus, Malchus, Lictorius, Fortunatus, Donatus, Pontianus, Saturnius, Cresconius, Lucius, Honorius, Servius, Therentius, Cresconius, Sperantius, Quadratus, Lucillus, Sabinus, likewise Sabinus, Cresconius, Victor, Honoratus, Donatus, Petrus, Praesidius, Cresconius, Lampadius, and Delphinus, from the Council of Milevis, send greetings in the Lord. [Col. 0729B]

Because the Lord has granted you, as a special gift of his grace, to be such a man in the Apostolic See in our own times that it would bring guilt upon us through negligence if we remained silent before your veneration about what ought to be proposed for the Church—rather than that you should receive it with either disdain or negligence—we ask that you deign to apply pastoral diligence to the great dangers threatening Christ’s weakened members.

For a new and exceedingly pernicious heresy is attempting to rise: enemies of Christ’s grace are trying, through impious arguments, to take away from us even the Lord’s Prayer. For although the Lord taught:

“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12),

these people say that a human being in this life, once he has learned God’s commandments, can attain such perfection of righteousness without the help of the Savior’s grace, through free choice alone, that it is not even necessary to say, “Forgive us our debts.” [Col. 0729C]

As for what follows, “Do not bring us into temptation” (ibid., 13), they say that it should not be understood as though we ought to ask for divine assistance lest, when tempted, we fall into sin. Rather, they say that this lies within our own power and that human will alone suffices to fulfill it—as though the Apostle had said in vain:

“It depends not on human willing or running, but on God’s mercy” (Romans 9:16);

and:

“God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13). [Col. 0729D]

For the Lord would then have said in vain to the apostle Peter:

“I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32),

and to all his disciples:

“Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Mark 14:38).

If all this lies within human power, they also contend, in a thoroughly unchristian presumption, that infants and little children, if they receive none of the sacraments of Christian grace, will nevertheless possess eternal life. Thus they nullify what the Apostle says:

“Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12; source: 5:2);

and elsewhere:

“As all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:22). [Col. 0730A]

To omit the many other things they argue against the holy Scriptures, let us for the moment mention these two matters by which they are attempting entirely to overturn all that makes us Christians. What faithful hearts could endure the claim that we should not ask God to be our helper against the evil of sin and in the performance of righteousness, and that the sacrament of Christian grace does not assist little children in attaining eternal life?

In making these matters known to your apostolic heart, we do not need to say much or to enlarge upon such great impiety. Without doubt these things will move you, so that you cannot altogether refrain from correcting them, lest they spread more widely and contaminate—or rather destroy—many, while under Christ’s name they estrange them completely from Christ’s grace. [Col. 0730B]

Pelagius and Coelestius are said to be the authors of this most pernicious error. We would rather have them healed within the Church than cut off from the Church as people whose salvation was hopeless, if any necessity should compel that course. One of them, namely Coelestius, is said even to have attained the presbyterate in Asia. Your holiness will be better informed by the Church of Carthage about what happened concerning him a few years ago.

As for Pelagius, letters sent by some of our brothers report that, while established at Jerusalem, he is said to be deceiving certain people. Nevertheless, many more who have been able to investigate his views more carefully are contending against him on behalf of Christ’s grace and the truth of the catholic faith, especially your holy son, our brother and fellow presbyter Jerome.

We believe, however, that, with the mercy of our Lord God Jesus Christ assisting—the mercy that deigns to direct you when you deliberate and to hear you when you pray—those who hold such perverse and pernicious opinions will more readily yield to the authority of your holiness, drawn from the clear light of the Scriptures, so that we may rejoice over their correction rather than grieve over their destruction, most blessed lord. [Col. 0730C]

Even if they themselves choose certain others—or very many others whom they can entangle in their snares if they are ignored—your venerability sees that action must be taken urgently and swiftly.

We have sent this letter to your holiness from the Council of Numidia, following the example of the Church of Carthage and our fellow bishops of the province of Carthage. We have learned that they have written to the Apostolic See, which you, blessed one, illuminate, concerning this matter.

And in another hand:

May you increase in the grace of the Lord, mindful of us, most blessed lord, deservedly venerable and honored in Christ, most holy pope. [Col. 0730D]

## Rescript of Pope Innocent to the Council of Milevis

Innocent sends greetings in the Lord to the elder Silvanus, Valentinus, and the other most beloved brothers who took part in the synod of Milevis.

Among the other concerns of the Roman Church and the occupations of the Apostolic See, through which we handle the consultations of various people concerning the faith with measured discussion, our brother and fellow bishop Julius unexpectedly placed before me your letters of affection, which you sent from the Council of Milevis with our authority and with a particularly earnest concern for the faith. He appended to them, moreover, writings of similar complaints from the synod of Carthage. [Col. 0731A]

Certainly the Church rejoices that pastors show such concern for the flocks entrusted to them that they not only do not allow any of them to go astray, but, if some have been led astray by the grass of a sheep’s shameful delight and persist in error, either wish them to be entirely separated or, when they avoid what they formerly sought unlawfully, wish to protect them with the vigilance of their former custody. In either case they are providing for the Church: lest, by receiving such people, the rest be led into error by a similar example, or, by despising those who return, they appear to have served them up to the bites of wolves.

This is a very prudent and thoroughly catholic intention in seeking advice. For who could tolerate someone who is in error, or refuse to receive someone who is correcting himself? For just as I consider it harsh to show connivance toward sinners, so I judge it impious to deny a hand to those who have converted. [Col. 0731B]

You therefore consult carefully and appropriately the mysteries of apostolic honor—that honor, I mean, which, beyond the matters external to it, retains concern for all the Churches regarding anxious questions and the judgment that must be maintained. You have followed the form of the ancient rule, which you know has always been observed throughout the whole world together with me. But I shall pass over these matters, since I do not believe that they are hidden from your prudence. You confirmed them also by your action, knowing that answers always flow from the Apostolic source to those who seek them throughout all the provinces.

Especially whenever the faith is impaired, I think that all our brothers and fellow bishops ought to refer the matter only to Peter—that is, to the author of their name and honor—just as your affection has now referred what may benefit all the Churches throughout the whole world in common. [Col. 0731C]

For they must become more cautious when they see the inventors of evils separated from ecclesiastical communion by the decision of our statutes, in response to the report of two synods. Your charity will therefore gain a double benefit: you will possess the grace of the canons that have been preserved, and through your good service the whole world will be protected.

For who among catholics would wish to continue sharing speech with the adversaries of Christ? Who would not flee the authors of this new heresy, who would even share with them the light of life through communion? What more bitter thing could they have fabricated against the Lord than to put an end to divine assistance and remove the basis of daily prayer? This is to say: “Why do I need God?”

David rightly sings a hymn against them: [Col. 0731D]

“Behold, people who did not set God as their helper” (Psalm 51:9).

By denying God’s help, they say that a human being can suffice for himself and does not need divine grace. Deprived of that grace, he must necessarily perish, caught in the devil’s snares, while he struggles by freedom alone to fulfill all the commandments of life.

O perverse doctrine of most depraved minds! Let them at last notice that this freedom deceived the first human being in such a way that, while using its reins [180] too indulgently, he fell into the presumption of transgression. He could not be rescued from this except when the coming of Christ the Lord restored the condition of his original freedom through the providence of regeneration.

Let them hear David saying:

“Our help is in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 123:8);

and:

“You are my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, O God my Savior” (Psalm 26:9). [Col. 0732A]

He would have said these things in vain if what he plaintively asked from the Lord had depended solely upon his own will.

Since these things are so, and since throughout all the divine pages we read that God’s assistance must be joined to free will, and that free will can do nothing when deprived of heavenly support, how can you persistently defend this ability as belonging to free will alone, as you claim? You thereby cause injury not merely to yourselves but, more importantly, to the common grief.
