For Pelagius and Coelestius persuade many people of this. We could use many and varied examples to teach such a lesson, if we did not know that your holiness fully knows, understands, and has mastered all the Scriptures, especially the divine writings. Your report is so filled with such great and weighty testimonies that the present doctrine can be overturned by these alone. You recognize that no further work is needed, since you have presented the passages that will readily occur to you; they neither dare nor are able to oppose them. [Col. 0732B]

They therefore attempt to take away God’s grace, which we must seek even with the freedom established in our original condition. For we cannot otherwise avoid the devil’s devices except with that same grace helping us.

As for what your fraternity says they preach—that little children can be granted the rewards of eternal life without the grace of baptism—it is utterly foolish:

“Unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, they will not have life in themselves” (John 6:54).

Those who defend life in children without regeneration seem to me to want to abolish baptism itself, since they preach that these children possess, without baptism, the grace which they believe is conferred upon them only through baptism. If they maintain that not being reborn causes no harm, they must necessarily admit that the sacred waters of regeneration are of no benefit. [Col. 0732C]

But so that the perverse doctrine of superfluous people may be distinguished quickly by the method of truth, the Lord proclaims in the Gospel:

“Let the little children come, and do not prevent them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Mark 10:14).

Therefore, by the authority of apostolic vigor, we judge that Pelagius and Coelestius—that is, the inventors of new expressions, which, as the Apostle said, produce no edification but rather endless questions (1 Timothy 1:4)—are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion until they repent of the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will. In the meantime, they are not to be received into the Lord’s fold until they wish to abandon the path of perversity that they have followed. [Col. 0732D]

Those who disturb you must be cut off, for they wish to destroy the Gospel of Christ. At the same time, we decree that all who similarly attempt to defend matters belonging to this error are to be bound by an equal punishment.

“For not only those who do such things, but also those who approve of those who do them, are worthy of death” (Romans 1:32),

because I think there is little difference between the intention of the person who commits an act and the favor of the person who consents to it. I add something further: someone who has no one consenting to him often unlearns his error.

Let this judgment therefore remain fixed, dearest brothers. Let such people be absent from the courts of the Lord and, at least, deprived of pastoral custody, lest the dreadful contagion of two sheep perhaps spread through the unwary multitude, and lest a ravenous wolf rejoice in heart within the Lord’s fold. For, while such a wound is overlooked by the guardians among the many flocks spread throughout it, the wound of two is being maintained. [Col. 0733A]

We must therefore take care lest, by permitting the wolf, we appear more like hirelings than shepherds. We command this because Christ our Lord has declared with his own voice that he does not desire merely the death of the dying, but that he should return and live. Thus, if they ever recover their sound mind from the error of their perverse doctrine, and condemn the things by which they have condemned themselves through their own transgression, the Church must not deny them the usual medicine—that is, its own refuge—lest, while we perhaps prevent their return, they remain outside the fold and, waiting there, be swallowed by the jaws of the swift enemy, against which they have armed themselves with the darts of evil argument.

Fare well, brothers.

Issued on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Honorius and Constantius. [Col. 0733B]

## Also, a private letter of five bishops to Pope Innocent

To the most blessed and deservedly most honored lord and brother, Pope Innocent: Aurelius, Alippius, Augustine, Enodius, and Possidius send greetings in the Lord.

We have sent to your holiness letters signed by a considerable number of bishops from the two councils of the province of Carthage and of Numidia, against the enemies of Christ’s grace who trust in their own strength and, in a certain sense, say to our Creator:

“You created us human beings; we made ourselves righteous.”

They say that human nature is free for this reason: so that they need not seek a liberator; and sound for this reason: so that they may judge the Savior superfluous. For they say that it is so powerful that, through free choice, with nothing further assisting from the grace of the One who created them, they can, by the strength once received at the beginning of their creation, subdue and extinguish every desire and overcome every temptation. [Col. 0733C]

Many of them rise up against us and say to our soul:

“There is no salvation for him in his God” (Psalm 3:3).

But the family of Christ says:

“When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10),

and to it its Lord says:

“I am your salvation” (Psalm 34:3).

With hearts suspended in fear and trembling, this family awaits God’s assistance also through the charity of your veneration.

We have heard that in the city of Rome, where he lived for a long time, there are certain people who favor him for various reasons. Some—namely, those who are reported to have persuaded us of such things—favor him; but many more do not believe that he holds such opinions, especially because, since he lives in the East, one must suppose that ecclesiastical proceedings have taken place there—unless he is thought to have been cleared by those proceedings. In that case, if certain bishops declared him catholic, one must believe that this happened for no other reason than that he said he confessed God’s grace and did not deny that a human being could, by his own labor and will, live righteously in such a way as to be assisted by God’s grace for this purpose. [Col. 0733D]

When they heard these words, catholic bishops could understand no other grace than the grace which they were accustomed to read in God’s books and preach to God’s peoples—the grace of which the Apostle says:

“I do not nullify the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21).

Without doubt this is the grace by which we are justified from iniquity and saved from weakness, not the grace by which we were created with our own will. [Col. 0734A]

For if those bishops had understood that he meant the grace which we share even with the impious, with whom we are human beings, while denying the grace by which we are Christians and children of God, who among the catholic priests, I do not say would have patiently listened to him, but would have tolerated seeing him before his eyes?

Therefore the judges are not to be blamed. By ecclesiastical custom they heard the word “grace,” without knowing what such people habitually spread either in the books of their doctrine or into the ears of their followers.

The matter does not concern Pelagius alone, because perhaps he has been corrected—would that it were so—but everything is already everywhere full of very many people who argue noisily, drawing weak and uninstructed souls along with them as though joined to them, while exhausting through their very contention those who are firm and steadfast in the faith. [Col. 0734B]

Either he must be summoned to Rome by your veneration and carefully questioned about what grace he means, so that he may confess—if indeed he now confesses it—that human beings are helped by grace not to sin but to live justly; or this very matter must be dealt with through letters. When he is found to mean the grace taught by ecclesiastical and apostolic truth, he must then be absolved without any scruple on the part of the Church and without any hiding place of ambiguity. Then we should truly rejoice at his purification.

For whether he says that grace is free choice, or that grace is the forgiveness of sins, or that grace is the commandment of the law, he says none of the things that pertain, through the ministry of the Holy Spirit, to overcoming desire and temptations—the Spirit whom he poured out most richly upon us—he who ascended into heaven, took captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings (Ephesians 4:8). [Col. 0734C]

For this reason we pray that we may be able to overcome the temptation of sins, so that the Spirit of God, from whom we have received the pledge, may help our weakness.

But when someone prays and says:

“Do not bring us into temptation” (Luke 11:4; source: 2:4),

he is certainly not praying to remain what he was born to be. Nor is he praying for the free choice which he already received when nature itself was created. Nor is he praying for the forgiveness of sins, since that is said earlier:

“Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12; source: 8:12).

Nor is he praying to receive a commandment; rather, he is plainly praying to fulfill the commandment. For if he is brought into temptation—that is, if he fails in temptation—he commits the sin that is contrary to the commandment. [Col. 0734D]

He therefore prays not to sin, that is, not to do anything evil. This is what the Apostle prays for the Corinthians when he says:

“We pray to the Lord that you may do nothing evil” (2 Corinthians 13:7; source: 13:6).

It is therefore sufficiently clear that, although free choice of the will undoubtedly exists, its power is not sufficient for refraining from sin—that is, for not doing evil—unless weakness is helped.

That prayer itself is therefore the clearest testimony to this grace. He confesses this grace, and we shall rejoice over him whether he is upright or corrected.

Law and grace must be distinguished: the law knows how to command; grace knows how to help. The law would not command unless there were a will, nor would grace help if the will were sufficient.

We are commanded to possess understanding, where it says:

“Do not be like a mule or a horse, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9); [Col. 0735A]

and yet we pray to possess understanding, where it says:

“Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Psalm 118:73).

We are commanded to possess wisdom, where it says:

“Fools, become wise at last” (Psalm 93:8);

and yet we pray to possess wisdom, where it says:

“If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him” (James 1:5).

We are commanded to possess continence, where it says:

“When I knew that no one could be continent unless God granted it—and that it was itself wisdom to know whose gift this was—I approached the Lord and entreated him” (Wisdom 8:21).

Finally, to avoid making this too long by going through everything, we are commanded not to do evil, where it says:

“Turn away from evil” (Psalm 36:27); [Col. 0735B]

and yet we pray not to do evil, where it says:

“We pray to the Lord that you may do nothing evil” (2 Corinthians 13:7).

We are commanded to do good, where it says:

“Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27);

and yet we pray to do good, where it says:

“We do not cease praying and asking for you,”

and among the things he prays for them he says:

“that you may walk worthily of God in every way pleasing to him, in every good work and word” (Colossians 1:9–10).

Thus, just as we recognize the will when these things are commanded, so let him also recognize grace when they are requested.

We sent to Your Reverence the book which the devout and honorable young servants of God gave us. We do not suppress their names, for they are called Thimasius and Jacobus [Col. 0735C]. As we hear—and as you also know—they abandoned the hope they had in the world at Pelagius’s exhortation and now serve God in continence. When, through some work of ours, with the Lord’s inspiration, they had at some point been freed from that same error, they brought forward the book, saying that it was Pelagius’s, and earnestly begged that a reply be made to it. When that reply was written to them, they sent back a letter giving thanks; we have sent both documents: the one to which the reply was made and the reply itself.

And, so that we might not be excessively burdensome, we marked those places where we ask that you not hesitate to examine how, when confronted with the question of whether he denied God’s grace, he answered in such a way that he said it was nothing other than the nature in which God created us [Col. 0735D]. But if he denies that this is his book, or maintains that these passages are not in his book, let him anathematize that teaching and confess as entirely appropriate the grace which Christian doctrine demonstrates and proclaims to be proper to Christians: it is not nature, but that by which one is saved. This grace does not nourish us by doctrine sounding in the ears or by some visible assistance, as something is, so to speak, planted and watered from outside, but by the ministry of the Spirit and by hidden mercy, as does the one “who gives the growth, God” (I Cor. III, 7).

For if, in a manner that should not be rejected, the grace of God by which we were created is said to be that by which we exist at all—so that we are not something else, such as a corpse that does not live, a tree that does not feel, or an animal that does not understand, but human beings, who exist, live, feel, and understand, and are able to give thanks to our Creator for this one great benefit—then this too can rightly be called grace, because it was given not on account of the merits of any preceding works, but by the free goodness of God. Nevertheless, there is another grace by which we are called according to predestination, justified, and glorified, so that we may say: “If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 31–32). It was concerning this grace that the controversy arose when those whom Pelagius gravely offended and disturbed said to him that he was attacking it in his arguments, by which he asserted that human nature, through free will, was sufficient not only for doing but also for accomplishing the divine commandments [Col. 0736B].

Apostolic teaching rightly calls this grace by which we are saved and justified through faith in Christ by this name. Of it it is written: “I do not nullify the grace of God; for if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. II, 21). Of it it is written: “You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the law; you have fallen away from grace” (Gal. V, 4). Of it it is written: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (Rom. II, 6). Of it it is written: “But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness; but to the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace, but according to debt” (Rom. IV, 4–5). There are many other passages which you can better remember, understand more wisely, and proclaim more clearly.

As for that grace by which we were created human beings—even though we understand that it can rightly be called grace—it is nevertheless astonishing if we read it called by this name in any legitimate prophetic, Gospel, or apostolic writings. When, therefore, this final question concerning this grace was put to him by Christian and Catholic believers, so that he might cease attacking it, what is one to make of the fact that, when he himself had raised this objection in his book, as though speaking in the person of an opponent, in order to clear himself by answering, he replied with nothing other than that the nature of the created human being reflects the Creator’s grace [Col. 0736D]? He said that justice could be fulfilled without sin through free will with the help of divine grace because God had given this to humanity in the very possibility of nature.

He is rightly answered: “Then the offense of the cross has been abolished” (Gal. V, 11); then “Christ died for nothing” (Gal. II, 21). For if Christ had not died because of our sins and risen because of our justification (Rom. IV, 25), and if he had not “ascended on high and taken captivity captive and given gifts to human beings” (Eph. IV, 8), would this possibility of nature which he defends not have existed among human beings? Or perhaps God’s commandment was lacking—and therefore Christ died? On the contrary, this too was already holy, just, and good. It had already been said: “You shall not covet” (Exod. XX, 17); it had already been said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XIX, 19). The Apostle says that the whole law is fulfilled in this saying (Gal. V, 14), and since no one loves himself unless he loves God, the Lord therefore said that in these two commandments the whole law and the prophets are fulfilled (Matt. XXII, 40).

These two commandments had already been divinely given to human beings; but the eternal reward of righteousness had not yet been promised. He himself does not say this—although in his writings he might even be able to maintain that the kingdom of heaven had been promised in the Old Testament. If, then, the possibility of nature through free will already existed for doing and accomplishing righteousness, the holy, just, and good commandment of God’s law already existed, and the eternal reward had already been promised—then Christ died for nothing (Gal. II, 21). Therefore righteousness comes neither through the law nor through the possibility of nature, but through faith and the gift of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, the one mediator between God and human beings (I Tim. II, 5).

For since “through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12), undoubtedly no one has been or is freed from this body of death, where “another law wars against the law of the mind” (Rom. VII, 23), by the possibility of his own nature. That nature has been lost and needs a Redeemer; it has been wounded and needs a Savior. It is the grace of God, through faith in the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ, that frees us—he who, although he was God, made himself human, and, remaining God, having become human, himself remade what he had made [Col. 0737C].

I think it is not unknown to you that the faith of Christ, which later came into revelation, existed in hidden fashion in the times of our fathers. Through it, nevertheless, even those were freed by the grace of God who, throughout all the ages of the human race, were able to be freed by God’s hidden, though not blameworthy, judgment. Hence the Apostle says: “Having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: ‘I believed, therefore I spoke,’ we also believe, and therefore we speak” (II Cor. IV, 13). Hence the Mediator himself says: “Abraham longed to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII, 56). Hence, when the sacrament of Melchizedek was brought forth, he knew it to prefigure the eternal priesthood of the Lord’s table.

But when the law was given in writing—the law which the Apostle says entered in “so that the offense might abound” (Rom. V, 20), and concerning which he says: “If the inheritance is from the law, it is no longer from the promise; but God granted it to Abraham through the promise”—what, then, is the law? “It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one. Is the law therefore against the promises of God? Certainly not. For if a law had been given which could justify, righteousness would truly be from the law. But Scripture shut everything under sin, saying that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. III, 18–22).

Does it not clearly show that the law was given so that sin might be recognized and increased through transgression? For where there is no law, there is no transgression; thus, against the victory of sin, one would flee to the divine grace contained in the promises. The law, therefore, was not against the promises of God, because through it comes the knowledge of sin, and through transgression of the law the abundance of sin, so that the promises of God—which is the grace of God—might be sought for liberation, and righteousness might begin to exist in a human being, not his own righteousness, but God’s: that is, righteousness given as a gift by God.

Even now, as once was said concerning the Jews, it is said: “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X, 3). Through the law they too suppose that they are justified, since free will is sufficient for them to keep it—that is, they put forward a righteousness arising from human nature, not one bestowed by divine grace; for this reason it is called God’s righteousness. Hence it is written: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin. But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, testified to by the law and the prophets” (Rom. III, 20–21).

When he says “has been manifested,” he shows that it existed then also, but at that time it was hidden, as the rain which Gideon obtained (Judg. VI, 37) was then, as it were, hidden in the fleece, whereas now it is manifest, as it were, on the threshing floor. For without grace the law could not be the death of sin, but rather its power. Thus it was said: “The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law” (I Cor. XV, 56). Just as many now flee from the face of resisting sin to grace, as to a threshing floor now lying open, so then few fled to it, as to a fleece in which it lay hidden.

This distribution of the times refers to the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, concerning which it was said: “How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable his ways” (Rom. XI, 33). Therefore, if before the time of the law and during the time of the law the righteous fathers who lived by faith were justified not by the possibility of weak, unworthy, corrupted, and sin-enslaved nature, but by God’s grace through faith, then now, when that same grace has come into the open and been revealed, it justifies as well.

Let Pelagius, therefore, anathematize his writings in which he argues against this grace—whether through contumacy or through ignorance—by defending the possibility of nature for overcoming sins and fulfilling the commandments. Or, if he denies that those writings are his, or says that they were introduced into his writings or attributed to him by his enemies, let him anathematize and condemn them through the paternal exhortation and authority of Your Holiness [Col. 0738D].

If he wishes to remove from himself a burdensome and destructive scandal, let him learn to remove the scandal of the Church, which his hearers and perverse admirers do not cease spreading everywhere. For if they learn that the same book which they either think or know to be his has been anathematized and condemned by the authority of the Catholic bishops—and especially by that of Your Holiness, which we do not doubt carries the greatest weight with him [Col. 0739A]—we do not think that they will thereafter dare to speak against the grace of God revealed through the passion and resurrection of Christ, or disturb faithful and simply Christian hearts. Rather, with God’s mercy assisting, they will join with us in striving, burning with devotion and charity, and, through your prayers, trust that they may be not only eternally blessed but also just and holy—not in their own strength, but in that same grace.

For this reason we have thought it better to send to Your Beatitude the letter written to him by one man, to whom, through a certain Eastern deacon who is also a citizen of Hippo, he sent some writings as a kind of defense [Col. 0739B]. We judged it better and asked that you yourself deign to send it to him, since he will probably not disdain to read it, paying more attention to the one who sent it than to the one who wrote it.

As for what they say—that a human being can be without sin and easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes—although this seems more tolerable when it is said with the help of God’s grace, which is nevertheless said to have been revealed and given through the incarnation of his Only-Begotten Son, the question can rightly be asked where and when, through that same grace, this is accomplished in us, so that we are entirely without sin: in this life, when the flesh desires against the spirit, or in that life when the saying written in Scripture will be fulfilled: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (I Cor. XV, 55).

For the sting of death is sin. This must be examined more carefully because of certain others who thought wickedly and committed their view to writing: they maintained that even in this life a human being can be without sin—not from the beginning of birth, but by conversion from sins to righteousness and from a wicked way to a good life. For thus they understood what is written concerning Zachariah and Elizabeth: “They walked in all the commandments and ordinances of God without reproach” (Luke I, 6). They understood the phrase “without reproach” as meaning “without sin,” not indeed denying—indeed, piously confessing what is also found in other places in their writings—that the help of the grace of our Lord comes not through the natural spirit of the human being, but through the governing Spirit of God.

They seem not to have considered sufficiently that Zachariah himself was also a priest. “All priests at that time necessarily had to offer sacrifices from the law of God, first for their own sins and then for the people” (Heb. V, 3). Just as now, through the sacrifice of prayer, we are proved not to be without sin, since we have been commanded to say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI, 12), so then, through the sacrifices of animal victims, the priests were proved not to be without sin, since they were commanded to offer sacrifices for their own sins.

If, then, the matter stands as follows—that through the grace of the Savior we make progress in this life, desire diminishing and charity increasing, but are perfected in the life to come, desire being extinguished and charity completed—then the statement “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (I John V, 18) was spoken according to that charity which alone does not sin. For charity belongs to the birth that is from God, as it is increased and perfected; it is not the desire which must be diminished and consumed.

Nevertheless, so long as desire remains in our members, it wars by a law of its own against the law of the mind. But one who is born of God, neither obeying its desires nor presenting his members as weapons of iniquity to sin, can say: “It is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Rom. VII, 17).

But whatever the answer to this question may be—for even if no human being is found to be without sin in this life, it is nevertheless said to be possible through the help of grace and the Spirit of God—one must strive and pray for it to happen. Anyone who is deceived in this matter is tolerably mistaken; it is not diabolical impiety, but human error, to maintain and desire what ought to be pursued, even if one cannot show that what one maintains is possible. For he believes that something can happen which it is certainly praiseworthy to desire.

For us, however, it is enough that no faithful person in the Church of God, however excellent his progress and righteousness, is found who hears that the prayer of the Lord is unnecessary for him—“Forgive us our debts”—and says that he has no sin, lest “he deceive himself, and the truth not be in him” (I John I, 8). Who, then, lives without reproach? For it is not just any human temptations, but grave sin, that falls under reproach.

May Your Sweetness forgive us if perhaps we have sent Your Holiness a longer letter than you wished. We are not pouring our little stream back into your abundant fountain to increase it; rather, although ours is small, it flows from the same source from which your stream also flows abundantly. We wished to make this clear by showing that we are consoled by your replies through our common participation in the one grace.

## Pope Innocent’s Reply concerning Pelagius the Heretic

**INNOCENTIUS to AURELIUS, ALYPIUS, AUGUSTINE, EVODIUS, and POSSIDIUS, bishops.**

We received with great pleasure the letters sent by Your Holy Brotherhood, full of faith and strengthened by the entire vigor of Catholic religion, which you sent to us and to your councils through our brother and fellow bishop Julius. Their whole tenor and composition rest upon a sound consideration of God’s daily grace and upon the correction of those who think otherwise, so that every error may be removed from them and, by providing a suitable example from our law, they may be able to offer a teacher worthy of imitation. But concerning these matters, as I think, we have already said enough above.

Yet continually something comes to their aid and supplies material for reply; and there can never fail to be something that conquers when the matter is so wretched and impious that it is more fully overcome by the power of our faith and by the truth itself. For one who rejects and despises every hope of life, confusing his own heart through a hostile and damnable argument, believes that there is nothing to receive from God, lest anything remain for him to ask for healing. But once he has taken this away from himself, what has he left thereafter?

If, then, there are some whom such great perversity has fixed in self-defense, who give and attach themselves to this doctrine, hoping that what is utterly abhorrent and thoroughly judged contrary belongs to Catholic teaching, they will hasten to return to the right path of life, lest the error, having besieged their minds for too long, invade their senses like a pestilence. For if Pelagius, wherever he opposed them, deceived the minds of those who were inclined to believe easily or simply by this assertion—or if such people are here in the city, something we can neither disclose nor deny because, even if they exist, they remain hidden and do not at any time dare either to defend him preaching these things or to make such claims in the presence of any of us, and because in so great a multitude of people no one can easily be detected or recognized anywhere—or if they live in any part of the world [Col. 0741B], we trust in the mercy and grace of our God that they will easily be corrected when they hear the condemnation of the man who is found to have been stubborn and resistant, and the author of this doctrine. It makes no difference where these people are, provided that wherever they can be found, they may be healed.

Nevertheless, we cannot be persuaded that he has been cleared, although records have been brought to us by certain laymen, by whom he would have believed that he had been heard and acquitted. We doubt whether these things are true, because they did not come to us under the execution of that council, nor have we received any letters concerning this matter from those before whom he gave an account of it. If he could have trusted in his own defense, we believe he would have acted in this way all the more—something that could have been much more genuinely done by compelling through his letters those who had judged him to render judgment.

But since certain matters are contained in the records themselves which he partly suppressed by muttering, partly obscured in total confusion by turning many words back upon himself, partly cleared, as it might seem for the moment, by arguments more false than rational, partly by denial, and partly by twisting them through a false interpretation—would that, which is more desirable, he too might turn from the error of his own path to the true way of the Catholic faith, and desire and wish to be cleared, recognizing God’s daily grace and assistance, so that he might appear truly corrected and be approved by all through manifest reason: not by the judgment of the records, but by his heart turned toward the Catholic faith.

Therefore I can neither approve nor condemn their judgment, since we do not know whether the records are true, or, if they are true, whether it is established that he evaded them rather than fully clearing himself in every respect. If he has confidence and knows that what he says—or all that he has said—is not wholly deserving of indignation, he should not be summoned by us; rather, he himself ought to hasten so that he may be acquitted. For if he still thinks in this way, he will commit himself to our judgment, knowing that he must be condemned regardless of whatever letters are received.

If he were to be summoned, it would be better done by those who are nearer and not separated by a great distance of land. But care will not be lacking if he provides material for a remedy. He can condemn what he had thought and, by sending a letter concerning his error, ask pardon, as is fitting when returning to us, dearest brothers.

We carefully read the book said to be his, which Your Charity sent to us. It contained many blasphemies, nothing pleasing, nothing that did not thoroughly displease—something to be condemned and trampled upon by anyone, and such as no one other than the person who wrote it would take into his mind or hold as an opinion. In this place [Col. 0742B] we did not consider it necessary to discuss the law at greater length, as though Pelagius were present and resisting, since we are speaking with you, who know the entire matter and rejoice with us in an equal agreement. These examples are better set forth when we discuss them with those who are known to be wise in such matters.

For who could rightly finish discussing the possibility of nature, free will, the whole grace of God, and daily grace? Let him, therefore, anathematize the opinions he held, so that those who had collapsed under his words and commands may finally know what true faith possesses. They can be recalled more easily when they hear that these things have been condemned by their own author.

But if he persists stubbornly in this impiety, action must be taken so that help may be given even to those whom not their own error but his error chiefly led astray, lest this remedy also be lost to them—a remedy which he himself neither accepts nor seeks.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.

## A Familiar Letter to Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage

**INNOCENTIUS to AURELIUS, bishop of Carthage.**

True affection is expressed in familiar letters, and the duties of charity deserve greater strength when they are begun well. For this reason I was eager to reply through our brother Julius to the letter sent from abroad, lest perhaps there remain with me the offense of a particular greeting withheld. I therefore return the aforesaid brother to Your Charity, since you have judged him worthy, for the report of the two synods, to be received by the Apostolic See [Col. 0742D].

It remains that, at our prayer, the Lord may deign to grant that every stain of his Church may be wiped away through our continual labors. May the Lord keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.

# THE DECREES OF POPE ZOSIMUS BEGIN

[Col. 0741]

[Col. 0741D]

1. Monks or laymen should not attain the highest priesthood except through the ecclesiastical grades.  
2. If anyone disregards prohibitions, he shall be subject to the penalty of his grade.  
3. What periods of time are prescribed for each of the clerical grades.

**Bishop ZOSIMUS of the city of Rome to HESITIUS, bishop of Salona, greetings.**

Your affection requests an ordinance of the Apostolic See, with which the decrees of the Fathers agree [Col. 0743A], and reports that certain members of the monastic body—whose concern is indeed greater, though the reading is uncertain—and laymen are hastening to the priesthood.

## Chapter I

This matter, in particular, is known to have been prohibited both under our predecessors and recently by us, in letters sent to Gaul and Spain. In those regions this presumption is more common, although Africa too is not exempt from this admonition of ours: no one who had not been instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines in due order and trained in divine service through the testing of time should presume in any way to aspire to the highest priesthood contrary to the commands of the Fathers. Not only should such ambition be considered ineffective, but those who ordained him should also be deprived of the rank which, contrary to the commands of the Fathers, they had presumed to confer without due order.

We are therefore surprised that the statutes of the Apostolic See were not brought to Your Affection. We praise your steadfastness, dearest brother. No other kind of episcopal judgment, in accordance with the authority of ancient tradition, was to be expected from you than that, standing ready in the line of faith, you should confront such ambitions on behalf of the commands of the Fathers.

Therefore, if you think that anything was lacking in your authority—which we do not suppose—we supply it. Resist such ordinations; resist the pride and arrogance that is arising. The commands of the Fathers are with you; the authority of the Apostolic See is with you.

For if secular offices confer the principal place not upon someone who has merely entered the vestibule of public service, but upon one examined through many grades of temporal service, who is so arrogant and shameless as to wish immediately to be a commander in the heavenly army—which must be weighed with greater care and tested like gold through repeated fires—when he has not previously been a recruit, and wishes to teach before he has learned?

Let him become accustomed to the Lord’s camp, first in the rank of lector, in the rudiments of divine service. Let it not seem beneath him to become, in order, an exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon. Let him not make this ascent by a leap, but at the periods established by the ordination of his elders. Finally, let such a man approach the summit of the presbyterate that both his age may fulfill the title and his previously completed service may testify to the merit of his character. From that point he may rightly hope for the place of supreme pontiff.

This is caused by the excessive laxity of our fellow priests, who seek the pomp of a multitude and think that some dignity can be acquired for themselves from this crowd. Hence, everywhere, even in places where there is solitude, a numerous popular presence of such men is found, while they desire to enlarge parishes or confer the sacred orders upon those to whom they can provide nothing else. This ought always to be a matter of strict judgment, for whatever is great is rare [Col. 0743D].

## II

Accordingly, so that we might not detract from the merits of Your Affection, we have sent these writings especially to you, so that they may come to the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow bishops—not only those who are in that province, but also those who are attached to the neighboring provinces of Your Affection.

Anyone who, setting aside the authority of the Fathers and of the Apostolic See, neglects this shall know that we will punish it more strictly, so that he may have no doubt that accountability for his position will remain with him if he thinks that, after so many prohibitions, the attempt can be made with impunity. For whatever is repeatedly usurped after being so often prohibited is done out of a desire to insult.

## III

The following periods of time are to be observed for the individual grades if a person has given his name to ecclesiastical service from childhood and remains continuously among the lectors until his twentieth year of age. If an older and mature man comes forward, who nevertheless desires to be devoted to divine service immediately after baptism, he is to remain either among the lectors or among the exorcists for five years.

After that, he is to serve four years as acolyte or subdeacon, and thus, if he deserves it, he may approach the blessing of the diaconate [Col. 0744B]. If he has conducted himself blamelessly in that order for five years, he must remain in it. Thereafter, with the services rendered through all these grades supporting him and with the proofs of his own faith, he may merit the presbyterate. If, from that position, a life more exacting in good conduct has brought him onward, he should hope for the highest pontificate.

This law must nevertheless be observed: neither a man married twice, nor the husband of a widow, nor one who has performed penance may be admitted to these grades. Furthermore, the defenders of the Church who come from the laity are also to be held to the aforesaid observance if they deserve to belong to the clerical order.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the eighth time.

## A Warning to the Clergy of Ravenna

**ZOSIMUS, bishop of the city of Rome, sends a warning [Col. 0744C] to the presbyters and deacons who are at Ravenna.**

From the report of our brother Archidamus the presbyter, we have learned how you received him and what you did, and how those men were received who, contrary to the canons and against us, wished to go to the imperial court with some unknown audacity and presumption.

We had previously written the matters we now send to you, replying to the letters which they had sent insultingly. But since they could not remain in their own Church—that is, in our Roman Church—with our fellow presbyters, we are sending these letters to you for delivery to them. In them, by our decree, we establish that the aforesaid disturbers have been alienated from the communion of our Apostolic See and have received the sentence approved by our subscription.

As for those who wished to lend their agreement to this unrestrained deed and plan [Col. 0744D], it belongs to Your Charity to judge how they are to be regarded. You must charge them with this: they have forcefully run counter to the commands of the canons, and, by becoming rebellious, attempted what was unbecoming for presbyters.

We warn you, however, that you must remain watchful, and that the audacity of those whom the holy Apostolic Church knows to have been anathematized must not break forth. As for those who joined themselves to their association, when you have returned we shall consider with better counsel what action we ought to take.

And in another hand: Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius.

# THE DECREES OF POPE BONIFACE BEGIN (C)

[Col. 0745]

## Supplicatory Letter to the Emperor Honorius, requesting that the Emperor establish that no pontiff should ever be ordained in the city of Rome through factional ambition

[Col. 0745A]

**183 BONIFACE, bishop, to HONORIUS Augustus.**

The care of my Roman Church—which our God has assigned my priesthood to serve while you govern human affairs—constrains me, even though I am still detained by bodily illness, not to be absent from the causes of that Church when assemblies stirred up by all the priests, clergy, and disturbances of the Christian people are brought before the ears of the most Christian prince.

For if something should happen contrary to what is proper, it will not appear that you have done it—you who settle everything with equitable moderation—but that through our silent negligence we have allowed something capable of overturning the peace of the city and the tranquility of the Church. Since, by God’s command, as a worshiper of divine religion, you preside over human affairs, it will be our fault if what has been preserved through so long a succession of years, even under those emperors who were bound by no concern for our religion, is not maintained under your glory by a firm and stable right. It is certain that your mind has always been more ready to favor divine matters, so that what is lawful may be used with confidence and, under the rule of your clemency, unlawful things may not be feared.

The Church itself, most Christian emperor, calls upon your devotion in this speech, though with its own venerable affection, because Christ our Lord, the faithful ruler and governor of your empire, preserves one bride betrothed to him, an untouched virgin. You must not allow her to be dashed against the waves of any threatening storms, nor allow the calm face of the weather to be disturbed by the swelling of an unusual tempest, most glorious and most tranquil Emperor Augustus [Col. 0745C].

Therefore, that Church which is betrothed to one alone, yet is your mother, calls upon your piety through the embassy it has entrusted to its priests. It recalls the past and the present and says to you: “Under your devout rule, my people, who are now yours, have grown—faithful to God as well as to you, who are the prince of Christ.”

For behold, amid the very mysteries, amid the prayers it pours out for the prosperity of our empire, with the holy Peter as witness before whom and concerning whose see the matter is being conducted, it cries out in anxious words for the observance of religion. While it mingles earnest petition with prayer, it asks that we not be torn away into various affairs from our accustomed worship of God, as the ancient tempter urges discord.

It would say more, most Christian prince, if its causes were not secure with you, and if in the suppression of idols and the correction of heretics your faith had not flourished together with the worship of God and the empire. Your gentleness has become its refuge, joined with reverence for its religion, since whatever benefits this Church is what you do.

Receive this unblemished embassy from my brothers and fellow priests, men approved by me and by all who make up the Church, as they plead the cause of sacred religion in the city of your gentleness. With the same disposition by which you are asked by many, provide for the universal Church to be established perpetually.

Given on the Kalends of June.

## Constitution of the Emperor Honorius Sent to Pope Boniface, Providing That If Two Bishops Are Ordained Again at Rome, Both Are to Be Expelled from the City

[Col. 0746A]

**Victor HONORIUS, illustrious triumphant, ever Augustus, to the holy and venerable BONIFACE, pope of the city of Rome.**

We received the writings of Your Beatitude with the reverent joy that was due. After reading them, we gave the greatest thanks to Almighty God because we learned that Your Holiness, restored as we had wished after a long illness, had returned to health. Therefore, in sacred rescripts addressed to the reverend and venerable men, we attest our joy and ask that your apostolate deign, through daily prayers, to devote its zeal and prayers to our safety and empire [Col. 0746B].

Know, moreover, that we are greatly pleased by this expression of our piety: that Your Holiness is concerned about any disturbance of the Churches or the people. Your Holiness has rightly judged that sufficient provision must be made so that this cannot happen in any way.

Finally, with Your Beatitude proclaiming it, we wish this to come to the knowledge of all the clergy: if anything should happen to your religion—which we do not wish—through human fate, let everyone know that ambition must cease. And if, contrary to law, two men should happen to be ordained through the rashness of rival claimants, neither of them is to become a priest in any respect. Only the man whom divine judgment and the consent of the whole body of clergy choose in a new election from among the clergy is to remain in the Apostolic See.

Therefore this must be observed: all are to preserve a tranquil mind and peaceful dispositions in response to the admonition of our serenity, and no one should attempt anything through seditious conspiracies, since it is certain that the efforts of neither party will benefit them.

## Letter of Pope Boniface to the Bishops of Gaul Concerning Bishop Maximus, Accused of Various Crimes
BONIFACE, bishop, to Patroclus, Remigius, Maximus, Hilary, Severus, Valerius, Julian, Castorius, Leontius, Constantine, John, Montanus, Marinus, Maurice, and the other bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces.

The clerics of the city of Valence approached us, presenting in a petition the crimes which, with the whole province as witness, they assert that Maximus committed. Although the investigation had so often been delegated and a trial repeatedly arranged, he always evaded the judgments, [Col. 0746D] lest, distressed in conscience, he should hasten to appear so that, if innocent, he might be cleared after everything had been examined—as often as we learned the decrees also from the information contained in our own documents. On the contrary, he proved against himself the things that had been alleged; and since there were innumerable charges to refute, the provincial investigation was delegated by my predecessors.

He is also said to have avoided the assembly and to have been entirely unwilling to attend. No one doubts that an innocent man evades judgment in this way just as an innocent man seeks to be acquitted—or whether this is the crafty quibbling of those who think matters must be handled by cunning devices, it will never receive the name of innocence. For whoever thinks that he can evade judgment by delays confesses everything. Yet this man, who is reported to be such, will eventually come forward; and it does him no good to have hidden and evaded judgment so often. Wherever he may flee, his own actions and the crimes he committed pursue him, if the charges brought against him are true.

I ought even now to have delivered a sentence worthy of the acts with which he has been accused in our judgment, since, by repeatedly avoiding the investigation and the judgment, he has thought them worthy of mockery. But lest anyone say that this sentence had been reserved as a public proclamation for one whom we might perhaps judge, and for him who is absent—although he has been sought by us—we preferred, after allowing an interval of time, to defer it.

His accusers further asserted that, the more secure Maximus was regarding their intentions and character, the more he should be condemned for committing such acts, since he had presented himself for the appointed trial only after so long a delay. They accuse him of being wrapped in the darkness [Col. 0747B] of the Manichaeans and belonging to a shameful sect. They produce synodal records as proof of the matter alleged, showing that he had long ago so defiled his mind that no subsequent action could cleanse him; and they bring forward records alleging that, enveloped in every kind of disgraceful offense, he had shown no regard for soundness, but that in his fury and insane recklessness he had gone so far as to be subjected to examination before the tribunals of secular judges—a charge disgraceful even in the case of a lowly person—and that he had been condemned for homicide.

They bitterly complain that such a man, after committing so many and such great offenses, still claims for himself the name of bishop in his hiding places, to the disgrace of his own city, and wishes to defile the holy name by claiming it for himself. Therefore, dearest brothers, since he refused to present himself here to be heard, perhaps so that, once convicted by the clerics accusing him, he could not finally, after being brought before an episcopal court, receive the appropriate sentence of a fitting judgment—even though he had been informed of these matters, and even though the loss of what sort of reputation this name could have for a man who is reported never to have possessed the shame appropriate to a priest, and never to have guarded his office even for a brief time.

We have granted only a delay, and we have decreed that the judgment must be yours within the province. A synod is to be assembled before the first day of November, so that, if he wishes to attend in person, he may answer the charges if he has confidence. If he neglects to attend, he shall gain no postponement of the sentence by his absence. For it is evident that a man confesses his crime when, although a trial has been granted and repeatedly delegated for his purification, he does not make use of the opportunity to clear himself. It makes no difference whether all that has been alleged is proved in a present examination, since even his repeated absence, arranged as it was for his defense, plainly stands as a confession.

We shall send letters throughout all the provinces, so that he cannot plead ignorance as an excuse, and so that he may be compelled to come to the province and present himself there [Col. 0748A] before the appointed court. Whatever your charity decides should be determined in this case, once it has been reported to us, must necessarily be confirmed by our authority, as is fitting.

Given on the day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Monarius II.

## So that no bishop may be ordained in contempt of the metropolitan

BONIFACE, bishop of the city of Rome, to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne: greetings.

It is difficult indeed to give credence to complaints whose purpose assails the priests of the Lord, especially when they allege that those priests have attempted something contrary to the statutes of the Fathers; yet, as the present multitude of complainants asserts, such things occur frequently. For behold, as your charity recognizes, the clerical order and the people subject to the Church of Lucubis have sent us their petitions and tears, as far as can be understood, with great sorrow. They say that our bishop Patroclus, despite their petition, ordained someone unknown in place of the deceased bishop, in a province not his own, having passed over the metropolitan, contrary to the rules of the Fathers. We cannot tolerate this at all, since it is appropriate that we be diligent guardians of the sanctions of the Fathers.

No one, surely, is unaware of the decree of the Council of Nicaea, which commanded—and we shall set down its very words—that throughout each province the metropolitan bishops should each possess their proper jurisdiction, and that no one should have two provinces subject to him. Since it is not permissible to believe otherwise, they judged that this should be observed, with the Holy Spirit suggesting it to them.

Therefore, dearest brother, if matters are as reported, and if the boundary of your province encloses the aforesaid Church, strengthen it by our authority—which indeed you ought willingly to do, out of regard for the wishes and will of those who supplicate you. Go to the same place where such an ordination is said to have been celebrated, fortified by the right of the metropolitan and relying on our instructions. Understand that, according to the rules of the Fathers, we have entrusted to your judgment whatever must be done, so that, once everything has been completed, whatever you determine may become known to the apostolic see through your report; for it is clear that the ordination of the entire province has been committed to it.

Let none of them, therefore, boldly and rashly overstep their boundaries, nor defend in their own districts anything that does not appear to have been granted to them, to the insult of the others. Let the presumption of such men, forestalled by our authority, cease: they extend a finger beyond the limit of their dignity. We say this so that your charity may understand how carefully we observe the commands of the canons: this decree of ours likewise determines that each province must always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of the emperors Honorius XII and Theodosius X.

The decrees of Pope Boniface end.

# The Decrees of Pope Celestine Begin (C)

[Col. 0747]

[Col. 0747D] 1. Concerning Prosper and Hilary, who accuse certain presbyters of Gaul.  
2. A remarkable testimony of praise concerning Saint Augustine, the bishop.  
3. The authority of former bishops of the apostolic see concerning the grace of God against the followers of Pelagius.  
4. That Adam injured all human beings, and that no one can rise by free choice unless the grace of God raises him. [Col. 0748D]  
5. That no one is good by his own powers unless by participation in him who alone is good.  
6. That unless we are continually aided by the grace of God, we cannot avoid the devil’s snares.  
7. That through Christ we make good use of free choice. [Col. 0749A]  
8. That all the merits of the saints are gifts of God.  
9. That every holy thought and movement of a pious will comes from God.  
10. That the grace of God not only forgives sins but also helps to prevent them from being committed and enables the law to be fulfilled—not as Pelagius says, “easily,” as though without the grace of God it could be fulfilled only with greater difficulty.  
11. That, apart from the decrees of the apostolic see, all the prayers of the Church resound with the grace of Christ, by which the human race is restored and led back from eternal condemnation.  
12. That the instituted purification of those being baptized, when unclean spirits are driven out from them by exorcisms and breathings, also bears witness to the grace of God. [Col. 0749B]  
13. That deeper questions are neither to be despised nor asserted absolutely.

To the most beloved brothers Venerius, Marinus, Leontius, Auxonius, Arcadius, Sillucius, and the other bishops of Gaul: Celestine.

The words of apostolic instruction require that we be without offense among Jews and Gentiles; every Christian preserves this with the full strength of his soul. Since this is so, no small danger may await before the Lord one who refuses even to display this toward the faithful. For how could we, who desire that no one perish, be distressed by those things which, according to the authority of Christian teachers, surpass Christian minds? The Lord’s word in the Gospel bears witness to this.

For the Savior himself says that “it is better for the one who causes one of the little ones to stumble to be drowned in the depth of the sea (Matt. 18:6).” Let us therefore ask what punishment already belongs to the man for whom we read that such a penalty is better.

## Chapter I

Our sons Prosper and Hilary, whose concern for our Lord is worthy of praise, * have reported to us that certain presbyters there are permitted—though I do not know why—to promote dissension within the Churches, bringing undisciplined questions before the public and stubbornly preaching doctrines opposed to the truth. Yet we more justly attribute this to your responsibility, since they have the opportunity to dispute above you.

We read, “A disciple is not above his teacher (Matt. 10:24)”; that is, no one ought to claim a doctrine for himself as an insult to his teachers. We also know that these very men were appointed by our God to teach, since, as the Apostle teaches, “the third place” is assigned to them within the Church (1 Cor. 12:28).

What kind of propriety is there when these men speak while their teachers are silent? If this is indeed the case, they have not been their disciples. I fear that silence here may be complicity; I fear that those who allow them to speak in this manner are themselves speaking through them. In such matters silence is not free from suspicion, for truth would intervene if falsehood were displeasing. Rightly, then, the matter concerns us if we favor error by our silence.

Therefore let such men be corrected; let them not have freedom to speak according to their own will. If matters are as reported, let novelty cease attacking antiquity. Let agitation cease disturbing the peace of the Churches. They often attempt to plunge into shipwreck those whom a secure station keeps safe while they stand within the harbor. Secure indeed is the station of all whose footsteps do not move from their firm paths.

The men mentioned above have appealed to the apostolic see, complaining to us of this very disturbance that is troubling them. Dearest brothers, take care that your handling of this matter serves the peace of the Catholic people. Let them know—if they are indeed considered subject to you in the dignity of the presbyterate. Let all who teach wrongly know that it is more fitting for them to learn, ever more and more, than to teach.

For what are you doing in the Churches if they hold the highest authority to preach? Unless perhaps this is prevented by the fact that, without authority and without adequate reasoning, it is not yet established that some of the brethren, recently admitted from the company of laymen into our college, do not know what they ought to claim for themselves. Much has already been said concerning these matters at the time when we gave a written reply in defense of a brother.

Even now, however, we repeat the warning more insistently: such men, who labor throughout the lands to sow something other than what our Agricola commanded, must be forbidden. Nor can we wonder that they now dare to attempt these things against the living, since they also strive to scatter the memory of brothers who have entered into rest.

## II

Augustine, a man of holy memory, whom because of his life and merits we have always held in our communion, and whom not even a rumor of sinister suspicion ever touched; whom we remember to have once possessed such great learning that even among the finest teachers he was always esteemed by my predecessors—concerning him all have rightly held a common opinion, since everywhere he was both loved and honored.

It is therefore necessary to resist such men, whom we see growing in evil; it is a sacrilege to allow religious souls to endure these things. Since they are our members, their affliction must also make us suffer, although the blessedness promised to all who are proved by enduring persecution for righteousness remains for them. The following word declares what the Lord promises them in the future.

This is not merely the cause of those acting in the matter; it is the cause of the universal Church, which is shaken by every novelty. Let us understand that what displeases us also displeases you. We shall be able to prove this only if, once silence has been imposed on the wicked concerning such matters, complaints of this kind cease thereafter.

May the Lord keep you safe and unharmed, dearest brothers.

## III

Because some boast of the Catholic name while remaining in the condemned opinions of heretics, whether through perversity or ignorance, they presume to oppose pious disputation. Although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Coelestius, they nevertheless speak against your teachers as though those teachers had exceeded the necessary measure. They profess that they follow and approve only what the most sacred see of the blessed Apostle has decreed and taught against the enemies of God’s grace through the ministry of its bishops.

It will therefore be necessary to inquire carefully what the rulers of the Roman Church judged concerning the heresy that arose in their time, and what they determined should be believed concerning the grace of God against the most pernicious defenders of free choice. We shall also join to these the judgments of certain African councils, which the apostolic bishops certainly made their own and approved.

Thus, so that those who doubt in any respect may be more fully instructed, we shall set forth in a concise catalogue the constitutions of the holy Fathers. If anyone is not excessively contentious, let him recognize that the connection of all these disputations depends upon the brevity of the authorities set out below, and that no ground for contradiction remains for him if he believes and speaks with Catholics.

## IV

By Adam’s transgression, all human beings lost their natural ability and innocence; and no one can rise by free choice from the depth of that ruin unless the grace of the merciful God raises him. This was pronounced by Innocent of blessed memory, who said in his letter to the Council of Carthage:

“For that free choice, while using its goods too heedlessly, fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression. It found no way by which it could rise from there; and, deceived in its freedom forever, it would have remained overwhelmed and hidden beneath this ruin, unless the coming of Christ had afterward restored it through his grace. Through the cleansing of a new regeneration, he purified every stain of past sin by the washing of his baptism.”

## V

No one is good through himself unless he is granted participation in him “who alone is good (Mark 10:18).” The judgment of the same pontiff, in the same writings, declares this, saying:

“Can we thereafter judge the minds of those people to be right who think that they themselves are responsible for being good, and do not consider him whose grace they receive daily, while they confidently believe that they can attain so much without him?”

## VI

No one, even when renewed by the grace of baptism, is capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and conquering the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily assistance, he receives perseverance in a good manner of life. The teaching of the same bishop confirms this in the same pages, saying:

“For although he redeemed a human being from past sins, yet, knowing that the person could sin again, he preserved many remedies for his restoration, by which he might also correct him afterward, providing him daily remedies. Unless we rely upon and trust in these, we can in no way overcome human errors. For necessarily, by the help of him through whom we conquer, if he does not again assist us, we are conquered.”

[Col. 0751D] VII

No one uses free choice well except through grace. The same teacher proclaims this in a letter sent to the Council of Milevis, saying:

“Consider at last, O perverse doctrine of the most depraved minds, that freedom itself so deceived the first human being that, while using its reins too indulgently, it advanced into the presumption of transgression. Nor could it be rescued from this except when the coming of Christ the Lord, through the providence of regeneration, restored the condition of its former freedom.”

## VIII

All the aspirations, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the grace and praise of God, because no one pleases him from any other source than what he himself has granted. In this judgment the authoritative rule of Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, directs us. Writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says:

“We have reported everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise.”

The African bishops venerated the speech radiant with the light of the most sincere truth with such honor that they wrote back to the same man concerning what you had placed in the letters that you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, saying: “We nevertheless act at God’s prompting,” and so forth.

“We understood this statement in such a way that you had, as if passing swiftly by, cut away with the sword of truth those who exalt human free choice against God’s help. For what have you attributed so much to free choice as this: that you referred everything to the conscience of our humility, and yet faithfully and wisely saw that it was done at God’s prompting? Truly and faithfully you said this, precisely because ‘the will is prepared by the Lord (Prov. 19:21),’ and because he himself touches the hearts of the faithful with paternal inspirations so that they may do something good.

“For ‘as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God (Rom. 8:14).’ Thus we do not feel that our free choice is absent, and yet in every good act of the human will, in each person, we do not doubt that his help is more powerful.”

## IX

God works in human hearts and in free choice itself in such a way that every holy thought, pious counsel, and movement of a good will comes from God, because through him we can do something good, “without whom we can do nothing (John 15:5).”

The same teacher instructed us in this confession when, speaking to the bishops of the whole world about the assistance of divine grace, he said:

“What time, then, intervenes when we do not need his help? In all our acts, cases, thoughts, and movements, we must pray for him as helper and protector. For it is proud for human nature to presume anything for itself, while the Apostle cries: ‘Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this air, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.’ And as he himself says again: ‘Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 7:24, 23).’ And again: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty; but I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me (1 Cor. 15:10).’”

## X

We also embrace as belonging properly to the apostolic see what was established among the decrees of the Council of Carthage—namely, what was defined in its third chapter: that whoever says that the grace of God by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord avails only for the remission of sins that have already been committed, and not also for assistance so that they may not be committed, let him be anathema.

Again, in the fourth chapter it says:

“If anyone says that the grace of God through Jesus Christ assists us in not sinning only because through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to desire and what we ought to avoid, but that through it we are not enabled, once we have recognized what must be done, both to love doing it and to be capable of doing it, let him be anathema.”

For although the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love greatly builds up (1 Cor. 8:1),” it is impious to believe that we have the grace of Christ for what puffs us up but not for what builds us up, since both are gifts of God: knowing what we ought to do and loving it so that we may do it, so that, while love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up.

As it is written concerning God, “He teaches human beings knowledge (Ps. 93:10),” so it is also written, “Love is from God (1 John 4:7).”

Likewise, in the fifth chapter: if anyone says that the grace of justification is given to us for this reason—that we may more easily fulfill by grace what we are commanded to do through free choice—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily, let him be anathema.

The Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do this with greater difficulty,” but said, “Without me you can do nothing (John 15:5).”

## XI

Beyond those inviolable sanctions of the most blessed apostolic see, by which the most devout Fathers, having cast down the arrogance of destructive novelty, taught us to refer to the grace of Christ both the beginnings of a good will, the growth of worthy endeavors, and perseverance in them to the end, let us also consider the sacraments of priestly supplication. Handed down from the apostles, these are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in the common Catholic Church, so that the law of prayer may establish the law of belief.

When the bishops of holy peoples, carrying out the commission entrusted to them, act as advocates for the human race before the divine mercy, the whole Church groaning with them asks and prays that faith be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, once the veil has been removed from the Jews, the light of truth may appear; that heretics may recover their senses through acceptance of the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that the remedy of repentance may be granted to the fallen; and finally that, when catechumens have been led to the sacraments of regeneration, the heavenly court of mercy may be opened to them.

The effects of these things show that they are not requested from the Lord superficially or in vain. For from every one of these groups God deigns to draw many whom he transfers, rescued from the power of darkness, “into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Col. 1:13),” and whom he makes vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. The whole of this is so clearly understood to be the work of God that, when God brings it about, thanksgiving and confession of praise are always rendered for the illumination or correction of such people.

## XII

We do not contemplate without serious attention what the holy Church uniformly performs throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether children or young people come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not approach the font of life before the unclean spirit has been driven from them by the exorcisms and breathings of the clergy. Then it truly becomes apparent how “the ruler of this world” is cast out, how the strong man is first bound, and afterward his vessels are seized and transferred into the possession of the victor, “who led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings (Eph. 4:8).”

Strengthened, therefore, by these ecclesiastical documents drawn from divine authority, and with the Lord’s help, we have been so confirmed that we confess God to be the author of all good affections and works, of all endeavors and virtues by which a person turns toward God from the beginning of faith. We do not doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good.

Yet by God’s help and gift free choice is not taken away; rather, it is freed, so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes sound, and what was shameless becomes prudent.

For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wishes the merits that are his gifts to be ours, and, for the things he has bestowed, he is going to grant eternal rewards. He works in us so that we may both will and do what he wills, nor does he permit the gifts he has granted for exercise to remain idle in us or to be neglected. Thus we may be fellow workers with God’s grace; and if we see something in us growing weak through our own negligence, we must earnestly return to him who heals all our illnesses and redeems our life from destruction, and to whom we say each day, “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil (Matt. 6:13).”

## XIII

As for the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise, which those who resisted the heretics treated at greater length, we do not dare to despise them; yet we do not consider it necessary to establish them absolutely. * For we believe that, in confessing the grace of God—a grace from whose work and favor nothing whatsoever should be withdrawn—it is fully sufficient to affirm whatever, according to the rules stated above, the writings—not we—of the apostolic see have taught, so that we should by no means consider anything Catholic that appears contrary to the judgments set forth.

## Another Letter of the Same [Celestine] to the Bishops of Gaul

1. That priests or clerics should not minister in churches wearing cloaks and girded about the loins.  
2. That final penance should be denied to no one.  
3. That a person should reach the office of bishop through the ecclesiastical grades.  
4. That each province should be content with its own metropolitan. [Col. 0754D]  
5. That no bishop should be ordained against the will of the clergy or people.  
6. That illicit ordinations must be avoided.

Celestine sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne.

We would indeed desire to rejoice so greatly in the ordering of your Churches that we might congratulate ourselves on advancement rather than grieve that anything had been done contrary to ecclesiastical discipline. Good deeds anticipate our joy, while wrongdoing pierces us with the goads of sorrow. Nor can we remain silent when the prompting of our office urges us to recall some people from illicit actions. We have been appointed by God as watchmen, so that, demonstrating the diligence of our vigilance, we may cut away what must be restrained and establish what must be observed.

Although spiritual concern for distant places does not fail but extends everywhere that the name of God is proclaimed, matters attempted through the authority of a novel presumption to overthrow the rules do not escape our notice.

## I

We have learned that certain priests of the Lord serve a superstitious form of worship rather than purity of mind or faith. It is not surprising that they act contrary to ecclesiastical custom, since they did not grow up in the Church but came by another path, bringing into the Church with them practices that they had maintained in another way of life. Wearing a cloak and girding their loins, they believe that they embrace the faith of Holy Scripture not through the spirit but through the letter.

For if these commands were given so that they should be observed literally in this fashion, why are the things that follow not carried out in the same way—why are burning lamps not held in the hands together with a staff? Let these things have their own mystery; to those who understand, they are so clear that they are observed according to a meaning greater than is appropriate to their outward form.

The girding of the loins signifies chastity; the staff, pastoral rule. The burning lamps indicate the radiance of good works, concerning which it is said, “So let your works shine (Matt. 5:16).”

Perhaps those who live in more remote places and dwell far from others have this form of worship, following custom rather than reason. But should this practice be introduced into the Gallican Churches, so that the custom of so many years and of so many bishops is changed into another form of dress? We ought to be distinguished from the people and from others by our teaching, not our clothing; by our manner of life, not our attire; by purity of mind, not outward adornment.

For if we begin to pursue novelty, we shall trample upon the order handed down to us by the Fathers, making room for superfluous superstitions. We must not lead the inexperienced minds of the faithful into such things; they should be taught rather than mocked. Instruction must not be imposed upon their eyes but poured into their minds.

There are many things that we could say about ecclesiastical discipline and the reasoning behind the matter itself, but from these we are being called back to other concerns.

## II
