We have learned that penance is being denied to the dying, and that the wishes of those who desire, at the time of their death, to have this remedy supplied to their souls are not being granted. I confess that we shudder to find anyone guilty of such great impiety as to despair of God’s mercy, as though he could not come to the aid of someone who turns to him at any time and redeem a person endangered beneath the burden of sins, when that person desires to be released and set free.

What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying, and through one’s own belief to kill the person’s soul so that it cannot be absolved, when God is most ready to help and, inviting repentance, promises the sinner in this way: “On whatever day he turns back, his sins will not be reckoned against him (Ezek. 33:12)”; and again: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. 33:11).”

Whoever denies repentance at the time of death therefore takes salvation away from a human being. And he despairs of God’s mercy if he does not believe that God is sufficient to aid the dying, or able to do so even in a moment.

The thief hanging on the cross at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward if repentance for a single hour had not helped him. Though he was in punishment, he repented, and through the promise contained in a single utterance, by God’s promise, he obtained the dwelling of paradise.

True conversion to the Lord at the end of life must therefore be judged by the mind of the sinner rather than by the length of time, as the prophet asserts in these words: “When you have turned back and groaned, then you will be saved.” Since the Lord examines the heart, repentance must not be denied to anyone who asks for it at any time, when that person binds himself to the Judge to whom he knows that all hidden things are revealed.

## III

We have learned, dearest brothers, that certain men have been ordained bishops even though they had not been formed through any ecclesiastical orders for such a pinnacle of dignity, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers. Whoever recognizes that he has done this has usurped the office. Yet provision should very frequently have been made for reaching the episcopate through these grades, so that those initiated in lesser offices might be strengthened for greater ones.

Anyone who wishes to be a teacher must first be a disciple, so that he may teach what he has learned. Every arrangement of life confirms itself according to this principle in relation to the goal toward which it strives. Someone who has given no attention to letters cannot be a teacher of letters. One who has not advanced through each period of service cannot reach the rank earned through service.

Is the priesthood alone, I ask, cheaper than all these offices—an office more easily bestowed even though it is more difficult to fulfill?

But it is now not enough that laymen are ordained, which no ecclesiastical order permits; even men whose crimes are widely known throughout almost all the provinces are being ordained as bishops.

For recently Daniel was accused before us, in a report sent from the eastern regions, by the entire monastery of virgins over which he had presided, with many charges of many disgraceful offenses. Inquiry was made in what part of the world he was hiding, so that, if he trusted in his innocence, he might not evade the judgment that had been sought.

Instructions were sent to the bishop of Arles through our subdeacon Fortunatus, so that Daniel might be assigned to an episcopal trial. Burdened by such weighty testimonies and struck by such an accusation of crimes, this bishop, polluted—as is said—by incest with sacred virgins, is asserted to have been ordained; and, as is contained in the documents of our archive, copies of which we have also sent to you, he insinuated himself into the dignity of the episcopate at the very time when, by letters sent by us, he was being summoned to answer the case. May no injury be done to the sacred name.

* It is more likely that, by conferring this dignity upon such a man, the one ordained has himself lost it than that, once ordained, he should possess it. The person who believed that such a man should be joined to him by granting him the episcopate will be associated with him after his conviction. For whoever ordains such a man reveals what sort of person he himself is.

Now that these matters have been brought forward, and since many among us know the statutes of the apostolic see and have spent some time with us, let your fraternity hasten, by our exhortations, to restore everything to the standard of discipline.

## IV

First, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, let each province be content with its own metropolitan, as the regulations contained in the letter of our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne establish. Let no priest be granted an opportunity for usurpation to the injury of another.

Let each person be content with the boundaries granted to him. Let no one presume to do anything in another’s province. Let foreigners and outsiders who have served out their terms in their own Churches, and those who were previously unknown, not be placed ahead of those who deserve well by the testimony of their fellow citizens, lest some new sort of college from which bishops are made appear to have been created.

## V

Let no bishop be given against the will of the people. The agreement and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order must be sought. Only then may someone be chosen from another Church if, among the clergy of the city in which a bishop is to be ordained, no worthy person can be found—which we do not believe will happen.

First, those clergy must be rejected, so that someone from another Church may rightly be preferred. Let each person receive the fruit of his service in the Church in which he has passed his entire life through all the offices. Let no one intrude upon another’s service, nor dare to claim for himself the reward owed to someone else.

Let the clergy have the freedom to resist if they see themselves being overburdened, and let them not fear to reject those whom they recognize as being thrust upon them from outside. If they do not receive their proper reward or freedom, those whom they are to govern must have the power to judge them.

## VI.

Let him also abstain from unlawful ordinations. No layman, no bigamist, no man who is or has been the husband of a widow is to be ordained; rather, let the candidate be blameless and such as the Apostle chose. Through Moses [Col. 0757C] the Lord commanded: “The priest shall take a virgin as his wife” (Leviticus 21:13). The Apostle, speaking by the same Spirit, follows and supplements this: “A bishop must be consecrated as the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2). Let priests therefore be chosen according to this rule; and if any ordinations have been performed unlawfully, let them be removed, since they cannot stand and will not be able to evade our investigation, although those who have attained office in this manner think that they can remain concealed.

And so that the reverence due to religion may not be disguised beneath obscurity, let there be no empty boasting by men wearing a cloak of respectability; let those who are bishops follow episcopal custom. Daniel, as we have said, who believed that he could evade accusation by pontifical rank and reached the summit only by concealing himself from his accusers, should meanwhile know that he has been separated from the assembly of your holiness [Col. 0757D]. If he knows that he possesses confidence in his conscience, he ought to submit himself to our judgment.

As for the priest of the church of Massilia, who is said—an abomination to say it—to have rejoiced so greatly at the death of his brother that he went to meet the man who had come stained with his brother’s blood, intending to share a portion with him, we delegate him to be heard by your assembly. [Col. 0758A] Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Felix and Taurus.

## Letter of the same Celestine to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria

1. That no priest may be ignorant of the canons.  
2. That it is not proper to ordain bishops from among the laity while the clergy of the churches are despised.  
3. That the people must be taught, not followed.

### Chapter I

Celestine to all the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria.

No priest may be ignorant of the canons, nor may anyone do what could conflict with the regulations of the Fathers. For what matter worthy of reservation will remain to us if the standard of the decrees is broken at the pleasure of certain people, with permission granted to the populace?

[Col. 0758B]

### II

We have heard that certain cities deprived of their own rulers wish to seek bishops from among the laity, and consider so exalted an office so worthless that they think it cannot be conferred upon men who have served not God but the world. In doing so, they judge not only badly of their own clergy, whom they despise by this action, but most badly of us, whom they believe capable of approving such a practice. They would never dare this if the opinion of certain people, consenting to unlawful acts, did not join with them.

Thus the decrees that have so often been issued accomplish nothing, since people behave as though nothing had ever been written on this matter. What benefit is there in clergy having served through the successive ranks and spent their whole lives in the Lord’s army, if those who are to preside are sought from among the laity? Such men, having been disengaged from the world and knowing nothing of the entire ecclesiastical order, seek in their unrestrained ambition to leap directly into another person’s honor and to pass into another kind of life, trampling underfoot the reverence owed to ecclesiastical discipline.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since we guard the helm of our jurisdiction—that is, of the canons—we must oppose such men. By this letter we admonish your fraternity that no one should admit a layman to the clerical order or allow this to happen, thereby deceiving him and creating for himself grounds on which he may become liable under the established decrees. [Col. 0758C]

### III

The people must be taught, not followed. If they do not know what is permitted and what is not, we must admonish them rather than give our consent to them. Whoever attempts to try what is forbidden should know that the censure of the Apostolic See will certainly not be lacking. For what we do not correct by the authority of admonition, we must necessarily punish with a severity appropriate to the regulations.

We therefore wish this to be made known throughout all the churches that lack their own rulers, so that no one, perhaps flattering himself with some hope, may deceive himself. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius.

# The Decrees of Pope Sixtus Begin (C)

[Col. 0757]

## Sixtus, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the eastern bishops

[Col. 0757D] We give thanks to your holiness because, amid our tribulation [Col. 0758D] and persecution, you sent to visit us, desired to learn that our case had reached a good conclusion, and prayed to God that he might come to my aid in my tribulation [Col. 0759A], assist me, and free me from my rivals who were troubling and persecuting me.

O how good is charity, which makes those who are absent present to one another through the likeness created by love; which also unites what is divided, sets in order what is confused, joins together what is unequal, and strengthens what is incomplete. How rightly the eminent preacher, the Apostle Paul, calls it “the bond of perfection”: for although the other virtues produce perfection, charity binds them so firmly that they can no longer be dissolved from the mind of the one who loves.

By this virtue also, brothers, I find you full of the grace of the Holy Spirit, since I feel that you are comforting me in my anxieties. Nor is it surprising, dearest ones, if my rivals persecute me, since the head of us all, who is Christ, was formerly persecuted by the enemies of the holy Church of God and of his servants. Hence Truth itself says: “If they have called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household!” (Matthew 10:25). Again it says: “If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own. But because you are not of this world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19).

Since we know these things and proclaim them so that others may know them, and since we do not doubt that you know them perfectly, we must not turn either to the right or to the left because of the insults or accusations of those who lie in wait, or because of the praises of flatterers. Rather, amid the words of those who praise or blame, we must always return to the conscience; and if the good attributed to us is not found there, it ought to produce great sadness. Conversely, if the evil that people say about us is not found there, we ought to leap for joy.

What does it matter if everyone praises us while conscience accuses us, or if everyone accuses us while conscience proves us innocent? We have Paul saying: “Our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12). Job also says: “Behold, my witness is in heaven” (Job 16:20). If, then, we have a witness in heaven and a witness in our heart, let us allow fools outside to say what they wish.

For what else do slanderers do except blow upon dust and raise earth into their own eyes? The more they breathe forth slander, the less they see any truth. Nevertheless, they too must be summoned and calmly admonished, and every effort must be made to satisfy them, remembering what Truth says concerning the Jews: “Lest we cause them to stumble.” But if they are unwilling to be satisfied by the truth, you have the consolation found in the Gospel. When the Lord had been told, “You know that when they heard this saying they were offended,” he replied: “Let them alone; they are blind leaders of the blind” (Matthew 15:14).

The Apostle Paul also admonishes us, saying: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Romans 12:18). By saying “live at peace with all people,” he showed that this is difficult; therefore he prefaced it with “if it is possible” and added “so far as it depends on you,” because if we wish to preserve charity in our hearts toward those who hate us, then, even if they are not at peace with us, we nevertheless are certainly at peace with them.

As for what you commanded: that I should write to you about how, and by whom, the dispute now stirred up against me arose, so that it might be driven away through your assistance and my case strengthened, know that I am accused and unjustly persecuted by a certain Bassus. When the Emperor Valentinian heard this, he ordered a synod to be convened by our authority. After the council had been held with thorough investigation, I could have escaped in another way; nevertheless, avoiding suspicion, I cleared myself before everyone, freeing myself from suspicion and rivalry, though not by compelling others who were unwilling or had not voluntarily chosen this course. I did so as a model and example, since it is written: “If anyone wishes to bring an accusation, let him first write that he will prove it”; and elsewhere: “Let no one receive accusations against a teacher.”

Again: “If any bishop, priest, deacon, or any cleric has been accused before a bishop by any person, whoever he may be—whether a man of exalted rank or a person of any other condition who has undertaken this kind of blameworthy charge—let him know that he must bring forward what he alleges, to be shown by more reliable proofs.” [187] If anyone therefore brings charges against such persons that cannot be proved, let him understand that he will suffer the loss of his reputation and be carried into exile under major excommunication.

I set all these matters aside, not for the sake of giving others an example, as was mentioned above, but in order to free myself from the infamy and suspicion just described.

[Col. 0760C] The aforesaid Bassus was condemned by the synod already mentioned, yet in such a way that, because of the humble mercy of the Church, the viaticum was not to be denied him on his final day.

The aforementioned emperor Valentinian also condemned him in writing. Together with his Augusta mother Placidia, he joined all Bassus’s estates and possessions to the Catholic Church, giving future men of this kind a model for acting in the same way.

The often-mentioned Bassus died not long afterward by divine will. Although he was not worthy of burial, nevertheless, out of mercy, I buried him in the chamber of his parents. Although he had acted foolishly and imprudently toward me, I acted mercifully toward him, reflecting on what the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6:15).

And in the Lord’s Prayer itself, which our Savior taught the disciples to pray, we daily beseech the Lord, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 7:12). There are many other sayings like these.

Having therefore set aside and completed these matters concerning me—because, against the will of the bishops who were with us, I did this out of the humility of my judgment, compelled by no decision or force but choosing it voluntarily, and not giving others an example, as has been said, but purifying myself—nevertheless, in the case of other bishops, appropriate treatment must be applied to wounds of this kind. Otherwise, an immature eagerness to heal may accomplish nothing against a deadly disease of the head, while an illness treated too slowly may involve both the wounded and those treating them in the guilt of an illegitimate cure.

For this reason we establish and decree that those who are not of good conduct and whose life is blameworthy, or whose faith, life, and liberty are unknown, may not accuse the Lord’s priests; nor may persons of low status be admitted to accuse them.

Likewise, those who are entangled in any crimes, or who are suspect, shall have no voice to accuse their elders, because a suspicious voice, being hostile to truth, generally suppresses it.

We also prohibit by a general decree foreign judgments, while preserving in every respect the authority of the Apostolic See. For it is unworthy that someone should be judged by outsiders when he ought to have provincial judges chosen by himself, unless an appeal has been made. Therefore, if any bishop is accused of specific crimes, he ought to be heard by all the bishops who are in the province, since an accused person ought not to be heard anywhere except in his own jurisdiction.

If anyone finds that a judge is hostile to him, let him present a formal appeal. The appellant must not be harmed by any affliction or injured by detention in custody; rather, the appellant must be allowed to raise a corrupted case through the remedy of appeal. It must also be permitted to appeal in criminal cases, and the right of appeal must not be denied even to one whom a sentence has destined for punishment.

Let the accused state his case before his own judge. If he is accused before a judge who is not his own, let him be permitted to appeal if he wishes; and whenever the accused appeal, let them be granted delays.

If anyone, being angry, rashly brings any charge against another, the insult is not to be regarded as an accusation. Rather, after a period has been allowed for reflection, let him declare in writing that he will prove what he said in anger. Thus, if perhaps he comes to his senses and is unwilling to repeat or write what he said in anger, he is not to be held liable as a criminal.

Everyone who brings an accusation must write that he will prove it. In truth, the case must always be heard where the crime was committed. And whoever does not prove what he has alleged must suffer the punishment he himself sought to impose.

It was also decided that if an accused bishop appeals to the Apostolic See, whatever the pontiff of that See decrees must be established.

Nevertheless, this rule must be observed in every case involving priests, so that no one may be bound by a sentence pronounced by a judge who is not his own. Every faithful person must also come to the aid of those crushed by ruin, and offer the miserable such counsel as may enable them, through the disclosure of another’s vengeance, to remove God’s vengeance from themselves.

He therefore enjoys prosperity who drives adversity away from the afflicted, as it is written: “A brother helping a brother shall be exalted.” “For the Church of God ought to exist without stain or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27). Therefore it ought not to be trampled upon or stained by certain people, because it is written: “One is my dove, my perfect one” (Song of Songs 2:10).

Again the Lord says to Moses: “There is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock” (Exodus 33:21). What place is not the Lord’s, since all things are contained in him through whom they were created? Yet the place beside him is, specifically, the unity of the holy Church, in which one stands upon the rock when the firmness of confession is held humbly.

We also admonish you and all our brothers who govern the Church of Christ, redeemed by his blood, to restrain by whatever means you can all those who fall headlong through words by slandering and persecuting their brothers and the Lord’s shepherds; do not allow them to slip into the depths, for it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). Again it is said: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19).

I do not doubt that, with God as your author, you observe all these things. But since an occasion for admonition has arisen, I stealthily join myself to your good works and desires, so that what you do without being admonished, when admonition is added to you, you may no longer do alone.

Therefore, brothers, you and all the faithful ought to love one another and not slander or accuse one another. For it is written: “Love your neighbor” (Matthew 5:43), and: “Join faith with him; if you uncover his secrets, do not pursue him afterward.”

As a person who loses his friend is, so is one who loses his neighbor’s friendship. And as one who lets a bird go from his hand, so is one who abandons his neighbor and does not seize him or follow him, because he is far away. For he escapes like a doe from a snare, because his soul has been wounded; you will no longer be able to bind him to yourself.

Cursed is the agreement to strip bare the secrets of a friend; it is despair for an unfaithful soul. He who signals with his eye contrives wickedness, and no one will cast him away. In the sight of your eyes he will trample his own mouth, and he will marvel at your words. At last he will pervert his mouth and bring scandal through your words.

I have heard many things and have not equated them with him, and the Lord will hate him. He who throws a stone upward will have it fall upon his own head, and a deceitful blow will inflict wounds. He who digs a pit will fall into it, and he who sets a stone for his neighbor will stumble over it. He who lays a snare for another will perish in it. The evil counsel devised against another will roll back upon its author, and he will not recognize from where it will come upon him.

Mockery and reproach will lie in wait for the proud like a lion; those who take pleasure in the downfall of the righteous will perish by a snare. Sorrow will consume them before they die. Anger and fury alike are detestable, and the sinful person who harbors them will be possessed by them.

Whoever wishes to avenge himself will find vengeance from God, and he will surely preserve his sins. Forgive your neighbor who has harmed you, and then, when you pray, your sins will be released. One person preserves anger against another and seeks healing from God. He has no mercy on a person like himself, yet prays for his own sins to the Most High? Though he is flesh, he preserves anger and asks God for pardon? Who will plead for his offenses?

Remember the last things and cease from hostility. For decay and death threaten the commandments. Remember the fear of God and do not be angry with your neighbor. Remember the covenant of the Most High and disregard your neighbor’s ignorance. Abstain from strife and you will diminish sins.

For an angry person kindles quarrels; a sinful person disturbs friends and introduces hostility among those who have peace. As are the trees of the forest, so the fire will blaze; according to a person’s strength will be his anger, and according to his substance he will exalt his wrath. A hastened contest will kindle fire; a quarrel hastening forward will pour out blood; and a tongue that bears witness will bring death.

If you blow upon it, it will blaze like fire; if you spit upon it, it will be extinguished—and both proceed from the mouth. The whisperer and the double-tongued person are accursed; they have disturbed many who were at peace. The third tongue has stirred up many and scattered them from nation to nation. It has destroyed the fortified cities of the rich and dug up the houses of the great; it has overthrown the strength of peoples and dissolved strong nations.

The third tongue has driven out spirited women and deprived them of their labors. Whoever watches it will have no rest and will not dwell in peace. The blow of a whip makes a bruise, but the blow of the tongue crushes bones.

Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not as many as those who have perished by their own tongue. Blessed is the one who is sheltered from an evil tongue, who has not passed into its anger, who has not drawn its yoke, and who has not been bound by its chains.

For its yoke is an iron yoke, and its chain is a bronze chain. Its death is a most evil death, and hell is preferable to it. Its persistence will not endure, but it will obtain the paths of the unjust, and its flame will not burn the righteous.

Those who forsake God fall into it; it will blaze among them and will not be extinguished. It will be sent against them like a lion and will hurt them like a leopard.

Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue. Make doors for your mouth and bolts for your ears. Refine your gold and silver, make a scale for your words, and straight bridle-reins for your mouth. Take care lest you slip with your tongue and fall before enemies lying in wait for you, and lest your fall be incurable, unto death.

Let everyone beware of these things and restrain his tongue from evil, and let his lips not speak deceit.

“Finally, dearest ones, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil; for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having accomplished everything, to stand firm.

Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth; put on the breastplate of righteousness; and having shod your feet for the preparation of the Gospel of peace in all things, take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:10–17).

These things, brothers, we have written to you and wish them to become known generally to all, so that what concerns some may become known to everyone. May almighty God protect you and the other brothers established everywhere until the end—Jesus Christ our Lord, who deemed it worthy to redeem the whole world, and who is blessed forever. Amen.

Given on the Kalends of April, in the fourth consulship of Valentinian and the consulship of Florentius.

# The Letters of Pope Leo Begin

[Col. 0763]

## I. To Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, against the Nestorian heresy

[Col. 0763C]

To his dearest son Eutyches the priest, Leo the bishop.

[188] You have brought to our attention, in a letter expressing your affection, that the Nestorian heresy was again sprouting through the efforts of certain people. We replied that your concern in this matter pleased us, since the words we received are an indication of your mind. Therefore we do not doubt that the author of the Catholic faith, the Lord, will be with you in all things.

When, with the Lord’s help, we have been able to learn more fully through whose wickedness this is being done, we must take care that the abominable and long-condemned poison may be eradicated from its roots. May God preserve you unharmed, dearest son.

## II. To the Emperor Theodosius

Leo to the Emperor Theodosius.

How much protection the Lord has prepared for his Church in the faith of your clemency is also shown by the letters that you sent to me, so that we rejoice that you possess not only a royal but also a priestly spirit.

For amid your imperial and public concerns, you show the most devout care for the Christian religion, lest schisms, heresies, or any scandals grow strong among the people of God. For then the condition of your kingdom is at its best, when the eternal and unchanging Trinity is served with confession of one deity.

What disturbance has occurred in the church of Constantinople, and what could have moved our brother and fellow bishop Flavian to deprive the priest Eutyches of communion, I have not yet been able to learn clearly. Although the aforesaid priest sent a complaint to the Apostolic See in a petition expressing his grief, he nevertheless briefly indicated certain matters, asserting that he had been wrongly accused of diversity in faith while observing the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.

But the petition of Eusebius, the bishop who accused him, copies of which the aforesaid priest sent to us, contained nothing that clearly demonstrated the charge. Although it brought against the priest the accusation of heresy, it did not clearly state what opinion of ours he had contradicted, even though both the priest and the bishop professed that in this matter they were subject to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. Therefore we had no basis on which to say anything.

And since the merits of the case, the concern for the faith, and your praiseworthy devotion require this, there must now be no opportunity for underhanded proceedings. We must first be informed of the matters for which he is considered blameworthy, so that a proper judgment may be made concerning facts that are well known.

I have sent letters to the aforesaid bishop in which he may recognize that I disapprove of his having concealed, even through excessive silence, the events that had taken place in so important a matter, when he ought first to have made everything known to us. We believe that, after this admonition, he will report everything to our knowledge, so that, once what still appears hidden has been brought into the light, judgment may be given according to what accords with evangelical and apostolic teaching.

Given toward the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes.

## III. To Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, asking why Eutyches was separated from the Church

To his dearest brother Flavian, Leo, and the rest.

Since the most Christian and clement emperor, concerned for the peace of the Catholic Church and for the holy and praiseworthy faith, has sent us a letter concerning those who have raised the tumult of disturbance among you, we are astonished that your fraternity could remain silent toward us about whatever that scandal may have been, instead of arranging matters so that your report might first inform us, lest we be able to doubt the reliability of what had occurred.

For we have received the petition of Eutyches the priest, who complains that he was deprived of communion undeservedly at the accusation of the bishop Eusebius, especially since he testifies that he was present when summoned and did not refuse to appear. Indeed, he asserts that at the very hearing he presented his petition of appeal, yet that it was not accepted; and for this reason he was compelled to post petitions of protest in the city of Constantinople.

In view of these circumstances, we still do not know by what justice he was separated from communion with the Church. But, considering the cause of your action, we wish to know the reason and to have everything brought to our knowledge.

For we, who desire the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, can decide nothing concerning anyone to the prejudice of either side on the basis of unknown facts, before we have truthfully heard everything that took place. Therefore let your fraternity, especially through a suitable and appropriate person, make known to us in a most complete report what novelty has emerged against the ancient faith and what deserved to be punished by a more severe sentence.

The moderation of the Church and the faith of the most religious ruler impose great concern for Christian peace upon us, so that, once disagreements have been cut off, the Catholic faith may be preserved inviolate, and those who defend what is wrong may be recalled from error while those whose faith has been approved are protected by our authority.

Nor can any difficulty arise from this side, since the aforementioned priest has declared in his own petition that he is ready to correct anything found in him deserving of reproach. For in such cases it is especially appropriate to ensure that both charity is preserved and truth defended without the tumult of contentious disputes, dearest brother.

Therefore, since your affection sees that we are necessarily concerned about so great a matter, let it hasten to indicate to us as fully and clearly as possible everything that it ought previously to have reported, lest we be deceived by some ambiguity among the assertions of the parties, and lest the disagreement, which ought to be abolished at its beginning, be nourished.

For this observance remains in our heart, by God’s inspiration: that the constitutions of the venerable Fathers, divinely strengthened and pertaining to the solidity of the faith, must not be violated by anyone’s perverse interpretation. May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

## IV. Flavian’s Reply to Blessed Pope Leo

1. Concerning the snares of the deceitful enemy.  
2. Concerning the fraudulent subtlety of heretics.  
3. Concerning the blasphemies of Eutyches.  
4. Concerning his entirely just excommunication.

To the most blessed and God-beloved Lord Leo, Flavian sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

### Chapter I

No circumstance restrains the devil’s poisons or holds back his deadly arrows. Flying upward and downward, he seeks those whom he may kill, whom he may overcome, whom he may devour. For this reason we must keep watch in prayers and work toward being able to avoid foolish inquiries.

It is proper to follow our Fathers and not alter the perpetual definition of those whose rule we have learned from the sacred Scriptures. Having therefore set aside weeping and tears, because a cleric occupying the highest rank was attacked by a savage demon and I could neither free him nor take him away from such a wolf—although I was prepared to lay down my life for him—I shall now begin to relate how he was seized, how he recoiled from the divine purpose, and how he ran to the one who is accustomed to destroy, turning away from the precepts of the Fathers and despising their decrees.

### II

There are certain people who signify sheep by their clothing but are inwardly ravenous wolves; we must recognize them by their fruits. At first sight these people appear to belong to our number, but they do not belong to our number. For if they belonged to our number, they would have remained with us.

But as soon as they began to assume impiety, what had been hidden within them was revealed, and all their deceit became manifest to everyone. They are found to be people weak in faith, ignorant of the divine writings, and dragging others with themselves into destruction. They scatter and disparage the teachings of the Fathers and the rest of the sacred Scriptures, to their own destruction.

We must anticipate such people and beware greatly of them, lest some who become entangled in their wickedness fall from their own firmness: “They have sharpened their tongue like serpents, and they have the poison of asps under their lips” (Psalm 139:4). Concerning these the Prophet cried out.

[Col. 0766D]

### III

Such a man appeared among us in Eutyches, formerly a priest and archimandrite. He seemed to hold and promote the position of our religion, but he confirmed the impiety of Nestorius and girded himself to fight on behalf of Nestorius in the battle being prepared against Nestorius.

He attempted to uproot the exposition of the faith made by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, and the letter written by Cyril of holy memory to Nestorius, or to those like him, to which everyone assented. In doing so he sought to restore the ancient sect of the impious Valentinus and Apollinaris, and he did not fear the command of the true God, who says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be fastened around his neck and that he be sunk into the depth of the sea” (Matthew 18:6).

He cast away all modesty and, stripping off the skin of unbelief that he wore, persistently asserted in the holy synod:

“The Lord Jesus Christ ought not to be confessed as being of two natures after the assumption of humanity, since he is recognized by us as being of one substance and one person. Nor does the flesh of the Lord subsist as coessential with us, as though taken from us and united to the Word of God according to substance.

Rather, he said that the Virgin who gave birth to him according to the flesh is indeed consubstantial with us. But the Lord himself did not assume from her flesh consubstantial with us; rather, the body of the Lord is not the body of a human being, though it is a human body that is from the Virgin.”

### IV

But, so that I may not make the letter long by saying much, long ago we sent everything that we had done to your blessedness. In those letters we explained that he had been stripped of the priesthood, because he had been caught in this error; we ordered that he have no association with the monasteries; and we excluded him from our communion.

Your holiness, knowing what was done concerning him, should graciously make his impiety known to all the bishops living under your blessedness, lest any of them, unaware of what he believed, speak to him as though he were orthodox, whether by letter or through any association.

## V. Pope Leo’s Reply to Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople, against the Heresy of Eutyches

1. How ignorance of the holy Scriptures made Eutyches a heretic.  
2. Against those who attempt to divide the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation into two sons.  
3. Against those who dare to assert that the divinity of the only-begotten Son of God is passible.  
4. Against those who argue for mixture or confusion in Christ’s two natures.  
5. Against those who, in their madness, assert that the form of a servant which he assumed from us is heavenly or of some other substance.  
6. Against those who deliriously say that God had two natures before the union but invent one after the union.

Leo, bishop, to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople.

[Col. 0767D] Having read the letter of Your Affection—which we are surprised was so long delayed—and having reviewed the sequence of the episcopal proceedings, we have at last learned what scandal had arisen among you against the integrity of the faith; and what previously seemed hidden has now been laid open and made clear to us. In these proceedings Eutyches, who appeared respectable by virtue of the presbyteral name, is shown to have been extremely imprudent and excessively ignorant, so that even of him the Prophet’s words may be said: “He refused to understand how to act well; he meditated iniquity upon his bed” (Ps. 35:4–5).

What, indeed, is more wicked than to hold impious opinions and refuse to believe those wiser and more learned? Yet those who, when some obscurity prevents them from recognizing the truth, turn not to the prophetic utterances, nor to the apostolic writings, nor to the authority of the Gospels, but to themselves, fall into this folly. They become teachers of error because they have not been disciples of the truth.

What learning did he acquire from the sacred pages of the New and Old Testament who has not even grasped the beginnings of the Creed itself? And although it is proclaimed throughout the whole world by the voice of all who are to be reborn, it is still not understood by this old man’s heart. Since, therefore, he did not know what he ought to believe concerning the incarnation of the Word of God, and was unwilling to labor through the breadth of the holy Scriptures in order to obtain the light of understanding, he should at least have received with attentive hearing that common and undivided confession by which the entire body of the faithful professes that it believes in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

These three statements destroy the devices of almost all heretics. For when God is believed to be both almighty and the eternal Father, the Son is shown to differ in nothing from the Father: God from God, almighty from almighty, born eternal from the eternal. He is not later in time, inferior in power, unlike in glory, or divided in essence.

This same eternal Only-Begotten of the eternal Begetter was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. That temporal birth neither diminished nor added anything to his divine and eternal birth; rather, it devoted itself wholly to restoring the deceived human being, so that he might conquer death and by his power destroy the devil, who held the authority of death. For we could not overcome the author of sin and death unless he took our nature and made it his own—he whom neither sin could defile nor death retain.

He was conceived, therefore, of the Holy Spirit within the womb of his virgin mother, who brought him forth while preserving her virginity, just as she had conceived him while preserving her virginity.

But if he could not draw a sound understanding from this purest source of the Christian faith, because through his own blindness he had darkened the brightness of evident truth, he should have submitted himself to the teaching of the Gospel. When Matthew says, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1), he should also have sought instruction from apostolic preaching. Reading in the Epistle to the Romans, “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:1–3), he should have directed his devout attention to the prophetic pages and found God’s promise to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 26:4).

And lest he doubt the particular identity of this “seed,” he should have followed the Apostle, who says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed” (Gal. 3:16). He does not say “to seeds,” as though to many, but as though to one: “and to your seed,” which is Christ.

He should also have grasped inwardly the preaching of Isaiah, who says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14). He should have faithfully read the words of the same prophet: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us; whose power is upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come” (Isa. 9:6).

He should not, by speaking deceptively, have said that the Word became flesh in such a way that Christ, born from the Virgin’s womb, possessed the appearance of a human being but did not possess the reality of maternal flesh. Or did he perhaps think that our Lord Jesus was not of our nature because the angel sent to blessed Mary said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35)—as though, because the Virgin’s conception was the work of God, the flesh conceived could not have come from the nature of the one conceiving?

But that uniquely wondrous and wondrously unique generation must not be understood in such a way that the novelty of the Creator removes the proper character of the race. The Holy Spirit gave the Virgin fruitfulness, but the reality of the body was taken from the body; and, as Wisdom built a house for itself, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14)—that is, in the flesh which he took from the human being and which the spirit of rational life animated.

## II

While, therefore, the proper character of both natures was preserved and both came together in one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by strength, and mortality by eternity. In order to discharge the debt imposed by our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that, as was fitting for our healing, one and the same mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, could both die by virtue of one nature and not die by virtue of the other.

Thus, in the complete and perfect nature of a true human being, true God was born—entirely in what was his own, entirely in what was ours. By “ours” we mean what the Creator established in us from the beginning and what he assumed in order to restore. But those things which the deceiver introduced and the deceived human being admitted left no trace in the Savior. Nor, because he entered into communion with human weaknesses, was he therefore a participant in our sins.

He assumed the form of a servant without the stain of sin, enhancing what was human without diminishing what was divine. For that self-emptying by which the invisible made himself visible, and the Creator and Lord of all things willed to become one of mortal beings, was an inclination of mercy, not a failure of power.

Accordingly, he who, remaining in the form of God, made the human being, himself became human in the form of a servant. Each nature therefore retains its proper character without defect; and just as the form of God does not take away the form of a servant, so the form of a servant does not diminish the form of God.

The devil had gloried that the human being, deceived by his fraud, had been deprived of divine gifts and stripped of the endowment of immortality, had undergone the harsh sentence of death, and that he himself had found some consolation in his evils through the fellowship of the transgressor. It was therefore necessary, by the arrangement of a hidden plan, that God, whose justice required it, should alter his sentence concerning the human being whom he had created in such great honor. Thus the unchangeable God—whose will cannot be deprived of its goodness—might complete his first dispensation of mercy toward us through a more hidden sacrament, and the human being, driven on by the devil’s wicked cunning, might not perish in guilt against God’s purpose.

## III

The Son of God, therefore, descends from his heavenly seat and enters the lowest regions of this world, without departing from the Father’s glory, generated in a new order and by a new birth.

In a new order, because he who was invisible in what was his own became visible in what was ours. The incomprehensible willed to become comprehensible; he who existed before the ages began to exist in time; the Lord of the universe assumed the form of a servant, while the immensity of his majesty was veiled.

God who is impassible did not disdain to be a passible human being, nor did the immortal disdain to submit to the laws of death.

He was generated by a new birth because inviolate virginity, which knew no lust, supplied the material of flesh. From the Lord’s mother, therefore, he assumed nature, not sin. Nor, because the birth is wondrous, is the nature of the Lord Jesus Christ, born from the Virgin’s womb, unlike ours. For he who is true God is likewise true human being, and in this unity there is no falsehood, since the humility of humanity and the height of divinity are mutually present.

For just as God is not changed by mercy, so the human being is not consumed by dignity. Each form acted in communion with the other according to what was proper to it: the Word performing what belonged to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belonged to the flesh.

One of these natures shines with miracles; the other submits to insults. And just as the Word did not withdraw from equality with the Father’s glory, so the flesh did not abandon the nature of our race.

For one and the same person is, as must often be said, truly the Son of God and truly the son of a human being:

- God, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1);
- human being, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14);
- God, because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3);
- human being, because he was made from a woman and made subject to the law.

The birth of the flesh is the manifestation of human nature. The Virgin’s delivery is a sign of divine power. The infancy of the child is displayed in the humility of the cradle. The greatness of the Most High is declared by the voices of angels.

He is like the beginnings of human life, whom the impious Herod attempts to kill; yet he is Lord of all, whom the Magi rejoice to worship in submission.

When he came to the baptism of his forerunner John, and it was not hidden that he was covered by the veil of flesh, the Father’s voice thundered from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

The one whom the devil’s cunning tests as a human being is served by angelic ministries as God. To hunger, thirst, grow weary, and sleep is evidently human. But to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves, to give the Samaritan woman living water whose drink ensures that the one who drinks will never thirst again, to walk upon the back of the sea without his feet sinking, and to silence the surging waves by rebuking the storm—these things are unmistakably divine.

Thus, to pass over many examples, it is not of the same nature to weep from compassion for a dead friend and, at the command of his voice, raise that same friend alive after removing the barrier of a four-day burial; to hang upon wood and make all the elements tremble when daylight is turned into night; to be pierced with nails and to open the gates of paradise to the believing thief.

Likewise, it is not of the same nature to say, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and to say, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

Although there is one person of God and human being in the Lord Jesus Christ, the source of the insult is one, while the source of the shared glory is another. His humanity is from us, and therefore he is less than the Father; his divinity is from the Father, and therefore he is equal with the Father.

## IV–V

Because of this unity of person, which must be understood in both natures, the Son of Man is read as having descended from heaven, although the Son of God assumed flesh from the virgin from whom he was born. Again, the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried, although he suffered these things not in the divinity itself—in which he is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father—but in the weakness of human nature.

For this reason we all confess, even in the Creed, that the only-begotten Son of God was crucified and buried, according to the Apostle’s words: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

When our Lord and Savior was instructing the faith of his disciples by his questions, he said: “Who do human beings say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:13). After they had reported the various opinions of others, he said: “But who do you say that I am?”

Then blessed Peter, divinely inspired and destined by his confession to benefit all nations, said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16).

The Lord rightly pronounced him blessed. From the principal Rock he drew both the firmness and the name of his strength, for by the Father’s revelation he confessed him to be both the Son of God and the Christ. One of these truths, received without the other, would not have brought salvation.

It was equally dangerous to believe that the Lord Jesus Christ was God alone without humanity, or a human being alone without God.

After the Lord’s resurrection—which was certainly the resurrection of a true human being, since no other was raised than the one who had been crucified and died—what else was accomplished during the interval of forty days except that the integrity of our faith might be cleansed of every obscurity?

He spoke with his disciples, lived with them, ate with them, and allowed himself to be handled with careful and searching touch by those whom doubt had unsettled. For this reason he entered to the disciples through closed doors, gave them the Holy Spirit by his breath, and, granting the light of understanding, opened the hidden meanings of the holy Scriptures.

Again, he displayed the wound in his side, the marks of the nails, and all the most recent signs of his passion, saying: “See my hands and my feet, for I am he; touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

Thus it might be recognized that the proper character of the divine and human nature remained undivided in him, and we might know that the Word is not the same as the flesh, so that we would confess one Son of God as both Word and flesh.

Eutyches must be judged utterly empty of this sacrament of faith, for he recognized neither our nature in the only-begotten Son of God through the humility of mortality nor through the glory of resurrection. He did not heed the sentence of blessed Paul and the evangelist John, who say: “Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God, and this is the Antichrist” (1 John 4:2–3).

But what does it mean to “dissolve Jesus” except to separate the human nature from him and to empty, through the most foolish fabrications, the sacrament of faith by which we have been saved?

If, being blind concerning the nature of Christ’s body, he necessarily raves with the same blindness concerning his passion. If he does not consider the Lord’s cross false, and does not doubt that the punishment undertaken for the salvation of the world was real, let him acknowledge the flesh whose suffering he believes. Let him not deny that the human being whom he recognizes as having suffered possessed our body.

For denial of true flesh is also denial of bodily suffering. If he has accepted the Christian faith and has not turned his hearing away from the preaching of the Gospel, let him see what nature hung, pierced by nails, upon the wood of the cross. When the crucified one’s side was opened by the soldier’s spear, let him understand from where the blood and water flowed, so that the Church of God might be watered by the bath and the cup.

Let him hear the blessed Apostle Peter preaching that sanctification of the Spirit takes place through the sprinkling of Christ’s blood. Let him not read casually the words of the same apostle: “Knowing that you were redeemed from the vain conduct inherited from your ancestors, not with corruptible silver and gold, but with the precious blood, as of an unstained lamb, of Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 1:18–19).

Nor let him resist the testimony of the blessed Apostle John, who says: “But the blood of Jesus, the Son of God, cleanses us from every sin” (1 John 1:7). And again: “This is the victory that conquers the world, our faith. And who is the one who conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because Christ is the Truth. For there are three who bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one” (1 John 5:4, 6, 8).

The Spirit, of course, is the Spirit of sanctification; the blood, of redemption; and the water, of baptism. These three are one and remain undivided; none of them is separated from its connection with the others.

For the Catholic Church lives and advances by this faith: that in Christ Jesus humanity is not believed to exist without true divinity, nor divinity without true humanity.

## VI

When, in response to the questioning of your examination, Eutyches answered by saying, “I confess that our Lord existed from two natures before the union; but after the union I confess one nature,” I am astonished that the judges’ rebuke did not condemn so absurd and perverse a profession, and that a statement so foolish and so blasphemous was passed over as though nothing offensive had been heard.

For it is just as impious to say that the only-begotten Son of God existed from two natures before the incarnation as it is wicked to assert that, after the Word became flesh, there is in him a single nature. Lest Eutyches therefore consider this statement correct or tolerable merely because he was not refuted by our judgment, we urge the diligence of Your Concern, dearest brother, that, if by God’s merciful inspiration the case is brought to a satisfactory conclusion, the imprudence of this ignorant man may also, through you, be cleansed of this stain in his thinking.

As the sequence of the proceedings made clear, he had begun well to withdraw from his own persuasion when, constrained by your decision, he professed that he was saying what he had not previously said and assenting to the faith from which he had previously been alien. But when he had been willing to give his assent by anathematizing the impious doctrine, your brotherhood realized that he remained in his own error and was worthy to receive a sentence of condemnation.

If he truly and profitably grieves over this, and recognizes either that episcopal authority was rightly moved or that he himself is guilty; or if, for the fullness of satisfaction, he condemns aloud and in a present subscription everything that he has wrongly thought, then however great the mercy shown toward one who has been corrected will not be blameworthy.

Our Lord, the true and good shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:15), and who came to save human lives, not to destroy them (Luke 9:56), wishes us to imitate his mercy, so that justice may restrain sinners, but mercy may not reject those who have turned back. True faith is defended most fruitfully when even by its own followers a false opinion is condemned.

To carry out the entire case piously and faithfully, we have sent our brothers Julian, bishop, and Renatus, presbyter of the title of Saint Clement, as well as my son Hilary, deacon, in our place. We have joined to them our notary Dulcitius, whose fidelity has often been tested by us. We trust that divine assistance will be present, so that the one who had gone astray may be saved after condemning the perversity of his thinking.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes, in the year 486.

## VI. Again, another letter of the same pope to Julian, bishop of Cos

[Col. 0773D]

To his most beloved brother Julian, bishop, Leo, and so forth.

Although through our representatives, whom we sent from the city on behalf of the faith, we sent our fullest letter to our brother Flavian against the error of excessive impiety, nevertheless, because through our son Basil the deacon we received a writing from Your Affection which greatly pleased us by the fervor of its Catholic understanding, we have added this page as well, in harmony with that letter, so that you may resist with one mind and steadfastly those who wish to corrupt the Gospel of Christ.

For the instruction of the Holy Spirit is one in us and in you, and the teaching is the same; whoever does not receive it is not a member of Christ’s body and cannot glory in that head in whom he asserts that his own nature is not present.

What benefit does it bring this most imprudent old man to tear apart, under the name of the Nestorian heresy, the opinion of those whose most pious faith he cannot overthrow? For to the extent that Nestorius departed from the truth by separating the divinity of the Word from the substance of the assumed human being, this man likewise departs from the right path when he proclaims that the only-begotten Son of God was born from the womb of the blessed Virgin in such a way that he bore a spiritual body, but that the reality of human flesh was not united to the Word.

Who would not see what monstrous opinions arise from this prodigy of falsehood? For one who denies the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ, must necessarily be filled with many impieties. Apollinaris will claim him, or Valentinus appropriate him, or Manichaeus possess him—none of whom believed in Christ the reality of human flesh.

If that flesh is not received, not only is it denied that he who remained in the form of God was born a human being according to flesh and rational soul, the same person in the form of a servant; it is also denied that he was crucified, died, and was buried, that he rose on the third day, and that he will come in that body to judge the living and the dead—the body in which he was judged.

These sacraments of our redemption are emptied if Christ is not believed to have assumed the true and complete nature of a true human being.

Or, because the divine signs were manifest, will the bodily evidence be called false, while the testimonies of both natures avail for the creature’s salvation? What belongs to divinity the flesh does not diminish; what belongs to the flesh divinity does not destroy.

The same person is eternal from the Father and temporal from his mother: inviolable in his own power, passible in our weakness. In divinity he is of one and the same nature with the Trinity, with the Father and the Holy Spirit. In the assumption of humanity he is not of one substance, but is one and the same person, so that the same person was rich in poverty, almighty in lowliness, impassible in punishment, and immortal in death.

For the Word was not converted, in any part of itself, either into flesh or into soul, since the simple and unchangeable nature of divinity is always wholly in its own essence, receiving neither loss nor increase. It so blesses the nature it assumed that, glorified, that nature remains in the one who glorifies it.

Why should it seem inappropriate or impossible that both flesh and soul should be one Jesus Christ and one Son of God and human being, if flesh and soul, though they are of dissimilar natures, form one person even without the incarnation of the Word? It is much easier for divine power to grant this unity to God and the human being than for the weakness of humanity alone to possess it in its substances.

The Word, therefore, was not changed into flesh, nor was flesh changed into the Word. Rather, both remain in one, and one is in both—not divided by distinction, nor confused by mixture. One is not from the Father and the other from the mother; rather, the same person is from the Father in one way before all beginnings, and from his mother in another way at the end of the ages, so that he might be the mediator of God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ.

In him the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily. The exaltation belonged to the one who was assumed, not to the one who assumed: “God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9–11).

When Eutyches dared to say in episcopal judgment that before the incarnation there were two natures in Christ, but after the incarnation one, it was necessary that he be pressed, through repeated and careful questioning by the judges, to give an account of his profession, lest something empty should simply pass away which clearly flowed only from the draught of revered doctrines.

I think that, when he speaks in this way, he is persuaded that the soul assumed by the Savior dwelt previously in heaven before being born from the Virgin, and that the Word joined it to himself in the womb.

But Catholic minds and ears do not tolerate this, because the Lord, coming from heaven, displayed nothing of our condition that had previously existed elsewhere. He did not assume a soul that had existed earlier, nor flesh that did not belong to his mother’s body.

Our nature was not assumed in such a way that it was first created and then assumed; rather, it was created through the assumption itself. Therefore, what was rightly condemned in Origen—who asserted that souls, before being inserted into bodies, had not only lives but also various activities—must necessarily be punished in this man as well, unless he prefers to renounce that opinion.

The Lord’s birth according to the flesh, although it has certain features by which it surpasses the beginnings of human existence—whether that he alone was conceived and born of the Holy Spirit and an inviolate Virgin without sexual desire, or that he was brought forth from his mother’s womb in such a way that both fertility gave birth and virginity remained—was nevertheless not of another nature than ours.

Nor was another soul breathed into him at the beginning than into other human beings, a soul that excelled by difference of kind rather than by sublimity of virtue. He had nothing opposed to him in his own flesh. Nor did conflicting desires produce a struggle of wills. His bodily senses were vigorous without the law of sin, and the reality of his affections remained under the governance of divinity and mind. He was not tempted by seductions, nor did he yield to injuries.

A true human being was truly united to God. He was not brought down from heaven according to a soul that had previously existed, nor was he created from nothing according to the flesh. He possessed in God the Word the same person of the Word of God, while retaining with us the common nature of body and soul.

For he would not be the mediator of God and human beings unless the same person were both God and human being, one and true in both.

The magnitude of the subject certainly urges us to expand our discussion, but in the presence of your learning there is no need for labor. Especially now, since through our representatives we have sent sufficient letters to our brother Flavian to strengthen the minds not only of priests but also of laypeople.

As we believe, God’s mercy will grant that, without harm to anyone’s soul, the healthy may be defended against the devil’s deceptions and the wounded healed.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes.

## VII. To Theodosius Augustus

To Caesar Theodosius, most religious and most devout Augustus, Leo, pope of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome.

How greatly divine providence deigns to care for human affairs is shown by Your Clemency’s concern, stirred by the Spirit of God. It desires that nothing in the Catholic Church be unsettled and nothing be divided, since the faith, which is one alone, cannot be unlike itself in any respect.

Accordingly, although Eutyches, as the sequence of the episcopal proceedings revealed, was discovered to be erring through ignorance and imprudence, and ought rightly to have withdrawn from his reprehensible persuasion, nevertheless, because Your Piety, which loves Catholic truth with the greatest religious devotion in honor of God, established at Ephesus a synodal council so that his ignorance might be enlightened concerning what he understands so poorly, I sent my brothers Julian, bishop, and Renatus, presbyter, and my son Hilary, deacon.

They would adequately represent my presence according to the nature of the case, and they would carry with them a disposition of justice and kindness, so that, since there can be no doubt about the integrity of the Christian confession, the perversity of the entire error might be condemned; and if the one who had gone astray came to his senses and pleaded for pardon, priestly benevolence might assist him.

In the petition which he sent to us, he at least reserved this as a means of obtaining pardon: he promised that he would correct whatever our judgment rejected in the opinions he had wrongly held.

What the Catholic Church universally believes and teaches concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s incarnation is more fully contained in the writings that I sent to our brother and fellow bishop Flavian.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes.

## VIII. To Pulcheria Augusta

LEO TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA

[Note: [Col. 0775] The old edition reads *Pulcherrimae Augustae* (“to the most beautiful Augusta”), here and below.]

The Lord’s provision for his Church in your clemency we have often demonstrated by many proofs; and whatever priestly diligence achieves in our time against the assailants of Catholic truth will redound above all to your glory, since, as you have learned from the Holy Spirit, you submit your authority in all things to him by whose gift and protection you reign.

Accordingly, when I learned from the report of our brother and fellow bishop Flavian that a certain dissension against the integrity of the Christian faith had been generated in the Church of Constantinople by Eutyches, so that the character of the whole case was displayed by the text of the synodal proceedings, it is worthy of your glory that this error—which, as I think, arose more from ignorance than from deceit—should be removed before it acquires any strength for itself through the agreement of the imprudent and the obstinacy of perversity. For ignorance too sometimes falls into serious errors, and unwary simplicity often rushes into the devil’s snares. Through this simplicity I understand that the spirit of falsehood has insinuated itself into the man mentioned above: while he thinks that he is holding a more reverent view of the majesty of the Son of God, he does not acknowledge that the truth of our nature is present in him, and therefore supposes that everything expressed by the words “the Word became flesh” belongs to one and the same substance.

But just as Nestorius fell away from the truth by asserting that Christ, who was born from his mother, was merely a man, so this man likewise departs from the Catholic path by refusing to believe that what was born from the same Virgin was our substance. He evidently does not wish it to be understood as belonging solely to the Godhead, so that what he performed in the form of a servant, and what made him like and conformed to us, would be merely an image of our nature and not its reality.

It is of no avail to call our Lord Jesus Christ the true and perfect man, if he is not believed to be a man of that race which the Gospel proclaims. Matthew says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1). He follows the order of human descent in such a way that he traces the lines of generation as far as Joseph, to whom the Lord’s mother was betrothed. Luke, however, reading backward through the stages of succession, returned to the very founder of the human race, showing that the first Adam and the last Adam are of the same nature.

The Son of God’s omnipotence could indeed have appeared to instruct human beings in the same way in which he appeared to the patriarchs and prophets in the form of flesh: when he entered into a struggle or engaged in conversation, when he accepted the duties of hospitality, or even when he took food that had been set before him. But those appearances were images of this man, whose reality the symbolic signs announced as something to be taken from the stock of the preceding fathers.

Yet the sacrament of our reconciliation, ordained before eternal ages, was fulfilled through a thousand figures because the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon the Virgin, nor had the power of the Most High overshadowed her, so that, while Wisdom built a house for itself within her undefiled womb, the Word might become flesh; and, with the form of God and the form of a servant meeting in one person, the Creator of the ages might be born in time, and he through whom all things were made might himself be begotten among all things.

For unless the new man, made in the likeness of sinful flesh, had taken upon himself our old condition, and, being consubstantial with the Father, had also deigned to be consubstantial with his mother; unless he, alone free from sin, had united our nature to himself, the whole of human captivity would have remained under the devil’s yoke. Nor could we otherwise possess the victory of the triumphant one, if that victory had been accomplished outside our nature.

From this participation he granted us the wondrous sacrament of regeneration, so that through the same Spirit by whom Christ was conceived and born, we too—who have been begotten through the desire of the flesh—might be born again through a spiritual origin. Therefore the evangelist says of believers: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:13).

Whoever is not a participant in this ineffable grace cannot attain the adoption of the children of God, if he excludes from his faith that which principally saves us. For this reason I grieve greatly and am deeply saddened that this man, who previously seemed praiseworthy for his profession of humility, dares to assert against our one hope and that of our fathers something so vain and foolish.

When he saw that the sense of his folly displeased Catholic ears, he ought to have withdrawn from his opinion, and he ought not to have so stirred up the rulers of the Church as to deserve to receive a sentence of condemnation. If he chooses to remain in his opinion, no one will be able to release him from that sentence. For the moderation of the Apostolic See observes this restraint: it acts more severely toward the obstinate and desires to grant pardon to those who have corrected themselves.

Because, therefore, I have great confidence in your most sincere faith, I beseech your clemency’s glory: just as Catholic preaching has always been aided by your holy zeal, so now also favor its freedom. Perhaps the Lord permitted it to be struck by this trial precisely so that it might be recognized what sort of people lie concealed within the Church. Their cure must certainly not be neglected, lest we also be saddened by the loss of bishops.

The most august and Christian emperor, desiring that the disturbances be settled as quickly as possible by an episcopal council which he wishes to hold at Ephesus, has appointed an excessively short and restricted time by fixing the meeting for the Kalends, since, from the third day of the Ides of May, when we received the letters of his Serenity, most of the remaining time must be consumed in arranging the departure of priests who are adequate for the business.

As for the fact that his Piety also believed that I ought to take part in the council, even if some earlier precedent demands this, it cannot in any way be fulfilled now, because the exceedingly uncertain condition of present affairs would not permit me to be absent from the people of so great a city; and the minds of those in turmoil would be thrown into a kind of despair if, under the pretext of an ecclesiastical case, I appeared willing to abandon my homeland and the Apostolic See.

Since, therefore, you recognize that this concerns the public welfare, judge—with your clemency’s pardon—that, for the sake of my affection and the petitions of the citizens, I am not absent from these brothers of mine whom I have sent as my representatives, but am present with the others. In accordance with the case, which has been made sufficiently clear to me from the sequence of the proceedings and from the profession of the man concerned, I have plainly and fully shown what ought to be preserved.

For it is not some small portion of our faith, shining with exceptional clarity, that is in question; rather, this most foolish contradiction dares to attack what our Lord wished no one in the Church, of either sex, to be ignorant of.

Indeed, the brief and perfect confession of the Catholic creed, marked by the corresponding twelve statements of the twelve apostles, is so fortified with heavenly defenses that all the opinions of heretics can be cut down by its sword alone. If Eutyches had wished to receive the fullness of this creed with a pure and simple heart, he would not have deviated at all from the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. He would have understood that the holy Fathers established this: against the apostolic faith, which is one and only one, no ingenuity and no eloquence may raise itself.

Therefore, according to your customary piety, deign to labor so that what blasphemous folly has uttered against the unique sacrament of human salvation may be driven from the minds of all. And if the man who has fallen into this temptation should come to his senses, so that through a generous satisfaction he condemns his own error, let the communion of his own order be restored to him.

Let him also know that I have written this to the holy Bishop Flavian, so that charity may not be denied if the error is abolished.

## IX. — To Dioscorus, Bishop of Alexandria

**LEO TO DIOSCORUS, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF ALEXANDRIA.**

You will be able to confirm how much affection of the Lord’s charity we devote to your beloved person from the fact that we desire to establish your beginnings more firmly, so that nothing may appear lacking in your charity’s progress, since, as we have proved, the merits of a special grace support you.

Therefore a paternal and fraternal exchange ought to be most welcome to your holiness, and you should receive it in such a way that you understand it to proceed from us. For we ought to think and act as one, so that, just as we read, it may also be shown in us that there is “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

Since the blessed Peter received from the Lord the apostolic primacy, and the Roman Church remains in his institutions, it is wrong to believe that his holy disciple Mark, who first governed the Church of Alexandria, formed the decrees of his traditions according to other rules.
