The spirit of the disciples and of the master came from the same source of grace, and the one who was ordained could not hand down anything other than what he had received from the one who ordained him.

We therefore do not permit that, while confessing that we are one body and one faith, we should disagree in anything, or that the institutions of the teacher should appear to be one thing and those of the disciple another.

What we know to have been preserved by our fathers with especially careful observance, we wish to be guarded by you also: priestly or levitical ordination is not to be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but is to be assigned to the beginning of the first day of the week that dawns after the Sabbath night; and on that occasion the sacred blessing is to be conferred upon those who are to be consecrated while they are fasting and by ministers who are fasting.

The same observance will be maintained if the morning itself of the Lord’s Day is celebrated with the Sabbath fast continued. From that point, the beginnings of the preceding night do not depart; they belong to the day of resurrection, as is unquestionably also shown by the Lord’s Passover.

For, besides the authority of custom—which we know comes from apostolic teaching—Sacred Scripture also makes clear that, when the apostles Paul and Barnabas were being sent to preach the Gospel at the command of the Holy Spirit, “after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them” (Acts 6:6). Thus we understand how much devotion both those who give and those who receive must exercise, lest the sacrament of so great a blessing appear to have been fulfilled negligently.

Therefore you will have acted piously and laudably in following apostolic institutions if you yourself observe this form for ordaining priests throughout the churches over which the Lord has willed you to preside: blessings are never to be given to those being consecrated except on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, whose beginning is acknowledged to be assigned to the evening of the Sabbath, and which has been consecrated by such great mysteries of divine arrangements that whatever has been established by the Lord as especially significant has been accomplished in the dignity of this day.

On this day the world received its beginning. On this day, through Christ’s resurrection, death received its destruction and life its beginning. On this day the apostles received from the Lord the trumpet of the Gospel to be preached among all nations, and received the sacrament of regeneration to be carried throughout the whole world.

On this day, as the blessed evangelist John testifies, when the disciples were gathered together behind closed doors and the Lord entered among them, “he breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose you retain, they are retained’” (John 20:22–23).

Finally, on this day the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord came upon the apostles, so that we may understand that, by a kind of heavenly ordinance, it was indicated and handed down that the mysteries of priestly blessings are to be celebrated on that day on which all gifts of grace were bestowed. [192]

So that our observance may agree in all respects, we also wish the following to be maintained: when a more solemn festival calls for an assembly of a numerous people, and so great a multitude gathers for it that a single basilica cannot contain them all at once, the offering of the sacrifice must unquestionably be repeated. Otherwise those who arrive later might appear not to have been admitted to this devotion, since it is entirely consistent with piety and reason that, whenever the basilica in which the service is being conducted is filled by the presence of a new congregation, the succeeding sacrifice should be offered.

A portion of the people must necessarily be deprived of their devotion if, while the custom of only one Mass is maintained, the sacrifice cannot be offered except for those who assembled in the first part of the day.

We therefore earnestly and familiarly admonish your beloved person: what has become established in our custom through the form of paternal tradition must not be neglected by your care, so that all things may correspond between us in faith and practice.

For this reason we have given this letter to our brother, the presbyter Possidonius, who is returning, to deliver to your fraternity. He has often taken part in our processions and ordinations, and, having been admitted on so many occasions, has learned what we maintain in all things by the authority of the Apostolic See.

Given on the Kalends of July.

## X. — To the Second Synod at Ephesus, in which he urges the bishops to condemn the blasphemies of Eutyches

**LEO, BISHOP, TO THE HOLY SYNOD ASSEMBLED AT EPHESUS.**

The devout faith of the most excellent prince, knowing that it especially belongs to his glory if no seed of error should arise within the Catholic Church, paid this reverence to the divine institutions: for the fulfillment of his holy purpose, he brought in the authority of the Apostolic See, as though he desired blessed Peter himself to declare what was praised in his confession, when the Lord said: “Who do men say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:13).

The disciples indeed recalled various opinions of different people. But when they were asked what they themselves believed, the prince of the apostles embraced the fullness of faith in a brief statement: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). That is: You who are truly the Son of Man are likewise truly the Son of the living God. You, I say, are true in divinity, true in the flesh, and, with the distinct properties of both natures preserved, you are one.

If Eutyches believed this intelligently and wholeheartedly, he would never have deviated from the path of this faith, on account of which the Lord answered him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” And I say to you: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:17–18).

He is exceedingly foreign to the structure of this building who does not grasp the confession of blessed Peter and contradicts the Gospel of Christ. He shows that he has never had any zeal for learning the truth, and that he was honored in vain as one whose old age he did not adorn with any authority of heart.

Yet because even the care of such people must not be neglected, the most Christian emperor wished an episcopal council to be held, so that every error might be abolished through fuller judgment. I have sent our brothers Julian, bishop, and Renatus, presbyter, and our son Hilary, deacon, together with Dulcitius, a notary of proven faith, so that they may attend your holy assembly in my place and, together with your fraternity, establish what is pleasing to the Lord.

The purpose is this: first, after the destructive error has been condemned, consideration should also be given to restoring the man who erred through imprudence—provided that, embracing the doctrine of truth, he fully and openly condemns, in his own voice and by his signature, the heretical opinions in which his ignorance had become entangled.

He also professed this in the statement which he had sent to us, promising that in all things he would follow our judgment. After receiving the letters of our brother and fellow bishop Flavian, we wrote back to him more fully about the matters which he appears to have reported to us, so that, once this error—which seemed to have been born—has been abolished, there may be throughout the whole world one faith and one identical confession, and “at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:10–11).

Given on the Ides of June, under the consulship of the most distinguished men Asterius and Protogenes, in the same era as above.

## XI. — To the Constantinopolitans

[Col. 0781D]

**LEO, BISHOP, AND THE HOLY SYNOD ASSEMBLED IN THE CITY OF ROME, TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE RESIDING IN CONSTANTINOPLE.**

Although we are deeply grieved by what is reported to have been done in the council of priests at Ephesus, because, as consistent rumor has spread and the actual outcome of events demonstrates, neither moderation in justice nor reverence for the faith was preserved there, we nevertheless rejoice in the pious devotion of your community. From the acclamations of the holy people, examples of which have been brought to us, we approve the affection of all of you, because the just love of the best of fathers lives and endures among good sons, and because you do not allow the instruction of Catholic doctrine to be corrupted in any respect.

For you know, as the Holy Spirit has revealed to you, that they are plainly allied with the error of the Manichaeans: they deny that the only-begotten Son of God assumed a true man of our nature, and they wish all his bodily actions to have been the appearance of an illusion.

So that you might not give the slightest assent to this impiety, we have already sent exhortatory letters to your beloved community through my son Epiphanius and Dionysius, notaries of the Roman Church. In them we freely granted the confirmation you requested, so that you might not doubt that we exercise paternal care for you and labor in every way so that, with the help of God’s mercy, all the scandals raised by the ignorant and foolish may be destroyed.

Let no one dare to flatter himself on his priestly honor if he can be convicted of the impiety of holding execrable opinions. For if ignorance is scarcely tolerable in laypeople, how much less is it excusable or pardonable in those who preside—especially when they presume not only to defend the inventions of perverse opinions but also, through error or favor, to lead the incurable into agreement with themselves.

Let such people be separated from the holy members of Christ’s body, and let Catholic freedom not endure the yoke of unbelievers being imposed upon it. For those who deny the nature of our flesh in Christ, contradicting the Gospel and resisting the creed, must be regarded as outside the gift of divine grace and outside the sacrament of human salvation. In their blindness they do not perceive that they are being led into this precipice, so that they have no share either in the reality of the Lord’s passion or in that of his resurrection. Both are emptied in the Savior if it is not believed that in him there is flesh of our race.

In what darkness of ignorance, in what torpor of negligence, have these people lain until now, that they have neither learned what they heard nor recognized by reading what is so consonant in the Church of God and in the mouth of all, that even the tongues of infants do not remain silent about the truth of Christ’s body and blood amid the sacramental communion?

For in that mystical distribution of spiritual nourishment, this is imparted: we who receive the power of the heavenly food pass into the flesh of the one who became our flesh.

Therefore, to strengthen your charity, which by praiseworthy faith withstands the enemies of truth, I shall fittingly and seasonably use the words and affection of the Apostle and say:

“For this reason I too, having heard of your faith which is in Christ Jesus and your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, enlightening the eyes of your heart, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his strength which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and power and virtue and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. And he subjected all things under his feet and gave him as head over all the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all” (Eph. 1:15–23).

Let these adversaries of the truth say: according to what nature, or with respect to what nature, did the almighty Father exalt his Son above all things? To what substance did he subject all things?

The divinity of the Word is equal in all respects and consubstantial with the Father; the power of the Begetter and the Begotten is eternal and timelessly one and the same. For he is the Creator of all natures, since “through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). He is above everything he created, and what he fashioned was never not subject to its Creator. To him it is proper and eternal to be, and he is from the Father alone, not something other than what the Father is.

If power was added to him, dignity enhanced, or sublimity exalted, then the one who grew was lesser than the one who advanced him, and he did not possess the riches of the nature whose generosity he needed.

But when one holds such views, Arius takes him into his fellowship. This impiety greatly supports Arius’s perversity, denying that the Word of God possesses human nature, so that, while it despises humility in the divine majesty, it either asserts that the bodily image in Christ was falsified, or that all his bodily actions and sufferings belonged rather to the Godhead than to the flesh.

Whatever such a person dares to defend is insane, because neither the piety of faith nor the reason of the sacrament admits that the Godhead suffered anything or that truth was false in any respect.

The Son of God, therefore, is impassible: he is God, and with the Father and the Holy Spirit he possesses the one essence of the immutable Trinity; for him, being is perpetual. In the fullness of time that had been appointed by the eternal plan and promised through the symbolic meaning of prophetic words and deeds, he became the Son of Man—not by a transformation of his own substance, but by assuming our nature—and “came to seek and to save what had been lost” (Matt. 18:11).

He came not by a local movement, nor through bodily change, as though he became present from a place where he had been absent or were about to depart from the place from which he had come. Rather, he came through what was visible and was to be made known to those who saw him by participation: he received human flesh and a human soul in the womb of the Virgin Mother, so that, while remaining in the form of God, he might unite to himself the form of a servant and the likeness of sinful flesh. Through this he did not diminish divine things by human things, but increased human things by divine things.

Such was the condition of all mortals, derived from their first ancestors, that, with original sin passing through their descendants, no one would escape the punishment of condemnation unless the Word became flesh and dwelt among us—in that nature which was truly of our blood and our race.

Therefore the Apostle says: “Just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all people, so through one act of righteousness justification came upon all people. For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man the many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5:18–19).

And again: “For since death came through a man, resurrection of the dead also came through a man; and just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22).

These are all those who, although born in Adam, are nevertheless found reborn in Christ, possessing the testimony of faith both concerning the justification of grace and concerning communion of nature. Whoever denies that this nature was assumed by the only-begotten Son of God in the womb of the Virgin descended from David is a stranger to the whole sacrament of the Christian religion; and, recognizing neither the bride nor understanding the bride, he cannot take part in the wedding feast.

For Christ’s flesh is the veil of the Word, with which everyone who confesses Christ is completely clothed. But whoever is ashamed of it and rejects it as though it were unworthy will receive no adornment from it. [193] Even if he intrudes into the royal celebration and presumptuously mingles with the sacred banquet, the shameless guest will not be able to deceive the king’s judgment. Rather, as the Lord himself declared, “he will be taken away, bound hand and foot, and cast into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:13).

Therefore, whoever does not confess human flesh in Christ should know that he is unworthy of the mystery of the incarnation and has no share in that sacrament which the Apostle proclaims, saying: “We are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh” (Eph. 5:30–31).

Explaining what this signifies, he added: “This mystery is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32).

From the very beginning of the human race, therefore, Christ was announced as one who would come in the flesh. In that flesh, as it was said, “the two will be one flesh.” The two are certainly God and man, Christ and the Church, who proceed from the bridegroom’s flesh when, from the side of the crucified man, as blood and water flowed forth, she received the sacrament of redemption and regeneration.

This is the new condition of the human creature: in baptism it is stripped not of the garment of true flesh, but of the contamination of condemned antiquity, so that a human being may become the body of Christ, because Christ too is the body of man.

Therefore we do not call Christ God alone, as the heretics the Manichaeans do, nor man alone, as the heretics the Photinians do; nor do we call him man in such a way that something is lacking in him which certainly belongs to human nature—whether a soul, a rational mind, or flesh. Nor do we say that he did not take flesh from a woman, but that flesh was made from the Word by the Word’s being converted and changed into flesh. These three false and empty claims were variously put forward in three forms by the heretics who follow Apollinaris.

Nor do we say that the blessed Virgin Mary conceived a man without divinity, who, having been created by the Holy Spirit, was afterward assumed by the Word—as Nestorius preached, and as we rightly and justly condemned him for preaching.

Rather, we say that Christ, the Son of God, is true God, born from God the Father without any beginning in time, and the same person is true man, born from his mother, a man born in the fullness of time. His humanity, through which the Father is greater, does not diminish anything of that nature through which he is equal to the Father.

These two together are one Christ, who most truly said, with reference to God: “I and the Father are one”; and with reference to man: “The Father is greater than I.”

Beloved, hold steadfastly and assert firmly this true and indissoluble faith, which alone makes true Christians, and which, as we understand and approve, you defend with devout zeal and laudable love.

And since, after divine assistance, you ought also to obtain the favor of Catholic rulers, ask humbly and wisely that the most merciful emperor deign to assent to our petition, by which we request that a full synod be convened, so that, with God’s mercy assisting, strength may be increased for the healthy and medicine supplied to the sick, if they consent to be healed.

## XII. — To Theodosius Augustus

**LEO, BISHOP, AND THE HOLY SYNOD ASSEMBLED IN THE CITY OF ROME, TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS.**

From the letters of your clemency, which some time ago you sent to the See of the blessed apostle Peter out of love for the Catholic faith, we gained such confidence in your defense of truth and peace that, in a matter so simple and so small, we thought nothing could arise to cause harm—especially since those sent to the episcopal council which you ordered to be held at Ephesus were so well equipped that, if the Alexandrian bishop had allowed the letters they brought either to the holy synod or to Bishop Flavian to be read aloud before the bishops, the tumult of every dispute would have fallen silent through the purest manifestation of the faith which we have received and hold as divinely inspired. Then neither ignorance would continue to act foolishly nor rivalry find an opportunity to do harm.

But while private cases were pursued under the pretext of religion, the impiety of a few committed an act that would wound the whole Church.

We have learned this not through an uncertain report, but from the most faithful narrator of the events that occurred: our deacon Hilary, who scarcely escaped being forced to sign. Many priests had assembled at the synod, and their large number would certainly have benefited the discussion and judgment if the man who claimed the chief place for himself had been willing to preserve priestly moderation. Then, as is customary, all could have expressed their opinions freely, and a calm and impartial examination could have established what was consistent with the faith and would assist those who had erred.

We have learned, however, that not all who had assembled took part in the judgment. Some, we understand, were rejected; others were admitted because, at the will of the priest mentioned above, they had surrendered their hands to impious signatures and knew that harm would result unless they did what was commanded.

And he is said to have issued such a sentence that, while one man was attacked, the whole Church was assaulted.

Our representatives, sent from the Apostolic See, saw that this was so impious and contrary to the Catholic faith that no oppression could compel them to consent. In that synod they steadfastly protested, as was proper, that the Apostolic See would never accept what was being decreed. For in truth the entire sacrament of the Christian faith would be cut away—God forbid—from the time of your Piety unless this most wicked crime, which surpasses every sacrilege, were abolished.

Since, however, the devil’s wickedness subtly deceives the unwary and mocks the imprudence of some through an appearance of piety, persuading them that harmful things are beneficial, we ask you to remove your ear from whatever endangers the conscience of your Piety, religion, and faith. What the equity of your laws permits to be done in secular matters must also be observed in dealing with divine things, so that human presumption may not use force against the Gospel of Christ.

Behold, most Christian and venerable emperor: together with my fellow priests I am fulfilling toward the reverence due to your clemency the duty of sincere love, and I desire you in all things to please God, for you are prayed for by the Church. Let us not be judged guilty before the tribunal of Christ the Lord for our silence.

Before the inseparable Trinity of the one Godhead—which is injured by such an act, since it is itself the guardian and author of your empire—and before the holy angels of Christ, we implore you to order everything to remain in the condition in which it was before any judgment, until a larger number of priests from the whole world has assembled.

Do not allow yourselves to be burdened by another’s sin, for we fear that, although we must say what is necessary, the one whose religion is being scattered may be provoked to anger.

Keep before your eyes, and receive with reverent attention, the glory of blessed Peter, the crowns shared with him by all the apostles, and the palms of all the martyrs. Their only cause for suffering was the confession of true divinity and true humanity in Christ.

Because a few imprudent people are now impiously opposing this sacrament, all the priests of the churches of our regions, together with all their communities, beseech your gentleness with groans and tears. Since our representatives faithfully protested and Bishop Flavian delivered to them the written appeal, order a general synod to be held within Italy. Let it either remove or mitigate all offenses in such a way that nothing further remains doubtful in the faith or divided in charity.

Let the bishops of the eastern provinces assemble; and if any of them, overcome by threats and insults, have deviated from the path of truth, let them be restored to wholeness by salutary remedies. Let those whose case is more difficult, if they accept better counsel, not depart from the unity of the Church.

That this should necessarily be demanded after an appeal has been lodged is attested by the decrees enacted at Nicaea, which were established by the priests of the whole world and are appended below.

Favor Catholics in accordance with the custom of yourself and your parents. Give freedom to the defense of the faith—a freedom which, without violating the reverence due to your clemency, no force and no worldly fear can take away.

Since we are conducting the cause of the Church and of salvation so that you may possess your provinces in peaceful security, defend the Church’s unshaken condition against heretics, so that the right hand of Christ may also defend your empire.

Given on the third day before the Ides of October, under the consulship of the most distinguished men Asterius and Protogenes, in the same era as above.

## XIII. — To Pulcheria Augusta

**LEO, BISHOP, AND THE HOLY SYNOD ASSEMBLED IN THE CITY OF ROME, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.**
[Col. 0787A] If the letters sent to Your Piety concerning the matter of the faith had reached you through our clerics, it is certain that, with the Lord assisting you, you could have provided a remedy for these actions committed against the faith. When have you ever failed priests, or the Christian religion, or the faith? But since those who were sent were unable to reach your gentleness to such an extent that scarcely one of them, our deacon Hilary, returned to us as a fugitive, we have believed that the letters must be sent again, so that our prayers might deserve to be more effective; and we have appended the examples of those who did not reach Your Clemency. We beseech you with still greater appeals: in proportion as the deeds are more bitter—deeds for which you ought to intervene before the royal throne—with that much greater glory may you take care of the religion in which you excel, lest the integrity of the Catholic faith be violated by any occasion of human disputes.

For the remedies of peace which, when the synod had been assembled at Ephesus, were believed capable of calming and healing matters have advanced not only to greater losses of peace but also—something which must be grievously lamented—to the destruction of the very faith by which we are Christians. Those who were sent, one of whom, fleeing the violence of the Alexandrian bishop who claimed everything for himself, faithfully reported to us the course of events, protested in the synod, as was proper, against the fury rather than the judgment of one man. They declared that actions carried out through force and fear could not prejudice the sacraments of the Church or the Creed itself established by the apostles, and that they could not be separated by any injury from the faith which they had brought, fully expounded and arranged, from the See of the blessed apostle Peter to the holy synod.

When the bishops requested that this confession be read, its recitation was not admitted. Thus, with that faith removed which crowned patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs, the birth according to the flesh of Jesus Christ our Lord, and the confession of his true death and resurrection—horrible to say—would be undone. We have written about this matter, as best we could, to the most glorious ruler and, most importantly, to a Christian ruler. We have appended copies of that letter as well, so that he would not permit the faith in which he reigns, reborn through God’s grace, to be corrupted by any novelty.

Since Bishop Flavian remains in communion with all of us, no consideration permits what has been done to be ratified without regard for justice and against the discipline of all the canons. And since the synod at Ephesus did not remove the scandal of dissension but increased it, a place and time should be established for a council within Italy, with all the complaints and prejudices of both parties suspended, so that everything that generated offense may be examined more carefully and they may return to the peace of Christ without wounding the faith and without injury to religion; let the priests remain, and let errors alone be removed.

That we may deserve to obtain this, may your piety—whose faith has been thoroughly proven to us and which has always assisted the labors of the Church—deign to affirm our supplication before the most clement ruler, or the embassy entrusted to us especially by the blessed apostle Peter, so that, before this destructive civil war within the Church grows strong, he may, with God’s help, grant the opportunity of restoring unity, knowing that whatever he bestows by his benevolent disposition upon Catholic liberty will benefit the strength of his empire. Given on the day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the illustrious men Asterius and Protogenes, in the era stated above.

XIV.—To the Same.

LEO, bishop, to PULCHERIA Augusta, etc.

Your letters have made me greatly rejoice and exult in the Lord. They clearly show how much you love the Catholic faith and how deeply you detest heretical error. For that heresy is exceedingly impious and hostile to the Gospel of truth: it attempts not to injure some portion, but to tear up the very foundations of the Christian religion, denying that the eternal Son of the eternal Father took true flesh of our nature from the womb of the blessed Virgin, his mother; and it strikes with condemnation those who could not be led away by any error from the evangelical and apostolic faith. It vainly claims that it holds the faith of the Nicene synod, although it is clear, most glorious Augusta, that it is alien from that faith.

Therefore, because divine protection does not abandon its Church, as the Lord says, “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20), at the same time and by the same action the Spirit of God kindled both the concern of Your Clemency and the care of our heart, so that we should desire the same remedies to be provided, which I previously requested. Now also I ask more urgently, with greater confidence in making my plea, since I have received the support of your venerable exhortation. I hope that God’s mercy will be present, so that, with Your Clemency cooperating, the disease of this deadly error may be removed; and that whatever can salutarily be done by his inspiration and assistance may be accomplished to the praise of your faith. For human affairs cannot otherwise be secure unless both royal and priestly authority defend what pertains to the confession of God. Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the seventh time and the illustrious man Anienus, in era 488.

XV.—To the Presbyters Martianus and Faustus.

LEO, bishop, to the presbyters MARTIANUS and FAUSTUS.

There can be no doubt that God is the author of good works and spiritual endeavors; he both stirs the minds of those whom he assists in their actions. This has clearly appeared to us through present experience. For although the intervals between our distant regions are so great, our hearts have taken one counsel, so that what you desired from us reached you at the very time when your letters were being sent—provided, of course, that our writings were able to be delivered to Your Love. They were sent not only with the authority of the Apostolic See but also with the unanimity of the holy synod that had assembled frequently with us, so that it might become clear from them how great a concern we have for the whole Church: namely, by exhorting the minds of all the faithful and seeking the support of the most clement rulers for the defense of the faith. We do not doubt that their pious and Catholic minds will extend their aid and authority to just petitions, so that, with the Lord’s help, the pernicious heresy—long ago condemned by the authority of the holy Fathers and recently badly supported at Ephesus—may more quickly be removed.

Meanwhile, let Your Love make every effort that it may become known to all the sons of the Church that, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic teaching, we denounce the impious doctrine. Although we have written fully what the Catholic position has always been and remains, we have now also added no small measure of exhortation to strengthen everyone’s minds. For I remember that I preside in the name of him whose confession was glorified by the Lord Jesus Christ, and whose faith destroys all heresies, but especially attacks the impiety of the present error. I understand that I am permitted nothing else than to devote all my efforts to the cause in which the salvation of the universal Church is threatened.

Lest our writings have been unable to reach you through some occasion of negligence, we have now decided to send copies of them, so that our preaching of the faith we defend may in no way be withheld from your knowledge. Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus VII and Ameno.

XVI.—To Theodosius Augustus.

LEO, bishop, to THEODOSIUS Augustus, etc.

In all your letters, amid the anxieties we suffer on behalf of the faith, you have provided us with the greatest hope of security by commending the Nicene council, to such an extent that, as you have often written, you do not permit the priests of the Lord to deviate from it. But lest I seem to have done anything prejudicial to the defense of Catholic truth concerning the ordination of the one who has begun to preside over the Church of Constantinople, I have meanwhile thought it improper to write rashly in either direction—not denying affection, but awaiting a manifestation of Catholic truth. I ask that Your Clemency bear this patiently, so that, when he has shown himself toward the Catholic faith as we desire, we may rejoice more fully and securely in his sincerity.

But lest any sinister suspicion about our disposition trouble him, I remove the occasion of the whole difficulty. I demand nothing that might seem arduous or doubtful, but invite him to what no Catholic would reject. For throughout the world there are known and evident those who before us shone in preaching Catholic truth, whether in the Greek or Latin language. Some even of our own age yield to their knowledge and teaching, and from their writings equal and manifold instruction is offered. Just as this instruction destroyed the Nestorian heresy, so it also cut off the error that is now sprouting again.

Let him therefore carefully reread what faith concerning the Lord’s incarnation was always preserved and likewise preached by the holy Fathers. Let him read the letter of Cyril, of holy memory, bishop of Alexandria, in which he wished to correct and heal Nestorius, exposing his perverse teachings and setting forth more clearly the faith of the Nicene definition. Although the archives of the Apostolic See had received the letter sent by him, let him perceive that it agrees with the teaching of those who preceded him. Let him also examine the acts of the synod at Ephesus, in which testimonies concerning the Lord’s incarnation from Catholic priests were both inserted by Cyril, of holy memory, and cited against the impiety of Nestorius.

Let him not disdain to reread my letter as well, which he will find entirely in agreement with the piety of the Fathers. When he recognizes that this is being sought and desired for his own benefit, let him consent with all his heart to the judgments of the Catholics. In this way, before all the clergy and the entire people, let him declare by an absolutely complete subscription his sincere profession of communion in the faith, to be published to the Apostolic See, to all the priests of the Lord, and to the churches. Then, with the world pacified through one faith, we may all say what the angels sang when the Savior was born of the Virgin Mary: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Because we and our blessed Fathers, whose teaching we both venerate and follow, are united in the concord of one faith, as the bishops of all the provinces testify, may the most devoted faith of Your Clemency act so that writings from the bishop of Constantinople—such as those of an approved and Catholic priest ought to be—may reach us as soon as possible. Let them clearly and plainly declare that if anyone believes or asserts anything concerning the incarnation of the Word of God other than what all Catholics and my profession declare, he separates that person from his communion, so that we may rightly extend to him fraternal love in Christ.

To ensure that these salutary concerns may be fulfilled more quickly and completely through the faith of Your Clemency, with the Lord’s help, I have sent to Your Piety our brothers and fellow bishops Abundius and Asterius, and also the presbyters Basil and Senator, whose devotion has been tested by me. Through them, by the instructions we have sent, you may graciously recognize the form of our faith. If the bishop of Constantinople wholeheartedly consents to the same confession, we may rejoice securely, as is proper, in ecclesiastical peace; nothing else would seem to remain doubtful, and we would not have to labor over perhaps superfluous suspicions.

But if any dissent from the purity of our faith and from the authority of the Fathers, may Your Clemency grant what I and the synod that assembled at Rome for this reason request: that a universal council be held within Italy, so that all who have fallen through ignorance or fear may come together and be assisted by remedies of correction. Let it no longer be permitted to anyone to speak of the Nicene synod in such a way that he is found to be contrary to its faith. For it will benefit both the universal Church and your empire if one God, one faith, and one sacrament of human salvation are held in the confession of the whole world. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August.

XVII.—To Pulcheria Augusta.

LEO, bishop, to PULCHERIA Augusta.

I rejoice in the faith of Your Clemency because you graciously devote religious zeal to the renewal of ecclesiastical peace, which appears to have been disturbed by the dissensions of those same men. This is especially owed to your glory: once all the scandals that the enemy had stirred up against the Catholic faith have been removed, there should be one and the same confession of truth throughout the whole world. This will be restored more easily and securely if no seeds and no traces of perverse doctrines remain.

Nevertheless, I must not pass over what belongs to my responsibility: I must learn what the bishop of Constantinople holds concerning the incarnation of the Son of God, especially since harsh events preceded his ordination and he ought to send us writings that would clearly show him to be free from the contagion of this error that recently emerged. Wishing to have secure concord with him and to extend to him the grace of fraternal love, I have meanwhile delayed writing to him—not denying affection, but awaiting a manifestation of Catholic truth.

What I ask is simple and unequivocal: setting aside the labor of lengthy disputes, let him accept the letter of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, of holy memory, which he himself had sent to Nestorius. In it he condemned the error of Nestorius and expounded the faith of the Nicene definition. Let him also agree with my letter sent to Flavian, bishop of holy memory. Having carefully examined these, let the bishop of Constantinople recognize without hesitation that he must repudiate what unlearned folly dared to define against the pure and singular faith; for my confession and that of the holy Fathers concerning the Lord’s incarnation are shared, wholly concordant, and one. If anyone judges that this confession should not be followed, he cuts himself off from the structure of Catholic truth, although we desire that everything be restored to its proper condition.

To obtain the effect of these salutary arrangements more quickly, I have sent my brothers and fellow bishops Abundius and Asterius, and also the presbyters Basil and Senator, most proven men. They will present to Your Clemency the form of the faith we preach according to the teaching of the venerable Fathers, and, removing circumlocutions by which truth is usually obscured, will show what the approved priests of the whole world have defended concerning the incarnation of the Son of God.

After divine grace, it is proper that they be assisted by the holy support of Your Piety, lest imprudent conflict arise to the disturbance of the whole Church. Once correction has been applied, all ought to return to concord in one confession. If perhaps some dissent from it, may Your Clemency order, with your assent, that a universal council of priests be held within Italy, so that, once the art of deception has been removed, it may at last become clear, through more profound deliberation, what ought either to be restrained or healed. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus VII and Ameno, illustrious men, in the era stated above.

195 XVIII.—To Pulcheria Augusta, through Theostichus the Master of Offices.

I fully recognize the religious concern of Your Clemency, which you continually devote to the Catholic faith; and I give thanks to God that I see you taking such care for the universal Church that I may confidently bring forward what I believe accords with justice and benevolence, so that, with Christ favorable, what has thus far been done irreproachably through the zeal of Your Piety may more quickly be brought to a gratifying result.

Accordingly, although Your Clemency ordered the Council of Chalcedon to be held, while Your Gentleness retained my request that it be held in Italy, so that all the bishops of our regions might be summoned and meet if the security of the times permitted it, I nevertheless received the order with such approval that I appointed two of my fellow bishops and fellow presbyters who would be sufficient to fulfill my role. I gave them suitable writings for the venerable synod, by which the assembled brethren might learn what procedure they ought to observe in this judgment, so that no rashness might obstruct either the rules of the faith, the decrees of the canons, or the remedies of benevolence.

For, as I have written very frequently from the beginning of this matter, I wished this moderation to be observed amid discordant opinions and carnal rivalries: nothing might be removed from the integrity of the faith, and nothing might be added to it; but when people returned to unity and peace, the remedy of pardon would be granted. For the works of the devil are then destroyed when human hearts are recalled to love of God and neighbor.

It would take much explanation to describe how contrary to these instructions and precautions of mine the actions then were. Nor is there any need to set down in an epistolary page what could be perpetrated in that Ephesian gathering—not a judgment, but a robbery. There the leaders of the synod spared neither brethren who resisted them nor those who assented. To undermine the Catholic faith and strengthen an execrable heresy, they stripped some of the privilege of their honor and infected others through association with impiety. They were plainly more savage toward those whom they separated from innocence by persuasion than toward those whom they made blessed confessors by persecuting them.

Nevertheless, since such men chiefly harmed themselves through their own iniquity, and greater wounds require more diligent medicine, I have never determined by any letters that pardon should be denied even to such men if they repented. Although we unchangeably detest the heresy that is most hostile to the Christian religion, we do not judge the men themselves, if they correct themselves and cleanse themselves through worthy satisfaction, to be excluded from the ineffable mercy of God. Rather, we groan with those who groan and weep with those who weep, and we use the justice of indignation in such a way that we do not lose the remedies of charity.

As Your Piety knows, this is promised not only in words but also demonstrated by deeds. Nearly all those who had either been induced or compelled into agreement with the presiding bishops, by repudiating what those men had decreed and condemning what they themselves had written, obtained perpetual abolition of guilt and the grace of apostolic peace.

Therefore, if Your Clemency deigns to consider our purpose, you will approve that we conducted everything in that council so that, without harm to anyone’s soul, only the extinction of heresy might be achieved. For this reason we diminished something of our customary severity toward the authors of the fiercest storms, so that their slowness might be stirred by some compunction to seek pardon. Although, after that judgment—both impious and unjust—they are no longer as honorable to the Catholic brotherhood as they were, they still retain their sees and enjoy the honor of their episcopates. They will either recover the peace of the Church through true and necessary satisfaction, or, if—as may it not happen—they defend the heresy, they will be judged according to the merit of their profession. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Helpidius, an illustrious man.

XIX.—To Faustus, Martinus, and the Others.

LEO, bishop, to FAUSTUS, MARTINUS, PETRUS, MANOHEL, JOB, ANTIOCHUS, ABRAHAM, THEODORUS, PIENTIUS, EUSEBIUS, HELPIDIUS, PAULUS, ASTERIUS, and CHARASUS, presbyters and archimandrites, and to JACOBUS, deacon and archimandrite.

[Col. 0793B] The cause of the faith, in which Christian salvation consists, compels me to labor under great anxiety, fearing that the perversity which ought to have been cut off at its beginnings may, as time passes, become both more obstinate and more widespread. For when the most clement emperor sent us writings demonstrating his concern for the peace of the universal Church, neither the bishop of Constantinople himself nor those who had consecrated him indicated anything to us, apart from what pertained to the rank of the new bishop, concerning errors that had been suppressed or renounced—as though no scandal or offense had arisen in that Church; or as though he had not especially been ordained to demonstrate his worth by teaching that doctrines opposed to Catholic understanding were alien from himself.

Therefore, lest—as can happen between distant regions—excessive delays prolong the examination of the truth, we have sent our brothers and fellow bishops Habundius and Asterius, and also the presbyters Basil and Senator, most proven men, to the most proven ruler, with sufficient instruction from the authority of the Fathers. We wish you, dearest brothers, to assist them in every way with your diligence and concern, so that the impiety which, through blind audacity, has advanced into deadly abysses may no longer have the power to deceive simple people. At the same time, we desire that those who have fallen through ignorance or been led astray by error be helped by remedies of correction.

Therefore, you who are justified by faith, who love Catholic truth, and who have been taught by the Holy Spirit concerning the singular sacrament of human salvation, cooperate with us. With as much devotion as you can, act so that, once falsehood has been destroyed and the solidity of the faith defended, we may enjoy God’s secure peace throughout the world. Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus VI and Anienus, illustrious men, in the era stated above.

XX.—To Martian Augustus.

LEO to MARTIAN Augustus.

I received with such pleasure Your Clemency’s holy zeal, by which you wished to hold a synod for the restoration of ecclesiastical peace, that although I had requested that it be held within Italy and had hoped for a more suitable time—one at which many bishops, even from distant provinces, might be summoned—as soon as the writings of Your Piety were delivered to me, I sent Boniface, one of my fellow presbyters, from the city, and arranged for my brother Paschasius, one of the bishops, to sail from Sicily. They would adequately fulfill my role. I also gave them letters to those who had previously accepted the embassy, so that they too might join the aforesaid men in completing the duties of my presence.

Although a very short period was appointed for the synod, I nevertheless hope that the help of the Almighty will be present, enabling all to arrive by the appointed time and, with the assent of the holy brotherhood, unanimously define what accords with the universal Church. For once the disturbance and perversity of the few have been suppressed or removed, an approved concord will easily be strengthened if all hearts converge upon the faith which we received and hold, declared by evangelical and apostolic preaching through our ancient Fathers. Let no discussion whatsoever admitting reconsideration be allowed, lest through empty and deceitful cunning those things appear weak or doubtful which are founded upon Christ himself, the cornerstone, and will remain without end.

We continually pray that no one be found alien from the sacrament of the singular faith, but that, with the impiety of heresy condemned, the Catholic Church may suffer no loss through anyone’s destruction.

What I begged Your Piety concerning those through whom I sent my letters, I now also ask with similar confidence: deign to keep those who will act in my place commended to you in every respect, so that what has been arranged through the excellent zeal of your faith may more easily and carefully be fulfilled with salutary effect. Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Adelphius, an illustrious man.

XXI.—To the Same.

LEO, bishop, to MARTIAN Augustus, etc.

Although I had previously written to Your Piety through the clerics of Constantinople, I received great cause for rejoicing when I received Your Clemency’s letters through the illustrious prefect of the city, my son Tatianus, because I recognized you as most devoted to ecclesiastical peace. To this holy desire justice fittingly contributes: whatever state of religion you wish to have, may you possess the same in your kingdom. For when concord among Christian rulers is confirmed by the Spirit of God, a twofold confidence is strengthened throughout the world, because the increase of charity and faith makes the power of both armies invincible. Thus, with God propitiated through one confession, both heretical falsehood and barbarian hostility may be destroyed, most glorious emperor.

Therefore, with hope of heavenly assistance increased through imperial friendship, I dare to encourage Your Piety more confidently on behalf of the sacrament of human salvation. Do not permit anyone’s shameless and insolent cunning to make it seem that inquiry must be conducted as though it were uncertain what should be followed. Since it is not permitted to depart by even one word from evangelical and apostolic doctrine, or to understand the divine Scriptures otherwise than the blessed Apostles and our Fathers learned and taught, must undisciplined and impious questions now at last be stirred up—questions which the Holy Spirit, through the disciples of truth, extinguished long ago, as soon as the devil stirred them through hearts suited to them?

It is exceedingly unjust that, through the foolishness of a few, we should be recalled to conjectures of opinion and to conflict, as though, with the dispute reopened, it were necessary to consider whether Eutyches thought impiously and whether Dioscorus judged impiously—he who struck Flavian, of holy memory, down in his condemnation and caused the simpler people to stumble so that they might be plunged into the same ruin. Since many of them, as we have learned, have already turned to remedies of satisfaction and are asking pardon for their wavering fearfulness, the question is not what kind of faith must be discussed, but how their petitions should be received.

Therefore, through the embassy which, with God’s favor, will soon reach Your Clemency, everything that I believe pertains to the usefulness of the case will be suggested to Your most devout concern more fully and at a suitable time. Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Adelphius, an illustrious man, in the era stated above.

XXII.—To the Same.

LEO, bishop, to MARTIAN Augustus.

I had indeed asked Your Glorious Clemency to order that the synod which you judged necessary for restoring peace to the Eastern Church, and which had also been requested by us, be postponed for a while until a more suitable time, so that those bishops whom fear of hostility detains might come with minds freer from every disturbance. But since you piously place divine matters before human affairs, and reasonably and religiously believe that it will benefit the strength of your kingdom if there is no dissonance in the minds of priests and no discord in the preaching of the Gospel, I too do not resist your arrangements. I desire that the Catholic faith, which can only be one, be firmly established in the hearts of all.

From its integrity both Nestorius earlier and Eutyches now have deviated by different paths, though equal in impiety, drawing their utterly abhorrent persuasions from the muddy pools of diabolical falsehood against the source of the pure, true light. The earlier synod at Ephesus rightly and justly condemned Nestorius together with his doctrine, and whoever persisted in that error can hope for no remedy.

But I cannot call the later gathering in that city a council. It is clear that it was conducted for the overthrow of the faith, and Your Clemency, in your love of truth and in support of the Catholics, weakened it by establishing something else, most glorious emperor. Therefore, by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is the author and ruler of your kingdom, I appeal to and beseech Your Clemency: do not permit the faith which our blessed Fathers preached as handed down to them by the apostles to be reconsidered in the present synod as though it were doubtful, and do not permit what was once condemned by the authority of our ancestors to be revived through renewed efforts.

Rather, order that the decrees of the ancient Nicene synod remain, with heretical interpretation removed. Do not think that I am absent from that council, as Your Clemency wished, since in these brothers whom I have sent—namely, the bishops Paschasius and Lucentius, the presbyters Boniface and Basil, and also my brother Julian, whom I wished to share in their mission—my own participation must also be reckoned.

With Christ’s help, I trust that they will act so that decisions pleasing to our Lord may be made, with the zeal of Your Piety assisting, a zeal that may benefit peace and serve as a guardian of religion and truth. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Adelphius, an illustrious man, in the era stated above.

XXIII.—To the Same.

LEO, bishop, to MARTIAN Augustus.

Your letters, which I received with reverence, and my fellow bishops returning from Constantinople have given me great confidence to write to Your Clemency. They have demonstrated, not merely by verbal assertion but by the very results of their actions, that divine protection is active in you for the defense of the Catholic faith. Through this, not only the state of the Church but also the strength of your empire is fortified, so that you rightly expect the protection of him whose truth you honor, most glorious emperor.

For the integrity of my brother Anatolius to be revealed more quickly; for the renewed advocate of an error once condemned to have no place in the Church of Christ; for the Catholic bishops whom the persecution of the heretics recently could not crush to be recalled from unjust exiles; and for the condemned man to acknowledge his impiety when the relics of Flavian, of blessed memory, were received with due honor—all this is the title of your courage and the fruit of your piety. I trust that the insignia of further victories will also be added to you.

As the Church of Constantinople rejoices in having recovered the freedom of apostolic faith, so may all the provinces of your kingdom glory in having been cleansed from the contagion of the devil’s doctrine. As I indicated in my preceding letters, I have sent my brothers Lucentius, bishop, and Basil, presbyter, who can fulfill the responsibilities of my concern. I commend them in every respect to the favor of Your Piety in the matters that must be carried out.

For when I learned both from the writings of my brother Anatolius and from the report of our men that many of those who at Ephesus, compelled by the faction of Dioscorus, had consented to the established decrees and now regretted their inconstancy, were seeking pardon and desiring Catholic communion through the satisfaction of correction, their conversion was not to be neglected. They are known to have fallen into these things not through their own judgment but through the impulse of an impious usurper, in circumstances in which they had no free choice.

Therefore, lest a long delay weary the desires of those who are repenting, or careless ease rashly and indiscriminately receive some people, the Apostolic See has instructed those who were sent to summon the bishop of the city of Constantinople into their deliberations, so that neither the contagion of the disease might be admitted nor the remedies of health denied. This diligence will, with the Lord’s help, quickly achieve the correction of all that was wickedly done, if Your Piety deigns to add its aid to the restoration of ecclesiastical peace.

Thus, while you reign on earth, may you deserve to possess God’s kingdom within you through honor; may no falsehood violate the Catholic faith; may no heresy disturb it; and may no one be permitted to abandon evangelical doctrine while enjoying priestly honor.

As Your Clemency remembers, we ourselves also requested that a synod be held. Yet the necessity of the present time in no way permits the priests of all the provinces to assemble, since the provinces from which they especially ought to be summoned are disturbed by war and do not allow them to depart from their churches. Therefore, when the Lord has been propitiated and security has been restored more firmly, may Your Clemency order that the synod be reserved for a more suitable time. Those whom I have sent will be able to explain this matter more fully, among other things, to Your Piety. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Adelphius, an illustrious man, in the era stated above.

XXIV.—To Bishop Anatolius.

[Col. 0797B]

1. His faith proved by writings that were sent.  
2. Concerning those who fell into heresy through fear, that they should be received if they are converted.  
3. Concerning the names of heretics not being recited at the altar.  
4. Concerning the commendation of Bishop Julian and of those clergy who remained attached in faith to Bishop Flavian.

CHAPTER I. LEO, bishop, to ANATOLIUS, bishop.

We rejoice in the Lord and glory in the gift of his grace. As we have learned from the letters of Your Love and from the report of our brothers whom we had sent to Constantinople, he has shown you to be a follower of evangelical instruction. Through the credible faith of a priest, we may rightly presume that the whole Church entrusted to you will have neither wrinkle of anyone’s error nor stain, as the Apostle says: “For I betrothed you to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

That virgin is the Church, the bride of one man, Christ. She does not allow herself to be corrupted by any error. In her we embrace the fellowship of Your Love, and we have approved the sequence of the acts we received, duly fortified, as was proper, by the necessary subscriptions.

Therefore, so that the mind of Your Love might be strengthened by our greetings in return, we have sent our sons, the presbyter Casterius and the deacons Patricius and Asclepiades, who brought your writings to us together with our letters, after the venerable day of the feast of Easter. We have informed you that, as we said above, we rejoice in the peace of the Church of Constantinople. We have always devoted this care to it: that we do not wish it to be violated by any deceit of heretics.

## II. Concerning the brothers whom we have learned from your letters and from the report of our legates to desire our communion

We have learned that they grieve because, unable to maintain their steadfastness against power and threats, they gave their consent to another’s crime, fear having so disturbed them that, in the condemnation of a Catholic and innocent bishop and in the reception of detestable wickedness, they served with trembling obedience. We approve what was established in the presence and through the agency of our representatives: that, for the time being, they should be content with the communion of their own churches. But we wished the matter to be arranged in consultation with you and our legates whom we sent, so that those who condemn their evil deeds with full satisfaction, and choose rather to accuse themselves than to defend them, may rejoice in the restoration of peace and of our communion. Thus, what was accepted contrary to the Catholic faith must first be condemned by a fitting anathema.

For otherwise, in the Church of God, which is the body of Christ, neither priesthoods are valid nor sacrifices true, unless the true High Priest reconciles us in the reality of our nature, and the true blood of the spotless Lamb cleanses us. Although he is seated at the right hand of the Father, in the same flesh which he assumed from the Virgin he carries out the sacrament of propitiation, as the Apostle says: “Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again, who is at the right hand of God and who also intercedes for us” (Romans 8:34).

Our kindness cannot rightly be criticized when we receive those who, by making satisfaction, we have judged to have been deceived. The grace of our communion must therefore neither be harshly denied nor granted recklessly: for just as it is wholly an act of piety to restore the Lord’s charity to the oppressed, so it is just that everything be charged to the authors of the disturbance. [Col. 0798B]

## III. Concerning the names of Dioscorus, Juvenal, and Eustathius being recited at the holy altar

Your Fraternity should observe what our representatives established there and declared ought to be done. This does not conflict with the honoring of the holy memory of Flavian, nor does it turn the minds of the Christian people away from your Grace.

For it is exceedingly unjust and improper that those who persecuted innocent Catholics should be indiscriminately mingled among the names of the saints. By refusing to abandon the impiety that has been condemned, they condemn themselves by their own depravity; they ought either to be struck with terror because of their perfidy or to labor for pardon. [Col. 0798C]

## IV. Concerning Julian and the clergy who adhered to the holy memory of Flavian

We wish our brother and fellow bishop Julian, and the clergy who remained faithful in their service to Flavian of holy memory, also to be joined to your Fraternity, so that they may recognize Flavian—whom by the merits of his faith we know to live with our Lord—as present to them in you.

We also wish your Fraternity to know that our brother and fellow bishop Eusebius, who endured many dangers and hardships for the sake of the faith, is meanwhile staying with us and continuing in our communion. We wish his church to be protected by your care, so that nothing should suffer loss during his absence and no one should presume to prejudice him in any respect, until he arrives among you with the delivery of our letters.

And, so that a greater affection for you—both ours and that of the whole Christian people—may be aroused, we wish what we have written to your Fraternity to become known to everyone, so that those who do not serve God may rejoice in the peace of the Apostolic See confirmed through you. Concerning the remaining matters and persons, your Fraternity will be more fully instructed by letters which you will receive through our representatives.

Given on the Ides of April, in the era stated above.

## XXV.—To Natholius, bishop of Constantinople

### Leo, bishop, to Anatolius, bishop

We approve the diligent and necessary care which your Fraternity displays in directing letters to us. Having received, through our son Olympius, the pages of your letters, we perceive that priestly concern is active in you; and we too, insofar as the Lord grants us ability, do not fail to support it. We beseech your Fraternity to persevere in holy vigilance, since we announce a time of labor, until the Lord’s right hand accomplishes a mighty deed and crushes the tempter beneath the feet of his Church.

The faith of the most merciful prince, divinely prepared for every circumstance, consoles us greatly. I have again exhorted him, as was fitting, in an address, so that with firmer resolve he may confront the attempts of the most impious robbers, who must not presume so much upon his favor as to dare to rage even at Constantinople.

Yet this has been permitted them by divine providence so that it may become increasingly clear by what spirit they are driven, and so that no one may doubt to what audacity they would break forth if, after the condemnation of their most impious heresy, they were granted the power to argue against the faith. Thus, insofar as they are able, they would spread more widely the fury which our brothers and fellow bishops, who recently fled to us from the regions of Egypt, report that they have endured.

I would not doubt that both the most Christian prince and your Fraternity have offered them the consolations of piety pleasing to God, even if you had not written to me. I therefore thought it appropriate to send them letters also, which might strengthen them in their commitment to the common faith and enable them to recognize what they deserve as a heavenly reward for their endurance. As the blessed Apostle teaches: “Receive them therefore with joy in the Lord, and hold such men in honor, because for the faith of Christ they came near to death” (Philippians 2:29–30). [Col. 0799C]

I declare that I am deeply displeased by the report that some among the clergy of your Fraternity connive at the wickedness of the adversaries, so that vessels of wrath are mingled with vessels of mercy. Your vigilance must persist in investigating and restraining them with appropriate severity. Thus, where correction cannot help, excision must not be spared. [197]

We ought indeed to remember the evangelical commandment, prescribed by Truth itself: “If an eye, or a foot, or a right hand causes us to stumble, let the hand be removed from the body’s structure” (Matthew 18:8). It is better to lack such members in the Church than to go with them into eternal punishment.

For we resist those placed outside the Church to no purpose if, through those who are within, we are wounded by the very people whom they deceive. This deadly indulgence must altogether be rejected by priestly vigor; by sparing the sins of others, it does not spare itself.

Thus, in former times, the priest Eli, by tolerating the sins of his sons, deserved to experience with them the sentence of divine justice, because through sluggish indulgence he neglected to punish sinners.

Therefore, whenever the opportunity of duty invites, your Fraternity should diligently visit the most religious prince and persist in entreating not only his royal mind but also his priestly mind with my prayers, so that, mindful of the common faith which we have received under the teaching of the Holy Spirit, he may shatter all the schemes of the heretics and allow them no power in the churches of Christ. Otherwise the divine mysteries would lie in the power of those who, in the house of God, possess neither the right to dwell nor to pray, in proportion to the enormity of their crimes. [Col. 0800A]

Given on the day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Constantinus and Rufus.

## XXVI.—To the same

### Leo, bishop, to Anatolius, bishop

Although I hope that your Fraternity is devoted to every good work, nevertheless, so that your activity may become more effective, it was appropriate—as we promised—to send my brothers, the bishop of the Lucensians and the presbyter Basil, so that your Fraternity might cooperate with them.

In all matters concerning the condition of the universal Church, whether doubtful or requiring action, everything should be conducted with moderation while you remain with those to whom we entrusted the execution of our decision. Thus neither the claims of benevolence nor those of justice will be neglected, and in everything the divine judgment will be kept in mind without respect of persons.

For this to be preserved through right observance, the integrity of the Catholic faith must first be maintained. Since “narrow and difficult is the way that leads to life” (Matthew 7:14), no one must deviate from its path either to the left or to the right.

The evangelical and apostolic faith overcomes every error: on one side it casts down Nestorius, and on the other it crushes Eutyches and his associates. Remember that this rule must be observed. Those who, at that synod which neither could nor deserved to bear the name of a synod, where Dioscorus displayed his malevolence and Juvenal his ignorance, were compelled by fear and terror to consent to the most criminal judgment—as we have learned from your report—and now desire to obtain Catholic communion, should be granted fraternal peace upon making satisfaction. They must unequivocally condemn Eutyches, his teaching, and his associates with the execration of an anathema. [Col. 0800C]

As for those who sinned more gravely in this affair, and on that account claimed for themselves the higher place in that unhappy synod, so that they might burden the simplicity of their humbler brothers by the prejudices of their arrogance: if they come to their senses and, ceasing to defend their action, turn instead to condemning their own error, then, provided their satisfaction is such as not to appear rejectable, they should be reserved for the more deliberate councils of the Apostolic See. After everything has been examined and weighed, it should be determined from their own acknowledgments what ought to be established concerning them.

Before then, as we have already written, no name belonging to any such person is to be recited at the altar in the Church over which the Lord has wished you to preside, until the course of events shows what decision ought to be made concerning them.

As for the memorandum submitted to us by the clergy of your Fraternity, it was not necessary to include in our letters what we thought about it, since it was sufficient to entrust everything to our legates, through whose report you would be more fully informed about all matters.

Therefore, dearest brother, strive faithfully and effectively to carry out, with those brothers whom we have chosen as suitable agents in so great an affair, whatever is fitting for the Church of God. The very nature of the case and the hope of divine assistance encourage you to do so, especially since the most merciful princes possess such holy faith and such religious devotion that in them we experience not only a Christian but also a priestly disposition.

Because of the piety by which they glory in being servants of God, they will graciously receive all your suggestions that may benefit the Catholic faith, so that through their aid Christian peace may be restored and impious error abolished.

If any matters require further deliberation, let a report be sent to us promptly, so that, after the nature of the cases has been considered, our concern may determine what ought to be observed.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelphius, in the era stated above.

## XXVII.—To the Council of Chalcedon

[Col. 0801B]

### Leo to the holy synod established at Chalcedon

Dearest brothers, I had wished, out of the charity of our common fellowship, that all the Lord’s priests would persevere in one devotion to the Catholic faith, and that no one, through the favor or fear of secular powers, would be corrupted and depart from the way of truth.

But since many things often arise which can bring about fullness, and since God’s mercy surpasses the offenses of sinners—on account of which punishment is delayed so that correction may have opportunity—the wholly religious plan of the most merciful prince must be embraced. He wished your holy Fraternity to assemble in order to destroy the devil’s plots and restore ecclesiastical peace, while preserving the right and honor of the blessed Peter.

Indeed, he invited me by letter to offer my presence to the venerable synod. Yet neither the urgency of the time nor any established custom allowed this. Nevertheless, in these brothers—Paschasinus and Lucentius, bishops, and Boniface and Basil, presbyters—who have been sent by the Apostolic See, let your Fraternity consider me presiding over your synod. My personal presence, which I now supply through my representatives, has not been withheld from the task imposed upon me; long ago I did not fail in proclaiming the Catholic faith.

Since you cannot be unaware of what we believe according to ancient tradition, you cannot doubt what I desire. Therefore, dearest brothers, let the audacity of disputing against the faith divinely inspired be wholly rejected, and let the empty unbelief of the erring fall silent. What may not be believed must not be defended.

For, according to the evangelical authorities, the prophetic voices, and the apostolic teaching, the pious and sincere confession concerning the mystery of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ was fully and clearly set forth in the letters which we sent to the bishop Flavianus of blessed memory.

Since we know that the condition of many churches was disturbed by wicked rivalries, and that many bishops who refused to receive heresy were expelled from their sees and deported into exile, while others were substituted in the places of those who survived, let the medicine of justice first be applied to these wounds. No one should be deprived of what belongs to him so that another may use what belongs to someone else.

If, as we desire, everyone abandons error, no one’s honor ought to perish. Rather, the rightful position of those who labored for the faith must be restored to them with every privilege. [Col. 0802A]

The decrees of the earlier synod of Ephesus, over which the bishop Cyril of holy memory then presided, concerning Nestorius must remain specially in force, lest the impiety condemned at that time flatter itself in any respect merely because Eutyches is struck down by a deserved execration.

For the purity of faith and doctrine which we proclaim in the same Spirit as our holy Fathers condemns and persecutes equally the wickedness of Nestorianism and of Eutychianism, together with their authors.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelphius.

## XXVIII.—To Anatolius

### Leo, bishop, to Anatolius, bishop

Since, as we desired, the light of evangelical truth has been manifested through God’s grace, and the night of the most destructive error has been driven away from the universal Church, we rejoice ineffably in the Lord that the labor of the stewardship entrusted to us has reached its desired outcome. The text of your letter also expresses this: that, according to apostolic teaching, we should all say the same thing and that there should be no divisions among us, being perfect in the same understanding and in the same judgment.

We rejoice that your Fraternity shares in the devotion to this work: your diligence has contributed to the correction of matters, and you have cleansed yourself from every participation and faction of those who deviated.

When your predecessor, Flavianus of blessed memory, was expelled for defending Catholic truth, it was not without reason believed that those who ordained you seemed, contrary to the decrees of the holy canons, to have consecrated one like themselves. But God’s mercy was present, restoring and confirming you in this respect, so that you might use your evil beginnings well and show that you had advanced not by human judgment but by God’s gracious favor. [Col. 0802C]

This must be understood in the proper way: you must not lose the grace of this divine gift through another offense. Just as a Catholic man, and especially a priest of the Lord, ought not to be entangled in any error, so he must not be corrupted by any desire.

For holy Scripture says: “Do not follow your desires, and restrain yourself from your will” (Ecclesiasticus 18:30). You must resist the many enticements and vanities of this world, so that the integrity of continence may truly be attained. Its first stain is pride, the beginning of transgression and the source of sin.

A mind greedy for power knows neither how to abstain from what is forbidden nor how to rejoice in what is permitted. Through an uncontrolled and perverse advance, the excesses of unpunished transgressions increase, and faults multiply—faults which were tolerated in the interest of restoring the faith and out of love for concord.

After those blameless beginnings of your ordination, and after you claimed for yourself the consecration of the bishop of Antioch contrary to canonical rule, I grieve that your Fraternity has also fallen into this: you attempted to violate the most sacred constitutions of the Nicene canons, as though this moment had conveniently offered itself to you, when the see of Alexandria had lost the privilege of second honor and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of third rank, so that all metropolitan bishops subject to those sees might be deprived of their own honor. [Col. 0802D]

Through unheard-of and unprecedented excesses you have deprived them, drawing the holy synod—assembled by the zeal of the most Christian prince solely to extinguish heresy and confirm the Catholic faith—into an occasion for ambition.
