You tried to compel it to grant you its connivance, as though what the multitude had illicitly desired could not be rejected, and as though the ordinance established at Nicaea by the truly Holy Spirit could be dissolved in any respect by anyone.

Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because their gatherings are larger. Let no number of priests more numerous than those three hundred and eighteen dare to compare itself with or prefer itself to them, since the Council of Nicaea was consecrated by so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are held by fewer or by more, whatever differs from its constitution is utterly devoid of authority. [Col. 0803B]

These actions are therefore exceedingly wicked and exceedingly perverse, since they are found to contradict the most sacred canons. This proud arrogance tends toward the disturbance of the whole Church: it sought to misuse the synodal council by compelling brothers who had been summoned solely for the business of the faith to agree with it through corruption.

For this reason our brothers sent from the Apostolic See, who presided over the synod in my place, rightly and steadfastly resisted these unlawful attempts. They openly cried out that presumptuous and reprehensible innovation must not arise against the ordinances of Nicaea. There can be no doubt about their opposition, since in your letter you yourself complain that they wished to obstruct your efforts.

By writing this, you commend them to me greatly; but you accuse yourself unnecessarily by refusing to obey them while plotting unlawful measures, pursuing what must not be granted and desiring what is salutarily opposed. Such desires could never obtain the consent of any of us.

Far be it from my conscience that such a wicked ambition should be aided by my efforts. Rather, it must be overthrown by my work and by the work of all who do not set their minds on high things but consent to humility.

Those holy and venerable Fathers who, after condemning the sacrilegious Arius and his impiety at Nicaea, established ecclesiastical-canonical laws destined to remain until the end of the world, and secured them throughout the whole world in their constitutions, made provision for us. Whatever is presumed elsewhere contrary to what they established is cancelled without hesitation.

What has been generally established for perpetual benefit must not be altered by any change, nor must what was fixed for the common good be diverted to private advantage. While the boundaries established by the Fathers remain, no one should invade what belongs to another.

Within his own proper and legitimate boundaries, each person may exercise himself in the breadth of charity as he is able. The bishop of Constantinople can acquire abundant fruits of this charity if he strives more through the virtue of humility than if he is inflated by the spirit of ambition.

Do not set your mind on high things, brother, but fear. Cease to trouble the pious ears of the most Christian princes with wicked petitions. I am certain that you will please them more by modesty than by arrogance.

The signature which, as you boast, was made by certain bishops more than sixty years ago lends no support whatever to your persuasion. It was never sent by your predecessors to the knowledge of the Apostolic See; from its beginning it had already become invalid and long since collapsed, yet you have now sought to apply late and useless supports to it, drawing from the brothers an appearance of consent which their wearied modesty offered you to their own injury.

Remember what the Lord threatens against the person who causes one of the little ones to stumble, and wisely understand what judgment of God you will face if you do not fear to cause scandal to so many churches and so many priests.

I confess that I am bound by love to the whole brotherhood in such a way that I agree with no one in matters which he demands against it. You can clearly recognize that I oppose your Fraternity with a benevolent disposition, so that, through sounder counsel, you may restrain yourself from disturbing the universal Church. [Col. 0804B]

Let the rights of provincial primacies not be overthrown, nor metropolitan bishops be deprived of privileges established in ancient times.

Let nothing be lost from the dignity which the see of Alexandria merited through the holy evangelist Mark, the disciple of the blessed Peter. Nor, when Dioscorus has fallen through the obstinacy of his impiety, should the splendor of so great a Church be obscured by alien darkness.

The Church of Antioch also, where the Christian name first arose through the preaching of the Apostle Peter, must remain within the order established by the Fathers and, placed in the third rank, must never make itself inferior.

For sees are one thing and those who preside over them another. The integrity proper to each is a great honor. If, in any place, it does not lose its own adornments, how much more glorious can it be in the magnificence of the city of Constantinople if, through your observance, many priests possess the protection of the paternal canons and the example of uprightness? [Col. 0804C]

Writing this to you, brother, I exhort and admonish you in the Lord: lay aside the desire for ambition and burn instead with the spirit of charity, adorning yourself productively with its virtues according to apostolic teaching.

“Charity is patient and kind; it is not jealous, it does not act improperly, it is not puffed up, it is not ambitious, it does not seek what is its own” (1 Corinthians 13:4–5).

If charity does not seek what is its own, how greatly does the person sin who covets what belongs to another?

I wish you to abstain altogether from these things, remembering the saying: “Hold fast to what you hold, lest another receive your crown.” For if you seek what has not been granted, you will by your own action and judgment be deprived of the peace of the universal Church.

Our brother and fellow bishop Lucianus and our son Basil, the deacon, did everything within their power and diligently assisted in the matters you had entrusted to them. But justice denied their action its effect.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Herculianus, in the era stated above.

## XXIX.—To the emperor Marcianus

### Leo to Marcianus Augustus, through the bishop Lucianus and the deacon Basil, concerning Anatolius’s ambition

By the great gift of God’s mercy, the joys of the whole Catholic Church have multiplied. Through the holy and glorious zeal of your Clemency, the most destructive error has been extinguished, so that our labor might more quickly reach its desired result, aided by a principate that serves God and by faith and power.

Although, through the power of the Holy Spirit, the freedom of the Gospel had to be defended amid every kind of dissension through the service of the Apostolic See, God’s grace nevertheless appeared more clearly in what he granted to the world: in the victory of truth, only the authors of violated faith perished, while the Church was restored to its integrity.

The war which our enemy had stirred up has therefore been happily concluded by God, with the Lord’s right hand fighting. With Christ triumphing, it became the one victory of all priests; and, as the light of truth flashed forth, the darkness of error and its defenders were driven away.

For just as, at the very resurrection of the Lord, great security was added for strengthening the beginnings of the faith because some of the Apostles had doubted the bodily reality of our Lord Jesus Christ, and, by seeing and touching the marks of the nails and examining the wound of the lance, removed the uncertainty of all who doubted, so now also, when the unbelief of some is refuted, the hearts of all who hesitate are strengthened. What brought blindness to some has advanced everyone toward illumination.

In this work your Clemency rightly and justly rejoices, since you faithfully and properly took care that the devil’s plots should not harm the Churches of the East, but that more effective offerings should everywhere be presented for propitiating God, when the confession of the peoples, of the priests, and of the kings was one and the same through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

When the matters for which so great an assembly of priests had been convened had been settled with a good and desirable outcome, I am astonished and grieved that the peace of the universal Church, restored by God, is again disturbed by the spirit of ambition.

Although my brother Anatolius may seem to have acted prudently for himself by abandoning the error of those who ordained him and passing, through salutary correction, into agreement with the Catholic faith, he nevertheless ought to have taken care that what he is known to have obtained through your beneficence should not be disturbed by any wicked desire.

Because we had regard for your faith and intervention, when the beginnings of his consecration were troubled by the very men responsible for it, we wished to be more kindly than strictly just toward him, so that we might soothe all the disturbances raised by the devil through the application of remedies. These remedies ought to have made him modest rather than immoderate.

Even if he had been legitimately and solemnly ordained with outstanding merits and excellent judgment, he could nevertheless have received no support against the reverence due to the paternal canons, against the institutions of the Holy Spirit, or against the examples of antiquity.

I speak before a Christian, truly religious, and truly orthodox prince. Bishop Anatolius greatly diminishes his own merit if he wishes to increase it by an unlawful addition.

May Constantinople possess, as we desire, all its glory, and, under the protection of God’s right hand, may it long enjoy your merciful rule. Yet the affairs of this world are one thing and divine affairs another; and no structure will be stable apart from that rock which the Lord placed as its foundation.

The person who covets what is not due loses what is his own. Let it be enough that, through the previously mentioned assistance of your piety and the agreement of my favor, he obtained the episcopate of so great a city.

Let him not disdain the royal city, which he cannot make an Apostolic See. Nor should he hope in any way to increase himself through offenses against others. The privileges of the churches, established by the canons of the holy Fathers and fixed by the decrees of the venerable Council of Nicaea, cannot be overthrown by any wickedness or altered by any innovation.

In faithfully carrying out this work, with Christ’s help, I must continue to offer my service, since a stewardship has been entrusted to me. It would become my guilt if, with my connivance—God forbid—the rules of the paternal sanctions established at Nicaea for the governance of the whole Church under the instruction of God’s Spirit were violated, and if the will of one brother were more important to me than the common welfare of the entire household of the Lord. [Col. 0806B]

Knowing, therefore, that your glorious Clemency is devoted to ecclesiastical concord and gives its most pious consent to whatever peacefully serves unity, I beseech and earnestly implore you to withdraw every support of your piety from reckless attempts opposed to Christian unity and peace. I ask you salutarily to restrain the ambition of my brother Anatolius, which, if he persists, will harm him himself.

He desires what is hostile to your glory and your times, wishing to be greater than his predecessors. Let him be free to shine with whatever virtues he can possess; but he will share in those virtues only if he chooses to be adorned by charity rather than swollen by ambition.

He ought never to have received this conception of wicked desire within the secrecy of his heart. When the brothers and my fellow bishops who were present in my place opposed it, he should at least have withdrawn from the unlawful desire in response to their salutary contradiction.

Both the letters of your piety and his own writings make clear that the legates of the Apostolic See resisted him, as was fitting, with the most just opposition. Thus his presumption is all the more inexcusable, since even when reproved it would not restrain itself.

Since it accords with your faith and glory that, just as heresy was destroyed through God’s agency by you, so every ambition should also be blunted, do what is worthy both of Christian integrity and of royal authority. Let the bishop mentioned above obey the Fathers and consult the interests of peace. Let him not think himself permitted to ordain a bishop of Antioch without precedent and contrary to the statutes of the canons—a matter which, out of love for restoring the faith and devotion to peace, we have refrained from pursuing.

Let him therefore refrain from injuring ecclesiastical regulations and avoid unlawful excesses, lest, by attempting what is hostile to peace, he cut himself off from the universal Church.

I wish to love him acting without reproach rather than see him persist in this presumption, which could separate him from everyone.

My brother and fellow bishop Lucianus, who brought your letters to me together with my son Basil, the deacon, fulfilled every part of the legation entrusted to him with complete devotion. A person should not be thought to have failed in a task when the cause itself abandoned him.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Herculianus.

## XXX.—To the empress Pulcheria

### Leo to Pulcheria Augusta, concerning Anatolius’s ambition

[Col. 0807A]

We rejoice ineffably with your Piety that, through the holy and God-pleasing efforts of your Clemency, the Catholic faith has been defended against the heretics and peace restored to the whole Church. We give thanks to the mercy of almighty God, who, except for those who loved darkness more than light, allowed no one to be defrauded of evangelical truth.

When the fog of error had been wiped away, the purest light arose in everyone’s hearts. That dark enemy could not exult over the weakness of certain minds: not only those who had stood unharmed but also those whom he had caused to waver overcame him. Thus, with error abolished, true faith reigned throughout the world, “and every tongue confessed that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).

Once the whole world had been confirmed in the unity of the Gospel and the hearts of all priests had been directed by the same Spirit and understanding, the best course would have been to introduce nothing contrary to the great good achieved through the holy synod’s assembly, nor to seek collectively, under cover of an episcopal council, what was not permitted to be desired.

For my brother and fellow bishop Anatolius gave too little consideration to the great benefit he had received from your Piety and to the agreement of my favor by which he obtained the priesthood of the Church of Constantinople. He rejoiced less in what he had attained than he departed beyond the measure of his honor in pursuing excessive ambitions.

He believed that this uncontrolled desire could be advanced by a certain signature which is said to have been obtained from some persons as their consent, although the opposition of the brothers and of my fellow bishops acting in my place faithfully and laudably confronted those efforts at once. [Col. 0807C]

Since nothing may be added to the provisions of the ancient canons of the Fathers, which were established long ago by the sacred decrees at Nicaea. Thus, if anyone wishes to decree something different, he should diminish himself rather than corrupt those provisions. If they are preserved inviolate, as they ought to be, by all bishops, peaceful harmony will exist throughout all the churches: there will be no disagreements concerning their boundaries, no disputes over ordinations, no uncertainties regarding privileges, no contests over the usurpation of another’s rights. Rather, that unanimity which is rightly owed in charity, conduct, and duties will be preserved.

And he will truly be great who is free from every ambition, as the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your minister.” And: “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant. Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve” (Matthew 20:26–28). Yet these things will then be impressed upon those who wished to rise from small beginnings and pass from the lowest places to the highest.

But as for the bishop of the Church of Constantinople, since he desires more than he has attained, what could satisfy him if the magnificence and renown of so great a city are not enough? It is exceedingly proud and immoderate to extend oneself beyond one’s proper bounds, to trample antiquity, and to seek to seize another’s right; and, so that the dignity of one man may increase, to attack the primacies of so many metropolitans, to bring a war of new disturbance upon provinces that have long been at peace and were arranged by the moderation of the holy Council of Nicaea, and, in order that the decrees of the venerable Fathers may be dissolved, to produce the consent of certain bishops—a consent to which the succession of so many years has denied effect.

For this vaunted claim is said to be nearly sixty years old, by which the aforementioned bishop supposes himself to be assisted, foolishly wishing that what no one, even if he dared to desire it, was ever able to obtain should benefit him. Let him recognize whose successor he is, and, rejecting every spirit of exaltation, imitate Flavian’s modesty and Flavian’s humility, which raised him even to the glory of a confessor. If he wishes to shine with that man’s virtues, he will be praiseworthy and will gain abundant affection in every place—not by coveting human things, but by deserving divine things.

This observance, moreover, should be joined to the disposition which he professes, as should his love for the Apostolic See, which we have always shown toward the Church of Constantinople and which must not be violated by any fickleness. For although excessively ambitious bishops sometimes fall into certain faults, the full grace of the Churches of Christ nevertheless endures.

But the agreements of bishops that conflict with the rules of the holy canons established at Nicaea, with the pious unity of your faith joined to ours, we declare null and, by the authority of blessed Peter the Apostle, completely annul by a general decision. In every ecclesiastical matter, let us obey these laws which the Holy Spirit established for the pacification of all bishops through the three hundred and eighteen prelates, so that, even if many others should decide to establish something beyond what those men established, whatever differs from the constitution of the aforementioned Fathers is to be held in no regard.

I therefore ask that, through my brother and fellow bishop Lucian, who, insofar as it depends on him, has faithfully carried out the responsibility of the embassy he undertook, and through my son Basil the deacon, your Piety graciously receive the length of my letter, in which I have necessarily explained what I think. And since it is your custom to labor for the peace and unity of the Church, beneficially restrain my brother Bishop Anatolius, whom your communication has shown to be beloved, in those matters that will be advantageous to him, so that the glory of your Clemency may be proclaimed for ambition restrained just as it is magnified for faith restored.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the illustrious man Herculanus.

### XXXI.—To the Emperor Marcian

**Leo, bishop, to the Emperor Marcian.**

There is much in all the letters of Your Clemency that gives me cause for joy, since, through the great mercy of divine providence, I perceive that what Your Piety graciously endeavors to do is being granted for human affairs: namely, to assist ecclesiastical peace, which is preserved only through unity in the preaching of the Gospel, with devout zeal, so that the glory of your faith may increase not only through the benefit of the state but also through the advancement of religion.

Most glorious Emperor, I therefore give ineffable thanks to God, who, foreseeing the scandals of heretics that were about to arise, placed you at the summit of imperial power, so that, for the salvation of the whole world, both royal power and priestly diligence might be vigorous. For it was chiefly through your work that, by the synodal council’s condemnation of the defenders of impious doctrine, sacrilegious error lost all its strength. To the palm of that same devotion belongs the destruction, even in whatever remnants remain, of the evil that has been suppressed in its leaders.

Your Clemency may more easily judge this to be accomplished if it is shown that the decrees of the holy Council of Chalcedon have pleased the Apostolic See. There was certainly no reason for doubt about this, since the agreement of all in subscribing to that faith had been added to it—the faith that was sent to me in accordance with apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers. Through my brother Bishop Lucian I sent to Your Glory and to the bishop of Constantinople letters that clearly demonstrated that I approved what had been defined concerning the Catholic faith at the aforementioned council.

But because in those same letters I had censured what had been wrongly attempted under the pretext of the council, the aforementioned bishop preferred to conceal my congratulation rather than publicize his own ambition.

For my part, God working through you, I have been granted great confidence because I had approved that you indicated, in the expressions of your Piety, your observance in guarding the canons of the Fathers. My joy is rightly doubled when I learn that it is most religiously pleasing to you that the faith of Nicaea retain its firmness and that the privileges of the Churches remain unimpaired.

Although Your Piety did not inform me of anything concerning your splendid work for the faith, nevertheless I indicate, through the venerable man who is spiritually united with me, that I have learned through my brother Bishop Julian how piously you deigned both to restrain and to instruct the minds of the ignorant monks by your reply, so that, if divine mercy has not entirely abandoned them, they may realize that they have learned both what they should believe and what they should fear.

Since Your Piety and your most religious will must be obeyed in every way, I gladly added my judgment to the synodal decrees that pleased me concerning the confirmation of the Catholic faith and the condemnation of heretics. If Your Clemency deigns to order that this be brought to the knowledge of all bishops and Churches, I believe and hope that the grace of God will be present, granting so holy a care on the part of so great a ruler the fullest fruit of its desire, so that, once every opportunity for dissent has been removed, peace and truth may reign everywhere according to apostolic teaching.

Your Clemency should know that I have specifically entrusted my brother Bishop Julian with this task: whatever he proves to concern the safeguarding of the faith there, he is confidently to bring to the attention of Your Piety in my name. For I am certain that, with God’s help, you are sufficient to correct or defend all these matters.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the illustrious man Opilio, in the year 416 of the era.

### XXXII.—To the Same

**Leo, bishop, to the Emperor Marcian.**

You demonstrate the purity of the Christian faith with which Your Clemency shines forth also in these letters, delivered by my brother and fellow bishop Nestor­ianus, in which you extend the most just favor to my brother Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, thereby making him in every respect more acceptable to me. Anyone to whom Your Piety deigns to bear witness would undoubtedly have to be approved, even if he were silent. But his grace is increased by the fact that he is also known through his own speech, and that he is a sincere preacher of Catholic doctrine is made clear by his own profession.

Therefore, with the fullest affection, I embrace the love of this orthodox brother and give thanks to God, who, after removing him who wished to oppose the Gospel of Christ and to dissent from the understanding of the holy Fathers, provided the Church of Alexandria with such a bishop that he agrees with his predecessors both in faith and in life. For when he professes with all his heart that he embraces my letter which I sent against the impious Eutyches to Flavian of blessed memory, what else does he show himself to be than a disciple of the apostles? The doctrine of truth remains in its own light, and what is one and divine cannot be different from itself.

I have therefore written to the aforementioned brother what I ought to write and exhorted him to persevere in his holy devotion. He will undoubtedly be more steadfast if Your Clemency also supports him with exhortations, and the ignorant dissent of certain men should not frighten him in any way—men whom the instigation of a few heretics, through their ignorance, makes liable to error.

What they cannot attain by their own diligence should suitably be brought to their hearing. And, lest he appear to be introducing something new or asserting something of his own, let the writings of the venerable Fathers who presided over that Church be read again, and let them recognize what blessed Athanasius, Theophilus, Cyril, and also the Eastern teachers thought concerning the Lord’s incarnation. Let them not be deceived by errors sprouting again, errors that were once struck down by the power of evangelical speech.

For nearly all the heresies that have arisen at different times, by failing to understand the mystery of Christ’s bodily birth, passion, and resurrection, show themselves to have departed from the Gospel. We could labor less in rejecting heretics if those falsehoods that antiquity destroyed did not themselves disturb inexperienced minds.

But now, as I have said, the best method of instruction is that the line of the Fathers’ teaching should become known to the ears of the Alexandrian people and clergy. If there are any who despise our writings, let them at least yield to those who agree with us in apostolic understanding. I shall rejoice greatly in the devotion of my fellow priest in this work, and I shall always be glad of his unanimity, because fraternal peace is preserved only by one confession of faith.

Since, however, the cunning wickedness of certain heretics is said to have falsified the letter that I sent to Flavian of blessed memory, in order to disturb the simplicity of others, so that, by changing certain words or syllables, they might claim that I accepted the error of Nestorius, I beseech Your Venerable Clemency to order that the same letter, fully and carefully translated into Greek by my brother Bishop Julian or by those whom Your Piety selects as suitable for the task, be delivered by a trustworthy bearer under the impression of your seal to the judges of Alexandria. They are to have it read to the clergy and people of that city together with the preaching of the aforementioned bishops, who also agree with my writing, so that they may recognize that they ought no longer to be deceived by the fraud of deceitful men and may prove themselves sincere disciples of the Apostolic See, where neither Eutyches nor Nestorius has any place. For, just as it condemned other heretics, so the universal Church has condemned these men also.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the illustrious men Aetius and Studius, in the year 492 of the era.

### 200. XXXIII.—To the Same

**Leo, bishop, to the Emperor Marcian.**

That the holy zeal of Your Piety for the Christian religion persists and grows through many glorious increases, as has been demonstrated very often by numerous proofs, and that this faith of Your Clemency consoles and strengthens not only me but also all the priests of the Lord, is evident while we experience priestly devotion in a Christian emperor. If the priests of the Eastern regions strive to imitate you, neither peace nor the Christian faith will suffer any scandals.

Accordingly, since the bishop of Constantinople is instructed by the present example of Your Clemency toward every advancement in piety, if he faithfully follows your exhortations, he has in me a disposition of sincere favor—provided that he fulfills in his heart what he promises in words. But if he deliberately chooses what displeases God and Your Piety, then, with due respect for your gentleness, I shall act with greater freedom against the proud man, together with all and on behalf of all, while you also strive against him. As I must often say, I would rather embrace him in brotherly charity for his holy actions, most glorious Emperor.

Since you have willingly received my petitions for the tranquility of the Catholic faith, know what has been reported to me by the speech of my brother and fellow bishop Julian: that the impious Eutyches is indeed exiled according to his deserts, but in the very place of his condemnation is pouring forth many poisons of blasphemy against Catholic integrity, and is vomiting up, with even greater shamelessness so that he may deceive the innocent, what the whole world shuddered at and condemned in him.

I therefore consider it entirely reasonable that Your Clemency order him to be transferred to a more distant and more secluded place. As for his monastery established at Constantinople, where its inhabitants, the monks themselves, need to be strengthened more frequently and more fully in evangelical and apostolic teaching, I believe it will be beneficial if the man said to be placed in charge of that monastery does not withdraw from the company of your venerable Julian, the bishop whom I appointed to be there as a watchman for the faith. Through his constant visitation, the progress of the servants of God who live there may be increased.

I rejoice that my request concerning the date of Easter was received by Your Piety in such a way that you immediately sent an *agent in public affairs* to Alexandria to remove the error that the constitution of Theophilus of blessed memory appears to have introduced. Concerning this matter, since you deign to write that whatever is brought to Your Piety’s attention should be reported to me, order me to know it, so that the universal Church may recognize what is especially to be observed concerning a practice that must not differ.

I also ask what I know accords with Your Clemency: that you especially protect against every plot those whom you recognize to be pleasing to me and to your gentleness for the love of God, so that the bishop of Constantinople may have no power to harm them.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of the illustrious men Aetius and Studius, in the year of the era stated above.

### XXXIV.—To Julian, Bishop of Cos

**Leo to Julian, bishop of Cos, concerning Aetius and Andrew.**

I recognized in your letter the affection of fraternal charity, since you share with us in pious grief over the many and severe evils that we have endured. But may those things which the Lord has either permitted or willed us to suffer contribute to the correction of many, so that adversities may cease and offenses come to an end. Both will be the result of God’s great mercy if he removes the scourges and turns the hearts of his people back to himself.

Just as the hostility that existed among us saddened the brotherhood, so it makes me anxious that, as your letters indicate, the plots of heretics do not cease in the Church of Constantinople and that, when opportunities are sought, those who were defenders of the Catholic faith are harassed. For while Aetius is removed from the office of archdeacon under the pretext of promotion, and Andrew, who had been rejected because of his association with heretics, is appointed in his place; while honor is restored to the accusers of Flavian of blessed memory, and the companions or disciples of the most pious confessor are despised, it is shown all too openly what pleases Christ in his Church.

I defer acting against him according to the merits of the case. I am awaiting what he himself will do with me in the letters which our son Aetius has indicated that he will send, allowing room for voluntary correction, by which I desire my grief to be mitigated. Nevertheless, I have written to the most clement emperor and the most pious Augusta concerning matters belonging to the preservation of ecclesiastical peace. I do not doubt that, through their devotion to the faith, they will take precautions so that condemned heresy cannot sprout again against the glory of their work.

Therefore, dearest brother, let your Love diligently devote a pious and necessary care to the concern of the Apostolic See. It entrusts to you, as one nurtured in its household, the Catholic cause against the heretics Nestorians and Eutychians by maternal right. Supported by divine assistance, do not cease to keep watch over the advantageous position of the city of Constantinople, so that the impious disturbance of those doctrines may never arise.

And since the Clemency of the glorious rulers is so great that you can confidently bring to their attention whatever ought to be reported, use their piety for the benefit of the universal Church. If your Love consults me concerning matters about which you think there may be uncertainty, my instructions will not be lacking in response to your reports. Thus, setting aside their proceedings, you may exercise this special care in my place in cases that ought to be established by the judgment of their bishops in whatever Churches they occur, so that the Nestorian or Eutychian heresy may not revive in any region.

For there is no Catholic vigor in the bishop of Constantinople, nor is he greatly concerned either for the mystery of human salvation or for his own reputation. If he possessed any spiritual diligence, he ought to consider both by whom he was ordained and whose successor he became, so that he might follow blessed Flavian rather than the authors of his own honor.

And therefore, since the most pious rulers deigned, in accordance with my entreaties, to rebuke my brother Anatolius concerning matters that rightly provoke complaint, let your Love persevere in its diligence, so that all the scandals may be reviewed with the fullest correction and the injury to our son and to you may cease.

For in the case of a Catholic bishop, even if the archdeacon possessed some degree of priestly distinction, he ought, out of reverence for the faith, to have been advanced rather than have the place of a Catholic occupied by a most wicked heretic. When I learn what follows, I shall judge more clearly what ought to be done. For the time being, restraining my grief, I prefer to allow patience, so that there may be room for pardon.

As for the monks of Palestine, who are said to have been in an uproar of dissension for some time, I do not know with what attitude they are still moved. Nor has anyone’s speech disclosed to me what causes they appear to advance in support of their former discord: whether they serve Eutychian perversity with such fury, or whether they are implacably grieved that their own man could be handed over to this impiety, which has departed from the truth of the Lord’s incarnation contrary to the testimony of those holy places by which the whole world is instructed, and whether they think that what it pleased us to cure in others through indulgence is not pardonable in him.

I therefore wish to be more fully informed about these matters, so that suitable correction may also be undertaken in their case. For it is one thing to arm oneself impiously against the faith, and another to be held in some error.

You should also know that the documents which the presbyter Actius previously indicated had been sent, and the summary of the faith which you say you sent, have not yet reached me. Therefore, if a more convenient opportunity presents itself, I shall gladly receive bearers, so that whatever instruction appears useful may be sent to me as soon as possible.

I wish to know how peaceful the Egyptian monks are and what their faith is, and what true reports reach you concerning the peace of the Church of Alexandria. I wished you to know, by copies having been sent, what other letters I have directed to its bishop, to those who ordained him, and to the clergy. The copies will also show what my present message is to the most clement emperor and the most religious Augusta.

I wish to know whether the letter concerning the faith of the Lord’s incarnation, which I sent to your Love through the deacon Basil while Flavian of holy memory was still alive, was delivered to your brotherhood, since I suspect this because you have never rendered any judgment concerning its text.

The instruction we possess concerning the acts of the synod conducted on every day of the council in the city of Chalcedon is not sufficiently clear because of the difference of language. Therefore I specifically charge your Brotherhood to have all the proceedings gathered into a single codex, translated into Latin in a completely finished version, so that we may have no doubt about any part of the acts and there may in no way be ambiguity concerning what, through your diligence, has been brought to full understanding.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the illustrious man Opilio.

### XXXV.—To the Emperor Marcian

**Leo to the Emperor Marcian, concerning Aetius and Andrew.**

The whole world recognizes with what outstanding piety and glorious zeal of Your Clemency the Christian faith has recently been restored in its entirety, and that through you the Lord has restored a singular safeguard for its salvation. If anything contrary to the completion of so great a work is perceived to arise from an opposing spirit, it is necessary that it be referred to the aid of Your Piety, which divine providence prepared for the protection of Catholic truth. Since it belongs to Your Piety to cut off scandals even when they arise far away, all the more must you not allow those that dare to arise beneath your eyes to grow.

The authors of the consecration of Bishop Anatolius had made me suspicious of his ordination, as God is my witness, and I considered the one elected to be no different from those who elected him. It followed that, while he remained separated from the communion of the Apostolic See, I refrained for a long time from sending him letters of peace.

But when the testimony of Your Piety supported him, and when he promised everything desirable and pleasing concerning his faith and unanimity, I believed his profession to be so sincere that I did not cease to remind him of the observance by which he ought to act. I earnestly and carefully impressed upon him that he should dare to keep no one in his company who had persecuted Flavian of blessed memory, and that he should declare the defender of the Eutychian heresy to have been expelled by him.

It then followed that, concerning what had been defined in the synodal council for the Catholic faith, he wrote me such things as it was fitting for a Catholic bishop to write.

Since these things had preceded in order to commend his beginnings, what cause or occasion arose that he should, under the pretext of honor, so resolutely degrade a man of the Catholic faith and an opponent of the Nestorian and Eutychian heretics, even in the case of an archdeacon, and suddenly transfer the administration of the entire ecclesiastical case and responsibility to Andrew the Eutychianist? He was so disturbed by excessive agitation that he inflicted the ordination which he gave as an injury on the sixth day of the week, contrary to apostolic tradition, as though ignorant or forgetful—as if the fault of that ordination belonged more to a bishop than to a presbyter, who, finding nothing in the man’s faith to accuse and nothing in his conduct to condemn, carried out the degradation of an innocent man under the appearance of promotion, adding this insult to his sentence: that he condemned him to exile by assigning him to a cemetery.

Nevertheless, I venture to commend him [Aetius] to Your Piety, so that the bishop may no longer be able to oppress him with further injuries or plot against one whom, as I have learned, the Lord has placed under your protection.

I also add this petition: deign necessarily to rebuke the aforementioned bishop, who is discordant with his own profession and has forgotten too greatly the testimony and favor you gave him. Let him cease harassing Catholics. Let him cease crushing those who pleased Flavian of holy memory and choosing the company of those whom Flavian rejected. We shall be able to show him brotherly charity only if he proves that he detests the enemies of the Catholic faith and cuts off their companionship and association from himself. Even if that man had been cleansed by great satisfaction, yet having returned to error after “doubt” [reading uncertain], he ought to be placed after Catholic deacons, not before them.

I also ask the benevolence of Your Clemency to hold our venerable brother Bishop Julian in your affection, as you graciously do, so that through his services the image of my presence may be restored to you. Confident in the sincerity of his faith, I have delegated my role to him against the heretics of our time, and, for the protection of the Churches and of peace, I required that he not be absent from your court. Deign to hear his petitions for the harmony of Catholic unity as though they were mine, pleasing God, who may grant you, beyond the royal crown, also the priestly palm.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the illustrious man Opilio.

### XXXVI.—To the Empress Pulcheria

**Leo to Pulcheria Augusta, concerning Aetius and Andrew.**

Since there are many documents by which Your Piety’s affection for the Church of God is shown, it is rightly desired, whenever any scandal becomes known, that your assistance be given, so that the faith which, with your support, was defended against the inventions of heretics may possess the lasting firmness of secure peace.

For what benefit is it that the adversaries of truth have been crushed outside if we have them revived within the Lord’s enclosure?

What I have learned to have been done concerning my son Aetius makes me exceedingly anxious and compels me, for good reason, to fear that I may have cause to regret having accepted, at your urging, better expectations concerning the bishop of Constantinople, who had been ordained by the opponents of the faith, when he was being supported by so great a testimony of Your Piety, lest the weakness of his ordination burden him where your intervention was present.

I had therefore begun to rejoice that he honored the memory of blessed Flavian and was said to resist the efforts of heretics. But I grieve that he has changed for the worse, as the aforementioned lamentable complaint shows, and that he has now appointed as archdeacon the very man whom he himself professed to have rejected, who had revealed himself among us as a defender of the Eutychian heresy.

Since he has now placed this man in charge of ecclesiastical affairs, he is proved, on account of his heretical perversity, to be granting him his favor. Even if that man could have merited pardon through great satisfaction, he should by no means have been placed before those who had remained in the faith.

Therefore, since it is not hidden from Your Clemency how much danger is being nourished either by shameful negligence or by deceitful wickedness, deign by the authority of Your Clemency to recall the bishop to the profession of his faith, lest he impose these stains upon himself, lest he despise the reputation he acquired through your favor, and lest he fail to sever his association with the heretic whom he formerly removed from himself.

I rejoice that you so stood by Aetius’s innocence that Your Piety came to his grief with worthy consolation.

Concerning my brother, your venerable Bishop Julian, judge how greatly your favor ought to increase toward him in the Apostolic See. In the cause of the faith, to which your glory ministers, I have delegated my role to him to such an extent that, without departing from the observance owed to you, he may not cease to present me to Your Piety. In the safeguarding of the faith and ecclesiastical discipline he carries out every aspect of this responsibility, and through timely petitions he makes known whatever may benefit the universal Church, so that through him neither your protection may be lacking to the Catholics whom we wish to assist, nor my service to you.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the illustrious man Opilio.

### XXXVII.—To the Same

**Leo, bishop, to Pulcheria Augusta.**

What we have always presumed concerning the mind of Your Piety, we have learned fully by experience: although the Christian faith was attacked by the various plots of the wicked, it could not be disturbed while you were present and prepared by the Lord for its defense.

For God does not abandon either the mystery of his mercy or the merit of your labor. Through it you once drove the deceitful enemy of holy religion from the very entrails of the Church, when Nestorian impiety could not defend its heresy, because the servant and disciple of truth was not deceived by how much poison was poured into the simple through the disguised falsehoods of that loquacious man.

From this struggle of virtues it came about, through your vigilance, that what the devil contrived through Eutyches did not remain hidden, so that those who had chosen the separate parts of a twofold impiety might fall by the single power of the Catholic faith.

This, therefore, is a second victory for you over the destroyed error of Eutyches. If he had possessed any soundness of heart, he could long ago have avoided it, struck down in its authors and overthrown in the past, so that he would not attempt to stir up renewed fires from buried ashes, by passing into the company of those whose example he had followed, most glorious Augusta.

I therefore gladly exult with joy and offer worthy vows to God for the prosperity of Your Clemency, since throughout all the regions of the world where the Gospel of the Lord is preached he has already bestowed upon you both a double palm and a double crown.

Let Your Clemency therefore recognize that the entire Roman Church greatly rejoices in all the resources of your faith: both because you assisted our embassy in every respect with pious affection, and because you restored the Catholic bishops who had been unjustly expelled from their Churches, and because you caused the relics of Flavian of holy memory, an innocent and Catholic bishop, to be brought back with due honor to the Church over which he had rightly presided.

In all these things the increase of your glory is multiplied, since you both venerate the saints according to their merits and wish thorns and thistles to be removed from the Lord’s field.

We have learned through reports, both of our representatives and of my brother and fellow bishop Anatolius, to whom you deign to bear witness, that certain bishops who appear to have given their consent to impious affairs are seeking reconciliation and desiring communion with the Catholics. We grant effect to their desires in such a way that, once they have been corrected and have condemned by their own signatures the things wrongly done, communion may be granted to them through the care shared by our representatives and the aforementioned bishop for the sake of peace. For both belong to Christian devotion: truth should justly restrain the obstinate, and charity should not reject those who have converted.

Since we know how much your gentleness deigns to bestow its pious solicitude upon Catholic bishops, we have considered it necessary to inform you that our brother and fellow bishop Eusebius lives with us and shares in our communion. We commend to you his Church, which, it is said, is being devastated by the man unjustly asserted to have been substituted for him.

We also ask this of Your Piety—something which we do not doubt you would do of your own accord—that you favor both my brother and fellow bishop Julian and the clergy of Constantinople who adhered to Flavian of holy memory with faithful service, with the favor that you ought to show them.

Concerning all these matters we have instructed Your Piety through our representatives about what ought to be done or avoided.

Given on the Ides of April, in the consulship of the illustrious man Adelphius, in the year 488 of the era.

### XXXVIII.—To Julian, Bishop of Cos

**Leo to Julian, bishop of Cos.**
The letter of your Affection, which you sent through my son, the illustrious man Isicius, I received at the time when I had already replied to your more recent letters on a renewed occasion [Col. 0817C]. Since in this address also you complained with righteous grief about the same most impious heretics, it was fitting, while the opportunity for writing presented itself, not to remain silent.

In the matter of the faith, whatever our office has required—and, with the Lord’s help, is able to accomplish—we carry out both diligently and willingly, so that we may serve the Gospel irreproachably and so that no part of the Catholic Church may seem neglected through our indolence. For this reason, as is known to all, I have not ceased laboring so that, once the truth of the Lord’s Incarnation had been made manifest and defended, the entire brotherhood might recognize what, according to apostolic teaching, must everywhere be held and taught. The zeal of the most glorious rulers, inspired by God, contributed to this end, so that, when a synod had assembled in the city of Chalcedon [Col. 0817D], heretical impiety might be condemned, and neither any follower of Nestorius nor any disciple of Eutyches might be able to maintain free association with Catholics. With regard to the authority of the holy council, no disagreement has anywhere remained.

If, however, some people, blinded by their own hardening, have passed into the madness of a reprobate mind so completely that they prefer to rage rather than be healed, it belongs to the imperial power to ensure that the disturbers of the Church’s peace, and enemies of the state—which rightly glories in its Christian rulers—are more diligently restrained. Just as it is, as we have said, the duty of imperial authority to suppress public disturbances and sacrilegious seditions with greater severity, so it belongs to priestly authority not to allow monks any license to preach something contrary to the faith, and to resist every form of presumption [Col. 0818A], lest they dare to claim for themselves what belongs to priests.

For this reason we are astonished that our brother Bishop Thalassius should have permitted some capacity for writing or preaching to a certain George—whoever he may be—who, by presuming upon what was unlawful, has lost both the monastic profession and the name. If it seems good to your Affection, let us send suitable letters on this matter to that bishop.

Let your Fraternity therefore act through appropriate representations, so that the most clement ruler may order what is pleasing to the Lord and command that the instigators of bloody seditions be suitably restrained, so that neither those whose hands perpetrated the crimes nor those who make use of such madness may go unpunished. But if judicial investigation and the confession of the guilty lead to persons by whose advice or incitement such great evils were committed [Col. 0818B], no protection of favoritism is to be granted them. For the better their reputation was believed to be, the more detestable they are, since their impiety, which had been concealed under hypocrisy, is now exposed.

Therefore let the most Christian and most devout emperor do what he understands will benefit ecclesiastical peace. Trust that he will be instructed by heavenly inspiration in such a way that he may recall the restless to discipline and order that their blood be spared, although those who have dared to oppose both divine and human constitutions deserve every punishment.

### XXXIX—To Eudocia Augusta

**Leo to Eudocia Augusta concerning the monks of Palestine.**

I do not doubt that your Piety knows how great is my concern for the Catholic faith and with what care, insofar as the Lord assists, one must guard against the Gospel of truth ever being resisted by the ignorant and impious [Col. 0818C]. Therefore, together with the greeting by which I must always address your Clemency in prayer, I beseech the Lord to make me increasingly able to assist your well-being in the cause of the faith, in which the hearts of certain monks throughout the province of Palestine had been disturbed, so that, as far as can be accomplished through the zeal of your Piety, every confidence may be removed from heretical perversity.

For those whom neither the reasoning of the sacraments, nor the authority of the Scriptures, nor even the testimony of the consecrated places moved—what could be feared for them except utter ruin? May it therefore benefit the churches, as by God’s favor it does and will benefit them, and may it benefit the human race, that your will is there in the words of God where they speak to you of our Lord Jesus Christ as true God and also true man in the unity of person, and speak to you both of the judgments of his miracles and of the evidences of his sufferings [Col. 0818D].

If, then, the aforesaid men venerate and love the Catholic name, and wish to be called members within the Lord’s body, let them condemn the perverse errors which they rashly admitted and do penance for their impious blasphemies and bloody deeds. Let them submit, for the salvation of their souls, to the synodal decrees confirmed in the city of Chalcedon. And because no one reaches an understanding of the mystery of human salvation except through true faith and a quiet humility, let them believe in the Gospel, which they confess in the Creed, and not mingle with impious doctrines.

For the Catholic faith [Col. 0819A], just as it condemns Nestorius, who dared to proclaim two persons in our one Lord Jesus Christ, so it also condemns Eutyches together with Dioscorus, because they deny that the reality of human flesh was assumed from the Virgin Mother in the womb by the only-begotten Word of God.

If your exhortation has achieved anything concerning the conversion of the aforesaid men—a result that will win you eternal glory—I ask that you inform me of it by letters from your Clemency, so that I may rejoice both in the fruit of good work in you and in the fact that the Lord’s mercy has not perished for them.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Opilio.

### XL—Pope Leo’s Letter

I have very frequently urged your Affection in my letters to devote yourself to this concern and diligence, so that you might continually inform me about what was being done regarding the faith, while I myself never cease writing on every occasion [Col. 0819B]. Yet I have received no reply from your Fraternity to certain letters of mine delivered through our son Rodanus, *domesticus* of our son, the illustrious man Aspiratius—as though the circumstances of the time had not allowed you to report what had occurred after my letters.

Therefore, through my son Rodanus, I greet you in this letter and admonish you not to neglect the opportunity for writing; in this matter the complaint of my concern is revealed. Since those in Constantinople possess in you a certain portion of me, it is worthy both of our common friendship and of your love for the whole Church that you watch with unceasing vigor, lest anything concerning the state of the faith remain hidden from me.

Therefore labor through suitable representations to ensure that what I wrote through the aforesaid persons either to the most glorious ruler or to your Affection [Col. 0819C] is brought into effect as quickly as possible. And whatever, with God’s help, has been arranged, let me know, so that, once the measures reasonably ordained have been carried out, the peace of the faith and the observance of the canons may everywhere be both more secure and stronger.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Opilio.

### XLI—To the Palestinians

**Leo to the Palestinians.**

It has been made clear to my concern—which I owe to the universal Church and to all her children—through the reports of many that something has caused offense in the minds of your Affections. Either inexperienced interpreters, as it appears, or malicious ones have caused you to understand certain things differently from what I said, being unable to translate Latin aptly and precisely into Greek [Col. 0819D]. In explaining subtle and difficult matters, each disputant can scarcely suffice even in his own language.

This, however, has produced one good result for me: when we understand that you are more friendly toward the truth than toward falsehood, we recognize that you rightly reject what even Eutyches himself detests on the basis of the ancient doctrinal tradition.

Although my letter to the bishop Flavian of holy memory, once delivered, is itself entirely sufficient to make its meaning clear and requires no purification or exposition in any respect, other writings of mine nevertheless agree with it, and in them likewise the sense of my teaching is openly expressed. For I was obliged to argue against the heretics who had disturbed many peoples of Christ [Col. 0820A], and I made clear both to the most clement rulers, to the holy synodal council, and to the Church of Constantinople what we ought to know and believe concerning the Incarnation of the Word according to evangelical and apostolic teaching. In no respect did I depart from the confession of the holy Fathers, because the Catholic faith is one, true, unique, perfect, and inviolable; nothing can be added to it or taken from it.

Nestorius first, and now Eutyches, have attempted to attack this faith with different assertions but similar impiety, and they have tried to introduce into the Church of God two heresies opposed to one another. Both were rightly condemned by the disciples of truth, because what they both believed, though in differing falsehoods, was exceedingly insane and sacrilegious.

Let Nestorius therefore be anathematized, because he believed the blessed Virgin Mary to be merely the mother of a man, making one person of the flesh and another of the divinity. He did not understand one Christ in the Word of God and in the flesh, but separately and apart proclaimed one Son of God and another son of man. Yet the immutable essence of the Word, which is timeless and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, remained unchanged; and the Word became flesh within the Virgin’s womb in such a way that, by one conception and one birth, the same Virgin, according to the union of both substances, was both the Lord’s handmaid and his mother.

Elizabeth also understood this, as the Evangelist declares, and said: “And whence is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43).

Let Eutyches also be struck by the same anathema. Having been tossed about amid the impious errors of the ancient heretics, he chose the third doctrine of Apollinaris, so that, by denying the reality of human flesh and soul, he might assert that our entire Lord Jesus Christ is of one nature—as though the divinity of the Word itself had been converted into flesh and soul. Thus, according to him, it would belong solely to that one essence to be conceived and born, nourished and to grow, crucified and to die, buried and to rise again, ascend into heaven, and sit at the Father’s right hand, from which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

But the nature of the Only-begotten is the nature of the Father and the nature of the Holy Spirit; it is simultaneously impassible and immutable, the undivided unity and consubstantial equality of the eternal Trinity.

Thus, although this heretic departs from the perversity of Apollinaris so as not to be convicted of believing the divinity to be passible and mortal, nevertheless, daring to proclaim one nature of the incarnate Word—that is, of the Word and the flesh—he unmistakably passes into the madness of Mani and Marcion. He believes that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, acted only in appearance, and that there was not a human body in him but merely a phantom-like bodily form appeared to the eyes of those who saw him.

Because the Catholic faith has long detested these impious falsehoods, and because the sacrileges of such men have been condemned by the concordant judgments of the blessed Fathers throughout the world, let all who are so blinded and alienated from the light of truth that they deny the Word of God to possess, from the time of the Incarnation, a human—that is, our—nature show in what respect they claim the Christian name [Col. 0821A]. And let them show on what grounds they claim the Christian name, and, in accordance with the Gospel of truth, by what reasoning divinity is—or whether divinity arose—without flesh [the Latin is syntactically corrupt].

For if it cannot be denied that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (Matthew 1:14, as cited in the source), neither can it be denied that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. What reconciliation could there be by which God might be propitiated toward the human race unless the mediator between God and humanity assumed the cause of all? And how could he fulfill the truth of mediation unless he were a participant in us in the form of a servant? Thus, through one new human being, the renewal of the old might take place, and the bond of death contracted through one transgression might be dissolved by the death of the one person who alone owed nothing to death.

For the shedding of the blood of the just one on behalf of the unjust was so powerful for privilege and so rich as a price that, if the whole company of captives believed in its Redeemer, no one would remain held by tyrannical bonds. As the Apostle says: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Romans 5:20). And although those born under the condemnation of sin received the power to be reborn into righteousness, the gift of freedom became stronger than the debt of slavery [Col. 0821B].

What hope, then, do they leave themselves in the protection of this mystery who deny the reality of human substance in the body of our Savior? Let them say in what sacrifice they were reconciled; let them say by what blood they were redeemed. Who is he “who gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling aroma” (Ephesians 5:2)? Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true high priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh?

Although “the death of many saints has been precious in the sight of the Lord” (Psalm 115:15), the killing of that innocent one was nevertheless the propitiation of the world. The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. From the courage of the faithful came examples of patience, not gifts of righteousness.

For their deaths were individual, each one belonging to a single person, and no one paid another’s debt by his own end. But among the children of human beings there has been one Lord alone, Jesus Christ, in whom all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised. Of them he himself said: “When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

True faith, which justifies the ungodly and creates the righteous, seeks salvation for humanity by drawing it into participation in his humanity—in him alone in whom the human being finds himself innocent. Through God’s grace, humanity is free to glory in his power: he confronted the proud enemy in the humility of our flesh and granted his victory to those in whose body he triumphed [Col. 0821D].

Although in the one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and true son of man, there is one person of the Word and the flesh, and although both essences possess common actions, the qualities of those actions must nevertheless be understood. With the contemplation of sincere faith, we must discern toward what the humility of weakness is raised and toward what the height of power inclines: what the flesh does not do without the Word, and what the Word does not accomplish without the flesh.

Without the power of the Word, the Virgin would neither conceive nor give birth; without the reality of the flesh, infancy wrapped in swaddling clothes would not lie there. Without the power of the Word, the Magi would not adore the child revealed by the new star; without the reality of the flesh, the child would not be ordered to be carried into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution.

Without the power of the Word, the voice of the Father sent from heaven would not say, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17); without the reality of the flesh, John would not testify: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

Without the power of the Word there would be neither the restoration of the weak nor the giving of life to the dead; without the reality of the flesh, neither food would be necessary for one who was fasting nor sleep for one who was weary. Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not declare himself equal to the Father; without the reality of the flesh, he would not say that the Father is greater than he. The Catholic faith accepts and defends both statements: according to the proper character of the divine and human substance, it believes the one Son of God to be both human and the Word [Col. 0822B].

Although, therefore, from that beginning when the Word became flesh in the Virgin’s womb there has never been any division between the divine and human substance, so that through all bodily development the actions of the entire period belonged to one person, we must nevertheless not confuse what was inseparably done through any mixture. Rather, from the character of the works we discern what belongs to which form. For the divine things do not prejudice the human, nor the human the divine, since both converge into one in such a way that neither their proper character is removed nor the person multiplied.

Let these phantom-Christians say, then, what substance was fastened to the wood, what substance lay in the tomb, what flesh rose on the third day when the stone of the monument had been rolled away, and what sort of body Jesus brought before the eyes of his disciples when he entered while the doors were shut. To dispel the disbelief of those who saw him, he demanded that the still-open marks of the nails and the freshly pierced wound in his side be examined with the eyes and handled with the fingers [Col. 0822C].

And if heretical obstinacy does not abandon its darkness in so great a light of truth, let them show from where they promise themselves the hope of eternal life, to which no one can attain except through the mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ.

“For there is no other name given to human beings under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12); nor is there redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him who gave himself as a redemption for all.

As the blessed Apostle proclaims: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Ephesians 2:6–11, as cited in the source) [Col. 0822D–0823A].

Although, therefore, there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and although in him there is one wholly identical person of true divinity and true humanity, and although the integrity of this union cannot be separated by any division, we understand the exaltation by which God exalted him and gave him the name above every name to belong to that form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glorification.

In the form of God, the Son was equal to the Father; between the Begetter and the Only-begotten there was no distinction in essence and no difference in majesty. Through the mystery of the Incarnation, nothing had departed from the Word that could be restored to him as the Father’s gift. But the form of a servant, through which the impassible divinity fulfilled the mystery of great devotion, is human humility, and it was raised into the glory of divine power. From the very conception in the Virgin, divinity and humanity were joined in such unity that neither divine things were done without humanity nor human things without God.

Therefore, just as the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, so he who is eternally equal to God is said to have been exalted. It makes no difference from which substance Christ is named, since, with the unity of person remaining inseparable, the same one is wholly the son of man because of the flesh and wholly the Son of God because of the one divinity he shares with the Father.

Whatever Christ received in time, he received according to his humanity, to which were conferred the things it did not possess. According to the power of the Word, the Son possesses without distinction everything that the Father possesses; and what he received from the Father in the form of a servant, he himself also bestowed in the form of the Father. The same one is both rich and poor.

Rich, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3) [Col. 0823C]. Poor, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

What, then, is his emptying and what his poverty, except the taking of the form of a servant, through which, while the majesty of the Word was veiled, the dispensation of human redemption was fulfilled?

For since the original bonds of our captivity could not be undone or released from the power of the enemy unless there existed a human being of our race and our nature, whom the condemnation of the ancient debt did not hold and who might erase the deadly bond with his undefiled blood, what had been divinely ordained from the beginning and announced beforehand through the prophetic oracles was accomplished at the fullness of the appointed time. Thus the promise signified in many ways came to the long-awaited fulfillment, and what had always been announced through continuous signs could not remain uncertain [Col. 0823D].

Since so many heresies have therefore been destroyed—heresies which, through the holy devotion of the presiding Fathers, were cut off from the body of Catholic unity, and which deserved to be exiled from Christ because they made the Incarnation of the Word, the unique salvation of those who rightly believe, for themselves “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Romans 9:36, as cited in the source)—I am astonished that your Affection struggles to discern the light of truth.

Since it has been made clear through so many manifestations how rightly the Christian faith condemned both Nestorius and Eutyches with Dioscorus, no one who assents either to the impiety of the former or to that of the latter can be called a Christian.

I grieve that, as I hear, you resist evangelical and apostolic teaching, stirring up cities through seditions, disturbing churches, and inflicting not only injuries but even killings upon presbyters and bishops [Col. 0824A], so that, through the fury and savagery of your purpose, you have forgotten your profession.

Where is the rule of gentleness and quiet? Where is the patience of long-suffering? Where is the tranquility of peace? Where is the foundation of love and the strength of endurance? What persuasion has drawn you away from the Gospel of Christ, or what persecution has separated you from it? What such great cunning of the deceiver has arisen that, forgetting the prophets and the apostles, forgetting the saving Creed and the confession by which, in the presence of many witnesses, you received the sacrament of baptism, you have subjected yourselves to diabolical illusions?

What would claws have accomplished against you, what savage tortures, if the empty inventions of heretics were sufficient to overthrow the integrity of your faith [Col. 0824B]? You believe that you act for the faith, yet you oppose the faith. You arm yourselves in the name of the Church, yet you fight against the Church.

Did you learn this from the prophets, the evangelists, and the apostles: to deny the flesh of Christ, to subject the very essence of the Word to suffering and death, to make our nature alien from its restorer, and to claim that everything brought about by the cross, wounded by the lance, and received and returned by the stone of the tomb was solely the work of divine power and not also of human humility?

For this reason the Apostle says: “I am not ashamed of the Gospel” (Romans 1:16), because he knew what reproach the enemies would cast upon Christians. Therefore the Lord testified, saying: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess him before my Father” (Matthew 10:32) [Col. 0824C].

Those who are now ashamed of Christ’s flesh will not be worthy of the confession of the Son and the Father. They will prove that they have received no power from the wood of the cross, since they are ashamed to utter with their lips what they received to carry upon their foreheads.

Turn away, children, from these diabolical persuasions; turn away. No circumstance violates God’s truth, but the truth does not save us except in our flesh. For “truth,” as the prophet says, “has sprung from the earth” (Psalm 84:12). Thus the Word was conceived by Mary, so that she might provide from her own substance the flesh to be united to him—neither with the addition of another person nor with the dissolution of nature. He who was in the form of God took the form of a servant in such a way that one and the same Christ exists in both forms: God inclining himself to the lowest things of humanity, and humanity advancing to the highest things of divinity.

As the Apostle says: “Theirs are the Fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5). Amen.

### XLII—To Bishop Theodoric

**Leo to Theodoric, bishop, concerning perseverance in the faith.**
[Col. 0825A] When our brothers and fellow priests whom the See of blessed Peter had sent to the holy council returned to us, we recognized that your devotion, with heavenly assistance, had proved victorious with us over both Nestorian impiety and Eutychian madness. Therefore we glory in the Lord, singing with the Prophet: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 123:8).

He did not permit us to suffer any loss in our brothers, but confirmed by the irrevocable assent of the whole brotherhood what he had previously established through our ministry, thus truly showing that it was advantageous that the judgment first framed by the foremost of all sees should receive the judgment of the entire Christian world, so that in this matter too the members might agree with the head.

[Col. 0825B] This gives us all the greater cause for rejoicing, since the enemy was struck all the more heavily when a servant rose up against the ministers of Christ. For, lest the absence of agreement from the other sees with the one which the Lord established to preside over all the rest should appear significant, or lest any other unfavorable suspicion should insinuate itself, there were first found men who doubted our judgments. And while some, incited to dissension by the author of contradiction, rush into mad conflicts, his evil is turned toward a greater good by the dispensation of the Author of all goodness.

Indeed, the gifts of divine grace come more sweetly whenever they are acquired only after great exertions. Peace maintained through leisure is usually thought less valuable than peace restored after labor. Truth itself also shines more clearly and is held more firmly when examination subsequently confirms what faith had previously taught.

[Col. 0825C] Finally, the dignity of priestly office shines greatly when the authority of the highest is preserved in such a way that the liberty of those below is not thought to have been diminished at all. The conclusion of the examination also contributes to greater glory when the confidence to undertake it was accepted for this purpose: that adversity might be overcome, lest what is proved in itself should seem to have been suppressed by the prejudice of silence.

Rejoice, therefore, dearest brother; rejoice as victor in the only Son. He won through us whose true flesh was being denied; he won through us, and for us, he for whom we won.

This is the world’s second festival after the Lord’s coming. With the despoiler struck down, the mystery of the divine incarnation has been restored to the world—a mystery which the enemy of the human race, since he could not take it away in reality, obscured by calumnies. Indeed, the immortal mystery had perished from the hearts of unbelievers, because so great a salvation benefits unbelievers nothing, as Truth itself says to his disciples: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16).

[Col. 0825D] The radiance of the Sun of Justice, obstructed in the East by the dense clouds of Nestorius and Eutyches, has shone forth purely from the West, where he principally established fellowship through the apostles and teachers, although it must not be thought ever to have been absent there, since he preserved for himself outstanding confessors.

Thus, while the ancient enemy again attempted, through the impenitent heart of a second Pharaoh, to destroy Abraham’s seed and the children of faith, by God’s mercy he became enfeebled and could do nothing except harm himself. The Almighty also accomplished something even more marvelous concerning him: those whom he had summoned as his accomplices to the seats of the Israelite people, he did not drown together with the author of the tyranny, but gathered them together with his own people; and, as the source of mercy knew to be worthy and possible to him alone, he made those conquered by us destined to live with us as victors.
