[Col. 0826A] For since the spirit of falsehood alone is truly the enemy of the human race, there is no doubt that all those whom Truth has claimed for itself now triumph over him. Now the divine authority of those words of our Redeemer is completely apparent, since they apply so aptly against the enemies of the faith that there can be no doubt about the words themselves: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to carry out your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from what belongs to him, because he is a liar and its father” (John 8:44).

[Col. 0826B] There is therefore nothing surprising in the fact that those who, against God’s truth, believed the falsehood concerning our nature agree with their father in these matters also. Whatever was seen, whatever was heard, whatever, finally, according to the Gospel, was touched and handled in the only Son of God, they assert was not the substance of the one whose reality was proved, but of a substance coeternal and consubstantial with the Father—as though the nature of divinity had been pierced by the wood of the cross, or the immutable could grow through the stages of life and progress in wisdom, or eternal Wisdom, or God who is spirit, could subsequently be filled with spirit.

In this too his bitter madness reveals from whom it proceeded, since, as far as it could, it attempted to harm everyone. For the man who afflicted us by persecuting us corrupted the others by driving them toward agreement in his crime. Yet although he wounded us in individual brothers, because they are our members, he did not leave us free from special grief when he attempted, with new, unheard-of, and incredible audacity, to inflict an injury against his own head.

[Col. 0826C] Would that, even after so many atrocities, he had repented, and not also saddened us by the ruin of his eternal damnation. What measure of crime did he leave unattempted? It was not enough for him that, sparing neither the living nor even the dead, he had already stained his hands with the blood of an innocent and catholic priest, after abandoning truth and approving falsehood. And although it is written, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 2:11), he devoted himself to completing by deeds what he had already done through hatred, as though he had heard neither that command nor the other saying of the Lord: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden light” (Matt. 11:29–30).

[Col. 0826D] He was found to be an Egyptian destroyer, worthy as a preacher of diabolical error, because, like a most savage tyrant, through the violent mob of the seditious and the bloody hands of soldiers he imposed upon the venerable brethren impious blasphemies against the Church. And although the voice of our Redeemer has established that the same person is the author of murder and falsehood, he fulfilled both in his own way, as though the words had been written not to warn against these acts but to bring them about. He drew to the increase of his own destruction what the Son of God had taught for salvation, passing over with an excessively deaf ear that other saying of the same Lord: “Therefore what I have seen with my Father I speak, and you therefore do what you have seen with your father” (John 8:38).

[Col. 0827A] Thus, while he plotted to take away the life of Flavian of holy memory, he deprived himself of the light of a peaceful life. While he attempted to expel you from your churches, he separated himself from the fellowship of Christians. While he dragged and impelled many toward agreement with error, he wounded his own soul with multiple wounds—alone guilty beyond all others, through all others, and on behalf of all, since he was the cause of guilt for them all.

Although your brotherhood, strengthened by solid food, hardly appears to need these things, nevertheless we fulfill what belongs to our position in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Besides those external matters, there is my daily pressure and concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Cor. 11:28–29).

[Col. 0827B] On the present occasion we especially believe that you should be admonished, dearest brother, so that whenever, with divine grace supplying the means, we either overwhelm or cleanse those who are outside by the fountain of doctrine, we may, with every precaution, keep our discourse free from the novel language of unbelief between the two enemies, departing in no respect from the rules of faith which the divinity of the Holy Spirit set forth at the Council of Chalcedon.

We must not, God forbid, dispute as though these matters were uncertain, but assert with authority what has been properly defined. We know that the letter of the Apostolic See, confirmed by the universal assent of the holy synod, contains such a mass of testimonies to divine authority that no one can doubt any longer, unless he prefers to bring upon himself the darkness of error. The acts of the synod—both those in which the definition of the faith was first formed and those by which the aforesaid letter of the Apostolic See, defended also through the efforts of your brotherhood, was upheld—and especially the address to the most pious rulers on behalf of the entire council, are so strongly fortified by the testimonies of the Fathers who preceded us that they can persuade even an imprudent and stubborn mind, provided that it has not already been condemned with the devil for its impiety.

[Col. 0827C] It is therefore fitting that we also take proper precautions against the enemies of the Church, leaving them no opportunity whatsoever, so far as we are concerned, for calumny. Nor, when acting against the Nestorians or Eutychians, should we ever appear to turn our backs on either of them. Let us avoid and condemn both enemies of Christ with equal measure.

[Col. 0827D] Whenever the usefulness of our hearers requires it, let us strike their doctrines with a fitting anathema, promptly and unmistakably, lest what is done by us should be considered unwilling because it appears obscure or delayed. Although the matter itself should be sufficient to admonish your prudence, experience has now taught this as well.

Blessed, therefore, is our God, whose invincible truth has shown you to be pure from every stain of heresy according to the judgment of the Apostolic See. You will offer him worthy gratitude for so many labors if you preserve yourself, for the defense of the universal Church, as the man whom we have proved and continue to prove you to be.

[Col. 0828A] For since God has exposed the deceptions of all calumniators, we all recognize the greatest care of blessed Peter on our behalf. Before he confirmed the judgment of his see in the definition of the faith, he did not permit any of you who labor with us for the catholic faith to appear rejected. Since the Holy Spirit was indicating this, no one could fail to emerge victorious, whose faith had already conquered.

For the rest, we exhort you: since we have learned that some remnants of Eutychian and Nestorian error remain there, now also cooperate with the Apostolic See. The victory which our God has granted to his Church, although it gives greater confidence while we remain in this world, does not wholly remove anxiety; it was not granted so that we might sleep, but so that we might labor more peacefully.

We therefore wish the concern of your vigilance to be assisted in this matter, so that, as your report circulates, you may hasten to inform the Apostolic See how far the teaching of the Lord’s religion is advancing among them, so that we may assist the priests of that religion in whatever circumstances require.

[Col. 0828B] Concerning the things which, in the aforesaid council, were attempted unlawfully and presumptuously against the venerable Nicene canons, we have written to our brother and fellow bishop, the bishop of the see of Antioch. We added what you had entrusted to us concerning the misconduct of certain monks of your religion, establishing through our representatives, and specifically, that apart from the priests of the Lord no one should dare to preach—whether he be a monk or a layman boasting of any kind of learning.

Nevertheless, for the benefit of the universal Church, we wish these letters to come to everyone’s knowledge through the aforesaid brother and our fellow bishop Maximus. For this reason we do not wish to append a copy of them, since we do not doubt that what we entrusted to the aforesaid brother will be carried out.

*In another hand:* [Col. 0828C] May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Opilio.

## XLIII. To Bishop Julian

[Col. 0828D] **Leo to Julian, bishop.**

We have often demonstrated by the clearest evidence the faith of the most Christian ruler, and I give thanks to our Lord who, in his piety, has deigned to grant such a governor to human affairs—one who defends the causes of the faith and the highest interests of the state with the utmost vigilance, always resisting the attempts of heretics and permitting nothing of their madness against the catholic faith.

To his benefits, after God, is owed the fact that the bishop of Jerusalem has been received and that imperial authority has recalled to health the monks whom the perfidy of heretical falsehood had invaded.

As soon as I received your letters containing these matters, I hastened to reply, not merely on that day but almost on the very day itself, so that you might receive certainty about everything you had written.

I rejoice that our brother Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, has sent us a letter full of satisfaction concerning his faith and has clearly indicated what he holds. Because of the sincerity of his faith, I must show him appropriate favor, so that he may in no respect lose the honor of his church, but may possess the privileges of his see according to the untouched rights of the canons and following the example of ancient tradition.

Concerning Easter in the present year, we could have had no doubt. But concerning the future date, we learned that Theophilus, bishop of the city of Alexandria, believed it should be assigned to the ninth day before the Kalends of May—a date on which it had never been celebrated since the Lord’s resurrection.

[Col. 0829A] It is therefore appropriate to investigate the matter more carefully, so that every opportunity for error may be removed. For in our records Easter is most suitably both established and celebrated by our Fathers on the day of the Kalends of May. And lest diversity arise from this matter either among us or among the Easterners, may your devotion deign to act with even greater urgency on our behalf with the most Christian ruler. Indeed, the most merciful ruler himself has deigned to inform us that he had entrusted this matter to his Egyptian bishops for the most diligent investigation.

[Col. 0829B] You reported in your letters that my letter to the Council of Chalcedon had been read in the presence of your bishops and clergy, but only up to the chapter in which my agreement appears to have confirmed the acts concerning the faith. I was therefore surprised that the remaining matters which followed were not likewise brought to the knowledge of those to whom the letter was read, since it should above all have been made known to everyone that we had censured improper ambition and that the established rights, which we have always commanded to be preserved inviolate, were being maintained against new usurpations.

We also rejoice that the presbyter whom you say was examined was, after the inquiry, found to have been cleared in every respect.

You should also know that I sent another letter to the most Christian ruler, in which I thanked him because he had deigned to make known to me his concern both for the cause of the faith and for the security of the state.

[Col. 0829C] He also sent us another letter, intervening on behalf of Bishop Anatolius, so that he might receive the favor of our disposition, since he permits his correction and promises that he will satisfy in every respect the requirements pertaining to the observance of the faith.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius and Studius.

## XLIV. To Bishop Anatolius, sent through the Deacon Patricius

[Col. 0829D] When I read the letter of your devotion which you sent through our son, the deacon Patricius, I understood that you were displeased by the zeal of my concern. In accordance with the Lord’s charity, which you have acknowledged through many proofs to have been shown you by us, I had warned you to beware of those who were said to be adversaries of the common faith, lest it be attributed to the negligence of a ruler if anyone in the catholic Church should presume to preach what agreed with the opinions of heretics.

Whether rumor was reporting this truthfully, I delegated the matter for investigation to the judgment of your devotion. Nor did I in any way injure your honor, since I entrusted to you the examination of what had been reported to me, namely, that the presbyter Atticus, whom I had learned dared to undertake such things, should be excluded from communion unless he cleared himself by complete satisfaction and condemned the heretics not only by word but also by a written subscription in his own hand.

By sending writings of uncertain faith and ambiguous profession, he confirmed rather than dispelled everything rumor had brought us concerning him. If he had wished to prove his conscience sincere, he ought to have confessed not merely that Eutyches was hateful to him, but that he rejected and condemned Eutyches’ perfidy. For human quarrels, even among Catholics, are one thing; the diabolical errors condemned by the catholic faith are another.

[Col. 0830A] Therefore, dearest brother, you must in no respect doubt our affection if you follow the Prophet’s example and say: “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and do I not waste away because of your enemies?” (Ps. 139:21).

I wish you to be completely certain that, just as I desire my own good reputation to remain unharmed, so I also wish you to be found irreproachable in every respect.

[Col. 0830B] The aforesaid man, so that he may appear free from every contrary suspicion, must clearly show what he anathematizes and condemns in Eutyches and must subscribe, without any doubt, to an explicit condemnation of the error. He must also profess that he will preserve in every respect the definition of faith in the Chalcedonian symbol, to which your devotion also gave assent by subscription and which the authority of the Apostolic See confirmed. His own-hand subscription must be added, and the profession must be recited in church in the presence of the Christian people, so that neither we may be considered negligent concerning the catholic faith nor he himself suspected even in appearance.

If he persists in the same perversity and refuses to obey salutary commands, he will receive the sentence of the Council of Chalcedon, against whose definitions he rebels.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the emperor Majorianus Augustus.

## XLV. To the same

**Leo, bishop, to Anatolius, bishop.**

[Col. 0830C] If your devotion had maintained the care of the common grace with a firm and unchangeable purpose, nothing would have arisen to cause you any anxiety. Reason did not permit me to disregard the affection of one whom, out of love of peace and zeal for restoring the catholic faith, I had assisted from the very beginning of his episcopate.

I desired to have in ecclesiastical concerns such a companion that I should feel none of your holy predecessors lacking to me: neither the particular and abundant teaching of John, nor the authority of Atticus, nor the diligence of Proclus, nor the faith of Flavian of blessed memory. I made use of your efforts in such a way that no one would dare either to oppose the catholic faith or to contravene the venerable regulations of the Nicene Fathers.

But when, as you acknowledge, things were attempted against the canons which would bring the greatest scandal upon all the churches, what could I do more suitably and moderately than first to warn you, with brotherly feeling and by letters, to withdraw from this intention? When you did not reply to those letters, you yourself separated me from the fellowship of my conversation.

[Col. 0830D] After that I remained silent, but I repeatedly urged the most merciful ruler, guardian of the faith, by letters and petitions, so that, for the peace of the churches—which you recognize to be especially beneficial to you—the matters now undertaken by your devotion might be carried out.

I give him boundless thanks because, according to the instruction of the Holy Spirit, with whose power he is filled, he deigns to devote himself to priestly concord. He knows that the prayers of those who beseech him will benefit him more abundantly if the servants of one Lord are in no respect divided from the true unity of peace.

[Col. 0831A] You indicate that certain matters in the offices of the clergy of the Constantinopolitan Church have been corrected: that you have restored a presbyter to your favor and affection, and that you have removed Andrew from the office of archdeacon. I write that this has pleased us, because it greatly elevates and commends your reputation, as I wished. After correction, what appeared deserving of criticism is rightly consigned to oblivion, since the advancement of heretics and the injury inflicted upon Flavian of holy memory had burdened you; now these matters have altogether ceased to cause offense, with your praise, as I desired, because what had been disturbed has returned to its proper order.

As for Andrew, who was reasonably deprived of the office of archdeacon, and Euphrates, who, as I have learned, was the unscrupulous accuser of Flavian of holy memory: if, in fully written professions, they condemn the Eutychian heresy no less than the abominable Nestorian doctrine, then, since pardon must be granted to those who have corrected themselves, you may consecrate them as presbyters, so that they may recognize that they have benefited from the remedy of the catholic faith.

[Col. 0831B] First, however, choose and approve someone capable of fulfilling the office of archdeacon—namely, one whom no rumor has ever stained with either of the aforementioned impieties. The others, likewise implicated in equal guilt, should be restored to their orders if they seek pardon through a similar profession and with satisfaction; but only those who are demonstrably free from every error should be admitted to the chief offices.

Your devotion would have removed more effectively and sincerely the fault which, as you say, you incurred through another’s exhortation to enlarge your power, if you had not transferred to the counsels of the clergy what could not have been attempted without your consent. For just as one sins through evil persuasion, so one sins through evil agreement.

[Col. 0831C] But it is pleasing to me, dearest brother, that your devotion professes its displeasure at what it ought not then to have approved either. Your profession of devotion, together with the testimony of the Christian ruler, is sufficient for your return to the common favor, so that correction is not denied to one whom so venerable an advocate has supported.

Let the desire for an ungranted right, which had caused dissension, be entirely cast aside. Let the boundaries established by the most prudent decrees of the holy Fathers suffice, so that the dignity of all priests may remain tranquil in its merits and be renewed according to its ancient privileges.

May the affection of the Lord’s charity remain in you—the affection to which I have often exhorted your devotion together with our brother and fellow bishop Julian, who has always desired the common favor. Through his diligence your concerns will be relieved and the catholic faith fortified.

[Col. 0831D] Above all, I exhort and admonish you in brotherly charity to preserve those matters which concern the glory and protection of priestly office and which, by maintaining the peace of the universal Church, were decreed by the canons of Nicaea. For charity will remain inviolate among the priests of the Lord if the institutions of the holy Fathers are preserved with equal zeal.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius and Studius.

## XLVI. To Juvenal of Jerusalem and the other bishops assembled at the holy Council of Chalcedon

[Col. 0832A] I do not doubt that all of you, my brothers, know that I embraced with my whole heart the definition of the holy synod celebrated in the city of Chalcedon for the confirmation of the faith. Reason did not permit me, since I grieved that the unity of the catholic faith had been disturbed by heretics, not to rejoice exultantly when it was restored.

You could have recognized this not only from the effect of the most blessed confession itself, but also from my letters which, after the return of my representatives, I sent to the bishop of the city of Constantinople, if he had wished to make known to you the reply of the Apostolic See.

Therefore, lest it appear doubtful through malicious interpreters whether I approve what was established concerning the faith at the Council of Chalcedon through your unity, I have sent this letter to all our brothers and fellow bishops who attended the aforesaid council. The most glorious and merciful ruler, as I requested, will deign to send it to your knowledge for the love of the catholic faith, so that the brotherhood as a whole and the hearts of all the faithful may know that I have reached the same judgment with you—not only through the brothers who carried out my commission, but also through my approval of the synodal acts—solely in the matter of faith, as must often be stated.

[Col. 0832B] For this reason it pleased us that the general council should be assembled, both at the command of the Christian rulers and with the agreement of the Apostolic See. The heretics were condemned; had they been willing to be in agreement, no doubt at all concerning the true incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ would remain.

Therefore, if anyone should ever dare either to defend the perfidy of Nestorius or to uphold the impious doctrine of Eutyches and Dioscorus, let him be cut off from the communion of Catholics and have no share in the body whose reality he denies.

[Col. 0832C] I also admonish your holiness to observe the statutes of the holy Fathers, which were fixed by inviolable decrees at the Council of Nicaea, so that the rights of the churches may remain ordered as they were divinely established by those 318 Fathers.

Let improper ambition desire nothing alien, and let no one seek his own advancement through the diminishment of another. However much the elevation of vanity may equip itself with emerging agreements, and however much it may judge its desires strengthened by the name of councils, whatever differs from the canons mentioned above will be weak and void.

[Col. 0832D] Your holiness can learn from a reading of my writings, by which I repelled the attempts of the bishop of Constantinople, how reverently the Apostolic See uses their regulations, and that, with the assistance of our Lord, I am a guardian both of the catholic faith and of the traditions of the Fathers.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Opilio.

## XLVII. To Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem

[Col. 0833A] After receiving the letter of your devotion, which our sons, the presbyter Andrew and the deacon Peter, brought to me, I rejoiced that you had been permitted to return to the seat of your episcopate. But when all the matters that caused you to suffer through certain excesses came back to mind, I grieved that you yourself had become the source of your adversities and had lost the steadfastness to resist heretics. They think that you are not free to rebuke those whom you have professed to have pleased you in their error.

For what was the condemnation of Flavian of blessed memory and the reception of the most impious Eutyches, if not a denial of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh? In his great mercy, the Lord caused this to be undone when he destroyed that detestable judgment of the Council of Ephesus through the authority of the holy Council of Chalcedon, in such a way that none of the corrupt were excluded from the remedy of correction.

Since, therefore, at the time of indulgence you chose repentance rather than obstinacy, I rejoice that you sought heavenly medicine, so that at last you may be a defender of the faith attacked by heretics.

[Col. 0833B] Although no priest is permitted not to know what he preaches—for “whoever is ignorant will be ignored”—yet every Christian living in Jerusalem is more inexcusable than all the unlearned. There he is instructed to know the power of the Gospel not only by the words of the pages but also by the testimony of the very places; and what elsewhere may not be disbelieved, there cannot fail to be seen.

What need is there for intellectual labor where sight itself is the teacher? Why should what is read or heard be doubtful where so many mysteries of human salvation present themselves to sight and touch? It is as though the Lord were still addressing each hesitant person in a bodily voice and saying: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, because it is I myself. Touch and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh as you see me having” (Luke 24:38–39).

[Col. 0833C] Use, therefore, dearest brother, the invincible proofs of the catholic faith, and defend the preaching of the evangelists by the testimony of the holy places in which you dwell.

Bethlehem is with you, where the life-giving birth of David’s Virgin shone forth; wrapped in cloths, he was received by a manger amid the narrowness of an inn. With you is the infancy of the Savior, announced by angels, adored by the Magi, and sought by Herod through the deaths of many infants.

With you is the place where his childhood grew, where his adolescence matured, and where, through every bodily stage of development, the nature of a true human being advanced to perfect manhood—not without the nourishment of learning, not without the sleep of rest, not without the tears of compassion, nor without the fear of dread.

For one and the same person worked great miracles of power in the form of God and endured the cruelty of suffering in the form of a servant.

[Col. 0833D] The cross itself speaks this to you without ceasing; the stone of the tomb cries it aloud—the tomb in which the Lord lay under the condition of a human being and from which he rose by divine power. And when you approach the Mount of Olives to venerate the place of his ascension, does not that angelic voice resound in your hearing, by which the astonished disciples were told at the Lord’s elevation: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11)?

The true birth of Christ is therefore confirmed by the true cross, because the one who was born in our flesh is the one crucified in our flesh. Since no sin intervened, he could not have been mortal unless he belonged to our race.

[Col. 0834A] In order to restore the life of all, he accepted the cause of all and, by paying on behalf of all what only he among all did not owe, he canceled the force of the ancient bond. Thus, just as through the guilt of one all had been made sinners, so through the innocence of one all might be made innocent.

From there justice flowed into humanity, where human nature had been assumed. For there is no rational basis for separating from the truth of our body the one concerning whom the evangelist begins his proclamation by saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1).

And he who declares to the Samaritan woman that salvation is from the Jews agrees with the teaching of the blessed Apostle Paul when he says: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

[Col. 0834B] Likewise, to Timothy: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David according to the flesh” (2 Tim. 2:8).

But you, dearest brother, clearly recognize, given the length of your priesthood, by how many authorities of both the New and Old Testaments these things are declared, since the faith of the Fathers and my writings sent to Flavian of holy memory—which you yourself mentioned—together with the confirmation of the universal synod, should suffice.

[Col. 0834C] Your devotion must therefore take care that no one murmur against the ineffable mystery of our redemption and hope. If there are people who are still darkened by ignorance or divided by perversity, let them be instructed by the authoritative writings of those whose apostolic teaching in the Church of God was and remains clear. Let them learn that concerning the incarnation of the Word of God we must believe what those men believed.

Let them not, through their hardness, place themselves outside the body of Christ, in which we died and rose again together with him. For neither the piety of faith nor the reason of the sacrament permits us to believe either that the Godhead was passible in its own essence or that the truth lied in assuming our nature.

I reverently received a portion of the Lord’s cross together with the tokens of your devotion.

Given on the day before the Nones of September, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius and Studius.

## XLVIII. Letter of Ravennius and the other bishops of Gaul to Pope Leo, praising his faith which he sent to the East

[Col. 0834D] To the truly holy lord, deservedly most blessed in Christ and venerable in apostolic honor, Pope Leo:

Ravennius, Rusticus, Venerius, Constantinus, Maximus, Armatarus, Florus, Gavinus, Valerianus, Constantius, Nestorius, Maximus, Asclepius; likewise Maximus, Ursus, Ingenulus, Justus, Valerius, Superventus, Crisaphius, Fonteius, Petronius, Hydacius, Etherius, Glalius, Euticius, Fraternus, Venturus, Eugenius, Hilarius, Verus, Amandus, Gerontius, Proculeianus, Julianus, Helladius, Amentarius, Honoratus, Hepartius, Amenius, Dinatius, Maximus and Hernantius, Palladius.

The letter of your Blessedness, which you sent to the East in defense of the Catholic faith, has been delivered to us. We would have wished to return thanks immediately to your Apostolate for so immense a gift, had not the difficulty by which we were unable to assemble quickly in one place [Col. 0835A], or the long distances of the lands separating us—together with the unseasonable severity of the weather in our regions—prevented this. Let your Apostolate therefore pardon our delay, which arose not from idleness or evasiveness but from genuine necessity. Although it deprived us of the grace of speed, it could not take away the occasion for rejoicing.

We therefore rejoice with the Christian people after reading the letter of your Blessedness; and, once its instruction had been made known to all, we immediately caused all who are established throughout Gaul to rejoice, while grieving at the same time for those among us who, having abandoned the light of the Catholic faith, have fallen into the darkness of error. Your Apostolate’s writings have been inscribed upon the tablets of the heart by everyone who does not neglect the mysteries of redemption, as a creed of faith, and have been entrusted to a tenacious memory, so that they might be better prepared to confound the errors of heretics [Col. 0835B].

Many, rejoicing and exulting together in them, recognized the meaning of their faith, and rightly rejoice that they have always held it according to the paternal tradition, just as your Apostolate has explained. Others, made more attentive by the admonition of your Blessedness, congratulate themselves in every way on having been instructed; and they rejoice that an opportunity has been given them to speak freely and confidently, with the authority of the Apostolic See also supporting them, and for each person to declare what he believes.

Who, however, could judge that adequate thanks can be rendered to your Apostolate for so great a gift, which has adorned not only Gaul but the whole world as though with precious jewels? After God, the faithful owe it to your teaching [Col. 0835C] that they may steadfastly hold what they believed; the unbeliever also owes it to you, so that, having recognized the truth, he may depart from his faithlessness and, illumined by the light of apostolic instruction, abandon the darkness of his error. Let him follow and believe rather what our Lord Jesus Christ teaches through your mouth concerning the mystery of his incarnation than hold what the devil, the enemy of human salvation and truth, instills.

We would also have wished to write on this same matter to your glorious and most faithful son, the emperor, congratulating him on his faith and making known also the concern of our humility by which we follow you in Christ, had we not thought this entirely unnecessary after news reached us from the East. Through the merits of your Apostolate, however, the merciful Lord has granted that a heresy long secretly nurtured should be exposed in your time [Col. 0835D]. It is a credit to your vigilance that the evil of error could not remain hidden, and it redounds to the glory of the faith that the perverse persuasion either found no participants or lost those whom it had found.

May the merciful Lord look upon his Church, spread throughout the whole world, while preserving your Apostolate. For, while you watch over these matters in this way, those who care for their souls are made more attentive in the faith, and those who are somewhat negligent are kindled to vigilance by so great an example. Keeping this always before our eyes, we shall not cease to give thanks to God and our Lord, and likewise to pray, rejoicing that he has given to the Apostolic See—whence, with Christ propitious, the fountain and origin of our religion has flowed—a bishop of such holiness, such faith, and such teaching [Col. 0836A]. We also ask that he preserve the gift granted and bestowed upon you as pontiff for the very longest time, for the building up of his churches.

Although unequal in merits, we are equal in faith. If anything—which God forbid—should be attempted against the Catholic Church by profane assault, we are prepared, with the Lord strengthening us, to lay down our souls with your Blessedness for the truth of the faith and to devote this life to the author of our salvation and giver of eternity.

And in another hand:

Pray for me, most blessed lord, rightly venerable for your apostolic honor. Rusticus the bishop: I salute your Apostolate in the Lord, venerable one, and humbly ask that you deign to pray for me.

Venerius: I salute you, my lord in Christ, most reverend one, and humbly ask that you deign to pray for me.

Constantine the bishop: I salute your Blessedness.

Likewise all the bishops written above sent their greetings.

## XLIX. — Letter of Leo to all the bishops of Gaul concerning the condemnation of the heretics

**LEO to Ravennius, Rusticus, Venerius, Constantine, Maximus, Armentarius, Florus, Samius, Valerianus, Constantine, Nectarius, Maximus, Asclepius, Maximus, Ursus, Ingenulus, Justus, Valerianus, Superventus, Crisaphius, Fonteius, Petronius, Hydacius, Etherius, Eulalius, Euticius, Fraternus, Venturus, Eugenius, Hilary, Verus, Amandus, Gerontius, Proculeianus, Julianus, Helladius, Armentarius, Honoratus, Hepartius, Amenius, Dinatius, Maximinus, Hernantius, and Palladius, bishops established throughout Gaul.**

We certainly wished to receive your Fraternity’s letter at the time when you had promised it, so that the profession of your judgment might also be joined to that of our brothers departing for the East, whom we sent in our place to the holy synod for the defense of the Catholic faith. But since many obstacles brought us an unforeseen delay, we gratefully received your letters—late and long awaited though they were—through our brother and fellow bishop Ingenulus. Reviewing them with joy, we approved them, just as we had trusted that, through the instruction of the Holy Spirit, heavenly teaching flourished in you. In the Eastern churches, the cunning of the ancient enemy has attempted to weary this teaching through those in whom it found followers of its falsehood; yet the Catholic faith, which is unchangeable in every part of itself, is always made stronger and clearer through the very exercises of its opponents. The grace of God brings this about, so that those who perhaps were less equipped and less vigilant to evade the enemy’s subtle darts, once they have received the weapons of truth, may become stronger against the lies of the impious [Col. 0836D].

Therefore we rejoice with great exultation that, as the case required, you have faithfully and obediently strengthened in the Lord the confidence we have in you. We rightly recognize that we have informed our brothers and fellow bishops in the East that, according to the evangelical and apostolic tradition, there is one and undivided confession among all of us concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. We are not to be detained by any of their disputations so as to think about the truth of this supreme and saving mystery otherwise than we have learned and teach from the preaching of the holy Fathers and the authority of the unchangeable creed.

Eutyches has been condemned by the universal Church, as Nestorius was previously. Whoever chooses to cling to the intolerable impieties of either cuts himself off from the body of Christian unity. No one is now granted the refuge of excuse on the grounds of ignorance, lack of knowledge, or difficulty of understanding. For this very synod, assembled from nearly six hundred of our fellow bishops and brothers, promised that no art of reasoning and no eloquence of debate could inspire anything against the foundation of the faith. Through the assistance of God’s grace, our brothers serving as our representatives showed the fullest devotion in every action, and it became fully and clearly apparent to Christ’s priests, to Christian rulers and authorities, and to all clerics, peoples, and orders that this is truly the apostolic faith, flowing from the fountain of divine mercy [Col. 0837B].

We preach it as sincere and free from every stain of error, as we received it, and defend it now with the agreement of the whole world. Throughout the world the doctrines have been extinguished which either the earlier heretic dared to introduce or the later one, though with a different invention, equal in impiety.

For just as Nestorius was not tolerated when he asserted that blessed Mary was merely the mother of a man who was afterward assumed by the Word of God—two natures being distinguished according to separate persons, so that the Son of Man who was the Son of God would not himself be one, and there would not be one Christ in both natures, but one eternal from the Father and another temporal from the mother—so evangelical authority proclaims the Word to have become flesh in such a way that it presents to us not two Christs or two sons, but in one Lord Jesus Christ the truth of both God and man. Thus the proper character of both substances—that of the one who saves and that of the one who is saved—can neither be confused nor the person doubled [Col. 0837C].

Therefore, just as Nestorius is accursed in his doctrine, so also Eutyches, following the error once condemned and blaspheming with another profanation, has been cut away from the structure of Catholic solidity. He attempted to persuade certain ignorant and excessively simple people that the Word of God became flesh in such a way that he did not take true flesh from the Virgin’s womb, nor possess a body of our race, but that his divinity and his flesh had one nature. Thus he would say that our one Lord Jesus was both a false man and a passible God.

Neither the devotion of faith nor the reason of the mystery accepts this: either that the deity was passible in its own nature, or that the truth was false in the assumption of humanity [Col. 0837D]. The holy synod, agreeing with the writings of our humility, now strengthened by the authority of my most blessed lord, the apostle Peter, and by his merit, has cut away from the Church of God these monstrous inventions of diabolical ideas as abominable.

It has also condemned Dioscorus of Alexandria, who persisted in his impiety, lest that Church which, at the very beginnings of the Gospel, had the blessed Mark, disciple of the most blessed apostle Peter, as its founder—consonant in every teaching with the instruction of his teacher—and which afterward, in more recent times, had Athanasius, Theophilus, and most recently Cyril as highly approved bishops, should suffer unworthy captivity under the domination of a heretic [Col. 0838A].

Therefore, according to the great mercy of God, know that all the efforts of the devil by which he attempted to disturb the Lord’s Church have been destroyed.

Give thanks, therefore, most beloved brothers, worthy thanks to God, and let your love pray with us that we may rejoice as soon as possible that our brothers, whose return we await with longing, have come back safely. Then, with the Lord’s help, we shall be able to instruct you more fully concerning everything that has been accomplished.

For we do not wish brother Ingenulus to be delayed by this expectation, since for this very reason he ought to return more quickly. Nor should the entire subject of our joys remain unknown to you any longer; we wish it, through the care of your love, also to reach our brothers, the bishops of Spain, so that what God has accomplished may be unknown to no one.

Given on the Kalends of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Herculanus.

## 207. L. — To the Emperor Marcian concerning Easter

Your piety’s faith has become known throughout all the churches of Christ through so many proofs that, whenever any concern arises for the common religion, it rightly seeks your assistance. Since I am mindful of my stewardship, I must, believe me, anticipate my concerns even regarding matters that are still future. I therefore reasonably desire to be assisted by your Clemency’s efforts, so that in this observance—which is always varied according to a definite calculation—no error may be incurred [Col. 0838C].

For although the Paschal feast, which contains above all the mystery of human salvation, must always be celebrated in the first month, it is nevertheless so changeable because of the condition of the lunar cycle that the choice of the most sacred day often runs uncertainly. From this it often happens that what is not permitted occurs: the whole Church does not observe together what ought to be one and the same.

The holy Fathers endeavored to remove the occasion of this error, entrusting the whole matter to the bishop of Alexandria, since among the Egyptians expertise in this calculation seemed to have been handed down from ancient times. Through it, the day on which the aforesaid solemnity would occur each year was reported to the Apostolic See, and the judgment of this written record was generally circulated to the more distant churches [Col. 0838D].

But Theophilus, of holy memory, bishop of the city and church of Alexandria, after collecting one hundred years of this observance, determined that the Paschal feast in the seventy-sixth year was to be kept far differently from what the others had decreed. Beginning with the first consulship of the elder Theodosius, of august memory, he arranged the successive cycles of the sacred observance, so that the calculation of a longer period might be preserved in his letters. The seventy-fourth year of this cycle is now in progress. In that year we celebrated Holy Easter on the day before the Ides of April; in the following year, with God’s favor, the same feast is to be held on the day before the Nones of April, as the regular order of the hundred-year calculation declares [Col. 0839A].

But in the year that will be the seventy-sixth, a day is found assigned to Easter which the authority of no precedent and no regulation permits since the Passion of the Lord. For we know that the eighth day before the Kalends of May has been prescribed by him, and that it exceeds the limit established in antiquity, whereas others have assigned the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May to this feast.

Indeed, the legitimate interval has been fixed from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April through the tenth day before the Kalends of May. The necessity of all variations must be contained within this interval, so that we can have the Lord’s Pascha neither earlier nor later.

The fact that the feast sometimes seems to have reached the tenth or ninth day before the Kalends of May can be defended by a certain reasoning: although the day of the Resurrection seems to have passed beyond the limit, the day of the Passion will nevertheless not be found to have exceeded the established boundary [Col. 0839B].

But to extend the Paschal observance to the eighth day before the Kalends of May is highly unusual and an obvious transgression. Since, therefore, as I have said, in that hundred-year calculation of Theophilus the seventy-sixth year is shown to have established the day of Easter contrary to ecclesiastical custom, and since it is no slight offense if the truth and unity of the mystery are not maintained by the universal Church at its beginning, I beseech your Clemency to deign to offer your efforts, so that the Egyptians—or any others who appear to possess certain knowledge of this calculation—may resolve the scruple of this concern. May general observance determine a day that neither abandons the rule of the paternal regulations nor wanders beyond the prescribed limits.

Whatever your piety learns concerning this inquiry, command that it be immediately brought to my knowledge, so that no fault of discord may arise in the divine mysteries.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Opilio.

## LI. — To the Empress Eudocia concerning Easter

**LEO to Eudocia Augusta.**

Theophilus, of holy memory, writing to the elder Emperor Theodosius, arranged the order of the feast for one hundred years beginning with the first consulship of the aforesaid emperor. The seventy-fourth year of this calculation is now passing, in the consulship of Opilio. The sacred solemnity was celebrated on the day before the Ides of April; from this, in the following year, the same feast appropriately falls on the day before the Nones of April [Col. 0839D].

But the year known as the seventy-sixth in the annotation of that bishop contains a date that disagrees with the example of all antiquity and with every authority of the Fathers. For he has transferred the Lord’s Pascha to the eighth day before the Kalends of May, exceeding the limits fixed by antiquity with excessive boldness, although he could have recorded the Paschal solemnity on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, as others established.

Since this gives rise to no small concern for me, lest this opinion be approved among the Egyptians, we have sent a letter to the most Christian and most merciful emperor. In it I carefully explained the cause of my anxiety and humbly requested that, as he is accustomed to do, he graciously devote his efforts to the worship of religion; that he order those who appear to possess perfect knowledge of this calculation to assemble; and that he command them to investigate carefully, lest this determination perhaps be maintained, and this excess—which seems contrary to earlier times—be attributed to our connivance or negligence, so that something never previously presumed might be attempted in our days [Col. 0840A].

Since your Fraternity ought to share this concern with me and guard against anything of this kind occurring, deign frequently to make representations to the most religious and faithful emperor, so that he may unmistakably order the Egyptians to be admonished not to sin, on the day of the highest solemnity, either through disagreement or through transgression.

Whatever your diligence is able to investigate more carefully concerning this matter, may the most glorious emperor command that it quickly reach my knowledge, since it concerns both his salvation and that of all people that the worship of God not be harmed by any error.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Opilio, most illustrious man.

## LII. — To the Emperor Leo

**LEO the bishop to Leo Augustus.**

My mind exults in the Lord with great joy, and I have abundant reason for boasting, when I recognize that your Clemency’s outstanding faith is increased in every way by the gifts of heavenly grace and that, through the growth of your diligence, I experience in you the devotion of a priestly spirit.

For it is plainly evident in the addresses of your piety that the Holy Spirit works through you for the salvation of the whole Church. How greatly all the prayers of the faithful ought to desire that your empire be extended to every glory—you who, beyond the care of temporal affairs, steadfastly devote yourself as a servant of religious providence to divine and eternal dispositions [Col. 0840C]. Your purpose is that the Catholic faith, which alone gives life and alone sanctifies the human race, may remain in one confession, and that the dissensions arising from the variety of earthly opinions may be driven away from the firmness of that rock upon which the city of God is built.

These gifts of God will finally be bestowed upon us in a divine manner only if we are not found ungrateful for what has been granted, expecting instead—almost as though we had acquired nothing—the opposite. To seek what has been revealed, reconsider what has been completed, and tear down what has been defined: what else is this than to fail to give thanks for what has been received and to extend wicked desires of deadly greed toward the food of the forbidden tree? [Col. 0840D]

Since you deign to look with heightened concern toward the peace of the universal Church and the preservation of the Catholic faith, you clearly recognize that the greater danger lies in the plots of the heretics: that a more detailed discussion might be held between the disciples of Eutyches and Dioscorus and the one whom the Apostolic See has sent, as though nothing had previously been defined; and that what all the priests of the Catholic world approve and rejoice to have been confirmed by the holy Council of Chalcedon should, even to the injury of the most sacred Council of Nicaea, be rendered uncertain.

For what was confirmed in our time at Chalcedon concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ was also defined at Nicaea by that mystical number of Fathers [Col. 0841A]: namely, that the confession of Catholics should not believe the only-begotten Son of God unequal to the Father in anything, nor believe that, when he became the Son of Man, he did not possess the true nature of our flesh and soul.

What the fraud of heresy strives to obtain must therefore be detested by us and steadfastly avoided. Matters piously and fully defined must not be recalled for debate, lest, at the will of the condemned, we ourselves seem to doubt matters that plainly agree in every respect with prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic authorities.

If there are any who dissent from what has been established from heaven, let them be left to their own opinions and depart from the unity of the Church with the perversity they have chosen. For it can in no way happen that those who dare to contradict the divine mysteries should be joined to us in any communion [Col. 0841B].

Let them boast in the vanity of their eloquence and glory in the cunning of their arguments, which is hostile to faith. We are pleased to obey the apostolic commands, which say: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deception of human beings” (Col. 2:8).

For, according to the same Apostle, “If I rebuild the things I destroyed, I show myself to be a transgressor” (Gal. 2:18), and I subject myself to those conditions of punishment which not only the authority of the emperor Marcian, of blessed memory, but I also have confirmed by my agreement. For, as you have said reverently and truthfully, perfection admits no increase, and fullness no addition.

Since I know you, venerable emperor, to be imbued with the purest light of truth, wavering in no part of the faith, but discerning what is right from what is perverse through holy and perfect judgment, and separating what is to be embraced from what must be rejected, I beseech you not to regard my humility as blameworthy for lack of confidence. My caution serves not only the universal Church but also your glory, lest under your imperial rule the wickedness of heretics appear to increase and the security of Catholics be disturbed [Col. 0841C].

Although, therefore, I have complete confidence in your pious heart in all things and perceive that, through the Spirit of God dwelling in you, you are sufficiently instructed so that no error could deceive your faith, I shall nevertheless strive to obey your command by sending some of my brothers who may represent my presence before you and, although—as I said—you know it well, demonstrate what the rule of the apostolic faith is. They will make clear and prove in every respect that those who do not follow the definition of the venerable Council of Nicaea or the regulations of the holy Council of Chalcedon must not be counted among Catholics at all, since it is evident that the holy decrees of both councils proceed from the evangelical and apostolic fountain. Whatever does not come from Christ’s irrigation is the drink of a viper [Col. 0841D].

Let your piety therefore know beforehand, venerable emperor, that those whom I promise to send will not depart from the Apostolic See to fight with the enemies of the faith or contend against them. We dare not undertake any discussion concerning matters defined at Nicaea and Chalcedon, as though they were doubtful or insecure—matters which, as it pleased God, such authority through the Holy Spirit established [Col. 0842A].

We do not, however, deny the support of our ministry to the instruction of our little ones, who, after the nourishment of milk, desire to be filled with more solid food. Just as we do not despise the more simple, so we abstain from rebellious heretics, mindful of the Lord’s command: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before pigs” (Matt. 7:6).

For it is exceedingly unworthy and exceedingly unjust that those be admitted to the freedom of debate whom the Holy Spirit signifies through the prophet by saying: “Foreign sons have lied to me” (Ps. 17:46). Even if they did not resist the Gospel, they would nevertheless show themselves to be among those of whom it is written: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

While the blood of the just Abel still cries out against the impious Cain [Col. 0842B], who, rebuked by the Lord, did not rest in repentance but burned for murder, we wish his punishment to be reserved to the Lord’s judgment in such a way that the wicked and cruel parricide may recoil upon himself and may not prevail over us; nor should you allow the lamentable captivity of the holy Church of Alexandria to be prolonged any further. Its freedom must be restored through the protection of your faith and justice, and throughout all the cities of Egypt the dignity of the Fathers and the right of the priesthood must be restored.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the consulships of Calippus and Majorian Augustus.

## LIII. — To the same

1. On the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches and their deserved anathema.  
2. That in the one person of the Lord the twofold nature of divinity [Col. 0842C] and humanity must be affirmed.  
3. On chapters of the faith collected from the books of the holy Fathers.

**LEO the bishop to Leo Augustus.**

### Chapter I

I remember that I promised, venerable emperor, in the matter of the faith concerning which I know your Clemency to be piously concerned, to send a fuller statement of my humility. With the Lord’s help, I now fulfill that promise at a suitable opportunity, so that instruction useful, as I judge, may not be lacking to the holy zeal of your piety.

Although I know that your Clemency has no need of human instruction and has drawn the purest teaching from the abundance of the Holy Spirit, it is nevertheless my duty both to make clear what you understand [Col. 0842D] and to proclaim what you believe. Thus may that fire which the Lord, when he came, sent upon the earth be stirred by frequent meditation until it grows hot, and be kindled until it gives light.

The Eutychian heresy has attempted to bring great darkness upon the regions of the East and has tried to turn the eyes of the ignorant away from that light which, as the Gospel says, “shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it” (John 1:5). Although it has fallen back into its own blindness, what failed in its author now breaks out afresh in his disciples.

For within no long interval of time, the Catholic faith—which is singular and true, and to which nothing can be added or taken away—was attacked by two enemies [Col. 0843A]. First Nestorius arose, and Eutyches second. They sought to bring into God’s Church two heresies opposed to one another, so that both might rightly be condemned by the preachers of truth, since what both believed, though with different falsehoods, was exceedingly insane and sacrilegious.

Let Nestorius therefore be anathematized. He believed that the blessed Virgin Mary was not the mother of God but merely the mother of a man, thereby making one person of the flesh and another of the deity. He did not perceive one Christ in the Word of God and in the flesh, but separately and distinctly preached one Son of God and another son of man.

Yet the unchangeable essence of the Word, which is timeless and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, remained unchanged. The Word became flesh within the Virgin’s womb in such a way that, through the ineffable mystery, by one conception and one birth, according to the truth of both natures, that virgin was both the handmaid of God and his mother.

Elizabeth also understood this, as the evangelist Luke declares, and said: “And how has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:45.)

Eutyches too must be struck by the same anathema. Having been rolled about in the impious errors of the ancient heretics, he chose the third doctrine of Apollinaris, so that, by denying the reality of human flesh and soul, he would assert that our whole Lord Jesus Christ was of one nature. It would then be as though the deity of the Word itself had changed into flesh, and that it belonged solely to the divine essence to be conceived and born, nourished and to grow, crucified and to die, buried and to rise again, ascend into heaven, and sit at the Father’s right hand, whence he will come to judge the living and the dead [Col. 0843C].

But none of these things can be received by the divine essence without the truth of flesh, since the nature of the Only-Begotten is the nature of the Father and the nature of the Holy Spirit. At once impassible and at once unchangeable, it is the undivided unity and consubstantial equality of the eternal Trinity.

Therefore, if some Eutychian departs from the perversity of Apollinaris so as not to be convicted of regarding the deity as passible and mortal, yet dares to declare that the incarnate Word—that is, the Word and the flesh—has one nature, he plainly passes into the madness of Valentinus and Manichaeus. He believes that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, acted out everything deceptively, and that he did not possess a human body, but that a phantasmal appearance of a body was displayed to the eyes of those who saw him [Col. 0843D].

Since the Catholic faith has long detested these impious lies, and the sacrileges of other assertions have already been condemned by the harmonious judgments of the blessed Fathers throughout the world, there is no doubt that we preach and defend the faith which the holy Council of Nicaea confirmed, saying:

“We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, the Only-Begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father: God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father”—which the Greeks call *homoousion* (“of the same substance”)—“through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth.

“Who for us and for our salvation descended from heaven, and was incarnate and became man; he suffered, and rose again on the third day; he ascended into the heavens, and will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.”

This confession most clearly contains what we also confess concerning the Lord’s incarnation. We believe that, in order to restore the human race to salvation, he did not bring true flesh of our frailty with him from heaven, but assumed it in the womb of the Virgin mother [Col. 0844A].

## II

Therefore, let all who are so blinded and alienated from the light of truth that, from the time of the incarnation of human flesh, they deny the reality of flesh to the Word of God show in what respect they claim for themselves the Christian name. And how do they agree with the Gospel of truth if, through the blessed Virgin’s childbirth, either flesh without deity or deity without flesh was brought forth?

For just as it cannot be denied, as the Evangelist declares, that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), so it cannot be denied, as the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims, that “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19). But what could this reconciliation have been, by which God was made propitious to the human race, unless the Mediator of God and human beings undertook the cause of all? And how could he fulfill the truth of the Mediator unless he who is equal to the Father in the form of God also shared in our condition in the form of a servant, so that the bond of death contracted through the transgression of one might be loosed by the death of one—who alone owed nothing to death? [Col. 0844B]

For the shedding of the blood of the Just One on behalf of the unjust was so powerful as a privilege and so abundant as a price that, if the whole body of captives believed in its Redeemer, no bonds of the devil would hold them, since, as the Apostle says, “where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Romans 5:20). And when those born under the sentence of sin received the power to be reborn into righteousness, the gift of freedom became stronger than the obligation of servitude. [Col. 0844C]

What hope, then, do they leave themselves in the protection of this sacrament when they deny the reality of a human body in our Savior? Let them say by what sacrifice they were reconciled; let them say by what blood they were redeemed. “Who,” as the Apostle says, “gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant odor” (Ephesians 5:2)? Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true and eternal high priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh?

Although the death of many saints has been precious in the sight of the Lord, the killing of no innocent person was the redemption of the world. The righteous received crowns; they did not bestow them; and from the courage of the faithful arose examples of endurance, not gifts of righteousness. For their deaths were individual deaths, each belonging to the individual, and no one paid another’s debt by his own end. Among the children of human beings, our one Lord Jesus Christ alone truly existed as the spotless Lamb, in whom all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised. Of these things he himself said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw everything to myself” (John 12:32). [Col. 0844D]

For your faith, which justifies the ungodly and creates the righteous, drawn into participation in his humanity, obtains salvation in him, in whom alone a human being finds himself innocent. Through God’s grace, he is free to glory in the power of the one who, having engaged the enemy of the human race in the lowliness of our flesh, granted his victory to those in whose body he triumphed. [Col. 0845A]

Although, therefore, in the one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and human being, there is one person of the Word and flesh, which inseparably and indivisibly possesses their common actions, the qualities of those actions must nevertheless be understood; and through the contemplation of sincere faith it must be discerned to what the lowliness of the flesh is raised and toward what the loftiness of the deity inclines: what it is that flesh does not do without the Word, and what it is that the Word does not accomplish without flesh. [Col. 0845B]

Without the power of the Word, the Virgin would neither have conceived nor given birth; and without the truth of the flesh, infancy wrapped in swaddling clothes would not lie there. Without the power of the Word, the Magi would not have worshiped the child revealed by the sign of the star; and without the truth of the flesh, the child would not have been ordered to be carried into Egypt and taken away from Herod’s persecution.

Without the power of the Word, the voice of the Father sent from heaven would not have said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 3:17). And without the truth of the flesh, John would not have testified: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). [Col. 0845C]

Without the power of the Word, the restoration of the weak and the giving of life to the dead would not occur; and without the truth of the flesh, food would not be necessary for the fasting person, nor sleep for the fatigued.

Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not declare himself equal to the Father; and without the truth of the flesh, he would not likewise say that the Father is greater. Catholic faith accepts and defends both, and, according to the confession of the blessed Apostle Peter, believes in one Christ, the Son of the living God, both as human being and as Word.

Although, therefore, from the beginning when the Word became flesh in the Virgin’s womb there was never any division between the two forms, and throughout all bodily growth the actions of the whole period belonged to one person, we nevertheless do not confuse the very things that were done inseparably through any commingling; rather, from the character of the actions we discern what belongs to which form. [Col. 0845D]

Let these hypocrites, then, who refuse to receive the light of truth with blind minds, say in what form Christ, the Lord of majesty, was fastened to the wood of the cross; what lay in the tomb; and, when the stone of the monument had been rolled away, what flesh rose on the third day. Let them say in what form, after his resurrection, he reproved certain disciples who did not believe and refuted the hesitation of those who doubted when he said: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). And to the Apostle Thomas: “Put your hand into my side, and see my hands and feet, and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John 20:27). [Col. 0846A]

With what manifest evidence of his body was he already destroying the lies of the heretics, so that the whole Church of Christ, which was to be instructed in these teachings, would not hesitate to believe what the apostles had received and were preaching?

But if, in so great a light of truth, heretical obstinacy does not abandon its darkness, let them show from where they promise themselves the hope of eternal life—for to whom can one come except through the Mediator of God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ? For, as the blessed Apostle Peter says, “There is no other name given among human beings under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12); nor is there redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him “who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6), and who, as the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims, “though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:6–11). [Col. 0846B]

Since, therefore, there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and in him the true deity and the true humanity are altogether one and the same person, nevertheless we understand that the exaltation by which, as the Teacher of the Gentiles says, God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, belongs to that form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glorification. [Col. 0846C]

For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father, and between the Begetter and the Only-Begotten there was no distinction in essence and no difference in majesty; nor had anything been taken away from the Word through the mystery of the incarnation that could be restored to him as the Father’s gift. But the form of a servant, through which the impassible deity fulfilled the sacrament of great piety, is the humanity that was raised into the glory of divine power. From the very conception in the Virgin, deity and humanity were joined into such unity that neither divine things were done without the human being, nor human things without God.

Therefore, just as the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, so he who is eternally equal to God is said to have been exalted, because, while the unity of the person remains inseparably, he is one and the same, and wholly the Son of God because of his one deity with the Father. [Col. 0846D]

Whatever Christ received in time, he received according to his humanity, to which things it did not possess were conferred. For according to the power of deity, the Son also possesses indiscriminately everything that the Father has; and what he received from the Father in the form of a servant, he himself also bestowed in the form of God.

## III

According to the form of God, he and the Father are one; but according to the form of a servant, “he did not come to do his own will, but the will of him who sent him” (John 6:38).

According to the form of God, “as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26).

[Col. 0847A]

According to the form of a servant, “my soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38), and “the same one,” as the Apostle says, “is both rich and poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

He is rich because, as the Evangelist says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3).

But he is poor because, for our sake, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). What, then, is his self-emptying, and what is his poverty, except the assumption of the form of a servant? Through this form, while the majesty of the Word was veiled, the administration of human redemption was accomplished.

For since the original bonds of our captivity could not be loosed unless there existed a human being of our race and of our nature, whom the sentence of sin did not hold and who would erase the deadly bond with his immaculate blood, so, just as it had been divinely ordained from the beginning, it was accomplished at the fullness of the appointed time. Thus the promise, signified in many ways, came to the long-awaited fulfillment, and what had always been announced through continual testimonies could not remain uncertain. [Col. 0847B]

The impiety of the heretics shows that they are involved in great sacrilege when, under the pretext of honoring the deity, they deny the reality of human flesh in Christ, and consider it a religious belief to say that, in our Savior, what saves is not real. Yet, in accordance with the promise that preceded all the ages, the world has been reconciled to God in Christ, so that unless the Word deigned to become flesh, no flesh could be saved. [Col. 0847C]

For the whole sacrament of Christian faith is greatly disfigured by darkness, as the heretics would have it, if the light of truth is thought to have been hidden under the lie of an apparition.

Therefore no Christian should be ashamed of the reality of our flesh in Christ, since all the Apostles and the disciples of the Apostles, and all the distinguished teachers of the churches who deserved to attain the crown of martyrdom or the glory of confession, shone in the light of this faith, proclaiming everywhere with harmonious agreement that one person of deity and flesh must be confessed in the Lord Jesus Christ.

But by what likeness of reasoning, and by what passage of the divine books, does heretical impiety think that it is supported when it denies the truth of Christ’s body, although neither the Law ceased to testify to this, nor prophecy to announce it beforehand, nor the Evangelist to teach it, nor Christ himself to demonstrate it? [Col. 0847D]

Let them search through the whole sequence of the Scriptures to find where they may flee from their darkness and in what place obscure the true light. Throughout all the ages they will find the truth flashing forth so brightly that they will see this great and wondrous sacrament believed from the beginning and fulfilled at the end.

Since no part of the sacred writings is silent about it, it is enough that certain harmonious signs of truth have been made manifest, by which the diligence of faith may be guided in the fullest brilliance and, in the clear light of sincere understanding, may perceive that Christians ought not to be ashamed but most steadfastly to glory in the Son of God, who continually professes himself to be the Son of Man and a human being.

But so that your Piety may recognize that we agree with the preaching of the venerable Fathers, I have decided to append to this discourse some of their statements. If you deign to attend to them as they are read, you will find that we preach nothing other than what our holy Fathers taught throughout the world, and that no one differs from them except impious heretics. [Col. 0848A]

Having touched on these matters, therefore, most glorious and venerable Emperor, with as much brevity as I could, recognize that our preaching is also united with the faith divinely inspired in you, and that we differ in no respect from evangelical and apostolic teaching or from the symbol of the Catholic confession. For, as the blessed Apostle Paul teaches, “great is the sacrament of piety: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). [Col. 0848B]

What, then, is more useful to your salvation, or more fitting for your authority, than that by your decree you should provide for the peace of the churches of the Lord, defend God’s gifts among all those subject to you, and in no way permit the ministers of the devil, through the devil’s envy, to rage against the destruction of anyone? Thus, since you now hold preeminence in this holy temporal kingdom, you may deserve to reign eternally with Christ.

## Saint Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers and Confessor, Book Two, among other passages

This, then, is the one immovable foundation, this the one blessed rock of faith confessed by Peter’s mouth: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (John 11:27). It sustains within itself as many arguments for truth as questions of perversity will be raised by the calumny of unbelief. [Col. 0848C]

Let the administration of the Father’s will be found in the remaining matters: the Virgin, the childbirth, and the body; afterward, the cross, death, the underworld, and our salvation.

For the Son of God was born from a Virgin for the sake of the human race. With the Holy Spirit himself serving him in this work, and with his own divine power overshadowing it, he sowed in himself the beginnings of a body and established the origins of flesh. Thus, having become human from a Virgin, he might receive human nature in himself through the flesh, so that through the fellowship of this union the body of the entire human race might be sanctified in him. Just as all were established in him through the fact that he willed himself to be corporeal, so he might again be extended into all through that which is invisible in him.

Therefore the image of the invisible God did not refuse the shame of human beginnings, and through conception, childbirth, crying, and the cradle he passed through all the humiliations of our nature. [Col. 0848D]

What, then, will be rendered in return for such condescension? The one and only-begotten God, whose origin is ineffable from God, grows in the form of a tiny human body within the womb of the holy Virgin. He who contains all things, and within whom and through whom all things exist, is brought forth according to the law of human birth. At his voice archangels and angels tremble; heaven and earth and all the elements of this world are dissolved; yet he is heard in the cry of an infant.

He who is invisible and incomprehensible, who cannot be circumscribed by sight, perception, or touch, is wrapped in swaddling clothes. If anyone recalls these things as unworthy of God, he will confess himself subject to a greater benefit precisely because these things are so far below the majesty of God. [Col. 0849A]

He did not need to become human, through whom humanity was made; we needed God to become flesh and dwell among us—that is, through the assumption of one flesh, to dwell within all flesh. His humility is our nobility; his humiliation is our honor. What he was as God dwelling in flesh, we in turn are renewed as those who dwell in the Lord’s flesh.

## The same author, Book Nine, among other passages
