Certainly he does not know his own life who does not know Christ Jesus as both true God and true human being. It is the same danger to deny Christ Jesus either as God the Spirit or as flesh of our body:

“Everyone, therefore, who confesses me before human beings, I will also confess before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before human beings, I will also deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:32–33). [Col. 0849B]

The Word made flesh was speaking these words, and the human being Jesus Christ, the Lord of majesty, was teaching them. He himself was established as Mediator for the salvation of the Church, and through that very sacrament of mediation between God and human beings he existed as one, while he himself, from the two natures united in one, is the same reality. Yet he lacked neither nature in either respect, lest perhaps God, by being born as man, should cease to be God, and man, while remaining God, should cease to be man.

This, certainly, is the true faith of human blessedness: to proclaim God and human being, to confess the Word and the flesh; neither to be ignorant that God is also human, nor to fail to recognize that the flesh is also the Word.

## The same author, in the same book, among other passages

The only-begotten God, therefore, born human from a Virgin, and destined, in the fullness of time, to advance humanity in himself into God, maintained throughout the whole manner of evangelical speech that he might teach himself to be believed as the Son of God and indicate that he should be proclaimed as the Son of Man. As a human being he spoke and did all that belongs to God; then, as God, he spoke and did all that belongs to humanity. Yet in that speech concerning both kinds, whenever he spoke, he did so with an indication both of humanity and of deity.

## The same author, elsewhere in the same book, among other passages

Here, then, the heretics find an opportunity to deceive the simple and ignorant: they falsely claim that what he said as a human being was spoken because of weakness in the divine nature, and, because one and the same person speaks everything that he speaks about himself, they insist that he spoke everything in the same manner. [Col. 0849C]

Certainly, we do not deny that the whole discourse belongs to him who remains in his own nature. But if Jesus Christ is both man and God—neither God only when he became man, nor, when he was both man and God, not also God, nor, after his humanity, in God not wholly man and wholly God—the mystery of his sayings must necessarily be one and the same as that of his kinds. When in him, according to time, you distinguish the man from God, then distinguish the speech of God and of man. And when you confess God and man in time, judge the sayings of God and man in time.

But when, again, from man and God you understand the time of the whole man now wholly God, if anything was said to demonstrate that time, fit what was said to the time to which it is suited. Thus, since before the man God is one thing, man and God another, and after the man and God, wholly man and wholly God, another, do not confuse the mystery of the dispensation in its times and kinds. For according to the quality of the kinds and natures, he necessarily had one speech in the mystery of man when unborn, another when still about to die, and another when already eternal. [Col. 0849D]

For our sake, therefore, Jesus Christ, remaining what he was and born human in our body, spoke according to the customary manner of our nature, without nevertheless abandoning what belongs to his own nature, namely, that he is God. For although in his birth, passion, and death he carried out realities belonging to our nature, he nevertheless accomplished all those realities through the power of his own nature. And so forth.

## The same author, elsewhere in the same book, among other passages

Do you see how God and human being are proclaimed, so that death is attributed to the human being, but the exercise of the flesh to God? Yet not in such a way that the one who died is different from the one through whom the dead man rises again. Christ died stripped of his flesh, and, in raising Christ from the dead, the same Christ is the one stripping himself of flesh. [Col. 0850A]

Understand the nature of God in the power of the resurrection; recognize the dispensation of the human being in the death. Although both were accomplished according to their respective natures, remember that the one who is both is one Christ Jesus. [Col. 0850B]

## The same author, shortly afterward

These matters had to be demonstrated by me briefly, so that we might remember that the person of both natures is treated in the Lord Jesus Christ, because, while remaining in the form of God, he assumed the form of a servant.

## Saint Athanasius, Bishop and Confessor of the Church of Alexandria, to Epictetus, Bishop of Corinth

How, then, did those who are called Christians dare even to doubt whether the Lord who proceeded from the Virgin Mary is indeed the Son by the substance and nature of God, while, according to the flesh, he is from the seed of David and from the flesh of holy Mary? [Col. 0850C]

## Saint Ambrose, Bishop and Confessor of the Church of Milan, in Book Two of *On the Faith*, which he sent to the Emperor Gratian, among other passages

Let us not suppose that the one statement we have read—that the Lord of majesty was crucified—means that he was crucified in his majesty. Rather, because the same one is God and the same one is human being, Christ Jesus the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified: God through his deity, human being through his assumption of flesh. As a participant in both natures, that is, the human and the divine, he underwent suffering in the nature of the human being. Thus the Lord of majesty who suffered and the Son of Man, as it is written, who descended from heaven, are indiscriminately said to be the same. [Col. 0850D]

## The same author, elsewhere in the same book, among other passages

Let empty disputes about words, therefore, be silent, because “the kingdom of God,” as it is written, “is not in persuasive speech but in a demonstration of power” (1 Corinthians 2:4).

Let us preserve the distinction between deity and flesh. The Son of God speaks as one in both, because both natures are in the same person; and although the same person speaks, he does not always speak in the same manner. Consider with me now the glory of God, now the sufferings of the human being. As God he speaks divine things, because he is the Word; as a human being he says human things, because he was speaking in that substance.

## The same author, in *On the Incarnation of the Lord against the Apollinarists*

But while we refute these people, others emerge who say that the Lord’s flesh and deity are of one nature. What sacrilege has the underworld vomited forth? The Arians are now more tolerable, since through these people the strength of their perfidy grows, so that they may assert with greater force that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not of one substance, because these people have attempted to say that the Lord’s deity and flesh are of one substance. [Col. 0851A]

## The same author, below

These people often remind me that they hold to the teaching of the Council of Nicaea. But in that teaching our Fathers said not that the flesh, but that the Word of God, is of one substance with the Father. They confessed that the Word proceeded from the Father’s substance, but that the flesh was from the Virgin.

How, then, is the name of the Council of Nicaea brought forward as a pretext while new doctrines are introduced that our ancestors never held? And so forth.

## The same author, to Bishop Sabinus, among other passages

The Apostle beautifully used repetition of the same word when he said of the Lord Jesus Christ: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). [Col. 0851B]

What does “in the form of God” mean except in the fullness of deity, in that expression of divine perfection? Therefore, while he was in the fullness of divinity, he emptied himself and assumed the fullness of human nature and perfection. Just as nothing was lacking in God, so neither was anything lacking for the human being to be perfect in both forms.

Hence David also says: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of human beings” (Psalm 44:3). The Apollinarist is confuted and has nowhere to turn; he is enclosed in his own nets. For he himself said, “He received the form of a servant,” not “the servant spoke.”

Again, therefore, I ask: What does “in the form of God” mean? He answered: “In the nature of God.” For, as the Apostle says, “There are those who are not gods by nature” (Galatians 4:8). [Col. 0851C]

I ask what it means that he received the form of a servant: undoubtedly, the perfection of human nature and condition, as I have said, so that he might exist in the likeness of human beings. And beautifully he said not “the likeness of flesh” but “the likeness of human beings,” because in flesh he is the same.

But because he alone was without sin, while every human being is in sin, he appeared in the form of a human being. Hence the prophet also says: “And he is a human being, and who knows him?”—a human being according to the flesh, but divine action beyond humanity.

Thus, when he touched the leper, he appeared to be a human being, but he acted beyond humanity when he cleansed him. And when he wept for the dead Lazarus, he wept for the dead as a human being, but he was beyond humanity when he ordered the bound dead man to come out on his feet. He appeared to be a human being when he hung upon the cross, but he acted beyond humanity when, after the tombs had been opened, he raised the dead. [Col. 0851D]

## Saint Augustine, Bishop of the Church of Hippo, to Dardanus, among other passages

Do not therefore doubt that the human being Christ is now there from where he is to come. Recall carefully and hold faithfully the Christian confession: he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and from nowhere other than there will come to judge the living and the dead.

He will come in the manner witnessed by the angelic voice, just as he was seen going into heaven—that is, in the same form and substance of flesh to which he certainly gave immortality without removing its nature.

## The same author, in his letter to Volusianus, among other passages

Now he appeared in such a way as Mediator between God and human beings, joining both natures through the unity of the person, that he elevated ordinary things through extraordinary ones and tempered extraordinary things with ordinary ones. [Col. 0852A]

## The same author, in his exposition of the Gospel according to John, among other passages

What, then, heretic, when Christ is God and human being, does he speak as a human being, and you bring accusation against God? He commends the human nature in himself; you dare to deform the divine nature in him.

And again below:

Let us recognize the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father, and the human, by which he is less than the Father. Yet both together are not two but one Christ, lest God should be a quaternity rather than a Trinity.

For just as one human being consists of a rational soul and flesh, so one is God, Christ, and human being; and by this reasoning Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh. We confess Christ in all these things and Christ in each of them.

Who, then, is the one through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Christ Jesus, but in the form of a servant. [Col. 0852B]

## The same author, as above

Who was not abandoned in the underworld? Christ Jesus, but in the soul alone. Who lay in the tomb for three days, destined to rise again? Christ Jesus, but in the flesh alone.

Christ is therefore spoken of in each of these particulars. Yet all these things are not two or three, but one Christ.

Therefore he says: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice because I am going to the Father” (John 14:28), because human nature ought to rejoice, since it was assumed by the only-begotten Word in such a way that it was established immortal in heaven, and the earth was so exalted that incorruptible dust sat at the right hand of the Father. [Col. 0852C]

## Saint John, Bishop of Constantinople and Confessor, in the homily on the Cross and the Robber

But let us see why he will come with the cross: clearly, so that those who crucified him may perceive the blindness of their own madness. Therefore the sign of their shamelessness is carried.

Hence the prophet says: “Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn” (Matthew 24:39; presumably 24:30), seeing their accuser and recognizing their sin. And what is surprising if he will come bearing the cross, when the wounds of his body themselves also show this? “Then,” he says, “they will see him whom they pierced.”

And just as after the resurrection he wished to refute Thomas’s disbelief, showed him the places of the nails, revealed the wounds of his side, and said, “Put your hand here and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39), so then also, showing his wounds and displaying the cross, he will demonstrate that he is the one who had been crucified. [Col. 0852D]

## The same author, in the homily on the Ascension of the Lord

For just as, when two people separated by a quarrel have a mediator placed between them, he dissolves their dispute and discord, so Christ acted for us. God was justly angry with us, while we despised him in his anger and turned away from the merciful Lord. Christ placed himself in the middle, joined the two natures, and himself endured the punishment that threatened us.

## The same author, in the same homily, among other passages

Christ, therefore, offered the firstfruits of our nature to the Father, and the Father marveled at the gift that had been offered: at the great dignity of what was offered, and at the fact that what was offered was defiled by no stain. [Col. 0853A]

For he received the offering with his own hands, made it share in his own seat, and, what is more, placed it at the Father’s right hand.

Let us recognize who it is that heard, “Sit at my right hand”; what nature it is to which he said, “Be a participant in my seat.” It is that nature which heard, “You are earth, and to earth you will return.”

## The same author, in the same homily, among other passages

What speech shall I use? By what word can I say what I cannot find? A fragile nature, a despised nature, a nature shown to all as inferior, has today conquered all things, surpassed all things, and deserved to be found higher than all things.

Today the angels received what they had long desired; today the archangels were able to behold what they had longed for over so much time: our nature shining with immortal glory in the Lord’s seat. [Col. 0853B]

## Saint Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, from the Paschal Letter that he sent throughout Egypt

The witness to this is the one who says: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Psalm 13:3). And the prophets, imploring Christ’s help, say: “Lord, bend your heavens and descend” (Psalm 17:10).

This was not so that he who is in all things might change places, but so that, for the sake of our salvation, he might assume flesh of human frailty.

The Apostle Paul sings the same thing: “Although he was rich, for our sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), so that we might be enriched by his poverty. He came to earth, and, having emerged as a human being from the virginal womb that he had sanctified, he confirmed through his dispensation the interpretation of his name, Emmanuel—that is, “God with us.” In a wondrous manner he began to be what we are and did not cease to be what he was. [Col. 0853C]

Thus he assumed our nature without losing what he himself was. For although John writes, “The Word became flesh”—that is, in other words, “God became human”—the Word was not changed into flesh, because he never ceased to be God.

To him the Holy Spirit also says: “But you are the same” (Hebrews 1:12). And the Father testifies from heaven and says: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Thus, having become human, he remains, according to our confession, what he was before he became human, as Paul likewise proclaims with us: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8).

For when he says “the same,” he shows that he did not change his former nature or diminish the riches of his deity, because, having become poor for our sake, he had assumed the complete likeness of our condition. [Col. 0853D]

## The same author, in another Paschal Letter against Origen, among other passages

“One Son of our Father is the Mediator. He neither lost his nature nor was separated from our fellowship. Invisible God and visible human being, hidden in the form of a servant and acknowledged by the confession of believers as the Lord of glory.

“For the Father did not deprive him of the name of his nature after he became human and poor for our sake, nor, when he was baptized in the Jordan River, did he call him by another name, but ‘only-begotten Son’: ‘You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matthew 3:17).

“Nor was our likeness changed into the nature of deity, nor was deity changed into the likeness of our nature.” [Col. 0854A]

## Saint Gregory, Bishop of Nazianzus, in the homily on the Epiphany, among other passages

When God, therefore, had proceeded from the Virgin in the human nature that he had assumed, one being from two mutually contrary things—flesh and spirit—one of these is taken up into God, while the other bestows the grace of deity.

## The same author, below

He was indeed sent, but as a human being, for there were two natures in him. Hence he also labored from the journey, and likewise became hungry and thirsty, was sorrowful, and wept according to the law of the human body.

## Saint Basil, Bishop of Cappadocia

When, therefore, we see certain things in Christ that are so human that they seem to differ in nothing from the common frailty of mortals, and other things so divine that they belong to no one else except that ineffable nature of deity, the narrowness of the human intellect is confounded and, struck by amazement at so great a wonder, does not know where to turn, what to hold, or in what direction to go.

If it considers him human, it sees him returning from the dead, having conquered the kingdom of death and brought back its spoils.

Therefore, with all fear and reverence, we must contemplate him, so that the truth of both natures may be demonstrated in one and the same person in such a way that neither anything unworthy or unfitting is thought about that divine and ineffable substance, nor, on the other hand, are the things that occurred thought to have been enacted through deceptive appearances. [Col. 0854B]

## Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria

He was called human although by nature he is God, the Word of God the Father, because he shared in blood and flesh in the same way as we do. For if he appeared on earth, he did not lose what he was, but assumed the nature of humanity, perfect in its own reality.

## The same author, in the book called *Colia*

There is therefore one and the same true God both before the incarnation and the one who remained in the deity in which he was, is, and will be.

We must not therefore distinguish one Lord Jesus Christ as a human being separately and as God separately, but we say that Jesus Christ is one and the same—not ignoring the differences of the natures, but preserving them without confusion between them. [Col. 0854C]

## The same author, as above

He is said, then, as though one thing dwelled in another—that is, as though the divine nature dwelled in humanity—without undergoing commingling, so that it might become what it was not.

For whatever is said to dwell in another is not itself such as the thing in which it dwells; rather, one thing is understood to be in another. But in the person of the Word, the diversity of the natures indicates to us merely the distinction of divinity and humanity. For Christ is understood to be one from both.

Therefore, as I said earlier, he says that the Word dwelled in us while preserving the distinction without confusion. For he knows that there is one only-begotten Son, made flesh and human being. [Col. 0854D]

## The same author, as above, to Nestorius
The holy and great synod therefore says that he who was naturally begotten from God the Father, the only-begotten Son, is true God from true God, light from light. Through him and with him the Father made all things; this one descended, was incarnate and made man, suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended once more into heaven. We must follow these words and obey these doctrines, considering what it means that the Word of God was incarnate and made man.

[Col. 0855A] For we do not say that the nature of God was changed or transformed into flesh, nor that it was transformed entirely into the man consisting of soul and body. Rather, we say that the Word joined to himself flesh endowed with a rational soul, and that he became man substantially, ineffably, and irreproachably, and was also called the Son of Man—not by bare will, nor by the assumption of a person alone, but because different natures came together into one. Yet one Christ and Son proceeded from both, without the difference of the natures being annulled or removed by the conjunction, but because divinity and humanity together made one Lord, Christ, and Son among us through that mysterious and ineffable union of conjunction.

Thus he who before all ages [Col. 0855B] was born from the Father is also said to have been physically begotten from a woman. This is not because his divine nature took its beginning from the holy Virgin, nor because, for its own sake, it needed to be born a second time after the birth it had from the Father. It would be senseless and foolish to say that he who is coeternal with the Father before all ages needed a second generation in order to begin to exist. Rather, because for us and for our salvation he joined the human nature to the Son’s nature and proceeded from a woman, he is therefore said to have been born physically.

For a common man was not first born from the holy Virgin and only afterward did the Word dwell in him. Rather, in the very womb and virginal uterus he joined flesh to himself and accepted physical kinship, making the birth of his flesh his own birth. Thus we say that he both suffered and rose again—not because God the Word suffered in his own nature, or the piercing of nails, or other wounds—for God, being incorporeal, is beyond suffering—but because that body which became his own suffered. Therefore he himself is said to have suffered all these things for us. God, who could not suffer, was present in the body that suffered.

In the same way we understand his death. The Word of God, who is life and gives life, is naturally immortal and incorruptible. But because his own body, by the grace of God, in Paul’s words, “tasted death for everyone” (Heb. 2:9), he is therefore said to have suffered death for us—not because, insofar as his nature is concerned, he experienced death in himself. To think or say this is madness. Rather, as we said above, his flesh tasted death.

So also, when his flesh rose again, we speak of his resurrection—not because, perish the thought, what was incorruptible fell into corruption, but because his body rose. Thus we confess one Christ and Lord. We do not worship a man together with the Word, lest an appearance of division be introduced; rather, we worship one and the same person, because his body is not alien to the Word, with whom it also sits at the Father’s side. Nor do we say this as though two sons were sitting there, but one Son with his flesh, because of the unity.

If we refuse to accept such a conjunction as having taken place substantially, or as though it were passible, or as though it were somehow dishonorable, we fall into the position of saying that there are two sons. For it would then be necessary to distinguish and say that the man was honored separately by the person of the Son, and again that the Word who is from God is, both in name and in truth, the Son of God. Yet we must not divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons.

This does not support the correct rule of faith, even though some people assert some kind of division of persons. Scripture did not say that the Word of God assumed the person of a man for himself, but that he became flesh. This means that the Word of God likewise shared in flesh and blood with us, made our body properly his own, and proceeded as a man from a woman—not having cast aside or laid down either his divinity or the generation he had from the Father, but remaining, even in the assumption of flesh, the Lord that he was.

[Col. 0856B] The rule of correct faith everywhere bears witness to this, and we find that the holy Fathers held this understanding. For that reason they did not hesitate to call the holy Virgin *theotokos*—“God-bearer”—not because the nature and divinity of the Word took their beginning from the holy Virgin, but because from her was born that sacred body, endowed with a rational soul, to which the Word of God was substantially united and of which he is said to have been physically born.

## LIV. — Pope Leo’s decretal letter to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica

If you truly discerned and rightly weighed how much had been entrusted to your fraternity by the most blessed apostle-father, and what responsibilities had also been committed to you through our favor, we could greatly rejoice in the devoted care imposed upon you.

For just as my predecessors delegated authority to your predecessors, so I too, following the example of those before me, have entrusted to your affection a share in my administration, so that, imitating our gentleness, you might assist in the care that by divine institution we principally owe to all the churches, and might in some manner extend the presence of our visitation to provinces distant from the Apostolic See. In this way, through continuous and timely progress, it would be easy for you to recognize what you should settle by your own diligence and in which matters you should reserve judgment for us.

Since it was open to you to suspend greater matters and more difficult outcomes of cases while awaiting our decision, there was neither reason nor necessity for you to deviate into something that exceeded your measure. [Col. 0856D] You have abundant written records of our instructions, by which we have frequently taught you moderation in all actions, so that through an exhortation of charity you might urge the churches entrusted to you toward wholesome obedience.

Even if matters often arise among negligent or sluggish brothers that must be treated with greater severity, correction must nevertheless be applied in such a way that charity is always preserved. Therefore the blessed apostle Paul, instructing Timothy in ecclesiastical governance, says: “Do not rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all purity” (1 Tim. 5:1–2).

If this moderation is owed, by apostolic instruction, even to the humbler members, how much more must it be rendered without offense to brothers and fellow bishops? Even when matters sometimes occur in priestly persons that deserve reproof, benevolence should nevertheless be more active toward correction than severity, exhortation more than agitation, and charity more than power.

But those who seek what is their own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ are easily distinguished from this rule. While they seek more to be honored than to serve their subjects, honor pleases them, pride inflates them, and what was intended for concord tends toward harm.

We are compelled to say this with no small grief of heart. I in some way feel myself at fault when I learn that you have deviated even slightly from the rules handed down to you. If you were not sufficiently concerned for your own reputation, you should at least have spared mine, lest what was done solely on your own initiative appear to have been done by our judgment.

Let your fraternity reread our pages, and let it run through all the letters sent to your predecessors, the bishops of the Apostolic See. There you will find, either from me or from my predecessors, an order concerning what I have learned was presumed upon by you.

For our brother Atticus, metropolitan bishop of ancient Epirus, came to us with the bishops of his province and complained, in a tearful statement, about the most unjust constraint he had endured. He did so in the presence of your deacons, who, by offering no response against his tearful complaints, showed that the matters reported to us were not without credibility.

Your letter, which those same deacons brought, was also read. It said that Brother Atticus had come to Thessalonica and had confirmed his consent by a written declaration, so that we could understand his coming and his written pledge of obedience as nothing other than the act of his own free will and spontaneous devotion.

Yet the very mention of that document revealed a sign of injury. It was not necessary to bind in writing one who had already proved his obedience by the service of his voluntary arrival. Thus these words of your letter gave testimony to the complaints mentioned above. What had been left unspoken was thereby exposed: namely, that the prefecture of Illyricum, invested with the highest authority among worldly offices, had been stirred up to produce an innocent bishop, so that, through a terrifying enforcement carrying every public office into the execution of the order, a priest accused of no crime—or of a false one—might be dragged from the sacred recesses of the Church.

No delay was granted him because illness and the severity of winter obstructed him. Instead, he was forced to travel by a road full of dangers, over impassable cliffs. What need was there for so much labor and so great a danger that some of those who accompanied the bishop are said to have collapsed?

I am greatly astonished, dearest brother, and also deeply grieved, that you could be moved so atrociously and violently against a man of whom you had reported nothing more than that, although summoned, he had delayed coming and pleaded an excuse of illness—especially since, even if he deserved such treatment, you ought to have awaited his reply to your inquiries.

But, as I see, you judged well of my character and most accurately foresaw how civilly I would respond in order to preserve priestly concord. For that reason you hastened to carry out your impulse without delay, lest, once you had received letters in which our moderation ordered something else, you should no longer have the freedom to do what was done.

Or had some crime of the brother become known to you, and was the metropolitan bishop burdened in your judgment by the weight of a new offense? You yourself confirm that this was foreign to him by bringing no charge against him. But even if he had done something intolerable, our judgment ought to have been awaited, so that you would decide nothing before learning what pleased us.

We entrusted our authority to your affection in such a way that you were called to share in our care, not to possess the fullness of our power. Therefore, just as the things you have piously managed greatly gladden us, so the things wrongly done distress us exceedingly.

After the experience of so many cases, it is necessary to look ahead more anxiously and take precautions more carefully, so that through the spirit of charity and peace every source of scandal may be removed from the churches of the Lord that we have entrusted to you. Let the dignity of your episcopate take precedence in those provinces, but let every excess of usurpation be cut away.

Therefore, in accordance with the canons of the holy Fathers—established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world—we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces, to whom the care of their brothers has been extended through our delegation, retain inviolate the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them, [Col. 0858C] so that they depart from the prescribed rules neither through negligence nor through presumption.

In cities whose rulers have died, the following procedure shall be observed in appointing bishops. The man to be ordained, even if he has a testimony of good conduct, must not be a layman, a recent convert, or the husband of a second wife, nor one who has or has had only one wife whom he married as a widow.

The election of priests is so excellent that qualifications which are not counted as faults in other members of the Church must nevertheless be considered unlawful in them. For while those outside the clerical order are free to pursue marriage and the begetting of children, even subdeacons are not permitted carnal marriage, so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who do not have wives may remain unmarried.

If this is rightly guarded in the order that is fourth from the top, how much more must it be observed in the first, second, and third, so that no one may be judged suitable for Levitical ministry, presbyteral honor, or episcopal excellence when he is found not yet to have restrained himself from conjugal pleasure.

When, therefore, the election of the chief priest is under consideration, let the man be placed before all others whom the clergy and people have jointly and harmoniously requested. If their votes should happen to be divided among several persons, the metropolitan’s judgment shall give preference to the one supported by greater numbers, zeal, and merits.

Only let no one be ordained against the wishes of those who neither desire nor request him, lest the city despise or hate a bishop it did not want and thereby become less religious than it ought to be, because it was not permitted to have the man it chose.

Concerning the person to be consecrated bishop and the agreement of clergy and people, the metropolitan bishop shall report to your fraternity and inform you of what has been approved in the province, so that your authority too may confirm that the ordination is to be properly celebrated. This authority must impose no delay or difficulty upon right arrangements, lest the flocks of the Lord lack the care of pastors for a long time.

When the metropolitan has died and another must be substituted in his place, the provincial bishops shall gather in the metropolitan city. After the will of all the clergy and citizens has been examined, the best man shall be chosen from among the presbyters or deacons of that church. The provincial priests shall report his name to you, ready to fulfill the wishes of those making the request if they learn that what pleased them has also pleased you.

For just as we do not wish just elections to be wearied by any delays, so we permit nothing to be presumed upon without your knowledge.

Regarding episcopal councils, we judge no differently from what the holy Fathers wisely ordained: namely, that two assemblies be held each year, in which judgment shall be given concerning all complaints that commonly arise among the various orders of the Church.

If a matter should arise among those who preside concerning serious offenses—which God forbid—and it cannot be resolved by provincial examination, the metropolitan shall take care to instruct your fraternity about the whole affair. [Col. 0859C] If, after the parties have appeared before you, the matter is not settled by your judgment, whatever it may be shall be transferred to our consideration.

If a bishop, disdaining the modesty of his own city, seeks the administration of a more distinguished place and on any pretext transfers himself to a larger people, he shall indeed be expelled from the foreign see, but he shall also lose his own, so that he may preside neither over those whom he coveted through greed nor over those whom he despised through pride. Let each person therefore be content with his own boundaries and not seek to increase himself beyond the measure of his jurisdiction.

Let no one receive another bishop’s cleric against that bishop’s will, and let no one solicit him, unless perhaps the matter has been agreed between the giver and receiver by an arrangement motivated by charity. For he is guilty of grave injury who dares either to lure away or retain from a brother’s church what is more useful or more valuable.

If the matter takes place within the province, let the metropolitan compel the fugitive cleric to return to his own church. If he has gone farther away, he shall be recalled by the authority of your command, so that no opportunity may remain either for greed or ambition.

When summoning bishops to you, we wish you to be most moderate, lest under the appearance of greater diligence you seem to glory in injuries inflicted upon your brothers. Therefore, if some greater matter arises that makes it necessary to summon a fraternal assembly, it will be sufficient for two bishops from each province—those whom the metropolitans judge should be sent—to come to your fraternity.

Those who have assembled must not be detained beyond fifteen days at the appointed time. If, however, in the matter you judge must be discussed and decided with the brothers, their opinion differs from your own, everything must be reported to us with the testimony of the official records, so that, once ambiguities have been removed, what pleases God may be determined.

Toward this end we direct all our activity and care: that whatever pertains to the unity of concord and whatever pertains to the preservation of discipline may be violated by no disagreement and neglected by no sluggishness.

Therefore I exhort and admonish you, dearest brother, and those brothers of ours who are offended by your excesses—although the grounds of all their complaints are not alike—not to disturb by contention what has been piously ordered and wholesomely arranged.

Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another, as the Apostle says: “Let each of you please his neighbor for his good, to build him up” (Rom. 15:2). For the firm structure of our truth cannot endure unless the bond of charity binds us into inseparable solidity.

Just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another. This connection requires unanimity throughout the whole body, but it especially demands concord among priests.

Although they share a common dignity, their order is not general or undifferentiated. For even among the most blessed apostles there was, despite the similarity of their honor, a certain distinction of authority. Although all were chosen equally, one was nevertheless given precedence over the others.

From this pattern also arose the distinction among bishops. By a great ordering it was provided that all should not claim everything for themselves, but that in each province there should be one whose judgment held first place among the brothers. Again, certain men established in the greater cities were to undertake a broader care, through whom the concern of the universal Church would flow toward the one See of Peter, and nothing would ever dissent from its head.

Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over certain people should not resent having someone placed over him. Let him also render the obedience he requires, and just as he does not wish to carry a burden too heavy, so let him not dare to impose an unbearable weight upon another.

For we are disciples of the humble and gentle teacher who says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:29–30). How shall we experience this unless we also observe what the same Lord says: “The greater among you shall be your servant” (Matt. 23:11), and “whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11)?

## LV. — To Septimus, bishop of Altinum

**LEO to Septimus, bishop of Altinum.**

Having read the letters of your fraternity, we have recognized the vigor of your faith, which we had known for a long time. We rejoice with you that you vigilantly carry out pastoral care for the safeguarding of Christ’s flocks, lest wolves who enter under the appearance of sheep tear the innocent apart with the ferocity of beasts. Such men would not only make no progress through correction themselves, but would also corrupt what is sound.

So that this viperous deceit may not prevail, we have sent a letter to the metropolitan bishop of the province of Venetia, informing him that it would endanger his own position if anyone coming from the company of the Pelagians or Coelestians were received into Catholic communion without a legitimate declaration of satisfaction.

It is most wholesome and full of the benefit of spiritual medicine that presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any order who wish to appear corrected should plainly acknowledge that they condemn both their own error and the authors of that error. Thus no opportunity for hope will remain to perverse and long-condemned teachings, and no member of the Church will be able to be defiled by association with such people, once their own profession has everywhere begun to oppose them.

Concerning them we also command that the canonical constitution be observed: they must not be permitted to depart from the churches to which they properly belong and, according to their own will, move to places not assigned to them. If this is rightly forbidden to those who are free from blame, much less should it be permitted to those under suspicion.

Therefore let your affection, whose devotion gives us joy, join its care to our arrangements. Together with the aforesaid metropolitan, take care that the measures which have been laudably enacted and wholesomely ordered for the safety of the whole Church are carried out promptly and carefully.

## LVI. — The same to the same

[Col. 0861C]

From the report of our brother and fellow bishop Septimus, contained below, we have learned that certain presbyters, deacons, and clerics of various orders who had been entangled in the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy entered your province and were admitted to Catholic communion without any condemnation of their own error being required from them. Thus, while pastoral watchmen were sleeping too deeply, a wolf clothed in sheep’s skins entered the Lord’s sheepfold without laying aside his bestial dispositions.

Even the innocent are not granted, by the authority of the canons and our decrees, the right to usurp such freedom that, abandoning the churches in which they had either received or regained the clerical office, they might be carried about through different places by their instability, always loving to wander and never remaining upon the apostolic foundation.

Because they have been bound by no examination and no prior judgment concerning their profession, they seek above all to obtain this advantage: that under the cover of communion they may visit many houses and, through knowledge falsely so called, corrupt the hearts of many.

They could not accomplish this if the bishops of the churches exercised the necessary care in receiving such persons and permitted none of them to wander. Therefore, lest this happen again, and lest the harm introduced through the negligence of some extend toward the destruction of many souls, by the authority of this command we instruct your fraternity to convene a provincial synod of the priests.

All those—whether presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any order—who, coming from the company of the Pelagians or Coelestians, were imprudently admitted to Catholic communion without first being compelled to condemn their error must now, since their hypocrisy is partly exposed, be compelled to true correction, which can benefit them without harming anyone.

Let them openly condemn, in formal declarations, the authors of their proud error, and detest whatever the universal Church has abhorred in their teaching. Let them declare, in full, open, and personally signed statements, that they embrace and approve in every respect all the synodal decrees which the authority of the Apostolic See has confirmed for the eradication of the heresy.

Nothing obscure or ambiguous must be found in their words. For we know that this is the cunning of such people: in whatever fragment of the detestable doctrine they use to distinguish themselves from the company of the condemned, they consider that none of their opinions has been left unpreserved.

Although they pretend to reject and abandon all their definitions with such apparent ease, they secretly reserve this point, by their entire art of deception, unless it is understood otherwise: that the grace of God is given according to the merits of those who receive it.

But if grace is not given freely, it is not grace, but payment and recompense for merits. The blessed Apostle says: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, so that we might walk in them” (Eph. 2:8–10).

All devotion to good works is therefore a divine preparation, and no one is justified by his own power, since grace is for each person the beginning of righteousness and the fountain and source of merits.

But these people say that grace is preceded by natural effort, so that what is already made bright by one’s own zeal before grace may appear not to have been wounded by original sin.

For this reason they also say that infants, if they depart from this world without baptism, cannot be condemned and are not held guilty in Adam’s sin, but come without delay to the kingdom of God or eternal life. Yet the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings” (Rom. 5:12). For this reason infants too are baptized.

Although several sins may be understood in that one sin, if that one sin itself is divided, as it were, into its individual members:

There is pride in it, because man preferred to belong to himself rather than to remain under God’s authority;

sacrilege, because he did not believe God;

murder, because he cast himself headlong into death;

spiritual fornication, because the integrity of the human mind was corrupted by the serpent’s persuasion;

theft, because he appropriated the food that had been forbidden;

and greed, because he desired more than ought to have been sufficient for him;

as well as anything else that careful consideration may discover in that one offense.

It is also reasonably said that infants are bound not only by the sins of the first human beings, but also by the sins of their own parents, from whom they were born.

For that sentence, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children,” holds them before, through generation, they begin to belong to the New Testament. That Testament was foretold when it was said through Ezekiel that children would no longer bear the sins of their parents, and that the proverb would no longer exist in Israel: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (Jer. 31:29).

They are therefore reborn so that whatever sin they were born with may be released in them. Sins committed afterward through wrongful action can be healed through repentance, as we also see happening after baptism.

For this reason regeneration was not instituted unless generation were defective, so much so that even one born of a legitimate marriage says: “I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother nourished me in sins in the womb” (Ps. 50:6).

Here he did not say “in iniquity” or “in sin,” although that could rightly have been said; rather, he preferred to say “in iniquities” and “in sins,” because in that one sin which passed into all human beings, and which is so great that human nature was changed by it and turned toward the necessity of death, as I explained above, several sins are found, as well as other sins of the parents. These cannot change nature, but they nevertheless bind children by guilt unless free grace and divine mercy come to their aid.

From the newly born infant to the decrepit old man, whatever bodily age they bear, just as no one should be barred from baptism, so no one exists who does not die to sin in baptism.

Infants die to original sin; adults, however, die also to all the sins they have added by wrongful living to what they brought with them by birth.

Your affection must therefore be on guard and provide with the greatest diligence lest, through such people, scandals long extinguished be revived, and from a doctrine once cut off some new growth of the same evil arise in the province. It might not only grow from its roots but also infect the offspring of the holy Church with the poison of its stench.

Those who wish to appear corrected must cleanse themselves of every suspicion and show through obedience to us that they are ours. If any one of them refuses to satisfy wholesome commands—whether he is a cleric or a layman—let him be expelled from the fellowship of the Church, lest one who destroys his own soul lie in wait for the salvation of another.

We also admonish you to restore that part of ecclesiastical discipline which was formerly decreed by the holy Fathers and by us many times: no one is free to pass from the Church in which he was ordained, whether in the rank of presbyter, in the order of deacon, or in any subsequent clerical office.

Let each person remain where he was ordained, not enticed by ambition, led astray by greed, or corrupted by human persuasion. If anyone, seeking what is his own rather than what is Jesus Christ’s, neglects to return to his own church, let him be regarded as an outsider both with respect to the privilege of honor and with respect to the bond of communion.

Your affection should not doubt that, if the measures we decree for the protection of the canons and the integrity of the faith are neglected—as we do not suppose they will be—we shall be moved with even greater force. For the faults of lower orders must be attributed above all to negligent and careless rulers, who often nourish a great disease by refusing to apply the harsher medicine.

## LVII. — To all the bishops throughout Campania

**LEO to all the bishops throughout Campania, Samnium, and Picenum.**

I am moved by great indignation and deeply grieved that I have learned some of you have forgotten the apostolic tradition and devoted yourselves to your own error, so that, apart from the feast of Easter—which alone is matched by the solemnity of Pentecost—you dare, not compelled by any necessity arising from human weakness but solely by the freedom of undisciplined choice, to claim the right of baptism for yourselves.

You even celebrate the mysteries of regeneration on the birthdays of martyrs, whose end must be honored in a manner different from the day of the Lord’s Passion. You hand over the sacrament to the ignorant and inexperienced without any spiritual instruction or preparation, so that nothing of ecclesiastical teaching, nothing of the imposition of hands in exorcisms, and nothing of the fasts by which the old man is destroyed has any effect upon those being renewed.

Nor is any exception made in so great a mystery of human salvation for the day on which that very gift was established for those being reborn.

We therefore admonish you, and declare—not without danger to the standing of those who do these things—that this presumption must cease. Confer this supreme and most powerful grace of God only on those who desire and believe, on the days of Easter and Pentecost.

At all other times, however, consideration must be given to serious necessities and dangers, according to which assistance ought to be provided, lest weakness constrained by mortal condition be deprived of necessary liberation. Although, as we have said, reverence for only these two festivals is to be preserved, care must nevertheless be taken, because of the many dangers, lest regeneration be denied through the Lord’s priests to anyone overtaken by unexpected illness, an enemy attack, or fear of shipwreck.

If anyone, after the prohibition, is discovered persisting in the same usurpation, he shall suffer a punishment worthy of his obstinacy, since he has shown that he pursued shameful profit rather than religious observance.

I also decree that, by every means, another presumption against apostolic rule, which I have recently learned is being committed by some through unlawful usurpation, must be removed. I mean the penitence requested from the faithful: a written declaration of the sins of each person, arranged by category, must not be publicly recited, since the guilt of consciences is sufficiently indicated to the priests alone through private confession.

Although the fullness of faith appears praiseworthy when, out of fear of God, it is not ashamed to blush before human beings, nevertheless not all sins of this kind are such that those who require penance are unafraid to publish them. This improper custom must therefore be removed, lest many be kept from the remedies of penance because they are either ashamed or afraid to disclose their deeds to their enemies, who could strike them through the provisions of the law.

The confession that is first offered to God is sufficient; then the sinner approaches the priest concerning the offenses for which he is doing penance. More people will then be able to be called to penance if the conscience of the one confessing is not made public to the ears of the people.

## LVIII. — To the bishops established throughout Campania and elsewhere

[Col. 0865A]

1. No bishop shall promote another person’s slave to the clerical office.

2. Whoever has been promoted to the priesthood despite being the husband of a widow or having contracted numerous marriages shall be barred from ecclesiastical offices.

3. Clerics must not exact interest, and neither must laymen.

4. A cleric must not engage in lending at interest, either in his own name or in another’s.

5. If any priest acts against these prohibitions, he shall be removed from his office.

**LEO, bishop of the city of Rome, to all the bishops established throughout Campania, Picenum, Tuscany, and all the provinces: greeting in the Lord.**
## Chapter I

Just as the condition of the churches, arranged in a sound disposition, gives us cause for rejoicing, so it grieves us deeply whenever we learn that something has been attempted or committed contrary to the canonical statutes and ecclesiastical discipline. If we do not examine such matters with the vigilance we ought to show, we cannot excuse ourselves before him who wished us to be watchmen, allowing the pure body of the Church—which we ought to guard free from every blemish—to be defiled by the wicked contagion of those who surround it, while the very structure of its members fails to cohere through dissimilarity.

Men are indiscriminately admitted to the sacred order who possess no dignity of birth and no distinction of character; and those who have been unable to obtain their freedom from their masters are advanced to the height of the priesthood, as though servile status could acquire honor, and as though someone could be thought capable of pleasing God who has not yet been able to prove himself to his own master. There is therefore a double guilt in this matter: both the sacred mystery is polluted by the baseness of such an association, and the rights of masters are violated insofar as this involves the rashness of an unlawful usurpation.

Accordingly, dearest brothers, let all the priests of your province abstain from such men; indeed, we wish them to refrain not only from these, but also from those who are bound by an original status or by any other condition, unless perhaps the request or consent of those who claim some authority over them should have been given. Anyone who is to be enrolled in divine service ought to be free from the control of others, so that he may not be withdrawn by any bonds of necessity from the Lord’s camp, to which his name is entered.

[Col. 0865C]

## II

We have learned both from the Apostle’s teaching, from divine command, and from the rules of the canons what sort of integrity of birth and character must belong to each person who is to be joined to the mystery of the sacred altar. Yet we have found that many of our brothers have departed from these rules and utterly strayed from them.

For it is clear that husbands of widows have attained the priesthood, and that some who have had several marriages have also been admitted to the sacred order, with every obstacle removed and with complete license for a freer life. This is contrary to the blessed Apostle’s statement concerning such men: “The husband of one wife”; and contrary to the command of the ancient Law, which says and prescribes: “The priest shall take a virgin as his wife, not a widow, not one who has been divorced” (Leviticus 21:13–14).

Therefore, by the authority of the Apostolic See, we command that all such men who have been admitted be excluded from ecclesiastical offices and from the priestly title. They cannot claim at their own discretion an office of which they have not been made worthy, because of the very impediment that stood in their way.

We specifically reserve to ourselves the responsibility for investigating this matter, so that any offenses that may have been committed may be corrected, that no one may thereafter be permitted to commit them, and that no excuse based on ignorance may arise—although a priest ought never to have been ignorant of what has been defined by the rules of the canons.

We have therefore sent these instructions in writing to your provinces through our brothers and fellow bishops Innocentius, the legitimate representative, and Segetius, so that whatever is known to have grown up wickedly may be uprooted from the roots, and no tares may corrupt the Lord’s harvest. For the sincere things will produce abundant fruit only if those practices that customarily destroy the growing crop are cut away with greater care.

[Col. 0866A–B]

## III

Nor did we think this should be passed over: some, seized by a shameful desire for profit, practice usury and wish to grow rich through interest. We grieve that this occurs not merely among those established in clerical office, but even among laymen who wish to be called Christians. We decree that harsher punishment be imposed upon those who are proved guilty, so that every opportunity for sinning may be removed.

## IV

We have also judged it necessary to give this warning: just as no cleric may conduct the business of interest in his own name, so no one may attempt to do so in another’s name. It is an indecent crime to devote one’s own wrongdoing to another’s advantage. The only “interest” we ought to consider and practice is that what we mercifully give here [214], we may receive from the Lord, who will repay it many times over and forever according to his measure.

[Col. 0866C]

## V

Our admonition therefore declares that if any of our brothers acts or attempts to act against these decrees, and dares to admit what has been forbidden, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and that he will not share in our communion, since he refused to be a partner in discipline.

Moreover, lest anything be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that your devotion guard all the decretal constitutions—those of blessed memory, Innocentius, as well as those of all our predecessors—which have been established concerning ecclesiastical ordinations and the discipline of the canons. If anyone despises them, he must know that forgiveness will henceforth be denied him.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Maximus and Paterius.

---

## LIX. To Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia

**Leo, to Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia.**

My son, the deacon Adeodatus, having returned to us, reported that your Belovedness had asked to receive from us the authority of the Apostolic See concerning matters that appear to present considerable difficulty for judgment. Yet, in view of temporal necessities, appropriate care must be applied, so that wounds inflicted by the violence of hostility may be healed especially through religious concern.

You have told us that, through the devastation of war and the most grievous assaults of the enemy, certain marriages were so divided that, after their husbands had been carried into captivity, their wives were left without support. They thought their husbands had either been killed or would never be freed from captivity, and, compelled by anxiety, they entered into marriages with other men. Now, with the state of affairs, by the Lord’s help, turned for the better, some of those who had been thought dead have returned. Your charity is therefore rightly uncertain what we ought to determine concerning the women who have been joined to other husbands.

But since we know that Scripture says that a woman is joined to a man by God, and since we recognize the command, “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6), we must believe that the bonds of lawful marriage are to be restored. Once the evils brought about by hostility have been removed, each person must be restored to what he or she lawfully possessed.

[Col. 0867A]

Every effort must be made so that each person receives what is his or her own. Yet the man who assumed the position of a husband whom he believed no longer existed must not be judged guilty as though he had invaded another’s right. In this way, many things belonging to those who were led into captivity could have passed into another’s possession; nevertheless, it is entirely just that, when those people return, their property be restored to them.

If this rule is properly observed with regard to slaves, fields, houses, and possessions, how much more must it be observed in the restoration of marriages, so that what was disturbed by the necessity of war may be restored by the remedy of peace?

Accordingly, if any men return after a long captivity and remain so devoted to their wives that they wish them to return to their marital union, what necessity brought about must be disregarded and judged blameless, while what fidelity demands must be restored.

[Col. 0867B–C]

If, however, some women have become so attached to their later husbands that they prefer to remain with them rather than return to their lawful marital union, they are rightly to be censured and even deprived of ecclesiastical communion, because they have inexcusably chosen the pollution of sin. They have shown that, through their lack of self-control, they preferred what a just remission could have expiated.

Let marriages therefore return voluntarily to their proper state. What necessity compelled must in no way be turned into a reproach for evil intention. For just as those women who refuse to return to their husbands must be regarded as impious, so those who return to the affection established by God are rightly to be praised by judgment.

Concerning those Christians who are said to have been defiled among their captors by food sacrificed to idols, we believe that this also must be answered to your charity: they should be cleansed through the satisfaction of penance. This must be assessed not so much by the length of time as by contrition of heart. Whether terror compelled it or hunger persuaded it, there should be no doubt that the act is to be abolished, since such food was consumed because of fear or want, not out of religious veneration.

[Col. 0867D–0868A]

Regarding those whom your Belovedness likewise believed should be brought to our attention—those who were compelled by fear or led astray by error to repeat baptism, and who now recognize that they acted against the sacrament of the Catholic faith—the following procedure must be observed: they are to be received into our fellowship and restored to the unity of communion only through the remedy of penance and the laying on of the bishop’s hand.

The length of their penance should be moderated according to your judgment, depending on how devoted you perceive the converts’ hearts to be. You should also take into account advanced age and the needs arising from any dangers or illnesses. If someone is so severely afflicted that, while still doing penance, his salvation is despaired of, priestly care must come to his aid with the grace of communion.

Those who received baptism from heretics without having previously been baptized are to be confirmed solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, because they received only the form of baptism, without the power of sanctification.

[Col. 0868B]

We proclaim this rule to all the churches as something to be observed: the washing once begun must not be violated by repetition. The Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5). Its washing must not be attempted again; rather, as we have said, only the sanctification of the Holy Spirit is to be invoked, so that what no one receives from heretics may be obtained from Catholic priests.

You shall arrange for this letter, which we have sent in response to your fraternal inquiry, to reach all the bishops of your province, so that the authority given for the observance of all may prove beneficial.

---

## LX. To Julian, Bishop of Aquileia

**Leo, Bishop, to Julian, Bishop of Aquileia.**

Having read the letters of your fraternity, we have recognized the strength of your faith, which we knew of old, and we rejoice that you vigilantly carry out pastoral care for the protection of Christ’s flocks, lest wolves who enter under the appearance of sheep tear the simple apart with bestial savagery, and not only make no progress themselves through correction but also corrupt what is sound.

To prevent this viperous deception from prevailing, we have thought it necessary to admonish your Belovedness, making clear that it endangers the soul if anyone who has fallen from us into the sect of the heretics and has in some way defiled himself with the contagion of heretical communion is accepted, after repentance, into Catholic communion without the legitimate satisfaction having first been carried out.

For it is most salutary and completely beneficial as spiritual medicine that presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any order who wish to appear corrected and desire to return to the Catholic faith—which they formerly abandoned—should first confess without ambiguity that they condemn both their own errors and the very authors of those errors. Once their false opinions have also been destroyed, no opportunity for hope should remain that any member of the Church might be corrupted by association with such men, since their own profession will have begun to confront them in every respect.

[Col. 0868C–D]

We also command that the following canonical constitution be observed concerning them: they should regard it as a great benefit if, after all hope of promotion has been entirely taken from them, they remain permanently in the order in which they are found—provided they have not been defiled by a second baptism.

Anyone who judges that such men should be promoted to the sacred orders incurs no slight offense before God. If promotion is granted to the blameless only after rigorous examination, it must be even less permissible for the suspect.

Therefore, your Belovedness, whose devotion gives us joy, should join your care to our directives and ensure that the measures proposed laudably and ordained salutarily for the safety of the whole Church are carried out carefully and promptly.

Your Belovedness should not think that we would be moved only weakly if—as we do not believe—those things we decree for the protection of the canons and the integrity of the faith were neglected. The faults of lower orders must be attributed above all to idle and negligent rulers, who often nurture a great pestilence while failing to apply the necessary medicine.

Given on the day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Alipius and Ardabur.

---

## LXI. To Dorus, Bishop of Beneventum

[Col. 0869B]

**Leo, Bishop, to his most beloved brother Dorus.**

We are grieved that the judgment we had hoped for concerning you has been disappointed, since we see that you have committed acts that, through a culpable novelty, would defile every rule of ecclesiastical sanction. You know very well how earnestly we wish the commands of the ancestral canons to be preserved throughout all the churches of the Lord, and that this care belongs especially to the priests of all peoples, so that the rules of the sacred constitutions may not be corrupted by any excesses.

We are therefore astonished that you, who ought to have been most observant of the authority of the Apostolic See, acted so negligently—or rather arrogantly—that you became not the guardian but the transgressor of the laws entrusted to you.

For from the petition of your presbyter Paul, who is counted among your subjects, we have learned that the order of the presbyterate was disturbed among you by a novel intrigue and shameful collusion. One of them was hurriedly and prematurely promoted, thereby causing the downfall of others, whose age commended them and no fault diminished them.

If ambition prompted this action, or if the inexperienced zeal of supporters demanded what custom had never allowed—that a beginner should be preferred to men of long service and a newcomer to an elder—then it was your duty, through prudence and instruction, to restrain the desires of those who made an unjust request by rational authority, lest the man whom you hastily advanced to priestly honor should begin his career by injuring those with whom he was associated.

I am surprised that, if this had occurred, the virtue of humility rather than the vice of arrogance would have been strengthened in him. You could not have been unaware that the Lord said: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted, but whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11). He also said: “You seek to grow from a small beginning and to become greater in honor.”

Both arrangements are disorderly and perverse. All the fruit of labor is taken away, and every measure of merit is emptied, if someone pursues these dignities only to the extent that he has obtained flattery—so that the desire to excel not only diminishes the proud man but also the one who indulges him.

[Col. 0869C–D]

If, as is asserted, the first and second presbyters were so eager to have Epicarpius preferred to themselves that they flattered him and asked that he be honored at their own disgrace, even this ought not to have been granted to them when they were casting themselves down by their own judgment. You should have opposed such a wretched desire rather than yielded to it.

Such ugly and cowardly submission could not prejudice the grace of God in men conscious of their good standing and not making God’s grace void, by allowing those men to exchange their precedence with one another by whatever arrangement, thereby diminishing the dignity of those who followed them; and because they had placed the last before themselves, they would consequently stand above the others.

Therefore, although the aforementioned presbyters, having declared themselves unworthy of the order of their honor, deserved even to be deprived of the priesthood, nevertheless, out of the Apostolic See’s compassion, let them be spared and be regarded as the last among all the presbyters of the Church.

And so that they may bear the sentence of their own judgment, they will stand below even the man whom, by their own decision, they preferred to themselves, while all the other presbyters remain in the order assigned to each by the date of his ordination. [215]

[Col. 0870A–B]

Let no one except the two men named above suffer any injury through diminished dignity. Let this disgrace fall only upon them: they chose to become inferior to one who had been ordained as a newcomer and prematurely, so that they may recognize the evangelical sentence as applying to themselves: “With the judgment you judge, you will be judged, and with the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matthew 7:2).

As for the presbyter Paul, whose order he did not abandon with praiseworthy steadfastness, let him retain it. Let him not thereafter presume anything to the injury of anyone. Your Belovedness, whom the disapproval of the entire affair rightly assails, should hasten to remedy the matter at least by ensuring that these decrees are carried out without delay or evasion. Otherwise, if a just appeal should once again be brought to us, we will necessarily be moved more severely, since we prefer to restore discipline by correcting what has been badly done rather than increase punishment.

Know that we have entrusted the execution of our commands to our brother and fellow bishop Julius, so that everything may be confirmed through him according to our decision.

Given on the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Postumianus.

---

## LXII. To all the bishops established throughout Sicily

**Leo, to all the bishops established throughout Sicily, greetings in the Lord.**

We are urged by divine commands and apostolic admonitions to watch tirelessly over the condition of all the churches, and, wherever something liable to censure is found, to remove it promptly, whether it has arisen from ignorance and lack of understanding or from presumptuous usurpation.

For the command of the Lord’s voice instructs us through the blessed Apostle Peter, who was imbued by a threefold repetition with a mystical ordinance: the one who loves Christ must feed Christ’s sheep. We are encouraged by the reverence due to the very See over which we preside through the abundance of divine grace to avoid, as far as we can, the danger of negligence, lest the confession of the chief Apostle—who testified that he was a lover of the Lord—not be found in us.

Anyone who is negligent toward a flock entrusted to him so many times is shown not to love its shepherd.

When, therefore, as I was fraternally concerned about the actions of your charity, reliable indications made known to me that you differed from the custom of apostolic institution in what is the principal matter among the Church’s sacraments—celebrating the sacrament of baptism more frequently on the day of Epiphany than during the season of Easter—I am astonished that you or your predecessors could have adopted so unreasonable an innovation. By confusing the mysteries of the two seasons, you seem to have thought that there was no difference between the day on which Christ was adored by the Magi and the day on which he rose from the dead.

[Col. 0870D–0871A]

You could never have fallen into this fault if you had taken the law of all observance from the same source from which you receive the consecration of your honor, and if the See of the blessed Apostle Peter—which is the mother of your priestly dignity—had been your guide in ecclesiastical instruction.

Your departure from its rules could have been tolerated with less equanimity if some written admonition from us had preceded it. But now, since correction is not despaired of, gentleness must be maintained. Although a priestly excuse that pleads ignorance is scarcely tolerable, we have nevertheless preferred both to temper the necessary censure and to instruct you by the clearest reasoning of the truth.

The restoration of the human race remained eternally and unchangeably preordained in God’s eternal plan. Yet the temporal order of events to be accomplished through Jesus Christ our Lord took its beginning from the incarnation of the Word.

Accordingly, one time is that when, at the angel’s announcement, blessed Mary believed that she would conceive through the Holy Spirit and conceived; another is that when, her virgin integrity preserved, the child was born and, amid the rejoicing of the heavenly ministers, was announced to the shepherds; another is that when the infant was circumcised; another is that when the prescribed offering was made for him; another is that when the three Magi, stirred from the East by the brightness of a new star, arrived at Bethlehem and reverently adored the child with the mystical offering of their gifts.

[Col. 0871B–C]

Nor are the days the same on which he was taken away from the impious Herod by the divinely ordained journey into Egypt and on which, after the persecutor’s death, he was recalled from Egypt to Galilee.

Amid these varied stages of the divine dispensation, his bodily growth also advanced. As the Evangelist testifies, the Lord increased in age and grace. During the days of Passover he went with his parents to the Temple; when he was absent from their company on the return journey, he was found seated among the elders and teachers, who marveled at him. When he explained the reason for remaining behind, he said: “Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” He signified that he was the Son of the one whose Temple it was.

When, at a more mature age, he openly sought the baptism of his forerunner John, what ambiguity remained concerning his divinity, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him and remained in the form of a dove, and the Father’s voice was heard from heaven saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Mark 1:11)?

We have touched on all these matters as briefly as we could, so that your Belovedness may know that all the days of Christ were consecrated by innumerable acts of power and that the mysteries of the sacraments shone forth in all his actions. Yet some things are announced by signs and others fulfilled in reality, and not everything numbered among the works of the Savior pertains to the time of baptism.

For if we were to honor indiscriminately even those things we know were done by him after the baptism of blessed John, all times would have to be counted as festivals, since all are full of miracles.

[Col. 0871D–0872A]

But because the Spirit of wisdom and understanding so instructed the Apostles and the teachers of the whole Church that Christian observance should contain nothing disorderly or confused, the reasons for the solemnities had to be distinguished, and in all established practices a reasonable discrimination of our fathers and leaders had to be preserved.

For we are not one flock and one shepherd in any other way than by saying, as the Apostle teaches, all the same thing. We must be perfect in the same understanding and in the same knowledge.
