Although the things that belong to Christ’s humility and those that belong to his glory proceed through one and the same person, and everything in him—both divine power and human weakness—tends toward our restoration, nevertheless the power of baptism establishes a new creation from the old specifically in the death of the crucified one and in the resurrection of the dead one. Thus, for those who are reborn, both Christ’s death and his life become effective.

The blessed Apostle Paul says: “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been united with the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be united with the likeness of his resurrection” (Romans 6:3–5).

And so on through the rest of what the teacher of the nations set forth at greater length to commend the sacrament of baptism. It was thereby made clear, through the spirit of this teaching, that for the rebirth of the human race and its adoption as children of God, that day and that time were chosen in which, through the likeness of the mystery, the things accomplished in the Head itself might be understood as corresponding to its members.

In the rule of baptism, death intervenes for the killing of sin; the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial; and washing with water is in the likeness of rising from the tomb.

[Col. 0872B–C]

The very character of the action therefore teaches that the proper day for the general celebration of grace is the day on which both the power of the gift and the form of the action arose.

For confirmation of this, it is especially significant that the Lord Jesus Christ himself, after rising from the dead, gave to the disciples—in whom all the leaders of the churches were being instructed—both the form and the authority to baptize, saying: “Go therefore now, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

He could certainly have instructed them about this even before his Passion, unless he wished the grace of regeneration to be understood as having begun with his own resurrection.

To this observance is also added the solemnity of Pentecost, consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit. It depends upon the celebration of Easter, and although other festivals belong to other days, this one always returns on the same day distinguished by the Lord’s resurrection. It extends, as it were, the hand of assisting grace, so that those whom illness, the length of a journey, or the difficulty of travel by sea kept unwillingly from Easter, or whom any other necessity hindered, may receive through the gift of the Holy Spirit the fulfillment of their desire.

[Col. 0872D–0873A]

The only-begotten Son of God wished there to be no distance between himself and the Holy Spirit in the faith of believers or in the power of works, because there is no diversity in nature. He said: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17). Again: “The Paraclete, the Spirit whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything and remind you of all that I have said to you” (ibid.). And again: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13).

Since Christ is the truth, the Spirit of truth is the Holy Spirit, and the name Paraclete belongs properly to both, the festival is not dissimilar where the sacrament is one.

We do not defend this merely from our own persuasion; we prove that it is to be observed on apostolic authority by a sufficiently suitable example. We follow the blessed Apostle Peter, who, on the day when the promised Spirit filled the whole number of believers, consecrated through the washing of baptism about three thousand people converted by his preaching.

The Holy Scripture containing the Acts of the Apostles teaches this in a faithful account, saying: “When they heard this, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the other Apostles, ‘What shall we do, brothers?’ Peter replied to them, ‘Repent,’ he said, ‘and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far away, everyone whom the Lord our God will call.’ With other words also he bore witness and exhorted them, saying, ‘Save yourselves from this crooked generation.’ Therefore those who received his word were baptized, and about three thousand persons were added on that day” (Acts 2:37–41).

[Col. 0873B–C]

Since it is therefore entirely clear that these two seasons of which we have spoken are the proper times for the chosen to be baptized in the Church, we admonish your Belovedness to introduce no other days into this observance.

Although there are also other festivals to which much reverence is owed in honor of God, we must nevertheless preserve the mystical distinction of the principal and greatest sacrament. This does not prohibit the freedom by which aid is given through baptism at any time to those in danger.

Thus we defer the free vows of those who are safe and living in the security of peace to these two festivals, which are joined and related to one another, but in danger of death, in the peril of siege, amid the hardships of persecution, or in fear of shipwreck, we deny no one at any time this remedy of true salvation.

If anyone thinks that the festival of Epiphany—which is to be venerated in its proper order with due honor—has the privilege of baptism because some say that on that very day the Lord approached the baptism of Saint John, let him know that the grace and purpose of that baptism were different and did not belong to the same power by which those are reborn through the Holy Spirit of whom it is said: “They were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:13).

[Col. 0873D–0874A]

For the Lord, who needed no remission of sin and sought no remedy of rebirth, wished to be baptized just as he wished to be circumcised and to have an offering of purification made for him, so that he who “was made from a woman,” as the Apostle says, “might be made under the law” (Galatians 4:4)—the law which he “had not come to abolish but to fulfill” (Matthew 5:17), and, by fulfilling it, to bring it to completion, as the blessed Apostle proclaims: “The end of the law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4).

He established in himself the sacrament of his baptism, because, holding the first place in all things, he taught that he was the beginning. He also confirmed the power of the principle of regeneration [216] when blood for redemption and water for baptism flowed from his side.

Just as the Old Testament was a testimony to the New, and the Law was given through Moses while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, so the various sacrifices prefigured one sacrifice, and the slaughter of many lambs came to an end in the offering of the one of whom it is said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

Thus John—not Christ, but Christ’s forerunner; not the bridegroom, but the bridegroom’s friend—was so faithful, seeking not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ, that he declared himself unworthy to loosen the straps of Christ’s sandals. John baptized with water for repentance, but Christ was to baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, by a twofold power both restoring life and consuming sins.

[Col. 0874B–C]

With so many and such great testimonies before you, brothers, by which you can recognize clearly and without any ambiguity that, in the baptism of the chosen—who, according to apostolic rule, must be examined by exorcisms, sanctified by fasts, and instructed by frequent preaching—only two seasons are to be observed, namely Easter and Pentecost, we make this known to your charity so that you may no longer depart in any excess from the apostolic institutions.

For after this there can be no great excuse if anyone believes that the apostolic rules may be neglected in any respect.

Therefore, as the first requirement for safeguarding the most harmonious unity, we insist that, since it has been most salutarily established by the holy Fathers that bishops should hold two assemblies each year, three of you should always come to Rome on the third day before the Kalends of October to join in a fraternal council, and that this custom be observed by you without evasion.

With the help of God’s grace, it will thus be easier to ensure that no scandals and no errors arise in the churches of Christ, since, in the presence of the blessed Apostle Peter, all matters may always be discussed in communion, so that all the institutions and canonical decrees may remain inviolate among all the Lord’s priests.

[Col. 0874D]

We wish the matters which, with the Lord inspiring us, we have thought necessary to make known to you to reach your awareness through our brothers and fellow bishops Bachillus and Paschasius. Through their report, we shall learn how reverently the institutions of the Apostolic See are observed by you.

---

## LXIII. To the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy

**Leo, to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy, greetings in the Lord.**
We summon you, dearest brothers, to share in our concern, [Col. 0875A] so that, with pastoral vigilance, you may more diligently care for the flocks entrusted to you, lest the devil’s cunning be able to accomplish anything. The disease which, through the mercy of the Lord revealing it, is being removed from our sheep by our care must not spread through your churches while you remain unwarned and still unaware of what is happening, nor find hidden passageways into its lairs, so that what is extinguished by us in the city may be planted among you with roots in darkness.

Our investigation discovered very many teachers who were followers of Manichaean impiety in the city; our vigilance exposed them, and authority and discipline restrained them. Those whom we were able to correct, we corrected, and we compelled them, by a public confession in the church and by their own signatures, to condemn Manichaeus together with his teachings and disciples. [Col. 0875B] Thus, after they had confessed their guilt, we lifted them from the abyss of their impiety by granting them penance. A few, however, had plunged themselves so deeply that no assistance from anyone could come to their aid. Subjected to the laws according to the enactments of Christian rulers, they were condemned by public judges to perpetual exile, lest they pollute the holy flock by their contagion.

We also displayed before the eyes of the Christian people, with clear disclosure, everything profane or disgraceful that they possess both in the Scriptures and in their secret traditions, so that the people might know what to shun or avoid. Indeed, the man who was said to be their bishop, when he was detained by us, revealed the shameful practices he maintained in their rites, as the record of the proceedings can inform you. For your instruction we have also sent these materials, and when you have read them, [Col. 0875C] you will be able to know everything that we discovered.

And because we learned that some of those whom a more severe guilt had prevented from being absolved had fled, we have sent this letter to your affection through our acolyte, so that, once your holiness has been more fully informed, you may act with greater diligence and caution, and so that men of Manichaean perversity may find no opportunity among your people to cause harm or to act as teachers of this sacrilege. For we cannot govern those entrusted to us otherwise than by pursuing with zeal for the Lord’s faith those who are destroyers and destroyed, and by cutting them off from sound minds, with whatever severity we can employ, lest the plague spread more widely.

Therefore I exhort, appeal to, and admonish your affection to watch with the concern that you owe and are able to exercise, in order to investigate them, and not to allow them any opportunity to conceal themselves. For just as the one who has diligently carried out whatever may benefit the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive an exceedingly great reward, so whoever has been unwilling to protect his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will not be able to excuse himself before the tribunal of the Lord on account of the guilt of negligence.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Theodosius, for the eighteenth time, and Aluinus.

### LXIV.—To Neonias, bishop of Ravenna.

Leo, to Neonia, bishop of Ravenna, concerning those returning from captivity who are uncertain whether they received baptism before their captivity.

We have often strengthened the wavering hearts of brothers amid the uncertainty of various questions, under the instruction of the Spirit of God, gathering the form of our answer either from the teaching of the holy Scriptures or from the rules of the Fathers. But recently, at a synod, a new and previously unheard-of kind of consultation arose. For, through the report of certain brothers, we learned that some captives returning to their homes and freedom—those who had entered captivity at an age when they could not have possessed firm knowledge of anything—were asking for the remedy of baptism. Yet, because of the ignorance of childhood, they could not remember whether they had received the sacrament of that remedy before their captivity. Thus, under this uncertainty concerning a hidden memory, they were bringing their souls into danger, while grace was denied them under the pretext of caution—grace which was not being given precisely because it was thought to have been given already. [Col. 0876A]

Since, therefore, the fear of certain brothers reasonably hesitated to confer upon such people the sacrament of the Lord’s mystery, we received, in the synodal assembly, as we have said, a consultation of this kind. We wished it to be carefully examined and considered with attentive reasoning according to each person’s understanding, so that, by the reflection of many, we might reach the truth with greater certainty. Accordingly, what divine inspiration brought to our mind was also confirmed by the frequent agreement of the brothers.

First, therefore, we must take care lest, while we maintain some appearance of caution, we incur the loss of souls that ought to be regenerated. Who is so devoted to his suspicions that he would define as true what, when all evidence is lacking, he merely suspects on the basis of uncertain opinion? When the person who desires regeneration does not remember that he was baptized, and no other person can testify about him concerning something he does not know, nothing is consecrated in which sin could intrude, since in this matter neither the one who is consecrated nor the one who consecrates is guilty in conscience.

We certainly know that it is an inexpiable crime whenever, in accordance with the practices condemned by the holy Fathers among heretics, someone is compelled to undergo twice the washing that is granted once for regeneration. Apostolic teaching protests against this, proclaiming for us one divinity in the Trinity, one confession of faith, and one sacrament in baptism. But in this case nothing similar is to be feared, since what is entirely unknown to have been done cannot become the crime of repetition.

Therefore, whenever such a person is encountered, investigate the matter first by careful examination, and for a long period—unless perhaps the final hour is approaching—inquire whether anyone can be found who, by his testimony, could swear to the ignorance of the person who does not know. When it has been established that the person who needs the sacrament of baptism is being prevented only by a groundless suspicion, let him approach without fear to obtain the grace of which he knows that he bears no trace within himself. We do not hesitate to open to him the door of salvation, which he is never shown to have entered.

But if it is established that someone was baptized by heretics, the sacrament of regeneration must not in any way be repeated for him. Instead, only what was lacking there is to be conferred, so that through the laying on of the bishop’s hands [Col. 0877A] he may receive the power of the Holy Spirit.

For this reason, dearest brother, we wish this matter to come generally to the knowledge of all of you, lest, while God’s mercy is feared more than is right, it be denied to those who desire to be saved.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of the emperor Martianus Augustus.

### LXV.—To the bishops of Africa.

Leo, to all the bishops established throughout Africa, greeting in the Lord.

Since widespread report repeatedly declared that certain practices had been illicitly usurped among you in the ordination of priests, the reasonableness of piety required us, in accordance with the concern that by divine institution we owe to the universal Church, to make every effort to learn the truth of these matters. We therefore entrusted the responsibility of our care to our departing brother and fellow priest, Potentius, [Col. 0877B] who, according to the letters that we sent to you through him concerning the bishops whose election was reported to be blameworthy, was to investigate what the truth might be and faithfully report everything to us.

Since he has now fully disclosed everything to our knowledge, and has revealed to us in a truthful report under what kinds of rulers certain Christian communities are governed in the regions of the province of Caesarea, it was necessary for us, by letters sent to you, to express the grief of our heart with which we burn on account of the dangers threatening the Lord’s flocks. We are astonished that, among you, either the presumption of ambitious men or popular tumult has prevailed so greatly under the pretext of troubled times that the pastoral dignity and government of the Church have been entrusted to unworthy men, situated far outside priestly merit. This is not to care for the peoples but to harm them; it is not to provide governance but to increase danger.

For the integrity of those who preside is the salvation of those subject to them, and where obedience is secure, there the form of teaching is sound. A principate that sedition has extorted or ambition has seized is pernicious because of the example of its very beginning, even if it does not offend by its morals and actions; and it is difficult for matters to end well when they have been begun with a bad beginning.

If it is necessary to take prudent and knowledgeable care in every rank of the Church that nothing in the Lord’s house be disordered or perverse, how much more must we labor to avoid error in the election of the one who is placed above all the ranks? For the condition and order of the entire household of the Lord will totter if what follows in the body is not found in the head.

Where is the command issued by the blessed apostle Paul through the Spirit of God, by which, in the person of Timothy, the entire company of Christ’s priests is instructed, and which is therefore addressed to each of us: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5:22)? What does it mean to lay hands hastily, except to grant priestly honor to those not tested before the age of maturity, before the time of examination, before the merit of labor, and before experience of discipline? And what does it mean to share in the sins of others, except to make the ordainer like the one who has not deserved to be ordained?

For just as the person who follows sound judgment in choosing a priest gains the fruit of a good work for himself, so the person who raises an unworthy man into the fellowship of his dignity inflicts grave harm upon himself. [Col. 0878A]

217. What is contained in the general regulations must not be disregarded in anyone’s case, nor should that honor be considered legitimate which has been conferred through transgression. For the Apostle says that, among the rules of election, a bishop must be ordained whom it has been established “to have been, or to be, the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2).

This command has always been held so sacred that the same condition is understood to apply when the wife of a priest is chosen: she must not previously have experienced marriage to another man before marrying the man who had had no other wife. Who, then, would dare to overlook the injury committed against so great a sacrament? [Col. 0878B] Even the prescriptions of the Law did not fail to provide for this great and venerable mystery; they clearly establish that the priest is to take a virgin and that the woman who is to become the wife of a pontiff must not know the bed of another husband.

Already then the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church was being prefigured in priests, so that, since the man is the head of the woman, the Bride of the Word might learn to know no other man than Christ, who chooses one, loves one, and does not join another to himself in companionship. If, therefore, this form of priestly marriage was observed even in the Old Testament, how much more, now that grace has been revealed, must we who are established under it obey the apostolic commands? Thus, however gifted with good morals someone may be found, and however adorned with holy works, he must in no way rise either to the rank of deacon, the honor of presbyter, or the height of the episcopate if it becomes clear either that he himself was not the husband of one wife or that his wife had not been the wife of one man. The Apostle also admonishes and says: “And let these first be tested, and then let them serve” (1 Timothy 3:10).

What else should we understand this to mean except that, in these promotions, we must consider not only the privileges of marriage but also the merits of labor? We must not entrust pastoral office either to those inexperienced from baptism or to those suddenly converted from secular activity, since every rank of Christian service ought to be assessed according to the growth of one’s progress, to determine whether greater responsibilities can be entrusted to anyone.

The venerable sanctions of the holy Fathers, when they spoke about the election of priests, rightly judged only those fit for sacred administration whose entire lives, from childhood beginnings to advanced age, had passed through the stages of ecclesiastical discipline. In this way, their earlier life would provide testimony for each of them, and no one could doubt the advancement of a man to whom, because of many labors, chaste morals, and energetic actions, the reward of a higher position was owed.

For if it is unworthy to attain worldly honor without the support of time and without the merit of labor, and those whom proofs of integrity do not support are ordinarily marked as ambitious, how careful and prudent must be the administration of divine gifts and heavenly dignities, lest apostolic and canonical decrees be violated in any respect, and the Church of the Lord be entrusted to men who, ignorant of legitimate institutions and strangers to all humility, do not wish to advance from the lowest places but want to begin from the highest? It is extremely unjust and absurd that the inexperienced should be preferred to their teachers, the new to the old, and the untrained to those who have earned their position.

“As there must be,” as the Apostle says, “in a great house vessels of various kinds, some of gold and silver, but others of wood and clay” (2 Timothy 2:20), their service is nevertheless distinguished according to the quality of the material, and the use of precious vessels is not the same as that of worthless ones. Everything is disordered if vessels of clay are preferred to vessels of gold, and wooden vessels to silver ones.

Just as the forms of all those who do not yet shine with any virtues are represented in the wooden and clay vessels, so in the gold and silver vessels are undoubtedly represented those who, refined through the long fire of instruction and through the furnace of prolonged labor, have deserved to be proven gold and pure silver. If these do not receive a reward for their devotion, all ecclesiastical discipline is dissolved and every order is disturbed, while, through the perverse judgment of those making elections, men who have undergone no ministry obtain the principate owed to others.

Since, therefore, popular enthusiasm or the ambition of proud men has prevailed among you to such an extent that we know not only laymen but also husbands of second wives and husbands of widows to have been advanced to pastoral office, do not the circumstances most appropriately demand that the churches in which these things were committed be cleansed by a stricter judgment, and that appropriate vengeance be pronounced not only against such prelates but also against those who ordained them? [Col. 0879C]

But gentleness of mercy surrounds us on one side, and the strictness of justice on the other. And because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10), we are compelled, in keeping with the piety of the apostolic see, to temper our judgment in such a way that, after weighing the gravity of the offenses—for it is clear that they are not all of the same measure—we define some as tolerable for the time being and cut off others entirely.

Neither apostolic nor legal authority permits those who have entered into a second marriage or joined themselves in marriage to widows to hold the priesthood. Still more must this apply to the man—if your judgment has convicted him—who, as has been reported to us, is simultaneously the husband of two wives, or to the man who, after being dismissed by his first wife, is said to have married another.

As for the others whose advancement incurs only this criticism, that they were selected from among the laity for episcopal office, and who cannot be considered blameworthy merely because they have wives, we permit them to retain the priesthood they have undertaken. In doing so, we do not prejudice the statutes of the apostolic see, nor the decrees of our predecessors and of ourselves, by which it was beneficially established that no layman, however many supporters he might have, should ascend to the first, second, or third rank in the Church before reaching the requisite merit through legitimate stages of advancement.

For although we tolerate both matters as venial, it will not long remain so if anyone presumes to usurp what we altogether prohibit. The remission of sin does not grant permission to sin, nor may what was permitted for some reason thereafter be committed with impunity. [Col. 0880A]

As for Donatus of Salicina, who, as we have learned, converted from Novatianism together with his people, we wish him to preside over the Lord’s flock on the condition that he remember to send us a statement of his faith, in which he condemns the error of Novatian teaching and fully confesses the Catholic truth.

We likewise will not remove Maximus, although he was blameworthily ordained from the laity, from the episcopal dignity he acquired in some manner, provided that he is no longer a Donatist and is alien to the spirit of schismatic depravity. He too must make known, by a statement submitted to us, that he is Catholic.

As for Aggarus and Tyberianus, whose case differs from that of the others ordained from the laity in this respect—that their ordination is said to have been accompanied by fierce disturbances and savage seditions—we have entrusted everything to your judgment, so that, once we have received a trustworthy report of the inquiry conducted among you, we may know what should be decided concerning the men mentioned above.

As for those servants of God who lost the integrity of their chastity through barbarian assault, they will be more praiseworthy in humility and modesty if they do not dare to compare themselves with undefiled virgins. Although every sin arises from the will, and the mind may not be polluted against its will by the corruption of the flesh, they will nevertheless suffer less harm if they grieve that they have lost in body what they were able not to lose in spirit.

Since, therefore, you will see that nearly everything contained in the report of our brother Potentius has been fully communicated to your affection through our brother and fellow bishop David, who has been approved by us both for the merit of his priesthood and for his character, [Col. 0880C] it remains, brothers, for you to receive these salutary exhortations with united obedience. Do nothing through contention, but, united in every effort of devotion, obey the divine and apostolic constitutions, and do not allow the pious decrees of the canons to be violated in any respect.

For what we have now relaxed after careful consideration of particular cases must henceforth be guarded according to the ancient rules, lest what we have granted for a time in pious leniency we later punish with just retribution.

### LXVI. Pope Leo on the privilege of bishops and presbyters, to all the bishops of the churches of Germany and Gaul.

When, in the name of God, we had held in the Roman Church an assembly of bishops, other fellow priests, and the faithful of Christ, and had diligently dealt with illicit ordinations—about which increasingly frequent reports had reached us from those parts who came here—as well as with other ecclesiastical needs and affairs, carefully rereading the holy canons, many men reported to us with tearful faces that certain bishops of the cities of Germany and Gaul frequently sent fellow bishops—who, according to the canons of Neocaesarea or the decrees of other Fathers, are the same as presbyters—or presbyters, to erect altars and consecrate basilicas in the absence of the pontiff. [Col. 0880D]

It is not surprising that men ignorant of ecclesiastical discipline, who had been transferred and promoted directly from secular service to priestly ministry, prescribed what is contrary to canonical rule. Therefore, lest such license be further usurped by you, it was necessary to establish by common judgment—and you should know this—that just as the consecration of an altar is illicit for a fellow bishop or presbyter, so also is its establishment.

For in the divine Scriptures, when the Lord commanded it, Moses alone erected the altar in the tabernacle of God; he alone anointed it, since he was indeed the high priest of God, as it is written concerning him: “Moses and Aaron among his priests” (Psalm 99:6). Therefore, what was commanded to be done only by the chief priests, whose type was represented by Moses and Aaron, is entirely forbidden to fellow bishops or presbyters who bear the figure of Aaron’s sons to presume to undertake.

Although they share with bishops the administration of very many ministries, they must nevertheless recognize that certain things are forbidden to them by the authority of the ancient Law and others by the ecclesiastical rules of the new covenant: for example, the consecration of presbyters and deacons or of virgins, as well as the establishment of an altar and its blessing or anointing.

They are not permitted to erect altars, consecrate churches or altars, or, by the laying on of hands, give the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, to the faithful being baptized or converted, or to those coming from heresy. Nor may they prepare chrism, mark the foreheads of the baptized with chrism, publicly reconcile a penitent during Mass, or send letters of authorization to anyone.

All these things are illicit for fellow bishops, who are known to exist according to the example and form of the seventy disciples, and for presbyters, who bear the same figure. For although they possess consecration, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate. The authority of the canons prescribes that all these matters belong solely to the supreme pontiffs, so that both the distinction of ranks and the height of the supreme pontiff’s dignity may thereby be demonstrated.

Nor is it permitted for presbyters to enter the baptistery in the presence of a bishop, to baptize or sign a child while the bishop is present, to reconcile a penitent without the command of his bishop, or, in the bishop’s presence, to celebrate the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood unless the bishop orders it. Nor may they, while he is present, teach, bless, or greet the people, or exhort the congregation.

We are moved especially and more earnestly against those who have neglected the statutes of the holy Fathers in ordaining bishops and have consecrated men whom they ought to have rejected. Therefore, if any bishops have consecrated as a priest someone whom it was not permitted to consecrate, even if they have in some way escaped the loss of their own honor, they will nevertheless no longer possess the right to ordain, nor may they take part in the sacrament that they conferred undeservedly, having disregarded divine judgment. [Col. 0881D]

We especially wish the following statute concerning priestly dignity to be observed among all the canons: where the populations are smaller and the assemblies smaller, the care of presbyters is sufficient. Episcopal governance, however, ought to preside only over larger populations and more populous cities, lest the priestly dignity—which the decrees of the holy Fathers, inspired by God, have forbidden to be assigned to hamlets and estates, or to obscure and isolated municipalities—be diminished by excessive multiplication, and the honor to which greater responsibilities ought to be entrusted become cheapened by its very numbers.

The bishop restored to his diocese has now claimed that this has occurred and has reasonably requested that, if the bishops of those places where they ought not to have been ordained should die by the course of nature, those very places be returned to the jurisdiction of that bishop. They had previously belonged to him. It is useless for priestly dignity to be diminished by the thoughtless freedom of ordainers and by unnecessary multiplication.

Concerning those who had been established in the sacred purpose of virginity but suffered barbarian violence and lost the integrity of their chastity not in mind but in body, we believe that this moderation should be observed: they should neither be cast down into the rank of widows nor be counted among sacred and persevering virgins. If, however, they persevere in every respect in their virginal commitment and preserve the firmness of chastity in their minds, communion in the sacraments must not be denied them, since it is unjust to accuse or mark them for what their will did not admit but hostile force took away. [Col. 0882B]

We also order that the case of Bishop Lupicinus be heard there. Although he repeatedly and earnestly requested communion, we restored it to him for this reason: because he had appealed to our judgment, we saw that he had been suspended from communion unjustly while the case remained pending.

It has also been added that a man is known to have been rashly ordained over him, although he ought not to have been ordained before Lupicinus, who was still present, had either been convicted or, at least, confessed and thereby become subject to a just sentence, so that the man being consecrated might receive the vacant place, as ecclesiastical discipline requires. [Col. 0882C]

If other matters arise that concern the condition of the churches and the concord of the priests, we wish them to be examined there under the fear of the Lord, and a full report concerning everything resolved and settled is to be sent to us, so that whatever has been defined justly and reasonably according to ecclesiastical custom may also be confirmed by my judgment.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of August.

### LXVII.—To the bishops established throughout the province of Vienne.

Leo, to his dearest brothers, all the bishops established throughout the province of Vienne.

The worship of the divine religion, which God’s grace willed to shine upon all peoples and every nation, was instituted by our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, [Col. 0882D] in such a way that the truth which had previously been contained in the proclamation of the Law and the Prophets might go forth through the apostolic trumpet for the salvation of all, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 3). Yet the Lord willed the sacrament of this ministry to belong to the office of all the apostles in such a way that he placed it principally in blessed Peter, the supreme head of all the apostles, so that from him, as from a kind of head, he might diffuse his gifts throughout the whole body. Thus he would understand himself to be excluded from the divine mystery who dared to withdraw from Peter’s firmness.

For when he had taken him into the fellowship of indivisible unity, he willed that what he himself was should exercise dominion, saying: [Col. 0883A] “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18), so that the building of the eternal temple, through the wondrous gift of God’s grace, might stand upon Peter’s firmness. Strengthening his Church with this stability, he ensured that neither human recklessness could assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it.

But since God, as we have said, built and established this most sacred firmness of the rock, whoever attempts to weaken its authority by indulging his own desires, failing to follow what he received from the ancients, and believing himself subject to no law or bound by no rule of the Lord’s institution—departing from your and our custom through the ambition of a new usurpation, presuming upon what is unlawful and neglecting what he ought to preserve—seeks to violate it with an exceedingly impious presumption.

Nevertheless, with God, as we believe, assisting us, we strive to correct these matters concerning you through more mature counsel, preserving the grace of our charity which the Apostolic See has always shown to your holiness, as you remember, and to settle the condition of your Churches through labor shared with you—not instituting new things, but renewing the old—so that we may continue in the established order of the custom handed down to us by our fathers and, through the ministry of good works, please God by removing the scandals of disturbances.

Let your fraternity therefore acknowledge with us that, out of reverence for the Apostolic See, the priests of your province have consulted it in innumerable communications, and that, in accordance with the ancient custom concerning appeals in various cases, judgments have either been reconsidered or confirmed, so that, while the unity of the Spirit was preserved in the bond of peace, letters passing back and forth might advance the holy work of perpetual charity. Our solicitude, seeking not its own interests but those of Christ, did not arrogate to itself the dignity divinely bestowed upon either the Churches or the priests of the Churches.

But Hilary departed from this course, which had always been both approved and beneficially established among our predecessors, intending to disturb the condition of the Churches and the concord of the priests through new presumptions. Once again he desired to subject you to his authority, refusing to allow himself to be subject to the blessed apostle Peter. He claimed for himself the ordinations of all the Churches throughout Gaul and transferred to his own jurisdiction the dignity owed to metropolitan priests, while also diminishing, through overly arrogant language, the reverence due to the most blessed [Col. 0883D] Peter. Although the power of binding and loosing was entrusted to him above all others, he was nevertheless specially charged with the care of feeding the sheep. Whoever thinks that his primacy should be denied can in no way diminish Peter’s dignity; rather, swollen with the spirit of his own pride, he plunges himself into the depths below.

What was done and concluded among us in the case of Bishop Celedonius, and what Hilary said when he was heard in the presence of that bishop, is shown by the order of events entered in the records. After Hilary had no reasonable answer that he could give in the council of holy priests, he turned to the hidden matters of his heart—matters that no layman could speak of and no priest could hear. We grieved, I confess, brothers, and attempted to treat this fear, which his deserts merited, with the remedies of our patience. We did not wish to aggravate the wounds which he repeatedly inflicted upon his own soul through insolent speeches; and we strove to soothe him, whom we had received as a brother, rather than distress him with our replies, although his own answers invited such a response.

Bishop Celedonius was acquitted, because, through the clear testimony of witnesses, and in Hilary’s own presence, he had shown that he had been unjustly deprived of the priesthood, so that Hilary, seated with us, had nothing he could bring against him. The judgment formerly pronounced in this matter was therefore removed—the judgment according to which a priest could not retain his office if he had been the husband of a widow.

In preserving the legal constitutions, we had indeed wished this rule to be observed carefully not only among priests but also among clerics of lower rank: men were not to be admitted to the sacred service who had contracted such a marriage or who could be shown, contrary to apostolic discipline, not to have been husbands of only one wife. But just as we decree that those whose conduct cannot be excused are either not to be admitted or, if admitted, are to be removed, so we must clear from this examination those against whom this charge is falsely brought, and not allow them to lose their office. The sentence pronounced against him would have remained had the truth of the accusations been established.

Our fellow bishop Celedonius was therefore restored to his own Church and to the dignity which he ought not to have lost, as the sequence of the proceedings and the judgment [Col. 0884C] pronounced by us after the inquiry had been completed testify.

When this matter had been concluded, the complaint of our brother and fellow bishop Projectus followed. He sent us a tearful and grievous letter concerning the bishop imposed over him. A letter was also submitted by his fellow citizens, confirmed by the numerous signatures of individuals, and filled with the most hostile complaints against Hilary: with their bishop Projectus, it had not been lawful even to fall ill; his priesthood had been transferred to another without his knowledge; and, while he was still alive, an heir had been introduced by Hilary the perverter into the vacant possession.

We should like to hear what your fraternity thinks of this, although our judgment ought not to doubt your sentiments. You see a brother lying on his sickbed, afflicted not so much by bodily illness [Col. 0884D] as by another grief. What hope of life remains for a man who, while another is substituted for him, is driven to despair concerning his priesthood?

It is therefore clear how gentle-hearted Hilary is: he thought that the delay of his brother’s death hindered his presumption. For as far as lay within him, he deprived him of light and took away his life; he inflicted this grief by substituting another in his place, so that the sick man would have no avenue of return to recovery.

Even if the customary departure of human life should soon come upon our brother, what does Hilary seek in another province? Why does he usurp what none of his predecessors, not even Patroclus, possessed, when even what appeared to have been temporarily granted to Patroclus by the Apostolic See was later removed by a better judgment? The wishes of the citizens should certainly have been awaited, the testimony of the people sought, the judgment of the distinguished consulted, and the election of the clergy obtained. In episcopal ordinations, these are accustomed to preserve among themselves the rules of the Fathers which they know, so that the norm of apostolic authority might be observed in all things. That authority commands that the priest who is to preside over a Church be supported not only by the testimony of the faithful but also by that of those outside, and that no opportunity for scandal be left, when the future teacher of peace is ordained through peace pleasing to God and through the united efforts of all.

But Hilary arrived unexpectedly, without their knowledge, and departed without warning, traveling rapidly, as we have learned, covering many routes and rushing through distant provinces with such premature haste that he seems to have sought glory more through clownish speed than priestly moderation.

These are the words of the citizens’ letter sent to us: “He departed before we knew that he had come. This is not returning but fleeing; it is not providing the care of pastoral diligence but inflicting the violence of a robber and thief, as the Lord says: ‘Whoever does not enter the sheepfold by the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber’ (John X, 1).”

Hilary therefore showed greater eagerness not to consecrate a bishop than to kill the one who was ill, and by wrongly ordaining the man he set over him, to deceive him.

Nevertheless, trusting that what we decide will be pleasing to you under God’s judgment, and consulting all our brothers in communion, we have decreed that the wrongly ordained man should be removed and that the deposed bishop should remain in his priesthood [Col. 0885C] and office.

We establish also that, if any of our brothers should die in any province, the right to ordain his successor belongs to the priest who is established as metropolitan of that province. For, as we see, cases have been concluded in which many things appear to have been committed contrary to ecclesiastical reason and ought to await the censure of a just judgment.

But we cannot linger here any longer, since we are summoned to other matters that must be discussed with your holiness.

As we have learned, an armed force follows the priest through the provinces, supported by armed men in his presumption, to invade Churches in the service of God which have lost their own bishops. Those who are to be ordained are dragged before this office, unknown to the cities over which they are to preside. Just as a known and approved man is sought peacefully, so, by force, it is necessary that an unknown man be brought and imposed.

I entreat and beseech you, and under God’s invocation I appeal to you, brothers: prohibit such things and remove every source of dissension from your provinces. Before God we certainly absolve ourselves, since we have warned you not to permit these things any longer.

Let future priests be sought in peace and quiet. The subscription of the clergy, the testimony of the distinguished, the agreement of the order, and the consent of the people must be secured. Let the man who is to preside over all be chosen by all.

As we have already said, let each metropolitan defend his right to ordination within his own province, together with those who by the antiquity of their priesthood precede the others, once that right has been restored to him [Col. 0886A]. Let no one dare claim another’s right for himself. Let each person be content with his own boundaries and limits. Let him understand that he may not transfer to another the privilege owed to himself.

If anyone, neglecting the apostolic decrees and showing greater favor to a person, should wish to abandon the privileges of his own office, believing that he can transfer his privilege to another, the power to ordain belongs not to the person to whom he yielded it but to the one within the province who precedes the other priests in episcopal seniority. The ordination is to be celebrated not arbitrarily but on the lawful day.

Let him know that the stability of his position cannot stand if he has been ordained on a day other than Saturday evening, as it dawns into the first day of the week, or the Lord’s Day itself. For our predecessors judged only the day of the Lord’s Resurrection worthy of honor, so that priests chosen on that day might especially be entrusted with their office [Col. 0886B].

Let every province be content with its own councils, and let Hilary no longer dare to convene synodal assemblies or disturb the judgments of the Lord’s priests by intruding himself. He must know not only that he has been excluded from another’s right but also that he has been deprived of authority over the province of Vienne, which he had wrongly usurped.

For it is fitting, brothers, that the statutes of antiquity be restored, since the man who claimed for himself the ordination of a province to which he had no right has now also been proved to be such that, although he repeatedly sought a sentence of condemnation through rash and insolent words, our instruction, out of the Apostolic See’s compassion, preserved for him the priesthood of his own city alone.

Let him therefore belong neither to the ordination nor to the order, since, conscious of his own deserts, when he was being sought in order to accuse, he believed that he should withdraw by shameful flight from the communion of the Apostolic See, of which he was not worthy to be a participant. God, as we believe, brought this about: when we thought he would appear before our judgments, he was drawn to them; and during the examinations that took place, God secretly caused him to depart, so that he would not become a sharer in our communion.

Communion should not easily be denied to any Christian, nor should it be left to the arbitrary decision of an angry priest—something which the mind of the one who inflicts punishment, unwillingly and sorrowfully, ought in a certain sense to reserve for the avenging of a grave offense.

We have learned that some have been excluded from the grace of communion for slight offenses and words, and that the soul for which Christ’s blood was poured out has been wounded by the imposition of so harsh a penalty, exposed, as it were, disarmed and stripped of every protection to the attacks of the devil, so that it might easily be captured.

Certainly, if a case should arise in which the nature of a committed crime justly requires someone to be deprived of communion, only the person whom guilt implicates should be subjected to that penalty; no one who is not shown to have shared in the offense should share in the punishment.

But why is it surprising that he behaves so toward laymen, when he is accustomed to take pleasure in dominating priests? Since our intention is evidently quite different—for we desire the condition of all the Churches and the concord of the priests to be preserved—we exhort and beseech you, bound together by the bond of charity, and admonish you with fitting affection, to preserve, for the sake of your peace and dignity, what has now been decreed by us, with God inspiring us and the most blessed apostle Peter, after all the cases had been examined and approved [Col. 0887A]. Be assured that our recognition of these decrees does not chiefly serve our own honor.

We are not defending the ordinations of your provinces for ourselves—something which Hilary may perhaps, according to his custom, falsely claim in order to corrupt the minds of your holiness—but through your vigilance we are vindicating them, so that novelty may no longer be permitted anything and no place remain for a presumptuous man to annul our privileges.

We declare that our one cause for rejoicing is that the diligence of the Apostolic See remains unimpaired among you, and that, through the preservation of priestly discipline, we do not allow what belongs to your office to perish from your mouth through new usurpations.

Since antiquity must always be honored, we wish our brother and fellow bishop Leontius, an approved priest, to be honored with this dignity, if it pleases you: no council of another province is to be proclaimed by your holiness without his consent, and all of you are to honor him as his age and integrity require, while the dignity of his metropolitan privilege is preserved [Col. 0887B].

For it is equitable, and appears injurious to no brother, that priests in their own provinces should show deference, in proportion to their age and merit, to those who precede them in seniority.

May God keep you safe and unharmed, my brothers.

### LXVIII.—To Ravennius, Archbishop of Arles

Know that we are pleased by the advancement of your belovedness, which has attained the dignity of the highest priesthood, so that we rejoice not only in the increase of your honor but also in that of the Church of Arles, over which the Lord has placed you [Col. 0887C].

For it redounds to the honor and benefit of all the faithful when such a bishop is held in office—one whose support benefits many and whose example inspires them. Since you are not unaware of what we have judged concerning the sincerity of your mind according to our present knowledge, you recognize that justice requires us to test what we have presumed concerning you, dearest brother.

Let the authority of your moderation be commended not by firmness but by gentleness; let leniency temper justice, and patience restrain freedom. Let pride, which is close to falling, be avoided, and let humility, which always ought to grow, be loved. Your choice is not ignorant of ecclesiastical laws, so contain all the rights of your authority within their rules and limits.

Yet it is said: “The law is not laid down for the just” (1 Tim. I, 9), because he fulfills the norm of the commandment through the judgment of his will, when true love of what is right possesses within itself both apostolic authorities and canonical decrees [Col. 0887D]. As their devoted follower and diligent executor, you will undoubtedly glory in the fellowship of those who deserved to hear, concerning the profit they had made from the talents entrusted to them: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXVII, 21).

So that you may have no doubt of our confidence in our affection for you, let us be informed more frequently of the progress of your actions, since, mindful of our judgment, we always desire to rejoice in the Lord over your advancement.

May God keep you safe and unharmed, dearest brother.

### LXIX.—To Theodore, Bishop of Fréjus

[Col. 0888A]

Leo to Theodore, Bishop of Fréjus.

The order of your concern ought to have been this: first, you should have consulted your metropolitan about the matter that appeared to require investigation; and, if your belovedness did not know what he himself also did not know, you should have asked that both of you be instructed together, since in cases relating to the general observance of all the Lord’s priests, inquiry ought to be made only with the primates.

Nevertheless, so that the uncertainty of the person consulting may in some way be instructed, I will not conceal what ecclesiastical rule teaches concerning the status of penitents. God’s manifold mercy assists human lapses in such a way that the hope of eternal life is restored not only through the grace of baptism but also through the remedy of penance. Those who had violated the gift of regeneration, condemning themselves by their own judgment, may reach the forgiveness of their sins through the divinely ordered aids of goodness; yet God’s indulgence cannot be obtained without the supplication of priests.

For the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, entrusted this power to the leaders of the Church: they are to impose an act of penance upon those who confess, and, once they have been cleansed by salutary satisfaction, admit them through the door of reconciliation to communion in the sacraments.

The Savior himself takes part in this work, and is never absent from what he has entrusted to his ministers to perform, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). Thus, if anything is fulfilled through our service in good order and with a rejoicing result, we should not doubt that it was granted through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0888C].

But if anyone for whom we implore the Lord is prevented by some obstacle from receiving the gift of present forgiveness, and, before reaching the appointed remedies, ends this temporal life according to the human condition, he will not be able, once stripped of the flesh, to obtain what he did not receive while remaining in the body.

Nor is it necessary for us to examine the merits and actions of those who have died in this way, since our Lord God, whose judgments cannot be grasped, has reserved to his own justice what the priestly ministry could not accomplish. He wishes his power to be feared in such a way that this fear benefits everyone, and that no one fail to fear what happens to certain lukewarm or negligent persons.

For it is highly useful and necessary that the guilt of sins be loosed through priestly supplication before the final day.

But those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger, implore the help of penance and immediately seek reconciliation must be denied neither the act of penance nor reconciliation, because we can impose neither measures upon God’s mercy nor limits upon its timing. With God, conversion suffers no delay, as the Spirit of God says through the prophet: “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved” (Ezek. III, 21). And elsewhere: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Ps. XXXI, 5); and again: “For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption” (Ps. CXXIX, 7).

In dispensing God’s gifts, therefore, we must not be harsh, nor neglect the tears and groans of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that penance itself is conceived through God’s inspiration, as the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (2 Tim. II, 26).

Therefore each Christian ought to exercise judgment over his own conscience, so that he does not postpone turning to the Lord from day to day or reserve the time of satisfaction for the end of his life. Human ignorance dangerously confines him, causing him to reserve himself for a few uncertain hours, and, although he could earn forgiveness through fuller satisfaction, to choose the narrow limits of a time in which scarcely any opportunity may be found either for the penitent’s confession or for the priest’s reconciliation.

Nevertheless, as I said, the necessity of such persons must be assisted in such a way that neither the act of penance nor the grace of communion is denied them [Col. 0889B], if they are shown to seek it even after losing the power of speech, through the judgment of an unimpaired mind.

But if some have been so weakened by illness that, in the presence of a priest, they cannot communicate what they had shortly before requested, the testimony of the faithful standing around them ought to benefit them, so that they may receive both the benefit of penance and that of reconciliation. The rule of the ancient canons must nevertheless be preserved regarding those who sinned against God by abandoning the faith.

Brother, you will bring to the attention of your metropolitan what I have answered to the questions of your belovedness, so that nothing contrary may be done under the excuse of ignorance. If there happen to be brothers who previously thought these matters uncertain, let them be instructed by him concerning everything that has been written to you.

### LXX.—To Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne

[Col. 0889C]

Leo, bishop, to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne.

I gladly received the letters of your fraternity, delivered by your archdeacon Hermes. They were lengthy, joined together from various cases, but not so burdensome to patience that anything in them was overlooked amid the anxieties pressing upon us from every side.

After considering the whole of your statement and reviewing the proceedings conducted in the presence of bishops and distinguished persons, we understood that the priests Savinianus and Leo lacked confidence in their own case, and that no just complaint remained to them, since they had voluntarily withdrawn from the disputes they had begun.

I leave it to your moderation to determine what form and measure of justice you should maintain toward them. Yet, with the encouragement of charity, I advise you to apply spiritual medicine to the sick, and, since Scripture says, “Do not be excessively just” (Ecclus. XXI, 20), to act more gently toward those who, in their zeal against immorality, seem to have exceeded the proper measure of punishment, lest the devil, who deceived the adulterers, rejoice over those who avenge adultery.

I am surprised that your belovedness should be so disturbed by the adversity of scandals arising from whatever cause that you say you desire release from the labors of the episcopate and prefer to spend your life badly in silence and leisure rather than remain in the responsibilities entrusted to you.

Yet the Lord says: “Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end” (Matt. XXIV, 13) [Col. 0890A]. And what perseverance can be blessed except that which arises from the virtue of patience? For, according to apostolic teaching, “Everyone who desires to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. III, 12).

Persecution is not to be understood only as what is inflicted against Christian piety by sword, fire, or any other punishment. The savagery of persecution is also supplied by differences of character, the stubbornness of disobedience, and the darts of malicious tongues. Since all the members of the Church are continually battered by these conflicts, and no portion of the devout is free here from temptation, dangers spare neither leisure nor labor.

Who will steer ships amid the waves of the sea if the helmsman departs? Who will guard the sheep from the ambushes of wolves if the shepherd’s care is not watchful? Who, finally, will resist robbers and thieves if love of rest draws the watchman, stationed before the lookout, away from his vigilant purpose?

One must therefore remain at the work entrusted and in the labor undertaken. Justice must be held firmly, and clemency kindly supplied. Let sins be hated, not people. At one time let the timid be corrected; at another let the weak be tolerated. What must be punished more severely because of sin should be punished not with the spirit of one who rages but of one who heals.

But if more intense tribulation should weigh upon us, let us not be so afraid as though that adversity had to be resisted by our own strength. Christ is both our counsel and our strength, so that through him, without whom we can do nothing, we may do all things, for he strengthens the preachers of the Gospel and the ministers of the sacraments. “Behold,” he says, “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20) [Col. 0890C]. And again: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me. In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John XVI, 33).

Since these promises are plainly certain, we must not be weakened by any scandals, lest we appear ungrateful to God’s choice, whose assistance is as powerful as his promises are true.

Regarding the questions of your belovedness, which your archdeacon delivered separately in writing, it would be more appropriate to determine our view of them in person, if we had the opportunity to see you. Since some questions seem to exceed the bounds of diligence, I understand that they are better suited to conversation than to writing.

For just as some matters cannot be shaken by any tradition, so many ought to be adjusted according to the consideration of ages or the necessities of circumstances, always preserving this condition: in matters that are doubtful or obscure, we must follow what is found to be contrary neither to the Gospel commandments nor to the decrees of the holy Fathers.

### The Answers Below Begin, In Response to the Inquiry of the Same Bishop

#### That those are not to be regarded as bishops whom neither the clergy elected, nor the people sought, nor the provincial bishops consecrated

No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clergy, nor requested by the people, nor consecrated by the provincial bishops with the judgment of the metropolitan.

Since the question of an honor wrongly assumed often arises, who could doubt that it must not be granted to those whose honor is not shown to have been conferred?

If any clerics were ordained by these pseudo-bishops in Churches belonging to their proper bishops, and their ordination was carried out with the consent and judgment of the presiding bishops, their ordination should be considered valid, so that they may remain in those Churches. Otherwise, an ordination is to be regarded as void when it is established neither in the proper place nor by an authorized person [Col. 0891A].

#### That presbyters or deacons who have fallen into some crime cannot obtain the remedy of penance through the imposition of hands

It is contrary to ecclesiastical custom that those who have attained the honor of the presbyterate or the rank of deacon should receive, through the imposition of hands, the remedy of penance for some crime of their own. This follows from the apostolic tradition, according to what is written: “If a priest should sin, who will pray for him?” (Lev. V, 18).

Therefore such persons who have fallen must withdraw privately in order to obtain God’s mercy, where their satisfaction may also be fruitful.

#### That a deacon, like a bishop and presbyter, must abstain from marital relations, but must not repudiate marriage

The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. When they were laymen or readers, they could lawfully marry wives and beget children [Col. 0891C]. But once they have reached the ranks mentioned above, what was lawful for them begins to be unlawful.

Therefore, so that a carnal marriage may become a spiritual one, they ought neither to dismiss their wives nor to live as though they did not have them. Thus the charity of marriage may remain while marital relations cease.

#### That a wife is one thing and a concubine another, and that no one is in error if he gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine

Not every woman joined to a man is his wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir.

The bonds of marriage among freeborn persons and between equals are legitimate, having been established by the Lord long before the beginnings of Roman law. Thus a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another [Col. 0891D].

For this reason the Apostle also cites testimony from Genesis to make clear the distinction between these persons, where it is said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son. For the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gen. XXI, 10).

Since the fellowship of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, apart from the union of slaves, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to a marriage in which the nuptial mystery is not shown to have existed.

Therefore, if a cleric of any place gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this must not be understood as though he had given her to a married man—unless perhaps that woman has been made free, lawfully endowed with a dowry, and honorably established through public nuptials [Col. 0892A].

Women joined to men by their fathers’ decision are free from guilt if the women whom the men kept were not wives in marriage, because a married woman is one thing and a concubine another.

#### That there is no duplication of marriage when a rejected slave woman is taken as a wife

To cast a slave woman from one’s bed and take as a wife a woman of certain free birth is not a duplication of marriage but an advancement in honorable conduct.

The negligence of such men is blameworthy, but it is not to be examined to the point of despair. Rather, stirred by frequent exhortations, they should faithfully carry out what they have rightly sought.

No one is to be despaired of while he remains in the body, because what is sometimes postponed through lack of confidence in one’s age may be accomplished through more mature counsel.

[Col. 0892B]

#### Concerning those deprived of communion, and concerning the dead

Their case must be reserved for God’s judgment. It was in his hand that the deaths of such persons were postponed until the remedy of communion could be received.

But we cannot give communion to the dead whom we did not communicate with while they were alive.

#### Concerning those who delay doing penance

This concealment may arise not from contempt for the remedy but from a more serious manner of sinning, so that, when the penance that was delayed is sought more earnestly, it should not be denied. In this way, somehow, the wounded soul may reach the remedy of forgiveness.

#### That one who asks forgiveness for unlawful acts must also abstain from many lawful acts

It is one thing justly to demand what is owed and another to renounce what is one’s own out of love for perfection.

Nevertheless, one who asks forgiveness for unlawful acts ought also to abstain from many lawful ones, as the Apostle says: “All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient” (1 Cor. VI, 12).

Therefore, if a penitent has a case that he ought not to neglect, he should prefer ecclesiastical judgment to a secular court [Col. 0892C].

#### That a penitent should not engage in profit-making commerce

The character of profit either excuses or condemns the merchant, for there is honorable gain and shameful gain.

Nevertheless, it is better for a penitent to endure losses than to bind himself to the dangers of commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the dealings between buyer and seller.

#### That one should not return to secular military service after penance

It is altogether contrary to ecclesiastical rules to return to secular military service after undertaking penance, since the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business” (2 Tim. II, 4).

Therefore, the person who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from its snares [Col. 0892D].

#### That a young man who undertook penance under pressure from some danger, but does not abstain from his wife’s embrace, may retain the remedy

If, while still a young man, someone undertook penance under pressure either of fear or of the danger of captivity, and afterwards, fearing a lapse into youthful incontinence, chose intercourse with a wife so as not to incur the crime of fornication, he appears to have done something pardonable—provided that he has had no relations at all except with his wife [Col. 0893A].

In this matter, however, we are not establishing a rule; we are judging what is more tolerable. For according to true understanding, nothing is more fitting for one who has undertaken penance than persevering chastity of both mind and body.

#### That if someone abandons his monastic commitment, he must be cleansed through public satisfaction

A monastic commitment, undertaken by one’s own judgment and will, cannot be abandoned without sin. For what one has vowed to God, one must also repay.

Therefore, anyone who, having abandoned the profession of solitude, turns either to military service or to marriage must be cleansed through the satisfaction of public penance. For although military service may be innocent and marriage honorable, abandoning the choice of better things is a transgression.

[Col. 0893B]

#### That girls who undertake a commitment to virginity voluntarily rather than under compulsion sin when they marry, even if they have not yet been consecrated

Girls who, not compelled by their parents’ command but by their own voluntary decision, have undertaken the commitment and habit of virginity, transgress if they later choose marriage—even if consecration has not yet followed. They would certainly not have been deprived of that gift had they remained in their commitment.

#### Concerning those whose baptism it is uncertain whether they received, and who therefore must be reborn
If there are no testimonies among relatives or family members, nor among clergy and neighbors, by which it might be established that those under inquiry had been baptized, they should be instructed, and action should be taken so that they may be reborn, lest they perish manifestly. In cases where what was done is not demonstrated, reason does not allow it to be regarded as repeated [Col. 0893C]. Those, however, who can remember that they used to come to church with their parents might recall whether they received what was given to their parents. But if even this is absent from their memory, it seems that what is not known to have been conferred should be conferred upon them. For the rashness of presumption does not intervene where there is the diligence of piety.

### Those who acknowledge that they were baptized but do not know in what faith should appropriately be received by the laying on of hands

But if those about whom you have written do not deny that they were baptized, yet profess that they do not know of what faith were those who baptized them, then, whatever form of baptism they received, they are not to be baptized again. Rather, after the power of the Holy Spirit has been invoked through the laying on of hands—a power which they could not have received from heretics—they are to be joined to the Catholics [Col. 0893D].

### Concerning those who have taken part in the banquets of the Gentiles and in sacrificial foods

If they have merely taken part in a Gentile banquet and eaten sacrificial foods, they can be cleansed by fasts and the laying on of hands, so that thereafter, abstaining from idolatrous practices, they may be admitted to participation in the sacred things of Christ. But if they have worshiped idols or been defiled by murders or fornications, they ought not to be admitted to communion except through public penance.

## LXXI.—To Tornulus, bishop of Astorigensis

### Leo to Tornulus, bishop of Austorigensis

How commendably you are moved on behalf of the truth of the Catholic faith, and how carefully you devote the service of your pastoral office to the Lord’s flock, is shown by the writings of your fraternity delivered to us by your deacon. In them you took care to make known to us what sort of error and disease, arising from the ancient remnants of the plague, has broken out in your regions. For both the wording of your letter, the sequence of the memorandum [221], and the text of your brief demonstrate that the most foul sewer of the Priscillianists has revived among you. There is no filth found in the minds of any impious people that has not flowed together into this doctrine, since they have mixed for themselves a manifold refuse from the mud of every earthly opinion, so that they alone might drink the whole of whatever others had tasted in part.

Finally, if all the heresies that arose before the time of Priscillian are examined more carefully, scarcely any error will be found from which this impiety did not draw contamination [Col. 0894B]. What invention of those who, under Christ’s name, deviated from the Gospel of Christ and plunged even into the darkness of paganism has this falsehood not received? Through the profane secrets of magical arts and the empty lies of astrologers, they placed religious faith and moral discipline under the power of demons and the influence of the stars.

If this may be believed and taught, then neither reward is owed to virtues nor punishment to vices; and all decrees, not only of human laws but also of divine ordinances, will be dissolved. For there can be no judgment concerning good or evil actions if fatal necessity drives the movement of the mind in either direction, and whatever human beings do belongs not to human beings but to the stars.

To this madness belongs that monstrous division of the whole human body among the twelve signs of the heavens [Col. 0894C], so that different powers preside over different parts, and the creature whom God made in his own image is subject to the bondage of the stars to the same degree as its limbs are joined together.

Our fathers, in whose time this abominable heresy burst forth, rightly acted throughout the world with persistent effort so that this impious frenzy might be expelled from the entire Church. Even the rulers of the world so detested this sacrilegious insanity that they struck down its author and many of his disciples with the sword of the public laws. For they saw that every concern for morality would be removed, every marital union dissolved, and divine and human law alike overturned if people of this kind were permitted anywhere to live while professing such beliefs.

This strictness long benefited ecclesiastical leniency [Col. 0894D]. Although the latter, content with priestly judgment, shuns bloody punishments, it is nevertheless supported by the stern enactments of Christian rulers, while those who fear bodily punishment sometimes have recourse to a spiritual remedy.

But since a hostile invasion has occupied many provinces, and the storms of war have prevented the enforcement of laws; since communication among the priests of God has become difficult and assemblies rare, secret perfidy has found freedom amid public disorder and has been stimulated toward the overthrow of many minds by the very evils by which it ought to have been corrected.

What portion, and how large a portion, of the people there is free from this plague, when—as your charity indicates—the hearts even of certain priests have been corrupted by the deadly disease [Col. 0895A], and those through whom falsehood should have been crushed and truth defended themselves subject the Gospel of Christ to the teaching of Priscillian, so that, with the piety of the sacred books perverted to profane meanings, what the Holy Spirit taught is not preached under the names of the prophets and apostles, but what the devil’s minister has inserted?

Therefore, since your love for the faith has, as far as possible, gathered the condemned opinions of old into seventeen chapters, let us too review everything briefly, so that none of these blasphemies may appear tolerable or doubtful.

### I
