The first chapter demonstrates how impiously they think about the divine Trinity: they assert that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same person [Col. 0895B], as though the same God were now called Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit; as though the one who begot, the one who was begotten, and the one who proceeded from both were not distinct, but a singular unity were to be understood under three names, though not as three persons.

They have taken this kind of blasphemy from the opinion of Sabellius, whose disciples are rightly also called Patripassians, because if the Son is himself also the Father, then the Son’s cross is the Father’s passion, and whatever the Son endured in the form of a servant while obeying the Father, the Father himself endured in its entirety.

This is unambiguously contrary to the Catholic faith, which confesses the Trinity as ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “of one essence”) with unity, believing the Father, Son, and Spirit to be undivided without confusion, eternal without time, and equal without difference; for their unity consists not in one person but in the same essence [Col. 0895C].

### II

In the second chapter he exposes the foolish and empty invention concerning certain emanations of powers from God, which God supposedly began to possess and which he himself preceded in his essence.

In this they support the error of the Arians, who say that the Father is prior to the Son because there was once a time when he existed without the Son, and that he began to be Father when he begot the Son. But just as the Catholic Church detests them, so it detests those who think that anything belonging to God’s own essence was ever lacking in God. It is impious to call him mutable, and equally impious to call him one who progresses. For just as what is diminished is changed, so too what is increased is changed.

### III

The statement of the third chapter indicates that these same impious people assert that the Son is called the only-begotten Son of God because he alone was born from a virgin [Col. 0895D]. They would certainly not dare to say this unless they had imbibed the poison of Paul of Samosata and Photinus, who said that our Lord Jesus Christ did not exist before he was born from the virgin Mary.

But if they wish something else to be understood from their own opinion and assign Christ his beginning from his mother, they must assert that the Son of God is not one, but that others too were begotten from the supreme Father, of whom this one alone was born from a woman, and that he is called only-begotten for this reason: no other son of God underwent this condition of birth.

However they turn, therefore, they rush toward the precipice of great impiety, whether they wish Christ God to have his beginning from his mother or deny that he is the only-begotten of God the Father. For the one who was born from his mother was God the Word, and no one was begotten from the Father except the Word [Col. 0896A].

### IV

The fourth chapter contains the claim that they do not truly honor Christ’s nativity, which the Catholic Church venerates according to the assumption of true humanity, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Rather, they pretend to honor it: they fast on that day just as they do on the Lord’s Day, which is the day of Christ’s resurrection.

They do this because they do not believe that the Lord Christ was born in a true human nature, but wish what was not real to appear to have been displayed through a kind of illusion. They follow the teaching of Cerdo and Marcion and agree in every respect with their kindred, the Manichaeans.

As they were exposed and convicted in our investigation, they devote the Lord’s Day, which the resurrection of our Savior consecrated for us [Col. 0896B], to the sorrow of fasting. As has been reported, they alone dedicate this abstinence to reverence, so that in every respect they may be at odds with the unity of our faith, and so that the day we observe with joy may be spent by them in affliction.

It is therefore fitting that the enemies of Christ’s cross and resurrection should receive the judgment corresponding to the doctrine they have chosen.

### V

The fifth chapter reports that they assert the human soul to be of divine substance, and that the nature of our condition does not differ from the nature of its Creator.

The Catholic faith condemns this impiety, which flows from the opinions of certain philosophers and of the Manichaeans. It knows that no created thing is so exalted or so eminent that God himself is its nature. Whatever is from himself—that is, whatever he himself is—belongs to the Son and the Holy Spirit as well [Col. 0896C].

Apart from this one consubstantial, eternal, and unchangeable divinity of the supreme Trinity, there is nothing among all created things that was not created from nothing at its beginning. Yet whatever excels among creatures is not therefore God; nor is anything great and wondrous thereby the One “who alone does great wonders” (Ps. 71:18).

No human being is truth, no human being is justice; many, however, participate in truth, wisdom, and justice. God alone is worthy of no participation. Whatever is worthily understood of him, in whatever manner, is not a quality but an essence.

Nothing is added to the unchangeable, and nothing is taken away, because what he is has always been proper to him eternally. Thus, remaining in himself, he renews all things, and receives nothing that he himself has not given [Col. 0896D].

They are therefore exceedingly proud and exceedingly blind when, by saying that the human soul is a divine substance, they do not understand that they are saying nothing other than that God is mutable and that he himself undergoes whatever can be inflicted upon his nature.

### VI

The sixth statement indicates that they say the devil was never good and that his nature is not God’s handiwork, but that he emerged from chaos and darkness. They claim that he has no author of his own and that he himself is the origin and substance of all evil.

The true faith, however, which is Catholic, confesses every creature—whether spiritual or bodily—to be a good substance, and declares that evil has no nature, because God, who is the creator of the universe, made nothing that was not good [Col. 0897A].

Thus the devil too would have been good if he had remained in what he was made. But because he used his natural excellence badly and did not remain in the truth, he did not pass into an opposite substance; rather, he departed from the supreme good to which he ought to have adhered. So too those who make such assertions rush from truth into falsehood, accusing nature in what they voluntarily do wrong and being condemned for their voluntary perversity.

The evil in them will indeed be evil, but evil itself will not be a substance; it will be the punishment of a substance.

### VII

In the seventh place follows their condemnation of marriage and their horror of the procreation of those who are born. In this they agree almost entirely with the profaneness of the Manichaeans. Their own practices prove it, since they detest conjugal union: there is no freedom for depravity where the modesty of marriage and offspring is preserved [Col. 0897B].

### VIII

Their eighth doctrine is that the fashioning of human bodies is a fabrication of the devil, and that the seeds of conception are shaped in women’s wombs by the work of demons. For this reason they say that the resurrection of the flesh should not be believed, since the formation of the body is not compatible with the dignity of the soul.

This falsehood is undoubtedly the work of the devil, and such monstrous inventions of opinion are fabrications of demons. They do not form human beings in women’s wombs; rather, such errors are manufactured in the hearts of heretics. The foulest poison proceeding especially from the source of Manichaean impiety was detected and condemned long ago by the Catholic faith [Col. 0897C].

### IX

The ninth statement makes clear that they say the children of promise were indeed born from women, but conceived from the Holy Spirit, so that the offspring born from the seed of the flesh might not appear to belong to God’s creation.

This is opposed and contrary to the Catholic faith, which confesses that every human being, both in bodily and spiritual substance, is formed and animated by the Creator of the universe within the mother’s womb. The contagion of sin and mortality does remain—the contagion that passes into offspring from the first parent—but the sacrament of regeneration comes to its aid, through which the children of promise are reborn from the Holy Spirit, not in the womb of the flesh but through the power of baptism.

Thus David, who was certainly a son of promise, says to God: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Ps. 118:73); and the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in your mother’s womb I consecrated you” (Jer. 1:5) [Col. 0897D].

### X

The tenth chapter reports that they assert that the souls inserted into human bodies previously existed in a body, sinned in a heavenly dwelling, and, falling from higher things to lower, came under rulers of diverse kinds. Through aerial and stellar powers—some harsher, others gentler—they were enclosed in bodies [222] according to a varied lot and unequal condition, so that whatever occurs variously and unequally in this life may seem to arise from preceding causes [Col. 0898A].

They have woven this impious tale from the errors of many, but the Catholic faith has steadily cut them all away from the body of its unity, proclaiming truthfully that human souls did not exist before they were breathed into their bodies, and that they are incorporated by no one except God the Maker, who is the creator both of the souls themselves and of the bodies.

And because the entire offspring of the human race has been corrupted through the transgression of the first human being, no one can be freed from the condition of the old human being except through the sacrament of Christ’s baptism. In it there is no distinction among the reborn, as the Apostle says: “For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. 3:27–28).

What do the courses of the stars accomplish? What do the inventions of fate accomplish? What does the mutable condition and restless diversity of worldly things accomplish? Behold, the grace of God makes so many unequal people equal. If they remain faithful amid whatever struggles of this life, they cannot be miserable, saying in temptation those apostolic words: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us” (Rom. 8:35–36) [Col. 0898B].

And therefore the Church, which is Christ’s body, fears nothing from the inequalities of the world and desires nothing from bodily goods. It does not fear being burdened by the empty tumult of fate, since it knows that through patience in tribulations it is strengthened.

### XI

Their eleventh blasphemy is that they think both human souls and bodies are bound by the fatal stars [Col. 0898C]. Through this madness they must become entangled in all the errors of the pagans, worshiping the stars that they suppose to favor them and striving to appease those that oppose them.

But there is no place in the Catholic Church for those who pursue such things, because whoever gives himself to such beliefs has entirely departed from the body of Christ.

### XII

The twelfth doctrine among these is that they assign parts of the soul to some powers and the limbs of the body to others, and establish the qualities of interior rulers under the names of the patriarchs. In opposition to these they set the signs of the stars, to whose power they subject bodies.

In all this they entangle themselves in an inextricable error, refusing to hear the Apostle who says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world and not according to Christ, because in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power” (Col. 2:8–10) [Col. 0898D].

And again: “Let no one deceive you, delighting in humility and the worship of angels, intruding into things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the sense of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, joined and supplied through its connections, grows with the growth of God” (Col. 2:18–19).

Why, then, is it necessary to admit into the heart what the law has not taught, prophecy has not sung, the truth of the Gospel has not proclaimed, and apostolic teaching has not handed down?

But these things are hidden from the minds of those about whom the Apostle says: “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but, according to their own desires, they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their ears; and they will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to fables” (2 Tim. 4:3–4) [Col. 0899A].

Let those who dare either to teach or to believe such things have nothing in common with us. They strive by every means to assert that the substance of the flesh is foreign to the hope of resurrection, and thus they dissolve the whole sacrament of Christ’s incarnation. For it would have been unworthy for the whole human being to be assumed if it were unworthy for the whole human being to be redeemed.

### XIII

The thirteenth position is that they say the entire body of the canonical Scriptures must be understood under the names of the patriarchs, because the twelve powers that work the reformation of the inner human being are indicated by those names. Without this knowledge, they claim, no soul can attain the state in which it may be reformed into the substance from which it emerged [Col. 0899B].

But Christian wisdom holds this impious vanity in contempt. It knows that the nature of the Godhead is truly inviolate and immutable, while the soul—whether living in the body or separated from the body—is subject to many afflictions. If it were of divine essence, nothing adverse could befall it.

Therefore, in an incorporeal respect, the Creator is one thing and the creature another. He is always the same and is changed by no variation; the creature, however, is mutable even when it has not changed, because it can possess as something given what is not proper to it.

### XIV

In the fourteenth chapter they are said to hold that the condition of the body is kept under the power of the stars and signs according to its earthly quality. For this reason, they claim, many things are found in the sacred books that pertain to the outer human being, so that within the Scriptures themselves there appears to be some conflict between divine and earthly nature, with one thing claimed by the rulers of souls and another by the creators of bodies [Col. 0899C].

These fables are expounded so that the souls may be declared to be of divine substance and the flesh believed to be of an evil nature. They also profess that the world itself, together with its elements, is not the work of the good God but the creation of an evil author. And, in order to cloak these sacrileges of their falsehoods with honorable titles, they have violated nearly all the divine utterances by inserting their wicked meanings.

### XV

The statement of the fifteenth chapter complains about this matter and rightly detests their diabolical presumption [Col. 0899D]. We ourselves have learned this through a true report of witnesses, and we have found many of their most corrupt books bearing the title “canonical.”

How could they deceive the simple unless they first smeared their poisoned cups with a kind of honey, so that the unpleasantness of what would later prove fatal might not be perceived in full?

Care must therefore be taken, and priestly diligence must especially provide, that falsified books, discordant with the sincere truth, be used for no reading. The apocryphal Scriptures, which under the names of the apostles contain a great seedbed of falsehoods, must not merely be cut out but entirely removed [Col. 0900A] and burned in the fire.

Although some things in them may appear to have the appearance of piety, they are never free from poisons. Through the allurements of stories they secretly work to ensnare those whom the narration of wonders has led astray in the traps of whatever error.

Therefore, if any bishop fails to prohibit apocryphal books from being kept in homes, or permits people to read under the name of canonical books those volumes corrupted by the adulterating revision of Priscillian, he must know that he is to be judged a heretic. For whoever does not recall another from error shows that he himself is in error.

### XVI

Finally, the sixteenth chapter justly complains that the treatises of Dicticinius, which he wrote according to the doctrine of Priscillian, were read by many with veneration [Col. 0900B]. If they think that anything should be attributed to Dicticinius’s memory, they ought rather to love his restoration than his fall.

They are therefore not reading Dicticinius but Priscillian; they approve what he taught while in error, not what he chose after correction.

Let no one presume to do this with impunity, and let no one who uses Scriptures condemned not only by the Catholic Church but also by their own author be counted among Catholics. The perverse must not be free to pretend what they invent, nor, under the cover of the Christian name, evade the provisions of imperial decrees.

For this reason they come together with the Catholic Church while so divided in heart: they seek to make their own as many as they can and to escape the severity of the laws while pretending to be ours. The Priscillianists do this, and so do the Manichaeans [Col. 0900C]. Their hearts are so closely allied with those of the Priscillianists that, though distinguished by name alone, they are found united in their sacrileges.

Although the Manichaeans reject the Old Testament—which these people pretend to accept—the intention of both nevertheless tends toward one end: the Priscillianists corrupt it by accepting it, while the Manichaeans attack it by rejecting it.

In their execrable mysteries—which, the more filthy they are, the more carefully they conceal them—there is altogether one crime, one obscenity, and a similar disgrace. Although we blush to speak of it, after the most diligent investigations and after it was revealed by the confessions of captured Manichaeans, we caused it to be made publicly known. Thus it could not in any way appear doubtful that the matter had been disclosed by the mouths of those who had perpetrated every crime, in our judgment, which was attended not only by the very frequent presence of priests but also by the dignity of distinguished men and by a portion of the senate and the people [Col. 0900D]. The proceedings that we have now sent to your charity demonstrate this.

What was discovered long ago and widely publicized concerning the foulest crime of the Manichaeans has likewise been discovered concerning the most incestuous practice of the Priscillianists. For those who are equal in the impiety of their beliefs cannot be different in their sacred rites.

Having therefore gone through everything contained in the sequence of the brief, which does not differ from the form of the memorandum, we have, as I believe, sufficiently shown what we judge concerning what your fraternity reported to us, and how intolerable it is if the hearts of certain priests even consent to such profane errors [Col. 0901A]—or, to put it more mildly, fail to resist them.

With what conscience do they claim for themselves the honor owed to them when they do not labor for the souls entrusted to them? Beasts rush in, and they do not close the sheepfolds; thieves lie in wait, and they do not set out guards; diseases multiply, and they prepare no remedies.

When they add that they refuse to agree with those who act more zealously, and dissemble in their signatures that they anathematize impieties condemned long ago throughout the world, what are they indicating about themselves except that they are not of the number of the brethren but belong to the side of the enemies?

### XVII

But concerning what you placed in the final part of your personal letter, I am astonished that the understanding of any Catholic should be troubled, as though it were uncertain whether, when Christ descended to the underworld, his flesh rested in the tomb [Col. 0901B].

Just as it truly died and was buried, so it truly rose again on the third day. The Lord himself had announced this when he said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). The evangelist adds: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (ibid., 21).

The prophet David had also foretold the truth of this matter. Speaking in the person of the Lord and Savior, he said: “Moreover, my flesh will rest in hope. For you will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10).

These words plainly show that the Lord’s flesh was truly buried and rested, yet did not undergo corruption, because, quickly brought to life by the return of the soul [Col. 0901C], it rose again.

It is sufficiently impious not to believe this, and there is no doubt that such disbelief belongs to the teaching of Mani and Priscillian, who, with sacrilegious understanding, pretend to confess Christ while removing the truth of his incarnation, death, and resurrection.

Let an episcopal council therefore be held among you, and let the priests of the neighboring provinces assemble at a place convenient for all, so that, in accordance with the responses we have given to your inquiries, it may be investigated by the fullest examination whether any bishops are polluted by the contagion of this heresy. They must without doubt be separated from communion if they refuse to condemn the most abominable sect in all the perversities of its beliefs.

For there is no reason to tolerate anyone who has undertaken the duty of preaching the faith yet dares to argue against the Gospel of Christ, against apostolic teaching, and against the creed of the universal Church [Col. 0901D].

What sort of disciples will there be where such teachers instruct them? What religion will exist there, what salvation for the people, where, against human society [223], the shame of broken modesty is removed; the bonds of marriage are taken away; the propagation of offspring is restrained; the nature of the flesh is condemned; and, against the true worship of God, the Trinity of the Godhead is denied, the distinct properties of the persons are confused, the human soul is proclaimed to be of divine essence, and the same soul is enclosed in flesh at the devil’s discretion?

The Son of God is proclaimed only-begotten because of what was born from the Virgin, not because of what was begotten from the Father; and the same person is asserted to be neither truly the offspring of God nor truly the Son of the Virgin, so that through a false passion and an untrue death even a deceptive resurrection of the flesh taken from the tomb may be affirmed [Col. 0902A].

They make vain use of the Catholic name, then, who do not resist these impieties. Those who can believe such things can also patiently hear them.

We have therefore sent letters to our brothers and fellow bishops in Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, and Gaul, and we have ordered them to convene a general synod. It will belong to the solicitude of your charity to convey the authority of our directive to the bishops of the aforementioned provinces.

But if anything—which God forbid—should prevent a general council from being held, let at least the priests of Galicia assemble in one place. When they have gathered, our brothers Hydacius and Ceponius, together with your joined effort, will attend to the matter, so that a remedy for such great wounds may be provided by a provincial assembly [Col. 0902B].

## Letter of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Byzacena and Arzigitana, concerning the condemnation of the heretics Pelagius and Coelestius

To our most beloved and longed-for brothers and fellow priests, Primianus, Gaianus, the other Gaianus, Januarius, and Victorinus, and to the rest established throughout the territory of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzigitana: Aurelius, bishop.

I have learned, most beloved and longed-for brothers, that your holy charity took part in the plenary council concerning the condemnation of Coelestius and Pelagius and their doctrines.

But since, for the honor of God—in whose hand the heart of the king is established—the authority of our most glorious Christian rulers, who preserve the true and Catholic faith, has intervened, I wished through my humility to make it known to all my bishops. For this reason I took care to instruct your honorable fraternity by sending copies [Col. 0902C], lest the serpent’s persuasion, excluded from the universal Church of the whole world, should perhaps creep into some part of the aforesaid province.

Your charity therefore ought not to have remained ignorant of this highly necessary enactment of the Christian rulers. From the letters sent to me by them, whose copies are being read along with them, your charity will learn how each of you ought to subscribe—whether you are already included among those whose signatures are recorded in the synodal proceedings, or whether you were unable to attend that plenary council of all Africa.

When the subscription of all of you has been completed in the condemnation of the aforesaid heretics, nothing at all will remain from which any suspicion of dissimulation, negligence, or perhaps concealed depravity on the part of any of you may reasonably be thought to persist.

In another hand: I wish you well, brothers; live well, remembering me. Given on the Kalends of August, at Carthage, in the consulship of Monaxius and Pluita.

## Excerpts from the proceedings held against the heretic Pelagius, together with other passages from his brief, which he was compelled to condemn when they were brought against him in Palestine

[Col. 0902D]

Just as the Lord cried out against Jerusalem, which was unwilling to gather her children, so we cry out against those who are unwilling to gather the children of the Church.

They were not corrected even after the judgment that was made concerning Pelagius himself in Palestine. He would have emerged condemned if he had not himself condemned the statements brought against him concerning the grace of God—statements that he could not obscure.

Besides those matters which, as best he could, he dared to defend by whatever argument, certain propositions were brought against him which, unless he had anathematized them without any evasion, would themselves have made him accursed.

## The doctrine of the heretic Pelagius

He said that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin; that his sin harmed only himself and not the human race; that infants newly born are in the same condition in which Adam was before his transgression; and that neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise again.

He also said that infants, if they are not baptized, nevertheless possess eternal life; that baptized rich people, unless they renounce everything, do not receive the reward for whatever good they may appear to have done and cannot possess the kingdom of God; that the grace and help of God are not given for each individual act, but are located in free choice or in the law and teaching; that God’s grace is given according to our merits; that people cannot be called children of God unless they have become entirely without sin; that there is no free choice if it needs God’s help, since each person has it in his own will to do or not to do something; that our victory comes not from God’s help but from free choice; and that forgiveness is not granted to penitents according to the grace and mercy of God, but according to the merit and labor of those who have become worthy of mercy through penance [Col. 0903B].

Pelagius anathematized all these propositions thus. The proceedings themselves sufficiently testify to this, so that he brought no argument whatsoever in any way to defend them. It follows, therefore, that anyone who is a follower of his must, by the authority of the episcopal judgment and by Pelagius’s own confession, hold what the Catholic Church has always held.

## The Catholic doctrine against Pelagius
That Adam, if he had not sinned, would not have died. Second, that his sin harmed not himself alone but also the human race. Third, that infants newly born are not in the condition in which Adam was before his transgression. Fourth, that what the Apostle briefly says also applies to them: “Through one man came death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead. For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:21–22). Hence it follows that unbaptized infants cannot possess not only the kingdom of heaven but eternal life as well. Fifth, that he should confess that baptized rich people, even if they do not lack their riches and are such as the Apostle describes to Timothy when he says, “Command those who are rich in this age not to be proud, nor to hope in the uncertainty of their riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment; let them be rich in good works, generous in giving, sharing, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19)—that such people cannot be deprived of the kingdom of God. Sixth, that he should confess that God’s grace and help are given even for each individual act, and that grace is not given according to our merits, so that it may truly be grace, that is, freely given through the mercy of him who said, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion” (Exod. 33:19). Seventh, that he should acknowledge that those who say daily, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), can be called children of God—for they certainly would not truthfully say this if they were entirely without sin. Eighth, that he should confess that free will exists even when it requires divine help. Ninth, that when we struggle against temptations and unlawful desires, although we have our own will in the matter, our salvation nevertheless comes not from that will but from God’s mercy; otherwise what the Apostle says would not be true: “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy” (Rom. 9:16). Tenth, that he should confess that forgiveness is granted to those who ask for it according to God’s grace and mercy, not according to their merit, since the Apostle called repentance itself a gift of God when he said of certain people, “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance.”

Let him confess all these things simply, without any evasions. If anyone agrees with the Catholic authority and with the explicit words of Pelagius himself recorded in the ecclesiastical proceedings—for it cannot be believed that the things contrary to these were truly anathematized unless these contrary doctrines are held in faith and in the heart and proclaimed in an open confession—

### LXXII.—To Rusticus, Ravennius, Venerius, and the Other Bishops of Gaul

When, through God’s mercy, our common prayers have been fulfilled, it is fitting that your fraternity should share in holy joys. For I inform you that the wishes which my brothers, who presided in my place over the Eastern synod, reported have been fulfilled, the Catholic faith having been confirmed and the triumph of apostolic preaching glorified. Those who had been led or driven astray into deviation are also rejoicing now that the light of truth has been received. Indeed, all the priests of the Lord, taught by the Holy Spirit, agreed in one judgment; and concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, about which the understanding of many had been clouded, the darkness of error has been removed in such a way that, in our one Lord, the true Son of God and man, there is no uncertainty either about the reality of his humanity or about the essence of his divinity.

As for the impious authors of this abominable error, who, judging themselves unworthy of God’s grace, refused to make use of the remedies of correction, the copies we have sent will inform you what sentence has been pronounced, so that your love, dearest brothers, may recognize that divine judgment was not absent from this holy examination: punishment was inflicted on the obstinate, and peace was extended to those who were corrected.

May the Lord keep you safe and unharmed, dearest brothers.

### LXXIII.—To Julian, Bishop

[Col. 0904C]

The letter of your love recently delivered to me shows with what spiritual affection you uphold the Catholic faith. It gives me great joy that devout hearts meet in the same judgment, so that, according to the teaching of the Holy Spirit, what the Apostle says may be fulfilled in us: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you. Rather, be perfected in the same understanding and in the same judgment” (1 Cor. 1:10).

Eutyches has made himself entirely alien to this unity if he grows old in his perversity and still does not understand by what bonds he is bound by the Lord. Although he thinks that a priest of the Lord can be found who will agree with his ignorance and madness, it long remained uncertain among us what exactly displeased Catholics in him. Since we had received no letters from our brother Flavian, while he himself complained in his writings that the Nestorian heresy was springing up again, we were unable fully to discover where such a deceitful accusation came from or toward what it was tending.

But after documents from the episcopal proceedings had reached us, everything that had been concealed under the veil of false complaints became clear as deserving detestation. And because the most merciful emperor, out of the benevolence and piety of his soul, wished the condition of this man—previously regarded as honorable—to be judged more carefully, and therefore considered that an episcopal council should be summoned, I sent sufficient letters, appropriate to the case, through our brothers Julian the bishop and Renatus the presbyter, and also through my son, the deacon Hilary, whom I sent from my side as my representatives to our brother Flavian. Through these letters both your love and the universal Church may learn what we hold as divinely handed down and what we preach immutably concerning the ancient and singular faith attacked by this unlearned assailant.

Nevertheless, because we must not neglect the claims of mercy, we thought it should be decreed with suitable moderation that, if the condemned presbyter is corrected through full satisfaction, the sentence by which he is bound should be relaxed. But if he chooses to lie in the same mire of his foolishness, let the decrees remain in force, and let him share the lot of those whose error he has followed.

Issued on the Ides of June, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

### 224. LXXIV.—Also to Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople

[Col. 0905B]

I have received the letter of your love, together with the records drawn up among you concerning the question of the faith. And because the most merciful emperor, concerned for the peace of the Church, wished a synod to be convened, although it is clearly evident that the matter under discussion in no way requires synodal deliberation, nevertheless, dearest brother, I inform you that those whom it pleased us to send in this matter have followed. Nor was it necessary to write anything more at present, since, with God’s favor, you will be more fully informed through the letters they themselves will carry concerning what we have thought appropriate to the case.

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Austurius and Protogenes.

### LXXV.—Also of the Same, to Theodosius Augustus

Having received the letters of your clemency, I foresaw that the universal Church ought to rejoice greatly, because you wish the Christian faith—which honors and worships the divine nature—to be in no respect different and in no respect divided. For what could more effectively obtain God’s mercy in human affairs than for one thanksgiving and the sacrifice of one confession to be offered to his majesty by all?

The full devotion of priests and all the faithful will be present in this only if, concerning what was accomplished for our redemption by the only Son of God, God the Word, nothing is believed except what he himself commanded to be preached and believed. Therefore, although no circumstance permits me to attend the day of the episcopal council appointed by your piety—especially since no precedent for this has come before and the necessity of the present time does not allow me to leave the city, while the matter of faith is so evident that the synod ought to have been avoided for rational reasons—nevertheless, insofar as the Lord deigns to assist my efforts, I have contributed what I could so that the decrees of your clemency might in some measure be obeyed.

For this reason I have appointed from here my brothers, with instructions sufficient, in accordance with the equity of the case, for cutting off scandals, and to fulfill the role of my presence, since no such question has arisen that can or ought to be doubted.

Issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

### LXXVI.—Of the Same, to Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople

Our representatives whom we sent to you concerning the faith have already departed, and through our son the deacon we received the letter of your love. You had rightly said little in it about the matter of common concern, since the records previously delivered had already informed us sufficiently about everything, and the speech of the aforesaid deacon was adequate for a personal inquiry. In returning our greetings to your love, therefore, we encourage you through the grace of God, in which we trust, using the Apostle’s words: “In nothing be frightened by your opponents; this is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation” (Phil. 1:28).

For what is more destructive than, by denying the truth of Christ’s incarnation, to seek to dissolve every hope of human salvation and to oppose the Apostle, who plainly says: “Great is the mystery of godliness that was manifested in the flesh” (1 Tim. 3:16)? What is more glorious than to fight for the faith of the Gospel against the enemies of Christ’s birth and cross?

In the letters already sent to your love concerning its most pure light and unconquered power, we have disclosed what was in our heart, so that no ambiguity might appear among us concerning the things we have learned and teach according to Catholic doctrine.

Since the testimonies of truth are so strong and so clear that anyone who does not immediately shake himself free from the darkness of falsehood at the radiance of light and reason must be considered exceedingly blind and hardened, we also wish to apply the medicine of patience to cure the madness of the ignorant. Let those who are children in mind though advanced in bodily age learn to obey their elders through paternal rebukes; and if, laying aside the vanity of their ignorance, they come to their senses and, after condemning every error, embrace the true and singular faith, let them not be denied the mercy of episcopal benevolence. The judgment already pronounced, however, shall remain if the impiety rightly condemned persists in its perversity.

Issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

### LXXVII.—Again to the Same Bishop of Constantinople

Your silence increases our concern, since for a long time we have received no letter from your love, although, as sharers in your cares and anxious for the defense of the faith, we have frequently sent letters to your love whenever suitable opportunities arose, so that we might strengthen you through the consolation of our exhortations and encourage you not to yield to the goads of your opponents in defense of the faith, while showing that we share in your labor.

We believe that our representatives reached your fraternity long ago. Through them you retain fuller instruction from our letters and commands, and we have also sent Basil back to you, as you requested. Now, lest you think that any opportunity had been neglected, we have given this letter through our son Esitius, an honorable man dear to us, so that you may answer our letters with all speed and subsequently make us more certain about your actions, ours, and the resolution of the whole case. Thus we may ease the concern we now bear for the defense of the faith through more favorable reports.

Issued on the third day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

### LXXVIII.—To the Clergy and People of Constantinople

LEO and the holy synod assembled in the city of Rome, to the honored clergy and the people of Constantinople.

[Col. 0907A]

When the acts carried out at Ephesus contrary to everyone’s expectation were reported to us, we confess that our spirit was overwhelmed with great sorrow. We could scarcely have believed that such license had been granted to iniquity, unless our son Hilary the deacon—who had been sent by us in our place with others to attend the synod—had fled and returned, refusing unjustly to become a participant in the sentence.

For a voice of contradiction was raised there by our representatives, but the Alexandrian bishop, who alone claimed everything for his own power, scorned to hear it. He dragged unwilling priests into participation in his will, so that, compelled by force, they might sign, although they had found no adequate cause for condemnation. But we trust that these acts of audacity will in no way please the pious and Christian emperor.

Now that we have learned that your Church has been dispersed in this manner, we believe that you must be consoled and encouraged by our letters to resist the wickedness of the treacherous in defense of the Catholic faith. We do not wish your love to be struck down by this sorrow, since greater glory will follow your steadfastness if no threats and no fear tear you away from your approved bishop.

For whoever, while your bishop Flavian is alive and remains in office, dares to seize his priesthood will never be regarded as being in communion with us, nor will he be able to be numbered among the bishops. For just as we anathematized Nestorius in his perversity, so we condemn with equal execration those who deny the truth of our flesh assumed by the Lord Jesus Christ.

Stand, therefore, in the spirit of Catholic truth, and receive the apostolic exhortation through the ministry of your own mouth: “For it has been granted to you for Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29). Do not think, dearest ones, that divine protection is absent or will be absent from its holy Church. The purity of faith shines forth when the stains of error are separated from it.

Therefore, again and again we solemnly appeal to you before the sight of the Lord and admonish you not to be moved by intrigues or anyone’s persuasion from the faith in which you have been established and in which we know the most Christian emperor to remain. Rather, in the person of your bishop, keep before the eyes of your heart the one who did not fear to suffer everything inflicted upon him. We wish you to be imitators of him in every respect, so that you may share with him the reward of faith.

Issued on the Ides of October, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

### LXXIX.—Also Pope Leo to Anastasius, Bishop of Thessalonica

As we have learned from the report of our deacon Hilary, a great crime was committed at the instigation or under the direction of the Alexandrian bishop: while ancient rivalries and private hatreds raged against our brother Flavian, neither the innocence of a most proven priest nor the Christian faith was spared.

We therefore greatly congratulate your love that, although you wished to go to that synod, the divine hand held you back through timely obstacles. Otherwise, having certainly abstained from participation in so great a crime, you might have been subjected to unworthy injuries and might have been unable to oppose the impious fury, supported—as we have learned—by soldiers and weapons.

Since, then, the treachery that had been concealed has burst forth at the proper time, and its followers have passed into the most abominable heresy of an utterly ignorant old man, we must recognize that the time of our testing has arrived and prepare steadfastness in our hearts, relying on heavenly defenses against the assaults of our adversaries.

We know, dearest brother, that divine protection will be present through the mystery of its great godliness. Therefore, if anything from the impious decrees has been brought before your fraternity, we protest and admonish you equally not to mingle the consent of your heart either in the condemnation of an innocent brother or in the acceptance of an abominable doctrine. For “greater is he who is in us than he who is against us.”

Rather, strive as far as the one who assumed and glorified our nature himself helps you, so that you may strengthen the hearts of all our brothers. For since we in no way depart from the Gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ’s birth, death, and resurrection, it is absolutely determined that those who attempt to tear up the foundations of the ancient Catholic faith will not be among the number of our communion.

Issued on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

### LXXX.—Also of the Same, to Theodosius Augustus

For the integrity of the Catholic faith, it is fitting that a Christian emperor should be concerned; and in unceasing prayers I ask God’s mercy to inspire your heart with what is true and not allow you to be deceived in anything through the rivalry of human cunning.

What the piety of the angelic faith defends on my part and on the part of all Catholic priests has been stated sufficiently fully and clearly in my letters, which I suppose your clemency received some time ago through your servant Epiphanius the tribune, who was sent for this purpose.

It is settled, and there can be no doubt, that we believe with complete purity and assert steadfastly what the venerable fathers once assembled at Nicaea, in accordance with the faith of the Creed, established by their most sacred authority as something to be believed and confessed.

For we, venerable emperor, just as we rightly anathematized the perverse doctrine of Nestorius, so we justly condemn the impiety of those who deny that the Lord Jesus Christ assumed the truth of our flesh.

Therefore, if your piety deigns to assent to our suggestion and supplication and orders that an episcopal council be held within Italy, then, with God’s help, all the scandals that have been stirred up to disturb the whole Church can quickly be cut away. Thus, with the integrity of the Catholic faith preserved throughout your realm, we may rejoice that Christian peace remains and that your glory before God increases.

Issued on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

### LXXXI.—Of the Same, to Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople

We have learned how much and what kinds of things your love is suffering in defense of the Catholic faith, through the deacon who slipped away secretly from Ephesus. Although we glorify God, who strengthens you by the power of his grace, we must nevertheless grieve over the downfall of those through whom the truth is attacked and the very foundations of the whole Church are shaken.

Since God’s providence always provides necessary help for his own, your fraternity should know that, for the common cause, we are neglecting none of the things that must be done, so that first we may deserve to reach those measures that benefit the whole body of the faithful.

Meanwhile, if this is the case, let your love courageously endure what you do not doubt will contribute to your eternal glory. The bearer of this brief letter will be able to explain in the language of faith whatever it is to which, with the Lord’s help, we are devoting our efforts in faith and charity.

Issued on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

### LXXXII.—The Preceding Letter of the Same, to Bishop Julian

[Col. 0909B]

Having learned what was done at Ephesus through the presumption of one man, we were indeed afflicted with great sorrow over the impious and furious deeds that were committed. But, directing our minds toward our Lord, we derive great confidence from the very truth that we follow, while not neglecting to do everything that, with God’s grace assisting, we believe will be beneficial.

We must therefore hold to what we hold; and while the storm of a single whirlwind rages, we must embrace the most serene tranquility of faith, until the truth spreads its rays throughout everything and consumes the darkness of unbelief. You will learn through the bearer’s report what has been arranged.

Issued on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

### LXXXIII.—To Faustus and the Other Archimandrites of Constantinople

[Col. 0909C]

LEO and the holy synod assembled in the city of Rome, to Faustus, Martin, Peter, Magnus, and Elijah, presbyters and archimandrites of Constantinople, beloved sons, greetings in the Lord.

Although the things we have written to the Church of Constantinople cannot be unknown to your devoted concern, nevertheless we thought that your love should also be encouraged by a special letter. Remember your holy profession, which consists particularly in faith and charity, and drive from your hearts every scandal that has arisen against the peace of the Church, retaining with devout mind the judgment of the blessed Apostle: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:8).

Maintain unity with our brother Flavian the bishop, whom the Lord permitted for a time to be tested by the faction of the impious, so that he might make his proven priest more illustrious through the merit of perseverance.

These disturbances must, with God’s grace assisting, be quickly destroyed, and everything that is rejected must be cast away from the purity of the Church, which admits neither stain nor wrinkle. This is especially necessary since ignorant madness has reached such a precipice that the truth of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, the mystery of human salvation, is denied, while the ancient preacher and defender of the faith is subjected to insults because he did not yield to blasphemies that our holy fathers once condemned in many heretics. In this, indeed, reverence for all the Lord’s priests is attacked and all the members of Christ’s body are struck.

But because it is glorious for us to endure for the sake of truth whatever God wills us to suffer, we call you into fellowship in this patience through paternal exhortations. Let what we have written become known through your love to all who serve God; resist the enemies of the Gospel, and do not abandon either love for your shepherd or the unity of the Catholic faith.

For no principle of the Catholic faith permits the things recently done at Ephesus, contrary to justice and the discipline of the canons, through the shamelessness of one man, to stand as valid.

Issued on the eighth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

### LXXXIV.—Also of Leo, to the Presbyter Martin

[Col. 0910B]

We give thanks to God and have received great confidence for devout rejoicing, since we know that your love and Catholic fraternity are so strong in the spirit of faith that no heretical temptation can bring weakness into your hearts. In order to destroy it by divine power, our concern has not been lacking, as you know, nor will it be lacking until the Almighty breaks all the weapons of the devil with his right hand.

The devil is permitted to dare something for this reason: so that he may be defeated by Christ’s faithful with greater glory. But whatever difficulties or delays intervene must be endured with equanimity, dearest brothers, since where truth is the teacher, divine consolations are never absent.

Although great distances separate us, we are nevertheless with you in the unity of faith, confessing with our whole heart Jesus Christ our Lord as true God and true man. We suffer no loss on your account when we glory in the harmony of your confession, provided only that steadfast perseverance continues, with the Apostle saying: “For it has been granted to you for Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29).

To strengthen the courage of holy minds, we believe that our brothers and legates whom we sent for the freedom of the apostolic faith, and whom we trust have long been with you, will be of great benefit. You will learn the disposition of our whole action, and you will join your concern and counsel to the work. There is no need to write more extensively about this now, since we have already sent sufficient letters through the aforesaid men, by which the whole Catholic fraternity may be instructed most fully.

It will belong to the power and grace of God that the Son of God, who made the nature of the human race his own, may assert the great mystery of his godliness more fully than we see or understand—a mystery which impious audacity has indeed defrauded itself of, but could not take away from upright hearts.

Issued on the Ides of September, in the consulship of Valentinian and Avennius.

### LXXXV.—Of the Same, to Marcian Augustus

I rejoice that I have received letters from your piety, and I recognize them as a sign of complete prosperity, since your words make you secure through your integrity. Therefore, recognize how great our thanks to your clemency are—not from our words but from your benefits, which you have bestowed upon the Church. Do not doubt what kind of retributor you have in all things, for whose sake you are concerned with such devout religion, and who, as the matter itself demonstrates, chose you so that the Catholic faith might be defended from the attacks of its enemies.

Let your piety graciously accept these brief words from me through the clergy of my brother Anatolius. We have sent fuller written communications through our legates concerning everything belonging to my care for the condition of the churches and the concord of the Lord’s priests.

Issued on the Ides of April, in the consulship of Adelphius.

### LXXXVI.—The Preceding Letter of the Same, to Bishop Julian

I received, through our sons, the Constantinopolitan clergy, a message in your fraternity’s letter concerning your welfare. You state that you were weighed down by great tribulations, since there was certainly no lack of material for anxiety and toil among the outspoken adversaries of the Catholic faith, who wearied a spirit clinging to the truth. As you write, your intention was to present yourself, through the opportunity provided by necessity, both to us and to your homeland.

I had hoped that this would happen, so that I might more suitably learn from your own mouth the evasions of all the heretics. But I give thanks to God that your safety and the cause of the Church have been accomplished in such a way that you were meanwhile free to live among those whose agreement has become known to us through their parables, just as the writings of our brother Anatolius declare and the proceedings conducted in his presence before our representatives demonstrate to our returning brothers.

I therefore return greetings for greetings, and I confidently exhort you to maintain persevering diligence against the cunning of falsehood, since both your own spirit and our authority support you in this.

Although better reports have been given concerning many—namely, that they regret having been deceived and, after condemning their treachery and its authors, seek the grace of our communion, which we have gladly accepted, intending to restore to them the communion they desire when they fulfill their promises—we have learned that some persist in their obstinacy. These must be restrained more strictly if they cannot be healed by kindness.

For this purpose we shall send our representatives after the venerable day; in consultation with you, they will carry out what we have decided.

Issued on the Ides of April, in the consulship of Adelphius, a man of illustrious rank.

### LXXXVII.—Leo to Pulcheria Augusta

[Col. 0911D]

I presume to encourage through more frequent messages the devout concern of your piety, by which, with God’s inspiration, you care for the whole world, so that the necessary completion may follow the progress of your works. Just as we rejoice over the condition of the Church of Constantinople, whose priest and people are now known to hold the faith of Catholic purity, so may the confession of others concerning the incarnation of the Word also be in harmony with us.

Therefore, as I had indicated in another letter that I would do, I have prepared to send my brothers the bishop of Lucera and the presbyter Basil. Joined to the devotion of my brother Anatolius, they will carry out my arrangements according to the rules they have received.

For, as has been made clear by the letters of the aforesaid bishop and by the reports of his clergy, there are many matters that must be treated with greater leniency and many that must be restrained more justly. In a case of such great disturbance, severity must not be too harsh, nor leniency insufficiently cautious, since one response is owed to those who offer satisfaction and another to the obstinate.

A worthy opportunity is therefore offered to your piety to exercise before the Lord the care of a holy heart and to multiply the crowns of your former merits by abolishing the present error as well.

Just as Nestorian impiety, so also Eutychian blasphemy must be removed from the fellowship of all Catholics. For it is just as impious to deny that the consubstantial and coeternal divinity of the Son with the Father was brought forth bodily from the womb of the Virgin mother, as to assert that there is one nature in the Son of God after the mystery of the incarnation—thereby rejecting either his humanity or his divinity. In the union of both essences, neither has been changed into the other, nor has the assumed nature been circumscribed within the one who assumed it.

Rather, the unchangeableness of the Word and the reality of flesh and soul remain inseparably in the unity of the person. Those who do not believe this, although the Law testifies to it, the patriarchs believe it, the prophets approve it, the Gospel preaches it, the apostles teach it, and the whole world confesses it, are outside the mystery of Christ’s body and outside the unity of the Christian name. As we grieve over their downfall, so we detest their treachery.

So that sound judgment may everywhere be preserved concerning such persons, and so that one response may be given to the corrected and another to the obstinate, may your piety deign to support our representatives sent from the apostolic see and assist all the actions we have entrusted to them. With the Lord’s help, they will carry out more quickly and easily whatever may advance your glory and the peace of the whole Church.

Concerning Eutyches, the author of all this scandal and perversity, let your clemency order that he be transferred farther away from the place that is too near the city of Constantinople, lest he enjoy frequent assistance from those whom he has drawn into his impiety. Also order that a Catholic abbot be placed over his monastery, which he presided over perniciously and unworthily, so that he may free that congregation of God’s servants from the corrupt doctrine and instruct it in the principles of truth.

Issued on the Ides of June, in the consulship of Adelphius, a man of illustrious rank.

### LXXXVIII.—Also of the Same, to Bishop Anatolius

### 226

To avoid the stain of error by which Nestorian impiety or Eutychian madness has shaken some people, our sons Basil and John, presbyters, took laudable care for their own reputation, so that amid the conflicting doctrines of falsehood they might rejoice in the true peace of the Catholic faith.

Indeed, after undertaking the long labor of pilgrimage, they disclosed the conviction of their hearts at the apostolic see, condemning both heresies mentioned above and accepting concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ nothing other than what, instructed by the Holy Spirit, we have learned and teach.

Through these men, therefore, dearest brother, returning to their homeland with our testimony, we have sent our letters to your love, confidently asking that those who are adorned with the grace of apostolic communion may also rejoice in being assisted in every way by your favor.

Issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Adelphius, a man of illustrious rank.

### LXXXIX.—The Preceding Letter of the Same, to Marcian Augustus

We believed that your clemency could grant our desire by ordering that, in view of the present necessity, the priestly synod be postponed to a more suitable time, so that, with priests summoned from all the provinces, it might truly be a universal council.

But since you wished the assembly to take place now out of love for the Catholic faith, I did not wish to appear to oppose your devoted decision. Therefore I sent my brother and fellow bishop Paschasius, summoned from the same province, which seems to be the safer one, so that he might fulfill the role of my presence. I associated with him our brother Boniface, a fellow presbyter, added those whom we had sent previously, and joined to them as a companion my brother Julian the bishop.

With the Lord’s help, we believe that they will conduct everything with such moderation that whatever has led to complaint and disturbance will be recalled to the unity of peace and faith, every dissension having been suppressed, and that no trace of either Nestorian or Eutychian impiety will remain in the hearts of any priests. For the Catholic faith, which, instructed by God’s Spirit, we learned from the blessed apostles through the holy fathers and which we teach, permits neither error to creep in.

Therefore, if there are any diseases or wounds, we wish to see whatever can be healed through sincere correction restored to true health. These matters would not now be doubtful, nor would they henceforth harm anyone’s simplicity, if no one wished to hide behind excuses, since forgiveness of sin is not obtained without true confession.

But because some of our brothers—as we do not say without sorrow—were unable to maintain Catholic steadfastness against the storms of falsehood, it is fitting that the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop preside over the synod in my place. I am confident that those to whom we have entrusted this task will labor there without hatred or favoritism, so that, with only heretical impiety destroyed, truth and charity may reign in all the churches of God.

Issued on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Adelphius, a man of illustrious rank.

### XC.—The Preceding Letter of the Same, to Pulcheria Augusta
Although I have not now received any letter from Your Piety, nevertheless, since the most glorious emperor has written, I have rejoiced in his graciousness no otherwise than if the greetings of Your Serenity had also been conveyed. Therefore, I ought to observe the customary duty belonging to my office, by which I might make known that I rejoice unreservedly in Your Clemency and continually ask God in prayer to preserve you and the Catholic Church of the Roman commonwealth in every prosperity.

As for the strength of your faith, because you continually offer the sacrifice of praise to the Lord, I cannot describe how great are the thanks I give to God, nor how much we recognize that the rulers of our time possess not only royal power but also priestly understanding. For, when my brother Bishop Julian was judging the matter, the most salutary enactments of Your Perception reached us in copies, by which you deigned, through mercy, to chastise the monks’ senseless ignorance and to punish it by instruction, so that, if divine mercy should turn them toward repentance, they might be cleansed with many tears both from their unspeakable slaughter and from the blasphemies of heretics.

As for the fact that the most devout emperor wished me to send written communications to all the bishops who had attended the Council of Chalcedon, by which I might confirm what had there been defined concerning the rule of faith, I willingly fulfilled this. Nor would any deceitful pretence wish my judgment to be regarded as uncertain, since, through the bishop of Constantinople, to whom I fully expressed my joy, what I had written could have become known to everyone—unless he preferred to conceal my joy rather than make public the rejection of his own ambition. To my brother and co-bishop Julian, to whom I have entrusted my concern in the matter of the faith, I ask that you deign to grant such confidence that he may suggest to Your Piety whatever things may benefit the universal Church.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Opilio, the most illustrious man.

### XCI.—To Maximus, Bishop of Antioch.

How much the sacred unity of the common faith and the tranquil harmony of ecclesiastical peace please Your Love is shown by the text of your letter, which our sons, the presbyter Martianus and the deacon Olympius, brought to us. It was all the more welcome to us because through it we mingle mutual greetings, and because the grace of God becomes increasingly manifest, by which it comes about that throughout the whole world we rejoice in the evident light of Catholic truth.

Although—we greatly grieve over this—as the report of the messengers indicates, some still love their darkness and, although the splendor of day has arisen everywhere, still take pleasure in the obscurity of their blindness, and, having lost the faith, remain Christians in name only, possessing no understanding by which to distinguish one error from another or to differentiate the blasphemy of Nestorius from the impiety of Eutyches.

Nor can any of their falsehood be considered excusable merely because they are opposed to one another in their perversity. For although the disciples of Eutyches detest Nestorius and the followers of Nestorius anathematize Eutyches, by the judgment of Catholics both sides are condemned, and both heresies together are cut away from the body of the Church, because neither falsehood can have fellowship with us.

It makes no difference by what sacrilege they disagree with the truth of the Lord’s incarnation, so long as what they perversely think is accepted neither by the authority of the Gospel nor by the reason of the mystery.

Therefore, dearest brother, Your Love ought to perceive with your whole heart over which Church the Lord has wished you to preside, and to remember the doctrine which the most blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles, founded throughout the world by a uniform preaching, but with a special teaching authority in the cities of Antioch and Rome. Thus, understanding him to be pre-eminent in the dwelling-place of his glorification, you should recognize him as demanding those institutions which he handed down, just as he received them from the very truth which he confessed.

Nor should you in any way allow the Gospel to be opposed by wicked heretics in the Eastern Churches, and especially in those which the sacred canons of the Fathers at Nicaea assigned to the see of Antioch; nor should you allow the doctrine either of Nestorius or of Eutyches to be defended by anyone.

For, as I have said, the rock of the Catholic faith, from which the blessed apostle Peter took his surname, receives from the Lord no trace of either impiety. Clearly and plainly it anathematizes Nestorius, who, separating the nature of the Word and of the flesh in their union with the blessed Virgin, divided the one Christ into two and wished there to be one person of the Godhead and another of the humanity, although it is altogether one and the same person who, according to his everlasting divinity, was born timelessly from the Father and, born from his mother, was born in time.

It likewise curses Eutyches, who, abolishing the reality of human flesh in the Lord Jesus Christ, asserts that the Word itself was transformed into flesh, so that birth, nourishment, growth, suffering, death, burial, and resurrection on the third day belonged to the divinity alone, which did not receive the reality of a servant’s form but only its appearance.

Therefore, it is fitting that you be guarded with the greatest vigilance, lest heretical perversity dare to claim anything for itself, since it is proper for you to resist such things with priestly authority and for us to be repeatedly informed by your reports of what is taking place concerning the progress of the Churches.

It is worthy of you to be a partner of the apostolic see in this concern and, for the strengthening of confidence, to recognize the privileges of the third see, so that they may not be diminished in anything by anyone’s ambition. For my reverence for the canons of Nicaea is so great that I have neither permitted nor will I tolerate that what was established by the holy Fathers be violated by any innovation.

Even though the merits of bishops may sometimes differ, the rights of the sees remain. Rival claimants may perhaps bring some disturbance against them, but they cannot diminish their dignity.

Therefore, whenever Your Love thinks that something ought to be done for the privileges of the Church of Antioch, you should explain it carefully in your own letters, so that we may be able to respond to your consultation fully and appropriately.

For the present, however, it is sufficient to declare generally that if anything has been attempted by anyone against the statutes of the canons of Nicaea in any synod, or if anything of this kind appears for a time to have arisen, it can inflict no prejudice upon the inviolable decrees. It will be easier to dissolve an agreement of whatever kind than to corrupt the rules of the aforesaid canons in any respect.

Ambition never fails to seek opportunities for creeping in, and whenever a general assembly of bishops has been convened because of pressing circumstances, it is difficult for the desire of the wicked not to attempt to seek something beyond its proper measure.

This was also the case with the synod of Ephesus, which endured the impious Nestorius together with his doctrine. Bishop Juvenal believed that he could secure the primacy of the province of Palestine and dared to strengthen his insolent claims by fabricated documents. The blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, rightly shuddering at this, informed me in his letters what the aforementioned ambition had dared to undertake and earnestly urged that no assent be given to unlawful efforts.

As for the letter of the blessed Cyril whose copies you sent to us, know that, after searching for it in our archive, we found it to be authentic.

This, however, is the particular principle of my decision: however large the number of bishops who may decree something through the secret manipulation of certain persons, if it is found to be contrary to the constitutions of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, it is annulled in consideration of justice. For the tranquility of universal peace cannot otherwise be preserved unless the reverence due to the canons remains inviolate.

If anything is said to have been done by these brothers, who were sent to the holy synod in my place, apart from what concerned the case of the faith, it will have no validity whatsoever, because they were sent from the apostolic see for this sole purpose: that, after the heresies had been exposed, they might be defenders of the Catholic faith.

Whatever is brought before the episcopal judgment apart from the specific matters of synodal councils may have some basis for adjudication if nothing concerning it was defined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. But whatever disagrees with their rules and constitution will never obtain the consent of the apostolic see.

You will learn with what diligence we guard this from a copy of the letter which we sent to the bishop of Constantinople to restrain his ambition. You should make it known to all our brothers and bishops, so that they may understand that ecclesiastical peace must be preserved through harmony pleasing to God.

Your Love must also take care that, apart from those who are the Lord’s priests, no one dare claim for himself the right to teach and preach, whether he is a monk or a layman who boasts in the name of some learning.

For although it is desirable that all the children of the Church should understand what is right and sound, it must not nevertheless be permitted that anyone established outside the priestly order assume the office of preacher. Everything in the Church of God ought to be ordered, so that in the one body of Christ the more excellent members may fulfill their office and the inferior may not oppose the superior.

Given on the third day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Opilio, the most illustrious man.

### 227. XCII.—The above letter to Leo Augustus.

After fulfilling the duties belonging to a congratulatory letter on your imperial rule, I have also added this page of necessary supplication, in which I ask for the protection of your favor, divinely prepared for the Catholic faith.

For from the report of my brother and co-bishop Anatolius I have learned that such things have been perpetrated in the Church of Alexandria that the whole Christian religion feels itself attacked and violated unless provision is made through your devotion to the universal faith, and unless the aforesaid Church, formerly renowned for its Catholic teachers, is restored to Christian freedom. Thus, once the assaults of heretics have ceased, the evangelical doctrine which flourished there before Dioscorus may be restored in unity with the peace of the whole Church.

This work, befitting your virtues and glory, will have a swift and God-pleasing result if you do not allow what was confirmed at the holy Council of Chalcedon concerning the Incarnation of the Lord Christ to be disturbed by any reconsideration.

For in that council, assembled through the Holy Spirit, everything was confirmed by full and perfect definitions, so that nothing may be added to or subtracted from the rule issued by divine inspiration.

We do not doubt that this is also clear to Your Clemency, since, as we have learned from the reports of many, you have allowed no attempt of the heretics against the authority of the aforesaid synod to dare anything.

Therefore, what you have voluntarily seen must be denied them, I confidently expect you to grant to the universal Church, and to provide immutably and perpetually: namely, that the things which, according to the Gospel of Christ and the truth of evangelical preaching, have been strengthened throughout all past ages by one faith and one understanding may no longer be overturned by any action.

Accordingly, as the mercy of God, through the counsel of his Spirit, instructs the mind of Your Piety, first provide for the restoration of peace to the holy Church of Alexandria, and order that a bishop be provided through Catholic priests in whom nothing blameworthy can be found either in the uprightness of his conduct or in the perfection of his faith. Thus, when everything has been properly arranged, the same preaching of truth may be preserved.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Constantius and Rufus.

### XCIII.—The same, to Leo Augustus.

Although recently I sent two letters to Your Clemency, one fulfilling the duty of greeting and the other making supplication for the condition of the Church, nevertheless, since an occasion has presented itself by God’s providence, it is fitting to repeat both.

Accordingly, in keeping with that confidence which, through divine inspiration, you have granted to the universal Church by establishing—before anyone’s petitions—what all most desired, we do not cease to give thanks and to bless God’s providence in the fervor of your faith. For, as I have learned from the words of my brother and co-bishop Anatolius, with a holy and Catholic spirit you resisted the shamelessness of the heretics so firmly that you declared yourself the guardian of the peace of the whole world established by the Council of Chalcedon.

Since this has most beneficially been determined according to the judgment of your faith, how much more zealously ought it to be bestowed upon the universal Church, so that the tranquility of the Christian faith may also benefit your empire and heretical wickedness may not glory in any undertaking of its own. Its persistent and treacherous contention will immediately fall silent if it is restrained by imperial power.

Given on the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Constantius and Rufus.

### XCIV.—Likewise, the same, to the same.

I reverently received the letters of Your Clemency, full of the strength of faith and the light of truth. I would have wished to obey also in the matter in which Your Piety considers my presence necessary, so that I might attain the greater benefit of beholding your splendor; but I think that what reason has shown should be chosen will please you more.

For, since you fortify the universal peace of the Church with holy and spiritual zeal, and nothing is more suitable for defending the faith than to adhere to the things which, under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, have been irreproachably defined in every respect, we ourselves would seem to be overturning the decrees and arbitrarily weakening the authorities embraced by the universal Church at the request of heretics. Thus we would impose no limit on the gathering together of the Churches, but, by granting permission for conflict, would prolong rather than quiet their struggles.
