Therefore, since after those impieties of the synod of Ephesus—in which, through the crime of Dioscorus, the Catholic faith was rejected and Eutychian perversity was received—nothing more useful could have been ordered for confirming the Christian faith than that the holy Council of Chalcedon should abolish the aforesaid crime, and since such heavenly care for doctrine was exercised there that nothing remained according to anyone’s opinion which was discordant with prophetic or apostolic preaching, with this moderation preserved—that only rebels and the obstinate were rejected from the unity of the Church, while pardon was denied to no one who corrected himself—what could Your Piety decide that would be more reasonable or more religious than that no one henceforth be allowed to attack what has been established not so much by human as by divine decrees? Otherwise those who dare to doubt the truth of God himself would truly deserve to lose God’s gift.

Since, therefore, the universal Church has become a rock through the building upon that principal rock, and the first and most blessed of the apostles, Peter, heard the Lord’s voice say, “You are Peter, and upon this Rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:16), who is he except either Antichrist or the devil who would dare assail the impregnable truth?

Persevering incorrigibly in his malice, through vessels of wrath suited to his deceit, under the false name of diligence—while falsely claiming to seek the truth—he desires to sow lies. Unrestrained madness and blind impiety have deservedly marked such persons as contemptible and to be avoided. By the devil’s instruction, what has raged against the holy Church of Alexandria has revealed what kind of people those are who desire to have the Council of Chalcedon reconsidered.

In no way could it have happened at Chalcedon that you should be thought to hold an opinion against the holy Council of Nicaea—contrary to what the heretics falsely claim, pretending that they uphold the faith of the Council of Nicaea. At Nicaea our holy and venerable Fathers, assembled against Arius, affirmed not that the Lord’s flesh but that the divinity of the Son is *homoousios*—“of the same substance”—with the Father.

At the Council of Chalcedon, however, it was defined against Eutychian impiety that the Lord Jesus Christ took the reality of our body from the substance of the Virgin Mother.

Therefore, before a Christian prince and one worthy to be numbered among the preachers of Christ, I use the freedom of the Catholic faith, and with confidence exhort you to the fellowship of the apostles and prophets: steadfastly despise and reject those who have deprived themselves of the Christian name, and do not allow impious parricides, through sacrilegious pretence, to deal with the faith when it is clear that they have deviated from the faith.

Since the Lord has enriched Your Clemency with such illumination of his mystery, you must understand without hesitation that royal power has been bestowed upon you not only for the governance of the world but especially for the protection of the Church, so that, by suppressing wicked attempts, you may defend what has been rightly established and restore true peace to what has been disturbed—namely, by driving out invaders of another’s rights and restoring to the Church of Alexandria the see of the ancient faith. Thus, with God’s anger appeased by your corrections, may he not repay the royal city for what has been committed but forgive it.

Set before the eyes of your heart, venerable emperor, all the Lord’s priests throughout the world, who beseech you for that faith in which lies the redemption of the whole world. In this matter especially, those who, as followers of the apostolic faith, desire to preside over the Church of Alexandria entreat you, asking Your Piety not to allow heretical men, rightly condemned for their perversity, to make use of their own persuasion.

Whether you consider the impiety of their errors or attend to the deed of their madness, they can be neither admitted to the honor of the priesthood nor allowed to retain the Christian name; rather, they deserve to be cut off from it.

For—if I may say this after having obtained Your Piety’s pardon—they darken the splendor of Your Serenity by a kind of contagion, when sacrilegious parricides dare to seek what even the innocent may not obtain.

Petitions have been presented to Your Piety, copies of which you appended to your letters. In these, the signatures of Catholics who lament are included, and, because their case is credible, the names of each person and the dignity of his office are openly set forth.

But in those which deceit did not fear to present to an orthodox prince, under the uncertain designation of a confused unity, the definite name is withheld, so that not only the small number of persons but also their worth may remain undisclosed. They consider it useful for themselves to conceal the number of those whose character has been judged, and, fearing to declare from what place they come, they conceal the fact that they deserved condemnation.

One petition, therefore, contains the case of Catholics; the other reveals the contrivances of heretics. In the former, the overthrow of the Lord’s priests, the whole Christian people, and the monasteries is lamented; in the latter, the continuation of monstrous crimes is displayed, so that what ought not to have been heard might be prolonged.

Is it not evident whom Your Piety ought to assist and whom to oppose, lest the Church of Alexandria, which has always been a house of prayer, now become a den of robbers?

It is plainly evident that through the most cruel and senseless violence all the light of the heavenly mysteries has there been extinguished. The offering of the sacrifice has been interrupted; the sanctification of the chrism has failed; and all the mysteries have withdrawn themselves from the murderous hands of the impious.

Nor can there be any doubt what ought to be decreed concerning those who, after unspeakable sacrileges, after the blood of a most upright priest had been shed and the ashes of his burned body had been scattered in insult through air and sky, dare to seek for themselves the right of an office they have seized and to summon the inviolable faith of apostolic teaching before councils.

It is a great thing for you if, in addition to your diadem, a crown of faith is also added to you from the hand of the Lord, and if you triumph over the enemies of the Church. For if it is praiseworthy for you to crush the weapons of hostile nations, how great will be the glory of freeing the Church of Alexandria from the most insane tyrant, whose destruction is an injury to all Christians?

So that my letters might offer Your Piety a conversation as though I were present, I judged that whatever I would have suggested concerning the common faith should be conveyed in the following writings. And, lest this letter’s page become excessively long, I have included in other letters matters appropriate to the defense of the Catholic faith, so that, although the things preached by the apostolic see would have been sufficient, these additions might also expose the plots of the heretics.

Your Piety’s priestly and apostolic spirit ought also to bring this evil to the justice of punishment: it pestilently obscures the purity of the Church of Constantinople, in which certain heretical clerics are found to agree in their thinking and, within the very entrails of the Catholics, to assist the heretics by their assertions.

In removing such men, my brother Anatolius is found to be too slow because he spares them with excessive kindness. Deign, for the sake of your faith, to provide this medicine also to the Church, so that such men may be expelled not only from the clerical order but also from residence in the city, lest the holy people of God be polluted any further by the contagion of perverse men.

At my request I commend to Your Piety Bishop Julian and the presbyter Eutychius, devotees of your piety, so that you may graciously hear their suggestions in defense of the Catholic faith, for they are truly such as may be found useful to your faith in every respect.

Given on the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Constantius and Rufus, the most illustrious men.

### XCV.—To Pulcheria Augusta.

228. We have often demonstrated by many proofs how much confidence the Church of God ought to claim for itself from the faith of Your Clemency, since, as you have learned under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, you subject your power in every respect to the one by whose gift and protection you reign.

Therefore, because from the report of my brother and co-bishop Anatolius I have learned that a certain dissension against the integrity of the Christian faith has been generated in the Church of Constantinople by the agency of Eutyches, and because the text of the synodal proceedings might reveal the character of the whole case, it is worthy of your glory that the error—which arose more from ignorance than from deceit—be removed before it acquires any strength from the agreement of the imprudent and from the obstinacy of perversity.

For just as Nestorius fell away from the truth when he asserted that the Lord Jesus Christ was born from the Virgin Mother as man alone, so this man too has deviated from the Catholic path, who did not believe that the one born from the same Virgin was of our nature. Thus, what bore the form of a servant, what was like us and conformed to us, would be some image of our flesh rather than its reality.

It is of no benefit to call our Lord the human son of the blessed Virgin Mary if he is not believed to be human of that same race and seed which is proclaimed at the very beginning of the Gospel.

Therefore I greatly grieve and am deeply distressed that this man, who previously seemed praiseworthy because of his purpose of humility, now dares to assert, against our single hope and that of our fathers, empty and exceedingly perverse things. When he saw that the meaning of his folly displeased Catholic ears, he ought to have recalled himself from his opinion, lest he move the bishops of the Church to such a degree that he should receive a sentence of condemnation.

If he wishes to remain in his opinion, no one will be able to release him from that sentence. The moderation of the apostolic see preserves this balance: it acts more severely with the hardened, but desires to grant pardon to those who correct themselves.

Because, therefore, I have great confidence in the most sincere faith of Your Piety, I beseech Your Clemency: just as Catholic preaching has always been assisted by your holy zeal, so now also favor its freedom.

For it is not some small portion of our faith, less clearly expressed, that is being attacked. Rather, this insolent opposition dares to assail what the Lord wished no one in his Church to ignore.

Therefore, according to the customary practice of Your Piety, deign to labor so that what blasphemous folly has brought forth against the unique mystery of human salvation may be driven from the minds of all. If the man who has fallen into this temptation should come to his senses, so that he condemns by his own voice and signature what he had wrongly thought, let him be restored to the communion of his order.

Your Clemency should also know that I have entrusted this matter to my brother and co-bishop Favianus and to those whom we sent, so that pardon may be granted if the error is abolished.

And lest our presence seem to have been lacking from the arrangement of the most devout prince, who wished an episcopal council to be convened, I have sent my brothers Bishop Julian and the presbyter Renatus, together with my son the deacon Hilary, who would be sufficient to fulfill the role of my presence.

But the man who is in error will be better helped if he comes to his senses in the very place where he went astray and receives indulgence there where he earned condemnation.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes, illustrious men.

### XCVI.—To all the bishops established throughout Gaul and Spain.

[Column 0921C]

Leo to his most beloved brothers, all the Catholic bishops established throughout Gaul and Spain, concerning Easter.

Since priestly observance ought to be harmonious in carrying out all the rules of the divine commandments, we must take special and primary care that, on the day of the paschal feast, neither ignorance nor presumption should incur the sin of diversity.

Since the time of the most sacred solemnity has its boundaries arranged in such a way that the saving mystery must sometimes be celebrated earlier and sometimes later, the solicitude of the apostolic see does not cease to take care lest ecclesiastical devotion be disturbed by uncertainty.

When, therefore, in certain records of the Fathers, the coming Easter of the Lord was found to have been assigned by some to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May and by others to the eighth day before those same Kalends, this difference so disturbed me that I disclosed my concern in this matter to the most merciful emperor Marcian. I asked that, on his instruction, those who possessed expertise in this calculation should investigate the reasoning more carefully and determine on which day the venerable solemnity could be celebrated more correctly.

When he replied, the day was fixed as the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

Therefore, because, for the sake of unity and peace, I preferred to assent to the decision of the Easterners rather than to disagree in the observance of so great a festival, let your Fraternity know that the Lord’s resurrection is to be celebrated by all on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. You are also to make this known to the other brothers, so that, joined by the fellowship of divine peace as we are united in one faith, we may likewise rejoice in one solemnity.

### XCVII.—To Samartio, Carathon, and others.

To the most blessed lords and venerable brothers in Christ, Samartio, Carathon, Desiderius, the bishops and presbyters of all the churches established within the province of Thrace:

Leo, Victor, and Eustathius, bishops.

The powers of this world have shown such reverence toward the priestly order—even those whom divine power has commanded to rule the earth under the imperial name—that, in accordance with imperial constitutions, they have permitted holy bishops the right to deal with legal matters.

Although this has frequently been brought forward in the formulas of ancient law and confirmed by statutes, we find that it has especially been trampled upon in recent times. For, with priestly judgment set aside, cases are indiscriminately transferred to secular examination.

Therefore it seemed to us that this insult both to sacred law and to our order should, for the present, be punished by full severity and that a rule should be established for future observance.

We decree, therefore, that whoever, bypassing the priest of his own church, comes before a secular tribunal for judgment shall be expelled from the sacred thresholds and excluded from the heavenly altar. After this decision, no one who has sat in judgment by common agreement should attempt to claim anything further for himself beyond what has been prescribed.

In this way, those who previously went astray may correct themselves by suitable amendment. But whoever is proven to serve the heavenly office under clerical discipline is to be expelled from the clergy if, bypassing the judgment of the priests, he approaches secular authority.

We wish all and each to know this, so that what has been established in the full order of justice and law may attain complete force in all matters concerning clerics.

If a cleric brings a case against a layman, let him first ask to be heard by the bishops. Then, if he sees the layman resisting his petition, let him, with the permission of his bishop, engage in litigation before the secular authorities.

Leo, bishop, writes.

Victor, bishop, writes.

Eustathius, bishop, writes.

[Column 0921]

## THE DECREES OF POPE HILARY BEGIN. (C)

## THE CHAPTERS BEGIN.

[Column 0921D]

1. That the canons of Nicaea and the decrees of the apostolic see be observed.

2. That bigamists, or men married to widows or to defiled women, may not enter the ecclesiastical orders.

3. That penitents or those ignorant of letters, or those who through bodily defect or amputation lack something, may not advance to a higher order.

4. That whatever a bishop or his predecessor has ordained unlawfully be corrected by the one who remains.

5. That no bishop choose his own successor.

## Decree

[Column 0923A]

### Chapter I

In the consulship of Flavius Basiliscus and Hermineicus, the most illustrious men, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

In the basilica of Saint Mary, with the venerable Pope Hilary seated together with fifty bishops, all the presbyters also seated and the deacons standing nearby, Hilary, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, presiding over the synod, said:

Since this religious assembly, gathered by the Holy Spirit, urges us to deal with more diligent care with certain matters necessary for ecclesiastical discipline, if it pleases you, brothers, let us, with the Lord’s help, establish permanently whatever pertains to the order of ordination, according to the commandments of divine law and the constitutions of the canons of Nicaea. Let no one be permitted, at the peril of his status, to violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the apostolic see.

For guilt in such transgressions will fall upon us, who administer the offices of the most powerful priest, if we are found negligent in the matters of God, since we remember that we must fear how the Lord threatens the negligence of priests.

Indeed, the one who enjoys the greater honor commits the greater offense, and the loftiness of dignities makes the vices of sinners more serious.

### II

Therefore, above all, care must be taken lest anyone aspire to the sacred orders who has not married a virgin, as was previously written in the proceedings. All who have entered into a second marriage contrary to the apostolic commandments are likewise to be rejected.

[Column 0923C]

### III

Let penitents, those ignorant of letters, those who have suffered loss through some bodily defect, and those who are themselves from among the penitents not dare to aspire to the sacred orders. Whoever should prove to be the consecrator of any such person shall himself annul his own act.

### IV

But whatever anyone has done unlawfully, or has found to have been committed by his predecessors, he must condemn if he wishes to avoid personal danger. We do not wish to exercise the severity of punishment in any matter.

But whoever has sinned in the matters of God either through defiance or through some lapse, or has refused to abolish what his immediate predecessor did, will find in himself whatever he did not cut away in another.

So that this may henceforth be more firmly observed, if it pleases you, furnish all your judgments and your individual subscriptions, so that access to unlawful acts may be closed by synodal judgment.

All the bishops and presbyters acclaimed:

“Christ, hear us; life to Hilary!”—said six times.

“We confirm and teach this.”—said eight times.

“These things must be held; these things must be observed.”—said five times.

“We give thanks for your teaching.”—said fifteen times.

“We ask that these things be observed forever.”—said fifteen times.

“Through Saint Peter we ask that these things be observed forever.”—said eight times.

“Let this presumption never occur.”—said ten times.

“Whoever violates these things will find the consequence in himself.”

After silence had been made, Bishop Hilary said:

### V

Moreover, brothers, as has reached us through letters sent from Spain in a definite report, new and unheard-of seeds of perversion are continually arising in certain places.

Indeed, some consider the episcopate—which is granted only on the basis of preceding merits—not a divine gift but an inheritance to be acquired. They believe that, like perishable and mortal possessions, the office of priests can be transferred as though by legacy or testamentary right.

For many priests, even when standing at the threshold of death, are said to designate others by name to be substituted in their place, so that what is expected is not a legitimate election but the favor of the deceased, which is treated as the consent of the people.

Consider how serious this is. Therefore, if it pleases you, let us remove this permission generally from the Churches, lest—shameful as it is to say—anyone think that what belongs to God is owed to a human being.

But so that what has been reported to us may also come to your knowledge, let the writings of our brothers and co-bishops from Spain be read.

The notary Paul recited them.

And it was decreed that no priest should henceforth presume anything of this kind.

### 229. Letter of the same Pope Hilary to the bishops of Tarragona.

1. That no bishop be ordained without the consent of the metropolitan bishop.

2. That no bishop leave his own Church and transfer to another.

3. That Hireneus, removed from Artimoniensis, return to his own place.

4. Concerning the removal of bishops who have been ordained unlawfully, and that two bishops not be held in one Church.

5. Concerning the condemnation of Hireneus if he does not return to his own Church.

To our most beloved brother Ascanio and all the bishops of the province of Tarragona:

Hilary, bishop.

After receiving the letter of Your Charity, in which you requested that the presumptions of Silvanus, bishop of the Church of Calagurris, be restrained, and again sought the confirmation of the excessively illicit petitions of the honorati and landowners of Barcino, Tiriasona, Castana, Calagurris, Viriges, and Tricio, together with written statements from various persons, we find that letters were submitted to us in which they excused what your complaint had brought forward against Silvanus. Yet their submission likewise did not lack very just grounds for censure, since it became clear that priests had been ordained in certain cities without the knowledge of our metropolitan brother and co-bishop Ascanius. Therefore, since we see that whatever has been reported by either side is confused by every kind of perversity, having taken into account the necessity of the times, we decree for this reason that what has been done is to be treated with pardon, so that henceforth nothing may be attempted against the commands of the blessed Apostle or against the decrees of the canons of Nicaea.

### I

This, however, we first wish to be observed in accordance with the rules of those same Fathers: that no bishop may in any way be consecrated without the knowledge and consent of our brother Ascanius, the metropolitan, since the ancient order has maintained this. The authority of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers defined this; whoever stretches out his hands against it declares himself unworthy of their fellowship, since he resists their prescriptions.

### II

In insult to them, that other provision is also despised in a proud spirit—namely, the provision that forbids anyone to presume to leave his own Church and transfer to another. Bishop Hireneus is attempting to admit this, with the shameless connivance of some and, even more grievously, with your assertion of it.

Since you wish to strengthen this by our authority, although you are shown to be greatly indignant at illicit matters, you will learn, when your letters have been read in the assembly of the brothers whom the feast of my birth had gathered, what judgment regarding the ordination of bishops, in accordance with the statutes of the canons and the decrees of my predecessors, was approved in the proceedings whose text we likewise sent.

### III

Therefore, once Bishop Hireneus has been removed from the Church of Barcino and sent back to his own, and once the desires that seek what is unlawful through ignorance of ecclesiastical laws have been quieted by priestly moderation, a bishop must immediately be ordained for the people of Barcino from their own clergy—one whom you, Brother Ascanius, ought especially to choose and whom it is fitting for you to consecrate. Otherwise, should something different perhaps be done, our command will rebuke it, especially in relation to your name, not without reproach, since we have learned that something has been admitted to the injury of God, from whom alone the grace of priestly dignities is specially bestowed. Nor should episcopal honor be regarded as hereditary right, since it is conferred upon us solely by the kindness of our God.

### IV

Accordingly, we now confirm this concerning the bishops who have been ordained: although, because they were advanced without your knowledge, they might have deserved to be removed together with those responsible for them, they may remain provided that none of them has been the husband of a widow or has entered into a second marriage and its vows, as the legal regulations also command, saying: “Let a priest take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one who has been divorced.” Likewise, the blessed Apostle, the teacher of the nations, did not leave silent his own instruction concerning those who desire to become priests, saying: “the husband of one wife.”

You must, of course, my dearest brothers, be so instructed in this matter that, among the other things that must be avoided, you strive especially to preserve what you know has been commanded above all. Among these things it must also be seen to that there are not simultaneously two priests of one Church, nor one who is ignorant of letters, nor one lacking any part of his limbs, nor anyone who has been among the penitents allowed at all to enter the sacred ministry.

Nor should you think that the petitions of the peoples have such force that, when you wish to comply with them, you abandon the will of our God, which forbids us to sin. His indignation is stirred more gravely by this because his kindness is offended, while illicit acts are being committed by those who are interpreters of reconciliation.

### V

To ensure that everything is corrected in accordance with what we have written, we have sent this present letter with the arrival of our subdeacon Trajan. If Bishop Hireneus, once he has been restored to his own Church, neglects to return to it through the ambition of his wickedness, let him know that he is to be removed from the fellowship of bishops—a removal that will be imposed upon him not by judicial sentence but by humane consideration.

May God keep you safe and unharmed.

## Another letter of Hilary to Ascanius, concerning the matters written above

To his dearest brother Ascanius, Hilary, bishop.

We must remember the divine grace toward us, which through the mercy of its favor has raised us to the summit of priesthood for this purpose: that, adhering to its commands and stationed, as it were, upon a watchtower of its priesthood, we may prohibit what is illicit and teach what must be followed.

Accordingly, by letters sent through our subdeacon Trajan, we warn that what has been wrongly done must be corrected. We are greatly astonished that Your Charity not only reported the petitions of the people of Barcino without any authority, but also, by letters sent to us, requested the completion of their wicked desire, introducing in the preface of your letters a reference to the council—as though the excesses of guilt were diminished by a multitude of ignorant people—even though each person had also added his own name alongside yours and individually supplied his own signature.

Yet the matter displeased Your Charity most profoundly, because, on account of the position and honor owed to you, the other priests ought to have been instructed by you, not followed. Therefore, as I indicated in the general letter, Hireneus must return to his own Church, and a bishop must immediately be consecrated for the people of Barcino from their own clergy, provided that he agrees with the statutes of the canons and the apostolic commands.

Although those priests who were ordained with the knowledge and consent of Your Charity ought to have been removed together with those responsible for them, nevertheless, so that we may not decree anything harsh in such great necessity, we wish those who have become bishops to remain, provided that they are not found liable under the apostolic commands and the statutes of the holy Fathers, and provided that henceforth nothing contrary to ecclesiastical discipline is perpetrated, as has been done until now.

It is your responsibility, dearest brother, to preserve the authority owed to you, not merely to refuse assent to illicit acts, but also to restrain everything that you discover to have been done contrary to the rule. Above all, in accordance with what we decree solely for the sake of unity, compel Hireneus to return to his own Church. He ought rather to return there willingly if he has deserved to be separated from the fellowship of priests, and two bishops must not be permitted to belong to one Church.

We have entrusted the more timely execution of this matter to the aforesaid subdeacon, whose diligence our authority has arranged to travel to Spain also for the preservation of ecclesiastical discipline.

May God keep you safe and unharmed, dearest brother.

## Letter of Pope Hilary to Leontius, Veranus, and Victurius, bishops

To his dearest brothers Veranus, Leontius, and Victurius, bishops, Hilary, pope.

We are moved by the consideration of justice, which, although it ought to be observed by all who think rightly, must not be rashly neglected especially by the Lord’s priests, whose institutions it is fitting should shape the conduct of others.

Our brother and co-bishop Ingenuus, bishop of Ebredunum in the province of the Maritime Alps, always supported by metropolitan honor, reports that, to his own prejudice—as an attached document has shown—we established certain things at the request of our brother and co-bishop Auxamius, things that would contradict every defense in this same case.

For, when the reports submitted for our judgment were reviewed—reports which our brother and co-bishop Veranus sent to my predecessor of holy memory together with the other priests of the province—and when the response of the Apostolic See that had then been sent was disclosed, it was made clear that nothing ought afterward to have been attempted and that nothing should have been established by the recent act of concealment, to the injury of synodal regulations.

Although even what was elicited from us on this matter may be considered invalid, since it was insinuated by the one who deserved to carry it out, nevertheless, so that we may not be moved by hatred or favor—neither of which ought to have a place in the examination of cases—we entrust the investigation of the attached complaint to Your Charity, so that nothing contrary to the venerable canons and nothing against the judgment of my predecessor of holy memory may have force, whatever is shown to have been concealed from us.

For we do not wish, dearest brothers, that the privileges of the Churches, which must always be preserved, be thrown into confusion. Nor do we permit one priest to possess a right in another’s province, because by this one sins against the sanctions of the holy traditions no less than one rushes into an affront to the Lord himself, whose expectation of the fruits of our ministry rests not upon the breadth of regions but upon the acquisition of souls.

Let our brother and co-bishop Ingenuus therefore have the episcopate of his province; he was formerly censured by the Apostolic See for an illicit cession. With everything preserved that, as we have said, the authority of my predecessor of holy memory defined concerning the Churches of the city of Ceruelena and the castle of Nicaea, let nothing harm the rights of the Churches because a bishop was recently consecrated over one of the aforesaid places by the aforementioned brother, in order to exclude ambition, just as he forbade the ambition of another. Let the established form of correction remain: the aforesaid places must return to the governance of one bishop, since it was not fitting for them to be divided between two priests.

May the Lord keep you safe and unharmed, dearest brothers.

## Letter of the bishops of Tarraco to Pope Hilary

To the most blessed pope Hilary, whom we honor in Christ with apostolic reverence, Ascanius and all the bishops of the province of Tarraco.

Since we have learned, through the report of our son in Christ, the illustrious Vincentius, governor of our province, that Your Apostolate cares for the priests of its provinces, his prompting caused our petition to rise with willing devotion to the boldness of writing.

Therefore, bringing the due services of the provincials in written speech to Your Crown, we ask that, with the favor by which you also regard other people, you deign, most blessed father whom we honor in Christ with apostolic reverence, to keep our humility in your prayers and in your mind.

We especially beseech you to deign to strengthen by your favorable assertions our action, which nearly the whole province nevertheless brings to our knowledge, both as a petition and as an example of antiquity.

And when it was read, all the bishops and priests cried out:

“Answer, O Christ; may Hilary live!”—said ten times.

“May this presumption never occur!”—said six times.

“What belongs to God cannot be given by man!”—said six times.

“Through the Lord Peter we ask that these things be preserved forever!”—said six times.

“We ask that these matters be kept secure.”

Bishop Hilary said: “Read.”

The notary Paul read:

The holy Nundinarius, bishop of the city of Varohia, paid the debt of human condition. He had earlier established our venerable brother Bishop Hireneus in his own diocese with our consent, and wished him to be installed in his own place, leaving him, under the provision of his final will, whatever his poverty could possess.

Yet the judgment of the deceased does not waver in its merit.

When Bishop Probus read this, he rose from the assembly and said:

“That was permitted. This was not permitted. God gives successors. Resist this matter through your apostolate by your authority.”

Bishop Hilary said: “Continue what you began.”

The notary Paul read:

Indeed, all the clergy and people of the same city, as well as the best and most numerous provincials, hoped that he would occupy the deceased man’s place, and they gave their consent.

Considering the judgment of the deceased, approving his life, and taking into account the nobility and multitude of those who were petitioning, as well as the advantage of the Church in question, we judged it best that a bishop of no lesser merit should be substituted for so great a priest who had departed to the divine realm—especially since it is clear that the church of that municipality, in which he had previously been ordained, had always belonged to the diocese of the Church of this city.

Therefore, we humbly beseech Your Apostolate to confirm by your authority what appears rightly to have been done by us in our humility.

Some time ago we had also complained in our letters to you about the presumption of Bishop Salvinus, and we are astonished that we have received no response from Your Correspondence. Now, repeating this same petition, we ask that you deign to instruct us by apostolic words concerning what must be observed in these matters.

And lest perhaps, through the negligence of the bearer or the difficulty of the long journey, our humble letter concerning this matter should not have reached you, we have preferred to repeat our petition.

And the subscription:

Pray for us. May the divine eternity preserve your holy Apostolate forever, for us all and for his Church, truly our Lord, apostolic pope.

## Letter of the bishops of Tarraco to Pope Hilary

To the most blessed lord Pope Hilary, whom we honor in Christ with apostolic reverence, Ascanius and all the bishops of the province of Tarraco.

Even if no necessity of ecclesiastical discipline dictated it, we truly ought to have sought that privilege of your See through which, after receiving the keys of the kingdom, the unique preaching of the most blessed Peter, following the Savior’s resurrection, has provided illumination for the whole world. Just as the primacy of his representative stands out, so it must be feared and loved by all.

Therefore, first worshiping God within ourselves, whom you serve without complaint, we turn back to the faith praised by the apostolic mouth, seeking answers from the place where nothing is commanded through error or presumption, but everything through episcopal deliberation.

Although matters stand thus, there is nevertheless among us a false brother. Just as necessity did not permit us to remain silent about his presumption for any longer, so the necessity of the future judgment compelled us to speak.

A certain Silvanus, bishop of Calagurris, situated in the farthest part of your province, has arrogated to himself unwarranted divinations and has driven our humility to the point that, against his utterly empty superstition, we demand the unique remedy of your See.

For already more than eight or perhaps seven years ago, setting aside the rules of the Fathers and disregarding your statutes, he ordained a bishop when no people had requested one. We thought that his rash action could be healed by fraternal and peaceful admonition, but he made it worse.

Finally, contrary to the antiquity of the canons and the decrees of the synod, inflamed with such a spirit of presumption, he made a bishop in the same place that had been designated for another brother of ours, a presbyter, upon whom he had laid hands against his will and resistance and who had already been added to our assembly.

It thus came about that our brother of the city of Caesaraugusta reported to us everything concerning his most wretched recklessness; with great diligence and concern he had foreseen what might be of some use. Indeed, he repeatedly opposed all the bishops situated nearby, so that they would not join themselves to the schismatic. But with damnable obstinacy that man alone did not blush to commit everything that was illicit—and what we are ashamed to say.

Therefore, because these presumptions, which divide unity and create schism, must be swiftly confronted, we ask Your See to instruct us through apostolic utterances concerning what you wish observed in this matter, so that, once our brotherhood has been gathered and the venerable decrees of the synod have been brought forward, strengthened by your authority against the spirit of rebellion, we may—with God’s help—understand what ought to be done both with the ordination and with the one ordained.

Your apostolate will certainly have its triumph in your time if the Catholic Church hears what the chair of Saint Peter holds, and if the new seeds of weeds are uprooted.

And the subscription:

May the divine eternity preserve your holy Apostolate forever, as you pray for us.

“We ask that these matters be corrected!”—said six times.

“We ask that these matters be cut off!”—said seven times.

“We ask that discipline be preserved!”—said five times.

“We ask that the canons be guarded!”—said seven times.

“We ask that punishment be imposed for presumptions!”—said seven times.

“Let apostolic ordination be preserved inviolate!”—said seven times.

“Answer, O Christ; may Hilary live!”—said five times.

“A worthy pope, a worthy teacher!”—said eight times.

“We ask that antiquity be preserved!”—said seven times.

“We ask that discipline be preserved!”

Bishop Hilary said:

“Now that what was read has been received from all, brothers, bring forward your individual judgments, with God inspiring you.”

Maximus, bishop of the Church of Taurinum, said:

“In guarding all the disciplines that pertain to sacred ordinations, I declare more clearly, by my profession, my judgment: that I will never do any of the things that are forbidden. Concerning the rest, I judge that whoever does such things, or refuses to remove from the Churches what has been discovered there, must know that he will have to answer for grave matters before the judgment of the Apostolic See. In that judgment he will necessarily undergo its sentence.”

Ingenuus, bishop of Ebredunum, said:

“My judgment also is the same in every respect, by which I bind myself, so that I may never attempt anything forbidden in these matters, since I know my position and my profession. Concerning the rest also I judge that whoever becomes a transgressor must know that he is bound by the snares of ecclesiastical rule and incurs the guilt of the Apostolic See.”

Paul, bishop of Aquae Vivae, said:

“I likewise bind myself by the same law. Concerning the rest, I judge similarly that transgressors may not attempt anything of this kind without danger to themselves—anything that rightly ought to be punished.”

Primus, bishop of the Church of Atella, said:

“I too judge that this must be observed.”

Pallidius, bishop of the Church of Salpina, said:

“I promise that I will do nothing against ecclesiastical discipline or the statutes of the holy canons.”

Tiberius, bishop of the Church of Sabina, said:

“I declare that I will observe the statutes of the Apostolic See in everything. And if in my Church I discover any cleric who, contrary to the commands of the holy canons, has married a woman or has two wives, I will separate him from ecclesiastical office.”

All the bishops said:

“We all follow the judgments of the brothers; we all confirm them, and we decree that they must be observed.”

“Answer, O Christ; may Hilary live!”—said six times.

“May what has been wrongly admitted be corrected through you!”—said eight times.

“Let what is not permitted not be done!”—said eight times.

Hilary, bishop of the Church of the city of Rome, presiding over the synod, said:

“Since we have decided that the form of the present definition, established according to the judgment of the holy statutes, should reach the knowledge of all the Churches, so that no one may, through ignorance, be permitted to do what is not permitted, the diligence of the notaries will ensure that the proceedings are recorded.”

# THE DECREES OF POPE SIMPLICIUS BEGIN

## To Zeno, bishop of Spalatum, concerning the apostolic vicariate entrusted to him

To his dearest brother Zeno, Simplicius.

From the report of many we have learned that Your Charity is a governor of the Church through fervor and holiness of spirit, so that, with God as its author, it may not suffer the losses of shipwreck.

Therefore, rejoicing in such judgments, we have considered it fitting that you be supported by the vicarious authority of our See. Strengthened by its power, do not in any way permit the decrees of apostolic instruction or the boundaries established by the holy Fathers to be transgressed, since you ought to be increased with a worthy reward of honor, through whom it has become known that the worship of God is divinely growing also in these regions.

May God keep you safe and unharmed, dearest brother.

## Letter of Pope Simplicius to John, bishop of Ravenna

If you had any regard for ecclesiastical discipline, or if any priestly moderation were maintained in you, such punishable excesses would never have been committed. If you could not restrain yourself from them by the commands of the rules handed down by the Fathers, at least you should have been recalled by the example of your predecessor of holy memory.

Although he had sinned somewhat by making a presbyter against that man’s will, he nevertheless recognized that a judgment deserved for such usurpation was fitting.

Where did you learn these practices, which you perpetrated against our brother and co-bishop Gregory—not through election but through envy? You allowed him to be dragged to you and harassed by inexcusable violence, so that you might inflict honor upon him—not through peace of mind, but through madness, as it must be called. Such acts could not have been committed with sound counsel.

We do not wish to exaggerate what was done, lest we be compelled to issue the judgment that is deserved. For he deserves to lose his privilege who abuses the power entrusted to him.

Yet one consideration makes us render a milder judgment—one that we preferred to learn through the report of our brother and co-bishop Projectus rather than publish the matter publicly in our letters because of its disgrace.

Our moderation restrained the scandals of which you are acknowledged to be the author in such a way that my brother and co-bishop Gregory, who is clearly not one who was promoted but one who was driven out, will have no case to pursue with you, as he requested, and will govern the Church of Mucira. He will not refuse to accept the spiritual companionship that he ought not to have been forced to assume.

If any dispute should perhaps arise for him, let our examination be requested concerning it or against him.

We also provide for the necessities that he is compelled to endure because of you by this decree: after he has returned the estate that, as he states, was given to him a year ago, and after he has returned to the Church of Ravenna, possession in the territory of Bononia yielding thirty solidi in free income shall without hesitation be handed over to him for the duration of his life—while the ownership rights of the Church of Ravenna remain intact. After his death, it shall return to that Church.

If you do not understand what will remain after your transgression under the provisions established by us for the parties, you yourself perceive that you are being obstinate.

We declare, moreover, that if you henceforth presume anything of this kind, and should happen to think that you may make anyone—whether bishop, presbyter, or deacon—against his will, you must know that the ordinations of the Church of Ravenna or of Emilia will be taken away from you.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the illustrious Severianus.

## Letter of Pope Simplicius to Florentius, Equitius, and Severus, bishops

Simplicius, bishop, to Florentius, Equitius, and Severus, bishops.

Your Charity’s report instructed us and informed us through the sequence of the proceedings that Gaudentius, priest of the Church of Aufinium, had carried out illicit ordinations contrary to the statutes of the canons and our commands. We order that all power of ordination be taken away from him entirely.

For we have written to our brother and co-bishop Severus that, if necessary, he himself should carry out in the aforesaid Church, after considering the rules of the Fathers, the office of which Gaudentius was convicted of having abused, so that those who were advanced illicitly by him may be removed from ecclesiastical ministries.

Likewise, since he does not know what is proper concerning the revenues of the Church or the offerings of the faithful, he must be permitted nothing in these matters; only one quarter of them is to be assigned to him. Two portions are to be administered by the presbyter Ovagius, under threat to his own order, for the benefit of the Church’s buildings and for distribution to pilgrims and the poor. The final portion is to be divided among the clergy according to the merits of each.

Moreover, the usurper must be compelled, through the diligence of the aforesaid brother, to restore the Church’s ministries that we have discovered to have been alienated. We specifically command him also to ensure that Gaudentius return the three portions that he is said to have claimed solely for himself for three years.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, after the consulship of Leo Augustus.

## 231. Simplicius to Acacius

To his dearest brother Acacius, Simplicius.

We have no leisure from our thoughts, nor does the matter allow us to rest; for if we abandon it, we are inexcusable before Christ our Lord, whose concern it is.

It is astonishing that Your Charity, after so much time had passed and so many opportunities had arisen from it, did not wish to give us any information concerning the Church of Alexandria, which is being shaken so severely. We have not ceased to admonish and rebuke you, urging you, with shared concern, to pursue my letters before the most Christian ruler by means of the present addresses of Your Charity, and, mindful of the ancient institution, to labor with us in defense of the orthodox, lest any of us incur the guilt of surrender while the Christian people perish.

Therefore we exhort Your Charity not to cease, at opportune and inopportune times, to impress this upon pious ears, so that the desired peace may be restored to the Church of Alexandria and the fruit of your vigilance may be brought about quickly.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Severinus; sent through Restitutus.

## Acacius’s reply to Simplicius, archbishop of the city of Rome

To the holy lord and father, Archbishop Simplicius, Acacius.

You continually exhort us, in accordance with the Apostle, to carry the concern of all the Churches, although we are watching willingly and taking the initiative; but you show yourselves concerned with divine zeal by seeking more certain information about the state of the Church of Alexandria, so that, in accordance with the paternal canons, you may undertake the labor, pouring forth pious sweat on behalf of these matters, as has always been approved.

But Christ our God, who works all things for good for those who love him, presiding over our thoughts and recognizing that we have one mind and the same glory in these matters, himself brought every victory to completion, making us partners with the most tranquil ruler.

He removed from human life Timothy, your predecessor, who breathed storms and appeared to disturb ecclesiastical tranquility, as was evident, saying to him: “Be silent and hold your tongue.”

He also scattered Peter, who had risen from Alexandria like a similar storm, and, with the Holy Spirit blowing, turned him into eternal flight—one of those who had formerly been condemned.

For, as has been found in our archives and councils, and as you will be able to learn from our records if you deign to inquire, you may recognize what subsequent reports concerning the same man were sent back and forth from the Alexandrian bishop to Rome.

Peter, being a son of night and appearing to have no share in the works that shine in the day, found the darkness wholly suitable for carrying out robbery and acting as its accomplice. While it was still the middle of the night, with the corpse of the man who had overturned the paternal canons still lying unburied, he slipped into the see, as he himself supposed, with only one person present—one who was a partner in his madness and who afterward disappeared completely and nowhere appeared again.

But Timothy, who followed the example of David’s gentleness and remained patient to the end, restored by Christ to his own authority, rejoices in the honor of his own see. Hearing the voices of his spiritual children, he awaits the grace of healing, honored by Christ, the prince of priests, with multiplied honor; for Christ’s sake he has bound upon himself the crown of endurance.

Therefore, let Your Beatitude pray more earnestly for the most Christian emperor and for us ourselves.

I, together with those who are with me, greet in Christ the whole brotherhood that is with you.

And in another hand:

In the Lord, pray for us, most just father.

# THE DECREES OF POPE FELIX BEGIN

## To the bishops of Sicily

1. Concerning those who were baptized, grieved over it, and afterward refused to repent.  
2. Concerning presbyters or deacons who, after falling into heresy, submitted themselves to baptism.  
3. Concerning those who impiously submitted themselves to be rebaptized.  
4. Concerning those who were rebaptized through ignorance of their age.  
5. Concerning those who, baptized or rebaptized by heretics, are not to advance to ecclesiastical service.  
6. Concerning penitents, that they are not to be received by other bishops.

On the third day before the Ides of March, during the consulship of the illustrious Flavius and Boethius, in the basilica of Constantine, with the venerable Pope Felix presiding, all the presbyters seated together with forty bishops and the deacons also standing by, Felix, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, presiding over the synod, said:

“It is a common grief and a universal groaning that we have learned that in Africa even bishops, presbyters, and deacons have been rebaptized. This matter has doubtless also reached the standard of our holiness, and it is fitting that we determine what must be observed concerning it.

Therefore, so that our judgment on this matter may be clear, let what has seemed right to us be read.”

The deacon Astasius read:

To all our dearest brothers in Christ Jesus, the bishops established throughout the various provinces.

How the devil’s cunning raged against the Christian people in the regions of Africa, and how it broke out through manifold deception, so that it plunged not only the unwary populace but even the priests themselves into the depths of death—there is no part of the world that did not lament it, no land that did not know it.

Therefore, placed in great sorrow, we cannot conceal the danger of souls that are perishing and that will be required from us. Accordingly, suitable medicine must be applied to wounds of this kind, lest an immature readiness to heal accomplish nothing against the deadly plague of the head; but lest destruction, treated too slowly, envelop both the wounded and those administering the remedy in the guilt of illegitimate treatment.

### I

First, then, the confession of the person coming to you and requesting a remedy must be carefully examined, as must the identity of the deceived person, so that an appropriate cure may be provided.

If someone who wishes to satisfy God through repentance grieves that he was rebaptized unlawfully, it must be investigated whether he ran toward this crime or approached it under compulsion, knowing that the one who deceives himself is the very person who deceives others.

Nothing is to be taken away through our leniency from the judgment of the exalted tribunal, for those things are valid before it that are pious, true, and just. The circumstances of necessity must be handled differently from those of the will.

The case of one who was perhaps enticed by payment in order to perish is worse. For the enemy left nothing unattempted; and, lest he be allowed to rejoice in his capture, those caught in his nets must be rescued, and the hunter’s snare must be crushed, so that the lamenters’ unfeigned fall may, through both the moderation of justice and the compassion of contrition, be restored to the court they had abandoned.

They should not perhaps be ashamed or reluctant to obey during the appointed periods of fasting and lamentation, or to comply with other commands of salutary observance, because grace is given to the humble, not to the proud.

Let anyone who seeks to become chosen in Christ therefore be prostrated by grief over his ruin. Through the mystery of our arrangement—which it is fitting for Your Charity to follow, and which no one may lawfully wish or be able to overstep—the causes of the person who, contrary to apostolic teaching, subjected himself to the deeply disastrous repetition of baptism, or of the person who has cunningly thought that his own consent should be excused by certain arguments, must be dealt with.

By priestly vigor and humanity, with the help of the Lord who judges, let the faith in them be restored to salvation—the faith which, unless it is one, is no faith at all—without impairment through our action. For when the satisfaction of the sinner is prolonged by us, his mind is found purer for pardon, not without our praise and joy.

Therefore remember that this is our judgment concerning these matters: while preserving discrimination among sinners, not all who have fallen are to be weighed on the same scale. For a greater penalty must be exacted from the one to whom the discipline of the Lord’s house has been entrusted.

### II

To begin, then, with the highest offices of the Church: those who are shown to have been bishops, presbyters, or deacons, and who, whether willingly or under compulsion, are found to have suffered the loss of that one and saving washing, and consequently to have stripped off Christ, whom they had put on not only through the gift of regeneration but also through the grace of their ordained honor—none of these could have approached a second baptism unless he had openly denied that he was a Christian and professed himself to be a pagan.

Although this is universally detestable in all people, it is much more horrifying when heard or even reported of bishops, presbyters, and deacons.

But because the same Lord and Savior is most merciful and wishes no one to perish, if they repent, they should remain in penance until the day of their death. They must not participate in prayer—not even in the prayer of the faithful, and certainly not in that of the catechumens.

At death, lay communion is to be restored to them. The care of a highly approved priest must investigate and administer this matter more diligently.

### III

Concerning clerics and monks, the maidens of God, and secular persons, we decree that the rule established by the Council of Nicaea concerning those who have fallen or will fall must be observed: namely, that those who, without any necessity or fear or danger of anything, have impiously handed themselves over to heretics to be rebaptized, if they nevertheless sincerely repent, are to remain for three years among the hearers.

For seven years they are to remain among the penitents under the hands of priests. For two years they are in every way forbidden to offer oblations; they are to join the secular people only in prayer.

Let no one be ashamed to submit his neck to God who was not afraid to deny him.

But if, as mortal beings, they begin to be pressed by the end of life within the limits of the appointed period, help must be given to the one who implores it. Whether from the bishop who imposed the penance, or from another who can nevertheless verify that it was imposed, or similarly from a presbyter, viaticum must not be denied to the person departing from this world.

[Col. 0935D] **IV.** To boys who, because they are still beardless, are designated by the term “underage,” whether clerics or laymen, and likewise to girls of similar age, whose ignorance is supported by their years, communion is to be restored after they have been kept for some time under the laying on of hands; nor is penitence to be awaited from those whom the censure exempts from punishment. This has been prudently established by us, lest those who still have more or less of the contagion of earthly defilement remaining to them for life should, while still in penitence, commit further acts requiring penitence.

But if, before the appointed period of penitence, someone—having been given up by physicians or overcome by clear signs of death—recovers after receiving the grace of communion, we shall observe what the Nicene canons ordained: that such a person be counted among [Col. 0936A] those who communicate by prayer alone, until the period of time prescribed for him has been completed.

Nor do we pass over our catechumens who were baptized under such a profession, because the case is not different. The same holy canons ordained this concerning one who, having once confessed Christ, renounced him in any manner whatsoever. Let them remain three years among the hearers; afterward let them be permitted to pray with the catechumens, so that through the laying on of hands they may receive the grace of Catholic communion. The sole exceptions are bishops, presbyters, and deacons, whom we have already decided are to be reconciled only at the time of their death.

As for the others—that is, clerics, monks, or lay persons of either sex—who are shown to have undergone a repetition of baptism under compulsion and danger, [Col. 0936B] or who have said by some subterfuge that they were not bound by the guilt of this crime, we decree that their penitence shall last three years and that, through the laying on of hands, they shall be received into participation in the sacrament.

**V.** Let this rule be observed in every respect: none of those who, at any age, have been baptized or rebaptized anywhere other than in the Catholic Church shall ever be permitted to enter the ecclesiastical service. It should be sufficient for them that they have been received into the number of Catholics, since whoever violates this—whether a bishop who does so or one who fails to remove a person whom he knows to have insinuated himself from among them into clerical ministry—will be seen to bear judgment concerning his rank and communion.

**VI.** Above all, care must be taken, and every precaution provided, [Col. 0936C] lest any of our brothers and fellow bishops, or even presbyters, receive in another’s city or diocese a penitent, one placed under the hand of a priest, or one who claims to have been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of a bishop or presbyter; nor should a presbyter receive such a person in a parish, or a bishop in a city, without them.

If this is neglected through any sort of concealment, the fault also touches the clergy who reside in places where the matter has been insufficiently attended to. Therefore, once these matters have been properly arranged and conveyed by our deliberation to the notice of your Churches, it is fitting that you obey them. Although nothing concerning the restoration of souls may seem to be lacking, if anything new should be revealed to anyone—something that may have escaped us—then, according to blessed Paul the Apostle, let the one who comes later faithfully make it known while the former is silent, [Col. 0936D] because the Spirit blows where he wills, especially when his own cause is being handled; nor will we be reluctant to listen. If anything has been omitted, let us not reject it arrogantly, but order it reasonably.

May God keep you, beloved brothers.

Given on the Ides of March, in the fourth consulship of Divanius and Sinidius.

---

### Letter of the same to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, in which he condemns him on account of communion with the Eutychians

**FELIX, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, to ACACIUS.**

You are found guilty of many transgressions and have often been involved in contempt for the venerable Council of Nicaea. Rashly you claimed the rights of provinces belonging to others; you thought that heretics and usurpers, those ordained by heretics, and those whom you yourself had condemned and had asked the Apostolic See to condemn, were not merely to be admitted to your communion, but even to preside over other Churches—something that could not have been done even with Catholics—and you increased them with honors they did not deserve.

John bears witness to this: although he had not been received by the Catholics of Apamea and had been driven from Antioch, you placed him over the Tyrians. Likewise Humerius, who had then been expelled from the diaconate and deprived of the name of Christian, was advanced by you to the office of the presbyterate. And as though these things seemed small to you, you extended your audacity and arrogance even against the truth of apostolic doctrine, so that Peter—whom you yourself had reported as condemned by my predecessor of blessed memory—should, as the attached documents testify, at your command again invade the see of the blessed Evangelist; and, after the orthodox bishops had been driven out, should undoubtedly ordain clerics like himself and, having expelled the man who had been regularly established there, hold the Church captive.

You have such a favorable opinion of this man, and find his ministry so acceptable, that you are shown to have afflicted many orthodox bishops and clerics who were then coming to Constantinople; to have supported his representatives; and, although that same Peter anathematized the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and violated the burial of Timothy of holy memory, to have believed—just as messengers have now again reported to us through Messenius and Vitalis—that he should be excused. You did not cease to praise him and to extol him with many commendations, even declaring that his condemnation, which you had previously reported, was not true.

You have persisted so greatly in defending this perverse man that you allowed Vitalis and Messenius—once bishops, but now deprived of honor and communion, whom we had sent specifically for his expulsion—to be seized and committed to custody. You then had them brought to the procession that you hold with the heretics and, as their statements have revealed, disregarding the embassy—which ought to have been protected even by the law of the nations—you dragged them into communion with the heretics and with yourself and corrupted them with rewards. Thus, to the injury of blessed Peter the Apostle, from whose see they had departed, you not only caused them to return ineffective but also displayed them as opponents of everything that had been commanded.

In their deception you revealed your wickedness. You refused to answer according to the canons the letter of my brother and fellow bishop John, who attacked you with the gravest charges, and instead confirmed what you had cast aside. You also judged Felix, our most faithful defender, unworthy of your attention because necessity had compelled him to follow your servants. You have testified that you communicate by letter with those who are plainly heretics. For what else are those who, after the death of Timothy of holy memory, return to the Church under Peter, or those who handed themselves over to him from the Catholic Church, than Peter himself, who had been judged by the universal Church and by you?

Have your portion, therefore, with those whom you willingly embrace. By the present sentence, which we have sent to you through the defender of your Church, recognize that, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by our apostolic authority, you have been separated from priestly honor and Catholic communion, as well as from the number of the faithful; that the name and office of the priestly ministry have been removed from you; and that you have been condemned and can no longer be released from the bonds of anathema.

---

### Pope Felix to Zeno

**Felix, bishop, to his most beloved brother Zeno.**

My son Terentianus, a most distinguished man, came to Italy some time ago and proved himself an exceptional herald of your affection. He proclaimed you to be such a man, overflowing with the grace of Christ, that amid the storms of the world you appeared as an outstanding governor of the Church.

Therefore, dearest brother, when he was traveling to the province and earnestly requested that we send our letter to your affection, we gladly consented. We wished both to embrace a bishop worthy of God in speech and, especially through him, to accomplish what he had made known to us through his praises.

Although, then, this man has supported your fraternity in every respect by his testimony concerning your holy works, and although he held great confidence in your goodwill, it is right that he should obtain what he greatly desired: that the man who was once pleasing to your heart should, out of regard for us, become still more acceptable; that he should at the same time be encouraged by maternal and priestly consolation; and that he should find the protection of pastoral kindness during his journey.

Thus, through the affection of your dignity, it may become evident to your sincerity that our salutary conversation has also been of no little benefit. May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

I, Celius Felix, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the second consulship of Venantius.

At the same time sixty-seven bishops, excluding the pope, subscribed.

---

## Letters of Pope Gelasius (C)

[Col. 0937]

### Letter of Pope Gelasius to the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily

1. Concerning ecclesiastical institutions moderately arranged according to the circumstances of the times.  
2. That, where no pressing necessity exists, the ordinances of the Fathers be preserved inviolate.  
3. That, when clerics are lacking, men be chosen from among the monks. [Col. 0938D]  
4. If laymen are chosen for the clergy, how much time is to be observed.  
5. Concerning bigamists and other persons who may in no way be admitted to clerical ministry.  
6. That new basilicas not be dedicated without the pope’s instruction.  
7. That no fees be demanded from those being baptized or signed with the sacrament. [Col. 0939A]  
8. Concerning presbyters, that they presume nothing belonging to bishops.  
9. That deacons preserve their proper measure according to the decrees of the Fathers.  
10. That deacons may not sit in the presbyterium.  
11. That the Apostolic See preserve the canons of the Fathers with pious devotion.  
12. That no one presume to baptize except during Easter and Pentecost, unless extreme illness compels it.  
13. Concerning the ordinations of presbyters and deacons, to be celebrated at appointed times.  
14. Concerning when sacred virgins are to be veiled.  
15. That widows not be veiled. [Col. 0939B]  
16. That slaves not be received into the clergy or monasteries under the pretext of religion.  
17. That clerics not pursue dishonorable commerce or shameful profits.  
18. That no illiterate person, or one impaired in any part of the body, be promoted to the clergy.  
19. Concerning those who castrate themselves.  
20. Concerning criminals, that they not be promoted to the clergy.  
21. That those entangled in demonic possession or other disorders may not handle sacred ministries.  
22. That those who join themselves to sacred virgins and contract incestuous unions may not communicate unless they have performed public penance.  
23. That widows, as stated above, not be veiled, [Col. 0939C] but, if they trample upon their professed continence after changing their intention, let them themselves render an account for themselves.  
24. That second marriages not be denied to laymen, although such men are not at all permitted to enter the clergy.  
25. If anyone receives a deserter from his own Church and promotes him to some dignity, that both persons be subject to the sentence prescribed by the canons.  
26. Concerning laymen or monks who are ordained for payment, so that the crime of Simon Magus may involve both the giver and the receiver.  
27. That no basilica established under the name of the dead be dedicated.  
28. Concerning women, that they not serve at the sacred altars [Col. 0939D] or presume to undertake any of the offices assigned to men.  
29. Concerning the revenues of the Church and the offerings of the faithful, which are to be divided into four portions.  
30. That a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who acts against these statutes shall suffer the loss of his honor.

### CHAPTER I

**To all our most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily. Gelasius.**

We are pressed by the necessity of arranging matters and constrained by the moderation of the Apostolic See to weigh the decrees of the ancestral canons and measure the commands of our predecessors and former bishops in such a way that, with careful consideration, we may temper as far as possible whatever the necessity of the present times demands should be relaxed for the restoration of the Churches.

Thus we may neither appear to exceed the entire form of the ancient rules nor fail to restore the offices of the clerical order, which the incursions of war and famine have so consumed throughout various parts of Italy that, as we have learned from the frequent report of our brother and fellow bishop John, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, the service of ministers is altogether failing in many Churches. Unless the intervals anciently established for ecclesiastical promotion are relaxed for a time, the sacred orders cannot be administered in Churches that have been utterly deprived of them. Moreover, in many places, through the lack of suitable assistance, the saving aid of redeeming souls is absent; and we would incur great guilt if, under the pressure of so great a danger, we did not provide some remedy. [Col. 0940B]

**II.** Therefore, while the ancient ordinances remain in force out of reverence for them—and where no difficulty of circumstances or times presses, it is fitting that they be observed according to rule—we grant that the intervals for establishing and providing clerical service may be so administered in Churches that are either entirely deprived of ministers or so stripped of adequate service that they cannot supply the divine offices to the peoples belonging to them.

**III.** If someone trained in a religious vocation and in monastic disciplines comes forward for clerical office, his life in former times must first be investigated: whether he is shown to be stained by no serious crime; whether he has perhaps not had a second wife, nor is shown to have taken as wife one rejected by her husband; whether he has performed public penance; whether he appears impaired in any part of his body; whether he is not subject to servile or hereditary status; whether he is shown to be free from the bonds of public office; and whether he has acquired literacy, without which he could scarcely perhaps fulfill even the office of doorkeeper.

If he is supported in all the matters mentioned above, let him immediately become a lector or notary, or at least a defender; after three months let him become an acolyte. Especially if his age also supports this, let him receive the title of subdeacon in the sixth month. If he is of modest conduct and honorable intention, let him become a deacon in the ninth month, and, once the year is complete, a presbyter. His freely undertaken devotion to the holy vocation is thereby shown to have supplied what the intervals of years would have contributed. [Col. 0940D]

**IV.** If a layman is to be added to the ecclesiastical offices, his person should be examined with all the more care in each of the matters described above, in proportion to the difference known to exist between worldly and religious life. For the suitable ministries of the Church are to be restored, not imposed upon persons whose merits are unsuitable. The more the time normally required for attaining these offices is shortened, the more it is necessary to seek in the candidate’s formation evidence of the moral uprightness that prolonged custom would otherwise have produced. We must not, under the pretext of supplying the clerical shortage, be judged to have introduced vices into divine worship rather than to have procured legitimate support.

For their promotions, nevertheless, we add six months beyond the limits of a year, since, as has been said, there ought to be a distinction between a person devoted to divine worship and one coming from lay conduct. We have thought this indulgence should extend only so far as to renew the ministries in those Churches where the devastation of war has left either no service at all or only a scant one. Once these have been restored, God willing, the ancient form of the ancestral canons is to be preserved in appointing persons to the ecclesiastical grades.

Nor should anyone in any way prevail against them on the ground that provision is being made for a contingent remedy: a deficiency is being supplied, not a new law proposed against the statutes of the elders. Other Churches, which have not been devastated by a similar calamity, must refrain from using this occasion and should retain the former judgment when ordinations are carried out. [Col. 0941B] Rather, having been reminded by this opportunity, we entrust to you more earnestly the observance of the venerable canons, admonishing the conscience of each grade not to attempt unlawful excesses.

**V.** Let no bishop presume that it is lawful for him to admit to divine ministry bigamists; men who have taken women abandoned by other husbands; persons who have performed penance; illiterate persons; persons impaired in body; persons of servile status; persons entangled in the bonds of public office or public affairs; or persons examined indiscriminately without waiting for the appropriate period of time. Nor should they strive, according to their own pleasure, to invade the rights of others without a just command and disposition of the Apostolic See.

**VI.** Let no one dare to dedicate newly established basilicas without requesting the customary instructions, nor let bishops seek to claim for themselves clerics belonging to another authority.

**VII.** Let no fees be fixed for those being baptized or signed with the sacrament, nor let them seek to harass those being reborn by imposing any exactions. For we are commanded to give freely what we have received freely. Therefore let them not attempt to demand anything at all from the persons mentioned above, lest those deterred by poverty or turned away by indignation disdain to hear the means of their redemption. Let them be certain that those discovered to have committed what is forbidden, or who do not voluntarily correct their offenses, will suffer the danger of losing their own honor.

**VIII.** We likewise forbid presbyters to extend themselves beyond their proper measure or boldly to assume for themselves what belongs improperly to the episcopal dignity. They must not claim the power of making chrism or of carrying out episcopal confirmation; nor, in the presence of any bishop, may they presume to undertake a prayer or sacred action unless they have been ordered to do so. In his presence they must not presume either to sit or to handle the venerable mysteries unless commanded.

Let them remember that they are in no way permitted, without the chief bishop, to have the right of making a subdeacon or acolyte. Nor should they doubt that, if they undertake on their own initiative anything specifically belonging to episcopal ministry, they will immediately be deprived of the dignity of the presbyterate and of sacred communion.

We consider this necessary if such transgression is proved by the report of their bishop. The bishop himself will not be free from the guilt of connivance and punishment if he neglects to punish those who act immoderately. [Col. 0942A]

**IX.** We likewise require deacons to observe the proper measure established for them and not to attempt anything beyond the tenor assigned by the ancestral canons. We permit them to apply to their ministry none of the functions that antiquity decreed properly for the higher orders.

They must not presume to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, unless perhaps extreme necessity compels them to perform these offices when the persons mentioned above are at a considerable distance. This is also often permitted to Christian laymen.
