**X.** We do not permit them to sit in the presbyterium while divine worship is being celebrated or any ecclesiastical matter is being conducted. They do not possess the privilege of the sacred Body in the presence of a bishop or presbyter, unless, in the absence of these persons, they have the right to exercise it. For while we ourselves strive with the greatest care to preserve the decrees of the venerable sanctions, we also concede, without impairing them, those matters which may perhaps seem relaxable for the sake of some useful advantage.

**XI.** Since we wish nothing rashly to be permitted to us against the reverence due to salutary rules, and since the Apostolic See, superior to all these matters, strives, with the Lord’s favor, to preserve what has been established by the ancestral canons with pious and devoted purpose, it is most unworthy for any bishop or person of a subsequent order to reject this observance, which he sees the See of blessed Peter both following and teaching.

It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree in this observance, which it sees flourishing where the Lord established the primacy over the whole Church, as Scripture says: “Order charity in me” (Song of Songs II, 4). And again: “Let all things be done in proper order” (Genesis XLI, 28). Again the Psalmist proclaims:

> “Surround Zion and encompass her; tell it in her towers. Set your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her houses, that you may recount it to another generation; for this is our God forever and ever, and he himself will rule us for ages” (Psalm XLVII, 13–15).

Here, without doubt, the one who is proclaimed in the height of ecclesiastical dignities, and in whose strength hearts are to be set through good works, is our God and ruler of the people, to be proclaimed by all Christians through the grades duly distributed. Let no one think that anything has been diminished for him, since nothing is lost through the advancement of each grade, and since, by suitably retaining what has been granted through heavenly dispensation, God grants that he be made known to us both as God and as ruler.

For if something is conceded concerning the length of time, it is balanced by the vigorous diligence joined to good conduct. If the purpose of life also contains what ought to be sought in view of the person’s age, this is acceptable, provided that those matters whose presence would rightly prove a person unworthy of the clerical insignia do not insidiously enter under any pretext.

Sometimes, indeed, those things may be permitted which, if the integrity of the others is established, cannot by themselves cause harm. Nevertheless, those things must be guarded against with the greatest care which cannot be admitted without manifest disfigurement. If even those matters that are sometimes thought permissible without detriment are excused either by consideration of circumstances and times or by the need for swift provision, how much more must those matters not be mutilated which no necessity whatsoever, and no ecclesiastical utility at all, compels us to alter? [Col. 0943A]

**XII.** Let no one presume that he has unrestricted confidence to baptize at any time whatsoever. Apart from the solemn sacrament of Easter and Pentecost, this is forbidden except in the event of the gravest illness, when there is fear that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person may depart, overtaken by death, without the saving remedy.

**XIII.** Ordinations of presbyters and deacons likewise must not be performed except at appointed times and on appointed days. They are to be celebrated at the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, as well as at the beginning of Lent and on the Saturday fast in the middle of Lent, toward Vespers. No one is to prefer either a presbyter or a deacon to those who were ordained before him, whatever advantage may be claimed.

**XIV.** Sacred veils are not to be placed upon dedicated virgins except on Epiphany, during the white garments of Easter, or on the anniversaries of the apostles. Nevertheless, as was said concerning baptism, if they are afflicted by serious illness and ask that they not depart from the world without this gift, it is not to be denied them.

**XV.** Let no bishop attempt to veil widows, since neither divine authority permits it nor the form of the canons establishes it. It must therefore not be usurped at all, because ecclesiastical protections must be conferred in such a way that nothing unlawful is committed.

**XVI.** The presumption giving rise to a general complaint must also be avoided: nearly everyone complains that slaves and hereditary dependants, fleeing the rights of their masters and their possessions, are indiscriminately admitted—often with the connivance of bishops—either to monasteries or to ecclesiastical service under the pretext of religious conduct. This evil must be removed in every way, lest, under the institution of the Christian name, another’s property appear to be invaded or public discipline overturned.

This is especially important because it is now appropriate to suspect that the dignity of clerical ministry itself is burdened by this obligation and compelled to quarrel over the status and condition of those serving, or—God forbid—to appear liable to such charges.

When these persons have been prohibited by suitable and careful interdiction, any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or any of those known to preside over monasteries, who keeps such persons with him and thinks of neither returning them to their patrons nor thereafter assigning them to ecclesiastical service or religious communities—unless they have first been released from the masters’ authority under the testimony of Scripture, or granted by a lawful settlement—must not doubt that he will incur the danger of his own honor and communion if anyone’s truthful complaint brings this matter before us.

For, according to the blessed Apostle, we must take great care lest the faith and discipline of the Lord be blasphemed.

**XVII.** It was consequently necessary that we should not now pass over what a report recently sent to us from the regions of Picenum announced: namely, that very many clerics are occupied with dishonorable commerce and shameful profits, looking upon the Gospel reading without any sense of shame. The Lord himself is said to have driven the merchants from the temple after scourging them with whips, yet they do not recall the Apostle’s words:

> “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs” (II Timothy II, 4).

They also ignore with deaf ears the Psalmist David singing:

> “Because I have not known commerce, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Psalm LXX, 16).

Accordingly, let them know that they must abstain from such and other dishonorable gains and cease from every practice or desire of commerce. Otherwise, whatever grade they may hold, they must immediately be compelled to withdraw from clerical offices. For the house of God, which is and ought to be called a house of prayer, must not become a workshop of commerce [Col. 0944B] and rather a den of thieves.

**XVIII.** We have also learned that illiterate persons and those impaired in some part of the body are coming without restriction into ecclesiastical service. Neither ancient tradition nor the ancient practice of the Apostolic See accepts this, since a person lacking literacy cannot be suitable for sacred offices, and the legal precepts have decreed that nothing defective is to be offered to God.

Therefore, such practices must henceforth be avoided in every way, and no such person is to be received into the clergy. If any have already been received through their own presumption or through the negligence of their superiors, let them remain in the places in which they have been established, but let them never seize any further promotion. Let them consider it sufficient that, out of excessive mercy, this very thing has been permitted to them.

**XIX.** Concerning those who castrate themselves, the ancestral canons have clearly laid down what must be followed. It is enough to state their provision: they say that, as soon as such persons have been recognized, they must be excluded from clerical office. We must preserve this in every respect, since no one is permitted to judge anything beyond what the memorable rule has decreed.

**XX.** We have also discovered that persons entangled in certain horrible crimes, with all discrimination set aside, not only fail to perform the necessary penance for atrocious deeds, but that no one, even after correction has entirely followed, strives for divine ministry and honor. Some who have already been established in the orders and have committed serious crimes are not rejected, although the Apostle commands that hands be laid quickly on no one and that no one share in the sins of others; the venerable ordinances of the elders likewise declare this.

If such persons have perhaps slipped in, those who previously sinned and have been exposed must be rejected; and those who have forgotten their sacred profession and betrayed their holy vocation must undoubtedly be removed.

**XXI.** We have found that unlawful practices have advanced so far that sacred ministries are entrusted to persons entangled in demonic possession and other disorders. If some personal necessity should arise for those engaged in this work, who could have confidence concerning his own salvation and that of the faithful? Where has anyone seen the ministers themselves afflicted by such a calamity requiring human treatment?

Therefore they must necessarily be removed, lest scandal be generated among the weak, for whom Christ died. [Col. 0945A] Finally, if divine law does not at all permit one wounded or debilitated in body to touch holy things, how much less is it fitting for those struck by a worse affliction of mind to be dispensers of the gift?

**XXII.** We have learned that some men rashly join themselves to sacred virgins and, after their vocation has been dedicated to God, mingle incestuous and sacrilegious unions with them. It is right that such men be immediately driven from holy communion and not received at all except through public and approved penance. Nevertheless, if they have repented, viaticum is not to be denied them as they depart from the world.

**XXIII.** Concerning widows who are not to be veiled under any blessing, we have already spoken above at length and sufficiently. If, by their own will and with changeable intent, they trample upon the chastity of their former marriage that they had professed, it will be a matter of their own peril to determine by what satisfaction they ought to appease God, since, according to the Apostle, they have invalidated their first faith.

Having deliberated with themselves in this way, they ought to preserve the pledge of chastity promised to God. We, however, must not cast any snare upon such women, but should set before them only exhortations concerning eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their intention may render an account to God for itself.

We must beware of what the blessed Apostle Paul testifies concerning their conduct and actions. We pass over explaining it more fully, lest the unstable sex seem to be less deterred than admonished.

**XXIV.** Just as laymen are permitted to enter second marriages, so after such marriages no one is permitted to enter the clerical fellowship. One permission is granted generally to human weakness; another kind of life must belong to those devoted to the service of divine matters.

**XXV.** Whoever thinks that he may leave his own Church and transfer to another without any existing cause, and is rashly received and promoted, will not escape the provisions of the venerable canons—neither he himself, nor the one who receives and promotes him—which have prescribed what must be observed concerning such presumptuous persons.

**XXVI.** Concerning monks and laymen, the first and more extensive part of this instruction has already set out what concessions may be made to them according to the needs of circumstances and times, and how, where no necessity is shown to intervene, only the ancient institution is to be preserved.

Those who are shown to have bought sacred dignity for a price despite being unworthy in merit must, once convicted, be excluded; for those who commit such a deed do not do so without peril, since the condemnation of Simon, as sacred Scripture testifies, involves both the giver and the receiver. [Col. 0945D]

**XXVII.** Although the consecration of holy places was briefly covered above, it has also been revealed to us that some presume, without a command of the Apostolic See, to consecrate churches or oratories that have been built.

We are moved by an even more detestable judgment because, under whatever name of the dead—and, as it is said, not entirely of the faithful—some are reported boldly to establish buildings constructed as sacred institutions. Since these matters are so bitter and so harsh that our hearing can scarcely endure them, if a genuine and firm Christian spirit exists in those regions, let these things be investigated more strictly and let those by whom they were done be disclosed. For as long as the names remain hidden in this atrocity, there is no one against whom the proper sentence can be pronounced; but when the perpetrator has been exposed by clear evidence, he will in no way avoid the punishment demanded by the enormity of so great a crime.

**XXVIII.** We have likewise heard with indignation that such contempt for divine matters has arisen that women are said to serve at the sacred altars and to perform for a sex to which it does not belong all the duties assigned exclusively to the service of men.

For every offense and crime that we have touched upon individually falls upon those priests who either commit these things themselves or, by failing to make public those who commit them, show that they favor wicked excesses—if, indeed, those who strive to overthrow the religious office entrusted to them in this way, pursuing every perverse and profane precipice without regard for Christian rule, are still to be called priests.

Since it is written, “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus XIX, 1), what should be thought of those who, through immense and manifold masses of depravity, have produced a great ruin driven on by many impulses?

Those who have dared to practice these things, and also those who have remained silent about matters previously known to them, must not doubt that they are lying under the loss of their own honor unless they hasten with all possible speed to heal these lethal wounds with suitable medicine.

For by what custom do they claim to hold the rights of bishops when they neglect the duties entrusted to episcopal watchfulness, to such an extent that they instead act against the house of God over which they preside? Let them consider what they would be able to obtain from the Lord if they provided what was fitting for him, and what they deserve when they pursue the opposite with detestable zeal.

It is as though this were more truly the rule by which Churches ought to be governed: that whatever is committed against ecclesiastical rules should be carried out, even though every bishop who knows the canons ought to preserve them under inviolate guardianship.

**XXIX.** It is agreed that four portions are to be made from both the revenues and the offerings of the faithful. One is to belong to the bishop, another to the clergy, a third to the poor, and a fourth to the repair and construction of the buildings.

As it is the priest’s responsibility to ensure that the full amount mentioned is paid to the ministers of the Church, so let the cleric know that he must not insolently demand anything beyond the sum assigned to him.

Let the manifest restoration of holy places plainly show that what has been allotted to ecclesiastical buildings has truly been devoted to that work. Even if the bishop seems able to show that he has administered the portion assigned to the poor according to divine accounting, nevertheless, according to what is written, “So that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V, 16), the work too must be publicly attested and not left unmentioned amid the praises of good repute.

XXX. Therefore no cleric should imagine that he will be free from blame for this offense if, when he sees any bishop, presbyter, or deacon [Col. 0947A] exceeding the bounds in the matters which we have set forth as salutary obligations, he does not promptly take care to report it to our ears. Every bishop, moreover, will in every respect be a destroyer of his rank and honor if he thinks that these matters ought to be suppressed from any cleric or from the hearing of the whole Church. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the fourth consulship of Asterius and Praesidius.

## Letter of Gelasius to the Sicilians

1. On the proper administration of the Church’s affairs by bishops.  
2. On the thirty-year prescription.

**Gelasius, bishop of the Roman Church, to his most beloved brothers, bishops established in Sicily, united in the love of Christ with one accord.**

### Chapter I

The authority of our predecessors established that they should have power to administer the resources of the Church of Christ. They must nevertheless distribute them for the support of widows, orphans, and the poor, as well as of the clergy. We decree that what has hitherto been established should be given to them. Let them claim the remainder for themselves, so that, as we said before, they may be able to act as benefactors to strangers and captives. [Col. 0947B]

### II

It has seemed good to add this: if—God forbid—any bishops should claim as their own the property of the Church, or likewise dioceses possessed by certain bishops, they may do so by right, because the thirty-year law has settled the matter, and because the authority of our imperial sons has likewise decreed that, after thirty years, no one may appeal in cases excluded by the statutory period. Given on the Ides of May, in the fourth consulship of Asterius and Praesidius.

Here begins Gelasius the pope’s book on the bond of anathema.

Lest they say what they are accustomed to say—that if the Council of Chalcedon is admitted, everything that appears to have been set forth there must be accepted, or else, if it is rejectable in part, it cannot be regarded as wholly authoritative—let them understand that what was done there according to the holy Scriptures and the tradition of the ancestors, according to the canons and rules of the Church, for the common faith and Catholic and apostolic truth, for which the apostolic see commissioned that council to be held and confirmed what was done, must be accepted without hesitation by the whole Church. [Col. 0947C]

But the other matters which were produced there—or rather, debated there—through incompetent presumption, and which the apostolic see entrusted to be dealt with, were immediately opposed by the representatives of the apostolic see. It is evident that the apostolic see did not approve them in any way, even when the emperor Marcian requested it. Anatolius, then bishop of the Church of Constantinople, neither professed that he had presumed such things nor denied that he had placed himself under the authority of the bishop of the apostolic see. [Col. 0947D]

For this reason the apostolic see did not receive them, as has been said: whatever is shown to be contrary to the privileges of the venerable Church cannot be tolerated for any reason. What then? In the holy books which we venerate and follow, certain profanities are also said to exist and crimes are reported as having been committed. Are we therefore to venerate or follow all these things alike merely because they are contained in those holy and venerable books?

The holy apostle Peter, thinking that the grace of the New Testament should be preached without departing from the institutions of the old law, is read to have acted in a certain way, through dissimulation, among Jews and Gentiles. Does this mean that those actions of his must also be followed—actions which his fellow apostle rightly rebuked and which he later consistently avoided—and that they must be adopted together with what he preached as salutary in his capacity as the first apostle? Or should his sound teaching be rejected along with what had been added on the human level? Or should that earlier weakness of ignorance be received together with his perfected teaching? [Col. 0948A]

Are not many things pertaining to the truth also found written in the books of the heretics? Is the truth therefore to be rejected because the books in which depravity is present are rejected? Or are the depraved books to be accepted merely because the truth inserted in them is not denied?

The Apostle says: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good” (1 Thess. 5:21). We know that the Apostle also quoted certain things from the books of the pagans. Does this mean that everything brought forth alongside those things must likewise be accepted? [Col. 0948B]

The Apostle himself says that many preachers proclaim Christ in different ways, and that nevertheless Christ must be accepted, however he is preached. Yet he does not thereby fail to warn us to avoid the manner in which Christ was not preached rightly. He complains of wicked workers, teaching that some of what they say must be rejected and other things followed.

These and similar examples, confirmed by divine testimonies, teach us not to accept indiscriminately everything said by anyone or written anywhere in the worst possible way, but to retain what is good and reject what is harmful.

Death was imposed upon the sinful human being; yet when death was imposed upon the man Jesus Christ, it made the devil guilty, because where there was no cause of death, there was no punishment of sin due.

[Col. 0948C] A sentence is always fixed, or has been fixed, against error. The sentence fixed against this error will never be entirely rescinded. For just as error itself, insofar as it is error, never ceases to be error, so it will never be released from the sentence once fixed against it. For error that is recognized as condemned is shown to remain bound by that same sentence for as long as it remains error.

Therefore those who are in that error are bound by the sentence against error, and for as long as they remain in it they are in no way absolved, just as the error in which they are is itself not absolved. Error itself never earns pardon; rather, pardon belongs to the one who truly abandons it and withdraws from participation in it.

Therefore, for as long as error is in them, they retain its condemnation, and it is never rescinded, because error always deserves punishment. Those who participate in it are always participants in its punishment if they do not cease to persist in it. But if they withdraw from it, then, to the extent that they have become separated from the error and distinguished from participation in it, they will consequently be separated from its punishment as well. [Col. 0948D]

When punishment is fixed against one who errs, for as long as he remains one who errs, he is constrained by that same punishment, because one cannot be an erring person without the punishment of error. This same punishment is perpetual and can never be released for as long as he persists in being one who errs.

But if he ceases to be one who errs, the punishment that was fixed against the erring person—perpetual for the erring person—cannot be perpetual for one who is no longer erring, that is, for one who has become someone else; indeed, it is no longer even punishment. For he is no longer the person against whom it was fixed. It was fixed against the erring person, not against one who is no longer erring.

What is fixed against the erring person is perpetual and perpetually constrains the erring person; it can no longer hold one who is not erring. Let it be said that it was decreed to be perpetual for the erring person; let it be said that it was decreed never to be released for the erring person. It remains altogether and truly so, and what was fixed in it is certain; nor can it be released at all for as long as it is owed to the erring person who remains in the condition against which it was fixed. [Col. 0949A]

For one who is no longer erring, however, it cannot be punishment, since what is not owed to one who is no longer erring cannot be inflicted. The punishment owed to the erring person is neither changed nor rescinded. Thus, in its own proper condition, it has been fixed and cannot in any way be released according to its own right. But outside that condition, in which it can no longer exist, it is shown to have been emptied of force and to have no right at all where it has no cause for existing.

The holy Scriptures are full of this form of justice. It is said: “Let sinners perish from the earth, so that they may be no more” (Ps. 67:3)—so that they may no longer be sinners, so that they may cease to be sinners. According to the prophet’s sentence, they would perish utterly, so that those who could be saved by our Redeemer would no longer exist substantially—[Col. 0949B] not the righteous, but sinners, whom he came to call—or those of whom the Apostle says: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost,” and, “When we were sinners, God sent his Son” (1 Tim. 1:15; Gal. 4:4), and other passages of this kind.

Here indeed very many sinners perished substantially, remaining in their sins. The true sentence spoken against them remained in force and was never rescinded. Yet, while that same sentence remained perpetual in such persons, against whom it had been fixed, it nevertheless came about in a certain way that the sentence fixed against them did not remain in persons who did not continue altogether in that condition or endure altogether in their sins.

For they perish, but they perish as sinners—not in a punitive way, as has been said, but in a remedial way, and in a certain sense they themselves perished. In a certain sense the sentence fixed against them also remained in them until, while remaining in force, it made them cease to be sinners, or brought about their ceasing to be sinners. [Col. 0949C]

The sentence was fulfilled in them; and, once that condition had been completed, the sentence remained in force concerning the sinners who perished, so that they were no longer sinners. It could no longer remain in those who were no longer sinners, because it had no right to remain in those upon whom it had not been inflicted.

Thus the sentence was in no way rescinded with respect to its own right or course. While remaining in force in those upon whom it had been inflicted, it became entirely separate from those who had been distinguished from its jurisdiction, so that, while preserving its own condition, it had no right to remain in those upon whom it had not been inflicted.

[Col. 0949D] The Lord said that those who sin against the Holy Spirit would be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come. Yet how many do we know who sinned against the Holy Spirit—various heretics, Arians and Macedonians—who returned to the Catholic faith, received here the forgiveness of their blasphemy, and gained hope of obtaining indulgence in the future? Nor is the Lord’s sentence thereby untrue, or should it be thought to have been rescinded in any way, since it persists as something never to be released with regard to those who remain such, but is not inflicted upon those who have become otherwise.

The same is true, consequently, of that saying of the blessed apostle John: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for it. There is sin not unto death; I do say that one should pray for it.” There is sin unto death for those who remain in the same sin. For there is no sin for which the Church does not pray that it be forgiven, or which, by the power divinely given to it, it cannot absolve those who desist from it, or release from it those who repent. To the Church it is said: “Whatever you forgive on earth will be forgiven in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:18). [Col. 0950A]

In these words, “whatever,” all things are included, however great and of whatever kind they may be. Nevertheless, the sentence remains true which is declared never to be rescinded: it remains in force for those concerned. In the sentence against Acacius, this must reasonably be observed: the statement does not also say that one who later withdraws from him is to be bound by it.

Even if it was said to him that he would never be released, it was not added, “even if you repent, even if you withdraw from error, even if you cease to be a transgressor.” Therefore it is clear that he was said to be never releasable if he remained such as he was when bound, not if he became other than he was—as one who ought not to have been bound was shown to be one who could be absolved.

Just as he was free from obligation when he had ceased to have the cause of obligation, so he would certainly exist as absolved. Thus it appeared that he could no longer, in a certain sense, be released by the necessity of the sentence pronounced against him unless he became such that, free from the obligation, he was absolved; and the sentence fixed against such persons would in no way be made rescindable. [Col. 0950B]

For did he not send, inquire, seek, and get rejected? Thus he himself made the sentence in his own case irretractable by choosing to remain such that he truly could not be absolved. He chose to become such a person that, once the sentence concerning such a person remained in force, it would not remain irretractable concerning one who was no longer such, since it would have no authority to remain concerning someone who had become otherwise.

How many examples did Acacius have in the bishops who had fallen in the Ephesian Robber Council and who, by whatever means, had broken with their consent to perversity? Even if it had not been stated that they could bear perpetual condemnation, they deserved to have the condemnation against them rescinded when, by repenting, they became unlike those whom they had become there and who deserved perpetual condemnation. Those who persisted made the condemnation irretractable against themselves; those who withdrew from the cause of perpetual condemnation deserved to have it rescinded for themselves. [Col. 0950D]

Therefore it makes no difference whether one says that an ecclesiastical sentence binds the guilty and transgressors. For just as what has not been said cannot benefit him—namely, that he is never to be released—but if he remains in error it persists in every way as irretractable, and he can be absolved from it only by becoming otherwise, so it cannot prejudice anyone merely because it was said that he would never be released. The evident reasoning shows that he is never to be released if he persists as one who is bound, or that he is never to be released in the condition in which he is bound.

But if he has not been rejected, even if he repents and corrects himself, it is plainly clear and beyond doubt that the way is open and free for him to become unlike the one of whom it was said that he would never be released. He may become one of whom it was not said that he would never be released—that is, corrected and amended—and consequently he may be corrected and released. [Col. 0951A]

It should be noted that if those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit in any manner repent and correct themselves, they are forgiven both in this age and in the age to come. The Lord’s sentence is not thereby changed, since it was declared to remain concerning those who continue to be such, not concerning those who have become otherwise.

[Col. 0951B] For as long as they remain in this condition, they are such as those against whom it was fixed that forgiveness should not be granted. But when they withdraw from it, they become unlike those of whom it was declared that forgiveness should not be granted. Therefore, once they have become otherwise, they can now be forgiven both in this age and in the age to come.

Otherwise—God forbid—the Church would appear to receive such people into reconciliation in vain. But since it cannot be frustrated, this interpretation must in every respect be proclaimed, so far as concerns us, without compromising the Lord’s sentence.

Thus Acacius was said to be such as the one who was bound, never to be released. He remained such to the end; he did not cease to be such. Therefore he is today such as he was said to be. He cannot now cease to be such. Since he remained such, he must never be released. For if he ceased to be such, he would not have remained one who was not such; and the one who was said never to be released because he was not such as had been declared could never be absolved. If he withdrew from being one who could never be released, he would approach the condition in which he could be released.

What the apostolic see did not consent to, the emperor now imposed; nor did Anatolius usurp it. Everything, as has been said, lay within the authority of the apostolic see. What the apostolic see confirmed in the synod obtained strength; what it rejected could have no validity. It alone rescinded what the synodal assembly had presumed to usurp contrary to order. It was not the promulgator of a repeated sentence, but, together with the apostolic see, the executor of the earlier one. [Col. 0951C]

[Col. 0951D] What has been said about one and the same person—whether he remains such as the one who properly received the sentence, or becomes otherwise and is absolved from that sentence, which was not pronounced against one who had become otherwise—is likewise read as having been fixed in every city and, indeed, drawn from the people and the whole nation, which is a portion of the entire world.

The world is the same world of which it was said that it would perish; the word of God cannot pass away; and yet, when that same world withdraws from wicked intentions, the word is not thereby nullified. Thus Tyre, Berytus, Gaza, and Egypt were declared destined to perish, yet afterward we know them to have been saved through the Gospel.

They therefore perished in two ways: either by remaining in the condition in which they had received such a sentence, or by departing from the condition in which they had been such. In the latter case, that sentence consequently did not apply to those who had become otherwise, since it had not been fixed against those who were otherwise. [Col. 0952A]

So also concerning the Jewish people, it was pronounced with such finality through the prophet Isaiah: “Close their eyes and stop up their ears, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear” (Isa. 6:10), “lest at any time they understand, and I heal them.” Here correction and amendment are shown to have been forbidden, and even the hope of repenting is entirely cut off.

Yet we know that from that people the apostles and the primitive Church proceeded, and that so many thousands of people were saved through baptism in a single day.

Behold: in those who persisted, the sentence that had been pronounced remained such as it was. They were not admitted to come to the healing of correction; rather, they were adjudged to perish in their wickedness. While the divine sentence remained in force, they were not converted through their own amendment, understanding, movement, strength, or ability so that they might be healed. They were healed by grace so that they might be converted:

“Lest they be converted,” he says, “and I heal them”—lest they be converted by their own will or by their own works, in which they confidently trusted; lest, pursuing their own righteousness, they fail to be subject to the righteousness of God; lest, relying on their own powers, they refuse to submit themselves to divine mercy and illumination. [Col. 0952B]

Therefore the effect of proud presumption is restrained in them, so that they may not be converted by their own intentions and efforts, as they had supposed, and so that he may heal them—not so that saving grace might be given to them as though it came from their merits or their own ability, and so that grace would then no longer be grace, if it were not given freely to the undeserving, but were repaid as a wage to those who had merited it.

Therefore it is not that they themselves convert and are healed; [Col. 0952C] rather, having been healed by grace, they should recognize how they are converted to the humility of Christ.

Thus, in both groups—that is, both in those who remained in the condition in which they had received such a sentence and in those who were saved from it—the Lord’s sentence remained fixed and in force. Yet, while it remained in force against them, healing was introduced in a wondrous manner, so that the sentence appeared not to have been changed, while, with the sentence continuing, healing came not through their confidence but through the divine gift.

If they fear attempting these things and recognize that they do not belong to the measure of their authority—that they have been permitted to govern only human affairs, not divine ones—how do they presume to judge those through whom divine matters are administered?

These arrangements existed before the coming of Christ, when, in a figurative manner, though they were still established in carnal actions, there were at once kings [Col. 0952D] and priests. Sacred history records that holy Melchizedek was such a person. The devil also imitated this among his own followers, since he always strives to claim for his tyrannical spirit whatever is suited to divine worship, so that pagan emperors were called both emperors and supreme pontiffs.

But when the truth had come, although he was one and the same king and pontiff, neither did the emperor afterward impose upon himself the name of pontiff, nor did the pontiff claim royal eminence for himself.

For although his members—that is, the members of the true king and pontiff—are said, by participation, to have magnificently received both dignities in sacred nobility, so that royal and priestly orders might exist together, Christ, mindful of human weakness, wisely tempered what was fitting for the salvation of his own. He therefore distinguished the duties of the two powers through their proper activities and dignities, wishing his people to be saved by healing humility rather than once again destroyed by human pride.

Thus Christian emperors needed pontiffs for eternal life, while pontiffs relied upon imperial arrangements for the course of temporal affairs, so that spiritual action might remain distinct from carnal incursions. For this reason, the one serving God should not entangle himself in secular business, and, conversely, the one entangled in secular affairs should not appear to preside over divine matters. In this way the moderation of both orders would be preserved, so that neither would be exalted by being supported with both powers, and so that a profession suited to the particular qualities of each activity might be appropriately assigned. [Col. 0953A]

[Col. 0953B] When all these matters are properly considered, it is shown clearly enough that a pontiff can neither be bound nor released by secular power. This makes it still more evident that Peter of Alexandria could in no way have been completely absolved merely by an imperial sentence.

If the consent of the pontiffs was also joined to it, we ask whether that consent preceded or followed. If it followed, the matter nevertheless returns to this: an absolution ordered by secular power and begun chiefly by the emperor could not be valid, and the consent of the pontiffs that followed would have been an act of flattery rather than a legitimate sanction.

If it preceded, let it be shown by whom and where it was carried out; whether it was celebrated according to the rule of the Church, proceeded from the tradition of the fathers, was issued according to the custom of the ancestors, and was produced by competent examination. [Col. 0953C]

Here it must undoubtedly be asked whether it was carried out by a synodal assembly—a matter which, since the cause was new, is most certainly shown to have been condemned upon reception and brought about through the expulsion of the Catholic party; whether the case was referred, according to the rules, to the first see, whose concern was the sentence by which Peter was bound; whether the same authority that bound him also absolved him; and whether he could have been released by one who had not bound him, or even by one who did not know of the matter.

If these things were not done, by what custom or rite is Peter of Alexandria claimed to have been absolved, when he was neither lawfully released by the pontiffs according to ecclesiastical laws nor could he have been completely absolved by secular power outside the course of the Church?

All the more, when the emperor was making this request, the pontiffs ought to have advised him that, if he wished Peter to be lawfully absolved, a lawful absolution in accordance with ecclesiastical procedure should be carried out, and that all the matters mentioned above should be observed according to the Church’s course—especially since the case concerned the bishop of a second see, who could not lawfully be absolved by any inferior authority but could be absolved by the first see.

An inferior cannot absolve a superior; only the superior can suitably absolve the inferior. Therefore the pontiffs of inferior rank, who knew that they could in no way release one superior to themselves without the first see—and especially one whom they knew to be bound by its sentence—did not completely strip him of his bond through a transgressive absolution; rather, by their transgression they bound him still more. [Col. 0953D]

Thus Peter’s absolution is invalid from both perspectives. They could not absolve the guilty man through a transgressive absolution; and, after Catholic pontiffs had been expelled everywhere and [Col. 0954B] heretics, or those tainted by communion with heretics, had been substituted in their place, they could no more absolve their associate—men themselves polluted in the integrity of sacred religion—than they had themselves been absolved.

Accordingly, they were both transgressors against ecclesiastical rule and defilers of the integrity of the holy communion through association with the faithless. What sort of judgment could they have rendered concerning one who was guilty, when they were shown to have become guilty above all?

Throughout the entire East, either every Catholic pontiff who persisted was expelled, or the one who consented to error remained and withdrew himself from the contagion of those who erred. What judgment, then, could such men have rendered concerning anyone’s error, when they are shown never to have ceased from error, but, by mixing the confession of heretics and Catholics alike, to have disturbed every see of the true and sincere religion and confused Catholic and apostolic purity? [Col. 0954A]

Behold those who were to absolve the guilty, though they were shown above all to have become guilty themselves. Behold with whom a synod concerning the absolution of the guilty was to be held.

If the Catholic faith and communion were being preserved, why were the Catholic bishops expelled? How were only the heretics retained?

## Another letter of Gelasius the pope to Faustus, serving as envoy at Constantinople

I too have understood in my mind that the Greeks will remain in their obstinacy, lest what was previously known should appear unexpected to anyone. Therefore they are not so much striving to obstruct the public arrangements on account of the purposes of the embassy as, rather, using the occasion of the imperial embassy to attempt to overturn the Catholic faith, and by such a contrivance they strive to accomplish what they hope for. [Col. 0954C]

What does the emperor mean by saying that he was condemned by us in matters of religion, when, concerning this matter, not only did my predecessor scarcely mention his name, but, when he had first obtained and exercised royal power, my predecessor even wrote that he rejoiced in the advancement of his empire, and I, having never received any writing from him, have nevertheless taken care to greet him in letters of honor?

My priestly predecessors, who openly confessed that they had communicated with transgressors, removed them from communion. If he chooses to mingle with the condemned, it cannot be charged to us if he wishes to withdraw from them. All the more, he cannot have been condemned by us; rather, he has been admitted to the grace of sincere communion.

It belongs to the Roman senate to avoid, mindful of the faith which it remembers having received from its ancestors, the contagions of external communion, and not, for this reason—God forbid—to be made foreign to the communion of the apostolic see, while placing before itself the claim that pardon ought to be granted to it. [Col. 0954D]

Let it be read, from the time when the Christian religion began—or at least let an example be produced in the Church of God by any pontiffs, by the apostles themselves, or finally by the Savior himself—that pardon was granted to those who did not correct themselves.

It has never been heard under heaven, nor is it read or said anywhere, that what is drawn from their words is: “Grant us pardon, so that we may remain in error.” That is still not enough. Let those who attempt to oppose us with canons show us in which canons, in which rules, in what reading or document—whether from our ancestors, from the apostles themselves, whom no one doubts were superior in authority, or from the Lord and Savior himself, who is believed to judge the living and the dead—it was ever done or commanded as something to be done. [Col. 0955A]

We read that Christ raised the dead. We do not read that he absolved the dead in error. He alone possessed the assured power to do this, and he principally entrusted it to the blessed apostle Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:18).

“On earth,” he says. For in this binding he never says that a dead person is to be absolved. We therefore fear even to contemplate what was never done, knowing that it cannot be completely excused in the divine judgment.

But if, as they now claim, they are going to separate themselves from the Roman Church, they are shown to have done so long ago. For this reason I am all the less surprised if the man who says that Acacius could not be condemned by one person does not himself perceive his ignorance.

Does he not perceive that, according to the form of the Council of Chalcedon, Acacius was condemned? Does he not know—or does he pretend not to know—how many priests, the authors of this error, are plainly shown to have been condemned by a sentence of great number, just as the clear course of events shows that this has happened and continues to happen in every heresy from the beginning of the Christian religion? My predecessor was the executor of an old decree, not the author of a new constitution. [Col. 0955B]

This is permitted not only to the apostolic bishop but to any pontiff: according to the rule concerning the heresy itself, already condemned, they may separate anyone, or any place, from Catholic communion.

[Col. 0955C] Acacius was not the inventor of a new or personal error, so that new decrees should proceed against him; rather, he mingled his communion with the crime of others. Therefore he necessarily fell under the just sentence which the author of the error had received, together with his successors, through synodal connivance.

They oppose us with canons while not knowing what they are saying. Yet they themselves reveal that they act against those canons by refusing to obey the first see when it gives sound and righteous counsel. The canons themselves are what wished the appeals of the whole Church to be brought before the judgment of this see. But they decreed that no appeal should be made from it anywhere at all. Thus they established that it should judge the whole Church, that it should be subject to the judgment of no one, and that its judgment should never itself be judged. They also established that its sentence ought not to be rescinded, since they commanded that its decrees should rather be followed. [Col. 0955D]

In this very case, Timothy of Alexandria, Peter of Antioch, Peter, Paul, John, and the others—not merely one but several bearing the name of the priesthood—were deposed solely by the authority of the apostolic see. Acacius himself is also taught to be a witness to this, since he was the executor of that command.

Just as it is clear that the apostolic see acted according to the synodal form, so it is most certain that no one could have resisted it. In this way Acacius, having fallen back into association with the condemned, was condemned, although before becoming a transgressor he had carried out their condemnation. [Col. 0956A]

They have dared to mention the canons to us, although you are always shown to be held by illicit ambitions. In what synod, or according to the form of what synod, did they expel John of Alexandria from the Church to which he had been ordained? He could not be accused on any evident grounds, nor had he been summoned beforehand or challenged afterward in a competent court.

If they say, “The emperor did this,” by which canons and rules was this commanded? Why did Acacius consent to so wicked an act, when divine authority says that not only those who commit wicked deeds are guilty, but also those who consent to the perpetrators?

By which canons or rules was Calendion excluded, or the first Catholic priests of the various cities? By what tradition of the ancestors do they summon the apostolic see to judgment? [Col. 0956B]

Were the bishops of the second see, and of the third and other sees—priests fully conscious of their own standing—obliged to be removed, while one who was an enemy of religion was not to be expelled?

Let them see, then, whether they have other canons by which to carry out their absurdities. The canons that are called sacred, ecclesiastical, and legitimate not only do not permit the apostolic see to be summoned to judgment; they also show that the bishop of Constantinople—a city which, according to the canons, has received no rank among the sees—ought he not to have been removed when he fell back into communion with the faithless.

Were those who were said to have lied to the emperor and were alleged to have injured him to be expelled, while Acacius, who offended against God, the supreme Emperor, and sought to mingle the sincere communion of the divine sacrament with the faithless, ought not to have been excluded according to the synod by which faithlessness was condemned? [Col. 0956C]

Whether they wish it or not, the ancient constitution of the canons will be confirmed by his own judgment. Yet do religious and perfect men, according to the canons, attempt to tear away from the apostolic see the power granted to it, and strive to usurp that power for themselves against the canons?

O teachers and guardians of the canons! We are not permitted to enter into any contest with men of alien communion, since divine Scripture proclaims: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition, knowing that one who is such is condemned by his own judgment.”

Let them recognize that the heretic is condemned not only by another but also by himself. But what is especially shameless is that they fabricate the claim that Acacius sought pardon and that we proved difficult. [Col. 0956D]

Your brother, the illustrious man and my son Andromachus, is witness—he was also abundantly instructed by us to exhort Acacius, once he had laid aside his obstinacy, to come to his senses and return to the fellowship of the apostolic see. He testifies that under oath he made great efforts with him, yet could not bend him toward what is right, as the outcome of events proves.

Let the judgment be produced: when did he send word, when did he ask pardon, and when did he promise us that he would submit to correction? Unless, perhaps, he possessed the disposition which we see his successors possess. Yet if he had asked that pardon be granted, he would have wanted it granted in such a way that he might nevertheless persist in error; in that case he would appear not so much to be received by us as to be drawing us over into his own perversity.

What guilt did he say he would confess before the contest? If it is guilt, then certainly he must be corrected. If they do not think that he should be corrected, they falsely claim that he professes guilt—unless the more wretched possibility is that they both admit the guilt and do not consider it in need of correction.

I also found it amusing that he says: “If it should be necessary to ask pardon”—plainly thinking that he would then necessarily have to seek pardon for his sin if we allowed him not to cease sinning, or rather, God forbid, if we too agreed with him and thereby sinned. I do not know among what prodigies of the world such a statement could be admitted.

A past fault can certainly be forgiven, provided that correction follows. For if thereafter the perversity is allowed to remain, the remission is not the kindness of one who forgives, but the assent of one who consents. It is no wonder that these men dare to blaspheme the see of the blessed apostle Peter, since they either harbor such monstrosities in their hearts or pour them forth from their mouths; and they even declare us proud, although the first see never ceases to offer them everything that belongs to piety, while they trust that they can subjugate it by that very insolent spirit.

But it is not surprising that people whose minds are captive do such things. Frenzied people are accustomed to regard even those treating them as enemies, and either to attack or strike them. Yet I ask these men for the judgment they claim to demand: where could it be conducted? Among themselves, perhaps, so that the same persons might be enemies, witnesses, and judges? But not even human affairs ought to be entrusted to such a judgment, much less the integrity of divine law.

If the matter concerns religion, the supreme judgment of the whole belongs, according to the canons, only to the apostolic see. If, as concerns secular power, he must learn from the pontiffs, and especially from the vicar of blessed Peter, what pertains to divine matters, he cannot himself judge those same matters. Nor should any powerful man of this world, though he is a Christian, presume to claim this for himself—unless, perhaps, he is persecuting religion.

What would they say, however, if they were not defeated in every respect by their own writings? Let them keep their absurdities to themselves, unless they come to their senses, and instead reflect that Christ’s saying is not empty: through the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, he declared that the gates of hell would not prevail. Therefore we do not fear that the apostolic sentence will be overturned—a sentence upheld both by Christ’s voice, by the tradition of our forefathers, and by the authority of the canons—so that it may itself always judge the whole Church. [Col. 0957C]

But let them think more carefully, if they possess any understanding of that religion, lest, by refusing in any way to abandon their perversity, they be condemned before God and men by the perpetual constitution of the apostolic see. It is said that the matter was thus determined, so that henceforth nothing should be said about it—as though even now I had chosen to address them by name in particular, as you know. Nor should any contest be entered into with these men who refuse correction, just as combat must be rejected with the adherents of other heresies.

As for you, we continually ask God in our prayers to bring you back here as soon as possible, safe and unharmed.

## Letter of Gelasius to Anastasius Augustus

The servants of your piety, my sons, Faustinus the master and Hirenaeus, men of consular rank, together with their companions, having returned to Rome after carrying out a public embassy, are said to have sought your clemency concerning why I had not sent you letters of greeting.

I confess that this was not according to my usual practice. But when those who had long ago been sent from the regions of the East had spread throughout the whole City that, by your instructions, permission to see me had been denied them, I believed that I should refrain from writing, lest I should prove burdensome rather than dutiful. You therefore see that this did not result from any dissimulation on my part, but from appropriate caution, lest I inflict annoyance upon minds that were rejecting me.

But when, through the report of the aforementioned men, I learned that your serenity had graciously sought a conversation with my humility, I truly realized that I would rightly be held accountable if I remained silent. For, illustrious son, I love, honor, and receive you as a Roman ruler born at Rome; and as a Christian, I desire to possess with one who has zeal for God a zeal according to the knowledge of truth. As the representative, however unworthy, of the apostolic see, I strive, insofar as I am able, to supply through timely admonitions whatever I discover to be lacking in the fullness of Catholic faith.

For I have been entrusted with the administration of the divine word: “Woe is me if I do not preach the gospel.” If the blessed apostle Paul, the vessel of election, feared this, then I, insignificant as I am, must fear it much more if I were to withhold the ministry of preaching that has been divinely inspired and transmitted through paternal devotion. I beg your piety not to judge the duty of divine reason as arrogance. God forbid, I ask, that a Roman ruler should regard truth communicated to his own seat as an injury.

[Col. 0958C] There are, indeed, two powers, Emperor Augustus, by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and the royal power. The burden of the priests is so much heavier as they must render an account before the divine tribunal even for the rulers themselves.

For you know, most merciful son, that although by your dignity you preside over the human race, nevertheless, as a devoted servant, you bow your neck to the leaders of divine affairs. From them you await the causes of your salvation, and in receiving the heavenly sacraments and arranging them, as is fitting, you recognize that you must be subject to them by the order of religion rather than preside over them. Thus, in these matters, you depend upon their judgment; you do not wish to bring them under your will.

For if, insofar as public discipline is concerned, the ministers of religion, recognizing that authority over you has been conferred by heavenly disposition, obey your laws lest they appear to oppose an established decision even in human affairs, with what devotion, I ask, ought you to obey those who have been appointed to administer the venerable mysteries? Accordingly, just as a serious danger rests upon pontiffs if they remain silent about what is fitting for the worship of God, so—God forbid—a considerable danger rests upon those who, though they ought to obey, despise them.

And if it is fitting for the hearts of the faithful to submit generally to all priests who rightly administer divine matters, how much more must assent be given to the bishop of that see whom supreme divinity willed to be set before all priests, and whom the continuing devotion of the universal Church has perpetually honored? [Col. 0959A]

Here your piety clearly perceives that no one can ever raise himself, by any merely human counsel, to the privilege or confession of the one whom Christ’s voice placed above all. That venerable Church, having confessed him, survives and devoutly maintains the primacy. What has been established by divine judgment cannot be attacked by human presumption. Nor can it be overcome by the power of anyone.

Would that the audacity of those who resist it were not as destructive as it is impossible by any force to overthrow what has been established by the very author of sacred religion. “The foundation of God stands.” Has religion, however hostile some have been toward it, ever been overcome by however great an innovation? Has it not rather remained unconquered precisely when it was thought capable of yielding?

Therefore, I ask you, let certain men cease, in your time and under the pretext of disturbances, rashly to pursue ecclesiastical matters that are not permitted, lest they both fail entirely to obtain what they wrongly desire and lose their standing before God and men.

Accordingly, before God I sincerely beseech, implore, and exhort your piety not to receive my petition with indignation. I ask rather that in this life you hear me pleading than—God forbid—that in the divine judgment you find me accusing you. Nor am I unaware, Emperor Augustus, that your devotion was earnest during your private life. You always desired to become a participant in the eternal promise.

Therefore do not be angry if, precisely because I love you, I wish you to possess forever the kingdom that you have obtained temporarily, and, though you rule the world, to be able to reign with Christ. Certainly, Emperor, under your laws you allow nothing to perish, and you permit no harm to be inflicted upon the Roman name. Is it not true, excellent prince, that you desire not only Christ’s present benefits but also those to come, so that during your reign you will not allow anyone to inflict harm upon religion, truth, the sincerity of Catholic communion, or faith?

With what confidence, I ask, will you seek there the rewards of one whose losses you do not prevent here? I ask you, do not regard as burdensome the things said for the sake of your salvation. You have read: “The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy.” I ask your piety to receive them in your understanding with the same disposition with which I speak them.

Let no one deceive your piety. Scripture truly and uniquely testifies through the prophet: “My dove, my perfect one, is one” (Song of Songs 6:8). There is one Christian faith, which the entire Catholic Church venerates. Truly Catholic, however, is that faith which is separated, by sincere, pure, and undefiled communion, from all the faithless, from their successors, and from their associates.

Otherwise there will not be the distinction commanded by God, but a pitiable confusion. Nor will any reason remain, if we are willing to admit this in the case of any contagion, why we should not open an entrance and a door to all heresies.

“For whoever offends in one point is guilty of all, and whoever despises the least thing gradually falls” (James 2:10; Sirach 19:1). This is what the apostolic see has emphatically established: because the glorious confession of the Apostle is the root of the world, it must not be stained by any fissure of perversity or by any contagion whatsoever. For if—God forbid, though we trust that it cannot happen—something of this kind were to occur, from where would we dare to resist error, or from where could we demand correction from those who err?

Therefore, if your piety denies that the people of one city can be restored to peace, what shall we do concerning the whole community of the world, if—God forbid—it is deceived by our transgression? If the whole world was corrected after first rejecting the profane tradition of its own people, how could the people of one city fail to be corrected if the preaching of faith succeeds?

Therefore, glorious Emperor, I do desire the peace of the Churches; even if it could come about at the cost of my blood, I would embrace it. But I ask what kind of peace that peace itself ought to be. Let us weigh it, clearly, with a truly Christian mind. For what can be true peace if undefiled charity is absent?

The Apostle clearly teaches us what charity must be when he says: “Charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5). How, I ask you, can it come from a pure heart if that heart is infected by an external contagion? How from a good conscience if it has been mixed with perverse and evil things? How can it be from an unfeigned faith if it remains associated with the faithless?

Although these points have often been stated by us already, they must nevertheless be repeated without ceasing, and we must not be silent as long as the name of peace is being used as a pretext. It is not for us, as is maliciously asserted, to make peace; rather, let us show that we desire the kind of peace which alone can be peace, and apart from which no peace exists.

The Eutychian doctrine is vigilant against the precaution of the apostolic see. If it is believed that it can truly stand while the truth of the Catholic faith remains safe, let it be brought forward, asserted, and defended with whatever force may be possible, so that it may be shown not only by itself to be hostile to the Christian faith, but also that the many and deadly heresies contained in its filth may be exposed.

But if, as we are more confident, it is judged by Catholic minds to be excluded, I ask you: why do you not decree that the contagions of those who are proven to have been polluted by it must likewise be rejected? The Apostle says that not only those who do what ought not to be done are held guilty, but also those who consent to the perpetrators.

Accordingly, just as perversity cannot fail to be approved when one who communicates it is received, so perversity cannot be rejected when its accomplice is admitted. Certainly, brothers, under the laws, those who are aware of crimes and those who receive and shelter robbers are bound by the same judicial penalty; nor is a person considered free of the crime who, although he did not commit it himself, nevertheless accepts the perpetrators into familiarity and alliance.

Accordingly, when the Council of Chalcedon, convened for the truth and communion of the Catholic and apostolic faith, condemned Eutyches, the author of detestable madness, it was not satisfied unless it also expelled his associate Dioscorus and the others with him.

Thus, as it is always either established or held beyond doubt in every heresy, the Church subsequently struck down their successors—Timothy, Peter, and the other Peter of Antioch—not by convening a separate council for each individual, but by applying the rule once established by the synod.

How, then, is it not evident that all are likewise bound by the same principle, and that those who became their communicants and accomplices must all be rightly separated from Catholic and apostolic communion?

For this reason we rightly say that Acacius too must be removed from our fellowship: he preferred to pass over into the lot of the faithless rather than remain in the sincerity of Catholic and apostolic communion, although for nearly three years he had been suitably instructed by letters from the apostolic see so that this might not occur.

Once he had become part of an alien communion, he could not fail immediately to be cut off from Catholic and apostolic fellowship, lest, if we delayed even slightly on his account, we too might appear to have undergone the contagions of the faithless.

But perhaps, struck by such a punishment, he came to his senses, promised correction, and amended his error. Or should that man be disciplined more gently who did not feel even severe blows? While he remains in his faithlessness and condemnation, his name cannot be entered in the ecclesiastical recitation any more than the contagion of an external communion can be admitted.

Accordingly, let him either be shown to be free from heretical participation—if he mixed himself into their communion—or, if that cannot be shown, he must necessarily be rejected along with them.

If the bishops of the East whisper that the apostolic see did not write these things to them, as though they themselves had informed the apostolic see by their letters that Peter had been lawfully received, or as though they had not already likewise become accomplices in this disorderly reception, then, just as they truly cannot prove that he was cleansed from heretical perversity, so they will be unable to excuse themselves from being associates of heretics.

But if they perhaps assert that they unanimously reported to the apostolic see everything concerning Peter’s reception by Acacius, then through the same man they all acknowledge that an answer was given to them in equal measure. The authority of the apostolic see, however, is established as superior to all secondary Christian communities and to the universal Church by the succession of the ancestral canons and by manifold tradition.

Even if someone should claim from this that he has some power against the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, one person may be shown to belong to a communion that is not opened to the minds of those outside it.

If anyone among them has confidence, let him come forward and defeat and instruct the apostolic see on both points. Let the name that operates through the distinction of the Churches, far from Catholic communion, therefore be removed from consideration, so that sincere peace of faith and communion, and unity, may be restored.

Then, whoever among us has risen up—or attempts to rise up—against venerable antiquity may be investigated appropriately and lawfully. There it will become clear who guards with a modest purpose the form and tradition of our forefathers; who irreverently leaps above these; and who thinks that an equivalent seizure can be made.

But if the case of the Constantinopolitan people is put forward, by which it is claimed that the name of the scandal—that is, Acacius—cannot be removed, I pass over the fact that the Constantinopolitan populace chose to remain Catholic both when the heretic Macedonius was expelled and when Nestorius was recently cast out, rather than be held by affection for condemned bishops of earlier times.

[Col. 0962A] I pass over the fact that, although they had been baptized by those same condemned bishops, they were not disturbed by any agitation while remaining in the Catholic faith.

I remain silent about the fact that your piety’s authority has now restrained popular tumults arising from theatrical entertainments, and therefore the multitude of the Constantinopolitan city must obey us all the more necessarily for the salvation of their souls if you, the rulers, restore them to Catholic and apostolic communion.

For, Emperor Augustus, if someone should perhaps attempt something against the public laws—God forbid—you could not possibly tolerate any disturbance of pure and sincere devotion to unity. Do you not think it concerns your conscience that the people subject to you should be brought back into order?

Finally, if it is thought that the spirit of one city’s people should not be offended so that divine matters may not be corrected as the situation demands, how much more must we neither dare nor be able to offend the devout faith of all who bear the Catholic name, lest divine matters be violated?

And yet those same people demand that they be healed by our will. Let them therefore allow themselves to be treated by appropriate remedies. Otherwise—God forbid—we may pass into their destruction and perish with them, while we cannot save them.

At this point I leave to your consciences, under divine judgment, what should be followed: whether, as we desire, we should all return together to certain life, or, as they demand, return together to manifest death.

Yet they still insist on calling the apostolic faith proud and arrogant, although it offers them remedies. This is often the characteristic of the sick: they accuse physicians who call them back to health through appropriate disciplines rather than consent to disclose or reject their own harmful desires.

If we are proud because we administer suitable remedies for souls, what should those who resist be called? If we are proud because we say that the paternal institutions must be obeyed, by what name should those who oppose them be called? If we are arrogant because we desire to preserve divine worship in a pure and undefiled manner, let those who think even against divinity say what they should be called.

In the same way, those who are in error judge us and the others because we do not consent to their madness. But where the spirit of pride truly resides and fights, let truth itself declare.

## Again: Gelasius to the Bishops of Dardania: Acacius Was Rightly Condemned by the Apostolic See

[Col. 0962D] GELASIUS to all his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Dardania.

We were greatly surprised that your affection wished to know, as though it were a new and difficult question, and still as though it were something unheard of, that the communicants of the Eutychian plague, having no answer to offer in defense of their observance of perdition and having already been convicted by frequent argument, mutter in mere contentiousness—not because what they babble has any importance, nor because they have any real explanation to give.

Rather, we are more surprised that those who have been instructed in Catholic principles still remain hesitant than that those who have fallen away from the truth and deviated from the ancient tradition of the Church put forward profane novelties of speech and absurdities of fleeting perversity, which your affection reports that they boast—though they have absolutely nothing to say.

For this reason they think that Acacius was not rightly condemned because he does not appear to have been deposed by a special synod; and, childishly, they add to the madness of their vanity that he was especially the bishop of the royal city.

Therefore, rejecting the foolishness of empty complaints, you ought to go back to the blessed apostles themselves and consider carefully that our Catholic forefathers—learned pontiffs, that is—whenever any heresy arose, decreed once, after assembling in accordance with the path of Scripture and the preaching of their predecessors, whatever had been done for the faith, for truth, and for Catholic and apostolic communion. They wished it thereafter to remain firm and unshaken.

Nor did they permit what had been established in the same matter to be reconsidered through any recent presumption, wisely foreseeing that if anyone were allowed to repeat salutary decrees, no ecclesiastical constitution would remain stable against any particular error, and every complete definition would be disturbed by recurring attacks of the same madness.

For if the plagues had not been struck down by the boundaries established in the synodal rules once laid down, and if, by renewed conflicts, they had been allowed to rise against the foundation of truth and strike simple hearts, what would happen if the faithless were thereafter permitted to convene a council?

Even when the truth is manifest to them, they never lack some destructive falsehood to put forward. Though deficient in reason or authority, they nevertheless do not cease from their purpose. Seeing this by divine inspiration, our forefathers took necessary precautions: they did not permit what a synod had once promulgated for the faith, communion, and Catholic and apostolic truth to be altered thereafter by new recitations.

They did not wish to provide the wicked with an opportunity to attack what had been established as a remedy. Once the author of any madness and the error itself had likewise been condemned, they judged it sufficient that whoever at any time became a communicant of that error should be bound by the principal sentence of its condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized either by his profession or by his communion.

To pass over earlier matters, which a diligent investigator can easily discover, the synod condemned Sabellius. It was not then necessary for his followers to be condemned afterward in separate synods, each individually; rather, in accordance with the established ancient constitution, the universal Church declared that all who had participated either in that perversity or in its communion were to be rejected.

Thus, because of the blasphemies of Arius, once the form of Catholic faith and communion had been set forth by the Council of Nicaea, it condemned without reconsideration all Arians and everyone who had fallen into that plague either by agreement or by communion.

Similarly, once a synod had condemned Eunomius, Macedonius, and Nestorius, it did not permit new councils to be convened concerning them. Instead, the Church rejected all who had fallen in any way into these blasphemies, according to the synodal boundary handed down to it. It is clear that the Church never rightly yielded, under any necessity, to the rash renewal of what had been salutarily established.

We are not unaware that, during the storm of the Arian persecution, many pontiffs, breathing again after returning from exile when peace had been restored, assembled their brothers in various provinces and set their troubled Churches in order. Yet they did not thereby alter anything that the Council of Nicaea had defined concerning the faith and Catholic communion, nor did they strike anyone with a new condemnation after his lapse.

Rather, by the terror of that decree, they judged those who had not come to their senses to be condemned. Having weighed these matters appropriately, as has been said, according to the paternal tradition, we are confident that no one who is now truly a Christian is ignorant that, for every synodal constitution approved by the assent of the universal Church, no see ought to be preferred to the first see. That see confirms each synod by its authority and guards it through continuous moderation, in accordance with the primacy that the blessed apostle Peter received by the command of the Lord’s voice. The Church, following thereafter, has always held and continues to hold it.

When the apostolic see learned through reliable evidence that Acacius had long since deviated from apostolic truth—though it was slow to believe this, since it knew that he had often acted as the executor of necessary measures against heretics—it did not cease for nearly three years to admonish him by letters, as the familiar letters sent on various occasions testify.

At first he proposed to respond to these letters with what seemed the silence owed to them. Eventually, however, in a letter he admits that he had admitted the Alexandrian Peter into communion without the knowledge of the apostolic see, although he himself, as executor, had condemned Peter after seeking the authority of the apostolic see.

The see of blessed Peter, which knew that it had condemned the Alexandrian Peter but had not released him, did not receive him. Therefore, lest Acacius bring him into Peter’s fellowship, it also removed Acacius himself from its communion and in many ways made him an outsider to its fellowship as a transgressor.

If an examination is sought, no further judgment will be necessary after he himself has confessed in his letters.
