If the weight of authority is sought, the execution of that definition is found in the terms of the Council of Chalcedon: once someone had become a communicant of the error condemned there, he was nevertheless established as a participant in the condemnation, because the very error that was once condemned with its author carries, in anyone who becomes a participant in its perverse communion, both the curse and the punishment attached to it.

[Col. 0964D] By this same principle, Timothy and Peter himself—the latter being the Alexandrian Peter, who was recognized as holding the second see—are shown to have been condemned not by a repeated synod, but solely by the authority of the apostolic see, with Acacius himself seeking or carrying out the action.

But if Acacius should perhaps be said to have needed to establish whether they communicated with error or with transgression, we briefly offer this response: either let them show that Peter was lawfully and truly purified and duly separated from every contagion of heretics when Acacius communicated with him, if they think that Acacius, as his communicant, can in any way be excused; or, if they do not prove that Peter was properly cleansed—as is more truly the case—
[Col. 0965A] It remains that he was unpurified, and that the one who communicated with him was infected. Nor do we pass over in silence what the entire Church throughout the world knows: that the authority of blessed Peter the apostle’s see cannot be released by the sentence of any pontiffs whatsoever once it has been bound, since it has the right to judge concerning the whole Church, while no one is permitted to judge its judgment. Indeed, the canons wished appeals from every part of the world to be made to it, whereas no one is permitted to appeal from it. Therefore it must be sufficiently clear that Acacius had no pontifical judgments by which he could dissolve the apostolic see’s sentences without any knowledge on its part.

By what synod, then, did he presume to do this—something which it was not lawful for him to effect even by the authority of the apostolic see, whose bishop he was, and the bishop of what metropolitan city? Was it not the parish of the Church of Heraclea? [Col. 0965B] If it was certainly lawful for him, without a synod and without seeking any prior consultation, to break the sentence of the apostolic see, was it truly not lawful for the First See, in accordance with the decision established by the Council of Chalcedon, to exercise the authority appropriate to remove such a transgressor? Was it not right to do so?

Nor do we pass over the fact that, according to the custom of our ancestors, the apostolic see was frequently granted the power, even without any presiding synod, to release those whom an unjust synod had condemned, and to condemn those whom it ought to condemn even when no synod was in existence. Thus a synod of the East had condemned Athanasius of blessed memory. Yet the apostolic see, having excepted him because it did not consent to the Greeks’ condemnation, absolved him.

Likewise, a synod had condemned John of Constantinople, also of blessed memory, certainly a synod of Catholic bishops; but the apostolic see, because it did not consent, absolved him by itself in the same manner. Likewise, it absolved the holy Flavian, bishop of the Greeks, who had been condemned by an assembly, in the same way, because the apostolic see alone did not consent; rather, it absolved him than he should have been received there.

By its own authority it condemned Dioscorus, bishop of the Second See, and, by refusing consent, alone removed the impious synod; by its own authority alone it decreed that the Council of Chalcedon should be held. Therefore, just as it alone had the power to absolve those whom synodal decrees had condemned, so it is known also to have condemned, without a synod, very many metropolitans in this same matter.

If anyone censures these actions of the apostolic see as having been carried out contrary to a holy synod, then, apart from the fact that he is refuted by the evidence of ancient precedent, [Col. 0965D] he will admit all the more that Acacius was not permitted to act. Let him say, then, by what synod he judged it permissible to exclude a bishop of the Second See—certainly a Catholic of some kind and ordained by Catholics, who had in no way been accused concerning the Catholic faith and communion—and to allow the manifest heretic Peter, himself condemned by his own execution of the sentence, to be substituted for a Catholic bishop.

By what synod did he cause the holy Calendion, bishop of the apostolic Third See, to be expelled, and nevertheless allow Peter—so manifest a heretic that he openly claimed that he did not share communion with him—to be substituted for him by his own arrangement? Finally, by what synod, throughout the whole East, did he substitute for orthodox bishops, stained by no crime, various wicked men entangled in crimes, through his own provision? By what synod did that nefarious despoiler seize so many privileges belonging to others? The books would not suffice if we attempted to describe individually the tragedies he brought about throughout the Churches of the entire East.

Or did he think that this argument should be brought against us: that he appeared to cast his crimes upon the imperial person? Why, then, when he wished, did he resist the tyrant Basiliscus, certainly a heretic and vehemently hostile to him? Why did he submit his will to the emperor Zeno himself, because Zeno did not wish to communicate openly with Peter of Antioch? Behold, he could resist others, but he did not wish to. Did not the Apostle say: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Romans 1:32), are likewise entangled in guilt?

But, leaving aside matters that would require fuller explanation, whatever the emperor Zeno himself declares in his letters—that he did everything in accordance with Acacius’s council—Acacius himself also bears witness in his own letters, and thereby does not deceive us. He wrote that Zeno had conducted everything correctly, and he did not conceal that these same things had been done by his council.

As though Acacius had become a transgressor only through communion with Peter of Alexandria, and not through all those whom he appointed; as though, after Catholic bishops had been driven out, he had not at some time placed tyrants over the Churches and so become joined by perverse communion to those thus appointed. According to the canons, these men should have been expelled from ecclesiastical communion precisely because they allowed successors to be installed while living priests were still in office.

Who, then, does not see that Christians who were introduced after Catholic bishops had been driven from their own sees could only have been heretics? Yet Acacius was either the author of the substitution of all these men, or joined them in communion after they had been substituted; and in this respect they did not differ at all from the communion of heretics.

Why, then, when he saw these things happening, did he not take care—as he had already done under Basiliscus—to refer the matter to the apostolic see, so that, if he himself could not act alone, he might, with those who shared his counsels and deliberations, bring before the emperor what was appropriate to the region? For if Basiliscus, as has been said, a tyrannical heretic vehemently hostile to the writings of the apostolic see, could be recalled from his approaches to it by repeated interventions, how much more could the legitimate emperor, who wished to appear Catholic, have been moderated by the apostolic see and by the measured representations of all the bishops—especially since he was a particular supporter and admirer of Acacius, and in his letters had praised both Acacius himself and the holy pope Simplicius highly for having resisted the heretics with the utmost firmness.

Why did Acacius remain silent for so long amid these events, unless he did not wish in any way to prevent what he desired to be accomplished?

Let us nevertheless suppose that no synod had preceded, though the apostolic see would rightly have been its executor. With whom was a synod concerning Acacius to be held? Was it with those who were already held to be Acacius’s associates and who had violently excluded Catholic priests throughout the whole East? Having sent their companions into various exiles, they were plainly partners in an enduring communion; nor did they transfer themselves to these associations before consulting the decisions of the apostolic see. With whom, then, was a synod to be held?

[Col. 0967A] Catholic bishops had already been driven out everywhere, and only the associates of the treacherous remained—men with whom it was not lawful to hold an assembly. The Psalmist says: “I have not sat in the council of vanity, and with those who do iniquity I will not enter” (Psalm 25:4). Nor is it ecclesiastical practice to mingle a council with those who have a polluted and adulterated communion, or to deliberate together with the treacherous.

Rightly, therefore, this sort of transgression was rejected through the form of the Council of Chalcedon, rather than being brought before a council which was neither necessary after the first synod nor permissible with such men. They could not have failed to understand what was being done concerning the Catholic faith, even if they wished to remain ignorant, when they saw Catholic bishops being driven out throughout the whole East without any synodal examination or council—especially since they recognized that new cases were involved, and the others could have learned from the character of those men what they themselves ought to guard against.

It remains, therefore, that it is clear that they belonged to that part of the heresy to which, after so many proofs, they surrendered themselves. Consequently, they should no longer be consulted by the apostolic see and the other Catholics, but rather marked out.

We laughed at their wish to compare Acacius’s prerogative with the fact that he was bishop of an imperial city. Did an emperor not reside for many years at Milan, Ravenna, Firmium, and Trier? Did the bishops of those cities ever in ancient times usurp anything for their own dignities beyond the measure assigned to them? Did Acacius, in order to expel John—however much a man, nevertheless a Catholic and ordained by Catholics—from Alexandria, and to receive Peter, already cast down into heresy and condemned, do so without consulting the apostolic see? Did he boldly undertake this on the basis of some synod held there? Is he shown to have done so by any synod in order to expel Calendion from Antioch and, although he himself had condemned the heretic Peter, to admit him again without the knowledge of the apostolic see?

[Col. 0967C] If the dignity of cities is at issue, the dignity of the bishops of the Second and Third Sees is greater than that of a city which is not only not counted among the sees, but is not even reckoned among metropolitan rights. For when you call it an imperial city, one power is the authority of secular rule, and another is the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities. Just as a small city does not diminish the prerogative of the present kingdom, so the emperor’s presence does not alter the measure of religious administration. Thus that distinguished city remains firm, free, and exalted in religious authority under the same imperial power, provided that, in the emperor’s presence, it retains its own proper measure without any disturbance.

Perhaps, however, it may be said concerning the Alexandrian and Antiochene cases that, for definite reasons, the prince ordered what was done, and not Acacius. But it was fitting for a Christian priest to advise a Christian prince—especially one who enjoyed his intimacy and favor—that vindication for the bishop’s injury and insult would remain secure, provided that the Christian ruler allowed the rules of the Church to be observed. For a new case had arisen concerning each bishop; consequently, a new examination was required. As had always been the outcome, judgments concerning priests should proceed from a priestly council, so that bishops, even if some error of human frailty had occurred, but without any transgression against religion, should not be driven out by secular power.

Or should these matters not also have been suggested in accordance with the prince’s position? If he had been exalted by the honor of an imperial city, he ought all the more to have been steadfast in making such representations. But if, in matters that had to be undertaken for religion, he proved contemptible, despised, sluggish, or lacking the confidence to speak plainly, in what respect did the imperial city make him greater?

The prophet Nathan openly and publicly declared to King David, face to face, the wrong he had committed; he did not conceal that David himself had committed it, and then absolved him after he had been corrected through confession (2 Samuel 12).

But this good man [Col. 0968B] and outstanding priest showed how much he could have advised and revealed how unwilling he was to do so—or rather, he made clear that he had been a participant—insofar as the emperor said that he had done everything on Acacius’s counsel, while Acacius himself raised the emperor, who was doing these things, with great praises, and exposed himself as having participated in their execution.

But let us grant that Calendion had removed the emperor’s name, and that he is alleged to have lied to John’s prince. Nevertheless, since these were new cases, a new ecclesiastical examination ought to have taken place. Those who were said to have sinned against a human emperor should by no means have been removed without coming to a synod; and should Acacius, who had sinned against God, the supreme and true Emperor, and who sought to mix sincere communion in the divine sacrament with the treacherous, not have been excluded by the holy synod in which this treachery was condemned?

What of the Catholic priests expelled from countless cities throughout the whole East and the heretics substituted for them? Were these not certainly cases, to which a single synod was consequently owed? Why, then, did it not occur to him to ask the prince to celebrate at least some sort of synod in such cases, so that bishops would not appear to have been excluded everywhere under any colored pretext of ecclesiastical procedure—not merely the priests of whatever cities, but metropolitan bishops without exception?

Since Acacius did not resist any of these matters by whatever representation he could make, he consented to them by communicating with all those who had been substituted as heretics in place of Catholic bishops. The Apostle says that not only “those who do such things,” [Col. 0968D] but also “those who consent to those who do them” (Romans 1:32), are unquestionably reckoned guilty.

Was it lawful for secular power, with Acacius consenting to such acts, to carry them out without any synod, although the novelty of the circumstances itself demanded one, and without consulting the apostolic see; yet was it not lawful for the apostolic see, in accordance with the tenor of the Council of Chalcedon, in an old case and under an old decree, to remove from its communion Acacius, who was justly condemned by the established definition and who communicated with the enemies of the Council of Chalcedon?

“But,” they say, “Acacius could not oppose the princes.” Why, then, did he oppose Basiliscus, because he wished to? Why did he not consent to Zeno himself, so that he would not appear to communicate openly with Peter of Antioch, although he did this secretly? Behold, the emperor did not resist him when he resisted. Behold, he did not use force against him when he refused. Behold, he granted escape from manifest contagion to one who was fleeing it.

Finally, why, while these things were being done, did he remain silent for so long, although he knew that the law had to be applied? Why did he not take care to refer the matter to the apostolic see, from which he knew that responsibility for those regions had been delegated to him? Instead, he himself first became a praiser of the deeds, rather than warning by law that such things were not to be attempted or opposing their attempted commission, as he had already done under Basiliscus.

Why did he consent to communicate with those others who, after Catholic priests had been expelled, had unquestionably been substituted as heretics in the individual cities? Finally, if he failed in his duties and did not take care to do what was incumbent upon a Catholic priest, for that reason the apostolic see could neither omit nor ought to have passed over what belonged to it. In whatever manner, it rejected the accomplice of the heretics and removed from its communion one who shared in their external communion.

[Col. 0969B] There was no need for a new synod, since the old decree sufficiently prescribed this procedure; nor was there any need to inform the bishops of the East that these things had to be done. It is clear that they were not unaware of the expulsion of the Catholics, which was being carried out in a matter of faith, and it is beyond doubt that, by communicating with the substituted heretics, they consented by that act, having likewise become participants in an external communion. Therefore the decisions of the apostolic see could neither be discussed nor ought to have been discussed with them any longer.

Behold, they recognized in the profession of those who persevered with the utmost firmness what was owed to the Catholic faith and communion. Behold, they recognized how Acacius, by withdrawing from such men—or rather, by devising measures contrary to them—had deviated from the Catholic and apostolic faith and communion, and they likewise subjected themselves with him to the same error.

Behold, they recognized for what just reasons Acacius was removed by the authority of the apostolic see from the Catholic and apostolic faith and communion, to which those who persevered in it conformed, while those who opposed the persevering were taught by that same authority to be alien. Likewise, all who proved to be his accomplices were separated from their communion on account of their deserts, from the communion from which he himself is known to have first separated by differing from the Catholic bishops and their associates.

He rightly received the sentence of condemnation that was to be pronounced against his other associates, since he alone, on behalf of all his associates, confessed in a letter sent to the apostolic see that he had fallen back into communion with treachery. If the Eastern bishops had communicated with him before he was reported here, they were undoubtedly shown to be involved in equal guilt; and rightly, through him, they received the sentence of transgression [Col. 0969D] as persons who had become partners with him in external communion. They should certainly no longer have been consulted as men of our communion, but rejected as placed in an opposing fellowship.

But if they had not communicated with Acacius before he was reported here, and ought to have marked the one who did communicate with him, then he himself should rather have reported the matter here and have shown that Acacius was rightly struck down by the force of the apostolic see. And they should have maintained concord with the apostolic see and with those great bishops. But because they had deserted their company and had undertaken to communicate with their successors, they were in no way in agreement with the apostolic see. For they had fallen back into the sect of the transgressor Acacius, and they clearly foresaw that they would consequently be bound by his sentence.

For this reason they did not want him to appear condemned: they recognized that they themselves had been condemned in the same transgression, in which they persist to remain even today. But just as men bound by the same condition cannot judge their accomplice to have been condemned unjustly, nor can the guilty competently absolve the guilty, so, once that transgressor had been justly condemned, these men also lie prostrate under an equal condemnation. They will be able to be absolved from it only if they repent.

For just as the transgression of all who had fallen back into the same act of treachery was published through one person who wrote on their behalf, so, through that one and the same person who had written—or, by writing, had exposed—the will of them all, the transgression of all was punished. We judge that these points, which we have confessed for the instruction of your Dilection, are more than sufficient, although, if the Lord grants us the opportunity, we shall strive to explain the same matters more fully, so that every one of the faithful may understand that the apostolic see did not, God forbid, act precipitously in its judgment.

This sentence, however, directed against Acacius, although it had been issued, especially since it appeared that it should be sent secretly, in the name only of the apostolic bishop whose lawful exercise of both powers had been established—lest, if the salutary disposition then present were displayed everywhere, its necessary effect should be obstructed by any difficulties—was nevertheless reasonably recognized by the assembly of many Catholic priests in Italy as having been pronounced against Acacius. For throughout the East the orthodox had been scattered everywhere, and only heretics and their associates remained; Catholic bishops either were entirely absent or possessed no freedom.

[Col. 0970C] This assembly of bishops did not convene against Chalcedon, nor as a new synod against the earlier and first one; rather, in accordance with the tenor of the old decree, it became a participant in the apostolic execution. Thus it becomes sufficiently clear that the Church and the apostolic see, since it could no longer act elsewhere, omitted nothing wherever and with whomever it could act that belonged to the fraternal treatment of the matter for the sake of undefiled faith and sincere communion.

What, then, did these prudent men, with their sharp minds probing the inner affairs of the whole region, do, once they learned that such a person had been installed in the Church of Antioch? Why did they give their consent to communicating with such men? Why did they not immediately protest? Why did they not withdraw themselves from such contagion, when they plainly perceived that Calendion had been expelled so that entrance might be opened to heretics?

Why did they discuss nothing about a synod, nothing about the matter itself, nothing about the Christian faith, and nothing about the examination of the persons involved? If they voluntarily submitted themselves to his communion, then they were certainly separated from the apostolic see together with such men; and, if it had been necessary to hold a synod among and concerning such persons, no synod could arise at all.

But if they say that they did not know what sort of bishop had succeeded Calendion at Antioch, what wonder is it if men situated in the East, who were unable to know what had happened in their own region, were likewise ignorant of what had been done at the apostolic see? Why, nevertheless, once they learned what sort of priest had been installed at Antioch, did they not immediately reject his association?

Why do they put forward an excuse under the guise of ignorance, when even today they pursue both the manifest contagion of the treacherous and the practices we have repeatedly reproached them for? This makes it sufficiently clear that even then, even if they had known, they would not have rejected him, since even now they do not reject what has been made public. However they may turn to any position or excuse, they are plainly opposed to the truth in matters that are being charged against them—matters that can be brought to a conclusion by their own words and actions—and nothing remains for them to ventilate except the sheer destruction of obstinate treachery.

[Col. 0971B]

These things, however, which have been said concerning the venerable Calendion, also apply, by a definite analogy, to the person of John of Alexandria. Indeed, if the matter is investigated more fully, such great tragedy and such great errors are found there that, if those who perpetrated these acts are themselves the judges, once they have been clearly refuted, they will not escape their own condemnation. For it is shown that the only matter sought there beforehand was how, once any sort of Catholic pontiff had been deposed, access might be opened to the heretic Peter. At that time no one examined the matter, no one demanded a synod; everything everywhere seemed permitted to anyone whatsoever. No distinction between cases was required, no ecclesiastical investigation was sought. Rather, as each person’s whim dictated, a bishop was expelled from Catholic cities—not only a metropolitan, but also a bishop of a third- or second-ranking see. In these matters no investigation was sought, no plans for action were discussed; heretics were substituted, and no one objected. Like dumb animals led into captivity, they followed perfidy under imposed commands. It is not surprising if they now try to defend those whose unexamined baseness they followed with holy-minded men. [Col. 0971C]

But we are astonished that they are not ashamed to complain, in condemning these men, that no synod was held, when they know that so many and such great pontiffs were expelled without any synod. If they complain, in rejecting these men, that a council was not convened, let them recognize that they are thereby open to accusation: why did they not demand this also in the rejection of the others? But if councils were not necessary for the rejection of the others, let them recognize that they were not necessary for these men either. Was a council unnecessary for the deposition of Catholics, yet very much necessary for the condemnation of those whom they confess to be transgressors?

[Col. 0971D]

What, then, remains except that they say these men were not heretics? Let them therefore not complain about a synod, since they openly declare themselves followers of an external communion. Why, then, should a synod have seemed necessary to them when they know that they are acting against the Council of Chalcedon? The Eutychian error was condemned, together with its authors, by the voice of the universal Church. There is no doubt that, as is continually necessary to repeat in every heresy—for no Christian doubts that this is firm—all accomplices, followers, and communicants of an error once condemned are judged to share the same lot. Therefore it follows that, just as Timothy and Peter, followers of such men, were condemned according to the tenor of that synod without any later gathering of pontiffs, so Acacius, because he communicated with Peter, became a participant in the crime and likewise a sharer in the punishment.

[Col. 0972A]

Why, then, do they cloak these matters with evasions and obscurities, striving more lethally to conceal their shamelessness and deranged mind with empty stories than medicinally to heal them by abandoning them? For you have no communion whatever with men of external communion. Every person is therefore summoned to a definite judgment, so that either he may admit the charges brought against him or be convicted by them. After Acacius had confessed, as the tenor of his letters revealed, that he had shared communion with Peter—whom he had requested to be condemned by command of the apostolic see—why should he have been summoned to judgment? Once he had become involved in external communion, he could no longer be believed, whether in his own defense, theirs, or Peter’s, since above he had mixed himself with Peter in that abominable association.

He had made himself, without doubt, party to Peter’s case; and if, after a prior and lawful examination, he had been joined to him following a legitimate purification, this would have been proper. But since he had joined himself in communion to one who had not been lawfully examined and purified, and had thereby still involved himself with the accused, he had no confidence to speak on that man’s behalf. For since Acacius had no privilege by which he could pass judgment from a second-ranking see, he could rightly be condemned in the same manner. Unless he had received authority from the first see, he possessed neither the right to examine Peter nor any power at all to receive him. For it was established according to the rule that, since we know that Peter had not been absolved by us, we likewise do not know that we had examined or absolved the one whom we had condemned.

[Col. 0972B]

It remains for us to demonstrate that this same Peter, whom Acacius claims to have received into communion after his purification, never ceased to be tainted by heretical communion. Nor was this true only at the time when Acacius communicated with him: Peter of Alexandria always remained in the company of heretics, and thus Acacius received through him the contagion of perfidious communion and, through that same communion, was infected with the same plague as those heretics with whom Peter communicated. Acacius presumed to receive Peter without observing the proper order; he did not receive him as an examined man, nor is he recognized to have received him as purified. Therefore he attempted to usurp for himself, without the permission of the apostolic see, an illegitimate reception of Peter, so that he could falsely claim, according to his own will, that Peter had been examined and purified, although he had in no way received him as either examined or purified.

[Col. 0972C]

If he truly wished to receive Peter as examined and purified, he would rather have observed the proper order in his examination and reception. Instead, the procedure appears to have been prolonged more for appearance than according to truth and law. [Col. 0972D]

Therefore, just as he did not previously condemn Peter before reporting the matter and requesting that he be condemned by apostolic authority, so in receiving him he ought to have observed the proper procedure: before joining himself to Peter’s communion, he ought to have requested through the apostolic see that Peter be examined and lawfully purified. Acacius himself had no pontifical authority to examine or receive him; he could accomplish this only through the authority and consent of that see, without whose authority he could not himself condemn Peter, and by whose principal diligence Peter could have been examined, purified, and admitted to suitable communion.

Since it is established that, by the authority of the apostolic see, such persons have either been examined and purified or absolved by other bishops competent to do so, but in such a way that their absolution nevertheless depended upon the consent of the apostolic see, where both elements were lacking it is clear that there was neither a legitimate examination nor a firm purification, and that the reception which followed was improper.

[Col. 0973A]

If you, disregarding me, judged Peter to be a Catholic without my communion and received him lawfully on your own authority, as you allege, what will you say if I, without your knowledge or consultation, rejected him from my communion—which you wished to be disregarded? If you are willing to comply, you are mine; if you are unwilling to comply, you are not mine. “For whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matthew 12:30).

[Col. 0973B]

I ask you: do you believe Peter was a heretic, or a Catholic, or that he was afterward corrected from heresy? If he was a heretic, you ought not to have communicated with him at all; and by communicating with him, it is clear that you became a participant in heresy and were consequently bound by the condemnation that followed him according to the tenor of the synod. If he was a Catholic, you are openly a defender of the whole doctrine which you declare Catholic. Yet you are judged to share that error if you define him as having been a heretic and claim that he was later corrected, declaring that you communicated with him after his purification.

Meanwhile, whose person did you think I should disregard? You cannot complain that I disregarded him in this same matter, and then claim that, without me, you possessed the right either to absolve or lawfully to receive such a person. For it is established that this person was neither legally purified nor regularly received; and just as he was not regularly received, so it is not established that he was legally purified. Therefore he was not purified lawfully, because he was not received legally.

[Col. 0973C]

My judgment concerning him remaining in force, you had no right, without my pontifical authority, to dissolve my judgment. By what power, then, is he said to have been examined, or by what authority received? Behold: in these matters your authority totters and collapses; and if this alone is considered, it will be utterly overthrown.

But bring forward still another point to add to the full measure of your disturbance. What if it is shown that, not only before you entered into his communion, but also when you entered into it, and afterward as well, he continued in the communion of heretics? Did heretical communion not reach you through him, or did you not pass, through your association with him, into the communion of heretics?

[Col. 0973D]

Show, then, that Peter of Alexandria ever withdrew from communion with Peter of Antioch, and that, until the day on which Peter of Antioch remained in this life, the two men did not continue in indivisible association with each other. Or will you say that Peter of Antioch too had been corrected? Why, then, did Acacius boast that the latter had never communicated to the end? But what did it accomplish that he himself did not wish to communicate with him, when he believed that, through Peter of Alexandria, he could communicate with the same man without incurring any blame?

What are we to make of so many and such great cities from which Catholic pontiffs were expelled? If Catholics were substituted for them, why were Catholics rejected? If it clearly appears that, when Catholics were rejected, non-Catholics were substituted, it follows that whoever succeeded them were not Catholics but heretics. Why did you rashly communicate with them? Why did you not act so that this new state of affairs and such a great tragedy concerning the succession of pontiffs might be examined by a living synod?

[Col. 0974A]

Do you grieve over one Acacius because he was not refuted by a special synod, even though he himself exposed his own crime in his letters and, having confessed it voluntarily, ought not to have been heard; yet do you not grieve over so many Catholic pontiffs who were excluded without any investigation? If you had known those whose communion they had avoided to be Catholics, you would have preferred to communicate with them rather than to drive away, by harsh persecution, those who did not communicate with them.

Behold: so many Catholic priests, by this very fact, judge themselves to have known and steadfastly approved what the apostolic see had decreed should be retained. They resounded with Catholic communion and continued to regard as their companions those who communicated with the apostolic see, even when persecution arose.

[Col. 0974B]

It is claimed that what the apostolic see had decreed was not known to the Eastern bishops. How, then, did so many and such great pontiffs, sharing the same judgment as the apostolic see and openly approving it as sacred in religious matters, make known that it had sanctioned the truth—things which they judged not only ought to be followed but also ought to be courageously practiced even unto persecution? Behold, you had men who brought you knowledge of the apostolic constitution and supplied examples of steadfastness in preserving it. If the apostolic see had sent messengers, it could scarcely have sent two or three. Behold, so many pontiffs following the decrees of the apostolic see bring its knowledge to us and offer examples of preserving the truth. You closed your eyes to so many men established there; how could you have listened to two or three?

[Col. 0974C]

Without doubt, by this very fact you recognized that those men pleased the apostolic see, since you saw that they displeased you. Therefore either follow those through whom you understood the will of the apostolic see, or cease altogether to make ignorance an excuse, since, despite relying upon so many and such weighty judgments proclaiming the decrees of the apostolic see, you preferred to reject rather than receive them.

[Col. 0974D]

Did all these bishops whom we have mentioned lie to the emperor? Did all of them remove the emperor’s name from the diptychs? While they were being expelled, and while Catholic pontiffs were still alive, heretical successors were installed—not merely in lesser cities, but even as metropolitan pontiffs—although the Catholic communion continued without interruption. Why, then, did you not sympathize with so many of your brothers? Why did you not approach the emperor? Why did you not continually lament, in public appeals, the cause of the Church and the pitiable dishonoring of the priesthood, arguing that the Church alone had ever judged such matters concerning pontiffs; that human laws had no authority to pronounce judgment on them without the Church’s prior determinations; that Christian rulers customarily obeyed the decrees of the Church and did not set their own power above it; that a ruler customarily subjected his head to bishops and did not judge those who were their heads; what they had committed, by what ecclesiastical decisions or by what synod they were expelled; and, finally, that so many leaders of churches ought not to be struck down at human whim and according to the discretion of secular power, unheard, unexamined, and un summoned?

[Col. 0975A]

This was especially so since a new case and a new state of affairs had appeared: the very rulers of peoples were suddenly deprived of their sacred dignities at the will of worldly power, without any previous cause, any collective charge of guilt, or participation in any error, so that they could be held and proved guilty as associates already condemned, as though bound by an earlier determination. Since none of them had previous cases against them, the charges for which they were being expelled ought to have been demonstrated. And if, at least in accordance with your position, you considered that their misery should be relieved, as ecclesiastical law always requires, you ought to have feared that what you saw happening to others might happen to you: that, if they were stained by a crime, they might be violently admitted contrary to established custom.

[Col. 0975B]

Something concerning an ecclesiastical examination ought to have been ascertained—about the rest I am silent—and the matter ought, according to custom, to have been referred to the apostolic see, lest we seem to be concerned only with our own privileges. It is enough to show what you ought to have done according to the rules of the Fathers and the canons, especially since even the public laws, following ecclesiastical regulation, have decreed that such persons may be judged only by bishops.

But if they were accused of any heresy, all the more ought those who were able to investigate such matters according to the requirements of religion, and who possessed the ancient pontifical authority of judgment preserved from the beginning of the Christian religion, to have examined them. For they were either Catholics or heretics—those against whom such mockeries were everywhere carried out and such detestable acts of brigandage raged. If they were heretics, they ought by every means to have been exposed, examined, and lawfully convicted, whether refuted by their own confessions or by the testimony of others. I say nothing of the fact that, according to the paternal custom, the matter ought to have been referred to us. I merely point out what ecclesiastical law required to be done.

[Col. 0975C]

But if they were proved to be Catholics, then you, who not only failed to intervene in their expulsion but also chose to communicate with those who were indisputably heretics substituted in their place, cannot have been ignorant of the cause of the faith and of Catholic communion, made manifest throughout the whole world through so many bishops. Yet knowingly and willingly, without any investigation of the facts, without any synodal examination, and without any reverence for or assent to the apostolic see, you gladly accepted heretics and patiently allowed Catholic bishops to be driven out in a previously unheard-of and pitiable manner.

[Col. 0975D]

If you thought that these men had strayed from the sound faith and Catholic communion, you ought, according to the decrees of the Fathers and as had always been done, to have referred the matter to the apostolic see—as Acacius is shown to have done concerning Peter of Alexandria, Peter of Antioch, John, and Paul. But since you knew that they shared the judgment of the apostolic see, and since it is evident that, through such great and distinguished bishops, the Eastern pontiffs could not have been ignorant of what the apostolic see had decided, they were revealed through those bishops as opponents of Catholic and apostolic communion and as having defected from it. You were not united with those bishops in their suffering; rather, you were bound by association with their persecutors.

[Col. 0976A]

Here a synod never came to your mind—and certainly the persons concerned were not bound by any old law. Here it never entered your mind that, through a priestly council, the Church of the entire East—not merely the Church of one city or one bishop—ought to be cared for. But you, who had fallen in the opposite direction with your entire purpose and inclination, deliberately avoided councils, even though they were necessary, lest through them some decision be reached by which, once your plainly offensive conduct had been lawfully refuted, it would be declared impermissible to enter into the fellowship of heretics.

Why, then, do you plead ignorance, when throughout the entire East you saw so many pontiffs not only recognize the Catholic faith and the sincere communion corresponding to the apostolic see, but also defend them with the greatest steadfastness to the very end? If you had not heard what we judged concerning the faith and Catholic and apostolic communion, you ought to have looked to those men and either followed them if you believed them to be Catholics, or accused them before the apostolic see if you believed that they had erred. [Col. 0976B]

You ought either to have followed, in your immediate presence, your colleagues and brothers who held that judgment by their own purpose or because they knew what the apostolic see had defined, or to have attacked them if you believed them to be in error. You ought not to have given your consent to those by whom they were harassed without distinction, until the truth concerning all of them had been made clear and the regular form of ecclesiastical judgment had proceeded against them.

But if, by following the rule of the apostolic see, you perceived that those men maintained this steadfastness, then through them you could not have been uncertain about what our definition contained. By agreeing with their persecutors, you withdrew from the fellowship of the apostolic see, even though you knew its judgment; and yet you still say that you do not know what the apostolic see had decided.

[Col. 0976C]

With those priests unwilling to abandon the Catholic faith and communion, you learned everything not through words or letters but from their presence. You appear to have separated yourselves from that communion by your own judgment, and yet you still say that a synod ought to have dealt with the person of one man, although you did not demand one when so many Catholic pontiffs were condemned.

Whom, then, do you want us to trust concerning the report of such cases: Catholics who are separated from every contagion of heretics, or heretics polluted by communion with heretics? Who does not see that those men are Catholic members of the Church and entirely alien to every heretical plague—men driven from their own cities and sent into exile—and that those who dared to become their successors while the Catholics were still alive are not Catholics at all, but either open Eutychians or communicants of the followers of Eutyches? This plague continues among them even today.

[Col. 0976D]

For those who succeeded the Catholics were indiscriminately joined in communion both with Peter of Alexandria and with Peter of Antioch, and to this day they are joined in communion with the successors of both Peters. Add also those who, although they did not succeed the Catholics, nevertheless joined themselves to the communion of such men while Catholic pontiffs were still recognized: this is that mixture. This is the confusion spread throughout the whole East, where no distinction is made between Catholic and heretical communion. Indeed, anyone who attempts to make a distinction is considered a heretic, struck by persecution, and punished with exile and affliction.

[Col. 0977A]

It therefore remains that, in this foul mixture of all things, just as anyone who is proved to have separated himself from it is accordingly Catholic and of sincere communion, so anyone found to be a participant in that detestable association is as far removed from Catholic and apostolic communion as he is from sincere communion. No one should plead that perhaps he did not communicate, or does not appear to communicate, with some particularly obvious heretic. What does it help if he does not communicate with that man but nevertheless joins himself in communion to those who differ in no way from that man’s communion? What if he has communicated with none of them, or does not communicate at all? Only then will he belong to sincere, Catholic, and apostolic communion and faith; otherwise he can in no way avoid the insincere contagion of that indiscriminate mixture.

In this way, the good man Acacius is also exposed as having communicated, through others and without any ambiguity, with Peter of Antioch, with whom he openly boasted that he did not communicate. For Acacius did not suspend himself from communion with all those who communicated with Peter of Antioch. What, then, did it accomplish that he wished to appear not to communicate openly with the man to whom he was bound through his accomplices under the sign of communion? Acacius communicated with Peter of Alexandria.

[Col. 0977B]

But as long as Peter of Antioch lived—for it is shown that he died after the pact was made between Acacius and Peter of Alexandria—Peter of Alexandria never ceased to communicate with Peter of Antioch. This is contained in the report of Catholic priests and holy men who remained in the Catholic faith. It cannot be hidden from the conscience of the whole East.

[Col. 0977C]

And, to say nothing of the fact that Acacius undoubtedly communicated through the emperor Zeno himself, who was joined in communion with Peter of Antioch—the man whom Zeno had introduced and whose priesthood he had approved—we can point to very many bishops of different cities who communicated with Peter of Antioch and with whom Acacius nevertheless communicated. Through them, consequently, he also communicated with Peter of Antioch.

But among the Greeks this easy mixture is considered blameless, since among them there is no distinction between truth and falsehood. And although they wish to be joined in fellowship with all the reprobate, they are shown to possess no integrity.

[Col. 0977D]

This is that Peter of Antioch whom Acacius did not request even the apostolic see to receive through repentance or Catholic communion. Consequently, when they complain to us that Acacius was condemned, the very profession set forth above shows that, by the winding paths through which he sought to have Peter of Antioch received into communion, Acacius himself condemned him.

In this matter Acacius is not the only one held guilty: all the pontiffs of the East are also held guilty, since they fell into these contagions in the same manner and are rightly bound by a similar condemnation. They can in no way free themselves from it unless, while they remain alive, they abstain from such men.

Nor ought we, in such cases, to trust anyone except those who either know that, by divine favor, they have kept themselves entirely separate from the bonds of this perfidy, or those who have withdrawn from the company of the perfidious. [Col. 0978A]

What confidence can we place in the testimony of those established in the contagion of the perfidious, as evidence of sincere communion, when we who are placed in sincere communion cannot rely for the truth on the testimony of those who strive to attack the truth with falsehoods? It remains, therefore, that we ought to trust only those who are free from every contagion.

[Col. 0978A]

## Letter of Pope Gelasius to Eunifimius

**To his most beloved brother Eunifimius, Gelasius.**

Your affection asserts what we plainly desire to have confirmed through the sincere restoration of faith and Catholic communion. Since hearing alone is not sufficient for one person unless, through letters, he has observed the one who provokes him, you have urged me to write concerning what divine providence has accomplished among us, so that, in favorable circumstances, I might offer a greeting in return.

[Col. 0978B]

We do not suppose that either your affection or anyone else could have hoped that, in reporting what had happened, we ought to have sought a response from someone superior, for it would have been judged excessively arrogant if he had thought in such a way about the first see.

But if we understand you to have meant instead that, as companions to whom the duty of presiding has been entrusted by Christ, we ought to have indicated in your letters that the apostolic see should have been led by a newly appointed priest, you should know that there was once among our Fathers an ancient ecclesiastical rule by which the one Catholic and apostolic communion remained free from every pollution of transgressors.

Now, however, you prefer to maintain an external association rather than return to the pure and undefiled fellowship of blessed Peter. “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm 136:4). How shall we offer to men of external communion the ancient covenants of the apostolic order? How will the one from whom you announce our ordination to have proceeded respond to us, when, even according to your own testimony, you place heretics and condemnation before him?

[Col. 0978C]

Perhaps your affection will say that Acacius and Peter are called condemned heretics. Why, if it is lawful, do we not at least discuss this through the present letters? Because we call those who participate in the Lord’s table by one name, and by another those who disagree with us in fellowship with him. The Lord himself spoke in one way to those separated from his preaching and in another way opened the secrets of the kingdom of heaven to his disciples. Accordingly, the Apostles also did not speak in the same manner to those separated from their company as they did to their associates and companions in the faith.

[Col. 0978D]

But your affection says that you held so much love toward me that you were not content merely to hear of your desire to write. Hear the sentence: “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Romans 10:17)—that is, through the Word who promised, in the confession of the blessed Apostle Peter, that “the gates of hell would never prevail” (Matthew 16:18).

For that reason you reasonably judged that the faithful God would not have promised anything of this kind in his words unless he intended it, and that he would fulfill the one promise of his pledge. Finally, your affection says that, through the grace of divine providence, he demonstrated that he does not abandon the love of the holy Churches, since he placed me upon the pontifical see—not, as you say, as one who needs instruction, but as one who attends to everything necessary for the unity of the ecclesiastical body.

[Col. 0979A]

I am indeed the least of all men and wholly unworthy of the office of so great a see, except that heavenly grace always accomplishes great things through the small. “What, then, should I think of myself, when the teacher of the nations himself testifies this concerning himself—he who declares that he is the last and not worthy to be called an apostle?” (1 Corinthians 15:9).

Nevertheless, to return to your words: if you have truly declared that these things were divinely bestowed upon me—and indeed whatever things are good are gifts of God—then follow the exhortations of one who does not need to be taught and who, according to heavenly disposition, observes everything that pertains to the unity of the Churches, resisting firmly, as you say, the devil, the disturber of true peace and harmony.

If, then, you make these statements about me, either you ought to follow what Christ established, as you forbid, or you openly reveal that you oppose Christ’s arrangements, or you are recognized as boasting these things about me in order to obtain pardon for your excess.

[Col. 0979B]

You add, accordingly, that I am able, by accommodating myself to you and through excellent arrangement, to restore harmony. Since you frequently use this word, let me investigate what it means. The excellent arrangement of the Catholic and apostolic Church is that which rises toward better things by advancing upward, not that which declines toward lower things by descending.

[Col. 0979B]

When you say that we ought to descend with you, you show that you are now either descending or have descended. From where, I ask, and to where is this descent? Clearly, from some higher place you have cast yourselves down to lower things. You see, you recognize, and you do not deny that you have fallen from Catholic and apostolic communion into heretical and condemned communion; and not only do you take pleasure in lying among the weak, but you also wish to drive down those who remain in the higher see.

[Col. 0979C]

You invite us to descend with you; we ask you to ascend with us from the depths to the heights. Let the human race now judge before that lofty justice which of us ought to obey the other.

Or will you say—to leave aside the rest for now—that the Lord himself descended from heaven? He certainly descended, but in order to free humanity from error, not to mix himself with its error. Did he not himself warn that those standing on the roof should not descend, nor go down to take away the things thought to be in the house? Did not the Apostle—“the one who labored more than all” (1 Corinthians 15:10)—cry out on behalf of everyone, when the preservation of the truth was at issue: “We did not yield in submission even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you”?

[Col. 0979D]

Do you see the heavenly Teacher refusing to accommodate himself to those who are harmful? Finally, let us suppose that someone has fallen and that a compassionate person wishes to bend down slightly in order to lift him up. It is fitting to incline oneself in compassion so that the one lying down may be raised, not so that one may fall with him into the pit.

Therefore, through the letters which you sent by the deacon Sinelicius, concerning those whom Acacius baptized and ordained, we offer you without difficulty the remedy prepared according to the tradition of the Fathers and especially suited to the true concern for religion. How much farther do you want us to descend? Why are you silent? Why are you ashamed to express in words what you carry in your hearts? That very shame ought at least sometimes to have warned you.

[Col. 0980A]

Perhaps you want us to agree that the names of condemned heretics and of those who communicate with them or with their successors should be admitted? This is not descending in order to provide assistance, but plainly plunging into hell. Spare, I beg you, both us and yourselves. But if you have so little concern for yourselves, grant us forgiveness.

We can and ought to grieve and weep, but we neither can nor ought to be led into these precipices. By the favor of our God, we desire to retain the sincere and pure faith and communion of the paternal tradition, kept separate from every contagion of transgressors, and, choosing—if God wills—to endure any hardship rather than incur grounds for eternal condemnation, even at the risk of death.

[Col. 0980B]

Grant forgiveness, I say, if you willingly incur these things for the love of some human being or through fear. We reject such things for the love of God and through fear of Gehenna. Nor should you think that, by concealing the cases and persons involved, you can steal them away under the cover of anyone’s friendship. You are not so subtle that you cannot be understood, and, by the favor of our God, you do not find us unwary.

Have you not often indicated in letters sent here that, along with the other heretics, you also reject Eutyches? If this is true, then either reject those who communicated with the successors of Eutyches, whom you have likewise condemned, or admit also those who communicate with the successors of other heretics. But, you say, Acacius is nowhere recorded as having said anything against the faith, as Eutyches and his successor did—as though it were not worse both to have known the truth and nevertheless to have communicated with the enemies of the truth.

For if someone who thinks rightly about the faith communicates with those heretics among whom you have placed Eutyches, or with their successors, it is not permissible to name them among the altars of Catholics. So, by communicating with the successors of that Eutyches, is he not likewise held liable to the same fate? Concerning such people it is appropriately said: “Let them descend alive into hell” (Psalm 54:16)—those who, while they are thought to live that true and catholic life by which the just man lives, suddenly incline either toward the precipice of depravity or toward the hell of heretical communion.

Behold the kind of people whom you say are to be preferred to Christ, although he does not command even our souls to be preferred to himself. Indeed, you still ask when Acacius was condemned, as though, even if no one had condemned him beforehand, he would not have deserved to be excluded from orthodox and apostolic communion, since by participation he became its transgressor and deserter. Likewise, anyone who was previously a Catholic but communicates with any heresy is rightly judged to be removed from our fellowship, and, if he dies in such a condition, is in no way to be counted among the names of Catholics.

Yet we are amazed at how you make these claims: you profess to accept the Council of Chalcedon on behalf of the catholic faith, but you do not think that those whom it condemned—the communicants of the sectarians—were likewise and universally condemned. Show, then, which council, in any heresy, does not condemn together with the errors their successors who communicate with them, and all their accomplices.

Thus your Acacius, who became a participant in the Eutychian heresies through detestable communion, was without doubt condemned by that same council. It overthrew Eutyches, Dioscorus, their successors, and those who communicated with them, in the language of its synodal decision. In the same way it also cast down their followers Timothy and Peter by a similar definition. Therefore, if you truly and certainly follow what was defined at the Council of Chalcedon, according to apostolic law, for the catholic faith and communion—as your repeated profession maintains—either reject the successors of those condemned by that council and those who communicate with them, or, if you admit them, understand that you not only falsely claim to retain matters that no council has established for the catholic and apostolic faith and communion, but even attempt to undermine them; and you relapse without reconsideration into the Eutychian heresy, and are rightly judged by Catholics to be people to be avoided.

For, so that we might always escape such a pestilence, the Catholic bishops not only of the apostolic see but also of the eastern regions have decreed that the things beneficially established against it by that assembly of holy Fathers must in no way be mutilated.

Do you say that Peter, with whom Acacius communicated, was purged? Prove it by your assertions. Show this; establish it. By what means, by what rules, was he cleansed from the Eutychian profession or communion? Once it has nevertheless become evident, established by a clear demonstration of the facts, you will be able openly and plainly to recognize either that you must yield to the truth or that you are fighting against it in manifest conflict.

Do not flatter yourselves that you hold the catholic faith because you have supported the name of Eutyches, on the grounds that you appear to preach things that orthodox antiquity preached. For that evangelical sentence cries out against you: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matthew 12:33). A tree is known by its fruits. Therefore, if by voice, faith, and catholic and apostolic profession you faithfully and truly glory in this faith, accept its communion as well. But if the communion of heretics—that is, of condemned persons—and of those who communicate with them or with their successors pleases you, why do you stand still? Why do you look around? Remove their obstacles openly and plainly, and defend their doctrine.

For what does it accomplish? Rather, it greatly burdens you to promise in words what your deeds deny. In this way you may recognize not only how destructive the Eutychian heresy itself is to the Christian sacrament, but also how great and how serious are the things that heresy contains in its own definition.

Behold the precipices toward which you provoke us to descend, and how you wish to incline us toward the dangers of eternal life. Is this descent the saving of a sick person, or is it perishing together with the sick?

Will that be the excellent arrangement for restoring concord which you mention? Or rather this: that, once the contagion of the faithless has been rejected, the catholic and apostolic communion may possess the fullness of its sincere faith; that, after the filth of the heretics has been driven away, it may strive to uphold an undefiled confession of its faith; and that there may be unity in orthodox profession and communion, mutually consistent with itself?

As your loving letter urges, I also implore, insofar as I am able, that this unity be preserved in my time—the unity that those glorious Fathers kept undefiled and untouched for so many years. For this is, as you yourself say, what our God foreordained would turn out well in every respect, what was to be governed according to his truth and rule, and what he fittingly adapted by his providence to each period.

This is the will of God, which you mention and which I too, according to the measure the Lord may graciously grant, desire entirely to fulfill, lest I be found guilty of diminishing this heavenly talent. In this talent, as you yourself also admonish us, I ask to attain an increase belonging to Christ and to suffer absolutely no loss.

For this reason, as your own page also indicated, I took upon myself sorrow for your salvation in my earlier letter of affection, when I discovered what was harmful to you and found it contrary to true peace. The Apostle grieves over the error of those who go astray and receives joy when they are corrected by his preaching.

But if your affection, as you said, is constrained by the necessity of I know not whom, forgive me for saying so: a priest who must speak the truth ought not at all to refrain from speaking. Forgive us, timid men that we are, if we are constrained by the terrible urgency of divine judgment—a great necessity that urges us, as befits whatever sort of ministers of Christ we may be, to lay down our lives so that they may be saved by the truth, rather than wishing to gain them by diminishing the truth and thereby losing them—not to mention surrendering them to the will of anyone whatsoever against the faith.

Those are the things which your affection commends to me: a sure faith and an enduring friendship in the heart of Christ with whoever has desired it. Here we do not so much wish, as you say, to be preferred to others as to share with all the faithful a fellowship that is holy and pleasing to God.

This is the solid peace that your affection enjoins upon me: unshaken and everlasting, this one salutary bond—which, as you yourself also desire, can unite the whole Church. May divine protection perfect those to whom this has been entrusted, as you too entreat.

This is the love of which it is said, “God is love” (1 John 4:8), and which you seek “from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5). How, then, can there be a pure heart if it has been polluted by participation with heretics? How can there be a good conscience if it has been mixed with the confusion of evil people? How can there be an unfeigned faith if it has been mingled with the faithless?

If your prudence carefully attends to this, as we proclaim God, it will perceive that the apostolic see does not avoid peace, but avoids the footsteps of heretics and condemned persons. You too, looking reasonably upon this, believe that the people of Constantinople should be reconciled, but do not permit them to be removed under the name of the faithless.

Who, I ask you, could hear this in the Church of God, when the flock ought certainly to follow the shepherd who calls it back to salutary pastures, not the shepherd who strays while the flock wanders off the path? Tell me, I beg you: are you going to give an account for the flock, or the flock for you?

Certainly, if this pleases you, our cause is much more just. We willingly listened to the Roman people, who would not at all permit themselves to depart from the faith they had laudably received through the tradition of their ancestors. If you do not wish to offend the people of Constantinople when they refuse to depart from heretical communion, but say that we ought to direct them because we can calm them, how will it listen to me, when it appears to regard me with suspicion? If it despises its own bishops when they admonish it, has it not been commanded even to the apostles in certain regions not to use the preaching of the word?

“But they were not to be listened to,” you say. We shall come, brother Eunifimus, without doubt we shall come to that fearsome tribunal of Christ. I shall say nothing of the vengeance that must be feared from this, nor of those who will stand around us—those by whom the faith itself was defended.

There it will not be a matter of denials, delays, or evasions, but it must be demonstrated most clearly whether the glorious confession of blessed Peter withheld anything necessary for salvation from any of those whom he received to govern, or whether obstinate wickedness, rebellious even at its own peril, wished to conceal it.

There it will certainly be made clear whether I am, as you think, bitter, harsh, excessively severe, difficult, and hard toward you, when I labor with reason for your salvation and cry out—even if the antidote seems bitter—“Take it, please; drink it; live. I do not want you to die.”

Or whether it is you who, prevented from harmful things, consider physicians accursed—indeed, who would rather have the physicians fall ill with you than receive health yourselves.

And with the other hand: May the Lord keep you safe and sound.

## The Order of the Old Testament

The order of the Old Testament, which the holy and catholic Roman Church receives and venerates, arranged by Pope Gelasius with seventy bishops.

One book of Genesis. One book of Exodus. One book of Leviticus. One book of Numbers. One book of Deuteronomy. One book of Joshua son of Nun. One book of Judges. One book of Ruth. One book of Kings. Two books of Chronicles. One book containing the 150 Psalms. Three books of Solomon: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Also, one book of Wisdom. One book of Ecclesiasticus.

Also, the order of the prophets: one book of Isaiah. One book of Jeremiah. One book of Lamentations [the source reads *Emoch*]. One book of Ezekiel. One book of Daniel. One book of Hosea. One book of Amos. One book of Micah. One book of Joel. One book of Obadiah. One book of Jonah. One book of Nahum. One book of Habakkuk. One book of Zephaniah. One book of Haggai. One book of Zechariah. One book of Malachi.

Also, the order of the historical books: one book of Job. One book of Tobit. One book of Ezra. One book of Esther. One book of Judith. One book of Maccabees.

Also, the order of the Scriptures of the New and eternal Testament: four books of the Gospels—one book according to Matthew, one according to Mark, one according to Luke, and one according to John. One book of the Acts of the Apostles.

The letters of the apostle Paul, fourteen in number: one letter to the Romans; two letters to the Corinthians; one letter to the Ephesians; two letters to the Thessalonians; one letter to the Galatians; one letter to the Philippians; two letters to Timothy; one letter to Titus; one letter to Philemon; one letter to the Hebrews.

Also, one book of the Apocalypse of John.

Also, seven catholic letters: two letters of the apostle Peter; one letter of the apostle James; three letters of the apostle John; one letter of Jude the Zealot, apostle.

## The Decrees of Pope Gelasius Begin

### Decree Held with Seventy Bishops Concerning the Apocryphal Scriptures

After the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures, upon which the catholic Church has been founded by the grace of God, we think it should also be made known that, although all the catholic Churches throughout the world constitute one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman, catholic, and apostolic Church has been set above the other Churches not by synodal decrees, but by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior it has obtained primacy:

“You are Peter,” he said, “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:18–19).

It was also granted the fellowship of the most blessed apostle Paul, the vessel of election. Contrary to the chatter of heretics, he did not die at a different time, but at one time and on the same day as Peter, crowned by a glorious death in the city of Rome, suffering under the emperor Nero. Together they consecrated the aforesaid holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord and, by their presence and venerable triumph, placed it above all the cities in the entire world.

The first see, therefore, is the Roman Church of the apostle Peter, having neither stain nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind. The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist. Sent by the apostle Peter into Egypt, Mark preached the word of truth and completed a glorious martyrdom.

The third see, at Antioch, is held in honor because it was there that the same most blessed apostle Peter lived before he came to Rome. There too the name of the Christians, that new people, first arose.

And although “no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3:11), nevertheless, for our edification, the same holy Roman Church, after the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament that we have regularly received, does not forbid the reception also of the following Scriptures:

The holy Council of Nicaea of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, held under the auspices of Maximus Constantine Augustus.

The holy Council of Ephesus, at which Nestorius was condemned, with the consent of the most blessed Pope Celestine, through Cyril, bishop of the see of Alexandria, and Arcadius, sent from Italy.

The holy Council of Chalcedon, held under the auspices of the emperor Marcian and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, at which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies were likewise condemned, together with Dioscorus and his accomplices.

And any councils instituted by the holy Fathers: after the authority of these, we command that they be both preserved and received.

Also, the works of blessed Cyril, Cyprian the martyr and bishop of Carthage.

Also, the works of blessed Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus.

Also, the works of blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia.

Also, the works of blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Also, the works of blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria.

Also, the works of blessed John, bishop of Constantinople.

Also, the works of blessed Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria.

Also, the works of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.

Also, the works of blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

Also, the works of blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo.

Also, the works of Jerome, presbyter.

Also, the works of Prosper, a most religious man.

Also, the letter of Pope Leo to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. If anyone disputes its text down to a single iota and does not receive it in every respect with reverence, let him be anathema.

Also, we decree that the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect departed from the fellowship of the holy Roman Church, nor separated from its faith or preaching, but by the grace of God remained participants in that communion until the final day of their lives, are to be read.

Also, the decretal letters that the most blessed popes issued from the city of Rome at different times for the consolation of various Fathers are to be received with reverence.

Also, the acts of the holy martyrs, who shine through the manifold torments of their sufferings and the wondrous triumphs of their confessions. What Catholic would doubt that they endured greater things in their struggles and bore everything not by their own strength but by the grace and assistance of God?

Nevertheless, according to ancient custom, they are not read in the holy Roman Church with special caution, because the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and because they are thought to contain material supplied by uneducated unbelievers that is excessive or less suitable than the order of events required—for example, the passions of Cyricus and Julitta, of George, and of others of this kind, which are said to have been composed by heretics. Therefore, as has been said, they are not read in the holy Roman Church, lest even a slight opportunity for mockery arise.

Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Church, we venerate with complete devotion all the martyrs and their glorious struggles, which are known more fully to them than to human beings.

Also, we receive with all honor the lives of the Fathers—Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—as they were written by the most blessed Jerome.

Also, the acts of blessed Silvester, bishop of the apostolic see. Although the name of the person who wrote them is unknown, we have learned that many Catholics in the city of Rome read them, and that many things in them have been changed according to the ancient custom of the Church.

Also, the writing concerning the discovery of the Lord’s cross, and another writing concerning the discovery of the head of John the Baptist, are certain recent accounts, and some Catholics read them. But when these come into the hands of Catholics, the sentence of the apostle Paul must precede them: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good.”

Also, Rufinus, a religious man, produced many books of ecclesiastical work and interpreted certain Scriptures. But since blessed Jerome censured him on certain matters concerning free choice, we hold those opinions that we know the aforesaid blessed Jerome held. This applies not only to Rufinus but also to various others whom that frequently mentioned man rebuked out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith.

Also, we have accepted for reading certain works of Origen that the most blessed Jerome does not reject. But all the rest, together with their author, we declare should be rejected.

The *Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea* and his book of *Ecclesiastical History*, although in the first book of his narrative he was lukewarm and later wrote a book in praise and defense of Origen the schismatic, nevertheless, because of the exceptional knowledge of events relevant everywhere to instruction, we do not declare them wholly to be rejected.

Also, we praise Orosius, a most learned man, because he composed a history that was highly necessary and suitable for us against the calumnies of the pagans, and wove it together with marvelous brevity.

Also, we venerate the Paschal work of Sedulius, which he wrote in heroic verse, and we hold it in high esteem with distinguished praise.

Likewise, we do not despise the laborious work of Juvencus, but marvel at it.

The catholic and apostolic Roman Church in no way receives the other works written or preached by heretics or schismatics. Of these, we believe that a few that come to mind, and that Catholics must avoid, should be set forth.

Also, a list of apocryphal books that are not received:

The Council of Ariminum, convened by Constantius Caesar, son of Constantine, through the prefect Taurus, it confesses to have been condemned then, now, and forever.

The itinerary under the name of the apostle Peter, which is called the *Books of Saint Clement*, ten books: apocryphal.

The Acts under the name of the apostle Andrew: apocryphal.

The Acts under the name of the apostle Thomas: apocryphal.

The Acts under the name of Philip: apocryphal.

The Gospel under the name of Matthias: apocryphal.

The Gospel under the name of the apostle Peter: apocryphal.

The Gospel under the name of James: apocryphal.

The Gospel under the name of Barnabas: apocryphal.

The Gospel under the name of Thomas, which the Manichaeans use: apocryphal.

The Gospel under the name of the apostle Bartholomew: apocryphal.

The Gospels falsified by Lucian: apocryphal.

The book concerning the infancy of the Savior: apocryphal.

The Gospels falsified by Esitius: apocryphal.

The book concerning the nativity of the Savior, Mary, and the midwife: apocryphal.

The book called *The Shepherd*: apocryphal.

All the books composed by Lucius, a disciple of the devil: apocryphal.

The book called *The Foundation*: apocryphal.

The book called *The Treasure*: apocryphal.

The book concerning the daughters of Adam, of Genesis: apocryphal.

The book called *The Acts of Thecla and the Apostle Paul*: apocryphal.

The book called *Nepos*: apocryphal.

The book of Proverbs written by heretics and entitled with the name of Saint Syrti: apocryphal.

The revelation called that of the apostle Thomas: apocryphal.
