The revelation called that of Stephen: apocryphal.

The revelation called that of Paul: apocryphal.

The book called *The Passing*, that is, the Assumption of Saint Mary: apocryphal.

The book called *The Repentance of Adam*: apocryphal.

The book of Ogias, named after the giant who is said to have fought with the dragon after the flood: apocryphal.

The book called *The Testament of Job*: apocryphal.

The book called *The Repentance of Saint Cyprian*: apocryphal.

The book called *The Repentance of Janua and Mambra*: apocryphal.

The book called *The Lots of the Apostles*: apocryphal.

The book called *The Praise of the Apostles*: apocryphal.

The book *Physiologus*, written by heretics and marked with the name of blessed Ambrose: apocryphal.

The history of Eusebius Pamphilus: apocryphal.

The works of Tertullian: apocryphal.

The works of Lactantius: apocryphal.

The works of Africanus: apocryphal.

The works of Postumianus and Gallus: apocryphal.

The works of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla: apocryphal.

All the works of Faustus the Manichaean: apocryphal.

The works of Commodianus: apocryphal.

The works of the other Clement of Alexandria: apocryphal.

The works of Thascius Cyprian: apocryphal.

The works of Arnobius: apocryphal.

The works of Tyconius: apocryphal.

The works of Cassian, presbyter of Gaul: apocryphal.

The works of Victorinus of Pettau: apocryphal.

The works of Faustus of Riez in Gaul: apocryphal.

The works of Frumentius the blind man: *Cento on Christ* composed in Virgilian verses [the wording is uncertain]: apocryphal.

The letter of Jesus to King Abgar: apocryphal.

The letter of Abgar to Jesus: apocryphal.

The passion of Cyricus and Julitta: apocryphal.

The passion of George: apocryphal.

The writing called *The Contradiction of Solomon*: apocryphal.

All phylacteries that, contrary to what those people fabricate, were written not by the craft of angels but rather by the craft of demons: apocryphal.

These and all similar works, Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, Paul of Samosata, Photinus, Bonosus, and those who fell away through similar error taught. Likewise Montanus with his most obscene followers; Apollinaris, Valentinus, Faustus, Africanus, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Sabbatius, Coelestius, Donatus, Eustathius, Jovinianus, Pelagius, Julian of Celanum, Coelestius, Maximinus, Priscillian of Spain, Nestorius of Constantinople, Maximus the One [the wording is uncertain], Lampetius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter and the other Peter—one of whom polluted Alexandria and the other Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople with his associates, and all heretics and the disciples of heretics or schismatics whose names are not retained.

These, we confess, have been not merely rejected but expelled from the entire Roman, catholic, and apostolic Church, and, together with their authors and the followers of their authors, condemned forever under the unbreakable bond of anathema.

# The Decrees of Pope Anastasius Begin

[Col. 0987]

1. That he acts as an ambassador on behalf of Christ while praying for the peace of the Church.  
2. That judgment must not rashly be passed on those who have departed to the Lord.  
3. That the name of Acacius should specifically be kept silent in the Church.  
4. That contention must be avoided with the greatest care.  
5. That the emperor should admonish the Alexandrians to return to sincere faith and catholic peace.  
6. That the emperor should be admonished to obey the ordinances of the apostolic see.  
7. That no share of injury affects those whom Acacius baptized or ordained after his condemnation.  
8. That evil people, by administering good things, harm only themselves and do not defile the sacraments of the Church.

## To Anastasius Augustus

To the most glorious and merciful son, Anastasius Augustus: Anastasius, bishop.

At the beginning of my pontificate, I first proclaim to the people the peace that has been offered. Confidently, on behalf of the catholic faith, I, a sinner, approach your humble piety. In this I trust that divine favor has first drawn near to me: that the consonance of your august name now undoubtedly provides assistance, so that, just as the exalted name of your piety shines throughout all nations and across the whole world, so, through the ministry of my humility, the see of the most blessed Peter may retain in the universal Church the primacy assigned to it by the Lord God, as it has always done.

Nor, because of one dead man, should that tunic of the Savior, woven from above throughout, continue for a longer time to suffer the uncertainty of an evil fate—especially while your serenity governs the commonwealth. Even in private life, he was devoted to the pursuit of sincere religion, so that, as reputation most certainly proclaimed, no one among the foremost priests was said to have guarded the rules of the Church established by the holy Fathers more carefully. We trust that this holy devotion has grown together with the majesty of the empire.

### I

We therefore act as ambassadors on behalf of Christ. Do not allow those whose merits or deeds cannot be hidden from that Judge, before whose judgment they now stand, to be publicly named because of offense or scandal. Nor should rash presumption intrude there into the mortal body that still remains, where not only open confession establishes the merits of each person, but even the secret of silence cannot remain hidden.

For without doubt our predecessor Pope Felix and Acacius are there, in the place where each person, under so great a Judge, cannot lose the quality of his merit.

### II

Therefore, since the most blessed Apostle admonishes us, let your tranquillity recognize that this must be observed: the Church must not be offended while we attempt to judge those who have already passed away, although we cannot do so.

For he says concerning those who presume to judge matters belonging to God alone:

“None of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. For whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s. For Christ rose from the dead for this purpose, that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead. But you, why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.’ Therefore each of us shall give an account of himself to God. Let us therefore no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling block or a scandal before your brother” (Romans 14:7–14).

The blessed Apostle therefore warns us not to presume to judge those concerning whom no one can judge better or more truly than God. No one should rashly usurp this judgment for himself and thereby cause the peace and unity of the Church to be dispersed.

For it is also said in the Book of Kings: “God does not see as man sees, because man sees the face, but God sees the heart” (1 Kings 16:7).

Likewise, in the First Book of Chronicles: “And now, Solomon, know the God of your fathers, and serve him with a perfect heart and a willing mind, for God searches all hearts and knows every thought” (1 Chronicles 28:9).

Likewise, in Ezekiel the Lord God says: “If you have said, O house of Israel, and I know the thoughts of your spirit” (Ezekiel 11:5).

Hence it is also said of the Lord who judges in the Gospel: “But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said: Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matthew 9:4).

### III

We therefore entreat your affection that the name of Acacius be kept silent in particular, so that what has stirred up scandal or offense in the Church for many reasons may be silenced by a specific designation. As we have said, however, when he is included in the generality of priests, his merit cannot be hidden from him who knows what must be assigned to each person according to the judged distribution of merits, and to whom even thoughts are manifest.

As for how many excesses and presumptions Acacius possessed, it may perhaps seem burdensome to suggest them one by one to your clemency. To my brothers and fellow bishops Cresconius and Germanus, whom we sent to your serenity concerning the individual matters of Acacius and the kind of man he was, we gave your clemency a full account, to be reviewed in greater detail if your piety should wish to investigate more carefully. Thus it may not appear that the truth was lacking in anything in our report, and, by your divine wisdom, you may clearly see that the sentence pronounced against Acacius did not proceed from pride or arrogance on the part of the apostolic see, but was extorted by definite crimes, insofar as we judge that judgment—which alone cannot err—to have been compelled chiefly by zeal for divine justice.

### IV

We, however, humbly beseech you: we do not wish controversy to remain in the Church, since contention must rather be avoided, as it is said in Proverbs: “Contention stirs up hatred” (Proverbs 10:12).

The friendship of my soul protects all who do not contend. For the Apostle also says to the Corinthians: “Since there are jealousies and contentions among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” (2 Corinthians 12:20).

Likewise, to the Philippians:

“If there is therefore any consolation in Christ, any appeal of love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any compassion and mercy, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, united in soul and intent on one purpose; doing nothing through contention or empty glory, but in humility of mind considering one another superior to yourselves, each looking not to his own interests but to those of others” (Philippians 2:1–5).

### V

This above all I make known to your most glorious and merciful serenity, Augustus, my son: when the case of the Alexandrians has been laid open to your most pious ears, cause them by your authority, wisdom, and divine admonitions to return to the catholic and sincere faith.

If you also command that what must be held in the catholic religion according to the definitions of the Fathers and the preaching of all the priests who have flourished in the Church be recalled to those who know it, we shall renew it in their memory; and we shall offer it, as our duty of instruction requires, to those who are ignorant, so that no boastfulness of intellect or depravity outside these things may be heard.

### VI

For the love of your empire and for the blessedness that its government may attain, which we proclaim as an apostolic benefit, we especially urge this: as is fitting and as the Holy Spirit dictates, let obedience be offered to our admonitions, so that all good things may come to your commonwealth, as is promised in Exodus:

“If you hear the voice of the Lord your God, do what is pleasing before him, obey his commandments, and observe all his justice, I will not bring upon you any of the weakness that I brought upon the Egyptians. For I am the Lord, who heals you” (Exodus 15:26).

And there again the most powerful trumpet sounds:

“Now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all his ways, love him, serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord your God and the ordinances that I command you?” (Deuteronomy 10:12–13).

May your piety not disregard these repeated admonitions. Keep before your eyes the word of the Lord in the Gospel:

“Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me; and whoever despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke 10:16).

The Apostle likewise, echoing our Savior, says:

“Therefore whoever despises these things does not despise man but God, who has also given his Holy Spirit among you” (1 Thessalonians 4:8).

The breast of your clemency is the sanctuary of public prosperity. May your excellence, whom the Lord has commanded to preside on earth as his representative, not resist the evangelical and apostolic commandments with harsh arrogance, but fulfill through obedience the things that bring salvation.

### VII

Now, according to the custom of the Catholic Church, let your most sacred and serene heart recognize that none of those whom Acacius baptized, nor of those whom he ordained priests or deacons according to the canons, suffers any portion of injury on account of Acacius’s name, so that the grace of the sacrament, perhaps conveyed through an unworthy person, might seem less secure. For even baptism administered far from the Church, whether by an adulterer or by a thief, reaches the recipient as an undefiled gift, because that voice which sounded through the dove excluded every stain of human pollution, when it declared and said: “This is he who baptizes with the Spirit and with fire” (John 1:33).

For if the visible rays of this sun, when they pass through the foulest places, are not stained by any contamination through contact, much more is the power of him who made this visible sun not constrained by any unworthiness of his minister. Judas, too, although he was sacrilegious and a thief, whatever he did among the apostles by virtue of the office entrusted to him, the benefits bestowed through an unworthy person suffered no diminution on that account, as the Lord himself declared in the clearest voice: “The scribes,” he says, “and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do, for they say things and do not do them” (Matthew 23:3).

Whatever, therefore, any minister in the Church appears to perform through his office for a perfected human being, all of it is contained in the fulfillment of the divine purpose. Thus Paul, through whom Christ speaks, affirms: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). God does not ask who preaches, or what sort of things he preaches, but whom he preaches; and he confirms that even the envious can preach Christ well—for by this very evil the devil himself was cast down, yet even so he does not cease to preach.

### VIII

Therefore, the man whose name we say must be retained here harmed himself by ministering good things badly. The inviolable sacrament that was given to others through him obtained the perfection of its power. Since this is so, the suspicious curiosity of some has extended so far that, after Pope Felix had issued his judgment, it imagines that Acacius thereafter acted ineffectively in the sacraments which he usurped [Col. 0991C–0992A]. Consequently, it makes those who received the mysteries conveyed either in consecration or in baptism fear that the divine gifts may appear void.

Let them remember that in this matter also the earlier ruling prevails in the same way, since he performed this act not without usurping the name of the priesthood, although the mysteries retained their power. In this matter also the guilty person did not harm himself. For the following, sung by the Davidic trumpet, applied to him: “Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of those who walk in their sins” (Psalm 67:22/68:21).

Pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon others, as the whole authority of the heavenly Scriptures bears witness. Thus it is also said through the Holy Spirit in the prophetic book: “He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Psalm 100:7). Therefore, when the condemned man claimed for himself the name of priest, the swelling of pride was inflicted upon his own head. The people who thirsted for the ministries of his house were not excluded; only that one soul which had sinned was, by the just judgment of its own guilt, liable to punishment.

What does the abundant instruction of the Scriptures everywhere attest? Therefore, setting aside the ambitions and craftiness of human beings who remain in this present frailty, in accordance with our prayers and with imperial authority, offer to our God one Catholic and apostolic Church. For this is the one thing by which you will be able to triumph without end, not only on earth but also in heaven.

After the subscription: May almighty God preserve your kingdom and your safety by perpetual protection, most glorious and most merciful, ever Augustus.

## THE DECREES OF POPE SYMMACHUS BEGIN

[Col. 0991]

[Col. 0991C]

1. That ecclesiastical property not be alienated, but be granted only for use to clerics, monks, or pilgrims.  
2. That no one obtain an office through bribes.  
3. That abductors of widows or virgins be expelled from communion with the Church.  
4. That widows or professed virgins who have vowed continence not marry thereafter.  
5. That no one approach the episcopate through canvassing.

### Symmachus to his most beloved brother Caesarius

The fairness of your request urges us gladly to grant the desire of your fraternity, since, concerning each of the matters for which you ask concessions from the Apostolic See, nothing is proposed that differs from the caution and provision of the Fathers. Although the rules of ecclesiastical punishment encompass everything, nevertheless we do not think it superfluous to repeat now what has so often been forbidden.

### Chapter I

We therefore do not permit possessions which anyone has given or left to his own church at its discretion to be alienated under any title or by any sale, or under any pretext whatsoever, unless perhaps necessity should require that they be granted to clerics on account of their meritorious service, to monasteries for the sake of religion, or indeed to pilgrims. Even then, they are to enjoy these things not perpetually but temporarily.

### II

We especially admonish that the ambitions of those who try to approach the priesthood not by the grace of God but through a prior promise of ecclesiastical property be restrained. Those who do not check themselves from such an intention must know that they will certainly be subjected to the penalties of the canons, so that they may not easily be permitted to approach the priesthood. For degrees and periods have been established through which they must aspire to this dignity. Whoever is promoted without the prescribed procedure does not easily escape offense, and without examination no one can obtain the judgment of a legitimate election.

### III

We detest abductors either of widows or of virgins because of the enormity of so great a crime, pursuing especially those who have attempted to join sacred virgins to marriage, whether willingly or unwillingly. Because of the atrociousness of this most wicked crime, we order them to be suspended from communion.

### IV

Nor do we permit widows to pass to marriage who have remained for a long time in a religious commitment. Likewise, we prohibit the marriage of virgins who have spent many years of their lives in monasteries.

### V

No one, therefore, shall be permitted to approach episcopal office through canvassing. For if this transgression is condemned in secular life, who doubts that it brings disgrace upon religious persons and those who serve God?

If anyone desiring the episcopate uses powerful persons as supporters by giving money, or compels clerics or citizens to subscribe to a decree made on his behalf by employing fear of any kind, or encourages them with any rewards, no decree shall be drawn up without the presence of a visitor, whose testimony can establish the unanimity of the clergy and citizens.

We therefore exhort all the faithful, for the sake of the Catholic religion and the peace of the Churches, to observe all these provisions with devoted hearts. For there is no doubt that, according to the venerable canons, transgressors of such prohibitions will suffer the loss of their own communion. We wish this, however, to be brought to the notice of all bishops.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of Probus.

## The chapters of the first Roman synod under Pope Symmachus begin

1. The proposal of Fulgentius, archdeacon of the Roman Church, concerning the synod assembled by order of Pope Symmachus.  
2. The intervention of Symmachus, that episcopal canvassing be eradicated.  
3. The synod’s judgment: if, while a pope is alive, anyone is proved to show favor in any manner to anyone for the Roman pontificate, he shall be deprived of his rank and of communion.  
4. If a pope, overtaken by death, has been unable beforehand to decide on the election of his successor, the bishop shall be ordained whom all the clergy, or at least the greater part, has chosen.  
5. If anyone exposes canvassers, or the supporters and conspirators of canvassers, he shall not merely be considered cleared if he was a participant, but shall also be judged most worthy of a reward.

After the consulship of Paulinus, a most illustrious man, on the Kalends of March, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, with the most blessed Pope Symmachus presiding over the synod, Fulgentius, archdeacon, said:

### Chapter I

Your Beatitude has often summoned a synod of the bishops of Italy by authorities previously sent throughout the provinces; their presence now appears before your eyes. May your Beatitude graciously arrange, through discussion, whatever concerns the protection of the Churches and the peace of the whole Church, or their harmony.

All the bishops and priests acclaimed: “Hear us, O Christ; life to Symmachus.” This was said ten times. “May his see and years [be preserved]”—this was said nine times. “We beg you to accomplish it”—this was said ten times.

### II

Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

Your concern for the protection of the Church has especially assembled this council of your affection, despite the severity of winter. We have gathered so that, through a common deliberation, we may firmly and vigorously cut off in the future the episcopal canvassing, the uncertainty of disorder, and the popular tumult which, through the devil’s deceit and the usurpation of certain persons, plainly arose at the time of my ordination.

Let us therefore take care in the future that the overturning of discipline or the audacity of presumptuous persons does not eagerly attempt similar things. With equal assistance, let us deal with the matter by expressly establishing, through our decisions, what must be observed concerning the ordination of the Roman bishop.

All the bishops and priests said: “We beg that it be done”—said ten times; “We beg that scandals be cut off”—said nine times; “We beg that canvassing be extinguished”—said ten times; “Hear us, O Christ; life to Symmachus”—said seven times. “May his see and years [be preserved]”—said five times; “Let it be done at once”—said ten times.

Bishop Symmachus said:

Since your fraternity has stirred up concern for our protection by its exhortations, and the contemplation of our God grants a like spirit concerning the tranquillity of the Church, as we have already said, inform us through your judgments of what seems appropriate concerning the liberation now under consideration, so that the decisions which are to be recited in the ecclesiastical proceedings may be set forth in this venerable council.

When they had risen and shortly afterward had sat down again, Emilianus, the synod’s notary, published the decrees.

### III

Because of the frequent canvassing of certain persons, the impoverishment of the Church, and the conflict among the people generated by the greed of those who improperly and distressingly desired the episcopate, the holy synod established the following provisions for the future, in order to extinguish such a destructive presumption:

If any priest, deacon, or cleric, while the pope is alive and without consulting him, attempts either to provide a subscription for the Roman pontificate, to promise payments, to give an oath, to promise any kind of support, or, after holding private meetings for this purpose, to deliberate or decide upon the matter, he shall be deprived of the dignity of his rank and of communion.

The whole synod rose and acclaimed: “Hear us, O Christ; life to Symmachus”—said ten times; “Peace here with Symmachus”—said fifteen times; “May his see and years [be preserved]”—said eight times.

The same severity shall strike anyone who, while this pontiff is alive, is convicted of having acted in any way as described, or of having attempted to do so; all equally guilty of this offense shall be punished by the sentence of anathema.

Bishop Symmachus said:

Does this judgment therefore please the whole assembly, and is it recognized and approved by all?

The whole synod said:

It pleases us; and what pleases all shall be done.

### IV

If, God forbid, the pope’s unexpected death should occur, so that he cannot previously decide concerning the election of his successor, as was agreed above, then, if the election of the whole ecclesiastical order should incline unanimously toward one person, the chosen bishop shall be consecrated. But if, as commonly happens, different preferences should arise among those over whom a dispute has emerged, let the decision of the greater number prevail.

The synod said: “Let it please”—said ten times.

### V

Because of the secret frauds which this strict decision seeks to prevent:

If anyone brings to the notice of the Church the plans of those who have engaged in canvassing for the pontificate against this synod, and proves by reasonable evidence that he was a participant in such an undertaking, let him not only be cleared from all guilt but also be supported with a reward that is not undeserved.

The whole synod said: “All these things please us.” And it added: “Hear us, O Christ; life to Symmachus”—said thirteen times; “We beg that these things be observed”—said ten times.

Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

Your acclamations and the judgment of the synod shall receive the acts now recorded.

And he added:

May the deliberation appropriate to religion and peace, which has restored firmness by calming the errors of inveterate presumption and the diseases of hostility to ecclesiastical affairs, with which the universal Church was infected, obtain lasting strength. Thus, by God’s favor—for he is known to be the guardian of good things—the synodal ordinance may flourish, and everyone who presumes to act, without distinction of person, contrary to the strict penalty stated above may be punished.

And they subscribed.

Caelius Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome: I have subscribed, consenting to these synodal constitutions after approving and confirming them.

Caelius Rusticus, bishop of the city of Minturnae: I have subscribed and consented to the synodal constitutions, and I profess that I remain in this judgment.

Caelius Bonifacius, bishop of the Church of Velitrae: I have subscribed and consented to the synodal constitutions, and I profess that I remain in this judgment.

Mesenus, Humanus, Rufinus of Camerinum, Cresconius of Tuder, Clarus of Allifae, Basilius of Toledo, Vitalis of Fundi, Decius of Tricabernum, Innocentius of Nubanatis, Vitalianus of Rosella, Maximus of Brescia, Constantius of Capua, Benignus of Aquinum, Fortunatus of Suessa, Palladius of Sulmo, Vindemius of Antium, Constantius of Utriculum, John of Ariminum, Germanus of Pisaurum, Martinus of Tarracina, Candidus of Tibur, Laurentius of Trebula, Titalianus of Narnia, Pachasius of Volsinii, Fortunatus, bishop of the Church of Anagni, for Sanctulus, bishop of the city of Signia, because he could not subscribe—I subscribed on his behalf; Valerius of Calenum, Felicissimus of Forum Sempronii, Valentinus of Amiternum, for the Roman bishop of the Church of Pitinum, I subscribed; Colonius of Forlì, Epiphanius of Beneventum, John of Spoleto, Constantius of Benevento, Maximianus of Perugia, Salustius of Camerinum, Lucianus of Tarquinii, Molensis of Centumcellae, Florentius of Plestia, Maximianus of Subaugusta, Fortunatus of Fulginium, John of Venafrum, Gaudentius of Tadinum, Mercurius of Sutrium, Serenus of Muranum, Justus of Aceruntia, Adeodatus of Ceronia, Stephanus of Mirsinum, Dulcitius of Sabina, Fortunatus of Anagni, Felix of Nepi, Serenus of Nola, Ancilpius of Puteoli, Timotheus of Abellinum, Rosarius of Sorrento, Stephanus of Naples, Rosarius, bishop, subscribed for my brother Ursus, bishop; Bellator of Ostia, Gaudentius of Volsinii, Marius of Tifernum.

## 247. Copy of the constitution made by Pope Symmachus concerning the preservation of ecclesiastical property

[Col. 0997A]

In the consulship of Flavius, a most illustrious younger man, on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, with the venerable man Pope Symmachus presiding, together with the venerable bishops Laurentius and Maximus, who were present, and also Petrus, Laurentius, Emilianus, Trigidius, Felix Bassianus, Cresconius, Pacatianus, Benignus, Rusentius, Innocentius, John, Maximus, Stephanus, John, Serenus, Eulalius, Proculeius, Fortunatus, Laurentius, Eustachius, Martianus, Jocundus, Candidus, Fortunatus, Felix, Euticius, Helpidius, Aprile, Innocentius, Mercurius, Hilarius, Fortunatus, Concordius, Asellus, Innocentius, Stephanus, Gerontius, Paschasius, Vitalis, Memor, Severinus, Hilarius, Veneriosus, Innocentius, Castus, Colonicus, Silvinus, Maximilianus, Aresto, Severius, Propinquus, Martinus, Valentinus, Sebastianus, Romanus, Vindemius, Dulcitius, Victor, Ursus, Mercurius, Asellus, Servus Dei, Adeodatus, Asterius, Martinianus, Felix, Eusebius, Augustus, Projecticius, Chrysogonus, Venantius, Rusticus, Salustius, Probus, Amandus, Basilius, and Florentius, bishops;

also present were Projectus, Martinus, Epiphanius, Sebastianus, Servus Dei, Octavianus, Epiphanius, Anastasius, Abundantius, Vicemalus, Paulinus, Julianus, Marcellus, Agatho, Benedictus, Crescentianus, Paschasius, Julianus, Severus, Paulinus, Adeodatus, John, Timothy, Laurentius, Hilarius, Marcus, Stephanus, Binantius, Petrus, Petrus Chrysogonus, Littorius and Chrysogonus, Timulus or Maximinus, and Fortunatus, priests; and the deacons Anastasius, Hormisdas, John, and Agapitus were also standing by.

Symmachus, bishop of the Church of the city of Rome, said:

Your fraternity has indeed obeyed the ecclesiastical laws. Under fear of the divine judgment, it has defined what needed to be established and has sufficiently brought it to the fullness of justice, since it embraces everything and its completeness needs no addition—especially concerning those clerics whom love of condemnation has seized and caused to reject the yoke of ecclesiastical discipline. It has become clear among you that these men therefore created a schism. Nevertheless, you did not deny them the mercy which God commands to be extended to all, as was fitting, unless the hardness of their hearts should acquire punishment for itself by despising the remedies offered.

It is difficult to recount their transgressions. Nevertheless, I shall not delay informing your venerable order of one matter that comes to mind. They said, among other things, that a certain document had been written by Basil, of illustrious memory, supposedly out of love for ecclesiastical property. In it, no bishop of the Roman Church either took part or subscribed, through whom it could have acquired legitimate validity.

I will not argue the matter myself. Let it be brought before your council, and let it be placed in the midst, so that by reading it you may recognize what sort of force it can possess.

The holy synod replied:

Let it be brought before us, so that its character may be recognized.

While they were speaking, the deacon Hormisdas read:

When they had assembled before the blessed apostle Peter, the eminent and most illustrious man Basilius, prefect of the praetorium and patrician, also acting as deputy for the most excellent king Odoacer, said:

Although it is in the interest of our zeal and religious duty that harmony should chiefly be preserved in the Church at the election of a bishop, and that the condition of the state should not be called into doubt through an occasion of sedition, nevertheless, at the admonition of our most blessed lord Pope Simplicius, whom we must always keep before our eyes, you reminded us that he had commanded us under solemn obligation that, should he happen to depart this life, no election of anyone should be celebrated without consulting us, and without any disturbance or detriment to the venerable Church.

As he was reading, Cresconius, bishop of the city of Tuder, rose from the assembly and said:

Let the holy synod weigh this matter: setting aside religious persons, whose chief concern it is, someone sought to bring such a great pontiff under his own power. It is plainly contrary to the canons.

The deacon Hormisdas likewise read:

We are astonished that, while our priest was still alive, anything should have been attempted without us, when nothing ought to have been undertaken. Therefore, if it pleases your greatness and holiness, let us preserve unharmed, with religious honor, everything that concerns the election of the future bishop.

We especially put forward this law, which we establish for ourselves and for our heirs, out of the devotion of a Christian mind: at no time shall any estate, whether rural or urban, or any ornaments or furnishings of the Churches, those now existing or those which have come to the rights of the Churches under any title, be alienated by the man who is now to be ordained bishop by common election, or by those who will follow in future ages, under any title or pretext. Let anathema fall upon the one who does this, the one who consents, and the one who accepts it.

Maximus, bishop of the Church of Pledana, said:

Now let the holy synod declare whether it was lawful for a layman to dictate an anathema within the ecclesiastical order, or whether a layman could pronounce an anathema against a priest and establish, contrary to the canons, something that did not belong to him. Tell us what you think: was it lawful for a layman to give a law?

The holy synod said:

It was not lawful.

And it added:

Read the following law.

The deacon Hormisdas read:

Anyone who has acquired a rural or urban estate belonging to ecclesiastical property shall know that he is protected by no law or prescription; the person who acquired it must restore it with its fruits, whether it was alienated by its former holder or he repeatedly attempts, against the holder's will, to reclaim such an alienated estate.

As he was reading, Stephanus, bishop of the Church of Venusia, rose from the assembly and said:

Let it be read in full.

The deacon Hormisdas read:

It was also agreed that the penalty should affect the heirs and successors of the recipient; in this matter, any cleric shall have free authority to object. For it is unjust and virtually sacrilegious that what each person has contributed to the venerable Church for the salvation or repose of his soul, or indeed has left to it, should be transferred into alien ownership by those whom it was especially appropriate to preserve it.

Clearly, whatever among gems, gold, silver, and clothing appears less suitable for the Church’s use or adornment, and cannot be preserved or endure for long, shall be sold at a fair valuation, and the proceeds shall be applied to religious purposes.

When these things had been read, Laurentius, bishop of the Church of Milan, said:

This document could not bind any pontiff of the Roman city, because it was not lawful for a layman establishing something in the Church to possess any authority apart from the Roman pope. The obligation to obey him remains; the authority to command does not. This is especially so since neither the Roman pope subscribed, nor is the assent of any metropolitan recorded according to the canons.

Petrus, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, said:

It is evident that the document which has been circulated in our assembly cannot be upheld by any force, because it does not agree with the canons and appears to have been conceived by a lay person. This is especially clear because no bishop of the apostolic see is shown to have taken part in it or confirmed it by his own subscription.

Eulalius, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, said:

The document read out in the priestly council is shown by the clearest evidence to be invalid. First, it appears to have been made contrary to the rules of the Fathers by laymen, even religious ones, to whom no authority to dispose of ecclesiastical resources is ever recorded as having been granted. Second, it is shown not to have been confirmed by the subscription of any bishop of the apostolic see.

The holy Fathers established that if a priest of any province, within his own boundaries and in a council held there, should testify to anything without the authority of his metropolitan or bishop, it must be invalid. How much more, then, must it be recognized as devoid of force—and in no way countable among ecclesiastical statutes—when, in the absence of a bishop at the apostolic see, whose primacy of priesthood throughout the world derives from the privilege of the blessed apostle Peter and who is accustomed to grant validity to synodal decisions, a matter has been presumed by laymen with the consent of some bishops who nevertheless could not prejudice the pontifical authority by which they are known to have been consecrated?

The holy synod said:

In accordance with the statements of our venerable brothers Laurentius, Petrus, Eulalius, Cresconius, Maximus, and Stephanus, it is fitting that this document, which we also regard as entirely without force, be weakened in every way and rendered void by the prudent judgment of your Beatitude in a synodal assembly, even if it could somehow be supported by an argument. It must not remain as an example encouraging any laymen, however religious or powerful, in any city and by any means, to decide anything concerning ecclesiastical resources. The care of disposing of these resources is taught to have been entrusted by God, without dispute, to priests alone.

Bishop Symmachus said:

Now, since God has granted me your desired presence on this occasion, I wish—if it pleases you—to make firm what I believe accords with ecclesiastical resources, so that all may know that, although empty madness has stirred certain people against me, I desire nothing more than that what has been entrusted to me by God under my stewardship may remain safe. It should also be pleasing to all who fear the Lord and should belong to the protection of ecclesiastical property.

The holy synod said:

We know that your provision is directed toward what is necessary; therefore it is in your power to arrange what must be followed.

Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

A great and venerable priestly care is owed to the office which has the responsibility of arranging what is right by deliberation, not by necessity. But because in some people, when they make claims upon another’s property, greed—the mother of vices—rejects the barriers of honesty and thinks every course expedient, they abuse the patience of heavenly mercy while greedily awaiting their prey. Since they believe that, while heaven regulates judgments, they are not held accountable for their actions, they fail to understand that the delay of the divine judgment becomes an opportunity for certain people to plunder.

But we, whom pastoral care binds and to whom an account must be rendered for the property entrusted to ecclesiastical administration, must extend our concern not only to the present but also to future ages, lest this result in the ruin of our souls. Those who, presuming upon freedom, have offended against the statutes and therefore ought to be innocent, can nevertheless be supported by the religious authority both of ourselves and of our successor, provided that they serve the ecclesiastical laws.

Having therefore weighed these matters, and with the decree remaining in force through the divine consideration of our God, we decree that, from this day onward, as long as the doctrine of the Savior concerning the Catholic faith remains by the Lord’s ordering, no bishop of the Apostolic See may transfer to another’s ownership any rural estate, whatever its size or smallness, under a perpetual alienation or exchange.

Nor may anyone be excused under the pretext of necessity. What we are saying is not personal, and no cleric or layman may use this occasion to protect himself. Nor may such property be given to anyone by way of usufruct, nor may property already given be retained by anyone except clerics, captives, and pilgrims. Let no opportunity for bad treatment be provided, since other avenues of generosity remain open to them.

Only houses situated in cities, whose condition necessarily requires substantial expenditure for their support, may, if the situation arises, be exchanged for revenues offered at a fair valuation, under fear of the divine judgment.

We likewise wish the priests, or whoever else they may be, who are guardians of the Churches throughout all the titles of the Roman city to be bound by the same law. For it has been said that it is impious that an obligation which the supreme pontiff binds himself to through the charity of Christ should not bind a man of the second order in the Church.

Anyone, therefore, who forgets God and disregards this decree—which we wish the priests of the Roman city to be bound to by religious obligations—and who, contrary to this present constitution, attempts in any way to alienate anything belonging to the rights of the titles or to the Churches mentioned above, except gold, silver, gems, clothing, and movable goods, whether already present or subsequently acquired, which do not pertain to divine adornment, shall suffer the loss of his office. This applies to the donor, the alienator, and the seller.

Furthermore, whoever seeks or receives such property, or whoever among the priests, deacons, or defenders subscribes to the donor, shall be struck with the anathema by which God strikes souls in anger. The recipient or subscriber, from among the persons identified above—that is, anyone whom we have judged liable to anathema—shall be subjected to the established penalty for associates, which we stated earlier as the punishment for the alienator, unless perhaps the alienator, while seeking its recovery, and the recipient, by prompt restoration, should each provide for his own correction.

If anyone, through insufficient concern for his own soul, should perhaps neglect the remedy offered, then, beyond the kinds of penalties set out above [Col. 1001B], if any document should be produced contrary to law—although it had no force at the outset—it shall be brought forward with every possible force. But it shall also be permitted to any ecclesiastical persons to offer a voice of opposition and to be supported by ecclesiastical authority, so that they may reclaim what was alienated together with its revenues, lest anyone fortify himself with some obstacle before the tribunal of Christ, since he scatters, contrary to law and without any consideration of mercy, the substance left to religious souls and to the poor.

We wish the law of this decree, however, to be observed only in the Apostolic See; throughout the provinces, let it be observed by all churches according to the consideration of souls and in the manner which their rulers judge fitting for the purpose of religion.

And they subscribed:

I, Celius Symmachus, bishop of the Roman Church [Col. 1001C], have written this decree made by us.

I, Celius Laurentius, bishop of the holy Milanese Church, have subscribed to this decree made by the venerable holy Pope Symmachus.

I, Peter, bishop of the Catholic Church of Ravenna, have subscribed to this decree made by the venerable holy Pope Symmachus.

I, Eulalius, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, have subscribed to this decree made by the venerable holy Pope Symmachus.

Felix of Terracina, Chrysogonus of Todi, Emilianus of Vercelli, Jocundus of Augusta, Tigridus of Turin, Vitalis of Fondi, Bassus of Modena, Pacatianus of Collemezzo, Maximus of Blera, Martyrius of Terracina, Rufentius of Segni, Vindemius of Anagni, Candidus of Tivoli, Fortunatus of Foligno, Proculeianus of Sepino, Fortunatus of Anagni,

Paschasius of Volturno, Martianus of Aecae, Maximianus of Perugia, Chrysogonus of Albano, Euticius of Trani, Laurentius of Vobia, Marcus of Samnium, Aprilis of Micernium, Memor of Cannae, Innocentius of Forum Sempronii, Florentinus of Palestrina, Felix of Nepi, Concordius of Mesenia, Amandus of Potenza, Ansellus of Plommis, Basilius of Tullia, Martianus of Ostia, Benignus of Aquinum, Fortunatus of Vessa, Severinus of Lunda, Eucarpius of Messina, John of Spoleto, Stephanus of Venosa, Valentinus of Amiternum, Romulus of Praeneste, Probus of Carmena, Colonius of Foroclaudium, Helpidius of Volterra, Projectus of Formiae, Veneriosus of Pella, Boniface of Forum Flaminius [Col. 1001D–1002A],

Sebastianus of Sora, Rusticus of Buxentum, Venantius of Senigallia, Victor of Duna, Innocentius of Tifernum Tiberinum, Sylvinus of Velitrae, Justus of Sessa, Arestonius of Ostia, Augustus of Lipari, Felix of Nepi for Ursus, Asterius of Aquinum, Propinquus of Trebia, Eusebius of Faventia, Romanus of Nomentum.

## Here begins the fourth Roman synod, assembled from various regions under King Theoderic

In the consulship of Rufus Magnus, Faustus, and Amenus, on the day of the Kalends of November, the holy synod, assembled in the city of Rome from various regions by command of the most glorious King Theoderic, spoke in the name of Christ:

When royal authority had ordered priests to come to the city of Rome from various provinces, so that the holy council might judge the matters which the adversaries of the venerable Pope Symmachus, bishop of the Apostolic See, were said to be bringing against him, we consulted the king concerning the bishops of Liguria, Emilia, and Venetia, whom the hope of making the journey had drawn to the presence of the ruler [Col. 1002B]. It had become necessary to consult him concerning why he had wished us, broken by age and weakened by bodily infirmity and incapacity, to be assembled.

The aforesaid most pious king replied, with the goodwill of a virtuous disposition, that many dreadful reports concerning the actions of Pope Symmachus had been brought to him, and that it was necessary for the synod to establish, by its investigation, whether the accusation of his enemies was true.

The pontiffs mentioned, upon whom the opportunity of presenting their case was impending, suggested that the person who was alleged to have been attacked ought himself to have summoned the synod, knowing that his see possessed first the merit and primacy of the Apostle Peter. Thereafter, following the Lord’s command, the authority of venerable councils had handed down a singular power in the churches; nor, they said, could anyone easily demonstrate by any similar precedent that the bishop of the aforesaid see had been subjected to the judgment of his enemies in the matter of an accusation [Col. 1002C].

But the most pious ruler indicated that he had also shown by letters that the pope himself had been willing to assemble the synod. Accordingly, the documents were requested from his clemency, since it was known that they had been sent by him. He ordered them to be given to the bishops without delay, together with whatever had been done in writing in the same affair and had, by God’s providence, reached Rome from different lands and regions.

While the venerable assembly was considering how the matter should be begun, in accordance with the requirements of the case [Col. 1002D], the holy Pope Symmachus entered the Basilica of Julius, where the gathering of bishops was being held, as heavenly care had directed him. He gave thanks to the most merciful king for the synodal summons and declared that the matter he had desired had come to pass.

Thus the cause of the priests’ distress concerning the council, which had not yet been firmly established, was removed. He declared that he would give his authority to the ordering of the assembly, as ecclesiastical statutes required, in the presence of all the bishops who had gathered there. He hoped that the visitor who had been accused by part of the clergy or by certain laymen of acting against religion, against the statutes of the ancients, or against the rules of their predecessors, would, through the arrangement of the bishops, as he said, strike the holy proposal with a resolute front; that all the things he had lost through the representations of his enemies would be restored to his power by the honorable council; that the bishop of so great a place would first be legally restored to his former status; and that only then would he come to the case and, if it seemed right, answer the propositions of his accusers [Col. 1003A].

This seemed worthy and deserving to the very large number of priests. Nevertheless, the synod did not presume to decree anything without the king’s knowledge. But a just request, through the negligence of the envoys, did not receive what it deserved; and, in accordance with the king’s wishes, Pope Symmachus was ordered to engage in dispute with his opponents before receiving back the patrimonies or churches which he had lost.

He did not wish on this occasion to resume the privileges of his power, or the things which he had submitted for the cleansing of his conscience, insofar as we judge them to have been just.

While the synod was convened in the Basilica of Jerusalem in the Sessorian Palace, some priests thought that the document which the accusers had prepared and which they were daily invoking amid seditions should be received by the synod. Once it had been received, it contained two matters which were either hostile to the truth or, as far as could be shown, contrary to the ecclesiastical purpose itself.

The first was that they said the crimes mentioned above concerning Pope Symmachus had come before the king’s knowledge. He declared this to be false. For he would not have entrusted the matter to a hearing as though it were a new case if, having been convicted in his conscience of error, he had known that he had only to await the sentence.

The second was that they said they could prove him guilty through the slaves concerning the matters they alleged, adding that he himself handed over slaves, by which, as they asserted, he could be defeated in the investigation. This was contrary both to the canons and to the public laws themselves, since the statutes of the Fathers had established that those whom the laws of the world do not admit to accusation must likewise be denied permission to speak in the inquiry or to obtain anything from it [Col. 1003C].

While it was being considered what should be done amid these circumstances, the aforesaid pope came forward to plead his case. When he arrived, he was treated by the mobs rushing upon him—mobs of his rivals—in such a way that the assault itself became the occasion of death for many priests who were with him. The illustrious Count Aligenius and the eminent men Gudila and Vedeulf, stewards of the royal household, saw the still-fresh traces of the wounds. He brought them with him, from the place where he had departed, to the enclosure of the blessed Apostle Peter [Col. 1003D].

After these events, and after affairs had been disturbed by various confusion, we again turned to the principal authority, knowing that the Lord himself governs by his divinity the ruler whom he had appointed to govern Italy. We laid everything before his gentleness in a report of events, as the matter required. We also informed him that the often-mentioned pope had been warned, at the place where he had remained with his followers, that, should he again wish to come out, he was to appear for judgment; but that, through the bishops sent to him, he had alleged that the canons permitted him, for the sake of his vindication, to lay aside the dignity of his office. Almost overwhelmed by such great dangers, he maintained that the lord king was free to do what he wished, but that he himself could not meanwhile be compelled, against the canonical statutes, to submit to judgment [Col. 1004A].

To this the most serene king replied, with God’s help, that the synod had authority to determine what ought to be followed in so great a matter, lest anything beyond reverence for ecclesiastical affairs should pertain to him. He also entrusted the bishops with the power to deliberate whether they wished to hear the case of the accused or not, and to decide what they considered more useful, provided that, through the care of the venerable council, peace might be restored to all Christians in the city of Rome.

When this is offered justly, the commands of God are fulfilled by giving Italy its ruler.

Recognizing that no labor remained for us except to exhort the dissenting parties, with humility of purpose, toward concord—for only one thing remained by which we might obey God, namely, to invite the most illustrious senate to comply with the holy ruler’s will—we sent an embassy as was fitting, warning and instructing them that the causes of God must be entrusted to God’s own judgment. He can kill the body and cast the soul into Gehenna; he said, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay”; before him conscience is bare, and hidden things are not concealed [Col. 1004B].

Wise men ought to consider how many inappropriate and prejudicial events had occurred in the affairs of this ruler, and that we should not open but close, by means of what they themselves called remission, a path toward sins. We preserve what is said to be the greater judgment, instructing them that, through us, Christ became known to them. It is not the part of sheep to foresee the ambushes of a wolf, but of a shepherd.

This was especially so because, in the case mentioned above, error had involved many who disdained to acknowledge and satisfy God; and because, on this occasion, the members of the Church could no longer be scattered further, but ought rather to be sustained by gentleness. Just as Paul, the teacher of good works, instructed us, saying that many must be healed by patience and teaching; and that those who are thought guilty and entangled in grave sins—although, as the Apostle John testifies, no one is without fault, “If I say that I have no sin, I am a liar”—ought nevertheless to be supported and restrained by human pressure, and that such sufferings should be held over for divine judgment [Col. 1004C].

Especially since the matters we set out above concerning the authority of the see stood in the way: what the former possessor of it, the blessed Peter, had merited was added to the nobility of its possession, and that ancient distinction is granted to Christ’s rulers. Let them devoutly proclaim what is written through the prophet in the person of God: “Is my hand not strong enough to destroy those who have gone astray?” [Col. 1004D].

We repeatedly reminded them of these things, as was necessary, so that, having considered their purpose, they might depart and not question the action God had inspired in us in accordance with the ruler’s command, but follow it as sons of the Church ought to do. They should not contend during this suspension, thereby increasing the losses of the Church, which the situation required to be relieved with haste. The necessity of this speed and of that obedience lay upon us.

This was especially so because we saw that nearly the whole people had adhered inseparably to his communion; and we were spurred by no small concern lest it should fall into any error [Col. 1005A].

After these arguments had been presented, we decree, bound by consideration of these necessities and religious concerns, and having weighed by heavenly inspiration all the hidden matters involved in the case, that Pope Symmachus, bishop of the Apostolic See, attacked by such propositions insofar as human beings are concerned—for, since all the matters obstructing the case have been set out above, it is clear that the whole affair was left to divine judgment [249]—shall be immune and free.

He shall administer the divine mysteries to the Christian people, without any imputation concerning the accusations brought against him, in all the churches belonging to the jurisdiction of his see. For we have recognized that he could not be bound by the petition of his opponents, nor by the causes set out above.

Therefore, in accordance with the royal commands which grant this authority to our power, we restore to him whatever ecclesiastical jurisdiction exists within the sacred city of Rome or outside it, reserving the entire case for God’s judgment. We exhort everyone to receive holy communion from him, as the situation requires, and to remember the God of their souls, because he is himself a lover of peace, and he himself is peace, who says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John XIV, 27). And wherever they affirm that peace must be established, they declare the peacemakers blessed.

Whoever, contrary to our instruction—which we do not think can either be disallowed or rejected—believes that it can be either disallowed or rejected, let him know that, as we trust in God, he will render an account of his contempt in the divine judgment.

Concerning the clergy of the aforesaid pope who departed from their bishop before the proper time, contrary to the rules, and created a schism, we decree that, if they make satisfaction to their bishop, his mercy shall follow them and they shall rejoice in being restored to their ecclesiastical offices. For the Lord and our Redeemer rejoices when he finds the lost sheep recovered from error, and the heavenly Mediator extends paternal generosity toward the son who had fled.

But if, after this form approved by us, any of the clergy should presume to celebrate Mass in the Roman Church at any consecrated place belonging to God, without the knowledge of Pope Symmachus, he shall be struck, while the pope lives, by canonical statutes as a schismatic.

Let these things suffice; now we have sincerely set them forth with God’s knowledge.

I, Laurentius, bishop of the Milanese Church, have subscribed to this statute of ours, in which we have entrusted the entire case to God’s judgment.

I, Peter, bishop of Ravenna, have subscribed to this statute of ours, in which we have entrusted the entire case to God’s judgment [Col. 1005D].

Felix of Terracina, Boniface of Aquae, Maximus of Blera, Emilianus of Furanum, Maximus of Ticinum, Cassianus of Modena, Gerontius of Fidenae, Stephanus of Venosa, Laurentius of Boae, Fortunatus of Foligno, Mercurius of Sutri, Stephanus of Naples, Hilarius of Tesenna, Maximilianus of Perugia, Innocentius Fortunatus, Concordius of Messina, Vitalis of Fondi, Castus of Porto, Aristus of Ostia, Martyrius of Terracina, Victor of Luni, Asterius of Aquino, Chrysogonus of Albano, Amandus of Potenza, Romanus of Nomentum, Ursus of Rieti, Paschasius of Volturno, Innocentius of Forum Sempronii,

Felix of Nepi, Hilarius of Temprana, Innocentius of Tarentum, of Tifernum, Severinus of Tundarita, Sylvanus of Velitrae, Sebastianus of Sora, Mercurius of Gavignano, Felix of Atella, Rusticus of Buxentum, Propinquus of Trebia, Adeodatus of Fornix, Boniface of Camerinum, Justus of Segni, Vindemius of Anagni, Augustus of Lipari, Valentinus of Amiternum, Fortunatus of Suessa, Jocundus of Augusta, Tigidius of Taurinum, Viticanus of Celano, John of Rimini, Proculeianus of Sepino, Candidus of Triportus, Cresconius of Todi, Innocentius of Venafrum, John of Spoleto, Eustasius of Cremona, Laurentius of Verginia, Eucarpius of Merysapa, Rufentius of Agnani, Serenus of Nola, Martianus of Acanum, Euticius of Trani [Col. 1006A],

Fortunatus of Anagni, Aprilis of Lateran, Asellus of Populonia, Memor of Cannae, Adrudatus of Silva Candida, Venerius of Pella, Rogatus of Taormina, Servusdei of Ferentum, Probus of Carmeia, Dulcitius of Sant’Antimo.

## Here begins Ennodius’s preface to the following book

The ardor of many matters often demands an eagerness to speak. But if a miser is eager for praise and desires to purchase favor through sweat, or through the flatteries of glory fails to recognize the cross of the narrator, or, bound by the fetters of profit, sells the service of his tongue, then, while his mind is subjected to the desire of possession and considers that it already holds the advantage it has presumed upon, it does not know how to fear the dangers that press upon it through the exercise of style.

Or, confined by necessity, it produces speech captive to every sort of polish and displays in public a brow ignorant of modesty; while it serves its purpose, it burns away care for elegance. For the ornaments of speech belong not to the business of the purpose but to repose; painted words belong not to military service but to leisure.

The battlefield demands a strong man; deep peace redeems ornament. Whoever asserts what will be useful despises speech colored by the peril of rhetorical art.

These matters being so, I present the subject of my narrative and commend the constrained voice of the wicked to religious minds, remembering that it is written: “A time to be silent, and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes III, 7). Or, after the authority of the prophetic oracle, I recall the example of a certain orator, who declares that the condition of speaking, unless it is necessary, is exceedingly foolish.

Accordingly, I have entrusted the ministry of speech to priests according to the strength of my intellect, against whom the poisons of hissing tongues have been poured out. Yet religious patience, protected by the shield of faith, does not fear the shower of darts, and the weapons directed without the art of warfare return to their author [Col. 1006C].

For those whose breastplate is Christ do not fear force, and by long endurance they overthrow their enemies. Yet let no one think that there is cause for fear in this battle line, in which a conflict is brought against God and the bishops without any reckoning of strength.

Let no one see a wavering and provocative enemy and, because of the circumstances of the battle, fear a weak adversary. The victor who refrains from attacking an enemy wounded in conscience envies himself victory. He advances to the advantage of his enemy who, in conflicts, does not first settle the causes before anything else.

Innocence gives strength to missiles, and purposes of combat arising from justice sharpen the sword. We know that the force of striking has been given more by a just grief than by arms; hence a multitude does not withstand the weapons of the few.

Therefore, with the prophet saying along with me, “Those who are with us are more numerous than those who are with him,” I shall begin the work which, as I judge, will please the good [Col. 1006D].

## Here begins the book of Ennodius, deacon of the holy Roman Church, against the detractors of the victorious fourth synod, held at Rome by Pope Symmachus under King Theoderic

[Col. 1007A]

It would indeed suffice that schismatic ignorance be overthrown by its proposition, especially since the objections themselves contain their answer, and since the title deserves authoritative condemnation without examination of the text, when the heading itself discloses the import of the work: the unseemly absolution of foul-mouthed speakers against the synod.

Nevertheless, I shall now act as though it were necessary for the one proposing evil to perish by another’s sword. This preface can be attributed only to the most merciful man’s ignorance.

And lest anyone besides you be counted among the ulcerous and wandering sheep, who might have attacked the great flock, the prophet speaks of the shepherds: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me” (Isaiah I, 2). And the Lord says concerning the apostles: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X, 16).

The prophet testifies that they were bishops when he says concerning Judas: “Let another receive his bishopric” (Psalm CVIII, 8); and the Apostle Paul likewise cries out: “Obey your leaders, for they watch over you” (Hebrews XIII, 17).

Let us not linger here, but return to the grave and venerable proposition, produced not merely from another matter but from a mystical one.

“They say: Not all the priests did royal authority summon to the council, nor did all take part in the judgment.”

Slaves of Tartarus, and plainly ministers of Satan, the written command of the ruler dragged along in new bonds and in the coils of your actions’ convolutions all whom it did not summon, like the tail of a serpent.

I do not wish to say what their vote was, or what their deliberation, when they departed; or what weariness that waiting produced in them, when they saw the venerable pope accept, contrary to law, long delays in his life. They saw the heavens beaten only by the darts they themselves directed.

Were these wretched men not permitted to hide secretly in the consolation of evil deeds? Your books strip away what was hidden, and through you they are not allowed to possess solitude in a disgraceful act, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Every evil person hates the light” (John III, 20).

After this, it should not have escaped you that the absent adversaries of the Roman pope—who, after the propositions mentioned above had been put forward, were making accusations—ought not to have been called his adversaries, since they were acting deceitfully. Canonical authority, speaking plainly in synodal decrees, declared that bishops ought not to admit hostile and suspect persons to bring an accusation against them. You joined faith to your assertions, saying that royal commands had not summoned them under this name [Col. 1007B].

O men fashioned with every refinement of art and baked in smiths’ furnaces, who labor to discover testimonies polished by the doctors!

We love the true judgment of the reverend men, and, as they say, we go on foot into it itself. We recognize the errors you mention: let someone call the accuser an enemy and give a tragic name to one who deserves no insult.

Then, by rhetorical argument, you bit into the question that followed, fastening it with a clasp when you added and alleged: “The Roman city is witness.”

If all the bishops who came together were old and weak, behold an argument relying upon the sinews of truth, and in the brilliance of its words to be preferred even to Cepasius.

Therefore, those who said that they were strong in age but weak in body themselves testify that they were inept for judgment, since they said that they were already suffering the losses of their limbs—especially if they presumed to press this upon the ears of the most merciful Lord [Col. 1007C].

You think that, expelled from the sight of all God’s people, their gatherings should everywhere be confused and narrated after the manner of those men, and that, before the ruler, others should have been preferred in speech concerning the assembly of bishops—unless those whom the maturity of age made authorities in refined speech, to whom long years had conferred reverence, and who were thought to have been preserved for a long time through the support of good merits.

It was therefore fitting that they should complain of the fatigue of advanced age, whom age had ordered to present their case.

Excellent men, you had already learned from the royal commands that the reason for the summons had been established and that the supreme ruler of Italy had not been called for consultation as though concerning a new matter. More was owed to writing and to the religious character of the document than to the ruler’s presence.

Thus no heading remained in the matter mentioned above from which, as they proceeded to investigate it, they might properly announce such an opening.

After this digression, you praise the king’s goodwill in good matters and honor with words an innocence which you ignore in deeds. If there is any honor in your speech, you plow it with a rough plowshare, as though working a field along a crooked path, commending weeds and darnel to a wasted soil, and destined to receive, for such expenditure, straw with which the fire of Gehenna will be kindled to your destruction [Col. 1007D–1008A].

But now, as someone is said to have asked, “What should I place before what?”

You say, contrary to the Apostle, that the opponents of the supreme pontiff were not heard, although, mindful of the heavenly command, they withdrew their portion from the adulterer’s company.

Here I do not attack your leaky ignorance or accuse your memory. I do not wish to say that you have attributed the prophet’s words to the Apostle, since I know that even those who were sent are rightly called apostles.

For David says: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm XLIX, 18).

Next, who among you can unravel the question which you put forward, namely, that in the accusations brought forward whatever is not excluded is approved? And what of the voice of the Roman Church, fitting for soldiers, in which one does not know whether to praise first its brilliance or its savor?

Do you think you have heard the law read: “What is just, you shall execute justly”? Have you heard, concerning the evil deeds of men—if human conduct has ever held you—that whatever is not approved according to its proper order is excluded?

Where is the prophet’s statement: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isaiah III, 14)? And concerning you it was said: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom [250]: woe to their souls.”

But what need is there of action whenever, in despair, no remedy comes to the rescue, unless the Lord is invoked, who promised through the Prophet that he would come upon every proud and exalted person and upon the arrogant, so that he might be humbled?

But I shall pursue your fetid work by its tracks and, if I can, crush it beneath an iron heel. To speak truthfully, matter will contend with matter, case with case, and reason with what they think is reason.

You allege that the priests spoke against the royal commands, and you consider it a kind of sacrilege that, not knowing how to distinguish the heavenly command from that of an earthly ruler, one should perceive something evil in the command of an earthly lord. You object: Who ought to have told the king that the pope should have summoned the synod?

Certainly, in this matter the example is especially clear in the man already oppressed by the criminal allegations of many: to condemn him was to accuse him, and the hostile outcry of his enemies had already stripped him of the prerogative assigned to him from heaven.

The stages of your evil deeds have led you to such indulgence that you believe it is the same thing to attack as to convict. Among you, hatred has no doctrine from truth; hatred often, contrary to merit, forms votes hindered by passions and obedient to no reason [Col. 1008C].

Where is this: “Before you know, do not judge anyone” (Ecclesiasticus XI, 7)?

Long ago the flock placed on the left received you as companions, among whom the one who deserved to be brought to examination is believed to have received a sentence beforehand, and to be guilty simply because he entered the balance of disputation [Col. 1008D].

Yet you inserted a divine example into your preface most skillfully, with such well-fitted language that one might think Chrysippus himself was maintaining the line in it.

God says to the sinner: “Why do you recount my justices?” (Psalm XLIX, 16).

Applying this saying, as though in an apostrophe to the priest who is regarded as the vicar of the blessed Apostle Peter, you forbid his chief physician to apply medicine to his body.

How do you refuse to provide healing for his soul? I do not know whether this is a great divine jest or the greatest lamentation.

You seek treatment for another’s fever; you wish to apply a remedy to a failing soul; and, placed near death, forgetful of yourselves, you concern yourselves with another’s salvation. What if the prophet has truly said this to you: “Is it too little for you to trouble human beings, since you trouble my God also?” (Isaiah VII, 13). And again: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke IV, 23).

But we know from elsewhere that one who has been declared hopeless and wicked, descending into the depths, cannot be healed; in astonishing recklessness he despises the warning. Yet I believe that in these men there still lives a council in the death of their evil conduct, and that one may wish for another what he himself has already lost [Col. 1009A].

Now we rightly say to you with the prophet: “Everything that this people says is a conspiracy; and do not fear its fear, nor be afraid.”

Far from us, away from us, be this itching of tongues that the same prophet truly rebukes: “Those who write injustice have written it.”

We do not judge that the blessed Peter received from the Lord, together with the privileges of his see, permission for himself or his successors to sin, as you claim. He sent to posterity an everlasting endowment of merits together with an inheritance of innocence.

What was granted to him because of the brightness of his deeds belongs to those whom a corresponding splendor of conduct illuminates. For who could doubt that he is holy whom the summit of so great a dignity raises up? Even if acquired virtues are lacking in him, those bestowed by the predecessor of the place are sufficient.

Either the dignity raises worthy men to these heights, or it illuminates those who are raised. For it foreknows what is suitable for the foundation of the churches, upon which the whole structure itself rests [Col. 1009B].

But from this you think that heavenly power supports our actions because you lend, as you say, an assisting right hand for the protection of the blessed Apostle Peter.

You do not know that the sun is not aided by torches, nor are lamps kindled to protect the light of day. For it is written: “God searches the kidneys and hearts” (Psalm VII, 10).

But in that authority who would dare answer your arguments, except that truth is spoken without art and faith is stitched to the artifices of lying speech?

“Why,” they say, “did you come to the ruler if it was not permitted for the accused to be heard?”

The fog of sin or divine dread so blinds you into an animal-like stupor that your modest excuse either passes through your mind by fraud or, pressed down by the dullness of beasts, fails to recognize itself.

Or perhaps you think that something else was meant when it was said that he himself ought to have summoned the synod: the work belonged to his office, so that, through pontifical examination, the divine sentence might prevail over you and those whom insane fury had cut away from the structure of their head, to their own loss of salvation.

After mentioning Esau, I do not know whether you introduced your work with words or with barking, comparing your bishop to him because he had lost the benefit of senior nature in exchange for a single meal and had surrendered the gray dignity of the firstborn in obedience to his appetite [Col. 1009C].

What shall I say in response to these things, when I am hemmed in on every side by the accusations? Who among you, I ask, took Symmachus’s blessing away because he served his father more devotedly? To whom was nobility granted in the role of Jacob through so many gifts?

Who among you came forward in obedience to the desires of the blind father? Which of you, through your devotion, made the venerable parent, whose eyes were captive, feel no loss of light?

Is not the night thought, by contrast with your darkness, to display a gleaming radiance through the clear sky? And does not every darkness, when compared with your actions, assume the beauty of the sun?

Moreover, at that time Jacob did indeed confer a blessing appropriate to the son’s character, but one that had already been promised.

Why do we dwell on these matters any longer, when those who have driven their heels against the goads are not to be taught? Believe me: the things you bring forward are enemies of peace and unfit for attack.

But there follows a bond with an enigma which I do not know by what art of repetition we can loosen. Having entered the sea of Ciceronian depth, they send the little boat of our barrenness, bearing a question, through the uncertain winds along the shores.

Yet with Christ holding the helm I shall enter the harbor, and I shall examine one by one all your whirlwinds, having in my guidance the ability of those men, not my own [Col. 1009D].

For they say: “If the assertion of the bishops is true—that the bishop of the Apostolic See has never been subject to the sentence of inferiors—why was he brought to judgment by a strict summons?”

A very old infancy labors greatly in you here. Who must be summoned to answer it is the one who always surpasses among us the weight of an inescapable proposition, since I openly cry out with the prophet on behalf of the priests:

“Will the axe boast against him who cuts with it, or will the saw exalt itself against him who draws it?” (Isaiah X, 15).

Thus the divine oracle may serve me: “Just as the tribute ceases when the exactor stops, so the Lord has crushed the rod of the wicked.”

Grant, Lord, what you foretold against him, so that, as a drunkard wanders and vomits, the unbeliever who acts faithlessly may perish.

For this reason the prophet, mocking you, cries out: “Hear the word of the Lord, you mocking men” (Isaiah XXVIII, 14). Does anyone establish the outcome of cases in advance through foreknowledge, and measure an end for furious conflicts in such a way that a swift decision, while it reveals itself to be older than the inquiry, anticipates it and accuses the favor of the judge? [Col. 1010A]

Now, although unworthy in years and conduct to speak with a mouth, I shall rebuke you with a pontifical voice.

We do not wish our statutes to stand before you on only one scale. The canons have spoken broadly concerning the character of accusers; among you it is a sacrilege to transgress the ancient definitions of the Fathers. It is written in the Council of Carthage:

“The authority of the Apostolic See, through Bishop Faustus, who was then present as its envoy, approved this: accusers who come from the house of an enemy are not to be believed. In them, a neighboring hostility set ablaze by hatred, through the dry fuel of persecution, kindles its flames and secretly constructs the entire machinery of deceit through expense and interconnected contrivances.”

What household would have vomited forth these men? How could our assembly have known, except through those present, and how could it have learned the character of the attack except from the written accusation? In these men, while they pretended to be persecuted, it would have recognized the cesspool of accusations and that they themselves owed persecution to their charges [Col. 1010B].

After the foregoing statements concerning the accusers, you added:

“Why were persons ordered to be brought forward whom the imperial authority had often demanded?” This pertains, you say, to the thwarting of the understanding of the man who now sits in the apostolic see as though in a fortress.
