Wisdom truly says to you: “A mortal is weak and short-lived and will not attain understanding, but must labor to know what is acceptable before the Lord” (Wisdom 9:5). And Proverbs likewise says: “He who neglects learning hates himself.” For death confronts the unlearned.

[Col. 1010C] Why do you pretend ignorance of that which descends into accessible knowledge? Why do you employ falsehood with the astonishing craft of brigands, or the tricks of deceit, displaying simplicity upon your face? It is of you that it is now said: “He who speaks falsehood speaks from his own resources.”

By the cunning foresight of your priest, you removed from his eyes that joyful appearance which came from the judgment of the courts, so that, armed with such defenses against your battle-lines and bearing before the whole world the weapons of innocence in his testimony, you might drive him from the very sanctuaries of judgment. You took care that the innocent man should neither live without opposition nor, when struck by the inquiry of incorrupt judges, possess the consolation of that inquiry.

You both granted and begrudged him the examination you had announced, since, by one and the same route, he is both forbidden and compelled to undergo the uncertainties of your disputes; and, by a singular path, he is summoned to the case only to be excluded from it. Thus he would obtain manifest safety either without being provoked or, once acquitted, by stealth.

I remember reading, in the days of my youth, a saying concerning someone: “You impose exile upon an exile, and do not grant it.” [Col. 1010D] The prophet’s sentence assails you: “These are the men who have troubled the earth and shaken kingdoms” (Isaiah 14:16). And again: “Their branches shall be cut off with sickles, and whatever is left shall be severed” (Isaiah 18:5). And once more: “While you do not expect it, your crushing will come, and your multitude will be shattered like a potter’s vessel” (Isaiah 30:13–14).

Moreover, the prophet spoke with a special reference to this case: “The Lord has inclined his hand, and he who brings aid to evils will fall; and he to whom he gives aid will fall, and all will be consumed together” (Isaiah 31:3).

Yet, after the support supplied by many examples, I return to the recent definitions of the canons. The Council of Carthage declares elsewhere that whatever persons the public laws do not admit for an accusation against another, we likewise remove from the possibility of bringing charges, and that no accusations are to be heard by ecclesiastical judges which the laws of the secular world prohibit.

[Col. 1011A] I ask you, men in whom—so you claim—polished perfection has been set down to the very last detail: what was the status of those slaves whom you reported, in official written petitions, as having been demanded? If servile bondage still held them under another’s power, and no traces of an obscene obligation, once released into freedom, loosened them—or if, while you were disputing, the words of the aforesaid persons had carried any credibility at all?

But, I suppose, you will answer that the truth—which a voice freely uttered by those men could not possess—had been extracted by a religious torturer from its hiding places through various torments, so that, while punishment loosened their bodies, the soul would not conceal what it knew to have been done.

But I ask you first to turn your faces toward the public laws, and then toward the judges. They can speak in their own defense as follows: We, whom the service of God has made free on account of our rejection of such things, either disdain or laugh at the insults of insolent slaves. Of servants the Apostle has written to us: “Remember that both your Master and theirs is in heaven” (Ephesians 6:9).

[Col. 1011B] Are we to be recalled to these evils of the secular world? We must do what we insist is profane when another does it—what, through the ministry of a command and the hand of another, would defile your sight, carried out by our authority.

Do not preserve this disposition toward all the Churches in the manner and nature of ravenous wolves; for after a bloody investigation had perhaps stained us according to your desires, it would not have achieved in these matters the result toward which you strive.

But the prophet says to you: “Let us put a ring in your nostrils and a bridle on your lips, and let us lead you back by the way you came” (2 Kings 19:28). You are assailed by the same prophet, who says: “They shall be as though they were not, and the men who oppose you shall perish” (Isaiah 41:11).

[Col. 1011C] You also added this new invention against us: that the Lord himself and our Redeemer submitted to the judgments of servants, and that the Maker of heaven willingly subjected himself to a small portion of earthly matter, when he testifies and says: “O Judah and Jerusalem, judge between me and my vineyard” (Isaiah 5:3). You relate that blessed Peter and the Apostle Paul likewise did not shrink from this, and you draw your own elegance of argument into the law by a chain of 251 examples preceding it—as though anything in this respect remained for you—although the opposition of the controversy and the powerful fingers of your eloquence force out what has been offered.

You also say that the miraculous prophet Samuel, in the serenity of his conscience, appealed to the testimony of the people. What did Samuel say? That the Lord knew he had never taken anyone’s property or driven away anyone’s animal; that he had opposed gifts and avoided presents that came spontaneously—things above the capacity of human beings—taking care, clearly, lest he should suffer loss of reputation (*opinionis*) through the prejudice of suspicion. [Col. 1011D: Merlin’s edition reads *Homirius*; elsewhere, *opinionis* (“reputation”).]

Finally, under divine attestation, he disclosed his innocence, lest he undergo human examination.

The judgment of our Redeemer—which he wishes to take place between himself and his vineyard—Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, invokes even more forcefully when, in condemning the envy of your associates, he recognized that the exercise allotted to him through the multitude of insults was an opportunity, not a cause for fear. He truly joined to the price of the crown what he had lowered from his dignity; and, before the heavenly sentence of acquittal, the good evaluator completed the status of the accused as innocent.

Thus the soldiers of Christ, by their sweat, bring forth for themselves an increase of honors, while they chastise the heights granted to them by a loftier humility, acquiring heaps of praise from the very source from which they regulate the dignities they have attained through sublime restraint.

But although the place shows blessed Athanasius to have been, so far as we know, unequal to the Roman bishop, in actual conduct they are compared. Athanasius was present before the judges; the other, as you yourselves say, summoned them. The former, as a servant of God, did not flee the investigation directed against him; the latter established his triumph in the collection of those who were investigated.

But why do we linger over these lengthy comparisons? He both desired and welcomed judgment; he drew it toward himself and entered into it. And, in a matter which could rouse faithful hearts with the goads of righteous sorrow, he even granted authority against himself, if he deserved it, to the venerable council.

[Col. 1012A] Who, upon the very face of his allegation, would not know that he had come to his fellow bishops supported by the testimonies of purity? He had recoiled from that which it was less permissible for their strictness to do, judging that what an incompetent censor had established ought rather to be weakened by any means.

Why did you assail the aforesaid man with canine loquacity? Why do you wound one who is not grieving? His desire is what you suppose to be your terror.

But in you the venom of a new serpent hisses more craftily than it did among Athanasius’s adversaries. They did not know what you understand perfectly well: how a triumph is taken away from the person attacked. They feared that, once summoned, he might appear and be heard.

You, unable to tolerate the custom by which they had their cases examined, repelled those who came with weapons, and exchanged the weariness prepared for you by the sentence for the taking up of avenging arms.

O recollection of evils, which both grants and overthrows speech! For while it forces those whom it has driven to cry out, the gravity of their own deed also confounds their words. Who could endure you chattering with an even temper?

[Col. 1012B] Therefore, according to your assertion, we do not love the advantages of a new usefulness, while you define that obedience must be rendered to the elders.

Here you suspend every sail of your ingenuity; here, with your neck thrown back, whatever breath of spirit your retreating breast contained belched forth. For you say:

“If you pursue only things of long standing, let the fasts of Moses and the miracles of Elisha—which he performed when he raised the dead—be brought against you and confound you.”

What has a competent investigator found here by way of reasoning? Even if a pale investigator of gold were to confront you, he would not discover the movements of the hidden veins in your minds; nor would a miner of discourse admit light into unfamiliar hiding places.

Therefore we do not approve ancient miracles if we refuse assent to youthful excesses. If, remembering that the servant is joined to the Lord and the disciple to the teacher of the Gospel, we neglect whatever could have been useful, then there are other things which, for the most shameless of men, we apply to recent use without injury to antiquity.

[Col. 1012C] You then opened up a new charge, one which our investigation had passed over: why did the pope summon a synod without the precedent of an established example, in order to inquire into the charge brought against him?

After this you accused us of falsehood before the emperor: “We learned what was written in the aforesaid case; we have read the petitions.”

Grant, Lord, that we may cross without error the winding turns of this labyrinth. Direct the path which the flexible serpent constructs beside the structure of its own body—or of its own mind—so that we may truly say: “The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our helper” (Psalm 45:8).

And let us rejoice with Solomon, who says: “The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory belongs to the Lord” (Proverbs 21:31).

It is indeed superfluous to answer absurd propositions, since the prophet says: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly” (Proverbs 26:4). But if something has passed by because of contempt, I fear that it may be thought powerful; I am afraid that not touching it may be mistaken for inability.

It is better for us to incur, with blessed Paul, the causes of insult and to testify in a full voice: “I have become a fool; you forced me to it” (2 Corinthians 12:11).

[Col. 1012D] Was there, then, no precedent at all for a pope to summon a council of priests, whose decision is a synodal assembly? Or were the crimes committed by you, with this great multitude, too insignificant to be condemned?

Are not the words of the canons explicit? “Whoever among the clergy departs from his bishop before the time of sentence, on account of doubtful suspicion, shall remain subject to manifest censure.”

For this purpose a devoted company ought to have come forward in the service of God, so that an army of physicians might assist the wounds of a lost and scattered flock. For whenever the violence of diseases hastens with swift step into the hidden places of the soul, salutary counsel cannot bring the necessary helping hands unless it proceeds from the consultation of many.

Your own allegation also demanded this from the king: that, once the prejudices against the clergy had been cut away, the supreme authority should judge through a human mouth concerning the merit of the pope’s accusers.

Let us nevertheless, if you please, reread those clever arguments of your little didactic treatise.

[Col. 1013A] The sanctions of the Fathers also stand before our eyes, by which the cesspool of your excesses may be weighed. Ecclesiastical law requires that a pontiff accused by others not be abandoned before the charges brought into the light have been established.

But you, supposedly mindful of divine law, despise minor errors because you take pleasure in the nobility of sin; lest guilt from the abandonment of the priest should touch you as well, you accuse him with additions to his crimes.

Your predecessor brought you to this condition, so that, after the pontiff had been deserted and attacked, you should believe that the censure of almost the whole of Italy’s bishops could be rejected without the severity of any sentence.

As someone said concerning your cohort: “He entrusted the hastening soul of your man to death.” Can a mind unlearned in crimes, already enriched by success and sterile through its detestable purpose, be brought to rest?

He made you rich in these evils—the man whose abundance of exaltation took away angelic wealth, and who begrudged the divine treasury the overflowing riches of harm.

But, mindful of our promise, let us touch upon all the matters which we recall as inserted into their work.

[Col. 1013B] Pope Symmachus is accused in a most splendid style: why, anticipating the assembly, did he enter into examination amid gatherings of the people, and why, after the judgments, did he disdain them when he had been summoned four times?

So completely has affection for truth departed from you that you suppose the testimony of the city to be enveloped in clouds of lies, and that words painted with the danger of falsehood possess more force, in your judgment, than the truth which Rome retains.

Did he, then, approach the dispute either uninvited or importunately, or did he flee when awaited? Did that multitude of the devout people come forth not out of Christian diligence for the faith, but rather because expectation summoned it—or fury?

Does anyone who runs to inflict violence have tears as companions, and does one who seeks to inspire fear display the face of someone afraid?

That multitude, bound by the duties owed to the priest, brought us laments, not weapons. It did not come threatening with missiles, but pitiable in its tears. It would burden your intention by a single display: through rivers flowing from abundant eyes, it showed how grievously, because of your harshness, the expelled man was to be pitied in his condition; and, in the sober and venerable examination, it [Col. 1013C] commended by its own affliction the man whom it could not commend by its voice.

But this matter gives you a clear indication of whom fury inflames with bile: he who came to the judgments almost acquitted, on whose behalf the world weeps, while you gather by speech an envy foreign to the facts against the aforesaid man. For a little while, your long-proud neck is compelled to bow to reverence.

You call it a sacred assembly when you wish to assert that Symmachus was our destroyer, and in cruel piety you think that it adds to our honor that, while seated in the fortress of the Churches, he destroyed us.

We have not perceived matters in this way; rather, we perceive the opposite. Turn the poisons of your protection elsewhere. He has no testimony as a defender who offers the service of his mouth to one who resists.

He loses the grace of the benefit he thinks he is granting who gives something to an unwilling recipient, since a gift is not a gift unless one wishes to receive it.

There is no need now to admonish you at length, since you are already lost. We owe hatred to the work of which nothing remains for its authors to condemn.

[Col. 1013D] You assert that crowds of women came with the aforesaid man to the judgments, using urban colors of description; and by that subtlety of yours the sex is exposed which ought to have shown greater affection toward the bishop.

Most profane of men, I retain what is written: “It is one thing to speak evil, another to accuse.” And the prophet says: “You rejected the word, you hoped in calumny and tumult, and you have persisted in it. Therefore this iniquity shall be for you like a breach, because God speaks on our behalf” (Isaiah 30:12–13).

“I will judge those who judge you.” And again he says to his servants: “Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies” (Matthew 10:26).

Again he cries out to you: “Come here, seed of adultery and fornication, against whom have you mocked? Against whom have you opened your mouth wide and thrust out your tongue? Are you not children of wickedness, a lying seed?” (Isaiah 57:3–4).

Observe what you join to what.

You say that, in the case in question, the defenders departed with the pope. In the present matter you offer examples from the forum and the streets, of which you are hypocrites:

[Col. 1014A] “It is written for us through the Apostle Paul: ‘For whom the world has been crucified’” (Galatians 6:14).

What have they to do with the forum? But you do not know these things, or, what is more serious, you knowingly despise them.

I suppose the pope departed while asking for something foreign and separated from reason. Did he not hope for this, bound by pastoral concern for the condition of the tottering Church, as both religious foresight and the order of the case demanded?

What form of judgment had preceded, so that, after you had been hostilely broken apart and, moreover, through your own suggestion, the resources of the Church had been removed—resources which for a long time had been food for the hungry—and the man who distributed nourishment seemed to have been made a slave of hunger, so that servitude might exist in domination and domination in servitude?

The character of the preceding age returned through memory to the center of the matter: what had happened under the earlier censure and what judgment had preceded the case in which the accused was condemned.

There was no privilege from which one who had already been stripped could be deprived. You think that one support alone remains for you in the sacred assembly: to attach priests as companions to yourselves in defending monstrous crimes, so that a crime might be rendered unpunishable through the pollution of many. [Col. 1014B]

A censor is never summoned at the proper time, because the guilty are called together when the case is almost decided. And if there is merit, the accuser removes it, since he wishes his fury to have greater license in that matter than the judge.

For the attacking prophet says to you: “This is the portion of those who laid us waste, and the lot of those who plundered us” (Isaiah 17:14)—“also swift messengers to the torn and ravaged flock, to a terrible people” (Isaiah 18:2).

A messenger has been sent to you, namely through priests, by whose voice and merit they receive gifts to be offered to Christ, and, when the Lord has been appeased, grant to mortals the requests they have obtained.

Through them gifts of rejected concord were offered to you; they brought to those who grieved the rewards of pleasure, while they considered themselves and looked upon nothing that you deserved.

“For who,” he says, “has ever seen him engage in open—so they call it—battle with his accusers?”

Most foolish of all, you who wish to contend with whomever you choose: look carefully, and, if any hope of salvation remains in you, consider the places, times, and persons of both parties. [Col. 1014C]

If the wealth wickedly heaped up in your still perverse hearts has not yet subdued you, lift your eyes for a little while toward the Lord and, even for a short time, disregard the commands of the sinister adviser.

Recognize that, by the commands of the supreme King, you are not protected in matters which rightly deserve punishment. For although the teachings dictate the character of the response, and the petition, while it exists, describes in advance what is to follow, you have never received, in your affairs, the free words of the ruler; never have imperial writings served your desires through the bird-catching of cunning.

As often as the ineffective bite of your empty gaping has snarled in its attempt to do harm, so often everything you held in hope concerning the accused has escaped, and the image seized by presumption has abandoned you empty-handed.

Thanks be to God, who has placed this foresight in the one to whom he entrusted the government of human affairs. The hope of peace is secure, and the wisdom of the governor is perfect for salvation.

[Col. 1014D] A ship whose master is prepared by the gift of understanding to direct the helm possesses everywhere, amid the waves, both a station and a harbor. There is sure security for the whole community when the state is governed by one trained in noble arts.

May the administration of our emperor, infused from heaven, extend a helping hand against minds famous for deceit. No labor is necessary before him, for whom naked truth long ago obtained a defender.

Let impious fabrications cease to pretend to simplicity through fraud in his presence. Whatever the matter may be, once he knows the justice of it, it is immediately held fast. Nothing is safer before the aforesaid ruler than innocence; he employs a powerful reading of the case, for he presents the matter suitably to equity.

An attack which is often serious for rulers is not bound by the flatteries of the less faithful. But these matters are better reported to God, from whom the plant of this fruit has sprung.

The hostile condition of the work I have undertaken brings me back to you, although until now I wished to range through better kinds of discourse, while imperious necessity demands captive speech.

[Col. 1015A] You said: “How will you first discuss the matter and its character, especially now that the synod still possessed validity?”

O forehead of unclean speech, and face of a little book, which ignorance alone has not stained! You both describe and question the province of our discussion. We were indeed uncertain, because, according to the way you speak, the synod did not possess validity.

The character of the case was passing before those who were to hear it, and more still remained in reverence for the man who had been struck than there was in the integrity of the assembly.

Then, after the torment of the questions, you repeat that the venerable bishops Laurentius and Peter suspended themselves from communion with the pope; and whatever the caution of those summoned provided, you turn into a charge against the accused.

Was there ever a time, while sacred Masses were being celebrated by them, when they ceased from mentioning his name? Did the bishops named ever, according to your desires, offer half-complete sacrifices without Catholic ritual and canonical custom?

Was an offense ever committed before the Lord through grace, to be attributed to your leader, and did an offering become the nurse of sin and the mother of forgiveness?

There were certain men, as you say, separated only by bodily assembly; [Col. 1015B] nevertheless, they did not avoid the presence of their souls. If you think that those whom the clasp of religion, biting with pious force, joins together were separated from communion by such a movement, an affection far removed from Catholic judgment has led you into the assessment of guilt.

Obedience to the heavenly command either joins or separates us. It makes no difference what intervals bring us together, if we are held in one chamber in the heavenly dwelling.

By this we truly prove that you are servants of the belly and the body; and through this baseness of your judgment you declare that you are slaves of earthly things. For it is written: “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

After this, with your ranks turned to flight and your speeches added in a frenzied manner, you said:

“Therefore the councils of priests, decreed annually throughout the provinces by ecclesiastical laws, have lost their force because they do not possess the presence of the pope.”

Read, most insane men, whether anything has ever been established in those councils apart from the sanction of the apostolic summit; and whether, in the greater matters, whatever arose was not reserved for consultation according to the judgment of the aforesaid see. [Col. 1015C]

For thus you have it: “If any bishop has been deposed by a provincial judgment, let him appeal again to the Roman pope, if he wishes; and he himself, if he thinks fit, may restore the judgments in aid of the condemned.”

Behold, the thing you prepared as a noose is plain—unless perhaps we are bound there by the tightest knots, and the paths of our replies are not opened to us, while the path that previously led forward is closed to these matters by a new obstruction.

For, as we walk through these thornbushes of speech, you hold us on level ground when you say that Jesus the prince—why did we wish, at the first appearance of the matter, to withdraw the appointed visitor contrary to ecclesiastical rules? Nothing further, you say, was permitted, lest the darnel harden through vices, lest the profane harvest, cut down by no disciplinary sickle before maturity, should fall, and lest what the judges did not forbid should be thought impermissible.

From this it is plainly evident that you are joined to no guilt outside the protection of the most pious king, which you desire in vain, and that you are supported by the authority of examples.

[Col. 1015D] It remains for me also to teach him that, in these excesses, what occurred for the good of all was not to be held against him, because he wished the directive to be not an occasion for litigation or fuel for quarrel, but a cause of concord. He foresaw, clearly, that unless he fortified the simple protection of his commands, your poisons would quickly steal it away as food for dissension.

For it is written: “The simple person believes every word.” Therefore he fixed the limit of the command, which no transgression was permitted to violate. He ordered that, once the aforesaid man had been brought to Rome, he should be met at the basilica of blessed Peter, thus making the king’s authority serve the priest’s wish.

Who would not have thought that the pontiff would willingly obey in that matter in which the prince did not believe it was permissible for him even to command? There, having ordered the pope to be greeted by him, he also ordered him to be addressed in such a way that the fellow bishop would hand over slaves who were to be subjected to no tortures, but were plainly to be preserved for the examination of the synodal judgment.

O purity of the command! While presenting its face to the present age, it forces the ancient shadow—which steals light from old things—into the shadow of the anticipated brightness of novelty.

[Col. 1016A] Who, rich in language, though deservedly poor or a fabricator of reputation, added this? Who enriched the Lord through such commendatory praises, when the truth of his deeds had left him poor in fame?

I do not detract from you, the chroniclers, through whose service it has happened that the distinguished deeds of our ancestors have been conveyed to us. But I will not be silent about God’s benefits, since our prince surpasses the adornments of speech. He examined the glory made subject to tongues, weighing the causes of those who could be rewarded, so that, while the result was skillfully granted to your petition, he nevertheless guarded ecclesiastical rights in every respect.

Whatever hearts sharper than others might suffice for this judgment, your desires were fulfilled at one time, in one writing, without injury to equity; and the same document was dispatched both for the service of religion and for your joy.

For the inquiry of the good prince foresaw that a slave’s testimony would not be approved by an innocent examination. In the selection of the venerable judges, he himself rejected the accusers through an extraordinary procedure; he himself restored the accused to hope.

[Col. 1016B] Let us nevertheless see whether these things were done—whether you were not enemies of God and also earthly lords, when with equal recklessness you despised Christ and the king, and one course of crimes led you to both insults.

The appointed bishop was snatched away from the boundary of fulfilling the command by the breath of your mouth and prepared as an incentive to confusion.

He had come to serve peace; yet, at the unseen threshold of the blessed Apostle, he was summoned, now ignorant of himself, for the use of your fury. The place which draws the devout from every quarter of the world because it is situated nearby was passed by; he was not permitted to approach the foundation of the Churches. The structure of a moderate hope of good fruits then lost its hope from the root when it was severed.

Perhaps you will say that this was done in opposition to the spirit of the Apostle, if it is thought that a citizen of heaven can be enclosed within earthly places.

Nevertheless, although blessing is bestowed everywhere upon those who ask, and faith and the devotion of the suppliant demand the presence of the martyr, it cannot be denied that greater diligence is attributed to his native soil, and that places from which one passes to the heavenly realm obtain greater affection. [Col. 1016C]

The multitude of healings has already provided this testimony to the allegation, and, after the devil’s siege, it makes use of witnesses who have now been healed.

Although these things are celebrated throughout the entire world through our Redeemer, the renown of that monument has nevertheless been increased in no small measure by the frequency of visits. Through him who changed a human being into an angel, the nature of the earth could be illuminated.

You begrudged this grace to your visitor, judging that he would cease to be a follower of your errors if he touched the inner sanctuaries of the venerable passion.

Behold, you have no support in the authority of the emperor. Behold, after the heavenly commotion, both the just and imperial censure—which you caused to be despised—strikes you.

Let us see whether any defense remains from your regular proposition.

“They say,” you continue, “that he also gave visitors to other bishops, and it is just that he should be bound by the law of his own action.”

[Col. 1016D] I do not attack you here under the heading of falsehood, nor do I accuse words that have long adhered to lies. I say, however, that unless the bearer of the legal definition wishes not to be enclosed within its limits, and unless the prince moderates the summit of his dignity, the law concerning what he gave to the clergy is invoked in vain.

It is the law of integrity and of the mind that chastises a living person without law; it properly applies to morals, because discipline ought not to be subordinated to necessity.

Perhaps God wished the cases of other people to be settled through human beings; but he reserved this bishop’s case, without question, for his own judgment. He wished the successors of the blessed Apostle Peter to owe innocence to heaven alone, and to present an utterly refined conscience inviolate to the scrutiny of the examiner.

Do not suppose that those souls whom God reserved for his own judgment above others have no fear of investigators.

Before him the defendant has no support from the brilliance of his allegation when he himself uses the facts as witness. Under such a judge, you may perhaps say, the condition of all souls was the same in that dispute.

I will reply with a saying addressed to one man: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:18–19).

[Col. 1017A] And again, through the voice of holy bishops, the dignity of his see was made venerable throughout the whole world: whatever belongs to the faithful submits to him everywhere, and he is designated as the head of the entire body.

Concerning this, I think the prophet said: “If this one is humbled, to whose help will you flee, and where will you leave your glory?”

What if I, having unclean lips and kindled by no coals—as was granted to Isaiah—were permitted, once those lips had been cleansed, to summon the Apostle Peter himself to defend the privileges of his possession, so that he might speak what he said through human speech and prayer?

If you listened to him, he would say: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? Know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful” (Psalm 4:3–4).

Why do you seek to overthrow foundations established by the hands of Christ? He dishonors the reverence due to the venerable name who claims to be an assistant in matters which he boasts have been entrusted to God.

It is a form of insult to stand, as though in consolation, beside one who is exalted, according to the Apostle: “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” (Romans 14:4).

[Col. 1017B] Why do you mock inexperienced ears, and make the appearance of vengeance seem more serious than that of guilt?

If you owe hatred to excesses, cleanse yourselves. Why do you condemn crimes more freely than you avoid them?

He is his own attacker who, through the services of fornication, presses adulteries upon others, and through the violation of souls accuses the flesh.

You surely retain what is written: “All who fornicate away from you are accursed” (Psalm 72:27).

The bond with the brightness of his Lord is therefore dissolved in the one who, according to the heavenly statutes, renders the duties of faith with insufficient purity.

The splendor of your possession, as I see, has stirred your envy; you transfer it through a feigned indignation against an evil possessor, while you labor and spend.

You proposed to overthrow the fortress in which you had been conspicuous, weakened by repeated blows, unless I resisted; and through its ruin to show how great was the structure established in heaven.

Do not await your victory in disaster. Do not lose, by conquering, the triumph obtained through my labors and my sweat. Whatever leads to triumph I have secured; whatever would make you illustrious in the see, I have gathered together.

[Col. 1017C] This torch grants you the splendor which you think can be extinguished by viperous poison. One who rages in such a way against the shoots of his own grace kindles the fire of his own destruction; in an anger freer than is just, he attacks the author more than others.

If the excesses of Symmachus, as you call them, are those which I too await with expectation, it is impious not to love the patience of the judge toward one who is sinning.

What else does the man demand but vengeance who, while himself guilty, complains of delays in vengeance against another?

This voice is owed by me to those endeavors, since I hold that God said that the human being is inclined toward wickedness and that all flesh is friendly toward sins.

I do not want dignity, which would provide innumerable occasions through a single person, to become a possession in disgrace, lest, while a human being is attacked, the divine law be broken. Believe me, if these are the things you say.

I consider what existed even in those against whom nothing of this kind was alleged; I have examined it.

He is mistaken who thinks that being deceived is close to God: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Hebrews 10:30).

You, rather, former sons, whose spiritual womb was burdened with childbirth, [Col. 1017D] return to the renounced concord.

May the Church, your mother, receive you in her pious embrace, as she has received you until now. Correction is never too late.

She knows how to await for a long time those acquired through immense labor; she does not know how, according to her strength, to despise those purchased at great price. There are many steps by which one returns to salvation.

No one is excluded except the one who despairs; the fruit of forgiveness is near to the crown.

Do not aid Pope Symmachus through your pressures. If he is guilty, believe me: when the ministry of human opposition has ceased, divine judgment will immediately follow.

Does not either punishment or reward belong to the aforesaid most splendid examiner’s balance?

Do not seek from me syllogisms of speech or rhetorical figures. I still use the ancient net for catching human beings, and I have not abandoned the little boat mocked by the wise men of the world.

It sustains me across the seas of the world; it enriches me—proved, as you rightly see, for the catching of human beings.

Return, therefore, because flight rescued you before you became wild. Run to the fold, and do not expose yourselves to the ambushes of wolves, lest through delay you lose the grace of those who come willingly, since Gehenna follows a rejected invitation.

[Col. 1018A] Therefore, if I owed you any sweetness, as is evident, or if, as an appointed teacher, I fulfilled any severity, take care that for no longer a time some corner of my cross be surrounded by a sparse band of Levites; lest a solitude grievous even to outsiders dominate for too long; lest the labor of my womb should have borne against you a hostile family in sterility, and a numerous offspring should display the barrenness of its parent through sinister deeds.

A few things have been asserted, but consider how much depends upon them:

> “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 33:12).

Look to Rome, which the outpouring of Christ’s blood freed from slavery to idols without payment in gold or silver; to whom he also commanded the death of me, his little servant, to be offered; which for many ages displayed worship in famous shrines; which for a long time venerated images of demons; which had placed its hands under the domination of a taskmaster who imposed terror through an oppressive census; which looked up to the power of deities purchased with the price of metals; for which the more skillful hand of the craftsman produced greater gods, and the divinity which man bestowed through manufacture possessed among men a greater form of godhood. [Col. 1018B]

Behold, now, with Christ propitious, the images have returned to new furnaces. Behold, now, from your obsolete superstition your practice has received something in which to rejoice. While new vessels are deservedly prepared from the old Thunderer.

Why do you strive to interrupt this peace? Why do you make happiness a game through vain intentions? This madness has no excuse if you believe. It does not matter by what paths he moves toward the prince of the world who dissents from holy unity. He sacrifices rich victims to the devil who troubles the Church. Reject, therefore, your vain snares: the love of peace has a simple defense. He is sufficiently armed who disregards the weapons supplied by the adversary of concord. Bare opposition in faith is enough against all the darts of quarrels.

Why, while you seek the consolations of evil, do you recall the times of Eulalius and Boniface? Why do you present ancient contagions by increasing your excesses [Col. 1018C], and by an unjust will make it permissible for old age to conceal no offenses? The cause of discord was different then. And when, by recounting it, you would compel us to endure what has passed, I must show you that no consolation comes from comparing the deeds: those whom zealous compliance with ambition had raised to the pontifical height, I rejected both. I chose this man because, as the outcome bears witness, none of those others pleased me; among these I made the man striving against the rules an exile. I preserved the one legitimately advanced, although the world opposed him.

You know these things, and they are not new, because while one was thrust aside, the other was strengthened, and your assent served me. Why, then, do you injure the priestly council to your own destruction? Why do you tear apart the judgment in which, Christ inspiring it, heavenly oracles were revealed, and in which the tongue of the pontiffs stood as interpreter between God and human beings? Why do you inflict pain upon the universal Church, although the offense was committed in the chief Church, yet in one place alone?

That heavenly court, enriched by the various endowments of its councilors and adorned with much gold and purple for our Redeemer [Col. 1018D], brought nothing forward in that deliberation on its own authority. Through the ministry of human speech it served the divine command; it understood that whatever it established under impulse was not its own; it has nothing in that judgment except what may rejoice in the solace of devotion. Its style recognized an alien eloquence and drew from it only this glory: that it both preserved and honored what had been infused into it.

What accusation have you prepared from these evangelical examples? As it is written concerning you:

> “They have erred through drunkenness; they have not known the seer; they have not understood judgment” (Isaiah 28:7).

For you strike the men mentioned with profane words, revealing ignorance and envy. These men, therefore, not believing in the resurrection of the body which they preach, mingled themselves with heretical contagions; whatever they renounce with their tongues, they pursue in their hearts.

Because they said that the one who can kill and cast the soul into Gehenna must be feared, they therefore wove this into an alien faith. Behold the depth of their ignorance. Behold blessed Luke, by whose assertion you can be convicted. What does he proclaim?

> “Fear him who, after he has killed the body [Col. 1019A], has power to cast the soul into Gehenna.”

Where is the error here, when the words of the example and the history agree in an equally fitting statement, and what is brought forward is not different from Catholic understanding and the readings? One should never search for a knot in a reed; the authors of the proclaimed light do not wrap it in mist.

You do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh because you confess that the body can be killed; because you say that the sinful soul can be handed over to Gehenna, your heart is choked by dense thorns. You struggle to attribute inward vices to others, and you boast that the writings of the apostle John are being violated because it is said in his words:

> “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

I ask nothing about the diversity of manuscripts. Are the apostle’s admonitions therefore corrupted because they have not added the words “we are liars,” and, because they have not added them, “we deceive ourselves”? You are ignorant not only of divine but also of human reasoning. He who does not possess the truth is rightly considered worthy of fear; and he who is recognized as empty of integrity is full of nothing but falsehood [Col. 1019B].

But these matters are not to be addressed to you through the speech of the tongue, but through groans. You should be shown not so much words as tears, because clearly the guilty person is harmful who opposes the innocent either a merit that condemns him or a name.

I shall not go over the remaining principal points of your objections; it is better that what deserves condemnation be buried in silence. He lends nobility to crimes who multiplies their exposure by transmitting the report of them to later ears. We must follow the judgment of blessed Paul, who admonishes everyone through his disciple and cries out:

> “Avoid empty questions.”

For there are many things in your propositions which the love of sin embraces with such filthy arms that they become unworthy of remembrance. Levity dishonors many things when, after the weights have been removed, your words are stripped bare, and inflated speech is composed about matters of religion.

An ear rightly endowed with gravity, amid an abundance of chaff that will bring no grain into the storehouses, gives birth to a luxuriance of stalks barren of crops and falsely promises the farmers hope from an excess of grass. From such things the winnowing-fans find no profit; they are destined for fire and destruction by burning. Of these it is written:

> “They have slept their sleep, and have found nothing” (Psalm 75:6).

There is nothing, dearest brothers, sweeter than peace, provided that a heart full of bitterness does not shut out its taste. I ought to have offered a brief rather than a lengthy admonition; but no small consideration of you, and a fountain stirred up for you by divine rebukes, has produced it. It is common for many sinners not to be corrected by a restrained address, and in admonitory speeches they seek an outpouring as great as that which they have shown in their sins.

For me, it is enough that I have obeyed both your diligence and the heavenly commands. I shall leave no further place for speeches in what follows, because I report that Rome, the head of the world, has been overthrown by your intentions, and that the chair which nourishes the pontiff has been despised as though it were seeing its final seat.

Blessed Paul heard its voice and thundered with the freedom of speech which he always used [Col. 1019D]. You attack the prince of the apostles for his gentleness, because he still preserved a father's affection toward minds weakened and ruined and did not come to their aid with the physician's knife when their wounds had been driven deep. He teaches that the hidden seats of diseases must be cut open, and that a healing wound must plainly be applied to despair, lest, while the physician’s hand is held back through impiety from cutting corrupted flesh, death be invited by withholding the instrument. For while the right hand spares the sick, it kills those whom it ought to cure. Nor is there much difference whether one inflicts death or permits it: one who, though able, does not avert death from the sick has inflicted it.

Thus someone opened the door of his mouth against them:

> “Everyone who judges, when you judge another, condemns yourself. For you do the very things which you judge. We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things.”

And again:

> “Blessed is the one who does not judge in what he approves of himself” (Romans 14:22).

What reason is there for someone who steals to proclaim that theft must not be committed, and to cover a shameless forehead with the cloud of an attack upon another? No one rightly assumes the role of admonisher except one who condemns error by his own actions and demonstrates love of innocence by his manner of life.

For even publicans find it congenial to condemn vices in speech, and criminals to punish through the services of the tongue what they love—as though it were not a kind of greater excess to give affection to the accused with one’s lips while despising him in one’s mind, and to cloak the poison of the intellect with the honey of conversation.

If I were to do this—if shame, chastity, and beauty could accuse a teacher before your eyes, and a bite from an envious mouth could be fitted against the chosen one—although, knowing what was to come, I had warned you in a letter addressed to you in a full voice:

> “Who will bring an accusation against God’s chosen? God, who justifies. Who is the one who condemns?” (Romans 8:33.)

And again:

> “O man, who judges those who do such things and yet does them yourself, do you suppose that you will escape the judgment of God?” (Romans 2:3.)

Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering?

You accuse malice while filled with iniquity, fornication, impurity, greed, wickedness, envy, murders, contention, deceit, malignity; proud and arrogant, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without mercy. You teach fornicators that no one is to associate with the adultery of Laurentius—whether they were his followers or those who preceded him, through whom he either practiced the poisons he possessed or, by pouring them out, displayed what he had received.

After that stain of seductive communion, a plague execrable throughout the whole world, you accuse the priests of God, comparing them to something obsolete because of their communion. You think those guilty who entered into the association, although convicted by no witness; and you follow a man pierced through by the entire ecclesiastical indictment—not merely by a stylus, but by a sword.

What is permitted is not permitted, and what is not permitted is permitted.

> “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted the truth” (2 Timothy 3:8),

so you too, with a mind rejected concerning the faith, reveal yourselves as proud and insolent betrayers, puffed up, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance [Col. 1020C] of piety but denying its power.

O force of inward grief, which cannot release what it has conceived; which, with the impulse to speak inserted deep in its entrails, breaks out under the command of force!

I shall say nothing further to you from what remains of this speech; lamentations will supply the rest. After this, if you are wasting away amid the care of physicians, some reflection upon the salvation begun now brings you back. At least look upon your city, the mother of the world. She herself, grieving after her apostolic defenders, approaches you. She herself calls upon you and, if there is any piety, begins a speech by which she may obtain what remains.

I, whom the temples of the highest God—rejoicing in the worship of his favor and the splendor of the new light—made conspicuous; whom, after filthy shrines polluted by the abundant gore of animals, he cleansed by the outpouring of the Lord’s and the apostles’ blood; whom the restoration of health after a long illness made despise the shrines; whom the offering freed from sacrifices [Col. 1020D]; I, who acquired Christ’s peace after hostility toward idols; to whom there were scarcely fewer gifts than deities; whom her own religion rendered needy through varied devotion; whom poverty oppressed while I repeatedly sought benefits from my gods; I, who sent Curii, Torquati, Camilli—whom the Church did not regenerate—and the rest of a very numerous offspring to Tartarus, a barren mother of a large progeny, while I, exhausted, withered away in my ill-bearing entrails; because Fabius, although he preserved his country, did not redeem its honor; because nothing remained of the glory won through much toil; innocence, driven away from its works, was joined to criminals; and Scipio, because he ignored Christ, was most observant of the horse.

I would carry the stylus through all these things, if grief-stricken feeling could bear not to sustain the infancy of its lamentation. But whoever rereads the events of the lamentation seems to desire the times of tears. No one is believed not to hate what does not wound him when it is reported, because one who recounts the funerals of his children with a dry face is convicted by a sure witness of cruelty.

Let us reread that posterity which, having been lost, brought more sorrow than the one acquired brought joy [Col. 1021A], and let us nevertheless consider by what successes these things were changed.

Behold, now, in that sanctuary of freedom nothing servile is found among the worship of idols. Behold the crown of the good, the genius of the world, the Roman flower, which for a long time was venerated, now treads the altars full of holiness. Behold, now my senate-house is called to heaven, praised, and received.

Nor can I say that I lost my offspring after the grace of baptism, whom sudden death took away. The supreme ruler embraces many possessors of the *trabea* and the curule offices without loss to worship or dignity. Almost now we deserve divine favor for the generosity of earthly triumphs; and what you strive to make venerable to the world advances the glory of Christ.

I lie if the needy ranks of our consulship do not await your arrival as support in their miseries. Indeed, your purple, by the generosity of clothing, drives away the cold that steals upon the years—the name of nobility; and already almost once more the ornaments of the official registers have become assistance to those in need. When the losses of wealth laid aside in the old infidelity are so prepared, they become profits for souls.

Behold, now candidates send tearful eyes toward the portable chair of the apostolic confession, and the gifts conferred by God’s favor are multiplied by abundant tears exacted through joy. Who, at a time when words are being directed toward the most precious members, when the eternal mother is again about to give birth to our offspring, now receives it—she whose womb, after the first birth, is filled with the tears of the aged; she who, by regenerating offspring, made that which I bore dear to me; she who makes those who come to her cast off old age and return, though broken, to the beginnings of life?

Who, I ask, would compromise this happiness through an intervention? Who, with a viperous mind composed through discord, orders the benefits of the age to perish from my hearing? Who secretly inspires my downfall amid renewal, and under the appearance of a gentle countenance gains strength for hostility? I do not recognize a noble lineage in such a matter.

If, nevertheless, there are some of the highest rank whom the storm of this tempest has joined to lowly persons, they are stained by participation in crimes instigated by others [Col. 1021C]. The splendor of their blood, even if it encounters communion with crimes, nevertheless does not know how to present itself as a leader to sinners. Perhaps it bears guilt for neglected caution, but it does not deserve punishment for ruling crimes. Under a certain shame, the one who is summoned to mature quarrels is joined to the delinquents. The lost person does not deserve despair in whom only easy cruelty is condemned.

Rather, I see in you the offspring of the streets. I recognize in you those in whom the baseness of nature has produced corresponding habits; you whom distinction itself had made degenerate; you who rejoice in the impunity of vices under the pretended title of religion; you whose lips have never been touched either by the taste of honors or by quietness; you who violate every sacred law by obeying your origin; you whom the present cause has revealed as produced from hiding places and caves.

Who, before the composition of this evil, recognized the secrets to which the night of your birth had long concealed you? Return instead to your former congenial blindness; leave us the serene and daylight. Provide concord to the Church either by your absence or by correction. If, nevertheless, you wish to be numbered among distinguished lineages, let them recognize you by the correction of your deeds.

## Proceedings of the fifth synod of 218 bishops begin, under Pope Symmachus, in the time of King Theoderic

After the consulship of Amantius, when, with the Lord’s assent, we had assembled before the confession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the holy synod said:

“Let the document composed by Ennodius, with synodal authority, against those who dared insolently to mutter against our fourth synod, which was held at Rome at the Palmaria, be brought forward before everyone, read in the presence of all, and confirmed.”

When it had been read aloud and confirmed by all with one accord, the holy synod [Col. 1022A] said:

“Let these things be preserved for future times, held by all, and observed in every respect. Let this document be held by everyone in its complete synodal form and inserted among the proceedings of our fourth and fifth synods. Let it be regarded just as the decrees of these synods, because it was composed and confirmed by synodal authority.”

To this the most blessed pope replied:

“Let it be done according to the will of you all; let its adjudged authority be held apostolic, and let what you say be inserted among the apostolic decrees and held by all like the other apostolic decrees.”

To this all replied three times with one voice:

“We ask that it be done.”

Afterward all the bishops and presbyters acclaimed:

“We ask that those who accused Pope Symmachus, attempted to bring condemnation upon him, judged him, or dared to chatter or write against our synod, be condemned.” [Col. 1022B]

A little later all the bishops and presbyters cried out in a loud voice:

“Hear us, O Christ: life to Pope Symmachus!”—said eight times.

“His see and his years!”—said ten times.

“We ask that it be done!”—said twelve times.

When these acclamations had ceased, Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

“Since your fraternity, venerable fathers, with a singular devotion of charity, pious and vigilant affection, tireless labors, and lively spirit, has taken pains to foster the protection of ecclesiastical affairs; since you have bravely defended the apostolic see, which has been established upon the solid confession of Peter; since, although unworthy, by the Lord’s arrangement we preside over it; and since you have defended our wickedness, long since driven by many afflictions, with manly protection, resisting our detractors and whisperers—those whom the spirit of division continually torments with its goads, who are enemies of peace and pleased by discord—

“Because your goodness has stirred your concern for our protection through its exhortations, and we ask that, in contemplation of our Lord, you show equal care for the tranquillity of the Church, we entreat you to act more mildly toward our plotters and persecutors. Although they are justly condemned, nevertheless let them be preserved through mercy, so that the Lord’s sentence may be displayed in us, by which he commands that brothers be forgiven as they wish to be forgiven by the Lord.

“Furthermore, let no one ever presume such things not only against the bishop of the apostolic see, but let them not be attempted against any Christian bishop. It is not therefore necessary to forge new rules concerning these matters, but to recite and confirm the old ones.

“For it has been decreed and confirmed synodally by many of our predecessors that the sheep entrusted to their shepherd must not presume to rebuke him unless he has deviated from the right faith, nor dare to accuse him for any other matter except his injustice. The shepherd’s actions are not to be struck by the sword of the mouth, although they may properly be judged worthy of rebuke.

“We decree also that bishops who have been stripped of their possessions or expelled from their sees by force, fraud, or any other device—as you judged us to have been—cannot be summoned to a provincial or general synod or judged in any matter before everything taken from them has been peacefully restored to their authority by law [Col. 1023A].

“First, therefore, everything must be restored to them according to law, and the Churches taken from them must be returned with all their privileges. Afterward, they must be granted not a short period of time but as much time as they appear to have been dispossessed or expelled, before they are summoned to a synod and heard by all the bishops of their province.

“For one who has been dispossessed or expelled can neither be summoned to trial nor judged, because there is no privilege by which one already stripped bare can be stripped further. Hence it was decreed in ancient times that all possessions, everything taken from him, and all revenues must be restored to the possessor by the *praeceptor* or *primas* before the lawsuit is formally contested [Col. 1023B].

“And elsewhere it is written:

> ‘Let the one who has suffered violence receive back everything in the condition in which it had been, and let him securely retain what he possessed.’

“And elsewhere, in the synodal decrees of the Fathers and in the edicts of kings, it is established that everything must be restored in the presence of the bishops to bishops who have been dispossessed or expelled, and that all the things which they are known to have lost—whether Church property, private property, or possessions—through the passage of time, fraud, captivity, the power of superiors, or any unjust causes must be completely recalled to their authority from which they departed, before their accusation or regular summons to a synod, and so forth.

“It is also decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that he who invades another’s property must not depart unpunished but must restore everything with increase.

“Hence it is written in the Gospel:

> ‘If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold’ (Luke 19:8).

“And in the laws of the world it is provided that he who steals another’s property must restore to the person whose property was seized what was taken elevenfold.

“And in the divine law it is written:

> ‘Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbor’s boundaries’; and all the people say, ‘Amen’ (Deuteronomy 27:17).

“Such things, therefore, must not be presumed without any punishment, nor practiced without their condemnation. As for accusers who are enemies, or who come from an enemy’s household, or who dwell with enemies, or who are suspect: they must not be believed, lest they desire to harm in anger or wish to avenge themselves because they have been injured.”

[Col. 1023D] “What seems to you, dearest brothers, in these matters? In your prudence, declare what you judge for ecclesiastical peace and for the protection of the whole Church.”

The whole synod said:

“Relying upon the authority stated above, the prohibition of all the holy Fathers, and your common consolation, we jointly and firmly cut off for the future, through deliberate and truthful discussion, the persecution of bishops, the devastation of Churches, and the harassment of the servants of God. We confirm the statutes of the holy Fathers and decree in explicit judgments that no one, in our time or in times to come, may ever presume such things.”

After silence had been made, Symmachus, bishop of the Church of the city of Rome, said:

“If some have transgressed these provisions and presumed such things, declare with united agreement what you judge concerning them.” [Col. 1024A]

When they had risen and shortly afterward sat down again, they said with one voice:

“If anyone should presume to violate or deliberately attempt to transgress these things prohibited today in this holy synod, then, if he is a cleric, let him be entirely deprived of his own rank; but if he is a monk or layman, let him be deprived of communion, and, if he does not correct himself, let him be struck with near-anathema.

“If anyone brings to the knowledge of the Church secret or open plots directed against pontiffs, or the matters contained in the judgment of this holy synod, let him obtain honor. But those who plot against them, as was long ago established by the holy Fathers and is today confirmed by synodal and apostolic authority, shall be completely rejected and handed over to perpetual exile with all their possessions taken away.

“We ask that these things established in this holy synod, and those contained in the document which Ennodius composed by our authority and which have been read again in our presence, be ratified by their own hands, preserved forever, and, as has been stated, confirmed by your apostolic authority.”

But Symmachus, Catholic bishop of the Church of the city of Rome, said:

“Your acclamations and the judgment of the synod will be received by the present acts.”

He added:

“Those provisions which a deliberation appropriate to religion and peace has established for dealing with the errors of inveterate presumption and the diseases of hostile presumption against pontiffs, by which the condition of the Church and of its servants is accustomed to suffer, shall possess perpetual firmness. With the Lord’s assent—for he is known to be the guardian of good things—let the synodal ordinance prevail. Anyone who presumes to come without distinction of person shall be punished by the severity imposed above.” [Col. 1024C]

The whole synod said:

“We ask that it be done”—said ten times.

“We ask that scandals be cut off and that plots and slanders against bishops be avoided”—said twelve times.

After silence had been made, all those assembled in the holy synod cried out:

“Hear us, O Christ: life to Symmachus!”—said eight times.

“This is peace with Symmachus”—said nine times.

“His see and his years”—said ten times.

“Let it be done at once”—said twelve times.

A little later, when they had sat down, the whole synod, after silence had been made, said:

“Whoever among the clergy, monks, or laypeople—whether of higher or lower rank—after this form has been issued to us, presumes to oppose these [Col. 1024D] decrees shall be struck, as a schismatic, by the canonical statutes.”

And they subscribed:

“Caelius Symmachus, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed to this statute, accomplished among us with the Lord inspiring us.

“Laurentius, bishop of the Church of Milan, have subscribed to this statute, accomplished among us with the Lord inspiring us.

“Petrus, of the Church of Ravenna, have subscribed to this statute, accomplished among us with the Lord inspiring us.

“Eulalius, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, have subscribed to this statute, accomplished among us with the Lord inspiring us.

“Felix, bishop of Terracina, have subscribed.

“Stephanus, bishop of the Church of Corduba, have subscribed.

“Fortunatus, bishop of the Church of Valeria, have subscribed.

[Col. 1025A]
