The fifth Roman synod under Pope Symmachus, in the ninth indiction, ends.

The sixth Roman synod under Pope Symmachus begins, held in the time of King Theoderic, on the Kalends of October.

When the holy Sixth Synod, canonically convened by the blessed Symmachus at Rome, had assembled and taken its seat in the Church of the blessed Apostle Peter [Col. 1026D], the aforementioned Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome and presiding over that synod, said:

“Since this religious assembly, brought together by the Holy Spirit, urges us to treat with the most diligent care whatever is necessary for ecclesiastical discipline, we are compelled both by the governance of the apostolic see and constrained by the ordering of the churches to release the decrees of the fathers’ canons and to measure the decrees of our predecessors and former bishops in such a way that, with careful consideration and as far as possible with the Lord’s help, we may temper whatever the necessity of the present times demands should be restored or relaxed for the churches. For we who administer the duties of the supreme priest will be answerable for the guilt of transgressions if we are found negligent in the affairs of God, since we remember what we must fear and how the Lord threatens [Col. 1027A] the negligence of priests. Indeed, the one who enjoys the greater honor commits the greater offense, and the loftiness of dignities makes the faults of sins more serious.

“Therefore we must not remain silent; rather, whatever we recognize as necessary, let us strive manfully to correct and amend, and whatever is harmful, let us not neglect to uproot, as the Lord grants.”

All the bishops and presbyters acclaimed: “Hear us, O Christ; life to Pope Symmachus!”—this was said seven times. “These things we confirm, and these things we teach”—this was said eight times. “We give immense thanks for your teaching”—this was said ten times. “We ask that these things be held and these things be observed”—this was said twelve times. “A worthy pope, a worthy teacher.”

And when silence had been made, Bishop Symmachus said:

“Common is the grief and general the lamentation over what we have learned has occurred within the Church, both in our own times and in former times: the seizure of ecclesiastical property and the harassment of priests. This matter concerns not us alone but all the priests of the Lord. Although these things have already been prohibited by our predecessors, and such presumptuous persons have been condemned and anathematized by the holy canons, nevertheless, lest they again be attempted, a judgment must also be pronounced concerning them, so that those who do not fear their downfall may at least fear their everlasting condemnation. What is often attempted must be prohibited all the more frequently.

“The holy synod said: ‘It is fitting that, by a prudent judgment of your blessedness in this synodal assembly, these things be prevented from happening again and be utterly uprooted, lest an example of presumption remain.’

“Bishop Symmachus said: ‘Now, because God has granted me your desired presence, it is necessary that this matter be made firm. I believe that it accords with ecclesiastical resources, so that all may recognize that those whom empty fury and avarice have stirred cannot presume to do such things without punishment.’

“The holy synod said: ‘We know that your prudence is devoted to what is necessary. Therefore it is in your power to arrange what must be followed.’

“Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

“‘Great reverence is owed to a venerable and priestly purpose when one is required to arrange what is right from devotion rather than from necessity. But since, when certain people demand what belongs to others, avarice—the mother of vices—after rejecting the barriers of honesty, thinks that anything whatsoever is expedient, and thus, while it gapes after plunder, abuses the patience of the heavenly city, those awaiting correction think that, while heaven regulates its judgments, they are not held accountable [Col. 1027D], although it is clear that, in the case of certain people, the delay of the divine sentence proceeds as an opportunity for plunder.

“‘But we, whom pastoral care and ecclesiastical duty bind, must render a definite account of our stewardship, so that our concern may extend not only to the present but also to future ages. Otherwise it may bring harm to our souls if those who, presuming upon their freedom, have violated what they owe to established laws and innocence can be supported by religious and ecclesiastical authority, and our successors can be supported by our power while serving the ecclesiastical laws.’

“The holy synod said: ‘We know that the Spirit of God has enkindled your heart and that you speak thus at God’s prompting. Therefore it is above all fitting that everyone observe that no one presume to claim the offerings of the faithful, and that no one attempt to possess or control them without the consent and will of the bishop in whose parish and authority they are known to lie. For some people, mindful of their own salvation, have handed over to the churches, for the remission of their sins and for paternal life [the transmitted wording is uncertain], portions of their property—some immovable goods, others by written instruments—and have given them to be held perpetually by God their Creator. Yet these goods are held with deadly cunning by those who fear God less in adversity, to such an extent that another person’s offering becomes their ruin. They cannot look in their hearts toward the day of judgment while they delight in the heat of excessive greed.

“‘Therefore we ask that you renew the rules of the ancient fathers, which now, because of the injury inflicted by certain people, are treated as though forgotten, so that such a judgment may be made against them that they shall either be openly regarded as heretics—those who tear apart the Church of God—and, having been anathematized, be held as exiles from the Church of God, or, through satisfaction rendered to the Church, be received into penance and thereafter, in accordance with the ecclesiastical rules, admitted to reconciliation.’”

Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

“Therefore, having duly considered these matters, lest they fall into ruin and be condemned to everlasting destruction, and lest the holy Church, redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, be restored while those who devoutly serve it are not oppressed but relieved, with due measure and in consideration of our God, together with our judgment, we decree that whoever—whether mindful or forgetful of his own destruction—shall henceforth presume to possess and retain, without the command of his own bishop, ecclesiastical property entrusted to the Church and offered to the Lord, wherever this fact is discovered, or shall conceal God’s property from his servants or refuse to restore it, shall first be barred by the bishop of that place from the threshold of the church. For one who dares to invade ecclesiastical property, or to possess it unjustly—that is, without the bishop’s permission—or to persist in an iniquitous or unjust defense of it, is unworthy to be permitted to approach God’s altar. Such persons are to be judged killers of the poor according to the fixed tenor of this decree, and, if they do not amend their fault, they are to be uprooted.

“Provision must nevertheless be made that admonition plainly precede vengeance, and that the one who unjustly took away the usurped property, or unjustly retains what was taken away, restore it under the protection of equity and the laws. But if he neglects this, and necessity eventually compels it, let the priestly coercion, hastened against the robber, strike him [Col. 1028D]. Let no one attempt to defend God through internal resources, for God’s power, by its singular dominion, encloses the boundaries of all kingdoms. If anyone presumes to do so, he shall suffer both the offense against God and the danger of the aforementioned condemnation.

“We also impose the restraints of this coercion upon the competitors who have invaded ecclesiastical property through wrongful stealth under the appearance of royal generosity or of the authority of anyone whatsoever. We are moved too late by repentance concerning these matters, since in times past the priests of the Lord, supported by the protection of the canons, ought to have risen against such persons, so that the mildness of indulgence would not daily provoke the audacity of the wicked to commit similar acts. Now, weighed down in our hearts by the burden of injuries and compelled by the damages themselves, we are roused.

“But if the person who lays claim to the Lord’s property customarily resides in territories other than those in which the matter is chiefly being handled, the priest of the place where he resides shall, without neglecting the case, inform the bishop of that place by letter [the transmitted Latin is corrupt]. Then that bishop, having learned of his brother’s concern, shall either correct the invader of the Lord’s property by admonition or condemn him by the canonical coercion prescribed above.

“Accordingly, in the canons established by apostolic authority in the Church of Gangra, it is written concerning the offerings of fruits owed to the ministers of the Church and concerning those things that are contributed for the use of the poor:

“‘If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church apart from the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, and does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.’

“And again, in the same council:

“‘If anyone gives or receives what has been offered to God apart from the bishop, or apart from the person appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, let both the giver and the receiver be anathema.’

“It is therefore exceedingly wicked and a great sacrilege that whatever anyone has contributed or left to a venerable church, whether for the remedy of sins, salvation, or the repose of souls, should be transferred or converted to another use by those to whom it is especially fitting that these things be preserved—that is, by Christians and God-fearing people, and above all by the princes and foremost men of the regions.

“Therefore whoever has not foreseen these matters and has sought, received, possessed, unjustly defended, or retained estates handed over to the churches in a manner other than what is written, unless he quickly corrects himself, shall be struck with the anathema by which God, when angry, strikes souls. Let there be anathema for the receiver, the giver, and the possessor, together with perpetual association with the prescribed penalty. Let no one who scatters, contrary to right and without any consideration of piety, what religious souls left for the support of the poor fortify himself with any defense before the tribunal of Christ.”

All the bishops and presbyters acclaimed: “We ask that these things be utterly cut off.” This was said five times. “We beseech that these things be severed.” This was said seven times. “We ask that the Church’s property be preserved with inviolate right by those to whom it was entrusted.” This was said seven times. “We ask that, while pursuing this matter, they become entirely unanimous in their prayers through the synodal assembly.” This was said eight times. “We ask that vengeance be taken upon the presumptuous.” This was said ten times. “We ask that discipline be preserved.” This was said eleven times. “Let what has been wrongly admitted be corrected through you.” This was said twelve times. “We ask that unlawful acts be cut off, so that henceforth they may not be committed.” This was said thirteen times. “Let the apostolic ordinance be preserved unimpaired.” This was said fourteen times. “A worthy pope: let what is not permitted not be done.” This was said fifteen times. “Hear us, O Christ; life to Symmachus.” This was said sixteen times. “We ask that the canons be guarded.” This was said fifteen times. “Let the apostolic ordinance be preserved”—this was said fifteen times. “A worthy pope, a worthy teacher”—this was said nineteen times. “We all unanimously confirm these things, and we ask that they be unanimously observed”—this was said twenty times. “Through the Lord Peter, we ask that they be preserved forever”—this was said twenty times. “Whoever violates these things, let him find upon himself the penalty prescribed above”—this was said twenty times.

And when silence had been made, Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

“We decree that the form of the present definition, established according to the judgment of the holy fathers, be brought to the knowledge of all the churches, so that no one may be permitted, through ignorance, to do what is not permitted, and so that those who presume such things may know that they are condemned in the manner prescribed above.

“Likewise, with the exhortation and judgment of all of you, we decree that this also be brought to the knowledge of the churches and firmly held by everyone: since the property of the churches is undoubtedly the property of the bishops, if the invaders of the aforesaid property are attacked by the punishment of the aforementioned canonical coercion with similar cruelty in their possessions [Col. 1030B], so that those who are not corrected by their own superiors or by any chastisement of conscience may at least be pierced by the barbs of ecclesiastical and canonical vengeance.

“Generally, however, whoever presumes to confiscate, claim, or invade ecclesiastical property through dangerous or persistent harassment, unless he corrects himself immediately through satisfaction rendered to the church concerned, shall be struck with perpetual anathema. Likewise, those who have retained ecclesiastical property by the command or generosity of princes, or of certain powerful persons, or through some invasion or tyrannical authority, and have left it to their sons or heirs as though hereditary—as we have heard certain people have already done—unless, after being admonished by the bishop and recognizing the truth, they quickly return God’s property, shall be struck with perpetual anathema.

“For we judge it unjust that we should be considered rather keepers of documents than defenders of the property entrusted to us, as has been commanded. The matter must therefore be healed more quickly, lest the execrable disease of the soul spread farther. When a physician sees that some sickness has arisen in an earthly body, he considers it a great proof of his art if, through his intervention, the person who was thought hopelessly ill quickly recovers; or, when he sees a wound, he applies remedies and whatever else may cover the wound that has arisen. But if, while it remains, it cannot be healed, lest it corrupt the rest of the body with its decay, he cuts away with iron what was harmful, so that he may preserve the remainder whole and untouched.

“Therefore that which has crept in like an excessive wound upon a pure and healthy body must be cut away [Col. 1030D], lest, if it is cleansed too slowly, the foul bilge-water of this evil become impossible to drain from the very entrails of punishment. Wounds that do not respond to remedies must be cut away with iron.

“Likewise, those who are not corrected by priestly admonition must be made exiles from the Church, as the Lord says: ‘Remove the evil from among you’ (Deut. 19:19).”

The whole synod acclaimed: “We ask that these things be done”—this was said eight times. “We beseech that these things be preserved”—this was said ten times. “We ask that they remain forever and be confirmed by your authority”—this was said twelve times. “Hear us, O Christ; life to Pope Symmachus”—this was said twelve times.

And when silence had been made, Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome and presiding over the synod, said:

“By this we all know that we love God: if we do his commandments [Col. 1031A]. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments, and his commandments are not burdensome. The Lord is just, and all his judgments are just; all his ways are mercy, truth, and judgment. In the hand of God is the power of the earth; to him every iniquity is detestable. In the hand of God is the power of man, and upon the face of the scribe he will place his honor. God destroys the memory of the proud and of those who do evil, and leaves the memory of the humble and good. Everyone who rightly worships God knows this with certainty: if his life is tested, he will be crowned; if it is afflicted, he will be delivered; and if it is subjected to correction, he will attain mercy.

“The Catholic Church defends everything that is irreprehensible. Therefore it is not permitted for an emperor or for anyone who guards piety to presume anything against the divine commandments, or to do anything that conflicts with the evangelical, prophetic, and apostolic rules. For an unjust judgment or an unjust decision arranged by judges through royal fear or command shall have no force; nor shall anything stand that has been done against the constitution of evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic teaching, whether by them or by the holy fathers. Whatever has been done by unbelievers or heretics shall be entirely annulled.

“Therefore my holy predecessors confidently strove to condemn what was harmful. My own insignificance, although unequal and least among them, nevertheless desires, in the ministry undertaken by divine favor, to follow in their footsteps. Woe to us if, having undertaken the burden of this ministry, we neglect to preach the truth of our Savior Jesus Christ, which the apostles proclaimed. Woe to us if we suppress by silence the truth when we are commanded to distribute it to the money-changers—that is, to instruct and teach Christian peoples.

“What shall we say at Christ’s future judgment if we are ashamed to preach the truth of his words? What will become of us when our just judge, our God, strictly demands an account concerning the souls entrusted to us and concerning the office we have undertaken? Therefore we must always cut away what is harmful and, with the Lord’s help, raise up what is beneficial.

“Accordingly, by rebuking, exhorting, persuading, encouraging, and advising, let us hasten to benefit those whom we can. Let our tongue be a remedy for the good and a goad for the wicked; let it restrain the fearful, calm the angry, sharpen the sluggish [Col. 1031D], kindle the negligent through exhortation, and persuade those who withdraw. Let it be gentle toward the harsh and console the despairing, so that, since we are called teachers, we may show the way of salvation to those who walk in it.

“Let us be watchful in our guard; let us carefully fortify the entrances against the enemy’s ambushes. If error ever leads a lost sheep away from the flocks entrusted to us, let us strive with all our strength to call it back to the Lord’s folds, so that from the name of shepherd which we bear we may receive not punishment but reward.

“Since, therefore, we need the help of divine grace in all these matters, let us beseech the mercy of almighty God with continual prayers, that he may grant us both the will and the ability to carry these things out, and may direct us along that road with the fruit of good works by which he testified that he is the Shepherd of shepherds [Col. 1032A], so that through him, without whom we can do nothing, we may be able to accomplish all things.”

The whole synod rose and acclaimed: “All these things please us; we ask that they be confirmed with perpetual stability”—this was said eight times. It added: “Hear us, O Christ; life to Symmachus”—this was said eight times. “Let these things be preserved inviolate”—this was said ten times. “We beseech that these things be guarded with inviolate right”—this was said twelve times. “We ask that whoever willingly violates these things be struck with perpetual anathema”—this was said fifteen times. “We beseech you to confirm our decrees”—this was said eighteen times.

And when silence had been made, Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

“The acts of the present session receive your acclamations and the judgment of the synod.”

And he added:

“Let those things which the deliberation, appropriate to religion and peace, has established with perpetual firmness for calming the errors of long-standing presumption and the diseases of hostility toward ecclesiastical property, by which the universal Church was afflicted, be joined together, so that, with God granting his aid—for he is known to be the guardian of good things—the synodal ordinance may remain in force, and so that everyone who presumes to come without distinction of person may be punished by the coercion imposed above.”

And they subscribed:

“Caelius Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, assenting to these synodal constitutions, approved and confirmed by me, subscribes.

“Peter, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, assenting to these synodal constitutions, approved and confirmed by us, subscribes.

“Innocentius of the Tiberine Dertona; Felix of Trarva; Severinus of Tundaris; Boniface of Aquileia; Silianus of Velitrae; Maximus of Blera; Sebastianus of Furanum; Aemilianus of Furanum; Mercurius of Ganina; ## Letter of the same pope to Laurentius, archbishop of Milan

[Col. 1033B]

To his most beloved and dearest brother Laurentius, archbishop of the Church of Milan, Symmachus, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

“The mind devoted to praise reveals the vow of a religious conscience; the assertion of talent is to devote what we say to those who obey God. In their praises, perhaps, a narrow speech displays its lack of skill. Yet if childish inadequacy is held back, who would judge the account poor when vows enrich it? Often the vein of the preacher is found poor in the gifts of eloquence, while conversely the treasure of the heart shines through poverty of words.

“One who judges in God’s place does not seek embellished speeches, but what unadorned brilliance of talent commends, for in some things eloquence flatters even without love, while in others naked truth commends its own splendor. Whether you are deceived or not, everything dictated by affection is fashioned to perfection; that which we desire seeks not so much to possess the appearance of what is right as its likeness.

“Above all, my speech is addressed to you, venerable bishop, whose virtue has acquired a name through the testimony of those who did not deserve it, in whom conduct speaks, or rather, whom the one who pronounces your name calls by that name. The provident diligence of your parents wished you to be chosen before you were tested. In former times, while you clung to secular titles, military labor cultivated you. Then the opposing party established you at the helm of the Church, as the Lord speaks through the prophet: ‘He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much’ (Luke 16:10).

“You were found worthy to be a sacred judge and a companion in counsel and labor. As one rightly to be initiated into the altars, you chose what was sacred even in lay conduct. At that age you were found a guardian of chastity, at an age in which the law also submits to desires. It is enough that the ambition of youth, which license supports, should be feared. Christ seeks soldiers whom he may raise up as beloved persons amid the hostile battle lines.

“Having been called to the Church, you filled the office of bishop with your conduct before the time of your dignity. Your kindness was not an outsider’s gift; resting upon the roots of nature, it displayed a shoot from an aged blossom. Everything fashioned is temporary; what matures with age is everlasting.

“We do not believe that the priesthood came to you as a gift, but as a reward. Others are commended by the enticement of ordinary favor; to you, a stern discipline toward the guilty gave affection. You possess singular wisdom, which, although generally desirable, nevertheless exists in a teacher. The monitor needlessly assumes the role of adviser if he cannot assess the weight of the duty imposed upon him; unless he excels in knowledge, he must be considered most insignificant who is superior in honor.

“Your judgment gave you the summit; the love worthy of a bishop is not that of favor but that which censure brings about. The character of an instructor is disfigured when he wishes to please solely through favor. You, instructed and formed by these gifts of heaven, teach the people more by doing than by teaching. Those admonitions educate the conscience of disciples which are approved by example. Without shame, he invites others to innocence who has himself pursued it.

“Let those who intend to sin fear you among the hidden chambers of the sanctuary, even where they fear no witness. Your fear and reverence prevent faults from taking effect at their beginnings; you meet vices at their outset, remove the opportunity for falls, and cleanse the source of desire.

“I have dedicated these words to your blessedness, as a brief commendation through the medium of my tongue. If the success of your life smiles upon my prayers, I shall consecrate you with a full account of your deeds, so that what is known to all may be preserved in lasting writings for the future, and so that what follows may rejoice in the deeds that remain.”

## Another letter of the same pope to the patrician Liberius

Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, sends greetings to the patrician Liberius.

“When you directed words arising from the reverence of your conscience concerning the election of a bishop at Aquileia, and, with a tongue initiated into divine worship, devoted yourselves to his consecration, your diligence held us bound by the ties of speech, since nothing surpasses riches whenever a worthy person brings something forth.

“For what could the judgment of those who follow leave behind when it obeys justice, whose decision is not summoned for examination? You act from the goodness of your conscience in a matter scarcely denied to your authority. Among the arbiters there emerged the venerable colleague Marcellinus, the greatest of men, made more exalted by humility. And lest favor be attributed to power, he joined to the price the testimony that he had drawn from his own talent.

“You acted with moderation, lest an excessively elevated commendation be undertaken. The testimony of the most illustrious is restrained so that high office may receive strength. Blessed is the priesthood to which a mind full of light has given precedence. Blessed is the conduct that was brought into examination for this reason: that, with so great a man speaking in its favor, it might prevail. It would not have learned the taste of victory had it not been subjected to uncertainties. Adversity has always produced glory for the innocent; moderate opposition provides the strongest defenders.

“But why have I prolonged the bounds of the letter with loquacity, exceeding the pages imposed by convention in human composition? I too join myself, according to the measure of my smallness, to your most exalted parts, with heaven consenting. And because what is regarded as marvelous among human beings draws me, through consideration of you, toward love, an affection inspired in me by another makes it pleasing to approve, while charity remains implanted in the deepest entrails. Though the person is absent, heavenly grace nevertheless joins itself as a companion to his desires; and while you desire it, affection is granted: either the good of the bishopric may come, or may bring it about.”

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends, in the eighth indiction.

# THE DECREES OF POPE HORMISDAS BEGIN

[Col. 1035]

[Col. 1035A]

1. Against the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches.  
2. Concerning the mystery of the Trinity: what the persons and what the substances signify.  
3. Concerning the divinity and humanity of the Lord Jesus Christ.

To the most glorious and most merciful son Justin, Augustus, Hormisdas, bishop.

“Among the matters that pertain to the unity of the Church, for whose sake God chose your mercy’s imperial rule, you included in your letter this further concern, venerable emperor: since you have declared that you devote yourself in many ways to the care of the faith, you added that the petitions of certain persons should be brought to the notice of my humility. Thus I might learn either what question had arisen or might return an answer suited to a religious judgment for removing the ambiguity of the proposed inquiry.

“I read everything with the diligence that was fitting. Although it could have sufficed for a full answer if I had merely subscribed to what had been defined by the authorities, nevertheless, in order to reward the devotion of your religious purpose, I judged that I too should not withhold the service of speech.”

## Chapter I. Against the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches

“For what is there that the instruction of the fathers omitted when the poisons of Nestorius and Eutyches emerged? Nearly all the impieties, together with the inventors of such wicked doctrines, were crushed by concordant synodal decrees, and no place remained for such dreadful seeds of perfidy once they had been cut off: either to believe that Christ the Lord existed without the truth of flesh, or to deny that the same Lord came forth both God and man from the undefiled fruitfulness of his mother’s womb.

“One of them, by denying the dispensation through which we were saved, rendered it ineffectual, so far as lay in him; the other, with an opposing opinion but comparable impiety, excluded divine power from true humanity in the same Lord Jesus Christ. The former did not remember that Christ had shown his flesh to be touched; the latter did not remember the Gospel’s declaration that the Word became flesh. The voice of the Lord should have sounded unfailingly in his ears, since he said and taught: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven’ (John 3:13).

“These matters have often been set forth in many judgments of those who came before us. But your clemency, although they have already been stated, will not disdain to hear them repeated, nor should we be ashamed to rehearse what our predecessors proclaimed. For there can be no diversity of preaching where there is one form of truth; nor will it rightly be judged foreign if, in agreement with those with whom we concur, we agree in faith and doctrine.

“Let the synodal decrees be recalled to the pious ears of your gentleness, together with the constitutions of the blessed Pope Leo that accord with the sacred faith. You will find in those decrees the same things that you will recognize in ours. What, then, is to be established after that fountain of the faithful? What more is there to inquire, if any curious investigator nevertheless preserves the boundaries of the faith? There is no need for addition for the common people or instruction for the perfected—unless someone should prefer to doubt rather than believe, to contend rather than know, and to follow uncertainties rather than preserve the decrees.”

## II. Concerning the mystery of the Trinity

“For if God is the Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and yet God is one, as the Lawgiver expressly says: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one’ (Deut. 6:3), whoever holds otherwise must either divide divinity into many parts or attribute suffering in a particular way to the very essence of the Trinity. May this be far from the minds of the faithful: either to introduce several gods in the manner of profane paganism, or to transfer sensible punishment to that nature which is free from all suffering.

“The holy Trinity is one. It is not multiplied by number, nor increased by augmentation; nor can what God is be comprehended by the intellect or separated by distinction. Who, then, would attempt to introduce profane division into that secret of the eternal and impenetrable substance, which the nature of no visible or invisible creature has been able to investigate, and reduce the mystery of the divine secret to the reckoning of human custom?

“Let us adore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: the undistinguished One distinctly, the incomprehensible and ineffable substance of the Trinity. Here, although reason admits the number of persons, unity nevertheless does not admit separation of essence.

“Yet let us preserve what is proper to the divine nature, and preserve what is proper to each person, so that neither the singularity of divinity is denied to the persons nor what is proper to the names transferred to the essence.

“Great is the holy and incomprehensible mystery of the Trinity: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, an undivided Trinity. Nevertheless, it is known that it is proper to the Father to beget the Son; proper to the Son of God to be born from the Father, equal to the Father; and proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son, under the one substance of the Godhead.”

### III.

It is also proper to the Son of God that, according to what is written, “in the last times the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” so that within the womb of the holy virgin Mary, Mother of God, the two natures were united without any confusion. Thus he who before the ages was the Son of God became the son of man and was born in time, without opening the womb of his human mother and without dissolving his mother’s virginity through the power of his divinity. Truly, it was a mystery worthy of God at his birth: he preserved the birth without corruption, just as he caused the conception to occur without seed, preserving what he was from the Father and displaying what he received from his mother.

For while he lay in a manger, he was seen in heaven; wrapped in swaddling clothes, he was worshiped by the Magi; born among animals, he was announced by angels; scarcely having entered infancy, he proclaimed a mystical teaching without an instructor; amid the beginnings of childhood he performed signs of heavenly powers. For the same one was God and man—not, as unbelievers say, through the introduction of a fourth person, but the very Son of God, God and man, at once power and weakness, humility and majesty, redeeming and sold, placed upon the cross and bestowing the kingdoms of heaven. He shared in our weakness so that he could be put to death; he was Lord of innate power so that death could not consume him.

He was buried in accordance with that by which he wished to be born as man; and in accordance with that by which he was like the Father, he rose again: enduring the wounds and Savior of the sick, one and the same among the dead and giver of life to those who die, descending to the underworld and not departing from the bosom of the Father. Thus, too, the soul which he laid down according to the common condition, he soon took up again through his singular virtue and wondrous power.

That these things are so and ought to admit no doubt—that is, lest our Lord Jesus Christ be thought not to be God amid the sufferings of the body, or lest, being regarded as God alone, he not also be regarded as man amid the works of wondrous and astonishing powers—he instructed us by the example of two apostles, declaring Christ our Lord to be God through Peter’s faith and man through Thomas’s doubt.

What purpose was served by his wishing to ask the disciples whom men said he was, unless, when Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (John XI, 27), he was confessing that this had not been disclosed by flesh and blood, but revealed by God the Father inspiring it, so that through the testimony of the praised response faith might reveal the truth? What purpose was served, moreover, by Thomas being so far from the others when the Lord appeared after the resurrection that he alone doubted, unless, when the Lord allowed himself to be touched by the hands of one man, it might be recognized by the whole community of believers who he was?

The doubt, therefore, was not introduced in order to test the disciple, but instruction for posterity was sought. Or does he expect something else when that same Lord inserted himself into the conversation of Cleopas and another disciple as they journeyed toward Emmaus and spoke about him? Although they had learned of the Lord’s resurrection from the women who had first gone to the tomb, nevertheless, in order that through their doubt he might provide future ages with firmness of belief, beginning with Moses and all the prophets he interpreted that “it was necessary for Christ to suffer and thus enter into his glory” (Luke XXIV, 26).

Through his suffering he showed human nature to be in him, and through his glory he showed the divine nature to be in him. These things are suggested by many examples from the holy Scriptures. Nor are they spoken as though unknown to your religious conscience, venerable emperor. The faith which you yourself constantly assert gives you this gift: it brings its own devotion into your understanding and pours into you the knowledge by which you may assert it more diligently.

Nevertheless, it belongs to the office entrusted to me that I too should not remain silent about what is known even to those who know it, so that, as the Catholic proclamation of these truths succeeds from age to age, what is unceasingly asserted may be believed without end. I could have discussed at greater length those matters concerning the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the unity in him of natures without confusion, according to the definitions of the ancients, if I had been arguing against those who dispute these things. But since everything is at hand—the synodal decisions and the teachings of the blessed Pope Leo—I have thought it more fitting to touch briefly upon everything rather than unfold it all.

Now it is sufficient to recognize and guard this point: that the properties and the essence must be contemplated in such a way that it is understood what we ought to attribute to the person and what to the substance. Those who improperly fail to understand this, or conceal it through cunning impiety, while omitting what is proper to the Son within the Trinity, plot against the unity. But if the things that have been proclaimed are held fixed with strong roots, if one does not depart from the tradition of the fathers, and if questions are met with steadfastness—

### The Sacred Letter of the Emperor Justin to Pope Hormisdas

To the most sacred and blessed archbishop of the revered city of Rome and patriarch, Hormisdas, Justin, emperor.

[Col. 1038B] Know, most religious Father, that what had long been sought with the greatest zeal has been disclosed, even before those whom we have sent have arrived: John, our most blessed bishop of New Rome, together with the clergy, agrees with you, differing in no ambiguities and divided by no disagreements.

Know that he has signed the libellus which you had indicated should be offered, and that it is in accord with the council of the most holy Fathers. All are hastening eagerly to undertake the vows, both of our see and of the see of Constantinople, whom the radiant splendor of truth enlightens. All hasten most willingly, delighted by the clear path, to follow the decisions of the Fathers and their most holy and approved laws. With the counsels of some thus confirmed—those who held the right path—and others who wandered thus corrected, the matter is brought together so that they too may worship the unity of the undivided Trinity in the unity of their minds.

It has been denied that any future remembrance be made amid the divine mysteries of the libellus mentioned above, belonging to Acacius, once the bishop of this royal city and a transgressor, as well as of the other priests who either were the first to act against the apostolic constitutions or became successors in error and were never corrected by repentance until the final day. And since all who belong to our religion must be admonished to imitate the example of the royal city, we have ordered that imperial commands be sent everywhere.

With such ardor do we burn for the duty of religion, with such zeal do we desire the peace of the Catholic faith, that we may swiftly restore peace, and the peace of our republic through the heavenly protection granted to my subjects. For what could be found more pleasing, more just, more illustrious than that the same kingdom should contain the same faith, and that those whom the same worship of faith illumines should not contend in opposing ways, but should venerate institutions established in the same convictions—not introduced by human thought, but inspired by the spirit of divine providence?

Let your religious holiness therefore pray that what is procured through vigilant zeal for the concord of the Churches and the Catholic faith may, through the assistance of the divine gift, be preserved with perpetual continuity.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, at Constantinople.

### The Libellus of Faith of John, Bishop of Constantinople, Sent to the Holy Pope Hormisdas

In it he anathematizes the blasphemies of Nestorius, Eutyches, and the remaining heretics.

Having received the letters of your holiness in Christ, dearest brother, through the most beloved Count Gratus, and now through Germanus and John, most reverend bishops, and Felix and Dioscorus, most holy deacons, and Blandus, presbyter, I rejoiced at the special holiness of your charity: that you seek the unity of the most holy Churches of God according to the tradition of the ancient Fathers, and hasten, out of love, to drive away those who tear apart Christ’s rational flock.

Know with certainty, therefore, most holy Father, that in every respect, according to what I wrote to you, agreeing with you in the truth, I reject all the heretics whom you have rejected. Loving peace and the most holy Churches of God—that is, your Church above and this New Rome—I acknowledge them to be one. I define the see of the apostle Peter and that of this august city to be one.

I assent to everything established by the four most holy synods, namely, those of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, for the confirmation of the faith, and I allow nothing to waver from what has been rightly judged. I also know that those who attempt or strive to disturb even one point of their decisions have fallen away from the holy, universal, and apostolic Church of God.

Using your rightly spoken words clearly in this present writing, I say that the first means of salvation is to preserve the rule of the true faith and in no way to deviate from the tradition of the Fathers. For the sentence of our Lord Jesus cannot be passed over, when he says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI, 18). These words are proved by their effects, because in the apostolic see the Catholic religion has always been preserved inviolate. This, therefore, is the faith.

Not wishing to fall, but following the constitutions of the Fathers in all things, and anathematizing all heresies, we especially anathematize Nestorius the heretic, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, condemned at the Council of Ephesus by the blessed Pope Celestine of the city of Rome and by the venerable Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria; together with him we anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of the city of Alexandria, condemned at the holy Synod of Chalcedon, which we venerate, follow, and embrace. This synod, following the holy Synod of Nicaea, proclaimed the apostolic faith.

Together with these we anathematize Timothy the parricide, surnamed Hellurus, and likewise condemn his disciple and follower in all things, Peter of Alexandria. We likewise anathematize Acacius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, who became their accomplice and follower, as well as those who persevered in their communion and participation. For whoever embraces the communion of such persons receives a similar judgment in condemnation.

In the same way, condemning Peter of Antioch, we anathematize him together with his followers and all those listed above. Therefore we approve and embrace all the letters of the blessed Pope Leo of the city of Rome which he wrote concerning the true faith.

Accordingly, as we have said, following the apostolic see in all things, and proclaiming everything decreed by it, I hope that I shall be in the one communion with you which the apostolic see proclaims. In it is the complete devotion and perfect firmness of the Christian religion. I promise that, in the time to come, the names of those who have been separated from communion with the Catholic Church—that is, those who do not agree with the apostolic see—will not be recited amid the sacred mysteries.

But if I should attempt to deviate in any part of my profession, I confess that, by my own judgment, I am an accomplice [p. 259] of those whom I have condemned. I have subscribed this profession with my own hand and sent it in writing to you, Hormisdas, holy and blessed brother and pope of great Rome, through the aforementioned Germanus and John, venerable bishops, Felix and Dioscorus, deacons, and Blandus, presbyter.

And in another hand: John, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, consenting to this profession of mine, have subscribed to all the foregoing, sound in the Lord. Pray for us, most holy and blessed brother.

Given in the month of March, on the twenty-eighth day, in the eleventh indiction, during the consulship of our lord Justin, august emperor, and Heradius IV. CC. Era DC.

### Letter of Pope Hormisdas to John, Bishop of the Church of Militana, Concerning the Communion of the Church of Constantinople

We do not wish your charity to remain unaware of our hopes, lest one who shared in our anxiety be excluded from the fruit of our joy. Therefore, with the Lord’s favor, we announce through these letters that the Church of Constantinople has returned to our communion, and that the entire sequence of the instructions which we gave to our legates has been fulfilled.

So that the joy of this completed matter might reach your affection more fully, we have likewise thought it right to send copies of the libellus of our brother and fellow priest, John, bishop of Constantinople, and of the sacred letters of Justin, the most gracious ruler of the East. We judge, moreover, that very many bishops throughout the East have acted in the same way.

It remains for us to pray that, when the divinity has been entreated with fitting petitions, he may grant us to rejoice also in the restoration of the other Churches. You will take care to convey what we have deemed necessary to make known to the priests who are near your fraternity, so that they too may not cease to give thanks with us for the accomplishment of so great a matter, through the benefits of heavenly mercy.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

### Also to John the Bishop, Concerning the Instructions Sent and the Authority Delegated

[Col. 1040D]

To his most beloved brother John, Hormisdas.

Your affection did something suited to charity and faith when, by letters sent to us, it announced your arrival in Italy and showed the full extent of your religious intention. Would that, for the satisfaction of a fuller affection, the joy of your presence had also been granted to us, so that we might rejoice in enjoying both conversation and your presence, which we have already embraced through your letters.

Nevertheless, dearest brother, you have demonstrated the devotion with which you venerate the Christian faith. You desire to preserve without any transgression those things which belong to the regulations of the Fathers and to the Catholic commands, hoping that, once the general constitutions have been extended to the Churches of Spain, we may establish what is appropriate concerning ecclesiastical disciplines, whether they have been carried out too carelessly or irreligiously.

For what is sweeter to us than to speak with the faithful, or more fitting to God than to recall those who have strayed from error? Therefore, greeting the charity by which we are joined, through Cassian, your deacon, we signify that we have sent general constitutions. In them we have both suitably decreed what ought to be observed according to the canons and sufficiently instructed you about the caution that must be exercised toward those who come from the Greek clergy.

The order and explanation of the matter itself will teach you fully through the ecclesiastical decrees, so that, recognizing both the transgression of the impious and the care of the apostolic see, which keeps watch over the regulations of the Fathers, you may show that you detest the fellowship of the condemned and love the faithful.

And because, through your affection’s disclosure, the prudence of this course has been made clear to us, we reward your diligence. While preserving the privileges established for metropolitans by the holy Fathers, we delegate to you the authority of the apostolic see to this extent: that, after examination, you may ensure that both those things which pertain to the canons and those which have recently been commanded by us are observed, and that whatever has occurred concerning ecclesiastical cases that has come to your attention may be disclosed to us through your report.

It will be the task of your zeal and diligence to show yourself in the matters entrusted to you in such a way that you may watch over the faith and integrity of each person whose care you undertake.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of April, during the consulship of Agapitus II, Era DCXLVIII.

### Also the Letter of Hormisdas to the Bishops of Spain

1. Concerning the ordination of priests according to the regulations of the canons.  
2. That no payment be received for the episcopate.  
3. Concerning the annual celebration of a council.

To his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Spain, Hormisdas.

Blessed is the Trinity, our God, who through his mercy has spread the tranquility of his peace throughout every part of the Roman commonwealth and has also granted us a way of demonstrating charity toward one another. Thus, while we are united by the firmness of faith, we may also be joined by the desired joy of conversation, so that, as we reach you through the service of letters, we may likewise stir your hearts to religious worship through apostolic admonitions. In returning the pledge of our affection, we may show a certain complete debt of devotion toward the Lord.

Let us therefore join, dearest brothers, in continuous and humble prayers. Entreating our Lord with tears of mouth and heart, let us ask him in continual supplication that, both in institution and in practice, we may cling to him whose members we desire to be, and that we may never turn aside by a wayward path from that way which is Christ, lest we be justly abandoned by him whom we impiously abandon.

With the aid of heavenly favor, this can happen to us if we preserve the apostolic teachings and the commands of the Fathers. For our Lord said: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

Although these words, spoken generally, might be sufficient either to make us avoid errors or to preserve the Catholic constitutions, nevertheless, because it has been reported to us through John, our brother and fellow bishop, that certain things are being presumed against the reverence due to the canons, I have thought it right to issue general constitutions. In this way I avoid the danger which threatens teachers through silence and, pierced by the prophetic voice that says, “Speak; do not be silent,” I shall give instruction.

### Chapter I

In ordaining priests, consider those things which have been prescribed and defined by the Fathers. For just as Christ is the head of the Church and priests are Christ’s vicars, so there must be evident care in choosing them. Those who must preside over people requiring correction ought to be irreproachable, and nothing should be lacking in that person in whom rests the whole of religion and the substance of discipline.

Let each person estimate the price of the Lord’s flock, so that he may know what merit is fitting for the one appointed as shepherd. This will happen if the rank of the priesthood is not transferred indiscriminately to laymen by some kind of sudden leap.

He to whom the helm of the Church is entrusted ought to demonstrate his life through a long period of testing. We do not deny that there are ways of life among laymen pleasing to God, but faithful institutions seek tested soldiers for themselves. Everyone ought to learn before teaching and to offer others, rather than presume upon them, an example of religious conduct drawn from his own life.

The one who must pray for the people ought to be more correct than the people. Religious worship should be handed on through long observance, and he should be trained through clerical service, so that, having been brought to the highest venerable rank, he may show what fruit humility produces.

It was neither insignificant nor pointless that, even among the ancients, only men of the Levitical race were admitted to the holy altars, lest one unworthy of sacred worship should approach through contemptible merit, payment, or presumption. Then the privilege of families passed into the institutions of worshipers; now doctrine takes the place of birth. What birth was for them, formation is for us. Nature gave them to the tabernacle; discipline brings us forth for the altars.

Nor do we merely prohibit laymen from being consecrated; we also prohibit any penitent from presuming, as a profane violator, to aspire to such a rank. Let pardon be sufficient for the one who seeks it. With what conscience can one absolve the guilty man who knows that he has confessed his sins before the people as witnesses? Who would venerate as a bishop the one whom he had seen lying prostrate only a short time before? He who bears the stain of a pitiable crime does not possess the bright dignity of the priesthood.

[Col. 1042D]

### II.

We add this also to what has been said above: no one should purchase with money the blessing given through the laying on of hands, which is believed to be divine, since it is fitting that the example of Simon should be before our eyes. When he wished to buy the Holy Spirit with money, he was struck by the Apostle’s detestation.

Who, then, does not regard as vile what is sold? The election of those to be ordained priests should preserve this reverence, so that, amid the solemn acclamation of the people, the judgment may be believed to be divine. For God is there where there is simple consent without perversity.

Yet we do not omit this part of our concern and admonition either: no one should consider himself free of guilt if, although he himself began the priest’s initiation with a mystical blessing without being involved in a purchase, he nevertheless consented to the will of another who had purchased it—whether willingly or under compulsion. What does it profit him not to be polluted by his own error if he gives his consent to the one who errs? Without doubt, both the one who has his own sin and the one who follows another’s sin act against the commands. The mind resists desire in vain if it does not also resist fear.

With God’s help, provision will more easily be made against these things if the privileges established by the holy Fathers for metropolitans remain in force, and if metropolitans preserve their proper order regarding their parishes with the reverence that is fitting. Thus neither may the election of a bishop be purchased for money, nor may it be sought through the works of one who serves him; rather, these principles must be fixed in their hearts just as they are read in the Scriptures.

If there are no seeds of buying and selling in the churches, there will be no fuel for discord. But when charity reigns, let us live in the peace which God promised us and repaid to us.

### III.

For this reason, moved by the providence through which the Holy Spirit has deigned to prick the consciences of his worshipers, the Fathers taught that councils should be held twice each year in every parish. Thus, gathered together according to the principles of salutary instruction, they might meet freely to discuss ecclesiastical matters. If everything remains in accordance with their desire, they might praise God with united voices, who grants what they seek.

For it is difficult for anyone’s heart to become so hardened by evil thoughts that he permits blameworthy things to be done by him, when he knows that the judgment of the council will come. Let them always have their loins girded for this journey, knowing that an account of their actions must be given. Let them be restrained from illicit things by fear, and those whom fear cannot restrain, by shame.

It is known that the holy canons established that they should meet twice a year, and this fixed requirement ought, if possible, to be observed inviolably. But if either the necessity of the times or emerging circumstances do not allow it to be fulfilled, we command that they meet at least once; no excuse whatsoever is permitted.

These things, dearest brothers, and the other matters contained in the regulations of the Fathers, let us meditate upon with undivided reflection on our lips and in our hearts. As it is written, let us recount them to our children, so that they may meditate upon them in their hearts, sitting in the house, walking on the road, sleeping and rising, because “blessed is the one who meditates on his law in the Lord day and night” (Psalm I, 2).

The teacher of the nations likewise instituted this when he admonished his disciple: “Meditate on these things; devote yourself to them,” adding the fullness of the instruction: “Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching.” For if we apply ourselves without interruption to the institutions of the faithful, we shall be separated from vices, while devoted care for the divine work leaves no room for human error.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of April, during the consulship of Agapitus II.

### Also the Letter of Pope Hormisdas to the Bishops of Spain, in Which He Sends Them the Profession of John, Bishop of Constantinople, on Account of the Eastern Clerics Who Had Sought Their Communion

260. To his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Spain, Hormisdas.

Meanwhile, our brother and fellow bishop John, acting out of ecclesiastical concern, has brought the following matter to our attention. Out of devotion to the Catholic faith and reverence for the apostolic see, he also sought advice concerning the procedure by which holy communion should be granted to those coming from the Greek clergy, on account of Acacius, who was condemned by our predecessors for communion with heretics. Those who do not separate themselves from his contagion are to be excluded from our communion.

I praise the intention of this man, who burns with such zeal for the faith and the apostolic institutions that he would not allow himself, even through ignorance, to be plunged into the filth of another’s error. Such care is worthy of the faithful, that they should always watch with anxious diligence and preserve themselves blameless from every perversity. This is the innocence of faith: to foresee that it cannot fall into error even by accident.

Therefore, satisfying the laudable desires of the aforesaid man and mindful, as we ought to be, of our office, we have taken various documents from the archives of the Church and sent them to your council for the instruction of all. From them you may learn more fully what was done and separate yourselves from every communion with those who err.

For this sentence against impious transgressors was not spoken from personal hatred; it was inspired by God. In this matter we have never ceased to preach: by entreating rulers, priests, and peoples, and by admonishing them, so that the transgressors, once absolved, might return to the true faith through love of God and fear of judgment. But their pitiable obstinacy had brought them to the point where deadly poisons could not be overcome by any means, and evil seeds, fixed in roots, grew ever more deeply toward destruction.

Therefore, dearest brothers, instructed in all appropriate matters, preserve yourselves and the Church of God, pierced by the Apostle’s exhortation.

We have sent a libellus under which any member of the Eastern clergy who seeks your communion may be admitted to it. According to this same rule, people from the regions of Thrace, Scythia, and Illyricum, or from Old Epirus, may be received; likewise, it is already established that many from Syria have been received, rejoicing to come to what is right and to turn away from what is deviant.

Accordingly, we command, lest anything be concealed, that every care and every concern remain vigilant. Let no one now claim ignorance; let no one use the excuse of former simplicity. For the one who sins knowingly must make confession. The person shown to have persisted on a perverse path must write out his error for himself.

Boniface, notary of the holy Roman Church, has prepared copies of the libellus from the archives.

The first means of salvation is to preserve the rule of the true faith and in no way to deviate from the constitutions of the Fathers. Since the sentence of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over—he says, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI, 18), and so forth—the things that have been said are proved by their effects, because in the apostolic see the Catholic religion has always been preserved without stain.

Wishing in no way to be separated from this hope and faith, and following the constitutions of the Fathers, we anathematize all heresies, especially Nestorius the heretic, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, condemned at the Council of Ephesus by the blessed Pope Celestine of the city of Rome and by the venerable Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria.

Likewise we anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus of Alexandria, condemned at the holy Synod of Chalcedon, which we follow and embrace. Following the holy Council of Nicaea, it proclaimed the apostolic faith.

We detest Timothy the parricide, surnamed Hellurus, and we also condemn his disciple and follower in every respect, Peter of Alexandria. We likewise anathematize Acacius, formerly bishop of Constantinople, condemned by the apostolic see, their accomplice and follower, and those who have remained in their communion.

Acacius deserved to receive, in his condemnation, a sentence like that of those whose communion he joined. We likewise condemn Peter of Antioch with his followers and all those listed above.

We accept and approve all the letters of the blessed Pope Leo which he wrote concerning the Christian religion. As we have said, we follow the apostolic see in all things and proclaim all its constitutions. In every respect I hope that I may be worthy to be in the one communion with you which the apostolic see proclaims, in which there is the integrity and truth of the Christian religion, and perfect firmness.

I promise that the names of those who have been separated from communion with the Catholic Church—that is, those who do not agree with the apostolic see—will not be recited amid the sacred mysteries.

But if I should attempt to deviate in any respect from my profession, I confess, by my own judgment, that I am an accomplice of those whom I have condemned.

I have subscribed this profession with my own hand and sent it to Hormisdas, holy and venerable pope of the city of Rome.

### Concerning the Reconciliation of the Roman and Constantinopolitan Churches

[Col. 1045C]

To his most beloved brother Epiphanius, Hormisdas.

I am filled with great joy that you have indicated by letter such earnest concern for the peace of the Church, for the most holy emperor, and for your affection—concern that I have also recognized as confirmed by the statements of my legates. For this reveals the evidence of heavenly mercy: worldly rulers join matters of faith with the ordering of the state, while the leaders of the churches carry out what pertains to the administration of their office, mindful of their duty. After the storms of discord, the Christian religion needed such leaders—leaders who, by prudent administration, would restrain the whirlwinds and, once the tempest had been driven away, restore the peace that had long wandered in exile, so that in ages to come those who strive toward the examples of their purpose might confidently show themselves what they had done for imitation by posterity in accordance with God’s will.

[Col. 1045D] Let us bless the Lord, dearest brothers, that this has been granted in our days, and let us strive with all the strength of our prayers and labors so that what has been well begun by God’s work may, with his help, be completed in every respect. For we must hope that the remaining members still lacking will hasten toward the joining of the body, and that the lesser will not disagree with the greater. Since your affection urges me to this with the zeal of Christian charity, what invites must be followed, and what it counsels us to love must be embraced. Since we already share the same concern for the faith, through religious patience we likewise hope for an equal reward from our devotion to good works.

[Col. 1046A] Nor must we yield to difficulties. Faith is not wearied by hardships; no one presses onward to the heights of heaven along an easy path, nor does anyone deserve recompense without the exercise of labor. Therefore, lest we grow weary in doing good, we are specially admonished, as the Psalmist also testifies: “Blessed are those who observe judgment and practice justice at all times” (Psalm 105:3). For it is not the beginning of labor that customarily receives the reward of recompense, but its completion.

Therefore, take up the vigilant concern appropriate to those who share one communion and one belief. Just as we rejoice in the Lord over the unity of the Apostolic See and the Church of Constantinople, so let us also rejoice, as you urge us, over the restoration of the others, and let us take care first to preserve our faith and integrity unstained by every pollution. [Col. 1046B] For you know, dearest and most holy brother, that the bonds of the Church preserve concord and protect us from the snares of heretics; through them also the integrity of the canons is maintained. When these are preserved in their full strength with every precaution, remedies are granted to those who hope for them.

The order of ecclesiastical rules and the very form of justice require that reasonable medicine not be denied to those who hope for it kindly and faithfully; nor is anyone so removed from humanity that prudent simplicity cannot incline him away from the severity of strict judgment. But so that you may carefully resolve this and the other complaints or errors of anyone, dearest brother, you must assume my person in this matter, knowing, as has been said, what must be avoided in such cases. [Col. 1046C] You must foresee everything in such a way that you do not doubt that you will have to render an account of this administration to God. At the same time, those who have been joined to you in communion—or who, through you, declare in writing their adherence to your Apostolic See to us—must be recorded; among them also let those be included who have offered the text of their petitions.

Thus we shall absolve the errors of Severus, Sulpicius, and their accomplices or associates, and we shall not suffer loss to befall those who can be healed. We have especially entrusted this to you, transferring this responsibility from our burden to your diligence, because you have already given no small proofs of resistance to the heretics. Nor should there be doubt about one who has been properly examined. At the same time apply the remedy of medicine and gird yourself with the authority of justice. Deal so gently with the simple that [Col. 1046D] those who persist in the contagion of heresy, or who pretend innocence and agree with our people only in words, may be excluded from those for whom the restoration of the Church is being advised and arranged.

For it is not expedient to temper ecclesiastical censure toward such people. The good acts of mercy that ought to be bestowed according to need will no longer be good if they are indiscriminately shared by the good and the wicked.

Since your affection mentioned in your letter that something should be done concerning the people of Jerusalem, whose profession has also been conveyed to us in part, we have thought it necessary to reply with what is appropriate. Those who observe the ordinances of the holy Fathers, if they venerate the foundations of the faith, must not be removed from what was defined through those Fathers by the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1047A] Either those ordinances are complete and require no addition, or they are fully sound and therefore must not be changed, since through them every poison of the heretics has been suppressed. Nor did the Council of Chalcedon omit anything useful that could have been undertaken with any diligence. It either made the doctrines of its predecessors clearer or confirmed them by repeated authority. It undertook a particular contest against Nestorius and Eutyches: one separated the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ from his flesh and therefore avoided proclaiming holy Mary the Mother of God; the other rejected the reality of the Lord’s flesh.

Our Lord Jesus Christ is the same Son of God and the same son of man, one person in two natures, divinity and flesh, without confusing the natures into unity. Nor is he a fourth person added to the Trinity; rather, “the Son of God himself emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). Therefore we confess one and indivisible essence of the Trinity, yet we know that each person retains its own property. We confess one person of the Father, one person of the Son of God with the flesh he assumed, and one person of the Holy Spirit. We designate the persons by their properties and, through the unity of essence, confess the inseparable mystery of the Trinity.

There can be no doubt that the Word of God assumed human nature through flesh within the Virgin’s womb, nor that he was divided within the womb by the safeguard of the natures when he was brought forth by the midwife. For just as humanity was not brought forth in him without God, so at the cross the impassible divinity was not separated from the suffering of the flesh. This is declared by the Virgin’s childbirth, her undefiled fecundity, his singular resurrection from the dead, and his ascent to heaven.

[Col. 1047C] If they believe these things as they were established by the Fathers and do not go beyond what was defined, those who depart from this path themselves spread before themselves a cloud of doubt. But, contemplating the apostolic teaching, we do not need to answer contentious people: “We have no such custom, nor the Church of God.”

I have defined these matters briefly because it is not fitting to doubt things so often settled by faith, and an argument offered to those already instructed is almost superfluous, especially since we have already touched on these matters at some length in writing to the most merciful emperor.

[Col. 1047D] Since we have answered concerning the profession of the people of Jerusalem, we have also judged it appropriate to add this for their salvation: if they give themselves to the unity of apostolic communion and indicate their profession in writing, they must offer it for your representatives stationed at Constantinople to read, or send it to us through their own people, or hand it over to your fraternity. It must nevertheless be written in the same form, as we have said, and delivered to us in every respect under our direction.

Concerning the Thessalonians, whose legates came to us by the arrangement of the most merciful and faithful emperor, our son, we wish you to know, lest we be thought to have omitted anything, that the whole matter is to be handled according to what pleases our Lord Jesus Christ under his inspiration, and is to be ordered for fulfillment as is fitting. [Col. 1048A] We are content to have sent a rescript concerning the matters pertaining to the case through our brother and fellow bishop, the venerable man John, and through our sons Heraclius, Probus, and Constantine, deacons most worthy of ecclesiastical honor.

We rejoiced that in a man of our order we had found both merit and a religious purpose, and that, together with the commission of the legation, his wisdom and conduct were appropriate. Their desired mission, full of joy, is a matter of thanksgiving, since they are as commendable as we had judged them to be and have proved worthy to share in the ministry of holy communion.

[Col. 1048B]

## Another letter of Hormisdas to Salustius, bishop of Hispalis, concerning the authority entrusted to him over the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania

### Hormisdas to his dearest brother Salustius

We have received the communications of your fraternity with full and welcome joy; they have made us glad by indicating your good health in body together with your spiritual duties. We have therefore seen that it is appropriate to express in words the joy that we bear in our mind.

You have given proof of a good bishop, both by doing what ought to be proclaimed and by not delaying to commend it. We have gained a prerogative for our judgment when we learned that you willingly embrace what we command to others. We pray that divine mercy may cause all to recognize this, and we have sent these instruments of our ecclesiastical peace.

You received our wishes with faithful understanding and immediately fulfilled them through the devotion of your office, making known to all the brothers what you had recognized as beneficial to all through heavenly grace.

[Col. 1048C] Since so many merits of pious diligence and labor support you, it now gives us pleasure to entrust to you what clearly belongs to the care of our office, so that, in provinces separated by such great distance, you may represent our person and preserve the regulations of the Fathers.

Therefore, by our present authority we entrust our authority over the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania to you, without prejudice to the privileges that antiquity decreed for metropolitan bishops. By this participation in our ministry we increase your dignity and lighten our own vigils through the remedy of this administration.

Although you do not need to be instructed about individual matters, since we have already found that you carefully preserve everything, it is nevertheless more welcome when the path is shown again and the form of the labor entrusted is set forth above.

Therefore we command that the paternal rules and decrees defined by the holy councils be observed by everyone. [Col. 1048D] In these matters we extend your vigilance and your care through fraternal admonition and exhortation. When these are guarded with the reverence they deserve, no room for fault remains, nor any obstacle to holy observance. There the lawful and unlawful are prescribed; there is what is forbidden, toward which no one may dare aspire; there is what is permitted and what a mind pleasing to God ought to undertake.

Whenever the cause of universal religion requires it, let all the brothers summon you to a council and let you attend. If any of them is troubled by a spiritual matter, restrain disputes that have arisen among them by examining and determining the controversies according to the sacred laws.

Whatever you prescribe to them concerning the faith in accordance with ancient decrees or prudent arrangement, or whatever you establish by the authority of our person, must all reach our knowledge through a report supported by written testimony. [Col. 1049A] Thus it will come about that our mind may enjoy the charity of the office entrusted, and yours the security of the office received.

May God preserve you safe, dearest brother.

## Rescript of Pope Hormisdas to the bishops of the province of Baetica concerning rejoicing over peace

### Hormisdas, bishop, to all the beloved bishops established throughout the province of Baetica, greeting in the Lord

What could be as sweet to one who is concerned as learning from you the things I desire? What is more fitting for religious institutions than that priests should preserve among themselves the peace that, in accordance with their office, they must announce to others?

I confess that I received with complete joy your indication in writing of the welcome affection existing among you and of the peace of the churches. Whatever could encourage me, whatever could admonish me, was freely conveyed to me. [Col. 1049B] “May God confirm what he has accomplished in you.” May he himself accomplish, for the salvation of souls, what he has commanded to be done, through that piety by which he redeemed us; and in this good news we too have repaid the duty of religious messengers.

Whatever we have indicated in writing and sent concerning the Easterners, whom by the help of our God we have recalled to the unity and body of the Church, we shall communicate again with you in due course through appropriate reports.

Soon after the return of our representatives, a legation was sent from the East. It made definite requests and sought definite counsel. We shall summarize what had to be said, rather sending you the replies that we gave, so as to inform you. Thus neither opinion nor error may claim anything from the greater distance of the lands, [Col. 1049C] since it is enough to hold to the truth itself concerning the facts.

As for the contents of your letter, it would indeed have been appropriate to explain your wishes more fully, so that, after everything had been considered, a response corresponding to reason might be given. But because in that same letter you mentioned the ancient privileges and paternal statutes, we have sent a rescript on this point to our brother and fellow bishop Salustius. We also indicate briefly to you what was stated more fully to him, so that we might not overturn privileges that had been granted and might judge nothing more consonant with the faith than that the decrees of the Fathers be preserved in their own honor.

May God preserve you safe, dearest brothers.

## The Emperor Justinus to Pope Hormisdas

[Col. 1049D]

The zeal that we recently possessed, and still possess, for reconciling the opinions of those who cultivate the Catholic faith, so that all may venerate the undivided divinity of the Trinity with one mind, has plainly been made known. Now, for this very purpose, we are voluntarily sending to your Blessedness Gratus, master of the scrinium (the imperial chancery/archive office), as envoy.

At last, so that a remedy may be found for the dissensions of those who contend in different ways, we now receive with ready and willing affection the most religious men whom your Apostolic See has judged suitable to send as intermediaries for unity.
