Indeed, we have looked upon them with joyful eyes as though they were peace itself, and we have embraced them with outstretched hands.

[Col. 1050A] Moreover, we have arranged everything with the utmost care so that the venerable Church of Constantinople, as well as many other churches, may accept your wishes—not only in other matters but also in removing from the sacred diptychs the names that you most insistently requested to be removed.

There were, however, certain cities and churches, both of Pontus and Asia, and especially of the East, whose clergy or peoples, though assailed by every kind of threat and persuasion, nevertheless could not be moved to remove the names of bishops or reject the names of those whose reputation flourished among them. They judge life harder than death if they condemn the dead whose rights among the living they gloried in.

What, then, are we to do with such obstinacy, which neither listens to God nor so greatly despises torments that [Col. 1050B] it considers it a great and festive occasion if it should cease from its religious resolve only after surrendering its body? It seems to us that we must act more gently and mercifully. If such an approach cannot be found in your holiness, it will not be found elsewhere.

For we have not accepted a petition from those eager for blood and punishments—though even saying this is severe—nor do we wish the hopes of concord to remain incomplete because of a small difference. Rather, we seek, in every way available to us, to extend the union of the Church’s members.

Which, then, will be more advantageous: that such great multitudes be wholly accepted by us for the sake of the lesser matters, or that, once the small concessions have been granted and the greater matters relaxed, those things be corrected by every possible means, so that what could not be obtained in every respect may at least be represented in the necessary parts?

[Col. 1050C] We therefore ask indulgence concerning the names—not of Acacius, not of either Peter, not of Dioscorus or Timothy, whose names were contained in the letters sent to us by your Blessedness—but of those whom the reverence of bishops has honored in other cities. This is excepted in the cities where your Blessedness’s petitions have already been fully accepted, unless your benevolence should also decide to correct this part more gently.

Nor is the matter without the judgment of the Apostolic See, so that it should be called pardon rather than a considered and deliberate decision. For Anastasius, of most religious memory, openly and clearly established the position of your Church’s summit when he wrote that it was enough for our predecessor, who desired peace, if Acacius’s name alone were kept silent.

[Col. 1050D] He therefore follows the earlier decrees of your See, which does not judge that all memorials of the dead must be despised, so that it should be considered unworthy and unfitting if your gentleness, made known throughout the whole world, were not more gracious toward everyone—not only the dead but also the living.

We have no doubt that this will be so pleasing to you that the world will immediately be restored to joy by a peaceful response. Your Holiness should also remember what we wrote some time ago: that petitions had been sent to us from the East, expressing their wishes and the decision in which they show that they will remain firm, and from which they judge that they must not withdraw for any reason.

[Col. 1051A] Accordingly, in fulfillment of our promises, we have rightly entrusted this document to be sent to you at present through John, the most reverend bishop, so that, once its wording has also been accepted by your See, it may contribute to gathering and uniting the venerable churches everywhere, and especially the Church of Jerusalem. All show such favor toward that church, as toward the mother of the Christian name, that no one dares separate himself from it.

It is therefore fitting that your Holiness declare your own agreement also in an epistolary document, so that, once it has become known and clear to all that you too approve and steadfastly preserve the wording of this document, the world may be made more joyful.

Given at Chalcedon on the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the consulship of Rusticus; received on the day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of the same.

## Copy of the petition

[Col. 1051B] To the God-beloved and most pious emperor, Augustus by God’s grace, the most Christian prince Justinus: a prayer and petition from the people of Jerusalem and Antioch, and from the clergy, abbots, and landholders of the province of Syria Secunda:

“Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation” (Isaiah 12:3), the prophet Isaiah cries aloud, clearly displaying the springs of salvation, the proclamations of evangelical truth. From these the blessed Apostles, their successors in discipleship, and the wise teachers of the Church drew the saving water of faith and watered the whole holy Church of God.

Established upon the rock of the chief of the Apostles and preserving a straight and unbending confession, she cries out confidently with him at all times to the only-begotten Son of God, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (John 11:27).

[Col. 1051C] Receiving this saving confession from the four holy synods honored by evangelical precepts, by the grace of Christ we have never departed from the right doctrines handed down to us, as the proof of events testifies and the steadfastness of our faith demonstrates in the time of necessity.

Therefore, most pious lord, if as Christians we share in the rationality of faith and hasten toward common peace and unity, through this declaration we make manifest to your piety the faith that we received from the beginning, so that it may be known that we join in peace and, with God’s help, do not turn away from the right faith. Rather, we equally abhor every heresy. [Col. 1051D] We anathematize and detest with our whole heart not only the Eutychianists and Acephali, but also the Nestorians and those who worship a mere human being.

We, most Christian emperor, as stated above, having been baptized and believing from the beginning in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, adore one essence of God in three subsistences. Believing according to the teaching and creed of the holy Fathers, we believe in one Lord God the almighty Father, and likewise in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Lord, the Word; and in one Holy Spirit; and, in accordance with this divine teaching, in the definition promulgated by the holy Council of Chalcedon.

[Col. 1052A] We also understand, confidently accept, and confess that the one substance or person—this is what the same holy synod proclaimed in two natures, namely divinity and humanity, indivisibly and without confusion—is God the Word. Our Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy Trinity, of one essence.

For thus we have received the Lord in three subsistences, as has been said. The Father was not incarnate, nor was the Holy Spirit; God the Word was incarnate and became man. According to the property of sonship, he is one of the holy Trinity, of one essence.

Thus, believing according to the aforementioned four holy synods, we do not refuse to confess the second birth of God the Word according to the flesh. Hence the holy Virgin is properly believed to be the Mother of God, since she gave birth to the Lord Word, the Son of the Father, who by nature and in truth is of one essence with the Father and who became man from her through an unchangeable nature.

[Col. 1052B] We confess two natures in Christ, united according to essence or substance, as in one person or substance. Nor do we remove their distinction or proper characteristics after the union; neither have we been taught by the union to divide them into two persons and substances.

We know the same only-begotten Son of God both before his incarnation and afterward as equally God and man: passible in the flesh, impassible in divinity; bounded by the body, not bounded in spirit—that is, earthly and heavenly; the one whom the world received as man but could not contain as Lord; mortal and immortal. Nowhere has the diversity of the natures been removed, nor do we divide the union according to essence.

[Col. 1052C] This is truly the great mystery of piety: God the Word, one of the holy Trinity and of one essence, was incarnate and became man. He is recognized and adored in both natures, divinity and humanity, indivisibly and without confusion. He did not undergo conversion or change, but preserves within himself the proper character of each nature in one person.

Therefore, accepting and preserving the aforementioned holy synods on account of this faith, we anathematize all who, at any time or in any manner, have written anything against them—especially John Egotas [the reading/name is uncertain], who, as a Nestorian, spewed forth many blasphemies against the aforementioned holy Council of Chalcedon. Likewise we condemn Timothy, surnamed the Cat, as an Eutychianist, barking against that council with his followers.

[Col. 1052D] Thus, with God’s help, we have always held and now hold the following confession: certain heretics, while hastening to conceal their evil faith, attempt to disparage our freedom in Christ and our right faith.

We therefore implore your clemency to take care and concern for the perfect union of the holy churches, so that, once the unity has been accomplished with God’s help, peace may not afterward be disturbed by any reasonable or unreasonable pretext. May the God of all fulfill your pious desire for his glory and for the order of the state.

# THE DECREES OF POPE JOHN BEGIN

[Col. 1053]

[Col. 1053A] ## John, bishop of the city of Rome, to Zacharias, archbishop, greeting

Your affection, dearest brother, demands the precept of the Apostolic See, in which the decrees of the Fathers agree—something that we believe it is lawful to deny neither to you nor to any priest who lives and believes rightly.

Although, in view of the merit and honor of the priesthood in which you greatly excel, all the rules of ecclesiastical life and teaching are known to you, nevertheless, because you have strongly requested the norm and authority of the Roman Church in your letters, we have taken care to reply briefly.

For it is unjust rashly to judge the hidden matters of another’s heart. Indeed, when someone’s works appear to be nothing but good, it is sinful to accuse him on the basis of suspicion.

Therefore, sheep entrusted to their shepherd ought not to rebuke him unless he has deviated from the right faith, and they can in no way accuse him. [Col. 1053B] The deeds of shepherds must not be struck down by the sword of the mouth, even if they appear rightly subject to correction.

We say this because in your letters we have found that certain bishops in your regions were accused by their own sheep: some, evidently, on suspicion, and others on certain grounds. For this reason, some were stripped of their property and others driven from their own sees.

You should know that such men can be summoned neither to a provincial synod nor to a general synod, nor can anything be judged concerning them, until everything that was taken from them has been restored to their legal authority.

First, therefore, all those things must be restored according to law, and the churches that were taken from them must be returned with all their privileges. Then they must be granted not a short period of time but as much time as they appear to have spent stripped of their property or expelled, before they are summoned to a synod and heard by all the bishops of their province.

[Col. 1053C] For one who has been stripped or expelled can neither be summoned to judgment nor judged, since there is no privilege by which one already stripped can be stripped. Hence it was decreed in ancient times that all possessions, everything taken from him, and all revenues must be restored by the prelate or chief bishop to the possessor before the case is formally opened.

It is written elsewhere: “He who has suffered violence shall receive everything in the condition in which it was, and shall securely retain what he possessed.”

Elsewhere, in the synodal decrees of the Fathers and in the edicts of kings, it is established and read: “Everything must be restored to bishops who have been stripped or expelled, immediately [Col. 1053D] by the ordinance of the bishops, and they must be fully recalled to possession of the places from which they departed—whatever the circumstances of time, fraud, captivity, the power of the great, or any unjust causes by which they are known to have lost Church property, personal property, or their own estates—before their accusation or regular summons to a synod,” and so forth.

[Col. 1054A] It is also decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that one who seizes another’s property must not go unpunished but must restore everything with increase. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8).

The laws of the world likewise provide: “Whoever steals another’s property shall restore to the person whose property was taken elevenfold what was removed.”

And it is written in the divine law: “Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbor’s boundary marker. And the people shall say, Amen” (Deuteronomy 27:17).

Such acts, therefore, must not be presumed without punishment or carried out without condemnation.

You, dearest brother, must take care not to transgress these provisions, and you must firmly teach the other bishops entrusted to your care, as well as the others, to observe them. For they cannot transgress the Apostolic statutes without endangering the transgressor’s rank.

[Col. 1054B] Accusers who are enemies, or who come from the household of an enemy, or who dwell with enemies, must not be believed, lest they desire to inflict harm in anger or seek revenge for an injury. Such accusers too must be rejected, not approved.

Hold fast to these things, dearest brother, and always beware of what is prohibited. Strive to fulfill what was rightly said to Jesus, son of Sirach: “Fight for the truth unto death, and the Lord God will fight for you always.”

For this reason the holy Church has been entrusted both to you and to us, so that we may not neglect to labor for everyone and provide help in every matter. For while a strong man armed guards his courtyard, everything he possesses is at peace.

Therefore, with such necessity pressing, it is especially incumbent upon you, by your authority and that of the Apostolic See, to restrain hostile bishops and [Col. 1054C] raise up the oppressed, so that, with the Lord’s help and without serious difficulty, we ourselves may always deserve to offer sacrifice to him unharmed and with joy.

The friendly circumstance of the work undertaken also compels me to turn back to you. Until now I have wished to renew my work through better words, since the poisoned necessity requires such an account. The dwelling of the heavenly command either joins us or separates us; and it does not matter what distances divide us, if we are held together by the key of the heavenly dwelling.

Nor will such men be able to harm you if you do not delay in providing one another assistance. For it is an unheard-of form of sacrilege when rivals disguise themselves under the appearance of false religious honor.

The one who boasts that he has been entrusted as an assistant in matters concerning God dishonors the reverence due to the venerable name. It is a kind of insult, as though one were in lofty consolation [Col. 1054D], in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Who are you to judge another’s servant?”

Why do they deceive inexperienced ears and make the appearance of vengeance seem more serious than the fault? If they have hatred, let them correct their excesses. Why, then, do they condemn crimes more freely than they avoid them?

Everyone who attacks the Fathers or does not fear to disparage them is surely his own assailant. For, with the Lord’s help, there is no weapon of the enemies that you cannot overcome [Col. 1055A], if, in accordance with the voice of truth and as the Lord commanded, you maintain love for one another.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the fourth consulship of Maximus and Olibrius.

## To the bishops of Italy concerning King Theodoric

John, bishop, to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy, greeting in the Lord.

I have learned through very frequent and extensive experience that your holy devotion to the Christian religion grows glorious and expands through great increase; and the right faith, which consoles and strengthens not only me but all the priests of the Lord, is recognized and enlarged in your minds and actions through your priestly work.

Therefore, brothers, I exhort and admonish you to arm yourselves against Arian treachery, which was condemned not merely once but often and which now revives in some places, with the sword of the Holy Spirit, so that, with divine grace assisting us, we may be able to crush and eradicate it, so that its root may not be found hereafter. Wherever you find churches of the Arians, consecrate them as Catholic churches without any delay through divine prayers and works. For when we were at Constantinople, persuaded and urged both by Catholic religion and by the cause of King Theodoric, and while the most devout, Christian, and supremely just orthodox Emperor Justin was uprooting the Arians, we consecrated, with the Lord’s help, whatever churches we were able to find in those regions as Catholic churches.

And although the aforesaid King Theodoric, inwardly struck and enveloped by their plague, threatens outwardly to destroy us and our whole region, consuming it with sword and fire, do not therefore lose heart. Rather, strive manfully in the Lord’s field, and, according to the voice of Truth:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28).

And the eminent Apostle of the Gentiles says:

> “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord; and ourselves as your servants through Jesus. For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has himself shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus. But we possess this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may belong to God and not to us. In everything we suffer affliction, but are not crushed; we are perplexed, but not driven to despair. We endure persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but do not perish, always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. Thus death is at work in us, but life in you. Since we have the same spirit of faith, as it is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke,’ we also believe, and therefore we speak, knowing that he who raised Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and establish us with you. For everything is for your sake, so that grace, abounding through many acts of thanksgiving, may abound to the glory of God” (2 Corinthians 4:1–18).

Therefore we do not lose heart. Although our outward self is being corrupted, our inward self is renewed day by day. For this slight, momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, since we look not to the things that are seen but to those that are unseen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

> “For we know that if our earthly house, this tent, is dissolved, we have a building from God, an eternal house in the heavens, not made by human hands. For in this also we groan, longing to be clothed with our dwelling that is from heaven—if indeed we are found clothed and not naked. For we who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be stripped but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Now the one who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit. Therefore, always confident and knowing that while we are in this body we are away from the Lord—for we walk by faith and not by sight—we are confident, and we have the good will rather to be away from the body and present with the Lord. And therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him. For we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to him through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade human beings, but to God we are manifest; and I hope that we are also manifest in your consciences. We do not commend ourselves to you again, but give you an occasion to glory on our behalf, so that you may have something to say to those who glory in appearance and not in heart. For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you. For the love of Christ presses upon us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose for them. Therefore, from now on we know no one according to the flesh. And even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we now know him no longer in that way. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become true. But everything is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: namely, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and placing in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:1–21).

> “As fellow workers, we also exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: ‘At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.’ Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Giving no one any cause for offense, so that our ministry may not be reviled, but in everything let us present ourselves as God’s ministers: in great patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in prisons, in riots, in labors, in vigils, in fasts, in purity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through honor and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful, as unknown and yet known, as dying—and behold, we live; as chastised and yet not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Corinthians 6:1–10).

> “Finally, brothers, rejoice; be perfected; be encouraged; keep peace, and the God of peace and love will be with you always” (2 Corinthians 13:11).

Amen.

Given on the third day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Maximus and Olibrius.

# THE DECREES OF POPE FELIX BEGIN

[Column 1057]

[Column 1057B]  
1. That the celebration of Mass ought not to take place anywhere except in places dedicated to God, unless great necessity compels it.  
2. Concerning uncertainty about the consecration of churches: what must be done.

To his most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout the various provinces, Felix, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

By the great gift of God’s mercy, the joys of the whole Catholic Church have been multiplied, since the condition of the churches flourishes in the order established by the successors of the apostles. And when we recognize that this order is disturbed by the cunning of the ancient enemy, we are saddened with no small grief.

For this reason, brothers, we exhort, admonish, and urgently ask you never to depart from the path of apostolic institution and not to disagree with the Head, but without any hesitation to hold fast the faith and order established by the apostles and apostolic men. For if the columns of some great house should fall, the house itself will afterward not stand. So also you are the columns of the Church: if you begin to be shaken, the holy Church governed through you wastes away and collapses.

These matters, brothers, which I mention, are greatly to be feared, weighed with the utmost care, and guarded against lest they occur. For Truth itself says:

> “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt should lose its savor, with what will it be salted?” (Matthew 5:13).

Behold the earth. Therefore, dearest brothers, I admonish you because I am your debtor and love you greatly. When I hear good things about you, I rejoice exceedingly; conversely, when I hear evil things, I am deeply troubled. Although I am separated from you by long intervals of land and sea, I am nevertheless altogether joined to you in heart. I trust in every way that this is also true because of your blessedness toward me: since you love me in return, you are not far from me.

Therefore we give thanks to that mustard seed which, from the appearance of a small and contemptible seed, grows from the same root into branches that spread so widely and are extended everywhere that all the birds of heaven nest in them (Matthew 13:31–32). We also give thanks to that leaven which, placed in three measures of flour, leavened the whole mass of the human race in unity (ibid. 13:33); and to the small stone cut from the mountain without hands, which filled the whole face of the earth (Daniel 2:34–35). It extended itself everywhere so that, when the whole human race had been brought into unity, it might perfect the body of the entire Church, and so that this mutually shared distinction of the members might contribute to the advantage of the whole structure.

Therefore we too are not far from you, because in him who is everywhere we are one. Let us therefore give thanks to him who, having destroyed hostilities in his flesh (Ephesians 2:14), made one flock and one fold throughout the whole world under one shepherd. Let us always remember what the eminent Preacher admonishes when he says:

> “Carefully preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3).

I received with gratitude the letter of your Holiness, which you sent to the apostolic see concerning certain questions, as to the Head, so that you might receive answers from the place from which the whole Church took the beginning of its religion. I have taken care to respond to you briefly.

## Chapter I

Concerning the consecration of churches and the celebration of Masses, it is clear to all who know the precepts of the New and Old Testaments that these ought not to take place anywhere except in places consecrated to the Lord, unless great necessity intervenes.

We read that Moses made the tabernacle at the Lord’s command and consecrated it, together with its table, altar, and the other vessels and utensils required for divine worship. We know that he consecrated these not only through divine prayers but also, at the Lord’s command, anointed them with holy oil.

How these things were done, and that no others handled, carried, raised, or set down the sacred objects except priests clothed with sacred anointing and consecrated to the Lord in holy vestments, together with the Levites, is found in the very institutions written through Moses at the Lord’s command.

How David, the most devout of kings, enlarged the worship of God and wished to build a temple for the Lord, but was forbidden because of the great amount of blood he had shed, and how he himself collected the expenses; and how his son Solomon, at God’s command and with his help, completed what David had wished to do, consecrating the temple with its altar and the rest of what was required for divine worship, is read, among other places, in the Third Book of Kings as follows:

> “Building,” says Solomon, “I have built a dwelling for you, O Lord, a most firm sanctuary, your everlasting throne.” Then the king turned his face and blessed the whole assembly of Israel. And the whole assembly of Israel was standing. He said:
>
> “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David my father and fulfilled it with his hands, saying: ‘From the day when I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I did not choose a city from all the tribes of Israel so that a house might be built and my name might be there; but I chose David to be over my people Israel.’ David my father wished to build a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, and the Lord said to David my father: ‘Because you considered in your heart the building of a house for my name, you did well to have this in mind. Nevertheless, you will not build the house; rather, your son who will come forth from your loins will build the house for my name.’ The Lord confirmed the word he had spoken. I therefore have taken the place of David my father and have sat upon the throne of Israel, as the Lord said; and I have built a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, and I have appointed there a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the Lord that he made with our fathers when they came out of the land of Egypt.
>
> “Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord in the presence of the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven. He said: ‘Lord God of Israel, there is none like you in heaven above or on earth below, keeping covenant and mercy with your servants who walk before you with their whole heart. You have kept for David my father what you spoke to him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hands you fulfilled it, as this day proves. Now therefore, Lord God of Israel, preserve for David your servant, my father, what you spoke to him, saying: “There shall not fail you a man before me who sits upon the throne of Israel, provided that your sons guard their way, walking before me as you have walked in my sight.” And now, Lord God of Israel, let your words be confirmed which you spoke to David your servant, my father.
>
> “‘Can it be thought that God truly dwells upon the earth? If heaven and the heavens of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built! Yet look upon the prayer of your servant and upon his supplications, Lord my God. Hear, Lord, the hymn and prayer that your servant prays before you today, so that your eyes may be open over this house night and day, over the house of which you said, “My name shall be there,” so that you may hear the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, whatever they pray for in this place. Hear in the place of your dwelling, in heaven, and when you hear, be merciful.
>
> “‘If someone sins against his neighbor and is bound by an oath, and comes because of the oath before your altar in your house, hear in heaven, act, and judge your servants, condemning the wicked and bringing his way upon his own head, vindicating the just and repaying him according to his justice.
>
> “‘If your people Israel flee before their enemies because they will have sinned against you, and then, doing penance and confessing your name, they come and pray and plead with you in this house, hear in heaven, forgive the sin of your people Israel, and bring them back to the land that you gave to their fathers.
>
> “‘If heaven is shut and it does not rain because of their sin, and they pray in this place, do penance in your name, and turn back from their sins because of their affliction, hear them in heaven. Forgive the sins of your servants and of your people Israel, show them the good way in which they should walk, and give rain upon the land that you gave to your people as a possession.
>
> “‘If famine arises in the land, or pestilence, or corrupt air, or blight, locust, or mildew; if their enemy afflicts them, besieging the gates; if any plague, illness, devouring calamity, or curse befalls any person among your people Israel; if anyone recognizes the plague of his heart and spreads out his hands in this house, hear in heaven, in the place of your dwelling, and be propitious. Act and give to each according to his ways, as you see his heart—for you alone know the hearts of all the children of human beings—so that they may fear you all the days they live upon the face of the land that you gave to our fathers.
>
> “‘Moreover, even the foreigner who is not of your people Israel, when he comes from a distant land because of your name—for your great name, your mighty hand, and your outstretched arm will be heard of everywhere—when he comes and prays in this place, hear in heaven, in the firmament of your dwelling, and do everything for which the foreigner calls upon you, so that all the peoples of the earth may learn to fear your name, as your people Israel does, and may know that your name has been invoked over this house that I have built.
>
> “‘If your people go out to battle against their enemies by whatever road you send them, and they pray to you in the direction of the city that you have chosen and of the house that I have built for your name, hear their prayer and supplication in heaven and execute their judgment.
>
> “‘But if they sin against you—for there is no one who does not sin—and, being angry, you deliver them to their enemies, and they are taken captive to the land of their enemies, whether far or near; if they repent in their heart in the place of their captivity and, turning back, plead with you in their captivity, saying, “We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have behaved impiously”; if they return to you with all their heart and soul in the land of their enemies to which they were led captive; if they pray to you toward the direction of their land that you gave to their fathers, and of the city that you chose, and of the temple that I built for your name, hear in heaven, in the firmament of your throne, their prayer and supplication; execute their judgment; be merciful to your people who sinned against you and to all their iniquities by which they transgressed against you; and grant them mercy in the sight of those who took them captive, so that they may have compassion on them.
>
> “‘For they are your people and your inheritance, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace. Let your eyes be open to the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, hearing them in everything for which they call upon you. For you separated them to yourself as an inheritance from all the peoples of the earth, as you spoke through Moses your servant when you brought our fathers out of the land of Egypt, Lord God.’
>
> “When Solomon had finished praying this prayer and supplication to the Lord, he rose from before the altar of the Lord. For he had fixed both knees upon the ground and spread out his hands toward heaven. He stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel in a loud voice, saying:
>
> “‘Blessed is the Lord, who has given rest to his people Israel, according to everything that he spoke; not one word has failed of all that he spoke through Moses his servant. May the Lord our God be with us, as he was with our fathers, not abandoning or rejecting us, but inclining our hearts toward himself, so that we may walk in all his ways and keep his commandments, ceremonies, and judgments, whatever he commanded our fathers. May these words of mine, by which I have pleaded before the Lord, draw near to the Lord our God day and night, so that he may execute judgment for his servant and his people Israel each day, so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord himself is God, and there is no other besides him. Let our heart also be perfect with the Lord our God, so that we may walk in his decrees and keep his commandments, as also today.’
>
> “Then the king and all Israel with him sacrificed victims before the Lord. Solomon slaughtered peace offerings, which he offered to the Lord: twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred twenty thousand sheep. And the king and the sons of Israel dedicated the temple to the Lord. On that day the king sanctified the middle of the court that was before the house of the Lord. For he made there the burnt offering, the sacrifice, and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the Lord was too small and could not contain the burnt offering, the sacrifice, and the fat of the peace offerings.
>
> “At that time Solomon held a solemn festival, and all Israel with him, a very great multitude, from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt, before the Lord our God, for seven days and seven days—that is, fourteen days. On the eighth day he dismissed the people” (3 Kings 8:13–66).

Therefore the Jews considered the places in which they sacrificed to the Lord consecrated through divine supplications, and they offered gifts to the Lord nowhere except in places dedicated to God.

If the Jews, who served the shadow of the law, did these things, how much more must those to whom the truth has been revealed, and to whom grace and truth have been given through Jesus Christ, build temples for the Lord and adorn them as well as we can; and must devoutly and solemnly consecrate them through divine prayers and holy anointings, together with their altars, vessels, vestments, and the other utensils required for divine worship. We ought not to celebrate Masses or offer sacrifices anywhere except in places consecrated to the Lord by bishops; nor may chorepiscopi, who have often been forbidden, do so, unless, as stated above, the greatest necessity demands it.

And even if the greatest necessity should compel this, it must not be done in houses, because the sacred canons forbid sacrifices to be offered in houses. Rather, it must be done in tents dedicated by bishops through divine prayers and on tables consecrated to the Lord and anointed with holy oil by bishops, for the extreme necessity mentioned above—not according to anyone’s preference or laziness.

It is therefore better not to sing or hear Mass than to do so in places where it ought not to be done, unless, as has often been stated, the greatest necessity happens to require it, since necessity has no law. Hence it is written:

> “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place that the Lord your God will choose” (Deuteronomy 12:13).

And in Exodus it is read:

> “You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves. You shall make an altar of earth for me, and upon it you shall offer your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen, in every place where the memory of my name shall be” (Exodus 20:22–24).

Just as only priests consecrated to the Lord ought to sing Masses and offer sacrifices, so it is lawful to sing Masses or offer sacrifices nowhere except in the places mentioned above, which have been consecrated to the Lord.

If, as is read in canon 26 of the Council of Laodicea, those who have not been ordained by bishops cannot exorcize either in churches or in houses, then much more may ministries of a higher rank be performed, or sacrifices offered, only by bishops who have been consecrated for the grades whose offices they are to exercise.

That offerings ought not to be made in houses, as was briefly stated above, is prohibited in canon 59 of the same council in these words:

> “Offerings ought not to be celebrated in houses by bishops and priests.”

The solemn anniversaries of the dedications of churches, however, are to be celebrated each year, with the Lord himself providing the example. When he came to celebrate the same festival with the rest of the people, he gave everyone a model for celebrating the feast of the dedication of the temple, as it is written:

> “The feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter. Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico” (John 10:28).

That the feast of Dedication is to be celebrated for eight days may be found in the Book of Kings after the dedication of the temple had been completed.

## II

Whenever there is doubt about the consecration of churches, and neither a certain document nor reliable witnesses exist by whom their consecration may be known, know without any doubt that they must be consecrated. Such hesitation should not lead to deterioration, since what is not known to have been done is not shown to have been repeated.

Brothers, let it suffice that I have briefly answered your questions with these testimonies of Scripture, examined according to apostolic authority. Nevertheless, you and everyone must take care and preach that unlawful things not be done, and that the Lord’s commands be preserved and faithfully carried out.

We ask you, brothers, to repeat the words of the Apostle:

> “Correct the disorderly, console the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient toward everyone. See that no one repays evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good for one another and for all. Rejoice always; pray without ceasing; give thanks in everything. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you. Do not extinguish the Spirit; do not despise prophecies. Test everything; hold fast what is good. Keep yourselves from every form of evil. May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, so that your spirit, soul, and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:14).

Given on the Kalends of March, in the fourth consulship of Lampadius and Orestes.

# Letter of the same man of exhortation to Sabina

It is sufficiently clear to everyone that you are a unique member of your Church’s religious greatness and are held in the highest reverence by us. At the very summit of nobility, you offer a far nobler devotion to the Church; with an increasingly joyful recognition of Christ, you obey his commandments; and you rejoice in faith rather than boast of the splendor of so great a lineage.

It is the highest virtue to have conquered the glory of the flesh, and it is a great grace of Christ to have surpassed nobility through moral character, my deservedly illustrious lady and daughter.

Therefore, being certain, dearest daughter, strive to illuminate whatever spans of this life there may be with eternal and divine duties, so that he who has made you distinguished may render you more glorious for ever.

For this reason we exhort your affection not to delay in continually fulfilling the good work you have begun, because the beginning is not praised, but the end.

We exhort you to love and investigate wisdom, so that you may arrange and judge rationally and wisely the matters entrusted to you, since the Lord says through the Prophet:

> “Learn wisdom, you who judge the earth” (Psalm 2:10).

Therefore fear the Lord, keep his commandments, love him with all your inward being, and love your neighbor as yourself.

> “The Most High God created wisdom in the Holy Spirit; he saw and numbered her, measured her, and poured her out upon all his works and upon all flesh according to his gift; and he provided her for those who love him. The fear of the Lord is glory and glorification, joy, and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart and give joy and gladness for length of days. It will be well with the one who fears the Lord at the end, and on the day of his death he will be blessed. The love of God is honorable wisdom; those to whom she appears in vision love her through seeing her and through knowing her great works. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and she is conceived in the womb with the faithful; she walks with chosen women and is recognized with the just and faithful. The fear of the Lord is religious devotion to knowledge. Religious devotion will guard and justify the heart and will give pleasantness and joy. It will be well with the one who fears the Lord, and he will be blessed in the days of his completion. The fullness of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and her fruits are fullness. She will fill his whole house through the generations and his storehouses with her treasures. The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling one with peace and the fruit of salvation. He saw and numbered her. Both are gifts of God. Wisdom acquires knowledge and understanding of prudence and exalts the glory of those who fear her. The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and her branches are long-lived. In the treasures of wisdom are understanding and religious devotion to knowledge; but wisdom is an abomination to sinners. The fear of the Lord drives out sin; for the one who is without fear cannot be justified, since the anger of his indignation is his overthrow. The patient will endure until the appointed time, and afterward there is a return of gladness. Good sense will hide his words for a time, and the lips of many will declare his understanding. In the treasures of wisdom is the meaning of discipline, but the worship of God is an abomination to the sinner.
>
> “My son, if you desire wisdom, preserve justice, and God will give it to you. For wisdom and discipline are the fear of the Lord; and what pleases him is faith and gentleness, and he will fill his treasures. Do not be stubborn and unbelieving toward the fear of the Lord, and do not approach him with a divided heart. Do not be a hypocrite before human beings, and do not give offense by your lips. Pay attention to these matters, lest you fall and place a stumbling block for your soul, bring dishonor upon yourself, and God reveal your hidden things” (Ecclesiasticus 1:9–40).

Always strive steadfastly for faith and justice and for the salvation of your soul, and act manfully for the assistance of your brothers, so that you may receive recompense from the Lord.

For it is written:

> “My son, preserve the opportunity and avoid evil. Do not be ashamed to speak the truth for the sake of your soul. For there is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings grace and glory. Do not accept a person’s face against your own face, nor a lie against your soul. Do not be ashamed of your neighbor in your fall, and do not withhold a word in a time of salvation. Do not hide your wisdom in its beauty. For wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and teaching are recognized in the tongue through words of truth, and strength is recognized in works of justice. Do not oppose the truth in any way, and be ashamed of the ignorance of your falsehood. Do not be ashamed to confess your sins, and do not submit yourself to a human being because of sin. Do not resist the face of the powerful, and do not strive against the force of a river. Fight for justice on behalf of your soul, and struggle for justice unto death, and God will fight your enemies for you. Do not be hasty with your tongue, useless and negligent in your works. Do not be like a lion in your house, overturning your household and oppressing those subject to you. Let your hand not be extended for receiving and closed for giving” (Ecclesiasticus 4:23–36).

Supported by these authorities of Scripture, always stand upright and do not turn away from the way of truth, so that you may acquire God’s grace and honor, enjoy the friendship of human beings, and so that your will may more easily depart from love of this world, the more it is driven onward while it is being called.

For we wish to see you present and desire at least to converse with you by letter when you are absent. Therefore we also wish that blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, may happily lead you to his threshold, so that we may deserve to enjoy your presence in the grace of the Almighty.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the fourth consulship of Lampadius and Orestes.

# THE DECREES OF POPE BONIFACE BEGIN

[Column 1065]

## Letter of the same man, addressed to Eulalius, bishop of Alexandria, concerning the reconciliation of the Church of Carthage

[Column 1065A]

BONIFACE, bishop, sends greetings to EULALIUS, his fellow bishop.

Long ago, and from the beginning, we received such great confidence from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that, with the Lord’s help, we possess authority to assist the universal Church and to correct and amend by apostolic authority whatever is harmful.

For this purpose divine providence established and distinguished different ranks, so that, while inferiors showed reverence to superiors and superiors bestowed love upon inferiors, a single harmony might be woven from diversity and the proper administration of individual duties might arise. Indeed, the whole cannot subsist by any other arrangement unless an order of this kind, with its great distinctions, preserves it.

Since creation cannot be governed or live in one identical equality, the examples of the heavenly armies instruct us. Although there are angels and archangels, it is clear that they are not equal, but that one differs from another in power and order, as you know.

If, then, among those who are without sin this distinction is established, who among human beings would refuse willingly to submit to the arrangement? From this, peace and mutual love embrace one another in turn, and firm harmony remains in a sincere affection that is reciprocal and pleasing to God.

Since each office is then fulfilled beneficially when there is one superior to whom one may have recourse, we do not wish your affection to be unaware of our wishes, lest one who shared the concern should be excluded from the fruits of joy.

Therefore we inform you by our letter that, with the Lord’s favor, the Church of Carthage has returned to our communion, and that the entire series of the commands which we gave to our legates has been fulfilled.

So that the joy might reach your affection more fully and completely, we have also decided to send the petition of our brother and fellow priest Eulalius, bishop of Carthage, together with copies of the sacred letters of Justin, the most merciful ruler of the East. We judge, moreover, that many bishops throughout the eastern regions have acted in the same way.

It remains for the Divinity, entreated by our fitting prayers, to grant that we may also rejoice over the restoration of other churches.

You should make the matters we have taken care to report known to those priests who are near your fraternity, so that they too may not cease to give thanks with us for the benefits of heavenly mercy upon the accomplishment of so great a matter.

For Aurelius, formerly bishop of the Church of Carthage, together with his colleagues, began, at the instigation of the devil, to grow proud against the Roman Church during the times of our predecessors Boniface and Celestine. But now, seeing himself separated from the communion of the Roman Church because of the sins of Aurelius, Eulalius humbled himself, recognized his fault, and, seeking peace and communion with the Roman Church, subscribed—together with his colleagues—to condemn by apostolic authority all writings that had been produced by any means against the privileges of the Roman Church.

## Copy of his petition and that of the aforesaid ruler Justin.

«The first means of salvation is to preserve the rule of right faith, and in no respect to deviate from the decrees of the Fathers; and since the sentence of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over, when he says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18).»

[Col. 1066B] These words are proved by the effects of events, because in the apostolic see the Catholic religion has always been preserved without blemish. Desiring in no way to be separated from this hope and faith, and following the decrees of the Fathers, we anathematize all who, in their pride, raise their necks against the holy Roman and apostolic Church, following the apostolic see in all things and proclaiming all its decrees. And in every respect I hope that I may deserve to be in communion with you, the communion which the apostolic see proclaims, in which there is the complete and true integrity and perfect solidity of the Christian religion. I promise that the names of those separated from communion with the Catholic Church—that is, those who do not consent to the apostolic see—are not to be recited among the sacred mysteries.

But if I should attempt to deviate in any respect from my profession, I declare by my own judgment that I am an accomplice of those whom I have condemned. I have subscribed this profession with my own hand and sent it to the holy and venerable Boniface, pope of the city of Rome, condemning both my predecessors and successors and all who strive to annul the privileges of the holy Roman and apostolic Church.»

From this, then, the evidence of heavenly mercy is fully made known: worldly rulers unite matters of faith with the administration of the commonwealth, and the leaders of the churches carry out what belongs to the administration of their office, mindful of their duty. After the storms of discord, the Christian religion needed such leaders—men who, by prudent administration, would restrain the whirlwinds and, when the storm had been driven away, restore the peace that had long wandered abroad—so that, in future generations, those who aimed at the examples of their purpose might plainly show that whatever they did, pleasing to the Lord, for the imitation of posterity, was unquestionably to be credited to them.

[Col. 1066D] Let us bless the Lord, dearest brothers, that this has been granted in our days, and let us strive with all the strength of our prayers and cares so that what has been well begun by God’s work may, with his help, be completed in every respect. For we must hope that the remaining members, which are still divided, will hasten to the joining together of their body, and that the lesser will not be separated from the greater. Since your Christian affection urges me to this with the zeal of charity, what invites must follow, and what it persuades us to love must be embraced. For, already sharing a similar care for the faith, through religious patience we also hope for the reward that will come from the accomplishment of the good work.

Nor must we yield to difficulties. Faith is not wearied by hardships, nor does one reach the heights of heaven by an easy path; no one deserves a reward without the exercise of labor. Therefore we are specially admonished not to grow weary in doing good, as the Psalmist also bears witness: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times” (Ps. VIII, 32), because it is not the beginning of labor that customarily receives the reward of recompense, but its completion.

[Col. 1067B] Therefore, taking up the zeal of vigilance, since we share one fellowship and one faith in communion, just as we rejoice together in the Lord over the unity of the apostolic see and the Church of Constantinople, so let us also rejoice in the restoration of the others, as your affection urges, and let us seek the reward: that we may preserve our faith and integrity unstained by every defilement.

For you know, dearest and most holy brother, that the bonds of the Church preserve concord, which protects us from the attacks of heretics; through it, the integrity of the canons is also maintained. When these things have been preserved in their strength with every caution, remedies remain available to those who hope for them. For the order of ecclesiastical rules, and justice itself in its proper form, requires that rational medicine not be denied kindly and faithfully to those who hope for it; nor is anyone so estranged from humanity that cautious simplicity does not incline him away from the rigor of strictness.

But so that you may cautiously resolve this and the other complaints or errors of any age, dearest brother, you ought in this matter to assume my person, knowing in such cases, as has been said, what must be avoided, and providing for everything in such a way that you cannot doubt that you will have to render an account to God for this administration. Yet do so in such a way that those who have been joined to you in communion, or through you to the apostolic see, declare this to us in writing; and let it also be entered what written petitions they have submitted and what their contents were.

[Col. 1068B] We must likewise keep humility in mind, so that by it we may preserve the dignity of our rank in honor, in such a way that among us there is neither humility to be feared nor a proud exercise of reason. May almighty God, dearest brother, guard you with his protection and lead you to the homeland of heavenly recompense through the abundant fruit of souls. May God keep you safe, most reverend brother. Amen.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Valentinian II and Orestes IV.

# THE DECREES OF POPE JOHN BEGIN

[Col. 1067]

[Col. 1067C] John to his most reverend brother Valerius, bishop.

On receiving your letters, I found them full of that rule of faith in which your holiness first excels, and I gave thanks to God when I learned that you were in good health in soul and body. Certainly, concerning what you reported—that some say that the Son is not equal to the Father, and that it is written in the Gospel, “The Father is greater than I”—you should know that such men do not understand the rules of the faith rightly, nor do they possess the right faith.

The apostle Paul does not indicate that Christ was created according to the nature of his divinity, but affirms that he was created according to the substance of human nature. He writes to the Ephesians: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind and put on the new man, who was created according to God in justice and the holiness of truth” (Eph. IV, 23). And to the Hebrews: “For in that he himself suffered and was tempted, he is also able to help those who are tempted. Therefore, as participants in a holy calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus, faithful to him who created him” (Heb. II, 18).

And to the Colossians: “But now put away all these things as well: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy; and let no shameful speech proceed from your mouth. Do not lie to one another, stripping off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new, which is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created it” (Col. III, 8).

Could the one who created and brought forth the whole creation, visible and invisible, by the power of his own authority, have created or been able to make himself either before or afterward—which it is impious to say? The Son is lesser than the Father in the form of the man he assumed, but equal to the Father in the substance of the nature of his divinity, as he himself testifies: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30). And again: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9). And again: “Whoever hates me hates my Father also” (John XV, 23). And again: “That all may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (John V, 23). And again: “That they may be one in us, as we also are one” (John XV, 21). And again: “You are in me and I in them” (ibid.). And again: “All that is mine is yours” (ibid., 10). And again: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (ibid.). And again: “The Father, remaining in me, does these works” (John XIV, 10).

The evangelist John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). And again, he himself says to the Parthians: “There are three who bear witness on earth: water, blood, and spirit. There are three in us, and there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit. And these three are one.”

Therefore, in the nature of the divinity, since the Father and the Son are one, we do not believe that the Father preceded the Son at any time, lest he be greater than the Son; nor that the Son was born later, so that he might be lesser than the Father in divinity.

If the Son is not equal to the Father, why did the evangelist John testify concerning him in this way: “For this reason the Jews were seeking all the more to kill Jesus, because he not only was breaking the Sabbath, but also was calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God”? And the apostle Paul says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus. Though he existed in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 5).

And in Solomon: “He who begot me rested in my tabernacle” (Ecclus. XXIV, 12). And Isaiah: “As he was from the beginning, so he remains unto eternity; nothing has been added to him, nor will anything be diminished from him. For he is the lord of his creation, who needed nothing from anyone.” And in Psalm LXXII: “For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?”

All these passages demonstrate that the Son is not inferior by nature, but proclaim the equality of his divinity, since the one who spoke both things spoke truly, for Truth could not lie.

Act always in this way, dearest brother, and urge all others to act likewise, so that, once this error—which appeared to have been born—has been abolished, there may be throughout the whole world one faith and one identical confession, to the praise and glory of God: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 10).

Given on the … day before the Nones of August, in the consulship of Justinian and Athalaric IV.

# THE LETTER OF POPE AGAPITUS TO ANTHEMIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, ON THE TWO NATURES IN ONE CHRIST, BEGINS

[Col. 1069]

[Col. 1069B] Agapitus to Anthemius, bishop, greeting.

I would have been filled with great joy if I had found you concerning the peace of the Church and the teaching of the most glorious emperor and people as I heard that you were at the beginning. But now, because we have learned from most reverend brothers that you teach the emperor and the other peoples contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, so that, denying the reality of human flesh and soul, you assert that our Lord Jesus Christ is of one nature alone, as though the divinity of the Word itself had changed into flesh and soul, and as though his conception and birth, nourishment and growth, crucifixion and death, burial and resurrection, ascension into heaven, sitting at the right hand of the Father, and coming to judge the living and the dead had belonged solely to the divine will—which received none of these things in itself without the reality of flesh; a nature united to the nature of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, likewise impassible and likewise immutable, the undivided unity and equality of the eternal Trinity and of one will.

If, therefore, anyone through an evil will, or any unbeliever, departs from this so as not to be convicted of believing the divinity to be passible and mortal, and yet dares to proclaim one nature of the incarnate Word—that is, of the Word and flesh—he plainly passes into an open and therefore detestable madness. He believes that Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and human beings, acted everything fictitiously, and that a true body was not in Christ, but that the appearance of his body appeared as a phantom to the eyes of those who saw it.

Since the Catholic faith has long detested these impious falsehoods, and since such sacrilegious assertions were long ago condemned by the concordant judgments of the blessed Fathers throughout the world, there is no doubt that we proclaim and defend the faith taught by the holy apostles, and that this holy Roman and apostolic Church, following them and their successors, has held and continues to hold, has taught and continues to teach, this doctrine.

For if they have been so blinded and alienated from the light of truth that they deny the truth of the Word of God from the time of the incarnation, let them show in what respect they appropriate the Christian name to themselves and how they agree with the Gospel of truth, if through the Virgin’s childbirth either flesh arose without divinity or divinity arose without flesh.

For just as it cannot be denied—as the evangelist says—that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” so it cannot be denied—as the blessed apostle Paul proclaims—that “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” But what reconciliation could there be by which God might be reconciled to the human race, if the mediator between God and human beings did not undertake the cause of humanity? And how does he fulfill the truth of the mediator, unless he who is equal to the Father in the form of God also shared our condition in the form of a servant, so that the bond of death contracted through the transgression of one might be dissolved by the death of one who alone owed nothing to death?

For the outpouring of Christ’s righteous blood was so rich as a price that, if the entire multitude of captives believed in their redeemer, no bond of the devil would retain any of them; for, as the Apostle says: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (I Tim. I, 14). And although those born under the sentence of sin received the power to be reborn into righteousness, the gift of freedom became stronger than the debt of slavery.

What hope, then, do those leave themselves in the protection of this sacrament who deny the truth of the human body in our Savior? Let them say by what sacrifice they were reconciled, by what blood they were redeemed. “Who,” as the Apostle says, “gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance”? Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true and eternal High Priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh?

In the sight of the Lord, the death of the righteous was precious, yet the killing of no innocent person was the redemption of the world. The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. From the steadfastness of the faithful arose examples of endurance, not gifts of righteousness. Their deaths were individual, each for each; no one paid another’s debt by his own end, since the Son of Man, our one and only Lord Jesus Christ, alone existed as the truly spotless Lamb.

In him all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised—of whom he himself said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32). For faith, which justifies the impious and creates the righteous, having been recalled to participation in humility, obtains salvation in him in whom alone a human being finds himself innocent, having through the grace of God the freedom to glory in his power. He fought against the enemy of the human race in the humility of our flesh and granted his victory to those in whose body he triumphed.

Although, therefore, in our one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and human being, there is one person of the Word and flesh, which inseparably and indivisibly possesses common actions, the qualities of those works must nevertheless be understood. By contemplation of the true faith, it must be discerned toward what the humility of the flesh is raised and toward what the height of the divinity inclines; what the flesh does not do without the Word, and what the Word does not accomplish without the flesh.

Without the power of the Word, the Virgin would neither have conceived nor given birth; and without the truth of the flesh, infancy would not have lain wrapped in swaddling clothes. Without the power of the Word, the magi would not have worshiped the child, made known by the sign of the star; and without the truth of the flesh, the child would not have been commanded to be taken into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution.

Without the power of the Word, the voice of the Father sent from heaven would not have said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. III, 17); and without the truth of the flesh, John would not have testified: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I, 29).

Without the power of the Word, the restoration of the weak and the giving of life to the dead would not have occurred; and without the truth of the flesh, food would not have been necessary for one who was fasting, nor sleep for one who was weary.

Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not have declared himself equal to the Father; and without the truth of the flesh, that same Lord would not have said that he was lesser than the Father. Catholic faith accepts and defends both, for, according to the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, it believes in one Christ, the Son of the living God, both human and true.

Christ our true God appeared as mediator between God and humanity in such a way that, joining both natures in the unity of his person, he both raised ordinary things through extraordinary ones and tempered extraordinary things through ordinary ones.

What, then? Since Christ is God and human, the human being speaks, and you bring an accusation against God? He commends the human nature in himself, and in him you dare to deform the divine nature?

Christ’s substance is therefore twofold: divine, by which he is equal to the Father, and human, by which he is lesser than the Father. Yet both together are not two Christs, but one Christ, lest God become a quaternity. For just as one human being consists of a rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and human; and by this very fact Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh. We confess Christ in all these things, and Christ in each of them.

May God convert you to what is good, brother, and grant that you hold and teach the rule of right faith in all things. Amen.

Given on the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Justinian IV and Theodatus IV.

# THE DECREES OF POPE SILVERIUS BEGIN

[Col. 1071]

## A letter of Amator, bishop, to the same

[Col. 1071C]

Amator, bishop, to the most blessed Silverius.

Most beloved Father, we have heard from certain Fathers who arrived there that you have been unjustly driven from the see of Saint Peter and sent into exile. Bearing this very heavily, we have sent a small gift—namely, thirty pounds of silver—for the support of you and your companions. We ask that you receive it with as grateful a spirit as the intention with which it is sent is grateful.

We also ask that you not disdain to inform us by letter how things have been done and are now being done concerning you, so that I may learn a reliable account about you and be able to report it to the brothers. For what do you think will happen to us, supreme Father, when such things are done to the supreme shepherd and vicar of Saint Peter? Nevertheless, do not grieve too much, but always take comfort in the Lord, for the divinity is powerful enough to remove the uncertainties of an immense storm and bring about the good calm.

Pray for us, most blessed pope.

## His reply to Amator, bishop

[Col. 1072D] Silverius to his most beloved and dearest Amator, bishop.

Oh, how good is charity, which through love makes absent persons present to one another in their likeness. It touches what is divided, orders what is confused, joins what is unequal, and perfects what is incomplete. How rightly the distinguished preacher calls it the bond of perfection, because the other virtues indeed generate perfection, but charity binds them together so that they can no longer be dissolved from the mind of the one who loves.

By this virtue, therefore, dearest brother, I find you full of charity, since you not only care for my restoration and visitation, but also do not cease to support and sustain me with your goods. I cannot fully recount or write to you all the evils that have been inflicted upon me.

Above all, however, the patrician was hostile to me because I did not restore Anthemius, formerly patriarch of Constantinople, whom my predecessor Agapitus, of holy memory, condemned on his own merits. At her command, certain false witnesses also came forward, bringing accusations against me in which I had no part.

[Col. 1073A] But while many persisted in the same accusation, our patrician Julisarius became afraid and ordered me to come peacefully to him concerning certain ecclesiastical arrangements at the imperial palace. At the first and second veil he detained all the clergy and people who were coming with me, and allowed no one to enter except me alone and my deacon Vigilius.

While I was being held by force and brought before the aforesaid patrician, they sent me into exile, where I am now sustained by the bread of tribulation and the water of anguish.

Nevertheless, for this reason I neither abandoned nor do I abandon my office. With the bishops whom I was able to assemble, I anathematized those who had acted in this way against me. Together with them, by apostolic synodal authority, I decreed that no one should ever again be deceived in such a way as I was deceived; and if anyone should henceforth deceive any bishop in such a manner, let him be anathema maranatha in the presence of God and his holy angels.

Likewise, strengthening the decrees of the holy Fathers, we decreed—although it has already been decreed very frequently—that neither false accusers nor enemies or suspected accusers or witnesses should ever be accepted against bishops, nor be able in any way to harm them, because the holy Fathers judged that a false, hateful, or rather deadly accusation should be prohibited rather than heard.

You must avoid and turn away from such persons with the greatest care, dearest brother, and reject them if they appear guilty, because not only ecclesiastical laws but also the laws of the world do not accept such persons, but repel them. Hence it is written: “The mouth of the impious devours iniquity” (Prov. XIX, 28). And the Lord speaks through the prophet, saying: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will act innocently. With the elect you will be elect, and with the perverse you will become perverse” (II Kings XXII, 26). And the Apostle says: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV, 33).

Therefore, as has already been said, the wicked must always be avoided, and one must cling to the good and benevolent, so that, as far as we can, we may avoid the danger of negligence. And lest this pestilence spread more widely, let us cut it off with whatever severity we can, since there is no rashness of presumption where there is diligent piety.

Let each of you, strengthened by this apostolic instruction, act according to his ability, preserve his conduct in holy religion through brotherly love, help one another in communion, remain in charity, and strive unceasingly to cling to the will of God, so that together we may always praise the Lord and give him tireless thanks.

Farewell always in Christ, and strive, with the Lord’s help, to fulfill the foregoing as well as you can and to instruct the remaining brothers by apostolic authority.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Justinian V and Julisanus IV.

## Letter of Pope Silverius to Pope Vigilius

Silverius, bishop, to Vigilius.

The general body of the priesthood has long known you to be entangled in many transgressions. Many of the faithful also know that, after wronging our predecessors by your obstinacy, you presumed to keep watch over the Levitical mysteries with hands [*cruenti*, “bloodstained”] by human blood.

For when, contrary to canonical law, during the time of Pope Boniface, of holy memory, you attempted, while he was still alive, to have his successor designated, then, unless the justice of the most distinguished Senate had opposed you, your beginnings ought already to have been cut short by pastoral foresight and pontifical authority.

But because a small wound in you was neglected, an incurable abscess grew, which, unless cut away more deeply with the knife, cannot feel the medicine of poultices. For, conceiving the frenzy of ambition through the audacity of the most wicked spirit, you insult that apostolic physician to whom the power of binding and loosing souls has been granted and entrusted, and you again strive to introduce a new crime into the apostolic see.

[Col. 1074C] In the manner of Simon, whose disciple you show yourself to be by your deeds, with money given, * you strive to invade my term of office without dislodging him who, by the Lord’s favor, has already continuously completed three terms in that protection [the transmitted wording is defective].

Receive, therefore, with those who consent to you, the sentence of punishment and condemnation; and recognize that the name and office of priestly ministry have been taken away from you by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, and that you have been condemned by us with apostolic authority.

For thus the faith of the holy Fathers ought to be preserved in the Catholic Church: that he who, with reprehensible presumption, has assumed what he did not receive should lose what he possessed.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the principate of Basil.

I, Caelius Silverius, pope of the eternal city, have subscribed to this decree of anathema made against Vigilius the usurper, giving my consent to all its provisions; and four bishops also subscribed, namely, those of Terracina, Fundi, Ferentinum, and Meterrensis. This document was delivered through Anastasius, subdeacon.

# THE DECREES OF POPE VIGILIUS BEGIN

[Col. 1073]

[Col. 1073D]

1. Concerning the Priscillianists who abstain from eating meat.  
2. Concerning triple immersion.  
3. Concerning those who are baptized again by the Arians.  
4. Concerning what must be observed in the restoration of churches, whether in their structures or in their dedication.  
5. Concerning the feast of Easter, the order of prayers, and the solemn celebrations of Masses.  
6. That baptism ought to be administered in the name of the Trinity.  
7. That the priestly see of the blessed apostle Peter—that is, the see of the Roman Church—is the mother of ecclesiastical dignity and the teacher of ecclesiastical reason.

## Chapter I. Vigilius to his dearest brother Euterus

We gladly receive the letters of your affection addressed to us, full of the solicitude of Catholic inquiry, blessing the mercy of our God, because he deigns to provide shepherds for his sheep in the remotest parts of the world—shepherds through whom they may abound in salutary pastures and be preserved from the rapacity of the ancient enemy, so that they may not fall into the snares of his deception.

Hence it is certain that the grace of the promised blessedness follows you, since the perfection of heavenly teachings is sought from you with such desirable eagerness. For it is written: “Blessed are those who search out his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (Ps. CXVIII, 2).
