Therefore, dearest brother, considering the purpose of your consultation with our whole mind, we maintain that this also proceeds from you: you strive to hold the rule of the Catholic faith in the same footsteps by which you know it to have been founded upon apostolic faith.

Although the sound of those teachings has spread throughout the whole world and their words have reached the ends of the earth, proving the heart of your affection faithful to Christ, nevertheless, if any matter concerning these things has not yet shone with full clarity in the Church entrusted by God’s help to your governance, you return to the same fountain from which that health-giving stream flowed. We rightly embrace this with charity, because you have confidently wished our response to confirm those matters concerning which, as you said, observance among them remained uncertain.

Therefore, greeting your affection in the Lord, we believe that you should be instructed concerning each matter: what the authority of the apostolic see holds according to Catholic discipline, with certain chapters of the holy rules also appended. First, you rightly judge that those whom you have indicated to be stained by the vices of the Priscillianist heresy must be accused with holy and appropriate detestation by the Catholic religion—those who, under the pretext of simulated abstinence, appear to withdraw themselves from eating meat in such a way that they are shown to do this rather from an execrable disposition than from devotion.

Since in this matter they are shown to be like the utterly impious Manichaeans, they have rightly been prohibited from this superstition under the threat of anathema by the decrees of the venerable Fathers, since they believe that something is polluted by the contagion of flesh, whereas of all the things which God’s mercy has provided for human nourishment, nothing should appear unclean to Catholics.

Thus the apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, admonishes Titus, saying: “To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, but their mind and conscience are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him; they are detestable and unbelieving, and unfit for every good work” (Tit. I, 15).

Likewise, in another place, he preached to Timothy concerning the avoidance of such errors, saying: “In the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to spirits of error and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage and abstaining from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth, because every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (I Tim. IV, 1).

Following these decrees of the venerable Fathers, they specifically judged those to be condemned who, while abstaining from meat, also believed that those things which appeared to have been mixed with meat were to be avoided. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself gave this warning: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth—this is what defiles a person” (Matt. XV, 11).

Therefore, we do not reject abstinence that is pleasing to God, but neither do we admit into our fellowship those who execrate the Lord’s creation.

## Concerning the triple immersion of those being reborn

### II

Concerning the solemn completion of baptism, your affection will clearly recognize below what the apostolic authority has either decreed or preserved in the same way. We judge the following to be an innovation of recent error: although all Catholics customarily say at the end of the psalms, “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” certain people, as you report, remove the connecting syllable and attempt to diminish the complete term “Trinity”: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

Although reason itself clearly teaches us that, with one syllable removed, they somehow indicate that the person of the Son and that of the Holy Spirit are one, it is nevertheless sufficient to refute the error of such people that the Lord Jesus Christ, indicating that baptism was to be celebrated through invocation of the Trinity, said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

Since he did not say, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” but commanded that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit be named with equal distinctions, it is clear that those who wish to detract anything from this confession deviate altogether from God’s teaching. If they persist in their error, they cannot be our companions.

### III

Concerning those also who, after receiving the saving grace of baptism, were baptized again among the Arians and plunged into the death of a deep abyss, we have sent you below the chapters of our predecessors’ decrees, arranged in various ways according to the several orders and ages, and brought forth from our archive.

Nevertheless, in these matters it is especially appropriate to observe this: since, on account of the many sins among the nations, iniquity itself has arisen, the matter should be left to the judgment of your fraternity and of the other bishops throughout their dioceses, so that, if the condition and devotion of the penitent are approved, it may also be brought near to the remedy of indulgence.

Their reconciliation, however, is not to be effected through that laying on of hands which operates through invocation of the Holy Spirit, but through that by which the fruit of penance is acquired and restoration to holy communion is accomplished.

### IV

Concerning the restoration of any church building if it has been destroyed, and whether the solemnity of consecration ought to be repeated in that place.

Where there have been no sanctuaries, we judge that it accomplishes nothing, and therefore blessed water should not be sprinkled there. For we know that the consecration of any church in which an altar of the Holy Spirit is not placed consists only in the celebration of Masses. Therefore, if any basilica of the saints has even been renewed from its foundations, there is no doubt that, once the solemn celebration of Masses has taken place in it, the sanctification of the entire consecration will be completed.

But if the sanctuaries that it possessed have been removed, it will again receive the honor of sanctification through their reinstallation and the solemn celebration of Masses.

## Concerning the solemnity of Easter and the order of prayers

[Col. 1077B] **V.** Know that, if God wills, we shall celebrate the coming Easter on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. We also state that at no time and on no feast do we have a divided order of prayers in the celebration of Masses, but always consecrate the offerings made to God according to the same form.

Whenever the feast of Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, Epiphany, or any feast of God’s saints is to be celebrated, we add individual chapters suited to those days, by which we make commemoration either of the holy solemnity or of those whose anniversaries we celebrate; the remaining parts we continue in the customary order.

Therefore, we have also sent below the text of the canonical prayer, which, by God’s favor, we received from apostolic tradition. And so that your affection may know at which places you should connect matters suited to the feasts, we have likewise appended the prayers for Easter day.

Having answered the inquiries of your fraternity, we earnestly beseech our Lord, as far as we can, to multiply the gifts of his grace among all the Churches of the Catholic religion and among all whom he makes faithful to himself, and to deign to preserve all his peoples immune from every ambush of the spiritual and carnal enemy.

We also indicate that, as we hope, we have sent to your holy affection relics of the blessed apostles and martyrs, presuming that henceforth your faith will be more fully aided by their merits.

### VI

If any bishop or presbyter, according to the Lord’s command, does not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but in one person of the Trinity, or in two, or in three fathers, or in three sons, or in three paracletes, let him be expelled from the Church of God.

### VII.

No one who has even a slight understanding, or who possesses full wisdom, is in doubt that the Roman Church is the foundation and model of the churches; nor is any right-believing person unaware that all the churches have derived their origin from her. For although the election of all the apostles was equal, blessed Peter was nevertheless granted precedence over the others, [Col. 1078B] and hence he is also called Cephas, because he is the head and first of all the apostles. What went before in the head must necessarily be followed in the members.

Therefore the holy Roman Church, consecrated by the Lord’s own voice on account of Peter’s merit and strengthened by the authority of the holy Fathers, holds primacy over all the churches. To it the most important episcopal affairs, judgments, and complaints, as well as the greater questions of the churches, must always be referred, as to the head. For one who knows that he has been placed over others ought not to resent having someone placed over him.

Indeed, that Church which is first has granted the other churches their respective functions in such a way that they are called to share in its solicitude, not in the fullness of its power. Hence it is clear that the judgments of all bishops appealing to the apostolic see, and all the affairs of the greater cases, have been reserved to that same holy see, especially since in all such matters its counsel must always be awaited. If anyone attempts to oppose its course, let him know that he will have to answer for the causes of the priests before that same holy see, not without danger to his own honor.

Given on the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Wisilianus and John IV.

## THE DECREES OF POPE PELAGIUS BEGIN.

[Col. 1077]

### Letter of Pope Pelagius to Vigilius

[Col. 1077D]

Pelagius, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to his fellow bishop Vigilius.

I rejoice in the devotion of your faith, because you diligently and reverently perform religious study and divine service, and especially because you rival the enemies of the faith by seeking the examples of the apostolic see. I have learned, both from the bearer of your letters and from your letters themselves, that there are certain people among you who chatter, saying: “How can the Father and the Son be one God, since there is no other God besides the Father, who is called unbegotten and invisible?”

If these people knew the gift of God and understood the rules of the true faith, they would never mutter such things. But since they do not possess pure hearts capable of seeing the hidden things of God and understanding the divine mysteries, their hearts must first be cleansed through repentance, so that afterward they may be able to understand and receive the light of truth.

Nevertheless, for their illumination and that of many others, their error must be corrected and answered by apostolic authority as follows: Why do you refuse to confess the Father and the Son as one? We also demonstrate from the prophets and apostles that they were preached as one and true God; from those same witnesses we believe that the Holy Spirit is not separate from them. The prophet Isaiah says:

> “I am God, and there is no other besides me. By myself I swear: truth has gone forth from my mouth, and my word shall not be turned back, because every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall swear by the Lord, saying: ‘Justice and glory shall come to him’” (Isa. XLV, 21–25).

And so that you may recognize that in this testimony the Father and the Son are spoken of together, hear Paul saying:

> “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. And every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the almighty Father” (Phil. II, 11).

But if this Son is less than his Father, then the Father’s glory has been diminished in the Son. And where is that which Scripture says in Solomon:

> “Just as you have been magnified in our sight, so you shall be magnified in their sight, so that they may know you as we also have known you, because there is no God besides you, Lord” (Ecclus. XXXVI, 4).

Pay close attention and recognize that it is the Son who will be magnified in judgment when he comes to judge the living and the dead.

Isaiah likewise says:

> “Hear me, house of Jacob and remnant of the house of Israel, you who come forth from my womb and are instructed from childhood even to old age. From the beginning I am, and until you grow old I am. I made you, and I sustain you. I will forgive, and I will receive you,” says the Lord.

And again:

> “I am the Lord God, and there is no other God besides me, announcing the last things before they occur; and as soon as they were announced, they were accomplished.”

Again elsewhere:

> “Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I have made. I am the Lord God, and there is no other besides me.”

Again elsewhere:

> “I am the Lord your God, the first, and I am the last, and in the things that are to come at the end, I am he.”

Again elsewhere:

> “I am God, who created you, who approached you and strengthened you with my right hand.”

And, assigning the unity of the Father and the Son, he says:

> “You are my witnesses,” says the Lord God, “and my servant whom I have chosen, so that you may know and believe that I am he. Before me there was no other God, and after me there shall not be.”

Heretic, choose one of these two alternatives: either confess that the Father and the Son are one God; or, if you insist that the Father alone is God, then the Lord God Jesus Christ, the Son of God, will not be God for you, because it is written: “Before me there was no other God, and after me there shall not be.”

If this is so according to you, why does the Apostle proclaim such things and imply that the same Son is God, blessed above all?

> “Their are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. IX, 5).

Isaiah also says:

> “The Lord God of Israel, who will deliver him from Egypt. I am the first, and I am after these things, and besides me there is no God. I am he who stands, calls, and prepares for me the one from whom I made man forever.”

Again there:

> “This is God, and we did not know it; God, and there is no other god besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it; God of Israel, the one Savior.”

The Father and the Son are not gods, because there is God in whom God is said to exist; the prophet repeatedly declares that there is no other God besides another God.

And Jeremiah says:

> “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted alongside him. He discovered every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III, 36).

And in Solomon:

> “Have mercy on us, God of all, and show us the light of your mercy, and send your fear upon the nations that have not sought you, so that they may know that there is no other God but you” (Ecclus. XXXVI, 1).

Again there:

> “Lord God of Israel, there is none like you in heaven above or on earth below” (Deut. IV, 39).

And in Psalm XVII:

> “For who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?”

And in Genesis:

> “And the Lord rained fire and brimstone from the Lord upon Sodom and Gomorrah, and he overthrew those cities” (Gen. XIX, 24).

If the Father alone is God, who rained fire and brimstone from the Lord, or overthrew the cities mentioned above? I ask you, answer.

And Deuteronomy says:

> “The Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign god with them.”

And the Apostle Paul says:

> “One God who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith” (Rom. III, 30).

And to the Corinthians:

> “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19).

And again:

> “There is no God except one.”

And to the Galatians:

> “Now a mediator is not of one; but God is one” (Gal. III, 30).

Demonstrating the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he confirms it in his letter to the Ephesians:

> “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God” [Col. 1080C] (Eph. IV, 3).

For if the aforementioned heretics are willing to receive the unity of faith with a simple heart, from this testimony they can already learn the unity of the Father and the Son in one Spirit.

Thus, although they say that they have found the Father expressly designated in the divine Scriptures as unbegotten, they can neither read nor prove this fully. Yet because Christian faith demands it, he is believed without any doubt to be unbegotten; nevertheless, according to the sequence of the Scriptures, he is shown to have been seen in the Son begotten from him.

The Apostle Paul, foreseeing from far off the sending of the Son of God in the Holy Spirit, testified to this in writing to the Roman Church:

> “For what was impossible for the law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled” (Rom. VIII, 3).

Do you see that the Son was not sent by the Father according to his divinity, but according to the flesh, which in his mercy and goodness he did not disdain to assume for us?

That the Son himself emptied himself of the power of his majesty and sent himself, the Apostle testifies, saying:

> “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. II, 7).

And Isaiah says:

> “Not an ambassador, nor an angel, but the Lord himself will come and save them.”

Again there:

> “I appeared openly to those who did not seek me.”

And in Jeremiah:

> “I abandoned my house, I dismissed my inheritance, and I came and became an object of disgrace to them.”

And in Micah:

> “Behold, the Lord will come, and the mountains will be shaken beneath him.”

And in Zechariah:

> “Rejoice and exult, daughter of Zion, for behold, I am coming and I will dwell in your midst,” says the Lord.

And the Apostle says to Timothy:

> “This saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (I Tim. I, 15).

And Malachi:

> “Behold, suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. III, 1).

And in the Gospel:

> “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

Again there:

> “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to destroy us?” (Matt. VIII, 29.)

Again there:

> “The Son of Man came to seek and save what had been lost” (Luke XIX, 10).

Again there:

> “I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.”

Again there:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13).

In these many and such great testimonies, in which the Son of God testified that he came by his own initiative, will you be able to say that he came from another and not from himself? It is clear that he who graciously assumed our flesh came voluntarily and was not sent by another.

For he who, while remaining in the Father, exists everywhere by his own power, had no place to which he could be sent by the Father. We know that no part of heaven or earth is excluded from the Father’s presence, so that, according to their view, the Son could be sent by the Father.

[Col. 1082A] Meanwhile, let your affection do everything possible so that all the sons of the Church may know what we preach against this impious doctrine according to evangelical and apostolic teaching. Although we have written out fully what has always been and is the opinion of Catholics, we now also add no small exhortation to strengthen the minds of all.

I remember that I preside in the name of that Church whose confession was glorified by the Lord Jesus Christ, and whose faith indeed destroys all heresies, but especially attacks the impiety of the present error. I understand that I may do nothing else than devote all my efforts to the cause in which the salvation of the universal Church is endangered.

And lest our writings have been unable to reach you because of some negligence, we believe that copies of them should now be sent, so that the preaching of the faith which we defend may in no way be withheld from your knowledge.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of May, in the consulship of John and Narses IV.

## THE DECREES OF POPE JOHN BEGIN.

[Col. 1081]

[Col. 1081C]

John, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Germany and Gaul.

I had wished, dearest brothers, out of love for our collegial fellowship, that all the priests of the Lord should remain united in one devotion, that no one should, in opposition to the grace that has been forbidden, follow the favor of priests or depart from the right path. Although we believe that your affection is prepared for every good work, nevertheless, so that it may become more effective, we have thought it appropriate, following the letters of the apostolic see and imitating the footsteps of our predecessors, to admonish you to carry out manfully the divine commands and the institutions of the apostolic see, to avoid what is forbidden and not touch it, and never to abandon the teaching of the Fathers while rejoicing in priestly honor.

It has been reported to the apostolic see that a practice has arisen and is again reviving which was prohibited and must be uprooted entirely. This practice was condemned by both Saint Damasus and Saint Leo, apostolic men, and by bishops universally through synodal authority; it is blameworthy and thoroughly unusual. Certain chorepiscopi—who have been prohibited by the holy apostolic Fathers and men mentioned above, by their predecessors, and by those same authorities and by us, as their decrees have thus far testified—are exceeding the limits of their office by conferring the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands and by performing unlawfully other acts that belong solely to pontiffs.

This is especially improper since, among the seventy disciples whose role they represent in the Church, none is read to have conferred the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. That it belongs specifically to the apostles and their successors to confer the Holy Spirit is taught by the book of the Acts of the Apostles.

In the Council of Caesarea the following is written concerning chorepiscopi:

> “The chorepiscopi also seem to correspond to the example and pattern of the seventy, so that, as fellow ministers, they may be honored on account of the zeal they show toward the poor. If you think yourselves better and holier than the holy apostles, do what they did not do and exalt yourselves above them. But if you belong to the same order and wish to make yourselves equal to them, do not do what they did not do. Rather, imitate, as well as you can, their examples and footsteps. Since the Lord commanded and charged them that they and their successors alone should confer the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, and since they knew that it would be unlawful for any of the seventy ever to do so—the chorepiscopi, as stated above, bore the type of the seventy in the Church before they were prohibited—they allowed no such conferral of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, giving their successors an example never to presume such things.”

Thus it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had arrived, they prayed for them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (Acts VIII, 14–17).

Therefore, as has already been said, they did not send anyone from the seventy, although the apostles were few for the completion of this work. Rather, they sent the apostles Peter and John to confer the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. Bishops represent their office in the Church, not chorepiscopi, who represented the form of the seventy disciples before their prohibition.

Do not do what they did not do, lest you appear unlike them and unworthy of their succession and ministry. For, as the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke XI, 23).

Thus Peter, prince of the apostles, took Linus and Cletus as assistants. Nevertheless, he did not grant them the power of the episcopate, nor did he give them the authority of binding and loosing. He granted this to his successor, Saint Clement, who deserved to hold the apostolic see and episcopal authority after him, when blessed Peter handed these over to him.

Linus and Cletus served in external matters, while Peter, prince of the apostles, devoted himself to the word and prayer, and to the duties appropriately connected with conferring the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. Hence it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “It is not right for us to abandon the word of God and serve tables” (Acts VI, 2).

For this reason seventy disciples were chosen to carry out external tasks, while the apostles themselves devoted themselves to the word and prayer. Accordingly, it is written in the Gospel according to Luke:

> “After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two before him into every city and place where he himself was about to come. And he said to them: ‘The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest. Behold, I am sending you like lambs among wolves. Carry neither purse, nor bag, nor sandals, and greet no one along the way. Into whatever house you enter, first say: “Peace to this house.” And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you. Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have, for the laborer is worthy of his wage. Do not move from house to house. Into whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat what is set before you, cure the sick who are there, and say to them: “The kingdom of God has drawn near to you.” But into whatever city you enter and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say: “Even the dust that clings to us from your city, we wipe off against you.” Yet know this: “The kingdom of God has drawn near.” I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Sodom on that day than for that city’” (Luke X, 1–12).

And in Matthew the evangelist it is written:

> “Behold, I am sending you like sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and simple as doves. But beware of people, for they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you. You will be led before governors and kings on my account, as a testimony to them and to the nations. When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you should speak, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. Brother will hand brother over to death, and father his son; children will rise against parents and put them to death. You will be hated by all on account of my name. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 16–27).

Linus and Cletus are never read to have exercised any part of the episcopal ministry with authority. They did only as much as blessed Peter commanded them.

For it is also written in the Nicene canon:

> “A bishop should, as far as possible, be ordained by all the bishops in the province. But if this is difficult, either because of pressing necessity or because of the length of the journey, at least three bishops must assemble for this purpose, while those who are absent likewise decree and consent in writing; then the ordination shall take place. The confirmation of what is done in each province shall be entrusted to the metropolitan bishop.”

All the greatest councils likewise affirm that one is not a bishop who has been made bishop by fewer bishops than the Fathers require, even with the authority of the metropolitan. Therefore, since those whom you call chorepiscopi, as we have heard, are made bishops by one bishop, it is evident that they are not bishops and ought not to exercise anything belonging to episcopal privilege. For if they do not possess the name, how can they possess the office?

If, therefore, they are not bishops, and they disdain being presbyters whose place they occupy because they were formerly made according to the example and pattern of the seventy, what will they be? Clearly, something devoid of reason, or something scarcely advanced at all.

If anyone wishes to know more about them, and about what ought not to be done, let him read the decrees of the aforementioned apostolic men; there he will find it.

We have thought it worthwhile to insert some of those decrees here. If we desire to be disciples of the Lord, let us imitate his footsteps, so that it may be said of us:

> “I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and I call them by name, and my sheep know me” (Luke X, 14), etc.

And again, in obedience to the command of the Lord’s voice, by which the most blessed apostle Peter was instructed through the mystical sanction of a threefold repetition to feed Christ’s sheep diligently and with the greatest care, we exhort you, for love and reverence toward that holy see over which we preside through the abundance of divine grace, to avoid as far as possible the danger of so great a superstition, which, as has often been said, is supported by no authority.

Otherwise the love of our blessed teacher Peter, the supreme apostle, by which he testified that he was a lover of God, would be found vain in us. For everyone who feeds negligently the Lord’s flock entrusted to him, although it has been commended to him so many times, is convicted of not loving the supreme Shepherd and of not wishing to become the disciple of one whose examples he neglects to imitate.

Indeed, greater grace is acquired if the shepherd’s solicitude offers God gain from the sheep entrusted to him. We also remember blessed Jacob, who had served for a long time for his wives, saying:

> “For twenty years I was with you; your sheep and goats were not barren; I did not eat the rams of your flock. I did not show you anything seized by a wild beast; I myself made good every loss, and whatever was stolen, you demanded from me. By day and by night I was consumed by heat and frost, and sleep fled from my eyes” (Gen. XXXI, 38–40).

If, then, the one who feeds Laban’s sheep labors and keeps watch, with how much labor and how many vigils must the one who feeds God’s sheep persevere?

But in all these matters may he himself instruct us, who gave his life for his sheep, and may he help us so that he may grant us to bring back to eternal joys abundant fruit and overflowing measure from those entrusted to us. May such love for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, inflame us that, in his sheepfold—to which all creatures have been entrusted—you may hasten with the greatest longing, through your holy efforts, to restore all who have gone astray and presumed upon unlawful and prohibited things, so that their souls, redeemed by Christ’s precious blood, may not perish through their deception.

It remains also that these men did not enter through the door at all, because they had no door through which they could enter. For, as has been said, if they are not bishops but aspire to be more than presbyters, through what door will they enter? Yet these orders are read to exist in the Church, and no further door to the pastoral office is open through which a pastor may enter.

Hear, brothers, not me but Truth itself speaking:

> “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John X, 1), etc.

And since the distinguished preacher also says:

> “No one can lay any other foundation besides that which has been laid” (I Cor. III, 11),

and since only the two aforementioned foundations are found to have been laid in the Church, whatever else is found to have been placed upon them will in no way be able to stand. Therefore it is necessary that it be uprooted with all its foundations, actions, and roots, so that it may no longer sprout or germinate.

Therefore, brothers, do not let the repeated statement produce weariness in you. It is a supreme necessity that what is so often unlawfully usurped should be prohibited repeatedly; truth, when frequently attacked, shines more brightly into the light; and what is repeatedly admonished is less often usurped.

Much has already been said about these matters by our predecessors, by whom such men were condemned and prohibited, just as they are now by us and were formerly by them. For that reason, by repeating our admonition, we warn all to avoid such persons and to abstain from them, if they do not wish, together with them as rebels, to become alien to the priestly ministry.

We shall be able to prove this only if you strive to uproot such men and do not favor them. Then complaints about this matter will cease, because whatever is repeatedly forbidden and nevertheless repeatedly usurped is done out of a desire for insult.

We command you, and all bishops and all priests generally, to observe all these decretal writings and all the constitutions of our predecessors promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons. If anyone violates them, let him know that forgiveness will henceforth be denied him. For truth would prevail if falsehood were displeasing.

And rightly the matter concerns us, who ought to hold the supreme helm of the Church, if we favor error by our silence.

[Col. 1086C] Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Justinian VI and Narses IV.

## THE DECREES OF POPE BENEDICT BEGIN.

[Col. 1085]

[Col. 1085C]

To the most reverend brother David, bishop: Benedict sends greetings in the Lord.

I had considered replying to your letters more fully, but while I was reflecting on this, such grief touched me that I found myself more inclined to weep than to say anything. Nevertheless, lest the matter remain entirely unanswered, I have taken care to write you a brief reply, suitably inviting you to better times.

Your letters testify that there are certain people within the province of Baetica who say that no one can truly prove that the Trinity becomes unity, since no one can properly demonstrate either three as one or one in three. For these reasons, dearest son, we have sent you the consultations of the apostolic see, so that you may either convert them to the right faith or drive them from the Church before this pestilence spreads more widely.

Brother, recognize the unity of the Trinity through these testimonies of Scripture, and cease to follow the depravity of the Arians, so that you may thereby obtain forgiveness of sins. The prophet Isaiah says:

> “I saw the Lord Sabaoth seated upon a lofty throne, and Seraphim stood around him. Six wings belonged to one, and six wings to the other; with two they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew. And they cried to one another, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Sabaoth’” (Isa. VI, 1–2).

If there is no Trinity, why did they say “holy” three times? And if there is no unity, why, under the threefold repetition, did they indicate one God and Lord?

If there is no Trinity, why does Genesis say:

> “God said, God made, and God blessed” (Gen. I, 24, 27)?

But if there is no unity, why did it say “God” three times, and not commend three gods in the plural?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said three times in Exodus:

> “Lord, Lord, Lord, compassionate and merciful” (Exod. XXXIV, 6)?

If there is no unity, why, after saying “Lord” three times, does it then say *miserator* (“compassionate”) in the singular, rather than *miseratores* (“compassionate ones”), if it intended to indicate several?

If there is no Trinity, why did Abraham, sitting by the oak of Mambre and meeting three, say “Lord” to one (Gen. XVII, 3), rather than return the courtesy of greeting to the three whom he had seen?

If there is no unity, why, when he had said three times to Moses, “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” did he, indicating unity, say, “This is my name” (Exod. III, 15)? Are these not the things that designated our names?

If there is no Trinity, why did David say three times:

> “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” (Ps. LXVIII, 8)?

If there is no unity, why, after naming “God” three times, did he add *benedicat* (“may he bless”), and not *benedicant* (“may they bless”)?

If there is no Trinity, why did Isaiah again say:

> “Lord, God Sabaoth, God of Israel, who sit upon the cherubim?” (Isa. XXXVII, 16.)

If there is no unity, why did he say *sedes* (“you sit”), and not *sedetis* (“you sit,” plural)?

If there is no Trinity, why does the Book of Kings say:

> “Lord God almighty, God of Israel, your words are faithful?” (II Kings XXII, 3.)

If there is no unity, why is *tui* (“your,” singular) said, and not rather *vestri* (“your,” plural)?

If there is no Trinity, why is it sung in Psalm LVIII:

> “Lord of hosts, God of Israel, attend to visit all the nations?”

If there is no unity, why did it use *intende* (“attend,” singular), and not *intendite* (“attend,” plural), if it intended to proclaim plurality?

If there is no Trinity, why did the Apocalypse say three times:

> “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who is and who was?” (Apoc. IV, 8.)

If there is no unity, why did it designate not *qui sunt* (“those who are”) in the plural, but *qui erat* (“who was”)?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in Deuteronomy:

> “The Lord your God is a merciful God, and he will hear your voice” (Deut. IV, 31)?

If there is no unity, why did it use *audiet* (“he will hear”), and not *audient* (“they will hear”)?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in the Book of Joshua:

> “The Lord God of gods is” (Deut. X, 17)?

If there is no unity, why did it say *est* (“is”), and not introduce *sunt* (“they are”) according to the plural manner of speech?

If there is no Trinity, why did Elijah, exhorting, say:

> “Lord, Lord, Lord, God of Israel, show that you are my God” (III Kings XVIII, 36)?

If there is no unity, why did he use *ostende* (“show,” singular), and not *ostendite* (“show,” plural)?

If there is no Trinity, why did Mordecai, praying, say:

> “Lord, almighty God, all things are in your power” (Esth. XIV, 12)?

If there is no unity, why did he use *tua* (“your,” singular), and not indicate *vestra* (“your,” plural)?

If there is no Trinity, why did Judith also say in prayer:

> “Lord, Lord, God of all powers, look upon my prayer?” (Judith IX, 3.)

If there is no unity, why did she use *respice* (“look,” singular), and not indicate *respicite* (“look,” plural)?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in Jeremiah:

> “The Lord your God is the true God?” (Jer. X, 10.)

If there is no unity, why is it written in the Apocalypse:

> “The Lord God and the Spirit of the prophets sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place?” (Apoc. XXII, 6.)

If there is no unity, why, after naming the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, did it say *misit* (“he sent”), and not *miserunt* (“they sent”), introducing the name under the pretext of three persons?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in Deuteronomy:

> “The Lord your God—this is God?” (Deut. I, 30.)

If there is no unity, why did it say *hic est* (“this is”), and not indicate *hi sunt* (“these are”) in the plural?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in the same book:

> “The Lord your God is a great and powerful God?” (Deut. X, 17.)

If there is no unity, why are “great and powerful” not expressed in the plural?

If there is no Trinity, why is Tobias taught to have said the following when he sent his son with the angel Raphael to the city of Rages, blessing them:

> “May the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob himself fulfill his blessing in you?” (Tob. VII, 15.)

If there is no unity, why did he say *ipse impleat* (“may he himself fulfill”), and not indicate *ipsi impleant* (“may they fulfill”)?

Finally, if there is no Trinity, why did the Lord command his disciples to baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit? (Matt. XXVIII, 19.)

If there is no unity, why did he say *in nomine* (“in the name”), and not instruct them to do so *in nominibus* (“in the names”)?

If there is no Trinity, why does the Apostle Paul say:

> “From him, and through him, and in him are all things?” (Rom. XI, 36.)

If there is no unity, why did he use *ex ipso* (“from him”), and not construct the phrase *ex ipsis* (“from them”)?

For if you wish with complete certainty to recognize the unity of the Trinity from the frequently mentioned teacher of the nations, the apostle, you can learn everything and follow the catholic faith while rejecting the depravity of the Arians. He says:

> “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit” (III Cor. XIII, 13).

This is that of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. How are they one in the Trinity? Because they share one nature and cannot be separated from one another.

For the rest, dearest brother, you will be able to gather almost everything contained in your letter from the statements set out below. It is necessary, dearest brother, that the divine be present where human assistance ceases. And, to speak in accordance with [Col. 1088C] the Apostle, even if we repeat the words that he himself writes to Timothy, saying:

> “The Church of the living God is the pillar and foundation of the truth. And manifestly great is the sacrament of piety: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:15–16).

> “Now the Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, and having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage, requiring abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if [Col. 1088D] it is received with thanksgiving, for it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer. By setting these things before the brethren, you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and of the good doctrine that you have attained. But avoid foolish and empty fables, and train yourself in piety. For bodily training is useful for a little, but piety is useful for everything, possessing the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance. For to this end we labor and are reviled, because we hope in the living God, who is the Savior of all human beings, especially of the faithful. Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, in chastity. Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching. Do not neglect the grace that was given you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbyter. Meditate on these things; be devoted to them, so that your progress may be manifest to all. Attend to yourself and to your teaching; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (1 Tim. 4:1–16).

For [the source is corrupt here:] he is exceedingly afflicted by report rather than by calamity; and, harassed by other anxieties, I have been quite unable to write a long letter. At a suitable time, send again if it should be necessary, and receive what you have desired. May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Amen.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of Justinian and Libio for the fourth time.

## HERE BEGIN THE DECREES OF POPE PELAGIUS II

[Col. 1089]

[Col. 1089A] To his dearest brothers, all the bishops who, by the illicit summons of John, bishop of Constantinople, assembled at Constantinople for a synod, Pelagius.

[Col. 1089B] Manifestly, as we desired, by the grace of God the light of evangelical truth has driven the night of the most pernicious error away from the universal Church; we rejoice in the Lord beyond expression. Yet we are saddened by no slight grief, because things that were formerly trampled underfoot and utterly condemned, and that ought never to have been done, are sprouting and flourishing again from renewed roots. And since many things are occurring that can generate repentance, it is necessary to denounce what is known to have been done against order and every authority.

Therefore, brothers, let the vain hearts of those who err, abandoning altogether the audacity that was taken up against the apostolic see and against the very voice of the Lord and Savior—by which it was said, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18)—of disputing against the Lord’s commands, come to rest. Let it not be permitted to defend what it is not permitted to do.

[Col. 1089C] It has therefore been reported to the apostolic see that John, bishop of Constantinople, has been subscribing himself “universal,” and that, relying on this presumption of his, he summoned you to a general synod, although the authority to summon general synods has been entrusted, by the singular privilege of blessed Peter, to the apostolic see, and no synod is ever read to have been valid that was not supported by apostolic authority.

Accordingly, whatever you established in that gathering of yours—which could not be a synod, since it was presumed in such a manner—I command, by the authority of holy Peter, chief of the apostles, and by the voice of the Lord and Savior, by which the Savior himself gave blessed Peter the power of binding and loosing, a power that has unquestionably passed to his successors, to be vain and annulled, so that henceforth it may neither appear nor be debated.

For the Savior himself said to blessed Peter, as the Truth himself speaks through his own person:

> “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (ibid., 19).

[Col. 1089D] We are instructed anew by many apostolic, canonical, and ecclesiastical rules that councils ought not to be held without the judgment of the Roman pontiffs. Therefore, as has now rightly been said, it is not a council that is annulled, but your gathering or [Col. 1090A] little council; and whatever was done in it is held to be invalid and void.

You also, henceforth, take care never to presume such things at anyone’s urging, if you do not wish to be deprived of communion with the apostolic see. For the present, however, [Col. 1090B] punishment is suspended so that correction may have an opportunity to take place.

271 John’s predecessors, and John himself, sent letters and booklets, subscribed with their own hands, not once but very frequently, to our holy predecessors. In them they solemnly declared before the Lord that they had never acted insolently against the apostolic see, nor usurped anything belonging to its privileges or those of other bishops. These documents remain intact to this day in the archive of the holy Roman Church, authenticated by their seals and handwritten subscriptions.

In those letters and booklets they bound themselves and their successors with the bond of anathema if they should ever presume anything against them, or in any way undertake anything adverse against the apostolic see or the see of any other bishop. Therefore it is not necessary to excommunicate or [Col. 1090C] anathematize them, since they themselves bound their professions and writings, authenticated by their own hands, with the bond of anathema.

Nevertheless, John himself should know that, unless he quickly corrects his error, he will be excommunicated by us and deprived of communion with the apostolic see and with all holy bishops. Do not heed the title of “universal” that he has illicitly usurped, nor ever come to a synod at his summons without the authority of the apostolic see, if you wish to enjoy communion with the apostolic see and with the other bishops.

Let no patriarch ever use this profane title, for if one patriarch is called universal, the name of patriarch is taken away from the others. But may this be far from the mind of any faithful person: that anyone should wish or seize this for himself in such a way that he appears, even in the smallest degree, to diminish the honor of his brothers.

Therefore, let your Charity never call anyone “universal” in your letters, lest you take away what is due to one person while offering another an honor that is not due.

[Col. 1090D] “For the adversary, the devil,” raging against the humble, “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). Yet now, as we see, he no longer prowls around the sheepfolds; rather, he fixes his tooth so forcefully in certain necessary members of the Church that no one can doubt that, unless the vigilant company of all shepherds comes together with the Lord’s unanimous support, the entire flock—which God forbid—will soon be torn apart.

[Col. 1091A] You understand, dearest brothers, what follows in the vicinity of this matter, when such perverse beginnings break out even among priests. For nearby is he of whom it is written: “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25). I am compelled to say this with profound grief: our brother and fellow bishop John, scorning the Lord’s commands, the apostolic precepts, and the rules of the Fathers, attempts in his arrogance to run through all things in the name of that one title.

May almighty God reveal to your Blessedness with what grievous groaning of reflection I am tormented: that the man who was once very well known to me, who was loved by everyone, who appeared to be occupied with prayers and fasts, has taken from the ashes with which he reeked, and from the humility that he displayed, an occasion for boasting. Thus he tries to attribute everything to himself, and, by the election of pompous language, seeks to subject to himself the members of Christ—all the things that belong to one head alone, namely Christ.

[Col. 1091B] It is not surprising that the tempter, who knows “pride to be the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15), first used it above all in the first human being, and now places it in certain people at the end of their virtues. He who seemed for a time to have escaped his most savage hands through the good pursuits of life now sets a snare for them in the very substance of their good work, and, so to speak, at the very conclusion of their perfection.

Therefore we must pray earnestly and implore almighty God with continual prayers to turn this error away from his mind, to remove from the unity and humility of the Church this evil of pride and confusion, and, with God’s favor, to strive and take precautions with all our strength, lest living members in the body of Christ die from the poison of one man’s words.

[Col. 1091C] For if this is freely permitted to be said, the honor of all patriarchs is denied; perhaps the one who is called “universal” will perish in error, and no bishop will any longer be found to have remained in the condition of truth.

It is therefore necessary that you steadfastly and without prejudice preserve the Churches as you received them, and not permit this diabolical temptation of usurpation to claim anything for itself among you. Stand firm; stand secure. Do not presume ever either to give or to receive false writings bearing the title “universal.”

Prohibit all the bishops subject to your care from the pollution of this flattery, so that the whole Church may recognize you as patriarchs, not only in good works but also in the authority of truth.

[Col. 1091D] If some adversity should perhaps follow, by remaining unanimous even unto death we must show that, when the common body suffers loss, we do not love anything special for ourselves. Let us say with Paul: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21).

Let us hear what the first of all the apostles says: “If you suffer because of righteousness, you will be blessed” (1 Pet. 3:14). Believe me: the honor that we have accepted in order to proclaim the truth, if necessity demands it, we will relinquish for that same truth more securely than we hold it.

Pray, brothers, that ecclesiastical honor may not be emptied out in our days, and that the Roman see—which, by the Lord’s institution, is the head of all the Churches—may never anywhere be deprived of or stripped of its privileges.

[Col. 1092A] “But we are confident about you, beloved, of better things and things closer to salvation” (Heb. 6:9), because, as the Apostle to the Gentiles teaches, “neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the right faith that is in him” (Rom. 8:38–39).

“Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward.” For patience is necessary for us in our struggles with adversaries, so that, preserving our faith undefiled to the end, we may receive the promise that he made to those who hasten to fight lawfully.

“For yet a very little while, and he who is to come will come, and he will not delay” (Heb. 10:37). “For behold, the judge stands before the door” (Jas. 5:9), promising cheerfully crowns to those who submit to sufferings for his sake. But if anyone withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him; rather, he will fall away from the promise because of denial.

[Col. 1092B] “But we are not children of withdrawal unto perdition, but of faith unto the acquisition of the soul” (Heb. 10:39). “Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day” (Eph. 6:13) against all the enemies of God’s holy Church and your own, “and put on the breastplate of righteousness, with your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Holy Spirit, which is the word of God, through every prayer and supplication” [Col. 1092C] (ibid., 14–18), “rooted and founded” (Eph. 3:17) in the consolation of the brethren for Christ Jesus our Lord.

But now also, brothers, we commend you all to the Lord and to the word of his grace, which is able to perfect you and to give you an inheritance with all the saints. “May the God of peace and consolation grant you to think the same thing toward one another” (Rom. 15:5), so that you may assist one another and not be divided, but, with one mind, one mouth, and one heart, honor him in concord and in the consolation of the brethren. He is able to strengthen you according to his Gospel and according to the revelation of the mystery through eternal—that is, perpetual—times, in which the gifts of future joys are to be bestowed upon you.

[Col. 1092D] You must also consider most carefully that those who envy their brothers and wish to condemn or destroy them are themselves destroyed by their own doctrines. For the Lord says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand” (Matt. 12:25); and every knowledge and law divided against itself will not stand.

Therefore it is necessary that you receive these salutary exhortations in concord, doing nothing through contention, but unanimously obeying the divine and apostolic constitutions in every effort of devotion. Do not allow the most provident decrees of the canons to be violated in any respect, so that the constitutions of the Nicene canons—which have been prudently and beneficially decreed by us or by our predecessors—may remain undefiled in the future.

And in the Apocalypse the Lord speaks through John, saying:

> “Do not be afraid. I am the first and the last, and the living one. I was [Col. 1093A] dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever, and I hold the keys of death and of hell” (Rev. 1:17–18).

And a little later:

> “To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. 2:7).

Likewise:

> “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (ibid., 10).

And again:

> “The one who conquers and keeps my works to the end, I will give him authority over the nations, and he will rule them with an iron rod, and they will be broken like a potter’s vessel” (ibid., 26–27).

Likewise:

> “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me. To the one who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat with my Father on his throne” (Rev. 3:20–21).

[Col. 1093B] Brothers, if you do not wish to be condemned with him—for not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are guilty (Rom. 1:32)—exhort and admonish him to withdraw from the aforesaid unlawful acts, to remember from where he has fallen, to repent, and to do his first works (Rev. 2:5).

If not, I am not speaking my own words, but those of the Lord and Savior himself, which he spoke through the aforesaid John in the book already mentioned. Repeating them, I say:

> “I will come and move your lampstand from its place, unless you repent” (ibid.).

For he more closely follows the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel (Num. 22:7), just as this man teaches you to cause the holy mother Church and the entire assembly of priests to stumble.

[Col. 1093C] Therefore, in the book mentioned above, it is also written as follows. I always prefer to strike and instruct you with the words of the Lord and Savior rather than with my own, although these too are filled with weight by apostolic authority:

> “I know your works, that your last works are worse than the first. But I have this against you: you put forward the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, but she does not wish to repent of her fornication. Behold, I cast her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great tribulation, unless they repent of their works. And I will strike her children with death. And all the Churches will know that I am the one who searches hearts and kidneys, and I will give to each of you according to your works” (Rev. 2:19–23).

These things, brothers, must be avoided with great care, and the commands of the Lord and of the holy apostolic see—which acts in the Lord and Savior’s place as his representative—must be faithfully embraced and carried out.

[Col. 1093D] For the rest, brothers, concerning the matter of the province about which you formerly wished to consult the apostolic see, it appears to us to have been sufficiently dealt with by our holy predecessors. But since you have again judged it worthwhile to inquire of our mediocrity about the same matter, know that a province is properly constituted when it has ten or eleven cities, one king, and an equal number of lesser authorities under him, as well as one bishop and ten or eleven other suffragan bishops as judges. All cases of bishops, the other priests, and the cities are to be referred to their judgment, so that they may be decided justly by the harmonious voice of all, unless those who are to be judged appeal to a higher authority.

[Col. 1094A] Accordingly, no province ought to be degraded or dishonored; rather, each should have within itself its own judges, priests, and individual bishops, according to their respective ranks. Whoever has a case should be judged by his own judges and not by strangers—that is, by the just judges of his own province and not by outsiders—unless, as has already been stated, an appeal has been made from the judgment.

If questions arise in any province, and the administration of affairs begins to differ among that province’s bishops, so that the dissenting bishops cannot reach agreement, the matter should then be referred to a higher see. If it is not easily and justly decided there, it should be judged canonically and justly wherever a synod has been regularly assembled.

[Col. 1094B] But greater and more difficult questions, as the holy synod has decreed and venerable custom requires, must always be referred to the apostolic see.

Moreover, following the statutes of the holy Fathers, by synodal authority we judge all who arm themselves against the Fathers to be infamous as invaders and slaughterers of the Fathers, since wounds that cannot be healed by poultices must be cut away or treated with the knife.

Therefore, brothers, let unjust rivalries cease; let ambushes cease; let false accusations cease. Let no weak person, for whom Christ died, be torn apart by such snares; let no sheep redeemed at Christ’s price be wounded by a brother’s wolfish bites.

It rightly concerns us if we begin to favor such things. Let such practices always be corrected. Those who try to engage in them, or who lie in wait for Fathers or brothers, must not be freely permitted to speak, nor allowed to put forward speech according to their own will.

[Col. 1094C] It is entirely clear that those who permit them to speak in such a manner connive at them, since truth would intervene if falsehood, slander, or hatred were displeasing.

Let falsehood therefore cease to attack truth; let suspicion, which is rightly rejected, cease to lie in wait; let hatred and hostility cease to pursue Fathers or brothers; let conspiracy, which everyone must reject, cease to harass teachers.

The authors and perpetrators of these vices, therefore, are not to be admitted as accusers of pontiffs but must be completely rejected. For the canonical decrees of the Fathers command that the accusation or testimony of those who pursue anyone out of hatred, or who are considered enemies or suspect, must in no way be received.

We, too, confirming their statutes, decree that the same provisions must be observed inviolably by everyone for all future times.

[Col. 1094D] Whatever our Fathers deemed worthy to be decreed concerning this matter must, when it begins to be shaken or weakened, necessarily be strengthened and renewed again by apostolic authority and given to the brethren.

Given on the Kalends of March, in the fifteenth indiction.

## Another letter of Pope Pelagius II to Archbishop Benignus, concerning the transfer of bishops

Pelagius, bishop, to his dearest brother Benignus, archbishop.

Having read the letters of your Brotherhood, we have recognized the vigor of your faith, which we had known for a long time. We rejoice with your affection that, in guarding Christ’s flock, you diligently devote yourself to pastoral care and show concern for those entrusted to you.

[Col. 1095A] Matters that bring benefit reach us to our joy; if anything occurs otherwise than it ought, it troubles us with no slight sorrow. Divine grace grants great cause for thanksgiving when it allows us, through letters, to confer the rule of salutary discipline among ourselves and leads us toward the desired pursuits of those who seek peace.

Your affection therefore requests the counsel of the apostolic see: whether it would be lawful for a bishop to pass or be transferred from one city to another, since certain canons, as it appears to you, prohibit this.

You have also indicated in your letters that you wish, for the sake of usefulness, to transfer one of the brethren, named and in conduct a servant of God, to the place and city of a deceased man, although some say that this cannot be done unless you have the consent of the apostolic see.

[Col. 1095B] Therefore know, dearest brother, that the cause of necessity and usefulness is one thing, and the cause of presumption and personal will another. He does not therefore change his see who does not change his mind—that is, one who does not move from city to city out of avarice, domination, personal will, or his own choice, but is transferred for the sake of necessity or usefulness.

For the usefulness of the many must be preferred to the usefulness or will of one person.

To transfer is one thing, and to be transferred another, just as to minister is one thing and to be ministered to another. Hence the Lord speaks in the Gospel, saying:

> “I did not come to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matt. 20:28).

[Col. 1095C] When the canons are read as saying that a bishop ought not to pass or be transferred from one city to another, this is not said of those who do so because they have been expelled by force, compelled by necessity, or directed by the authority of their superiors. It is said of those who, inflamed by the ardor of avarice, leap forward of their own accord and desire to serve ambition rather than the usefulness of the Church, and to persist in exercising domination.

Thus the canons also contain the following:

> “If anyone should prove so rash as perhaps to offer the excuse that he received letters from the people and therefore migrated, although it is manifest that a few people without sincere faith could have been corrupted by reward and payment, so that they might shout in the Church and appear to request him, we judge that such frauds must altogether be removed.”

By these words and many other examples it is clear—as was stated a little earlier—that this does not refer to those who, having been expelled or not received by their citizens or by anyone else, or compelled by necessity or by the authority of their superiors, pass from city to city. It refers to those who leap forward of their own accord and do this because of rashness or ambition.

[Col. 1095D] For it is one thing to come under compulsion or necessity. Such men do not change cities; they are changed, because they do this not voluntarily but under compulsion.

Who would ever dare to say that holy Peter, chief of the apostles, did not act rightly when he changed his see from Antioch to Rome? Or who would deny that he was holy because of this, or that he ever lost the dignity or merit of his apostleship either in heaven or on earth?

Or who denies that many other bishops are holy who have been transferred from cities to cities, or that they lost the merit of their episcopate? If I began to enumerate their names, the days would pass before I could write all of them down, and the letter would become longer than necessary.

[Col. 1096A] Or who could ever approve the claim that Alexander was not holy, although he was transferred to Jerusalem from another city? Or that Gregory of Nazianzus was not holy, although he was established at Nazianzus? Or that Proclus was not holy, although he was transferred from Cyzicus and enthroned at Constantinople?

Those who deny that this can be done for the sake of usefulness or necessity, whenever common usefulness or necessity persuades it, therefore do not properly understand ecclesiastical rules.

For we do not find that any of these men, or any others who changed cities through a better judgment because of some necessity or ecclesiastical or secular usefulness, were deprived of communion; nor should this ever in any way happen.

[Col. 1096B] The judgment contained in the Council of Antioch—that a bishop should by no means move from one parish to another—retains in its entirety, as do all the judgments concerning this matter, the force explained above. They do not harm transfers of bishops carried out or to be carried out in the manner already described; rather, the authority of the Savior, which surpasses all canonical books, gives them strength and approval.

Such questions, however, appear to arise more from envy than from charity or usefulness, since the Truth himself says:

> “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10:23),

and what follows.

No Catholic can anywhere contradict this judgment, which is known to have been spoken and confirmed not by someone else but by the Lord himself, from his own mouth. If anyone contradicts it, let him be expelled from the Church not only as an exile but also as one anathematized.

And elsewhere the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness” (Matt. 5:10).

If the Lord calls blessed those who suffer persecution for righteousness, who can condemn them? And if he himself commanded them to flee from city to city because of persecution, who dares or is able to disparage or condemn them for obeying the Lord’s words?

[Col. 1096C] Indeed, whoever contradicts or resists this condemns himself, because he is rebellious against the Lord’s mouth and disobedient.

Hence the Truth himself says:

> “Which of you will convict me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me? Whoever is from God hears the words of God. For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God” (John 8:46–47).

It is altogether necessary “to obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29). Are we therefore to be condemned because, obeying God, we pass from city to city at his command, for the sake of persecution—that is, of necessity or usefulness? Certainly not. Rather, we are to be honored and supported, since this cannot be charged even against the bishops themselves.

[Col. 1096D] “Whoever resists these things resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:2), and “is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8), because it is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back.

The Lord himself also withdrew from place to place—that is, he passed from one place to another—when the Jews were seeking him: “fleeing from those who sought and pursued him” (John 8:59). And he commanded that people pass from city to city, saying:

> “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matt. 10:23),

and other similar things.

[Col. 1097A] For if fleeing is evil, persecution is much worse. One person hides so that he may not die; another persecutes in order to kill and compels him to flee. The one who seeks to kill violates the law and provides all the more reason for flight.

If persecutors reproach those who flee, let them instead be ashamed of themselves, cease their ambushes, and the fugitives will immediately cease fleeing. No one ever flees from a gentle person, but rather from one who is both savage and cunning.

Everyone who groaned and was harassed by Saul fled and came to David (1 Sam. 31:7). If therefore the most pious and just David had known that it was a sin to flee from persecution and to pass from place to place and from city to city, he would certainly not have received such people, kept them with him, or settled them in other cities.

[Col. 1097B] Those who persecute the Lord’s bishops and compel them to pass from cities to cities persecute not only them but our Lord Jesus Christ, “whose ambassadors they are” (2 Cor. 5:20). Nor do the bishops themselves sin in this, since they do it not voluntarily but under compulsion. Rather, those by whom they are persecuted are at fault. This cannot be charged against the bishops themselves but against those who compel them to act in this way.

The holy protomartyr Stephen was being stoned, but Jesus was receiving the blows (Acts 7:58). Therefore everyone must take care not to persecute, judge, or punish anyone unjustly, lest he persecute, judge, and punish Jesus.

Those who deny that mercy should be shown to fugitives and to those suffering necessity deny Christ himself, who is mercy and truth and who commands everyone to assist those suffering necessity.

[Col. 1097C] These are few things, brother, that I have asserted, but you will be able to judge how much depends upon your prudence.

Why do the malicious strive to interrupt this mercy? Why do they injure happiness with empty intentions? This frenzy has no longer any excuse among believers, nor does it matter by what paths he runs toward “the ruler of the world” (John 12:31), whoever withdraws from the goodwill of the brethren or denies mercy to those suffering necessity.

He denies mercy to those in need who does not permit divine mysteries to be provided to needy peoples who lack a bishop of their own to instruct them for the sake of usefulness and necessity; or who does not permit a more learned or more useful bishop to pass by better judgment, not voluntarily but at the exhortation of his superiors, from another city—even if it is a smaller one—to a city that has no bishop; or who does not permit an expelled and persecuted bishop to be enthroned for the sake of usefulness or necessity.

[Col. 1097D] Among the ancients, a bishop moved from one city to another without any distinction whenever usefulness or necessity summoned him.

Therefore it has pleased us to insert that very rule into this letter, so that it may be shown that those who said that a bishop could not be enthroned were lying. Thus it is also read in the canons:

> “If a bishop has been ordained for a parish but does not proceed to the parish for which he was ordained—not through his own fault, but because the people reject him or for any other reason not arising from necessity—he is nevertheless to share in the honor and ministry; nor is he to be involved in the affairs of the Church in which he celebrates the gatherings, but is to await what the synod of the province determines by its judgment.”

[Col. 1098A] No one can contradict this rule, which also commands that, for the sake of usefulness or necessity, a bishop may be enthroned and may be transferred and pass from one city to another that does not have its own bishop.

He offers fat victims to the devil who strives to resist these things or denies the mercy and usefulness of the Church described above—that is, to bishops and peoples alike.

In vain, therefore, will they henceforth set snares against the simple, who formerly prohibited the performance of these things while saying them, since, armed with these and other supports, they know what must be done concerning them and what must be avoided.

He is exceedingly well armed who despises the weapons that the adversary supplies against mercy, usefulness, and concord.

[Col. 1098B] Therefore a bare opposition of faith is sufficient against all the missiles of quarrels.

I know, brother, that you are not unaware that the canonical judgments mentioned above are not new in the evangelical decrees, but are committed to our assent.

Why do those who contradict these things and prohibit bishops’ migrations for the sake of usefulness and necessity—as has often been said, and not for avarice or rashness, to the destruction of priests and peoples—injure the council of priests?

Why do they tear apart the judgment in which, with Christ inspiring it, heavenly oracles were revealed, and in which the tongue of the pontiffs became an interpreter between God and human beings?

[Col. 1098C] That court of heaven, enriched with the various gifts of the curule offices and adorned with much gold and purple of our Redeemer, put forward nothing in that decision on its own authority; rather, through the ministry of the human tongue, it served the divine command.

It understood that whatever it established under compulsion was not its own, and that it had nothing in that judgment except what allowed it to rejoice over its devotion alone.

For when one yields to the profane words of those already mentioned, they reveal both the ignorance of their madness and their envy. What place is there here for error, when the words of example and of history converge along a corresponding course? What is put forward is not different from Catholic understanding and the readings.

The knot is not properly sought in a reed while a cloud obscures the 273 authors of the proclaimed light; for he who performs his duties with less than pure faith according to heavenly statutes is freed from a foul obligation by the radiance of his Lord.

[Col. 1098D] The words or prohibitions of such people therefore become unworthy even of mention.

Their ignorance, then, is exceedingly profound: “their throat is an open grave, for they acted deceitfully with their tongues” (Ps. 5:11). There is no rightness in their mouth; their inner parts are snares; their heart is suffocated by dense thorns, and they strive to attribute their inner vices to others.

He gives nobility to crimes who takes their agitation in such matters as an example, or transmits it to later ears in a report deemed worthy of preservation.

But you should not concern yourself with such questions. Follow the judgment of blessed Paul the apostle, who admonishes everyone through his disciple and cries out, saying:

> “Avoid empty questions.”

Always avoid empty questions, as the Apostle teaches, and do what you have discerned should usefully be done by better judgment—not for avarice or rashness, but, as has often been said, for the sake of usefulness and necessity.

[Col. 1099A] Therefore, dearest brother, supported by these apostolic authorities, transfer, for a reason of necessity or usefulness, the bishop concerning whom you wished to consult us, and teach our other brothers, whom necessity or usefulness has compelled to do this, to act accordingly. For what we write to you alone, we command all generally to observe. Just as we have the authority regularly to assign titles to bishops and priests and to ordain them, so, as has been said, in a case of necessity or usefulness you have authority to transfer and translate them from one title to another, even if the transfer is from a smaller city to a greater one. This, however, must be guarded against with the utmost care: it must never be done out of arrogance or greed. Those condemned by the aforesaid canons are the men who act from such motives, not those who do so from necessity or usefulness, on the counsel of their superiors, with sound and pure intention pleasing to God.

You, brother, always pursue justice, piety, faith, charity, patience, and gentleness. Fight also the good fight of faith and seize eternal life, to which you were called; for the spirit of those who fear the Lord is sought by him, and they are blessed in his sight.
