Their hope is in the one who saves them, and the eyes of the Lord are upon those who love him. Whoever fears the Lord will fear nothing and will not be afraid, because he himself is his hope. Blessed is the soul that fears the Lord. Upon whom does he look, and who is his strength? The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him: a protector of power, a stronghold of strength, a shelter from heat, a midday shade, a safeguard against stumbling, and a help in falling; he lifts up the soul, enlightens the eyes, and gives health, life, and blessing.

The offering of one who sacrifices from injustice is defiled, and the mockeries of the unjust are not pleasing. The Lord alone is with those who support him in the way of truth and justice. The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked, nor regard the offerings of the unjust, nor will he be appeased for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices. Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who slaughters a son in the presence of his father. The bread of the needy is the life of the poor; whoever defrauds him is a man of blood. Whoever takes away bread by sweat, and food from one who is sweating, is like one who has killed his neighbor. Whoever sheds blood and whoever cheats a hired worker are brothers: one builds and the other destroys; what benefit does he gain except labor?

What profit is there for one who is washed after contact with a dead person and then touches him again? What benefit is there in his washing? So too, what benefit is there for a person who fasts for his sins and then commits the same sins again? What does he gain by humbling himself? Who will hear his prayer? Whoever keeps the law multiplies prayer. A saving sacrifice is to heed the commandments and to withdraw from every iniquity; an atoning sacrifice is offered in reparation for injustice, and a supplication for sins is to withdraw from injustice. Whoever offers fine flour repays grace, and whoever practices mercy offers a sacrifice. It is pleasing to God to withdraw from iniquity, and to withdraw from injustice is a supplication. You shall not appear before the presence of God empty-handed, for all these things are done because of the Lord’s command.

[Col. 1099D] “The offering of the righteous makes the altar fat, and its fragrance is sweet in the presence of the Most High. The sacrifice of the righteous is acceptable, and the Lord will not forget its memory. With a good heart give glory to God, and do not diminish the firstfruits of your crops. In every gift make your face cheerful, and in exultation sanctify your tithes. Give to the Most High according to his gift, and with a generous eye make an offering from the work of your hands, for the Lord is one who repays, and he will repay you sevenfold.

“Do not offer corrupt gifts, for he will not accept them; and do not look upon an unjust sacrifice, for the Lord is judge, and with him there is no respect for persons. The Lord will show no partiality against the poor, and he will hear the prayer of the one who has been wronged. He will not despise the prayers of the orphan or of the widow if she pours out a lamenting utterance. Do not the widow’s tears descend upon her cheek, and does not her cry rise against the one who causes them? For from her cheek they ascend to heaven, and the Lord, who hears, will not be pleased with them.

“Whoever worships the Lord will be accepted in his offering, and his prayer will draw near to the clouds. The prayer of one who humbles himself will pierce the clouds; it will not be comforted until it draws near, nor will it depart until the Most High looks upon it, and the Lord will not delay. Rather, he will judge the unjust and execute judgment, and the Mighty One will not be patient with them, but will break their backs and repay vengeance to the nations, until he removes the fullness of the proud and breaks the scepters of the wicked; until he repays all according to their deeds, according to the works of Adam, and according to his presumption; until he judges the judgment of his people and gladdens the righteous with his mercy” (Ecclus. 35:8–25).

May God, dearest brother, fulfill your desire and the ministry divinely entrusted to you according to his riches in glory, in Christ Jesus our Lord. To God our Father be glory forever and ever. Amen. Given on the thirteenth day of August, in the fourteenth indiction.

### Likewise, a letter of Pope Pelagius to all the bishops of Italy

To all our dearest and most beloved brothers, the bishops, and especially to all those serving the Lord throughout Campania and the provinces of Italy, Pelagius sends greetings.

Bearing, according to the Apostle, concern for all the churches, we ought to remember the divine grace toward us: the Lord, through the mercy of his gracious favor, has raised us to this priestly eminence so that, adhering to his commandments and standing as a kind of mirror of his priests, we may prohibit what is unlawful and teach what must be followed.

All, dearest brothers, who wish to live devoutly in Christ must suffer reproaches from the impious and those unlike them, and must be despised as fools and madmen—those who lose present goods in order to acquire invisible things that will benefit them. But this contempt and mockery will be turned back upon the mockers, when their abundance passes into poverty and their pride into disgrace.

For by a just judgment power is often given to sinners by which they persecute his saints, so that those who are helped and led by the Spirit of God may become more illustrious through the exercise of hardships. And although, brothers, these things are so, those who either criticize or accuse their superiors must not therefore be tolerated but rejected. Accordingly, following and strengthening the canonical statutes of the holy Fathers, lest the pillars of holy Church totter, we remove entirely from any accusation all infamous persons, all who are suspect or hostile, those who are not of their people, those whose faith, life, and liberty are unknown, those who are not of good conduct, and those whose life is liable to every accusation.

Likewise, we judge that all whom the divine laws call dead must be removed from the same accusation and subjected to public penance. Nor, while the possessions or property of any Church’s bishop are being unjustly detained by his rivals or by anyone else, should anything be brought against him, or could anything be brought by anyone, before all his property has been restored. First everything must be restored to him according to the laws; afterward, at the time fixed by the Fathers, the cases are to be examined.

Robbers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, adulterers, and their like must also be rejected. For it is clear that such people always pursue discord rather than peace. No monk, moreover, should ever seize such matters or presume to disturb secular or ecclesiastical affairs, for in such matters their voice is dead. The Lord always wishes his chief preachers to remain immovable, not to be assailed by certain persons, but to serve him freely and peacefully. Hence he himself says: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zech. 2:8). And: “Whoever grieves you grieves me.” And: “Whoever commits an injury will receive what he has done unjustly.” Elsewhere also: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Matt. 10:40).

Thus, too, pastors and preachers of the Church must generally be feared, struck down, and venerated by the peoples and by all others, so that, under the discipline of good will, temporal things may be endured and eternal things hoped for. The one who does not violate his purpose but increases his devotion increases the merits of virtue. Charity, however, always calls out to a person. Just as malice makes people old, so love makes them new. The faith of those who are going to see God believes what it does not see; for if it sees, it is not faith. Merit is gathered for the believer, while reward is given to the one who sees.

Then the shepherd’s diadem is precious, when the ecclesiastical flock, as it advances toward uprightness under his exhortation, does not resist. The one who follows his instructions loves his admonisher without deceit and with an open face. They provide human beings with instruction in nature, and the dumb with an answer; a return of clamorous concern comes back to mortals, because each person will receive according to what he has done. For what the tongue has received perishes; a benefit is useless unless the undertaking has been lawfully begun and canonically completed.

With confidence in our party, what apostolic authority commands is being sent: that you, prelates of Christ, should always provide kindness, while preserving the fairness of your ears and hearts and your good will. To help against assaults and to restore the traveler after intervals is justice. Whoever drives adversity away from the afflicted offers prosperity to the Lord.

The appointed fruit of labor must be rendered to judgment with the utmost purity, venerable prelates, so that in both respects a fitting brightness neither disfigures the recipient if it has come through unworthy authority nor unjustly stains the giver when it is bestowed. Let there always be a free voice against the wicked, the impious, and the persecutors of God’s servants. Let them be struck and rebuked with the sword of the mouth; let them be pursued and repelled, confounded and turned away, and let them have no power to harm those who live devoutly.

What appear to be safest are often full of dangers. See with how many snares such people struggle. Therefore what we add must not be concealed. Our manifest persecution had already been hidden; mercy has been preserved for the persecutors, and strictness for the criminals.

Therefore grant rest to sleep, and drive away the enemy of the heavenly commandments, lest the bright conduct of those dwelling with you be stained by the dark contagion of one who intrudes. Remedies must be provided before the disease grows. Let us also seek the assistance of the holy apostles and the other priests, and close the mouths of the aforesaid persecutors.

The conduct of the world is restrained by fear of the laws; ecclesiastical custody is likewise preserved and governed by the reins of regulations. May God, dearest brothers, always keep envy far away. Arm yourselves, therefore, according to the Apostle, with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, and with the shield of apostolic authority, so that the rights of ecclesiastical fruitfulness may not be overturned by any assault of a raging storm. Never burden anyone with any prejudice; always examine what is declared by the testimony of the regulations.

What remains, once salvation has been set first, is that you, brothers, should always hasten devotedly toward joys, because divine benefits often approach by degrees, and to those to whom he grants good things he promises better things. One always ascends by stages toward the summit, where heavenly favor provides the beginning. May almighty God always preserve what has been granted and increase it with successes that will benefit you. May everything always be done among you in charity. Do not slander those who slander, for it is not good to slander those who slander, lest, stirred by what has been written, they engage in conflict at all.

274. We must not fear the reproach of human beings or be overcome by their insults, because the Lord commands this for us through the prophet Isaiah: “Hear me, you who know judgment, my people in whose hearts is my law: do not fear the reproach of human beings, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies” (Isa. 51:7). Let us consider what is written in the Psalm: “Will God not require these things? For he knows the hidden things of the heart and the thoughts of such people, because they are vain. Everyone has spoken vain things to his neighbor; with deceitful lips and with a double heart they have spoken evil. But may the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things. They said: ‘We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is our lord?’” (Psal. 43:22; 93:11; 11:3–5).

For if they kept these things in mind, they would by no means rush into such great iniquity. They do not do this on the basis of sound and ancient teaching, but in order to exercise their vengeance against the servants of God. For it is written: “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes” (Prov. 12:15); and: “There are ways that seem right to a person, but their end leads to death” (Prov. 14:12).

We who suffer these things must reserve them for the judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his works. He also thundered through his ministers, saying: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. 12:19). You, however, should assist one another in right faith and pure and good will, and let no one withdraw his hand from helping his brother, because, the Lord says, by this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.

Given on the Kalends of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## THE DECREES OF POPE GREGORY BEGIN

[Col. 1103]

### On triple immersion in baptism

[Col. 1103B]

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and most holy brother Leander, fellow bishop.

I would have wished to answer your letters with undivided attention, unless the burden of pastoral care so wearied me that I would rather weep than say anything. Your Reverence will also perceive this attentively in the very text of my letter, when I speak negligently to one whom I love intensely. For I am so shaken here by the many waves of this world that I am altogether unable to steer into port the old and crumbling ship which, by God’s hidden dispensation, I undertook to govern.

Now waves rush upon it from one direction; now heaps of the foaming sea swell from the side; now a storm pursues from behind. Amid everything, in confusion, I am compelled sometimes to steer the ship among the very masses of the waves, and sometimes, by inclining the side of the ship, to avoid the threats of the waves obliquely.

But I groan because I perceive that, through my negligence, the bilge of vices is increasing. With the storm vehemently opposing us, the planks already creak from decay and threaten shipwreck. Weeping, I recall that I have lost the calm shore of my peace; sighing, I see the land, yet, because events oppose me, I cannot hold to it.

Therefore, dearest brother, if you love me, stretch out to me in these waves the hand of your prayer, so that you may help me in my labor, and by this exchange may yourself become stronger in your own labors. I cannot express in words the joy I feel at having learned that our common son, the glorious King Reccared, has been converted to the Catholic faith with complete devotion.

When you describe his character to me in your letters, you have made me love even one whom I do not know. But since you know the snares of the ancient enemy, and know that he prepares a harsher war against victors, let your holiness now watch carefully over this same son of ours, so that he may complete what he has begun well and not exalt himself over his accomplished good works. Let him hold the faith he has come to know also through the merits of his life, and show by his works that he belongs to the eternal kingdom, so that after many cycles of years he may pass from kingdom to kingdom.

Concerning triple immersion in baptism, nothing truer can be answered than what you yourself have perceived: in one faith, a diversity of custom does no harm to the holy Church. We immerse three times, however, signifying the sacrament of the three-day burial, so that when the infant is lifted from the water three times, the resurrection after the three days may be expressed.

### Likewise, to Leander, bishop of Spalatum

I received your letter, written with the pen of pure charity. Your tongue had dyed from the heart what it poured out upon the page. When it was read, good and wise men were present, and their inward parts were immediately stirred to compunction. Each began, with the hand of love, to draw you into his heart, because in that letter it was not merely possible to hear the sweetness of your mind but to see it.

They were each kindled and amazed, and the very fire of the listeners showed what the ardor of the speaker had been. For unless torches first burn within themselves, they do not kindle another. There, therefore, we saw how greatly your mind had burned with charity, since it kindled others in this way.

They did not know your life, which I always recall with great veneration, but the height of your heart was revealed to them through the humility of your speech. Your letter says that my life is worthy of imitation by all. But although it is not as you say, let it be so because you say it, lest one who is not accustomed to lying should lie.

In response to this I briefly repeat the words of a certain old woman: “Do not call me Naomi—that is, beautiful—but call me Mara, because I am full of bitterness” (Ruth 1:20). Nor, good man, am I today the one whom you knew. I confess that, while outwardly progressing, I have inwardly fallen, and I fear that I belong to those of whom it is written: “You cast them down while they were being lifted up” (Ps. 72:18). For the one who advances in honors but falls in character is cast down even while being lifted up.

Following the ways of my Lord, I had resolved above all to be the reproach of human beings and the outcast of the people, and to run in the lot of the one of whom the Psalmist again says: “You have appointed ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears”—so that I might rise inwardly with all the greater force the more humbly I lay outwardly in the valley of tears.

But now burdensome honor greatly weighs me down; countless cares make a din. When the mind gathers itself toward God, these cares tear it apart with their impulses as with swords. There is no rest of heart. Prostrate in the depths and weighed down by the burden of its own thoughts, contemplation’s wing lifts it into the heights only very rarely, or not at all.

The mind grows numb through sluggishness and, already almost reduced to stupor by cares that bark around it, is compelled sometimes to conduct earthly affairs and sometimes even to administer carnal matters. At times, because weariness demands it, it is compelled to arrange certain things even with guilt.

Why say more? Overcome by its own weight, it sweats blood. For unless guilt were understood by the name “blood,” the Psalmist would not say: “Deliver me from bloodguilt” (Ps. 50:16). When we join sins to sins, we also fulfill what was said through another prophet: “Blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:2). Blood is said to touch blood when one guilt is added to another, so that the accumulation of iniquity may multiply.

Amid these things I beseech almighty God that, having escaped the waves of turmoil, I may feel the hand of your prayer. For I was sailing, as it were, with a favorable wind when I lived a tranquil life in the monastery. But suddenly the storm seized me in its confusion through violent movements, and I lost the prosperity of my journey: having lost peace, I suffered shipwreck of the mind.

Now I am tossed among the waves and seek the plank of your intercession, so that I who did not deserve to reach the shore safely in an intact ship may at least, after my losses, be brought back to land on a plank.

Your Reverence is afflicted, as you write, by the trouble of gout; I too have been severely worn down by its continual pain. But consolation will be easy if, amid the scourges we suffer, we recall the sins we have committed and recognize that the scourges are no longer scourges but gifts, if the sins we committed through the pleasure of the flesh are cleansed through the pain of the flesh.

Moreover, by the blessing of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, we have sent you a pallium, to be used only for the solemn celebrations of Mass. In sending it, I ought certainly to have admonished you how you should live, but I suppress my words because your conduct surpasses words.

May almighty God guard you with his protection and lead you, with abundant fruit of souls, to the reward of the heavenly homeland. How greatly I am weighed down by occupation and weakness is shown by this brief letter, in which I speak little even to one whom I love greatly. May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

### To Reccared, king of the Visigoths

1. On praise of the same ruler, through whom the Gothic people were converted to the Catholic faith.  
2. On the gifts sent by the aforementioned ruler to blessed Peter the Apostle.  
3. On his decree against the Jews, which was not corrupted by a gift of gold.  
4. That rulers should possess humility of heart.  
5. That rulers should devote themselves to bodily chastity.  
6. That rulers should be moderate and gentle toward their subjects.  
7. On the key of the little door of blessed Peter, and on the cross of the Lord that was sent, as well as on the pallium sent to blessed Leander, bishop.

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his most glorious and excellent son Reccared, king of the Goths and Suevi.

### Chapter I

I cannot express in words, most excellent son, how much I delight in your work and your life. In our own days I have heard of a miraculous deed accomplished through your excellence: the entire Gothic people has been transferred from the error of the Arian heresy to the firmness of the true faith. I long to exclaim with the prophet: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76:11).

Whose breast, even if it were made of stone, would not immediately soften into praise of almighty God and love for your excellence after learning of a deed so great? I confess that I often delight in telling my assembled sons what has been accomplished through you, and often in wondering at it together with them.

These things frequently stir me even against myself, because I, lazy and useless, grow numb in idle leisure at the very time when kings are laboring in the gathering of souls for the gain of the heavenly homeland. What, then, shall I say to the Judge who comes at that terrible examination, if I arrive there empty, while your excellence leads after you flocks of the faithful whom you have now drawn to the grace of the true faith through diligent and continual preaching?

Yet, good man, I have great consolation in this gift of God: I love in you the holy work which I do not possess in myself. When I rejoice with great exultation in your good deeds, what belongs to you through labor becomes mine through charity. Therefore, concerning the conversion of the Goths through your work and our rejoicing, I wish to exclaim with the angels: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). Through you, as I judge, we are more deeply indebted to almighty God in thanksgiving, because although we have done nothing with you, by rejoicing with your work we share in it.

### II

How gladly blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, received the gifts of your excellence is so clear that your obligations themselves testify to it. For it is written: “The vows of the righteous are pleasing” (Prov. 15:8). In the judgment of almighty God, it is not what is given but by whom it is given that is considered.

Hence it is written: “God looked upon Abel and his gifts, but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look” (Gen. 4:4). In saying that the Lord looked upon the gifts, Scripture carefully first stated that he looked upon Abel. From this it is plainly shown that it was not the offerer who pleased because of the gifts, but the gifts because of the offerer.

You show how welcome your offering is, because, before giving your gift, you first gave the disposition of your mind through the conversion of the people subject to you. As for your statement that the abbots you sent to carry your offering to blessed Peter the Apostle, having been wearied by the journey at sea, returned to Spain, the gifts that arrived later were not rejected; rather, the steadfastness of those who had been sent was tested, so that they might learn to overcome dangers placed in the way of holy desire and not grow weary in mind through bodily fatigue. Adversity placed in the way of good vows is a testing of virtue, not a judgment of rejection.

For who does not know how favorable it was that blessed Paul the Apostle was coming to Italy to preach? Yet he suffered shipwreck, while the ship of his heart remained intact amid the waves.

### III

I further declare that, through your work, what I learned concerning my beloved son Probino has increased the praises of God. When your excellence had issued a certain decree against Jewish perfidy, those against whom your integrity had been tested attempted to bend your upright mind by offering a sum of money. Your excellence despised it and, seeking to please almighty God, preferred innocence to gold.

This brings to my mind the deed of King David. When his soldiers, eager to serve him, had brought him the water he desired from the cistern at Bethlehem, which lay among enemy ranks, he immediately said: “Far be it from me to drink the blood of these men” (2 Sam. 23:16–17). Because he poured it out and refused to drink it, it is written: “And he poured it out to the Lord” (ibid. 23:16).

If water rejected by an armed king was turned into a sacrifice to God, let us consider what sort of sacrifice the king offered to almighty God who, for love of him, refused to accept not water but gold. Therefore, most excellent son, I shall say confidently: you poured out to the Lord the gold that you refused to possess against him.

### IV

These are great deeds and must be proclaimed to the praise of almighty God. But amid them the snares of the ancient enemy must be avoided with vigilant care. The greater the gifts he sees in people, the more subtly he seeks to take them away. Highway robbers do not seek empty travelers, but those who carry vessels of gold or silver. The present life is indeed a road, and the greater the gifts each person carries, the more necessary it is for him to beware the spirits lying in wait.

Your excellence must therefore guard with the utmost care the great gift received through the conversion of the people subject to you: first, humility of heart, and then purity of body. Since it is written, “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14), it is plainly clear that the one who truly loves high things does not sever his mind from the root of humility.

Often the evil spirit, unable to destroy the good things to which he previously could not oppose himself, comes afterward to the mind of the one who performed the work. Through silent thoughts he shakes it with certain praises of his own, so that the deceived mind marvels at how great are the things it has done. When, through hidden swelling, it exalts itself before itself, it is deprived of the grace of the one who gave the gift.

Hence it is said through the prophet’s voice to the proud heart: “Trusting in your beauty, you committed fornication in your name” (Ezek. 16:15). For the soul to trust in its own beauty is to presume upon its righteous action within itself. It fornicates in its own name when, in what it has done rightly, it does not seek to magnify the praise of the Creator but seeks the glory of reputation.

Again it is written through the prophet: “The more beautiful you are, descend” (Ezek. 32:19). The soul descends from the very place where it is more beautiful, because from the beauty of virtue by which it ought to have been exalted before the Lord, it falls from his grace through its own exaltation.

What, then, must be done in these matters except that, whenever the evil spirit brings back to us the good things we have done in order to lift up our mind, we should always recall our evil deeds? And although we recognize as our own the things we did by sinning, when we avoid sins we should recognize them as gifts belonging solely to almighty God.

### V

Purity of body must also be guarded in the pursuit of good action, because, according to the voice of the preaching Apostle, “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17). Again he says: “This is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thess. 4:3). Showing what sanctification he meant, he immediately completed the statement: “that you abstain from fornication, and that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire” (ibid. 4:5).

### VI

The reins of government toward subjects must also be tempered with great moderation, lest power steal into the mind. A kingdom is governed well when the glory of ruling does not rule the mind. Care must also be taken lest anger intrude and quickly do whatever is permitted.

Even when anger seeks the faults of those who have transgressed, it must not go before the mind as a mistress; rather, it must serve behind the back of reason like a maidservant, coming forward when commanded. For if it once begins to possess the mind, it considers even what it does cruelly to be just.

Hence it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (Jas. 1:20). Again it is said: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (ibid. 1:19).

With God as author, I do not doubt that you observe all these things. But since an occasion for admonition has arisen, I furtively attach myself to your good actions, so that when admonition is added to what you do without being admonished, you may no longer do it alone.

May almighty God protect you in all your deeds by the extension of his heavenly arm, and grant you both the prosperity of the present life and, after many cycles of years, eternal life.

### VII

We have sent you, as a blessing, a small key from the most sacred body of blessed Peter the Apostle. It contains iron enclosed from his chains, so that what had bound his neck for martyrdom may free you from everything.

We have also given the present bearer a cross to carry to you. It contains wood from the Lord’s cross and hairs of blessed John the Baptist, so that through the intercession of his Forerunner you may always have the consolation of our Savior.

To the most reverend man, Father and our fellow bishop Leander, we have sent a pallium from the see of blessed Peter the Apostle. By ancient custom, by your customs, and by his goodness and dignity, we owed it to him.

### Likewise, a letter of the same man to Secundinus the enclosed monk

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother Secundinus, servant of God and enclosed monk.

I received the letters of your affection, which tasted, in my judgment, as though seasoned with the honey of love. O how full of inspiration for life are the things spoken through the grace of the Spirit! No cultivation of eloquence and no stylistic form of words appeared in them; rather, because they held fast to the root of truth and charity, everything they said burned with love for the heavenly homeland.

In them your affection earnestly asked me to write an exhortatory booklet. But you must know, dearest son, that I am oppressed by such pains of gout and such tumult of cares that, although I may remember that I once was something, I nevertheless see very clearly that I am no longer what I was.

Your affection also asserts that, even beyond the age of fifty, you remain subject to youthful desires. In this too you fulfill the command of the divine oracle, in which it is written: “The righteous person is first an accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17).

Yet I do not doubt that you suffer greater snares from the crafty enemy, against whom you have prepared greater battles. For he seeks the devices of deception with all the greater ardor the more fervently he recognizes that you long for the heavenly homeland.

We, indeed, who live our life among many people, although fearful and timid, nevertheless stand as if in battle array because we have undertaken wars against the ancient enemy. But you, who lead a solitary life—and what else should I call you but a monk?—hasten through the fervor of virtue to go out before the battle line. Why, then, should the enemy not attack singly the one from whom he expects to be attacked singly?

We who live among human beings are often tempted by the crafty enemy through another person. But you, who now live the present life outside the company of human beings, must endure greater battles, because the master of temptations himself approaches you.

For you cannot devote yourselves to prayers and praises of God without some interruption of time. Even if intention is continually ready, human weakness itself nevertheless falls back upon itself, so that at times it lies exhausted and grows numb from exercising its discipline.

As soon as the ancient enemy finds an idle mind, he comes to it under certain pretexts to speak with it. He brings certain things from past deeds back to its memory, makes words once heard resound indecently in thought, and places before the eyes of the heart the images of whatever was once shamefully done, so that he may stain with past evils the mind he cannot defile through present things.

The deceived mind often restores affection for the very things from which it has long afflicted itself through repentance, so that it truly says with the Psalmist: “My wounds have stunk and festered because of my foolishness” (Ps. 37:6). A scar is the image of a wound, but of one that has been healed. The scar therefore returns to putrefaction when, through the wound of sin already healed by repentance, the mind is shaken into delight in that sin.

Often, through the snares of the crafty enemy, we see with the eyes of the heart what we have done. When delight imperceptibly steals into this, although the unhappy mind already mourns what it has done, it is nevertheless grieved that it has done certain things which it mourns.

These are the darknesses of our heart which, whether we wish it or not, we endure in this life. Who must be sought against them except the one who is “a helper in times of trouble” (Ps. 9:10)?

[Col. 1110A] I received with great pleasure the inquiry with which your Charity questioned me about its doubt: whether the Churches of the East follow the faith and teaching of blessed memory Leo, or whether perhaps their opinions are divided among themselves in defense of the Three Chapters. Therefore I wish your devoted affection to be certain that the most holy Eastern Churches, with one understanding and one teaching, hold the faith of the same holy Leo, and guard and venerate the holy Council of Chalcedon together with us in such a way that no one is considered a bishop who has not been its defender and follower.

For this reason, whenever bishops are ordained in the four principal sees, they send synodal letters to one another, in which they profess that they preserve the holy Council of Chalcedon together with the other general councils. We likewise reject and judge subject to anathema anyone who presumes either to diminish anything concerning the faith of that council or to add anything else to it. For the council subsequently held as a general council is preserved by us for this reason: as a follower of that council, it preserves in all things its honor and authority.

Therefore your affection, dearest to me, must consider all the more diligently this point: that the person who excels especially in holy conduct, who afflicts himself through abstinence, and who applies himself most earnestly to the teaching of God, must take care lest, by following the error of schismatics, he be found separated from the communion of the holy universal Church. And what benefit will all those labors bring if those who chiefly guard their souls in good works before the eyes of almighty God are not found in the unity of the faith? [Col. 1110C] Hence it is said: “My dove is one” (Song 6:8).

Again the Lord says to Moses: “There is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock” (Exod. 33:21). What place is not the Lord’s, since all things are contained in him through whom they were created? Yet there is a place beside him—namely, the unity of the holy Church—in which one stands as upon a rock, while the firmness of confession is humbly maintained. Concerning this place it is added: “Then you shall see my back” (ibid., 23). For standing upon the rock—that is, the holy Church—we shall see God’s back when we contemplate the joys of the heavenly homeland, those things promised at the end.

But perverse men, finding an occasion in the Three Chapters, flee ecclesiastical discipline, fear being reproved for their carnal deeds, and refuse to be subject to the apostolic see; yet they reprove us concerning a faith which they themselves do not know. Although they are neither sound in faith nor devoted to good works, they strive to appear to be contending for the faith. Thus they become worse each day, as guilt grows coarse within them. They seek also to become praiseworthy, as though through the zeal of fervor; but, as it is written: “You will know them by their works” (Matt. 7:20). Let your Charity display their manner of life and examine the merit of their intention.

To speak briefly to your affection about this matter: the entire Council of Chalcedon, up to the definition of the faith and the promulgation of the canons, dealt with general questions. After [Col. 1111A] the canons had been examined, it took care to settle the particular disputes of the bishops.

You know the letter which the most reverend Ibas denies to be his, and which lies at the end of the council. That letter asserts that Nestorius was condemned unheard and without an investigation, while it suspects Cyril of having fallen into the doctrine of Apollinaris. If the whole preceding text of the council is read, it becomes clear how greatly this letter contradicts that council. The holy council declares Nestorius to be a heretic, as he truly was, and venerates blessed Cyril as a catholic Father.

Therefore a letter that defends one condemned by the council and accuses one venerated by the council is unquestionably shown to oppose the definition of the holy council. [Col. 1111B] Those who do not preserve the judgment defined by so many Fathers unquestionably oppose the Church.

Your Holiness has therefore asked us to write to you concerning the possibility of rising again to priestly office after a fall, since you say that you have read differing judgments in various canons: some permitting restoration, others asserting that it is entirely impossible. For this reason we venerate the general councils, beginning with Nicaea and together with the remaining four, because, following them, they agree unanimously in all their judgments; because we follow the Fathers who preceded us; and because, with God as our guide, we do not depart from their sacred teaching.

Beginning, then, with the highest rank and proceeding down to the fourth minister of the altar, we understand this to be the rule to be followed: the one who is lower in rank should give precedence to the one who is higher. But just as the higher person surpasses him in honor, so also in guilt: the one whose guilt is greater must be subjected to a greater punishment, and after penance he should be believed capable of bearing fruit.

For what benefit is there in sowing wheat without gathering its fruit? Or in building a house without dwelling in it? After worthy satisfaction, we believe that one may return to honor, as the Prophet says: “Shall not one who falls rise again?” (Ps. 40:9). And will one who has turned away not return? He likewise says: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 33:12).

Hence the Psalmist says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 51:12–13). When he asked not to be cast away from him, he trembled and was terrified at the guilt of his fall, because he, king and prophet alike, had seized another man’s wife. When his crime had been exposed, the prophet added in doing penance: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit” (ibid., 14).

For if he had not done worthy penance before God, he would never have preached to others. He says: “I will teach the unjust your ways, and the ungodly will turn back to you” (ibid., 15). When the Prophet saw that his own sins had been cleansed through penance, he did not hesitate to heal the sins of others by preaching. He also endeavored to offer himself as a sacrifice to God, saying: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (ibid., 19).

These things would have been sufficient, but every judgment is more readily believed the more fully it is confirmed by testimonies of sacred Scripture. Concerning this, the prophet says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11). And this is said to sinners: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, all his iniquities shall be consigned to oblivion” (Ezek. 18:21–22).

If the Redeemer, who came not at all to destroy sinners but to justify them (Luke 9:56), does not abandon sinners to oblivion, who among men reserves them for condemnation, when the Apostle says: “If God justifies, who is he that condemns?” (Rom. 8:33–34).

Returning to the fountain of mercy, let us recall the evangelical judgment: “I tell you, I rejoice more over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance” (Luke 15:7). He also says that he carries the lost sheep upon his shoulders, leaving the ninety-nine that had not gone astray [Col. 1112B] behind (ibid., 4–5).

If the wandering sheep, after being found, is carried upon the shoulders to the fold, why should a sinner not be recalled to the ministry of the Church after undergoing the punishment of penance? What is more serious: to commit a carnal offense, without which few among the many are found, or to deny the Son of God through fear? In this one matter we know that blessed Peter himself, prince of the apostles, at whose body we now sit unworthy, fell. Yet after the denial came penance, and after penance mercy was given (Luke 22:57–61), because he did not remove him from the apostolate, although he had foretold that he would deny him before himself (Matt. 26:75).

Let these things, dearest son, be sufficient for you, so that when you see one wiping away his offenses with tears, you may not doubt that he obtains mercy in the sight of the divine Majesty. For he who came to redeem sinners despises no sinner who has been converted.

You asked that an image of the one whom you worship be sent to you through Dulcerius, your deacon. Your request pleased us greatly, because you seek with your whole intention in your heart the one whose image you desire to have before your eyes. So that bodily sight may daily make the desired one present and, while you look upon the painting, you may burn inwardly toward the one whose image you desire to see, we do nothing inappropriate if through visible things we demonstrate invisible realities.

Thus, when someone ardently desires to see another person, and according to custom loves and longs to see his bride, if it happens that she goes to the bath or proceeds to church, he quickly prepares himself on the way so that he may depart rejoicing from seeing her.

We know that you do not ask for an image of our Savior in order to worship it as though it were God, but for the remembrance of the Son of God, so that you may grow warm in love for the one whose image you desire to see. We do not prostrate ourselves before the image itself as though before divinity; rather, we adore the one whom through the image we remember either as born, or suffering, or seated upon the throne. And while through the painting itself, as through writing, we recall the Son of God to memory, it gladdens our spirit concerning the resurrection or soothes it concerning the Passion.

Therefore we have sent you, through the aforementioned Dulcerius, our son and deacon, two *surtiriae* [the term is uncertain], containing images of the Savior, of holy Mary the Mother of God, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, together with one cross and a key, as a blessing from the most holy body of Peter, prince of the apostles. May you be defended through him from the evil enemy, since you believe yourself fortified by the holy wood; and may he protect you from the one who suggests youthful passions to you.

Remember that, persevering in your good works, you should kindle others to his love, for whose sake you have made yourself dwell in solitude, so that, having cast back whatever evils of this life the enemy suggests in your heart, you may burn inwardly with the advances of the mind like torches, for love of him, and may even wish to end your life. May he himself also protect you to the end—the Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to redeem the whole world and who lives forever.

**Also, Gregory to the patrician Theotista. On calming discord.**

[Col. 1113B]

We must give great thanks to almighty God that our most devout and gracious emperors have such close relatives of their own family beside them, from whose manner of life great joy may arise for all of us. Therefore we must continually pray for these lords, that their life, together with all that belongs to them, may be kept peaceful for a long time under the protection of heavenly grace.

I report that I learned from certain informants that, through the fickleness of the people, a disturbance of defamatory speech had arisen against you. Because of this, I hear that your Excellence was greatly troubled. If this is so, I am very surprised that, although you have fixed your heart in heaven, the words of men should agitate you on earth.

For blessed Job, when his friends who had come to console him broke out into reproach, said: “Behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who knows me is on high” (Job 16:20). Whoever has the witness of his life in heaven ought not to fear human judgments on earth.

Paul, the leader of the good, also says: “Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another” (Gal. 6:4). For if we rejoice in praise or are broken by blame, we have placed our glory not in ourselves but in the mouth of others.

Again: “The foolish virgins did not take oil in their vessels, but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps” (Matt. 25:3–4). Our lamps are good works, concerning which it is written: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

We take oil in our vessels with our lamps when we do not seek the splendor of glory from those near us who praise our good deeds, but preserve these things within the testimony of our conscience. Whatever is said about us outwardly, we must return to the hidden places of the mind. Even if everyone blames a person, he is free if his conscience does not accuse him; and even if everyone praises him, he cannot be free if his conscience accuses him.

The Truth says concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see—a reed shaken by the wind?” (Matt. 11:7). This is said by way of negation, not affirmation, as what follows makes clear: “But what did you go out to see—a man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (ibid., 8).

Although, according to the truth of the Gospel, John was clothed in a rough garment (Matt. 3:4), by symbolic meaning those clothed in soft garments are people who delight in flattery and praise. It is denied that John was a reed shaken by the wind, because no breeze from human mouths bent the strength of his mind.

If we are lifted up by praise and humbled by blame, we are reeds shaken by the wind. But may this be far from us—far from the heart of your Excellence. I know that you diligently read the teacher of the nations, who says: “If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10).

If, nevertheless, even a small sadness has arisen in your mind from this matter, I believe that almighty God kindly permitted it to happen. For he did not promise his chosen ones joys of delight in this life, but bitterness and tribulations (Matt. 24:19), so that, as by a medicine, they might return through a bitter drink to the sweetness of eternal salvation.

What does he say? “The world will rejoice, but you will mourn” (John 16:20). And with what hope and promise does he add shortly afterward: “I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (ibid., 22). Again he says to the disciples: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

Consider, I ask you, where there will be patience if there is nothing to endure. I do not suppose that Abel existed without Cain’s wickedness exercising him. For if the good were without the evil, they could not be perfectly good, since they would not be purified. The company of the wicked itself is the purification of the good.

There were three sons of Noah in the ark; one became a mocker of his father (Gen. 9:22), and although he himself had been blessed, he received the sentence of the curse in his son (ibid., 25). Abraham had two sons before he took Cethura as his wife, yet the son of his carnal promise persecuted the other. The great teacher explains this, saying: “As the one who was according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the Spirit, so it is now” (Gal. 4:29).

Isaac had two sons, but one, who was spiritual, fled before the threats of his carnal brother (Gen. 27:43). Jacob had twelve sons, but ten of them sold into Egypt the one who lived more uprightly (Gen. 37:36). In the case of the prophet David, because there was something in him that needed purification, it happened that he suffered a persecuting son [Col. 1114D] (2 Sam. 15:16).

Blessed Job says concerning the company of the reprobate: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches” (Job 30:29). The Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, unbelievers and subverters are with you, and you dwell among scorpions” (Ezek. 2:6). At times one reprobate was mixed among the twelve apostles (John 6:71), so that there might be one through whose persecution the eleven would be tested.

Peter, prince of the apostles, says to the disciples: “He rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the abuse of the wicked; for by sight and hearing he was righteous while living among those who from day to day tortured the soul of the righteous with iniquitous deeds” (2 Pet. 2:7–8).

The Apostle Paul also says to the disciples: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. 2:15–16).

Since, therefore, Scripture bears witness that the good cannot be without the evil in this life, your Excellence must not be disturbed at all by the words of fools. Above all, one has firm confidence in almighty God when one receives some adversity in this world for a good work, so that a full reward may be preserved in eternal recompense.

Hence the holy Gospel says: “Blessed will you be when men speak every evil against you, lying for my name’s sake” (Matt. 5:11). He who deigned to offer his own reproaches as an example for our consolation said: “If they called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more his domestics” (Matt. 10:25).

[Col. 1115B] There are many who perhaps praise the lives of the good more than they ought. To prevent any pride from creeping in through praise, almighty God permits the wicked to break out into disparagement and abuse, so that if some fault is born in the heart from the mouths of those who praise, it may be strangled by the mouths of those who blame.

Thus the Teacher of the nations testifies that he runs in his preaching “through dishonor and good repute” (2 Cor. 6:8). He also says: “As deceivers and yet truthful” (ibid.). If there were people who imposed an evil reputation upon Paul and called him a deceiver, what Christian ought to consider it unworthy to hear insults for Christ?

We know how great was the virtue of the forerunner of our Redeemer, who through sacred speech is called not only more than a prophet but also an angel (Matt. 11:9–10). Yet, as ecclesiastical history testifies, after his death his body was burned by persecutors.

But if we speak of these things concerning all the saints, let us speak also concerning the Holy One of holy ones himself—that is, concerning God, who became human for us (John 1:14). Before the outrage he heard that he had a demon (John 8:48); after his death he was called a deceiver by his persecutors, who said: “We know that that deceiver said, ‘After three days I shall rise again’” (Matt. 27:63).

How much, then, must we sinners endure from the tongues and hands of wicked men, since we shall be judged at the coming of the eternal Judge, if even he who came as Judge endured so much after death?

I have said these things briefly, dearest and most excellent daughter, so that whenever you learn that foolish people are disparaging you, you may not be touched by any, even the smallest, sadness of mind. But since the murmur of foolish people can be quieted by calm reasoning, I believe it would be a sin to neglect doing whatever good can be done. For when we can calm deranged minds and lead them back to salvation, we must not scandalize them at all.

There are, indeed, certain scandals that must be utterly disregarded; others, however, when they cannot be avoided without sin, must not be disregarded, lest they be preserved together with sin.

We have learned this from the preaching of the sacred Gospel. When the Truth said: “Not what enters the mouth defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth defiles a person” (Matt. 15:11), and the disciples replied: “Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard this word, were scandalized?” (ibid., 12), he immediately answered: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them; they are blind and leaders of the blind” (ibid., 13–14).

Yet when tribute was demanded, he first explained why they ought not to pay it (Matt. 17:24), and immediately added: “But so that we do not scandalize them, go to the sea, cast in a hook, and take the fish that first comes up; when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it for me and for you” (ibid., 26).

What does it mean that, concerning some who were scandalized, he says, “Leave them; they are blind and leaders of the blind,” while for others, lest they be scandalized, the Lord pays tribute, even though it was not owed? What does it mean that he permitted one scandal but forbade another, except that he wished to teach us both to disregard those scandals that entangle us in sin and, by every means, to mitigate those that we can calm without sin?

Therefore, with the Lord’s protection, your Excellence can avoid the scandals of wicked people with great tranquility. First they should be summoned privately by you, and an explanation should be given to them. Certain erroneous propositions which they think that we hold should be anathematized in their presence.

If, as is said, they suspect that the anathema is being offered falsely, you must also confirm by oath that you neither hold nor have ever held those propositions. Nor should it seem unworthy of you to satisfy them in this way, nor should pride arising from your imperial lineage be directed against them in your mind.

For we are all brothers, created under the power of one Emperor and redeemed by his blood. Therefore we must not despise our brothers, however poor and lowly they may be.

Peter had certainly received the power of the heavenly kingdom, so that whatever he bound or loosed on earth would be bound or loosed in heaven (Matt. 16:19). He walked upon the sea (John 21:7), healed the sick by his shadow (Acts 5:15), put sinners to death (ibid., 5:10), and raised the dead by prayer (Acts 9:40). Yet because, at the prompting of the Spirit, he had entered the house of Cornelius the Gentile (Acts 10:19), the faithful questioned him: why he had entered the house of Gentiles and eaten with them; why he had received them in baptism [Col. 1116D] (ibid., 28).

Nevertheless, he—the first of the apostles—filled with such an abundance of gifts and supported by such power of miracles, answered the complaint of the faithful not by authority but by reason. He explained the matter in order: how he had seen a vessel like a linen sheet descending from heaven, containing four-footed animals of the earth, beasts, reptiles, and birds; how he had heard a voice: “Rise, Peter, kill and eat”; how three men had come, calling him to Cornelius; how the Holy Spirit had commanded him to go with them; and how the same Holy Spirit, who customarily came upon those baptized in Judaea after baptism, had come upon the Gentiles before baptism (ibid., 11–48).

If, when he was blamed by the faithful, he had answered by appealing to the authority he had received in the holy Church, so that the sheep would not dare to reproach their shepherd, but had said something of his power in response to the complaint of the faithful, he would certainly not have been a teacher of gentleness. Therefore he calmed them by humble reasoning and, in the matter of his reproach, even produced witnesses, saying: “These six brothers also came with me” (Acts 11:12).

[Col. 1117A] If, then, the shepherd of the Church and prince of the apostles, who uniquely performed signs and miracles, did not disdain humbly to give an account when he was reproached, how much more ought we sinners, when we are reproved in some matter, to calm our reprovers with humble reasoning?

As you know, when I was staying in the royal city at the feet of the lords, many of those who were accused concerning the aforementioned propositions used to come to me. But, with my conscience as witness, I confess that I never found in them any wickedness or error concerning those things that were alleged against them. Therefore, disregarding the opinion held about them, I made a practice of receiving them familiarly and of defending them especially from their pursuers.

It was said against them that under the pretext of religion they dissolved marriages; that they claimed baptism did not entirely remove sins; that if someone performed penance for three years for his iniquities, he was afterward permitted to live wickedly; and that if, under compulsion, they anathematized something of which they were accused, they claimed that they were in no way held by the bond of the anathema.

If there are people who most certainly hold or believe such things, there is no doubt that they are not Christians. Both I and all catholic bishops, and the universal Church, anathematize them, because they think and speak things contrary to the truth.

If they say that marriages ought to be dissolved for the sake of religion, it must be understood that, although human law has permitted this, divine law has forbidden it. The Truth himself says: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6). He also says: “It is not permitted to dismiss one’s wife except on account of fornication” (ibid.).

Who, then, could contradict this heavenly Lawgiver? We know that it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). If husband and wife are one flesh, and for the sake of religion a man dismisses his wife, or a woman her husband who remains in this world or perhaps goes over to unlawful practices, what sort of conversion is this, in which the same one flesh partly passes over to continence while partly remains in pollution?

But if both agree to lead a continent life, who would dare to condemn this, when it is certain that almighty God, who has permitted lesser things, has not forbidden greater ones? We know many saints who first led a continent life with their wives and afterward entered the governance of the holy Church.

Holy men customarily abstain even from lawful things in two ways: sometimes to increase their merit before almighty God, and sometimes to wipe away the sins of their former life.

The three young men who had been brought into the service of the king of Babylon asked for vegetables to eat (Dan. 1:12) and refused the royal foods (ibid., 5), not because it would have been sinful to eat what God created. They refused, therefore, to take what was permitted, so that their virtue might grow through abstinence.

David, however, who had taken another man’s wife and had been severely scourged for his guilt, later refused to drink water from the cistern at Bethlehem (2 Sam. 23:16). When the bravest soldiers brought it to him, he refused to drink it and poured it out as a libation to the Lord (ibid.). He could have drunk it if he had wished, but because he remembered that he had yielded to what was unlawful, he laudably abstained even from what was lawful.

He who earlier, because of his guilt, had not feared to shed the blood of dying soldiers afterward judged that, if he drank the water, he would also have drunk the blood of soldiers who had died on his account, saying: “Shall I drink the blood of these men who went at the risk of their lives?” (ibid., 17).

Therefore, when good spouses desire either to increase their merit or to wipe away the sins of their former life, they may bind themselves to continence and seek a better life. But if the husband refuses the continence desired by his wife, the marriage may not be divided, because it is written: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does” (1 Cor. 7:4).

If there are people who say that sins are forgiven in baptism only superficially, what could be more faithless than this teaching? By it they hasten to dissolve the very sacrament of faith, in which the soul is principally bound to the mystery of heavenly purity, so that, radically freed from all sins, it may cling to him alone concerning whom it is written: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 73:28).

Certainly the passage through the Red Sea was a figure of holy baptism (1 Cor. 10:2). In it the enemies died behind them, but others were found before them in the wilderness. Thus, for all who are immersed in holy baptism, all their former sins are loosed, because, like the Egyptians, their enemies die behind them.

But in the wilderness we encounter other enemies before we reach the land of promise. Many temptations weary us and hasten to block the path of those journeying toward the land of the living.

Therefore, whoever says that sins are not completely forgiven in baptism should say that the Egyptians did not truly die in the Red Sea. But if he admits that the Egyptians truly died, he must admit that sins completely die in baptism, since the truth is plainly more powerful in our absolution than the shadow of truth.

In the Gospel the Lord says: “He who has been washed needs only to wash his feet, but is entirely clean” (John 13:10). If sins are not completely forgiven in baptism, then the one who has been washed is not entirely clean. For one cannot be called entirely clean if something of sin remains in him. But no one can resist the voice of the Truth, which says: “He who has been washed is entirely clean” (ibid.). Therefore nothing of the contamination of sin remains in the one whom the Redeemer himself declares to be entirely clean.

If there are people who say that for any sin one must do penance for three years and then live in pleasures after the three years, they have not yet understood either the precepts of the true faith or the commands of sacred Scripture.

The eminent preacher Paul speaks against them: “He who sows in his flesh will also reap corruption from his flesh” (Gal. 6:8). Again he says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. 8:8). Then he adds to the disciples: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit” (ibid., 9). Those are in the flesh who live in carnal pleasures.

Against them it is said: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:50). But if they say that a short period of penance ought to suffice for sin, so that afterward one may return to sin, the judgment of the first shepherd rightly strikes them: “What happened to them is according to the true proverb: The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mire” (2 Pet. 2:22).

Penance is a great virtue against sin, but only if a person perseveres in that same penance. For it is written: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

Hence it is written: “He who is baptized by a dead person and again touches him, what does his washing profit him?” (Sir. 34:30). Every perverse work that leads to death, that does not live the life of righteousness, is dead. Therefore he is baptized by a dead person and again touches him who mourns the evil works he remembers having committed but becomes entangled in the same works again after his tears.

The washing of that dead person profits such a soul nothing, because by doing again what it lamented, it does not rise to the uprightness of justice even through the lamentation of penance. Truly to do penance is to mourn what has been committed and to avoid again the things that must be mourned.

If there are people who say that, when someone under compulsion anathematizes something, he is not held by the bond of the anathema, they are themselves witnesses that they are not Christians. They think that the bonds of the holy Church can be loosened by empty efforts, and therefore they do not consider the absolution of the holy Church—which it grants to the faithful—to be genuine if they do not believe that its commission has force.

There is no need to dispute at length against them, because they must be utterly despised and anathematized, so that, in the very matter through which they believe they are deceiving the truth, they may truly be bound in their sins.

Therefore, if there are people who, under the Christian name, dare either to preach these propositions of error that we have mentioned or silently to hold them within themselves, we unquestionably anathematize them.

[Col. 1119D] Nevertheless, among all the propositions, I found absolutely no one of the aforementioned errors in those who used to come to me in the royal city, as I have said; nor do I think that such an error existed among them, for if it had existed, I would have recognized it.

Since, however, there are many of the faithful who are inflamed by ignorant zeal, and who, while pursuing certain people as though they were heretics, often create heresies, we must take care of their weakness. As I have said, they must be calmed by reason and gentleness.

They are like those of whom it is written: “I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2).

Therefore your Excellence, who continually lives in reading, tears, and almsgiving, ought, as I have requested, to calm their ignorance through gentle exhortations and answers, so that you may find the glory of eternal recompense not only from yourself but also from them.

Excessive love moved me to say these things to you, because I consider myself to grow in your joy and to diminish in your sadness. May almighty God protect you by heavenly grace and, with the Lord’s mercy preserved and the Lord’s most devout tranquility, prolong your life for the nourishment of your little lords.

**Letter of Pope Gregory to Augustine**

To the most reverend and most holy brother AUGUSTINE, GREGORY, servant of the servants of God.

Denual, a devout presbyter sent by you, brought me welcome news when he reported that you were safe and, by God’s favor, informed me that he was making progress in the ministry for which he had been sent. He also delivered letters sent by you, in which you indicated that the Lord’s field, lying uncultivated and overgrown with the thorns of unbelief, had received the seed of the word under the plough of your teaching and had produced a fruitful harvest of faithfulness. In the same letters you appended certain chapters, asking how this holy apostolic Roman Church holds or teaches these matters.

It is entirely fitting, since the blessed apostle Peter was the beginning both of the apostolate and of the episcopate, and since you have consulted me about the condition of the Church—not from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but from the grace “which opens the mouth of the dumb and makes the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wis. X, 21)—that we should declare, by the teaching of apostolic vigor, how you ought to act.

First, it was asked how many generations of relatives may be joined in marriage. We say that, certainly, so long as they recognize one another as related, they ought not to enter into such a union. But because moderation is preferable to strict severity, especially among so barbarous a people, it should be permitted that they marry after the fourth generation.

You also stated that if a woman, overcome by illness, is unable to render to her husband the marital debt, what should her husband do. It would be good if he remained so that he might devote himself to continence. But because this is the practice of the strong, let the man who cannot remain continent marry instead; nevertheless, he must not withdraw assistance from the woman whom illness hinders, and whom no detestable guilt excludes.

If a presbyter or any priest is accused by the people, and there are no certain witnesses [Col. 1120D] who can establish the truth of the charge brought against him, an oath shall be required, and he shall produce as witness to the purity of his innocence him “to whom all things are naked and open” (Heb. IV, 13); thus he shall remain in his own rank. For a man who has been confirmed by a bishop must not again be subjected to such a repetition of the procedure.

At the solemn celebration of Mass, the practice given by our Lord Jesus Christ to his holy disciples must be observed: for he took the cup and gave it to them, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this whenever you receive it” (Matt. XXVI, 28). Therefore it is not appropriate to place two or three cups on the altar when the solemn celebration of Mass is being performed.

You also consulted us about sacrificial foods, asking whether, when the faithful are told what was mentioned above, they should make the life-giving sign of the cross over them or not. It is sufficient to answer with what the blessed Apostle says: “If anyone says, ‘This has been sacrificed,’ do not eat it, on account of the one who pointed it out and on account of conscience” (1 Cor. X, 28).

You further added that if a father or mother entrusts a son or daughter, during the years of childhood, within the enclosure of a monastery, to formation under a rule, are they permitted, after completing the years of puberty, to leave and marry? We absolutely reject this, because it is wrong that children offered to God by their parents should later be allowed to loosen the reins of desire.

Indeed, you have confessed that certain people were baptized without being questioned about the Creed, by adulterous and unworthy presbyters. In these cases let your beloved self observe the ancient custom of the Church: whoever has been baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit may not be baptized again. For he received the gift of this grace not in the name of the one who baptized him, but in the name of the Trinity. Let what the Apostle says be upheld: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV, 5). We charge you, moreover, to impart spiritual teaching to such people with particular diligence.

## The questions of Saint Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury, begin, together with the responses of Pope Gregory

### Question of the blessed Augustine, bishop of the Church of Canterbury, concerning how bishops should conduct themselves with their clergy, what portions should be made of the offerings that come to the altar through the prayers of the faithful, and how a bishop should act in the Church

### Gregory’s response

Holy Scripture bears witness—a text I do not doubt you know well—and especially the blessed Paul’s Letters to Timothy, in which he took pains to teach how Timothy ought to conduct himself in the house of God. It is the custom of the apostolic see to give ordained bishops this instruction: from every income that comes in, four portions are to be made—one for the bishop and his household, for the sake of hospitality and reception; another for the clergy; a third for the poor; and a fourth for the repair of churches.

But because your fraternity, instructed in the rules of monasteries, ought not to live separately from its clergy, you should establish among your clergy in the English Church—which, by God’s authority, has recently been brought to the faith—the manner of life that existed among our fathers at the beginning of the newborn Church, among whom “none of them said that any of the things he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common” (Acts IV, 32).

If there are clergy outside the sacred orders who cannot maintain continence, they ought to take wives and receive their stipends separately. For we know that it is written concerning those whom we have mentioned above, “it was distributed to each according to his need” (ibid., 35). Their stipends, too, must therefore be considered and provided for, and they must be kept under ecclesiastical discipline, so that they may live uprightly, devote themselves to the singing of psalms, and, with God’s help, preserve their hearts, tongues, and bodies from every unlawful act.

For those living a common life, what need is there for us to speak about making portions, offering hospitality, or fulfilling mercy, when everything that remains must be distributed for pious and religious purposes, as the Lord and Master of all teaches: “Give what remains as alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI, 41)?

### Augustine’s question

Since the faith is one, why are the customs of the Churches different? Why is the custom of Mass observed one way in the holy Roman Church and another way in the Churches of Gaul?

### Gregory’s response

Your fraternity knows the custom of the Roman Church, in which you remember having been nourished and which you greatly love. But I would have you choose carefully, whether in the Roman Church, in the Churches of Gaul, or in any other Church, whatever you have found that may please almighty God more, and introduce into the English Church, which is still new to the faith, the principal institutions that you have been able to gather from many Churches.

Things are not to be loved on account of places, but places on account of good things. Therefore choose from each Church whatever is pious, religious, and right, and, having gathered these things as though into a bundle, establish them as a custom among the minds of the English.

### Augustine’s question

I ask what penalty should be imposed if someone steals something from a church.

### Gregory’s response

Your fraternity can judge how the thief may be corrected according to the person of the thief. Some commit theft despite possessing adequate means, while others offend in this matter because of poverty. Thus some must be corrected by fines, others by blows; some more strictly, others more lightly.

When the correction is somewhat severe, it must be carried out from charity, not from anger, since it is done for the benefit of the one being corrected, so that he may not be handed over to the fires of Gehenna. We must maintain discipline among the faithful as good fathers customarily do with their earthly children: they strike them for their faults, yet seek to have as heirs those whom they afflict with pain, and preserve for those whom they seem to pursue in anger whatever they possess.

This charity must therefore be held in mind, and it must itself determine the measure of correction, so that the mind does absolutely nothing outside the rule of reason.

You also ask how those who have stolen things from churches should return them. But far be it from the Church to receive with increase what it appears to have lost from earthly goods, and to seek profits from empty things.

### Augustine’s question

May two full brothers each marry one of the sisters descended from those brothers through a long line of ancestors?

### Gregory’s response

This is entirely permissible. For nowhere in the sacred writings is anything found that appears to contradict this matter.

### Augustine’s question

Up to what generation may a believer marry a relative, or a stepmother, or a kinswoman, if such a marriage is permitted?

### Gregory’s response

Indeed, the civil law in the Roman state permits the son and daughter of a brother and sister, or of two full brothers, or of two full sisters, to marry. But experience has taught us that offspring cannot flourish from such a union, and the sacred law forbids exposing the shame of kinship. Therefore it is necessary that believers should be permitted to marry in the third or fourth generation. The second generation, as we have said, must entirely refrain from intermarriage.

To have relations with one’s stepmother is a grave offense, because it is also written in the Law: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father” (Lev. XVIII, 7). A son cannot literally uncover his father’s nakedness; but because it is written, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24), whoever presumes to uncover the nakedness of his stepmother, who was one flesh with his father, will clearly uncover his father’s nakedness.

It is also forbidden to have relations with a kinswoman, because through the union of those who came before her she became the flesh of a brother. For this reason John the Baptist was beheaded and crowned with holy martyrdom (Matt. XIV, 10). He was not told to deny Christ, nor was he killed for confessing Christ. But because our Lord Jesus Christ had said, “I am the truth” (John XIV, 6), and John was killed for the truth, he evidently shed his blood for Christ.

Since there are people among the English who, while they were still unbelievers, are said to have entered into this wicked union, once they come to the faith they must be admonished to abstain from it, to recognize that it is a grave sin, and to fear God’s terrible judgment, lest for the sake of carnal pleasure they incur the torments of eternal punishment.

Nevertheless, they must not on this account be deprived of communion in the sacred body and blood of the Lord, lest we appear to punish in them what they bound themselves to through ignorance before the washing of baptism. In the present age the holy Church corrects some things with zeal, tolerates others with gentleness, and overlooks and bears still others with discernment, so that often, by bearing and overlooking the evil it detests, it may restrain it.

All who come to the faith must be admonished not to dare to commit anything of this kind. If they have committed it, they must be deprived of communion in the body and blood of the Lord, because, just as guilt is to some extent tolerated in those who acted through ignorance, so it must be vigorously pursued in those who were not afraid to sin knowingly.

### Augustine’s question
