If a great distance lies between us, so that bishops cannot easily meet, may bishops be ordained without the presence of other bishops?

### Gregory’s response

Indeed, in the English Church, in which you alone are found to be a bishop, you cannot ordain a bishop in any other way than without bishops. For when bishops come from Gaul, who will be present as witnesses at the ordination?

But we wish your fraternity to ordain bishops in such a way that the bishops themselves are not separated from one another by great distances, so that there may be no necessity preventing them from meeting at the ordination of a bishop. Since the presence of some pastors is also extremely useful, they ought to be able to meet with the greatest ease.

Therefore, when, by God’s authority, bishops have been ordained in neighboring places, an episcopal ordination should in every respect not take place without the gathering of three or four bishops.

For the wise and mature ordering of spiritual matters, we can take an example even from earthly affairs. Certainly, when marriages are celebrated in the world, married couples are invited, so that those who have already preceded others on the path of marriage may share in the joy of the subsequent union. Why, then, should not those who may rejoice in the advancement of the bishop being ordained, and who may together pour out prayers to the Lord for his protection, come together with us at this special ordination, through which a man is joined to God by sacred ministry?

### Augustine’s question

How should we deal with the bishops of Gaul and Britain?

### Gregory’s response

We grant you no authority over the bishops of Gaul, because from the ancient times of my predecessors the bishop of Arles has received the pallium, and we must not deprive him of the authority he has received.

If, therefore, your fraternity happens to go into the province of Gaul, you should act together with that same bishop of Arles, so that any faults among the bishops may be corrected. If he should perhaps prove lukewarm in the vigor of discipline, he must be kindled by the zeal of your fraternity. We have also written to him, so that, when your holiness is present in Gaul, he too may assist with his whole mind and restrain from the conduct of the bishops whatever is contrary to the command of our Creator.

You yourself, however, will not be able to judge the bishops of Gaul by your own authority. Instead, by persuasion, gentleness, and showing them your good works as an example for imitation, reform the minds of the wicked toward the pursuit of holiness. For it is written in the Law: “When you pass through another man’s harvest, you shall not put in the sickle, but you shall pluck the ears with your hand and eat” (Deut. XXIII, 25).

You cannot put the sickle of judgment into a field that appears to have been entrusted to another. But through the effect of good works, strip the Lord’s grain of the chaff of its vices, and by urging and persuading, as though by chewing, convert it into the body of the Church.

Whatever must be done by authority should be done together with the aforementioned bishop of Arles; nor may what the ancient constitution of the Fathers established be omitted.

We entrust all the bishops of Britain to your fraternity, so that the unlearned may be taught, the weak strengthened by persuasion, and the perverse corrected by authority.

### Augustine’s petition

I ask that relics of the holy martyr Sixtus be sent.

### Gregory’s concession

We have done what you requested, so that the people who formerly claimed to venerate the body of the holy martyr Sixtus at that place—although the body seems to your fraternity neither genuine nor truly holy—may receive the certain benefits of a most holy and proven martyr and not worship an uncertain one.

It nevertheless seems to me that, if the body which the people believe to belong to a certain martyr shines there with no miracles, and if there are no older people who claim to have heard of his passion from their parents, the relics you requested should be deposited separately, while the place in which the aforesaid body lies should be closed off in every way. The people must not be permitted to abandon what is certain and venerate what is uncertain.

### Augustine’s question

Should a pregnant woman be baptized, or, after she has given birth, how long should she wait before entering the church, or even before being baptized, lest she be overtaken by death? If she has given birth, after how many days may she receive the sacrament of holy baptism? After how long may her husband unite with her in sexual intercourse? And if she is subject to her menstrual period, may she enter the church, receive the sacrament of holy communion, or unite with her husband before she has been washed with water? If she may enter the church, may she also approach the mystery of holy communion? All these matters ought to be made known to the inexperienced English people.

### Gregory’s response

I have no doubt that your fraternity has asked this of me, although I think I have already given you an answer. But since you yourself were able to say and think these things, I believe that you wished my response to confirm them for you.

Why should a pregnant woman not be baptized, since, in the eyes of almighty God, the fruitfulness of the flesh is not a fault? When our first parents sinned in paradise, they lost the immortality they had received through God’s just judgment. Yet almighty God did not wish to destroy the human race completely because of its sin: he took immortality away from humanity because of its offense, but in the kindness of his mercy he preserved for it the fruitfulness of offspring.

Therefore, how can what was preserved for human nature by the gift of almighty God be forbidden the grace of holy baptism? In that mystery, in which every fault is utterly extinguished, it would be exceedingly foolish to suppose that the gift of grace could be opposed.

When a woman has given birth, after how many days she should enter the church you have learned from the command of the Old Testament: she is to abstain for thirty-three days in the case of a male child (Lev. XII, 4), and sixty-six in the case of a female child (ibid., 5). This, however, must be understood symbolically. If she enters the church at the very hour after giving birth to give thanks, she is not burdened by any weight of sin. The fault lies in the pleasure of the flesh, not in the pain; for pleasure occurs in sexual intercourse, while in bringing forth offspring there is groaning. Hence the Lord himself, the first teacher of all, said: “In pain you shall give birth” (Gen. III, 16).

If we forbid a woman who has given birth to enter the church, we turn her very penitence into a fault. But neither a woman who has given birth, nor what she has given birth to, may be prevented from being baptized if the danger of death is pressing. Nor may she herself be prevented from being baptized at the very hour when she gives birth, or the child at the same hour in which it is born. For just as the grace of the holy mystery must be provided with great discernment to those who are living and capable of understanding, so it must be offered without any delay to those whose death is imminent, lest, while time is still being sought for providing the mystery of redemption, a slight delay should intervene and no one remain to be redeemed.

Her husband must not approach her for intercourse until the child who has been born has been weaned. A wicked custom, however, has arisen among married people: women disdain to nurse the children they bear and hand them over to other women to be nourished. This appears to have arisen solely from lack of continence, because women who refuse to remain continent disdain to nurse the children they have borne.

Women who, through this wicked custom, hand their children over to others to be nourished must not unite with their husbands until the time of purification has passed. Indeed, even apart from childbirth, women who are undergoing their customary menstrual period are forbidden to unite with their husbands, so that the sacred law strikes with death any man who approaches a menstruating woman.

A woman, however, while suffering her menstrual period, must not be forbidden entry into the church, because the natural excess that she experiences cannot be counted as her fault. Since she suffers it unwillingly, it is not right that she be deprived of entrance into the temple.

We know that the woman who suffered from an issue of blood came humbly behind the Lord, touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her illness departed from her (Matt. IX, 20, 22). If, therefore, a woman in an issue of blood could rightly touch the Lord’s garment, why should a woman suffering the flow of menstrual blood not be permitted to enter the Lord’s church?

But you say: “Illness compelled that woman, whereas custom binds those of whom we speak.” Consider, dearest brother, that everything we suffer in this mortal flesh is, because of the weakness of nature, ordered by the just judgment of God as a consequence of sin. To hunger, thirst, be hot, be cold, or grow weary belongs to the weakness of nature. What else is it to seek food against hunger, drink against thirst, breezes against heat, clothing against cold, and rest against weariness, than to seek certain remedies against illnesses?

A woman’s menstrual flow is also an illness. If, therefore, it was rightly presumed that the woman, placed in illness, touched the Lord’s garment, and what was granted to one infirm person is not denied, why should it not be granted to all women who are infirm through the defect of their nature?

They must not be forbidden to receive the mystery of holy communion during those same days. If, out of great reverence, a woman does not presume to receive it, she is to be praised; but if she does receive it, she is not to be judged.

It is characteristic of good minds to recognize their faults in some way even where there is no fault, because often something that comes from fault is done without fault. Thus, when we hunger, we eat without fault, although hunger came to us through the fault of the first human being.

A woman’s menstrual period is not itself any fault, since it occurs naturally. But the fact that nature itself has been corrupted, so that a woman appears to be polluted without any intention of her will, derives from sin. In this defect human nature recognizes what it has become through judgment, and the human being who willingly committed the fault bears the guilt of that fault unwillingly.

Therefore, when women consider themselves and, during their menstrual period, do not presume to approach the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, they are to be praised for their proper reverence. But when, through the custom of a religious life, they are carried by love of the same mystery toward receiving it, they must not be restrained, as we have already said.

Just as external works are observed in the Old Testament, so in the New Testament attention is directed not so much to what is done outwardly as to what is thought inwardly, so that judgment may be passed with subtle discernment.

Although the Law forbids the eating of many things as unclean, the Lord nevertheless says in the Gospel: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but the things that come out of the mouth are what defile a person” (Matt. XV, 11). A little later he explains: “From the heart come evil thoughts” (ibid., 19). It must be judged abundantly from this that what is shown to be polluted in action by almighty God is generated from the polluted root of thought.

The apostle Paul likewise says: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus I, 15). Immediately afterward, declaring the causes of their defilement, he adds: “For both their mind and their conscience are defiled” (ibid.).

If food is not unclean for one whose mind is pure, why should what a woman suffers naturally with a pure mind be counted as defilement for her?

A man who sleeps with his own wife must not enter the church unless he has washed with water; yet even after washing he should not enter immediately. The Law commanded the ancient people that a man who had intercourse with a woman should wash with water and not enter the church before sunset. This can be understood spiritually in a particular way: a man unites with a woman when his mind, through illicit desire, joins itself to her in thought by pleasure. Unless the fire of desire has first cooled in his mind, he ought not to consider himself worthy of the assembly of the brethren, since he sees himself burdened by the wickedness of improper pleasure.

Although different peoples have different opinions about this matter and appear to observe different practices, it has always been the custom of the Romans, from ancient times, after intercourse with one’s own wife, to seek purification by washing and then, out of reverence, to abstain for a short time from entering the church.

In saying this we do not declare marriage itself to be a fault. But because even lawful intercourse with one’s wife cannot take place without carnal pleasure, one must abstain from entering the sacred place, since pleasure cannot exist without some fault.

The one who said, “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. L, 7), was not born of fornication or adultery. Because he knew himself to have been conceived in iniquities, he lamented that he had been born in sin: a tree bears in its branch the corruption that it drew from its root.

In these words, however, he does not call the intercourse of married couples iniquity, but the pleasure itself. There are many lawful and legitimate unions, yet in the act of them we are defiled to some degree, just as we often pursue faults in anger and disturb the tranquillity of our minds. What is done may be right, yet the disturbance of mind accompanying it is not commendable.

He was angry against the vices of sinners when he said, “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. VI, 8). Since a tranquil mind alone can raise itself to the light of contemplation, he grieved that his very eye had been troubled by anger: while pursuing evil deeds below, he was forced to be confused and disturbed and was unable to contemplate higher things.

Anger against vice is therefore praiseworthy, yet also burdensome, because the person who experienced it judged that, by becoming troubled, he had incurred guilt.

Thus lawful sexual intercourse ought to be for the sake of offspring, not pleasure; the union of flesh ought to be for the grace of producing children, not the satisfaction of vice.

If someone uses his wife not seized by the desire for pleasure but solely for the sake of producing children, he must be left to his own judgment concerning either entering the church or receiving the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood. We must not forbid him to receive it, since he does not know how to be burned even when placed in fire.

But when pleasure, rather than love of producing offspring, dominates the act of intercourse, married people have something to lament even in their union. Holy preaching permits this to them, yet fear still shakes the mind because of the permission itself.

When the apostle Paul said, “Let him who cannot remain continent have his own wife” (1 Cor. VII, 2), he immediately took care to add: “But I say this by way of concession, not by command” (ibid., 6). What is lawful and just is not conceded as an indulgence. Therefore, by saying that it is conceded, he showed that it involves fault.

It must also be weighed with vigilant attention that on Mount Sinai the Lord commanded the people to abstain from women (Exod. XIX, 15). If there, where the Lord spoke through a creature subject to human beings, bodily purity was required with such care that those who were to receive God’s words were not to have intercourse with women, how much more ought women who receive the body of the almighty Lord preserve themselves in bodily purity, lest they be burdened by the immeasurable greatness of the mystery itself?

For this reason the priest also says to David concerning his young men that, if they are pure from women, they may receive the bread of the Presence; they would certainly not receive it unless David first declared them pure from women (1 Sam. XXI, 4).

A man who, after intercourse with his wife, has washed with water may receive the mystery of holy communion only when, according to the judgment established above, he is also permitted to enter the church.

### Augustine’s question

After the nocturnal emission that commonly occurs in sleep, may anyone receive the Lord’s body, or may a priest celebrate the sacred mysteries?

### Gregory’s response

The Testament of the ancient law calls such a person unclean, as we have already said in the preceding chapter, and does not permit him to enter the church until evening unless he has washed with water.

This, however, must be understood specifically with reference to that people and spiritually according to the same interpretation we have already given: the person who is tempted by impurity and defiled in his thoughts by empty images is, as it were, polluted through a dream.

He must be washed with water so that he may cleanse the faults of his thought with tears. Unless the fire of temptation has first withdrawn, he should recognize himself as guilty, as it were, until evening.

But in this same nocturnal emission very careful discernment is necessary. One must subtly consider from what cause it arose in the sleeping mind. Sometimes it occurs from overeating, sometimes from an excess of nature, sometimes from thought, and sometimes through illness.

When it results from an excess of nature or from illness, this occurrence is not at all to be feared, because it is more a matter for grief that someone has suffered it without the knowledge of his mind than that he has caused it.

But when the appetite for food is carried beyond measure in eating, and the reservoirs of bodily fluids are consequently burdened, the mind incurs some guilt. Nevertheless, this does not go so far as to prohibit receiving the holy mystery or celebrating the solemnities of Mass, especially when a feast day requires it or necessity compels the priest to perform the mystery because no other priest is present.

If others are available who can perform the ministry, an emission caused by overeating should not prevent the reception of the sacred mystery. But, in my judgment, the priest should humbly abstain from offering the sacred mystery if shameful images have disturbed the mind of the sleeper.

There are some in whom such an occurrence usually arises without their mind being defiled by shameful images even while their body sleeps. In this matter one thing is revealed: the mind itself is not guilty, yet it is not free by its own judgment, because although, while the body slept, it remembers seeing nothing, during wakefulness it remembers having fallen into gluttony.

But if the emission arises from the shameful thought of the sleeper, the mind’s guilt is evident. For it is clear from what root that defilement proceeded: what he consciously thought, he suffered unconsciously.

The thought itself must also be weighed: did it fall into suggestion, into pleasure, or, which is more serious, into consent to sin? Every sin is completed in three ways: by suggestion, by pleasure, and by consent. Suggestion comes through the devil, pleasure through the flesh, and consent through the spirit. For when the serpent first suggested the fault, Eve, as the flesh, took pleasure in it, while Adam, as the spirit, consented.

The mind must therefore disclose its own condition by exercising great discernment between suggestion, pleasure, and consent. When the evil spirit suggests sin to the mind, if no pleasure in sin follows, the sin has not been committed at all. When the flesh begins to take pleasure, sin begins to be born. But if the mind, after deliberation, descends even to consent, then sin is known to be complete.

In suggestion there is the beginning of sin; in pleasure, its nourishment; in consent, its completion. It often happens that what the evil spirit sows in thought is drawn by the flesh into pleasure, while the soul nevertheless does not consent to that pleasure.

Although the flesh cannot take pleasure without the soul, the mind itself, resisting the pleasures of the flesh, is nevertheless bound in some way by carnal pleasure against its will, so that it contradicts it by reason and does not consent, yet remains bound by pleasure and deeply laments that it is bound.

Hence that chief soldier of the heavenly army also lamented, saying: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” (Rom. VII, 23).

If he was captive, he was not fighting; yet he was fighting. Therefore he was both captive and not captive, and he was fighting. The law in his members was thus warring against the law of his mind. If he was fighting, he was not captive.

Behold, a human being is, so to speak, both captive and free: free because of the righteousness he loves, captive because of the pleasure he bears unwillingly.

## The Roman synod held by Pope Gregory I begins

While our Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever, in the time of the most pious and serene lords Maurice and Theodosius Tiberius, Augusti, in the thirteenth year of the reign of that same Lord Maurice, in the thirteenth indiction, on the fifth day of the month of July, Pope Gregory, seated before the most sacred body of the blessed apostle Peter with all the bishops of the Roman Church and the presbyters, while the deacons and the entire clergy stood present, said:

In this holy Roman Church, over which divine providence has willed me to preside, a highly reprehensible custom has arisen for some time: certain singers are chosen for the mystery of the sacred altar and, having been constituted in the order of deacons, devote themselves to vocal melody, although it would have been fitting for them to be free for the ministry of preaching and the pursuit of almsgiving.

Thus it frequently happens that, while an attractive voice is sought for the sacred ministry, a suitable life is neglected; and the singer, the servant of the Lord, is stimulated in his conduct while he delights the people with his voice.

Therefore, by the present decree I establish that in this see the ministers of the sacred altar must not sing. During the solemn celebration of Mass, they are to perform only the ministry of reading the Gospel. I decree that the psalms and the other readings be delivered by subdeacons or, if necessity requires, by those in the minor orders.

If anyone attempts to act contrary to this decree of mine, let him be anathema. And they all replied: Let him be anathema.

A disgraceful custom, arising from the sluggishness of indiscretion, has grown up: lay boys and secular persons attend upon the pontiffs of this see in the private services of the bedchamber. Since the life of a pastor must always be an example to his disciples, it often happens that the clergy do not know what the life of their pontiff is like in private, although, as has been said, secular boys know it.

Therefore, by the present decree I establish that certain men selected from the clergy or even from the monks shall attend upon the pontifical bedchamber, so that the one who occupies the place of governance may have as witnesses men who see his true conduct in private and who, through attentive observation, may take from it an example for their own progress.

A new and highly reprehensible custom has broken out in this church: whenever its administrators suspect that urban or rural estates may lawfully belong to them as part of their patrimony, they affix titles to them in the manner of the treasury and defend by force what they judge to belong to the poor rather than by judgment.

And since Truth says through its preachers, “Do nothing through contention (Phil. II, 2),” even the evil of contentious dispute is being surpassed, and whatever is judged capable of belonging to the Church is seized by force. Therefore, by the present decree I establish that if any ecclesiastic ever presumes, on his own initiative, to affix titles either to a rural or to an urban estate, let him be anathema. And all replied: Let him be anathema.

But if the one who presides over the Church either himself orders this to be done, or neglects to punish with fitting severity what has been done without his order, let him be anathema. And all replied: Let him be anathema.

Just as the minds of the faithful venerate us as unworthy through reverence for the blessed apostle Peter, so it is fitting for our weakness always to recognize itself and to avoid the burdens of the veneration bestowed upon it. For, through the affection of the faithful, a custom has arisen among the rulers of this see beyond what they deserve: when their bodies are carried out for burial, people cover them with dalmatics, then, out of reverence for their sanctity, tear those same dalmatics apart among themselves; and although many coverings are present for the sacred bodies of apostles and martyrs, something is taken from the body of sinners and preserved as though it were worthy of great reverence. Concerning this matter, by the present decree I establish that the bier on which the body of the Roman pontiff is carried for burial shall be covered by no covering. We decree that the presbyters and deacons of this see are to take responsibility for observing this decree. If anyone from their order neglects to attend to this, let him be anathema. And all replied: Let him be anathema.

Following the ancient rule of the Fathers, I establish that nothing is ever to be received for ordinations—neither for the giving of the pallium, nor for the delivery of documents, nor for that term which a new pretense born of ambition has invented, called the *pastellus*. For since the pontiff lays his hand upon the bishop being ordained, while a minister reads the Gospel lesson and a notary writes the letter of confirmation, just as it is not fitting for the pontiff to sell the hand that he lays upon someone, so the minister or notary ought not, in his ordination, to sell either his voice or his pen. Therefore I entirely prohibit the person who is to be ordained, or who has been ordained, from giving anything for ordination, the pallium, documents, or the *pastellus*. If anyone should presume to demand or request any advantage under the name of these things, let him be subject to guilt at the strict judgment of almighty God. But if the person who has been ordained, after receiving the documents and the pallium, wishes to offer something to anyone from the clergy solely as a gesture of gratitude—not because it was agreed upon, exacted, or requested—we in no way prohibit its acceptance, because his offering incurs no stain of guilt when it did not arise from the recipient’s ambition.

We know that many from the ecclesiastical household hasten to the service of almighty God, so that, freed from human servitude, they may be able to live in monasteries in the divine ministry. If we dismiss them indiscriminately, however, we provide everyone with an opportunity to escape the authority of ecclesiastical law. But if we carelessly retain those who are hastening to the service of almighty God, we are found to deny something to the one who gave all things. Therefore, if anyone wishes to turn from servitude under ecclesiastical law to the service of God, he must first be tested while living in lay clothing; and if his character and conduct bear witness to his good desire, he is to be permitted, without any hesitation, to serve almighty God in a monastery and to depart free from human service—he who, for the sake of divine service, desires to undertake a stricter servitude.

## Here begins the letter of Felix, bishop of Sicily, addressed to holy Gregory, pope of the Romans

[Col. 1132B]

To the most blessed Lord and honorable holy Father Gregory, Felix, a lover of your salvation.

The rights of your most blessed salvation and holiness are manifest before God, since, clearly, the whole earth has been filled with apostolic preaching and with the cultivation of the doctrine of true faith. Yet, through instruction in divine eloquence and through your exhortatory admonition, the orthodox Church of Christ—founded upon apostolic institution and most firmly strengthened by the faithful Fathers—is built up further. To this Church all the most blessed apostles, endowed with an equal fellowship of honor and power, brought the armies of the peoples, leading those whom divine predestination had foreknown, through saving precepts and admonitions, piously and holily “from darkness to light (I Pet. II, 9),” from the fall of unbelief to true faith, and from death to life.

Following the honored merits of these holy apostles and more perfectly fulfilling their examples, your fraternity adorns the Church of God with upright character and holiness of deeds. Flourishing in sacred faith and Christian conduct, it continually labors through pontifical efforts and accomplishes what it commands to be pleasing to God, observing the precepts of divine law, because, as the Apostle says, “it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified (Rom. II, 13).”

While we were reflecting on these matters, it was reported to us—as we learned from certain people coming from Rome—that your venerable holiness later ordained Augustine, our companion, as bishop for the English people and sent him there, and that you wrote to the English, whom we have learned were formerly converted to the faith through you, that those related in the fourth generation should not separate. This custom did not formerly exist among them or in these regions when I was brought up and instructed with you from childhood; nor have I read it in any decrees of your predecessors or in the institutions of the other Fathers, whether general or particular; nor have I hitherto learned that it was granted by any wise men. Rather, I have always found that the holy predecessors of your see and the other holy Fathers, assembled both at the Council of Nicaea and at other holy councils, determined that this should be observed as far as the seventh degree of their origin, and I have learned that upright and God-fearing people carefully take precautions concerning it.

While these matters were occupying our thoughts, other questions also arose, about which it seems necessary for us to consult your authority. Benedict, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, and some other brethren came to us, weeping and saying that they had been greatly troubled and distressed in mind by secular people and laymen because of their excessive actions, for which certain charges were also being brought against them. There are also certain churches in our province concerning whose consecration there is doubt; because of the antiquity of the matter and the negligence of their custodians, it is not known whether they were consecrated by bishops or not. Concerning all these matters we beg to be instructed by your holiness and by the authority of your see.

We also seek to be informed by your letters whether what we have heard you wrote specifically to the aforementioned Augustine, our companion and bishop, and to the English people was written generally to everyone. We desire to be fully informed about this and about the other matters mentioned above. We do not report to you what we have read and have learned is observed by the faithful in order to rebuke you—far be that from us—but we seek to know what we ought reasonably and faithfully to observe concerning these matters. And since no small murmur is circulating among us about this affair, we seek an answer from you, as from our head, concerning what we should reply to our brethren and fellow bishops, so that we may not remain uncertain about these matters, nor should any murmur remain among us and others, either in our own times or among posterity; nor should your reputation, which has always been good and excellent, be torn or gnawed by slander, or your name—far be it from us—be blasphemed in times to come.

For our part, humbly observing, with God as author, what is right, and bound to you by one bond of charity, we defend your religious authority in all things as faithful disciples and seek from you what is right. We know that, as the prelates of the holy see have always done—first the apostles, then their successors—you are charged with the care of the universal Church, and especially of the bishops, who are called its eyes because of contemplation and watchfulness; and that you continually think about religion and your law, as it is written: “Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. I, 2).”

This meditation is recognized not merely as observed in you through reading the written letters, but as firmly implanted in your conscience through Christ’s overflowing grace. The law of Christ and the sacred justice of the Lord never depart from your heart, as the Prophet says in the Psalms: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment. The law of his God is in his heart (Ps. XXXVI, 30–31).” It is written in your hidden places not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God—not on tablets of stone but on tablets of the heart.

We pray that every darkness of ignorance may be extinguished by your most wise responses and assistance, so that through you, most holy Father, the morning star may shine upon us, and so that a doctrinal definition may bring joy everywhere to all, by which the glorious Fathers of the holy Church are known to have proclaimed their own devout doctrines as a firm inheritance of eternal life.

And the subscription: May the Lord preserve you forever, holy Father of Fathers, safe and pleasing to God and praying for us. Amen.

## Reply of holy Pope Gregory to Felix, bishop of Sicily

To the most reverend brother Felix, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

Christ, our head, willed us to be his members for this purpose: that through his abundant charity and faith he might make us one body in himself. We ought to cling to him in such a way that, since without him we can be nothing, through him we may be what we are called. Let nothing divide us from the fortress of the head, lest, if we refuse to be his member, we be abandoned by him and, like branches cast from the vine, wither.

Therefore, if we wish to deserve to be the dwelling place of our Redeemer, let us remain in his love with the full devotion of our minds. For he himself says: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him (John XIV, 23).”

Your love, dearest brother, has therefore required that we respond to your inquiries by the authority of the apostolic see. Although we would have hastened to do this briefly and concisely, certain burdensome circumstances, which have come upon us through the hindrance of our sins, have prevented it. Nevertheless, we entrust to your diligence the task of investigating and examining these matters more extensively through the remaining institutions of the holy Fathers. For a mind weighed down by burdens and oppressive circumstances cannot accomplish as much good as one that is delighted and freed from oppression.

We have not endured these things in order to deny your holiness these or other matters that we recognize to be necessary, but so that what is found here in lesser measure may be investigated more broadly. Following the examples of your predecessors, you believed that the apostolic see in which you were nourished and instructed should be consulted on three matters: the union of blood relations, the harassment of bishops by their subjects, and uncertainty concerning the consecration of churches.

Regarding what I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English people and, as you recall, your own disciple, concerning unions between blood relatives, you should understand that I wrote specifically to him and to the English people, who had recently come to the faith, so that they would not withdraw in fear of harsher measures from the good undertaking they had begun; I did not write generally to the others. The entire city of Rome is witness to this.

Nor did I give them this written instruction with the intention that, once they had been firmly rooted and fully established in the faith, they should not separate if they were found within their own blood-relationship, or that they should marry within the line of affinity, that is, as far as the seventh generation. Rather, while they were still neophytes, it was necessary first to teach them repeatedly what was unlawful, to instruct them by words and examples, and thereafter reasonably and faithfully to exclude them from such conduct.

For, in accordance with the Apostle who says, “I gave you milk to drink, not food (I Cor. III, 2),” we granted this for them to observe now—not, as stated above, in later times—so that the good which had been planted while still weakly rooted would not be uprooted, but would be strengthened in its beginning and preserved until perfection. If in these matters we acted otherwise than we ought, you should understand that we did so out of compassion, not in order that this practice might be retained in the future. I therefore call upon God as witness, who knows the thoughts of all people, “before whose eyes all things are naked and open (Heb. IV, 13).”

For if I were to destroy what our predecessors established, I would rightly be shown to be not a builder but a destroyer, as Truth testifies when it says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand (Luke XI, 17).” Every knowledge and every law divided against itself will likewise be destroyed. Therefore it is necessary that we hold together all the statutes of our holy Fathers, doing nothing through contention, but united in every effort of good devotion and, with the Lord’s assistance, obeying the divine and apostolic constitutions.

O how good is charity, which presents absent persons through their image and present persons to one another through love; which unites what is divided, orders what is confused, joins what is unequal, and completes what is imperfect! How rightly the distinguished preacher calls it “the bond of perfection (Col. III, 14),” because the other virtues indeed produce perfection, but charity binds them together so that they cannot be separated from the love of the one who loves.

Having properly considered these matters, I granted what I have said out of charity. I did not issue a command, but advice; nor did I hand down a rule to be observed by any future generations in these matters. I merely showed which of two dangers would be easier to avoid. If, therefore, in secular affairs each person’s right and proper order must be preserved, how much more must no confusion be introduced into ecclesiastical arrangements, lest discord find a place where the blessings of peace ought to proceed? This will be preserved if nothing is attributed to power, but everything to equity.

For this reason our heart greatly rejoices with your greatness, because we find you so diligent in your actions that you both care for us and strive to investigate such matters by raising them, so that these efforts may obtain for you, with everyone’s assistance, not only glory among human beings but also rewards from almighty God.

As for the harassment of bishops, about which you wished to consult us, we know that the lives of prelates ought not to be disturbed by anyone’s excesses, because it is exceedingly unworthy that those who are called the thrones of God should be troubled by any agitation from others or from their subjects. Since David, the most just of kings, did not presume to lay a hand upon Saul, whom it was already clear had been rejected and cast away by the Lord (I Sam. XXIV, 7), how much more must care be taken lest anyone lay a hand of detraction, blame, lack of discernment, or dishonor upon the Lord’s anointed or upon the preachers of the holy Church, because their harassment or defamation concerns Christ, in whose place they exercise an embassy in the Church (II Cor. V, 20).

Therefore all the faithful must take the greatest care not to tear apart their bishop—that is, the Lord’s anointed—secretly or publicly through detraction or reproach, considering the example of Mary. Because she spoke against Moses, the servant of the Lord, on account of the Ethiopian woman (Num. XII, 1), she was punished with the most unclean leprosy (ibid., 10). There is also the saying of the Psalmist: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets (Ps. CIV, 15).” And it is written in the divine law: “You shall not speak evil of the gods, nor curse the ruler of your people (Exod. XXII, 28).”

Therefore subjects—both clerics and laypeople—must be especially careful not to dare to criticize the life of their bishops or superiors, lest, in rebuking evil, they be driven by pride into deeper evils. They must also be admonished that, when they observe the faults of their superiors, they should not become more audacious against them, but should judge their wrong actions privately, so that, restrained by fear of God, they do not refuse to bear the yoke of reverence under them.

The deeds of bishops or superiors are not to be struck down by the sword of the mouth, even when they appear rightly subject to criticism, because we know that our predecessors and many other holy men established that sheep should not lightly criticize their shepherds, nor presume to accuse or charge them. For when we sin against our superiors, we resist the ordinance of the one who placed them over us (Rom. XIII, 2). Thus, when Moses learned that the people were complaining against him and Aaron, he said: “What are we? Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord (Exod. XVI, 8).”

Therefore subjects of both orders must be admonished that, when they observe the actions of their teachers, they should return to their own hearts and not presume to rebuke them, because “a disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord (Matt. X, 24).”

Regarding the uncertainty about the dedication of churches, about which you wished to consult us among other matters, you should rightly hold to what we received as handed down by our predecessors: whenever there is doubt concerning the baptism or confirmation of certain persons, or concerning the consecration and dedication of churches, and no certain account exists either in writing or through witnesses as to whether the persons were baptized or confirmed, or whether the churches were consecrated, such persons should be baptized and confirmed, and the churches should be canonically dedicated. This is so that such uncertainty may not become a ruin for the faithful, since something is not shown to have been repeated when there is no reliable evidence that it was properly performed in the first place.

By the support of divine grace, we desire to hold to these principles, and, as you requested, we command you to hold and teach them. We also command you not arrogantly to interrupt what the holy Fathers before us established, but faithfully to preserve it. Therefore we implore the mercy of our Redeemer, that his grace may assist you in all things and grant you to accomplish what he has permitted you to desire.

As for each person’s descendants, among those who have been faithfully instructed and now stand firmly rooted, we decree that the seventh generation is to be observed without disturbance; and for as long as they recognize themselves as related by affinity, they must not enter into the union of such a marriage. Nor is it or will it ever be permitted to any Christian to take in marriage a woman whom someone had as a wife from his own blood-kindred, or whom he had defiled by any unlawful pollution. Such intercourse is incestuous and abominable to God and to all good people.

We read that the incestuous are not to be counted under the name of marriage, and we do not wish to be reproached by God in this matter by the other faithful, because what we granted to the English people in these matters was done not by establishing a model, but out of consideration, so that they would not abandon as incomplete the good of Christianity that they had begun.

Since, therefore, the benefits of reward increase in this matter in proportion as the labor of diligence increases, we greet you with paternal affection and exhort you to take advantage of the opportunity presented and to strive with greater effort in your effectiveness. By every possible means, insofar as it can be done, endeavor to act with the diligence of all, so that, with everyone’s assistance and the Lord’s help, you may fulfill your commendable desire.

Nor do we omit this part of our concern: all incestuous persons are to be separated from the thresholds of the holy Church until, through satisfaction and the prayers of the priests, they are canonically reconciled to that same holy Church. The wicked must be separated from the good and the unjust from the just, so that at least through their shame they may recognize their consciences and turn from their perversities.

If they appear incorrigible, they are to be separated from the faithful until they offer satisfaction, in accordance with the judgment of the Lord Savior, who says, among other things, concerning a brother who sins against him: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. If he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. But if he does not listen to them, tell it to the Church. And if he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector (Matt. XVIII, 15–17).”

By these and many other authorities of the holy Fathers, the wicked must be separated from the good, lest the just perish on account of the unjust, as it is written: “The just man perished for the unjust (I Pet. III, 18).” Distinction must always be made between the good and the wicked, just as there is a distinction between goats and sheep.

Manifest sins are not to be cleansed by secret correction; those who do harm openly must be rebuked openly, so that, while they are healed through public correction, those who sinned by imitating them may be corrected. When one person is rebuked, many are amended. It is better that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through one person’s license.

Nor is it surprising that this principle is maintained among human beings, since we often observe it among animals. Those that appear to have mange or scab are separated from the healthy, lest the others be condemned or perish through their disease. It is therefore better that the wicked be corrected openly than that the good perish on their account.

For this reason we wished all of you bishops to meet together, so that disputes might be held concerning cases that arise and a salutary discussion might take place concerning ecclesiastical observance. In this way, while past matters are corrected and future matters receive a rule, almighty God may everywhere rejoice through the concord of the brethren.

Know that if you observe these things, his presence will be with you, for it is written: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them (Matt. XVIII, 20).” If he deigns to be present where two or three are gathered, how much more will he not be absent where many priests assemble?

It is indeed not unknown that the rules establish that a council of the Fathers should be held twice each year. Nevertheless, lest there perhaps be any excuse, we decree that it be assembled once, so that, while a council is expected, nothing wicked and nothing unlawful may be presumed. For often, even if people refrain from something not out of love for justice, they nevertheless refrain through fear of judgment from what everyone knows could displease the tribunal.

Let us preserve this observance, dearest brother, for our successors. It is certain that if we devote ourselves wholeheartedly to saving commands, we shall escape every stain of vice. Therefore you ought to show yourselves especially diligent in all things toward the brethren and subjects, so that everyone may recognize that you—because you were brought up with us and know the teachers of the holy Roman Church—obey the precepts of the apostolic see and make its commands widely and openly known.

What we write in response to your letters specifically to you and to the charity of your brethren, we command all generally to observe. Let your fraternity be vigilant concerning the actions of your subjects. Let your example be their instruction, and your life their teacher. Through the exhortation of your tongue, let them learn what they should fear and be taught what they should love. Thus, when the profit of the entrusted talent is multiplied, may you deserve, on the day of recompense and by the favor of divine grace, to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord (Matt. XXV, 21).”

Moreover, we wish to know that you take full care of everything that we have written to you, to your other brethren, and generally to all concerning the prohibition of unlawful things. It is necessary that these matters be fulfilled with every effort and exertion through the vigilance of your fraternity, and that everything we have written there for the salvation of souls be faithfully reviewed. In this way you will show both your zeal and how displeasing unlawful acts are to you, and we shall appear to have made wise provision in choosing your person above others for this task.

May almighty God guard you with his protection and grant you to preserve the honor entrusted to you through your conduct. Amen.

[NOTE.]

[Col. 1138D] As may be inferred from the preface that Isidore placed before this work, this is where the collection of the decrees of councils and the sanctions of pontiffs, which the same presbyter and author brought together and collected into one volume, concludes.

The remaining constitutions that follow—namely, those of Gregory the Younger, Vitalian, Martin, Gregory III, and Zachary, Roman pontiffs—have been appended to the aforementioned collection because the old codices contain them in this form. Their authors likewise contributed many distinguished and excellent things to the Church, so that I judged it unworthy for the acts of such eminent prelates to be obliterated and passed over untouched.

## HERE BEGIN THE DECREES OF GREGORY THE YOUNGER

[Col. 1139A]

1. That no one dare take a presbyteress in marriage.  
2. Likewise, concerning a deaconess.  
3. Likewise, concerning a nun whom they call a servant of God.  
4. Concerning a spiritual co-mother.  
5. Concerning a brother’s wife.  
6. Concerning a niece.  
7. Concerning a stepmother or daughter-in-law.  
8. Concerning a female cousin.  
9. Concerning one’s own kinship, or a woman whom a kinsman had possessed.  
10. That no one abduct a widow as a wife.

[Col. 1139B]

11. Likewise, that no one abduct a virgin as a wife.  
12. Concerning diviners, soothsayers, enchanters, or amulets.  
13. Concerning the observance of the precepts of the Church.  
14. Concerning Adrian, son of Exhilaratus.  
15. Concerning Epiphania, a deaconess.  
16. That no one dare give consent.  
17. Concerning the hair of clerics, which is not to be left loose.

In the name of the Lord our Savior, Jesus Christ our God, while the most pious Lord Augustus Leo, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the sixth year, and in the seventeenth year after his consulship; and also in the second year of Constantine, his son and emperor; in the month of April, in the fourth indiction; with the most holy apostolic pope Gregory presiding in the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before the confession; and with the most holy bishops also seated: Agnellus of Ferentinum, Agnellus of Sutri, John of Beliternum, Triburatio of Filaris, Vitalis of Alatri, Anastasius of Tibur, Opportunus of Mauriana, John of Blera, Mauricianus of Sabina, Wiliarit of Narni, George of Portus, Sergius of Praeneste, Tiberius of Silva Candida, Peter of Camerino, Gregory of Anagni, Sindered, archbishop of Spama, George of Nepi, Sedulus, bishop of Britain, John of Signia, Fergustus, bishop of Scotland, Andrew of Albano, and Maurinus of Palmaria; as well as the venerable presbyters Sisinnius, John, another John, Eustratius, George, Thalassius, Marinus, Constantine, Gregory, John, Epiphanius, Marinus, John, and John; with the deacons also standing by—Peter the archdeacon, George of Orascho, and Benedict—and the entire clergy, Gregory, most holy and most blessed pope, seated in synod before the body of the most blessed Peter, said:

Since, through the heavenly mercy of the Lord, we are rulers of the Christian people, it is especially fitting that we repeatedly implore God’s protection for their salvation, lest—God forbid—because of the souls entrusted to us and frustrated by us, we be compelled to render a strict account before the shepherd of all, unless correction precedes us by preventing offenses.

When I consider or call to mind how watchfully we must stand on guard against the wickedness of each person’s crime, and how, whenever the enemy attacks in order to disturb the minds of the faithful, we must resist his assault with heavenly assistance, I am greatly shaken and waste away with anxiety, lest, through serpentine cunning, he deceive the more careless—God forbid. Yet, trusting in God’s great favor and concern, we must strive with a more tranquil mind, with divine help, for the salvation of all, so that we may deserve to stand before the eternal Judge with an unconfounded face, not struck down by anyone’s deceit, and hear the voice saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your Lord (Matt. XXV, 21).”

For this reason I say with a groan that I hear that certain Christian people living throughout the province of Italy are rashly acting against the Catholic faith and the statutes of the Fathers, to the extent that they presume to take women consecrated to God as wives and join close relatives in marriage. It is fitting that this be cut away with a spiritual sword and, if it pleases your holiness, uprooted from the roots, lest the crop of the good farmer, mixed with weeds, be defiled by dreadful thickets.

The most holy bishops and the venerable clergy replied: We truly recognize that, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the heart of your apostolate burns; and, so that the filth of such great misery may be wiped from the minds of the faithful from its roots, and so that the wound fixed in the body may be healed with a salutary antidote by closing the entrance of such misery, as has rightly been foreseen, through the prohibition of anathema, no Roman, Lombard, or person of any other nation washed in the waters of holy baptism should attempt this again. Thus, lest anyone oppressed by the burden of so great a crime fall through rashness or be swallowed in the abyss of iniquity, it must be avoided and uprooted from the roots.

After this unanimous response of all, Gregory, the apostolic pope, before the body of the aforesaid venerable chief of Christ’s apostles, pronounced the sentence:

I. If anyone takes a presbyteress in marriage, let him be anathema. And all replied: Let him be anathema.

II. If anyone takes a deaconess in marriage, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

III. If anyone takes in marriage a nun whom we call a servant of God, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

IV. If anyone takes a spiritual co-mother in marriage, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

V. If anyone takes his brother’s wife in marriage, let him be anathema. And all replied: Let him be anathema.

VI. If anyone takes a niece in marriage, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

VII. If anyone takes a stepmother or daughter-in-law in marriage, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

VIII. If anyone takes a female cousin in marriage, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

[Col. 1141A]

IX. If anyone takes as a wife a woman from his own kinship, or one whom a kinsman had had [as wife], let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

X. If anyone abducts a widow as a wife, or consents to such an act, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

XI. If anyone, unless he has betrothed her, abducts a virgin or carries her off as a wife, or consents to such an act, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

XII. If anyone consults diviners, soothsayers, or enchanters, or uses amulets, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

[Col. 1141B]

XIII. If anyone violates in any respect our apostolic commands previously issued to the Church concerning the Olive Groves and various places, and does not observe them in all things, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

XIV. Adrian, son of Exhilaratus, who, after the oath given in the apostolic confession, unlawfully and audaciously has Epiphania, the deaconess, as his wife, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

XV. Epiphania, the deaconess, who, after the aforementioned oath, fled away and became the wife of Adrian, son of Exhilaratus, let her be anathema. And all replied three times: Let her be anathema.

[Col. 1141C]

XVI. If anyone gave consent to him in so cruel an act, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

XVII. If anyone from the clergy lets his hair grow loose, let him be anathema. And all replied three times: Let him be anathema.

And the subscription: I, Gregory, bishop of the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, have subscribed to this constitution promulgated by us. I, Agnellus, bishop of the holy Church of Ferentinum, have subscribed to this constitution promulgated by us. I, John, humble bishop of the holy Church of Beliternum, have subscribed to this constitution promulgated by us. And the remaining fourteen bishops and four deacons [subscribed], on the Nones of April, in the fourth indiction.

## HERE BEGIN THE LETTERS OF POPE VITALIAN

Vitalian, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Paul, archbishop of Crete.

On the nineteenth day of the month of December of the present indiction, the eleventh, John, bishop of the city of Lampeon, presented to us within the venerable basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, a petition by which he earnestly requested and implored us—“by the terrible coming of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ,” as he said—that, according to the most sacred canons and the regulations of the holy Fathers, we should investigate the merits of his case and pronounce judgment. Immediately he also presented the judgment drawn up by your fraternity and subscribed by the hand of its author and by the hands of those bishops. Therefore, after some days, acceding to his requests, we caused a gathering of prelates to assemble in this city of Rome, so that, sitting with us, they might examine both his petition and the proceedings in priestly fashion.

While that synod of bishops was assembled in this Roman city to hear and deal with such a matter, copies of the same proceedings sent by your fraternity were immediately reported to us. Having received and compared them with one another, we found that they agreed in words and meaning with what the aforesaid bishop had presented to us, subscribed by the hands of the bishops and by your affection. We were therefore astonished that he had not sent this to you through his cleric. For if perhaps the unsuitable timing prevented this, why did he not send it to us without his written submission?

When the judgment had been read before our brother bishops, it seemed to us and to them that the case of the same John, bishop of Lampeon, had not been investigated and concluded according to the fear of God, nor according to the regulations of the Fathers and the sacred canons, and that his person had been subjected to penalties. For this reason we were deeply grieved, especially because the same John, bishop of Lampeon, had been sent under guard for several days and was thereafter brought to the secretariat of your fraternity so that, as he said, he might speak whatever you wished; then he was again led under guard to confinement, as the confession of the defender of your affection states in the judgment issued by him.

Moreover, although this was contrary to the commands of the canons and the provisions of the laws, he was urged to provide a surety. Then, at the time when he requested to come to us, your fraternity ought, in accordance with the force of the canons, to have released him by your letters. You not only refused to release him canonically so that he could come to the threshold of the prince of the apostles, but answered him indecently, saying, “Because you are not making a proper request.” Are the things sanctioned by the holy Fathers, then, indecent? Or are things pleasing to you deemed proper?

Finding the aforesaid John, the bishop, equally blameless, according to the wording of the judgment sent to us by you, we therefore caused him, together with us and the bishops, to proceed into the churches of God for the solemn celebration of Mass. Accordingly, by the authority of this command of ours, we establish and confirm that everything done or prepared by you and your synod contrary to the regulations of the canons and the decrees of the laws, as well as the judgment pronounced against him, is empty and void. Whatever is shown to have been taken from him or from his church by anyone, let your affection have it restored to him, preserving him entirely from loss.

We release herewith the named John, since he is innocent, by this our penitential command, so that, like the other bishops of your affection, he may conduct the affairs of his church with the fear of God and in conformity with the institution of the sacred rules.

Indeed, dearest brother, indeed we ought to repay like with like. Yet we believe that these things were done more through ignorance than through cunning. Therefore, strive to carry out immediately, according to God and for the Lord, what we command you and your synod to do, lest we be compelled to conduct ourselves not mercifully, but according to the force of the most sacred canons.

For it is written: “The Lord said: ‘Peter, I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brethren’” (Luke 22:32); and again: “Whatever you bind, Peter, on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

After your affection has reread this command of ours, let it surely return it through the penitential bearer to John the bishop, for the protection of himself and of his Church.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the eleventh indiction.

## Another letter of the same.

**Vitalian, to Vaani, chamberlain and imperial chartulary.**

Your Highness has always offered support to devout men, and has always willingly extended aid to those who live irreproachably. We have therefore judged it fitting, through this present letter of ours, to commend to you in all respects John, bishop of the Church of Lampeon, situated on the island of Crete, so that, with divine assistance going before him and supported by your help, he may be able to return quickly to the holy Church.

During the present month of September, in the eleventh indiction, he came to this city of Rome to the threshold of the apostles, the protectors of our eminence, and presented us with a petition in which he humbly begged us, after investigating the merits of his case, to conclude it canonically. He also presented to us the judgment which his metropolitan, together with his bishops, had pronounced against the same John, intending to show him blameworthy; by this judgment he subjected him to penalties contrary to the decrees of the canons. The same metropolitan also sent us a copy of it.

Therefore, having caused bishops to assemble in this city, we investigated his case, having read his petition. When the aforesaid judgment, sent to us by the same metropolitan, had also been read, it seemed to us that the judgment had not been pronounced according to the sacred canons. We therefore decreed that it should be empty and void, determining that the same John was innocent and that we found him to have undergone this without any fault on his part at the hands of his metropolitan. We rightly released him to return to his Church, writing to the metropolitan mentioned above that what he had done against John through simplicity, contrary to the decrees of the canons, was empty and void. [284]

Accordingly, commending the same John, the bishop, to your distinguished charity through these letters of ours, we release him here, so that he may proceed to your presence. We ask that you then hasten to release him with your letters to his Church, commending him to those whom you deem appropriate, so that he may remain unharmed. Indeed, together with me, he will pray throughout all the days of his life to the Lord for the prosperity and longevity of your most excellent charity.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh indiction.

## Another letter of the same to Paul of Crete.

**Vitalian, to Paul, bishop of Crete.**

We have judged it fitting to bring to the knowledge of your affection that John, bishop of the Church of Lampeon, has reported to us that two monasteries belonging to his parish—one called Palea and the other Arsilli—have been seized by your Church. Therefore, if this is so, we urge your most dear fraternity to have them restored to him according to the boundaries established by the holy canons, because we wish what is just to be preserved for each person, especially by our brethren.

We have also learned that a certain deacon named John, after he had been ordained a minister, took a wife, and not only this, but serves in two Churches. Therefore, if this is so, let your most beloved fraternity correct the matter for the love of God, lest such a crime occur again as an example to those who live wickedly.

Moreover, we have learned that you have a certain court official named Eulampius as an adviser. For, as has been reported to us, he is not known to be of good conduct. He is said to sow discord daily among the brethren, in order to fill his purse from their dissension. Therefore, if this is so, we urge your fraternity to cast him away from you, so that your reputation may flourish before God and men.

Given as above.

## Another letter of the same.

**Vitalian, to George, bishop of Syracuse.**

We have received from our beloved son Gaudentius, the primicerius, the proceedings—or judgment—sent by your fraternity, which had been transmitted to him by the bishop of the island of Crete concerning the case of the bishop of the Church of Lampeon. We were therefore astonished that the bishop of Crete had not sent this to us either through his cleric or by his letters, nor indicated what was necessary.

For the aforesaid John, of the Church of Lampeon, presented to us with his petition a judgment of this kind, subscribed by the hand of his metropolitan and by those of the bishops, requesting that the merits of his case be investigated canonically. Moved by his prayers, we caused a synod to assemble in this city concerning such a matter, so that the case might be examined.

When it had assembled, John’s petition and the judgment sent by your fraternity were read. It seemed to us and to them that these proceedings had been promulgated against the aforementioned bishop of the Church of Lampeon neither according to the most sacred canons nor according to the regulations of the Fathers. Therefore, by the authority of our command, we decreed that it was empty and void, releasing him to return to his Church with the command we addressed to his metropolitan.

Accordingly, when he comes there and joins your fraternity, let him receive such assistance from you that, with the commendatory letters of our excellent son Vaani, the imperial chamberlain and chartulary, he may return safely to his Church. In person he will certainly explain his case carefully to your fraternity when questioned by you, showing you a copy of our command sent to the metropolitan of Crete.

For this reason, Sylvinus will inform you of everything stated above, lest we be seen to overstep the bounds of the letters.

Given as above.

# Copy of a letter of Pope Martin to Amandus

**To his dearest brother Amandus, Martin.**

Receiving your letter, filled with the zeal of piety on the part of your fraternity, we recognize that our spirits are refreshed. For, despising the fleeting and transitory pleasures of this world, you are plainly intent on seeking those perpetual and sublime gifts which are granted in service to the Lord our God.

From the report of the bearer of this letter, according to the content of your fraternity’s letter, we have learned of the struggle of your labors. Through these labors, with the heavenly homeland approving, gifts of future joys are to be granted to you, whose minds are humble and whose bodies are contrite.

For nothing can at all be compared with what our Creator recompenses for good service. Since the labors that we endure for love of him are brought to an end within a brief and small span of time, we ought, in view of the refreshment to come, willingly to endure the hardships of the present life.

But just as the work of your labors brings us great abundance of joy, so we are distressed by the hardness of the priests of that people: setting aside the aids of their salvation and despising the service of our Redeemer, they are weighed down by the stench of vices. In order to prepare salvation, we must press upon them with untiring preaching as insistently as the doubling of the talents entrusted to us demands the completion of our stewardship, and as the Lord’s words urge us to receive his rest.

For it has been reported to us that presbyters, deacons, and others of priestly office fall into defilement after their ordination. Consequently, your fraternity is bound by excessive grief and wishes to lay down pastoral service because of their disobedience, choosing the labors of the episcopate and a life of silence and leisure rather than remaining in what has been entrusted to you. Yet the Lord says: “Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end” (Matthew 10:22).

From what does blessed perseverance arise, if not from the virtue of patience? For, according to apostolic preaching, “all who desire to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecutions” (2 Timothy 3:12).

Therefore, dearest brother, do not let the bitterness of afflictions constrain you from advancing in the purpose of your devout mind. Consider how much our Creator and Lord endured for our release and liberation, and to what insults he delivered himself, so that he might free us from the bonds of the devil’s power. Therefore, do not show compassion, to the destruction of the canons, toward those who fall into sins of this kind.

For anyone who has once fallen after his ordination shall thereafter remain deposed and will be able to attain no priestly rank. It is enough for him to continue in the same repentance throughout his life with constant lamentation and tears, so that by divine grace he may extinguish the offense committed.

If we seek for promotion to the sacred orders men whom no wrinkle and no taint of life impedes, how much more, if someone falls after his ordination and is found liable for the sin of transgression, must he be altogether forbidden to handle the mystery of our salvation with muddy hands and in a polluted state. According to the decrees of the sacred canons, let such a man remain deposed throughout this life, so that when the one who searches the inner depths of the mind—and who rejoices in none of the sheep going astray—sees his sincere repentance, he may find him reconciled at the terrible judgment.

Therefore, again we urge your charity, by the example of him who was willing to suffer and die for us, to remain ready in all the services of the one who did this. Let us not shrink from enduring temporal torments for Christ’s name; rather, let the benefits of future recompense persuade us to endure the troubles of this world.

For it is written: “What shall I repay to the Lord for all that he has repaid me? I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115:12).

As much is required of us as we are able to contribute through the service of our ministry. Since, through the clemency of the heavenly Majesty, everything that could be supplied by us to strengthen the hearts of your fraternity has undoubtedly been made clear to you, it remains for us to inform your fraternity about the other matters on which it consulted us by its letters.

We believe that it has reached you how, about fifteen years ago, during the disturbance of the true faith and the trampling down of the Catholic Church, an accursed and abominable heresy arose through Sergius, the false bishop of Constantinople, who had the then-ruling Heraclius as his ally. He renewed the errors of the Apollinarists, Severians, Eutychians, and Manichaeans. His successor, Pyrrhus—the same bishop who seized the see of Constantinople through the arrogance of ambition—increased it for the worse.

For this reason the apostolic see repeatedly admonished them through exhortations, protests, and many rebukes, so that they might withdraw from such error and return to the light of piety from which they had fallen.

And not only did they entirely refuse to do this, but now his successor Paul, the bishop of Constantinople and violator of the faith, devised an even worse attempt against the Catholic faith. As though destroying what had been heretically set forth by his predecessors, he persuaded our most clement prince to produce, by sacrilegious audacity, an imperial *type* completely filled with perfidy. In it was promulgated that all Christian peoples ought to believe.

Therefore, lest through some negligence we be bound by guilt for the ruin of the souls entrusted to us, we had to assemble in this city of Rome a general gathering of our brethren and bishops. In their presence, the criminal writings of the aforesaid heretics were examined and exposed. With one voice and one spirit, by the apostolic sword and the definitions of the Fathers, we condemned them, so that all, recognizing the error contained in them, might not be defiled in any way by their pollution.

For this reason we have decided to send you the volumes of the synodal proceedings, together with our encyclical, from which you can learn everything in detail, and extinguish their darkness with us as children of light.

Therefore let your fraternity strive to make these matters known to everyone, so that they may join us in execrating so abominable a heresy and learn the sacraments of their salvation; and, once a synodal undertaking of all the brethren and our fellow bishops in those regions has been completed according to the content of the encyclical sent by us, let them join in sending written acts to us together with your own writings, confirming and assenting to what we have recently established for the orthodox faith and for the destruction of the newly arisen madness of the heretics.

Let them also most wisely admonish and entreat our most excellent son Sigebert, king of the Franks, for the welfare of his Christian faith, to send us from among our brethren beloved bishops who, by a legation of the apostolic see and with God’s merciful favor, may discharge this office and may without doubt carry to our most clement prince what has been accomplished by our counsel together with these synodal writings of ours, so that, becoming a participant in our labors, he may attain an abundance of reward and find as protector of his kingdom Him whose aid he is known to invoke.

We have learned that this is also urged upon him in his letter.

As for the relics of the saints about which the bearer of this letter reminded us, we have ordered that they be given. For the books in our library have already been exhausted, and we had no way at all to give him any from there. Nor could he have copies made, since he hastened to leave this city.

Having thus prefaced these matters, we urge your fraternity to put into effect what has been written to you by us in this letter. May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

## 285. Decrees of Popes Gregory III and Zachary

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, while the lord Leo, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the sixth year after his consulship, and while Constantine, his son, the great emperor, was likewise in the fourth year, in the sixth indiction.

I, Boniface, bishop by the grace of God, promise to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to your vicar, blessed Pope Gregory, and to his successors, by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the indivisible Trinity, and by this most sacred body of yours, that I will offer every faithfulness and the purity of the holy Catholic faith, and, with God working, persevere in the unity of that same faith, in which the salvation of Christians is undoubtedly established.

In no way will I, persuaded by anyone, consent to act against the unity of the common and universal Church. Rather, as I have said, I will offer my faithfulness, purity, and support in every respect to you and to the interests of your Church, to which the power of binding and loosing has been given by the Lord God (Matthew 16:19), and to your aforesaid vicar and his successors.

If I recognize bishops conducting themselves contrary to the ancient regulations of the holy Fathers, I will have no communion or association with them. Rather, if I am able, I will prevent them; if I am not, I will report them faithfully to my apostolic lord.

But if—which may it never happen—I should in any way or on any pretext attempt to do anything contrary to the terms of this permission, may I be found guilty at the eternal judgment and incur the vengeance of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:5–10), if I should presume to defraud you even of my own possessions or to speak falsely.

I, Boniface, an insignificant bishop, have subscribed this little document of the oath with my own hand. Having placed it above your most sacred body, as written above, with God as witness and judge I have rendered the oath, and I promise to preserve it.

## Letter of Pope Gregory to the presbyter Boniface

**Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Boniface, religious presbyter.**
