You also asked how long one must wait before eating bacon. The Fathers have not established this for us. But to you, who ask our advice, we say that it ought not to be eaten before it has been dried over smoke or cooked by fire. If, however, one wishes to eat it uncooked, it may be eaten after the Paschal feast.

As for the condemned bishop about whom you inquired, who is an aggressor and fornicator and attempts, after his degradation, to claim the property of the Church for himself, he must be rejected altogether and with abhorrence. “For what partnership has the unbeliever with the believer? Or what communion has Christ with Belial?” (2 Corinthians 6:15). The traditions of the holy Fathers and the provisions of the sacred canons have condemned such things.

Concerning the ordination of priests and deacons whom, compelled by necessity and by the poverty of those making the request, you ordained outside the lawful times and days, and concerning which you indicated that you had some scruple, we say to you, brother: you know well that the sacred canons teach that priests are to be ordained at suitable times. Nevertheless, since what you did was done out of zeal for the faith, we ask our Lord God to grant forgiveness.

Concerning the tax of the churches—that is, receive one solidus from each farmstead—and have no hesitation, so long as from it you are able to give alms, distribute to Christ’s poor, and complete the work of the holy churches, according to the provisions of the canons.

If there are priests who were promoted from the laity and who, having previously been entangled in criminal causes, concealed their sin and were ordained, but whose wicked conduct was later exposed, strip them of the priestly garb and subject them to penance. For God does not hate the sinner who confesses, but the sinner who denies.

You also asked whether it is permissible to flee persecution by the pagans. For this, brother, we give salutary counsel. If it can be done and you find a place, persist in preaching to them. But if you cannot endure their persecution, you have the Lord’s commandment that you should enter another city (Matthew 10:23).

You also asked what should be done with an excommunicated bishop who disregards apostolic authority. He is detestable before God and human beings; no one who is not condemned shall share in his condemnation. For they themselves will be condemned on the day of the wrath and revelation of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, when he shall sit in judgment upon the human race (Romans 2:5), as it is written: “I resist the proud, says the Lord” (1 Peter 5:5).

You asked, brother, whether tribute ought to be collected from the Slavs inhabiting the land of Christians. This requires no counsel, since the matter is clear. For if they remain without tribute, they will eventually claim the land as their own. But if they pay tribute, they acknowledge that the ruler possesses the land.

You also requested, most holy brother, that in preaching concerning the sacred canon we indicate in how many places crosses should be made. Graciously inclining to your wishes, we marked in the roll given to your religious priest Lul, at the various places, how many signs of the holy cross should be made.

These matters having been arranged, although we are sinners, we beseech the Lord’s mercy to strengthen and protect you by his aid, and to grant that we may always receive joyful news of your prosperity. May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

Given on the second day before the Nones of November, during the reign of the most pious Lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, great emperor, in the thirtieth year, in the eleventh year of his reign, in the fourth indiction.

## Letter of Pope Zacharias to Bishop Boniface

Zacharias, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy brother Boniface, bishop.

Having received the letters of your holiness through Deneard, your religious priest, and having learned that you are safe and well, as we always desire, we gave great thanks to our almighty and most merciful God, who deigns to prosper you in all good things. You pour great joy into our hearts whenever writings from your holiness are sent to us, when we find in them matters directed toward the salvation of souls, while new peoples are daily added, through your preaching, to the bosom of holy Mother Church.

We have also learned that you have ordained three bishops in the several places, according to the sequence of your letters, who are to preside over the same people whom our Lord God has deigned, through your holiness, to gather to himself; and you asked that, by the authority of our see, episcopal sees should be established there.

But let your holy fraternity consider the matter maturely and discern with careful judgment whether it is expedient, and whether the places or the crowds of people are shown to be such that they deserve to have bishops. For remember what we are commanded to observe in the sacred canons: we must not ordinarily ordain bishops in villages or small cities, lest the name of bishop become cheapened.

Nevertheless, moved by your most sincere words, which are beloved by us, we allow without delay what you have proposed, and by apostolic authority we establish episcopal sees there, where succession may produce bishops worthy of the office, who may preside over the peoples and cause the word of preaching to be proclaimed to their subjects: namely, in the fortress called Mürzburg, another in the settlement called Büraburg, and a third in the place called Erphesfurt.

Henceforth no one shall be permitted in any way to violate what has been decreed by us, which we have determined shall stand firm by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter.

You also informed us that our son Carloman asked you to come to him so that you might hold a synod in a city of the Frankish kingdom situated under his jurisdiction and authority, because every ecclesiastical rule and discipline had been utterly abolished throughout that province. This is a matter greatly to be lamented: for over long periods no synod of priests had been held there, and consequently no one knew what the priesthood was among those who considered themselves priests.

But when, with God’s help, what our aforesaid son has promised has been brought to completion, and your fraternity has sat in council with that most excellent man, if your holiness finds that any bishops, priests, or deacons have transgressed the canons or the statutes of the Fathers—that is, through adultery, or by having several wives, or by shedding the blood of Christians or pagans, or in any other matters in which you find them to have acted contrary to the canons—do not permit them under any circumstances, by apostolic authority, to exercise the priesthood.

For such men are falsely called priests by their own mouths and are known to be worse and more depraved than secular people: they neither abstain from fornication nor from wicked marriages, nor do they keep their hands innocent of the shedding of human blood. What sort of priests do they think themselves to be, or what do they understand by the office, when God says, “My priests shall marry only once,” and the Apostle says, “the husband of one wife,” and so forth (Titus 1:6)—and this before receiving the priesthood, when it is lawful?

From the day on which they receive the priesthood, they must even be prohibited from their own marriage. How can those who are shown to be entangled in such crimes consider themselves fit to exercise the priesthood, when we do not wish even secular believers involved in such offenses? How do they not fear touching the divine mysteries, or how do they presume to approach in order to pray for the sins of the people, when the sacred canons do not even permit a pure cleric who is not a priest to enter a second marriage?

These men, on the contrary, not only refuse to abstain from one wife after receiving the priesthood, but, wrapped in lust, commit crimes worse than those of secular people, daring to have several wives, although they are not permitted to touch even one after receiving the ministry. Disregarding these matters and provoking God to anger, they commit still greater crimes, killing Christians and pagans with their own hands.

Thus it happens that those to whom they ought to have administered the bath of regeneration for the remission of sins and given the sacrament of Christ, so that they might not perish eternally, are themselves destroyed by their sacrilegious hands. What wise person with understanding would judge those to be priests who neither abstain from fornication nor keep their hands innocent of bloodshed? And who would believe that God is pleased by their sacrifices, when the Prophet says: “The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit” (Psalm 5:7)?

As I said above, we admonish you not to permit such men to exercise the priesthood or touch the divine mysteries. Whatever else you find them to have transgressed against ecclesiastical rule, as has been said, keep the canons and the statutes of the Fathers before you, and judge according to what you have been taught in them.

You also said that you had appointed a successor for yourself, so that, at your command, a bishop might be chosen in your place. We cannot permit this under any circumstances, because it is shown to be contrary to every ecclesiastical rule and to the statutes of the Fathers. Rather, we wish him to assist you and to be your helper in the Gospel of Christ, as the Apostle says: “If anyone serves well, he acquires for himself a good standing” (1 Timothy 3:13).

It is plainly most reprehensible that, while you are alive, we should substitute another for you. But we admonish you that, as long as divine mercy commands you to remain, you should not cease praying without interruption that God may grant you such a successor as will be acceptable to him, who may irreproachably govern the people whom he wished to call to his grace through the work of eternal holiness and may strive to lead them to the way of life.

For how can we grant what you have asked, even if we wished to do so, when we are frail human beings subject to death, ignorant of what the coming day will bring, and unable to discover which of us will depart this present age first?

But if divine mercy should wish him to outlive the day of your departure, and if you recognize him as suitable and the decision has been fixed according to your will, at the hour when you know that you are about to depart this present age, designate your successor in the presence of all, so that he may come here to be ordained. We permit this to no one else, but, compelled by affection, we have judged it right to grant it to you.

Concerning the man who is shown to have taken as wife his uncle’s widow, who had herself been the wife of his cousin, and who was also shown to wear the sacred veil, and who publicized that permission had been granted to him by our predecessor of blessed memory so that he might take her in a pernicious marriage: far be it from us to believe that our predecessor commanded such a thing. Matters that are said to be contrary to the institutions of the Fathers or the canons are not issued by the apostolic see.

Do not cease, brother, to admonish, exhort, and rebuke them, so that they may withdraw from such a wicked marriage and not perish forever. Let them remember that they have been redeemed by Christ’s blood and must not willingly surrender themselves to the devil’s power, but withdraw from that incestuous marriage and surrender themselves instead to God himself, to Christ his Son, and also to the Holy Spirit, in whose name they were rescued from the power of that ancient enemy.

Work diligently among them, most holy brother, for you know what is written: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:20). We too have sent him a letter of admonition concerning this.

### 292

Concerning the Kalends of January, and other omens, amulets, incantations, and various other observances that you said are practiced in the pagan manner at the shrine of the blessed apostle Peter or in the city of Rome, we judge this to be detestable and harmful, both by us and by all Christians, since God says: “You shall not practice augury, nor shall you observe dreams” (Leviticus 19:26). And again: “There is no augury in Israel, nor divination in the house of Jacob” (Numbers 23:23).

We therefore judge that we too must guard against these things, so that we pay attention to no omens or observances, because we have been taught by the Fathers that all such practices have been cut away. Since, through the instigation of the devil, they had begun to sprout again from the day on which divine mercy commanded us—although we consider ourselves unworthy—to act as the apostle’s representative, we immediately cut them all off.

In the same way we wish your holiness to preach to the peoples subject to you and lead them toward the way of eternal life. All these things, together with very many other practices that were sprouting at the devil’s prompting in Christ’s sheepfold, were piously and faithfully cut away by the constitution of our predecessor and guardian of blessed memory, Pope Gregory; we have hastened to send you a copy of it for the salvation of that people.

As for those priests who hold false opinions, who are also proved to be adulterers and fornicators, and who claim that an indulgence was granted to them by the apostolic see and, conversely, that permission to preach was bestowed upon them, let your holy fraternity believe this under no circumstances. Rather, exercise canonical punishment upon them in the same way as you have been instructed above concerning such men.

For we do not wish you to do anything other than what the sacred canons command or what you are recognized as having been instructed in by this apostolic see.

At your holiness’s request, we have also sent separate letters of confirmation to your three bishops, which we wish to have you distribute to them with your own hands. We have sent another letter to our son Carloman, urging him to hasten to fulfill what he promised you and to provide assistance.

But concerning all the chapters set out above, dearest brother, we have answered everything, as the Lord has granted, in order to cut away every scandal of diabolical deceit. If anything further should occur, let your holy fraternity take care to correct it among the congregations entrusted to you by God, as the sacred canons teach. For it is not fitting for us to preach anything other than what we have been taught by the holy Fathers.

But if, through the cunning of the enemy, something new should occur that your holy fraternity cannot discern by the provisions of the canons, do not hesitate to inform us, so that, with God’s help, we may hasten to answer you without delay concerning whatever may contribute to the correction of the new congregation.

For know, dearest brother, that your holy fraternity is held by us in such affection within our hearts that we desire to see you bodily every day, and that we count you as one of our company, truly as a minister of God and steward of the Churches of Christ.

For the future, then, take courage in the Lord, dearest brother, and be strong (Deuteronomy 31:7), and labor at the work to which divine mercy has wished to call you. A great hope of reward awaits you, which God has promised to those who love him (James 2:5).

And although we are sinners, we nevertheless do not cease to beseech without interruption the immense mercy of our God, that he who began the good work in you may bring it to completion even now (Philippians 1:6). May the blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, cooperate with you in all the good things that you desire to prepare for him.

May God keep you safe, most reverend and most holy brother.

Given on the Kalends of April, during the reign of the most pious Lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, great emperor, in the twenty-fourth year, in the second year of his reign, in the eleventh indiction.

## [Note]

### [Col. 1177]

Be grateful, diligent reader, that you now have at hand both the acts of councils and the writings of pontiffs, which Isidore of Seville gathered into one volume from Greek and Latin repositories, with the enactments of the supreme pontiffs added: Gregory II, Vitalian, Martin, Gregory III, and Zacharias. The industrious printer and honorable citizen of Cologne, Peter Quentell, brought them to completion in the year of the Lord 1530, on the third day before the Kalends of April.

# Marcus Valerius Probus

### [Col. 1177]

## Historical Notice

Concerning Marcus Valerius Probus, the following is read in the edition of the little work *On Ancient Abbreviations*, published at Paris in the year 1510 under the supervision of Godefredus Torin:

“Marcus Valerius Probus, a native of Berytus, long sought a military command until, wearied of it, he turned to study. In Provence he had read certain old little books at the house of a grammarian, while the memory of the ancients still survived there and had not yet been wholly obliterated, as it had at Rome. Since he wished to reread these more carefully and afterward to become acquainted with others, although he noticed that he was despised and that this activity brought its practitioners more reproach than glory or profit, nevertheless he remained steadfast in his purpose. He took care to correct, distinguish, and annotate many collected copies, devoting himself exclusively to this and to no other branch of grammar.

He had a few followers rather than pupils; he never taught in such a way as to assume the role of a master. He was accustomed to admit one or two, or at most three or four, during the afternoon hours; while lying down, amid long and ordinary conversations, he would read some things, and even that very rarely. He published far too little and only brief material concerning certain small questions. He left behind, however, no inconsiderable forest of observations on the ancient language.”

### [Col. 1177]

## Godefredus Torinus Bituricus, Greetings to the Reader

From the time when I began, as I think, under favorable auspices, to print Valerius Probus, it occurred to me to compress a few additional matters not unworthy of knowing, lest the book should emerge less suitable than a handbook of one or two codices. These include a treatise on weights and measures from Priscian; and, from Columella, how the prescribed forms of fields ought to be measured . . .

I ask you, good reader, to take care lest I have placed a “glaucoma” before your eyes, as Plautus also says enigmatically in *The Soldier*. Farewell.

### [Col. 1177]

## Dedication Letter of the Same

Godefredus Torinus Bituricus greets the most distinguished Philibert Babou and the younger Joannes Alemanus, citizens of Bourges, united to one another by equal friendship.

To you, men filled with singular virtue, are owed all the labors that I can undertake, by night and by day, even deliberately. Since you make use of and take pleasure in ancient customs—that is, honorable and truly good ones—to no small degree, behold: I willingly entrust Valerius Probus, the most diligent collector and most reliable interpreter of the ancient scripts and abbreviations that were elegantly recorded in antiquity on coins, tombs, and tablets, to your ever-beloved name, in characters and impressions revised by our modest—would that it were as fortunate as it is diligent—reconsideration, so that I may be able to benefit the commonwealth at least a little.

Permit, I beg, this highly exceptional author first to pass conveniently and cheerfully into your hands, which are most suited to every virtue, and then into the hands of all other students.

Farewell.

Paris, at the College of Plessis, on the sixth day before the Ides of May, 1510.

A CITIZEN

### [Col. 1179]

# The Little Work of the Grammarian M. Valerius Probus on Ancient Abbreviations

### [Col. 1179A] The little work of the grammarian Valerius Probus on interpreting the ancient abbreviations, or letters, of the Romans happily begins

There is also a necessary concern with writing words in full or marking them with fewer letters. This is done partly according to each person’s preference, and partly according to public usage and common practice.

Among the ancients, when the use of abbreviations did not yet exist, because of the practical need for writing—especially among those present in the senate—certain words and names were marked by their initial letters, so that they might be recorded quickly; and it was readily understood what each letter signified. This practice remains in names, public laws, the records of the pontiffs, and the study of civil law.

Alongside these public abbreviations there is also the inclination of students, so that each person might mark familiar things with abbreviations according to preference. To comprehend all such abbreviations is impossible. Those that are public must certainly be retained, since they are found in many monuments, books of history, and public sacred records. They are as follows.
