## X

[Col. 1195B] X.V. a decemvir, or decemvirs (members of a board of ten). X. ten, or denarii. XV.VIR.S.F. the quindecemvir for performing sacred rites. XXII.S. twenty-two and a half. IXI signifies one thousand, as is seen on marble.

The names, praenomina [printed *pronomina*, literally “pronouns”], and cognomina of Roman citizens, and those of their magistracies, which are found written in ancient codices, are expressed by abbreviated letters, as will appear below. By the first name you are to understand the *praenomen*; by the second, the proper name; and by the third, the *agnomen*. Sometimes the same is also the surname, as in the example:

C. IVLIUS CAESAR CN. POMPEIVS MAGNVS  
[Col. 1195C] L. STATIVS DIODORVS  
L. POMPEIVS CORNELIANVS.

And all these must be placed and pronounced in the case in which the words to which they refer are written:

M. CICERO IM. CAES. AVG.  
Marcus Cicero, commander (*imperator*). Caesar Augustus [the printed punctuation is retained].

HIRCIVS ET PANSA IMPP.  
Hircius and Pansa, commanders (*imperatores*).

[Col. 1196A] SYLVANVS ET MVRENA COSS. DESIG.  
Sylvanus and Murena, consuls-designate.

## On Numbers

One is expressed by I, two by II, five by V, and ten by X. The letter I, as in IX, signifies nine; if it is placed afterward, it signifies eleven, XI. L signifies fifty, C one hundred, D fifty [the source prints *quinquaginta*, “fifty”; this is erroneous for the usual value five hundred], and M one thousand. Note that if a straight transverse line is placed over any numeral, it signifies as many thousands as the numeral by itself signifies units: thus I signifies one thousand; V, five thousand; X, ten thousand. Or CC signifies two hundred; [Col. 1196B] M, or [infinity sign], one thousand [the numeral forms and missing overbars are retained as transmitted]. I.CC signifies five thousand. CCICC; X; CMC; IMI signify ten thousand. DMICCC; D signify fifty thousand. CCCICCC signifies one hundred thousand, or C, or CM. CMC or CQC signifies one million.

## Other Abbreviations

P.I.R.P.Q.I.S.I.F.P.R.E.A.D.P.  
The people requested by law, and the people accepted by law, in the forum before the Rostra, and on the preceding day.

E.H.O.L.N.R.  
*ejus hac omnibus legem nihilum rogatur*: “of him … by this … for all … law … nothing … is asked” [the printed words do not form a secure continuous construction].

S.R.L.E.E.C.Q.O.R.E.  
*si rem lex ex ejus causaque omnium rerum esto*: “if … the matter … law … from his … and cause … of all things … let it be” [the printed construction is corrupt].

[Col. 1196C] M.E.M.D.D.E.  
Let the municipal citizen of that municipality be condemned to give.

C.E.D.  
It will be said to be joined.

S.Q.M.D.E.R.A.P.P.V.O.E. CONSPR. TR.P.L.Q.N.S.Q.E.V.A.P.PL.F.  
*Si quod me de ea re ad populum plebum valeto opus est conspreto*: “If anything … me … concerning that matter … before the people/plebs … let it be valid … there is need …” [the construction and *conspreto* are uncertain]. “Let the tribunes of the plebs who are now in office bring before the people of the plebs whatever shall seem [appropriate] concerning it” [*ad populum plebis*, as printed]. And so on indefinitely.

[Col. 1195]

# Carolingian-Age Poems

## I. Verses in praise of Emperor Lothar, placed at the front of the Gospel text, which Emperor Lothar himself presented to the monastery of Saint Martin of Metz

[Note: [Col. 1195D] That Gospel codex, given by Lothar to the monastery of Saint Martin of Metz, is presently preserved in the Royal Library. At its beginning [Col. 1196D] is placed an image of Lothar, concerning which verse 22 says, “He is shown painted,” and so forth. — Baluze.]

[In Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. II, col. 1565.]

[Col. 1195D]

Judge enthroned on high, fashioner and creator of the world,  
who preserve the heavens and powerfully sustain all things and all ages;  
you who command kings to reign through the ages of the world,  
exalt with your lofty right hand and defend and adorn  
[Col. 1196D] Lothar, who now, supported by your gracious piety,  
is regarded throughout the world as emperor and Augustus king.  
May he hold, extend, strengthen, and unite the empire;  
may he use it well, enjoying peace and prosperity,  
and may he prosper, flourish, and live happily through the ages.

For this pious Augustus, guided by the love of Christ,  
foresaw that this beneficent ornament should belong  
to the Church, in reverence for the blessed bishop Martin,  
[Col. 1197A] and ordered that this beautiful book be written within the flock.  
He commanded it, the venerable book, to be adorned with gold and paintings,  
so that it might make known how powerful that place is.  
But Sigilaus, zealously obeying the king’s commands,  
ordered this entire Gospel to be written there.  
The Caesar wished to be a brother of the aforementioned flock,  
so that, being humble, he might receive the heavenly gift.

Indeed, the entire flock with all its strength prays to the Almighty  
for the virtue and perpetual prosperity of Augustus,  
and likewise for his venerable wife and offspring.  
For this reason the king is also depicted on this page,  
so that whoever should ever behold Augustus’s face here  
may humbly say to God: “[Praise, supplied in the text] to the Almighty!”

[Col. 1197B] “May Lothar deserve to possess everlasting rest  
through our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns everywhere.”

## II. Verses placed at the front of the Bible and written in letters of gold in a very ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Denis, now preserved in the Royal Library

[Baluze, cited above.]

The illustrious King Charles clothed this series of Bible books in gold,  
cherishing it with a pure heart.  
O exceedingly wondrous wisdom of the supreme Lord,  
which was present when he himself was preparing the heavens!  
Nor is it less worthy of contemplation that you thus arrange all things  
in an arranged order under our authority … [the printed *nostri sub jure coapto* is grammatically uncertain].

[Col. 1197C] You seem to have set stars among stars,  
marking out celestial boundaries with varied distinction,  
and ordaining that the sun be set before all lights.  
You also, circling around, thus encompass the whole circuit of heaven,  
and have fastened the earth in the middle beneath the vault.  
You placed the sea, flowing with waves, in its separate region.  
Thus different peoples preserve different customs and ways.  
Yet you alone hold equal primacy among all peoples,  
restraining the proud by your own power.  
You have always given laws to kings and kingdoms;  
and whichever king obeyed your commands  
has himself shone higher from a lofty summit.  
They are called happy, and they are also made happy.  
Those who have clung to you reign, your praise and glory.

[Col. 1197D] In the series of the Bible books, many things are related about many persons,  
some corrected and many finally rejected.  
You guided certain kings, glorifying them by name.  
But it is clear to the wise of the world  
that you have specially preserved for yourself one Charles as your own,  
whom, alone like the sun, bright in royal form,  
you, O Wisdom, set conspicuous in light and foremost.

Now it is permitted and pleasing to examine him thoroughly,  
the manner in which kings are known to have pleased you,  
and how your Charles may be called or regarded as yours;  
let this at least be disclosed in a few simple words.

For mighty David reigned and acted through you,  
the weapon of the blessed and likewise the standard of the guilty,  
teaching the saints to stand and the fallen to rise again.  
You do not allow the humble entirely to perish,  
[Col. 1198A] those whom you confess to have accepted sufficiently in your heart.  
You rebuke and restrain those whom you correct, and likewise raise them up.  
You exercise all whom you love with gracious spirit,  
and by strong powers you bestow welcome virtues.  
Foolish people think that those whom you deeply love have displeased you.

King Solomon, because he asked for your gifts in order to become wise [the printed *potus*, “having drunk,” is uncertain here],  
surpassing all others and becoming greater than kings,  
was powerful in abundant riches.  
With sound judgment he established many good things with you,  
and by your teaching richly adorned the world (*redimivit*, “wreathed/adorned”).  
He also deserved to build a wondrous temple for the Lord.  
When he departed from you, he suffered loss in himself;  
yet the doctrine he drew from you shines through the ages.

Do you, then, not willingly love your Charles?  
Or is he second to any person in humility of heart?  
[Col. 1198B] Or has anyone else been or become so ardent in piety?  
He remembers all things so deeply in his heart  
that forgetfulness seizes nothing he has heard or seen.  
Only a personal injury inflicted upon him remains hidden in his mind.

Shall I speak, or be silent, about the tenor of his justice?  
If anything is perhaps lacking, I confess that compassion prevails.  
Come, free voice, proclaim his generous hand:  
the orphan and the ward will now be truthful witnesses.  
Thus, deservedly, I mark all of these in their name,  
since no one is excluded and no one is driven away.

Nor could the seething sea in its vast whirlpool  
ever have held back this hand, nor will it ever do so.  
Different languages speak of this in different regions;  
different customs praise it harmoniously.

Happy, then, is the hand, but happier still the mind of this man,  
[Col. 1198C] which, rather than being rich, stands poor and needy within itself,  
not swollen with pride in the emblem of royal rank.  
But while his flesh shines adorned with gems and gold,  
he meditates on this continually, night and day:  
that he may shine for Christ more brightly than the sun itself.

Thus, O Wisdom, you make your Charles a sun.  
For where the treasure is, there the heart is rightly said to be;  
and his heart constantly cleaves to its lord,  
in whom he stores all that he possesses with tender piety.

What if he were now to see Christ himself on earth in the flesh?  
With what love, with what devotion, would he press Christ’s feet to his mouth,  
when he venerates the law he has given with such honor?

What shall I say in repetition of the revered Gospel text?  
Behold, he surrounds its very letters with gems and gold.  
[Col. 1198D] O how ardently this mind loves Christ,  
for whose love all the things of the world become worthless to him!

There is a way in which one who possesses does not possess, nor desire to possess;  
and there is one who possesses as though he did not possess, yet gives freely.  
This virtue adorns the man with a fitting name.

Behold, O Wisdom, it is evident that Solomon did not love you  
more than Charles, whom you bless without end.  
Nor did you, O Wisdom, approve David so greatly in each respect [the compressed *tantisper quaeque* is uncertain].  
Among these matters, concerning a certain deed of grace,  
much thanks must be offered to you with the whole heart.

David lost his kingdom and received it again.  
Yet he grieved deeply in sorrow at the death of his son;  
but you restored his paternal kingdoms to your Charles.  
No grief came near him; rather, brotherly love remained with him.

[Col. 1199A] Therefore you will always preserve your Charles everywhere.  
Thus it plainly appears that neither this David nor Job was more approved,  
nor did they endure more things for you

than your Charles—mild, pious, and kind,  
temperate, wise, brave, and just:

**ΝΗΦΑΔΕΟϹ ΦΡΟΝΙΜΟϹ ϹΠΟΥΔΑΙΟϹ ΚΑΙΔΕ ΔΙΚΑΙΟϹ**  
“Temperate, prudent, diligent, and also just.”

Deprived of worthy offspring in his namesake Charles [sense uncertain],  
he showed indulgence, for your sake, toward a fierce and crooked tyrant.  
Toward all his own people who deprived him of the kingdom  
he showed such proven goodness and such great piety.  
Indeed, he restored very substantial estates to his enemies,  
and gave even more to some of them.

What does so great a lord deserve, O Wisdom? [The printed *sancti* is grammatically uncertain.]  
In our judgment he stands first above kings.  
With pious purpose I ask and open the hearts of peoples:  
[Col. 1199B] May distinctive excellence benefit the renowned man [sense uncertain].

## III. Verses written in golden letters at the front of the Bible in a very ancient manuscript of the Colbert Library, formerly belonging to Saint Stephen of Metz

[Baluze, cited above, col. 1568.]

Blessed King, Charles, may this library please you,  
which bears two Testaments to be read again.  
It brings what you love, what you ought to love, what is useful to learn,  
what you may grasp, hold, and frequently practice.  
It corrects, exhorts, restores, chastens, and ennobles;  
it reproves, entreats, rebukes, adorns … [the printed *alii*, “others/to another,” is syntactically uncertain].

[Col. 1199C] It arranges speech, morals, study, and actions;  
it is food, drink, a rule, a way, weapons, and salvation.  
It brings forth the inner things of a person and reveals heavenly things;  
full of God’s gifts, it adapts each to the other.  
It sings of things past while showing things present.  
It is silent about individual laws, yet makes each one resound.

Though its lover be unstable, it will afterward make him steadfast,  
if he is devoted to what he has confessed [printed *fassis … suis*, with an uncertain reference].  
[lacuna]us, so that he may believe as true what it contains in its entirety;  
from this, the hope of the pious follower of truth may become firm.

May exceedingly sweet love duly advance as a third in those two  
and itself join the three together.  
May those things now enter the mind that were harmful through guilt,  
born through tears and through the labor of sorrow.

Thus, yes, thus, let the grace of Christ be sought with prayers,  
[Col. 1199D] for whatever good exists in the world is his gift.  
What we desire, ask for, do, know, or possess  
is given from him to us, not according to our merits.

All is vain or empty or nothing, and nowhere praiseworthy,
unless the Holy Spirit comes to it as its active author [the compressed Latin construction is irregular].  
Under his guidance, what lay hidden becomes openly clear,  
when he opens it by his own will.  
With him the mind has power; without him it grows dark in shadow,  
as though deprived of light or the faculty of reason.

Moreover, let the body be rightly weakened by fasting,  
and everywhere by chaste vigils of the night.  
[Col. 1200A] Thus the intellect may grow together with the sharpness of perception,  
when wasting flesh passes away and, worn thin, perishes.  
When the flesh is fatigued, the acuteness of the heart gradually grows  
and begins to receive what has been granted.

A whetstone sharpens iron—believe me—so that it may cut a hair  
or likewise shave the head without effort.  
No less does the body, governed by proper discipline,  
raise, heal, and strengthen the understanding.

Finally, while your riches remain and your means are abundant,  
while you long for greater things and ask for more useful ones,  
give to those in need; become a defense for the wretched.  
Let the poor, needy, and destitute cry out through your compassion.  
Through your compassion let every little sufferer cry out and live,  
who asks you to be the help of his life.

Be father, brother, mother, sister, and lamb on either side,  
[Col. 1200B] the greatest hope, substance, glory, and day for the weak.  
Love justice; may a friend of justice’s path accompany you,  
first with you in every good [the printed word order is compressed].

Exalt, fortify, guard, gather, and praise;  
raise up or venerate your clergy.  
Thus show worthy honors to sacred buildings,  
in holy places, so that you may deserve assistance.

Eat, drink, sleep, rise, and work at the proper time;  
everything must be done in its own season.

With these and other good things established in the triune name  
of the Almighty Lord together with his divinity,  
I ask you to examine from the beginning of this volume  
his writings with pious mind, deed, and faith—I ask you.

Here is the fountain, here the powerful teaching, here the rich streams  
of the holy Church, whiter than snow.

[Col. 1200C] Certainly, the five books of Moses, of lofty song,  
shine joined together and sing of his death to the end.  
Joshua the leader arises, strong in arms, leading the people  
into their homeland, where they rightfully hold their place [the printed case construction is irregular].  
Behold the seventh book, which recounts the names of the judges  
whose power was over the Hebrews.  
Their deeds, lineage, time, places, wars, and triumphs  
are inserted there with the honor due to them.

The noble woman Ruth sits there as a companion,  
whom Job of extraordinary faith follows.  
Gladly imitate him, since pure patience  
was found in him and he became a great example for us.

And the four books of Kings before the twice-eight prophets,  
with David the hymn-singer joined to them [the printed syntax is elliptical; their exact ordering is not unambiguous].  
David sang the hymnic songs of the Psalms,  
[Col. 1200D] often speaking many mystical things about Christ;  
from his royal seed came the virgin Mary,  
the blessed virgin who bore God.

The peace-loving Solomon, and Wisdom beside him,  
is followed by Jesus as the third.  
After Chronicles, Ezra, or Nehemiah,  
then Esther, Judith, and Tobias sing.  
Next the renowned Maccabean wars thunder forth,  
once undertaken for law, fatherland, and salvation.

This ancient Scripture, briefly recalled, stands here,  
though in a modest and rustic style.

The precepts of the New Testament are begun  
by the four holy writers, in harmonious speech:  
Matthew, Mark, Luke, and exalted John,  
[Col. 1201A] proclaiming the teaching of God in equal meaning.  
Their persons are various, but their doctrine is one;  
their tenor is one, and the path to be followed is one.

They all teach what, what sort of things, how great, and in what manner  
the Son, descending from the Father, did everywhere.  
Hence the first face of a man is assigned to the first,  
because he begins sufficiently with the Lord’s genealogy.  
The form of a lion is beautifully shaped in the second,  
because he touched the remote countryside with his voice.  
Since the third concerns sacred matters,  
the form of a calf is now impressed upon him.  
Because the fourth rises above the stars like an eagle,  
he himself bears the image of that exalted sign.

Luke also adds the Acts of the Apostles,  
where the whole people is instructed.  
[Col. 1201B] From this come the seven Catholic epistles, fragrant with wonder,  
which the apostolic style shaped through its work.  
To these are joined Paul’s fourteen writings,  
whose voice, once wolfish, now shines as sheep-like.

This work is now concluded by the holy vision of John,  
a holy vision sufficiently memorable and greatly worthy of remembrance.

This new series rightly shines, joined to the earlier one,  
of which the former is the shadow and the latter the cause.  
Thus the effect of both is one double path,  
by which, when he grants it, ascent to the lofty heaven is given.

Here, because eternal riches fill the living table  
entirely with perpetual nectar;  
here, O paradise, your manifold and honey-bearing place  
is revealed with radiant understanding.

Here the thirsty will find drink, the hungry bread,  
and likewise the anxious person [Col. 1201C] will find joy—and from it will become joyful.  
Yet whoever dwells in this mortal body  
and possesses these things desires more from love.

Thus, if more wood is supplied, the fire burns more fiercely.  
Thus, the more each person drinks, the more he thirsts for wine.  
But when hope becomes reality, then the lover of these things  
will be completely full; then I shall be satisfied.

Toward this, let the mind truly strive—this house, this teaching, this path—  
under the help of the Godhead.

In physics, logic, and also morals,  
everything is here for you, reader, in brief.  
Here are silver, gold, gems, vessels, garments,  
and whatever on earth can be considered more precious.

Here too is the precious law. Nothing is more precious than it,  
[Col. 1201D] nor does anything exist, flourish, shine, or give off fragrance more sacredly.  
It commands what is just, forbids what is unjust, drives away all evils,  
and is powerful in nobility among all good things.

Schism, fury, anger, deceit, discord, and strife  
can be made to depart by the counsel of this Law.  
It teaches the unlearned, making some equal to the wise,  
and thus supplies the doctrine of salvation to those in between.

It rains great things upon the great and assigns small things to the small.  
In both cases the style of justice is strong.  
A pure confession provides knowledge of Jesus.  
It stands as a venerable law for humankind.  
It stands as a light for humankind along the roads of the world,  
a light and its source, with terrifying voice.

In liberal arts this law surpasses all others worthily:  
[Col. 1202A] in art, origin, eloquence, power, reason, and function.  
It touches upon what is useful, seemly, and honorable;  
it imbues, adorns, instructs, arms, and loves.

After the whole world has been transformed, it reveals  
what the Church will soon be when it returns there.  
There it terrifies many, and there it soothes some,  
marking out fixed future things that are by no means doubtful.

Yet beforehand it clearly discloses the beginnings of the cosmos  
and through what wisdom it came into being.  
At the beginning, the creator of heaven, earth, and sea,  
and his Son, and the Holy Spirit.

From his stream divine knowledge flows widely,  
stripping the world of its pestilential darkness  
and showing how every person, protected by weapons,  
may beware of the exceedingly hostile darts of the perverse enemy.

[Col. 1202B] It produces the noble fourfold path of virtue,  
by which it sends the earthly race to the stars.  
By speech of many kinds it continually draws and urges toward what is salutary,  
or commands while urging.

It commands, drives away darkness, then expels deceit;  
it seeks heavenly truths: these it practices, those evils it flees.  
The exile is consoled in exile by rich banquets,  
when he reads or rereads, and when, rereading, he understands.

It counts the accumulated evils of this present time as worthless,  
and does not judge them worthy of eternal goods;  
or it fears to look upon them, fearing only am[lacuna]a [fragment uncertain]  
as much as it fears not to be among the heavenly assemblies.

Here the Lord speaks; here let us speak to him in our hearts,  
to which nothing greater approaches or can approach.

Whoever you are, instructed in these worldly matters,  
[Col. 1202C] with which Solomon shone richer in possessions,  
The wisdom granted to him made him rich  
and set him before kings and all others.

You too, though humble, prudent, and devoted in holy purpose,  
love, seek, and receive her for her wisdom.

Is not that for which something else exists more than the action itself?  
Yet this Wisdom could not have anything greater than herself [the compressed Latin is uncertain].

Therefore, O triune God, peace, or true Wisdom—  
beyond this there is no praise, nor any poetic summit.

You adapt yourself to this great work with great efforts,  
illustrious King Charles, dearer than light,—

[Source ends here.]

He is the splendor of the people, the light of the world, the glory of the kingdom,

Greater in goodness, and no less in piety,

Now also, more justly preferred to all humankind

In endeavor, achievement, skill, and faith.

[Col. 1202D] In strength David, in understanding blessed Solomon,

In appearance Joseph, in hope a rejoicing emperor.

May He who contains the sea, the earth, and the whole world

Preserve you, love you, and lead you even to heaven.

May honor, peace, order, dignity, patience, and kingship be yours,

Every prosperity, and an unending farewell.

## At the beginning of the New Testament

Rejoice and be glad enough, illustrious King David,

Everywhere possessing the excellent wish that is yours.

Charles, glory of the kingdom, torch of the universe, glory of the clergy,

Supporter of the Church and ornament of the army.

Behold, the sequence of ancient things now read to you has ended,

But what follows, new in due order, now lies open to be read.

[Col. 1203A] At whose beginning Matthew clearly sings

The bright origins of the Lord from Genesis.

Like a lion roaring through the wilderness, threatening the desert,

So does your voice, Mark, resound, supported forever by its God.

Through the four parts of the world, sacred mystical teaching

Is carried by Luke’s devotion from the citadel of holy light.

To the Father’s Begotten One above the heavens, exalted John,

You ascend, and from the Word you sing words worthy of reverence.

These eminent men cast forth far and wide the mysteries of Christ,

And agree with one another in equal understanding.

Whether they sound more, less, or equally, thus they unfold what is their own;

Yet the new effect is one in either case.

This Gospel heals, consoles, honors,

Corrects, renews, strengthens, ennobles, and nourishes.

Here are the manner of speaking, the power, the pure action,

[Col. 1203B] Here the food, here the drink, here blessed salvation.

Here are life, charity, the way, hope, truth, and faith,

Or rather, all good things joined together flourish here.

Accustom yourself to these for a long time; meditate on them; love them;

Strive to make them dwell in speech and in action.

Good king, wise king, prudent king, venerable king,

Good King Charles, farewell, with the aid of piety.

May Jesus give you your father’s scepters, confirm and unite them,

So that you may deserve the rewards of the saints. Amen.

## At the end of the codex

O glory, O venerable salvation, O splendid David,

Good King Charles, flourish through the aid of the Almighty.

Glory, praise, honor, everything fitting, and merciful compassion—

You are depicted here through the devoted skill of an outstanding artist.

[Col. 1203C] But since this radiant image can do no more than portray

A true likeness of your whole person, which yields to it,

You are superior in appearance, superior in understanding, arts, and songs;

Whether superior in these or in those, the matter remains uncertain.

And this ignorance is pleasing to your people, David:

Everywhere the place shines with extraordinary joy.

It also plainly shows them that you are greater on both sides

Than all the great men throughout the world.

You command what is just, forbid what is unjust, and cut away every evil:

In your words and deeds, the holy way is yours.

What you yourself sing, you also do, and in these matters there is no blemish,

Except that in both cases the action is God’s pure action.

Supporter of the Church, relief to clergy and peoples,

And, among the sacred orders, sufficiently a sacred order yourself.

[Col. 1203D] Through you the pontiffs can rightly renew boys

In Christ’s name with the holy chrism;

You grant them the honors due to their merits and to the Godhead,

While submitting yourself to them in heart, deed, speech, and faith.

Therefore you know and preserve what portion must go first

To your Lord, who gave you being.

To the poor, needy, destitute, widow, orphan, afflicted, and bereaved—

To these and others you have been given as father and provider.

You continually contemplate the final day of judgment,

And that you are corruptible flesh and a perishing human being.

Therefore you are just, prudent, brave, and temperate:

Your hand is always generous, and your work is one of piety.

He who knows the drops of rain and counts the grains of sand

[Col. 1204A] Can praise you fully and deservedly.

As lead is distinguished from silver, bronze from gold, the countryside from a star,

And a jewel from glass, so your fame rises higher still.

Before a Briton becomes steadfast, or a wall-mouse [*musio muri*],

Good peace will come before your name and honor are lacking.

Now, for so great and such a king, may the whole world

Pour out abundant prayers with me,

That he may prosper, flourish, and live happily through the ages,

Enjoying peace and prosperity,

That he may possess, hold, enlarge, strengthen, and adorn the kingdom,

And add to it the laws’ rights from the holy citadel.

Moreover, once these things have been nobly secured, at the time of death

May he deserve everlasting rest here. Amen.

## On the last page of the book, before the image mentioned in the note to the first poem

[Col. 1204B]

This painting also discloses how the hero Vivianus

Now offers this work together with his company.

Before you stand, after the father, the firstborn beloved by the world,

The just Siguald and the eminent Aregarius.

In these three are honesty, piety, truth, and faith,

Together with all other honorable qualities.

A fourth, most holily joined to these, is David,

Who loves you with all the strength of his mind.

Behold, these blessed men, prostrate before you, Lord, on behalf

Of Martin and the brothers, give you this book;

In whose honor they ask that it please you to receive it, praise it, love it,

Examine it, make it beneficial, assist it, and nourish it;

In which there is nothing other than the brothers’ sole wish,

[Col. 1204C] which your command had restored to them from your estates.

You return them, Caesar, out of reverence for Martin,

And because of the ever-loving prayers of the Lord,

And under the protection of holy Brictius,

And for the sake of your other saints, O Paradise.

Indeed, rather, for your own sake, beloved Jesus the Savior,

May you finally be life everlasting for him.

Also for us, servants fit to offer prayers,

Whom thirst, cold, and black hunger had overwhelmed.

O king, O revered one, may a fixed renewal come

From your reward or from your salvation.

May royal dignity prevail, and may the power of kings

Who, according to custom, have cherished goodness, surpass all else.

You renewed the commandment of your father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.

May this stand, remain, and never be allowed to perish.

[Col. 1204D] May what your holy hand recently honorably confirmed

By the series of the commandment proceed wholly as something lasting.

What will others do after so great a king’s change,

If, while evil is prevailing, this deed should be undone?

Go far away, far away, from this cruel crime everywhere.

With justice near you, overcome what harms and drive it away.

What praises, what thanks, what songs can sing for you, David—

What equal sweet melody, voice, or lyre-string?

For our part, we specially pray through psalms and Masses;

We shall sing for you, for your wife, and for your offspring, O devout one.

Thus all who truly will come after us

Will pour forth constant and manifold prayers.

May Christ be your hope, strength, light, and victory;

Peace and continual praise—good King David, hail.

## IV. On the death of Hugh, son of Charlemagne by the concubine Regina

[In Lebeuf, *Collection of Various Writings, etc. Historical Monuments on Charlemagne and Charles the Bald*.]

[Col. 1205A]

### NOTICE

Those who work on history ordinarily regard canticles or songs as monuments containing the most reliable facts, because they were composed by contemporary authors and were public writings into which one would not have dared to insert falsehoods, since the interested families would immediately have exposed them. I would not today present one of these ancient canticles to the public if I did not have before my eyes the example of Dom Mabillon, who printed one from the ninth century in the Benedictine *Annals*. [Col. 1205B] The one I am about to give is from the same century and is in the Latin language; but in the manuscript from which I took it, which is approximately from the same period, the first stanza is notated with the characters then used to transmit song—that is, with small dots and small hooks, extremely difficult to decipher. Readers who may share the taste of the celebrated M. de Tillemont, whom I know to have loved song at least as much as history [Note: [Col. 1205] These are the words of that famous historian in one of his letters of 3 July 1685, which I preserve in the original.], would have something to satisfy them in both genres. First, in the song, the number of syllables may enable them to guess the melody if they wish to consult the manuscript. They will notice in the third, seventh, and eighth stanzas a repetition of the same words, which shows that such canticles were sometimes sung in the form of a rondeau. This one is a kind of lament, composed on the occasion of the tragic death of Prince Hugh, a famous ninth-century abbot. The melody was apparently sad and languid, [Col. 1205C] as the subject required. What concerns history is limited to the circumstances of this death, which we did not know, and to some details of the prince’s life. The same canticle also contains certain particulars concerning Pepin, king of Aquitaine.

Hugh died at the siege which Charles the Bald was conducting against the city of Toulouse. But these modern authors are mistaken, and on this point one must follow the annals of Prudentius, called the Annals of Saint-Bertin, which state that it occurred in the region of Angoumois in the year 844. Hugh wished to help lead troops to Charles the Bald so as to advance in the siege; King Pepin’s army came against them and defeated them without any loss of its own. It killed Hugh and another abbot related to the princes, named Richboton, as well as Counts Eccard and Ravan, together with others, and took several notable prisoners, among them Ebroin, bishop of Poitiers, and Ragenaire, bishop of Amiens.

The first two stanzas of the canticle add [Col. 1205D] nothing to the historians of the period. The third indicates that Abbot Hugh was cruelly pierced with lances and that his body was torn apart. The following stanzas add that Pepin, king of Aquitaine, who had been the aggressor, could not hold back his tears when he saw Hugh’s body lying naked on the ground. He even remarks that the prince would have wished it to have cost him a hundred talents of gold and for Hugh still to have been full of life. In any case, Pepin says that he should be carried to Charroux, where he had been a priest, so that he might receive burial from the hands of the religious, among whom, while alive, he had asked to be buried. The final two stanzas praise this abbot’s bodily beauty and his gentle, beneficent character, which caused everyone to mourn him.

[Col. 1206A] This lament appears to be in the same style as the one composed by Angelbert on the battle of Fontenay, and I believe it to be by the same author, who lived in the kingdom of Aquitaine and was probably the son of Angelbert, an officer (*primicerius*) of Pepin’s palace, to whom Alcuin’s forty-second letter is addressed. Here is the piece:

### Lament of Abbot Hugh

Hugh, a sweet name,

Hugh, noble offspring

Of mighty

And serene Prince Charles,

Innocent beneath arms,

So suddenly wounded,

You fell.

But why did you presume

[Col. 1206B] To approach Charles,

Whom Louis,

The illustrious emperor,

Was evidently pleased

To establish as king

Through his son?

Yet for that reason you were not

To be pierced by lances,

Nor were your limbs

To be torn apart,

Since you always loved

To benefit everyone

More than to harm them.

For King Pepin

[Col. 1206C] Is said to have wept

When he saw you,

Without any garments,

Lying naked

Shamefully amid

The dust of the field.

Indeed, he followed this

By adding about you:

“If I now saw him

Safe in body,

A hundred talents

Of gold would not please me

As much as this.”

Let him be honorably

[Col. 1206D] Placed in a tomb

By the monks,

At Charroux,

Where he had been

A priest,

And where, while alive,

He had asked

To be buried.

O how graceful

And how beautiful an appearance

You carried among all,

Beyond the rest,

Since you always loved

To benefit everyone

More than to harm them.

[Col. 1207A] You had committed

No crime,

No sort of robbery,

Since you were

Most gentle,

Since you always loved

To benefit everyone

More than to harm them.

## V. Epitaph of Clodarius, the boy king, “salvage” [as printed] [Note: [Col. 1207D] Son of Charlemagne.]

[At Abbot Lebeuf, in the work cited above.]

Here, sown in the green field, is preserved this little flower,

More beautiful than milk and whiter than snow.

Until the Most High Judge comes through the ages,

Who will reap the everlasting roses with his purple-bearing sickle.

[Col. 1207B] Your consecrated water, Jordan, brought him forth;

The vine of Engaddi refreshed him with dew.

Living bilberries, encircled by purple roses,

Bloom; from the soil the womb grows toward every beauty.

Whether pale sandyx gleams among the viburnums,

Or high Cynthus pours down waters rich with rain,

Or gold, baked in a burning furnace, glows,

Or the Indian stone shines with varied splendor.

Beside these there flashed the slender childhood of a son,

Whom the almighty Father sent to the stars of heaven.

Here was lofty love; an arrow, steeped in honey,

Pierced the father’s heart with its wounding point.

Alas, it violated the mother’s joys of life

And scorched her breast, burning it deeply.

Yet one blessed confidence in hope remains:

That such a spirit of heaven seeks the stars.

[Col. 1207C] A helmeted phalanx did not draw him into the weapons of battle:

An everlasting soldier reigns in the court of God.

He did not drain the riches of treasures or estates,

Nor, captivated by love of the world, seize its banquets.

Content with Christ’s cradle, a most welcome hero,

He earned the riches of milk from the river of heaven.

Born of royal blood with a radiant lineage,

He was not able to see his father’s golden scepters.

Overcome by excessive love for the ancient kings,

His father gave him the name Lotharius.

As twin flowers rise from a single seed,

So the mother poured both forth from her womb:

One, remaining here, flourishes on the springtime turf;

The other, flying to the stars, possesses golden ages.

[Col. 1207D] For you, dear Charles, your father,

The king mighty with the sword, issued this tearful song.

But I, Hildegard, your mother and queen, send you

Kisses, my sweet love.

Six months had scarcely passed before the year turned,

And the little gem withered, night having driven it away . . .

This snowy gift I offer first on the sacred altar;

I pray, virgin Mary, to the Judge enthroned on high.

O you worshipers of Christ who bear offerings to the temple,

Pray with us from your hearts for the mother, I beg you,

That she may deign, by her sacred prayers,

To associate the father with those of the lofty name.

Written below by the same hand:

[Col. 1208A] “He died on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the tenth year of the reign of his father Charles, the glorious king.”

## VI. Verses by an unknown poet on the succession of co-provincial bishops

[In Mabillon, *Old Analecta*, new edition, col. 316.]

### 1. Bishops of Salzburg

This place was once called Juvavum, a metropolitan city,

Which the noble Hrodbert first founded and governed.

After him Bishop Vitalis governed the same place.

Then came Flobargisus, supported by the honor of his office.

John was fourth, governing the see,

And the newcomer Virgil, establishing many things, was fifth.

Arno, accomplishing far more than all, was sixth.

[Col. 1208B] Next, Adalram succeeded as the seventh, an excellent shepherd,

For in his time he beautifully established many things.

Liuphrammus came as the eighth, bishop of the sheepfold,

Renewing the Lord’s service with equal and greater beauty.

### 2. Archbishops of Salzburg

This place, as is said, was once called Juvavum;

It was great in honor, as its present signs demonstrate,

When Bishop Hrodbert governed this people

And built here the sacred sheepfold of the see.

Afterward, when many bishops had properly sat there,

Arno succeeded, rejoicing as ruler and governing the fold.

Prince Charles increased his honor within the kingdom,

So that he might become more worthy as archpriest.

Pope Leo clothed him in the garment of his honor,

And, granting privileges, immediately established him firmly.

[Col. 1208C] So that he might be the summit of the region and its highest bishop,

And that this city might forever be a metropolitan see.

Adalram, the beloved bishop, succeeded him,

Whom Pope Eugenius adorned with pious honor.

After him Liuphrammus properly succeeded as priest,

Having fulfilled the office of Gregory the Apostolic.

For, remaining in the see as archpriests,

And legitimately exercising apostolic authority,

They built many monuments in different forms of activity,

Each succeeding most effectively in his own place.

Thus it is fitting that all their successors who will occupy the see

Should always possess such wishes together.

For all the fathers who have passed and all those yet to come,

May God grant great joys in the citadel of heaven,

[Col. 1208D] And grant forgiveness of sins to those subject to them,

And allow them all continually to rejoice in rest.

### 3. Bishops of Regensburg

This is called the see of Reginensis from the city

Which that bishop Wicterpus first governed.

After him came another, called Cauvipaldus by name.

The third was Sigiricus, consecrated to the court.

After him Sindbertus had already been fourth in succession.

Adalwinus was fifth, governing the see.

After him the pious Baturicus held the see most excellently.

Erchanfredus, rejoicing, follows as an excellent shepherd.

### 4. Bishops of Freising

This place is called the hall of the see of Frisingensis,

[Col. 1209A] Which the noble Corbinian first governed.

Then the servant of God Ermperht sat there by name.

Next came Joseph, a distinguished teacher.

Arpeo was fourth, relying upon eloquent speech.

The pious Atto, fifth, held the apostolic chair.

After him the blessed father Hitto governed the see.

Then Erchanperht succeeded, a beloved shepherd.

Behold, the pious Anno now governs the present see.

### 5. Bishops of Passau

Therefore this hall is dedicated to the see of Passau,

Which Vivolvus himself, already a priest, first held.

After him came the bishop Beatus in due order.

The third is Sidonius, advanced in honor.

Anthelmus was fourth, great in merits and doctrine.

Then the rejoicing Wisuricus ascended the honor of the see.

[Col. 1209B] Recently Waldricus, a fortunate man, was sixth in succession.

Now Urolfus, the great bishop, occupies the honor of this see. [Note: [Col. 1209D] Urolfus.]

### 6. Bishops of Säben

This see is called Säben, the valley of Noricum,

Which the blessed Ingenuinus first governed.

Mastulo was second and sat governing the chair.

After him John preserved the sheepfold as shepherd.

Bishop Alimus, fourth, sat there, distinguished by merits and doctrine.

Heinrich sits fifth, invested with the same honor. [Note: [Col. 1210D] Heinricus.]

### Epitaph of Virgil, bishop of Salzburg

Here rests in body Virgil,

Father and shepherd, humble, learned priest,

Whom the land of Ireland, by God’s arrangement,

Sent to these regions;

He joyfully governed the heights of the present see

[Col. 1209C] For nearly forty years with his beloved brothers.

He was loved by them, and piously loved them.

Meanwhile he also raised many things with beautiful construction,

Among them temples that can now be seen in this place.

Moreover, he was generous and helpful to all the unfortunate.

Therefore, whoever reads these verses, remember to pray.

### Epitaph of Arno, archbishop of Salzburg

If you wish, traveler, pausing at the crypt, to know us,

Know that I, Arno, built this crypt while alive,

I who had been ruler of the government of this see,

And had enjoyed many riches and great honor.

Now, having left all these things behind, my limbs rest here.

I ask you: remember to call upon the Lord in prayer,

That he may grant me forgiveness for whatever sins I committed,

[Col. 1209D] So that I may deserve to dwell in everlasting rest.

### Epitaph of Adalram, archbishop of Salzburg

[Read: “You are what I was”;] now consider, traveler,

And share my grief over our common lot.

Now you live, breathe, and perhaps do what you desire,

And the world itself lies open to your uses.

Riches serve your wishes, the elements yield,

And the threefold machinery of things is subject to you.

I too made use of these things while my present life remained,

And possessed all these things, with God supplying them.

But when Fortune turned her deceptive face,

It became clear that I no longer possessed what I had.

[Col. 1210A] Yet I have not lost what is now mine: I feel that what is mine is with me;

Groan over our like condition.

Bend the Thunderer with prayers for me, now and always,

And, I beg you, pray forgiveness for my soul.

I am called Adalram, who was ruler of the sheepfold

Of this church of the present Lord.

The body of Adalram, through whose episcopate this city flourished,

Lies beneath this mass; seize my soul, O Christ.

### Another poem by the same author

If you cannot now recount aloud

What the bishop’s merits once were,

Still release sighs, moved as a grieving friend,

Because so great a father, so loving, departed quickly.

His name was Adalram; he governed this see,

And his limbs lie buried in this hall.

[Col. 1210B] He was vigorous in sacred service above all others,

As was fitting, for three lustres.

It is believed that his soul now rejoices in the heights of heaven,

Where the Lord bestows rewards according to merits.

For him, whoever recites these verses, say with a pure heart:

“Merciful Lord, grant this soul rest,

So that, when the final trumpet gives life to this flesh,

You may make him enjoy the twofold joy in its fullness.”

### Epitaph of Liuphrammus, archbishop of Salzburg

Palm of priests, learned in good things,

Prince of the Church, a star shining in the world,

O Father Liuphrammus, father of the poor, protector of the wretched,

You accomplish everything as the Lord commanded.

With you as shepherd, the wolf had torn away the empty belly,

While you nourished the ignorant whelps of the barking pack.

And because all your deeds please Christ in his serenity,

He now blows away the filth, so that you may be his own.

He chastises the offspring whom the ruler receives into his hall,

So that he may scatter the stains of dust from their feet.

The empty body falls, but its better part rises from it:

Now eternal things flourish, and mortal things collapse.

[Col. 1210C] The spirit rejoices; the battle with vices withdraws.

The soul’s virtue will not thereby be perfected.

So also joys shine forth, and sins will perish.

Despise sorrows, seeing the prosperous destinies.

O how sweet the kingdom will become, the kingdom established forever—

Which remains free from corruption and holds every good thing!

In it the companies of noble ancestors rejoice,

And wish to keep us in their homeland.

[Col. 1210D] Likewise the holy mothers and chaste sisters,

Desiring us to return by a peaceful road.

Moreover, the Almighty, source of all goodness,

Commands us to hasten and assists us with his piety.

May he lead you, perpetually sound, to that place,

So that you may praise Christ’s name in the citadel of heaven.

### On Bishop Aries

May Aries, noble and called by his ancestral name,

Kindly read this document with his sacred mouth.

Rightly, Father, are you called by such a holy name,

You who well feed the Lord’s sheep in their folds.

Aries, leader of the flock toward life, whom no one resists,

You shine, made a shepherd with apostolic honor.

From this place Aelim overflows with a fountain twelvefold,

And is fruitful ten times over with seven palms.

Therefore, shepherd, bishop, father, and priest,

In the prayer you pour forth, remember me, I beg you.

Though I am a foreigner, insignificant, most worthless, and witless,

I am nevertheless weak in your service.

Therefore, if I can do anything, remember to command me

To perform it with a ready heart of service.

So that I may be believed more certainly, I beg you to permit

A little salt to be used for our needs.

For salt must season the faithful earth;

I ask you also to let this be done for me by you.

The bodily salt signifies the just thing I request;

Dear Father, I humbly ask you to grant it.

[Col. 1211B] For you are powerful in imparting the flavor of salt,

So that our food may not be excessively tasteless.

May you, acting graciously through ages without end,

As perpetual bishop, live in everlasting peace, I beg.

## HL. REX

We wish to give you immense thanks, Baldo,

Because your great faith remains so unshaken,

As you confirmed it with us in words long ago.

For your pious writings gladden our mind,

Which you often send us and by which you encourage us excellently,

And through your goodness reveal to us in benign affection

What your great skill sends us in this way.

But recently you sent such writings

That our understanding could not comprehend them completely,

Because the whole composition is firmly shrouded in riddling language.

[Col. 1211C] What need is there, when one knows your words, to learn anything further from them?

This, however, we ask: explain it clearly to us.

## NOTES

From the verses given above, which are known to have been written in the ninth century, the published lists of the bishops of the metropolitan see of Salzburg must be corrected.

First, Ansalogus, Savolus, and Ezius must be removed from the class of Salzburg bishops, since they are listed by Hundius after Vitalis. Next, Bertricus must also be removed after Virgil.

Second, there is also a great discrepancy in the commonly published catalogue of the bishops of Regensburg, of whom there are two classes. One consists of bishops who governed that Church, as it were, outside the regular succession—eight in number: Saint Lupus, Ratharius, Saint Rudpertus, Saint Emmerammus, Saint Erhardus, Albertus, Velipholaegus, Vioterbus, and Saint Winifridus, or Boniface. The other class consists of the ordinary bishops after these, [Col. 1211D] whose first is called Saint Garibaldus; here he is called Cauvibaldus, or Gauvibadus.

There is no difference among the bishops of Freising, except in the reading of their names; but among those of Passau there is a major discrepancy. For before Vivolus, or Vivilon, who is counted first here, Hundius lists twelve bishops; and after Vivilus, Beatus is missing.

In the succession of the bishops of Säben, commonly called Seben, whose see later moved to Brixen, Saint Cassianus is placed before Ingenuinus; and after Ingenuinus there are eleven others before Mastulo, who is second in these verses.

Who Bishop Aries is—whether the name is fictitious or genuine—and where Aelim is, where his see was located, are unknown to us. The poet calls himself a foreigner and perhaps an Englishman. [Col. 1212A] Yet Aries is called *Aramme* in the English language. Is he Adalram, archbishop of Salzburg? I confess that I am perplexed, especially since I do not know how the word Aelim could in any way be attributed to Salzburg.

There is nearly the same difficulty concerning Bishop Baldo, to whom the following verses are addressed. He would seem to be Bardo, the eleventh-century bishop of Mainz, were it not for the antiquity of the codex, as well as the name of King Louis written in the verses, which I interpret as referring to Louis, king of Germany. For this reason these verses cannot apply to Waldo, bishop of Basel, who ceased to live before Charlemagne. But these matters are not important enough for us to dwell on them longer.

## VII. Rhythmic verses on the destruction of the monastery of Glonn

[Note: [Col. 1211D] Saint-Florent-le-Vieil, in the district of Anjou. The monastery of Glonn was reduced to ashes in the year 818 by Nomenoius, duke of the Britons, after he had inflicted much damage on Brittany and the neighboring regions. [Col. 1212D]]

[Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, appendix, p. 753.]

[Col. 1212B]

Offer sweet melodies and songs,

O Thracian lyre,

With which the stirred peaks

Mourned in the northern regions.

Let the mountains and rivers together

Now deem them Orphic;

Let songs answer,

Let the forests sing honey-sweetly,

Let the heavy trumpet provide its music;

Let the pipe resound aloft;

Let every harmony sing;

Let the nightingale offer songs.

Once shining most brightly,

And most famous throughout the lands,

The outstanding basilica

Of Saint Father Florentius

Suffered savage fires

At the hands of the most cruel people,

Truly brutish Brittany;

All of you, mourn such things.

For when all Gaul

Bent its head and sought

The aid of Florentius,

That impious people despised it.

Once the pious King Charles,

Great and most powerful,

Devoutly established this place

For the virtues of the blessed man.

Having given fertile lands,

He greatly increased its honor,

And at that time presented a magnificent vessel

For the Lord’s Supper.

Through him illness is often driven away

From those who suffer,

And health is immediately granted

To the faithful from this source.

Afterward Louis ruled,

The son of great Charles;

He honored this place more generously

With pious adornments.

Shaken by rebellious sons,

By deep waves,

And by disturbances troubling Francia,

He died and left the kingdom.

When these four men soon divided

The kingdom among themselves,

And quarreled throughout Francia,

The war became more terrible.

Thus, under a troubled empire,

The faction of evils grew;

Then dissension arose

And mixed everyone together in strife.

One attacks his allies,

Evils grow over the good,

Every tyrant roars,

Honors are given to the impious.

[Col. 1213B] There is devastation of many,

Plunder of holy places,

Disruption of all good things,

And confusion of everything.

At that time there was a man

Named Nomenoius,

Previously poor in birth,

Who cultivated a field with the plow.

But he discovered a very great

Treasure hidden in the earth,

Which joined to himself

The support of many rich men.

Then he began to deceive by cunning

And soon began to grow,

Until by power

He surpassed everyone.

Thus, while the Franks and their kings

Were quarreling together,

Together with the other rebels

He became opposed to Charles.

This Charles often waged war

With his brothers,

But he did not prevail against the enemy,

Driven back by such great disasters.

Therefore the impious man grew confident;

Nomenoius carried off plunder,

Pressing upon the people of Rennes

And likewise those of Nantes.

Then he attacked the district of Médalgis,

Beyond the Loire, where the Poitevins

Were settled,

And the most beautiful place of Glonn.

He summoned the monastic community,

Gave a large sum of money,

And immediately ordered his own statue

To be fashioned splendidly.

They were to place it upon the pinnacle,

Open toward the east,

As a sign that he did not fear

Charles, his lord.

They immediately reported these things

To their own king, Charles,

Who, hearing of the man’s arrogance,

Marveled at his audacity.

Then he ordered that all the money be set out for him,

With that man’s image, carved in white stone,

As an object of ridicule,

Which they were to place on the pinnacle

Open toward the east,

As a sign that the impious man

Was to be subjected to Charles.

Angered by such things,

He hastened to the place;

He ordered his soldiers to plunder

And immediately kindled a fire.

The Britons soon spread

Savage flames everywhere:

The holy place was burned,

And so much beauty consumed.

Alas for me! The sufferings of the homeland!

Alas for me! The honors of glory,

Which the former world knew!

Alas for me! Now tears flow.

Then Saint Florentius,

Stirred from heaven, appeared;

He looked upon the Britons

Setting his place ablaze.

O how great the vengeance would have been,

Had there not been permission!

But the impious man was struck

With weakness in his feet.

He prayed for forgiveness,

That he might return to his homeland;

Having returned to Brittany,

He gave an enormous sum of money.

The abbot was the good Dido,

Close to King Charles,

Who, having summoned the brothers,

Approached the king as quickly as possible.

He explained the Britons’ anger

And the great crime of their cruelty.

Then the king, grieving in his heart,

Immediately sought to repay it.

From there he hastened to Angers,

Most sorrowful;

He gave the abbey of the place

Dedicated to Saint John.

[Col. 1214D] But this seemed too little,

And soon he gave another,

Named for Saint Gundulf,

Which lies in the regions of Francia.

Having given great gifts,

He became attentive to the place,

Restored it more happily,

And adorned it more beautifully.

Rejoice, all of you, in your hearts;

Sing with great voices.

Saint Florentius, we beg you,

Be present to us from heaven.

Amen.

## VIII. Verses on the battle [Note: [Col. 1215D] Thus the codex] fought at Fontenay

[Lebeuf, *Dissertation on the Battle of Fontenay*.]

[Col. 1215A]

### NOTICE

Royal Codex 4458 contains a poem on the battle of Fontenay under the name of a certain Angelbert, who speaks as an eyewitness. It consists of trochaic verses, and certain dots placed above the first verses indicate a song marked with musical signs, or an ode. We give the poem as it is read in the manuscript codex, which appears to be attributable to approximately the tenth century. On the battle at Fontenay, see the narrative of Nithard in volume 116 of the *Patrologia*.

At dawn, with the first morning,

Dividing the dreadful night,

It was not that Sabbath,

But Saturn’s vat:

Because fraternal peace was broken,

The impious demon rejoices.

Wars cry out on this side and that;

A grievous battle arises:

Brother prepares death for brother,

An uncle for his nephew;

Nor does a son show his father

What he deserved.

No worse slaughter ever occurred,

Nor any worse on the field of Mars;

The law of Christians became

Drenched in a flood of blood . . .

From this the hands of hell

And Cerberus’s maw rejoice.

[Col. 1215C] The all-powerful right hand of God

Protected Lotharius;

He, victorious by his own hand,

Fought bravely;

If the others had fought in the same way,

There would soon have been peace.

Behold, once Judas

Betrayed the Savior;

So your own men, O king,

Betrayed you to the sword.

Be cautious, lest you be deceived—

A lamb before a prowling wolf.

They call it Fontenay’s spring . . . [Note: [Col. 1215] The final letters of this word have faded, but it should unquestionably be read as *fontem*, “spring.”]

And the peasants call it a village,

In which there was slaughter and ruin

From the blood of the Franks:

The fields shudder, the forests shudder,

The marshes themselves shudder.

May neither dew nor shower

Moisten that grass with rain,

Where the strong, most skilled in battle,

Fell in combat;

May they mourn those who died

In that catastrophe.

This crime, which I have described

In rhythmic form,

I, Angelbertus, saw,

And, fighting with the others,

Alone of many, I remained

[Col. 1216A] in the foremost line at Fontenay.

[Col. 1216B] I looked back over the bottom of the valley

And the summit of the hill,

Where the strong King Lotharius

Was overcoming his enemies

As they fled

As far as the stream’s ford.

But on Charles’s side,

And likewise on Louis’s,

The fields grew white with the linen garments

Of the dead,

As birds customarily whiten

In autumn.

The battle deserves no praise,

Nor should it be sung melodiously:

East, south,

West, and north

Will mourn those who died

There in that catastrophe.

Accursed be that day,

And let it not be counted

Among the cycles of the year,

But erased

From all memory;

May the sun’s radiance be absent from it,

And the dawn be like twilight.

And that night—bitter night,

And night exceedingly harsh—

In which the strong, most skilled in battle,

Fell,

Father, mother, sister, and brother,

Whom their friends mourned.

## IX. Victory song, or Germanic rhythm, acclaimed for Louis, son of Louis the Stammerer, after he defeated the Northmen in the year 883, with the Latin translation of Johann Schilter

[In Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. III, appendix, p. 684.] [Note: [Col. 1215] The German and Latin versions of the following poem are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1215]

### Germanic rhythm

[Col. 1215D] I know a king;

His name is Lord Louis,

Who gladly serves God,

Because God rewards him.

He became fatherless as a child;

That was very hard for him.

He served the Lord.

He became a great warrior.

[Col. 1217A] He gave him courage,

A noble inheritance,

A seat here in Francia.

May he use it for a long time.

Then he shared it

At once with Karloman,

His brother,

Who had won the kingdom.

The battle was then ended.

God wished to test him,

To see whether he could endure

Labor

For so long.

He let the pagan man

Suffer among them,

The people of Francia,

Serving his men.

Some were immediately lost,

Some were chosen.

Harsh hardship he endured,

He who had been ill-starred.

He who had then been a thief

And had acquired theft there,

Took his goods;

Afterward he became a good man.

One was a liar,

One was a robber,

Some were faithless, [text fragment ends here]

[Fragmentary opening: “And he … was born/begotten … of this” (the surviving reading is materially uncertain).]

The king was alarmed.

[Col. 1217C] The whole kingdom was thrown into confusion,

For Christ was angered,

And exacted payment for it in suffering.

Yet God took pity,

For he knew all their distress,

And commanded Lord Ludwig

To ride there swiftly.

“Ludwig, my king,

Help my people;

The Northmen

Have oppressed them harshly.”

Then Ludwig spoke:

“Lord, so shall I do;

May death not prevent me

From doing all that you command.”

[Col. 1217D] Then he received God’s permission,

Raised the war-banner,

And rode there into Francia,

Against the Northmen.

They gave thanks to God,

Having awaited him.

He said: “Come, Lord;

We have awaited you so long.”

Then the good Ludwig spoke:

“Take heart, companions,

My comrades,

For God has sent me here;

May he himself grant me grace,

[Col. 1219A] If you give counsel,

So that I may lead out the host here.

I shall not spare myself

Until I have rescued you.

Now I wish all God’s faithful

To follow me.

This earthly life is allotted

For as long as Christ wills.

For he preserves our bones

And watches over them.

Whoever here, in courage,

Does God’s will,

Shall come forth unharmed;

I shall reward him.

[Col. 1219B] If he remains here,

With his kin.”

Then he took shield and spear;

Bravely he rode.

He wished to avenge

His own adversaries.

Before much time had passed,

He found the Northmen.

“Praise be to God!” he said,

For he saw what he desired.

Then the king rode boldly;

He sang a noble song.

And all together they sang:

[Col. 1219C] “Kyrie eleison.”

The song was sung;

The battle began.

Blood shone upon the cheeks

Of the exultant Franks.

Here each warrior took vengeance in like manner;

No one did so as Ludwig did.

Swift and bold—

Such was his nature.

One he struck through;

Another he pierced through.

He gave his enemies

[Col. 1219D] A bitter draught.

Thus they departed from this life.

Blessed be God’s power!

Ludwig became victorious.

Give thanks to all the saints.

His was the victorious battle.

And Ludwig,

The king, was blessed.

As ready as he was,

As severe as necessity required,

Preserve him, Lord,

In his righteousness!

[RHYTHMUS TEUTONICUS.]

[Col. 1216D] I know a king,

Who is called Lord Ludwig,

Who willingly serves God,

Since he rewards him.

While still a minor, he was deprived of his father,

And this was very harmful to him.

The Lord took him up;

He became his leader.

[Col. 1218A] He gave him heroes,

Illustrious companions,

A seat here in Francia.

May he use them thus for a long time!

Afterward he divided these things

With Carolomannus,

His brother,

Without fraud, in shares.

When all this had been completed,

God wished to test him,

To see whether he could endure

Tribulations for some time.

He allowed a pagan army

To be led against them:

The people of Francia

[Col. 1218B] To serve their warriors.

Some immediately fell away;

Others were tempted and harassed.

Whoever lived otherwise

Suffered insults.

He who had then been a robber,

And had prospered amid these disturbances,

Seized the king’s camps;

From this he became a nobleman.

One was a liar, or deceiver;

Another was a murderer;

Another was a deserter;

And each exalted himself by that crime.

The king was terrified.

[Col. 1218C] The whole kingdom was thrown into confusion.

Christ was angered;

He permitted this tyranny.

But God had pity;

He knew all that distress.

He ordered Lord Ludwig

To ride there immediately.

“Ludwig, my king,

Help my people;

The Northmen

Have grievously oppressed them.”

Then Ludwig spoke:

“Lord, so I shall do;

May death not prevent me from doing

All that you command.”

[Col. 1218D] Then he received God’s permission,

Raised the war-banner,

And rode there into Francia,

Against the Northmen.

Giving thanks to God,

They awaited him.

He said: “Come, Lord;

We have awaited you so long.”

Then the illustrious Ludwig spoke aloud:

“Take heart, companions,

My fellow soldiers.

God has sent me here;

May he also show me favor!”

[Col. 1220A] May you give counsel,

So that I may lead out the army.

I shall spare neither myself

Until I have freed you.

Now I wish all God’s faithful

To follow me.

This life has been granted

For as long as Christ wills,

For he preserves our bones

And keeps watch over them.

Whoever here, with courage,

Does God’s will,

Shall come forth unharmed from the battle;

I shall reward him.

[Col. 1220B] If anyone dies here in battle,

I shall provide for his family.”

Then he seized shield and spear

And rode swiftly.

He truly wished to take vengeance

On his adversaries.

Before much time had passed,

He found the Northmen.

“Praise be to God!” he said,

Seeing what he had desired.

The king rode boldly;

He began a public song of praise.

And all together they sang:

[Col. 1220C] “Kyrie eleison.”

The song was sung;

The battle began.

Blood appeared upon the cheeks

Of the exultant Franks.

Here each warrior took vengeance in like manner;

No one did so as Ludwig did.

Swift and bold—

Such qualities were innate in him.

He struck one;

He pierced another.

Then he gave his enemies

[Col. 1220D] A bitter draught.

Thus they departed from this life.

Blessed be God’s power!

Ludwig became victorious.

Give thanks to all the saints.

His was the victorious battle.

And Ludwig,

The king, was blessed.

As ready as he was,

As severe as necessity required,

Preserve him, Lord,

In his righteousness!

## X. Asclepiadic verses with which the codex called Gothicus Vigilanus, or Albeldensis, is concluded

[Note: **[Col. 1221]** It is preserved in the Escorial Library. It contains sixty-one councils and decretal letters. All these were written by the monks Vigila and Sarracino of Albelda, and by a certain disciple of Vigila named Garcia. **[Col. 1222]** They indicate that the work was completed on 25 May in the era 1014, that is, in the year of Christ 976, during the reigns in Navarre of Lord Sancho and Lady Urraca and of Lord Ramiro in Viguera; special mention is made of them in these verses.]

[According to Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol. XXXIII, p. 471.]

[Col. 1221]

### I

The power of Christ indeed, granting comfort to me, most humble Vigila,  
Has enabled me diligently to bring the work of this book of sacred canon, begun by me, to its end.  
Behold, I have gathered the living, flowering, illustrious councils of the holy eastern fathers,  
And thereafter joined together the great life-giving works of the western kings and bishops.

The holy Church, illuminated and shining with the Lord’s light, gleams like the moon.  
Adorned with the clear teachings of the apostles, washed in sacred waters, she glows like the sun.  
She receives sound and radiant doctrine, accepting no stain from painted deceits.  
Free from the depraved doctrine of emanating things, she remains radiant in holy work.

By the ray of her example she illumines the world, together with a most pure life and the angels.  
She shines resplendent in the heavenly seat; through whose prayer may we at last be brought there.  
There we may often behold the life-giving hosts of holy spirits and martyrs,  
And the one united, radiant company of virgins and holy fathers, flowing with light.

By illustrious merit and work, together with the starry hosts and the dwellers in heaven,  
May our names be written in the book of life, that we may be summoned into their heavenly courts.  
There may we enjoy the pure, springlike and flower-bearing fruits of the living, in abundant harvest.  
Sarracino, son of Salbi, and Vigila himself, aided by the prayer of their excellent teachers,

We, the two scribes, have now arranged their illustrious names, which this book contains.  
United as one, may we continually rejoice with them in the company of the angels.  
Like an eastern host, twice a hundred in number, the community of Albelda shines exceedingly white.  
Behold, the one brotherhood of Saint Martin: may it fly together with the saints to heaven.

Proceeding under the guidance of the holy Gospel, let us follow the ways of the Lord,  
Who endured insults for us, whose footsteps we ought to follow.  
The era, one thousand and fourteen, was passing and had come to an end,  
And the time was marked on the twenty-fifth day of the Kalends of May, in the course of the moon.

This book was written while Ramiro, the brother, and Sancho, the orthodox king, were reigning,  
Together with the illustrious Queen Urraca, in the sixth year after the death of King García.  
Now, all you readers who bow down, we ask you to commend us, the insignificant,  
To the most holy Trinity, that together we may enjoy all glory throughout the ages.

### II

[Col. 1221] O Word of God, brought forth from the Father’s mouth,  
At whose command the world’s machine shines,  
That we may enjoy your eternity sweetly,  
Christ, we pray that you may now come to us.

We who write earnestly ask you, all together,  
To grant us here great joy and the protection of your gracious Martin.  
Behold, his radiant light shines always in these courts,  
And here may your life-giving glory shine,

And may the true and glorious light breathe upon us.  
May the hostile enemy, often defeated, depart from here.  
May your life-giving help be present to us,  
Immense Christ, living Son of the living God.

May we all be covered by your seals,  
And by the light brought to us from your light.

[Col. 1222] May the power of the supreme Son of God  
Always protect this place and the court of the saints.  
May it flourish, shining with the Lord’s light,  
Life-giving, vigorous, and enduring through the ages.

Now may the hall of God shine with glory.  
Christ, may splendor be present in our hearts,  
And in the sacred court of Martin the bishop.  
By whose prayer, protected by your hand,

May the life-giving company of monks here flourish,  
And, rejoicing in sacred virtues, bloom.  
Made celibate by your Holy Spirit,  
Filled with the goodness of your clemency,

May we, illumined, shine continually  
With sacred works of righteousness,  
So that we may be crowned with your life-giving glory.

[Col. 1223A]

May this house be the protection of the eternal King;  
There may we all be sheltered beneath his seals.  
We who dwell in this sacred court—  
May King Jesus Emmanuel grant us joy,

May he, shining forth, bestow from his gracious Spirit  
Glory also upon our king Sancho.  
Renowned Christ, provide protection  
To your humble angel Ramiro.

Mercifully impart the light of righteousness,  
So that they may always enjoy your grace.

[Col. 1224A]

This book was completed as the era was passing,  
With nine hundred reckoned three times over,  
With seventy years properly added,  
And six together counted in the course of time.

When the revolving circle had run its course,  
Let there be praise, honor, and glory to the Father,  
To the only Son, always equal to him,  
Who remains together with both eternally,

And equally to the life-giving Holy Spirit,  
Now and throughout future ages. Amen.

[Col. 1223]

One must not fast on Sundays, 63. Nor on Thursday, which is called the Lord’s Supper, 138. One must not fast during the months of July and August, 99. To fast on the day of the Lord’s birth has the character of heresy, 221. One who fasts on Sunday is to be regarded as a heretic, 83, 102, 143. The Church’s fasts must not be held in contempt, 63. During the periods of fasting, confirmation is to be given to those who request it, 83. The institution of the Ember fasts, 29. It is not permitted to break the fast on a weekday, 5. In the last week of Lent, fasting must not take place on Sunday, 55. Fasting must not be undertaken on Saturday, 99. The Lenten fast instituted by Pope Telesphorus, 23. A priest ought to celebrate fasting, 141. John, bishop of Lampsacus, is commended to the imperial chamberlain, 283. Decrees of Pope John, 262. The statement of faith of John of Constantinople, 258. The Jews accepted that Christ would come, 10. Jews coming to the faith, 96. The faith of the Jews must be free, 115. Jews must not have Christian wives or hold public offices, 110. Jews are excluded from every public office, 116. After accepting the faith, Jews who have transgressed must not be admitted as witnesses, 115. Jews may not have Christian slaves, 116. Unless he converts, a Jew cannot retain a believing wife, 115. One who supports a Jew out of greed is to be excommunicated, 115. One must not share in the Jews’ unleavened bread, 68. The blessings of Jews over fruits must not be permitted, 100. The sons or daughters of Jews must be separated from their association, 115. The believing children of heretical Jews must not be defrauded of their hereditary right, 115. An ecclesiastical judge must not decide against someone in his absence, 82. Ecclesiastical judges must not hear cases contrary to the laws, 158. We must not pass judgment on others but kindly come to their aid, 9, 244. Julius’s vindication against the Orientals, 165. One must not swear at all from personal desire, 38. The just are preserved by the Lord, 47. The sacred letter of the emperor Justin to Pope Hormisdas, 258. The justice of God must be sought above all, 10. Justice is from God as sin is from the devil, 14.

K

The superstition of the January Kalends among the Gauls, 292.

L

Milk must not be offered in the sacrifice of the Mass, 145. Laymen who are forbidden to advance, 173. How a layman is to be admitted to the priesthood, 233. A layman, however powerful, can establish nothing against the Roman pontiff, 247. How laymen are to be promoted to the priesthood, 139. A layman must presume to do nothing in the presence of clergy, 83. A layman who takes another woman after his wife must not be promoted to the clergy, 102. Women must not observe wool-working with vain superstitions, 144. Those led astray through ignorance or error must be helped, 195. How a lector is ordained, 82. If a lector takes a widow, 143. In what dress lectors ought to sing the psalms, 139. Once lectors have reached puberty, they must either marry or vow continence, 79. If a faithful lector takes a widow as wife, 104. Lectors and psalmists must not use oraria, 68. If lectors or doorkeepers associate with adulteresses, 101. Bishops serve as ambassadors of Christ, 244. Laws do not bind in necessity, 88. Progress in the law depends upon charity, 52. Whether the legislator is subject to his own laws, 252. The intention of the legislator, 252. Leo asks the Augusta that Eutyches be sent far from Constantinople, lest he contaminate others through his intimacy, 225. The emperor Leo, guardian of the Council of Chalcedon, 227. Letters of Pope Leo to various persons, 187–229. Communion is to be given to lepers, 287. A levite who lives incontinent with his wife is to be deposed, 93. The law is not laid down for the just, 219. The law of God must not be interpreted according to human desire, 12. The law promulgated in the Eighth Council of Toledo, 226. The drafting of a written charge in a criminal case, 47. Refutation of a certain didactic pamphlet against Pope Symmachus, 251. Those who publish defamatory pamphlets are to be excommunicated, 100. A book sent to Innocent, 180. The generosity of a bishop’s lover toward Pope Silverius, 266. Free will is not taken away by God’s gift, 185. No one can use free will for good except through the grace of God, 184. Freedmen owe service to the church from which they obtained the grace of freedom, 128. Freedmen of the Church must make a declaration of their status, 119. Freedmen of the Church who abandon its protection fall back into slavery, 116. Freedmen of the Church must render service to someone within the church, 119. If freedmen are promoted to the clergy, 109. Freedmen bound to the Church’s protection must be protected by it, 116. Freedmen of the Church can alienate nothing from the property they hold from the Church, 128. Freedmen whose patrons were secular persons, 101. Freedmen who take wives contrary to their marital status, 128. Freedmen of the Church cannot be dismissed from its protection, 116. A bishop cannot release the Church’s freedmen from their service, 116. The Church must defend those made free by their masters, 96. Books received by the Church, 68. Canonical books are to be read in the churches, 144. Moderation of the tongue is difficult, 50. The celebration of the litanies, 117. The second litanies are to be celebrated on the Kalends of November, 102. The address of Bishop Lucretius to his fellow bishops, 139. The penalty for those using pagan lustrations.
